Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

In the Vinaya Piṭaka

Pārājikakaṇḍa-aṭṭhakathā (paṭhamo bhāgo)

The Commentary on the Pārājika Section (First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Yo [P 1.0001][M 1.0001][V 1.0001] kappakoṭīhipi appameyyaṃ;

Kālaṃ karonto atidukkarāni;

Khedaṃ gato lokahitāya nātho;

Namo mahākāruṇikassa tassa.

Homage to that Greatly Compassionate Lord, who for the welfare of the world went to weariness, performing exceedingly difficult deeds for a time immeasurable even by crores of aeons.

Asambudhaṃ buddhanisevitaṃ yaṃ;

Bhavābhavaṃ gacchati jīvaloko;

Namo [V 1.0002] avijjādikilesajāla-

Viddhaṃsino dhammavarassa tassa.

Because the world of living beings, not comprehending that which is frequented by the Buddha, goes from one existence to another, homage to that excellent Dhamma, the destroyer of the net of defilements such as ignorance.

Guṇehi yo sīlasamādhipaññā-

Vimuttiñāṇappabhutīhi yutto;

Khettaṃ janānaṃ kusalatthikānaṃ;

Tamariyasaṅghaṃ sirasā namāmi.

I bow my head to that Noble Sangha, who is endowed with virtues such as morality, concentration, wisdom, deliverance, and knowledge, and who is an excellent field for people who desire what is wholesome.

Iccevamaccantanamassaneyyaṃ;

Namassamāno ratanattayaṃ yaṃ;

Puññābhisandaṃ vipulaṃ alatthaṃ;

Tassānubhāvena hatantarāyo.

Thus paying homage to the Triple Gem, which is exceedingly worthy of veneration, I have obtained a vast stream of merit. By its power, I am one whose obstacles are destroyed.

Yasmiṃ [M 1.0002] ṭhite sāsanamaṭṭhitassa;

Patiṭṭhitaṃ hoti susaṇṭhitassa;

Taṃ vaṇṇayissaṃ vinayaṃ amissaṃ;

Nissāya pubbācariyānubhāvaṃ.

When this Vinaya is established, the Dispensation of the Blessed One—who is not established in the two extremes but is well-established in the Middle Way—becomes firmly established. Relying on the authority of the ancient teachers, I shall expound that unmixed Vinaya.

Kāmañca pubbācariyāsabhehi;

Ñāṇambuniddhotamalāsavehi;

Visuddhavijjāpaṭisambhidehi[P 1.0002];

Saddhammasaṃvaṇṇanakovidehi.

Indeed, by the bull-like ancient teachers—whose stains and cankers are washed away by the water of knowledge, who possess purified higher knowledges and analytical insights, and who are skilled in expounding the good Dhamma—

Sallekhiye nosulabhūpamehi;

Mahāvihārassa dhajūpamehi;

Saṃvaṇṇitoyaṃ vinayo nayehi;

Cittehi sambuddhavaranvayehi.

who are not easily compared in the practice of effacement, who are like a banner for the Mahāvihāra—this Vinaya has been expounded with various methods in accordance with the lineage of the excellent Sambuddha.

Saṃvaṇṇanā sīhaḷadīpakena;

Vākyena esā pana saṅkhatattā;

Na [V 1.0003] kiñci atthaṃ abhisambhuṇāti;

Dīpantare bhikkhujanassa yasmā.

However, since this commentary, being composed in the language of the island of Sinhala, does not accomplish any benefit for the community of monks in other lands,

Tasmā imaṃ pāḷinayānurūpaṃ;

Saṃvaṇṇanaṃ dāni samārabhissaṃ;

Ajjhesanaṃ buddhasirivhayassa;

Therassa sammā samanussaranto.

Therefore, properly remembering the request of the Elder named Buddhasiri, I shall now begin this commentary in a manner that accords with the method of the Pāḷi.

Saṃvaṇṇanaṃ tañca samārabhanto;

Tassā mahāaṭṭhakathaṃ sarīraṃ;

Katvā mahāpaccariyaṃ tatheva;

Kurundināmādisu vissutāsu.

And in beginning that commentary, I shall make the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā its body, and likewise draw upon the decision stated in the Mahāpaccarī and in the famous commentaries such as the Kurundī.

Vinicchayo aṭṭhakathāsu vutto;

Yo yuttamatthaṃ apariccajanto;

Tatopi antogadhatheravādaṃ;

Saṃvaṇṇanaṃ samma samārabhissaṃ.

From that decision, without abandoning the suitable meaning, I shall properly begin this commentary, which has the Theravāda tradition included within it.

Taṃ [M 1.0003] me nisāmentu pasannacittā;

Therā ca bhikkhū navamajjhimā ca;

Dhammappadīpassa tathāgatassa;

Sakkacca dhammaṃ patimānayantā.

May the Elder, new, and middle monks, with serene minds, listen attentively to this work of mine, while respectfully honoring the Dhamma of the Tathāgata, the Lamp of the Dhamma.

Buddhena dhammo vinayo ca vutto;

Yo tassa puttehi tatheva ñāto;

So yehi tesaṃ matimaccajantā;

Yasmā pure aṭṭhakathā akaṃsu.

Because the Dhamma and Vinaya spoken by the Buddha were known in that very same way by His sons, and because the ancient commentary teachers, not abandoning the opinion of those sons, composed the commentaries in the past,

Tasmā [P 1.0003] hi yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ;

Taṃ vajjayitvāna pamādalekhaṃ;

Sabbampi [V 1.0004] sikkhāsu sagāravānaṃ;

Yasmā pamāṇaṃ idha paṇḍitānaṃ.

Therefore, because whatever is said in the commentaries—avoiding scribal errors due to negligence—is indeed the standard here for wise ones who are respectful towards the trainings,

Tato ca bhāsantarameva hitvā;

Vitthāramaggañca samāsayitvā;

Vinicchayaṃ sabbamasesayitvā;

Tantikkamaṃ kiñci avokkamitvā.

And therefore, from those ancient commentaries, having set aside only the other language, having condensed the lengthy method, having left out none of the decisions, and without skipping over any of the textual sequence,

Suttantikānaṃ vacanānamatthaṃ;

Suttānurūpaṃ paridīpayantī;

Yasmā ayaṃ hessati vaṇṇanāpi;

Sakkacca tasmā anusikkhitabbāti.

And because this commentary will also be one that clarifies the meaning of the words of the Suttantas in a manner that accords with the Suttas, therefore it should be respectfully and repeatedly studied.

Bāhiranidānakathā

The Discourse on the External Introduction

Tattha [M 1.0004] taṃ vaṇṇayissaṃ vinayanti vuttattā vinayo tāva vavatthapetabbo. Tenetaṃ vuccati – “vinayo nāma idha sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ adhippeta”nti. Saṃvaṇṇanatthaṃ panassa ayaṃ mātikā –

Therein, because it was stated, "I shall explain that Vinaya," the Vinaya should first of all be defined. Therefore, this is said: "Here, by 'Vinaya' is intended the entire Vinaya Piṭaka." Furthermore, for the purpose of its explanation, this is the matrix:

Vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmā, dhāritaṃ yena cābhataṃ;

Yatthappatiṭṭhitacetametaṃ vatvā vidhiṃ tato.

By whom it was spoken, when, and for what reason; by whom it was borne in mind and handed down; and in whom it was established—having stated this procedure, thereafter,

Tenātiādipāṭhassa, atthaṃ nānappakārato;

Dassayanto karissāmi, vinayassatthavaṇṇananti.

showing the meaning of the text beginning with "Tena" in various ways, I shall compose the explanation of the meaning of the Vinaya.

Tattha vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmāti idaṃ tāva vacanaṃ “tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatī”ti evamādivacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Idañhi buddhassa bhagavato attapaccakkhavacanaṃ na hoti, tasmā vattabbametaṃ [P 1.0004] “idaṃ vacanaṃ kena vuttaṃ, kadā vuttaṃ, kasmā ca vutta”nti? Āyasmatā upālittherena vuttaṃ, tañca pana paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle.

Therein, the statement "By whom it was spoken, when, and for what reason" was said referring to the words beginning with, "At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Verañjā." For this is not a statement made in the personal presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One. Therefore, this should be stated: "By whom was this statement spoken, when was it spoken, and for what reason was it spoken?" It was spoken by the Venerable Upāli Thera, and that, moreover, at the time of the First Great Council.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā

The Discourse on the First Great Council

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti [V 1.0005] nāma cesā kiñcāpi pañcasatikasaṅgītikkhandhake vuttā, nidānakosallatthaṃ pana idhāpi iminā nayena veditabbā. Dhammacakkappavattanañhi ādiṃ katvā yāva subhaddaparibbājakavinayanā katabuddhakicce kusinārāyaṃ upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane yamakasālānamantare visākhapuṇṇamadivase paccūsasamaye anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbute bhagavati lokanāthe, bhagavato parinibbāne sannipatitānaṃ sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassānaṃ saṅghatthero āyasmā mahākassapo sattāhaparinibbute bhagavati, subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitena “alaṃ, āvuso, mā socittha, mā paridevittha, sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena; upaddutā ca homa – ‘idaṃ vo kappati, idaṃ vo na kappatī’ti! Idāni pana mayaṃ yaṃ icchissāma taṃ karissāma, yaṃ na icchissāma na taṃ karissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 437; dī. ni. 2.232) vuttavacanamanussaranto “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati yaṃ pāpabhikkhū atītasatthukaṃ pāvacananti maññamānā [M 1.0005] pakkhaṃ labhitvā nacirasseva saddhammaṃ antaradhāpeyyuṃ, yāva ca dhammavinayo tiṭṭhati tāva anatītasatthukameva pāvacanaṃ hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

And although this, the so-called First Great Council, was spoken of in the Khandhaka on the Council of Five Hundred, nevertheless, for the sake of skill in the introduction, it should be understood here also in this way. For when the Blessed One, the Protector of the World—having completed the Buddha's duties, beginning with the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma up to the disciplining of the wanderer Subhadda—had passed into final Nibbāna by the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, at the time of dawn on the full-moon day of Visākha, between the twin Sāla trees in the Sāla grove of the Mallas at the Upavattana of Kusinārā, the Elder of the Saṅgha of the seven hundred thousand monks who had assembled, the Venerable Mahākassapa, when the Blessed One had been passed into final Nibbāna for seven days, recalling the words spoken by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age: "Enough, friends, do not grieve, do not lament. We are well-freed from that great ascetic. We were oppressed, being told, 'This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you!' But now we shall do what we wish, and what we do not wish, we shall not do," considered: "There exists this possibility, that evil monks, thinking 'the teaching is one whose teacher is past,' might gain a faction and before long cause the good Dhamma to disappear. And as long as the Dhamma and Vinaya stand, the teaching is one whose teacher is not past." For this was said by the Blessed One:

‘Yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto[P 1.0005], so vo mamaccayena satthā’ti (dī. ni. 2.216).

"Ānanda, that Dhamma and Vinaya which has been taught and laid down by me, that will be your teacher after my passing."

“Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyaṃ, yathayidaṃ sāsanaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ.

"What if I were to chant together the Dhamma and the Vinaya, so that this Dispensation might be long-lasting and endure for a long time?"

Yaṃ cāhaṃ bhagavatā –

And since I was by the Blessed One—

‘Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ, kassapa, sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanānī’ti vatvā cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena ceva,

'Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out, hempen, dust-heap robes?' and having said this, by the shared use of the robe, and

‘Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yāvade ākaṅkhāmi vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharāmi; kassapopi, bhikkhave, yāvade ākaṅkhati vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī’ti –

'Monks, for as long as I wish, being secluded from sensual pleasures… I enter and abide in the first jhāna; Kassapa too, monks, for as long as he wishes, being secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and abides in the first jhāna.'—

Evamādinā [V 1.0006] nayena navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāppabhede uttarimanussadhamme attanā samasamaṭṭhapanena ca anuggahito, tassa kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissati; nanu maṃ bhagavā rājā viya sakakavacaissariyānuppadānena attano kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ puttaṃ ‘saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako me ayaṃ bhavissatī’ti mantvā iminā asādhāraṇena anuggahena anuggahesī”ti cintayanto dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesi. Yathāha –

—I was honored by being placed as an equal to himself in the supramundane states divided into the nine successive abidings and the six super-knowledges, in this and other ways. For me, then, what else could be the means of becoming free from debt? Surely the Blessed One, thinking, 'This one will be the establisher of my lineage, the lineage of the good Dhamma,' honored me with this uncommon honor, just as a king honors a son who establishes his dynasty by bestowing his own armor and sovereignty. Reflecting thus, he generated enthusiasm among the monks for the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. As it was said:

“Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘ekamidāhaṃ, āvuso, samayaṃ pāvāya kusināraṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.231) sabbaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ vitthārato veditabbaṃ.

'Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks: "Friends, on one occasion I was traveling on the high road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a great Saṅgha of monks, with about five hundred monks."' The entire Subhadda section should be understood in detail.

Tato [P 1.0006][M 1.0006] paraṃ āha –

After that, he said:

“Handa mayaṃ, āvuso, dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāma. Pure adhammo dippati, dhammo paṭibāhiyyati; avinayo dippati, vinayo paṭibāhiyyati. Pure adhammavādino balavanto honti, dhammavādino dubbalā honti; avinayavādino balavanto honti, vinayavādino dubbalā hontī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

'Come, friends, let us communally recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, before the non-Dhamma shines forth and the Dhamma is obstructed; before the non-Vinaya shines forth and the Vinaya is obstructed. Before speakers of non-Dhamma become strong and speakers of Dhamma become weak; before speakers of non-Vinaya become strong and speakers of Vinaya become weak.'

Bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “tena hi, bhante, thero bhikkhū uccinatū”ti. Thero sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanapariyattidhare puthujjana-sotāpanna-sakadāgāmi-anāgāmi-sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavabhikkhū anekasate anekasahasse ca vajjetvā tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadhare paṭisambhidāppatte mahānubhāve yebhuyyena bhagavatā etadaggaṃ āropite tevijjādibhede khīṇāsavabhikkhūyeva ekūnapañcasate pariggahesi. Ye sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo ekenūnāpañcaarahantasatāni uccinī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

The monks said: 'In that case, venerable sir, let the Elder select the monks.' The Elder—avoiding many hundreds and many thousands of worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and dry-insight destroyers of the cankers who were bearers of the entire nine-limbed teaching of the Master—selected only four hundred and ninety-nine monks who had destroyed the cankers, who were bearers of all the divisions of the scriptural learning of the Tipiṭaka, who had attained the analytical knowledges, who were of great power, and who had for the most part been placed by the Blessed One in the foremost position in the various divisions beginning with the three knowledges. It was with reference to them that this was said: 'Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected five hundred Arahants less one.'

Kissa pana thero ekenūnamakāsīti? Āyasmato ānandattherassa okāsakaraṇatthaṃ. Tena hāyasmatā sahāpi vināpi na sakkā dhammasaṅgīti kātuṃ, so hāyasmā sekkho sakaraṇīyo, tasmā sahāpi na sakkā; yasmā panassa kiñci dasabaladesitaṃ suttageyyādikaṃ bhagavato asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā vināpi na sakkā. Yadi evaṃ sekkhopi samāno dhammasaṅgītiyā bahukārattā therena uccinitabbo assa. Atha kasmā na uccinitoti[P 1.0007]? Parūpavādavivajjanato. Thero hi āyasmante ānande ativiya vissattho ahosi, tathā hi naṃ [V 1.0007] sirasmiṃ palitesu jātesupi “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) kumārakavādena ovadati. Sakyakulappasuto cāyaṃ āyasmā tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto. Tatra hi bhikkhū chandāgamanaṃ viya maññamānā “bahū asekkhapaṭisambhidāppatte bhikkhū ṭhapetvā ānandaṃ sekkhapaṭisambhidāppattaṃ thero uccinī”ti upavadeyyuṃ, taṃ parūpavādaṃ parivajjento “ānandaṃ vinā saṅgīti [M 1.0007] na sakkā kātuṃ, bhikkhūnaṃyeva anumatiyā gahessāmī”ti na uccini.

Why then did the Elder leave out one? To grant an opportunity to the Venerable Ānanda. For with that venerable one, or without him, it was not possible to hold the communal recitation of the Dhamma. That venerable one was a learner with something further to do, therefore it was not possible with him; moreover, since there was no teaching declared by the Ten-Powered One—such as the discourses and verses—that he had received out of the Blessed One's presence, it was not possible without him. If that were the case, even though he was a learner, due to his great assistance in the communal recitation of the Dhamma, he should have been selected by the Elder. Then why was he not selected? To avoid criticism from others. For the Elder was very familiar with the Venerable Ānanda; indeed, even when gray hairs appeared on his head, he would admonish him with the address of 'young boy', saying, 'This young boy does not know his measure.' Moreover, this venerable one was born into the Sakyan clan and was the Tathāgata’s brother, the son of a paternal uncle. In that case, the monks, thinking it was a matter of partiality, might have criticized, 'The Elder, setting aside many non-learners who had attained the analytical knowledges, has selected Ānanda, a learner who has attained the analytical knowledges.' Avoiding such criticism from others, he did not select him, thinking, 'The communal recitation cannot be held without Ānanda; I shall select him with the monks' approval.'

Atha sayameva bhikkhū ānandassatthāya theraṃ yāciṃsu. Yathāha –

Then the monks of their own accord requested the Elder on Ānanda's behalf. As it is said:

“Bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ayaṃ, bhante, āyasmā ānando kiñcāpi sekkho abhabbo chandā dosā mohā bhayā agatiṃ gantuṃ, bahu cānena bhagavato santike dhammo ca vinayo ca pariyatto; tena hi, bhante, thero āyasmantampi ānandaṃ uccinatū’ti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantampi ānandaṃ uccinī”ti (cūḷava. 437).

The monks said to the Venerable Mahākassapa: 'Venerable sir, although the Venerable Ānanda is a learner, he is incapable of following a wrong course due to desire, hatred, delusion, or fear. Moreover, he has learned much of the Dhamma and Vinaya in the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder also select the Venerable Ānanda.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa also selected the Venerable Ānanda.

Evaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anumatiyā uccinitena tenāyasmatā saddhiṃ pañca therasatāni ahesuṃ.

Thus, with that venerable one chosen with the consent of the monks, there were five hundred elders.

Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “kattha nu kho mayaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāmā”ti. Atha kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “rājagahaṃ kho [P 1.0008] mahāgocaraṃ pahūtasenāsanaṃ, yaṃnūna mayaṃ rājagahe vassaṃ vasantā dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāma, na aññe bhikkhū rājagahe vassaṃ upagaccheyyu”nti. Kasmā pana nesaṃ etadahosi? Idaṃ amhākaṃ thāvarakammaṃ, koci visabhāgapuggalo saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā ukkoṭeyyāti. Athāyasmā mahākassapo ñattidutiyena kammena sāvesi, taṃ saṅgītikkhandhake vuttanayeneva ñātabbaṃ.

Then this thought occurred to the elder monks: 'Where, indeed, should we communally recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?' Then this thought occurred to the elder monks: 'Rājagaha has an extensive area for alms-gathering and plentiful lodgings. It would be good if we were to spend the rains-residence in Rājagaha while communally reciting the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and if other monks did not enter the rains-residence in Rājagaha.' But why did this occur to them? 'This is our enduring work; let no unsuitable person enter the midst of the Saṅgha and cause disruption.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made an announcement by means of a motion proposed for the second time. This should be understood according to the method stated in the Saṅgītikkhandhaka.

Atha tathāgatassa parinibbānato sattasu sādhukīḷanadivasesu sattasu ca dhātupūjādivasesu vītivattesu “aḍḍhamāso atikkanto, idāni gimhānaṃ diyaḍḍho māso seso, upakaṭṭhā vassūpanāyikā”ti mantvā mahākassapatthero “rājagahaṃ, āvuso, gacchāmā”ti upaḍḍhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gato. Anuruddhattheropi upaḍḍhaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gato. Ānandatthero pana bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiṃ gantvā rājagahaṃ gantukāmo yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Ānandattherena gatagataṭṭhāne mahāparidevo ahosi [V 1.0008] – “bhante ānanda, kuhiṃ satthāraṃ ṭhapetvā āgatosī”ti[M 1.0008]. Anupubbena pana sāvatthiṃ anuppatte there bhagavato parinibbānadivase viya mahāparidevo ahosi.

Then, after seven days of joyful celebration and seven days of paying homage to the relics had passed since the Tathāgata’s Parinibbāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa reflected: 'Half a month has passed. Now, one and a half months of the hot season remain, and the time for the rains-residence is approaching.' He said, 'Friends, let us go to Rājagaha,' and taking half the community of monks, he went by one road. The Venerable Anuruddha also took half and went by another road. The Venerable Ānanda, however, took the Blessed One’s bowl and robe and, surrounded by the community of monks, desiring to go to Rājagaha, set out on a journey in the direction of Sāvatthī. In every place the Venerable Ānanda went, there was great lamentation: 'Venerable Ānanda, where have you come from, having left the Teacher behind?' And when the elder gradually arrived in Sāvatthī, there was great lamentation, just as on the day of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna.

Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā ānando aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammiyā kathāya taṃ mahājanaṃ saññāpetvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā dasabalena vasitagandhakuṭiyā dvāraṃ vivaritvā mañcapīṭhaṃ nīharitvā papphoṭetvā gandhakuṭiṃ sammajjitvā milātamālākacavaraṃ [P 1.0009] chaḍḍetvā mañcapīṭhaṃ atiharitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā bhagavato ṭhitakāle karaṇīyaṃ vattaṃ sabbamakāsi. Atha thero bhagavato parinibbānato pabhuti ṭhānanisajjabahulattā ussannadhātukaṃ kāyaṃ samassāsetuṃ dutiyadivase khīravirecanaṃ pivitvā vihāreyeva nisīdi. Yaṃ sandhāya subhena māṇavena pahitaṃ māṇavakaṃ etadavoca –

There, the Venerable Ānanda, having consoled that great crowd with a Dhamma talk connected with impermanence and so on, entered Jetavana. He opened the door of the Fragrant Cottage where the One of Ten Powers had dwelt, removed the bed and seat, shook them out, swept the Fragrant Cottage, discarded the withered garlands and refuse, brought back the bed and seat, and placed them. He then performed all the duties that were to be done as when the Blessed One was present. Then, since the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, the elder's bodily elements had become aggravated due to frequent standing and sitting; to relieve his body, on the second day he drank a milk purgative and sat in the monastery. It was in reference to this that he addressed the young man sent by the youth Subha, saying:

“Akālo kho, māṇavaka, atthi me ajja bhesajjamattā pītā, appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāmā”ti (dī. ni. 1.447).

'It is not the right time, young man. Today I have taken a dose of medicine. Perhaps we might come tomorrow.'

Dutiyadivase cetakattherena pacchāsamaṇena gantvā subhena māṇavena puṭṭho dīghanikāye subhasuttaṃnāma dasamaṃ suttamabhāsi.

On the second day, having gone with the elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, he, upon being questioned by the youth Subha, spoke the tenth sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya, named the Subha Sutta.

Atha thero jetavanavihāre khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ kārāpetvā upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya rājagahaṃ gato. Tathā mahākassapatthero anuruddhatthero ca sabbaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gahetvā rājagahameva gato.

Then the elder, having had repairs done to the broken and dilapidated parts of the Jetavana monastery, went to Rājagaha as the time for entering the rains was drawing near. Likewise, the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Anuruddha, taking the entire community of monks with them, also went to Rājagaha.

Tena kho pana samayena rājagahe aṭṭhārasa mahāvihārā honti. Te sabbepi chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā ahesuṃ. Bhagavato hi parinibbāne sabbe bhikkhū attano attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vihāre ca pariveṇe ca chaḍḍetvā agamaṃsu. Tattha therā bhagavato vacanapūjanatthaṃ titthiyavādaparimocanatthañca “paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karomā”ti cintesuṃ. Titthiyā hi evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā satthari ṭhiteyeva vihāre paṭijaggiṃsu, parinibbute chaḍḍesu”nti. Tesaṃ vādaparimocanatthañca cintesunti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttampi [P 1.0010] hetaṃ –

At that time, there were eighteen great monasteries in Rājagaha. All of them had become heaps of discarded and fallen debris. Indeed, upon the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, all the monks, taking their own bowls and robes, had abandoned the monasteries and their precincts and departed. There, the elders, for the purpose of honoring the Blessed One's word and to be free from the accusations of the sectarians, thought, “For the first month, let us undertake the repairing of what is broken and dilapidated.” For indeed, the sectarians might say, “The disciples of the ascetic Gotama looked after the monasteries only while the Teacher was present; when he attained Parinibbāna, they abandoned them.” And it is said that they thought this also to be free from their accusations. Indeed, this has been said:

“Atha [M 1.0009] kho therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – ‘bhagavatā kho, āvuso, khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ [V 1.0009] vaṇṇitaṃ. Handa mayaṃ, āvuso, paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ khaṇḍaphullappaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ karoma, majjhimaṃ māsaṃ sannipatitvā dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyissāmā”ti (cūḷava. 438).

“Then this thought occurred to the elder monks: ‘Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repairing of what is broken and dilapidated. Come, friends, let us spend the first month repairing what is broken and dilapidated; in the middle month, having assembled, we shall rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya.’”

Te dutiyadivase gantvā rājadvāre aṭṭhaṃsu. Ajātasattu rājā āgantvā vanditvā “kiṃ, bhante, āgatatthā”ti attanā kattabbakiccaṃ paṭipucchi. Therā aṭṭhārasa mahāvihārapaṭisaṅkharaṇatthāya hatthakammaṃ paṭivedesuṃ. “Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā hatthakammakārake manusse adāsi. Therā paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ sabbavihāre paṭisaṅkharāpetvā rañño ārocesuṃ – “niṭṭhitaṃ, mahārāja, vihārapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Idāni dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ karomā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante, vissatthā karotha. Mayhaṃ āṇācakkaṃ, tumhākaṃ dhammacakkaṃ hotu. Āṇāpetha, bhante, kiṃ karomī”ti? “Saṅgahaṃ karontānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sannisajjaṭṭhānaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Kattha karomi, bhante”ti? “Vebhārapabbatapasse sattapaṇṇiguhādvāre kātuṃ yuttaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho rājā ajātasattu vissakammunā nimmitasadisaṃ suvibhattabhittitthambhasopānaṃ nānāvidhamālākammalataākammavicittaṃ abhibhavantamiva rājabhavanavibhūtiṃ avahasantamiva devavimānasiriṃ siriyā niketamiva ekanipātatitthamiva ca devamanussanayanavihaṅgānaṃ lokarāmaṇeyyakamiva sampiṇḍitaṃ daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḍaṃ maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā vividhakusumadāma-olambaka-viniggalantacāruvitānaṃ [P 1.0011] ratanavicittamaṇikoṭṭimatalamiva ca naṃ nānāpupphūpahāravicittasupariniṭṭhitabhūmikammaṃ brahmavimānasadisaṃ alaṅkaritvā tasmiṃ mahāmaṇḍape pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anagghāni pañca kappiyapaccattharaṇasatāni paññāpetvā dakkhiṇabhāgaṃ nissāya uttarābhimukhaṃ therāsanaṃ maṇḍapamajjhe puratthābhimukhaṃ buddhassa bhagavato āsanārahaṃ dhammāsanaṃ paññāpetvā dantakhacitaṃ bījaniñcettha ṭhapetvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ārocāpesi – “niṭṭhitaṃ, bhante, mama kicca”nti.

On the second day, they went and stood at the king’s gate. King Ajātasattu came, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable sirs, for what purpose have you come?” thus inquiring about the duty he should perform. The elders informed him of the need for manual labor for the repairing of the eighteen great monasteries. “Very well, venerable sirs,” said the king, and he provided men to do the work. Having had all the monasteries repaired during the first month, the elders informed the king: “Great king, the repairing of the monasteries is finished. Now we shall undertake the compilation of the Dhamma and the Vinaya.” “Very well, venerable sirs, proceed with confidence. Let mine be the wheel of authority, and yours be the wheel of the Dhamma. Command me, venerable sirs, what shall I do?” “A place of assembly for the monks performing the compilation, great king.” “Where shall I make it, venerable sirs?” “It is suitable to make it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the side of Mount Vebhāra, great king.” “Very well, venerable sirs.” Then King Ajātasattu had a pavilion constructed, like one created by Vissakamma, with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and staircases, adorned with various kinds of flower-work and creeper-work; as if overpowering the splendor of a royal palace, as if mocking the glory of a celestial mansion, like a home for all splendors, and like a single landing-place for the birds that are the eyes of gods and humans, like the world's delightfulness gathered into one place, a splendid sight to behold. Having had this pavilion made and adorned to be like a Brahmā’s mansion, with beautiful canopies from which hung various garlands of flowers, and its floor perfectly finished and adorned with offerings of various flowers, like a surface of polished gems variegated with jewels; and having prepared in that great pavilion five hundred priceless, suitable seat-coverings for the five hundred monks; having prepared the Elder's seat in the southern part, facing north, and in the middle of the pavilion, facing east, a Dhamma-seat worthy of the Blessed One, the Buddha; and having placed there a fan inlaid with ivory, he had it announced to the Sangha of monks: “Venerable sirs, my duty is finished.”

Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye ekacce bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sandhāya evamāhaṃsu – “imasmiṃ bhikkhusaṅghe eko bhikkhu vissagandhaṃ vāyanto vicaratī”ti. Thero taṃ sutvā “imasmiṃ bhikkhusaṅghe añño vissagandhaṃ vāyanto [M 1.0010] vicaraṇakabhikkhu nāma natthi, addhā ete maṃ sandhāya vadantī”ti saṃvegaṃ āpajji. Ekacce bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āhaṃsu – “sve, āvuso, sannipāto tvañca sekkho sakaraṇīyo, tena te na yuttaṃ sannipātaṃ gantuṃ, appamatto hohī”ti.

At that time, some monks, with reference to the Venerable Ānanda, said this: “In this community of monks, there is one monk who wanders about giving off a raw, fleshy smell.” The elder, having heard that, thought, “In this community of monks, there is no other monk who wanders about giving off a raw, fleshy smell; surely, they are speaking with reference to me,” and he felt a sense of spiritual urgency. Some monks said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend, tomorrow is the assembly, and you are a trainee with something further to do; therefore, it is not fitting for you to go to the assembly. Be heedful!”

Atha kho āyasmā ānando – “sve sannipāto, na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ yvāhaṃ sekkho [V 1.0010] samāno sannipātaṃ gaccheyya”nti bahudeva rattiṃ kāyagatāyasatiyā vītināmetvā rattiyā paccūsasamayaṃ caṅkamā orohitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā “nipajjissāmī”ti kāyaṃ āvajjesi. Dve pādā bhūmito muttā, appattañca sīsaṃ bimbohanaṃ, etasmiṃ antare anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci. Ayañhi āyasmā caṅkamena [P 1.0012] bahi vītināmetvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto cintesi – “nanu maṃ bhagavā etadavoca – ‘katapuññosi tvaṃ, ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja; khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo’ti (dī. ni. 2.207). Buddhānañca kathādoso nāma natthi. Mama accāraddhaṃ vīriyaṃ tena me cittaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvattati. Handāhaṃ vīriyasamathaṃ yojemī”ti caṅkamā orohitvā pādadhovanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā pāde dhovitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā mañcake nisīditvā “thokaṃ vissamissāmī”ti kāyaṃ mañcake upanāmesi. Dve pādā bhūmito muttā, sīsañca bimbohanaṃ asampattaṃ. Etasmiṃ antare anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuttaṃ, catuiriyāpathavirahitaṃ therassa arahattaṃ ahosi. Tena imasmiṃ sāsane anipanno anisinno aṭṭhito acaṅkamanto “ko bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto”ti vutte “ānandatthero”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Then the Venerable Ānanda thought, “Tomorrow is the assembly, and it is not fitting for me, being a trainee, to go to the assembly.” Having spent most of the night with mindfulness directed to the body, at the time of dawn he descended from his meditation walk, entered his dwelling, and thinking, “I will lie down,” he inclined his body. His two feet were lifted from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow. In that interval, without clinging, his mind was liberated from the taints. For this venerable one, having spent time outside on the meditation walk and being unable to bring about a special attainment, reflected: “Did not the Blessed One say this to me: ‘You have made merit, Ānanda. Apply yourself to the striving; you will quickly be without taints’? And there is no flaw in the words of the Buddhas. My effort is over-exerted; because of that, my mind tends towards restlessness. Come, let me balance my energy.” Descending from his meditation walk, he stood at the place for washing feet, washed his feet, entered his dwelling, sat on his couch, and thinking, “I will rest a little,” he laid his body down on the couch. His two feet were lifted from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow. In that interval, without clinging, his mind was liberated from the taints. The elder's Arahantship was free from the four postures. Therefore, in this Dispensation, when it is asked, “Which monk attained Arahantship without lying down, without sitting, without standing, and without walking?” it is fitting to say, “The Elder Ānanda.”

Atha kho therā bhikkhū dutiyadivase katabhattakiccā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā. Ānandatthero pana attano arahattappattiṃ ñāpetukāmo bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ na gato. Bhikkhū yathāvuḍḍhaṃ attano attano pattāsane nisīdantā ānandattherassa āsanaṃ ṭhapetvā nisinnā. Tattha kehici “etamāsanaṃ kassā”ti vutte “ānandattherassā”ti. “Ānando pana kuhiṃ gato”ti? Tasmiṃ samaye thero cintesi – “idāni mayhaṃ gamanakālo”ti. Tato attano ānubhāvaṃ [P 1.0013] dassento pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā attano āsaneyeva attānaṃ dassesi. Ākāsenāgantvā nisīdītipi eke.

Then, on the second day, the elder monks, having completed their meal and put away their bowls and robes, assembled in the Dhamma hall. The Elder Ānanda, however, wishing to make known his attainment of Arahantship, did not go with the monks. The monks, sitting down in their respective seats according to seniority, left the Elder Ānanda’s seat vacant. There, when some asked, “Whose seat is this?” it was said, “The Elder Ānanda’s.” “But where has Ānanda gone?” At that moment, the Elder thought, “Now is my time to go.” Then, displaying his psychic power, he dived into the earth and showed himself on his own seat. Some also say that he came through the sky and sat down.

Evaṃ [M 1.0011] nisinne tasmiṃ āyasmante mahākassapatthero bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso, kiṃ paṭhamaṃ saṅgāyāma, dhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā”ti? Bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “bhante mahākassapa, vinayo nāma buddhasāsanassa āyu, vinaye ṭhite sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ hoti; tasmā paṭhamaṃ vinayaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti,. “Kaṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti? “Āyasmantaṃ upāli”nti. “Kiṃ ānando nappahotī”ti? “No nappahoti; api ca kho pana sammāsambuddho dharamānoyeva vinayapariyattiṃ nissāya āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ etadagge ṭhapesi – ‘etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upālī’ti (a. ni. 1.219, 228). Tasmā upālittheraṃ [V 1.0011] pucchitvā vinayaṃ saṅgāyāmā”ti. Tato thero vinayaṃ pucchanatthāya attanāva attānaṃ sammanni. Upālittheropi vissajjanatthāya sammanni. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

When that venerable one was thus seated, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the monks: “Friends, what shall we chant first, the Dhamma or the Vinaya?” The monks said: “Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the life-force of the Buddha’s Dispensation. When the Vinaya stands, the Dispensation stands. Therefore, let us chant the Vinaya first.” “Having made whom the authority?” “The Venerable Upāli.” “Is Ānanda not capable?” “It is not that he is not capable; but furthermore, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was still living, with reference to the scriptural learning of the Vinaya, placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position, saying: ‘Foremost, O monks, among my monk disciples who are masters of the Vinaya is this one, namely Upāli.’ Therefore, having questioned the Elder Upāli, let us chant the Vinaya.” Then, the Elder appointed himself for the purpose of questioning on the Vinaya. The Elder Upāli also appointed himself for the purpose of answering. Herein, this is the Pāli text:

“Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa announced to the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ upāliṃ vinayaṃ puccheyya’nti.

“Friends, may the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli on the Vinaya.”

“Āyasmāpi upāli saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

The Venerable Upāli also announced to the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ āyasmatā mahākassapena vinayaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeyya”nti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer.”

Evaṃ attanāva attānaṃ sammannitvā āyasmā upāli uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā there bhikkhū vanditvā dhammāsane nisīdi, dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ gahetvā. Tato āyasmā mahākassapo therāsane nisīditvā āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ vinayaṃ pucchi – “paṭhamaṃ, āvuso upāli, pārājikaṃ kattha paññatta”nti[P 1.0014]? “Vesāliyaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kaṃ ārabbhā”ti? “Sudinnaṃ kalandaputtaṃ ārabbhā”ti. “Kismiṃ vatthusmi”nti? “Methunadhamme”ti.

Thus having appointed himself, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat down on the Dhamma-seat, holding an ivory-inlaid fan. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having sat down on the elder’s seat, questioned the Venerable Upāli on the Vinaya: “Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika laid down?” “In Vesālī, venerable sir.” “Concerning whom?” “Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka.” “In what matter?” “In the matter of sexual intercourse.”

Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ paṭhamassa pārājikassa vatthumpi pucchi, nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi, paññattimpi pucchi, anupaññattimpi pucchi, āpattimpi pucchi, anāpattimpi pucchi; yathā ca paṭhamassa tathā dutiyassa tathā tatiyassa tathā catutthassa pārājikassa vatthumpi pucchi…pe… anāpattimpi pucchi. Puṭṭho puṭṭho upālitthero vissajjesi. Tato [M 1.0012] imāni cattāri pārājikāni “pārājikakaṇḍaṃ nāma ida”nti saṅgahaṃ āropetvā ṭhapesuṃ. Terasa saṅghādisesāni “terasaka”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Dve sikkhāpadāni “aniyatānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Tiṃsa sikkhāpadāni “nissaggiyapācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Dvenavuti sikkhāpadāni “pācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Cattāri sikkhāpadāni “pāṭidesanīyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Pañcasattati sikkhāpadāni “sekhiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Satta dhamme “adhikaraṇasamathā”ti ṭhapesuṃ.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli about the story of the first Pārājika, he asked about the origin, he asked about the person, he asked about the regulation, he asked about the supplementary regulation, he asked about the offense, and he asked about the non-offense. And just as for the first, so too for the second, so too for the third, so too for the fourth Pārājika, he asked about the story… and so on… he asked about the non-offense. Whenever questioned, the Elder Upāli answered. Then, having brought these four Pārājikas into the compilation, they established them as “This is the Pārājika Section.” They established the thirteen Saṅghādisesas as “The Thirteen.” They established the two training rules as “The Indefinites.” They established the thirty training rules as “The Nissaggiya Pācittiyas.” They established the ninety-two training rules as “The Pācittiyas.” They established the four training rules as “The Pāṭidesanīyas.” They established the seventy-five training rules as “The Sekhiyas.” They established the seven principles as “The Adhikaraṇasamathas.”

Evaṃ [V 1.0012] mahāvibhaṅgaṃ saṅgahaṃ āropetvā bhikkhunīvibhaṅge aṭṭha sikkhāpadāni “pārājikakaṇḍaṃ nāma ida”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Sattarasa sikkhāpadāni “sattarasaka”nti ṭhapesuṃ. Tiṃsa sikkhāpadāni “nissaggiyapācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Chasaṭṭhisatasikkhāpadāni “pācittiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Aṭṭha sikkhāpadāni “pāṭidesanīyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Pañcasattati sikkhāpadāni “sekhiyānī”ti ṭhapesuṃ. Satta dhamme “adhikaraṇasamathā”ti [P 1.0015] ṭhapesuṃ. Evaṃ bhikkhunīvibhaṅgaṃ saṅgahaṃ āropetvā eteneva upāyena khandhakaparivārepi āropesuṃ. Evametaṃ saubhatovibhaṅgakhandhakaparivāraṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ saṅgahamārūḷhaṃ sabbaṃ mahākassapatthero pucchi, upālitthero vissajjesi. Pucchāvissajjanapariyosāne pañca arahantasatāni saṅgahaṃ āropitanayeneva gaṇasajjhāyamakaṃsu. Vinayasaṅgahāvasāne upālitthero dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ nikkhipitvā dhammāsanā orohitvā vuḍḍhe bhikkhū vanditvā attano pattāsane nisīdi.

Thus having brought the Mahāvibhaṅga into the compilation, in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga they established the eight training rules as “This is the Pārājika Section.” They established the seventeen training rules as “The Seventeen.” They established the thirty training rules as “The Nissaggiya Pācittiyas.” They established the one hundred and sixty-six training rules as “The Pācittiyas.” They established the eight training rules as “The Pāṭidesanīyas.” They established the seventy-five training rules as “The Sekhiyas.” They established the seven principles as “The Adhikaraṇasamathas.” Thus having brought the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga into the compilation, by this same method they also brought the Khandhakas and the Parivāra into the compilation. Thus, concerning this entire Vinayapiṭaka which had been brought into the compilation—comprising both Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra—the Elder Mahākassapa questioned and the Elder Upāli answered. At the conclusion of the questioning and answering, the five hundred Arahants performed a group chanting in the very way it had been brought into the compilation. At the end of the Vinaya compilation, the Elder Upāli, having put down the ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dhamma-seat, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat down in his own appointed seat.

Vinayaṃ saṅgāyitvā dhammaṃ saṅgāyitukāmo āyasmā mahākassapo bhikkhū pucchi – “dhammaṃ saṅgāyantehi kaṃ puggalaṃ dhuraṃ katvā dhammo saṅgāyitabbo”ti? Bhikkhū “ānandattheraṃ dhuraṃ katvā”ti āhaṃsu.

Having chanted the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa, wishing to chant the Dhamma, asked the monks: “When we chant the Dhamma, who should be appointed as the authority?” The monks replied: “The Elder Ānanda.”

Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa announced to the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ ānandaṃ dhammaṃ puccheyya”nti.

“Friends, may the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda on the Dhamma.”

Atha kho āyasmā ānando saṅghaṃ ñāpesi –

Then the Venerable Ānanda announced to the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ āyasmatā mahākassapena dhammaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeyya”nti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer.”

Atha [M 1.0013] kho āyasmā ānando uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā there bhikkhū vanditvā dhammāsane nisīdi dantakhacitaṃ bījaniṃ gahetvā. Atha mahākassapatthero ānandattheraṃ dhammaṃ pucchi – “brahmajālaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti? “Antarā ca, bhante, rājagahaṃ [P 1.0016] antarā ca nāḷandaṃ rājāgārake ambalaṭṭhikāya”nti. “Kaṃ ārabbhā”ti? “Suppiyañca paribbājakaṃ, brahmadattañca māṇava”nti. “Kismiṃ vatthusmi”nti? “Vaṇṇāvaṇṇe”ti. Atha kho [V 1.0013] āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ brahmajālassa nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi, vatthumpi pucchi. “Sāmaññaphalaṃ panāvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”nti? ‘Rājagahe, bhante, jīvakambavane”ti. “Kena saddhi”nti? “Ajātasattunā vedehiputtena saddhi”nti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sāmaññaphalassa nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi. Eteneva upāyena pañca nikāye pucchi.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and sat down on the Dhamma seat, holding an ivory-inlaid fan. Then the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Ānanda about the Dhamma: 'Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?' 'Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, venerable sir, at the royal resthouse in Ambalaṭṭhikā.' 'Concerning whom?' 'Concerning the wanderer Suppiya and the young man Brahmadatta.' 'On what subject?' 'On praise and dispraise.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda about the occasion for the Brahmajāla Sutta, the persons involved, and the subject matter. 'And the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, friend Ānanda—where was it spoken?' 'In Rājagaha, venerable sir, in Jīvaka’s mango grove.' 'With whom?' 'With Ajātasattu, son of the Videhī queen.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda about the occasion for the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and the persons involved. In this same way, he questioned him about the five Nikāyas.

Pañcanikāyā nāma – dīghanikāyo, majjhimanikāyo, saṃyuttanikāyo, aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakanikāyoti. Tattha khuddakanikāyo nāma – cattāro nikāye ṭhapetvā, avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Tattha vinayo āyasmatā upālittherena vissajjito, sesakhuddakanikāyo cattāro ca nikāyā ānandattherena. Tadetaṃ sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ rasavasena ekavidhaṃ, dhammavinayavasena duvidhaṃ, paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavasena tividhaṃ; tathā piṭakavasena, nikāyavasena pañcavidhaṃ, aṅgavasena navavidhaṃ, dhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassavidhanti veditabbaṃ.

The five Nikāyas are: the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya. Therein, the Khuddaka Nikāya is the remainder of the Buddha’s word, setting aside the four Nikāyas. Therein, the Vinaya was answered by the Venerable Elder Upāli; the remaining Khuddaka Nikāya and the four Nikāyas were answered by the Elder Ānanda. All this word of the Buddha should be understood as: onefold by way of taste; twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya; threefold by way of the first, middle, and last periods; likewise threefold by way of the Piṭakas; fivefold by way of the Nikāyas; ninefold by way of the divisions; and eighty-four thousandfold by way of the Dhamma aggregates.

Kathaṃ rasavasena ekavidhaṃ? Yañhi bhagavatā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā yāva anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati, etthantare pañcacattālīsavassāni devamanussanāgayakkhādayo anusāsantena paccavekkhantena vā vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekarasaṃ vimuttirasameva hoti. Evaṃ rasavasena ekavidhaṃ.

How is it onefold by way of taste? For whatever was spoken by the Blessed One—whether instructing or reviewing while teaching gods, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, and so on—in the forty-five years from the time he awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until he passed into the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining, all of that has a single taste, the taste of liberation. Thus, it is onefold by way of taste.

Kathaṃ [P 1.0017] dhammavinayavasena duvidhaṃ? Sabbameva cetaṃ dhammo ceva vinayo cāti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tattha vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayo, avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ dhammo; tenevāha – “yaṃnūna mayaṃ, āvuso, dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyeyyāmā”ti. “Ahaṃ [M 1.0014] upāliṃ vinayaṃ puccheyyaṃ, ānandaṃ dhammaṃ puccheyya”nti ca evaṃ dhammavinayavasena duvidhaṃ.

How is it twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya? All of this is reckoned as both Dhamma and Vinaya. Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya, and the remainder of the Buddha’s word is the Dhamma. Therefore it was said: 'Friends, let us now chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya.' And also: 'I would question Upāli about the Vinaya, and Ānanda about the Dhamma.' Thus it is twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya.

Kathaṃ paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavasena tividhaṃ? Sabbameva hidaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ, majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ, pacchimabuddhavacananti tippabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha –

How is it threefold by way of the first, middle, and last periods? All this is indeed of three kinds: the first word of the Buddha, the middle word of the Buddha, and the last word of the Buddha. Therein:

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

Through many a birth in saṃsāra I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Painful is birth again and again.

“Gahakāraka [V 1.0014] diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ;

Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti. (dha. pa. 153-154);

O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build a house again. All your rafters are broken, your ridgepole is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.

Idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ.

This is the first word of the Buddha.

Keci “yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā”ti khandhake udānagāthaṃ āhu. Esā pana pāṭipadadivase sabbaññubhāvappattassa somanassamayañāṇena paccayākāraṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannā udānagāthāti veditabbā.

Some say that the inspired utterance in the Khandhaka, 'When, indeed, phenomena become manifest,' is the first word. But this should be understood as the inspired utterance that arose on the day after enlightenment to him who had attained the state of an All-Knowing One, as he was reviewing the causal structure with knowledge accompanied by joy.

Yaṃ pana parinibbānakāle abhāsi – “handa dāni, bhikkhave, āmantayāmi vo, vayadhammā saṅkhārā, appamādena sampādethā”ti (dī. ni. 2.218) idaṃ pacchimabuddhavacanaṃ.

But what he spoke at the time of his final passing away—'Come now, bhikkhus, I address you: all formations are subject to decay; strive on with heedfulness'—this is the last word of the Buddha.

Ubhinnamantare yaṃ vuttaṃ etaṃ majjhimabuddhavacananti. Evaṃ paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavasena tividhaṃ.

Whatever was spoken between these two is the middle word of the Buddha. Thus, it is threefold by way of the first, middle, and last periods.

Kathaṃ [P 1.0018] piṭakavasena tividhaṃ? Sabbampi hetaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakanti tippabhedameva hoti. Tattha paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ saṅgītañca asaṅgītañca sabbampi samodhānetvā ubhayāni pātimokkhāni, dve vibhaṅgāni, dvāvīsati khandhakāni, soḷasaparivārāti idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ nāma.

How is it threefold by way of the Piṭakas? All of this is indeed of three kinds: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein, at the First Council, all that was chanted and not chanted was compiled together: the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras—this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Brahmajālādi catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho dīghanikāyo, mūlapariyāyasuttādi diyaḍḍhasatadvesuttasaṅgaho majjhimanikāyo, oghataraṇasuttādi sattasuttasahassa sattasata dvāsaṭṭhisuttasaṅgaho saṃyuttanikāyo, cittapariyādānasuttādi navasuttasahassa pañcasata sattapaññāsasuttasaṅgaho aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakapāṭha-dhammapada-udāna-itivuttaka-suttanipāta-vimānavatthu-petavatthu-theragāthā-therīgāthā-jātakaniddesa-paṭisambhidā-apadāna-buddhavaṃsa-cariyāpiṭakavasena [M 1.0015] pannarasappabhedo khuddakanikāyoti idaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ nāma.

The Dīgha Nikāya, a collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla; the Majjhima Nikāya, a collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta; the Saṃyutta Nikāya, a collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta; the Aṅguttara Nikāya, a collection of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta; and the Khuddaka Nikāya, which has fifteen divisions, namely: Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—this is called the Suttanta Piṭaka.

Dhammasaṅgaho, vibhaṅgo, dhātukathā, puggalapaññatti, kathāvatthu, yamakaṃ, paṭṭhānanti idaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ nāma. Tattha –

The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—this is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein:

Vividhavisesanayattā[V 1.0015], vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ;

Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto.

Because of its various and special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, this Vinaya is declared 'Vinaya' by those who know the meaning of Vinaya.

Vividhā hi ettha pañcavidha pātimokkhuddesa pārājikādi sattaāpattikkhandhamātikā vibhaṅgādippabhedā nayā, visesabhūtā ca daḷhīkammasithilakaraṇappayojanā anupaññattinayā[P 1.0019], kāyikavācasikaajjhācāranisedhanato cesa kāyaṃ vācañca vineti, tasmā vividhanayattā visesanayattā kāyavācānañca vinayanato “vinayo”ti akkhāto. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

For herein there are various methods, with divisions such as the fivefold Pātimokkha recitation, the seven groups of offenses beginning with Pārājika, the Mātikā, and the Vibhaṅga; and there are special methods, which are the supplementary regulations for the purpose of strengthening or making flexible; and by prohibiting bodily and verbal transgression, it disciplines the body and speech. Therefore, because of its various methods, its special methods, and its disciplining of body and speech, it is declared 'Vinaya'. For this reason, for the sake of skill in its etymology, this was said:

“Vividhavisesanayattā, vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ;

Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto”ti.

Because of its various and special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, this Vinaya is declared 'Vinaya' by those who know the meaning of Vinaya.

Itaraṃ pana –

As for the other:

Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, suttanti akkhātaṃ.

Because it indicates meanings, is well-spoken, yields, pours forth, protects well, and has the nature of a thread, it is declared 'Sutta'.

Tañhi attatthaparatthādibhede atthe sūceti, suvuttā cettha atthā veneyyajjhāsayānulomena vuttattā. Savati cetaṃ atthe sassamiva phalaṃ pasavatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sūdati cetaṃ dhenuviya khīraṃ, paggharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Suṭṭhu ca ne tāyati rakkhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Suttasabhāgañcetaṃ, yathā hi tacchakānaṃ suttaṃ pamāṇaṃ hoti; evametampi viññūnaṃ. Yathā ca suttena saṅgahitāni pupphāni na vikiriyanti na viddhaṃsiyanti; evametena saṅgahitā atthā. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

For it indicates meanings with divisions such as one's own benefit and the benefit of others; and herein, the meanings are well-spoken, being spoken in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained. And it yields benefits, just as a crop yields fruit—thus it is said. And it pours forth benefits, like a cow its milk, it gushes forth—thus it is said. And it protects them well, it guards them—thus it is said. And it has the nature of a thread; for just as a carpenter's thread is a measure, so too is this a measure for the wise. And just as flowers gathered on a thread are not scattered or destroyed, so too are the meanings gathered by this. Therefore, for the sake of skill in the etymology of this word, this was said:

“Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, suttanti akkhāta”nti.

Because it indicates meanings, is well-spoken, yields, pours forth, protects well, and has the nature of a thread, it is declared 'Sutta'.

Itaro [P 1.0020][M 1.0016] pana –

As for the other:

Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto.

Because herein are taught dhammas that are augmentative, characterized, venerated, delimited, and superior, it is therefore declared 'Abhidhamma'.

Ayañhi [V 1.0016] abhisaddo vuḍḍhilakkhaṇapūjitaparicchinnādhikesu dissati. Tathāhesa – “bāḷhā me āvuso dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti no paṭikkamantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.389; saṃ. ni. 5.195) vuḍḍhiyaṃ āgato. “Yā tā rattiyo abhiññātā abhilakkhitā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.49) lakkhaṇe. “Rājābhirājā manujindo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 558) pūjite. “Paṭibalo vinetuṃ abhidhamme abhivinaye”tiādīsu (mahāva. 85) paricchinne. Aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhamme ca vinaye cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Abhikkantena vaṇṇenā”tiādīsu (vi. va. 75) adhike.

For this prefix 'abhi' is seen in the senses of augmentation, characteristic, veneration, delimitation, and superiority. Thus, it is found in the sense of augmentation in passages such as: 'Friend, strong painful feelings are increasing in me, not decreasing.' In the sense of characteristic in passages such as: 'Those nights that are well-known and well-marked.' In the sense of veneration in passages such as: 'The king of kings, the lord of men.' In the sense of delimitation in passages such as: 'Capable of guiding in the delimited Dhamma and the delimited Vinaya.' This means in the Dhamma and Vinaya that are free from mutual confusion. In the sense of superiority in passages such as: 'With surpassing beauty.'

Ettha ca “rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti, mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 160 ādayo) nayena vuḍḍhimantopi dhammā vuttā. “Rūpārammaṇaṃ vā saddārammaṇaṃ vā”tiādinā nayena ārammaṇādīhi lakkhaṇīyattā salakkhaṇāpi. “Sekkhā dhammā, asekkhā dhammā, lokuttarā dhammā”tiādinā nayena pūjitāpi pūjārahāti adhippāyo. “Phasso hoti vedanā hotī”tiādinā nayena sabhāvaparicchinnattā paricchinnāpi. “Mahaggatā dhammā, appamāṇā dhammā, anuttarā dhammā”tiādinā nayena adhikāpi dhammā vuttā. Tenetametassa vacanatthakosallatthaṃ vuttaṃ –

And herein, dhammas that are augmentative are also taught, in the manner of: 'He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm; he dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.' Dhammas that are characterized are also taught, as they are to be characterized by their objects, etc., in the manner of: 'a form-object or a sound-object.' Dhammas that are venerated are also taught, in the manner of: 'dhammas of trainees, dhammas of non-trainees, supramundane dhammas'; the intended meaning is that they are worthy of veneration. Dhammas that are delimited are also taught, as they are delimited by their intrinsic nature, in the manner of: 'there is contact, there is feeling.' And dhammas that are superior are also taught, in the manner of: 'exalted dhammas, immeasurable dhammas, unsurpassed dhammas.' Therefore, for the sake of skill in the etymology of this word, this was said:

“Yaṃ ettha vuḍḍhimanto, salakkhaṇā pūjitā paricchinnā;

Vuttādhikā ca dhammā, abhidhammo tena akkhāto”ti.

Because herein are taught dhammas that are augmentative, characterized, venerated, delimited, and superior, it is therefore declared 'Abhidhamma'.

Yaṃ panettha avisiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ –

That which is common among these is:

Piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū, pariyattibbhājanatthato āhu;

Tena samodhānetvā, tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā.

Those who know the meaning of 'Piṭaka' declare it so from its meaning as 'scripture' and 'receptacle'. By combining with that term, the three beginning with Vinaya should be understood.

Pariyattipi [P 1.0021][M 1.0017] hi “mā piṭakasampadānenā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) piṭakanti vuccati. “Atha puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭakaṃ ādāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.228; a. ni. 3.70) yaṃ kiñci bhājanampi. Tasmā piṭakaṃ piṭakatthavidū, pariyattibbhājanatthato āhu.

For 'scripture' (pariyatti) is also called 'piṭaka' in passages such as: 'Do not be satisfied merely with proficiency in the scriptures.' And any kind of 'receptacle' (bhājana) is also called 'piṭaka' in passages such as: 'Then a man might come, bringing a spade and a basket.' Therefore, those who know the meaning of 'Piṭaka' declare it so from its meaning as 'scripture' and 'receptacle'.

Idāni tena samodhānetvā tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyāti. Tena evaṃ duvidhatthena piṭakasaddena saha [V 1.0017] samāsaṃ katvā vinayo ca so piṭakañca pariyattibhāvato tassa tassa atthassa bhājanato cāti vinayapiṭakaṃ, yathāvutteneva nayena suttantañca taṃ piṭakañcāti suttantapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammo ca so piṭakañcāti abhidhammapiṭakanti evamete tayopi vinayādayo ñeyyā.

Now, regarding 'By combining with that term, the three beginning with Vinaya should be understood': Having formed a compound with that word 'piṭaka' which has a twofold meaning, it should be understood thus: It is the Vinaya, and it is a Piṭaka—both because it is scripture and because it is a receptacle for its various meanings—thus it is the Vinaya Piṭaka. In the same way as stated, it is the Suttanta, and it is a Piṭaka, thus it is the Suttanta Piṭaka; it is the Abhidhamma, and it is a Piṭaka, thus it is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. In this way, these three beginning with Vinaya should be understood.

Evaṃ ñatvā ca punapi tesveva piṭakesu nānappakārakosallatthaṃ –

Having understood this, and again, for the sake of skill in various ways in these very Piṭakas:

Desanāsāsanakathā, bhedaṃ tesu yathārahaṃ;

Sikkhāpahānagambhīra, bhāvañca paridīpaye.

One should illuminate, as is appropriate in them, the distinctions of exposition, instruction, and discourse, and the nature of training, abandonment, and profundity.

Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiṃ cāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye.

One should also make clear all of this: in which Piṭaka, in what way, a bhikkhu attains a certain distinction of learning, accomplishment, or failure.

Tatrāyaṃ paridīpanā vibhāvanā ca, etāni hi tīṇi piṭakāni yathākkamaṃ āṇā vohāra paramatthadesanā yathāparādha-yathānuloma-yathādhammasāsanāni, saṃvarāsaṃvaradiṭṭhiviniveṭhanāmarūpaparicchedakathāti ca vuccanti.

Herein is this illumination and explanation: For these three Piṭakas, in order, are also called: the exposition by command, by conventional discourse, and by ultimate reality; the instruction according to offense, according to suitability, and according to the Dhamma; and the discourse on restraint and non-restraint, on the removal of wrong views, and on the delimitation of name-and-form.

Ettha hi vinayapiṭakaṃ āṇārahena bhagavatā āṇābāhullato desitattā āṇādesanā, suttantapiṭakaṃ vohārakusalena bhagavatā vohārabāhullato desitattā vohāradesanā, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ paramatthakusalena bhagavatā paramatthabāhullato desitattā paramatthadesanāti vuccati.

Herein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is called the exposition of command because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is worthy of giving commands, with an abundance of commands. The Suttanta Piṭaka is called the exposition of conventional discourse because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in conventional discourse, with an abundance of such discourse. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called the exposition of ultimate reality because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in ultimate reality, with an abundance of such reality.

Tathā [P 1.0022] paṭhamaṃ ye te pacurāparādhā sattā te yathāparādhaṃ ettha sāsitāti yathāparādhasāsanaṃ, dutiyaṃ anekajjhāsayānusayacariyādhimuttikā sattā yathānulomaṃ ettha sāsitāti yathānulomasāsanaṃ, tatiyaṃ dhammapuñjamatte “ahaṃ mamā”ti saññino sattā yathādhammaṃ ettha sāsitāti yathādhammasāsananti vuccati.

Furthermore, the first is called the 'instruction according to offense' because those beings who are abundant in offenses are instructed herein according to their offense. The second is called the 'instruction according to suitability' because beings with diverse inclinations, underlying tendencies, conduct, and dispositions are instructed herein according to what is suitable. The third is called the 'instruction according to the Dhamma' because beings who perceive a mere collection of phenomena as 'I' and 'mine' are instructed herein according to the Dhamma.

Tathā [M 1.0018] paṭhamaṃ ajjhācārapaṭipakkhabhūto saṃvarāsaṃvaro ettha kathitoti saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā, dutiyaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhipaṭipakkhabhūtā diṭṭhiviniveṭhanā ettha kathitāti diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā, tatiyaṃ rāgādipaṭipakkhabhūto nāmarūpaparicchedo ettha kathitoti nāmarūpaparicchedakathāti vuccati.

Furthermore, the first is called the 'discourse on restraint and non-restraint' because restraint and non-restraint, which are the antithesis of transgression, are taught herein. The second is called the 'discourse on the unraveling of views' because the unraveling of views, which is the antithesis of the sixty-two wrong views, is taught herein. The third is called the 'discourse on the discernment of mind and matter' because the discernment of mind and matter, which is the antithesis of lust and so forth, is taught herein.

Tīsupi ca cetesu tisso sikkhā, tīṇi pahānāni, catubbidho ca gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo[V 1.0018]. Tathā hi – vinayapiṭake visesena adhisīlasikkhā vuttā, suttantapiṭake adhicittasikkhā, abhidhammapiṭake adhipaññāsikkhā.

And in all three of these Piṭakas, the three trainings, the three kinds of abandoning, and the fourfold profundity should be understood. Indeed, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue is especially taught; in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind; and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom.

Vinayapiṭake ca vītikkamappahānaṃ kilesānaṃ, vītikkamapaṭipakkhattā sīlassa. Suttantapiṭake pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ, pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkhattā samādhissa. Abhidhammapiṭake anusayappahānaṃ anusayapaṭipakkhattā paññāya.

And in the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the transgression of the defilements, because virtue is the antithesis of transgression. In the Suttanta Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the obsession of the defilements, because concentration is the antithesis of obsession. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the latent tendencies of the defilements, because wisdom is the antithesis of latent tendencies.

Paṭhame ca tadaṅgappahānaṃ kilesānaṃ, itaresu vikkhambhanasamucchedappahānāni. Paṭhame ca duccaritasaṃkilesassa pahānaṃ, itaresu taṇhādiṭṭhisaṃkilesānaṃ.

And in the first, there is the abandoning of defilements by substitution of the opposite part; in the others, there are the abandonings by suppression and by eradication. And in the first, there is the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct; in the others, the abandoning of the defilements of craving and wrong view.

Ekamekasmiñcettha catubbidhopi dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīrabhāvo veditabbo. Tattha dhammoti pāḷi. Atthoti tassāyevattho. Desanāti tassā manasāvavatthāpitāya pāḷiyā desanā. Paṭivedhoti pāḷiyā pāḷiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho. Tīsupi cetesu ete dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhā [P 1.0023] yasmā sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo mandabuddhīhi dukkhogāhā alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā ca, tasmā gambhīrā. Evaṃ ekamekasmiṃ ettha catubbidhopi gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo.

And in each one of these, the fourfold profundity—of Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration—should be understood. Herein, 'Dhamma' is the Pāḷi text. 'Meaning' is the meaning of that very text. 'Teaching' is the exposition of that Pāḷi text which has been determined in the mind. 'Penetration' is the understanding of the Pāḷi text and its meaning as they really are. In all three of these Piṭakas, these—the Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration—are difficult for those of dull wisdom to fathom and have no attainable foundation, just as the great ocean is for hares and other small creatures; therefore, they are profound. Thus, in each one of these, the fourfold profundity should be understood.

Aparo nayo – dhammoti hetu. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti. Atthoti hetuphalaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti. Desanāti paññatti, yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpoti adhippāyo. Paṭivedhoti abhisamayo, so ca lokiyalokuttaro visayato asammohato ca atthānurūpaṃ dhammesu, dhammānurūpaṃ atthesu, paññattipathānurūpaṃ paññattīsu avabodho.

Another method: 'Dhamma' is cause. For this has been said: 'Knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma.' 'Meaning' is the result of the cause. For this has been said: 'Knowledge in the result of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning.' 'Teaching' is designation; the intention is the verbal expression in accordance with the phenomena. 'Penetration' is realization. And that, being both worldly and supramundane, is the unconfused knowledge, with respect to its object, that understands causes in accordance with their results, results in accordance with their causes, and designations in accordance with the path of designation.

Idāni yasmā etesu piṭakesu yaṃ yaṃ dhammajātaṃ vā atthajātaṃ vā, yā cāyaṃ yathā yathā ñāpetabbo attho sotūnaṃ ñāṇassa abhimukho hoti, tathā tathā tadatthajotikā desanā, yo cettha [M 1.0019] aviparītāvabodhasaṅkhāto paṭivedho sabbametaṃ anupacitakusalasambhārehi duppaññehi sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo dukkhogāhaṃ alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhañca, tasmā gambhīraṃ. Evampi ekamekasmiṃ ettha catubbidhopi gambhīrabhāvo veditabbo.

Now, because in these Piṭakas, whatever kind of Dhamma (cause) or meaning (result) there is; and the teaching that illuminates that meaning in whatever way a meaning that should be made known becomes accessible to the knowledge of the listeners; and the penetration herein, which is known as unerring understanding—all this, for those of little wisdom with an unaccumulated store of wholesome requisites, is difficult to fathom and has no attainable foundation, just as the great ocean is for hares and other small creatures; therefore, it is profound. In this way also, in each one of these, the fourfold profundity should be understood.

Ettāvatā [P 1.0024] ca –

And by this much:

“Desanā-sāsanakathā[V 1.0019], bhedaṃ tesu yathārahaṃ;

Sikkhāpahānagambhīrabhāvañca paridīpaye”ti.

“One should illuminate the teaching, instruction, and discourse, their divisions in these as is fit, and the profundity of training and abandoning.”

Ayaṃ gāthā vuttatthā hoti.

This verse has its meaning already explained.

“Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiñcāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye”ti.

“The division of learning, success and failure, which a bhikkhu attains, where and how—all that too one should make clear.”

Ettha pana tīsu piṭakesu tividho pariyattibhedo daṭṭhabbo. Tisso hi pariyattiyo – alagaddūpamā, nissaraṇatthā, bhaṇḍāgārikapariyattīti.

Now, herein, in the three Piṭakas, a threefold division of learning should be understood. For there are three kinds of learning: that which is like a water-snake, that for the purpose of liberation, and that of a treasurer.

Tattha yā duggahitā upārambhādihetu pariyāpuṭā, ayaṃ alagaddūpamā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko alagaddagavesī alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno, so passeyya mahantaṃ alagaddaṃ. Tamenaṃ bhoge vā naṅguṭṭhe vā gaṇheyya. Tassa so alagaddo paṭiparivattitvā hatthe vā bāhāya vā aññatarasmiṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅge ḍaṃseyya. So tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya, maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, alagaddassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacce moghapurisā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti suttaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ. Te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ na upaparikkhanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ anupaparikkhataṃ na nijjhānaṃ khamanti. Te upārambhānisaṃsā ceva dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca. Yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhonti. Tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitā dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.238).

Herein, that learning which is wrongly grasped, undertaken for the sake of criticism and the like, is that which is like a water-snake. Regarding this, it was said: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, searching for a water-snake, were to see a large water-snake. He might grasp it by its coils or its tail. That water-snake, turning back, would bite his hand or arm or one of his other limbs. From that cause he would meet with death or death-like suffering. What is the reason for that? Because of the wrong grasp of the water-snake, bhikkhus. So too, bhikkhus, some foolish men here learn the Dhamma—discourses… miscellanies. They learn that Dhamma and then do not investigate the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. For them, those teachings, not being investigated with wisdom, do not yield to contemplative insight. They learn the Dhamma only for the sake of criticism and for release from refutation in debate. They do not experience the goal for the sake of which they learn the Dhamma. Those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, conduce to their harm and suffering for a long time. What is the reason for that? Because of the wrong grasp of the teachings, bhikkhus.”

Yā [P 1.0025][M 1.0020] pana suggahitā sīlakkhandhādipāripūriṃyeva ākaṅkhamānena pariyāpuṭā na upārambhādi hetu, ayaṃ nissaraṇatthā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tesaṃ te dhammā suggahitā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Suggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.239).

But that learning which is well-grasped, undertaken by one aspiring only for the complete fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so forth, not for the sake of criticism and the like, this is for the purpose of liberation. Regarding this, it was said: “For them, those teachings, being well-grasped, lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. What is the reason for that? Because, bhikkhus, of the teachings being well-grasped.”

Yaṃ pana pariññātakkhandho pahīnakileso bhāvitamaggo paṭividdhākuppo sacchikatanirodho khīṇāsavo [V 1.0020] kevalaṃ paveṇīpālanatthāya vaṃsānurakkhaṇatthāya pariyāpuṇāti, ayaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikapaayattīti.

But that learning which one who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned defilements, developed the path, penetrated the unshakable, realized cessation, and whose taints are destroyed, undertakes merely for the sake of maintaining the continuity of the teaching and preserving the lineage of the Buddha—this is the treasurer’s learning.

Vinaye pana suppaṭipanno bhikkhu sīlasampattiṃ nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃyeva ca tattha pabhedavacanato. Sutte suppaṭipanno samādhisampadaṃ nissāya cha abhiññā pāpuṇāti, tāsaṃyeva ca tattha pabhedavacanato. Abhidhamme suppaṭipanno paññāsampadaṃ nissāya catasso paṭisambhidā pāpuṇāti, tāsañca tattheva pabhedavacanato. Evametesu suppaṭipanno yathākkamena imaṃ vijjāttayachaḷabhiññācatupaṭisambhidābhedaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇāti.

In the Vinaya, a bhikkhu who practices well, relying on the accomplishment of virtue, attains the three knowledges, for there is a detailed explanation of these very things therein. In the Suttas, a bhikkhu who practices well, relying on the accomplishment of concentration, attains the six direct knowledges, for there is a detailed explanation of these very things therein. In the Abhidhamma, a bhikkhu who practices well, relying on the accomplishment of wisdom, attains the four analytical knowledges, for there is a detailed explanation of these very things therein. Thus, one who practices well in these attains in due order this accomplishment distinguished as the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the four analytical knowledges.

Vinaye pana duppaṭipanno anuññātasukhasamphassaattharaṇapāvuraṇādiphassasāmaññato paṭikkhittesu upādinnaphassādīsu anavajjasaññī hoti. Vuttampi hetaṃ – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.234) tato dussīlabhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti. Sutte [P 1.0026] duppaṭipanno “cattārome, bhikkhave, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.5) adhippāyaṃ ajānanto duggahitaṃ gaṇhāti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “attanā duggahitena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati, attānañca khanati, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavatī”ti (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.236) tato micchādiṭṭhitaṃ pāpuṇāti. Abhidhamme duppaṭipanno dhammacintaṃ atidhāvanto acinteyyānipi cinteti, tato cittakkhepaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, acinteyyāni na cintetabbāni, yāni cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77). Evametesu duppaṭipanno yathākkamena imaṃ dussīlabhāvamicchādiṭṭhitā cittakkhepabhedaṃ vipattiṃ pāpuṇātīti.

In the Vinaya, however, a bhikkhu who practices wrongly, due to the similarity of touch with allowed things of pleasant contact such as floor coverings and robes, perceives as blameless the prohibited contacts that are clung to. For it has been said: “Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, that those things declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive are not obstructive when indulged in.” From this, he falls into immorality. In the Suttas, a bhikkhu who practices wrongly, not understanding the intended meaning in passages such as, “Monks, these four persons exist, are found,” grasps it wrongly. Concerning this, it is said: “Having wrongly grasped it himself, he both misrepresents us and harms himself, accumulating much demerit.” From this, he falls into wrong view. In the Abhidhamma, a bhikkhu who practices wrongly, overstepping the contemplation of phenomena, contemplates even the unthinkables. From this, he falls into mental distraction. For it has been said: “Monks, there are these four unthinkables that should not be contemplated, for whoever contemplates them would partake of madness or frustration.” Thus, a bhikkhu who practices wrongly in these attains in due order this ruin distinguished as immorality, wrong view, and mental distraction.

Ettāvatā [M 1.0021] ca –

And thus far—

“Pariyattibhedaṃ sampattiṃ, vipattiṃ cāpi yaṃ yahiṃ;

Pāpuṇāti yathā bhikkhu, tampi sabbaṃ vibhāvaye”ti.

“The distinctions of learning, the accomplishment, and the ruin, whatever and wherever; how a bhikkhu attains them, all that should be elucidated.”

Ayampi gāthā vuttatthā hoti. Evaṃ nānappakārato piṭakāni ñatvā tesaṃ vasenetaṃ buddhavacanaṃ tividhanti ñātabbaṃ.

This verse, too, has its meaning stated. Thus, having understood the Piṭakas in various ways, the Buddha’s word should be understood as threefold by way of them.

Kathaṃ [V 1.0021] nikāyavasena pañcavidhaṃ? Sabbameva cetaṃ dīghanikāyo, majjhimanikāyo, saṃyuttanikāyo, aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakanikāyoti pañcappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha katamo dīghanikāyo? Tivaggasaṅgahāni brahmajālādīni catuttiṃsa suttāni.

How is it fivefold by way of Nikāyas? All of this is fivefold: the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among these, what is the Dīgha Nikāya? The thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla, which are collected in three sections.

Catuttiṃseva suttantā, tivaggo yassa saṅgaho;

Esa dīghanikāyoti, paṭhamo anulomiko.

“Thirty-four discourses indeed, a collection of three sections; this first one is the Dīgha Nikāya, a suitable name.”

Kasmā panesa dīghanikāyoti vuccati? Dīghappamāṇānaṃ suttānaṃ samūhato nivāsato ca, samūhanivāsā hi nikāyoti [P 1.0027] vuccanti. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekanikāyampi samanupassāmi evaṃ cittaṃ; yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā; poṇikanikāyo, cikkhallikanikāyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.100) evamādīni cettha sādhakāni sāsanato ca lokato ca. Evaṃ sesānampi nikāyabhāve vacanattho veditabbo.

Why, then, is this called the Dīgha Nikāya? It is so called because it is a collection and a dwelling place of suttas of long measure. For indeed, collections and dwelling places are called ‘nikāya.’ Herein, examples brought from both the Teaching and from common usage are the proofs: “Monks, I do not see any other single collection so varied as these animals that live in the animal realm; the dwelling of the Poṇikas, the dwelling of the Cikkhallikas.” In this way, the meaning of the word in its sense as ‘nikāya’ should be understood for the remaining ones as well.

Katamo majjhimanikāyo? Majjhimappamāṇāni pañcadasavaggasaṅgahāni mūlapariyāyasuttādīni diyaḍḍhasataṃ dve ca suttāni.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? It consists of one hundred and fifty-two suttas of medium length, beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, which are collected in fifteen sections.

Diyaḍḍhasataṃ suttantā, dve ca suttāni yattha so;

Nikāyo majjhimo pañca-dasavaggapariggaho.

“Where there are one hundred and fifty-two discourses, that Nikāya, which embraces fifteen sections, is the Majjhima.”
