Katamo saṃyuttanikāyo? Devatāsaṃyuttādivasena ṭhitāni oghataraṇādīni satta suttasahassāni satta ca suttasatāni dvāsaṭṭhi ca suttāni.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? It consists of seven thousand, seven hundred and sixty-two suttas, such as the Oghataraṇa Sutta, arranged by way of the Devatāsaṃyutta and so forth.

Satta suttasahassāni, satta suttasatāni ca;

Dvāsaṭṭhi ceva suttantā, eso saṃyuttasaṅgaho.

“Seven thousand suttas, and seven hundred suttas, and sixty-two suttas indeed—this is the collection of the Saṃyutta.”

Katamo [M 1.0022] aṅguttaranikāyo? Ekekaaṅgātirekavasena ṭhitāni cittapariyādānādīni nava suttasahassāni pañca suttasatāni sattapaññāsañca suttāni.

What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? It consists of nine thousand, five hundred and fifty-seven suttas, such as the Cittapariyādāna Sutta, arranged by way of an increase of one factor at a time.

Nava suttasahassāni, pañca suttasatāni ca;

Sattapaññāsa suttāni, saṅkhyā aṅguttare ayaṃ.

“Nine thousand suttas, and five hundred suttas, and fifty-seven suttas—this is the number in the Aṅguttara.”

Katamo [V 1.0022] khuddakanikāyo? Sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ khuddakapāṭhādayo ca pubbe nidassitā pannarasabhedā ṭhapetvā cattāro nikāye avasesaṃ buddhavacananti.

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? The entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the fifteen divisions beginning with the Khuddakapāṭha previously indicated, and the remainder of the Buddha’s word after setting aside the four Nikāyas.

Ṭhapetvā [P 1.0028] caturopete, nikāye dīghaādike;

Tadaññaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, nikāyo khuddako matoti.

“Setting aside these four Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha, the other word of the Buddha is considered the Khuddaka Nikāya.”

Evaṃ nikāyavasena pañcavidhaṃ.

Thus, it is fivefold by way of Nikāyas.

Kathaṃ aṅgavasena navavidhaṃ? Sabbameva hidaṃ suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthā, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallanti navappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha ubhatovibhaṅganiddesakhandhakaparivārā suttanipāte maṅgalasutta-ratanasutta-nālakasutta-tuvaṭṭakasuttāni aññampi ca suttanāmakaṃ tathāgatavacanaṃ suttanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbampi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyanti veditabbaṃ. Visesena saṃyuttake sakalopi sagāthāvaggo, sakalaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ, yañca aññampi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi asaṅgahitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ taṃ veyyākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Dhammapadaṃ, theragāthā, therīgāthā, suttanipāte nosuttanāmikā suddhikagāthā ca gāthāti veditabbā. Somanassañāṇamayikagāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā dvāsīti suttantā udānanti veditabbaṃ. “Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā”tiādinayappavattā dasuttarasatasuttantā itivuttakanti veditabbaṃ. Apaṇṇakajātakādīni paññāsādhikāni pañca jātakasatāni jātakanti veditabbaṃ. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, acchariyā abbhutā dhammā ānande”ti (dī. ni. 2.209) -ādinayappavattā sabbepi acchariyaabbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttā suttantā abbhutadhammanti veditabbaṃ. Cūḷavedalla-mahāvedalla-sammādiṭṭhi-sakkapañha-saṅkhārabhājaniya-mahāpuṇṇamasuttādayo [P 1.0029] sabbepi vedañca tuṭṭhiñca laddhā laddhā pucchitasuttantā vedallanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ aṅgavasena navavidhaṃ.

How is it ninefold by way of constituents? Indeed, all this Word of the Buddha—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—is of nine kinds. Therein, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, the Niddesas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra; in the Suttanipāta, the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta; and any other word of the Tathāgata named 'sutta' are to be understood as Sutta. Any sutta that is accompanied by verses is to be understood as Geyya. Specifically, in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the entire Sagāthāvagga is to be understood as Geyya. The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, any sutta without verses, and any other Word of the Buddha not included in the other eight constituents are to be understood as Veyyākaraṇa. The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and in the Suttanipāta, the pure verses not designated by the name 'sutta' are to be understood as Gāthā. The eighty-two discourses connected with verses born of knowledge accompanied by joy are to be understood as Udāna. The one hundred and ten discourses that proceed in the manner beginning with, “This was said by the Blessed One,” are to be understood as Itivuttaka. The five hundred and fifty Jātakas, beginning with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, are to be understood as Jātaka. All discourses connected with wonderful and astonishing qualities that proceed in the manner beginning with, “Monks, there are these four wonderful and astonishing qualities in Ānanda,” are to be understood as Abbhutadhamma. The Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Saṅkhārabhājaniya Sutta, Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta, and others—all discourses wherein questions are asked having repeatedly gained knowledge and delight—are to be understood as Vedalla. Thus, it is ninefold by way of constituents.

Kathaṃ [M 1.0023] dhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassavidhaṃ? Sabbameva cetaṃ buddhavacanaṃ –

How is it eighty-four thousandfold by way of Dhamma-sections? Indeed, all this Word of the Buddha—

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti. (theragā. 1027);

“Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha, two thousand from the bhikkhus; eighty-four thousand are these teachings that are current for me.”

Evaṃ paridīpitadhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassappabhedaṃ hoti. Tattha ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ eko dhammakkhandho. Yaṃ anekānusandhikaṃ tattha anusandhivasena dhammakkhandhagaṇanā. Gāthābandhesu pañhāpucchanaṃ [V 1.0023] eko dhammakkhandho, vissajjanaṃ eko. Abhidhamme ekamekaṃ tika-duka-bhājanaṃ, ekamekañca cittavārabhājanaṃ, eko dhammakkhandho. Vinaye atthi vatthu, atthi mātikā, atthi padabhājanīyaṃ, atthi antarāpatti, atthi āpatti, atthi anāpatti, atthi paricchedo; tattha ekameko koṭṭhāso, ekameko dhammakkhandhoti veditabbo. Evaṃ dhammakkhandhavasena caturāsītisahassavidhaṃ.

Thus, by way of the Dhamma-sections thus explained, it is eighty-four thousandfold. Among these, a discourse with a single connection is one Dhamma-section. Where there are multiple connections, the counting of Dhamma-sections is by way of the connections. In verse compositions, the asking of a question is one Dhamma-section, and the answering is one. In the Abhidhamma, each division of a triad and a dyad, and each division of a consciousness-round, is one Dhamma-section. In the Vinaya, there is the basis, there is the mātikā, there is the analysis of terms, there is the intermediate offense, there is the offense, there is the non-offense, and there is the delimitation; therein, each portion is to be understood as one Dhamma-section. Thus, it is eighty-four thousandfold by way of Dhamma-sections.

Evametaṃ abhedato rasavasena ekavidhaṃ, bhedato dhammavinayādivasena duvidhādibhedaṃ buddhavacanaṃ saṅgāyantena mahākassapappamukhena vasīgaṇena “ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo; idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ majjhimabuddhavacanaṃ, idaṃ pacchimabuddhavacanaṃ; idaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, idaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ, idaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ; ayaṃ dīghanikāyo…pe… ayaṃ khuddakanikāyo; imāni suttādīni navaṅgāni, imāni caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti imaṃ pabhedaṃ vavatthapetvāva saṅgītaṃ. Na [P 1.0030] kevalañca ettakameva, aññampi uddānasaṅgaha-vaggasaṅgahapeyyālasaṅgaha-ekakanipāta-dukanipātādinipātasaṅgaha-saṃyuttasaṅgaha-paṇṇāsasaṅgahādianekavidhaṃ tīsu piṭakesu sandissamānaṃ saṅgahappabhedaṃ vavatthapetvāeva sattahi māsehi saṅgītaṃ. Saṅgītipariyosāne cassa – “idaṃ mahākassapattherena dasabalassa sāsanaṃ pañcavassasahassaparimāṇaṃ kālaṃ pavattanasamatthaṃ kata”nti sañjātappamodā sādhukāraṃ viya dadamānā ayaṃ mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā anekappakāraṃ kampi saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi, anekāni ca acchariyāni pāturahesunti ayaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītināma. Yā loke –

Thus, this Word of the Buddha, undivided by way of flavor as one, but divided into two or more divisions by way of Dhamma and Vinaya and so forth, was chanted by the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa only after distinguishing this classification: “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first Word of the Buddha, this is the middle Word of the Buddha, this is the last Word of the Buddha; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya… up to… this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine constituents, these are the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-sections.” And not only this much, but also other manifold classifications appearing in the three Piṭakas—such as summaries of contents, summaries of chapters, summaries by extended passages, summaries by single items, double items, and other numerical items, summaries of connected discourses, summaries by fifties, and so forth—were all distinguished before being chanted in seven months. At the conclusion of the chanting, this great earth, making the water its boundary, rejoiced as if giving applause, saying, “This teaching of the Ten-Powered One, established by the elder Mahākassapa, has been made capable of lasting for a period of five thousand years,” and it quaked, shook, trembled, and vibrated in many ways, and many wonders appeared. This is called the First Great Council. That which is in the world—

Satehi pañcahi katā, tena pañcasatāti ca;

Thereheva katattā ca, therikāti pavuccatīti.

“Made by five hundred, therefore it is called Pañcasata; and because it was made by the Elders, it is called Therikā.”

Imissā [M 1.0024] pana paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyā pavattamānāya vinayaṃ pucchantena āyasmatā mahākassapena “paṭhamaṃ, āvuso upāli, pārājikaṃ kattha paññatta”nti evamādivacanapariyosāne “vatthumpi pucchi, nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchī”ti ettha nidāne pucchite taṃ nidānaṃ ādito pabhuti vitthāretvā yena ca paññattaṃ, yasmā ca paññattaṃ, sabbametaṃ kathetukāmena āyasmatā upālittherena vuttaṃ “tena samayena [P 1.0031] buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatī”ti sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Evamidaṃ āyasmatā upālittherena vuttaṃ, tañca pana “paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vutta”nti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā ca “idaṃ vacanaṃ kena vuttaṃ, kadā vutta”nti etesaṃ padānaṃ attho pakāsito hoti.

While this First Great Council was proceeding, when the Venerable Mahākassapa, questioning the Vinaya, asked, “Friend Upāli, where was the first pārājika rule laid down?” at the conclusion of such words, it was said, “He asked about the basis, he asked about the origin, he asked about the individual.” Here, when the origin was questioned, the Venerable Elder Upāli, wishing to relate that origin in detail from the very beginning—by whom it was laid down, and because of what it was laid down—said, “At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā.” The whole account was to be told. Thus, this was spoken by the Venerable Elder Upāli, and it should be understood that “it was spoken at the time of the First Great Council.” By this much, the meaning of these terms, “by whom was this spoken, when was it spoken,” is made clear.

Idāni [V 1.0024] kasmā vuttanti ettha vuccate, yasmā ayamāyasmatā mahākassapattherena nidānaṃ puṭṭho tasmānena taṃ nidānaṃ ādito pabhuti vitthāretuṃ vuttanti. Evamidaṃ āyasmatā upālittherena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vadantenāpi iminā kāraṇena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā ca vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmāti imesaṃ mātikāpadānaṃ attho pakāsito hoti.

Now, regarding the question, 'Why was it spoken?', it is said: Because he was asked about the introduction by the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa, it was therefore spoken by him in order to elaborate on that introduction from the very beginning. Thus, it should be understood that this was spoken by the Venerable Elder Upāli at the time of the First Great Council, even while he was reciting, for this very reason. And by this much, the meaning of these mātikā terms—'by whom it was spoken, when, and why'—is made clear.

Idāni dhāritaṃ yena cābhataṃ, yatthappatiṭṭhitaṃ cetametaṃ vatvā vidhiṃ tatoti etesaṃ atthappakāsanatthaṃ idaṃ vuccati. Taṃ panetaṃ “tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatī”ti evamādivacanapaṭimaṇḍitanidānaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ kena dhāritaṃ, kenābhataṃ, kattha patiṭṭhitanti? Vuccate – ādito tāva idaṃ bhagavato sammukhā āyasmatā upālittherena dhāritaṃ, tassa sammukhato aparinibbute tathāgate chaḷabhiññādibhedehi anekehi bhikkhusahassehi parinibbute tathāgate mahākassapappamukhehi dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi. Kenābhatanti? Jambudīpe tāva upālittheramādiṃ katvā ācariyaparamparāya yāva tatiyasaṅgīti tāva ābhataṃ. Tatrāyaṃ [P 1.0032] ācariyaparamparā –

Now, for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of these mātikā terms—'By whom was it preserved and brought, and where was it established, and having stated the method thereof'—this is said. But this Vinaya Piṭaka, with its introduction adorned with words beginning, 'At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā'—by whom was it preserved, by whom was it brought, and where was it established? It is said: Firstly, this was preserved by the Venerable Upāli in the presence of the Blessed One. From him, while the Tathāgata had not yet attained Parinibbāna, it was preserved by many thousands of bhikkhus possessing various distinctions such as the six higher knowledges; and after the Tathāgata had attained Parinibbāna, by the Dhamma-reciting elders headed by Mahākassapa. By whom was it brought? In Jambudīpa, it was brought by the succession of teachers, beginning with the Elder Upāli, up to the Third Council. Herein is the succession of teachers:

Upāli dāsako ceva, soṇako siggavo tathā;

Tisso moggaliputto ca, pañcete vijitāvino.

Upāli and Dāsaka, Soṇaka and Siggava as well; and Tissa, son of Moggali—these five were conquerors.

Paramparāya vinayaṃ, dīpe jambusirivhaye;

Acchijjamānamānesuṃ, tatiyo yāva saṅgaho.

In the island named Jambu, they brought the Vinaya by succession, without interruption, up to the Third Council.

Āyasmā [M 1.0025] hi upāli imaṃ vinayavaṃsaṃ vinayatantiṃ vinayapaveṇiṃ bhagavato

Indeed, the Venerable Upāli, this lineage of the Vinaya, this thread of the Vinaya, this succession of the Vinaya of the Blessed One,

Sammukhā uggahetvā bahūnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hadaye patiṭṭhāpesi. Tassa hāyasmato santike vinayavaṃsaṃ uggahetvā vinaye pakataññutaṃ pattesu puggalesu puthujjana-sotāpanna-sakadāgāmi-anāgāmino gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā, khīṇāsavānaṃ sahassamekaṃ ahosi. Dāsakattheropi tasseva saddhivihāriko ahosi, so upālittherassa sammukhā uggahetvā tatheva vinayaṃ vācesi. Tassāpi āyasmato santike uggahetvā vinaye pakataññutaṃ pattā puthujjanādayo gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā, khīṇāsavānaṃ sahassameva ahosi. Soṇakattheropi dāsakattherassa saddhivihāriko ahosi, sopi attano upajjhāyassa dāsakattherassa sammukhā uggahetvā tatheva vinayaṃ vācesi. Tassāpi āyasmato santike uggahetvā vinaye pakataññutaṃ pattā puthujjanādayo gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā, khīṇāsavānaṃ sahassameva ahosi. Siggavattheropi soṇakattherassa saddhivihāriko ahosi, sopi attano upajjhāyassa [V 1.0025] soṇakattherassa santike vinayaṃ uggahetvā arahantasahassassa dhuraggāho ahosi. Tassa panāyasmato santike uggahetvā vinaye pakataññutaṃ pattā puthujjana-sotāpannasakadāgāmi-anāgāminopi khīṇāsavāpi ettakāni [P 1.0033] satānīti vā ettakāni sahassānīti vā aparicchinnā ahesuṃ. Tadā kira jambudīpe atimahābhikkhusamudāyo ahosi. Moggaliputtatissattherassa pana ānubhāvo tatiyasaṅgītiyaṃ pākaṭo bhavissati. Evamidaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ jambudīpe tāva imāya ācariyaparamparāya yāva tatiyasaṅgīti tāva ābhatanti veditabbaṃ.

having learned in His presence, established it in the hearts of many bhikkhus. Indeed, in the presence of that venerable one, among those individuals who had learned the lineage of the Vinaya and attained proficiency in the Vinaya, the worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners were beyond counting; there was one thousand of those whose taints were destroyed. The Elder Dāsaka was also his co-resident disciple; he, having learned in the presence of the Elder Upāli, taught the Vinaya in the same way. In the presence of that venerable one as well, those who had learned and attained proficiency in the Vinaya—worldlings and the rest—were beyond counting; there was a thousand of those whose taints were destroyed. The Elder Soṇaka was also the co-resident disciple of the Elder Dāsaka; he too, having learned in the presence of his preceptor, the Elder Dāsaka, taught the Vinaya in the same way. In the presence of that venerable one as well, those who had learned and attained proficiency in the Vinaya—worldlings and the rest—were beyond counting; there was a thousand of those whose taints were destroyed. The Elder Siggava was also the co-resident disciple of the Elder Soṇaka; he too, having learned the Vinaya from his preceptor, the Elder Soṇaka, became the foremost learner among a thousand arahants. But in the presence of that venerable one, those who had learned and attained proficiency in the Vinaya—worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and even those whose taints were destroyed—were immeasurable, whether by hundreds or by thousands. At that time, it is said, there was an exceedingly great community of bhikkhus in Jambudīpa. The power of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, however, will become manifest at the Third Council. Thus, it should be understood that this Vinaya Piṭaka was brought in Jambudīpa through this succession of teachers up to the Third Council.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the First Great Council is concluded.

Dutiyasaṅgītikathā

The Account of the Second Council

Dutiyasaṅgītivijānanatthaṃ pana ayamanukkamo veditabbo. Yadā hi –

Now, for the purpose of understanding the Second Council, this sequence should be known. For when—

Saṅgāyitvāna saddhammaṃ, jotayitvā ca sabbadhi;

Yāva jīvitapariyantaṃ, ṭhatvā pañcasatāpi te.

Having recited the True Dhamma and illuminated it everywhere, those five hundred, having remained until the end of their lives,

Khīṇāsavā [M 1.0026] jutīmanto, therā kassapaādayo;

Khīṇasnehapadīpāva, nibbāyiṃsu anālayā.

those elders headed by Kassapa, whose taints were destroyed and who were possessed of radiance, like lamps whose oil is spent, attained Parinibbāna without attachment.

Athānukkamena gacchantesu rattindivesu vassasataparinibbute bhagavati vesālikā vajjiputtakā bhikkhū vesāliyaṃ “kappati siṅgīloṇakappo, kappati dvaṅgulakappo, kappati gāmantarakappo, kappati āvāsakappo, kappati anumatikappo, kappati āciṇṇakappo, kappati amathitakappo, kappati jaḷogiṃ pātuṃ, kappati adasakaṃ nisīdanaṃ, kappati jātarūparajata”nti imāni dasa vatthūni dīpesuṃ. Tesaṃ susunāgaputto kāḷāsoko nāma rājā pakkho ahosi.

Then, as days and nights passed in succession, one hundred years after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, the Vajjian monks of Vesālī proclaimed these ten points at Vesālī: “The practice of storing salt in a horn is allowable; the practice of eating when the sun has passed the meridian by two finger-breadths is allowable; the practice of going to another village and eating again is allowable; the practice of holding separate Uposatha ceremonies within the same monastic boundary is allowable; the practice of performing a formal act and obtaining consent afterward is allowable; the practice of following the precedent of one's teachers is allowable; the practice of drinking milk that is no longer milk but not yet curd is allowable; the practice of drinking unfermented toddy is allowable; the practice of using a sitting cloth without a border is allowable; the practice of accepting gold and silver is allowable.” King Kālāsoka, son of Susunāga, was their supporter.

Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā yaso kākaṇḍakaputto vajjīsu cārikaṃ caramāno “vesālikā kira vajjiputtakā bhikkhū vesāliyaṃ dasa vatthūni dīpentī”ti sutvā “na kho panetaṃ patirūpaṃ yvāhaṃ dasabalassa sāsanavipattiṃ sutvā appossukko bhaveyyaṃ. Handāhaṃ adhammavādino [V 1.0026] niggahetvā dhammaṃ [P 1.0034] dīpemī”ti cintento yena vesālī tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā yaso kākaṇḍakaputto vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ.

At that time, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta, while wandering on tour among the Vajjis, heard: “It is said that the Vajjian monks of Vesālī are proclaiming ten points.” He thought: “It is not proper that I, having heard of this corruption of the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers, should remain unconcerned. Come now, having refuted those who speak against the Dhamma, I shall proclaim the Dhamma.” Thinking thus, he went to Vesālī. There, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta dwelt in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, at the Kūṭāgāra Hall.

Tena kho pana samayena vesālikā vajjiputtakā bhikkhū tadahuposathe kaṃsapātiṃ udakena pūretvā majjhe bhikkhusaṅghassa ṭhapetvā āgatāgate vesālike upāsake evaṃ vadanti – “dethāvuso, saṅghassa kahāpaṇampi aḍḍhampi pādampi māsakarūpampi, bhavissati saṅghassa parikkhārena karaṇīya”nti sabbaṃ tāva vattabbaṃ, yāva “imāya pana vinayasaṅgītiyā satta bhikkhusatāni anūnāni anadhikāni ahesuṃ, tasmā ayaṃ dutiyasaṅgīti sattasatikāti vuccatī”ti.

At that time, on the Uposatha day, the Vajjian monks of Vesālī filled a bronze bowl with water, placed it in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, and said to the lay followers from Vesālī who came: “Give, friends, to the Saṅgha a kahāpaṇa, or a half, or a quarter, or even a coin of māsaka value; there will be use for it by way of the Saṅgha’s requisites.” All this should be related up to the point where it is said: “At this Vinaya Council, there were seven hundred monks, no fewer and no more. Therefore, this Second Council is called the Sattasatikā, or the Council of Seven Hundred.”

Evaṃ tasmiñca sannipāte dvādasa bhikkhusatasahassāni sannipatiṃsu āyasmatā yasena samussāhitā. Tesaṃ majjhe āyasmatā revatena puṭṭhena sabbakāmittherena vinayaṃ vissajjentena tāni dasa vatthūni vinicchitāni, adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamitaṃ. Atha therā “puna dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyissāmā”ti tipiṭakadhare pattapaṭisambhide sattasate bhikkhū uccinitvā vesāliyaṃ [M 1.0027] vālikārāme sannipatitvā mahākassapattherena saṅgāyitasadisameva sabbaṃ sāsanamalaṃ sodhetvā puna piṭakavasena nikāyavasena aṅgavasena dhammakkhandhavasena ca sabbaṃ dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyiṃsu. Ayaṃ saṅgīti aṭṭhahi māsehi niṭṭhitā. Yā loke –

Thus, at that assembly, one million two hundred thousand monks gathered, encouraged by the Venerable Yasa. Among them, those ten points were adjudicated and the dispute was settled by the elder Sabbakāmī, who, being questioned by the Venerable Revata, gave answers on the Vinaya. Then the elders, resolving, “Let us recite the Dhamma and Vinaya again,” selected seven hundred monks who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka and had attained the analytical knowledges. Assembling in the Vālikārāma at Vesālī, just as the elder Mahākassapa had recited, they purified the entire Dispensation of all its impurities and then recited all the Dhamma and Vinaya again, classifying it by way of the Piṭakas, Nikāyas, Aṅgas, and Dhammakkhandhas. This council was completed in eight months. Which in the world—

Satehi sattahi katā, tena sattasatāti ca;

Pubbe kataṃ upādāya, dutiyāti ca vuccatīti.

Because it was held by seven hundred, it is called the ‘Seven Hundred’; and with reference to the one held before, it is called the ‘Second’.

Sā panāyaṃ –

Now, this council:

Yehi therehi saṅgītā, saṅgīti tesu vissutā;

Sabbakāmī ca sāḷho ca, revato khujjasobhito.

Of the elders by whom this council was recited, these were renowned: Sabbakāmī, Sāḷha, Revata, and Khujjasobhita.

Yaso [P 1.0035] ca sāṇasambhūto, ete saddhivihārikā;

Therā ānandatherassa, diṭṭhapubbā tathāgataṃ.

Yasa and Sāṇasambhūta—these elders were co-resident disciples of the elder Ānanda; they had previously seen the Tathāgata.

Sumano vāsabhagāmī ca, ñeyyā saddhivihārikā;

Dve ime anuruddhassa, diṭṭhapubbā tathāgataṃ.

Sumana and Vāsabhagāmī, these two should be known as the co-resident disciples of Anuruddha; they had previously seen the Tathāgata.

Dutiyo [V 1.0027] pana saṅgīto, yehi therehi saṅgaho;

Sabbepi pannabhārā te, katakiccā anāsavāti.

Those elders by whom this second collection was recited—all of them had laid down the burden, had done what was to be done, and were without taints.

Ayaṃ dutiyasaṅgīti.

This is the Second Council.

Evamimaṃ dutiyasaṅgītiṃ saṅgāyitvā therā “uppajjissati nu kho anāgatepi sāsanassa evarūpaṃ abbuda”nti olokayamānā imaṃ addasaṃsu – “ito vassasatassa upari aṭṭhārasame vasse pāṭaliputte dhammāsoko nāma rājā uppajjitvā sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ kāressati. So buddhasāsane pasīditvā mahantaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ pavattayissati. Tato titthiyā lābhasakkāraṃ patthayamānā sāsane pabbajitvā sakaṃ sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ paridīpessanti. Evaṃ sāsane mahantaṃ abbudaṃ uppajjissatī”ti. Atha nesaṃ etadahosi – “kinnu kho mayaṃ etasmiṃ abbude uppanne sammukhā bhavissāma, na bhavissāmā”ti. Atha te sabbeva tadā attano asammukhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ko nu kho taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametuṃ samattho bhavissatī”ti sakalaṃ manussalokaṃ chakāmāvacaradevalokañca olokentā na kañci disvā brahmaloke tissaṃ nāma mahābrahmānaṃ addasaṃsu [M 1.0028] parittāyukaṃ uparibrahmalokūpapattiyā bhāvitamaggaṃ. Disvāna nesaṃ etadahosi – “sace mayaṃ etassa brahmuno manussaloke nibbattanatthāya ussāhaṃ kareyyāma, addhā esa [P 1.0036] moggalibrāhmaṇassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gahessati. Tato ca mantehi palobhito nikkhamitvā pabbajissati. So evaṃ pabbajitvā sakalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā adhigatapaṭisambhido hutvā titthiye madditvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchitvā sāsanaṃ paggaṇhissatī”ti.

Having thus recited this Second Council, the elders, looking to see whether such a danger would arise for the Dispensation in the future, saw this: “In the eighteenth year after one hundred years from now, a king named Dhammāsoka will arise in Pāṭaliputta and will exercise kingship over the whole of Jambudīpa. Having gained faith in the Buddha’s Dispensation, he will cause great gain and honor to arise. Then, heretics, desiring gain and honor, will go forth in the Dispensation and proclaim their own respective views. Thus, a great danger will arise in the Dispensation.” Then this thought occurred to them: “When this danger arises, will we be present, or will we not?” Then, all those elders, knowing that they would not be present at that time, considered: “Who, indeed, will be capable of settling that dispute?” Surveying the entire human world and the six sense-sphere celestial worlds, and seeing no one, they saw in the Brahmā world a great Brahmā named Tissa, who had a short lifespan and had developed the path for rebirth in a higher Brahmā world. Seeing him, this thought occurred to them: “If we were to make an effort for this Brahmā to be reborn in the human world, surely he will take conception in the house of the brahmin Moggali. Then, enticed by mantras, he will go forth and become a monk. Having thus gone forth, he will master the entire word of the Buddha, attain the analytical knowledges, crush the heretics, adjudicate that dispute, and uphold the Dispensation.”

Te brahmalokaṃ gantvā tissaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ etadavocuṃ – “ito vassasatassa upari aṭṭhārasame vasse sāsane mahantaṃ abbudaṃ uppajjissati. Mayañca sakalaṃ manussalokaṃ chakāmāvacaradevalokañca olokayamānā kañci sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ samatthaṃ adisvā brahmalokaṃ vicinantā bhavantameva addasāma. Sādhu, sappurisa, manussaloke nibbattitvā dasabalassa sāsanaṃ paggaṇhituṃ paṭiññaṃ dehī”ti.

They went to the Brahmā world and said thus to the great Brahmā Tissa: “In the eighteenth year after a hundred years from now, a great danger will arise in the Dispensation. We, surveying the entire human world and the six sense-sphere celestial worlds, saw no one capable of upholding the Dispensation. Searching the Brahmā world, we saw only you. Good sir, we implore you, be reborn in the human world and give your promise to uphold the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers.”

Evaṃ vutte mahābrahmā, “ahaṃ kira sāsane uppannaṃ abbudaṃ sodhetvā sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ samattho bhavissāmī”ti haṭṭhapahaṭṭho udaggudaggo hutvā, “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā paṭiññaṃ adāsi. Therā brahmaloke taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā puna paccāgamiṃsu.

When this was said, the great Brahmā, thinking, “It seems I will be able to cleanse the danger that has arisen in the Dispensation and to uphold the Dispensation,” became joyful and exceedingly glad, elated and exhilarated. Consenting with “It is good,” he gave his promise. The elders, having completed that task in the Brahmā world, returned again.

Tena [V 1.0028] kho pana samayena siggavatthero ca caṇḍavajjitthero ca dvepi navakā honti daharabhikkhū tipiṭakadharā pattapaṭisambhidā khīṇāsavā, te taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ na sampāpuṇiṃsu. Therā “tumhe, āvuso, amhākaṃ imasmiṃ adhikaraṇe no sahāyakā ahuvattha, tena vo idaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ hotu – ‘tisso nāma brahmā moggalibrāhmaṇassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhissati, taṃ tumhākaṃ eko nīharitvā pabbājetu, eko buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhāpetū’”ti vatvā sabbepi yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā –

Now, at that time, the elder Siggava and the elder Caṇḍavajji were both junior, young monks, bearers of the Tipiṭaka, who had attained the analytical knowledges, and were destroyers of the taints. They did not arrive at that legal matter. The elders said: “Friends, you were not our helpers in this legal matter. Therefore, let this be a punitive act for you: ‘A Brahmā named Tissa will take conception in the house of the Brahmin Moggali. One of you, having led him out, should cause him to go forth; the other should cause him to learn the Buddha’s word.’” Having said this, all of them, having remained for the extent of their lifespans—

Sabbakāmippabhutayo, tepi therā mahiddhikā;

Aggikkhandhāva lokamhi, jalitvā parinibbutā.

Those elders, beginning with Sabbakāmī, of great psychic power, having blazed in the world like great masses of fire, attained Parinibbāna.

Dutiyaṃ saṅgahaṃ katvā, visodhetvāna sāsanaṃ;

Anāgatepi [P 1.0037] katvāna, hetuṃ saddhammasuddhiyā.

Having held the Second Council, having purified the Dispensation, and having also established a cause for the future purity of the True Dhamma.

Khīṇāsavā [M 1.0029] vasippatthā, pabhinnapaṭisambhidā;

Aniccatāvasaṃ therā, tepi nāma upāgatā.

Those whose cankers were destroyed, who had attained mastery, who possessed the differentiated analytical knowledges—even those elders, indeed, came under the sway of impermanence.

Evaṃ aniccataṃ jammiṃ, ñatvā durabhisambhavaṃ;

Taṃ pattuṃ vāyame dhīro, yaṃ niccaṃ amataṃ padanti.

Thus having known impermanence to be wretched and insuperable, the wise person should strive to attain that state which is permanent and deathless.

Ettāvatā sabbākārena dutiyasaṅgītivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā hoti.

Herewith, the explanation of the Second Council is concluded in all its aspects.

Dutiyasaṅgītikathā niṭṭhitā

The Account of the Second Council is concluded.

Tatiyasaṅgītikathā

The Account of the Third Council

Tissopi kho mahābrahmā brahmalokato cavitvā moggalibrāhmaṇassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Siggavattheropi tassa paṭisandhiggahaṇato pabhuti satta vassāni brāhmaṇassa gehaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Ekadivasampi uḷuṅkamattaṃ vā yāguṃ kaṭacchumattaṃ vā bhattaṃ nālattha. Sattannaṃ pana vassānaṃ accayena ekadivasaṃ “aticchatha, bhante”ti vacanamattaṃ alattha. Taṃdivasameva brāhmaṇopi bahiddhā kiñci karaṇīyaṃ katvā āgacchanto paṭipathe theraṃ disvā, “bho pabbajita, amhākaṃ gehaṃ agamitthā”ti āha. “Āma, brāhmaṇa, agamimhā”ti. “Api kiñci [V 1.0029] labhitthā”ti? “Āma, brāhmaṇa, labhimhā”ti. So gehaṃ gantvā pucchi – “tassa pabbajitassa kiñci adatthā”ti? “Na kiñci adamhā”ti. Brāhmaṇo dutiyadivase gharadvāreyeva nisīdi “ajja pabbajitaṃ musāvādena niggahessāmī”ti. Thero dutiyadivase brāhmaṇassa gharadvāraṃ sampatto. Brāhmaṇo theraṃ disvāva evamāha – “tumhe hiyyo amhākaṃ gehe kiñci aladdhāyeva ‘labhimhā’ti avocuttha. Vaṭṭati nu kho tumhākaṃ musāvādo”ti! Thero āha – “mayaṃ, brāhmaṇa, tumhākaṃ gehe satta vassāni ‘aticchathā’ti vacanamattampi alabhitvā hiyyo ‘aticchathā’ti vacanamattaṃ labhimha; athetaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ upādāya evamavocumhā”ti.

The Great Brahmā Tissa, having passed away from the Brahmā-world, took rebirth in the household of the brahmin Moggali. From the time of his rebirth, the Elder Siggava entered the brahmin’s house for alms for seven years. Not even on a single day did he receive so much as a dipperful of gruel or a ladleful of cooked rice. But at the end of seven years, one day he received just the words, “Please accept, venerable sir.” That very day, the brahmin, having gone outside for some business and returning, saw the Elder on the path and said, “O ascetic, did you go to our house?” “Yes, brahmin, we went.” “Did you get anything?” “Yes, brahmin, we did.” He went home and asked, “Did you give anything to that ascetic?” “We gave nothing.” The next day, the brahmin sat right at the door of his house, thinking, “Today I will subdue the ascetic with a false statement.” The Elder arrived at the brahmin’s door the following day. As soon as the brahmin saw the Elder, he said, “Yesterday, though you got nothing in our house, you said, ‘We did.’ Is speaking falsely proper for you?” The Elder replied, “Brahmin, for seven years we did not receive even the mere words ‘Please accept’ in your house. Yesterday we received the mere words ‘Please accept.’ Therefore, on account of this friendly reception, we spoke thus.”

Brāhmaṇo cintesi – “ime paṭisanthāramattampi labhitvā ‘labhimhā’ti pasaṃsanti, aññaṃ kiñci khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ [P 1.0038] labhitvā kasmā na pasaṃsantī”ti pasīditvā attano atthāya paṭiyāditabhattato kaṭacchumattaṃ bhikkhaṃ tadupiyañca byañjanaṃ dāpetvā “imaṃ bhikkhaṃ sabbakālaṃ tumhe labhissathā”ti āha[M 1.0030]. So punadivasato pabhuti upasaṅkamantassa therassa upasamaṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya pasīditvā theraṃ niccakālaṃ attano ghare bhattavissaggakaraṇatthāya yāci. Thero adhivāsetvā divase divase bhattakiccaṃ katvā gacchanto thokaṃ thokaṃ buddhavacanaṃ kathetvā gacchati. Sopi kho māṇavako soḷasavassuddesikoyeva tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū ahosi. Brahmalokato āgatasuddhasattassa āsane vā sayane vā añño koci nisajjitā vā nipajjitā vā natthi. So yadā ācariyagharaṃ gacchati, tadāssa mañcapīṭhaṃ setena vatthena paṭicchādetvā laggetvā ṭhapenti. Thero cintesi – “samayo dāni māṇavakaṃ pabbājetuṃ, cirañca me idhāgacchantassa, na ca kāci māṇavakena saddhiṃ kathā uppajjati. Handa dāni iminā upāyena pallaṅkaṃ nissāya uppajjissatī”ti gehaṃ gantvā yathā tasmiṃ gehe ṭhapetvā māṇavakassa pallaṅkaṃ aññaṃ na kiñci āsanaṃ dissati tathā adhiṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇassa gehajano theraṃ disvā aññaṃ kiñci āsanaṃ apassanto māṇavakassa pallaṅkaṃ attharitvā therassa adāsi. Nisīdi thero pallaṅke. Māṇavakopi kho taṅkhaṇaññeva ācariyagharā āgamma theraṃ attano pallaṅke nisinnaṃ disvā kupito anattamano “ko mama pallaṅkaṃ samaṇassa paññapesī”ti āha.

The brahmin thought: “These men, having received even a mere friendly greeting, praise it, saying, ‘We have received.’ Having received any other food, hard or soft, why would they not praise it?” Becoming pleased, he had a ladleful of alms-food and accompanying curry given from the food prepared for himself and said, “You will receive this alms-food at all times.” From the next day onward, seeing the tranquility of the approaching Elder, he became pleased to an even greater degree and requested the Elder to always perform the meal service at his house. The Elder, having consented, would, after performing his meal-duty each day, speak a little of the Buddha's word before departing. That young man, being about sixteen years of age, had become a master of the three Vedas. On the seat or bed of that pure being who had come from the Brahmā world, no one else would sit or lie. When he went to his teacher’s house, they would cover his couch and chair with a white cloth and set them aside. The Elder thought, “Now is the time to ordain the young man. It has been long that I have been coming here, and no conversation has arisen with the young man. Well now, by this stratagem, a conversation will arise based on the couch.” Having gone to the house, he made a determination that in that house, apart from the young man’s couch, no other seat would be seen. The people of the brahmin's house, seeing the Elder and not seeing any other seat, spread out the young man’s couch and gave it to the Elder. The Elder sat on the couch. At that very moment, the young man, having returned from his teacher’s house and seeing the Elder seated on his couch, became angry and displeased, and said, “Who has prepared my couch for this recluse?”

Thero bhattakiccaṃ katvā vūpasante māṇavakassa caṇḍikkabhāve evamāha – “kiṃ pana tvaṃ, māṇavaka, kiñci [P 1.0039] mantaṃ jānāsī”ti? Māṇavako “bho pabbajita, mayi dāni mante ajānante aññe ke jānissantī”ti vatvā, theraṃ pucchi – “tumhe pana mantaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Puccha, māṇavaka, pucchitvā sakkā jānitu”nti. Atha kho māṇavako tīsu vedesu sanighaṇḍukeṭubhesu [V 1.0030] sākkharappabhedesu itihāsapañcamesu yāni yāni gaṇṭhiṭṭhānāni, yesaṃ yesaṃ nayaṃ neva attanā passati nāpissa ācariyo addasa, tesu tesu theraṃ pucchi. Thero “pakatiyāpi tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū, idāni pana paṭisambhidāppatto, tenassa natthi tesaṃ pañhānaṃ vissajjane bhāro”ti tāvadeva te pañhe vissajjetvā māṇavakaṃ āha – “māṇavaka, ahaṃ tayā bahuṃ pucchito; ahampi dāni taṃ ekaṃ pañhaṃ pucchāmi, byākarissasi me”ti? “Āma, bho pabbajita, puccha byākarissāmī”ti. Thero cittayamake imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi –

The Elder, having finished his meal-duty, when the young man's harsh nature had subsided, said this: “Well then, young man, do you know any sacred texts?” The young man replied, “O ascetic, if I do not know the sacred texts now, who else will know them?” and then asked the Elder, “But do you know the sacred texts?” “Ask, young man; having asked, it can be known.” Then the young man asked the Elder about all the difficult points in the three Vedas, together with their Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha, with their analysis of letters, and with the Itihāsa as the fifth—those points whose method neither he himself could see nor his teacher had seen. The Elder, being by nature a master of the three Vedas and now having attained the analytical knowledges, had no burden in answering those questions. Having answered those questions right then, the Elder said to the young man, “Young man, I have been questioned much by you; I too will now ask you one question—will you explain it to me?” “Yes, O ascetic, ask; I will explain.” The Elder then posed this question from the Citta-yamaka:

“Yassa [M 1.0031] cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhati tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissati nuppajjissati; yassa vā pana cittaṃ nirujjhissati nuppajjissati tassa cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhatī”ti?

“For whom consciousness arises but does not cease, for him will consciousness cease and not arise? Or for whom consciousness will cease and not arise, for him does consciousness arise but not cease?”

Māṇavo uddhaṃ vā adho vā harituṃ asakkonto “kiṃ nāma, bho pabbajita, ida”nti āha. “Buddhamanto nāmāyaṃ, māṇavā”ti. “Sakkā panāyaṃ, bho, mayhampi dātu”nti. “Sakkā māṇava, amhehi gahitapabbajjaṃ gaṇhantassa dātu”nti. Tato [P 1.0040] māṇavo mātāpitaro upasaṅkamitvā āha – “ayaṃ pabbajito buddhamantaṃ nāma jānāti, na ca attano santike apabbajitassa deti, ahaṃ etassa santike pabbajitvā mantaṃ uggaṇhissāmī”ti.

The young man, being unable to grasp either the upper part or the lower part, said, “O ascetic, what is this mantra called?” “Young man, this is called the Buddha-mantra.” “Sir, is it possible for this to be given to me also?” “Young man, it is possible to give it to one who takes the going forth that has been taken by us.” Then the young man, having approached his parents, said: “This ascetic knows the Buddha-mantra, but he does not give it to one who has not gone forth in his presence. Having gone forth in his presence, I will learn the mantra.”

Athassa mātāpitaro “pabbajitvāpi no putto mante gaṇhatu, gahetvā punāgamissatī”ti maññamānā “uggaṇha, puttā”ti anujāniṃsu. Thero dārakaṃ pabbājetvā dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ tāva ācikkhi. So tattha parikammaṃ karonto nacirasseva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tato thero cintesi – “sāmaṇero sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito, abhabbo dāni sāsanato nivattituṃ. Sace panassāhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā katheyyaṃ, arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyya, appossukko bhaveyya buddhavacanaṃ gahetuṃ, samayo dāni naṃ caṇḍavajjittherassa santikaṃ pesetu”nti. Tato āha – “ehi tvaṃ, sāmaṇera, therassa santikaṃ gantvā buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇha. Mama vacanena tañca ārogyaṃ puccha; evañca vadehi – ‘upajjhāyo maṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pahiṇī’ti. ‘Ko nāma te upajjhāyo’ti ca vutte ‘siggavatthero nāma, bhante’ti vadeyyāsi. ‘Ahaṃ ko nāmā’ti vutte evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘mama upajjhāyo, bhante, tumhākaṃ nāmaṃ jānātī’”ti.

Then his parents, thinking, “Even having gone forth, let our son learn the mantras; having learned them, he will return again,” gave their permission, saying, “Learn, son.” The Elder, having ordained the boy, first taught him the meditation subject on the thirty-two parts of the body. While he was doing the preliminary practice on that, not long after, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then the Elder thought: “The novice is established in the fruit of stream-entry; he is now incapable of turning back from the Dispensation. However, if I, having developed his meditation subject, were to teach him, he might attain Arahantship and would become unconcerned with learning the Buddha’s word. Now is the time to send him to the Elder Caṇḍavajji.” Then he said: “Come, novice, go to the Elder’s presence and learn the Buddha’s word. By my word, inquire after his health, and speak thus: ‘Venerable Sir, my preceptor has sent me to you.’ And when asked, ‘What is the name of your preceptor?’ you should say, ‘Venerable Sir, his name is the Elder Siggava.’ When asked, ‘What is my name?’ you should speak thus: ‘Venerable Sir, my preceptor knows your name.’”

“Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho tisso sāmaṇero theraṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā anupubbena caṇḍavajjittherassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Thero sāmaṇeraṃ pucchi – “kuto [V 1.0031] āgatosī”ti? “Upajjhāyo maṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pahiṇī”ti. “Ko nāma te upajjhāyo”ti? “Siggavatthero nāma, bhante”ti. “Ahaṃ ko nāmā”ti? “Mama upajjhāyo, bhante, tumhākaṃ nāmaṃ jānātī”ti. “Pattacīvaraṃ dāni paṭisāmehī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti sāmaṇero pattacīvaraṃ [P 1.0041] paṭisāmetvā punadivase pariveṇaṃ sammajjitvā udakadantaponaṃ upaṭṭhāpesi. Thero tassa sammajjitaṭṭhānaṃ puna sammajji[M 1.0032]. Taṃ udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā aññaṃ udakaṃ āhari. Tañca dantakaṭṭhaṃ apanetvā aññaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ gaṇhi. Evaṃ satta divasāni katvā sattame divase puna pucchi. Sāmaṇero punapi pubbe kathitasadisameva kathesi. Thero “so vatāyaṃ brāhmaṇo”ti sañjānitvā “kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti āha. “Buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhatthāya, bhante”ti. Thero “uggaṇha dāni, sāmaṇerā”ti vatvā puna divasato pabhuti buddhavacanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Tisso sāmaṇerova hutvā, ṭhapetvā vinayapiṭakaṃ sabbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhi saddhiṃ aṭṭhakathāya. Upasampannakāle pana avassikova samāno tipiṭakadharo ahosi. Ācariyupajjhāyā moggaliputtatissattherassa hatthe sakalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā parinibbāyiṃsu. Moggaliputtatissattheropi aparena samayena kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattappatto bahūnaṃ dhammavinayaṃ vācesi.

“So be it, Venerable Sir,” said the novice Tissa. Having paid homage to the Elder and circumambulated him respectfully, he went in due course to the presence of the Elder Caṇḍavajji, and having paid his respects, he stood to one side. The Elder asked the novice, “From where have you come?” “Venerable Sir, my preceptor has sent me to you.” “What is the name of your preceptor?” “Venerable Sir, his name is the Elder Siggava.” “What is my name?” “Venerable Sir, my preceptor knows your name.” “Then put away the bowl and robes.” “Very well, Venerable Sir,” said the novice. Having put away the bowl and robes, on the next day he swept the monastic grounds and set out water and a tooth-stick. The Elder re-swept the place he had swept. Having discarded that water, he brought other water. And having removed that tooth-stick, he took another tooth-stick. Having done this for seven days, on the seventh day he asked again. The novice again spoke just as he had spoken before. The Elder, recognizing, “Indeed, this is that brahmin,” asked, “For what purpose have you come?” “To learn the Buddha’s word, Venerable Sir.” The Elder, having said, “Learn now, novice,” from the next day onwards began to teach the Buddha’s word. Tissa, while still a novice, setting aside the Vinaya Piṭaka, learned all the Buddha’s word together with the commentary. At the time of his higher ordination, while still being without a full year’s seniority, he became a bearer of the Tipiṭaka. His teacher and preceptor, having established the entire Buddha’s word in the hands of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, lived for the remainder of their lives and attained Parinibbāna. The Elder Moggaliputtatissa also, at a later time, having developed his meditation subject and attained Arahantship, taught the Dhamma and Vinaya to many.

Tena kho pana samayena bindusārassa rañño ekasataputtā ahesuṃ. Te sabbe asoko attanā saddhiṃ ekamātikaṃ tissakumāraṃ ṭhapetvā ghātesi. Ghātento ca cattāri vassāni anabhisittova rajjaṃ kāretvā catunnaṃ vassānaṃ accayena tathāgatassa parinibbānato dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ upari aṭṭhārasame vasse sakalajambudīpe ekarajjābhisekaṃ pāpuṇi[P 1.0042]. Abhisekānubhāvena cassa imā rājiddhiyo āgatā – mahāpathaviyā heṭṭhā yojanappamāṇe āṇā pavattati; tathā upari ākāse anotattadahato aṭṭhahi kājehi soḷasa pānīyaghaṭe divase divase devatā āharanti, yato sāsane uppannasaddho hutvā aṭṭha ghaṭe bhikkhusaṅghassa adāsi, dve ghaṭe saṭṭhimattānaṃ tipiṭakadharabhikkhūnaṃ, dve ghaṭe aggamahesiyā asandhimittāya, cattāro ghaṭe attanā paribhuñji; devatāeva himavante nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ nāma atthi siniddhaṃ mudukaṃ rasavantaṃ taṃ divase divase āharanti, yena rañño ca mahesiyā ca soḷasannañca nāṭakitthisahassānaṃ saṭṭhimattānañca bhikkhusahassānaṃ devasikaṃ dantaponakiccaṃ nippajjati. Devasikameva cassa devatā agadāmalakaṃ agadaharītakaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇañca gandharasasampannaṃ ambapakkaṃ āharanti. Tathā chaddantadahato pañcavaṇṇanivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ pītakavaṇṇahatthapucchanapaṭakaṃ dibbañca pānakaṃ āharanti. Devasikameva panassa nhānagandhaṃ [M 1.0033] anuvilepanagandhaṃ [V 1.0032] pārupanatthāya asuttamayikaṃ sumanapupphapaṭaṃ mahārahañca añjanaṃ nāgabhavanato nāgarājāno āharanti. Chaddantadaheva [P 1.0043] uṭṭhitassa sālino nava vāhasahassāni divase divase sukā āharanti. Mūsikā nitthusakaṇe karonti, ekopi khaṇḍataṇḍulo na hoti, rañño sabbaṭṭhānesu ayameva taṇḍulo paribhogaṃ gacchati. Madhumakkhikā madhuṃ karonti. Kammārasālāsu acchā kūṭaṃ paharanti. Karavīkasakuṇā āgantvā madhurassaraṃ vikūjantā rañño balikammaṃ karonti.

At that time, King Bindusāra had one hundred and one sons. Asoka, having slain all of them, excepting Prince Tissa, his brother by the same mother, ruled the kingdom for four years without being consecrated. At the passing of four years, in the eighteenth year after two hundred years from the Tathāgata’s Parinibbāna, he attained the sole consecration over all of Jambudīpa. And by the power of his consecration, these royal powers arose for him: his command prevailed for a yojana beneath the great earth, and likewise in the sky above. Daily, deities brought sixteen pitchers of drinking water from Lake Anotatta with eight carrying-poles. From these, having become one with faith arisen in the Dispensation, he gave eight pitchers to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, two pitchers to sixty thousand bhikkhus who were masters of the Tipiṭaka, two pitchers to his chief queen Asandhimittā, and he himself used four pitchers. Deities themselves daily brought from the Himavanta a smooth, soft, and flavorful tooth-stick called Nāgalatā, by which the daily duty of tooth-cleansing for the king, the queen, sixteen thousand dancing women, and sixty thousand bhikkhus was accomplished. And for him, daily, deities brought medicinal āmalaka fruit, medicinal harītaka fruit, and ripe mangoes that were golden in color and endowed with fragrance and flavor. Likewise, from Lake Chaddanta, they brought five-colored inner and outer garments, a yellow-colored cloth for wiping the hands, and a divine beverage. Moreover, daily, from the Nāga abode, the Nāga kings brought for him fragrant bathing water, fragrant ointment for anointing, a cloth with jasmine flower patterns not made of thread for wearing, and excellent collyrium. Daily, parrots brought nine thousand vāhas of sāli rice that had grown in Lake Chaddanta itself. Mice made it free of chaff and broken grains; there was not even one broken grain of rice. In all the king's places, this very rice was consumed. Honeybees made honey. In the smithies, bears struck with hammers. Karavīka birds, having come, singing with a sweet voice, performed the tribute for the king.

Imāhi iddhīhi samannāgato rājā ekadivasaṃ suvaṇṇasaṅkhalikabandhanaṃ pesetvā catunnaṃ buddhānaṃ adhigatarūpadassanaṃ kappāyukaṃ kāḷaṃ nāma nāgarājānaṃ ānayitvā setacchattassa heṭṭhā mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā anekasatavaṇṇehi jalaja thalajapupphehi suvaṇṇapupphehi ca pūjaṃ katvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitehi soḷasahi nāṭakitthisahassehi samantato parikkhipitvā “anantañāṇassa tāva me saddhammavaracakkavattino sammāsambuddhassa rūpaṃ imesaṃ akkhīnaṃ āpāthaṃ karohī”ti vatvā tena nimmitaṃ sakalasarīravippakiṇṇapuññappabhāvanibbattāsītānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasassirīkatāya vikasitakamaluppalapuṇḍarīkapaṭimaṇḍitamiva salilatalaṃ tārāgaṇarasmijālavisadavipphuritasobhāsamujjalitamiva gaganatalaṃ nīlapītalohitādibhedavicitravaṇṇaraṃsivinaddhabyāmappabhāparikkhepavilāsitāya [P 1.0044] sañcāppabhānurāgaindadhanuvijjulatāparikkhittamiva kanakagirisikharaṃ nānāvirāgavimalaketumālāsamujjalitacārumatthakasobhaṃ nayanarasāyatanamiva brahmadevamanujanāgayakkhagaṇānaṃ buddharūpaṃ passanto satta divasāni akkhipūjaṃ nāma akāsi.

Endowed with these powers, the king one day sent a golden chain for binding and had the Nāga king named Kāḷa, who had seen the forms of the four Buddhas and was an aeon in lifespan, brought before him. He had him seated beneath a white parasol on a couch worthy of great ones, made an offering with aquatic and terrestrial flowers of many hundreds of colors and with golden flowers, had him surrounded on all sides by sixteen thousand dancing women adorned with all ornaments, and said: “Pray, make the form of the Sammāsambuddha—who possesses infinite knowledge, the supreme wheel-turner of the good Dhamma—an object for these eyes of mine.” Then, beholding the Buddha-form created by that Nāga king—glorious with the thirty-two marks of a great man, adorned with the eighty minor characteristics produced by the power of merit scattered all over the entire body, like a water surface adorned with opened lotuses, blue lotuses, and white lotuses; like the surface of the sky, brightly shining with the splendor of the clear, radiant net of the host of stars; graced with the surrounding fathom-wide aura interwoven with variegated rays of blue, yellow, red, and other colors; like a golden mountain peak encircled by the glow of twilight, the rainbow, and flashes of lightning; having the beauty of a charming head-top, brightly shining with the flawless, variegated, and radiant rays of the ketumālā; like an elixir for the eyes of the hosts of Brahmās, devas, humans, nāgas, and yakkhas—for seven days, he performed what is called the eye-offering.

Rājā kira abhisekaṃ pāpuṇitvā tīṇiyeva saṃvaccharāni bāhirakapāsaṇḍaṃ pariggaṇhi. Catutthe saṃvacchare buddhasāsane pasīdi. Tassa kira pitā bindusāro brāhmaṇabhatto ahosi, so brāhmaṇānañca brāhmaṇajātiyapāsaṇḍānañca paṇḍaraṅgaparibbājakādīnaṃ saṭṭhisahassamattānaṃ niccabhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Asokopi pitarā pavattitaṃ dānaṃ attano antepure tatheva dadamāno ekadivasaṃ sīhapañjare ṭhito te upasamaparibāhirena ācārena bhuñjamāne asaṃyatindriye avinītairiyāpathe disvā cintesi – “īdisaṃ dānaṃ upaparikkhitvā yuttaṭṭhāne dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Evaṃ cintetvā amacce āha – “gacchatha, bhaṇe, attano attano sādhusammate [M 1.0034] samaṇabrāhmaṇe antepuraṃ atiharatha, dānaṃ dassāmā”ti. Amaccā “sādhu, devā”ti rañño paṭissuṇitvā te te paṇḍaraṅgaparibbājakājīvakanigaṇṭhādayo ānetvā “ime, mahārāja, amhākaṃ arahanto”ti āhaṃsu.

The king, it is said, having attained the consecration, for three years only investigated and patronized the external heresies. In the fourth year, he gained faith in the Buddha's Dispensation. His father, Bindusāra, it is said, was a devotee of brahmins, and he established a perpetual food-offering for sixty thousand brahmins and heretics of brahmin birth, such as the white-robed wanderers and others. Asoka also, while giving in his own palace the same donation established by his father, one day, standing at the lion-window, saw them eating with conduct external to tranquility, with unrestrained faculties, and with undisciplined deportment, and he thought: “It is proper to give such a donation after investigating, to suitable recipients.” Having thought thus, he said to his ministers: “Go, sirs, bring to the inner palace those ascetics and brahmins whom you yourselves deem to be good persons; we shall give a donation.” The ministers, assenting to the king with “Very well, Your Majesty,” brought those various white-robed wanderers, Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and others, and said, “These, great king, are our arahants.”

Atha [V 1.0033] rājā antepure uccāvacāni āsanāni paññapetvā “āgacchantū”ti vatvā āgatāgate āha – “attano attano patirūpe āsane nisīdathā”ti[P 1.0045]. Tesu ekacce bhaddapīṭhakesu, ekacce phalakapīṭhakesu nisīdiṃsu. Te disvā rājā “natthi nesaṃ anto sāro”ti ñatvā tesaṃ anurūpaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ datvā uyyojesi.

Then the king, having had high and low seats prepared in the inner palace, said, “Let them come.” To each one as they came, he said: “Sit on a seat suitable for yourself.” Among them, some sat on fine stools, and some on plank-seats. Seeing them, the king, knowing, “There is no inner substance within them,” gave them suitable hard and soft food and dismissed them.

Evaṃ gacchante kāle ekadivasaṃ rājā sīhapañjare ṭhito addasa nigrodhasāmaṇeraṃ rājaṅgaṇena gacchantaṃ dantaṃ guttaṃ santindriyaṃ iriyāpathasampannaṃ. Ko panāyaṃ nigrodho nāma? Bindusārarañño jeṭṭhaputtassa sumanarājakumārassa putto.

Thus, as time was passing, one day the king, standing at the lion-window, saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the royal courtyard—disciplined, guarded, with tranquil faculties, and endowed with inspiring deportment. Who, then, was this one named Nigrodha? He was the son of Prince Sumana, the eldest son of King Bindusāra.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

In this regard, this is the story in sequential order:

Bindusārarañño kira dubbalakāleyeva asokakumāro attanā laddhaṃ ujjenīrajjaṃ pahāya āgantvā sabbanagaraṃ attano hatthagataṃ katvā sumanarājakumāraṃ aggahesi. Taṃdivasameva sumanassa rājakumārassa sumanā nāma devī paripuṇṇagabbhā ahosi. Sā aññātakavesena nikkhamitvā avidūre aññataraṃ caṇḍālagāmaṃ sandhāya gacchantī jeṭṭhakacaṇḍālassa gehato avidūre aññatarasmiṃ nigrodharukkhe adhivatthāya devatāya “ito ehi, sumane”ti vadantiyā saddaṃ sutvā tassā samīpaṃ gatā. Devatā attano ānubhāvena ekaṃ sālaṃ nimminitvā “ettha vasāhī”ti adāsi. Sā taṃ sālaṃ pāvisi. Gatadivaseyeva ca puttaṃ vijāyi. Sā tassa nigrodhadevatāya pariggahitattā “nigrodho” tveva nāmaṃ akāsi. Jeṭṭhakacaṇḍālo diṭṭhadivasato pabhuti taṃ attano sāmidhītaraṃ viya maññamāno nibaddhavattaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Rājadhītā tattha satta vassāni vasi. Nigrodhakumāropi [P 1.0046] sattavassiko jāto. Tadā mahāvaruṇatthero nāma eko arahā dārakassa hetusampadaṃ disvā rakkhitvā tattha viharamāno “sattavassiko dāni dārako, kālo naṃ pabbājetu”nti [M 1.0035] cintetvā rājadhītāya ārocāpetvā nigrodhakumāraṃ pabbājesi. Kumāro khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So ekadivasaṃ pātova sarīraṃ jaggitvā ācariyupajjhāyavattaṃ katvā pattacīvaramādāya “mātuupāsikāya gehadvāraṃ gacchāmī”ti nikkhami. Mātunivāsanaṭṭhānañcassa dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā nagaramajjhena gantvā pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā gantabbaṃ hoti.

It is said that during the time of King Bindusāra's weakness, Prince Asoka, having abandoned the kingdom of Ujjenī which he had obtained, came and, having brought the entire city into his own hands, seized Prince Sumana. On that very day, Queen Sumanā, the wife of Prince Sumana, was with a full-term pregnancy. She, having gone out in the guise of an unknown person and heading toward a certain outcaste village not far away, was going along when, not far from the house of the chief outcaste, she heard the sound of a deity dwelling in a certain banyan tree, who said, “Come here, Sumanā!” Having heard this, she went near the deity. The deity, by her own power, created a hall and gave it to her, saying, “Dwell here.” She entered that hall, and on the very day she arrived, she gave birth to a son. Because he was taken under the protection of the banyan-tree deity, she gave him the name “Nigrodha.” The chief outcaste, from the day he first saw her, considering her to be like his master's daughter, established a constant provision of support. The princess lived there for seven years, and Prince Nigrodha also became seven years of age. At that time, a certain Arahant named Mahāvaruṇa Thera, while dwelling there, saw the boy’s perfection of the conditions for Arahantship and protected him. Thinking, “The boy is now seven years old; it is time to ordain him,” he had the princess informed and ordained Prince Nigrodha. The prince attained Arahantship at the very tip of the razor. One day, early in the morning, having attended to his body and performed his duties to his teacher and preceptor, he took his bowl and robe and set out, thinking, “I will go to the door of my mother, the lay devotee.” And his mother’s dwelling place had to be reached by entering the city through the southern gate, going through the middle of the city, and exiting through the eastern gate.

Tena [V 1.0034] ca samayena asoko dhammarājā pācīnadisābhimukho sīhapañjare caṅkamati. Taṅkhaṇaññeva nigrodho rājaṅgaṇaṃ sampāpuṇi santindriyo santamānaso yugamattaṃ pekkhamāno. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekadivasaṃ rājā sīhapañjare ṭhito addasa nigrodhasāmaṇeraṃ rājaṅgaṇena gacchantaṃ dantaṃ guttaṃ santindriyaṃ iriyāpathasampanna”nti. Disvā panassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ jano sabbopi vikkhittacitto bhantamigappaṭibhāgo. Ayaṃ pana dārako avikkhittacitto ativiya cassa ālokitavilokitaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇañca sobhati. Addhā etassa abbhantare lokuttaradhammo bhavissatī”ti rañño saha dassaneneva sāmaṇere cittaṃ pasīdi, pemaṃ saṇṭhahi. Kasmā? Pubbe hi kira puññakaraṇakāle esa rañño jeṭṭhabhātā vāṇijako ahosi. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

And at that time, Asoka, the righteous king, was walking back and forth at the lion-window, facing the eastern direction. At that very moment, Nigrodha arrived at the royal courtyard, with tranquil faculties, with a tranquil mind, looking a yoke's length ahead. Therefore it was said: “One day the king, standing at the lion-window, saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the royal courtyard—disciplined, guarded, with tranquil faculties, and endowed with inspiring deportment.” And upon seeing him, this thought occurred to the king: “All these people have distracted minds, like startled deer. But this boy has an undistracted mind, and his looking forward and glancing sideways, and his bending and stretching, are exceedingly graceful. Surely, within him there must be the supramundane Dhamma.” As soon as he saw the novice, the king’s mind became serene, and affection was established. Why? For it is said that previously, at a time of making merit, this one had been the king’s elder brother, a honey merchant. For this has also been said:

“Pubbe va [P 1.0047] sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā;

Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃ va yathodake”ti. (jā. 1.2.174);

“Through having lived together in the past, or through benefit in the present, thus is that affection born, just as a lotus is in the water.”

Atha rājā sañjātapemo sabahumāno “etaṃ sāmaṇeraṃ pakkosathā”ti amacce pesesi. “Te aticirāyantī”ti puna dve tayo pesesi – “turitaṃ āgacchatū”ti. Sāmaṇero attano pakatiyā eva agamāsi. Rājā patirūpamāsanaṃ ñatvā “nisīdathā”ti āha. So ito cito ca viloketvā “natthi dāni aññe bhikkhū”ti samussitasetacchattaṃ rājapallaṅkaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pattaggahaṇatthāya rañño ākāraṃ dassesi. Rājā taṃ pallaṅkasamīpaṃ upagacchantaṃyeva disvā cintesi – “ajjeva dāni ayaṃ sāmaṇero imassa gehassa sāmiko bhavissatī”ti sāmaṇero rañño hatthe pattaṃ datvā pallaṅkaṃ abhiruhitvā nisīdi. Rājā attano atthāya sampāditaṃ sabbaṃ yāgukhajjakabhattavikatiṃ [M 1.0036] upanāmesi. Sāmaṇero attano yāpanīyamattakameva sampaṭicchi. Bhattakiccāvasāne rājā āha – “satthārā tumhākaṃ dinnovādaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Jānāmi, mahārāja, ekadesenā”ti. “Tāta, mayhampi naṃ kathehī”ti. “Sādhu, mahārājā”ti rañño anurūpaṃ dhammapade appamādavaggaṃ anumodanatthāya abhāsi.

Then the king, with affection and great respect having arisen, sent his ministers, saying, “Summon this novice.” Thinking, “They are taking too long,” he again sent two or three, saying, “Let him come quickly.” The novice came at his own natural pace. The king, knowing a suitable seat, said, “Please sit.” He looked here and there, and knowing, “There are now no other monks,” he approached the royal throne with its raised white parasol and showed the king a gesture for taking the bowl. The king, seeing him just as he was approaching the vicinity of the throne, thought: “This very day, this novice will become the master of this house.” The novice, having given the bowl into the king’s hand, ascended the throne and sat down. The king offered all the varieties of gruel, hard food, and rice that had been prepared for himself. The novice accepted only as much as was sufficient to sustain himself. At the conclusion of the meal, the king asked: “Do you know the instruction given to you by the Teacher?” “I know it in part, great king.” “Dear one, please tell it to me as well.” Saying, “Very well, great king,” for the purpose of giving thanks for the meal, he recited the Appamādavagga from the Dhammapada, which was suitable for the king.

Rājā pana “appamādo amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno pada”nti sutvāva “aññātaṃ, tāta, pariyosāpehī”ti āha. Anumodanāvasāne ca “aṭṭha te, tāta, dhuvabhattāni dammī”ti āha. Sāmaṇero āha – “etāni ahaṃ upajjhāyassa dammi, mahārājā”ti. “Ko ayaṃ, tāta, upajjhāyo nāmā”ti? “Vajjāvajjaṃ disvā codetā sāretā ca, mahārājā”ti. “Aññānipi te, tāta, aṭṭha dammī”ti. “Etāni [P 1.0048] ācariyassa dammi, mahārājā”ti. “Ko ayaṃ, tāta, ācariyo nāmā”ti? “Imasmiṃ sāsane sikkhitabbakadhammesu patiṭṭhāpetā, mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu, tāta, aññānipi te aṭṭha dammī”ti. “Etānipi bhikkhusaṅghassa dammi, mahārājā”ti. “Ko ayaṃ, tāta, bhikkhusaṅgho nāmā”ti? “Yaṃ nissāya[V 1.0035], mahārāja, amhākaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānañca mama ca pabbajjā ca upasampadā cā”ti. Rājā bhiyyoso mattāya tuṭṭhacitto āha – “aññānipi te, tāta, aṭṭha dammī”ti. Sāmaṇero “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā punadivase dvattiṃsa bhikkhū gahetvā rājantepuraṃ pavisitvā bhattakiccamakāsi. Rājā “aññepi dvattiṃsa bhikkhū tumhehi saddhiṃ sve bhikkhaṃ gaṇhantū”ti eteneva upāyena divase divase vaḍḍhāpento saṭṭhisahassānaṃ brāhmaṇaparibbājakādīnaṃ bhattaṃ upacchinditvā antonivesane saṭṭhisahassānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ niccabhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi nigrodhatthere gateneva pasādena. Nigrodhattheropi rājānaṃ saparisaṃ tīsu saraṇesu pañcasu ca sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā buddhasāsane pothujjanikena pasādena acalappasādaṃ katvā patiṭṭhāpesi. Puna rājā asokārāmaṃ nāma mahāvihāraṃ kāretvā saṭṭhisahassānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ niccabhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Sakalajambudīpe caturāsītiyā nagarasahassesu caturāsītivihārasahassāni kārāpesi caturāsītisahassacetiyapaṭimaṇḍitāni dhammeneva, no adhammena.

The king, however, upon just hearing, 'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless, heedlessness the path to death,' said, 'It is understood, dear one, bring it to a conclusion.' And at the end of the thanksgiving sermon, he said, 'I give you, dear one, eight permanent portions of food.' The novice said, 'I give these to my preceptor, great king.' 'Who, dear one, is this preceptor?' 'One who, seeing faults, reproves and reminds one, great king.' 'I give you another eight, dear one.' 'I give these to my teacher, great king.' 'Who, dear one, is this teacher?' 'One who establishes one in the things that should be learned in this Dispensation, great king.' 'Good, dear one, I give you another eight.' 'These also I give to the community of monks, great king.' 'Who, dear one, is this community of monks?' 'That, great king, on which our teachers' and preceptors' and my own going forth and higher ordination depend.' The king, his mind pleased beyond measure, said, 'I give you another eight, dear one.' The novice, accepting with 'Good,' on the next day took thirty-two monks, entered the king's inner palace, and performed the meal service. The king said, 'Let another thirty-two monks receive alms with you tomorrow.' By this very method, increasing the number day by day, he cut off the food supply for sixty thousand brahmins, wanderers, and others, and, prompted by the very faith he had in Elder Nigrodha, he established a permanent food offering for sixty thousand monks within the royal residence. Elder Nigrodha, for his part, established the king and his retinue in the three refuges and the five precepts, and made his ordinary faith in the Buddha's Dispensation unwavering. Furthermore, the king had a great monastery named Asokārāma built and established a permanent food offering for sixty thousand monks. Throughout all of Jambudīpa, in eighty-four thousand cities, he had eighty-four thousand monasteries built, adorned with eighty-four thousand cetiyas, righteously and not unrighteously.

Ekadivasaṃ kira rājā asokārāme mahādānaṃ datvā saṭṭhisahassabhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe nisajja saṅghaṃ catūhi paccayehi pavāretvā imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi [M 1.0037] – “bhante, bhagavatā desitadhammo nāma kittako hotī”ti? “Aṅgato, mahārāja, navaṅgāni, khandhato caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti. Rājā dhamme pasīditvā “ekekaṃ dhammakkhandhaṃ ekekavihārena pūjessāmī”ti ekadivasameva [P 1.0049] channavutikoṭidhanaṃ visajjetvā amacce āṇāpesi – “etha, bhaṇe, ekamekasmiṃ nagare ekamekaṃ vihāraṃ kārāpentā caturāsītiyā nagarasahassesu caturāsītivihārasahassāni kārāpethā”ti. Sayañca asokārāme asokamahāvihāratthāya kammaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Saṅgho indaguttattheraṃ nāma mahiddhikaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ navakammādhiṭṭhāyakaṃ adāsi. Thero yaṃ yaṃ na niṭṭhāti taṃ taṃ attano ānubhāvena niṭṭhāpesi. Evampi tīhi saṃvaccharehi vihārakammaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Ekadivasameva sabbanagarehi paṇṇāni āgamiṃsu.

It is said that one day, the king, having given a great offering at the Asokārāma, sat in the midst of the community of sixty thousand monks, invited the Sangha with the four requisites, and asked this question: 'Venerable sirs, how much is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One?' 'By way of divisions, great king, there are nine divisions; by way of aggregates, there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.' The king, inspired by the Dhamma, thought, 'I shall honor each and every aggregate of the Dhamma with a separate monastery.' On that very day, he disbursed ninety-six crores of wealth and commanded his ministers: 'Come, sirs, having a monastery built in each and every city, have eighty-four thousand monasteries built in the eighty-four thousand cities.' He himself initiated the work in the Asokārāma for the Asoka Great Monastery. The Sangha appointed the Elder Indagutta—one of great psychic power, great might, and whose cankers were destroyed—as the supervisor of the new work. Whatever was not completed, the Elder completed by his own power. Even so, he completed the work on the monastery in three years. On one and the same day, letters arrived from all the cities.

Amaccā rañño ārocesuṃ – “niṭṭhitāni, deva, caturāsītivihārasahassānī”ti. Rājā nagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “ito sattannaṃ divasānaṃ accayena vihāramaho bhavissati. Sabbe aṭṭha sīlaṅgāni samādiyitvā antonagare ca bahinagare ca vihāramahaṃ paṭiyādentū”ti. Tato sattannaṃ divasānaṃ accayena sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitāya anekasatasahassasaṅkhyāya caturaṅginiyā senāya parivuto devaloke amaravatiyā rājadhāniyā sirito adhikatarasassirīkaṃ viya nagaraṃ kātukāmena ussāhajātena mahājanena alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ nagaraṃ anuvicaranto vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe aṭṭhāsi.

The ministers informed the king: 'Sire, the eighty-four thousand monasteries are completed.' The king had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: 'Seven days from now, there will be a festival for the monasteries. Let everyone, having undertaken the eight precepts, prepare for the monastery festival both inside and outside the city.' Then, after seven days had passed, the king, surrounded by a four-fold army numbering many hundreds of thousands and adorned with all ornaments, went about inspecting the city, which had been decorated and prepared by a great populace filled with enthusiasm and the desire to make it even more splendid than Amaravatī, the capital city in the world of the devas. He then went to the monastery and stood in the midst of the community of monks.

Tasmiñca [V 1.0036] khaṇe sannipatitā asīti bhikkhukoṭiyo ahesuṃ, bhikkhunīnañca channavutisatasahassāni. Tattha khīṇāsavabhikkhūyeva satasahassasaṅkhyā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ etadahosi – “sace rājā attano adhikāraṃ anavasesaṃ passeyya ativiya buddhasāsane pasīdeyyā”ti. Tato [P 1.0050] lokavivaraṇaṃ nāma pāṭihāriyaṃ akaṃsu. Rājā asokārāme ṭhitova catuddisā anuvilokento samantato samuddapariyantaṃ jambudīpaṃ passati caturāsītiñca vihārasahassāni uḷārāya vihāramahapūjāya virocamānāni. So taṃ vibhūtiṃ passamāno uḷārena pītipāmojjena samannāgato “atthi pana aññassapi kassaci evarūpaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppannapubba”nti cintento bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pucchi – “bhante, amhākaṃ lokanāthassa dasabalassa sāsane ko mahāpariccāgaṃ pariccaji. Kassa [M 1.0038] pariccāgo mahantoti? Bhikkhusaṅgho moggaliputtatissattherassa bhāraṃ akāsi. Thero āha – “mahārāja, dasabalassa sāsane paccayadāyako nāma tayā sadiso dharamānepi tathāgate na koci ahosi, taveva pariccāgo mahā”ti. Rājā therassa vacanaṃ sutvā uḷārena pītipāmojjena nirantaraṃ phuṭṭhasarīro hutvā cintesi – “natthi kira mayā sadiso paccayadāyako, mayhaṃ kira pariccāgo mahā, ahaṃ kira deyyadhammena sāsanaṃ paggaṇhāmi. Kiṃ panāhaṃ evaṃ sati sāsanassa dāyādo homi, na homī”ti. Tato bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pucchi – “bhavāmi nu kho ahaṃ, bhante, sāsanassa dāyādo”ti?

And at that moment, eighty crores of monks had gathered, along with ninety-six hundred thousand nuns. Among them, a hundred thousand were Arahant monks. This thought occurred to them: “If the king could see the full extent of his meritorious deeds, he would develop exceedingly great faith in the Buddha’s Dispensation.” Then, they performed the miracle known as the “Opening of the World.” Standing in the Asokārāma, the king looked around in all directions and saw the entire Jambudīpa up to the ocean’s edge, and eighty-four thousand monasteries, all resplendent with a magnificent great offering for the monasteries. Seeing this splendor, he was filled with sublime joy and gladness and wondered, “Has such joy and gladness ever arisen for any other person?” Reflecting thus, he asked the Saṅgha of monks, “Venerable sirs, in the Dispensation of our Protector of the World, the Ten-Powered One, who has made a great donation? Whose donation is said to be great?” The Saṅgha of monks entrusted the task to the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa. The Elder said, “Great king, in the Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One, no donor of requisites equal to you has ever existed, even when the Tathāgata was living. Your donation alone is great.” Hearing the Elder’s words, the king, his body continuously suffused with sublime joy and gladness, thought, “It seems there is no donor of requisites like me; my donation is indeed great. I uphold the Dispensation through donative offerings. But given this, am I an heir to the Dispensation, or am I not?” Then he asked the Saṅgha of monks, “Venerable sirs, do I become an heir to the Dispensation?”

Tato moggaliputtatissatthero rañño idaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā rājaputtassa mahindassa upanissayasampattiṃ sampassamāno “sace ayaṃ kumāro pabbajissati sāsanassa ativiya vuḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti cintetvā rājānaṃ etadavoca – “na kho, mahārāja, ettāvatā sāsanassa dāyādo hoti; apica kho paccayadāyakoti vā upaṭṭhākoti vā saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Yopi hi, mahārāja, pathavito yāva brahmalokaparimāṇaṃ paccayarāsiṃ dadeyya sopi ‘sāsane dāyādo’ti saṅkhyaṃ na gacchatī”ti. “Atha kathaṃ carahi, bhante, sāsanassa dāyādo hotī”ti? “Yo hi koci, mahārāja, aḍḍho [P 1.0051] vā daliddo vā attano orasaṃ puttaṃ pabbājeti – ayaṃ vuccati, mahārāja, dāyādo sāsanassā”ti.

Then the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa, hearing the king's words and perceiving the perfection of supporting conditions for Prince Mahinda, thought, “If this prince goes forth, the Dispensation will greatly increase.” He then said this to the king, “Great king, by this much one does not become an heir to the Dispensation; rather, one is counted as a donor of requisites or a supporter. Indeed, great king, even if someone were to give a heap of requisites as great as from the earth up to the Brahma world, that person is not counted as an ‘heir in the Dispensation’.” “Then how, venerable sir, does one become an heir of the Dispensation?” “Whoever, great king, whether rich or poor, causes their own legitimate son to go forth—this one, great king, is called an heir of the Dispensation.”

Evaṃ vutte asoko rājā “ahaṃ kira evarūpaṃ pariccāgaṃ katvāpi neva sāsanassa dāyādabhāvaṃ patto”ti sāsane dāyādabhāvaṃ patthayamāno ito cito ca viloketvā addasa mahindakumāraṃ avidūre ṭhitaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – “kiñcāpi ahaṃ imaṃ kumāraṃ tissakumārassa pabbajitakālato pabhuti oparajje ṭhapetukāmo, atha kho oparajjatopi pabbajjāva [V 1.0037] uttamā”ti. Tato kumāraṃ āha – “sakkhasi tvaṃ, tāta, pabbajitu”nti? Kumāro pakatiyāpi tissakumārassa pabbajitakālato pabhuti pabbajitukāmova rañño vacanaṃ sutvā ativiya pāmojjajāto hutvā āha – “pabbajāmi, deva, maṃ pabbājetvā tumhe sāsanadāyādā hothā”ti.

When this was said, King Asoka thought, “It seems that even having made such a great donation, I have not attained the state of being an heir to the Dispensation.” Desiring the state of being an heir in the Dispensation, he looked here and there and saw Prince Mahinda standing not far away. Having seen him, this thought occurred to him: “Although I have been desirous of placing this prince in the viceroyalty since the time of Prince Tissa's going forth, nevertheless, going forth is superior even to the viceroyalty.” Then he said to the prince, “Are you able, dear son, to go forth?” The prince, who by nature had been desirous of going forth since the time of Prince Tissa's going forth, having heard the king's words, became exceedingly joyful and said, “I will go forth, Your Majesty. By having me go forth, may you become heirs of the Dispensation.”

Tena ca samayena rājadhītā saṅghamittāpi tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne ṭhitā hoti. Tassā ca sāmiko aggibrahmā nāma kumāro yuvarājena tissakumārena [M 1.0039] saddhiṃ pabbajito hoti. Rājā taṃ disvā āha – “tvampi, amma, pabbajituṃ sakkhasī”ti? “Sādhu, tāta, sakkomī”ti. Rājā puttānaṃ manaṃ labhitvā pahaṭṭhacitto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ etadavoca – “bhante, ime dārake pabbājetvā maṃ sāsane dāyādaṃ karothā”ti. Saṅgho rañño vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā kumāraṃ moggaliputtatissattherena upajjhāyena mahādevattherena ca ācariyena pabbājesi. Majjhantikattherena ācariyena upasampādesi. Tadā kira kumāro paripuṇṇavīsativassova hoti. So tasmiṃyeva upasampadasīmamaṇḍale saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Saṅghamittāyapi rājadhītāya ācariyā āyupālittherī nāma, upajjhāyā pana dhammapālittherī nāma ahosi. Tadā [P 1.0052] saṅghamittā aṭṭhārasavassā hoti. Taṃ pabbajitamattaṃ tasmiṃyeva sīmamaṇḍale sikkhāya patiṭṭhāpesuṃ. Ubhinnaṃ pabbajitakāle rājā chabbassābhiseko hoti.

And at that time, the king’s daughter, Saṅghamittā, was also standing in that very place. Her husband, a prince named Aggibrahmā, had gone forth together with the heir-apparent, Prince Tissa. Seeing her, the king said, “You too, dear one, are you able to go forth?” “Yes, father, I am able,” she replied. The king, having ascertained his children’s minds, with a delighted heart, said this to the Saṅgha of monks: “Venerable sirs, by having these children go forth, make me an heir in the Dispensation.” The Saṅgha accepted the king’s words and had the prince go forth with the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa as preceptor and the Elder Mahādeva as teacher. He was given the higher ordination with the Elder Majjhantika as teacher. At that time, it is said, the prince was fully twenty years of age. Right there, within the ordination boundary, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. For the princess Saṅghamittā, the teacher was the Elderess Āyupālī, and the preceptor was the Elderess Dhammapālī. At that time, Saṅghamittā was eighteen years old. As soon as she had gone forth, they established her in the training within that very boundary. At the time of the going forth of both, the king was in the sixth year of his consecration.

Atha mahindatthero upasampannakālato pabhuti attano upajjhāyasseva santike dhammañca vinayañca pariyāpuṇanto dvepi saṅgītiyo ārūḷhaṃ tipiṭakasaṅgahitaṃ sāṭṭhakathaṃ sabbaṃ theravādaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ abbhantare uggahetvā attano upajjhāyassa antevāsikānaṃ sahassamattānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāmokkho ahosi. Tadā asoko dhammarājā navavassābhiseko hoti. Rañño pana aṭṭhavassābhisekakāleyeva kontaputtatissatthero byādhipaṭikammatthaṃ bhikkhācāravattena āhiṇḍanto pasatamattaṃ sappiṃ alabhitvā byādhibalena parikkhīṇāyusaṅkhāro bhikkhusaṅghaṃ appamādena ovaditvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvā parinibbāyi. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā therassa sakkāraṃ katvā “mayi nāma rajjaṃ kārente evaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paccayā dullabhā”ti nagarassa catūsu dvāresu pokkharaṇiyo kārāpetvā bhesajjassa pūrāpetvā dāpesi.

Then, from the time of his higher ordination, the Elder Mahinda, while learning the Dhamma and the Vinaya in the presence of his own preceptor, within three years mastered the entire Theravāda tradition—the Tipiṭaka as established in the two Councils, together with its commentaries. He became the foremost among the thousand or so monks who were disciples of his preceptor. At that time, Dhammāsoka, the righteous king, was in the ninth year since his consecration. However, in the eighth year of the king’s consecration, the Elder Koṇṭaputtatissa, while wandering on alms-round to treat an illness, did not obtain even a handful of ghee. With his life-formations exhausted by the power of the illness, he exhorted the community of monks with heedfulness, sat cross-legged in the air, entered into the fire-element, and attained Parinibbāna. The king, having heard of this event, performed honors for the Elder and thought, “While I am ruling, are requisites for monks truly so scarce?” He then had ponds constructed at the four gates of the city, had them filled with medicines, and had them given.

Tena kira samayena pāṭaliputtassa catūsu dvāresu cattāri satasahassāni, sabhāyaṃ satasahassanti divase divase pañcasatasahassāni rañño uppajjanti. Tato rājā nigrodhattherassa devasikaṃ satasahassaṃ visajjesi. Buddhassa cetiye gandhamālādīhi pūjanatthāya satasahassaṃ[V 1.0038]. Dhammassa [M 1.0040] satasahassaṃ, taṃ dhammadharānaṃ bahussutānaṃ catupaccayatthāya upanīyati. Saṅghassa satasahassaṃ, catūsu dvāresu bhesajjatthāya satasahassaṃ. Evaṃ sāsane uḷāro lābhasakkāro [P 1.0053] nibbatti.

It is said that at that time, a revenue of four hundred thousand arose for the king at the four gates of Pāṭaliputta, and one hundred thousand in the assembly hall; thus, five hundred thousand arose for the king daily. From that, the king disbursed a daily one hundred thousand to the Elder Nigrodha. One hundred thousand for the worship at the Buddha's cetiya with perfumes, garlands, and so on. One hundred thousand for the Dhamma, which was offered for the four requisites of the learned bearers of the Dhamma.
