One hundred thousand for the Saṅgha, and one hundred thousand for medicines at the four gates. Thus, great gain and honor arose in the Dispensation.

Titthiyā parihīnalābhasakkārā antamaso ghāsacchādanampi alabhantā lābhasakkāraṃ patthayamānā sāsane pabbajitvā sakāni sakāni diṭṭhigatāni “ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo”ti dīpenti. Pabbajjaṃ alabhamānāpi sayameva muṇḍetvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā vihāresu vicarantā uposathampi pavāraṇampi saṅghakammampi gaṇakammampi pavisanti. Bhikkhū tehi saddhiṃ uposathaṃ na karonti. Tadā moggaliputtatissatthero “uppannaṃ dāni idaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ, taṃ nacirasseva kakkhaḷaṃ bhavissati. Na kho panetaṃ sakkā imesaṃ majjhe vasantena vūpasametu”nti mahindattherassa gaṇaṃ nīyyātetvā attanā phāsuvihārena viharitukāmo ahogaṅgapabbataṃ agamāsi. Tepi kho titthiyā bhikkhusaṅghena dhammena vinayena satthusāsanena niggayhamānāpi dhammavinayānulomāya paṭipattiyā asaṇṭhahantā anekarūpaṃ sāsanassa abbudañca malañca kaṇṭakañca samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Keci aggiṃ paricaranti, keci pañcātapena tāpenti, keci ādiccaṃ anuparivattanti, keci “dhammañca vinayañca vobhindissāmā”ti paggaṇhiṃsu. Tadā bhikkhusaṅgho na tehi saddhiṃ uposathaṃ vā pavāraṇaṃ vā akāsi. Asokārāme sattavassāni uposatho upacchijji. Raññopi etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi – “vihāraṃ gantvā adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametvā uposathaṃ kārāpehī”ti. Amacco rājānaṃ paṭipucchituṃ avisahanto aññe amacce upasaṅkamitvā āha – “rājā maṃ ‘vihāraṃ gantvā adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametvā uposathaṃ kārāpehī’ti pahiṇi. Kathaṃ nu kho adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammatī”ti? Te āhaṃsu [P 1.0054] – “mayaṃ evaṃ sallakkhema – ‘yathā nāma paccantaṃ vūpasamentā core ghātenti, evameva ye uposathaṃ na karonti, te māretukāmo rājā bhavissatī’”ti. Atha so amacco vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātetvā āha – “ahaṃ raññā ‘uposathaṃ kārāpehī’ti pesito. Karotha dāni, bhante, uposatha”nti. Bhikkhū “na mayaṃ titthiyehi saddhiṃ uposathaṃ karomā”ti āhaṃsu. Atha amacco therāsanato paṭṭhāya asinā sīsāni pātetuṃ āraddho.

The sectarians, with their gain and honor diminished and not obtaining even food and clothing, desiring gain and honor, went forth in the Dispensation and expounded their own views, saying, “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya.” Even those not obtaining the going forth shaved their own heads, donned ochre robes, and, wandering about in the monasteries, entered into the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the formal acts of the Saṅgha, and the formal acts of the group. The monks did not perform the Uposatha with them. Then the Elder Moggaliputtatissa thought: “Now this dispute has arisen, and it will soon become severe. It is not possible to settle it while living among them.” Desiring to dwell in comfort, he entrusted his group of monks to the Elder Mahinda and went to Ahogaṅga Mountain. Those sectarians, though being restrained by the community of monks according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s Dispensation, were not established in the practice that accords with the Dhamma and Vinaya, and they caused various kinds of tumors, stains, and thorns to arise in the Dispensation. Some tended the fire, some tormented themselves with the fivefold heat, some revolved following the sun, and some upheld their views, declaring, “We will destroy your Dhamma and Vinaya.” At that time, the community of monks did not perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā with them. In the Asokārāma, for seven years, the Uposatha was interrupted. They informed the king of this matter. The king ordered a minister: “Go to the monastery, settle the dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.” The minister, not daring to question the king back, approached other ministers and said: “The king has sent me, saying, ‘Go to the monastery, settle the dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.’ How then is the dispute to be settled?” They replied: “We think thus: ‘Just as those who pacify the border regions kill robbers, even so the king must wish to kill those who do not perform the Uposatha.’” Then that minister went to the monastery, assembled the community of monks, and said: “I have been sent by the king to have the Uposatha performed. Now, venerable sirs, perform the Uposatha.” The monks replied: “We do not perform the Uposatha with the sectarians.” Then the minister, starting from the seat of the elders, began to cause their heads to fall with a sword.

Addasā [M 1.0041] kho tissatthero taṃ amaccaṃ tathā vippaṭipannaṃ. Tissatthero nāma na yo vā so vā, rañño ekamātiko bhātā tissakumāro nāma, taṃ kira rājā pattābhiseko oparajje ṭhapesi. So ekadivasaṃ vanacāraṃ gato addasa mahantaṃ migasaṅghaṃ cittakīḷāya kīḷantaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – “ime tāva tiṇabhakkhā migā evaṃ kīḷanti, ime pana samaṇā [V 1.0039] rājakule paṇītāni bhojanāni bhuñjitvā mudukāsu seyyāsu sayamānā kiṃ nāma kīḷitaṃ na kīḷissantī”ti! So tato āgantvā imaṃ attano vitakkaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “aṭṭhāne kukkuccāyitaṃ kumārena! Handa, naṃ evaṃ saññāpessāmī”ti ekadivasaṃ kenaci kāraṇena kuddho viya hutvā “ehi sattadivasena rajjaṃ sampaṭiccha, tato taṃ ghātessāmī”ti maraṇabhayena tajjetvā tamatthaṃ saññāpesi. So kira kumāro “sattame maṃ divase māressatī”ti na cittarūpaṃ nhāyi, na bhuñji, na supi, ativiya lūkhasarīro ahosi. Tato naṃ rājā pucchi – “kissa tvaṃ evarūpo jāto”ti? “Maraṇabhayena, devā”ti. “Are, tvaṃ nāma paricchinnamaraṇaṃ sampassamāno [P 1.0055] vissattho na kīḷasi? Bhikkhū assāsapassāsanibaddhaṃ maraṇaṃ pekkhamānā kathaṃ kīḷissantī”ti! Tato pabhuti kumāro sāsane pasīdi.

The Elder Tissa saw that minister behaving perversely in that way. This Elder Tissa was no ordinary person; he was the king’s maternal brother, Prince Tissa, whom, it is said, the king, upon his consecration, had appointed as viceroy. One day, while wandering in the forest, he saw a large herd of deer playing joyfully. Seeing this, it occurred to him: “If these deer, who feed on grass, play in this way, then what kind of play will these ascetics not engage in, after eating fine foods in the royal household and sleeping on soft beds?” Returning from there, he reported this thought of his to the king. The king thought: “The prince has become worried over an inappropriate matter! Well now, I shall make him understand in this way.” One day, pretending to be angry for some reason, he threatened him with the fear of death, saying, “Come, accept the kingdom for seven days, after which I will have you killed!” and thus made him understand the matter. It is said that the prince, thinking, “On the seventh day, he will kill me,” did not bathe to his heart’s content, did not eat, did not sleep, and his body became extremely gaunt. Then the king asked him: “Why have you become like this?” “Out of fear of death, Your Majesty.” “You there! Seeing a definite death, you do not play freely? How then can the bhikkhus play, who are contemplating a death that is tied to every in-breath and out-breath?” From that time on, the prince gained faith in the Dispensation.

So puna ekadivasaṃ migavaṃ nikkhamitvā araññe anuvicaramāno addasa yonakamahādhammarakkhitattheraṃ aññatarena hatthināgena sālasākhaṃ gahetvā bījiyamānaṃ nisinnaṃ. Disvā pāmojjajāto cintesi – “kadā nu kho ahampi ayaṃ mahāthero viya pabbajeyyaṃ! Siyā nu kho so divaso”ti. Thero tassāsayaṃ viditvā tassa passantasseva ākāse uppatitvā asokārāme pokkharaṇiyā udakatale ṭhatvā cīvarañca uttarāsaṅgañca ākāse laggetvā nhāyituṃ āraddho.

Again, on another day, having gone out on a hunt and while wandering in the forest, he saw the Elder Yonaka Mahādhammarakkhita seated, being fanned with a sāla branch by a certain great elephant. Seeing this, with joy arisen, he thought: “When, indeed, will I too go forth like this great elder! Might that day come?” The Elder, knowing his intention, while the prince was still watching, rose into the sky, and having stood on the surface of the water in the pond at the Asoka Monastery, he hung his lower and upper robes in the air and began to bathe.

Kumāro therassānubhāvaṃ disvā ativiya pasanno “ajjeva pabbajissāmī”ti nivattitvā rañño ārocesi – “pabbajissāmahaṃ, devā”ti. Rājā anekappakāraṃ yācitvāpi taṃ nivattetuṃ asakkonto asokārāmagamanīyamaggaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā kumāraṃ chaṇavesaṃ gāhāpetvā alaṅkatāya senāya parivārāpetvā vihāraṃ nesi. “Yuvarājā kira pabbajissatī”ti sutvā bahū bhikkhū pattacīvarāni paṭiyādesuṃ. Kumāro padhānagharaṃ [M 1.0042] gantvā mahādhammarakkhitattherasseva santike pabbaji saddhiṃ purisasatasahassena. Kumārassa pana anupabbajitānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo natthi. Kumāro rañño catuvassābhisekakāle pabbajito. Athaññopi rañño bhāgineyyo saṅghamittāya sāmiko aggibrahmā nāma kumāro atthi. Saṅghamittā taṃ paṭicca ekameva puttaṃ vijāyi. Sopi [P 1.0056] “yuvarājā pabbajito”ti sutvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “ahampi, deva, pabbajissāmī”ti yāci. “Pabbaja, tātā”ti ca raññā anuññāto taṃdivasameva pabbaji.

The prince, seeing the Elder’s power, became exceedingly faithful and, turning back, announced to the king: “I will go forth this very day, Your Majesty.” The king, though entreating him in many ways, was unable to dissuade him. He had the road to the Asoka Monastery decorated, had the prince dressed in festive attire, had him surrounded by an adorned army, and brought him to the monastery. Hearing, “It is said the crown prince will go forth,” many bhikkhus prepared their bowls and robes. The prince went to the meditation hall and went forth in the presence of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita himself, together with one hundred thousand men. There is no count of those who went forth following the prince. The prince went forth at the time of the king’s fourth-year consecration. Now, there was also another prince, the king’s nephew named Aggibrahmā, who was the husband of Saṅghamittā. On account of him, Saṅghamittā gave birth to only one son. He too, hearing, “The crown prince has gone forth,” approached the king and requested: “I too, Your Majesty, will go forth.” Having been permitted by the king with the words, “Go forth, my dear,” he went forth that very same day.

Evaṃ [V 1.0040] anupabbajito, uḷāravibhavena khattiyajanena;

Rañño kaniṭṭhabhātā, tissattheroti viññeyyo.

Thus, the king's younger brother, followed into homelessness by the noble people of great splendor, should be known as the Elder Tissa.

So taṃ amaccaṃ tathā vippaṭipannaṃ disvā cintesi – “na rājā there mārāpetuṃ pahiṇeyya; addhā imassevetaṃ amaccassa duggahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti gantvā sayaṃ tassa āsanne āsane nisīdi. So theraṃ sañjānitvā satthaṃ nipātetuṃ avisahanto gantvā rañño ārocesi – “ahaṃ, deva, uposathaṃ kātuṃ anicchantānaṃ ettakānaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ sīsāni pātesiṃ; atha ayyassa tissattherassa paṭipāṭi sampattā, kinti karomī”ti? Rājā sutvāva – “are! Kiṃ pana, tvaṃ, mayā bhikkhū ghātetuṃ pesito”ti tāvadeva sarīre uppannadāho hutvā vihāraṃ gantvā there bhikkhū pucchi – “ayaṃ, bhante, amacco mayā anāṇattova evaṃ akāsi, kassa nu kho iminā pāpena bhavitabba”nti? Ekacce therā, “ayaṃ tava vacanena akāsi, tuyhetaṃ pāpa”nti āhaṃsu. Ekacce “ubhinnampi vo etaṃ pāpa”nti āhaṃsu. Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ pana te, mahārāja, atthi cittaṃ ‘ayaṃ gantvā bhikkhū ghātetū’”ti? “Natthi, bhante, kusalādhippāyo ahaṃ pesesiṃ – ‘samaggo bhikkhusaṅgho uposathaṃ karotū’”ti. “Sace tvaṃ kusalādhippāyo, natthi tuyhaṃ pāpaṃ, amaccassevetaṃ pāpa”nti. Rājā dveḷhakajāto āha – “atthi nu kho, bhante, koci bhikkhu mametaṃ dveḷhakaṃ chinditvā sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ samattho”ti? “Atthi, mahārāja, moggaliputtatissatthero nāma, so [P 1.0057] te imaṃ dveḷhakaṃ chinditvā sāsanaṃ paggaṇhituṃ samattho”ti. Rājā tadaheva cattāro dhammakathike ekekabhikkhusahassaparivāre, cattāro ca amacce ekekapurisasahassaparivāre “theraṃ gaṇhitvā āgacchathā”ti pesesi. Te gantvā “rājā pakkosatī”ti āhaṃsu. Thero nāgacchi[M 1.0043]. Dutiyampi kho rājā aṭṭha dhammakathike, aṭṭha ca amacce sahassasahassaparivāreyeva pesesi – “‘rājā, bhante, pakkosatī’ti vatvā gaṇhitvāva āgacchathā”ti. Te tatheva āhaṃsu. Dutiyampi thero nāgacchi. Rājā there pucchi – “ahaṃ, bhante, dvikkhattuṃ pahiṇiṃ; kasmā thero nāgacchatī”ti? “‘Rājā pakkosatī’ti vuttattā, mahārāja, nāgacchati. Evaṃ pana vutte āgaccheyya ‘sāsanaṃ, bhante, osīdati, amhākaṃ sāsanaṃ paggahatthāya sahāyakā hothā’”ti. Atha rājā tathā vatvā soḷasa dhammakathike, soḷasa ca amacce sahassasahassaparivāre pesesi. Bhikkhū ca paṭipucchi – “mahallako nu kho, bhante, thero daharo nu kho”ti? “Mahallako, mahārājā”ti. “Vayhaṃ vā sivikaṃ vā abhiruhissati, bhante”ti? “Nābhiruhissati, mahārājā”ti. “Kuhiṃ, bhante, thero vasatī”ti? “Upari gaṅgāya, mahārājā”ti. Rājā āha – “tena hi, bhaṇe, nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ bandhitvā [V 1.0041] tattheva theraṃ nisīdāpetvā dvīsupi tīresu ārakkhaṃ saṃvidhāya theraṃ ānethā”ti. Bhikkhū ca amaccā ca therassa santikaṃ gantvā rañño sāsanaṃ ārocesuṃ.

That Elder, seeing that minister acting perversely in that manner, thought: “The king would not have sent someone to have the Elders killed; surely this will be a misdeed of this very minister.” Having gone, he himself sat on a seat near him. That minister, recognizing the Elder and not daring to bring the weapon down, went and reported to the king: “Your Majesty, I have caused the heads of so many bhikkhus who were unwilling to perform the Uposatha to fall. Then, the turn of the noble Elder Tissa arrived. What am I to do?” The king, as soon as he heard, said: “You there! Were you sent by me to kill the bhikkhus?” At that very moment, with a burning sensation having arisen in his body, he went to the monastery and asked the Elder bhikkhus: “Venerable sirs, this minister did so, though unordered by me. To whom, indeed, should this evil deed belong?” Some Elders said: “This one acted on your word; this evil is yours.” Some said: “This evil belongs to both of you.” Some said thus: “But, great king, did you have the thought, ‘Let this one go and kill the bhikkhus’?” “No, venerable sirs. I, having a wholesome intention, sent him, thinking, ‘Let the united Saṅgha of bhikkhus perform the Uposatha.’” “If you had a wholesome intention, there is no evil for you. This evil belongs to the minister alone.” The king, having become uncertain, said: “Is there, venerable sirs, any bhikkhu capable of cutting off this uncertainty of mine and upholding the Dispensation?” “There is, great king, the Elder named Moggaliputta Tissa. He is capable of cutting off this uncertainty of yours and upholding the Dispensation.” On that very day, the king sent four Dhamma-preachers, each with a retinue of a thousand bhikkhus, and four ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand men, saying, “Having fetched the Elder, come back.” They went and said, “The king summons you.” The Elder did not come. A second time, the king sent eight Dhamma-preachers and eight ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand, saying, “Having said, ‘The king summons you, venerable sir,’ fetch him and come back.” They spoke in that very way. A second time, the Elder did not come. The king asked the Elders: “Venerable sirs, I sent them twice; why does the Elder not come?” “Great king, he does not come because it was said, ‘The king summons you.’ But if it were said thus, he would come: ‘Venerable sir, the Dispensation is declining; be our helpers for the purpose of upholding the Dispensation.’” Then the king, having spoken thus, sent sixteen Dhamma-preachers and sixteen ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand. And he asked the bhikkhus in turn: “Venerable sirs, is the Elder old or is he young?” “He is old, great king.” “Will he ascend a covered cart or a palanquin, venerable sirs?” “He will not ascend one, great king.” “Where, venerable sirs, does the Elder reside?” “Upstream on the Ganges, great king.” The king said: “Well then, my men, having bound together a raft of boats and having seated the Elder right there, and having arranged a guard on both banks, bring the Elder.” The bhikkhus and the ministers went to the Elder and announced the king’s message.

Thero sutvā “yaṃ kho ahaṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya sāsanaṃ paggaṇhissāmīti pabbajitomhi. Ayaṃ dāni me so kālo anuppatto”ti cammakhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhitvāva uṭṭhahi. Atha “thero [P 1.0058] sve pāṭaliputtaṃ sampāpuṇissatī”ti rattibhāge rājā supinaṃ addasa. Evarūpo supino ahosi – “sabbaseto hatthināgo āgantvā rājānaṃ sīsato paṭṭhāya parāmasitvā dakkhiṇahatthe aggahesī”ti. Punadivase rājā supinajjhāyake pucchi – “mayā evarūpo supino diṭṭho, kiṃ me bhavissatī”ti? Eko taṃ, “mahārāja, samaṇanāgo dakkhiṇahatthe gaṇhissatī”ti. Atha rājā tāvadeva “thero āgato”ti sutvā gaṅgātīraṃ gantvā nadiṃ otaritvā abbhuggacchanto jāṇumatte udake theraṃ sampāpuṇitvā therassa nāvāto otarantassa hatthaṃ adāsi. Thero rājānaṃ dakkhiṇahatthe aggahesi. Taṃ disvā asiggāhā “therassa sīsaṃ pātessāmā”ti kosato asiṃ abbāhiṃsu. Kasmā? Etaṃ kira cārittaṃ rājakulesu – “yo rājānaṃ hatthe gaṇhati tassa asinā sīsaṃ pātetabba”nti. Rājā chāyaṃyeva disvā āha – “pubbepi ahaṃ bhikkhūsu viraddhakāraṇā assādaṃ na vindāmi, mā kho there virajjhitthā”ti. Thero pana kasmā rājānaṃ hatthe [M 1.0044] aggahesīti? Yasmā raññā pañhaṃ pucchanatthāya pakkosāpito tasmā “antevāsiko me aya”nti aggahesi.

The Elder, having heard, thought: “Indeed, I went forth thinking, ‘I shall uphold the Dispensation starting from its root.’ Now that time has arrived for me.” And taking only a piece of leather, he arose. Then, during the night, when it was said, “The Elder will arrive at Pāṭaliputta tomorrow,” the king saw a dream. The dream was of this nature: “A completely white majestic elephant, having come and stroked the king starting from the head, took hold of him by the right hand.” On the next day, the king asked the dream-interpreters: “A dream of this nature was seen by me. What will become of me?” One said: “Great king, a majestic ascetic will take hold of you by the right hand.” Then the king, as soon as he heard, “The Elder has arrived,” went to the bank of the Ganges, descended into the river, and while going to meet him, reached the Elder in knee-deep water and gave his hand to the Elder as he was descending from the raft of boats. The Elder took hold of the king by the right hand. Seeing that, the sword-bearers, thinking, “We shall cause the Elder’s head to fall,” drew their swords from their scabbards. Why? It is said to be the custom in royal families: “Of him who takes the king by the hand, his head must be made to fall by the sword.” The king, seeing just the shadow, said: “Previously also, because of the fault of having offended the bhikkhus, I find no pleasure. Do not offend the Elder.” But why did the Elder take the king by the hand? Because he had been caused to be summoned by the king for the purpose of asking a question, he took hold of his hand, thinking, “This one is my pupil.”

Rājā theraṃ attano uyyānaṃ netvā bāhirato tikkhattuṃ parivārāpetvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā sayameva therassa pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā therassa santike nisīditvā “paṭibalo nu kho thero mama kaṅkhaṃ chinditvā uppannaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametvā sāsanaṃ paggaṇhitu”nti vīmaṃsanatthāya “ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ daṭṭhukāmo”ti āha. “Kataraṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ daṭṭhukāmosi, mahārājā”ti? “Pathavīkampanaṃ, bhante”ti. “Sakalapathavīkampanaṃ daṭṭhukāmosi, mahārāja, padesapathavīkampana”nti? “Kataraṃ panettha, bhante, dukkara”nti? “Kiṃ nu kho, mahārāja, kaṃsapātiyā udakapuṇṇāya sabbaṃ udakaṃ kampetuṃ dukkaraṃ; udāhu upaḍḍha”nti? “Upaḍḍhaṃ, bhante”ti. “Evameva kho, mahārāja, padesapathavīkampanaṃ dukkara”nti. “Tena hi, bhante, padesapathavīkampanaṃ [P 1.0059] passissāmī”ti. “Tena hi, mahārāja, samantato yojane puratthimāya disāya ekena cakkena sīmaṃ akkamitvā ratho tiṭṭhatu; dakkhiṇāya disāya dvīhi pādehi sīmaṃ akkamitvā asso tiṭṭhatu; pacchimāya disāya ekena pādena sīmaṃ akkamitvā puriso tiṭṭhatu; uttarāya disāya upaḍḍhabhāgena sīmaṃ akkamitvā ekā udakapāti [V 1.0042] tiṭṭhatū”ti. Rājā tathā kārāpesi. Thero abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya “rājā passatū”ti yojanappamāṇapathavīcalanaṃ adhiṭṭhahi. Puratthimāya disāya rathassa antosīmāya ṭhito pādova cali, itaro na cali. Evaṃ dakkhiṇapacchimadisāsu assapurisānaṃ antosīmāya ṭhitapādāyeva caliṃsu, upaḍḍhupaḍḍhaṃ sarīrañca. Uttaradisāya udakapātiyāpi antosīmāya ṭhitaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgagatameva udakaṃ cali, avasesaṃ niccalamahosīti. Rājā taṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā “sakkhati dāni thero sāsanaṃ paggaṇhitu”nti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā attano kukkuccaṃ pucchi – “ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ amaccaṃ ‘vihāraṃ gantvā adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametvā uposathaṃ kārāpehī’ti pahiṇiṃ, so vihāraṃ gantvā ettake bhikkhū jīvitā voropesi, etaṃ pāpaṃ kassa hotī”ti?

The king led the Elder to his own park, had it surrounded three times from the outside and guards stationed, and personally washed the Elder’s feet and anointed them with oil. Having sat down near the Elder, for the purpose of investigating, “Is the Elder capable of dispelling my doubt, settling the arisen dispute, and upholding the Dispensation?” he said, “Venerable sir, I wish to see a miracle.” “What miracle do you wish to see, great king?” “An earthquake, venerable sir.” “Do you wish to see an earthquake of the entire earth, great king, or a localized earthquake?” “Which of these is more difficult to perform, venerable sir?” “What do you think, great king, is it more difficult to shake all the water in a bronze bowl full of water, or half of it?” “Half of it, venerable sir.” “In the same way, great king, a localized earthquake is more difficult to perform.” “In that case, venerable sir, I will see a localized earthquake.” “In that case, great king, within a yojana all around, let a chariot stand in the eastern direction with one wheel crossing the boundary; let a horse stand in the southern direction with two feet crossing the boundary; let a man stand in the western direction with one foot crossing the boundary; and let a water pot stand in the northern direction with half of it crossing the boundary.” The king had it done so. The Elder entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for the higher knowledges, and having emerged from it, he resolved, “Let the king see,” and willed the earth to shake for the extent of a yojana. In the eastern direction, of the chariot, only the wheel that stood within the boundary shook; the other did not. Similarly, in the southern and western directions, of the horse and the man, only the feet standing within the boundary shook, and half of their bodies. In the northern direction, of the water pot, only the water in the half that was within the boundary shook; the remainder was still. Seeing this miracle, the king came to the conclusion, “Now the Elder is able to uphold the Dispensation,” and asked about his own scruple: “Venerable sir, I sent a minister, saying, ‘Go to the monastery, settle the dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.’ He went to the monastery and deprived so many monks of life. Whose evil deed is this?”

“Kiṃ pana te, mahārāja, atthi cittaṃ ‘ayaṃ vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhū ghātetū’”ti? “Natthi, bhante”ti. “Sace te, mahārāja, natthi evarūpaṃ cittaṃ, natthi tuyhaṃ pāpa”nti. Atha thero rājānaṃ etamatthaṃ iminā suttena saññāpesi [M 1.0045] – “cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi. Cetayitvā kammaṃ karoti – kāyena vācāya manasā”ti (a. ni. 6.63).

“But did you, great king, have the thought, ‘Let this man go to the monastery and kill the monks’?” “No, venerable sir.” “If, great king, you had no such thought, there is no evil deed for you.” Then the Elder made the king understand this matter with this sutta: “Volition, O monks, I declare is kamma. Having willed, one performs kamma by way of body, speech, or mind.”

Tamevatthaṃ [P 1.0060] paridīpetuṃ tittirajātakaṃ (jā. 1.4.75) āhari – “atīte, mahārāja, dīpakatittiro tāpasaṃ pucchi –

To illuminate this very point, he recounted the Tittira Jātaka: “In the past, great king, the partridge Dīpaka asked an ascetic:

‘Ñātako no nisinnoti, bahu āgacchatī jano;

Paṭicca kammaṃ phusati, tasmiṃ me saṅkate mano’ti.

‘Thinking, “Our kinsman is sitting there,” many folk arrive. On my account, a deed is committed; about this, my mind is in doubt.’

Tāpaso āha – ‘atthi pana te cittaṃ mama saddena ca rūpadassanena ca āgantvā ete pakkhino bajjhantu vā haññantu vā’ti? ‘Natthi, bhante’ti tittiro āha. Tato naṃ tāpaso saññāpesi – ‘sace te natthi cittaṃ, natthi pāpaṃ; cetayantameva hi pāpaṃ phusati, nācetayantaṃ.

The ascetic said: ‘But do you have the thought, “By my sound and by the sight of my form, let these birds who have come be bound or be killed”?’ ‘No, venerable sir,’ said the partridge. Then the ascetic made him understand: ‘If you have no such thought, there is no evil deed; for an evil deed touches only one who has volition, not one who is without volition.

‘Na paṭicca kammaṃ phusati, mano ce nappadussati;

Appossukkassa bhadrassa, na pāpamupalimpatī’”ti.

‘A deed done on your account does not touch you, if your mind is not corrupted. For the virtuous one who does not strive in evil, evil does not cling.’”

Evaṃ thero rājānaṃ saññāpetvā tattheva rājuyyāne satta divasāni vasanto rājānaṃ samayaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Rājā sattame divase asokārāme bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā sāṇipākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā [V 1.0043] sāṇipākārantare nisinno ekaladdhike ekaladdhike bhikkhū ekato ekato kārāpetvā ekamekaṃ bhikkhusamūhaṃ pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “kiṃvādī sammāsambuddho”ti? Tatosassatavādino “sassatavādī”ti āhaṃsu. Ekaccasassatikā…pe… antānantikā… amarāvikkhepikā… adhiccasamuppannikā… saññīvādā… asaññīvādā… nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā [P 1.0061]… ucchedavādā… diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā “diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā paṭhamameva samayassa uggahitattā “nayime bhikkhū, aññatitthiyā ime”ti ñatvā tesaṃ setakāni vatthāni datvā uppabbājesi. Te sabbepi saṭṭhisahassā ahesuṃ.

Thus, having made the king understand, the Elder, while dwelling in that very royal park for seven days, had the king learn the doctrine. On the seventh day, the king had the community of monks assembled in the Asokārāma, had a cloth screen set up all around, and, sitting within the cloth screen enclosure, he had the monks of each particular view gathered into separate groups. Having summoned each group of monks one by one, he asked, “What is the doctrine of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One?” Then the eternalists said, “He is an eternalist.” The partial-eternalists… the finite-and-infinite theorists… the eel-wrigglers… the chance-originationists… the perceptionists… the non-perceptionists… the neither-perception-nor-non-perceptionists… the annihilationists… the theorists of Nibbāna-in-this-life said, “He is a theorist of Nibbāna-in-this-life.” Because the king had already learned the doctrine beforehand, he knew, “These are not monks, they are other sectarians.” Having given them white clothes, he had them disrobed. All of them numbered sixty thousand.

Athaññe bhikkhū pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “kiṃvādī, bhante, sammāsambuddho”ti? “Vibhajjavādī, mahārājā”ti. Evaṃ vutte rājā theraṃ pucchi – “vibhajjavādī, bhante, sammāsambuddho”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. Tato rājā “suddhaṃ dāni, bhante, sāsanaṃ; karotu bhikkhusaṅgho uposatha”nti ārakkhaṃ datvā nagaraṃ pāvisi.

Then he had other monks summoned and asked, “Venerable sirs, what is the doctrine of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One?” “He is an analyst, great king.” When this was said, the king asked the Elder, “Venerable sir, is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One an analyst?” “Yes, great king.” Then the king said, “Venerable sirs, the Dispensation is now pure; let the community of monks perform the Uposatha.” Having provided protection, he entered the city.

Samaggo [M 1.0046] saṅgho sannipatitvā uposathaṃ akāsi. Tasmiṃ sannipāte saṭṭhi bhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ. Tasmiṃ samāgame moggaliputtatissatthero parappavādaṃ maddamāno kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ abhāsi. Tato saṭṭhisatasahassasaṅkhyesu bhikkhūsu uccinitvā tipiṭakapariyattidharānaṃ pabhinnapaṭisambhidānaṃ tevijjādibhedānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sahassamekaṃ gahetvā yathā mahākassapatthero ca kākaṇḍakaputto yasatthero ca dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyiṃsu; evameva dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyanto sabbaṃ sāsanamalaṃ visodhetvā tatiyasaṅgītiṃ akāsi. Saṅgītipariyosāne anekappakāraṃ pathavī akampittha. Ayaṃ saṅgīti navahi māsehi niṭṭhitā. Yā loke –

The united Saṅgha, having assembled, performed the Uposatha. At that assembly, there were six million bhikkhus. In that gathering, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, while crushing the various views of others, expounded the Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa. Then, from among the bhikkhus numbering six million, having selected one thousand bhikkhus who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka scriptures, possessed of the distinguished analytical insights, and endowed with the distinctions of the threefold knowledge and so forth, just as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa, son of Kākaṇḍaka, had rehearsed the Dhamma and the Vinaya, even so, while rehearsing the Dhamma and the Vinaya and purifying all the defilements of the Sāsana, he held the Third Council. At the conclusion of the council, the earth shook in many ways. This council was completed in nine months. Which in the world—

Katā bhikkhusahassena, tasmā sahassikāti ca;

Purimā dve upādāya, tatiyāti ca vuccatīti.

Because it was held by a thousand bhikkhus, it is therefore also called the 'Sahassikā'; and taking into account the two previous councils, it is also called the 'Third'.

Ayaṃ tatiyasaṅgīti.

This is the Third Council.

Ettāvatā ca “kenābhata”nti etassa pañhassa vissajjanatthaṃ yaṃ avocumha – “jambudīpe tāva upālittheramādiṃ katvā ācariyaparamparāya [P 1.0062] yāva tatiyasaṅgīti tāva ābhataṃ. Tatrāyaṃ ācariyaparamparā –

And by this much, for the purpose of answering the question, 'By whom was it brought?', we have stated: 'In Jambudīpa, it was brought down through the succession of teachers, beginning with the Elder Upāli, up to the Third Council.' Therein, this is the succession of teachers:

“Upāli [V 1.0044] dāsako ceva, soṇako siggavo tathā;

Tisso moggaliputto ca, pañcete vijitāvino.

“Upāli, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, Siggava likewise, and Tissa Moggaliputta—these five were conquerors.

“Paramparāya vinayaṃ, dīpe jambusirivhaye;

Acchijjamānamānesuṃ, tatiyo yāva saṅgaho”ti.

“They maintained the Vinaya, unbroken in the lineage, on the island of Jambusirī, until the Third Council.”

Tassattho pakāsitova hoti.

The meaning of that has indeed been explained.

Tatiyasaṅgahato pana uddhaṃ imaṃ dīpaṃ mahindādīhi ābhataṃ. Mahindato uggahetvā kañci kālaṃ ariṭṭhattherādīhi ābhataṃ. Tato yāvajjatanā tesaṃyeva antevāsikaparamparabhūtāya ācariyaparamparāya ābhatanti veditabbaṃ. Yathāhu porāṇā –

However, after the Third Council, it was brought to this island by Mahinda and others. Having learned it from Mahinda, it was brought for some time by the Elder Ariṭṭha and others. From then until the present day, it should be understood that it has been brought by the succession of teachers which is the very lineage of pupils of those same elders. As the ancients have said:

“Tato mahindo iṭṭiyo, uttiyo sambalo tathā;

Bhaddanāmo ca paṇḍito.

“Then Mahinda, Iṭṭiya, Uttiya, Sambala likewise, and the wise one named Bhaddasāla.

“Ete nāgā mahāpaññā, jambudīpā idhāgatā;

Vinayaṃ te vācayiṃsu, piṭakaṃ tambapaṇṇiyā.

“These Nāgas of great wisdom came here from Jambudīpa; they caused the Vinaya Piṭaka to be recited in Tambapaṇṇi.

“Nikāye [M 1.0047] pañca vācesuṃ, satta ceva pakaraṇe;

Tato ariṭṭho medhāvī, tissadatto ca paṇḍito.

“They caused the five Nikāyas to be recited, and the seven treatises as well; then Ariṭṭha the intelligent, and Tissadatta the learned.

“Visārado kāḷasumano, thero ca dīghanāmako;

Dīghasumano ca paṇḍito.

“Kāḷasumana the confident, and the elder named Dīgha; and Dīghasumana the learned.

“Punadeva kāḷasumano, nāgatthero ca buddharakkhito;

Tissatthero ca medhāvī, devatthero ca paṇḍito.

“And again Kāḷasumana, the Elder Nāga, and Buddharakkhita; and the Elder Tissa the intelligent, and the Elder Deva the learned.

“Punadeva sumano medhāvī, vinaye ca visārado;

Bahussuto cūḷanāgo, gajova duppadhaṃsiyo.

“And again Sumana the intelligent, and confident in the Vinaya; Cūḷanāga of great learning, unassailable like an elephant.

“Dhammapālitanāmo [P 1.0063][V 1.0045] ca, rohaṇe sādhupūjito;

Tassa sisso mahāpañño, khemanāmo tipeṭako.

“And one named Dhammapālita, honored by the virtuous in Rohaṇa; his disciple of great wisdom, named Khema, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka.

“Dīpe tārakarājāva, paññāya atirocatha;

Upatisso ca medhāvī, phussadevo mahākathī.

“That elder shone exceedingly on the island with wisdom, like the king of stars; and Upatissa the intelligent, and Phussadeva the great preacher.

“Punadeva sumano medhāvī, pupphanāmo bahussuto;

Mahākathī mahāsivo, piṭake sabbattha kovido.

“And again Sumana the intelligent, Pupphanāma of great learning; Mahāsiva the great preacher, skilled in the entire Tipiṭaka.

“Punadeva upāli medhāvī, vinaye ca visārado;

Mahānāgo mahāpañño, saddhammavaṃsakovido.

“And again Upāli the intelligent and confident in the Vinaya; Mahānāga of great wisdom, skilled in the lineage of the good Dhamma.

“Punadeva abhayo medhāvī, piṭake sabbattha kovido;

Tissatthero ca medhāvī, vinaye ca visārado.

“And again Abhaya the intelligent, skilled in the entire Tipiṭaka; and the Elder Tissa the intelligent, and confident in the Vinaya.

“Tassa sisso mahāpañño, pupphanāmo bahussuto;

Sāsanaṃ anurakkhanto, jambudīpe patiṭṭhito.

“His disciple of great wisdom, named Puppha, of great learning; protecting the Sāsana, he was established in Jambudīpa.

“Cūḷābhayo ca medhāvī, vinaye ca visārado;

Tissatthero ca medhāvī, saddhammavaṃsakovido.

“And Cūḷābhaya the intelligent, and confident in the Vinaya; and the Elder Tissa the intelligent, skilled in the lineage of the good Dhamma.

“Cūḷadevo ca medhāvī, vinaye ca visārado;

Sivatthero ca medhāvī, vinaye sabbattha kovido.

“And Cūḷadeva the intelligent, and confident in the Vinaya; and the Elder Siva the intelligent, skilled in the entire Vinaya.

“Ete nāgā mahāpaññā, vinayaññū maggakovidā;

Vinayaṃ dīpe pakāsesuṃ, piṭakaṃ tambapaṇṇiyā”ti.

“These Nāgas of great wisdom, knowers of the Vinaya, skilled in the path; they made the Vinaya Piṭaka manifest on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.”

Tatrāyaṃ [M 1.0048] anupubbikathā – moggaliputtatissatthero kira imaṃ tatiyadhammasaṅgītiṃ katvā evaṃ cintesi – “kattha nu kho anāgate sāsanaṃ suppatiṭṭhitaṃ bhaveyyā”ti? Athassa upaparikkhato etadahosi – “paccantimesu kho janapadesu suppatiṭṭhitaṃ bhavissatī”ti. So tesaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [V 1.0046] bhāraṃ katvā te te bhikkhū tattha tattha pesesi. Majjhantikattheraṃ kasmīragandhāraraṭṭhaṃ pesesi – “tvaṃ etaṃ raṭṭhaṃ gantvā ettha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpehī”ti. Mahādevattheraṃ tatheva vatvā mahiṃsakamaṇḍalaṃ pesesi. Rakkhitattheraṃ vanavāsiṃ. Yonakadhammarakkhitattheraṃ [P 1.0064] aparantakaṃ. Mahādhammarakkhitattheraṃ mahāraṭṭhaṃ. Mahārakkhitattheraṃ yonakalokaṃ. Majjhimattheraṃ himavantadesabhāgaṃ. Soṇattherañca uttarattherañca suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ. Attano saddhivihārikaṃ mahindattheraṃ iṭṭiyattherena uttiyattherena sambalattherena bhaddasālattherena ca saddhiṃ tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ pesesi – “tumhe tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ gantvā ettha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpethā”ti. Sabbepi taṃ taṃ disābhāgaṃ gacchantā attapañcamā agamaṃsu “paccantimesu janapadesu pañcavaggo gaṇo alaṃ upasampadakammāyā”ti maññamānā.

Herein is the sequential account: It is said that the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, having held this Third Dhamma Council, thought thus: 'Where, indeed, in the future might the Sāsana be well established?' Then, as he was investigating, this occurred to him: 'It will be well established in the border regions.' Having assigned the responsibility to various bhikkhus, he sent those bhikkhus to those various places. He sent the Elder Majjhantika to the country of Kasmīra-Gandhāra, saying, 'Go to that country and establish the Sāsana there.' Having spoken in the same way, he sent the Elder Mahādeva to the Mahiṃsaka region. He sent the Elder Rakkhita to Vanavāsī. He sent the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita to Aparantaka. He sent the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita to Mahāraṭṭha. He sent the Elder Mahārakkhita to the Yonaka world. He sent the Elder Majjhima to the region of the Himavanta. He sent the Elder Soṇa and the Elder Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. He sent his own co-resident disciple, the Elder Mahinda, together with the Elder Iṭṭiya, the Elder Uttiya, the Elder Sambala, and the Elder Bhaddasāla, to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, saying, 'Go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Sāsana there.' All of them, while going to their respective regions, went as a group of five, thinking, 'In the border regions, a chapter of five is sufficient for the act of higher ordination.'

Tena kho pana samayena kasmīragandhāraraṭṭhe sassapākasamaye aravāḷo nāma nāgarājā karakavassaṃ nāma vassāpetvā sassaṃ harāpetvā mahāsamuddaṃ pāpeti. Majjhantikatthero pana pāṭaliputtato vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā himavati aravāḷadahassa upari otaritvā aravāḷadahapiṭṭhiyaṃ caṅkamatipi tiṭṭhatipi nisīdatipi seyyampi kappeti. Nāgamāṇavakā taṃ disvā aravāḷassa nāgarājassa ārocesuṃ – “mahārāja, eko chinnabhinnapaṭadharo bhaṇḍu kāsāvavasano amhākaṃ udakaṃ dūsetī”ti. Nāgarājā tāvadeva kodhābhibhūto nikkhamitvā theraṃ disvā makkhaṃ asahamāno antalikkhe anekāni bhiṃsanakāni nimmini. Tato tato bhusā vātā vāyanti, rukkhā chijjanti, pabbatakūṭāni patanti, meghā gajjanti, vijjulatā niccharanti, asaniyo phalanti, bhinnaṃ viya gaganatalaṃ udakaṃ paggharati. Bhayānakarūpā [P 1.0065] nāgakumārā sannipatanti. Sayampi dhūmāyati, pajjalati, paharaṇavuṭṭhiyo vissajjeti. “Ko ayaṃ muṇḍako chinnabhinnapaṭadharo”tiādīhi pharusavacanehi theraṃ santajjesi. “Etha gaṇhatha hanatha [M 1.0049] niddhamatha imaṃ samaṇa”nti nāgabalaṃ āṇāpesi. Thero sabbaṃ taṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ attano iddhibalena paṭibāhitvā nāgarājānaṃ āha –

At that time, in the land of Kasmīra and Gandhāra, during the crop-ripening season, a nāga king named Aravāḷa caused a hailstorm to fall, had the crops carried away, and sent them into the great ocean. The Elder Majjhantika, however, having risen into the sky from Pāṭaliputta, descended upon the Aravāḷa Lake in the Himalayas and walked, stood, sat, and lay down on the surface of the Aravāḷa Lake. The young nāgas, seeing him, reported to the nāga king Aravāḷa: 'Great king, a certain shaven-headed man wearing torn and tattered saffron robes is spoiling our water!' The nāga king, immediately overcome with anger, came forth and, upon seeing the Elder, unable to endure the disparagement, created many terrifying apparitions in the sky. From all directions, fierce winds blew, trees were broken, mountain peaks fell, clouds thundered, flashes of lightning issued forth, and thunderbolts split. Water poured down as if the expanse of the sky were rent asunder. Nāga youths of terrifying appearance assembled. He himself emitted smoke, blazed with fire, and unleashed a rain of weapons. He threatened the Elder with harsh words, such as: 'Who is this shaveling wearing torn and tattered robes?' He commanded the nāga army, saying: 'Come, seize this ascetic, strike him, expel him!' The Elder, having warded off all those terrifying things by his own psychic power, said to the nāga king:

“Sadevakopi ce loko, āgantvā tāsayeyya maṃ;

Na me paṭibalo assa, janetuṃ bhayabheravaṃ.

Even if the world with its devas were to come and threaten me, it would not be capable of generating fear and terror in me.

“Sacepi tvaṃ mahiṃ sabbaṃ, sasamuddaṃ sapabbataṃ;

Ukkhipitvā mahānāga, khipeyyāsi mamūpari.

Even if you, O great nāga, were to lift up the entire earth, with its oceans and mountains, and hurl it upon me,

“Neva [V 1.0047] me sakkuṇeyyāsi, janetuṃ bhayabheravaṃ;

Aññadatthu tavevassa, vighāto uragādhipā”ti.

you would still not be able to produce fear or dread in me; rather, O lord of serpents, it would only be your own vexation.

Evaṃ vutte nāgarājā vihatānubhāvo nipphalavāyāmo dukkhī dummano ahosi. Taṃ thero taṅkhaṇānurūpāya dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṃsetvā tīsu saraṇesu pañcasu ca sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi saddhiṃ caturāsītiyā nāgasahassehi. Aññepi bahū himavantavāsino yakkhā ca gandhabbā ca kumbhaṇḍā ca therassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Pañcakopi yakkho saddhiṃ bhariyāya yakkhiniyā pañcahi ca puttasatehi paṭhame phale patiṭṭhito. Athāyasmā majjhantikatthero sabbepi nāgayakkharakkhase āmantetvā evamāha –

When this was said, the nāga king, his power destroyed and his efforts fruitless, became sorrowful and dejected. Then the Elder, instructing, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening him with a Dhamma talk appropriate to the occasion, established him in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, together with eighty-four thousand nāgas. Many other beings dwelling in the Himalayas—yakkhas, gandhabbas, and kumbhaṇḍas—also heard the Elder's Dhamma talk and were established in the Refuges and the Precepts. The yakkha Pañcaka, together with his yakkhinī wife and their five hundred sons, was established in the first fruit. Then the venerable Majjhantikatthera, addressing all the nāgas, yakkhas, and rakkhasas, said:

“Mā dāni kodhaṃ janayittha, ito uddhaṃ yathā pure;

Sassaghātañca mā kattha, sukhakāmā hi pāṇino;

Karotha mettaṃ sattesu, vasantu manujā sukha”nti.

Henceforth, do not generate anger as you did before. Do not destroy the crops, for beings desire happiness. Cultivate loving-kindness towards beings; may human beings dwell in happiness.

Te [P 1.0066] sabbepi “sādhu bhante”ti therassa paṭissuṇitvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Taṃdivasameva ca nāgarājassa pūjāsamayo hoti. Atha nāgarājā attano ratanamayaṃ pallaṅkaṃ āharāpetvā therassa paññapesi. Nisīdi thero pallaṅke. Nāgarājāpi theraṃ bījayamāno samīpe aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe kasmīragandhāraraṭṭhavāsino āgantvā theraṃ disvā “amhākaṃ nāgarājatopi thero mahiddhikataro”ti therameva vanditvā nisinnā. Thero tesaṃ āsīvisopamasuttaṃ kathesi[M 1.0050]. Suttapariyosāne asītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi, kulasatasahassaṃ pabbaji. Tato pabhuti ca kasmīragandhārā yāvajjatanā kāsāvapajjotā isivātapaṭivātā eva.

All of them replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and practiced according to his instructions. That very day was the time for the nāga king's festival. Then the nāga king had his jeweled couch brought and prepared for the Elder. The Elder sat upon the couch. The nāga king stood nearby, fanning the Elder. At that moment, inhabitants from the regions of Kasmīra and Gandhāra arrived and, seeing the Elder, thought, "This Elder is even more powerful than our nāga king," and, after paying homage to him, sat down. The Elder taught them the Āsīvisopama Sutta. At the end of the discourse, eighty thousand living beings attained the penetration of the Dhamma, and one hundred thousand families went forth. From that time onward, the regions of Kasmīra and Gandhāra are, up to this day, radiant with the saffron robes and pervaded by the winds of the sages.

Gantvā kasmīragandhāraṃ, isi majjhantiko tadā;

Duṭṭhaṃ nāgaṃ pasādetvā, mocesi bandhanā bahūti.

Having gone to Kasmīra and Gandhāra, the sage Majjhantika then, having inspired faith in the malevolent nāga, freed many from bondage.

Mahādevattheropi mahiṃsakamaṇḍalaṃ gantvā devadūtasuttaṃ kathesi. Suttapariyosāne cattālīsa pāṇasahassāni dhammacakkhuṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, cattālīsaṃyeva pāṇasahassāni pabbajiṃsu.

The Elder Mahādeva also went to the Mahiṃsaka region and taught the Devadūta Sutta. At the end of the sutta, forty thousand beings attained the Dhamma-eye, and forty thousand went forth.

Gantvāna [V 1.0048] raṭṭhaṃ mahiṃsaṃ, mahādevo mahiddhiko;

Codetvā devadūtehi, mocesi bandhanā bahūti.

Having gone to the Mahiṃsa country, the greatly powerful Mahādeva, having exhorted them with the divine messengers, freed many from bondage.

Rakkhitatthero pana vanavāsiṃ gantvā ākāse ṭhatvā anamataggapariyāyakathāya vanavāsike pasādesi. Kathāpariyosāne panassa saṭṭhisahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Sattatisahassamattā [P 1.0067] pabbajiṃsu, pañcavihārasatāni patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Evaṃ so tattha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

The Elder Rakkhita, for his part, went to Vanavāsī and, standing in the sky, inspired the inhabitants of Vanavāsī with a discourse on the Anamatagga Pariyāya. At the end of his discourse, sixty thousand attained the penetration of the Dhamma. Seventy thousand in number went forth, and five hundred monasteries were established. Thus he established the Dispensation there.

Gantvāna rakkhitatthero, vanavāsiṃ mahiddhiko;

Antalikkhe ṭhito tattha, desesi anamataggiyanti.

Having gone to Vanavāsī, the greatly powerful Elder Rakkhita, standing in the sky there, taught the Anamataggiya.

Yonakadhammarakkhitattheropi aparantakaṃ gantvā aggikkhandhopamasuttantakathāya aparantake pasādetvā sattati pāṇasahassāni dhammāmataṃ pāyesi. Khattiyakulato eva purisasahassāni pabbajiṃsu, samadhikāni ca cha itthisahassāni. Evaṃ so tattha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

The Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita also went to Aparantaka and, having inspired the people of Aparantaka with a discourse on the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta, he caused seventy thousand living beings to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. A thousand men from the khattiya caste went forth, and more than six thousand women. Thus, he established the Dispensation there.

Aparantaṃ vigāhitvā, yonako dhammarakkhito;

Aggikkhandhopamenettha, pasādesi jane bahūti.

Having entered Aparantaka, the Yona Dhammarakkhita, with the Aggikkhandhopama, inspired faith in many people there.

Mahādhammarakkhitatthero pana mahāraṭṭhaṃ gantvā mahānāradakassapajātakakathāya mahāraṭṭhake pasādetvā caturāsīti pāṇasahassāni maggaphalesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Terasasahassāni pabbajiṃsu. Evaṃ so tattha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, for his part, went to Mahāraṭṭha and, by the discourse on the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka, having inspired faith in the people of Mahāraṭṭha, established eighty-four thousand beings in the paths and fruits. Thirteen thousand went forth. Thus, he established the Dispensation there.

Mahāraṭṭhaṃ isi gantvā, so mahādhammarakkhito;

Jātakaṃ kathayitvāna, pasādesi mahājananti.

Having gone to Mahāraṭṭha, that noble arahant Mahādhammarakkhita, having preached the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka, inspired faith in the great multitude.

Mahārakkhitattheropi [M 1.0051] yonakaraṭṭhaṃ gantvā kāḷakārāmasuttantakathāya yonakalokaṃ pasādetvā sattatisahassādhikassa pāṇasatasahassassa maggaphalālaṅkāraṃ adāsi. Santike cassa dasasahassāni pabbajiṃsu. Evaṃ sopi tattha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

The Elder Mahārakkhita also went to the Yona country and, by the discourse on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, inspired faith in the Yona people. He bestowed upon one hundred and seventy thousand beings the adornment of the path and its fruit. And in his presence, ten thousand went forth. Thus, he also established the Dispensation there.

Yonaraṭṭhaṃ tadā gantvā, so mahārakkhito isi;

Kāḷakārāmasuttena te pasādesi yonaketi.

Going then to the Yona country, that arahant Mahārakkhita, with the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, inspired faith in those Yonakas.

Majjhimatthero [P 1.0068][V 1.0049] pana kassapagottattherena aḷakadevattherena dundubhissarattherena mahādevattherena ca saddhiṃ himavantadesabhāgaṃ gantvā dhammacakkappavattanasuttantakathāya taṃ desaṃ pasādetvā asītipāṇakoṭiyo maggaphalaratanāni paṭilābhesi. Pañcapi ca therā pañca raṭṭhāni pasādesuṃ. Ekamekassa santike satasahassamattā pabbajiṃsu. Evaṃ te tattha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

The Elder Majjhima, together with the Elders Kassapagotta, Aḷakadeva, Dundubhissara, and Mahādeva, went to the Himalayan region. Through the discourse on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, they inspired faith in that region and caused eighty koṭis of beings to attain the jewels of the path and its fruit. The five elders also inspired faith in five countries. In the presence of each one, about a hundred thousand went forth. Thus, they established the Dispensation there.

Gantvāna majjhimatthero, himavantaṃ pasādayi;

Yakkhasenaṃ pakāsento, dhammacakkapavattananti.

The Elder Majjhima, having gone to the Himavanta, inspired faith in the host of yakkhas by proclaiming the Dhammacakkapavattana.

Soṇattheropi saddhiṃ uttarattherena suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ agamāsi. Tena ca samayena tattha ekā rakkhasī samuddato nikkhamitvā rājakule jāte jāte dārake khādati. Taṃdivasameva ca rājakule eko dārako jāto hoti. Manussā theraṃ disvā “rakkhasānaṃ sahāyako eso”ti maññamānā āvudhāni gahetvā theraṃ paharitukāmā āgacchanti. Thero “kiṃ tumhe āvudhahatthā āgacchathā”ti āha. Te āhaṃsu – “rājakule jāte jāte dārake rakkhasā khādanti, tesaṃ tumhe sahāyakā”ti. Thero “na mayaṃ rakkhasānaṃ sahāyakā, samaṇā nāma mayaṃ viratā pāṇātipātā…pe… viratā majjapānā ekabhattikā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā”ti āha. Tasmiṃyeva ca khaṇe sā rakkhasī saparivārā samuddato nikkhami “rājakule dārako jāto taṃ khādissāmī”ti. Manussā taṃ disvā “esā, bhante, rakkhasī āgacchatī”ti bhītā viraviṃsu. Thero rakkhasehi diguṇe attabhāve nimminitvā tehi attabhāvehi taṃ rakkhasiṃ [P 1.0069] saparisaṃ majjhe katvā ubhosu passesu parikkhipi[M 1.0052]. Tassā saparisāya etadahosi – “addhā imehi idaṃ ṭhānaṃ laddhaṃ bhavissati. Mayaṃ pana imesaṃ bhakkhā bhavissāmā”ti. Sabbe rakkhasā bhītā vegasā palāyiṃsu. Theropi te yāva adassanaṃ tāva palāpetvā dīpassa samantato rakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Tasmiñca samaye sannipatitaṃ mahājanakāyaṃ brahmajālasuttantakathāya pasādetvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpesi. Saṭṭhisahassānaṃ panettha dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Kuladārakānaṃ aḍḍhuḍḍhāni sahassāni pabbajiṃsu, kuladhītānaṃ diyaḍḍhasahassaṃ. Evaṃ so tattha sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Tato pabhuti rājakule jātadārakānaṃ soṇuttaranāmameva karonti.

The Elder Soṇa also went to Suvaṇṇabhūmi with the Elder Uttara. At that time, a female rākkhasī emerged from the ocean there and devoured every child born in the royal family. On that very day, a child was born in the royal family. Seeing the Elder, the people thought, “This is an ally of the rākkhasas,” and, taking up weapons, they came to strike him. The Elder asked, “Why do you come with weapons in hand?” They replied, “Rākkhasas devour every child born in the royal family, and you are their allies.” The Elder said, “We are not allies of the rākkhasas. We are ascetics, abstaining from killing living beings… abstaining from intoxicants, eating one meal a day, virtuous, and of good conduct.” At that very moment, the female rākkhasī emerged from the ocean with her retinue, thinking, “A child has been born in the royal family—I will devour it.” Seeing her, the terrified people cried out, “Venerable sir, that rākkhasī is coming!” The Elder created forms double the size of the rākkhasas and, placing that rākkhasī and her retinue in the middle, surrounded them on both sides with these forms. To her and her retinue, this thought occurred: “Surely, this place has been taken by them. We will become their food.” All the rākkhasas, terrified, fled with great speed. The Elder drove them away until they were out of sight and then set up a protective guard around the island. At that time, he inspired faith in the great crowd that had gathered with a discourse on the Brahmajāla Sutta and established them in the refuges and precepts. On this occasion, sixty thousand attained the penetration of the Dhamma. Three thousand five hundred young men of good family went forth, and one thousand five hundred young women of good family went forth. Thus, he established the Dispensation there. From then on, children born in the royal family were given the name Soṇuttara.

Suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gantvāna, soṇuttarā mahiddhikā;

Pisāce niddhametvāna, brahmajālaṃ adesisunti.

Having gone to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, the greatly powerful Soṇa and Uttara, having driven away the pisācas, taught the Brahmajāla.

Mahindatthero pana “tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ gantvā sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpehī”ti upajjhāyena ca bhikkhusaṅghena [V 1.0050] ca ajjhiṭṭho cintesi – “kālo nu kho me tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ gantuṃ no”ti. Athassa vīmaṃsato “na tāva kālo”ti ahosi. Kiṃ panassa disvā etadahosi? Muṭasivarañño mahallakabhāvaṃ. Tato cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā mahallako, na sakkā imaṃ gaṇhitvā sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ. Idāni panassa putto devānaṃpiyatisso rajjaṃ kāressati. Taṃ gaṇhitvā sakkā bhavissati sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ. Handa yāva so samayo āgacchati, tāva ñātake olokema. Puna dāni mayaṃ imaṃ janapadaṃ āgaccheyyāma vā na vā”ti. So evaṃ cintetvā upajjhāyañca bhikkhusaṅghañca vanditvā asokārāmato nikkhamma tehi iṭṭiyādīhi catūhi therehi saṅghamittāya puttena sumanasāmaṇerena bhaṇḍukena [P 1.0070] ca upāsakena saddhiṃ rājagahanagaraparivattakena dakkhiṇāgirijanapade cārikaṃ caramāno ñātake olokento cha māse atikkāmesi. Athānupubbena mātu nivesanaṭṭhānaṃ vedisanagaraṃ nāma sampatto. Asoko kira kumārakāle janapadaṃ labhitvā ujjeniṃ gacchanto vedisanagaraṃ patvā vedisaseṭṭhissa dhītaraṃ aggahesi. Sā taṃdivasameva gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā ujjeniyaṃ mahindakumāraṃ vijāyi. Kumārassa [M 1.0053] cuddasavassakāle rājā abhisekaṃ pāpuṇi. Sā tassa mātā tena samayena ñātighare vasati. Tena vuttaṃ – “athānupubbena mātu nivesanaṭṭhānaṃ veṭisanagaraṃ nāma sampatto”ti.

The Elder Mahinda, having been requested by his preceptor and the community of monks, “Go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Dispensation,” reflected: “Is it now the time for me to go to Tambapaṇṇi, or is it not?” Upon consideration, it occurred to him, “It is not yet the time.” What, then, did he see that this occurred to him? The old age of King Muṭasiva. Then he reflected: “This king is old; it is not possible to establish the Dispensation by winning him over. But soon his son, Devānaṃpiyatissa, will take the throne. By winning him over, it will be possible to establish the Dispensation. Well then, until that time comes, let us visit our relatives. For we may or may not be able to return to this country again.” Having thus reflected, he paid homage to his preceptor and the community of monks, departed from the Asokārāma, and together with those four elders—Iṭṭiya and the others—along with Saṅghamittā's son, the novice Sumana, and the lay follower Bhaṇḍuka, he spent six months wandering on tour in the Dakkhiṇāgiri country, visiting relatives, taking the road that circumambulates the city of Rājagaha. Then, in due course, he reached the city called Vedisa, his mother’s place of residence. It is said that Asoka, when he was a prince, having received a province, was going to Ujjenī when he arrived at the city of Vedisa and took the daughter of the Vedisa Seṭṭhi. She conceived on that very day and in Ujjenī gave birth to Prince Mahinda. When the prince was fourteen years old, the king attained his consecration. At that time, his mother was living in her relatives’ house. Therefore it was said: “Then, in due course, he reached the city called Vedisa, his mother’s place of residence.”

Sampattañca pana theraṃ disvā theramātā devī pādesu sirasā vanditvā bhikkhaṃ datvā theraṃ attanā kataṃ vedisagirimahāvihāraṃ nāma āropesi. Thero tasmiṃ vihāre nisinno cintesi – “amhākaṃ idha kattabbakiccaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ, samayo nu kho idāni laṅkādīpaṃ gantu”nti. Tato cintesi – “anubhavatu tāva me pitarā pesitaṃ abhisekaṃ devānaṃpiyatisso, ratanattayaguṇañca suṇātu, chaṇatthañca nagarato nikkhamitvā missakapabbataṃ abhiruhatu, tadā taṃ tattha dakkhissāmā”ti. Athāparaṃ ekamāsaṃ tattheva vāsaṃ kappesi. Māsātikkamena ca jeṭṭhamūlamāsapuṇṇamāyaṃ uposathadivase sannipatitā sabbepi – “kālo nu kho amhākaṃ tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ gamanāya, udāhu no”ti mantayiṃsu. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Furthermore, having seen the elder arrive, the elder's mother, the queen, bowed with her head at his feet, gave alms, and then offered to him the great monastery named Vedisagiri, which she herself had built. Seated in that monastery, the elder thought: “Our duty to be done here is finished. Is it now indeed the time to go to the island of Laṅkā?” Then he thought: “Let Devānaṃpiyatissa first experience the consecration sent by my father, and let him hear the virtues of the Triple Gem, and for the sake of the festival, having gone out from the city, let him ascend Missaka mountain; then we will see him there.” Then, for another month, he made his residence right there. And with the passing of the month, on the Uposatha day of the full moon of the Jeṭṭha-Mūla month, all who had assembled consulted: “Is it now indeed the time for our journey to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, or is it not?” Therefore the ancients said—

“Mahindo nāma nāmena, saṅghatthero tadā ahu;

Iṭṭiyo uttiyo thero, bhaddasālo ca sambalo.

“At that time there was the Elder of the Saṅgha, Mahinda by name; and the elders Iṭṭiya, Uttiya, Bhaddasāla, and Sambala.

“Sāmaṇero [P 1.0071] ca sumano, chaḷabhiñño mahiddhiko;

Bhaṇḍuko sattamo tesaṃ, diṭṭhasacco upāsako;

Iti hete mahānāgā, mantayiṃsu rahogatā”ti.

“And the novice Sumana, of great psychic power, possessing the six super-knowledges; and Bhaṇḍuka the lay follower, the seventh of them, who had seen the truths. Thus these great nāgas, having gone to a secluded place, consulted.”

Tadā [V 1.0051] sakko devānamindo mahindattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – “kālaṅkato, bhante, muṭasivarājā; idāni devānaṃpiyatissamahārājā rajjaṃ kāreti. Sammāsambuddhena ca tumhe byākatā – ‘anāgate mahindo nāma bhikkhu tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ pasādessatī’ti. Tasmātiha vo, bhante, kālo dīpavaraṃ gamanāya; ahampi vo sahāyo bhavissāmī”ti. Kasmā pana sakko evamāha? Bhagavā kirassa bodhimūleyeva buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketvā anāgate imassa dīpassa sampattiṃ disvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi – “tadā tvampi sahāyo bhaveyyāsī”ti ca āṇāpesi. Tasmā evamāha. Thero tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā attasattamo veṭisakapabbatā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā anurādhapurassa puratthimadisāya missakapabbate patiṭṭhahi. Yaṃ panetarahi “cetiyapabbato”tipi sañjānanti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Then Sakka, the lord of the devas, approached the elder Mahinda and said this: “Venerable sir, King Muṭasiva has passed away; now the great king Devānaṃpiyatissa rules the kingdom. And you were declared by the Fully Enlightened One: ‘In the future, a monk named Mahinda will inspire faith in the island of Tambapaṇṇi.’ Therefore, venerable sir, it is time for you to go to the excellent island; I too will be your companion.” But why did Sakka say so? Indeed, the Blessed One, right at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and having seen the future prosperity of this island, declared this matter to him and commanded, “Then you too should be a companion.” Therefore he said so. The elder, having accepted his word, he himself as the seventh, rose into the sky from Vedisaka mountain and established himself on Missaka mountain in the eastern direction of Anurādhapura, which now they also know as “Cetiya mountain.” Therefore the ancients said—

“Veṭisagirimhi [M 1.0054] rājagahe, vasitvā tiṃsarattiyo;

Kālova gamanassāti, gacchāma dīpamuttamaṃ.

“Having dwelt at Vedisagiri in Rājagaha for thirty nights, they thought, ‘It is indeed time for the journey; let us go to the excellent island.’

“Paḷīnā jambudīpā te, haṃsarājāva ambare;

Evamuppatitā therā, nipatiṃsu naguttame.

“Like a swan-king in the sky, they flew from Jambudīpa; thus having soared up, the elders alighted on the best of mountains.

“Purato puraseṭṭhassa, pabbate meghasannibhe;

Patiṃsu sīlakūṭamhi, haṃsāva nagamuddhanī”ti.

“Before the best of cities, on a mountain resembling a cloud, they alighted on the Silakūṭa peak, like swans on a mountain's summit.”

Evaṃ [P 1.0072] iṭṭiyādīhi saddhiṃ āgantvā patiṭṭhahanto ca āyasmā mahindatthero sammāsambuddhassa parinibbānato dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ upari chattiṃsatime vasse imasmiṃ dīpe patiṭṭhahīti veditabbo. Ajātasattussa hi aṭṭhame vasse sammāsambuddho parinibbāyi. Tasmiṃyeva vasse sīhakumārassa putto tambapaṇṇidīpassa ādirājā vijayakumāro imaṃ dīpamāgantvā manussāvāsaṃ akāsi. Jambudīpe udayabhaddassa cuddasame vasse idha vijayo kālamakāsi. Udayabhaddassa pañcadasame vasse paṇḍuvāsudevo nāma imasmiṃ dīpe rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha nāgadāsakarañño vīsatime vasse idha paṇḍuvāsudevo kālamakāsi. Tasmiṃyeva ca vasse abhayo nāma rājakumāro imasmiṃ dīpe rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha susunāgarañño sattarasame vasse idha abhayarañño vīsativassāni paripūriṃsu. Atha abhayassa vīsatime vasse paṇḍukābhayo nāma dāmariko rajjaṃ aggahesi. Tattha kāḷāsokassa soḷasame vasse idha paṇḍukassa sattarasavassāni paripūriṃsu. Tāni heṭṭhā ekena vassena saha aṭṭhārasa honti. Tattha [V 1.0052] candaguttassa cuddasame vasse idha paṇḍukābhayo kālamakāsi. Muṭasivarājā rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha asokadhammarājassa sattarasame vasse idha muṭasivarājā kālamakāsi. Devānampiyatisso rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Parinibbute ca sammāsambuddhe ajātasattu catuvīsati vassāni rajjaṃ kāresi. Udayabhaddo [P 1.0073] soḷasa, anuruddho ca muṇḍo ca aṭṭha, nāgadāsako catuvīsati, susunāgo aṭṭhārasa, tasseva putto kāḷāsoko aṭṭhavīsati, tato tassa puttakā dasa bhātukarājāno dvevīsati vassāni rajjaṃ kāresuṃ. Tesaṃ pacchato nava nandā dvevīsatimeva, candagutto catuvīsati, bindusāro aṭṭhavīsati[M 1.0055]. Tassāvasāne asoko rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa pure abhisekā cattāri abhisekato aṭṭhārasame vasse imasmiṃ dīpe mahindatthero patiṭṭhito. Evametena rājavaṃsānusārena veditabbametaṃ – “sammāsambuddhassa parinibbānato dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ upari chattiṃsatime vasse imasmiṃ dīpe patiṭṭhahī”ti.

Thus, it should be known that the venerable elder Mahinda, having come with Iṭṭiya and the others, was established on this island in the thirty-sixth year after two hundred years from the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened One. For in the eighth year of Ajātasattu, the Fully Enlightened One attained Parinibbāna. In that very year, Prince Vijaya, son of Prince Sīha and the first king of the island of Tambapaṇṇi, came to this island and established human habitation. In Jambudīpa, in the fourteenth year of Udayabhadda, Vijaya passed away here. In the fifteenth year of Udayabhadda, one named Paṇḍuvāsudeva attained kingship on this island. There, in the twentieth year of King Nāgadāsaka, Paṇḍuvāsudeva passed away here. And in that very year, a prince named Abhaya attained kingship on this island. There, in the seventeenth year of King Susunāga, the twenty years of King Abhaya's reign here were completed. Then, in the twentieth year of Abhaya, a rebel named Paṇḍukābhaya seized the kingdom. There, in the sixteenth year of Kāḷāsoka, the seventeen years of Paṇḍuka's reign here were completed. Those, together with one year before, are eighteen. There, in the fourteenth year of Candagutta, Paṇḍukābhaya passed away here. King Muṭasiva attained kingship. There, in the seventeenth year of King Asoka Dhammarāja, King Muṭasiva passed away here. Devānampiyatissa attained kingship. And after the Fully Enlightened One attained Parinibbāna, Ajātasattu ruled for twenty-four years. Udayabhadda for sixteen, Anuruddha and Muṇḍa for eight, Nāgadāsaka for twenty-four, Susunāga for eighteen, his son Kāḷāsoka for twenty-eight, then his sons, the ten brother-kings, ruled for twenty-two years. After them, the nine Nandas for exactly twenty-two, Candagutta for twenty-four, Bindusāra for twenty-eight. At the end of his reign, Asoka attained kingship. Four years of his were before the consecration, and in the eighteenth year from the consecration, the elder Mahinda was established on this island. Thus, by this royal lineage, this should be known: “He was established on this island in the thirty-sixth year after two hundred years from the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened One.”

Tasmiñca divase tambapaṇṇidīpe jeṭṭhamūlanakkhattaṃ nāma hoti. Rājā nakkhattaṃ ghosāpetvā “chaṇaṃ karothā”ti amacce ca āṇāpetvā cattālīsapurisasahassaparivāro nagaramhā nikkhamitvā yena missakapabbato tena pāyāsi migavaṃ kīḷitukāmo. Atha tasmiṃ pabbate adhivatthā ekā devatā “rañño there dassessāmī”ti rohitamigarūpaṃ gahetvā avidūre tiṇapaṇṇāni khādamānā viya carati. Rājā taṃ disvā “ayuttaṃ dāni pamattaṃ vijjhitu”nti jiyaṃ phoṭesi. Migo ambatthalamaggaṃ gahetvā palāyituṃ ārabhi. Rājā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhanto ambatthalameva abhiruhi. Migopi therānaṃ avidūre antaradhāyi. Mahindatthero rājānaṃ avidūre āgacchantaṃ disvā “mamaṃyeva rājā passatu, mā itare”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā “tissa, tissa, ito ehī”ti āha. Rājā sutvā cintesi – “imasmiṃ dīpe jāto maṃ ‘tissā’ti nāmaṃ gahetvā [P 1.0074] ālapituṃ samattho nāma natthi. Ayaṃ pana chinnabhinnapaṭadharo bhaṇḍu kāsāvavasano maṃ nāmena ālapati, ko nu kho ayaṃ bhavissati manusso vā amanusso vā”ti? Thero āha –

On that day, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the festival called the Jeṭṭhamūla constellation festival was taking place. The king, having proclaimed the festival and commanded his ministers, “Hold a festival,” departed from the city with a retinue of forty thousand men and proceeded towards Missaka Mountain, desiring to play the sport of hunting. Then, a certain deity dwelling on that mountain, thinking, “I shall show the Theras to the king,” took the form of a rohita deer and wandered nearby as if eating grass and leaves. The king, seeing it, thought, “It is improper to shoot one who is heedless,” and twanged his bowstring. The deer, taking the path to Ambatthala, began to flee. The king, following closely behind, ascended to Ambatthala itself. The deer also vanished not far from the Theras. The Thera Mahinda, seeing the king approaching nearby, made a resolution, “Let the king see only me; let him not see the others,” and called out, “Tissa, Tissa, come here!” Hearing this, the king thought: “In this island, there is no one born here who is capable of addressing me by the name ‘Tissa.’ But this one, a wearer of torn and tattered robes, a shaven-headed one clad in ochre garments, addresses me by name. Who indeed could this be? A human or a non-human?” The Thera said—

“Samaṇā mayaṃ mahārāja, dhammarājassa sāvakā;

Taveva anukampāya, jambudīpā idhāgatā”ti.

“We are recluses, Mahārāja, disciples of the King of Dhamma. Out of compassion for you alone have we come here from Jambudīpa.”

Tena ca samayena devānampiyatissamahārājā ca asokadhammarājā ca adiṭṭhasahāyakā honti. Devānampiyatissamahārājassa ca puññānubhāvena chātapabbatapāde ekamhi veḷugumbe tisso veḷuyaṭṭhiyo rathayaṭṭhippamāṇā uppajjiṃsu – ekā latāyaṭṭhi nāma, ekā pupphayaṭṭhi nāma, ekā [V 1.0053] sakuṇayaṭṭhi nāma. Tāsu latāyaṭṭhi rajatavaṇṇā hoti, taṃ alaṅkaritvā uppannalatā kañcanavaṇṇā khāyati. Pupphayaṭṭhiyaṃ pana nīlapītalohitodātakāḷavaṇṇāni pupphāni suvibhattavaṇṭapattakiñjakkhāni hutvā khāyanti. Sakuṇayaṭṭhiyaṃ haṃsakukkuṭajīvajīvakādayo sakuṇā nānappakārāni ca catuppadāni sajīvāni viya khāyanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ dīpavaṃse –

At that time, the great king Devānampiyatissa and the Dhamma-king Asoka were unseen friends. And by the power of the merit of the great king Devānampiyatissa, at the foot of Chāta Mountain, in a single bamboo grove, three bamboo stalks of the size of a chariot-goad arose—one called the creeper-stalk, one the flower-stalk, and one the bird-stalk. Among them, the creeper-stalk was silver in color; the creepers that arose adorning it appeared golden. On the flower-stalk, flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and black colors appeared, being well-distinguished with stalks, leaves, and filaments. On the bird-stalk, birds such as haṃsas, water-fowl, and jīvajīvakas, and various kinds of four-footed creatures appeared as if they were alive. This is also stated in the Dīpavaṃsa:

“Chātapabbatapādamhi[M 1.0056], veḷuyaṭṭhī tayo ahu;

Setā rajatayaṭṭhīva, latā kañcanasannibhā.

“At the foot of Chāta Mountain, there were three bamboo stalks. The white ones were like silver staffs; the creeper was similar in color to gold.

“Nīlādi yādisaṃ pupphaṃ, pupphayaṭṭhimhi tādisaṃ;

Sakuṇā sakuṇayaṭṭhimhi, sarūpeneva saṇṭhitā”ti.

“Whatever kind of flower there is, such as blue and so on, that kind of flower was on the flower-stalk. On the bird-stalk, the birds were established in their very own forms.”

Samuddatopissa [P 1.0075] muttāmaṇiveḷuriyādi anekavihitaṃ ratanaṃ uppajji. Tambapaṇṇiyaṃ pana aṭṭha muttā uppajjiṃsu – hayamuttā, gajamuttā, rathamuttā, āmalakamuttā, valayamuttā, aṅguliveṭhakamuttā, kakudhaphalamuttā, pākatikamuttāti. So tā ca yaṭṭhiyo tā ca muttā aññañca bahuṃ ratanaṃ asokassa dhammarañño paṇṇākāratthāya pesesi. Asoko pasīditvā tassa pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni pahiṇi – chattaṃ, cāmaraṃ, khaggaṃ, moḷiṃ, ratanapādukaṃ, aññañca abhisekatthāya bahuvidhaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ; seyyathidaṃ – saṅkhaṃ, gaṅgodakaṃ, vaḍḍhamānaṃ, vaṭaṃsakaṃ, bhiṅgāraṃ, nandiyāvaṭṭaṃ, sivikaṃ, kaññaṃ, kaṭacchuṃ, adhovimaṃ dussayugaṃ, hatthapuñchanaṃ, haricandanaṃ, aruṇavaṇṇamattikaṃ, añjanaṃ, harītakaṃ, āmalakanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ dīpavaṃse –

For him, from the ocean also, various kinds of gems such as pearls, jewels, and beryl arose. And in Tambapaṇṇi, eight kinds of pearls arose: horse-pearls, elephant-pearls, chariot-pearls, āmalaka-pearls, bracelet-pearls, finger-ring-pearls, kakudha-fruit-pearls, and natural pearls. He sent those stalks, those pearls, and many other gems to the Dhamma-king Asoka for the purpose of a gift. Pleased, Asoka sent him the five items of royal regalia—a parasol, a chowrie, a sword, a diadem, and jeweled sandals—and also various other gifts for the consecration ceremony; namely: a right-spiraling conch, water from the Ganges, cosmetic powder, a head-ornament, a golden pitcher, a Nandiyāvaṭṭa vessel, a palanquin, a maiden, a ladle, a pair of garments not needing to be washed, a hand-towel, golden sandalwood, fine clay the color of dawn, collyrium, chebulic myrobalan, and emblic myrobalan. This is also stated in the Dīpavaṃsa:

“Vālabījanimuṇhīsaṃ, chattaṃ khaggañca pādukaṃ;

Veṭhanaṃ sārapāmaṅgaṃ, bhiṅgāraṃ nandivaṭṭakaṃ.

“A chowrie and a turban, a parasol, a sword, and sandals; a head-wrap, an excellent jeweled fillet, a golden pitcher, and a Nandivaṭṭaka vessel.

“Sivikaṃ saṅkhaṃ vaṭaṃsañca, adhovimaṃ vatthakoṭikaṃ;

Sovaṇṇapātiṃ kaṭacchuṃ, mahagghaṃ hatthapuñchanaṃ.

“A palanquin, a conch, and a head-ornament, a pair of garments not needing to be washed; a golden bowl, a ladle, and a costly hand-towel.

“Anotattodakaṃ kaññaṃ, uttamaṃ haricandanaṃ;

Aruṇavaṇṇamattikaṃ[P 1.0076], añjanaṃ nāgamāhaṭaṃ.

“Water from Anotatta and a maiden, the finest golden sandalwood; fine clay the color of dawn and collyrium, brought by nāgas.

“Harītakaṃ [V 1.0054] āmalakaṃ, mahagghaṃ amatosadhaṃ;

Saṭṭhivāhasataṃ sāliṃ, sugandhaṃ suvakāhaṭaṃ;

Puññakammābhinibbattaṃ, pāhesi asokavhayo”ti.

“Chebulic and emblic myrobalan, a costly ambrosial medicine; sixty hundred cartloads of fragrant sāli rice, brought by parrots; produced by meritorious action—these the one named Asoka sent.”

Na kevalañcetaṃ āmisapaṇṇākāraṃ, imaṃ kira dhammapaṇṇākārampi pesesi –

And he did not send only this material gift; it is said he also sent this Dhamma-gift—

“Ahaṃ buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato;

Upāsakattaṃ desesiṃ, sakyaputtassa sāsane.

“I have gone to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha for refuge; I have declared my status as a lay follower in the Dispensation of the Son of the Sakyans.

“Imesu [M 1.0057] tīsu vatthūsu, uttame jinasāsane;

Tvampi cittaṃ pasādehi, saddhā saraṇamupehī”ti.

“You too, in the supreme Dispensation of the Victor, should gladden your mind towards these three objects; with faith, go for refuge.”

Svāyaṃ rājā taṃ divasaṃ asokaraññā pesitena abhisekena ekamāsābhisitto hoti.

On that day, one month had passed since that king had been consecrated with the consecration requisites sent by King Asoka.

Visākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ hissa abhisekamakaṃsu. So acirassutaṃ – taṃ sāsanappavattiṃ anussaramāno taṃ therassa “samaṇā mayaṃ mahārāja dhammarājassa sāvakā”ti vacanaṃ sutvā “ayyā nu kho āgatā”ti tāvadeva āvudhaṃ nikkhipitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathayamāno. Yathāha –

Indeed, they had performed his consecration on the full moon day of Visākha. While recollecting that account of the Dispensation which he had recently heard, upon hearing the Thera's words, “We are recluses, Mahārāja, disciples of the King of Dhamma,” he thought, “Have the noble ones indeed come?” At that very moment, laying down his weapon, he sat down to one side and engaged in courteous conversation. As it is said:

“Āvudhaṃ nikkhipitvāna, ekamantaṃ upāvisi;

Nisajja rājā sammodi, bahuṃ atthūpasañhita”nti.

“Having laid down his weapon, he sat down to one side. Seated, the king exchanged many pleasantries connected with what was beneficial.”

Sammodanīyakathañca kurumāneyeva tasmiṃ tānipi cattālīsapurisasahassāni āgantvā samparivāresuṃ. Tadā thero itarepi cha jane dassesi. Rājā disvā “ime kadā āgatā”ti āha[P 1.0077]. “Mayā saddhiṃyeva, mahārājā”ti. “Idāni pana jambudīpe aññepi evarūpā samaṇā santī”ti? “Santi, mahārāja; etarahi jambudīpo kāsāvapajjoto isivātapaṭivāto. Tasmiṃ –

And while that king was exchanging words of joyful greeting, those forty thousand men also arrived and surrounded them. Then the Elder showed the other six people. Seeing them, the king said, “When did these arrive?” “With me, great king.” “But now, are there other such ascetics in Jambudīpa?” “There are, great king; at present Jambudīpa is illuminated by the color of the saffron robe and swept all around by the wind from the sages. Therein—

“Tevijjā iddhipattā ca, cetopariyāyakovidā;

Khīṇāsavā arahanto, bahū buddhassa sāvakāti.

‘Possessing the three knowledges, having attained psychic power, skilled in discerning the minds of others, Arahants whose taints are destroyed—many are the Buddha’s disciples.’

“Bhante, kena āgatatthā”ti? “Neva, mahārāja, udakena na thalenā”ti. “Rājā ākāsena [V 1.0055] āgatā”ti aññāsi. Thero “atthi nu kho rañño paññāveyattiya”nti vīmaṃsanatthāya āsannaṃ ambarukkhaṃ ārabbha pañhaṃ pucchi – “kiṃ nāmo ayaṃ, mahārāja, rukkho”ti? “Ambarukkho nāma, bhante”ti. “Imaṃ pana, mahārāja, ambaṃ muñcitvā añño ambo atthi, natthī”ti? “Atthi, bhante, aññepi bahū ambarukkhā”ti. “Imañca ambaṃ te ca ambe muñcitvā atthi nu kho, mahārāja, aññe rukkhā”ti? “Atthi, bhante, te pana na ambarukkhā”ti. “Aññe ambe ca anambe ca muñcitvā atthi pana añño rukkho”ti? “Ayameva, bhante, ambarukkho”ti. “Sādhu, mahārāja, paṇḍitosi. Atthi pana te, mahārāja, ñātakā”ti? “Atthi, bhante, bahū janā”ti. “Te muñcitvā aññe keci aññātakāpi atthi, mahārājā”ti? “Aññātakā, bhante, ñātakehi bahutarā”ti. “Tava ñātake ca aññātake ca muñcitvā atthañño koci, mahārājā”ti[M 1.0058]? “Ahameva, aññātako”ti. Atha thero “paṇḍito rājā sakkhissati dhammaṃ aññātu”nti cūḷahatthipadopamasuttaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne rājā tīsu saraṇesu patiṭṭhahi saddhiṃ cattālīsāya pāṇasahassehi.

“Venerable sirs, by what means have you come?” “Neither by water nor by land, great king.” The king understood, “They have come through the air.” The Elder, wishing to test whether the king possessed sharp wisdom, asked a question concerning a nearby mango tree: “What is the name of this tree, great king?” “It is called a mango tree, venerable sir.” “But apart from this mango tree, great king, is there another mango tree, or not?” “There are, venerable sir, many other mango trees.” “And apart from this mango tree and those mango trees, great king, are there other trees?” “There are, venerable sir, but those are not mango trees.” “And apart from the other mango trees and the non-mango trees, is there another tree?” “This very one, venerable sir, is the mango tree.” “Good, great king, you are wise. But do you have relatives, great king?” “I do, venerable sir, many people.” “Apart from them, are there any others who are non-relatives, great king?” “Non-relatives, venerable sir, are more numerous than relatives.” “And apart from your relatives and non-relatives, is there anyone else, great king?” “Only I myself, venerable sir.” Then the Elder, thinking, “The king is wise; he will be able to understand the Dhamma,” taught the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king, together with forty thousand living beings, was established in the Three Refuges.

Taṃ khaṇaññeva ca rañño bhattaṃ āhariyittha[P 1.0078]. Rājā ca suttantaṃ suṇanto eva aññāsi – “na imesaṃ imasmiṃ kāle bhojanaṃ kappatī”ti. “Apucchitvā pana bhuñjituṃ ayutta”nti cintetvā “bhuñjissatha, bhante”ti pucchi. “Na, mahārāja, amhākaṃ imasmiṃ kāle bhojanaṃ kappatī”ti. “Kasmiṃ kāle, bhante, kappatī”ti? “Aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhikasamayā, mahārājā”ti. “Gacchāma, bhante, nagara”nti? “Alaṃ, mahārāja, idheva vasissāmā”ti. “Sace, bhante, tumhe vasatha, ayaṃ dārako āgacchatū”ti. “Mahārāja, ayaṃ dārako āgataphalo viññātasāsano pabbajjāpekkho idāni pabbajissatī”ti. Rājā “tena hi, bhante, sve rathaṃ pesessāmi; taṃ abhiruhitvā āgaccheyyāthā”ti vatvā vanditvā pakkāmi.

At that very moment, the king's meal was brought. And while listening to the discourse, the king realized, “This is not an allowable time for these venerable ones to eat.” But thinking, “It is not proper to eat without asking,” he asked, “Venerable sirs, will you eat?” “No, great king, it is not an allowable time for us to eat.” “At what time, venerable sirs, is it allowable?” “From the rising of the dawn up until midday, great king.” “Shall we go to the city, venerable sirs?” “Enough, great king, we will stay right here.” “If you, venerable sirs, are staying, let this boy come.” “Great king, this boy has attained the fruit, has understood the teaching, and is one who desires to go forth. He will go forth now.” The king said, “In that case, venerable sirs, tomorrow I will send a chariot; having mounted it, may you come.” Having spoken thus, he paid homage and departed.

Thero acirapakkantassa rañño sumanasāmaṇeraṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, sumana, dhammasavanassa kālaṃ ghosehī”ti. “Bhante, kittakaṃ ṭhānaṃ sāvento ghosemī”ti? “Sakalaṃ tambapaṇṇidīpa”nti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti sāmaṇero abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhahitvā samāhitena cittena sakalaṃ tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ sāvento tikkhattuṃ dhammasavanassa kālaṃ ghosesi. Rājā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā therānaṃ santikaṃ pesesi – “kiṃ, bhante, atthi koci upaddavo”ti. “Natthamhākaṃ koci upaddavo, dhammasavanassa kālaṃ ghosāpayimha buddhavacanaṃ kathetukāmamhā”ti[V 1.0056]. Tañca pana sāmaṇerassa saddaṃ sutvā bhummā devatā saddamanussāvesuṃ. Etenupāyena yāva brahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchi. Tena saddena mahā devatāsannipāto ahosi. Thero mahantaṃ devatāsannipātaṃ disvā samacittasuttantaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ devatānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Bahū nāgā [P 1.0079] ca supaṇṇā ca saraṇesu patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Yādisova sāriputtattherassa imaṃ suttantaṃ kathayato devatāsannipāto ahosi, tādiso mahindattherassāpi jāto. Atha tassā rattiyā accayena rājā therānaṃ [M 1.0059] rathaṃ pesesi. Sārathī rathaṃ ekamante ṭhapetvā therānaṃ ārocesi – “āgato, bhante, ratho; abhiruhatha gacchissāmā”ti. Therā “na mayaṃ rathaṃ abhiruhāma; gaccha tvaṃ, pacchā mayaṃ āgacchissāmā”ti vatvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā anurādhapurassa puratthimadisāyaṃ paṭhamakacetiyaṭṭhāne otariṃsu. Tañhi cetiyaṃ therehi paṭhamaṃ otiṇṇaṭṭhāne katattāyeva “paṭhamakacetiya”nti vuccati.

Not long after the king had departed, the Elder addressed the novice Sumana: “Come, Sumana, announce the time for hearing the Dhamma.” “Venerable sir, making it heard over how large an area should I announce?” “The entire island of Tambapaṇṇi.” “Very well, venerable sir,” the novice replied. Having entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for supernormal knowledge, he rose from it, made a determination, and with a concentrated mind announced the time for hearing the Dhamma three times, making it heard throughout the whole island of Tambapaṇṇi. Hearing that sound, the king sent a messenger to the elders: “Venerable sirs, is there some disturbance?” “There is no disturbance for us. We caused the time for hearing the Dhamma to be announced, as we wish to speak the Buddha’s word.” And hearing the novice’s voice, the earth deities relayed the sound. By this means, the sound rose as far as the Brahma world. By that sound, a great assembly of deities came to be. Seeing the great assembly of deities, the Elder preached the Samacitta Sutta. At the end of the discourse, there was the realization of the Dhamma for countless deities. Many nāgas and supaṇṇas were established in the refuges. Just such an assembly of deities as there had been when the Elder Sāriputta preached this discourse, so too did one arise for the Elder Mahinda. Then, when that night had passed, the king sent a chariot for the elders.
