The charioteer, having stationed the chariot to one side, informed the elders: “Venerable sirs, the chariot has come; please mount, we shall go.” The elders replied, “We will not mount the chariot. You go ahead; we will come later.” So saying, they rose into the air and descended at the site of the Paṭhamaka Cetiya to the east of Anurādhapura. Indeed, because that cetiya was built at the place where the elders first descended, it is called the ‘Paṭhamaka Cetiya’.

Rājāpi sārathiṃ pesetvā “antonivesane maṇḍapaṃ paṭiyādethā”ti amacce āṇāpesi. Tāvadeva sabbe haṭṭhatuṭṭhā ativiya pāsādikaṃ maṇḍapaṃ paṭiyādesuṃ. Puna rājā cintesi – “hiyyo thero sīlakkhandhaṃ kathayamāno ‘uccāsayanamahāsayanaṃ na kappatī’ti āha; ‘nisīdissanti nu kho ayyā āsanesu, na nisīdissantī’”ti? Tassevaṃ cintayantasseva so sārathi nagaradvāraṃ sampatto. Tato addasa there paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ pārupante. Disvā ativiya pasannacitto hutvā āgantvā rañño ārocesi – “āgatā, deva, therā”ti. Rājā “rathaṃ ārūḷhā”ti pucchi. “Na ārūḷhā, deva, api ca mama pacchato nikkhamitvā paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā pācīnadvāre ṭhitā”ti. Rājā “rathampi nābhirūhiṃsū”ti sutvā “na dāni ayyā uccāsayanamahāsayanaṃ sādiyissantī”ti cintetvā “tena hi, bhaṇe, therānaṃ bhūmattharaṇasaṅkhepena āsanāni paññapethā”ti vatvā paṭipathaṃ agamāsi. Amaccā pathaviyaṃ taṭṭikaṃ paññapetvā upari kojavakādīni cittattharaṇāni paññapesuṃ. Uppātapāṭhakā disvā “gahitā dāni imehi pathavī, ime tambapaṇṇidīpassa [P 1.0080] sāmikā bhavissantī”ti byākariṃsu. Rājāpi gantvā there vanditvā mahindattherassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā mahatiyā pūjāya ca sakkārena ca there nagaraṃ pavesetvā antonivesanaṃ pavesesi. Thero āsanapaññattiṃ disvā “amhākaṃ sāsanaṃ sakalalaṅkādīpe pathavī viya patthaṭaṃ niccalañca hutvā patiṭṭhahissatī”ti cintento nisīdi. Rājā there paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappetvā sampavāretvā “anuḷādevīpamukhāni pañca itthisatāni therānaṃ abhivādanaṃ pūjāsakkārañca karontū”ti pakkosāpetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Thero bhattakiccāvasāne rañño saparijanassa [V 1.0057] dhammaratanavassaṃ vassento petavatthuṃ [M 1.0060] vimānavatthuṃ saccasaṃyuttañca kathesi. Taṃ therassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā tāni pañcapi itthisatāni sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchākaṃsu.

The king, having sent his charioteer, ordered his ministers, 'Prepare a pavilion in the inner palace.' Immediately, all of them, overjoyed and delighted, prepared a very splendid pavilion. Then the king thought, 'Yesterday, the Elder, while teaching the section on virtue, said, "High and luxurious beds are not proper." Will the venerable ones sit on the seats, or will they not sit?' While he was still thinking this, the charioteer arrived at the city gate. There he saw the elders arriving first, fastening their waistbands and putting on their robes. Seeing them, he became exceedingly pleased and went to inform the king, 'The elders have arrived, Your Majesty.' The king asked, 'Did they ride in the chariot?' 'No, Your Majesty, but they left after me and arrived first, standing at the eastern gate.' Hearing that they did not even mount the chariot, the king thought, 'Now the venerable ones will not accept high and luxurious beds,' and said, 'Well then, sirs, prepare seats for the elders with simple ground coverings,' and went out to meet them. The ministers spread mats on the ground and placed fine coverings like woolen carpets and figured sheets on top. The interpreters of portents, seeing this, declared, 'Now the earth has been taken by these men; these will become the lords of the island of Tambapaṇṇi.' The king went, paid homage to the elders, took the bowl from the hand of the Elder Mahinda, and with great honor and offerings, led the elders into the city and into the inner palace. Seeing the arrangement of the seats, the Elder thought, 'Our Dispensation will spread throughout the entire island of Laṅkā like the earth, becoming firmly established and immovable,' and sat down. The king personally served the elders with excellent food and drink, and after having served them to their satisfaction, he summoned five hundred women, led by Anulādevī, to pay homage and honor to the elders, then sat to one side. At the end of the meal, the Elder rained down the jewel of the Dhamma upon the king and his retinue, teaching the Petavatthu, Vimānavatthu, and the Saccasaṃyutta. Hearing the Elder's Dhamma teaching, those five hundred women realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Yepi te manussā purimadivase missakapabbate there addasaṃsu, te tesu tesu ṭhānesu therānaṃ guṇe kathenti. Tesaṃ sutvā mahājanakāyo rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā mahāsaddaṃ akāsi. Rājā “kiṃ eso saddo”ti pucchi. “Nāgarā, deva, ‘there daṭṭhuṃ na labhāmā’ti viravantī”ti. Rājā “sace idha pavisissanti, okāso na bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “gacchatha, bhaṇe, hatthisālaṃ paṭijaggitvā vālukaṃ ākiritvā pañcavaṇṇāni pupphāni vikiritvā celavitānaṃ bandhitvā maṅgalahatthiṭṭhāne therānaṃ āsanāni paññapethā”ti āha. Amaccā tathā akaṃsu. Thero tattha gantvā nisīditvā devadūtasuttantaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne pāṇasahassaṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tato “hatthisālā atisambādhā”ti dakkhiṇadvāre nandanavanuyyāne āsanaṃ paññapesuṃ. Thero tattha nisīditvā āsīvisopamasuttaṃ kathesi. Tampi sutvā pāṇasahassaṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ [P 1.0081] paṭilabhi.

Those people who on the previous day had seen the elders on Mount Missaka, spoke of the elders' virtues in various places. Hearing them, a great crowd gathered in the royal courtyard and made a loud noise. The king asked, 'What is this noise?' 'Your Majesty, the citizens are lamenting, "We do not get to see the elders!"' The king, thinking, 'If they enter here, there will be no space,' said, 'Go, sirs, clean the elephant hall, spread sand, scatter flowers of five colors, hang up a cloth canopy, and set up seats for the elders in the place of the state elephant.' The ministers did so. The elder went there, sat down, and expounded the Devadūta Sutta. At the end of the discourse, one thousand beings were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, thinking, 'The elephant hall is too crowded,' they prepared seats at the southern gate in the Nandana Grove. The elder sat there and expounded the Āsīvisopama Sutta. Hearing that also, a thousand beings attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Evaṃ āgatadivasato dutiyadivase aḍḍhateyyasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Therassa nandanavane āgatāgatāhi kulitthīhi kulasuṇhāhi kulakumārīhi saddhiṃ sammodamānasseva sāyanhasamayo jāto. Thero kālaṃ sallakkhetvā “gacchāma dāni missakapabbata”nti uṭṭhahi. Amaccā – “kattha, bhante, gacchathā”ti? “Amhākaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhāna”nti. Te rañño saṃviditaṃ katvā rājānumatena āhaṃsu – “akālo, bhante, idāni tattha gantuṃ; idameva nandanavanuyyānaṃ ayyānaṃ āvāsaṭṭhānaṃ hotū”ti. “Alaṃ, gacchāmā”ti. Puna rañño vacanenāhaṃsu – “rājā, bhante, āha – ‘etaṃ meghavanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ mama pitu santakaṃ nagarato nātidūraṃ nāccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannaṃ, ettha therā vāsaṃ kappentū’”ti. Vasiṃsu therā meghavane uyyāne.

Thus, on the second day from their arrival, the Dhamma-realization of two thousand five hundred beings occurred. While the Elder was exchanging pleasantries in the Nandana Grove with the noblewomen, noble daughters-in-law, and noble maidens who kept coming, the evening arrived. The Elder, noting the time, rose, saying, 'Now we shall go to Mount Missaka.' The ministers asked, 'Venerable sirs, where are you going?' 'To our dwelling place.' They informed the king, and with the king's consent, they said, 'It is now the wrong time to go there, venerable sirs; let this very Nandana Grove be the venerable ones' residence.' 'Enough, we shall go.' Again, by the king's word, they said, 'The king says, venerable sirs: "This park named Meghavana, which belongs to my father, is convenient for coming and going from the city. Let the Elders dwell here."' The Elders dwelled in the Meghavana park.

Rājāpi kho tassā rattiyā accayena therassa samīpaṃ gantvā sukhasayitabhāvaṃ pucchitvā “kappati, bhante, bhikkhusaṅghassa ārāmo”ti pucchi. Thero “kappati, mahārājā”ti vatvā imaṃ suttaṃ āhari – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ārāma”nti. Rājā tuṭṭho suvaṇṇabhiṅgāraṃ gahetvā therassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā mahāmeghavanuyyānaṃ adāsi. Saha [M 1.0061] udakapātena pathavī kampi. Ayaṃ mahāvihāre paṭhamo pathavīkampo ahosi. Rājā bhīto theraṃ pucchi – “kasmā, bhante, pathavī kampatī”ti? “Mā bhāyi, mahārāja, imasmiṃ dīpe dasabalassa sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhahissati; idañca paṭhamaṃ vihāraṭṭhānaṃ bhavissati, tassetaṃ pubbanimitta”nti. Rājā bhiyyosomattāya [V 1.0058] pasīdi. Thero punadivasepi rājageheyeva bhuñjitvā nandanavane anamataggiyāni kathesi. Punadivase aggikkhandhopamasuttaṃ kathesi. Etenevupāyena satta divasāni kathesi. Desanāpariyosāne aḍḍhanavamānaṃ pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Tato paṭṭhāya [P 1.0082] ca nandanavanaṃ sāsanassa jotipātubhāvaṭṭhānanti katvā “jotivana”nti nāmaṃ labhi. Sattame pana divase therā antepure rañño appamādasuttaṃ kathayitvā cetiyagirimeva agamaṃsu.

The king, after that night had passed, approached the elder and inquired about his restful sleep. Then he asked, 'Venerable sir, is a monastery suitable for the community of bhikkhus?' The elder replied, 'It is suitable, great king,' and recited this discourse: 'I allow, bhikkhus, a monastery.' Delighted, the king took a golden water vessel, poured water on the elder’s hand, and donated the Mahāmeghavana pleasure park. Together with the pouring of the water, the earth trembled. This was the first earthquake at the Mahāvihāra. Frightened, the king asked the elder, 'Venerable sir, why does the earth tremble?' The elder reassured him, 'Do not fear, great king. The Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One will be established on this island, and this will be the first monastery site; this is the forerunner of that.' The king became even more exceedingly confident. The next day, the elder again ate in the royal palace and preached in Nandana Grove the discourses connected with the inconceivable beginning. On the following day, he taught the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta. In this way, he taught for seven days. At the conclusion of the discourse, eight thousand five hundred beings attained the penetration of the Dhamma. From then on, because it was the place where the Dispensation shone forth, Nandana Grove received the name 'Jotivana'. On the seventh day, the elders taught the Appamāda Sutta to the king in the inner palace and then went to Cetiyagiri itself.

Atha kho rājā amacce pucchi – “thero, amhe gāḷhena ovādena ovadati; gaccheyya nu kho”ti? Amaccā “tumhehi, deva, thero ayācito sayameva āgato; tasmā tassa anāpucchāva gamanampi bhaveyyā”ti āhaṃsu. Tato rājā rathaṃ abhiruhitvā dve ca deviyo āropetvā cetiyagiriṃ agamāsi mahañcarājānubhāvena. Gantvā deviyo ekamantaṃ apakkamāpetvā sayameva therānaṃ samīpaṃ upasaṅkamanto ativiya kilantarūpo hutvā upasaṅkami. Tato naṃ thero āha – “kasmā tvaṃ, mahārāja, evaṃ kilamamāno āgato”ti? “‘Tumhe mama gāḷhaṃ ovādaṃ datvā idāni gantukāmā nu kho’ti jānanatthaṃ, bhante”ti. “Na mayaṃ, mahārāja, gantukāmā; apica vassūpanāyikakālo nāmāyaṃ mahārāja, tatra samaṇena vassūpanāyikaṭṭhānaṃ ñātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Taṃdivasameva ariṭṭho nāma amacco pañcapaṇṇāsāya jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhabhātukehi saddhiṃ rañño samīpe ṭhito āha – “icchāmahaṃ, deva, therānaṃ santike pabbajitu”nti. “Sādhu, bhaṇe, pabbajassū”ti rājā anujānitvā theraṃ sampaṭicchāpesi. Thero tadaheva pabbājesi. Sabbe khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

Then the king asked his ministers, 'The elder is admonishing us with a strong admonition; might he be intending to depart?' The ministers replied, 'Your Majesty, the elder came to you of his own accord, unasked; therefore, he might depart without asking permission.' Thereupon, the king mounted his chariot, took his two queens with him, and went to Cetiyagiri with great royal majesty. Upon arriving, he had the queens step aside and approached the elders himself, appearing extremely weary. The elder then asked him, 'Great king, why have you come here so exhausted?' The king replied, 'Venerable sirs, I came to find out whether you, after giving me such a strong admonition, now intend to depart.' 'Great king, we do not wish to depart. However, this is the time for the rains-residence, and it is proper for a recluse to know a place for the rains-residence.' That very day, a minister named Ariṭṭha, standing before the king along with fifty-five elder and younger brothers, said, 'Your Majesty, I wish to go forth into homelessness in the presence of the elders.' The king granted permission, saying, 'Very well, my good man, go forth,' and entrusted them to the elder. The elder ordained them that same day. All of them attained Arahantship at the very tip of the razor.

Rājāpi kho taṅkhaṇeyeva kaṇṭakena cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ parikkhipitvā dvāsaṭṭhiyā leṇesu kammaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nagarameva agamāsi. Tepi therā [P 1.0083] dasabhātikasamākulaṃ rājakulaṃ pasādetvā mahājanaṃ ovadamānā cetiyagirimhi vassaṃ vasiṃsu. Tadāpi cetiyagirimhi paṭhamaṃ vassaṃ upagatā dvāsaṭṭhi [M 1.0062] arahanto ahesuṃ. Athāyasmā mahāmahindo vutthavasso pavāretvā kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ uposathadivase rājānaṃ etadavoca – “mahārāja, amhehi ciradiṭṭho sammāsambuddho, anāthavāsaṃ vasimha, icchāma mayaṃ jambudīpaṃ gantu”nti. Rājā āha – “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhe catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahāmi, ayañca mahājano tumhe nissāya tīsu saraṇesu patiṭṭhito, kasmā tumhe ukkaṇṭhitatthā”ti? “Ciradiṭṭho no, mahārāja, sammāsambuddho, abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, tenamha ukkaṇṭhitā”ti. “Nanu, bhante, tumhe avocuttha – ‘parinibbuto sammāsambuddho’”ti. “Kiñcāpi, mahārāja, parinibbuto; atha khvassa sarīradhātuyo tiṭṭhantī”ti. “Aññātaṃ, bhante, thūpapatiṭṭhānaṃ tumhe ākaṅkhathāti. Karomi[V 1.0059], bhante, thūpaṃ, bhūmibhāgaṃ dāni vicinātha; apica, bhante, dhātuyo kuto lacchāmā”ti? “Sumanena saddhiṃ mantehi, mahārājā”ti.

At that very moment, the king had the courtyard of the cetiya enclosed with thorns, initiated the work in sixty-two caves, and then returned to the city. Those elders, having inspired faith in the royal family which was crowded with the ten brothers, spent the rains-residence on Cetiyagiri while instructing the great multitude. At that time, there were sixty-two arahants who had undertaken the first rains-residence on Cetiyagiri. Then, the Venerable Mahāmahinda, having completed the rains-residence and performed the pavāraṇā, addressed the king on the Uposatha day of the Kattika full moon: 'Great king, it has been a long time since we saw the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. We are dwelling without a refuge; we wish to go to Jambudīpa.' The king replied, 'Venerable sirs, I attend to you with the four requisites, and this great multitude has been established in the three refuges by relying on you. Why then are you discontent?' 'It has been a long time since we saw the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, great king. There is no place to perform acts of reverence—such as saluting, rising, joining palms, or doing proper service. That is why we are discontent.' 'But, venerable sirs, did you not say that the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has attained Parinibbāna?' 'Though he has attained Parinibbāna, great king, his bodily relics still remain.' 'I understand, venerable sirs, that you desire the establishment of a stupa. I will make a stupa, venerable sirs. Now, select a site. Moreover, venerable sirs, where can we obtain the relics?' 'Consult with Sumana, great king.'

“Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā sumanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “kuto dāni, bhante, dhātuyo lacchāmā”ti? Sumano āha – “appossukko tvaṃ, mahārāja, vīthiyo sodhāpetvā dhajapaṭākapuṇṇaghaṭādīhi alaṅkārāpetvā saparijano uposathaṃ samādiyitvā sabbatāḷāvacare upaṭṭhāpetvā maṅgalahatthiṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ kārāpetvā upari cassa setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā sāyanhasamaye mahānāgavanuyyānābhimukho yāhi. Addhā tasmiṃ ṭhāne [P 1.0084] dhātuyo lacchasī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Therā cetiyagirimeva agamaṃsu. Tatrāyasmā mahindatthero sumanasāmaṇeraṃ āha – “gaccha tvaṃ, sāmaṇera, jambudīpe tava ayyakaṃ asokaṃ dhammarājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena evaṃ vadehi – ‘sahāyo vo, mahārāja, devānampiyatisso buddhasāsane pasanno thūpaṃ patiṭṭhāpetukāmo, tumhākaṃ kira hatthe dhātu atthi taṃ me dethā’ti. Taṃ gahetvā sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadehi – ‘tumhākaṃ kira, mahārāja, hatthe dve dhātuyo atthi – dakkhiṇadāṭhā ca dakkhiṇakkhakañca; tato tumhe dakkhiṇadāṭhaṃ pūjetha, dakkhiṇakkhakaṃ pana mayhaṃ dethā’ti. Evañca naṃ vadehi – ‘kasmā tvaṃ, mahārāja, amhe tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ pahiṇitvā pamajjasī’”ti?

“Very well, venerable sir,” said the king. Approaching Sumana, he asked, “Venerable sir, from where shall we now obtain the relics?” Sumana replied, “Great king, be without anxiety. Have the streets cleaned and adorned with banners, flags, and filled pots. Then, observe the Uposatha with your retinue, have all musical instruments and musicians assembled, have an auspicious elephant prepared, adorned with all ornaments, and raise a white umbrella above it. In the evening, proceed towards the Mahānāgavana pleasure park. Surely, you will obtain the relics there.” The king accepted, saying, “Very well.” The elders went to Cetiyagiri. There, the Venerable Mahinda Thera addressed the novice Sumana: “Go, novice, to Jambudīpa, approach your grandfather, King Asoka, the Dhamma king, and speak thus in my name: ‘Your friend, great king, Devānampiyatissa, is devoted to the Buddha’s Dispensation and wishes to establish a stupa. It is said that you possess relics; please give them to me.’ Then, take them and approach Sakka, the king of gods, and say: ‘Great king, it is said that you possess two relics—the right tusk and the right collarbone. From those, you should venerate the right tusk, but give me the right collarbone.’ And say this to him also: ‘Why, great king, having sent us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, are you negligent?’”

“Sādhu, bhante”ti kho sumano therassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tāvadeva pattacīvaramādāya vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pāṭaliputtadvāre oruyha rañño [M 1.0063] santikaṃ gantvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājā tuṭṭho sāmaṇerassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā gandhehi ubbaṭṭetvā varamuttasadisānaṃ dhātūnaṃ pūretvā adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ upasaṅkami. Sakko devarājā sāmaṇeraṃ disvāva “kiṃ, bhante sumana, āhiṇḍasī”ti āha. “Tvaṃ, mahārāja, amhe tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ pesetvā kasmā pamajjasī”ti? “Nappamajjāmi, bhante, vadehi – ‘kiṃ karomī’”ti? “Tumhākaṃ kira hatthe dve dhātuyo atthi – dakkhiṇadāṭhā ca dakkhiṇakkhakañca; tato tumhe dakkhiṇadāṭhaṃ pūjetha, dakkhiṇakkhakaṃ pana mayhaṃ dethā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho sakko devānamindo yojanappamāṇaṃ maṇithūpaṃ ugghāṭetvā dakkhiṇakkhakadhātuṃ nīharitvā sumanassa adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā cetiyagirimhiyeva patiṭṭhāsi.

“Very well, venerable sir,” Sumana accepted the elder's words. At that very moment, taking his bowl and robe, he rose into the sky, descended at the gate of Pāṭaliputta, and went to the king to convey this matter. The delighted king took the bowl from the novice's hands, rubbed it with perfumes, filled it with relics resembling excellent pearls, and gave it. Taking it, Sumana approached Sakka, the king of gods. Sakka, the king of gods, upon the very sight of the novice, said, “Why, Venerable Sumana, are you wandering about?” “You, great king, sent us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi—why are you negligent?” “I am not negligent, venerable sir. Tell me, what should I do?” “It is said that in your possession are two relics—the right tusk and the right collarbone. From those, you should venerate the right tusk, but give the right collarbone to me.” “Very well, venerable sir,” said Sakka, the lord of gods. He opened the jeweled stupa, which was a yojana in size, extracted the right collarbone relic, and gave it to Sumana. Taking it, he established himself on Cetiyagiri itself.

Atha kho mahindapamukhā sabbepi te mahānāgā [P 1.0085] asokadhammarājena dinnadhātuyo cetiyagirimhiyeva patiṭṭhāpetvā dakkhiṇakkhakaṃ ādāya vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya mahānāgavanuyyānamagamaṃsu[V 1.0060]. Rājāpi kho sumanena vuttappakāraṃ pūjāsakkāraṃ katvā hatthikkhandhavaragato sayaṃ maṅgalahatthimatthake setacchattaṃ dhārayamāno mahānāgavanaṃ sampāpuṇi. Athassa etadahosi – “sace ayaṃ sammāsambuddhassa dhātu, chattaṃ apanamatu, maṅgalahatthī jaṇṇukehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahatu, dhātucaṅkoṭakaṃ mayhaṃ matthake patiṭṭhātū”ti. Saha rañño cittuppādena chattaṃ apanami, hatthī jaṇṇukehi patiṭṭhahi, dhātucaṅkoṭakaṃ rañño matthake patiṭṭhahi. Rājā amateneva abhisittagatto viya paramena pītipāmojjena samannāgato hutvā pucchi – “dhātuṃ, bhante, kiṃ karomā”ti? “Hatthikumbhamhiyeva tāva, mahārāja, ṭhapehī”ti. Rājā dhātucaṅkoṭakaṃ gahetvā hatthikumbhe ṭhapesi. Pamudito nāgo koñcanādaṃ nadi. Mahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā pokkharavassaṃ vassi. Udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahābhūmicālo ahosi. “Paccantepi nāma sammāsambuddhassa dhātu patiṭṭhahissatī”ti devamanussā pamodiṃsu. Evaṃ iddhānubhāvasiriyā devamanussānaṃ pītiṃ janayanto –

Then all those great ones, led by Mahinda, having enshrined the relics given by King Asoka, the Dhamma king, on Cetiyagiri itself, took the right collarbone relic and, in the afternoon when the shadows lengthen, proceeded to the Mahānāgavana pleasure park. The king too, having performed the offerings and honors as instructed by Sumana, mounted on the back of the excellent elephant, himself holding a white parasol over the auspicious elephant's head, reached the Mahānāgavana. Then this thought occurred to him: “If this is truly a relic of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, let the parasol lower itself, let the auspicious elephant kneel on the ground with its knees, and let the relic casket rest upon my head.” Simultaneously with the arising of the king's thought, the parasol lowered, the elephant knelt with its knees, and the relic casket rested upon the king's head. The king, as if his body were anointed with ambrosia, possessed of supreme joy and delight, asked, “Venerable sirs, what shall we do with the relic?” “For now, great king, place it on the elephant's frontal globe.” The king took the relic casket and placed it on the elephant's frontal globe. The delighted elephant trumpeted a crane-like cry. A great cloud arose and rained a lotus-shower. A great earthquake occurred, reaching to the edge of the waters. “Indeed, even in the borderlands a relic of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One will be established!” Thus gods and humans rejoiced. In this way, generating joy in gods and humans with the splendor of his psychic power and majesty—

Puṇṇamāyaṃ mahāvīro, cātumāsiniyā idha;

Āgantvā devalokamhā, hatthikumbhe patiṭṭhitoti.

On the full-moon day of Cātumāsinī, the Great Hero, having come here from the world of the gods, was established on the elephant's frontal globe.

Athassa so hatthināgo anekatāḷāvacaraparivārito ativiya uḷārena pūjāsakkārena sakkariyamāno pacchimadisābhimukhova hutvā, apasakkanto [M 1.0064] yāva nagarassa puratthimadvāraṃ tāva gantvā puratthimena dvārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā sakalanāgarena [P 1.0086] uḷārāya pūjāya karīyamānāya dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā thūpārāmassa pacchimadisābhāge mahejavatthu nāma kira atthi, tattha gantvā puna thūpārāmābhimukhoyeva paṭinivatti. Tena ca samayena thūpārāme purimakānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ paribhogacetiyaṭṭhānaṃ hoti.

Then that noble elephant, surrounded by many musicians and musical instruments and being honored with exceedingly great offerings and respects, faced the western direction and, retreating, went as far as the eastern gate of the city. Entering the city through the eastern gate, while great offerings were being made by the entire city, it exited through the southern gate and went to a place called Mahejavatthu in the western part of the Thūpārāma. Having gone there, it turned back again to face the Thūpārāma. And at that time, in the Thūpārāma was the site of the cetiyas of use of the three previous Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones.

Atīte kira ayaṃ dīpo ojadīpo nāma ahosi, rājā abhayo nāma, nagaraṃ abhayapuraṃ nāma, cetiyapabbato devakūṭapabbato nāma, thūpārāmo paṭiyārāmo nāma. Tena kho pana samayena kakusandho bhagavā loke uppanno hoti. Tassa sāvako mahādevo nāma thero bhikkhusahassena saddhiṃ devakūṭe patiṭṭhāsi, mahindatthero viya cetiyapabbate. Tena kho pana samayena ojadīpe sattā pajjarakena anayabyasanaṃ āpajjanti. Addasā kho kakusandho bhagavā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ olokento te satte anayabyasanamāpajjante. Disvā cattālīsāya bhikkhusahassehi parivuto agamāsi. Tassānubhāvena tāvadeva pajjarako vūpasanto. Roge vūpasante bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi. Caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Bhagavā dhamakaraṇaṃ [V 1.0061] datvā pakkāmi. Taṃ anto pakkhipitvā paṭiyārāme cetiyaṃ akaṃsu. Mahādevo dīpaṃ anusāsanto vihāsi.

In the past, it is said, this island was named Ojadīpa, the king was named Abhaya, the city was named Abhayapura, Cetiyapabbata was named Devakūṭapabbata, and the Thūpārāma was named Paṭiyārāma. At that time, the Blessed One Kakusandha had arisen in the world. His disciple, the Elder Mahādeva, established himself on Devakūṭa with a thousand bhikkhus, just as the Elder Mahinda on Cetiyapabbata. During that time, the beings in Ojadīpa were falling into ruin and destruction due to a pestilence. The Blessed One Kakusandha, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw those beings falling into ruin and destruction. Having seen this, he went there accompanied by forty thousand bhikkhus. By his power, the pestilence subsided at that very moment. When the disease subsided, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma. Eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma. The Blessed One, having given a water-strainer, departed. Having enshrined it within, they made a cetiya in Paṭiyārāma. The Elder Mahādeva dwelt there, instructing the island.

Koṇāgamanassa pana bhagavato kāle ayaṃ dīpo varadīpo nāma ahosi, rājā sameṇḍī nāma, nagaraṃ vaḍḍhamānaṃ nāma[P 1.0087], pabbato suvaṇṇakūṭo nāma. Tena kho pana samayena varadīpe dubbuṭṭhikā hoti dubbhikkhaṃ dussassaṃ. Sattā chātakarogena anayabyasanaṃ āpajjanti. Addasā kho koṇāgamano bhagavā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ olokento te satte anayabyasanaṃ āpajjante. Disvā tiṃsabhikkhusahassaparivuto agamāsi. Buddhānubhāvena devo sammādhāraṃ anuppavecchi. Subhikkhaṃ ahosi. Bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi. Caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Bhagavā bhikkhusahassaparivāraṃ mahāsumanaṃ nāma theraṃ dīpe ṭhapetvā kāyabandhanaṃ datvā pakkāmi. Taṃ anto pakkhipitvā cetiyaṃ akaṃsu.

At the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, this island was called Varadīpa. The king was named Sameṇḍī, the city was Vaḍḍhamāna, and the mountain was Suvaṇṇakūṭa. During that time in Varadīpa, there was drought, famine, and poor harvests. Beings fell into ruin and destruction due to the disease of hunger. The Blessed One Koṇāgamana, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw those beings falling into ruin and destruction. Having seen this, he went there accompanied by thirty thousand bhikkhus. By the Buddha’s power, rain fell in proper showers. There was abundance. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma. Eighty-four thousand living beings attained realization of the Dhamma. The Blessed One, having established the Elder Mahāsumana, who was accompanied by a thousand bhikkhus, on the island, and having given a girdle, departed. Having enshrined it within, they built a cetiya.

Kassapassa pana bhagavato kāle ayaṃ dīpo maṇḍadīpo nāma ahosi, rājā jayanto nāma, nagaraṃ visālaṃ nāma, pabbato subhakūṭo nāma[M 1.0065]. Tena kho pana samayena maṇḍadīpe mahāvivādo hoti. Bahū sattā kalahaviggahajātā anayabyasanaṃ āpajjanti. Addasā kho kassapo bhagavā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ olokento te satte anayabyasanaṃ āpajjante. Disvā vīsatibhikkhusahassaparivuto āgantvā vivādaṃ vūpasametvā dhammaṃ desesi. Caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Bhagavā bhikkhusahassaparivāraṃ sabbanandaṃ nāma theraṃ dīpe patiṭṭhāpetvā udakasāṭakaṃ datvā pakkāmi. Taṃ anto pakkhipitvā cetiyaṃ akaṃsu. Evaṃ thūpārāme purimakānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ cetiyāni patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tāni sāsanantaradhānena nassanti, ṭhānamattaṃ avasissati. Tasmā vuttaṃ – “tena ca samayena thūpārāme purimakānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ paribhogacetiyaṭṭhānaṃ hotī”ti. Tadetaṃ vinaṭṭhesu cetiyesu [P 1.0088] devatānubhāvena kaṇṭakasamākiṇṇasākhehi nānāgacchehi parivutaṃ tiṭṭhati – “mā naṃ koci ucchiṭṭhāsucimalakacavarehi padūsesī”ti.

At the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, this island was called Maṇḍadīpa. The king was named Jayanta, the city was named Visāla, and the mountain was named Subhakūṭa. At that time, there was a great conflict in Maṇḍadīpa. Many beings, having become engaged in quarrels and disputes, fell into ruin and destruction. The Blessed One Kassapa, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw those beings falling into ruin and destruction. Having seen this, he arrived with an entourage of twenty thousand bhikkhus, pacified the conflict, and taught the Dhamma. Eighty-four thousand living beings attained realization of the Dhamma. The Blessed One, having established the Elder named Sabbananda, who was accompanied by a thousand bhikkhus, on the island, and having given a bathing-cloth, departed. They enshrined it and built a cetiya. Thus, in the Thūpārāma, cetiyas of the three previous Buddhas were established. These were destroyed with the disappearance of the Dispensation, leaving only the site. Therefore it is said: “At that time, in the Thūpārāma, there was the site of a cetiya for the use of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas.” Though those cetiyas have perished, by the power of the devas, the place remains surrounded by various bushes with thorn-covered branches—so that no one may defile it with leftovers, impurities, filth, and rubbish.

Atha khvassa hatthino purato purato gantvā rājapurisā sabbagacche chinditvā bhūmiṃ sodhetvā taṃ hatthatalasadisaṃ akaṃsu. Hatthināgo gantvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ purato katvā tassa pacchimadisābhāge bodhirukkhaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Athassa matthakato dhātuṃ oropetuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Nāgo oropetuṃ na deti. Rājā theraṃ pucchi – “kasmā, bhante, nāgo dhātuṃ oropetuṃ na detī”ti? “Ārūḷhaṃ, mahārāja, oropetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Tasmiñca kāle abhayavāpiyā udakaṃ [V 1.0062] chinnaṃ hoti. Samantā bhūmi phalitā hoti, suuddharā mattikāpiṇḍā. Tato mahājano sīghaṃ sīghaṃ mattikaṃ āharitvā hatthikumbhappamāṇaṃ vatthumakāsi. Tāvadeva ca thūpakaraṇatthaṃ iṭṭhakā kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Na yāva iṭṭhakā pariniṭṭhanti tāva hatthināgo katipāhaṃ divā bodhirukkhaṭṭhāne hatthisālāyaṃ tiṭṭhati, rattiṃ thūpapatiṭṭhānabhūmiṃ pariyāyati. Atha vatthuṃ cināpetvā rājā theraṃ pucchi – “kīdiso, bhante, thūpo kātabbo”ti? “Vīhirāsisadiso, mahārājā”ti.

Then, the king's men, going ahead of the elephant, cut down all the bushes, cleared the ground, and made it like the palm of a hand. The great elephant, having gone, placed that spot before it and stood in the western part, at the place of the Bodhi tree. Then, they began to bring down the relic from its head. The elephant would not allow it to be brought down. The king asked the elder, "Why, venerable sir, does the elephant not allow the relic to be brought down?" "It is not fitting, great king, to bring down what has been mounted." At that time, the water in the Abhaya tank had been cut off. The surrounding ground was cracked, and lumps of clay were easily extracted. Then, the great populace quickly brought clay and made a foundation the size of an elephant's forehead protuberance. At that very moment, they began making bricks for the purpose of building the stupa. For as long as the bricks were not yet finished, the great elephant stood for some days in the elephant stable at the place of the Bodhi tree during the day, and at night circumambulated the site where the stupa was to be established. After having the foundation constructed, the king asked the elder, "What kind of stupa, venerable sir, should be built?" "Like a heap of paddy, great king."

“Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā jaṅghappamāṇaṃ thūpaṃ cināpetvā dhātuoropanatthāya mahāsakkāraṃ kāresi. Sakalanagarañca janapado ca dhātumahadassanatthaṃ sannipati. Sannipatite ca pana tasmiṃ mahājanakāye dasabalassa [M 1.0066] dhātu hatthikumbhato sattatālappamāṇaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. Tehi tehi dhātuppadesehi channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ udakadhārā ca aggikkhandhā ca pavattanti, sāvatthiyaṃ kaṇḍambamūle bhagavatā dassitapāṭihāriyasadisameva [P 1.0089] pāṭihāriyaṃ ahosi. Tañca kho neva therānubhāvena, na devatānubhāvena; apica kho buddhānubhāveneva. Bhagavā kira dharamānova adhiṭṭhāsi – “mayi parinibbute tambapaṇṇidīpe anurādhapurassa dakkhiṇadisābhāge purimakānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ paribhogacetiyaṭṭhāne mama dakkhiṇakkhakadhātu patiṭṭhānadivase yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ hotū”ti.

“Excellent, venerable sir,” said the king, and had a stūpa built to the height of a pedestal. For the purpose of lowering the relic, he arranged a great veneration. The entire city and the country gathered for the purpose of seeing the great relic festival. And when that great populace had assembled, the relic of the One of Ten Powers, having ascended into the air to the height of seven palm trees from the elephant's frontal globe, displayed the twin miracle. From those various parts of the relic, streams of water and masses of fire of six colors proceeded; the miracle was just like the miracle shown by the Blessed One at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree in Sāvatthī. And this was not by the power of the Elder, nor by the power of deities; but indeed, it was solely by the power of the Buddha. It is said the Blessed One, while still living, made this resolution: “When I have attained Parinibbāna, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, in the southern quarter of Anurādhapura, at the place of the cetiya of use of the three previous Buddhas, on the day of the establishment of my right collarbone relic, let the twin miracle occur.”

“Evaṃ acintiyā buddhā, buddhadhammā acintiyā;

Acintiye pasannānaṃ, vipāko hoti acintiyo”ti. (apa. thera 1.1.82);

“Thus, Buddhas are inconceivable, the qualities of a Buddha are inconceivable; for those who have faith in the inconceivable, the result is also inconceivable.”

Sammāsambuddho kira imaṃ dīpaṃ dharamānakālepi tikkhattuṃ āgamāsi. Paṭhamaṃ – yakkhadamanatthaṃ ekakova āgantvā yakkhe dametvā “mayi parinibbute imasmiṃ dīpe sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhahissatī”ti tambapaṇṇidīpe rakkhaṃ karonto tikkhattuṃ dīpaṃ āvijji. Dutiyaṃ – mātulabhāgineyyānaṃ nāgarājūnaṃ damanatthāya ekakova āgantvā te dametvā agamāsi. Tatiyaṃ – pañcabhikkhusataparivāro āgantvā mahācetiyaṭṭhāne ca thūpārāmacetiyaṭṭhāne ca mahābodhipatiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne ca mahiyaṅgaṇacetiyaṭṭhāne ca mutiyaṅgaṇacetiyaṭṭhāne ca dīghavāpicetiyaṭṭhāne ca kalyāṇiyacetiyaṭṭhāne ca nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Idamassa catutthaṃ dhātusarīrena āgamanaṃ.

It is said that the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One visited this island three times even while living. First, for the purpose of subduing the yakkhas, he came alone, subdued the yakkhas, and thinking, “When I have attained Parinibbāna, the teaching will be established on this island,” he established a protection on the island of Tambapaṇṇi and circled the island three times. Second, for the purpose of subduing the nāga kings, his maternal uncle and nephew, he came alone, subdued them, and departed. Third, he came with an entourage of five hundred monks and sat down, having entered the attainment of cessation, at the site of the Mahācetiya, at the site of the Thūpārāma Cetiya, at the place where the Great Bodhi would be established, at the site of the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Cetiya, at the site of the Mutiyaṅgaṇa Cetiya, at the site of the Dīghavāpi Cetiya, and at the site of the Kalyāṇiya Cetiya. This was his fourth coming, by means of the relic-body.

Dhātusarīrato [V 1.0063] ca panassa nikkhantaudakaphusitehi sakalatambapaṇṇitale na koci aphuṭṭhokāso nāma ahosi. Evamassa taṃ dhātusarīraṃ udakaphusitehi tambapaṇṇitalassa pariḷāhaṃ vūpasametvā mahājanassa pāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā otaritvā rañño matthake patiṭṭhāsi[P 1.0090]. Rājā saphalaṃ manussapaṭilābhaṃ maññamāno mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ karitvā dhātuṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Saha dhātupatiṭṭhāpanena mahābhūmicālo ahosi. Tasmiñca pana dhātupāṭihāriye cittaṃ pasādetvā rañño bhātā abhayo nāma rājakumāro purisasahassena saddhiṃ pabbaji. Cetaraṭṭhagāmato pañca dārakasatāni pabbajiṃsu, tathā dvāramaṇḍalādīhi gāmakehi nikkhamitvā pañcapañca [M 1.0067] dārakasatāni sabbānipi antonagarato ca bahinagarato ca pabbajitāni tiṃsabhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Niṭṭhite pana thūpasmiṃ rājā ca rājabhātikā ca deviyo ca devanāgayakkhānampi vimhayakaraṃ paccekaṃ paccekaṃ pūjaṃ akaṃsu. Niṭṭhitāya pana dhātupūjāya patiṭṭhite dhātuvare mahindatthero meghavanuyyānameva gantvā vāsaṃ kappesi.

And by the water droplets that issued from his relic-body, there was no place whatsoever on the entire surface of Tambapaṇṇi that was untouched. Thus that relic-body of his, by means of the water droplets, having allayed the burning heat of the surface of Tambapaṇṇi and having displayed the miracle to the great populace, descended and established itself on the king's head. The king, considering the attainment of a human state to be fruitful, made a great veneration and had the relic established. Together with the establishment of the relic, there was a great earthquake. And having felt confidence in their hearts at that relic-miracle, the king's brother, the prince named Abhaya, went forth together with a thousand men. From the village of Cetaraṭṭha, five hundred boys went forth; likewise, having departed from the small villages of Dvāramaṇḍala and others, five hundred boys each went forth. All those who had gone forth from within the city and from outside the city amounted to thirty thousand monks. When the stūpa was completed, the king, the king's brothers, and the queens each individually made offerings that were astonishing even to the devas, nāgas, and yakkhas. When the relic veneration was concluded and the excellent relic was established, the Elder Mahinda went to the Meghavana park itself and took up residence.

Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye anuḷā devī pabbajitukāmā hutvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā tassā vacanaṃ sutvā theraṃ etadavoca – “anuḷā, bhante, devī pabbajitukāmā, pabbājetha na”nti. “Na, mahārāja, amhākaṃ mātugāmaṃ pabbājetuṃ kappati. Pāṭaliputte pana mayhaṃ bhaginī saṅghamittattherī nāma atthi, taṃ pakkosāpehi. Imasmiñca pana, mahārāja, dīpe purimakānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ bodhi patiṭṭhāsi. Amhākampi bhagavato sarasaraṃsijālavissajjanakena bodhinā idha patiṭṭhātabbaṃ, tasmā tathā sāsanaṃ pahiṇeyyāsi yathā saṅghamittā bodhiṃ gahetvā āgaccheyyā”ti.

Now at that time, Queen Anulā, desiring to go forth, informed the king. The king, having heard her words, said this to the Elder: “Venerable sir, Queen Anulā desires to go forth; please have her go forth.” “No, great king, it is not allowable for us to give the going forth to a woman. But in Pāṭaliputta there is my sister named the Elder Saṅghamittā; have her summoned. And moreover, great king, on this island the Bodhi trees of the three previous Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones were established. The Bodhi tree of our Blessed One, which emits a net of succulent rays, should also be established here. Therefore, you should send a message in such a way that Saṅghamittā might come bringing the Bodhi tree.”

“Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā therassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā amaccehi saddhiṃ mantento ariṭṭhaṃ nāma attano bhāgineyyaṃ āha – “sakkhissasi tvaṃ, tāta, pāṭaliputtaṃ gantvā mahābodhinā saddhiṃ ayyaṃ saṅghamittattheriṃ ānetu”nti? “Sakkhissāmi, deva, sace me pabbajjaṃ anujānissasī”ti. “Gaccha, tāta[P 1.0091], theriṃ ānetvā pabbajāhī”ti. So rañño ca therassa ca sāsanaṃ gahetvā therassa adhiṭṭhānavasena ekadivaseneva jambukolapaṭṭanaṃ gantvā nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddaṃ atikkamitvā pāṭaliputtameva agamāsi. Anuḷāpi kho devī pañcahi kaññāsatehi pañcahi ca antepurikāsatehi saddhiṃ dasa sīlāni samādiyitvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā nagarassa ekadese upassayaṃ kārāpetvā nivāsaṃ kappesi. Ariṭṭhopi taṃdivasameva rañño sāsanaṃ appesi, evañca avoca – “putto te, deva, mahindatthero evamāha – ‘sahāyakassa kira te devānampiyatissassa rañño bhātu jāyā anuḷā nāma devī pabbajitukāmā[V 1.0064], taṃ pabbājetuṃ ayyaṃ saṅghamittattheriṃ pahiṇatha, ayyāyeva ca saddhiṃ mahābodhi’”nti. Therassa sāsanaṃ ārocetvā saṅghamittattheriṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – “ayye, tumhākaṃ bhātā mahindatthero maṃ tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pesesi, devānampiyatissassa rañño bhātu jāyā anuḷā nāma devī [M 1.0068] pañcahi kaññāsatehi, pañcahi ca antepurikāsatehi saddhiṃ pabbajitukāmā, taṃ kira āgantvā pabbājethā”ti. Sā tāvadeva turitaturitā rañño santikaṃ gantvā evamāha – “mahārāja, mayhaṃ bhātā mahindatthero evaṃ pahiṇi, ‘rañño kira bhātu jāyā anuḷā nāma devī pañcahi kaññāsatehi pañcahi ca antepurikāsatehi saddhiṃ pabbajitukāmā mayhaṃ āgamanaṃ udikkhati’. Gacchāmahaṃ, mahārāja, tambapaṇṇidīpa”nti.

"Very well, venerable sir," said the king, accepting the elder’s words. Then, consulting with his ministers, he addressed his nephew named Ariṭṭha: "Dear one, will you be able to go to Pāṭaliputta and bring the revered elder nun Saṅghamittā along with the great Bodhi tree?" "I will be able, Your Majesty, if you grant me permission to be ordained." "Go, dear one, bring the elder nun and then be ordained." Taking the message of both the king and the elder, by the elder’s power of resolve, he reached Jambukolapaṭṭana in a single day, boarded a ship, crossed the ocean, and went straight to Pāṭaliputta. Queen Anuḷā, along with five hundred maidens and five hundred palace women, undertook the ten precepts, donned ochre robes, had a residence built in a certain part of the city, and took up her dwelling there. On that very day, Ariṭṭha delivered the king's message and also said this: "Your Majesty, your son, the elder Mahinda, says this: ‘It is said that Anuḷā, the wife of the brother of your friend, King Devānampiyatissa, wishes to be ordained. Please send the revered elder nun Saṅghamittā to ordain her, and also send the great Bodhi tree along with the revered one.’" Having delivered the elder’s message, he approached the elder nun Saṅghamittā and said this: "Revered lady, your brother, the elder Mahinda, has sent me to you. It is said that Anuḷā, the wife of the brother of King Devānampiyatissa, along with five hundred maidens and five hundred palace women, wishes to be ordained. Please come and ordain her." She, at that very moment, hurrying with great haste, went to the king and said this: "Great king, my brother, the elder Mahinda, has sent this message: ‘It is said that Anuḷā, the wife of the king’s brother, along with five hundred maidens and five hundred palace women, wishes to be ordained and awaits my arrival.’ I shall go, great king, to the island of Tambapaṇṇi."

Rājā āha – “amma, puttopi me mahindatthero nattā ca me sumanasāmaṇero maṃ chinnahatthaṃ viya karontā tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ [P 1.0092] gatā. Tassa mayhaṃ tepi apassantassa uppanno soko tava mukhaṃ passantassa vūpasammati! Alaṃ, amma, mā tvaṃ agamāsī”ti. “Bhāriyaṃ me, mahārāja, bhātu vacanaṃ; anuḷāpi khattiyā itthisahassaparivutā pabbajjāpurekkhārā maṃ paṭimāneti; gacchāmahaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi, amma, mahābodhiṃ gahetvā gacchāhī”ti. Kuto rañño mahābodhi? Rājā kira tato pubbe eva dhātuggahaṇatthāya anāgate sumane laṅkādīpaṃ mahābodhiṃ pesetukāmo, “kathaṃ nu kho asatthaghātārahaṃ mahābodhiṃ pesessāmī”ti upāyaṃ apassanto mahādevaṃ nāma amaccaṃ pucchi. So āha – “santi, deva, bahū paṇḍitā bhikkhū”ti. Taṃ sutvā rājā bhikkhusaṅghassa bhattaṃ paṭiyādetvā bhattakiccāvasāne saṅghaṃ pucchi – “gantabbaṃ nu kho, bhante, bhagavato mahābodhinā laṅkādīpaṃ no”ti? Saṅgho moggaliputtatissattherassa bhāraṃ akāsi.

The king said: "Dear daughter, my son, the elder Mahinda, and my grandson, the novice Sumana, have gone to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, making me as if with severed hands. The sorrow that arises for me in not seeing them subsides when I see your face. Enough, dear daughter, do not go." "Great king, my brother’s word is weighty to me; and the noble lady Anuḷā, surrounded by a thousand women, with ordination as her foremost aim, awaits me. I shall go, great king." "In that case, dear daughter, take the great Bodhi tree and go." From where did the king have the great Bodhi tree? It is said that before this, before Sumana had come for the purpose of taking the relics, the king desired to send the great Bodhi tree to the island of Laṅkā. Thinking, "How indeed shall I send the great Bodhi tree, which is not fit to be cut by a weapon?" and not seeing a way, he asked a minister named Mahādeva. He said: "Your Majesty, there are many wise monks." Hearing that, the king had a meal prepared for the community of monks, and at the conclusion of the meal, he asked the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, should the great Bodhi tree of the Blessed One go to the island of Laṅkā, or should it not?" The Saṅgha assigned the responsibility to the elder Moggaliputtatissa.

Thero “gantabbaṃ, mahārāja, mahābodhinā laṅkādīpa”nti vatvā bhagavato pañca mahāadhiṭṭhānāni kathesi. Katamāni pañca? Bhagavā kira mahāparinibbānamañce nipanno laṅkādīpe mahābodhipatiṭṭhāpanatthāya “asokamahārājā mahābodhiggahaṇatthaṃ gamissati, tadā mahābodhissa dakkhiṇasākhā sayameva chijjitvā suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhātū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi – idamekamadhiṭṭhānaṃ.

The elder said: "Great king, the great Bodhi tree must go to the island of Laṅkā." Having said this, he related the five great resolutions of the Blessed One. What are the five? It is said that the Blessed One, while lying on his great parinibbāna couch, for the sake of establishing the great Bodhi tree on the island of Laṅkā, resolved: "The great king Asoka will go for the purpose of taking the great Bodhi tree. At that time, may the right branch of the great Bodhi tree break off by itself and become established in a golden vessel." This is the first resolution.

Tattha patiṭṭhānakāle ca “mahābodhi himavalāhakagabbhaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhātū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi – idaṃ dutiyamadhiṭṭhānaṃ.

And at the time of its establishment therein, he resolved: "May the great Bodhi tree become established after entering into a mass of snowy clouds." This is the second resolution.

“Sattame [M 1.0069][V 1.0065] divase himavalāhakagabbhato oruyha suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhahanto pattehi ca phalehi ca chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo muñcatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi – idaṃ tatiyamadhiṭṭhānaṃ.

He resolved: "On the seventh day, descending from the mass of snowy clouds and becoming established in the golden vessel, may it emit six-colored rays from its leaves and fruits." This is the third resolution.

“Thūpārāme dakkhiṇakkhakadhātu cetiyamhi patiṭṭhānadivase yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi – idaṃ catutthaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ.

He resolved: "May the right collar-bone relic perform the Twin Miracle on the day of its establishment in the cetiya at the Thūpārāma." This is the fourth resolution.

Laṅkādīpamhiyeva me doṇamattā dhātuyo mahācetiyamhi patiṭṭhānakāle [P 1.0093] buddhavesaṃ gahetvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karontū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi – idaṃ pañcamaṃ adhiṭṭhānanti.

He resolved: "On the island of Laṅkā itself, at the time of their establishment in the Great Cetiya, may my relics, measuring one doṇa, take on the appearance of the Buddha, rise up into the sky, and perform the Twin Miracle." This is the fifth resolution.

Rājā imāni pañca mahāadhiṭṭhānāni sutvā pasannacitto pāṭaliputtato yāva mahābodhi tāva maggaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā suvaṇṇakaṭāhatthāya bahuṃ suvaṇṇaṃ nīharāpesi. Tāvadeva ca rañño cittaṃ ñatvā vissakammadevaputto kammāravaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā purato aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā “tāta, imaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā kaṭāhaṃ karohī”ti āha. “Pamāṇaṃ, deva, jānāthā”ti? “Tvameva, tāta, ñatvā karohī”ti. “Sādhu, deva, karissāmī”ti suvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā attano ānubhāvena hatthena parimajjitvā suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ nimmini navahatthaparikkhepaṃ pañcahatthubbedhaṃ tihatthavikkhambhaṃ aṭṭhaṅgulabahalaṃ hatthisoṇḍappamāṇamukhavaṭṭiṃ. Atha rājā sattayojanāyāmāya tiyojanavitthārāya mahatiyā senāya pāṭaliputtato nikkhamitvā ariyasaṅghamādāya mahābodhisamīpaṃ agamāsi. Senā samussitadhajapaṭākaṃ nānāratanavicittaṃ anekālaṅkārapaamaṇḍitaṃ nānāvidhakusumasamākiṇṇaṃ anekatūriyasaṅghuṭṭhaṃ mahābodhiṃ parikkhipi. Rājā sahassamatte gaṇapāmokkhe mahāthere gahetvā sakalajambudīpe pattābhisekānaṃ rājūnaṃ sahassena attānañca mahābodhiñca parivārāpetvā mahābodhimūle ṭhatvā mahābodhiṃ ullokesi. Mahābodhissa khandhañca dakkhiṇamahāsākhāya catuhatthappamāṇappadesañca ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ adassanaṃ agamāsi.

The king, hearing these five great resolutions, with a devout mind had the road prepared from Pāṭaliputta up to the Great Bodhi Tree and caused much gold to be brought out for a golden bowl. At that very moment, knowing the king's intention, the divine architect Vissakamma assumed the form of a goldsmith and stood before him. The king, seeing him, said, “My dear, take this gold and make a bowl.” “Do you know the measurements, sire?” “You yourself, my dear, knowing it, make it.” “Very well, sire, I will make it.” Taking the gold, he stroked it with his hand by his own power and fashioned a golden bowl—nine cubits in circumference, five cubits in height, three cubits in width, eight fingers thick, with a rim the size of an elephant's trunk. Then the king, with a great army seven leagues long and three leagues wide, set out from Pāṭaliputta. Taking the noble Sangha with him, he went to the vicinity of the Great Bodhi Tree. The army, with banners and flags raised, adorned with various jewels and many ornaments, strewn with all kinds of flowers, and resounding with many musical instruments, encircled the Great Bodhi Tree. The king, taking a thousand leading elders, and surrounding himself and the Great Bodhi Tree with a thousand kings who had received the ceremonial sprinkling from all over Jambudīpa, stood at the foot of the Great Bodhi Tree and looked up at it. Except for the trunk of the Great Bodhi Tree and a four-cubit portion of the southern great branch, the rest became invisible.

Rājā taṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā uppannapītipāmojjo “ahaṃ, bhante, imaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā tuṭṭho mahābodhiṃ sakalajambudīparajjena pūjemī”ti bhikkhusaṅghassa vatvā abhisekaṃ adāsi. Tato [P 1.0094] pupphagandhādīhi pūjetvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vanditvā uṭṭhāya añjaliṃ paggayha [M 1.0070] ṭhatvā saccavacanakiriyāya bodhiṃ gaṇhitukāmo bhūmito yāva mahābodhissa dakkhiṇasākhā tāva uccaṃ katvā ṭhapitassa sabbaratanamayapīṭhassa upari suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ ṭhapāpetvā ratanapīṭhaṃ āruyha suvaṇṇatulikaṃ gahetvā manosilāya lekhaṃ katvā “yadi mahābodhinā laṅkādīpe patiṭṭhātabbaṃ, yadi cāhaṃ buddhasāsane nibbematiko bhaveyyaṃ, mahābodhi [V 1.0066] sayameva imasmiṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhe oruyha patiṭṭhātū”ti saccavacanakiriyamakāsi. Saha saccakiriyāya bodhisākhā manosilāya paricchinnaṭṭhāne chijjitvā gandhakalalapūrassa suvaṇṇakaṭāhassa upari aṭṭhāsi. Tassa ubbedhena dasahattho khandho hoti catuhatthā pañca mahāsākhā pañcahiyeva phalehi paṭimaṇḍitā, khuddakasākhānaṃ pana sahassaṃ. Atha rājā mūlalekhāya upari tivaṅgulappadese aññaṃ lekhaṃ paricchindi. Tato tāvadeva pupphuḷakā hutvā dasa mahāmūlāni nikkhamiṃsu. Puna uparūpari tivaṅgule tivaṅgule aññā nava lekhā paricchindi. Tāhipi dasa dasa pupphuḷakā hutvā navuti mūlāni nikkhamiṃsu. Paṭhamakā dasa mahāmūlā caturaṅgulamattaṃ nikkhantā. Itarepi gavakkhajālasadisaṃ anusibbantā nikkhantā. Ettakaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ rājā ratanapīṭhamatthake ṭhitoyeva disvā añjaliṃ paggayha mahānādaṃ nadi. Anekāni bhikkhusahassāni sādhukāramakaṃsu. Sakalarājasenā unnādinī ahosi. Celukkhepasatasahassāni pavattayiṃsu. Bhūmaṭṭhakadeve ādiṃ katvā yāva brahmakāyikā devā [P 1.0095] tāva sādhukāraṃ pavattayiṃsu. Rañño imaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ passantassa pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭasarīrassa añjaliṃ paggahetvā ṭhitasseva mahābodhi mūlasatena suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhāsi. Dasa mahāmūlāni suvaṇṇakaṭāhatalaṃ āhacca aṭṭhaṃsu. Avasesāni navuti khuddakamūlāni anupubbena vaḍḍhanakāni hutvā gandhakalale oruyha ṭhitāni.

The king, seeing that miracle, was filled with joy and delight. He said to the Sangha of monks, “Venerable sirs, having seen this miracle, I am pleased and will honor the Great Bodhi Tree with the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa.” Having spoken thus, he performed the consecration. Then, having honored it with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, he circumambulated it three times, paid homage at eight places, and stood up with hands reverently joined. Wishing to take the Bodhi sapling by a solemn declaration of truth, he had a golden bowl placed upon a jeweled platform raised as high as the southern branch of the Great Bodhi Tree. Then, ascending the jeweled platform and taking a golden stylus, he made a mark with red arsenic and declared, “If the Great Bodhi Tree is to be established in the island of Laṅkā, and if I have unwavering faith in the Buddha’s dispensation, may the Great Bodhi Tree itself descend into this golden bowl and be established there.” No sooner had he made this solemn declaration than the Bodhi branch broke off at the marked spot and stood in the golden bowl filled with fragrant paste. Its trunk was ten cubits high, with five great branches, each four cubits long and adorned with five fruits, and a thousand smaller branches. Then the king made another mark three finger-widths above the original mark. Immediately, ten great roots emerged like buds. Again, at intervals of three finger-widths, he made nine more marks. From each of these, ten roots emerged, totaling ninety roots. The first ten great roots extended four finger-widths, while the others emerged, intertwining like a lattice window. Seeing this miracle while standing atop the jeweled platform, the king raised his hands in reverence and uttered a great shout. Thousands of monks acclaimed it. The entire royal army was tumultuous. A hundred thousand cloths were waved in celebration. From the earth-dwelling devas up to the Brahmā-world devas, all acclaimed it. As the king stood there, his body overflowing with continuous joy, his hands raised in reverence, the Great Bodhi Tree took root in the golden bowl with a hundred roots. The ten great roots reached the bottom of the golden bowl and stood firm, while the remaining ninety smaller roots gradually grew and descended into the fragrant paste.

Evaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhitamatte mahābodhimhi mahāpathavī cali. Ākāse devadundubhiyo phaliṃsu. Pabbatānaṃ naccehi devānaṃ sādhukārehi yakkhānaṃ hiṅkārehi asurānaṃ thutijappehi brahmānaṃ apphoṭanehi meghānaṃ gajjitehi catuppadānaṃ ravehi pakkhīnaṃ rutehi sabbatāḷāvacarānaṃ [M 1.0071] sakasakapaṭibhānehi pathavītalato yāva brahmalokā tāva ekakolāhalaṃ ekaninnādaṃ ahosi. Pañcasu sākhāsu phalato phalato chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo nikkhamitvā sakalacakkavāḷaṃ ratanagopānasīvinaddhaṃ viya kurumānā yāva brahmalokā abbhuggacchiṃsu. Taṃ khaṇato ca pana pabhuti satta divasāni mahābodhi himavalāhakagabbhaṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhāsi. Na koci mahābodhiṃ passati. Rājā ratanapīṭhato oruyha satta divasāni mahābodhipūjaṃ kāresi. Sattame divase sabbadisāhi himā ca chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo ca āvattitvā mahābodhimeva pavisiṃsu. Vigatahimavalāhake vippasanne cakkavāḷagabbhe mahābodhi paripuṇṇakhandhasākhāpasākho [P 1.0096] pañcaphalapaṭimaṇḍito suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhitova paññāyittha. Rājā mahābodhiṃ disvā tehi pāṭihāriyehi sañjātapītipāmojjo “sakalajambudīparajjena taruṇamahābodhiṃ pūjessāmī”ti abhisekaṃ datvā satta divasāni mahābodhiṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Thus, at the very moment the Great Bodhi was established in the golden bowl, the great earth shook. In the sky, celestial drums resounded. With the dances of the mountains, the cries of 'Sādhu' from the devas, the 'hiṅ, hiṅ' sounds of the yakkhas, the sounds of praise from the asuras, the clapping of hands by the brahmās, the thunder of the clouds, the roars of four-footed creatures, the calls of birds, and with the sounds from all musical instruments, each arising from the player's own inspiration—from the surface of the earth up to the Brahma world, there arose a single great uproar, a single resounding echo. From each and every fruit on the five branches, six-colored rays issued forth, rising up to the Brahma world, making the entire Cakkavāḷa as if it were interwoven with jeweled rafters. Furthermore, from that moment on, for seven days, the Great Bodhi entered into the womb of a snow-cloud and remained. No one saw the Great Bodhi. The king, descending from the jeweled seat, had worship of the Great Bodhi performed for seven days. On the seventh day, the snows and the six-colored rays from all directions turned back and entered the Great Bodhi itself. When the Cakkavāḷa-sphere was devoid of the snow-cloud and had become perfectly clear, the Great Bodhi, complete with trunk, main branches, and minor branches, adorned with five fruits, appeared as established in the golden bowl. The king, having seen the Great Bodhi, and with joy and delight having arisen on account of these miracles, thought, “I will honor the young Great Bodhi with the sovereignty of all Jambudīpa!” He gave an anointing and remained for seven days at the very place of the Great Bodhi.

Mahābodhi [V 1.0067] pubbakattikapavāraṇādivase sāyanhasamaye paṭhamaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhahi. Tato himagabbhasattāhaṃ abhisekasattāhañca vītināmetvā kāḷapakkhassa uposathadivase rājā ekadivaseneva pāṭaliputtaṃ pavisitvā kattikajuṇhapakkhassa pāṭipadadivase mahābodhiṃ pācīnamahāsālamūle ṭhapesi. Suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patiṭṭhitadivasato sattarasame divase mahābodhissa abhinavaṅkurā pāturahesuṃ. Te disvāpi pasanno rājā puna mahābodhiṃ rajjena pūjento sakalajambudīpābhisekamadāsi. Tadā sumanasāmaṇero kattikapuṇṇamadivase dhātuggahaṇatthaṃ gato mahābodhissa kattikachaṇapūjaṃ addasa. Evaṃ mahābodhimaṇḍato ānetvā pāṭaliputte ṭhapitaṃ mahābodhiṃ sandhāya āha – “tena hi, amma, mahābodhiṃ gahetvā gacchāhī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

The Great Bodhi was first established in the golden bowl in the evening on the Pavāraṇā day associated with the Pubbakattikā constellation. Then, after passing the seven days in the snow-womb and the seven days of anointing, the king entered Pāṭaliputta in a single day on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight. On the first day of the bright fortnight of Kattika, he placed the Great Bodhi at the foot of the great Sāla tree to the east. On the seventeenth day from the day it was established in the golden bowl, new shoots appeared on the Great Bodhi. Seeing them, the pleased king, while honoring the Great Bodhi again with the sovereignty, bestowed the anointing of all Jambudīpa. At that time, the novice Sumana, who had gone to obtain relics on the full-moon day of Kattika, saw the Kattika festival offering for the Great Bodhi. Thus, with reference to the Great Bodhi that was brought from the Mahābodhimaṇḍa and placed in Pāṭaliputta, he said, “Well then, mother, take the Great Bodhi and go.” She replied, “Very well,” and accepted.

Rājā mahābodhirakkhaṇatthāya aṭṭhārasa devatākulāni, aṭṭha amaccakulāni, aṭṭha brāhmaṇakulāni, aṭṭha kuṭumbiyakulāni, aṭṭha gopakakulāni, aṭṭha taracchakulāni, aṭṭha ca kāliṅgakulāni datvā udakasiñcanatthāya ca aṭṭha suvaṇṇaghaṭe, aṭṭha ca rajataghaṭe datvā iminā parivārena mahābodhiṃ [M 1.0072] gaṅgāya nāvaṃ [P 1.0097] āropetvā sayampi nagarato nikkhamitvā vijjhāṭaviṃ samatikkamma anupubbena sattahi divasehi tāmalittiṃ anuppatto. Antarāmagge devanāgamanussā uḷāraṃ mahābodhipūjaṃ akaṃsu. Rājāpi samuddatīre satta divasāni mahābodhiṃ ṭhapetvā sakalajambudīpamahārajjaṃ adāsi. Idamassa tatiyaṃ jambudīparajjasampadānaṃ hoti.

The king, for the protection of the Great Bodhi, gave eighteen families of devatās, eight families of ministers, eight families of brahmins, eight families of householders, eight families of Gopakās, eight families of Taracchas, and eight families of Kāliṅgas. For the purpose of pouring water, he also gave eight golden pots and eight silver pots. With this retinue, he placed the Great Bodhi onto a ship on the Ganges and, departing from the city himself, crossed the Vindhya forest and, in due course, reached Tāmalitti in seven days. Along the way, devas, nāgas, and humans made a magnificent offering to the Great Bodhi. The king also, having placed the Great Bodhi on the seashore for seven days, gave the great sovereignty of all Jambudīpa. This was his third bestowal of the sovereignty of Jambudīpa.

Evaṃ mahārajjena pūjetvā māgasiramāsassa paṭhamapāṭipadadivase asoko dhammarājā mahābodhiṃ ukkhipitvā galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ oruyha nāvāyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā saṅghamittattherimpi saparivāraṃ nāvaṃ āropetvā ariṭṭhaṃ amaccaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ, tāta, mahābodhiṃ tikkhattuṃ sakalajambudīparajjena pūjetvā galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ oruyha mama sahāyakassa pesesiṃ, sopi evameva mahābodhiṃ pūjetū”ti. Evaṃ sahāyakassa sāsanaṃ datvā “gacchati vatare, dasabalassa sarasaraṃsijālaṃ vimuñcanto mahābodhirukkho”ti vanditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā assūni pavattayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Sāpi kho mahābodhisamārūḷhā nāvā passato passato mahārājassa mahāsamuddatalaṃ pakkhantā. Mahāsamuddepi samantā yojanaṃ vīciyo vūpasantā; pañca vaṇṇāni padumāni pupphitāni; antalikkhe dibbāni tūriyāni pavajjiṃsu; ākāse jalajathalajarukkhādisannissitāhi devatāhi pavattitā ativiya uḷārā pūjā ahosi. Saṅghamittattherīpi supaṇṇarūpena mahāsamudde nāgakulāni santāsesi. Te ca utrastarūpā nāgā āgantvā taṃ vibhūtiṃ passitvā theriṃ yācitvā mahābodhiṃ nāgabhavanaṃ atiharitvā satta divasāni [V 1.0068] nāgarajjena [P 1.0098] pūjetvā puna nāvāyaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ. Taṃdivasameva nāvā jambukolapaṭṭanaṃ agamāsi. Asokamahārājāpi mahābodhiviyogadukkhito kanditvā roditvā yāva dassanavisayaṃ oloketvā paṭinivatti.

Thus, having honored it with great sovereignty, on the first day of the month of Māgasira, Asoka the Dhamma-king lifted up the Great Bodhi, descended into water up to the measure of his throat, and established it on the ship. He also had Saṅghamittā Therī together with her retinue board the ship and said this to the minister Ariṭṭha: “My dear sir, I, having honored the Great Bodhi three times with the sovereignty of all Jambudīpa, and having descended into water up to the measure of my throat, have sent it to my friend. May he also honor the Great Bodhi in this very same way.” Thus, having given the message for his friend, he stood, causing tears to flow, with his hands raised in añjali, paying homage, saying: “Alas, the Great Bodhi tree, releasing the net of potent rays of the one of Ten Powers, is going!” And that very ship, which the Great Bodhi had boarded, sped into the surface of the great ocean even as the great king watched. In the great ocean also, for a yojana all around, the waves were stilled; five-colored lotuses bloomed; in the sky, celestial musical instruments played; an exceedingly magnificent offering, set in motion by the devatās dwelling in aquatic and terrestrial trees and other such places, occurred in the sky. Saṅghamittā Therī also, in the form of a Supaṇṇa, terrified the nāga families in the great ocean. And those nāgas, being terrified, came, saw that splendor, and having requested the Therī, they carried the Great Bodhi to the nāga-abode, honored it for seven days with the sovereignty of the nāgas, and then established it again on the ship. On that very day, the ship reached the port of Jambukola. Great King Asoka also, afflicted with sorrow from the separation from the Great Bodhi, having cried and lamented, looked as far as sight could reach and turned back.

Devānampiyatisso mahārājāpi kho sumanasāmaṇerassa vacanena māgasiramāsassa paṭhamapāṭipadadivasato pabhuti uttaradvārato paṭṭhāya yāva jambukolapaṭṭanaṃ tāva maggaṃ sodhāpetvā alaṅkārāpetvā nagarato nikkhamanadivase uttaradvārasamīpe samuddasālavatthusmiṃ ṭhitoyeva tāya vibhūtiyā mahāsamudde āgacchantaṃyeva mahābodhiṃ therassa [M 1.0073] ānubhāvena disvā tuṭṭhamānaso nikkhamitvā sabbaṃ maggaṃ pañcavaṇṇehi pupphehi okirāpento antarantare pupphaagghiyāni ṭhapento ekāheneva jambukolapaṭṭanaṃ gantvā sabbatāḷāvacaraparivuto pupphadhūmagandhavāsādīhi pūjayamāno galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ oruyha “āgato vatare, dasabalassa sarasaraṃsijālavissajjanako mahābodhirukkho”ti pasannacitto mahābodhiṃ ukkhipitvā uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā mahābodhiṃ parivāretvā āgatehi soḷasahi jātisampannakulehi saddhiṃ samuddato paccuttaritvā samuddatīre mahābodhiṃ ṭhapetvā tīṇi divasāni sakalatambapaṇṇidīparajjena pūjesi, soḷasannaṃ jātisampannakulānaṃ rajjaṃ vicāresi. Atha catutthe divase mahābodhiṃ ādāya uḷāraṃ pūjaṃ kurumāno anupubbena anurādhapuraṃ sampatto. Anurādhapurepi mahāsakkāraṃ katvā cātuddasīdivase vaḍḍhamānakacchāyāya mahābodhiṃ uttaradvārena pavesetvā nagaramajjhena atiharanto [P 1.0099] dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā dakkhiṇadvārato pañcadhanusatike ṭhāne yattha amhākaṃ sammāsambuddho nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi, purimakā ca tayo sammāsambuddhā samāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdiṃsu, yattha kakusandhassa bhagavato mahāsirīsabodhi, konāgamanassa bhagavato udumbarabodhi, kassapasammāsambuddhassa ca nigrodhabodhi patiṭṭhāsi, tasmiṃ mahāmeghavanuyyānassa tilakabhūte sumanasāmaṇerassa vacanena paṭhamameva katabhūmiparikamme rājavatthudvārakoṭṭhakaṭṭhāne mahābodhiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

King Devānampiyatissa, by the word of the novice Sumana, from the first day of the month of Māgasira, starting from the northern gate, had the road cleared and adorned as far as the port of Jambukola. On the day of departure from the city, standing near the northern gate at the place of the Samuddasāla grove, with that splendor, he, by the power of the Elder, saw the great Bodhi tree while it was still arriving on the great ocean. With a delighted mind, he set out, causing the entire road to be scattered with flowers of five colors, placing flower stūpas at intervals, and reached the port of Jambukola in just one day. Surrounded by all kinds of musical instruments and worshipping with flowers, incense, perfumes, and scents, he descended into the water up to the measure of his throat. With a faithful heart, he exclaimed: “Oh, it has come! The great Bodhi tree, the emitter of the net of potent rays of the Ten-Powered One!” Having lifted the great Bodhi tree and established it on his head, the most excellent limb, he, together with the sixteen clans of high birth who had come surrounding the great Bodhi tree, ascended again from the ocean. Having placed the great Bodhi tree on the seashore, for three days he worshipped it with the sovereignty of the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, and he had the sixteen clans of high birth administer the kingdom. Then, on the fourth day, taking the great Bodhi tree and performing a grand worship, he arrived in Anurādhapura by stages. In Anurādhapura also, having made a great offering, on the fourteenth day, in the afternoon when the shadow was increasing, he had the great Bodhi tree enter by the northern gate. Carrying it through the middle of the city, he exited by the southern gate. At a place five hundred bow-lengths from the southern gate, where our Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, having entered into the attainment of cessation, sat, and where the three former Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, having entered into the attainment, sat; where the great Sirīsa Bodhi of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Udumbara Bodhi of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Nigrodha Bodhi of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Kassapa were established—there, at the site of the gatehouse of the royal park, which was like an ornament of the Mahāmeghavana park and where the ground preparation had been done beforehand by the word of the novice Sumana, he caused the great Bodhi tree to be established.

Kathaṃ? Tāni kira bodhiṃ parivāretvā āgatāni soḷasa jātisampannakulāni rājavesaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Rājā dovārikavesaṃ gaṇhi. Soḷasa kulāni mahābodhiṃ gahetvā oropayiṃsu. Mahābodhi tesaṃ hatthato muttasamanantarameva asītihatthappamāṇaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo muñci. Raṃsiyo sakaladīpaṃ pattharitvā upari brahmalokaṃ āhacca aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahābodhipāṭihāriyaṃ disvā sañjātappasādāni dasapurisasahassāni anupubbavipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ patvā pabbajiṃsu. Yāva sūriyatthaṅgamā mahābodhi antalikkhe aṭṭhāsi. Atthaṅgamite pana [V 1.0069] sūriye rohiṇinakkhattena pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi. Saha bodhipatiṭṭhānā udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī akampi. Patiṭṭhahitvā ca pana mahābodhi satta divasāni himagabbhe sannisīdi. Lokassa adassanaṃ agamāsi. Sattame [M 1.0074] divase vigatavalāhakaṃ nabhaṃ ahosi. Chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo jalantā vipphurantā nicchariṃsu. Mahābodhissa khandho ca sākhāyo ca pattāni [P 1.0100] ca pañca phalāni ca dassiṃsu. Mahindatthero ca saṅghamittattherī ca rājā ca saparivārā mahābodhiṭṭhānameva agamaṃsu. Yebhuyyena ca sabbe dīpavāsino sannipatiṃsu. Tesaṃ passantānaṃyeva uttarasākhato ekaṃ phalaṃ paccitvā sākhato mucci. Thero hatthaṃ upanāmesi. Phalaṃ therassa hatthe patiṭṭhāsi. Taṃ thero “ropaya, mahārājā”ti rañño adāsi. Rājā gahetvā suvaṇṇakaṭāhe madhurapaṃsuṃ ākiritvā gandhakalalaṃ pūretvā ropetvā mahābodhiāsannaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sabbesaṃ passantānaṃyeva catuhatthappamāṇā aṭṭha taruṇabodhirukkhā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Rājā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā aṭṭha taruṇabodhirukkhe setacchattena pūjetvā abhisekaṃ adāsi. Tato ekaṃ bodhirukkhaṃ āgamanakāle mahābodhinā paṭhamapatiṭṭhitokāse jambukolapaṭṭane ropayiṃsu, ekaṃ tavakkabrāhmaṇassa gāmadvāre, ekaṃ thūpārāme, ekaṃ issaranimmānavihāre, ekaṃ paṭhamacetiyaṭṭhāne, ekaṃ cetiyapabbate, ekaṃ rohaṇajanapadamhi kājaragāme, ekaṃ rohaṇajanapadamhiyeva candanagāme. Itaresaṃ catunnaṃ phalānaṃ bījehi jāte dvattiṃsa bodhitaruṇe yojaniyaārāmesu patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

How? It is said that those sixteen clans of high birth who had come surrounding the Bodhi tree took the guise of kings. The king took the guise of a doorkeeper. The sixteen clans, having taken the great Bodhi tree, lowered it. Immediately upon being released from their hands, the great Bodhi tree ascended into the sky to a height of eighty cubits and released rays of six colors. The rays, having spread over the entire island and reached the Brahma world above, remained there. Seeing the miracle of the great Bodhi tree, ten thousand men in whom faith had arisen, having established insight in sequence, attained Arahantship and went forth. Until sunset, the great Bodhi tree remained in the sky. When the sun had set, it was established on the earth under the Rohiṇī constellation. Simultaneously with the establishment of the Bodhi tree, the great earth trembled up to its water-boundary. And after being established, the great Bodhi tree remained for seven days within a womb of mist, becoming unseen by the world. On the seventh day, the sky became free of clouds. Rays of six colors, blazing and flashing about, issued forth. The trunk, branches, leaves, and five fruits of the great Bodhi tree became visible. The Elder Mahinda, the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā, and the king with his retinue all went to the place of the great Bodhi tree. And for the most part, all the inhabitants of the island assembled. While they were watching, one fruit from the northern branch ripened and was released from the branch. The Elder extended his hand. The fruit was established in the Elder's hand. The Elder gave it to the king, saying, “Plant it, great king.” The king, having taken it, poured sweet earth into a golden bowl, filled it with fragrant mud, planted it, and placed it in a spot near the great Bodhi tree. While everyone was watching, eight young Bodhi trees, four cubits in measure, arose. The king, seeing this wonder, honored the eight young Bodhi trees with a white parasol and bestowed a consecration. Then, one Bodhi tree they planted at the port of Jambukola, in the place where the great Bodhi tree was first established upon its arrival; one at the village gate of the brahmin Tavakka; one at the Thūpārāma; one at the Issaranimmāna Monastery; one at the site of the first cetiya; one on Cetiya Mountain; one in the village of Kājara in the Rohaṇa district; and one in the village of Candana, also in the Rohaṇa district. The thirty-two young Bodhi trees that grew from the seeds of the other four fruits they had established in monasteries within a yojana.

Evaṃ puttanattuparamparāya samantā dīpavāsīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya patiṭṭhite dasabalassa dhammadhajabhūte mahābodhimhi [P 1.0101] anuḷā devī pañcahi kaññāsatehi pañcahi ca antepurikāsatehīti mātugāmasahassena saddhiṃ saṅghamittattheriyā santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva saparivārā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Ariṭṭhopi kho rañño bhāgineyyo pañcahi purisasatehi saddhiṃ therassa santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva saparivāro arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

Thus, when the great Bodhi tree—the Dhamma-banner of the Ten-Powered One—was established all around for the welfare and happiness of the island-dwellers through the lineage of sons and grandsons, Queen Anuḷā, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the inner palace, thus with a thousand women, went forth in the presence of the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā and, not long after, was established in Arahantship with her retinue. And Ariṭṭha, the king's nephew, having gone forth in the presence of the Elder together with five hundred men, was also, not long after, established in Arahantship with his retinue.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā mahābodhiṃ vanditvā therena saddhiṃ thūpārāmaṃ gacchati. Tassa lohapāsādaṭṭhānaṃ sampattassa purisā pupphāni abhihariṃsu. Rājā therassa pupphāni adāsi. Thero pupphehi lohapāsādaṭṭhānaṃ pūjesi. Pupphesu bhūmiyaṃ patitamattesu mahābhūmicālo ahosi. Rājā “kasmā, bhante, bhūmi calitā”ti pucchi. “Ismiṃ, mahārāja, okāse saṅghassa anāgate uposathāgāraṃ bhavissati, tassetaṃ pubbanimitta”nti.

Then one day, the king, having paid homage to the great Bodhi tree, went with the Elder to the Thūpārāma. When he arrived at the site of the Lohapāsāda, men brought him flowers. The king offered the flowers to the Elder. The Elder honored the site of the Lohapāsāda with the flowers. As soon as the flowers fell upon the ground, a great earthquake occurred. The king asked, “Venerable sir, why did the ground shake?” The Elder replied, “Great king, in this place, in the future, there will be an Uposatha hall for the Saṅgha; this is its premonitory sign.”

Rājā [M 1.0075] puna therena saddhiṃ gacchanto ambaṅgaṇaṭṭhānaṃ patto. Tatthassa vaṇṇagandhasampannaṃ atimadhurarasaṃ ekaṃ ambapakkaṃ āharīyittha. Rājā taṃ therassa paribhogatthāya adāsi. Thero tattheva [V 1.0070] paribhuñjitvā “idaṃ ettheva ropethā”ti āha. Rājā taṃ ambaṭṭhiṃ gahetvā tattheva ropetvā udakaṃ āsiñci. Saha ambabījaropanena pathavī akampi. Rājā “kasmā, bhante, pathavī kampitthā”ti pucchi. “Imasmiṃ, mahārāja, okāse saṅghassa anāgate ‘ambaṅgaṇaṃ’ nāma sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissati, tassetaṃ pubbanimitta”nti.

As the king proceeded again with the Elder, he reached the site of the Ambaṅgaṇa. There, a single ripe mango fruit, endowed with color and fragrance and possessing an exceedingly sweet taste, was brought to him. The king offered it to the Elder for his consumption. The Elder consumed it right there and said, “Plant this here.” The king took the mango stone, planted it there, and poured water on it. Simultaneously with the planting of the mango seed, the earth trembled. The king asked, “Venerable sir, why did the earth shake?” The Elder replied, “Great king, in this place, in the future, there will be a gathering place for the Saṅgha named ‘Ambaṅgaṇa.’ This is its premonitory sign.”

Rājā tattha aṭṭha pupphamuṭṭhiyo okiritvā vanditvā puna therena saddhiṃ gacchanto mahācetiyaṭṭhānaṃ patto. Tatthassa purisā campakapupphāni abhihariṃsu. Tāni rājā therassa adāsi. Thero mahācetiyaṭṭhānaṃ pupphehi pūjetvā vandi. Tāvadeva mahāpathavī saṅkampi. Rājā “kasmā, bhante, pathavī kampitthā”ti pucchi. “Imasmiṃ, mahārāja, okāse anāgate buddhassa bhagavato asadiso mahāthūpo bhavissati, tassetaṃ [P 1.0102] pubbanimitta”nti. “Ahameva karomi, bhante”ti. “Alaṃ, mahārāja, tumhākaṃ aññaṃ bahukammaṃ atthi, tumhākaṃ pana nattā duṭṭhagāmaṇī abhayo nāma kāressatī”ti. Atha rājā “sace, bhante, mayhaṃ nattā karissati, kataṃyeva mayā”ti dvādasahatthaṃ pāsāṇatthambhaṃ āharāpetvā “devānampiyatissassa rañño nattā duṭṭhagāmaṇī abhayo nāma imasmiṃ padese thūpaṃ karotū”ti akkharāni likhāpetvā patiṭṭhāpetvā vanditvā theraṃ pucchi – “patiṭṭhitaṃ nu kho, bhante, tambapaṇṇidīpe sāsana”nti? “Patiṭṭhitaṃ, mahārāja, sāsanaṃ; mūlāni panassa na tāva otarantī”ti. “Kadā pana, bhante mūlāni otiṇṇāni nāma bhavissantī”ti? “Yadā, mahārāja, tambapaṇṇidīpakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ tambapaṇṇidīpe jāto dārako tambapaṇṇidīpe pabbajitvā tambapaṇṇidīpamhiyeva vinayaṃ uggahetvā tambapaṇṇidīpe vācessati, tadā sāsanassa mūlāni otiṇṇāni nāma bhavissantī”ti. “Atthi pana, bhante, ediso bhikkhū”ti? “Atthi, mahārāja, mahāariṭṭho bhikkhu paṭibalo etasmiṃ kamme”ti. “Mayā ettha, bhante, kiṃ kattabba”nti? “Maṇḍapaṃ, mahārāja, kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā meghavaṇṇābhayassa amaccassa pariveṇaṭṭhāne mahāsaṅgītikāle ajātasattumahārājena katamaṇḍapappakāraṃ rājānubhāvena maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sabbatāḷāvacare sakasakasippesu payojetvā “sāsanassa mūlāni otarantāni [M 1.0076] passissāmī”ti anekapurisasahassaparivuto thūpārāmaṃ anuppatto.

There, the king scattered eight handfuls of flowers, paid homage, and then, proceeding again with the Elder, reached the site of the Great Cetiya. There, his men brought him campaka flowers. The king gave them to the Elder. The Elder honored the site of the Great Cetiya with the flowers and paid homage. At that very moment, the great earth trembled. The king asked, “Venerable sir, why did the earth tremble?” “Great king, in this place in the future, there will be a great stupa for the Blessed One, the Buddha, that is without parallel. This is its premonitory sign.” “Venerable sir, I myself will do it.” “Let it be, great king. You have much other work to do. However, your grandson, the king named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, will cause it to be built.” Then the king said, “If, venerable sir, my grandson will build it, it is as if it were done by me.” He had a twelve-cubit stone pillar brought and, having had the words inscribed: “May the grandson of King Devānampiyatissa, named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, build a stupa in this place,” he had it set up, paid homage, and asked the Elder, “Venerable sir, has the Dispensation been established in Tambapaṇṇidīpa?” “Great king, the Dispensation has been established, but its roots have not yet descended.” “When, venerable sir, will the roots be said to have descended?” “Great king, when a child born in Tambapaṇṇidīpa to parents of Tambapaṇṇidīpa goes forth in Tambapaṇṇidīpa, learns the Vinaya in Tambapaṇṇidīpa itself, and teaches it in Tambapaṇṇidīpa—then the roots of the Dispensation will be said to have descended.” “Is there, venerable sir, such a bhikkhu?” “There is, great king. The bhikkhu Mahāariṭṭha is capable in this task.” “What should be done by me in this matter, venerable sir?” “Great king, it is fitting to have a pavilion made.” “Very well, venerable sir.” The king, at the site of the pariveṇa of the minister Meghavaṇṇābhaya, by his royal power, had a pavilion made in the manner of the pavilion made by King Ajātasattu at the time of the Great Council, and having engaged all the musicians in their respective skills, and thinking, “I will see the roots of the Dispensation descend,” arrived at the Thūpārāma surrounded by many thousands of men.

Tena kho pana samayena thūpārāme aṭṭhasaṭṭhi bhikkhusahassāni sannipatiṃsu. Mahāmahindattherassa āsanaṃ dakkhiṇābhimukhaṃ [P 1.0103] paññattaṃ hoti. Mahāariṭṭhattherassa dhammāsanaṃ uttarābhimukhaṃ paññattaṃ hoti. Atha kho mahāariṭṭhatthero mahindattherena ajjhiṭṭho attano anurūpena pattānukkamena dhammāsane nisīdi. Mahindattherapamukhā aṭṭhasaṭṭhi mahātherā dhammāsanaṃ parivāretvā [V 1.0071] nisīdiṃsu. Raññopi kaniṭṭhabhātā mattābhayatthero nāma “dhuraggāho hutvā vinayaṃ uggaṇhissāmī”ti pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ mahāariṭṭhattherassa dhammāsanameva parivāretvā nisīdi. Avasesāpi bhikkhū sarājikā ca parisā attano attano pattāsane nisīdiṃsu.

At that time, sixty-eight thousand bhikkhus assembled at the Thūpārāma. A seat for the Elder Mahāmahinda was prepared facing south. A Dhamma seat for the Elder Mahāariṭṭha was prepared facing north. Then, the Elder Mahāariṭṭha, having been invited by the Elder Mahinda, sat on the Dhamma seat according to the sequence appropriate to him. The sixty-eight great elders, with the Elder Mahinda as their chief, sat surrounding the Dhamma seat.
