The king’s younger brother, named the Elder Mattābhaya, thinking, “Taking the lead, I will learn the Vinaya,” sat with five hundred bhikkhus surrounding the very Dhamma seat of the Elder Mahāariṭṭha. The remaining bhikkhus, and the assembly together with the king, sat in their own respective seats.

Athāyasmā mahāariṭṭhatthero tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharati naḷerupucimandamūleti vinayanidānaṃ abhāsi. Bhāsite ca panāyasmatā ariṭṭhattherena vinayanidāne ākāsaṃ mahāviravaṃ ravi. Akālavijjulatā nicchariṃsu. Devatā sādhukāraṃ adaṃsu. Mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā saṅkampi. Evaṃ anekesu pāṭihāriyesu vattamānesu āyasmā ariṭṭhatthero mahāmahindapamukhehi aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyā paccekagaṇīhi khīṇāsavamahātherehi tadaññehi ca aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusahassehi parivuto paṭhamakattikapavāraṇādivase thūpārāmavihāramajjhe satthu karuṇāguṇadīpakaṃ bhagavato anusiṭṭhikarānaṃ kāyakammavacīkammavipphanditavinayanaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ pakāsesi. Pakāsetvā ca yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhamāno bahūnaṃ vācetvā bahūnaṃ hadaye patiṭṭhāpetvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Tepi kho mahāmahindappamukhā tasmiṃ samāgame –

Then the Venerable Mahāariṭṭhatthera recited the Vinaya Nidāna, beginning with, 'At that time the Blessed One was dwelling in Verañjā at the foot of the Naḷeru Pucimanda tree.' And as the Vinaya Nidāna was being recited by the Venerable Ariṭṭhatthera, the sky resounded with a great sound. Unseasonal lightning flashed forth. The devas gave their cries of approval. The great earth trembled up to its ocean boundary. While these numerous miracles were occurring, the Venerable Ariṭṭhatthera—surrounded by sixty-eight great elders who were destroyers of the taints and individual group leaders, headed by Mahāmahinda, and by sixty-eight thousand other bhikkhus—on the day of the first Kattika Pavāraṇā, in the middle of the Thūpārāma monastery, expounded the Vinaya Piṭaka, which reveals the Teacher's quality of compassion and is the subduer of the agitation of bodily and verbal actions for those who follow the Blessed One's instruction. And having expounded it, remaining for the extent of his lifespan, having taught it to many, having established it in the hearts of many, he attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. And those headed by Mahāmahinda, at that assembly—

“Aṭṭhasaṭṭhi [P 1.0104] mahātherā, dhuraggāhā samāgatā;

Paccekagaṇino sabbe, dhammarājassa sāvakā.

Sixty-eight great elders, foremost burden-bearers, assembled; all were individual group leaders, disciples of the Dhamma King.

“Khīṇāsavā vasippattā, tevijjā iddhikovidā;

Uttamatthamabhiññāya, anusāsiṃsu rājino.

Destroyers of the taints, who had attained mastery, possessors of the three knowledges, skilled in psychic power; having directly known the supreme goal, they instructed the king.

“Ālokaṃ dassayitvāna, obhāsetvā mahiṃ imaṃ;

Jalitvā aggikkhandhāva, nibbāyiṃsu mahesayo”.

Having shown the light, having illuminated this earth, blazing like masses of fire, the great seers attained Nibbāna.

Tesaṃ [M 1.0077] parinibbānato aparabhāge aññepi tesaṃ therānaṃ antevāsikā tissadattakāḷasumana-dīghasumanādayo ca mahāariṭṭhattherassa antevāsikā, antevāsikānaṃ antevāsikā cāti evaṃ pubbe vuttappakārā ācariyaparamparā imaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ yāvajjatanā ānesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

In the period after their Parinibbāna, other pupils of those elders—such as Tissadatta, Kāḷasumana, and Dīghasumana—and the pupils of the Elder Mahāariṭṭha, and the pupils of their pupils, thus in this way, the lineage of teachers of the kind previously mentioned brought this Vinaya Piṭaka down to the present day. Therefore it was said:

“Tatiyasaṅgahato pana uddhaṃ imaṃ dīpaṃ mahindādīhi ābhataṃ, mahindato uggahetvā kañci [V 1.0072] kālaṃ ariṭṭhattherādīhi ābhataṃ, tato yāvajjatanā tesaṃyeva antevāsikaparamparabhūtāya ācariyaparamparāya ābhata”nti.

But after the Third Council, it was brought to this island by Mahinda and others. Having learned it from Mahinda, it was transmitted for some time by the Elder Ariṭṭha and others. From then until today, it has been transmitted by the lineage of teachers which is the succession of their very pupils.

Kattha patiṭṭhitanti? Yesaṃ pāḷito ca atthato ca anūnaṃ vattati, maṇighaṭe pakkhittatelamiva īsakampi na paggharati, evarūpesu adhimattasati-gati-dhiti-mantesu lajjīsu kukkuccakesu sikkhākāmesu puggalesu patiṭṭhitanti veditabbaṃ. Tasmā vinayapatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ vinayapariyattiyā ānisaṃsaṃ sallakkhetvā sikkhākāmena bhikkhunā vinayo pariyāpuṇitabbo.

Where is it established? It should be known to be established in such persons in whom it exists undiminished both in text and in meaning, not leaking even a little, like oil poured into a jeweled pot; in persons possessed of exceptional mindfulness, wisdom, and energy, who are conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of the training. Therefore, for the purpose of establishing the Vinaya, a bhikkhu desirous of the training should master the Vinaya, having marked its benefits.

Tatrāyaṃ vinayapariyattiyā ānisaṃso – vinayapariyattikusalo hi puggalo sāsane paṭiladdhasaddhānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ mātāpituṭṭhāniyo hoti, tadāyattā hi nesaṃ pabbajjā upasampadā vattānuvattapaṭipatti ācāragocarakusalatā. Api cassa vinayapariyattiṃ nissāya attano sīlakkhandho sugutto hoti surakkhito; kukkuccapakatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hoti; visārado saṅghamajjhe voharati; paccatthike sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhāti; saddhammaṭṭhitiyā [P 1.0105] paṭipanno hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “pañcime, bhikkhave, ānisaṃsā vinayadhare puggale; attano sīlakkhandho sugutto hoti surakkhito…pe… saddhammaṭṭhitiyā paṭipanno hotī”ti (pari. 325).

Herein, this is the benefit of mastering the Vinaya: Indeed, a person skilled in mastering the Vinaya stands in the place of a mother and father to clansmen who have gained faith in the Dispensation, for their going forth, higher ordination, practice of the duties, and skill in proper conduct and resort depend on that person. Moreover, by relying on mastery of the Vinaya, one’s own aggregate of virtue becomes well-guarded and well-protected. One becomes a refuge for bhikkhus afflicted by scruples. One speaks confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha. One rightly restrains opponents with the Dhamma. One is practicing for the stability of the True Dhamma. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in a person who is a master of the Vinaya: one’s own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected… one is practicing for the stability of the True Dhamma.'

Ye cāpi saṃvaramūlakā kusalā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā, vinayadharo puggalo tesaṃ dāyādo; vinayamūlakattā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ. Vuttampi hetaṃ bhagavatā – “vinayo saṃvaratthāya, saṃvaro avippaṭisāratthāya, avippaṭisāro pāmojjatthāya, pāmojjaṃ pītatthāya, pīti passaddhatthāya, passaddhi sukhatthāya, sukhaṃ samādhatthāya, samādhi yathābhūtañāṇadassanatthāya, yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ nibbidatthāya, nibbidā virāgatthāya, virāgo vimuttatthāya[M 1.0078], vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanatthāya, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ anupādāparinibbānatthāya. Etadatthā kathā, etadatthā mantanā, etadatthā upanisā, etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ – yadidaṃ anupādācittassa vimokkho”ti (pari. 366). Tasmā vinayapariyattiyā āyogo karaṇīyoti.

And whatever wholesome states rooted in restraint have been spoken by the Blessed One, a person who is a master of the Vinaya is an heir to them, because those states are rooted in the Vinaya. For this was also said by the Blessed One: 'The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint; restraint is for the purpose of non-remorse; non-remorse is for the purpose of joy; joy is for the purpose of rapture; rapture is for the purpose of tranquility; tranquility is for the purpose of happiness; happiness is for the purpose of concentration; concentration is for the purpose of knowledge and vision of things as they truly are; knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is for the purpose of disenchantment; disenchantment is for the purpose of dispassion; dispassion is for the purpose of liberation; liberation is for the purpose of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the knowledge and vision of liberation is for the purpose of final Nibbāna through non-clinging. For this purpose is talk, for this purpose is counsel, for this purpose is the supporting condition, for this purpose is the lending of the ear—that is, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.' Therefore, exertion should be made in mastering the Vinaya.

Ettāvatā ca yā sā vinayasaṃvaṇṇanatthaṃ mātikā ṭhapitā tattha –

And thus far, with regard to the outline that was established for the purpose of expounding the Vinaya—

“Vuttaṃ yena yadā yasmā, dhāritaṃ yena cābhataṃ;

Yatthappatiṭṭhitaṃ cetametaṃ, vatvā vidhiṃ tato”ti.

By whom it was spoken, when, and from whom; by whom it was borne and brought; and where it is established—having stated this, then the method.

Imissā tāva gāthāya attho pakāsito vinayassa ca bāhiranidānavaṇṇanā yathādhippāyaṃ saṃvaṇṇitā hotīti.

Thus far, the meaning of this verse has been made clear, and the exposition of the external introduction to the Vinaya has been expounded according to intention.

Tatiyasaṅgītikathā niṭṭhitā.

The account of the Third Council is finished.

Bāhiranidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The account of the External Introduction is finished.

Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verañjā Section

1. Idāni [P 1.0106][M 1.0079][V 1.0074]

1. Now

“Tenātiādipāṭhassa, atthaṃ nānappakārato;

Dassayanto karissāmi, vinayassatthavaṇṇana”nti.

Explaining in various ways the meaning of the text beginning with 'tena', I shall now compose the commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya.

Vuttattā tena samayena buddho bhagavātiādīnaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Seyyathidaṃ – tenāti aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ. Tassa sarūpena avuttenapi aparabhāge atthato siddhena yenāti iminā vacanena paṭiniddeso kātabbo. Aparabhāge hi vinayapaññattiyācanahetubhūto āyasmato sāriputtassa parivitakko siddho. Tasmā yena samayena so parivitakko udapādi, tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Ayañhi sabbasmimpi vinaye yutti, yadidaṃ yattha yattha “tenā”ti vuccati tattha tattha pubbe vā pacchā vā atthato siddhena “yenā”ti iminā vacanena paṭiniddeso kātabboti.

To wit: 'tena' is a word of indefinite indication. Although not stated by its form, its specific reference should be made by this word 'yena', which is established by meaning in a later part. For in a later part, the thought of the Venerable Sāriputta, which became the cause for requesting the laying down of the Vinaya, is established. Therefore, the connection here should be understood thus: 'At the time when that thought arose, at that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Verañjā.' For this is the proper method throughout the entire Vinaya: wherever 'tena' is stated, there a specific reference should be made by the word 'yena', which is established by meaning, either before or after.

Tatridaṃ mukhamattanidassanaṃ – “tena hi, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmi, yena sudinno methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevi; yasmā paṭisevi, tasmā paññapessāmī”ti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tāva pubbe atthato siddhena yenāti iminā vacanena paṭiniddeso yujjati. Tena samayena buddho bhagavā rājagahe viharati, yena samayena dhaniyo kumbhakāraputto rañño dārūni adinnaṃ ādiyīti evaṃ pacchā atthato siddhena yenāti iminā vacanena paṭiniddeso yujjatīti vutto tenāti vacanassa attho. Samayenāti ettha pana samayasaddo tāva –

Herein is a brief illustration: 'Therefore, monks, I shall lay down a training rule for the monks for the reason that Sudinna engaged in sexual intercourse; since he engaged in it, therefore I shall lay it down'—this is what is meant. Thus, in the first place, a specific reference by this word 'yena', which is established by meaning beforehand, is proper. 'At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Rājagaha, at the time when Dhaniya, the potter's son, took the king's timber that was not given'—thus a specific reference by this word 'yena', which is established by meaning afterwards, is proper. In this way, the meaning of the word 'tena' has been stated. Now, in the word 'samayena', the term 'samaya' is first to be considered—

Samavāye [P 1.0107] khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetu-diṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati.

It is seen in the sense of concurrence, moment, time, assembly, cause and views; in acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.

Tathā [V 1.0075] hissa – “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.447) evamādīsu samavāyo attho. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”ti (a. ni. 8.29) evamādīsu khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo [M 1.0080] pariḷāhasamayo”ti (pāci. 358) evamādīsu kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”nti evamādīsu samūho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”ti (ma. ni. 2.135) evamādīsu hetu. “Tena kho pana samayena uggahamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.260) evamādīsu diṭṭhi.

Indeed, for this word: in such instances as 'Perhaps tomorrow we might go, having considered the time and the occasion', the meaning is concurrence. In such instances as 'Monks, there is but one moment, one occasion for living the holy life', the meaning is moment. In such instances as 'the hot season, the scorching season', the meaning is time. In such instances as 'A great assembly in the forest', the meaning is assembly. In such instances as 'Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate this reason: “The Blessed One is dwelling at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One will know of me that the monk named Bhaddāli is not a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.” This reason, Bhaddāli, was also not penetrated by you', the meaning is cause. In such instances as 'Now at that time, the wandering ascetic Uggahamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling in Queen Mallikā's park, in the single-hall building with a row of Tinduka trees, a place for debating views', the meaning is view.

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.129);

Whatever benefit is in this present life, and whatever benefit pertains to the life to come; through full understanding of the benefit, the steadfast one is called a sage.

Evamādīsu paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”ti (ma. ni. 1.28) evamādīsu pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.8) evamādīsu paṭivedho attho. Idha panassa kālo attho. Tasmā yena kālena āyasmato sāriputtassa vinayapaññattiyācanahetubhūto parivitakko udapādi, tena kālenāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

In such instances, the meaning is acquisition. In such instances as 'Through the complete abandonment of conceit, one made an end of suffering', the meaning is abandonment. In such instances as 'The meaning of suffering is oppression, that of being conditioned, of burning, of change; it is a matter for penetration', the meaning is penetration. Here, however, its meaning is time. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: at the time when the thought that was the cause for requesting the laying down of the Vinaya rules arose in the Venerable Sāriputta, at that time...

Etthāha – “atha kasmā yathā suttante ‘ekaṃ samaya’nti upayogavacanena niddeso kato, abhidhamme ca ‘yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacara’nti bhummavacanena, tathā akatvā idha ‘tena samayenā’ti karaṇavacanena niddeso kato”ti? Tattha tathā, idha ca aññathā atthasambhavato. Kathaṃ? Suttante tāva accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati. Yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā brahmajālādīni suttantāni desesi, accantameva taṃ samayaṃ karuṇāvihārena vihāsi; tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha upayoganiddeso kato. Abhidhamme ca adhikaraṇattho [P 1.0108] bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho ca sambhavati. Adhikaraṇañhi kālattho samūhattho ca samayo, tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa bhāvena tesaṃ bhāvo lakkhiyati. Tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha bhummavacanena niddeso kato. Idha pana hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo [M 1.0081] hi so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo [V 1.0076] sāriputtādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtena ca sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi; tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ idha karaṇavacanena niddeso katoti veditabbo. Hoti cettha –

Here, a critic asks: 'Then why is it that, unlike in the Suttanta where the exposition is made with the accusative 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', and in the Abhidhamma with the locative 'yasmiṃ samaye', here in the Vinaya the exposition is made with the instrumental 'tena samayena'?' This is because the meaning is suitable thus in those cases, and otherwise here. How so? In the Suttanta, the meaning of continuous connection is suitable. For during the time the Blessed One taught suttas such as the Brahmajāla, he dwelt in a state of compassion continuously throughout that time. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the accusative exposition is used there. In the Abhidhamma, the meanings of location and of one state being the mark of another are suitable. For time, in the sense of a period and in the sense of a collection, is the location for the phenomena such as contact mentioned there. And the existence of those phenomena is marked by the existence of 'samaya' in the sense of moment, concurrence, and cause. Therefore, to illuminate those meanings, the locative exposition is used there. Here in the Vinaya, however, the meanings of cause and instrument are suitable. For that time of laying down the training rules was difficult to discern even for Sāriputta and others. By means of that time, which served as cause and instrument, the Blessed One dwelt in various places, laying down the training rules and considering the reason for their establishment. Therefore, to illuminate those meanings, the instrumental exposition is used here. This should be understood. And on this there is the following:

“Upayogena bhummena, taṃ taṃ atthamapekkhiya;

Aññatra samayo vutto, karaṇeneva so idhā”ti.

With the accusative and the locative, having regard for each respective meaning, 'samaya' is stated elsewhere; here, it is by the instrumental alone.

Porāṇā pana vaṇṇayanti – ‘ekaṃ samaya’nti vā ‘yasmiṃ samaye’ti vā ‘tena samayenā’ti vā abhilāpamattabhedo esa, sabbattha bhummameva attho”ti. Tasmā tesaṃ laddhiyā “tena samayenā”ti vuttepi “tasmiṃ samaye”ti attho veditabbo.

The ancient masters, however, explain: 'Whether 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', 'yasmiṃ samaye', or 'tena samayena', this is merely a difference in expression; in all cases the meaning is only the locative.' Therefore, according to their doctrine, even when 'tena samayena' is stated, the meaning should be understood as 'tasmiṃ samaye'.

Buddho bhagavāti imesaṃ padānaṃ parato atthaṃ vaṇṇayissāma. Verañjāyaṃ viharatīti ettha pana verañjāti aññatarassa nagarassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tassaṃ verañjāyaṃ; samīpatthe bhummavacanaṃ. Viharatīti avisesena iriyāpathadibbabrahmaariyavihāresu aññataravihārasamaṅgīparidīpanametaṃ, idha pana ṭhānagamananisajjāsayanappabhedesu iriyāpathesu aññatarairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ, tena ṭhitopi gacchantopi nisinnopi sayānopi bhagavā viharaticceva veditabbo. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti, tasmā “viharatī”ti vuccati.

We shall explain the meaning of these words, 'Buddho, Bhagavā,' further on. Now, in the phrase 'dwells at Verañjā,' 'Verañjā' is the designation for a certain city. 'At that Verañjā' is a locative expression in the sense of proximity. The word 'dwells' is a term that, without distinction, indicates being endowed with any one of the abidings—postural, divine, sublime, or noble. Here, however, it indicates association with one or another of the postures, which are distinguished as standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. Therefore, whether the Blessed One is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, he should indeed be understood as 'dwelling.' For by cutting off the affliction of one posture with another posture, he carries on and maintains his personal existence so that it does not collapse. Therefore, he is said to 'dwell.'

Naḷerupucimandamūleti ettha naḷeru nāma yakkho, pucimandoti [P 1.0109] nimbarukkho, mūlanti samīpaṃ. Ayañhi mūlasaddo “mūlāni uddhareyya antamaso usīranāḷimattānipī”ti (a. ni. 4.195) -ādīsu mūlamūle dissati. “Lobho akusalamūla”nti (dī. ni. 3.305) -ādīsu asādhāraṇahetumhi. “Yāva majjhanhike kāle chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūla”ntiādīsu samīpe. Idha pana samīpe adhippeto, tasmā naḷeruyakkhena adhiggahitassa pucimandassa samīpeti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. So kira pucimando ramaṇīyo pāsādiko anekesaṃ rukkhānaṃ ādhipaccaṃ viya kurumāno tassa nagarassa avidūre gamanāgamanasampanne ṭhāne ahosi. Atha [M 1.0082] bhagavā verañjaṃ gantvā patirūpe ṭhāne viharanto tassa rukkhassa samīpe heṭṭhābhāge vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “verañjāyaṃ viharati naḷerupucimandamūle”ti.

As for 'at the root of Naḷeru's pucimanda tree,' here 'Naḷeru' is the name of a yakkha, 'pucimanda' is the nimba tree, and 'mūla' (root) means proximity. Indeed, this word 'mūla' is seen in the sense of a physical root in passages such as, 'one should uproot the roots, even if only as much as a blade of usīra grass.' In passages such as, 'greed is the unwholesome root,' it is seen in the sense of an uncommon cause. And in passages such as, 'as far as the shadow extends at midday, or where leaves fall when there is no wind, that much is the root of the tree,' it is seen in the sense of proximity. Here, however, proximity is intended. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'in the proximity of the pucimanda tree possessed by the yakkha Naḷeru.' It is said that this pucimanda tree was delightful and inspiring, as if exercising lordship over many other trees, and it stood in a place not far from that city, convenient for travel. Then, the Blessed One, having gone to Verañjā and dwelling in a suitable place, dwelt at the base, in the proximity of that tree. Hence it was said: 'He dwells at Verañjā, at the root of Naḷeru’s pucimanda tree.'

Tattha [V 1.0077] siyā yadi tāva bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharati, “naḷerupucimandamūle”ti na vattabbaṃ, atha tattha viharati, “verañjāya”nti na vattabbaṃ, na hi sakkā ubhayattha teneva samayena apubbaṃ acarimaṃ viharitunti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, nanu avocumha “samīpatthe bhummavacana”nti. Tasmā yathā gaṅgāyamunādīnaṃ samīpe goyūthāni carantāni “gaṅgāya caranti, yamunāya carantī”ti vuccanti; evamidhāpi yadidaṃ verañjāya samīpe naḷerupucimandamūlaṃ tattha viharanto vuccati “verañjāyaṃ viharati naḷerupucimandamūle”ti. Gocaragāmanidassanatthaṃ hissa verañjāvacanaṃ. Pabbajitānurūpanivāsanaṭṭhānanidassanatthaṃ naḷerupucimandamūlavacanaṃ.

Herein, a certain person might have this thought: 'If the Blessed One was dwelling in Verañjā, then "at the root of Naḷeru's pucimanda tree" should not be said. Or, if he was dwelling there, then "at Verañjā" should not be said. For it is not possible to dwell in both places at the very same time, neither before nor after, is it?' But this should not be understood in this way. Did we not say, "the locative expression is in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle wandering near rivers like the Ganges and Yamunā are said to be 'wandering at the Ganges, wandering at the Yamunā,' so too here, one dwelling at the root of Naḷeru's pucimanda tree, which is near Verañjā, is said to be 'dwelling at Verañjā, at the root of Naḷeru's pucimanda tree.' For the mention of Verañjā is for the purpose of indicating his alms-round village. The mention of the root of Naḷeru's pucimanda tree is for the purpose of indicating a dwelling place suitable for renunciants.

Tattha verañjākittanena āyasmā upālitthero bhagavato gahaṭṭhānuggahakaraṇaṃ dasseti, naḷerupucimandamūlakittanena pabbajitānuggahakaraṇaṃ, tathā purimena paccayaggahaṇato attakilamathānuyogavivajjanaṃ, pacchimena vatthukāmappahānato kāmasukhallikānuyogavivajjanupāyadassanaṃ; purimena ca dhammadesanābhiyogaṃ, pacchimena vivekādhimuttiṃ; purimena karuṇāya upagamanaṃ[P 1.0110], pacchimena paññāya apagamanaṃ; purimena sattānaṃ hitasukhanipphādanādhimuttataṃ, pacchimena parahitasukhakaraṇe nirupalepanaṃ; purimena dhammikasukhāpariccāganimittaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ, pacchimena uttarimanussadhammānuyoganimittaṃ; purimena manussānaṃ upakārabahulataṃ, pacchimena devatānaṃ; purimena loke jātassa loke saṃvaḍḍhabhāvaṃ, pacchimena lokena anupalittataṃ; purimena “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katamo ekapuggalo? Tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti (a. ni. 1.170) vacanato yadatthaṃ bhagavā uppanno tadatthaparinipphādanaṃ, pacchimena yattha uppanno tadanurūpavihāraṃ. Bhagavā hi paṭhamaṃ lumbinīvane, dutiyaṃ bodhimaṇḍeti lokiyalokuttarāya uppattiyā vaneyeva uppanno, tenassa vaneyeva vihāraṃ dassetīti evamādinā nayenettha atthayojanā veditabbā.

Therein, by mentioning Verañjā, the venerable elder Upāli shows the Blessed One's benefiting of householders; by mentioning the root of Naḷeru's pucimanda tree, he shows the benefiting of renunciants. Likewise, by the former, he shows the avoidance of the practice of self-mortification through the acceptance of requisites; by the latter, he shows the means of avoiding the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures through the abandoning of sensual objects. And by the former, he shows exertion in teaching the Dhamma; by the latter, the inclination towards seclusion. By the former, he shows approaching with compassion; by the latter, withdrawing with wisdom. By the former, he shows the inclination to accomplish the welfare and happiness of beings; by the latter, being unsullied in the act of bringing about the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, he shows a comfortable abiding as a sign of not abandoning righteous happiness; by the latter, a comfortable abiding as a sign of practicing the superhuman states. By the former, he shows being of great benefit to humans; by the latter, to devas. By the former, he shows being born in the world and growing up in the world; by the latter, being unsullied by the world. By the former, he shows the accomplishment of the purpose for which the Blessed One arose, according to the saying: 'Monks, one person, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Who is that one person? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One'; by the latter, he shows a dwelling suitable to where he arose. For the Blessed One, with both a worldly and a supramundane arising, arose in a forest: first in the Lumbinī grove, and second at the Bodhi-maṇḍa. Therefore, this shows his dwelling in a forest. In this and other ways, the application of the meaning should be understood here.

Mahatā [M 1.0083] bhikkhusaṅghena saddhinti ettha mahatāti guṇamahattenapi mahatā; saṅkhyāmahattenapi, so hi bhikkhusaṅgho guṇehipi mahā ahosi, yasmā yo tattha pacchimako so sotāpanno; saṅkhyāyapi mahā pañcasatasaṅkhyattā. Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅghena bhikkhusaṅghena; diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅkhātasaṅghātena samaṇagaṇenāti attho. Saddhinti ekato. Pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehīti pañca mattā etesanti pañcamattāni. Mattāti pamāṇaṃ vuccati. Tasmā yathā “bhojane [V 1.0078] mattaññū”ti vutte bhojane mattaṃ jānāti, pamāṇaṃ jānātīti attho hoti; evamidhāpi tesaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pañca mattā pañcappamāṇanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhūnaṃ satāni bhikkhusatāni, tehi pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi. Etena yaṃ vuttaṃ – “mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhi”nti, ettha tassa mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa saṅkhyāmahattaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Parato panassa [P 1.0111] “nirabbudo hi, sāriputta bhikkhusaṅgho nirādīnavo apagatakāḷako suddho sāre patiṭṭhito. Imesañhi, sāriputta, pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ yo pacchimako so sotāpanno”ti vacanena guṇamahattaṃ āvibhavissati.

"With a great community of monks"—here, "great" means great in virtue as well as great in number. For that community of monks was great in virtues, because the one who was last among them was a stream-enterer; and it was great in number, because of having the number of five hundred. "By the community of monks" means by the group of recluses, a combination designated as commonality of view and virtue. "Together" means as one. "With five hundred bhikkhus": this means that five is their measure (`mattā`), thus they are "five-measured" (`pañcamattāni`). "Matta" is said to mean "measure." Therefore, just as when it is said, "one who knows the measure in food," the meaning is that one knows the measure, knows the proper amount; so too here, the meaning should be understood thus: of those hundreds of bhikkhus, five is the measure, a quantity of five. "Hundreds of bhikkhus" means the hundreds of bhikkhus; with those five hundred bhikkhus. By this, what was said—"with a great community of monks"—shows the numerical greatness of that great community of monks. Furthermore, its greatness in virtue will become manifest later by the statement: "For, Sāriputta, this community of monks is without blemish, free from defect, pure, and established in the essence. Indeed, Sāriputta, of these five hundred monks, the one who is last is a stream-enterer."

Assosi kho verañjo brāhmaṇoti assosīti suṇi upalabhi, sotadvārasampattavacananigghosānusārena aññāsi. Khoti padapūraṇamatte avadhāraṇatthe vā nipāto. Tattha avadhāraṇatthena assosi eva, nāssa koci savanantarāyo ahosīti ayamattho veditabbo. Padapūraṇena pana byañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattameva. Verañjāyaṃ jāto, verañjāyaṃ bhavo, verañjā vā assa nivāsoti verañjo. Mātāpitūhi katanāmavasena panāyaṃ “udayo”ti vuccati. Brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo, mante sajjhāyatīti attho. Idameva hi jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ niruttivacanaṃ. Ariyā pana bāhitapāpattā “brāhmaṇā”ti vuccanti.

The brahmin Verañja heard: "Heard" means he listened, he received, he knew through the mind-door process that follows the sound of speech arriving at the ear-door. "Kho" is a particle used merely for filling out a phrase or for emphasis. Among these, in the sense of emphasis, the meaning to be understood is that he indeed heard, and there was no obstacle to his hearing. With the sense of filling out a phrase, however, it is merely for the elegance of the expression. He was called Verañja because he was born in Verañjā, originated in Verañjā, or had his residence in Verañjā. By the name given by his parents, however, he is called "Udaya." He is a "brāhmaṇa" because he recites the sacred texts (`brahmaṃ aṇati`); the meaning is that he recites the mantras. This is indeed the etymological explanation for brahmins by birth. The noble ones, however, are called "brāhmaṇas" because they have banished evil.

Idāni yamatthaṃ verañjo brāhmaṇo assosi, taṃ pakāsento samaṇo khalu bho gotamotiādimāha. Tattha samitapāpattā samaṇoti veditabbo. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “bāhitapāpoti brāhmaṇo (dha. pa. 388), samitapāpattā [M 1.0084] samaṇoti vuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 265). Bhagavā ca anuttarena ariyamaggena samitapāpo, tenassa yathābhuccaguṇādhigatametaṃ nāmaṃ yadidaṃ samaṇoti. Khalūti anussavanatthe nipāto. Bhoti brāhmaṇajātikānaṃ jātisamudāgataṃ ālapanamattaṃ. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

Now, to make clear what the brahmin Verañja heard, the text beginning "The recluse Gotama, it is said, sir..." was stated. Therein, "recluse" (`samaṇa`) should be understood as one who has stilled evil (`samitapāpa`). For this has been said: "One who has banished evil is a brahmin, and one is called a recluse because of having stilled evil." And the Blessed One has stilled evil by the unsurpassed noble path; therefore, this name, "recluse," is one he has acquired through his true virtue. "Khalu" is a particle in the sense of hearsay. "Bho" is merely a form of address that comes from the birth of those of the brahmin caste. For this too has been said:

“Bhovādī nāmaso hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano”ti. (Dha. pa. 396; su. ni. 625). Gotamoti bhagavantaṃ gottavasena parikitteti, tasmā “samaṇo khalu bho gotamo”ti ettha samaṇo kira bho gotamagottoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sakyaputtoti idaṃ pana bhagavato uccākulaparidīpanaṃ. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti saddhāpabbajitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ, kenaci pārijuññena anabhibhūto aparikkhīṇaṃyeva, taṃ kulaṃ pahāya saddhāya pabbajitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato paraṃ vuttatthameva. Taṃ kho panāti itthambhūtākhyānatthe [P 1.0112] upayogavacanaṃ, tassa kho pana [V 1.0079] bhoto gotamassāti attho. Kalyāṇoti kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato; seṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kittisaddoti kitti eva, thutighoso vā.

"One is called a 'bhovādī' (one who says 'bho') if one has impediments." By "Gotama," he proclaims the Blessed One by his clan name. Therefore, in the phrase "The recluse Gotama, it is said, sir," the meaning should be understood thus: "The recluse of the Gotama clan, it is said, sir, is dwelling." "Son of the Sakyans" (`Sakyaputta`), however, is an indicator of the Blessed One's high-born clan. "Gone forth from the Sakyan clan" is an indicator of his state of having gone forth out of faith; it is said that, not overcome by any decline, he went forth out of faith, having abandoned that clan while it was not in decline. After that, the meaning is as has been stated. "Taṃ kho pana" is a phrase in the accusative case used in the sense of describing a particular state; the meaning is "of that venerable Gotama." "Excellent" (`kalyāṇa`) means endowed with excellent qualities; it is said to mean "supreme" (`seṭṭha`). "Good repute" (`kittisadda`) is fame itself, or the sound of praise.

Itipi so bhagavātiādīsu pana ayaṃ tāva yojanā – so bhagavā itipi arahaṃ, itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavāti iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the passages beginning with "Thus indeed is that Blessed One," this, first, is the construction: That Blessed One, for this reason also, is an Arahant; for this reason also, a Sammāsambuddha... and so on... for this reason also, a Bhagavā. It is said to be because of this and that reason.

Idāni vinayadharānaṃ suttantanayakosallatthaṃ vinayasaṃvaṇṇanārambhe buddhaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammiyā kathāya cittasampahaṃsanatthañca etesaṃ padānaṃ vitthāranayena vaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ – “so bhagavā itipi araha”ntiādi; tattha ārakattā, arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti imehi tāva kāraṇehi so bhagavā arahanti veditabbo. Ārakā hi so sabbakilesehi suvidūravidūre ṭhito, maggena savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattāti ārakattā arahaṃ; te cānena kilesārayo maggena hatāti arīnaṃ hatattāpi arahaṃ. Yañcetaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhipuññādiabhisaṅkhārāraṃ jarāmaraṇanemi āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā tibhavarathe samāyojitaṃ anādikālappavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ, tassānena bodhimaṇḍe [M 1.0085] vīriyapādehi sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakaraṃ ñāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā sabbe arā hatāti arānaṃ hatattāpi arahaṃ.

Now, for the benefit of the Vinaya-holders' skill in the method of the Suttas, and at the commencement of the Vinaya commentary, to gladden the mind with a Dhamma talk connected with the Buddha's virtues, I shall provide a detailed explanation of these terms. Therefore, regarding what was said—"That Blessed One, for this reason also, is an Arahant," and so on—therein, that Blessed One is to be known as an "Arahant" first for these reasons: because of being far (`ārakattā`), because of having destroyed the enemies (`arīnaṃ hatattā`) and the spokes (`arānaṃ hatattā`), because of being worthy (`arahattā`) of requisites and so on, and because of the absence of secrecy (`rahābhāva`) in doing evil. For he is far from all defilements, standing at a great, great distance, because the defilements with their latent tendencies have been destroyed by the path; thus, because of being far, he is an Arahant. And by him those enemies, the defilements, have been destroyed by the path; thus, because of having destroyed the enemies, he is also an Arahant. And as for this wheel of saṃsāra, which has rolled on since beginningless time, yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence, pierced by the axle made of the arising of the taints, with its hub made of ignorance and craving for existence, its spokes made of meritorious and other volitional formations, and its rim made of aging and death—of that wheel, he, at the seat of enlightenment, standing on the ground of virtue with the feet of energy, taking the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma with the hand of faith, destroyed all the spokes; thus, because of having destroyed the spokes, he is also an Arahant.

Atha vā saṃsāracakkanti anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭaṃ vuccati, tassa ca avijjā nābhi, mūlattā; jarāmaraṇaṃ nemi, pariyosānattā; sesā dasa dhammā arā, avijjāmūlakattā jarāmaraṇapariyantattā ca. Tattha dukkhādīsu aññāṇaṃ avijjā, kāmabhave ca avijjā kāmabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti. Rūpabhave avijjā rūpabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti. Arūpabhave avijjā arūpabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave saṅkhārā kāmabhave [P 1.0113] paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paccayā honti. Esa nayo itaresu. Kāmabhave paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ kāmabhave nāmarūpassa paccayo hoti, tathā rūpabhave. Arūpabhave nāmasseva paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave nāmarūpaṃ kāmabhave saḷāyatanassa paccayo hoti. Rūpabhave nāmarūpaṃ rūpabhave tiṇṇaṃ āyatanānaṃ paccayo hoti. Arūpabhave nāmaṃ arūpabhave ekassāyatanassa paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave saḷāyatanaṃ kāmabhave chabbidhassa phassassa paccayo hoti. Rūpabhave tīṇi āyatanāni rūpabhave tiṇṇaṃ phassānaṃ; arūpabhave ekamāyatanaṃ arūpabhave ekassa phassassa paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave cha phassā kāmabhave channaṃ vedanānaṃ paccayā honti. Rūpabhave tayo tattheva [V 1.0080] tissannaṃ; arūpabhave eko tattheva ekissā vedanāya paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave cha vedanā kāmabhave channaṃ taṇhākāyānaṃ paccayā honti. Rūpabhave tisso tattheva tiṇṇaṃ; arūpabhave ekā vedanā arūpabhave ekassa taṇhākāyassa paccayo hoti. Tattha tattha sā sā taṇhā tassa tassa upādānassa paccayo; upādānādayo bhavādīnaṃ.

Alternatively, the beginningless round of saṃsāra is called the wheel of saṃsāra. Of this, ignorance is the hub, because it is the root; aging-and-death is the rim, because it is the end; the remaining ten states are the spokes, because they have ignorance as their root and aging-and-death as their end. Therein, not knowing concerning suffering and so on is ignorance. And in the sense-sphere existence, ignorance is a condition for formations in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, ignorance is a condition for formations in the fine-material existence. In the immaterial existence, ignorance is a condition for formations in the immaterial existence. In the sense-sphere existence, formations are a condition for relinking-consciousness in the sense-sphere existence. This is the method in the other cases. In the sense-sphere existence, relinking-consciousness is a condition for mentality-materiality in the sense-sphere existence; likewise in the fine-material existence. In the immaterial existence, it is a condition for mentality only. In the sense-sphere existence, mentality-materiality is a condition for the six sense bases in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, mentality-materiality is a condition for three sense bases in the fine-material existence. In the immaterial existence, mentality is a condition for one sense base in the immaterial existence. In the sense-sphere existence, the six sense bases are a condition for the sixfold contact in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, the three sense bases are a condition for three contacts; in the immaterial existence, the one sense base is a condition for one contact. In the sense-sphere existence, the six contacts are a condition for the six feelings in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, the three contacts are a condition for three feelings right there; in the immaterial existence, the one contact is a condition for one feeling right there. In the sense-sphere existence, the six feelings are a condition for the six classes of craving in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, the three feelings are a condition for three classes of craving right there; in the immaterial existence, the one feeling is a condition for one class of craving in the immaterial existence. In each respective existence, that particular craving is a condition for that particular clinging; clinging and the rest are conditions for becoming and the rest.

Kathaṃ? Idhekacco “kāme paribhuñjissāmī”ti kāmupādānapaccayā kāyena duccaritaṃ carati, vācāya manasā duccaritaṃ carati; duccaritapāripūriyā apāye upapajjati. Tatthassa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammanibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo, khandhānaṃ nibbatti jāti, paripāko jarā, bhedo maraṇaṃ.

How? Here, a certain person, thinking, 'I will enjoy sensual pleasures,' conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures, engages in misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Due to the fulfillment of misconduct, they are reborn in a state of deprivation. Therein, for that person, the kamma that has become the cause of rebirth is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming; the manifestation of the aggregates is birth; their maturation is aging; their breaking up is death.

Aparo [M 1.0086] “saggasampattiṃ anubhavissāmī”ti tatheva sucaritaṃ carati; sucaritapāripūriyā sagge upapajjati. Tatthassa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavoti so eva nayo.

Another person, thinking, 'I will experience heavenly attainment,' likewise engages in good conduct. Due to the fulfillment of good conduct, they are reborn in heaven. Therein, for that person, the kamma that has become the cause of rebirth is kamma-becoming. This is the same method.

Aparo pana “brahmalokasampattiṃ anubhavissāmī”ti kāmupādānapaccayā eva mettaṃ bhāveti, karuṇaṃ… muditaṃ… upekkhaṃ bhāveti, bhāvanāpāripūriyā brahmaloke nibbattati. Tatthassa nibbattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavoti soyeva nayo.

But another person, thinking, 'I will experience the attainment of the Brahma world,' develops loving-kindness, develops compassion, develops appreciative joy, develops equanimity. Due to the fulfillment of this development, they are reborn in the Brahma world. Therein, for that person, the kamma that has become the cause of rebirth is kamma-becoming. This is the same method.

Aparo “arūpavabhasampattiṃ anubhavissāmī”ti [P 1.0114] tatheva ākāsānañcāyatanādisamāpattiyo bhāveti, bhāvanāpāripūriyā tattha nibbattati. Tatthassa nibbattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammanibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo, khandhānaṃ nibbatti jāti, paripāko jarā, bhedo maraṇanti. Esa nayo sesupādānamūlikāsupi yojanāsu.

Another person, thinking, 'I will experience the attainment of the immaterial existence,' likewise develops the attainments of the base of infinite space, and so on. Due to the fulfillment of this development, they are reborn there. Therein, for that person, the kamma that has become the cause of rebirth is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming; the manifestation of the aggregates is birth; their maturation is aging; their breaking up is death. This is the method also for the applications rooted in the remaining clingings.

Evaṃ “ayaṃ avijjā hetu, saṅkhārā hetusamuppannā, ubhopete hetusamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ; atītampi addhānaṃ, anāgatampi addhānaṃ; avijjā hetu, saṅkhārā hetusamuppannā, ubhopete hetusamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti etena nayena sabbapadāni vitthāretabbāni. Tattha avijjā saṅkhārā eko saṅkhepo, viññāṇa-nāmarūpa-saḷāyatana-phassa-vedanā eko, taṇhupādānabhavā eko, jāti-jarā-maraṇaṃ eko. Purimasaṅkhepo cettha atīto addhā, dve majjhimā paccuppanno, jātijarāmaraṇaṃ anāgato. Avijjāsaṅkhāraggahaṇena cettha taṇhupādānabhavā gahitāva hontīti ime pañca dhammā atīte kammavaṭṭaṃ; viññāṇādayo pañca dhammā etarahi vipākavaṭṭaṃ. Taṇhupādānabhavaggahaṇena [V 1.0081] avijjāsaṅkhārā gahitāva hontīti ime pañca dhammā etarahi kammavaṭṭaṃ; jātijarāmaraṇāpadesena viññāṇādīnaṃ niddiṭṭhattā ime pañca dhammā āyatiṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ. Te ākārato vīsatividhā honti. Saṅkhāraviññāṇānañcettha antarā eko sandhi, vedanātaṇhānamantarā eko, bhavajātīnamantarā eko. Iti bhagavā evaṃ catusaṅkhepaṃ, tiyaddhaṃ, vīsatākāraṃ, tisandhiṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sabbākārato jānāti passati aññāti paṭivijjhati. Taṃ ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, pajānanaṭṭhena paññā. Tena vuccati – “paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti. Iminā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇena bhagavā te dhamme yathābhūtaṃ ñatvā tesu [M 1.0087] nibbindanto virajjanto vimuccanto vuttappakārassa imassa saṃsāracakkassa are hani vihani viddhaṃsesi. Evampi arānaṃ hatattā arahaṃ.

Thus: 'This ignorance is a cause, formations are cause-originated; both these are cause-originated.' The wisdom in grasping conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena. This applies to the past period and to the future period as well: 'Ignorance is a cause, formations are cause-originated; both these are cause-originated.' In this way, all terms should be expanded. Therein, ignorance and formations are one summary; consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are one summary; craving, clinging, and becoming are one summary; birth, aging-and-death are one summary. Herein, the first summary is the past period; the two middle ones are the present period; birth, aging-and-death is the future period. And herein, by the inclusion of ignorance and formations, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included; thus, these five phenomena in the past are the kamma-round. The five phenomena beginning with consciousness are the result-round in the present. By the inclusion of craving, clinging, and becoming, ignorance and formations are also included; thus, these five phenomena in the present are the kamma-round. Because the phenomena beginning with consciousness are indicated by the terms birth, aging-and-death, these five phenomena in the future are the result-round. They are of twenty modes. And herein, there is one connection between formations and consciousness, one between feeling and craving, and one between becoming and birth. Thus, the Blessed One knows, sees, understands, and penetrates dependent origination in all its aspects: with four summaries, three periods, twenty modes, and three connections. That is knowledge in the sense of knowing, and wisdom in the sense of discerning. Therefore it is said: 'The wisdom in grasping conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.' With this knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the Blessed One, having known those phenomena as they truly are, and becoming disenchanted with them, dispassionate towards them, and liberated from them, has destroyed, struck down, and demolished the spokes of this wheel of saṃsāra described above. In this way also, because of having destroyed the spokes (arānaṃ hatattā), he is an Arahant.

Aggadakkhiṇeyyattā ca cīvarādipaccaye [P 1.0115] arahati pūjāvisesañca; teneva ca uppanne tathāgate ye keci mahesakkhā devamanussā na te aññattha pūjaṃ karonti. Tathā hi brahmā sahampati sinerumattena ratanadāmena tathāgataṃ pūjesi, yathābalañca aññepi devā manussā ca bimbisārakosalarājādayo. Parinibbutampi ca bhagavantaṃ uddissa channavutikoṭidhanaṃ visajjetvā asokamahārājā sakalajambudīpe caturāsītivihārasahassāni patiṭṭhāpesi. Ko pana vādo aññesaṃ pūjāvisesānanti! Evaṃ paccayādīnaṃ arahattāpi arahaṃ. Yathā ca loke keci paṇḍitamānino bālā asilokabhayena raho pāpaṃ karonti; evamesa na kadāci karotīti pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvatopi arahaṃ. Hoti cettha –

And because of being the foremost recipient of offerings, He is worthy of requisites such as robes and of special offerings. For this very reason, when a Tathāgata has arisen, whatever devas and humans of great power there are, they do not make offerings to anyone else. Indeed, Brahmā Sahampati honored the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland the size of Mount Sineru, and other devas and humans, such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala, did likewise according to their ability. And even with the Blessed One who had attained Parinibbāna as the object, King Asoka, having spent ninety-six crores of wealth, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout all of Jambudīpa. What, then, is to be said of other special offerings! Thus, because of being worthy of requisites and so on, He is an Arahant. And just as in the world some fools who fancy themselves wise commit evil in secret out of fear of ill repute, so this one never commits evil. Therefore, because of the absence of a secret place for doing evil, He is an Arahant. And here there is this:

“Ārakattā hatattā ca, kilesārīna so muni;

Hatasaṃsāracakkāro, paccayādīna cāraho;

Na raho karoti pāpāni, arahaṃ tena vuccatī”ti.

Because He is far from defilements, and because the defilement-enemies have been slain; that Sage, having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, is also worthy of requisites and so on. He does no evil deeds in secret; therefore, He is called 'Arahaṃ'.

Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā pana sammāsambuddho. Tathā hesa sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho, abhiññeyye dhamme abhiññeyyato buddho, pariññeyye dhamme pariññeyyato, pahātabbe dhamme pahātabbato, sacchikātabbe dhamme sacchikātabbato, bhāvetabbe dhamme bhāvetabbato. Teneva cāha –

Furthermore, because He has rightly and by Himself awakened to all dhammas, He is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddho). Indeed, this one has rightly and by Himself awakened to all dhammas: He has awakened to the dhammas to be directly known as to be directly known; He has awakened to the dhammas to be fully understood as to be fully understood; He has awakened to the dhammas to be abandoned as to be abandoned; He has awakened to the dhammas to be realized as to be realized; He has awakened to the dhammas to be developed as to be developed. For that reason, He said:

“Abhiññeyyaṃ [V 1.0082] abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇā”ti. (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 563);

What was to be directly known has been directly known; and what was to be developed has been developed; what was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me. Therefore, O brahmin, I am a Buddha.

Apica cakkhu dukkhasaccaṃ, tassa mūlakāraṇabhāvena taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnamappavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhappajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccanti evaṃ ekekapaduddhārenāpi sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho. Esa nayo sota-ghāna-jivhā-kāyamanesupi. Eteneva nayena rūpādīni cha āyatanāni, cakkhuviññāṇādayo cha viññāṇakāyā, cakkhusamphassādayo cha phassā, cakkhusamphassajādayo cha vedanā, rūpasaññādayo cha saññā, rūpasañcetanādayo cha cetanā, rūpataṇhādayo cha [M 1.0088] taṇhākāyā, rūpavitakkādayo cha vitakkā, rūpavicārādayo cha vicārā[P 1.0116], rūpakkhandhādayo pañcakkhandhā, dasa kasiṇāni, dasa anussatiyo, uddhumātakasaññādivasena dasa saññā, kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, kāmabhavādayo nava bhavā, paṭhamādīni cattāri jhānāni, mettābhāvanādayo catasso appamaññā, catasso arūpasamāpattiyo, paṭilomato jarāmaraṇādīni, anulomato avijjādīni paṭiccasamuppādaṅgāni ca yojetabbāni.

Furthermore, the eye is the truth of suffering; the prior craving, by being its root cause that gives rise to it, is the truth of origin; the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; and the practice for the distinct knowing of cessation is the truth of the path. Thus, even by the extraction of each single term, He has known all dhammas rightly and by Himself. This is the method also in the cases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. By this very method, the six sense bases beginning with forms; the six bodies of consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness; the six contacts beginning with eye-contact; the six feelings beginning with those born of eye-contact; the six perceptions beginning with perception of forms; the six volitions beginning with volition regarding forms; the six bodies of craving beginning with craving for forms; the six applied thoughts beginning with applied thought on forms; the six sustained thoughts beginning with sustained thought on forms; the five aggregates beginning with the form aggregate; the ten kasiṇas; the ten recollections; the ten perceptions, such as the perception of a bloated corpse; the thirty-two parts beginning with the hair of the head; the twelve sense bases; the eighteen elements; the nine kinds of existence beginning with sensual existence; the four jhānas beginning with the first; the four immeasurables beginning with the development of loving-kindness; the four formless attainments; and the links of dependent origination—in reverse order beginning with aging and death, and in forward order beginning with ignorance—should be connected.

Tatrāyaṃ ekapadayojanā – “jarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, jāti samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnampi nissaraṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhappajānanā paṭipadā maggasacca”nti. Evaṃ ekekapaduddhārena sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho anubuddho paṭividdho. Tena vuttaṃ – sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā pana sammāsambuddhoti.

Herein, this is the application to a single term: 'Aging and death are the truth of suffering; birth is the truth of origin; the escape from both is the truth of cessation; the practice for the distinct knowing of cessation is the truth of the path.' Thus, by the extraction of each single term, He has rightly and by Himself awakened to, awakened in detail to, and penetrated all dhammas. Therefore it was said: 'Furthermore, because He has rightly and by Himself awakened to all dhammas, He is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.'

Vijjāhi pana caraṇena ca sampannattā vijjācaraṇasampanno; tattha vijjāti tissopi vijjā, aṭṭhapi vijjā. Tisso vijjā bhayabheravasutte (ma. ni. 1.34 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbā, aṭṭha vijjā ambaṭṭhasutte (dī. ni. 1.278 ādayo). Tatra hi vipassanāñāṇena manomayiddhiyā ca saha cha abhiññā pariggahetvā aṭṭha vijjā vuttā. Caraṇanti sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, satta saddhammā, cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānānīti ime pannarasa dhammā veditabbā. Imeyeva hi pannarasa dhammā, yasmā etehi carati ariyasāvako gacchati amataṃ disaṃ tasmā, caraṇanti vuttā. Yathāha – “idha, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sīlavā hotī”ti (ma. ni. 2.24) vitthāro. Bhagavā imāhi vijjāhi iminā ca caraṇena samannāgato, tena vuccati vijjācaraṇasampannoti[V 1.0083]. Tattha vijjāsampadā bhagavato sabbaññutaṃ pūretvā ṭhitā, caraṇasampadā mahākāruṇikataṃ. So sabbaññutāya sabbasattānaṃ atthānatthaṃ ñatvā mahākāruṇikatāya anatthaṃ parivajjetvā atthe niyojeti, yathā taṃ vijjācaraṇasampanno. Tenassa sāvakā suppaṭipannā honti no duppaṭipannā, vijjācaraṇavipannānañhi sāvakā attantapādayo viya.

Furthermore, because He is endowed with the knowledges and with conduct, He is 'Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct' (Vijjācaraṇasampanno). Therein, 'knowledge' refers to the three knowledges and also the eight knowledges. The three knowledges should be understood according to the method stated in the Bhayabherava Sutta, and the eight knowledges according to the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. For in the latter, the eight knowledges are stated by including the six supernormal knowledges together with insight-knowledge and the power of the mind-made body. 'Conduct' should be understood as these fifteen dhammas: restraint of virtue, guardedness of the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, application to wakefulness, the seven true dhammas, and the four form-sphere jhānas. Indeed, because a noble disciple fares on and goes to the deathless direction by means of these fifteen dhammas, they are called 'conduct.' As was said: 'Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is virtuous...'—the detailed explanation should be understood. The Blessed One is endowed with these knowledges and this conduct; therefore, He is called 'Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct.' Therein, the accomplishment in knowledge stands, having fulfilled the Blessed One's omniscience, while the accomplishment in conduct stands, having fulfilled His great compassion. Through omniscience, He knows the welfare and non-welfare of all beings, and through great compassion, He avoids what is not for their welfare and engages them in what is for their welfare, as is befitting one accomplished in knowledge and conduct. Therefore, His disciples are of good practice, not of bad practice, for the disciples of those deficient in knowledge and conduct are of bad practice, like the self-tormentors and so on.

Sobhanagamanattā, sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā, sammāgatattā, sammā ca gadattā sugato. Gamanampi hi gatanti vuccati, tañca bhagavato sobhanaṃ parisuddhamanavajjaṃ[M 1.0089]. Kiṃ [P 1.0117] pana tanti? Ariyamaggo. Tena hesa gamanena khemaṃ disaṃ asajjamāno gatoti sobhanagamanattā sugato. Sundaraṃ cesa ṭhānaṃ gato amataṃ nibbānanti sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattāpi sugato. Sammā ca gato tena tena maggena pahīne kilese puna apaccāgacchanto. Vuttañcetaṃ – “sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato…pe… arahattamaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato”ti (mahāni. 38). Sammā vā āgato dīpaṅkarapādamūlato pabhuti yāva bodhimaṇḍo tāva samatiṃsapāramipūritāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbalokassa hitasukhameva karonto sassataṃ ucchedaṃ kāmasukhaṃ attakilamathanti ime ca ante anupagacchanto āgatoti sammāgatattāpi sugato. Sammā cesa gadati, yuttaṭṭhāne yuttameva vācaṃ bhāsatīti sammā gadattāpi sugato.

Because of his excellent going, because he has gone to a beautiful place, because he has gone rightly, and because he speaks rightly, he is the Sugata (Well-Gone). For even the act of going is called 'gone,' and that of the Blessed One is excellent, utterly pure, and blameless. What, then, is that going? The Noble Path. For by this going he has gone to the secure destination without getting stuck; thus, because of his excellent going, he is the Sugata. And he has gone to the beautiful place—the deathless Nibbāna; thus, because he has gone to a beautiful place, he is also the Sugata. And he has gone rightly, not returning again to the defilements abandoned by each respective path. And this was stated: 'The defilements that are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, to those defilements he does not return, he does not go back, he does not revert; thus he is the Sugata… (and so on until) …the defilements that are abandoned by the path of Arahantship, to those defilements he does not return, he does not go back, he does not revert; thus he is the Sugata.' Or, he has gone rightly from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the Bodhi-seat, fulfilling the thirty perfections through right practice, bringing about only the welfare and happiness of the entire world, and not approaching these two extremes—eternalism and annihilationism, indulgence in sensual pleasure and self-mortification; thus, because he has gone rightly, he is also the Sugata. And he speaks rightly, uttering only suitable speech in a suitable place; thus, because he speaks rightly, he is also the Sugata.

Tatridaṃ sādhakasuttaṃ – “yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya. Yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāyā”ti (ma. ni. 2.86). Evaṃ sammā gadattāpi sugatoti veditabbo.

Herein is the corroborating Sutta: 'The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unpleasant to others—such speech the Tathāgata does not utter. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, but unbeneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unpleasant to others—that speech, too, the Tathāgata does not utter. But the speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unpleasant to others—therein the Tathāgata is a knower of the right time for uttering that speech. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, but which is agreeable and pleasant to others—such speech the Tathāgata does not utter. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, but unbeneficial, and which is also agreeable and pleasant to others—that speech, too, the Tathāgata does not utter. But the speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, and which is also agreeable and pleasant to others—therein the Tathāgata is a knower of the right time for uttering that speech.' In this way, because he speaks rightly, he is to be understood as the Sugata.

Sabbathā viditalokattā pana lokavidū. So hi bhagavā sabhāvato samudayato nirodhato nirodhūpāyatoti [V 1.0084] sabbathā lokaṃ avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi. Yathāha – “yattha kho, āvuso, na jāyati [P 1.0118] na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjati, nāhaṃ taṃ gamanena lokassa [M 1.0090] antaṃ ñāteyyaṃ daṭṭheyyaṃ patteyyanti vadāmi; na cāhaṃ, āvuso, appatvāva lokassa antaṃ dukkhassa antakiriyaṃ vadāmi. Api cāhaṃ, āvuso, imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññapemi lokasamudayañca lokanirodhañca lokanirodhagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ.

Moreover, because he has known the world in every way, he is the Lokavidū (Knower of the World). For that Blessed One has in every way known, understood, and penetrated the world: in terms of its nature, its origin, its cessation, and the way to its cessation. As was said: 'Friend, I do not say that the end of the world—where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn—can be known, seen, or reached by going. Yet, friend, I do not say that there is an end to suffering without having reached the end of the world. Rather, friend, it is in this very fathom-long body, with its perception and mind, that I make known the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.'

“Gamanena na pattabbo, lokassanto kudācanaṃ;

Na ca appatvā lokantaṃ, dukkhā atthi pamocanaṃ.

The end of the world can never be reached by going; and without reaching the world's end, there is no release from suffering.

“Tasmā have lokavidū sumedho;

Lokantagū vusitabrahmacariyo;

Lokassa antaṃ samitāvi ñatvā;

Nāsīsatī lokamimaṃ parañcā”ti. (a. ni. 4.45; saṃ. ni. 1.107);

Therefore, indeed, the wise one, the knower of the world, who has gone to the world's end and lived the holy life; the pacified one, having known the end of the world, does not long for this world or the next.

Apica tayo lokā – saṅkhāraloko, sattaloko, okāsalokoti; tattha “eko loko – sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.112) āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhāraloko veditabbo. “Sassato lokoti vā asassato lokoti vā”ti (dī. ni. 1.421) āgataṭṭhāne sattaloko.

Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of space (okāsaloka). Therein, in the passage, 'There is one world: all beings are sustained by nutriment,' the world of formations is to be understood. In the passage, 'The world is eternal, or the world is not eternal,' the world of beings is to be understood.

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā, pariharanti disā bhanti virocanā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko, ettha te vattatī vaso”ti. (ma. ni. 1.503) –

As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world; therein your power prevails.

Āgataṭṭhāne okāsaloko, tampi bhagavā sabbathā avedi. Tathā hissa – “eko loko – sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Dve lokā – nāmañca rūpañca. Tayo lokā – tisso vedanā. Cattāro lokā – cattāro āhārā. Pañca lokā – pañcupādānakkhandhā. Cha lokā – cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni. Satta lokā satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Aṭṭha lokā – aṭṭha lokadhammā. Nava lokā – nava sattāvāsā. Dasa lokā – dasāyatanāni. Dvādasa lokā – dvādasāyatanāni[V 1.0085]. Aṭṭhārasa lokā – aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.112). Ayaṃ saṅkhāralokopi sabbathā vidito.

In the passage just quoted, the world of space is to be understood. That too the Blessed One knew in every way. For indeed, to him: 'There is one world: all beings are sustained by nutriment. There are two worlds: name and form. There are three worlds: the three feelings. There are four worlds: the four nutriments. There are five worlds: the five aggregates of grasping. There are six worlds: the six internal sense bases. There are seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. There are eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. There are nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. There are ten worlds: the ten sense bases. There are twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases. There are eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements.' This world of formations, too, was known in every way.

Yasmā [M 1.0091] panesa sabbesampi sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānāti, anusayaṃ jānāti, caritaṃ jānāti, adhimuttiṃ jānāti, apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye mudindriye svākāre dvākāre suviññāpaye duviññāpaye bhabbe abhabbe satte jānāti, tasmāssa sattalokopi sabbathā vidito. Yathā ca sattaloko [P 1.0119] evaṃ okāsalokopi. Tathā hesa ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ āyāmato ca vitthārato ca yojanānaṃ dvādasa satasahassāni tīṇi sahassāni cattāri satāni paññāsañca yojanāni. Parikkhepato –

Furthermore, because he knows the disposition of all beings, knows their latent tendencies, knows their conduct, knows their inclinations; because he knows beings with little dust and with much dust, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, of good character and of bad character, easy to teach and difficult to teach, capable and incapable—therefore, the world of beings is also known to him in every way. And just as the world of beings, so too the world of space. For this one world-system is, in length and in breadth, one million, two hundred and three thousand, four hundred and fifty yojanas. In circumference—

Sabbaṃ satasahassāni, chattiṃsa parimaṇḍalaṃ;

Dasañceva sahassāni, aḍḍhuḍḍhāni satāni ca.

The entire circumference is three million, six hundred and ten thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas.

Tattha –

Therein—

Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharā.

Two hundred thousand, and four myriads; by such a measure of thickness is this earth reckoned.

Tassā eva sandhārakaṃ –

Its very support—

Cattāri satasahassāni, aṭṭheva nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, jalaṃ vāte patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Four hundred thousand, and indeed eight myriads; by such a measure of thickness is the water established on the wind.

Tassāpi sandhārako –

Its supporter as well—

Navasatasahassāni, māluto nabhamuggato;

Saṭṭhi ceva sahassāni, esā lokassa saṇṭhiti.

The wind has risen into the sky for nine hundred thousand and sixty thousand yojanas; this is the foundation of the world.

Evaṃ saṇṭhite cettha yojanānaṃ –

And thus constituted, here, in terms of yojanas—

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato tāvadeva, sinerupabbatuttamo.

Eighty-four thousand yojanas, submerged in the great ocean; risen up just as much, is the excellent Mount Sineru.

Tato [V 1.0086] upaḍḍhupaḍḍhena, pamāṇena yathākkamaṃ;

Ajjhogāḷhuggatā dibbā, nānāratanacittitā.

From that, by a measure of successive halves, in due order, are the divine mountains, submerged and risen up, variegated with various jewels.

Yugandharo īsadharo, karavīko sudassano;

Nemindharo vinatako, assakaṇṇo girī brahā.

Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara, Vinataka, and Assakaṇṇa—these are the great mountains.

Ete satta mahāselā, sinerussa samantato;

Mahārājānamāvāsā, devayakkhanisevitā.

These seven great mountains are around Sineru, the abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by devas and yakkhas.

Yojanānaṃ [M 1.0092] satānucco, himavā pañca pabbato;

Yojanānaṃ sahassāni, tīṇi āyatavitthato;

Caturāsītisahassehi, kūṭehi paṭimaṇḍito.

The Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high, and three thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks.

Tipañcayojanakkhandha, parikkhepā nagavhayā;

Paññāsa yojanakkhandha, sākhāyāmā samantato.

The Jambu tree, also known as Naga, has a trunk fifteen yojanas in girth; its trunk and main branches are fifty yojanas in length all around.

Satayojanavitthiṇṇā, tāvadeva ca uggatā;

Jambū yassānubhāvena, jambudīpo pakāsito.

One hundred yojanas in breadth, and risen up just as high; the Jambu tree by whose power Jambudīpa is made known.

Dve asīti sahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato tāvadeva, cakkavāḷasiluccayo;

Parikkhipitvā taṃ sabbaṃ, lokadhātumayaṃ ṭhito.

The Cakkavāḷa rock mountain is submerged eighty-two thousand yojanas in the great ocean and rises up just as much; it stands encompassing that entire world-system.

Tattha candamaṇḍalaṃ ekūnapaññāsayojanaṃ, sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ paññāsayojanaṃ, tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ dasasahassayojanaṃ; tathā asurabhavanaṃ, avīcimahānirayo, jambudīpo ca. Aparagoyānaṃ sattasahassayojanaṃ; tathā pubbavideho. Uttarakuru aṭṭhasahassayojano, ekameko cettha mahādīpo pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāro; taṃ sabbampi ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ[P 1.0120], ekā lokadhātu, tadantaresu lokantarikanirayā. Evaṃ anantāni cakkavāḷāni anantā lokadhātuyo bhagavā anantena buddhañāṇena avedi, aññāsi, paṭivijjhi. Evamassa okāsalokopi sabbathā vidito. Evampi sabbathā viditalokattā lokavidū.

Therein, the moon's disk is forty-nine yojanas, the sun's disk is fifty yojanas, and the Tāvatiṃsa realm is ten thousand yojanas; likewise the Asura realm, the great Avīci hell, and Jambudīpa. Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas; likewise Pubbavideha. Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas, and each of these great continents is surrounded by five hundred lesser islands. All of this is one Cakkavāḷa, one world-system, and in the spaces between them are the Lokantarika hells. Thus the Blessed One knew, understood, and penetrated infinite Cakkavāḷas and infinite world-systems with his infinite Buddha-knowledge. In this way, the spatial world was fully known to him. Thus, because the world was known in every way, he is the 'Knower of the World'.

Attano [V 1.0087] pana guṇehi visiṭṭhatarassa kassaci abhāvā natthi etassa uttaroti anuttaro. Tathā hesa sīlaguṇenāpi sabbaṃ lokamabhibhavati, samādhi…pe… paññā… vimutti… vimuttiñāṇadassanaguṇenāpi, sīlaguṇenāpi asamo asamasamo appaṭimo appaṭibhāgo appaṭipuggalo…pe… vimuttiñāṇadassanaguṇenāpi. Yathāha – “na kho panāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samanupassāmi sadevake loke samārake…pe… sadevamanussāya attanā sīlasampannatara”nti vitthāro.

Furthermore, because there is no one superior to him in virtues, 'there is no superior to him' (natthi etassa uttaro), thus he is 'Unsurpassed' (anuttaro). For indeed, he surpasses the entire world by the quality of his virtue, by the quality of his concentration... (and so on)... by the quality of his wisdom... by the quality of his liberation... by the quality of his knowledge and vision of liberation. By the quality of his virtue he is unequal, of unequal equality, without peer, without counterpart, without a rival individual... (and so on)... by the quality of his knowledge and vision of liberation. As he said: “Bhikkhus, I do not perceive in this world with its devas, its Māras... (and so on)... with its generation of ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, anyone more accomplished in virtue than myself.” The detailed account should be understood.

Evaṃ [M 1.0093] aggappasādasuttādīni (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) “na me ācariyo atthī”tiādikā gāthāyo (ma. ni. 1.285; mahāva. 11) ca vitthāretabbā.

In the same way, the Aggappasāda Sutta and others (AN 4.34; Iti 90), and the verses beginning “I have no teacher” (MN 26; Mv 1.6.7), should be elaborated upon.

Purisadamme sāretīti purisadammasārathi, dameti vinetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha purisadammāti adantā dametuṃ yuttā tiracchānapurisāpi manussapurisāpi amanussapurisāpi. Tathā hi bhagavatā tiracchānapurisāpi apalāḷo nāgarājā, cūḷodaro, mahodaro, aggisikho, dhūmasikho, dhanapālako hatthīti evamādayo damitā, nibbisā katā, saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpitā. Manussapurisāpi saccakanigaṇṭhaputta-ambaṭṭhamāṇava-pokkharasāti-soṇadaṇḍakūṭadantādayo. Amanussapurisāpi āḷavaka-sūciloma-kharaloma-yakkha-sakkadevarājādayo damitā vinītā vicitrehi vinayanūpāyehi. “Ahaṃ kho, kesi, purisadammaṃ saṇhenapi vinemi, pharusenapi vinemi, saṇhapharusenapi vinemī”ti (a. ni. 4.111) idañcettha suttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Atha vā visuddhasīlādīnaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīni sotāpannādīnañca uttarimaggapaṭipadaṃ ācikkhanto dantepi dametiyeva.

He is the 'Guide for Persons to be Tamed' (purisadammasārathi) because he guides persons who are to be tamed (purisadamme sāreti); this is to say, he tames and disciplines them. Herein, 'persons to be tamed' refers to untamed beings suitable for taming—animal-men, human-men, and non-human men. For indeed, the Blessed One tamed animal-men such as the nāga kings Apaḷāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, and Aggisikha, and the elephant Dhanapāla; he made them non-venomous and established them in the refuges and moral precepts. He also tamed human-men such as Saccaka son of the Nigaṇṭhas, the youth Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, and Kūṭadanta. He also tamed non-human men such as the yakkhas Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma, and Sakka, king of the devas; they were disciplined by various skillful means of training. And here this sutta should be elaborated: 'Kesi, I discipline a person to be tamed with gentleness, with harshness, and with both gentleness and harshness' (AN 4.111). Furthermore, by explaining the first jhānas and so on to those of pure virtue, and the path to the higher stages of awakening to stream-enterers and so on, he tames even those who are already tamed.

Atha vā anuttaro purisadammasārathīti ekamevidaṃ atthapadaṃ[P 1.0121]. Bhagavā hi tathā purisadamme sāreti, yathā ekapallaṅkeneva nisinnā aṭṭha disā asajjamānā dhāvanti. Tasmā “anuttaro purisadammasārathī”ti vuccati. “Hatthidamakena, bhikkhave, hatthidammo sārito ekaṃyeva disaṃ dhāvatī”ti idañcettha suttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.312) vitthāretabbaṃ.

Alternatively, 'Unsurpassed Guide for Persons to be Tamed' is a single term of meaning. For the Blessed One guides persons to be tamed in such a way that, while sitting in one cross-legged posture, they run unimpeded towards the eight directions, which are the eight attainments. Therefore, he is called the 'Unsurpassed Guide for Persons to be Tamed'. And here this sutta should be elaborated: 'Bhikkhus, an elephant to be tamed, when guided by an elephant tamer, runs in only one direction...' (MN 125).

Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ anusāsatīti satthā. Apica satthā viyāti satthā, bhagavā satthavāho. “Yathā satthavāho satthe kantāraṃ tāreti, corakantāraṃ tāreti, vāḷakantāraṃ tāreti, dubbhikkhakantāraṃ tāreti, nirudakakantāraṃ tāreti, uttāreti nittāreti patāreti [V 1.0088] khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpeti; evameva bhagavā satthā satthavāho satte kantāraṃ tāreti jātikantāraṃ tāretī”tiādinā (mahāni. 190) niddesanayenapettha attho veditabbo.

He is the 'Teacher' (satthā) because he instructs (anusāsati) appropriately in matters concerning this present life, the next life, and the ultimate good. Moreover, he is a 'Teacher' (satthā) because he is like a caravan leader (satthavāha); the Blessed One is a caravan leader. “Just as a caravan leader guides a caravan across a wilderness—guides them across a wilderness of thieves, a wilderness of beasts, a wilderness of famine, a wilderness of drought; leads them across, leads them out, leads them through, and brings them to a land of safety—so too the Blessed One, the Teacher, the caravan leader, guides beings across a wilderness, guides them across the wilderness of birth,” and so on. By this method from the Niddesa (Mahāni 1.93), the meaning should be understood here.

Devamanussānanti [M 1.0094] daevānañca manussānañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ, bhabbapuggalaparicchedavasena ca. Bhagavā pana tiracchānagatānampi anusāsanippadānena satthāyeva. Tepi hi bhagavato dhammasavanena upanissayasampattiṃ patvā tāya eva upanissayasampattiyā dutiye tatiye vā attabhāve maggaphalabhāgino honti. Maṇḍūkadevaputtādayo cettha nidassanaṃ. Bhagavati kira gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre campānagaravāsīnaṃ dhammaṃ desayamāne eko maṇḍūko bhagavato sare nimittaṃ aggahesi. Taṃ eko vacchapālako daṇḍamolubbha tiṭṭhanto tassa sīse sannirumbhitvā aṭṭhāsi. So tāvadeva kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane dvādasayojanike kanakavimāne nibbatti. Suttappabuddho viya ca tattha accharāsaṅghaparivutaṃ attānaṃ disvā “are, ahampi nāma idha nibbattosmi! Kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ akāsi”nti āvajjento nāññaṃ kiñci addasa, aññatra bhagavato sare nimittaggāhā. So [P 1.0122] taāvadeva saha vimānena āgantvā bhagavato pāde sirasā vandi. Bhagavā jānantova pucchi –

The term 'of devas and humans' is spoken by way of distinguishing superior beings, and also by way of distinguishing individuals capable of liberation. However, the Blessed One is indeed the Teacher even of animals by giving instruction. For they, by hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One, attain the perfection of a supporting condition, and through that very perfection of a supporting condition, in their second or third existence, they become partakers of the path and fruit. The devaputta who was a frog and others serve as an example here. It is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the inhabitants of Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā pond, a frog grasped the sign in the Blessed One’s voice. A cowherd, standing leaning on a stick, pressed down on its head and stood there. At that very moment, it died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size. And there, as if awakened from sleep, it saw itself surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs and reflected, “Oh! I too have been reborn here! What kamma, I wonder, did I perform?” Reflecting, it saw nothing else apart from having grasped the sign in the Blessed One’s voice. At that very moment, it came with its celestial mansion and bowed its head at the Blessed One’s feet. The Blessed One, although knowing, asked—

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti.

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with psychic power and retinue, with surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions?”

“Maṇḍūkohaṃ pure āsiṃ, udake vārigocaro;

Tava dhammaṃ suṇantassa, avadhi vacchapālako”ti. (vi. va. 857-858);

“Once I was a frog, an aquatic creature with water as my pasture. While I was listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me.”

Bhagavā tassa dhammaṃ desesi. Desanāvasāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Devaputtopi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya sitaṃ katvā pakkāmīti.

The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma. The devaputta also, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry, smiled and departed.

Yaṃ pana kiñci atthi ñeyyaṃ nāma, tassa sabbassa buddhattā vimokkhantikañāṇavasena buddho. Yasmā vā cattāri saccāni attanāpi bujjhi, aññepi satte bodhesi; tasmā evamādīhipi kāraṇehi buddho.
