Imassa catthassa viññāpanatthaṃ “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”ti evaṃ pavatto sabbopi niddesanayo (mahāni. 192) paṭisambhidānayo (paṭi. ma. 1.162) vā vitthāretabbo.

Furthermore, whatever knowable thing exists, because he has understood all of it by means of the knowledge culminating in liberation, he is 'Buddha'. Or, because he himself understood the four truths and caused other beings to understand, for these and similar reasons he is 'Buddha'. To make this meaning known, this entire method of the Niddesa or the Paṭisambhidāmagga which proceeds thus: “He is ‘Buddha’ because he has understood the truths; he is ‘Buddha’ because he awakens the populace,” should be elaborated.

Bhagavāti [V 1.0089] idaṃ panassa guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Now, this term 'Bhagavā' is a designation of weightiness and reverence for him who is supreme among beings and distinguished by virtues. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Bhagavāti [M 1.0095] vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garu gāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“The word 'Bhagavā' is excellent, the word 'Bhagavā' is supreme; He is weighty and endowed with reverence, therefore he is called 'Bhagavā'.”

Catubbidhañhi nāmaṃ – āvatthikaṃ, liṅgikaṃ, nemittikaṃ, adhiccasamuppannanti. Adhiccasamuppannaṃ nāma lokiyavohārena “yadicchaka”nti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha “vaccho dammo balibaddo”ti evamādi āvatthikaṃ. “Daṇḍī chattī sikhī karī”ti evamādi liṅgikaṃ. “Tevijjo chaḷabhiñño”ti evamādi nemittikaṃ. “Sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhako”ti evamādi vacanatthamanapekkhitvā pavattaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ. Idaṃ pana bhagavāti nāmaṃ nemittikaṃ, na mahāmāyāya na suddhodanamahārājena na asītiyā ñātisahassehi kataṃ, na sakkasantusitādīhi devatāvisesehi. Vuttañhetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā – “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ…pe… vimokkhantikametaṃ [P 1.0123] buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikāpaññatti, yadidaṃ bhagavā”ti (mahāni. 84).

For names are of four kinds: based on a condition, based on a sign, based on a reason, and arisen by chance. A name that has arisen by chance is what is called 'random' in worldly usage. Among these, 'calf', 'tameable', 'bullock', and so on are based on a condition. 'Staff-bearer', 'umbrella-bearer', 'crested one', 'trunked one (elephant)', and so on are based on a sign. 'Possessor of the three knowledges', 'possessor of the six supernormal knowledges', and so on are based on a reason. 'Sirivaḍḍhaka', 'Dhanavaḍḍhaka', and so on, which are used without regard to the meaning of the words, have arisen by chance. But this name 'Bhagavā' is based on a reason. It was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana, nor by the eighty thousand relatives, nor by distinguished deities like Sakka and Santusita. For this was said by the General of the Dhamma: 'This name "Bhagavā" was not given by his mother... it is a name culminating in liberation for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, along with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience. It is a designation based on direct realization, this name "Bhagavā".'

Yaṃguṇanemittikañcetaṃ nāmaṃ, tesaṃ guṇānaṃ pakāsanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ vadanti –

And to reveal those virtues which are the reason for this name, they recite this verse:

“Bhagī bhajī bhāgī vibhattavā iti;

Akāsi bhagganti garūti bhāgyavā;

Bahūhi ñāyehi subhāvitattano;

Bhavantago so bhagavāti vuccatī”ti.

“He is a possessor of blessings (bhagī), he resorts (bhajī), he is a partaker (bhāgī), and he has analyzed (vibhattavā); he has effected the breaking (bhaggaṃ akāsi), he is weighty (garu), and he is fortunate (bhāgyavā); his self is well-developed by many methods; he has gone to the end of existence (bhavantago): therefore he is called Bhagavā.”

Niddese vuttanayeneva cettha tesaṃ tesaṃ padānamattho daṭṭhabbo.

And here, the meaning of those respective words should be understood precisely according to the method spoken in the Niddesa.

Ayaṃ pana aparo nayo –

But this is another method:

“Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti.

“Because he is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has broken (bhaggavā), is endowed with blessings (bhagehi yutto), and has analyzed (vibhattavā); he has frequented (bhattavā) and has vomited out the going in existences (bhavesu vantagamano), therefore he is Bhagavā.”

Tattha vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyayoti etaṃ niruttilakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā saddanayena vā pisodarādipakkhepalakkhaṇaṃ [V 1.0090] gahetvā yasmā lokiyalokuttarasukhābhinibbattakaṃ dānasīlādipārappattaṃ bhāgyamassa atthi, tasmā “bhāgyavā”ti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vuccatīti ñātabbaṃ. Yasmā pana lobha-dosa-moha-viparītamanasikāra-ahirikānottappa-kodhūpanāha-makkha-paḷāsaissā-macchariya-māyāsāṭheyya-thambha-sārambha-mānātimāna-mada-pamāda-taṇhāvijjā [M 1.0096] tividhākusalamūla-duccarita-saṃkilesa-mala-visamasaññā-vitakka-papañca-catubbidhavipariyesaāsava-gantha-ogha-yogāgati-taṇhuppādupādāna-pañcacetokhīla-vinibandha-nīvaraṇābhinandanachavivādamūla-taṇhākāya-sattānusaya-aṭṭhamicchatta-navataṇhāmūlaka-dasākusalakama diṭṭhigata-aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritappabheda-sabbadaratha-pariḷāha-kilesasatasahassāni, saṅkhepato vā pañca kilesa-abhisaṅkhārakhandhamaccu-devaputta-māre abhañji, tasmā bhaggattā etesaṃ parissayānaṃ bhaggavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati. Āha cettha –

Here, by taking the characteristic of etymology—that is, the addition or alteration of letters—or by the method of grammar, taking the characteristic of inclusion in the `pisodara` group and so on, it should be known that because he possesses the fortune which produces worldly and supramundane happiness and which has reached perfection through giving, virtue, and so on, therefore, though he should be called 'bhāgyavā' (the fortunate one), he is called 'bhagavā'. Furthermore, because he broke greed, hatred, delusion, wrong attention, lack of shame, lack of fear of wrongdoing, anger, resentment, contempt, hypocrisy, envy, stinginess, deceit, trickery, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, heedlessness, craving, ignorance, the three unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains, distorted perceptions, thoughts, mental proliferation, the fourfold perversions, the taints, the fetters, the floods, the yokes, wrong courses, the arising of craving, clinging, the five mental barrennesses, bondage, the hindrances, delighting, the six roots of dispute, the body of craving, the seven underlying tendencies, the eight wrongnesses, the nine things rooted in craving, the ten unwholesome courses of action, the sixty-two kinds of wrong views, the one hundred and eight kinds of craving-conduct, and all the hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause fever and burning heat—or, in brief, because he broke the five Māras: the Māra of defilements, the Māra of formations, the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of death, and the Māra that is the devaputta—therefore, because of having broken these perils, though he should be called 'bhaggavā' (the breaker), he is called 'bhagavā'. And it is said here:

“Bhaggarāgo bhaggadoso, bhaggamoho anāsavo;

Bhaggāssa pāpakā dhammā, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

He has destroyed passion, destroyed hatred, destroyed delusion, and is without taints; his evil states are destroyed, therefore he is called Bhagavā.

Bhāgyavantatāya [P 1.0124] cassa satapuññajalakkhaṇadharassa rūpakāyasampattidīpitā hoti, bhaggadosatāya dhammakāyasampatti. Tathā lokiyaparikkhakānaṃ bahumatabhāvo, gahaṭṭhapabbajitehi abhigamanīyatā, abhigatānañca nesaṃ kāyacittadukkhāpanayane paṭibalabhāvo, āmisadānadhammadānehi upakāritā, lokiyalokuttarasukhehi ca sampayojanasamatthatā dīpitā hoti.

And by his fortune, the perfection of the physical body of him who bears the marks born of hundreds of meritorious accumulations is revealed; by his having destroyed hatred, the perfection of the Dhamma body is revealed. Likewise, the following are revealed: the state of being highly esteemed by the worldly wise, the state of being approachable by householders and renunciants, the state of being capable of removing the bodily and mental suffering of those who have approached him, the state of being beneficial through the gifts of material things and the Dhamma, and the state of being capable of connecting them with worldly and supramundane happiness.

Yasmā ca loke issariya-dhamma-yasa-sirī-kāma-payattesu chasu dhammesu bhagasaddo vattati, paramañcassa sakacitte issariyaṃ, aṇimā laghimādikaṃ vā lokiyasammataṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ atthi tathā lokuttaro dhammo lokattayabyāpako yathābhuccaguṇādhigato ativiya parisuddho yaso, rūpakāyadassanabyāvaṭajananayanappasādajananasamatthā sabbākāraparipūrā sabbaṅgapaccaṅgasirī, yaṃ yaṃ etena icchitaṃ patthitaṃ attahitaṃ parahitaṃ vā, tassa tassa tatheva abhinipphannattā icchiticchi, tattha nipphattisaññito kāmo, sabbalokagarubhāvappattihetubhūto sammāvāyāmasaṅkhāto payatto ca atthi; tasmā imehi bhagehi yuttattāpi bhagā assa santīti iminā atthena bhagavāti vuccati.

And because in the world the word 'bhaga' applies to six things—sovereignty, Dhamma, fame, glory, wish-fulfillment, and effort—and he possesses supreme sovereignty over his own mind, or worldly-acknowledged power complete in all aspects such as minuteness and lightness; likewise, the supramundane Dhamma; fame that pervades the three worlds, obtained through genuine virtues, and is exceedingly pure; the glory of all major and minor limbs, complete in all aspects, capable of producing clarity in the eyes of people diligent in seeing the physical body; wish-fulfillment, so-called because whatever benefit for self or others is wished or aspired to by him is fulfilled just so; and effort, called right endeavor, which is the cause for attaining the state of being revered by the whole world; therefore, because of being endowed with these fortunes (bhaga), he is also called 'Bhagavā' with the meaning 'He has fortunes'.

Yasmā pana kusalādīhi bhedehi sabbadhamme, khandhāyatana-dhātusacca-indriyapaṭiccasamuppādādīhi [V 1.0091] vā kusalādidhamme, pīḷana-saṅkhata-santāpavipariṇāmaṭṭhena vā dukkhamariyasaccaṃ, āyūhana-nidāna-saṃyoga-palibodhaṭṭhena samudayaṃ, nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhata-amataṭṭhena [M 1.0097] nirodhaṃ, niyyāna-hetu-dassanādhipateyyaṭṭhena maggaṃ vibhattavā, vibhajitvā vivaritvā desitavāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā vibhattavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati[P 1.0125].

Furthermore, because he has analyzed all phenomena by classifications such as wholesome and so forth; or wholesome and other phenomena by classifications such as the aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so forth; or the Noble Truth of Suffering by way of the meaning of oppression, the conditioned, torment, and change; the Noble Truth of the Origin by way of the meaning of accumulation, source, bond, and obstruction; the Noble Truth of Cessation by way of the meaning of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless; and the Noble Truth of the Path by way of the meaning of leading out, cause, vision, and sovereignty; and having analyzed, elucidated, and taught them, it is said. Therefore, when 'Vibhattavā' (he who has analyzed) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā ca esa dibbabrahmaariyavihāre kāyacittaupadhiviveke suññatappaṇihitānimittavimokkhe aññe ca lokiyalokuttare uttarimanussadhamme bhaji sevi bahulamakāsi, tasmā bhattavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati.

And because he resorted to, frequented, and cultivated abundantly the divine, brahma, and noble abidings; the seclusions of body, mind, and substrata; the liberations of emptiness, the undirected, and the signless; and other worldly and supramundane states superior to the human; therefore, when 'Bhattavā' (he who has frequented) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā pana tīsu bhavesu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamanamanena vantaṃ, tasmā bhavesu vantagamanoti vattabbe bhavasaddato bhakāraṃ, gamanasaddato gakāraṃ, vantasaddato vakārañca dīghaṃ katvā ādāya bhagavāti vuccati. Yathā loke “mehanassa khassa mālā”ti vattabbe “mekhalā”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, because the going, known as craving, in the three existences has been expelled by him, therefore, when 'bhavesu vantagamano' (one who has expelled going in existences) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā' by taking the letter 'bha' from the word 'bhava', the letter 'ga' from the word 'gamana', and the letter 'va' from the word 'vanta'. Just as in the world, when 'mehanassa khassa mālā' should be said, it is called 'mekhalā'.

So imaṃ lokanti so bhagavā imaṃ lokaṃ. Idāni vattabbaṃ nidasseti. Sadevakanti saha devehi sadevakaṃ; evaṃ saha mārena samārakaṃ; saha brahmunā sabrahmakaṃ; saha samaṇabrāhmaṇehi sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ; pajātattā pajā, taṃ pajaṃ; saha devamanussehi sadevamanussaṃ. Tattha sadevakavacanena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, samārakavacanena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇīvacanena sāsanassa paccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ, samitapāpa-bāhitapāpa-samaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇañca, pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ, sadevamanussavacanena sammutidevaavasesamanussaggahaṇaṃ. Evamettha tīhi padehi okāsaloko, dvīhi pajāvasena sattaloko gahitoti veditabbo.

'So imaṃ lokaṃ' means: that Blessed One, this world. By this, he now points out what is to be spoken of. 'With its devas' means together with the devas. Likewise, 'with its Māra' means together with Māra; 'with its Brahmā' means together with Brahmā; 'with its ascetics and brahmins' means together with ascetics and brahmins; 'its populace' means beings, because they are born (pajā); 'with its devas and humans' means together with devas and humans. Therein, by the expression 'with its devas', the devas of the five sense-sphere heavens should be understood. By the expression 'with its Māra', the devas of the sixth sense-sphere heaven should be understood. By the expression 'with its Brahmā', the Brahmās beginning with the Brahmakāyika realm should be understood. By the expression 'with its ascetics and brahmins', both the ascetics and brahmins who are opponents and adversaries of the Dispensation, and the ascetics who have pacified evil and brahmins who have banished evil should be understood. By the expression 'populace', the world of beings should be understood. By the expression 'with its devas and humans', conventional devas and the remaining humans should be understood. Thus it should be understood that here, by three phrases the world of space is included, and by two, by way of 'populace', the world of beings is included.

Aparo nayo – sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaradevaloko gahito, samārakaggahaṇena chakāmāvacaradevalokā, sabrahmakaggahaṇena rūpībrahmaloko, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇādiggahaṇena catuparisavasena sammutidevehi vā saha manussaloko, avasesasabbasattaloko vā.

Another method: by the inclusion of 'with its devas', the formless-sphere deva world is included; by the inclusion of 'with its Māra', the six sense-sphere deva worlds are included; by the inclusion of 'with its Brahmā', the form-sphere Brahmā world is included; by the inclusion of 'with its ascetics and brahmins, etc.', the human world is included by way of the four assemblies, or the human world together with conventional devas, or all the remaining world of beings.

Apicettha [M 1.0098] sadevakavacanena ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato sabbassāpi lokassa sacchikatabhāvaṃ sādhento tassa bhagavato kittisaddo abbhuggato. Tato yesaṃ siyā – “māro mahānubhāvo chakāmāvacarissaro vasavattī; kiṃ sopi etena sacchikato”ti? Tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamanto samārakanti [V 1.0092] abbhuggato. Yesaṃ pana siyā – “brahmā mahānubhāvo ekaṅguliyā ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷasahasse [P 1.0126] ālokaṃ pharati, dvīhi…pe… dasahi aṅgulīhi dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu ālokaṃ pharati, anuttarañca jhānasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, kiṃ sopi sacchikato”ti? Tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamanto sabrahmakanti abbhuggato. Tato yesaṃ siyā – “puthūsamaṇabrāhmaṇā sāsanapaccatthikā, kiṃ tepi sacchikatā”ti? Tesaṃ vimatiṃ vidhamanto sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajanti abbhuggato. Evaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhānaṃ sacchikatabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā atha sammutideve avasesamanusse ca upādāya ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena sesasattalokassa sacchikatabhāvaṃ pakāsento sadevamanussanti abbhuggato. Ayametthānusandhikkamo.

Moreover, here, by the expression 'with its devas', establishing the fact of his realization of the entire world by way of its highest division, the sound of that Blessed One's fame arose. Then, for those who might have the doubt, 'Māra is of great power, lord of the six sense-sphere heavens, a controller; has he too been realized by this one?', dispelling their doubt, the sound of fame 'with its Māra' arose. Furthermore, for those who might have the doubt, 'Brahmā is of great power; with one finger he can pervade one thousand world-systems with light, with two fingers... with ten fingers he can pervade ten thousand world-systems with light, and he experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative attainment; has he too been realized?', dispelling their doubt, the sound of fame 'with its Brahmā' arose. Then, for those who might have the doubt, 'There are many ascetics and brahmins who are opponents of the Dispensation; have they too been realized?', dispelling their doubt, the sound of fame 'its populace with its ascetics and brahmins' arose. Thus, having declared the realization of the highest of the high, then, taking into account conventional devas and the remaining humans, and proclaiming the realization of the rest of the world of beings by way of the highest division, the sound of fame 'with its devas and humans' arose. This is the sequential connection here.

Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetīti ettha pana sayanti sāmaṃ, aparaneyyo hutvā; abhiññāti abhiññāya, adhikena ñāṇena ñatvāti attho. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā, etena anumānādipaṭikkhepo kato hoti. Pavedetīti bodheti ñāpeti pakāseti. So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… pariyosānakalyāṇanti so bhagavā sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca hitvāpi anuttaraṃ vivekasukhaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Tañca kho appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desento ādikalyāṇādippakārameva deseti.

Furthermore, in the phrase, `Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti` (He himself, having directly known and realized it, declares it): `sayaṃ` means by himself, having become one not to be led by another. `Abhiññā` means having known with special knowledge, that is, having known with superior knowledge; this is the meaning. `Sacchikatvā` means having made it directly perceptible; by this, the rejection of inference and the like is accomplished. `Pavedeti` means he makes known, he informs, he reveals. As for `So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ` (He teaches the Dhamma that is lovely in the beginning… lovely in the end): That Blessed One, on account of compassion for beings, having relinquished even the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion, teaches the Dhamma. And whether teaching it in brief or in detail, he teaches it only in a way that is lovely in the beginning and so forth.

Kathaṃ? Ekagāthāpi hi samantabhadrakattā dhammassa paṭhamapādena ādikalyāṇā, dutiyatatiyapādehi majjhekalyāṇā, pacchimapādena pariyosānakalyāṇā. Ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ nidānena ādikalyāṇaṃ, nigamanena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ, sesena majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Nānānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ paṭhamānusandhinā ādikalyāṇaṃ, pacchimena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ, sesehi majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Sakalopi sāsanadhammo attano atthabhūtena sīlena ādikalyāṇo, samathavipassanāmaggaphalehi majjhekalyāṇo, nibbānena pariyosānakalyāṇo. Sīlasamādhīhi vā ādikalyāṇo, vipassanāmaggehi majjhekalyāṇo, phalanibbānehi pariyosānakalyāṇo[M 1.0099]. Buddhasubodhitāya vā ādikalyāṇo, dhammasudhammatāya majjhekalyāṇo, saṅghasuppaṭipattiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo. Taṃ sutvā tathattāya paṭipannena adhigantabbāya abhisambodhiyā vā ādikalyāṇo, paccekabodhiyā majjhekalyāṇo, sāvakabodhiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo. Suyyamāno cesa nīvaraṇavikkhambhanato savanenapi [P 1.0127] kalyāṇameva āvahatīti ādikalyāṇo, paṭipajjiyamāno samathavipassanāsukhāvahanato paṭipattiyāpi kalyāṇameva āvahatīti majjhekalyāṇo, tathā paṭipanno ca paṭipattiphale niṭṭhite tādibhāvāvahanato paṭipattiphalenapi kalyāṇameva āvahatīti pariyosānakalyāṇo. Nāthappabhavattā ca pabhavasuddhiyā ādikalyāṇo, atthasuddhiyā majjhekalyāṇo[V 1.0093], kiccasuddhiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo. Tasmā eso bhagavā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desento ādikalyāṇādippakārameva desetīti veditabbo.

How so? Indeed, even a single verse, due to its all-around excellence, is lovely in the beginning with its first line, lovely in the middle with its second and third lines, and lovely in the end with its final line. A discourse with a single thematic connection is lovely in the beginning with its introduction, lovely in the end with its conclusion, and lovely in the middle with the remainder. A discourse with various thematic connections is lovely in the beginning with its first connection, lovely in the end with its final connection, and lovely in the middle with the remaining connections. The entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is lovely in the beginning with virtue, which is its meaning; lovely in the middle with serenity, insight, the paths, and the fruits; and lovely in the end with Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is lovely in the beginning with virtue and concentration; lovely in the middle with insight and the paths; and lovely in the end with the fruits and Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is lovely in the beginning due to the Buddha's perfect enlightenment; lovely in the middle due to the excellent Dhamma-nature of the Dhamma; and lovely in the end due to the Sangha's good practice. Alternatively, for one who practices for its realization after hearing it, it is lovely in the beginning with the supreme enlightenment to be attained; lovely in the middle with the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha; and lovely in the end with the enlightenment of a disciple. Furthermore, when this Dhamma is being heard, by suppressing the hindrances, it brings forth only what is beneficial even through the hearing of it; thus, it is lovely in the beginning. When it is being practiced, by bringing the happiness of serenity and insight, it brings forth only what is beneficial even through the practice of it; thus, it is lovely in the middle. And for one who has so practiced, when the fruit of the practice is accomplished, by bringing the state of being 'such,' it brings forth only what is beneficial even through the fruit of the practice; thus, it is lovely in the end. Furthermore, it is lovely in the beginning due to the purity of its source, as it originates from the Protector; lovely in the middle due to the purity of its meaning; and lovely in the end due to the purity of its function. Therefore, it should be understood that whether the Blessed One teaches in brief or in detail, he teaches only in a way that is lovely in the beginning and so forth.

Sātthaṃ sabyañjananti evamādīsu pana yasmā imaṃ dhammaṃ desento sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyañca pakāseti, nānānayehi dīpeti; tañca yathānurūpaṃ atthasampattiyā sātthaṃ, byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Saṅkāsanapakāsana-vivaraṇa-vibhajana-uttānīkaraṇa-paññatti-atthapadasamāyogato sātthaṃ, akkharapada-byañjanākāraniruttiniddesasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Atthagambhīratā-paṭivedhagambhīratāhi sātthaṃ, dhammagambhīratādesanāgambhīratāhi sabyañjanaṃ. Atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāvisayato sātthaṃ, dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāvisayato sabyañjanaṃ. Paṇḍitavedanīyato parikkhakajanappasādakanti sātthaṃ, saddheyyato lokiyajanappasādakanti sabyañjanaṃ. Gambhīrādhippāyato sātthaṃ, uttānapadato sabyañjanaṃ. Upanetabbassa abhāvato sakalaparipuṇṇabhāvena kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ; apanetabbassa abhāvato niddosabhāvena parisuddhaṃ; sikkhattayapariggahitattā brahmabhūtehi seṭṭhehi caritabbato tesañca cariyabhāvato brahmacariyaṃ. Tasmā “sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ…pe… brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, in passages such as `sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ` (with meaning and with phrasing): Because in teaching this Dhamma he proclaims the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the path, and illuminates it in various ways, it is, as is appropriate, `sātthaṃ` (with meaning) due to its perfection in meaning, and `sabyañjanaṃ` (with phrasing) due to its perfection in phrasing. It is `sātthaṃ` because it is well-connected with the meanings of indication, exposition, disclosure, analysis, clarification, and designation. It is `sabyañjanaṃ` due to its perfection in letters, words, phrasing, style, language, and exposition. It is `sātthaṃ` due to the profundity of its meaning and the profundity of its penetration; it is `sabyañjanaṃ` due to the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the teaching. It is known to be `sātthaṃ` as it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of ready wit; it is known to be `sabyañjanaṃ` as it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and the analytical knowledge of language. It is `sātthaṃ` because, being knowable by the wise, it inspires confidence in discerning people; it is `sabyañjanaṃ` because, being worthy of faith, it inspires confidence in worldly people. It is `sātthaṃ` due to its profound intention; it is `sabyañjanaṃ` due to its clear wording. It is `kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ` (complete and perfect) because of its total completeness, as there is nothing to be added. It is `parisuddhaṃ` (utterly pure) because of its faultlessness, as there is nothing to be removed. It is `brahmacariyaṃ` (the holy life) because it is encompassed by the three trainings, because it is to be practiced by the supreme ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples—who have become noble, and because it is their very conduct. Therefore, it is said, 'He proclaims the holy life... with meaning, with phrasing.'

Apica yasmā sanidānaṃ sauppattikañca desento ādikalyāṇaṃ deseti, veneyyānaṃ anurūpato atthassa aviparītatāya ca hetudāharaṇayuttato ca majjhekalyāṇaṃ, sotūnaṃ saddhāpaṭilābhena nigamanena [M 1.0100] ca pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ deseti. Evaṃ desento ca brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti. Tañca paṭipattiyā adhigamabyattito sātthaṃ, pariyattiyā āgamabyattito sabyañjanaṃ, sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhayuttato kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ, nirupakkilesato nittharaṇatthāya [P 1.0128] pavattito lokāmisanirapekkhato ca parisuddhaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtānaṃ buddha-paccekabuddha-buddhasāvakānaṃ cariyato “brahmacariya”nti vuccati. Tasmāpi “so dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, because he teaches the Dhamma with its introduction and its origin story, he teaches what is lovely in the beginning. Because it is suitable for the trainees, undeviating in meaning, and endowed with reasons and examples, he teaches what is lovely in the middle. Because it leads to the listeners' acquisition of faith and has a conclusion, he teaches what is lovely in the end. And in teaching thus, he proclaims the holy life. That holy life is `sātthaṃ` (with meaning) due to the manifestation of attainment through practice; it is `sabyañjanaṃ` (with phrasing) due to the manifestation of the scriptural tradition through learning. It is `kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ` (complete and perfect) because it is endowed with the five aggregates of the Dhamma beginning with virtue. It is `parisuddhaṃ` (utterly pure) because it is free from defilements, because it proceeds for the purpose of crossing over, and because it is unconcerned with worldly gain. In the sense of 'supreme,' it is called `brahmacariyaṃ` (the holy life) because it is the conduct of those who have become noble: the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha's disciples. Therefore, it is also said, 'He teaches the Dhamma that is lovely in the beginning… and proclaims the holy life.'

Sādhu kho panāti sundaraṃ kho pana atthāvahaṃ sukhāvahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathārūpānaṃ arahatanti yathārūpo so bhava gotamo, evarūpānaṃ yathābhuccaguṇādhigamena loke arahantoti laddhasaddānaṃ arahataṃ. Dassanaṃ hotīti pasādasommāni akkhīni ummīlitvā “dassanamattampi sādhu hotī”ti evaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ katvā atha kho verañjo brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti.

`Sādhu kho pana` (It is indeed good) means: it is indeed excellent, beneficial, and brings happiness. `Tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ` (of such Arahants) means: of Arahants of such a nature as the venerable Gotama, who have gained the designation 'Arahant' in the world by attaining true qualities. The phrase `Dassanaṃ hoti` (the sight of them occurs) is explained by what follows: having formed the intention, 'Even the mere sight is good,' and having opened his clear and serene eyes, `atha kho verañjo brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami` (then the brahmin Verañja approached the Blessed One).

2. Yenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tasmā yattha bhagavā tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo[V 1.0094]. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya. Upasaṅkamīti ca gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gato tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti.

2. 'Yena' is a term in the instrumental case used in the sense of location. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'He approached wherever the Blessed One was.' Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'For that reason for which the Blessed One should be approached by gods and humans, for that reason he approached.' And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached? With the intention of attaining various kinds of special qualities, just as a great, ever-fruitful tree is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying its sweet fruits. And 'upasaṅkami' means 'he went.' 'Upasaṅkamitvā' is a term indicating the conclusion of the approaching. Or else, it is also said that having gone thus, from that place he went to a nearer place, designated as the presence of the Blessed One.

Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodīti yathā khamanīyādīni pucchanto bhagavā tena, evaṃ sopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi, sītodakaṃ viya uṇhodakena sammoditaṃ ekībhāvaṃ agamāsi. Yāya ca “kacci, bho, gotama, khamanīyaṃ; kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci bhoto gotamassa, ca sāvakānañca appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāro”tiādikāya kathāya sammodi, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātaṃ sammodaṃ jananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ. Atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ [P 1.0129] nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ araharūpato saritabbabhāvato ca sāraṇīyaṃ, suyyamānasukhato vā sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato [M 1.0101] sāraṇīyaṃ. Tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya sāraṇīyanti. Evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ kathaṃ vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhāpetvā yenatthena āgato taṃ pucchitukāmo ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

'He exchanged greetings with the Blessed One' means that just as the Blessed One, inquiring about matters such as his well-being, had a mutual exchange with him, so too did he have a mutual exchange with the Blessed One; they reached a state of oneness through their exchange, like cold water mixed with hot water becoming one. The conversation by which he exchanged greetings—'I hope, Venerable Gotama, you are well; I hope you are getting by. I hope you, Venerable Gotama, and your disciples are free from serious illness, free from affliction, are agile, strong, and dwelling in comfort' and so on—is called 'conducive to greeting' (sammodanīya) because it generates delight and joy and is thus fitting for exchange. Due to the sweetness of its meaning and expression, it is 'memorable' (sāraṇīya) because it is worthy of being prolonged for a long time, continuously engaged in, and worthy of being recollected. Alternatively, it is 'conducive to greeting' due to the pleasure of hearing it, and 'memorable' due to the pleasure of recollecting it. Likewise, it is 'conducive to greeting' due to the purity of its expression, and 'memorable' due to the purity of its meaning. Thus, having concluded this conversation, which was in many ways conducive to greeting and memorable, and wishing to ask about the matter for which he had come, he sat down to one side.

Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Tasmā yathā nisinno ekamantaṃ nisinno hoti tathā nisīdīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nisīdīti upāvisi. Paṇḍitā hi purisā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ nisīdanti. Ayañca tesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

'Ekamantaṃ' (to one side) is a neuter noun indicating manner, like 'visamaṃ' in passages such as 'the sun and moon revolve unevenly.' Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'He sat in such a way that one sitting would be sitting appropriately to one side.' Alternatively, this is a word in the accusative case used in the sense of location. 'Nisīdi' means 'he took a seat.' Indeed, wise persons, having approached one who is worthy of respect, sit to one side due to their skill in seating. And this one was one of them; therefore, he sat to one side.

Kathaṃ nisinno pana ekamantaṃ nisinno hotīti? Cha nisajjadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ – atidūraṃ, accāsannaṃ, uparivātaṃ, unnatappadesaṃ, atisammukhaṃ, atipacchāti. Atidūre nisinno hi sace kathetukāmo hoti uccāsaddena kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne nisinno saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti. Uparivāte nisinno sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese nisinno agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā [V 1.0095] ayampi ete cha nisajjadose vajjetvā nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”ti.

How, then, is one who is seated, seated 'to one side'? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. What are the six? Sitting too far, too close, upwind, in an elevated place, directly in front, and too far behind. Indeed, one sitting too far, if one wishes to speak, must speak in a loud voice. One sitting too close causes physical contact. One sitting upwind offends with body odor. One sitting in an elevated place displays disrespect. One sitting directly in front, if one wishes to look, must look with one's eyes making contact with the other's eyes. One sitting too far behind, if one wishes to look, must stretch one's neck. Therefore, this one also sat down, having avoided these six faults of sitting. For that reason, it is said: 'He sat down to one side.'

Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho verañjo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavocāti etanti idāni vattabbamatthaṃ dasseti. Dakāro padasandhikaro. Avocāti abhāsi. Sutaṃ metanti sutaṃ me etaṃ, etaṃ mayā sutanti idāni vattabbamatthaṃ dasseti. Bho gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati.

In the passage 'The brahmin Verañja, seated to one side, said this (etadavoca) to the Blessed One': 'etaṃ' (this) indicates the matter that is now to be spoken. The letter 'd' serves as a euphonic link between words. 'Avoca' means 'he spoke.' 'Sutaṃ metaṃ' means 'This has been heard by me,' or 'I have heard this,' indicating the matter that is now to be spoken. With 'Bho Gotama,' he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.

Idāni yaṃ tena sutaṃ – taṃ dassento na samaṇo gotamoti evamādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – brāhmaṇeti jātibrāhmaṇe. Jiṇṇeti jajjarībhūte [P 1.0130] jarāya khaṇḍiccādibhāvaṃ āpādite. Vuḍḍheti aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ vuḍḍhimariyādappatte. Mahallaketi jātimahallakatāya samannāgate, cirakālappasuteti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhagateti addhānaṃ gate[M 1.0102], dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe atīteti adhippāyo. Vayo anuppatteti pacchimavayaṃ sampatte, pacchimavayo nāma vassasatassa pacchimo tatiyabhāgo.

Now, showing what was heard by him, he spoke the words beginning with 'The ascetic Gotama does not...' Therein, this is the explanation of the unclear terms: 'brāhmaṇe' means brahmins by birth. 'Jiṇṇe' (aged) means decrepit, brought by old age to a state of being broken-toothed and the like. 'Vuḍḍhe' (elderly) means having reached the limit of growth of the major and minor limbs. 'Mahallake' (old) means endowed with great age by birth; it is said to mean 'born a long time ago.' 'Addhagate' (traveled the road) means having gone a long way in time; the intention is that two or three royal successions have passed. 'Vayo anuppatte' (attained to age) means having reached the final stage of life; the final stage of life is the last third part of a hundred years.

Apica – jiṇṇeti porāṇe, cirakālappavattakulanvayeti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuḍḍheti sīlācārādiguṇavuḍḍhiyutte. Mahallaketi vibhavamahattatāya samannāgate mahaddhane mahābhoge. Addhagateti maggappaṭipanne, brāhmaṇānaṃ vatacariyādimariyādaṃ avītikkamma caramāne. Vayoanuppatteti jātivuḍḍhabhāvaṃ antimavayaṃ anuppatteti evamettha yojanā veditabbā.

Furthermore: 'jiṇṇe' means ancient; it is said to mean 'of a lineage that has continued for a long time.' 'Vuḍḍhe' means endowed with the growth of qualities such as virtue and conduct. 'Mahallake' means endowed with greatness of wealth, having great riches and great possessions. 'Addhagate' means entered upon the path, conducting oneself without transgressing the bounds of the brahmins' duties and conduct. 'Vayoanuppatte' means having reached the final age, the state of seniority by birth. Thus the application of meaning here should be understood.

Idāni abhivādetīti evamādīni “na samaṇo gotamo”ti ettha vuttanakārena yojetvā evamatthato veditabbāni – “na vandati vā, nāsanā vuṭṭhahati vā, nāpi ‘idha bhonto nisīdantū’ti evaṃ āsanena vā upanimantetī”ti. Ettha hi vā saddo vibhāvane nāma atthe, “rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”tiādīsu viya. Evaṃ vatvā atha attano abhivādanādīni akarontaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā āha – “tayidaṃ bho gotama tathevā”ti. Yaṃ taṃ mayā sutaṃ – taṃ tatheva, taṃ savanañca me dassanañca saṃsandati sameti, atthato ekībhāvaṃ gacchati. “Na hi bhavaṃ gotamo…pe… āsanena vā nimantetī”ti evaṃ attanā sutaṃ diṭṭhena nigametvā nindanto āha – “tayidaṃ bho gotama na sampannamevā”ti taṃ abhivādanādīnaṃ akaraṇaṃ na yuttameva.

Now, words such as 'he pays homage' are to be understood by connecting them with the negative particle from the phrase 'the ascetic Gotama does not...', in the following manner: 'He neither pays homage, nor rises from his seat, nor invites them with a seat, saying, “Please, venerable sirs, be seated here.”' Here, the word 'vā' is in the sense called 'vibhāvana' (clarification), as in examples such as 'Is form permanent or impermanent?' and so forth. Having said this, then seeing the Blessed One not performing acts of homage and so on, he said, 'This, Venerable Gotama, is indeed so.' That which I have heard—it is indeed so; that hearing and seeing of mine correspond, accord, and reach a unity of meaning. 'Indeed, Venerable Gotama does not... nor does he invite with a seat' — thus, concluding what he had heard with what he saw, criticizing, he said, 'This, Venerable Gotama, is simply not seemly.' That non-performance of acts of homage and so forth is simply not proper.

Athassa bhagavā attukkaṃsanaparavambhanadosaṃ anupagamma karuṇāsītalahadayena taṃ aññāṇaṃ vidhamitvā [V 1.0096] yuttabhāvaṃ dassetukāmo āha – “nāhaṃ taṃ brāhmaṇa [P 1.0131]…pe… muddhāpi tassa vipateyyā”ti. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – “ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, appaṭihatena sabbaññutaññāṇacakkhunā olokentopi taṃ puggalaṃ etasmiṃ sadevakādibhede loke na passāmi, yamahaṃ abhivādeyyaṃ vā paccuṭṭheyyaṃ vā āsanena vā nimanteyyaṃ. Anacchariyaṃ vā etaṃ, yvāhaṃ ajja sabbaññutaṃ patto evarūpaṃ nipaccakārārahaṃ puggalaṃ na passāmi. Apica kho yadāpāhaṃ sampatijātova uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena gantvā sakalaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokesiṃ; tadāpi etasmiṃ sadevakādibhede loke taṃ puggalaṃ na passāmi, yamahaṃ [M 1.0103] abhivādeyyaṃ vā paccuṭṭheyyaṃ vā āsanena vā nimanteyyaṃ. Atha kho maṃ soḷasakappasahassāyuko khīṇāsavamahābrahmāpi añjaliṃ paggahetvā “tvaṃ loke mahāpuriso, tvaṃ sadevakassa lokassa aggo ca jeṭṭho ca seṭṭho ca, natthi tayā uttaritaro”ti sañjātasomanasso patināmesi; tadāpi cāhaṃ attanā uttaritaraṃ apassanto āsabhiṃ vācaṃ nicchāresiṃ – “aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmi lokassā”ti. Evaṃ sampatijātassapi mayhaṃ abhivādanādiraho puggalo natthi, svāhaṃ idāni sabbaññutaṃ patto kaṃ abhivādeyyaṃ vā…pe… āsanena vā nimanteyyaṃ. Tasmā tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, mā tathāgate evarūpaṃ nipaccakāraṃ patthayittha. Yañhi, brāhmaṇa, tathāgato abhivādeyya vā…pe… āsanena vā nimanteyya, muddhāpi tassa puggalassa rattipariyosāne paripākasithilabandhanaṃ vaṇṭā pavuttatālaphalamiva gīvato pacchijjitvā sahasāva bhūmiyaṃ vipateyyāti.

Then the Blessed One, without falling into the fault of praising oneself and disparaging others, with a heart cooled by compassion, wishing to dispel that ignorance and show what is proper, said: 'I, brahmin... his head would fall off.' Here is the brief meaning: 'Brahmin, even looking with my unobstructed eye of omniscience, I do not see in this world with its devas and so on any person whom I should pay homage to, rise for, or invite with a seat. It is not surprising that I, having today attained omniscience, do not see such a person worthy of reverence. Moreover, when I was just newly born and, facing north, walked seven steps and surveyed the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, even then I did not see in this world with its devas and so on any person whom I should pay homage to, rise for, or invite with a seat. Indeed, even the Arahant Mahābrahmā, whose lifespan is sixteen thousand aeons, raised his joined palms and, with a joyful mind, revered me, saying: “You are the Great Being in the world; you are the highest, the eldest, and the best in this world with its devas; there is none superior to you.” And even then, seeing no one superior to myself, I uttered the bull-like utterance: “I am the highest in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world.” Thus, even for me when I was just newly born, there was no person worthy of homage and so forth. So I, having now attained omniscience, whom should I pay homage to, rise for, or invite with a seat? Therefore, brahmin, do not desire such reverence from the Tathāgata. For, brahmin, if the Tathāgata were to pay homage to someone, rise for someone, or invite someone with a seat, by the end of the night, that person’s head—like a ripe palmyra fruit with its stalk loosened by ripeness, fallen from the stem—would suddenly be severed from his neck and fall to the ground.'

3. Evaṃ vuttepi brāhmaṇo duppaññatāya tathāgatassa loke jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ asallakkhento kevalaṃ taṃ vacanaṃ asahamāno āha – “arasarūpo bhavaṃ gotamo”ti. Ayaṃ kirassa adhippāyo – yaṃ loke abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ “sāmaggiraso”ti vuccati, taṃ bhoto gotamassa natthi[P 1.0132], tasmā arasarūpo bhavaṃ gotamo, arasajātiko arasasabhāvoti. Athassa bhagavā cittamudubhāvajananatthaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhāvaṃ pariharanto aññathā tassa vacanassatthaṃ attani sandassento “atthi khvesa brāhmaṇa pariyāyo”tiādimāha.

3. Even when this was said, the brahmin, due to his lack of wisdom, not considering the Tathāgata's seniority in the world and simply unable to bear that statement, said: 'Venerable Gotama is without savor.' His intention was this: 'That which in the world is called “the savor of harmony”—paying homage, rising, making añjali, and proper conduct—is not found in Venerable Gotama. Therefore, Venerable Gotama is without savor, of a savorless kind, of a savorless nature.' Then the Blessed One, to soften his mind, avoiding direct opposition and showing the meaning of that statement in another way with regard to himself, said: 'Indeed, brahmin, there is a way...'

Tattha pariyāyoti kāraṇaṃ; ayañhi pariyāyasaddo desanā-vāra-kāraṇesu vattati. “Madhupiṇḍikapariyāyotveva naṃ dhārehī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.205) hi esa desanāyaṃ vattati. “Kassa nu kho, ānanda, ajja pariyāyo bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.398) vāre. “Sādhu, bhante, bhagavā aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ ācikkhatu, yathāyaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho aññāya saṇṭhaheyyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 164) kāraṇe. Svāyamidha kāraṇe vattati[V 1.0097]. Tasmā ettha evamattho daṭṭhabbo – atthi kho, brāhmaṇa, etaṃ kāraṇaṃ; yena kāraṇena maṃ “arasarūpo [M 1.0104] bhavaṃ gotamo”ti vadamāno puggalo sammā vadeyya, avitathavādīti saṅkhyaṃ gaccheyya. Katamo pana soti? Ye te brāhmaṇa rūparasā…pe… phoṭṭhabbarasā te tathāgatassa pahīnāti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ye te jātivasena vā upapattivasena vā seṭṭhasammatānampi puthujjanānaṃ rūpārammaṇādīni assādentānaṃ abhinandantānaṃ rajjantānaṃ uppajjanti kāmasukhassādasaṅkhātā rūparasasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbarasā, ye imaṃ lokaṃ gīvāya bandhitvā viya āviñchanti, vatthārammaṇādisāmaggiyañca uppannattā sāmaggirasāti vuccanti, te sabbepi tathāgatassa pahīnāti. Mayhaṃ pahīnāti vattabbepi mamākārena attānaṃ anukkhipanto dhammaṃ deseti. Desanāvilāso vā esa bhagavato.

Here, 'pariyāya' means reason; for this term 'pariyāya' is used in the senses of teaching, turn, and reason. In phrases like, 'Remember it as the “Honeyball Discourse”,' it refers to teaching. In instances such as, 'Ānanda, whose turn is it today to advise the bhikkhunīs?' it refers to a turn. In statements like, 'Good, sir, may the Blessed One explain another reason so that this community of monks may be established in final knowledge,' it refers to a reason. So here, it is used in the sense of a reason. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: 'Indeed, brahmin, there is this reason—by which a person speaking of me as “Venerable Gotama is without savor” would be speaking rightly, and would be counted as one who speaks without falsehood. But what is it?' It is that those tastes of forms... and tastes of tactile objects, brahmin, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. What is being said? Those tastes of forms, sounds, odors, flavors, and tactile objects—which arise for ordinary people, even those esteemed as the best due to birth or status, who savor, delight in, and are infatuated with form-objects and the like, which are reckoned as the savor of sensual pleasure; which drag this world as if having bound it by the neck; and which, because they arise from the coming together of base, object, and so on, are called 'savors of harmony'—all these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Though it could be said, 'They have been abandoned by me,' he teaches the Dhamma without exalting himself in the manner of 'I' or 'mine.' Or, this is an elegance of the Blessed One's teaching.

Tattha pahīnāti cittasantānato vigatā jahitā vā. Etasmiṃ panatthe karaṇe sāmivacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ariyamaggasatthena ucchinnaṃ taṇhāvijjāmayaṃ mūlametesanti ucchinnamūlā. Tālavatthu viya nesaṃ vatthu katanti tālāvatthukatā. Yathā hi tālarukkhaṃ samūlaṃ [P 1.0133] uddharitvā tassa vatthumatte tasmiṃ padese kate na puna tassa tālassa uppatti paññāyati; evaṃ ariyamaggasatthena samūle rūpādirase uddharitvā tesaṃ pubbe uppannapubbabhāvena vatthumatte cittasantāne kate sabbepi te “tālāvatthukatā”ti vuccanti. Avirūḷhidhammattā vā matthakacchinnatālo viya katāti tālāvatthukatā. Yasmā pana evaṃ tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā honti, yathā nesaṃ pacchābhāvo na hoti, tathā katā honti; tasmā āha – “anabhāvaṃkatā”ti. Ayañhettha padacchedo – anuabhāvaṃ katā anabhāvaṃkatāti. “Anabhāvaṃ gatā”tipi pāṭho, tassa anuabhāvaṃ gatāti attho. Tattha padacchedo anuabhāvaṃ gatā anabhāvaṃ gatāti, yathā anuacchariyā anacchariyāti. Āyatiṃ anuppādadhammāti anāgate anuppajjanakasabhāvā. Ye hi abhāvaṃ gatā, te puna kathaṃ uppajjissanti? Tenāha – “anabhāvaṃ gatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā”ti.

Therein, 'abandoned' means departed or discarded from the mind-continuum. Furthermore, in this context, the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the agent in the instrumental case. Because their root, consisting of craving and ignorance, has been cut off by the weapon of the noble path, they are called 'those with root cut off.' Because their base has been made like the site of a palm tree, they are called 'those made like the site of a palm tree.' For just as when a palm tree is uprooted together with its root, and that place is made into its mere site, the arising of that palm tree is no longer apparent; even so, when the savors of form and so on, together with their root, are uprooted by the weapon of the noble path, and the mind-continuum is made into their mere site by virtue of their having arisen there before, all of them are called 'those made like the site of a palm tree.' Alternatively, because they have the nature of not growing, they are made like a palm tree cut at the top; thus, they are called 'those made like the site of a palm tree.' Furthermore, since they are thus made like the site of a palm tree, they are made into a state of non-becoming; they are made in such a way that there is no subsequent becoming for them. Therefore, He said: 'made into a state of non-becoming.' And here, this is the division of the word: `anu` + `abhāvaṃ` + `katā` becomes `anabhāvaṃkatā`. There is also the reading `anabhāvaṃ gatā`; its meaning is 'gone to a state of non-becoming hereafter.' Therein, the division of the word is `anu` + `abhāvaṃ` + `gatā` becomes `anabhāvaṃ gatā`, just as `anu` + `acchariyā` becomes `anacchariyā`. 'Of a nature not to arise in the future' means they have the nature of not arising in the future. Indeed, how could those things that have gone to a state of non-becoming arise again? Therefore, He said: 'gone to a state of non-becoming, of a nature not to arise in the future.'

Ayaṃ kho brāhmaṇa pariyāyoti idaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, kāraṇaṃ yena maṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya “arasarūpo samaṇo gotamo”ti. No ca kho yaṃ tvaṃ sandhāya vadesīti yañca kho tvaṃ sandhāya vadesi, so pariyāyo na hoti. Kasmā pana bhagavā evamāha? Nanu evaṃ vutte [M 1.0105] yo brāhmaṇena vutto sāmaggiraso tassa attani vijjamānatā anuññātā hotīti. Vuccate, na hoti. Yo hi taṃ sāmaggirasaṃ kātuṃ bhabbo hutvā na karoti, so tadabhāvena arasarūpoti vattabbo bhaveyya. Bhagavā pana abhabbova etaṃ kātuṃ, tenassa karaṇe abhabbataṃ pakāsento [V 1.0098] āha – “no ca kho yaṃ tvaṃ sandhāya vadesī”ti. Yaṃ pariyāyaṃ sandhāya tvaṃ maṃ “arasarūpo”ti vadesi, so amhesu neva vattabboti.

This, brahmin, is the reason; this, O brahmin, is the ground by which one, speaking rightly, might say of me, 'The ascetic Gotama is without savor.' But the reason to which you refer is not the case. But why did the Blessed One say so? Surely, when it is said thus, is it not that the existence in himself of that 'savor of harmony' spoken of by the brahmin is admitted? It is said: it is not so. For one who, being capable of producing that savor of harmony, does not do so, he could be called 'without savor' on account of its absence. The Blessed One, however, is simply incapable of producing this. Therefore, making clear his incapability in producing it, He said: 'But it is not that which you refer to when you speak.' The reason with reference to which you call me 'without savor' should not be spoken of in our case at all.

4. Evaṃ brāhmaṇo attanā adhippetaṃ arasarūpataṃ āropetuṃ asakkonto athāparaṃ nibbhogo bhavaṃ gotamotiādimāha. Sabbapariyāyesu cettha vuttanayeneva yojanakkamaṃ viditvā [P 1.0134] sandhāya bhāsitamattaṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Brāhmaṇo tameva vayovuḍḍhānaṃ abhivādanakammādiṃ loke sāmaggiparibhogoti maññamāno tadabhāvena bhagavantaṃ nibbhogoti āha. Bhagavā pana yvāyaṃ rūpādīsu sattānaṃ chandarāgaparibhogo tadabhāvaṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti.

4. Thus the brahmin, being unable to attribute the state of being without savor that he intended, then said the words beginning with, 'The venerable Gotama is without enjoyment.' And in all these sections, having understood the sequence of application by the method already stated, just the meaning spoken with a specific reference should be understood thus. The brahmin, thinking that this very act of paying homage, etc., to elders is 'communal enjoyment' in the world, called the Blessed One 'one without enjoyment' due to the absence of that. The Blessed One, however, seeing in himself the absence of that enjoyment of beings with regard to forms and so on, which is enjoyment through desire and passion, approved of another reason as well.

5. Puna brāhmaṇo yaṃ loke vayovuḍḍhānaṃ abhivādanādikulasamudācārakammaṃ lokiyā karonti tassa akiriyaṃ sampassamāno bhagavantaṃ akiriyavādoti āha. Bhagavā pana, yasmā kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ akiriyaṃ vadati tasmā, taṃ akiriyavādaṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti. Tattha ca kāyaduccaritanti pāṇātipāta-adinnādāna-micchācāracetanā veditabbā. Vacīduccaritanti musāvāda-pisuṇavācā-pharusavācā-samphappalāpacetanā veditabbā. Manoduccaritanti abhijjhābyāpādamicchādiṭṭhiyo veditabbā. Ṭhapetvā te dhamme, avasesā akusalā dhammā “anekavihitā pāpakā akusalā dhammā”ti veditabbā.

5. Again, the brahmin, seeing the non-performance of that customary family practice of paying homage, etc., to elders, which worldly people perform in the world, called the Blessed One a 'proponent of non-action.' The Blessed One, however, because he teaches the non-doing of bodily misconduct, etc., therefore, seeing that doctrine of non-action in himself, approved of another reason as well. And therein, 'bodily misconduct' should be understood as the volitions for killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. 'Verbal misconduct' should be understood as the volitions for false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. 'Mental misconduct' should be understood as covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. Setting aside those states, the remaining unwholesome states should be understood as 'the many kinds of evil, unwholesome states.'

6. Puna brāhmaṇo tameva abhivādanādikammaṃ bhagavati apassanto imaṃ “āgamma ayaṃ lokatanti lokapaveṇī ucchijjatī”ti maññamāno bhagavantaṃ ucchedavādoti āha. Bhagavā pana yasmā aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatacittesu pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa dvīsu akusalacittesu uppajjamānakadosassa ca anāgāmimaggena ucchedaṃ vadati. Sabbākusalasambhavassa pana niravasesassa mohassa arahattamaggena ucchedaṃ vadati. Ṭhapetvā te tayo, avasesānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ yathānurūpaṃ catūhi maggehi [M 1.0106] ucchedaṃ vadati; tasmā taṃ ucchedavādaṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti.

6. Again, the brahmin, not seeing in the Blessed One that very act of paying homage and so on, thinking, 'On account of this one, this worldly tradition, this worldly lineage, is cut off,' called the Blessed One a 'proponent of annihilation.' The Blessed One, however, because he teaches the cutting off, by the path of the non-returner, of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed, and of hatred arising in the two types of unwholesome consciousness; and furthermore, he teaches the cutting off, without remainder, by the path of arahantship, of delusion, which is the origin of all unwholesome states; and setting aside those three, he teaches the cutting off of the remaining evil, unwholesome states by the four paths, as is appropriate; therefore, seeing that doctrine of annihilation in himself, he approved of another reason as well.

7. Puna brāhmaṇo “jigucchati maññe samaṇo gotamo idaṃ vayovuḍḍhānaṃ abhivādanādikulasamudācārakammaṃ, tena taṃ na karotī”ti maññamāno bhagavantaṃ jegucchīti āha. Bhagavā pana yasmā jigucchati kāyaduccaritādīhi; kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti[P 1.0135]? Yañca tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, yañca catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ, yañca tividhaṃ manoduccaritaṃ, yā ca ṭhapetvā tāni [V 1.0099] duccaritāni avasesānaṃ lāmakaṭṭhena pāpakānaṃ akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpatti samāpajjanā samaṅgibhāvo, taṃ sabbampi gūthaṃ viya maṇḍanakajātiyo puriso jigucchati hirīyati, tasmā taṃ jegucchitaṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti. Tattha “kāyaduccaritenā”ti upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

7. Again, the brahmin, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama, I think, loathes this customary family practice of paying homage to elders; for that reason he does not do it,' called the Blessed One a 'loather.' The Blessed One, however, is a 'loather' because he loathes bodily misconduct and so on. What is meant by this? The threefold bodily misconduct, the fourfold verbal misconduct, the threefold mental misconduct, and—setting aside those misconducts—whatever attainment, entering into, and possession there is of the remaining states that are evil in the sense of being base, and unwholesome in the sense of arising from unskillfulness—all of that he loathes and is ashamed of, just as a person fond of adornment would loathe and be ashamed of excrement. Therefore, seeing that quality of being a 'loather' in himself, he approved of another reason as well. Therein, in the phrase `kāyaduccaritena`, the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of the object.

8. Puna brāhmaṇo tameva abhivādanādikammaṃ bhagavati apassanto “ayaṃ imaṃ lokajeṭṭhakakammaṃ vineti vināseti, atha vā yasmā etaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ na karoti tasmā ayaṃ vinetabbo niggaṇhitabbo”ti maññamāno bhagavantaṃ venayikoti āha. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – vinayatīti vinayo, vināsetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vinayo eva venayiko, vinayaṃ vā arahatīti venayiko, niggahaṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavā pana, yasmā rāgādīnaṃ vinayāya vūpasamāya dhammaṃ deseti, tasmā venayiko hoti. Ayameva cettha padattho – vinayāya dhammaṃ desetīti venayiko. Vicitrā hi taddhitavutti! Svāyaṃ taṃ venayikabhāvaṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti.

8. Again, the brahmin, not seeing in the Blessed One that very act of veneration and so forth, thinking, “This one abolishes and destroys this act of respect for the world's elders. Or else, because he does not perform this respectful act, he should be disciplined and restrained,” called the Blessed One “Venayiko.” Therein, this is the meaning of the word: He abolishes (vinayati), thus he is a `vinayo`; this means he destroys (vināseti), it is said. A `vinayo` itself is a `venayiko`. Or, he is worthy of discipline (vinayaṃ arahati), thus he is a `venayiko`; this means he is worthy of restraint (niggahaṃ arahati), it is said. The Blessed One, however, because he teaches the Dhamma for the removal and calming of passion and so on, is therefore a `venayiko`. And in this context, this very meaning of the word is: He teaches the Dhamma for removal, thus he is a `venayiko`. Indeed, the taddhita derivation is varied! He, seeing that state of being a `venayiko` in himself, approves of another explanation as well.

9. Puna brāhmaṇo yasmā abhivādanādīni sāmīcikammāni karontā vayovuḍḍhe tosenti hāsenti, akarontā pana tāpenti vihesenti domanassaṃ nesaṃ uppādenti, bhagavā ca tāni na karoti; tasmā “ayaṃ vayovuḍḍhe tapatī”ti maññamāno sappurisācāravirahitattā vā “kapaṇapuriso aya”nti maññamāno bhagavantaṃ tapassīti āha. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – tapatīti tapo, roseti vihesetīti vuttaṃ hoti, sāmīcikammākaraṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tapo assa atthīti tapassī. Dutiye atthavikappe byañjanāni avicāretvā loke kapaṇapuriso “tapassī”ti vuccati. Bhagavā pana ye akusalā dhammā lokaṃ tapanato tapanīyāti [M 1.0107] vuccanti, tesaṃ pahīnattā yasmā tapassīti saṅkhyaṃ gato, tasmā taṃ tapassitaṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – tapantīti tapā, akusaladhammānametaṃ [P 1.0136] adhivacanaṃ. Vuttampi hetaṃ – “idha tappati pecca tappatī”ti. Tathā te tape assi nirassi pahāsi viddhaṃsesīti tapassī.

9. Again, the brahmin, because those who perform respectful acts such as veneration please and delight the elders, while those who do not perform them torment, harass, and cause them displeasure, and the Blessed One does not perform those acts; therefore, thinking, “This one torments the elders,” or, due to being devoid of the conduct of good people, thinking, “This is a wretched man,” he called the Blessed One “Tapassī.” Therein, this is the meaning of the word: He torments (tapati), thus it is `tapo`; it is said that this means he angers (roseti) or harasses (viheseti); this is a name for the non-performance of respectful acts. He has this `tapo`, thus he is a `tapassī`. In the second interpretation of the meaning, without analyzing the components, a wretched man in the world is called a “tapassī.” The Blessed One, however, because those unwholesome states which, from tormenting the world, are called `tapanīyā` (tormenting) have been abandoned by him, has reached the designation of “Tapassī.” Therefore, seeing that state of being a `tapassī` in himself, he approves of another explanation as well. Therein, this is the meaning of the word: They torment (tapanti), thus they are `tapā`; this is a designation for unwholesome states. For this was also said: “Here he is tormented, hereafter he is tormented.” Likewise, because he has cast off, cast out, abandoned, and destroyed those torments (tape), he is a `tapassī`.

10. Puna brāhmaṇo taṃ abhivādanādikammaṃ devalokagabbhasampattiyā devalokapaṭisandhipaṭilābhāya saṃvattatīti maññamāno bhagavati cassa abhāvaṃ disvā bhagavantaṃ apagabbhoti āha. Kodhavasena vā bhagavato mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇe dosaṃ dassentopi evamāha. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – gabbhato apagatoti apagabbho, abhabbo devalokūpapattiṃ pāpuṇitunti [V 1.0100] adhippāyo. Hīno vā gabbho assāti apagabbho, devalokagabbhaparibāhirattā āyatiṃ hīnagabbhapaṭilābhabhāgīti, hīno vāssa mātukucchimhi gabbhavāso ahosīti adhippāyo. Bhagavato pana yasmā āyatiṃ gabbhaseyyā apagatā, tasmā so taṃ apagabbhataṃ attani sampassamāno aparampi pariyāyaṃ anujānāti. Tatra ca yassa kho brāhmaṇa āyatiṃ gabbhaseyyā punabbhavābhinibbatti pahīnāti etesaṃ padānaṃ evamattho daṭṭhabbo – brāhmaṇa, yassa puggalassa anāgate gabbhaseyyā, punabbhave ca abhinibbatti anuttarena maggena vihatakāraṇattā pahīnāti. Gabbhaseyyaggahaṇena cettha jalābujayoni gahitā. Punabbhavābhinibbattiggahaṇena itarā tissopi.

10. Again, the brahmin, thinking that this act of veneration and so forth leads to the perfection of conception in the deva world, and seeing its absence in the Blessed One, called the Blessed One “Apagabbho.” Or, through the power of anger, wishing to show a fault in the Blessed One's taking of conception in his mother's womb, he also spoke thus. Therein, this is the meaning of the word: He is departed from the womb (gabbhato apagato), thus he is `apagabbho`; the intention is that he is incapable of attaining arising in the deva world. Or, he has an inferior womb (hīno gabbho assa), thus he is `apagabbho`; because he is external to a deva-world conception, in the future he will be one who partakes in obtaining an inferior conception—this is one intention. Or, his dwelling in his mother's womb was inferior—this is another intention. For the Blessed One, however, because in the future, lying in a womb (gabbhaseyyā) has departed from him, he, seeing that state of being `apagabbho` in himself, approves of another explanation as well. And there, the meaning of these words—“O brahmin, for whom future lying in a womb and new arising in a future existence is abandoned”—should be seen thus: O brahmin, for whichever person, in the future, lying in a womb and new arising in a future existence is abandoned by the unsurpassed path, because its cause has been destroyed. And here, by the term `gabbhaseyyā`, womb-birth (jalābujayoni) is taken. By the term `punabbhavābhinibbatti`, the other three types of birth are also taken.

Apica gabbhassa seyyā gabbhaseyyā, punabbhavo eva abhinibbatti punabbhavābhinibbattīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yathā ca viññāṇaṭṭhitīti vuttepi na viññāṇato aññā ṭhiti atthi, evamidhāpi na gabbhato aññā seyyāti veditabbā. Abhinibbatti ca nāma yasmā punabbhavabhūtāpi apunabbhavabhūtāpi atthi, idha ca punabbhavabhūtā adhippetā. Tasmā vuttaṃ – “punabbhavo eva abhinibbatti punabbhavābhinibbattī”ti.

Furthermore, the lying (`seyyā`) of a fetus (`gabbhassa`) is `gabbhaseyyā`. A future existence (`punabbhavo`) itself is a new arising (`abhinibbatti`), thus `punabbhavābhinibbatti`; in this way the meaning should be understood here. And just as when `viññāṇaṭṭhiti` (station of consciousness) is said, there is no station (`ṭhiti`) other than consciousness (`viññāṇa`), so too here, it should be known that there is no lying (`seyyā`) other than the fetus (`gabbha`). And as for `abhinibbatti` (new arising), because it exists both as that which has become a future existence and that which has not become a future existence, and here that which has become a future existence is intended, therefore it was said: “A future existence itself is a new arising, thus `punabbhavābhinibbatti`.”

11. Evaṃ āgatakālato paṭṭhāya arasarūpatādīhi aṭṭhahi akkosavatthūhi akkosantampi brāhmaṇaṃ bhagavā dhammissaro dhammarājā dhammassāmī [M 1.0108] tathāgato anukampāya sītaleneva cakkhunā olokento yaṃ dhammadhātuṃ paṭivijjhitvā desanāvilāsappatto hoti, tassā dhammadhātuyā [P 1.0137] suppaṭividdhattā vigatavalāhake antalikkhe samabbhuggato puṇṇacando viya saradakāle sūriyo viya ca brāhmaṇassa hadayandhakāraṃ vidhamanto tāniyeva akkosavatthūni tena tena pariyāyena aññathā dassetvā, punapi attano karuṇāvipphāraṃ aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi akampiyabhāvena paṭiladdhaṃ, tādiguṇalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīsamacittataṃ akuppadhammatañca pakāsento “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo kevalaṃ palitasirakhaṇḍadantavalittacatādīhi attano vuḍḍhabhāvaṃ sañjānāti, no ca kho jānāti attānaṃ jātiyā anugataṃ jarāya anusaṭaṃ byādhinā abhibhūtaṃ maraṇena abbhāhataṃ vaṭṭakhāṇubhūtaṃ ajja maritvā puna sveva uttānasayanadārakabhāvagamanīyaṃ. Mahantena kho pana ussāhena mama santikaṃ āgato, tadassa āgamanaṃ sātthakaṃ hotū”ti cintetvā imasmiṃ loke attano appaṭisamaṃ purejātabhāvaṃ dassento seyyathāpi brāhmaṇātiādinā nayena brāhmaṇassa dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhesi.

11. Thus, from the time he arrived, even while the brahmin was reviling him with the eight grounds for abuse beginning with `arasarūpatā`, the Blessed One—the Lord of the Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata—gazed upon him with an eye cool with compassion. Because he had penetrated a certain Dhamma-element, he had attained the grace of exposition. Due to that Dhamma-element being well-penetrated, like the full moon fully risen in a cloudless sky and like the sun in the autumn season, he was dispelling the darkness in the brahmin's heart. Having shown those very grounds for abuse in another way through various reasons, and revealing the diffusion of his own compassion and his imperturbable nature—the state of having a mind like the earth, which is the characteristic of one possessing the quality of `tādi` (suchness), attained through being unshaken by the eight worldly conditions—he thought: “This brahmin perceives his own state of being old merely through having a white head, broken teeth, wrinkled skin, and so on. But he does not know himself to be followed by birth, entwined by old age, overwhelmed by sickness, struck by death, having become a stump for the round of existence, and that having died today, tomorrow he is liable to reach the state of an infant lying on its back. Yet he has come to my presence with great effort. May his coming be fruitful!” Having thought thus, and showing his own unequalled, first-born state in this world, he expanded the Dhamma teaching for the brahmin with the method beginning, “Just as, O brahmin…”

Tattha seyyathāti opammatthe nipāto; pīti sambhāvanatthe; ubhayenāpi yathā nāma brāhmaṇāti [V 1.0101] dasseti. Kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vāti ettha pana kiñcāpi kukkuṭiyā vuttappakārato ūnādhikānipi aṇḍāni honti, atha kho vacanasiliṭṭhatāya evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Evañhi loke siliṭṭhavacanaṃ hoti. Tānassūti tāni assu, bhaveyyunti vuttaṃ hoti. Kukkuṭiyā sammā adhisayitānīti tāya janettiyā kukkuṭiyā pakkhe pasāretvā tesaṃ upari sayantiyā sammā adhisayitāni. Sammā pariseditānīti kālena kālaṃ utuṃ gaṇhāpentiyā suṭṭhu samantato seditāni, usmīkatānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sammā paribhāvitānīti kālena kālaṃ suṭṭhu samantato bhāvitāni, kukkuṭagandhaṃ gāhāpitānīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, the word `seyyathā` is a particle in the sense of a simile; the word `pi` is a particle in the sense of making evident. By both, it demonstrates the meaning 'just as, Brahmin'. Now, in the passage 'a hen’s eggs, eight or ten or twelve,' although a hen may have fewer or more eggs than the stated number, it should be understood that it is said thus for the sake of elegant expression. For in this way, it is elegant speech in the world. `Tānassu` means `tāni assu`, that is, 'they should be,' is what is said. 'Properly sat upon by the hen' means that they are properly sat upon by that mother hen as she spreads her wings and lies upon them. 'Properly incubated' means that as she causes them to take on warmth from time to time, they are well warmed all around; 'made warm' is what is said. 'Properly imbued' means that from time to time they are well imbued all around; 'caused to take on the hen’s scent' is what is said.

Idāni yasmā tāya kukkuṭiyā evaṃ tīhi pakārehi tāni aṇḍāni paripāliyamānāni na pūtīni honti. Yopi nesaṃ allasineho so pariyādānaṃ gacchati. Kapālaṃ tanukaṃ hoti, pādanakhasikhā ca mukhatuṇḍakañca kharaṃ hoti, kukkuṭapotakā paripākaṃ gacchanti, kapālassa tanukattā bahiddhā [P 1.0138] āloko anto paññāyati. Atha te kukkuṭapotakā “ciraṃ [M 1.0109] vata mayaṃ saṅkuṭitahatthapādā sambādhe sayimha, ayañca bahi āloko dissati, ettha dāni no sukhavihāro bhavissatī”ti nikkhamitukāmā hutvā kapālaṃ pādena paharanti, gīvaṃ pasārenti. Tato taṃ kapālaṃ dvedhā bhijjati, kukkuṭapotakā pakkhe vidhunantā taṅkhaṇānurūpaṃ viravantā nikkhamanti. Evaṃ nikkhamantānañca nesaṃ yo paṭhamataraṃ nikkhamati so ‘jeṭṭho’ti vuccati. Tasmā bhagavā tāya upamāya attano jeṭṭhakabhāvaṃ sādhetukāmo brāhmaṇaṃ pucchi – “yo nu kho tesaṃ kukkuṭacchāpakānaṃ…pe… kinti svassa vacanīyo”ti. Tattha kukkuṭacchāpakānanti kukkuṭapotakānaṃ. Kinti svassa vacanīyoti so kinti vacanīyo assa, kinti vattabbo bhaveyya jeṭṭho vā kaniṭṭho vāti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

Now, because those eggs are protected by that hen in these three ways, they do not become rotten. Whatever wet moisture is in them is used up. The shell becomes thin, and the tips of their claws and the tip of their beak become hard. The chicks reach maturity, and because of the shell's thinness, the light outside becomes visible within. Then those chicks, thinking, 'For a long time, indeed, have we lain in this confined space with our wings and feet contracted. And this light outside is seen. Now, here will be our pleasant abiding,' desiring to emerge, strike the shell with their feet and stretch their necks. Thence, that shell breaks in two, and the chicks emerge, shaking their wings and chirping in a manner appropriate to that moment. And among those emerging thus, whoever emerges first is called the 'eldest.' Therefore the Blessed One, wishing to establish his own state of being the eldest by means of that simile, asked the brahmin: 'Now, among those chicken chicks... what should he be called?' Therein, `kukkuṭacchāpakānaṃ` means 'of the young chickens.' `Kinti svassa vacanīyo` means 'What should he be called? What should he be spoken of as—the eldest or the youngest?' The rest has a clear meaning.

Tato brāhmaṇo āha – “jeṭṭhotissa bho gotama vacanīyo”ti. Bho, gotama, so jeṭṭho iti assa vacanīyo. Kasmāti ce? So hi nesaṃ jeṭṭho, tasmā so nesaṃ vuḍḍhataroti attho. Athassa bhagavā opammaṃ sampaṭipādento āha – “evameva kho ahaṃ brāhmaṇā”tiādi. Yathā so kukkuṭacchāpako jeṭṭhoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati; evaṃ ahampi avijjāgatāya pajāya. Avijjāgatāyāti avijjā vuccati aññāṇaṃ, tattha gatāya. Pajāyāti sattādhivacanametaṃ. Tasmā ettha avijjaṇḍakosassa anto paviṭṭhesu sattesūti evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo. Aṇḍabhūtāyāti aṇḍe bhūtāya jātāya sañjātāya. Yathā hi aṇḍe nibbattā ekacce sattā aṇḍabhūtāti vuccanti; evamayaṃ sabbāpi pajā avijjaṇḍakose nibbattattā aṇḍabhūtāti vuccati. Pariyonaddhāyāti tena avijjaṇḍakosena samantato onaddhāya baddhāya veṭhitāya[V 1.0102]. Avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvāti taṃ avijjāmayaṃ aṇḍakosaṃ bhinditvā[P 1.0139]. Ekova loketi sakalepi lokasannivāse ahameva eko adutiyo. Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti anuttaranti uttaravirahitaṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ. Sammāsambodhinti sammā sāmañca bodhiṃ; atha vā pasatthaṃ sundarañca bodhiṃ; bodhīti rukkhopi maggopi sabbaññutaññāṇampi nibbānampi vuccati. “Bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho”ti (mahāva. 1; udā. 1) ca “antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhi”nti (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 1.285) ca āgataṭṭhānesu hi rukkho bodhīti vuccati. “Bodhi [M 1.0110] vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) āgataṭṭhāne maggo. “Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti (dī. ni. 3.217) āgataṭṭhāne sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. “Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhata”nti āgataṭṭhāne nibbānaṃ. Idha pana bhagavato arahattamaggañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Sabbaññutaññāṇantipi vadanti. Aññesaṃ arahattamaggo anuttarā bodhi hoti, na hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Asabbaguṇadāyakattā. Tesañhi kassaci arahattamaggo arahattaphalameva deti, kassaci tisso vijjā, kassaci cha abhiññā, kassaci catasso paṭisambhidā, kassaci sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ. Paccekabuddhānampi paccekabodhiñāṇameva deti. Buddhānaṃ pana sabbaguṇasampattiṃ deti, abhiseko viya rañño sabbalokissariyabhāvaṃ. Tasmā aññassa kassacipi anuttarā bodhi na hotīti. Abhisambuddhoti abbhaññāsiṃ paṭivijjhiṃ; pattomhi adhigatomhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Then the brahmin said: 'He should be called the eldest, Venerable Gotama.' This means: 'Venerable Gotama, he should be called "the eldest."' If asked why, it is because he is the eldest among them; the meaning is that he is the most senior among them. Then the Blessed One, applying the simile, said to him: 'Even so, Brahmin...' and so on. Just as that chick is reckoned as the 'eldest,' so too am I among a generation gone to ignorance. Regarding `avijjāgatāya`: `avijjā` is called non-knowledge; `gatāya` means gone into that. `Pajāya` is a term for beings. Therefore, the meaning here should be seen thus: 'among beings who have entered inside the eggshell of ignorance.' `Aṇḍabhūtāya` means 'egg-born,' that is, become, born, and produced in an egg. For just as some beings that have arisen in an egg are called 'egg-born,' so too this entire generation is called 'egg-born' because of having arisen in the eggshell of ignorance. `Pariyonaddhāya` means covered over, bound, and wrapped all around by that eggshell of ignorance. `Avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā` means having broken that eggshell made of ignorance. `Ekova loke` means in the entire abode of the world, I alone am without a second. `Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho`: Here, `anuttaraṃ` means without a superior, the best of all. `Sammāsambodhiṃ` means awakening rightly and by oneself; or, a praised and beautiful awakening. `Bodhi` can refer to the tree, the path, omniscient knowledge, and also Nibbāna. For in passages such as 'first awakened at the foot of the Bodhi tree' and 'between Gayā and the Bodhi,' the tree is called `bodhi`. In the passage '`bodhi` is called the knowledge in the four paths,' it refers to the path. In the passage 'the one of great wisdom attains `bodhi`,' it refers to omniscient knowledge. In the passage 'having reached `bodhi`, the deathless, the unconditioned,' it refers to Nibbāna. Here, however, the Blessed One's knowledge of the Arahant path is intended. Some also say omniscient knowledge is intended. Is the Arahant path of others unsurpassed awakening or not? It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. For among them, for some the Arahant path gives only the fruit of Arahantship; for some, it gives the three knowledges; for some, the six supernormal powers; for some, the four analytical knowledges; for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. Even for Paccekabuddhas, it gives only the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha's awakening. But for the Buddhas, the Arahant path gives the accomplishment of all qualities, just as a king's consecration gives sovereignty over the whole world. Therefore, the awakening of any other is not unsurpassed. `Abhisambuddho` means 'I have fully known, I have penetrated'; 'I have reached, I have attained' is what is said.

Idāni yadetaṃ bhagavatā “evameva kho ahaṃ brāhmaṇā”ti ādinā nayena vuttaṃ opammasampaṭipādanaṃ, taṃ evamatthena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā veditabbaṃ. Yathā hi tassā kukkuṭiyā attano aṇḍesu adhisayanāditividhakiriyākaraṇaṃ; evaṃ bodhipallaṅke nisinnassa bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato attano cittasantāne aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti tividhānupassanākaraṇaṃ. Kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyāsampādanena aṇḍānaṃ apūtibhāvo viya bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato tividhānupassanāsampādanena vipassanāñāṇassa aparihāni. Kukkuṭiyā [P 1.0140] tividhakiriyākaraṇena aṇḍānaṃ allasinehapariyādānaṃ viya bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato tividhānupassanāsampādanena bhavattayānugatanikantisinehapariyādānaṃ. Kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyākaraṇena aṇḍakapālānaṃ tanubhāvo viya bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato tividhānupassanāsampādanena avijjaṇḍakosassa tanubhāvo. Kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyākaraṇena kukkuṭacchāpakassa pādanakhasikhātuṇḍakānaṃ thaddhakharabhāvo viya bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato tividhānupassanāsampādanena vipassanāñāṇassa tikkhakharavippasannasūrabhāvo. Kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyākaraṇena [V 1.0103] kukkuṭacchāpakassa paripākakālo viya bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato tividhānupassanāsampādanena vipassanāñāṇassa [M 1.0111] paripākakālo vaḍḍhitakālo gabbhaggahaṇakālo veditabbo.

Now, this connecting of the simile with its subject, spoken by the Blessed One by the method beginning with, 'In the same way, O brahmin,' should be understood by correlating it with the meaning in this way. For, just as one should know of that hen's performing the threefold action beginning with sitting upon her own eggs; so too, one should know of the performing of the threefold contemplation—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—in his own mental continuum by the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta seated on the Bodhi-throne. As, through the hen's accomplishment of the threefold action, the non-rotting of the eggs is to be understood; so, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta, the non-decline of insight knowledge is to be understood. As, through the hen's performing of the threefold action, the exhaustion of the moist fluid from the eggs is to be understood; so, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta, the exhaustion of the fluid of craving and attachment that follows along with the three states of existence is to be understood. As, through the hen's performing of the threefold action, the thinning of the eggshells is to be understood; so, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta, the thinning of the eggshell of ignorance is to be understood. As, through the hen's performing of the threefold action, the state of the tips of the chick's claws and beak becoming hard and rough is to be understood; so, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta, the state of insight knowledge becoming sharp, hard, exceptionally clear, and heroic is to be understood. As, through the hen's performing of the threefold action, the time of the chick's maturation is to be understood; so, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta, the time of maturation, the time of growth, and the time of conception for the insight knowledge are to be understood.

Tato kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyākaraṇena kukkuṭacchāpakassa pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā pakkhe papphoṭetvā sotthinā abhinibbhidākālo viya bodhisattabhūtassa bhagavato tividhānupassanāsampādanena vipassanāñāṇaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpetvā anupubbādhigatena arahattamaggena avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā abhiññāpakkhe papphoṭetvā sotthinā sakalabuddhaguṇasacchikatakālo veditabboti.
