Then, just as the time is to be known when the chick, having split the eggshell with the tip of its claw or with its beak, having flapped its wings, breaks out safely; so too, the time is to be known when the Blessed One, who was a Bodhisatta, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation, having caused the conception of insight knowledge to be taken, and with the path of Arahantship attained in gradual succession, having split the eggshell of ignorance, having flapped the wings of mundane higher knowledge, safely realized all the qualities of a Buddha.

Svāhaṃ brāhmaṇa jeṭṭho seṭṭho lokassāti so ahaṃ brāhmaṇa yathā tesaṃ kukkuṭapotakānaṃ paṭhamataraṃ aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā abhinibbhido kukkuṭapotako jeṭṭho hoti; evaṃ avijjāgatāya pajāya taṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā paṭhamataraṃ ariyāya jātiyā jātattā jeṭṭho vuḍḍhataroti saṅkhyaṃ gato. Sabbaguṇehi pana appaṭisamattā seṭṭhoti.

Regarding the phrase 'I, brahmin, am the eldest, the foremost in the world': O brahmin, just as among those chicks, the chick that, having first split the eggshell, breaks out is the eldest; so too, among beings existing in ignorance, because of being the very first to be born with the noble birth after splitting that eggshell of ignorance, I have come to be reckoned as the eldest, the most senior. Furthermore, because of being without equal in all qualities, I have come to be reckoned as the foremost.

Evaṃ bhagavā attano anuttaraṃ jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ brāhmaṇassa pakāsetvā idāni yāya paṭipadāya taṃ adhigato taṃ paṭipadaṃ pubbabhāgato pabhuti dassetuṃ “āraddhaṃ kho pana me brāhmaṇā”tiādimāha. Imaṃ vā bhagavato anuttaraṃ [P 1.0141] jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ sutvā brāhmaṇassa cittamevamuppannaṃ – “kāya nu kho paṭipadāya imaṃ patto”ti. Tassa cittamaññāya “imāyāhaṃ paṭipadāya imaṃ anuttaraṃ jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ patto”ti dassento evamāha. Tattha āraddhaṃ kho pana me brāhmaṇa vīriyaṃ ahosīti brāhmaṇa, na mayā ayaṃ anuttaro jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvo kusītena muṭṭhassatinā sāraddhakāyena vikkhittacittena adhigato, apica kho tadadhigamāya āraddhaṃ kho pana me vīriyaṃ ahosi, bodhimaṇḍe nisinnena mayā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ ahosi, paggahitaṃ asithilappavattitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Āraddhattāyeva ca me taṃ asallīnaṃ ahosi. Na kevalañca vīriyameva, satipi me ārammaṇābhimukhībhāvena upaṭṭhitā ahosi. Upaṭṭhitattāyeva ca asammuṭṭhā. Passaddho kāyo asāraddhoti kāyacittapassaddhivasena kāyopi me passaddho ahosi[M 1.0112]. Tattha yasmā nāmakāye passaddhe rūpakāyopi passaddhoyeva hoti, tasmā nāmakāyo rūpakāyoti avisesetvāva passaddho kāyoti vuttaṃ. Asāraddhoti so ca kho passaddhattāyeva asāraddho, vigatadarathoti vuttaṃ hoti. Samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekagganti cittampi me sammā [V 1.0104] āhitaṃ suṭṭhu ṭhapitaṃ appitaṃ viya ahosi; samāhitattā eva ca ekaggaṃ acalaṃ nipphandananti. Ettāvatā jhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadā kathitā hoti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having revealed his own unsurpassed state of being the eldest and foremost to the brahmin, now, in order to show the practice by which he attained it, beginning from the preliminary part, spoke the words beginning with, 'Indeed, brahmin, my energy was aroused.' Alternatively, having heard of the Blessed One’s unsurpassed state of being the eldest and foremost, this thought arose in the brahmin’s mind: 'By what practice, indeed, did he attain this?' Knowing his thought, and showing, 'It was by this practice that I attained this unsurpassed state of being the eldest and foremost,' he spoke thus. Therein, the meaning of 'Indeed, brahmin, my energy was aroused' is: Brahmin, this unsurpassed state of being the eldest and foremost was not attained by me as one who was lazy, of lapsed mindfulness, with an agitated body, or with a distracted mind. Rather, for the sake of its attainment, my energy was indeed aroused. Seated at the Bodhi-seat, energy endowed with four factors was aroused by me; it was upheld and made to proceed without slackening, is what is meant. And because it was aroused, it was for me unshrinking. And not only energy, but my mindfulness, too, was established by way of facing its object. And because it was established, it was not lapsed. Regarding 'The body was calmed, not agitated': by the power of the tranquility of the mental and physical body, my body also became calmed. Therein, because when the mental body is calmed the physical body is also calmed, it was said 'the body was calmed' without making a distinction between the mental body and the physical body. Regarding 'not agitated': because it was calmed, it was not agitated; it was devoid of distress, is what is meant. Regarding 'The mind was concentrated, one-pointed': my mind, too, was well placed, rightly established, as if having reached absorption; and because it was concentrated, it was one-pointed, unshaken, and unmoving. By this much, the preliminary-part practice for jhāna has been spoken of.

Paṭhamajjhānakathā

Discourse on the First Jhāna

Idāni imāya paṭipadāya adhigataṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā vijjattayapariyosānaṃ visesaṃ dassento “so kho aha”nti ādimāha. Tattha vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehītiādīnaṃ kiñcāpi “tattha katame kāmā? Chando kāmo, rāgo kāmo, chandarāgo kāmo; saṅkappo kāmo, rāgo kāmo, saṅkapparāgo kāmo – ime vuccanti kāmā. Tattha katame akusalā dhammā? Kāmacchando…pe… vicikicchā – ime vuccanti akusalā dhammā. Iti imehi ca kāmehi imehi ca akusalehi dhammehi [P 1.0142] vivitto hoti pavivitto, tena vuccati – ‘vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehī’”tiādinā (vibha. 564) nayena vibhaṅgeyeva attho vutto. Tathāpi aṭṭhakathānayaṃ vinā na suṭṭhu pākaṭoti aṭṭhakathānayeneva naṃ pakāsayissāma.

Now, wishing to show the special attainment which is attained by this practice—beginning with the first jhāna and culminating in the three kinds of knowledge—he said the passage beginning, “So I…” Therein, regarding the passage beginning, “Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states…,” although the meaning has been stated in the Vibhaṅga itself by the method beginning, “Therein, what are sensual pleasures? Desire is a sensual pleasure, lust is a sensual pleasure, desire and lust is a sensual pleasure; intention is a sensual pleasure, lust is a sensual pleasure, intention and lust is a sensual pleasure—these are called sensual pleasures. Therein, what are unwholesome states? Sensual desire… doubt—these are called unwholesome states. Thus, he is secluded, fully secluded from these sensual pleasures and from these unwholesome states; therefore it is said, ‘Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states…’,” nevertheless, without the commentarial method, the meaning is not very clear. Therefore, I shall explain it only by the commentarial method.

Seyyathidaṃ – vivicceva kāmehīti kāmehi viviccitvā vinā hutvā apasakketvā. Yo panāyamettha evakāro, so niyamatthoti veditabbo. Yasmā ca niyamattho, tasmā tasmiṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇasamaye avijjamānānampi kāmānaṃ tassa paṭhamajjhānassa paṭipakkhabhāvaṃ kāmapariccāgeneva cassa adhigamaṃ dīpeti. Kathaṃ? “Vivicceva kāmehī”ti evañhi niyame kariyamāne idaṃ paññāyati. Nūnimassa jhānassa kāmā paṭipakkhabhūtā, yesu sati idaṃ na pavattati, andhakāre sati padīpo viya, tesaṃ pariccāgeneva cassa adhigamo hoti, orimatīrapariccāgena pārimatīrasseva, tasmā niyamaṃ karotīti.

As follows: ‘Quite secluded from sensual pleasures’ means having become secluded from sensual pleasures, having become without them, having moved away from them. The word ‘eva’ here should be understood as having a restrictive meaning. And because it has a restrictive meaning, it indicates that even when sensual pleasures are not present at the time of attaining and abiding in the first jhāna, sensual pleasures are the opponent of the first jhāna, and its attainment comes only through the abandonment of sensual pleasures. How so? For when the restriction is made thus, ‘Quite secluded from sensual pleasures,’ this becomes apparent: Indeed, sensual pleasures are the opponents of this jhāna. When they are present, this jhāna does not arise, just as a lamp does not arise when darkness is present. And its attainment comes about only through their abandonment, just as the far shore is reached only by abandoning the near shore. Therefore, it makes the restriction.

Tattha siyā – “kasmā panesa pubbapadeyeva vutto na uttarapade, kiṃ akusalehi dhammehi aviviccāpi jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyyā”ti? Na [M 1.0113] kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tannissaraṇato hi pubbapadeeva esa vutto. Kāmadhātusamatikkamanato hi kāmarāgapaṭipakkhato ca idaṃ jhānaṃ kāmānameva nissaraṇaṃ. Yathāha – “kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, yadidaṃ nekkhamma”nti (itivu. 72). Uttarapadepi pana yathā “idheva, bhikkhave, paṭhamo samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.139) ettha evakāro ānetvā vuccati, evaṃ vattabbo. Na hi sakkā ito aññehipi nīvaraṇasaṅkhātehi akusalehi dhammehi avivicca jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ[V 1.0105]. Tasmā “vivicceva kāmehi vivicceva akusalehi dhammehī”ti evaṃ padadvayepi esa daṭṭhabbo. Padadvayepi ca kiñcāpi “viviccā”ti iminā sādhāraṇavacanena tadaṅgavivekādayo kāyavivekādayo ca sabbepi vivekā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Tathāpi kāyaviveko, cittaviveko, vikkhambhanavivekoti tayo eva idha daṭṭhabbā. “Kāmehī”ti iminā pana padena ye ca niddese “katame vatthukāmā manāpiyā rūpā”tiādinā (mahāni. 1; vibha. 964) nayena vatthukāmā vuttā, ye ca tattheva vibhaṅge ca “chando [P 1.0143] kāmo”tiādinā (mahāni. 1) nayena kilesakāmā vuttā, te sabbepi saṅgahitā icceva daṭṭhabbā. Evañhi sati “vivicceva kāmehī”ti vatthukāmehipi viviccevāti attho yujjati. Tena kāyaviveko vutto hoti.

Herein, this might be said: “Why is this stated only in the first term and not in the second? Could one attain and abide in jhāna even without being secluded from unwholesome states?” But this should not be understood in that way. For it is stated only in the first term because this jhāna is the escape from them. For this jhāna is the escape from sensual pleasures themselves, because it transcends the sense-sphere and because it is the opponent of sensual lust. As it is said: “This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation.” But in the second term too, the word ‘eva’ should be brought in and recited, just as it is brought in and recited in the passage, “Here, monks, is the first ascetic, here the second ascetic.” For it is not possible to attain and abide in jhāna without being secluded from the other unwholesome states called the hindrances. Therefore, this should be understood as applying to both terms thus: “Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, and quite secluded from unwholesome states.” And although in both terms, by this general word ‘secluded,’ all kinds of seclusion are included—such as seclusion by substitution and bodily seclusion—nevertheless, only three should be understood here: bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression. Furthermore, by this term ‘from sensual pleasures,’ all are included: both the objective sensual pleasures spoken of in the Niddesa by the method beginning, “What are objective sensual pleasures? Agreeable forms…,” and the defilement-sensualities spoken of there and in the Vibhaṅga by the method beginning, “Desire is a sensual pleasure….” This is how it should be understood. For when this is so, the meaning, ‘quite secluded from objective sensual pleasures,’ is suitable for the phrase ‘quite secluded from sensual pleasures.’ By this, bodily seclusion is stated.

Vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti kilesakāmehi sabbākusalehi dhammehi vā viviccāti attho yujjati. Tena cittaviveko vutto hoti. Purimena cettha vatthukāmehi vivekavacanatoyeva kāmasukhapariccāgo, dutiyena kilesakāmehi vivekavacanato nekkhammasukhapariggaho vibhāvito hoti. Evaṃ vatthukāmakilesakāmavivekavacanatoyeva ca etesaṃ paṭhamena saṃkilesavatthuppahānaṃ, dutiyena saṃkilesappahānaṃ; paṭhamena lolabhāvassa hetupariccāgo, dutiyena bālabhāvassa; paṭhamena ca payogasuddhi, dutiyena āsayaposanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hotīti viññātabbaṃ. Esa tāva nayo “kāmehī”ti ettha vuttakāmesu vatthukāmapakkhe.

‘Secluded from unwholesome states’—the meaning ‘secluded from defilement-sensualities’ or ‘from all unwholesome states’ is suitable. By this, mental seclusion is stated. And here, by the former—the statement of seclusion from objective sensual pleasures—the abandonment of sensual pleasure is clarified. By the latter—the statement of seclusion from defilement-sensualities—the taking up of the bliss of renunciation is clarified. Thus, by this statement of seclusion from objective sensual pleasures and defilement-sensualities, the following is clarified: by the first, the abandonment of the basis of defilements; by the second, the abandonment of the defilements. By the first, the abandonment of the cause of fickleness; by the second, that of the cause of foolishness. And by the first, the purity of application; by the second, the purification of one’s underlying disposition. This is how it should be understood. This, so far, is the method regarding the aspect of objective sensual pleasures among those sensual pleasures spoken of in the phrase ‘from sensual pleasures’.

Kilesakāmapakkhe pana chandoti ca rāgoti ca evamādīhi anekabhedo kāmacchandoyeva kāmoti adhippeto. So ca akusalapariyāpannopi [M 1.0114] samāno, “tattha katamo kāmachando kāmo”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge jhānapaṭipakkhato visuṃ vutto. Kilesakāmattā vā purimapade vutto, akusalapariyāpannattā dutiyapade. Anekabhedato cassa kāmatoti avatvā kāmehīti vuttaṃ. Aññesampi ca dhammānaṃ akusalabhāve vijjamāne “tattha katame akusalā dhammā kāmacchando”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge (vibha. 564) uparijhānaṅgapaccanīkapaṭipakkhabhāvadassanato nīvaraṇāneva vuttāni. Nīvaraṇāni hi jhānaṅgapaccanīkāni, tesaṃ jhānaṅgāneva paṭipakkhāni, viddhaṃsakānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi “samādhi kāmacchandassa paṭipakkho, pīti byāpādassa, vitakko thinamiddhassa, sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccassa, vicāro vicikicchāyā”ti peṭake vuttaṃ.

But in the aspect of defilement-sensualities, it is sensual desire itself—with its many varieties such as ‘desire,’ ‘lust,’ and so on—that is intended by ‘sensual pleasure.’ And although it is included among the unwholesome, it is stated separately in the Vibhaṅga as an opponent to jhāna, by the method beginning, “Therein, what is the sensual desire that is a sensual pleasure?” Or, it is stated in the first term because it is a defilement-sensuality, and in the second term because it is included among the unwholesome. And because of its many varieties, it is stated as ‘from sensual pleasures’ (kāmehi) and not as ‘from sensual pleasure’ (kāmato). Furthermore, although other unwholesome states exist, only the hindrances are mentioned in the Vibhaṅga by the method beginning, “Therein, what are the unwholesome states? Sensual desire…,” because of showing their nature as adversaries and opponents to the jhāna factors to be mentioned. For the hindrances are the adversaries of the jhāna factors; the jhāna factors themselves are their opponents and destroyers. This is what is stated. Thus, it is said in the Peṭakopadesa: “Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire, rapture is the opponent of ill will, applied thought is the opponent of sloth and torpor, happiness is the opponent of restlessness and remorse, and sustained thought is the opponent of doubt.”

Evamettha “vivicceva kāmehī”ti iminā kāmacchandassa vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hoti. “Vivicca akusalehi dhammehī”ti iminā pañcannampi nīvaraṇānaṃ. Aggahitaggahaṇena pana [V 1.0106] paṭhamena kāmacchandassa, dutiyena sesanīvaraṇānaṃ. Tathā paṭhamena tīsu akusalamūlesu pañcakāmaguṇabhedavisayassa lobhassa, dutiyena [P 1.0144] āghātavatthubhedādivisayānaṃ dosamohānaṃ. Oghādīsu vā dhammesu paṭhamena kāmogha-kāmayoga-kāmāsava-kāmupādāna-abhijjhākāyagantha-kāmarāga-saṃyojanānaṃ, dutiyena avasesaogha-yogāsava-upādāna-gantha-saṃyojanānaṃ. Paṭhamena ca taṇhāya taṃsampayuttakānañca, dutiyena avijjāya taṃsampayuttakānañca. Apica paṭhamena lobhasampayuttaaṭṭhacittuppādānaṃ, dutiyena sesānaṃ catunnaṃ akusalacittuppādānaṃ vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hotīti veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāva “vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehī”ti ettha atthappakāsanā.

Thus, herein, by the phrase 'secluded from sensual pleasures,' the seclusion by suppression of the hindrance of sensual desire is spoken of. By the phrase 'secluded from unwholesome states,' the seclusion by suppression of all five hindrances is spoken of. Alternatively, by taking what was not taken before, by the first phrase, the seclusion by suppression of the hindrance of sensual desire is spoken of; by the second, that of the remaining hindrances. Likewise, among the three unwholesome roots, by the first phrase, the seclusion by suppression of greed, which has as its object the various kinds of the five sensual pleasures, is spoken of; by the second, that of hatred and delusion, which have as their objects the various grounds for resentment and so on. Or, regarding the dhammas such as the floods, by the first phrase, the seclusion by suppression of the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of sensual lust is spoken of; by the second, that of the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. And by the first, of craving and its associated states; by the second, of ignorance and its associated states. Moreover, by the first, the seclusion by suppression of the eight consciousnesses associated with greed is spoken of; by the second, that of the remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses. Thus it should be understood. This, for now, is the explanation of the meaning here regarding 'secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.'

Ettāvatā ca paṭhamassa jhānassa pahānaṅgaṃ dassetvā idāni sampayogaṅgaṃ dassento savitakkaṃ savicārantiādimāha. Tattha vitakkanaṃ vitakko, ūhananti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇo, āhananapariyāhananaraso. Tathā hi “tena yogāvacaro ārammaṇaṃ vitakkāhataṃ vitakkapariyāhataṃ karotī”ti vuccati. Ārammaṇe cittassa ānayanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Vicaraṇaṃ vicāro, anusañcaraṇanti [M 1.0115] vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo, tattha sahajātānuyojanaraso, cittassa anuppabandhanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Santepi ca nesaṃ katthaci avippayoge oḷārikaṭṭhena ghaṇṭābhighātasaddo viya cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto vitakko, sukhumaṭṭhena anuravo viya anuppabandho vicāro. Vipphāravā cettha vitakko paripphandanabhāvo cittassa, ākāse uppatitukāmassa pakkhino pakkhavikkhepo viya padumābhimukhapāto viya ca gandhānubandhacetaso bhamarassa. Santavutti vicāro nātiparipphandanabhāvo cittassa, ākāse uppatitassa pakkhino pakkhappasāraṇaṃ viya paribbhamanaṃ viya ca padumābhimukhapatitassa bhamarassa padumassa uparibhāge. So pana nesaṃ viseso paṭhama-dutiyajjhānesu pākaṭo hoti. Iti iminā ca vitakkena iminā ca vicārena saha vattati rukkho viya pupphena ca phalena cāti idaṃ jhānaṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti vuccati. Vibhaṅge pana “iminā ca vitakkena iminā ca vicārena upeto hoti [P 1.0145] samupeto”tiādinā (vibha. 565) nayena puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā katā. Attho pana tatrāpi evameva daṭṭhabbo.

And having thus far shown the factor to be abandoned of the first jhāna, now, showing its associated factor, He said, 'with vitakka and with vicāra,' and so on. Therein, thinking is vitakka; it is said to be pondering. This vitakka has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object; its function is striking and striking all around. For so it is said: 'By that, the yogāvacara makes the object struck by vitakka, struck all around by vitakka.' Its manifestation is the leading of the mind to the object. Examining is vicāra; it is said to be moving about continuously. This vicāra has the characteristic of rubbing the object again and again; its function is to repeatedly engage the co-arisen states with that object; its manifestation is the uninterrupted binding of the mind. And although they are inseparable in some consciousnesses, due to its coarseness, the mind's first impact is vitakka, like the sound of a bell being struck; due to its subtlety, the uninterrupted binding is vicāra, like the reverberation. Herein, vitakka is agitated, a state of the mind's trembling all around, like the flapping of wings of a great bird wishing to fly up into the sky, and like the flight of a bee, whose mind follows the scent, towards a lotus. Vicāra has a calm proceeding, a state of the mind's not trembling excessively, like the spreading of the wings of a bird that has flown up into the sky, and like the circling of a bee above a lotus after having flown towards it. But that distinction between them becomes evident in the first and second jhānas. Thus, just as a tree exists together with its flowers and fruits, so this jhāna exists together with this vitakka and with this vicāra; for this reason, this jhāna is called 'with vitakka and with vicāra.' In the Vibhaṅga, however, the teaching is given from the standpoint of a person, by the method beginning, 'He is endowed, fully endowed with this vitakka and with this vicāra...' But the meaning there too should be understood in just this way.

Vivekajanti ettha vivitti viveko, nīvaraṇavigamoti attho. Vivittoti vā viveko, nīvaraṇavivitto jhānasampayuttadhammarāsīti attho. Tasmā vivekā, tasmiṃ vā viveke jātanti vivekajaṃ. Pītisukhanti ettha pinayatīti pīti, sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā kāyacittapīnanarasā[V 1.0107], pharaṇarasā vā, odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā. Sukhanaṃ sukhaṃ, suṭṭhu vā khādati khanati ca kāyacittābādhanti sukhaṃ, taṃ sātalakkhaṇaṃ, sampayuttakānaṃ upabrūhanarasaṃ, anuggahapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Satipi ca nesaṃ katthaci avippayoge iṭṭhārammaṇapaṭilābhatuṭṭhi pīti, paṭiladdharasānubhavanaṃ sukhaṃ. Yattha pīti tattha sukhaṃ, yattha sukhaṃ tattha na niyamato pīti. Saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā pīti, vedanākkhandhasaṅgahitaṃ sukhaṃ. Kantārakhinnassa vanantodakadassanasavanesu viya pīti, vanacchāyappavesanaudakaparibhogesu viya sukhaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye pākaṭabhāvato cetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ayañca pīti, idañca sukhaṃ, assa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne atthīti idaṃ jhānaṃ “pītisukha”nti vuccati.

Herein, in the word 'vivekajaṃ' (born of seclusion), seclusion is viveka; the meaning is freedom from the hindrances. Or, it is secluded, therefore it is viveka; the meaning is the collection of states associated with jhāna that is secluded from the hindrances. It is 'born of seclusion' because it is born from that seclusion, or born in that seclusion. Herein, in the word 'pītisukhaṃ' (rapture-happiness), it delights, therefore it is pīti (rapture). It has the characteristic of endearment, the function of refreshing the body and mind, or the function of suffusion, and its manifestation is elation. Being happy is sukha (happiness). Or, it thoroughly eats up and digs up bodily and mental affliction, therefore it is sukha. It has the characteristic of gratification, the function of augmenting associated states, and its manifestation is support. And although they are inseparable in some consciousnesses, pīti is the contentment on gaining a desirable object, while sukha is the experiencing of the flavor of what has been gained. Where there is pīti, there is sukha; but where there is sukha, there is not necessarily pīti. Pīti is included in the aggregate of formations; sukha is included in the aggregate of feeling. Pīti is like that of a person exhausted in a wasteland upon seeing or hearing of a forest's edge and water; sukha is like entering the forest shade and making use of the water. And it should be known that this is said because of their prominence at those respective times. This pīti and this sukha exist in this jhāna, or belong to this jhāna; therefore, this jhāna is called 'pītisukha.'

Atha vā pīti ca sukhañca pītisukhaṃ, dhammavinayādayo viya. Vivekajaṃ pītisukhamassa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne atthīti evampi vivekajaṃpītisukhaṃ. Yatheva [M 1.0116] hi jhānaṃ, evaṃ pītisukhaṃ pettha vivekajameva hoti, tañcassa atthīti tasmā ekapadeneva “vivekajaṃ pītisukha”ntipi vattuṃ yujjati. Vibhaṅge pana “idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagata”ntiādinā (vibha. 567) nayenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Attho pana tatrāpi evameva daṭṭhabbo.

Or alternatively, pīti and sukha are 'pītisukha,' like the words 'Dhamma-Vinaya,' and so on. The rapture-happiness born of seclusion belongs to this jhāna, or exists in this jhāna; for this reason also, it is called 'vivekajaṃpītisukhaṃ.' For just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too the rapture-happiness herein is also born of seclusion, and that belongs to it. Therefore, it is also fitting to say with a single compound term, 'vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ.' In the Vibhaṅga, however, this was stated by the Blessed One by the method beginning, 'This happiness is accompanied by this rapture...' But the meaning there too should be understood in just this way.

Paṭhamanti gaṇanānupubbatā paṭhamaṃ, idaṃ paṭhamaṃ samāpajjatītipi paṭhamaṃ. Paccanīkadhamme jhāpetīti jhānaṃ, iminā yogino jhāyantītipi jhānaṃ, paccanīkadhamme ḍahanti gocaraṃ vā cintentīti attho. Sayaṃ vā taṃ jhāyati upanijjhāyatīti jhānaṃ, teneva upanijjhāyanalakkhaṇanti vuccati. Tadetaṃ ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ[P 1.0146], lakkhaṇūpanijjhānanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha ārammaṇūpanijjhānanti saha upacārena aṭṭha samāpattiyo vuccanti. Kasmā? Kasiṇādiārammaṇūpanijjhāyanato. Lakkhaṇūpanijjhānanti vipassanāmaggaphalāni vuccanti. Kasmā? Lakkhaṇūpanijjhāyanato. Ettha hi vipassanā aniccalakkhaṇādīni upanijjhāyati, vipassanāya upanijjhāyanakiccaṃ pana maggena sijjhatīti maggo lakkhaṇūpanijjhānanti vuccati. Phalaṃ pana nirodhassa tathalakkhaṇaṃ upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānanti vuccati. Imasmiṃ panatthe ārammaṇūpanijjhānameva jhānanti adhippetaṃ.

It is 'first' (paṭhama) by way of numerical sequence; also, because one enters this first, it is called 'first'. It burns up opposing states, thus it is 'jhāna'; by this, yogis contemplate, thus it is also 'jhāna'. The meaning is: they burn up opposing states, or they contemplate the object. Alternatively, it itself contemplates or closely examines that object, thus it is 'jhāna'. For that very reason, it is said to have the characteristic of close examination. That jhāna is of two kinds: object-contemplation and characteristic-contemplation. Therein, the eight attainments together with access concentration are called 'object-contemplation'. Why? Because of contemplating objects such as kasiṇas. Insight, path, and fruition are called 'characteristic-contemplation'. Why? Because of contemplating the characteristics. For herein, insight contemplates the characteristics of impermanence, etc., but the function of contemplation by insight is accomplished by the path; thus, the path is called 'characteristic-contemplation'. Fruition, however, contemplates the unfailing characteristic of cessation, thus it is called 'characteristic-contemplation'. In this context, however, only object-contemplation is intended as 'jhāna'.

Etthāha – “katamaṃ pana taṃ jhānaṃ nāma, yaṃ savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ…pe… pītisukhanti evaṃ apadesaṃ arahatī”ti? Vuccate – yathā sadhano saparijanotiādīsu ṭhapetvā dhanañca parijanañca añño apadesāraho hoti, evaṃ ṭhapetvā vitakkādidhamme aññaṃ apadesārahaṃ natthi. Yathā pana sarathā sapatti senāti vutte senaṅgesuyeva senāsammuti, evamidha pañcasu aṅgesuyeva [V 1.0108] jhānasammuti veditabbā. Katamesu pañcasu? Vitakko, vicāro, pīti, sukhaṃ, cittekaggatāti etesu. Etāneva hissa “savitakkaṃ savicāra”ntiādinā nayena aṅgabhāvena vuttāni. Avuttattā ekaggatā aṅgaṃ na hotīti ce tañca na. Kasmā? Vuttattā eva. Sāpi hi vibhaṅge “jhānanti vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti evaṃ vuttāyeva. Tasmā yathā savitakkaṃ savicāranti, evaṃ sacittekaggatanti idha avuttepi iminā vibhaṅgavacanena cittekaggatāpi aṅgamevāti veditabbā. Yena hi adhippāyena bhagavatā uddeso kato, so eva tena vibhaṅgepi pakāsitoti.

Here a questioner asks: "But what is that jhāna called, which is worthy of the designation 'with initial application, with sustained application... with rapture and pleasure'?" The reply is stated: Just as in expressions such as 'one with wealth', 'one with a retinue', setting aside the wealth and the retinue, there is another person worthy of designation, so too, setting aside the states such as initial application, there is no other thing worthy of designation. And just as when it is said, 'an army with chariots, with infantry', the convention 'army' is to be understood as referring only to the components of the army, so too here, the convention 'jhāna' is to be understood as referring only to the five factors. In which five? In these: initial application, sustained application, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind. For these very factors have been stated as its components by the method beginning 'with initial application, with sustained application'. If it is said that because it is not stated, one-pointedness is not a factor, that is not correct. Why? Because it is indeed stated. For it too is stated in the Vibhaṅga thus: "Jhāna is initial application, sustained application, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind." Therefore, just as it is said 'with initial application, with sustained application', so too, even though 'with one-pointedness of mind' is not stated here, through this statement from the Vibhaṅga, it should be understood that one-pointedness of mind is indeed a factor. For the very intention with which the summary was made by the Blessed One is clarified by him in the Vibhaṅga as well.

Upasampajjāti [M 1.0117] upagantvā, pāpuṇitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasampādayitvā vā, nipphādetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vibhaṅge pana “upasampajjāti paṭhamassa jhānassa lābho paṭilābho patti sampatti phusanā samphusanā sacchikiriyā upasampadā”ti vuttaṃ. Tassāpi evamevattho veditabbo. Vihāsinti bodhimaṇḍe nisajjasaṅkhātena iriyāpathavihārena itivuttappakārajhānasamaṅgī [P 1.0147] hutvā attabhāvassa iriyaṃ vuttiṃ pālanaṃ yapanaṃ yāpanaṃ cāraṃ vihāraṃ abhinipphādesinti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ vibhaṅge – “viharatīti iriyati vattati pāleti yapeti yāpeti carati viharati, tena vuccati viharatī”ti (vibha. 512).

'Having attained' (upasampajja) means 'having approached', 'having reached', so it is said. Or, 'having accomplished', 'having produced', so it is said. But in the Vibhaṅga it is said: "'Attaining' is the gain, attainment, reaching, achievement, touching, contact, realization, and accomplishment of the first jhāna." The meaning of that passage should also be understood in this same way. The meaning of 'He dwelt' (vihāsi) is: having become endowed with the jhāna of the kind thus described, by the posture-dwelling described as sitting at the Bodhi-seat, he brought about the body's posture, its proceeding, maintenance, sustenance, movement, and dwelling. For this is said in the Vibhaṅga: "'He dwells' (viharati) means he moves, proceeds, maintains, sustains, makes last, moves about, dwells; therefore it is said 'he dwells'" (Vibh. 512).

Kiṃ pana katvā bhagavā imaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsīti? Kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā. Kataraṃ? Ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ. Aññena tadatthikena kiṃ kātabbanti? Aññenapi etaṃ vā kammaṭṭhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇādīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ bhāvetabbaṃ. Tesaṃ bhāvanānayo visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.55) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Idha pana vuccamāne atibhāriyaṃ vinayanidānaṃ hoti, tasmā pāḷiyā atthappakāsanamattameva karomāti.

But having done what did the Blessed One attain and dwell in this jhāna? By developing a meditation subject. Which one? The meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing. What should be done by another who desires that? By another, either this meditation subject should be developed, or another one from among the earth kasiṇa, etc. The method for developing them should be understood only in the way stated in the Visuddhimagga. But if the method of development were to be stated here, this introduction to the Vinaya would become very heavy; therefore, we will provide only a clarification of the meaning of the Pāḷi.

Paṭhamajjhānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the first jhāna is concluded.

Dutiyajjhānakathā

The Exposition of the Second Jhāna

Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti vitakkassa ca vicārassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vūpasamā samatikkamā; dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe apātubhāvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi dutiyajjhāne sabbepi paṭhamajjhānadhammā na santi, aññeyeva hi paṭhamajjhāne phassādayo, aññe idha; oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamo [V 1.0109] hotīti dīpanatthaṃ “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ajjhattanti idha niyakajjhattamadhippetaṃ. Vibhaṅge pana “ajjhattaṃ paccatta”nti (vibha. 573) ettakameva vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana niyakajjhattaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā attani jātaṃ attano santāne nibbattanti ayamettha attho.

“Because of the stilling of initial application and sustained application” means: because of the stilling (vūpasamā), because of the transcending (samatikkamā) of these two, that is, of initial application and of sustained application; it is said to mean their non-manifestation at the moment of the second jhāna. Herein, although in the second jhāna all the factors of the first jhāna are not present—for, in the first jhāna contact and the other factors are different, and here they are different—it should be understood that the attainment of the subsequent second jhāna and so on from the first jhāna occurs because of the transcending of the grosser and grosser factor. For the purpose of clarifying this meaning, it is said thus: “because of the stilling of initial application and sustained application.” By “internal” (ajjhattaṃ), one's own internal state is intended here. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only this much is said: “internal, personal.” But since one's own internal state is intended, the meaning here is: “arisen in oneself, produced in one's own continuum.”

Sampasādananti sampasādanaṃ vuccati saddhā. Sampasādanayogato jhānampi sampasādanaṃ, nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viya. Yasmā vā taṃ jhānaṃ sampasādanasamannāgatattā vitakkavicārakkhobhavūpasamanena ceto sampasādayati, tasmāpi sampasādananti vuttaṃ. Imasmiñca atthavikappe sampasādanaṃ cetasoti evaṃ padasambandho veditabbo. Purimasmiṃ pana atthavikappe [M 1.0118] cetasoti etaṃ ekodibhāvena saddhiṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ atthayojanā – eko udetīti ekodi, vitakkavicārehi anajjhārūḷhattā aggo seṭṭho hutvā udetīti [P 1.0148] attho. Seṭṭhopi hi loke ekoti vuccati. Vitakkavicāravirahato vā eko asahāyo hutvātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha vā sampayuttadhamme udāyatīti udi, uṭṭhāpetīti attho. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena eko ca so udi cāti ekodi, samādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti imaṃ ekodiṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhayatīti idaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ ekodibhāvaṃ. So panāyaṃ ekodi yasmā cetaso, na sattassa na jīvassa, tasmā etaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvanti vuttaṃ.

By `sampasādana` (serenity) is meant faith. Because of its connection with serenity, the jhāna is also called `sampasādana`, just as a blue cloth is so called because of its connection with the color blue. Or, because that jhāna, being endowed with serenity and by the stilling of the agitation of applied and sustained thought, makes the mind serene, it is therefore also called `sampasādana`. In this latter alternative meaning, the connection of the words should be understood as `sampasādanaṃ cetaso` (serenity of the mind). In the former alternative meaning, however, `cetaso` (of the mind) should be connected with `ekodibhāvena` (with unification). Therein, this is the application of the meaning: `eko udeti` (one arises), thus `ekodi` (unification); the meaning is that because it is not overcome by applied and sustained thought, it arises as supreme, as excellent. For in the world, even that which is excellent is called `eko` (one). Or, it is also fitting to say that because it is devoid of applied and sustained thought, it arises as `eko` (one), without a companion. Or else, `udāyati` (it causes to rise) the associated states, thus `udi`; the meaning is 'it uplifts.' `Eko` in the sense of excellent, and that is also `udi`; thus `ekodi`. This is a synonym for concentration. Thus, 'it develops, it cultivates this `ekodi`'; therefore this second jhāna is `ekodibhāva` (the state of unification). But since this `ekodi` is of the mind, not of a being, not of a life-principle, it is therefore called `cetaso ekodibhāva` (the unification of the mind).

Nanu cāyaṃ saddhā paṭhamajjhānepi atthi, ayañca ekodināmako samādhi; atha kasmā idameva sampasādanaṃ “cetaso ekodibhāvañcā”ti vuttanti? Vuccate – aduñhi paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārakkhobhena vīcitaraṅgasamākulamiva jalaṃ na suppasannaṃ hoti, tasmā satiyāpi saddhāya sampasādananti na vuttaṃ. Na suppasannattāyeva cettha samādhipi na suṭṭhu pākaṭo, tasmā ekodibhāvantipi na vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana jhāne vitakkavicārapalibodhābhāvena laddhokāsā balavatī saddhā, balavasaddhāsahāyappaṭilābheneva ca samādhipi pākaṭo; tasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Vibhaṅge pana “sampasādananti yā saddhā saddahanā okappanā abhippasādo, cetaso ekodibhāvanti yā cittassa ṭhiti…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttena panetena saddhiṃ ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā yathā na virujjhati aññadatthu saṃsandati ceva sameti ca evaṃ veditabbā.

Is not this faith also present in the first jhāna, and this concentration named `ekodi` as well? Then why is only this jhāna called `sampasādana` and `cetaso ekodibhāva`? It is said: For that first jhāna, due to the agitation of applied and sustained thought, is not perfectly serene, like water agitated with ripples and waves. Therefore, although faith is present, it is not called `sampasādana`. And precisely because it is not perfectly serene, the concentration herein is also not very manifest; therefore, it is not called `ekodibhāva` either. But in this jhāna, because of the absence of the obstruction of applied and sustained thought, faith, having found its opportunity, is powerful. And precisely by gaining the support of powerful faith, concentration also becomes manifest. Therefore, it should be understood that only this jhāna is spoken of thus. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only this much is said: 'By `sampasādana` is meant the faith, the believing, the settling upon, the serene trust that exists. By `cetaso ekodibhāva` is meant the stability of mind... right concentration.' It should be understood that this commentary is presented in such a way that it does not contradict what is said there, but on the contrary, is consistent and in agreement with it.

Avitakkaṃ avicāranti bhāvanāya pahīnattā etasmiṃ etassa vā vitakko natthīti avitakkaṃ. Imināva nayena avicāraṃ. Vibhaṅgepi (vibha. 576) vuttaṃ “iti ayañca vitakko [V 1.0110] ayañca vicāro santā honti samitā vūpasantā atthaṅgatā abbhatthaṅgatā appitā byappitā sositā visositā byantīkatā, tena vuccati avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti.

“Without applied thought, without sustained thought” means: because it has been abandoned through development, in this jhāna or for this person, there is no applied thought; thus, it is “without applied thought.” In the same way, it is “without sustained thought.” In the Vibhaṅga also it is said: “Thus, this applied thought and this sustained thought are calmed, quieted, stilled, set, completely set, vanished, utterly vanished, dried up, thoroughly dried up, and brought to an end; therefore, it is called ‘without applied thought, without sustained thought.’”

Etthāha – nanu ca “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti imināpi ayamattho siddho, atha kasmā puna vuttaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti? Vuccate – evametaṃ siddho vāyamattho, na panetaṃ tadatthadīpakaṃ; nanu avocumha – “oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa [M 1.0119] aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ [P 1.0149] adhigamo hotīti dīpanatthaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti evaṃ vutta”nti.

Here one asks: “Is not this meaning already established by the phrase, ‘because of the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought’? Why then is it said again, ‘without applied thought, without sustained thought’?” It is replied: “It is so; this meaning is indeed established. But that phrase is not an elucidator of this specific meaning. Have we not said: ‘The attainment of the subsequent second jhāna and so on from the first jhāna occurs because of the transcending of the grosser and grosser factor; for the purpose of clarifying this, it is said thus: “because of the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought”’?”

Apica vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ sampasādanaṃ, na kilesakālusiyassa. Vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā ekodibhāvaṃ na upacārajjhānamiva nīvaraṇappahānā, na paṭhamajjhānamiva ca aṅgapātubhāvāti evaṃ sampasādanaekodibhāvānaṃ hetuparidīpakamidaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathā vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ, na tatiyacatutthajjhānāni viya cakkhuviññāṇādīni viya ca abhāvāti evaṃ avitakkaavicārabhāvassa hetuparidīpakañca, na vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakaṃ. Vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakameva pana “avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ, tasmā purimaṃ vatvāpi puna vattabbamevāti.

Furthermore, this jhāna is `sampasādana` (serenity) because of the stilling of applied and sustained thought, not because of the stilling of the impurity of defilements. And it is `ekodibhāva` (unification) because of the stilling of applied and sustained thought, not because of the abandoning of the hindrances, as in the case of access concentration, and not because of the manifestation of the factor, as in the case of the first jhāna. Thus, this phrase (`vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā`) is an elucidator of the cause for `sampasādana` and `ekodibhāva`. Likewise, this jhāna is 'without applied and sustained thought' because of the stilling of applied and sustained thought; it is not so because of their mere absence, as in the case of the third and fourth jhānas or as in the case of eye-consciousness and so on. Thus, that phrase is also an elucidator of the cause for the state of being without applied and sustained thought; it is not an elucidator of the mere absence of applied and sustained thought. The phrase 'without applied thought, without sustained thought,' however, is precisely an elucidator of the mere absence of applied and sustained thought. Therefore, even after saying the former phrase, the latter must be said again.

Samādhijanti paṭhamajjhānasamādhito sampayuttasamādhito vā jātanti attho. Tattha kiñcāpi paṭhamampi sampayuttasamādhito jātaṃ, atha kho ayameva “samādhī”ti vattabbataṃ arahati vitakkavicārakkhobhavirahena ativiya acalattā suppasannattā ca. Tasmā imassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ idameva “samādhija”nti vuttaṃ. Pītisukhanti idaṃ vuttanayameva.

“Born of concentration” (samādhija) means: born of the concentration of the first jhāna, or born of the associated concentration. Therein, although the first jhāna is also born of associated concentration, yet only this concentration deserves to be called “concentration.” Why? Because of the absence of the agitation of applied and sustained thought, and because of being extremely unmoving and perfectly serene. Therefore, for the purpose of speaking its praise, only this jhāna is called “born of concentration.” The phrase “rapture and happiness” (pītisukha) is to be understood in the way already explained.

Dutiyanti gaṇanānupubbato dutiyaṃ, idaṃ dutiyaṃ samāpajjatītipi dutiyaṃ. Jhānanti ettha pana yathā paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkādīhi pañcaṅgikaṃ hoti, evamidaṃ sampasādādīhi “caturaṅgika”nti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “jhānanti sampasādo, pīti, sukhaṃ, cittassekaggatā”ti (vibha. 580). Pariyāyoyeva ceso. Sampasādanaṃ pana ṭhapetvā nippariyāyena tivaṅgikamevetaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye tivaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti? Pīti, sukhaṃ, cittassekaggatā”ti (dha. sa. 161). Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Second (dutiyaṃ) means second according to the numerical sequence. It is also 'second' because one attains this for a second time. Regarding 'jhāna' here, just as the first jhāna has five factors beginning with applied thought, so this should be understood as having four factors beginning with serene confidence. As it is said: 'Jhāna is serene confidence, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.' And this is only a figurative expression. However, setting aside serene confidence, this is literally three-factored. As it is said: 'What at that time is the three-factored jhāna? Rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.' The rest is as has been explained.

Dutiyajjhānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discussion of the Second Jhāna is concluded.

Tatiyajjhānakathā

The Discussion of the Third Jhāna

Pītiyā [V 1.0111] ca virāgāti ettha vuttatthāyeva pīti. Virāgoti tassā jigucchanaṃ vā samatikkamo vā. Ubhinnamantarā “ca” saddo sampiṇḍanattho, so [M 1.0120] hi vūpasamaṃ vā sampiṇḍeti vitakkavicāravūpasamaṃ vā. Tattha yadā vūpasamameva sampiṇḍeti, tadā pītiyā virāgā ca, kiñca bhiyyo vūpasamā cāti evaṃ yojanā [P 1.0150] veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāyaṃ virāgo jigucchanattho hoti. Tasmā pītiyā jigucchanā ca vūpasamā cāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo. Yadā pana vitakkavicāravūpasamaṃ sampiṇḍeti, tadā pītiyā ca virāgā, kiñca bhiyyo vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāyaṃ virāgo samatikkamanattho hoti. Tasmā pītiyā ca samatikkamā, vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, in the phrase 'pītiyā ca virāgā' (and from the fading away of rapture), 'pīti' has the meaning already stated. 'Virāgo' means either disgust (jigucchanaṃ) with it or the transcending (samatikkamo) of it. The word 'ca' between the two has the meaning of combining; for it combines either 'subsiding' (vūpasama) or 'the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought' (vitakkavicāravūpasama). Therein, when it combines only 'subsiding,' the construction should be understood thus: 'and from the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, from its subsiding.' In this construction, 'virāgo' has the meaning of disgust. Therefore, this meaning should be understood: 'from disgust for rapture and from its subsiding.' When, however, it combines 'the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought,' the construction should be understood thus: 'and from the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, from the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought.' In this construction, 'virāgo' has the meaning of transcending. Therefore, this meaning should be understood: 'from the transcending of rapture and from the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought.'

Kāmañcete vitakkavicārā dutiyajjhāneyeva vūpasantā imassa pana jhānassa maggaparidīpanatthaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthañcetaṃ vuttaṃ. “Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti hi vutte idaṃ paññāyati – “nūna vitakkavicāravūpasamo maggo imassa jhānassā”ti. Yathā ca tatiye ariyamagge appahīnānampi sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānā”ti (ma. ni. 2.132) evaṃ pahānaṃ vuccamānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti tadadhigamāya ussukānaṃ ussāhajanakaṃ; evamevaṃ idha avūpasantānampi vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo vuccamāno vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti. Tenāyamattho vutto – “pītiyā ca samatikkamā, vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā”ti.

Although these applied thoughts and sustained thoughts have indeed subsided in the second jhāna itself, this is stated for the purpose of clarifying the path to this jhāna and for the purpose of commendation. For when it is said, 'from the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought,' this becomes clear: 'Surely, the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna.' And just as, in the case of the third noble path, speaking of the abandoning of things not yet abandoned, such as personality view and so on, in the words 'from the abandoning of the five lower fetters,' becomes a commendation that generates enthusiasm in those zealous for its attainment; so too here, speaking of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, which are not in the process of subsiding at this stage, becomes a commendation. For this reason, this meaning was stated: 'from the transcending of rapture, and from the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought.'

Upekkhako ca vihāsinti ettha upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā, samaṃ passati, apakkhapatitāva hutvā passatīti attho. Tāya visadāya vipulāya thāmagatāya samannāgatattā tatiyajjhānasamaṅgī “upekkhako”ti vuccati. Upekkhā pana dasavidhā hoti – chaḷaṅgupekkhā, brahmavihārupekkhā, bojjhaṅgupekkhā, vīriyupekkhā, saṅkhārupekkhā, vedanupekkhā, vipassanupekkhā, tatramajjhattupekkhā, jhānupekkhā, pārisuddhupekkhāti. Evamayaṃ dasavidhāpi tattha tattha āgatanayato bhūmipuggalacittārammaṇato, khandhasaṅgaha-ekakkhaṇakusalattikasaṅkhepavasena ca aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāya [P 1.0151] vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Idha pana vuccamānā vinayanidānaṃ atibhāriyaṃ karotīti na vuttā. Lakkhaṇādito pana idha adhippetupekkhā majjhattalakkhaṇā, anābhogarasā, abyāpārapaccupaṭṭhānā, pītivirāgapadaṭṭhānāti.

Herein, regarding 'upekkhako ca vihāsi' (and he dwells equanimously), 'upekkhā' is so-called because one looks on (ikkhati) appropriately (upapattito); the meaning is that one sees evenly, one sees having become impartial. Because one who has attained the third jhāna is endowed with that equanimity which is clear, abundant, and firm, they are called 'upekkhako' (equanimous). Now, equanimity is of ten kinds: six-factored equanimity, divine-abiding equanimity, enlightenment-factor equanimity, energy equanimity, formation equanimity, feeling equanimity, insight equanimity, neutrality-of-a-specific-concomitance equanimity, jhāna equanimity, and purification equanimity. Thus, these ten kinds are to be understood according to the method stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī commentary, the Aṭṭhasālinī, by way of their occurrence in various contexts based on planes, persons, consciousness, and objects, and by way of summary through inclusion in the aggregates, the single moment, and the wholesome triad. Here, however, to discuss them would make the Vinaya Nidāna overly burdensome, and so they are not stated. As for its characteristics and so on, the equanimity intended here has the characteristic of neutrality, the function of non-application, manifestation as non-concern, and the fading away of rapture as its proximate cause.

Etthāha [V 1.0112] – nanu cāyaṃ atthato tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti, sā ca paṭhamadutiyajjhānesupi atthi, tasmā tatrāpi “upekkhako ca vihāsi”nti evamayaṃ vattabbā siyā, sā kasmā na vuttāti? Aparibyattakiccato. Aparibyattañhi [M 1.0121] tassā tattha kiccaṃ, vitakkādīhi abhibhūtattā. Idha panāyaṃ vitakkavicārapītīhi anabhibhūtattā ukkhittasirā viya hutvā paribyattakiccā jātā, tasmā vuttāti.

Herein, one might ask: 'Is this not, in essence, simply equanimity as neutrality of concomitance (tatramajjhattupekkhā)? And that exists in the first and second jhānas as well. Therefore, should it not also be said there, "and he dwells equanimously"? Why, then, was it not stated?' Because its function is not distinct. For its function there is not distinct, being overwhelmed by applied thought and so on. Here, however, because it is not overwhelmed by applied thought, sustained thought, and rapture, its function has become distinct, like one who has raised their head. Therefore, it is stated.

Niṭṭhitā “upekkhako ca vihāsi”nti etassa sabbaso atthavaṇṇanā.

The complete explanation of the meaning of 'upekkhako ca vihāsi' is concluded.

Idāni sato ca sampajānoti ettha saratīti sato, sampajānātīti sampajāno. Puggalena sati ca sampajaññañca vuttaṃ. Tattha saraṇalakkhaṇā sati, asammussanarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā; asammohalakkhaṇaṃ sampajaññaṃ, tīraṇarasaṃ, pavicayapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi idaṃ satisampajaññaṃ purimajjhānesupi atthi, muṭṭhassatissa hi asampajānassa upacārajjhānamattampi na sampajjati, pageva appanā; oḷārikattā pana tesaṃ jhānānaṃ bhūmiyaṃ viya purisassa cittassa gati sukhā hoti, abyattaṃ tattha satisampajaññakiccaṃ. Oḷārikaṅgappahānena pana sukhumattā imassa jhānassa purisassa khuradhārāyaṃ viya satisampajaññakiccapariggahitāyeva cittassa gati icchitabbāti idheva vuttaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo? Yathāpi dhenupago vaccho dhenuto apanīto arakkhiyamāno punadeva dhenuṃ upagacchati; evamidaṃ tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ pītito apanītampi satisampajaññārakkhena arakkhiyamānaṃ punadeva pītiṃ upagaccheyya pītisampayuttameva siyā. Sukhe vāpi sattā rajjanti, idañca atimadhuraṃ sukhaṃ, tato paraṃ sukhābhāvā[P 1.0152]. Satisampajaññānubhāvena panettha sukhe asārajjanā hoti, no aññathāti imampi atthavisesaṃ dassetuṃ idaṃ idheva vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Now, regarding 'sato ca sampajāno' (mindful and clearly comprehending): herein, 'sato' (mindful) means one who remembers, and 'sampajāno' (clearly comprehending) means one who comprehends clearly. Mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña) are stated with reference to the person. Herein, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, the function of not forgetting, and manifestation as guarding. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion, the function of discerning, and manifestation as investigation. Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas—for one who is unmindful and not clearly comprehending, not even access concentration is achieved, let alone absorption—the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not distinct there. This is because, due to the grossness of those jhānas, the movement of the mind is easy, like a person on level ground. But with the abandoning of the gross factors, due to the subtlety of this jhāna, the movement of the mind should be one entirely guided by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a person on a razor’s edge. Therefore, this is stated specifically here. Furthermore, just as a calf that follows its mother, if taken from the cow and left unguarded, will return to the cow again, so too this pleasure of the third jhāna, though separated from rapture, if not guarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension, could return to rapture and become associated with it. Moreover, beings become attached to pleasure, and this pleasure is exceedingly sweet, for there is no pleasure beyond it. It is through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension that non-attachment to this pleasure occurs, and not otherwise. It should be understood that this was stated specifically here to show this special meaning as well.

Idāni sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesinti ettha kiñcāpi tatiyajjhānasamaṅgino sukhappaṭisaṃvedanābhogo natthi, evaṃ santepi yasmā tassa nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, yaṃ vā taṃ nāmakāyasampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānenassa yasmā atipaṇītena rūpena rūpakāyo phuṭo, yassa [M 1.0122] phuṭattā jhānā vuṭṭhitopi sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya, tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento “sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesi”nti āha.

Now, regarding 'sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesi' (and he experiences pleasure with the body): herein, although one endowed with the third jhāna has no mental advertence towards experiencing pleasure, it is nevertheless the case that there is for that person a pleasure associated with the mental body (nāmakāya). By the very refined physical form (rūpa) originating from that pleasure associated with the mental body, the physical body (rūpakāya) is pervaded. Because it is so pervaded, one would experience pleasure even after emerging from the jhāna. Therefore, to show this meaning, it was said, 'and he experiences pleasure with the body.'

Idāni yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti ettha yaṃjhānahetu yaṃjhānakāraṇā taṃ tatiyajjhānasamaṅgīpuggalaṃ buddhādayo ariyā ācikkhanti desenti paññapenti [V 1.0113] paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti uttānīkaronti pakāsenti, pasaṃsantīti adhippāyo. Kinti? “Upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī”ti. Taṃ tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsinti evamettha yojanā veditabbā.

Now, regarding “that which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, a dweller in happiness’”: because of which jhāna, for which jhāna’s reason, the noble ones, such as the Buddha, declare, teach, make known, establish, disclose, analyze, make clear, reveal, and praise that person endowed with the third jhāna—this is the intended meaning. How? As: “Equanimous, mindful, a dweller in happiness.” The connection here should be understood thus: “Having attained and entered upon that third jhāna, I dwelt.”

Kasmā pana taṃ te evaṃ pasaṃsantīti? Pasaṃsārahato. Ayañhi yasmā atimadhurasukhe sukhapāramippattepi tatiyajjhāne upekkhako, na tattha sukhābhisaṅgena ākaḍḍhīyati, yathā ca pīti na uppajjati; evaṃ upaṭṭhitassatitāya satimā. Yasmā ca ariyakantaṃ ariyajanasevitameva ca asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ nāmakāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, tasmā pasaṃsāraho. Iti pasaṃsārahato naṃ ariyā te evaṃ pasaṃsāhetubhūte guṇe pakāsentā “upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī”ti evaṃ pasaṃsantīti veditabbaṃ.

But why do they praise him thus? Because he is worthy of praise. Indeed, since this person, even in the third jhāna which has exceedingly sweet pleasure and has reached the ultimate limit of pleasure, is equanimous and is not drawn by attachment to that pleasure; and in such a way that rapture does not arise, he is thus mindful through well-established mindfulness. And since he experiences with the mental body a pleasure that is cherished by the noble ones, frequented by the noble ones, and is undefiled, he is therefore worthy of praise. Thus, because he is worthy of praise, it should be understood that the noble ones praise him in this way, as “Equanimous, mindful, a dweller in happiness,” while making manifest those qualities that are the cause for praise.

Tatiyanti gaṇanānupubbato tatiyaṃ. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ samāpajjatītipi tatiyaṃ. Jhānanti ettha ca yathā dutiyaṃ sampasādādīhi caturaṅgikaṃ; evamidaṃ upekkhādīhi pañcaṅgikaṃ. Yathāha – “jhānanti upekkhā sati sampajaññaṃ sukhaṃ cittassa ekaggatā”ti (vibha. 591). Pariyāyoyeva ceso. Upekkhāsatisampajaññāni pana ṭhapetvā nippariyāyena duvaṅgikamevetaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye duvaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti[P 1.0153]? Sukhaṃ, cittassekaggatā”ti (dha. sa. 163). Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Third (tatiyaṃ): it is the third according to numerical sequence. It is also the third because one attains this for a third time. And as for jhāna: here, just as the second jhāna has four factors, such as confidence, so this one has five factors, such as equanimity. As it was said: “Jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind” (Vibh 267). And this is only a figurative expression. Setting aside equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, it is, in the strict sense, only twofold. As it was said: “What at that time is the twofold jhāna? Pleasure and one-pointedness of mind” (Dhs 163). The rest is as has been explained.

Tatiyajjhānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third jhāna is concluded.

Catutthajjhānakathā

Explanation of the Fourth Jhāna

Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānāti kāyikasukhassa ca kāyikadukkhassa ca pahānā. Pubbevāti tañca kho pubbeva, na catutthajjhānakkhaṇe[M 1.0123]. Somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cetasikasukhassa ca cetasikadukkhassa cāti imesampi dvinnaṃ pubbeva atthaṅgamā pahānā icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Kadā pana nesaṃ pahānaṃ hoti? Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe. Somanassañhi catutthajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyati, dukkhadomanassasukhāni paṭhamadutiyatatiyānaṃ upacārakkhaṇesu. Evametesaṃ pahānakkamena avuttānaṃ, indriyavibhaṅge pana indriyānaṃ uddesakkameneva idhāpi vuttānaṃ sukhadukkhasomanassa domanassānaṃ pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

‘By the abandoning of pleasure and by the abandoning of pain’ means because of the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain. As for ‘previously,’ this abandoning is indeed previous, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna. ‘With the disappearance of joy and sorrow’ means that this is stated because of the previous disappearance and abandoning of these two as well, namely mental pleasure and mental pain. But when does their abandoning occur? At the access moments of the four jhānas. Indeed, joy is abandoned at the very access moment of the fourth jhāna, while pain, sorrow, and pleasure are abandoned at the access moments of the first, second, and third jhānas respectively. Thus, although they are not stated here according to the order of abandoning, the abandoning of this pleasure, pain, joy, and sorrow mentioned here should be understood according to the very order of exposition of the faculties in the Indriyavibhaṅga.

Yadi [V 1.0114] panetāni tassa tassa jhānassupacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyanti, atha kasmā “kattha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati. Kattha cuppannaṃ domanassindriyaṃ… sukhindriyaṃ… somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, etthuppannaṃ somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.510) evaṃ jhānesveva nirodho vuttoti? Atisayanirodhattā. Atisayanirodho hi nesaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu, na nirodhoyeva; nirodhoyeva pana upacārakkhaṇe, nātisayanirodho. Tathā hi nānāvajjane paṭhamajjhānūpacāre niruddhassāpi dukkhindriyassa ḍaṃsamakasādisamphassena vā visamāsanupatāpena vā siyā uppatti, na tveva antoappanāyaṃ. Upacāre vā niruddhampetaṃ na suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti; paṭipakkhena avihatattā. Antoappanāyaṃ pana pītipharaṇena sabbo kāyo sukhokkanto hoti. Sukhokkantakāyassa ca suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti dukkhindriyaṃ; paṭipakkhena vihatattā. Nānāvajjane eva [P 1.0154] ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre pahīnassa domanassindriyassa yasmā etaṃ vitakkavicārappaccayepi kāyakilamathe cittupaghāte ca sati uppajjati, vitakkavicārābhāve neva uppajjati. Yattha pana uppajjati tattha vitakkavicārabhāve. Appahīnā eva ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre vitakkavicārāti tatthassa siyā uppatti; appahīnapaccayattā. Na tveva dutiyajjhāne; pahīnapaccayattā. Tathā tatiyajjhānūpacāre pahīnassāpi sukhindriyassa pītisamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭakāyassa siyā uppatti, na tveva tatiyajjhāne. Tatiyajjhāne hi sukhassa paccayabhūtā [M 1.0124] pīti sabbaso niruddhāti. Tathā catutthajjhānūpacāre pahīnassāpi somanassindriyassa āsannattā, appanāppattāya upekkhāya abhāvena sammā anatikkantattā ca siyā uppatti, na tveva catutthajjhāne. Tasmā eva ca “etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti tattha tattha aparisesaggahaṇaṃ katanti.

But if these are abandoned at the very access moment of each respective jhāna, then why is it said: “Where does the arisen pain faculty cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna; here the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder. Where does the arisen sorrow faculty… pleasure faculty… joy faculty cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; here the arisen joy faculty ceases without remainder” (SN 48.40)? Why is cessation spoken of only in the jhānas? Because of surpassing cessation. Indeed, in the first jhāna and so on, there is surpassing cessation, not mere cessation; but in the access moment, there is only mere cessation, not surpassing cessation. For so it is: in the access to the first jhāna, which has diverse advertence, although the pain faculty has ceased, its arising might occur due to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or through the affliction of an uncomfortable posture; but it would certainly not occur within absorption. Or, though it has ceased in the access moment, it is not well ceased, because it has not been struck down by its opposite. But within absorption, through the suffusion of rapture, the whole body is pervaded by pleasure. And for one whose body is pervaded by pleasure, the pain faculty is well ceased, because it has been struck down by its opposite. And in the access to the second jhāna, which also has diverse advertence, although the sorrow faculty has been abandoned, it arises when there is bodily fatigue and mental affliction, which have initial and sustained thought as their condition, but it does not arise in their absence. But where it arises, it is because of the presence of initial and sustained thought. And in the access to the second jhāna, initial and sustained thought are not yet abandoned; therefore, its arising might occur there, because its condition has not been abandoned. But it would certainly not occur in the second jhāna, because its condition has been abandoned. Likewise, in the access to the third jhāna, although the pleasure faculty has been abandoned, its arising might occur for one whose body is touched by the refined matter produced by rapture; but it would certainly not occur in the third jhāna. For in the third jhāna, rapture, which is the condition for pleasure, has ceased in every way. Likewise, in the access to the fourth jhāna, although the joy faculty has been abandoned, its arising might occur due to its nearness and because it has not been properly transcended, owing to the absence of equanimity that has attained absorption; but certainly not in the fourth jhāna. And it is for this very reason that in each respective case, the term ‘without remainder’ is used, as in ‘here the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder.’

Etthāha – “athevaṃ tassa tassa jhānassūpacāre pahīnāpi etā vedanā idha kasmā samāharī”ti? Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ. Yā hi ayaṃ “adukkhamasukha”nti ettha adukkhamasukhā vedanā vuttā, sā sukhumā atidubbiññeyyā na sakkā sukhena gahetuṃ. Tasmā yathā nāma duṭṭhassa yathā vā tathā vā upasaṅkamitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa goṇassa gahaṇatthaṃ gopo ekasmiṃ vaje sabbe gāvo samāharati, athekekaṃ nīharanto paṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ “ayaṃ so, gaṇhatha na”nti tampi gāhāpayati; evameva bhagavā sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ sabbā etā samāhari. Evañhi [V 1.0115] samāhaṭā etā dassetvā “yaṃ neva sukhaṃ na dukkhaṃ na somanassaṃ na domanassaṃ, ayaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā”ti sakkā hoti esā gāhayituṃ.

Here one asks: “If these feelings are abandoned in the access of each respective jhāna, why are they brought together here?” For the purpose of easy grasping. Indeed, this feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure spoken of here is subtle, very difficult to discern; it cannot be grasped easily. Therefore, just as a cowherd, for the purpose of catching a fierce bull that cannot be caught by approaching it in any old way, gathers all the cattle into one pen, and then, while leading them out one by one, has that one caught which comes in its turn, saying, “This is it, catch it!”; so too the Blessed One brought all these feelings together for the purpose of easy grasping. For when these are brought together and shown thus: “Whatever feeling is neither pleasure nor pain, neither joy nor sorrow—this is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,” it becomes possible to have it grasped.

Apica adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā paccayadassanatthañcāpi etā vuttāti veditabbā. Sukhappahānādayo hi tassā paccayā. Yathāha – “cattāro kho, āvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu, sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthajjhānaṃ [P 1.0155] upasampajja viharati. Ime kho, āvuso, cattāro paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.458). Yathā vā aññattha pahīnāpi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo tatiyamaggassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ tattha pahīnāti vuttā; evaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthampetassa jhānassetā idha vuttātipi veditabbā. Paccayaghātena vā ettha rāgadosānaṃ atidūrabhāvaṃ dassetumpetā vuttāti veditabbā. Etāsu hi sukhaṃ somanassassa paccayo, somanassaṃ rāgassa, dukkhaṃ domanassassa, domanassaṃ dosassa. Sukhādighātena ca te sappaccayā rāgadosā hatāti atidūre hontīti.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these were stated also for the purpose of showing the conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. For the abandoning of pleasure and so on are its conditions. As it is said: “Friend, there are four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. Here, friend, a bhikkhu, having abandoned pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. These, friend, are the four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind” (MN 1.458). Or, just as identity view and so on, though abandoned elsewhere, are said to be abandoned there for the purpose of extolling the third path; so too it should be understood that these are stated here for the purpose of extolling this jhāna. Alternatively, it should be understood that these are stated to show the extreme remoteness of lust and hatred in this jhāna through the destruction of their conditions. For among these, pleasure is a condition for joy, joy for lust; pain is a condition for sorrow, sorrow for hatred. And through the destruction of pleasure and so on, that lust and hatred, together with their conditions, are destroyed; thus they become extremely remote.

Adukkhamasukhanti dukkhābhāvena adukkhaṃ, sukhābhāvena asukhaṃ. Etenettha dukkhasukhapaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tatiyavedanaṃ dīpeti, na dukkhasukhābhāvamattaṃ. Tatiyavedanā nāma – adukkhamasukhā, upekkhātipi vuccati. Sā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā, majjhattarasā, avibhūtapaccupaṭṭhānā, sukhanirodhapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā. Upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti upekkhāya janitasatipārisuddhiṃ. Imasmiñhi jhāne suparisuddhā sati. Yā ca tassā satiyā pārisuddhi, sā upekkhāya katā na aññena; tasmā etaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti vuccati. Vibhaṅgepi vuttaṃ – “ayaṃ sati imāya upekkhāya visadā hoti parisuddhā pariyodātā, tena vuccati – ‘upekkhāsatipārisuddhi’”nti (vibha. 597). Yāya ca upekkhāya ettha satiyā pārisuddhi hoti, sā atthato tatramajjhattatā veditabbā. Na kevalañcettha tāya satiyeva parisuddhā, apica kho sabbepi sampayuttadhammā; satisīsena pana desanā vuttā.

“Neither-painful-nor-pleasant” means not painful due to the absence of pain, and not pleasant due to the absence of pleasure. By this, it indicates here the third feeling, which is the opposite of pain and pleasure; it does not indicate the mere absence of pain and pleasure. The third feeling is named neither-painful-nor-pleasant; it is also called equanimity. It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing that which is contrary to the agreeable and disagreeable, the function of being neutral, the manifestation of being indistinct, and the cessation of pleasure as its proximate cause. “Purity of mindfulness through equanimity” means the purity of mindfulness generated by equanimity. For in this jhāna, mindfulness is exceedingly pure. And the purity of that mindfulness is brought about by equanimity and by nothing else; therefore, this is called “purity of mindfulness through equanimity.” In the Vibhaṅga it is also said: “This mindfulness, through this equanimity, becomes clear, purified, and bright; therefore, it is called ‘purity of mindfulness through equanimity’” (Vibh 597). And the equanimity by which the purity of mindfulness occurs here should be understood, in essence, as the mental factor of neutrality. And not only is mindfulness purified by it here, but indeed all associated states are as well; however, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the principal element.

Tattha [M 1.0125] kiñcāpi ayaṃ upekkhā heṭṭhāpi tīsu jhānesu vijjati, yathā pana divā sūriyappabhābhibhavā sommabhāvena ca attano upakārakattena vā sabhāgāya rattiyā alābhā divā vijjamānāpi candalekhā aparisuddhā hoti apariyodātā; evamayampi tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā vitakkavicārādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā alābhā vijjamānāpi paṭhamādijjhānabhedesu aparisuddhā [P 1.0156] hoti. Tassā ca [V 1.0116] aparisuddhāya divā aparisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo aparisuddhāva honti; tasmā tesu ekampi “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti na vuttaṃ. Idha pana vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavābhāvā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā paṭilābhā ayaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā ativiya parisuddhā, tassā parisuddhattā parisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo parisuddhā honti pariyodātā, tasmā idameva upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

In this regard, although this equanimity also exists in the three lower jhānas, it is like the crescent moon which, though present during the day, is not pure or bright, being overpowered by the sun's radiance and because it has not obtained its congenial night. So too, this crescent moon of the equanimity of neutrality, though present in the divisions of the first jhāna and so on, is not pure, being overpowered by the force of opposing factors such as initial and sustained thought, and because it has not obtained its congenial night, which is equanimous feeling. And of that impure equanimity, the co-arisen factors of mindfulness and so on are also impure, like the light of the impure crescent moon during the day. Therefore, not even one of those jhānas is called “purity of mindfulness through equanimity.” Here, however, due to the absence of being overpowered by the force of opposing factors such as initial thought, and due to obtaining the congenial night, which is equanimous feeling, this crescent moon of the equanimity of neutrality becomes exceedingly pure. Due to its purity, just like the light of a pure crescent moon, the co-arisen factors of mindfulness and so on become pure and bright. Therefore, it should be understood that this jhāna alone is called “purity of mindfulness through equanimity.”

Catutthanti gaṇanānupubbato catutthaṃ. Idaṃ catutthaṃ samāpajjatītipi catutthaṃ. Jhānanti ettha yathā tatiyaṃ upekkhādīhi pañcaṅgikaṃ; evamidaṃ upekkhādīhi tivaṅgikaṃ. Yathāha – “jhānanti upekkhā, sati cittassekaggatā”ti. Pariyāyo eva ceso. Ṭhapetvā pana satiṃ upekkhekaggatameva gahetvā nippariyāyena duvaṅgikamevetaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye duvaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti? Upekkhā, cittassekaggatā”ti (dha. sa. 165). Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

“Fourth” means fourth in the sequence of counting. It is also called “fourth” because one attains this fourth one. Regarding jhāna: here, just as the third is five-factored with equanimity and so on, so this one is three-factored with equanimity and so on. As it is said: “Jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.” And this is merely a figurative expression. However, setting aside mindfulness and taking only equanimity and one-pointedness, this is, in a direct sense, only two-factored. As it is said: “What at that time is the two-factored jhāna? Equanimity and one-pointedness of mind” (Dhs 165). The remainder is as has been explained.

Catutthajjhānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Fourth Jhāna is Concluded.

Pubbenivāsakathā

Exposition on Previous Abodes

12. Iti imāni cattāri jhānāni kesañci cittekaggatatthāni honti, kesañci vipassanāpādakāni, kesañci abhiññāpādakāni, kesañci nirodhapādakāni, kesañci bhavokkamanatthāni. Tattha khīṇāsavānaṃ cittekaggatatthāni honti, te hi samāpajjitvā “ekaggacittā sukhaṃ divasaṃ viharissāmā”ti [M 1.0126] iccevaṃ kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattenti. Sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ “samāpattito vuṭṭhāya samāhitena cittena vipassissāmā”ti nibbattentānaṃ vipassanāpādakāni honti. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā abhiññāpādakaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”ti vuttanayā abhiññāyo patthentā nibbattenti, tesaṃ abhiññāpādakāni honti. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā “nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā sattāhaṃ acittakā hutvā diṭṭheva dhamme nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ patvā sukhaṃ viharissāmā”ti nibbattenti, tesaṃ nirodhapādakāni [P 1.0157] honti. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā “aparihīnajjhānā hutvā brahmaloke uppajjissāmā”ti nibbattenti, tesaṃ bhavokkamanatthāni honti.

12. Thus, these four jhānas are for some for the purpose of mental unification; for some, they are the basis for insight; for some, the basis for higher knowledge; for some, the basis for cessation; and for some, for the purpose of proceeding to a new existence. Therein, for those whose taints are destroyed, they are for the purpose of mental unification. For they, having entered the attainment, think, 'With a unified mind, we will dwell happily for the day,' and with just this aspiration, having performed the kasiṇa preliminary work, they generate the eight attainments. For trainees and ordinary people who generate them thinking, 'Having emerged from the attainment, we will practice insight with a concentrated mind,' they are the basis for insight. As for those who, having generated the eight attainments and entered the jhāna that is the basis for higher knowledge, emerge from the attainment and, desiring the higher knowledges according to the method described as, 'Being one, he becomes many,' generate them, for them they are the basis for higher knowledge. As for those who, having generated the eight attainments, generate them thinking, 'Having entered the attainment of cessation, we will dwell for seven days without consciousness and, having reached cessation—Nibbāna—in this very life, we will dwell happily,' for them they are the basis for cessation. As for those who, having generated the eight attainments, generate them thinking, 'Without having lost the jhānas, we will be reborn in the Brahmā world,' for them they are for the purpose of proceeding to a new existence.

Bhagavatā [V 1.0117] panidaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ bodhirukkhamūle nibbattitaṃ, taṃ tassa vipassanāpādakañceva ahosi abhiññāpādakañca nirodhapādakañca sabbakiccasādhakañca sabbalokiyalokuttaraguṇadāyakanti veditabbaṃ. Yesañca guṇānaṃ dāyakaṃ ahosi, tesaṃ ekadesaṃ dassento “so evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādimāha.

Furthermore, this fourth jhāna was generated by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree. It should be understood that for him, it was the basis for insight, the basis for higher knowledge, the basis for cessation, the accomplisher of all tasks, and the giver of all mundane and supramundane qualities. And showing a portion of those qualities of which it was the giver, he spoke the words beginning with, 'He, with a mind thus concentrated...'

Tattha soti so ahaṃ. Evanti catutthajjhānakkamanidassanametaṃ. Iminā kamena catutthajjhānaṃ paṭilabhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Samāhiteti iminā catutthajjhānasamādhinā samāhite. Parisuddhetiādīsu pana upekkhāsatipārisuddhibhāvena parisuddhe. Parisuddhattāyeva pariyodāte, pabhassareti vuttaṃ hoti. Sukhādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ ghātena vihatarāgādiaṅgaṇattā anaṅgaṇe. Anaṅgaṇattāyeva ca vigatūpakkilese; aṅgaṇena hi cittaṃ upakkilissati. Subhāvitattā mudubhūte, vasībhāvappatteti vuttaṃ hoti. Vase vattamānañhi cittaṃ mudūti vuccati. Muduttāyeva ca kammaniye, kammakkhame kammayoggeti vuttaṃ hoti. Mudu hi cittaṃ kammaniyaṃ hoti sudhantamiva suvaṇṇaṃ, tadubhayampi ca subhāvitattā eva. Yathāha – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulīkataṃ mudu ca hoti kammaniyañca, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti (a. ni. 1.22).

Therein, `so` means 'that I.' `Evaṃ` is an indication of the sequence for the fourth jhāna. This means it is said: 'having attained the fourth jhāna by this sequence.' `Samāhite` means concentrated by this fourth-jhāna concentration. As for `parisuddhe`, etc., it is pure (`parisuddhe`) through the state of purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Because of its purity, it is said to be exceedingly pure (`pariyodāte`) and luminous (`pabhassare`). It is unblemished (`anaṅgaṇe`) due to the destruction of the conditions for pleasure and so on, and because the blemishes such as lust have been removed. And because it is unblemished, it is free from corruptions (`vigatūpakkilese`); for the mind is corrupted by a blemish. Because it is well-developed, it has become pliant (`mudubhūte`); this means it has attained mastery. For a mind that is under one's control is called 'pliant.' And because of its pliancy, it is workable (`kammaniye`); this means it is fit for the task and suitable for the task. For a pliant mind is workable, like well-refined gold, and both of these are due to being well-developed. As it is said: 'Monks, I do not see a single other thing that, when developed and cultivated, is so pliant and workable as this, monks: the mind' (A.N. 1.22).

Etesu [M 1.0127] parisuddhabhāvādīsu ṭhitattā ṭhite. Ṭhitattāyeva āneñjappatte, acale niriñjaneti vuttaṃ hoti. Mudukammaññabhāvena vā attano vase ṭhitattā ṭhite, saddhādīhi pariggahitattā āneñjappatte.
