Saddhāpariggahitañhi cittaṃ assaddhiyena na iñjati, vīriyapariggahitaṃ kosajjena na iñjati, satipariggahitaṃ pamādena na iñjati, samādhipariggahitaṃ uddhaccena na iñjati, paññāpariggahitaṃ avijjāya na iñjati, obhāsagataṃ kilesandhakārena na iñjati. Imehi [P 1.0158] chahi dhammehi pariggahitaṃ āneñjappattaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ cittaṃ abhinīhārakkhamaṃ hoti abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhiññāsacchikiriyāya.

Because it is steadfast (`ṭhite`) due to standing in these states of purity and so on. Because it is steadfast, it has reached the imperturbable (`āneñjappatte`); this means it is unmoving (`acale`) and unshaken (`niriñjane`). Alternatively, it is steadfast (`ṭhite`) because it stands in its own control through its state of pliancy and workability; it has reached the imperturbable (`āneñjappatte`) because it is encompassed by faith and other qualities. For a mind encompassed by faith is not shaken by lack of faith; a mind encompassed by energy is not shaken by laziness; a mind encompassed by mindfulness is not shaken by heedlessness; a mind encompassed by concentration is not shaken by restlessness; a mind encompassed by wisdom is not shaken by ignorance; a mind that has attained illumination is not shaken by the darkness of the defilements. A mind encompassed by these six qualities becomes one that has reached the imperturbable. Thus, a mind endowed with eight factors is capable of being directed to the direct realization through higher knowledge of those things to be directly realized by higher knowledge.

Aparo nayo – catutthajjhānasamādhinā samāhite. Nīvaraṇadūrībhāvena parisuddhe. Vitakkādisamatikkamena pariyodāte. Jhānappaṭilābhapaccayānaṃ pāpakānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ abhāvena anaṅgaṇe. Abhijjhādīnaṃ cittūpakkilesānaṃ vigamena vigatūpakkilese. Ubhayampi cetaṃ anaṅgaṇavatthasuttānusārena (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) veditabbaṃ. Vasippattiyā mudubhūte. Iddhipādabhāvūpagamena kammaniye. Bhāvanāpāripūriyā paṇītabhāvūpagamena ṭhite āneñjappatte[V 1.0118]. Yathā āneñjappattaṃ hoti; evaṃ ṭhiteti attho. Evampi aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ cittaṃ abhinīhārakkhamaṃ hoti abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhiññāsacchikiriyāya, pādakaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūtanti attho.

Another method: Concentrated (`samāhite`) by the fourth-jhāna concentration. Purified (`parisuddhe`) by being distant from the hindrances. Exceedingly pure (`pariyodāte`) by transcending thought-conception and so on. Unblemished (`anaṅgaṇe`) by the absence of evil, desire-led states that are conditions for attaining jhāna. Free from corruptions (`vigatūpakkilese`) by the departure of mental corruptions such as covetousness. Both of these should be understood in accordance with the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and Vattha Sutta. Having become pliant (`mudubhūte`) by the attainment of mastery. Workable (`kammaniye`) by undertaking the state of the bases of spiritual power. Steadfast (`ṭhite`) and having reached the imperturbable (`āneñjappatte`) by undertaking the state of excellence through the perfection of development. The meaning is: 'steadfast in such a way that it becomes imperturbable.' Thus, a mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of being directed to the direct realization through higher knowledge of those things to be directly realized by higher knowledge; the meaning is that it is a basis, having become a foundation.

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāyāti evaṃ abhiññāpādake jāte etasmiṃ citte pubbenivāsānussatimhi yaṃ ñāṇaṃ tadatthāya. Tattha pubbenivāsoti pubbe atītajātīsu nivutthakkhandhā. Nivutthāti ajjhāvutthā anubhūtā attano santāne uppajjitvā niruddhā nivutthadhammā vā nivutthā, gocaranivāsena nivutthā, attano viññāṇena viññātā paricchinnā, paraviññāṇaviññātāpi vā chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsu. Pubbenivāsānussatīti yāya satiyā pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, sā pubbenivāsānussati. Ñāṇanti tāya satiyā sampayuttañāṇaṃ. Evamimassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa atthāya pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya etassa ñāṇassa adhigamāya pattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Abhininnāmesinti abhinīhariṃ.

For the knowledge of recollection of past lives: When this mind has thus become a basis for higher knowledge, it is for the sake of that knowledge which is in the recollection of past lives. Herein, 'past lives' (pubbenivāsa) means the aggregates dwelt in previously, in past existences. 'Dwelt in' (nivuttha) means dwelt in (ajjhāvutthā), experienced (anubhūtā), having arisen and ceased in one's own continuity; or, things that have been dwelt in (nivutthadhammā), dwelt in by way of being an object-range (gocaranivāsena), known and defined by one’s own consciousness, or also known and defined by another’s consciousness, as in cases such as the recollection of those whose round of rebirths is cut off. 'Recollection of past lives' (pubbenivāsānussati) is the mindfulness by which one recollects past lives. 'Knowledge' (ñāṇa) is the knowledge associated with that mindfulness. Thus it is said: 'for the sake of this knowledge of recollection of past lives', for the attainment, for the reaching of this knowledge. As for 'I directed' (abhininnāmesiṃ): it means 'I brought forth' (abhinīhariṃ).

Soti [M 1.0128] so ahaṃ. Anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ, anekehi vā pakārehi pavattitaṃ saṃvaṇṇitanti attho. Pubbenivāsanti samanantarātītaṃ bhavaṃ ādiṃ katvā tattha tattha nivutthasantānaṃ. Anussarāmīti “ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo”ti evaṃ jātipaṭipāṭiyā anugantvā anugantvā sarāmi, anudeva vā sarāmi, citte [P 1.0159] abhininnāmitamatte eva sarāmīti dasseti. Pūritapāramīnañhi mahāpurisānaṃ parikammakaraṇaṃ natthi, tena te cittaṃ abhininnāmetvāva saranti. Ādikammikakulaputtā pana parikammaṃ katvāva saranti, tasmā tesaṃ vasena parikammaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā. Taṃ pana vuccamānaṃ atibhāriyaṃ vinayanidānaṃ karoti, tasmā taṃ na vadāma. Atthikehi pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.402 ādayo) vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Idha pana pāḷimeva vaṇṇayissāma.

'So' means 'that I'. 'Of many kinds' means of various sorts; or, the meaning is, brought about or described in many ways. 'Past lives' means the continuity dwelt in here and there, beginning with the immediately preceding existence. 'I recollect' shows this: 'I recollect by following back again and again in the order of births, as in "one birth, two births..."; or I recollect immediately upon inclining the mind; or I recollect just by directing the mind.' For great beings who have fulfilled the perfections, there is no need for preparatory work; thus, they recollect simply by directing the mind. But sons of good family who are beginners recollect only after doing the preparatory work; therefore, in connection with them, the preparatory work should be mentioned. However, if it were spoken of, it would make this Introduction to the Vinaya too burdensome; therefore, we do not speak of it. But those who are interested should take it according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, however, we will explain only the Pāli text.

Seyyathidanti āraddhappakāradassanatthe nipāto. Teneva yvāyaṃ pubbenivāso āraddho, tassa pakārappabhedaṃ dassento ekampi jātintiādimāha. Tattha ekampi jātinti ekampi paṭisandhimūlaṃ cutipariyosānaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannaṃ khandhasantānaṃ. Esa nayo dvepi jātiyotiādīsu. Anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappetiādīsu pana parihāyamāno kappo saṃvaṭṭakappo, vaḍḍhamāno vivaṭṭakappoti veditabbo. Tattha ca saṃvaṭṭena saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī gahito hoti tammūlakattā. Vivaṭṭena ca vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Evañhi sati yāni tāni “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyāni[V 1.0119]. Katamāni cattāri? Saṃvaṭṭo saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī, vivaṭṭo vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī”ti vuttāni tāni sabbāni pariggahitāni honti.

The word 'that is' (seyyathidaṃ) is a particle used in the sense of showing the variety of what has been commenced. For that very reason, since this recollection of past lives has been commenced, wishing to show its various kinds, He said, 'even one birth,' and so on. Here, 'even one birth' means one continuum of aggregates, having rebirth-linking as its root, death as its end, and included in a single existence. The same method applies in 'two births,' and so on. But in phrases like 'many contracting world-cycles,' a world-cycle that is declining is to be known as a contracting world-cycle (saṃvaṭṭakappa); a world-cycle that is developing is to be known as an expanding world-cycle (vivaṭṭakappa). And there, by 'contracting-cycle' the 'in-contraction cycle' is taken, because the former is its basis. And by 'expanding-cycle', the 'in-expansion cycle' is taken. For this being so, all those which were spoken of by the Blessed One—'Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of an aeon. Which four? The contracting-cycle, the in-contraction cycle, the expanding-cycle, the in-expansion cycle'—are included.

Tattha tayo saṃvaṭṭā – tejosaṃvaṭṭo, āposaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti. Tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmā – ābhassarā, subhakiṇhā, vehapphalāti. Yadā kappo tejena saṃvaṭṭati, ābhassarato heṭṭhā agginā ḍayhati. Yadā udakena saṃvaṭṭati, subhakiṇhato heṭṭhā udakena vilīyati. Yadā vātena saṃvaṭṭati, vehapphalato heṭṭhā vātena viddhaṃsiyati. Vitthārato pana sadāpi ekaṃ buddhakkhettaṃ vinassati.

Therein, there are three kinds of dissolution: dissolution by fire, dissolution by water, and dissolution by wind. There are three limits of dissolution: the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. When the aeon dissolves by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is burned by fire. When it dissolves by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it dissolves by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is destroyed by wind. In detail, however, it is always one Buddha-field that is destroyed.

Buddhakkhettaṃ nāma tividhaṃ hoti – jātikkhettaṃ, āṇākkhettaṃ, visayakkhettañca. Tattha jātikkhettaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ hoti, yaṃ tathāgatassa paṭisandhiādīsu kampati. Āṇākkhettaṃ [M 1.0129] koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ hoti. Yattha ratanaparittaṃ, khandhaparittaṃ, dhajaggaparittaṃ, āṭānāṭiyaparittaṃ, moraparittanti imesaṃ parittānaṃ ānubhāvo pavattati. Visayakkhettaṃ pana anantaṃ aparimāṇaṃ, “yaṃ [P 1.0160] yāvatā vā pana ākaṅkheyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) vuttaṃ yattha yaṃ yaṃ ākaṅkhati taṃ taṃ anussarati. Evametesu tīsu buddhakkhettesu ekaṃ āṇākkhettaṃ vinassati. Tasmiṃ pana vinassante jātikkhettampi vinaṭṭhameva hoti; vinassantañca ekatova vinassati, saṇṭhahantampi ekatova saṇṭhahati. Tassa vināso ca saṇṭhahanañca visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.404) vuttaṃ. Atthikehi tato gahetabbaṃ.

The Buddha-field is threefold: the birth-field, the authority-field, and the range-field. Among these, the birth-field has a limit of ten thousand world-systems, which trembles at the Tathāgata's conception and so on. The authority-field has a limit of one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, wherein the power of these protective chants—the Ratana Paritta, Khandha Paritta, Dhajagga Paritta, Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and Mora Paritta—prevails. The range-field, however, is endless and immeasurable, concerning which it was said, 'As far as he might wish.' Therein, whatever object he wishes to recollect, that he recollects. Thus, among these three Buddha-fields, one authority-field is destroyed. But when that is being destroyed, the birth-field is also destroyed. And being destroyed, it is destroyed together; and being established, it is established together. Its destruction and establishment have been described by me in the Visuddhimagga. Those who are interested should take it from there.

Ye panete saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭā vuttā, etesu bhagavā bodhimaṇḍe sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhanatthāya nisinno anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe sari. Kathaṃ? “Amutrāsi”ntiādinā nayena. Tattha amutrāsinti amumhi saṃvaṭṭakappe ahaṃ amumhi bhave vā yoniyā vā gatiyā vā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā vā sattāvāse vā sattanikāye vā ahosiṃ. Evaṃnāmoti vessantaro vā jotipālo vā. Evaṃgottoti bhaggavo vā gotamo vā. Evaṃvaṇṇoti odāto vā sāmo vā. Evamāhāroti sālimaṃsodanāhāro vā pavattaphalabhojano vā. Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedīti anekappakārena kāyikacetasikānaṃ sāmisanirāmisādippabhedānaṃ vā sukhadukkhānaṃ paṭisaṃvedī. Evamāyupariyantoti evaṃ vassasataparamāyupariyanto vā caturāsītikappasahassaparamāyupariyanto vā.

Now, as to these contracting and expanding cycles that have been mentioned, among them the Blessed One, seated at the Bodhi-dais for the purpose of fully awakening to perfect self-awakening, recollected many contracting-cycles, many expanding-cycles, and many contracting-and-expanding cycles. How? By the method beginning 'I was there...' Herein, 'I was there' means: 'In such-and-such a cycle, I was in such-and-such an existence, or womb, or destiny, or station of consciousness, or abode of beings, or group of beings.' 'I had such-and-such a name': I was Vessantara or Jotipāla. 'I was of such-and-such a clan': I was Bhaggava or Gotama. 'I had such-and-such a complexion': I was fair or golden. 'I had such-and-such food': my food was fine rice with meat, or I ate spontaneously arisen fruit. 'I experienced such-and-such pleasure and pain': I experienced in many ways bodily and mental pleasures and pains, of varieties such as worldly and unworldly. 'I had such-and-such a lifespan limit': I was one whose lifespan was at most one hundred years, or one whose lifespan was at most eighty-four thousand aeons.

So [V 1.0120] tato cuto amutra udapādinti so ahaṃ tato bhavato yonito gatito viññāṇaṭṭhitito sattāvāsato sattanikāyato vā cuto, puna amukasmiṃ nāma bhave yoniyā gatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā sattāvāse sattanikāye vā udapādiṃ. Tatrāpāsinti atha tatrāpi bhave yoniyā gatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā sattāvāse sattanikāye vā puna ahosiṃ. Evaṃnāmotiādi vuttanayameva.

'Having passed away from there, I arose elsewhere' means: 'Having passed away from that existence, or from that womb, or from that destiny, or from that station of consciousness, or from that abode of beings, or from that group of beings, I arose again in such-and-such an existence, or womb, or destiny, or station of consciousness, or abode of beings, or group of beings.' 'There too I was' means: 'Then, there too, in that existence, or in that womb, or in that destiny, or in that station of consciousness, or in that abode of beings, or in that group of beings, I was again.' 'Such was my name,' and so on, is to be understood in the same manner as stated before.

Atha vā yasmā amutrāsinti idaṃ anupubbena ārohantassa yāvadicchakaṃ saraṇaṃ. So tato cutoti paṭinivattantassa paccavekkhaṇaṃ. Tasmā idhūpapannoti imissā idhūpapattiyā anantaraṃ amutra udapādinti tusitabhavanaṃ sandhāyāhāti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmoti tatrāpi [M 1.0130] tusitabhavane [P 1.0161] setaketu nāma devaputto ahosiṃ. Evaṃgottoti tāhi devatāhi saddhiṃ ekagotto. Evaṃvaṇṇoti suvaṇṇavaṇṇo. Evamāhāroti dibbasudhāhāro. Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedīti evaṃ dibbasukhappaṭisaṃvedī. Dukkhaṃ pana saṅkhāradukkhamattameva. Evamāyupariyantoti evaṃ sattapaññāsavassakoṭisaṭṭhivassasatasahassāyupariyanto. So tato cutoti so ahaṃ tato tusitabhavanato cuto. Idhūpapannoti idha mahāmāyāya deviyā kucchimhi nibbatto.

Alternatively, since 'I was there' is the recollection of one ascending in sequence as far as one wishes, and 'Having passed away from there' is the reviewing of one descending, it should be understood that immediately after 'I was reborn here,' he said 'I arose there' with reference to the Tusita realm. 'There too I was of such name' means that even there, in the Tusita realm, I was a deva-son named Setaketu. 'Of such clan' means I was of the same clan as those deities. 'Of such complexion' means I had a golden complexion. 'Such was my food' means I had divine ambrosia as food. 'Such was my experience of pleasure and pain' means I experienced divine pleasure in this way. As for suffering, it was merely the suffering of formations. 'Such was the end of my lifespan' means my lifespan extended to fifty-seven koṭis and sixty hundred thousand years. 'Then I passed away from there' means I, having passed away from that Tusita realm. 'I was reborn here' means I was conceived here in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

Itīti evaṃ. Sākāraṃ sauddesanti nāmagottavasena sauddesaṃ, vaṇṇādivasena sākāraṃ. Nāmagottavasena hi satto “datto, tisso, gotamo”ti uddisīyati; vaṇṇādīhi odāto, sāmoti nānattato paññāyati; tasmā nāmagottaṃ uddeso, itare ākārā. Kiṃ pana buddhāyeva pubbenivāsaṃ sarantīti? Vuccate – na buddhāyeva, paccekabuddha-buddhasāvaka-titthiyāpi, no ca kho avisesena. Titthiyā hi cattālīsaṃyeva kappe saranti, na tato paraṃ. Kasmā? Dubbalapaññattā. Tesañhi nāmarūpaparicchedavirahato dubbalā paññā hoti. Sāvakesu pana asītimahāsāvakā kappasatasahassaṃ saranti; dve aggasāvakā ekamasaṅkhyeyyaṃ satasahassañca. Paccekabuddhā dve asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca. Ettako hi tesaṃ abhinīhāro. Buddhānaṃ pana paricchedo natthi, yāva icchanti tāva saranti. Titthiyā ca khandhapaṭipāṭimeva saranti. Paṭipāṭiṃ muñcitvā cutipaṭisandhivasena sarituṃ na sakkonti. Tesañhi andhānaṃ viya icchitappadesokkamanaṃ natthi. Sāvakā ubhayathāpi saranti; tathā paccekabuddhā. Buddhā pana khandhapaṭipāṭiyāpi cutipaṭisandhivasenapi sīhokkantavasenapi anekāsu kappakoṭīsu heṭṭhā vā upari vā yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ ākaṅkhanti, taṃ sabbaṃ sarantiyeva.

'Thus' means 'in this way.' 'With aspects and with designation' means designation by way of name and clan, and aspects by way of complexion and so on. For by name and clan a being is designated as 'Datta,' 'Tissa,' or 'Gotama'; and by complexion and so on, diversity is discerned as 'fair' or 'dark.' Therefore, name and clan are designation; the others are aspects. But do only Buddhas recollect past lives? It is said: not only Buddhas, but also Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and sectarians; but not without distinction. For sectarians recollect only forty eons, not beyond that. Why? Because of their weak wisdom. For their wisdom is weak due to the lack of discernment of name-and-form. Among disciples, however, the eighty great disciples recollect a hundred thousand eons; the two chief disciples, one incalculable eon and a hundred thousand eons. Paccekabuddhas recollect two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand eons. For such was their aspiration. But for Buddhas there is no limit; they recollect as far as they wish. And sectarians recollect only in the sequence of aggregates. They cannot recollect by way of death and rebirth, skipping the sequence. For them, like the blind, there is no proceeding to a desired place. Disciples recollect in both ways; and so do Paccekabuddhas. But Buddhas, whether in the sequence of aggregates, by way of death and rebirth, or by way of the lion's leap, across many koṭis of eons, below or above, whatever place they wish to recollect, they recollect all of it.

Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇātiādīsu meti mayā. Vijjāti viditakaraṇaṭṭhena vijjā. Kiṃ viditaṃ [V 1.0121] karoti? Pubbenivāsaṃ. Avijjāti tasseva pubbenivāsassa aviditakaraṇaṭṭhena tappaṭicchādakamoho vuccati. Tamoti sveva moho tappaṭicchādakaṭṭhena [P 1.0162] “tamo”ti vuccati. Ālokoti sāyevavijjā obhāsakaraṇaṭṭhena “āloko”ti vuccati. Ettha ca vijjā adhigatāti ayaṃ attho, sesaṃ pasaṃsāvacanaṃ. Yojanā [M 1.0131] panettha – ayaṃ kho me vijjā adhigatā, tassa me adhigatavijjassa avijjā vihatā, vinaṭṭhāti attho. Kasmā? Yasmā vijjā uppannā. Esa nayo itarasmimpi padadvaye.

In the phrase 'This, O brahmin...' and so on, 'me' means 'by me.' 'Knowledge' (vijjā) is so called because of the meaning of making known. What does it make known? Past lives. 'Ignorance' (avijjā) is the name for the delusion that conceals those very past lives, because of the meaning of making them unknown. 'Darkness' (tamo) is that very delusion; it is called 'darkness' because of the meaning of concealing. 'Light' (āloko) is that very knowledge; it is called 'light' because of the meaning of producing illumination. And here, the essential meaning is: 'Knowledge has been attained.' The rest is a statement of praise. The connection of sentences here should be understood thus: 'This knowledge has indeed been attained by me. For me, who has attained this knowledge, ignorance has been dispelled, has been destroyed'—this is the meaning. Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This is the method in the other pair of terms as well.

Yathā tanti ettha yathāti opammatthe. Tanti nipāto. Satiyā avippavāsena appamattassa. Vīriyātāpena ātāpino. Kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pahitattassa, pesitacittassāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato avijjā vihaññeyya vijjā uppajjeyya, tamo vihaññeyya āloko uppajjeyya; evameva mama avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā, tamo vihato āloko uppanno. Etassa me padhānānuyogassa anurūpameva phalaṃ laddhanti.

In 'yathā taṃ,' 'yathā' is a particle in the sense of a simile. 'Taṃ' is a mere particle. 'Heedful' (appamattassa) means through not being parted from mindfulness. 'Ardent' (ātāpino) means through the heat of energy. 'Of sent forth self' (pahitattassa) means through having no regard for body and life, having a directed mind—this is the meaning. This is what is said: Just as for one who dwells heedful, ardent, and of sent forth self, ignorance would be dispelled because knowledge would arise, and darkness would be dispelled because light would arise; in the very same way, for me, ignorance has been dispelled because knowledge has arisen, and darkness has been dispelled because light has arisen. A fruit indeed befitting this application to striving has been obtained by me.

Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa paṭhamā abhinibbhidā ahosi kukkuṭacchāpakasseva aṇḍakosamhāti ayaṃ kho mama brāhmaṇa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇamukhatuṇḍakena pubbe nivutthakkhandhapaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā paṭhamā abhinibbhidā paṭhamā nikkhanti paṭhamā ariyājāti ahosi, kukkuṭacchāpakasseva mukhatuṇḍakena vā pādanakhasikhāya vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā tamhā aṇḍakosamhā abhinibbhidā nikkhanti kukkuṭanikāye paccājātīti.

'This, O brahmin, was my first breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell' means: This, O brahmin, was my first breakthrough, first emergence, first noble birth—having broken, with the beak of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the aggregates formerly lived in—just as for a chick, having broken the eggshell with the tip of its beak or the tip of its claw, there is a breakthrough from that eggshell, an emergence, a rebirth into the flock of chickens.

Pubbenivāsakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on past lives is concluded.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathā

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

13. So evaṃ…pe… cutūpapātañāṇāyāti cutiyā ca upapāte ca ñāṇāya; yena ñāṇena sattānaṃ cuti ca upapāto ca ñāyati, tadatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittaṃ abhininnāmesinti parikammacittaṃ nīhariṃ. So dibbena…pe… passāmīti ettha pana pūritapāramīnaṃ mahāsattānaṃ parikammakaraṇaṃ natthi. Te hi citte abhininnāmitamatte eva dibbena cakkhunā satte passanti, ādikammikakulaputtā pana parikammaṃ katvā. Tasmā tesaṃ vasena parikammaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā. Taṃ pana vuccamānaṃ atibhāriyaṃ vinayanidānaṃ karoti; tasmā taṃ [V 1.0122] na vadāma. Atthikehi pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.411) vuttanayena gahetabbaṃ. Idha pana pāḷimeva vaṇṇayissāma.

13. So evaṃ…pe… cutūpapātañāṇāya means: for the knowledge of decease and rebirth. By which knowledge the decease and rebirth of beings are known, for that purpose is what is meant. Cittaṃ abhininnāmesinti means: I brought forth the preparatory mind. In the context of So dibbena…pe… passāmi, however, for great beings who have fulfilled the perfections, there is no making of preparation. For they see beings with the divine eye merely by directing the mind. But beginners from good families see after having done the preparation. Therefore, on their account, preparation should be spoken of. But that, being spoken of, makes the introduction to the Vinaya very heavy; therefore, we do not speak of it. By those who are interested, however, it should be understood according to the method spoken of in the Visuddhimagga. Here, however, we will explain only the Pāli text.

Soti [M 1.0132] so ahaṃ. Dibbenātiādīsu dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ[P 1.0163]. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattaṃ pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhaṃ upakkilesavinimuttatāya dūrepi ārammaṇasampaṭicchanasamatthaṃ dibbaṃ pasādacakkhu hoti. Idañcāpi vīriyabhāvanābalanibbattaṃ ñāṇacakkhu tādisamevāti dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ, dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbaṃ, ālokapariggahena mahājutikattāpi dibbaṃ, tirokuṭṭādigatarūpadassanena mahāgatikattāpi dibbaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ saddasatthānusārena veditabbaṃ. Dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu. Cakkhukiccakaraṇena cakkhumivātipi cakkhu. Cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddhaṃ. Yo hi cutimattameva passati na upapātaṃ, so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo upapātamattameva passati na cutiṃ, so navasattapātubhāvadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana tadubhayaṃ passati, so yasmā duvidhampi taṃ diṭṭhigataṃ ativattati, tasmāssa taṃ dassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhihetu hoti. Tadubhayañca bhagavā addasa. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ – “cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddha”nti.

Soti means: so I. In dibbenāti, and so on, dibbaṃ (divine) is so called because of its similarity to the divine. For the divine sensitive eye of deities, produced by wholesome deeds, is unimpeded by bile, phlegm, blood, and so on, and because of its freedom from corruptions, it is capable of receiving objects even at a distance. And this eye of knowledge, produced by the power of effort and development, is just like that; thus it is dibbaṃ because of its similarity to the divine. It is also dibbaṃ because it is attained by means of the divine abiding and because it is itself dependent on the divine abiding. It is also dibbaṃ because of its great brilliance through grasping the light. It is also dibbaṃ because of its wondrous nature in seeing forms that have gone beyond a wall, etc. All this should be understood in accordance with the grammatical treatises. Cakkhu (eye) is so called in the sense of seeing. It is also cakkhu because it is like an eye in that it performs the function of an eye. Visuddhaṃ (purified) is so called because it is a cause for the purification of view through seeing decease and rebirth. For one who sees only decease and not rebirth grasps the annihilationist view. One who sees only rebirth and not decease grasps the view of a new being's appearance. But one who sees both, because he overcomes both those kinds of wrong view, for him that seeing is a cause for the purification of view. And the Blessed One saw both. Therefore this was said: “Purified because it is a cause for the purification of view through seeing decease and rebirth.”

Ekādasaupakkilesavirahato vā visuddhaṃ. Bhagavato hi ekādasapakkilesavirahitaṃ dibbacakkhu. Yathāha – “so kho ahaṃ, anuruddha, ‘vicikicchā cittassa upakkileso’ti iti viditvā vicikicchaṃ cittassa upakkilesaṃ pajahiṃ. Amanasikāro…pe… thinamiddhaṃ… chambhitattaṃ… uppilaṃ… duṭṭhullaṃ… accāraddhavīriyaṃ… atilīnavīriyaṃ… abhijappā… nānattasaññā… ‘atinijjhāyitattaṃ rūpānaṃ cittassa upakkileso’ti iti viditvā atinijjhāyitattaṃ rūpānaṃ cittassa upakkilesaṃ pajahiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, anuruddha, appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto obhāsañhi kho sañjānāmi, na ca rūpāni passāmi. Rūpāni hi kho passāmi, na ca obhāsaṃ sañjānāmī”ti (ma. ni. 3.242-243) evamādi. Tadevaṃ ekādasupakkilesavirahato [P 1.0164] visuddhaṃ.

Or, it is visuddhaṃ (purified) because of its freedom from the eleven corruptions. For the Blessed One’s divine eye is free from the eleven corruptions. As it was said: “Then, Anuruddha, having understood, ‘Doubt is a corruption of the mind,’ I abandoned doubt, a corruption of the mind. Inattention… sloth and torpor… terror… elation… gross bodily inertia… over-exerted energy… too lax energy… longing… perception of diversity… ‘Excessive meditation on forms is a corruption of the mind,’ having understood this, I abandoned excessive meditation on forms, a corruption of the mind. Then, Anuruddha, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceive light but do not see forms; or I see forms but do not perceive light,” and so on. Thus, it is purified because of its freedom from the eleven corruptions.

Manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā rūpadassanena atikkantamānusakaṃ; mānusakaṃ vā maṃsacakkhuṃ atikkantattā atikkantamānusakanti veditabbaṃ. Tena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena.

It is atikkantamānusakaṃ (surpassing the human) because it sees forms by transcending the human sphere. Or, it should be understood as atikkantamānusakaṃ because it has transcended the human fleshly eye. With that divine, purified, human-surpassing eye.

Satte [V 1.0123] passāmīti manussamaṃsacakkhunā viya satte passāmi dakkhāmi olokemi. Cavamāne upapajjamāneti ettha cutikkhaṇe vā upapattikkhaṇe vā [M 1.0133] dibbacakkhunā daṭṭhuṃ na sakkā, ye pana āsannacutikā idāni cavissanti te cavamānā. Ye ca gahitapaṭisandhikā sampatinibbattā vā, te upapajjamānāti adhippetā. Te evarūpe cavamāne upapajjamāne ca passāmīti dasseti. Hīneti mohanissandayuttattā hīnānaṃ jātikulabhogādīnaṃ vasena hīḷite ohīḷite uññāte avaññāte. Paṇīteti amohanissandayuttattā tabbiparīte. Suvaṇṇeti adosanissandayuttattā iṭṭhakantamanāpavaṇṇayutte. Dubbaṇṇeti dosanissandayuttattā aniṭṭhākantaamanāpavaṇṇayutte; abhirūpe virūpetipi attho. Sugateti sugatigate, alobhanissandayuttattā vā aḍḍhe mahaddhane. Duggateti duggatigate, lobhanissandayuttattā vā dalidde appannapāne. Yathākammūpageti yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ upacitaṃ tena tena upagate. Tattha purimehi “cavamāne”tiādīhi dibbacakkhukiccaṃ vuttaṃ; iminā pana padena yathākammūpagañāṇakiccaṃ.

Satte passāmi means: just as humans see with the fleshly eye, so I see, behold, and look upon beings. Here, in cavamāne upapajjamāne (passing away, being reborn), it is not possible to see with the divine eye the very moment of decease or the moment of rebirth. Rather, those who are near to decease and will now pass away are intended by cavamāne (passing away). And those who have taken a rebirth-linking, or who have just been reborn, are intended by upapajjamāne (being reborn). Thus it shows: “I see those beings in such a state, passing away and being reborn.” Hīne (inferior) means despised, greatly despised, looked down upon, and greatly looked down upon by way of low birth, family, wealth, etc., because of being connected with the result of delusion. Paṇīte (superior) means the opposite of that, because of being connected with the result of non-delusion. Suvaṇṇe (of good complexion) means endowed with a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable complexion, because of being connected with the result of non-aversion. Dubbaṇṇe (of bad complexion) means endowed with an undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable complexion, because of being connected with the result of aversion; the meaning also includes well-formed or ill-formed. Sugate (fortunate) means gone to a good destination, or, because of being connected with the result of non-greed, affluent and of great wealth. Duggate (unfortunate) means gone to a bad destination, or, because of being connected with the result of greed, poor and with little food and drink. Yathākammūpage (faring according to their kamma) means gone to a state according to whatever kamma has been accumulated. Therein, by the former words, “cavamāne,” etc., the function of the divine eye is stated; but by this phrase, the function of the knowledge of beings faring according to their kamma is stated.

Tassa ca ñāṇassa ayamuppattikkamo – so heṭṭhā nirayābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nerayikasatte passati mahantaṃ dukkhamanubhavamāne, taṃ dassanaṃ dibbacakkhukiccameva. So evaṃ manasi karoti – “kinnu kho kammaṃ katvā ime sattā etaṃ dukkhamanubhavantī”ti? Athassa “idaṃ nāma katvā”ti taṃ kammārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tathā upari devalokābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nandanavana-missakavana-phārusakavanādīsu satte passati mahāsampattiṃ anubhavamāne. Tampi dassanaṃ dibbacakkhukiccameva. So evaṃ manasi karoti – “kinnu kho kammaṃ katvā ime sattā etaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavantī”ti? Athassa “idaṃ [P 1.0165] nāma katvā”ti taṃkammārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ yathākammūpagañāṇaṃ nāma. Imassa visuṃ parikammaṃ nāma natthi. Yathā cimassa, evaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇassapi. Dibbacakkhupādakāneva hi imāni dibbacakkhunā saheva ijjhanti.

And this is the sequence of arising for that knowledge: he, having extended light downwards towards hell, sees beings in hell experiencing great suffering. That seeing is solely the function of the divine eye. He reflects thus: “Having done what kamma, I wonder, do these beings experience this suffering?” Then, for him, the knowledge which has that kamma as its object arises, with the thought, “Having done such-and-such kamma.” Similarly, having extended light upwards towards the deva world, he sees beings in the Nandana grove, Missaka grove, Phārusaka grove, and so on, experiencing great fortune. That seeing, too, is solely the function of the divine eye. He reflects thus: “Having done what kamma, I wonder, do these beings experience this fortune?” Then, for him, the knowledge which has that kamma as its object arises, with the thought, “Having done such-and-such kamma.” This is called the knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma. For this, there is no separate preliminary practice. Just as for this knowledge, so too for the knowledge of the future. For these knowledges, having the divine eye as their basis, are accomplished together with the divine eye.

Kāyaduccaritenātiādīsu duṭṭhu caritaṃ duṭṭhaṃ vā caritaṃ kilesapūtikattāti duccaritaṃ; kāyena duccaritaṃ, kāyato vā uppannaṃ duccaritanti kāyaduccaritaṃ. Evaṃ vacīmanoduccaritānipi daṭṭhabbāni. Samannāgatāti samaṅgībhūtā. Ariyānaṃ upavādakāti buddha-paccekabuddha-buddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ antamaso gihisotāpannānampi anatthakāmā hutvā antimavatthunā [M 1.0134] vā guṇaparidhaṃsanena vā upavādakā; akkosakā, garahakāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha “natthi imesaṃ samaṇadhammo, assamaṇā ete”ti vadanto antimavatthunā upavadati. “Natthi imesaṃ jhānaṃ vā vimokkho vā maggo vā phalaṃ vā”ti vadanto guṇaparidhaṃsanena upavadatīti [V 1.0124] veditabbo. So ca jānaṃ vā upavadeyya ajānaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi ariyūpavādova hoti. Bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ saggāvaraṇaṃ maggāvaraṇañca, satekicchaṃ pana hoti. Tassa ca āvibhāvatthaṃ idaṃ vatthumudāharanti –

In the phrase beginning with `kāyaduccaritena`, `duccarita` is ‘badly conducted conduct,’ or ‘corrupt conduct’ because it is putrid with defilements. `Kāyaduccarita` is misconduct by way of the body, or misconduct arisen from the body. In this way, verbal and mental misconduct should also be understood. `Samannāgatā` means endowed. `Ariyānaṃ upavādakā` means accusers of noble ones: desiring the harm of noble ones—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha’s disciples, down to the last lay stream-enterer—they are accusers either by means of the final matter or by means of destroying their virtues; this means they are revilers and censurers. Therein, one who says, “These have no ascetic qualities; they are not true ascetics,” accuses by means of the final matter. It should be understood that one who says, “These have no jhāna or liberation or path or fruition,” accuses by means of destroying their virtues. And whether one accuses knowing or not knowing, in either case it is an accusation of a noble one. It is a weighty kamma, an obstruction to heaven and an obstruction to the path, but it is remediable. And to make this clear, they cite this story:

“Aññatarasmiṃ kira gāme eko thero ca daharabhikkhu ca piṇḍāya caranti. Te paṭhamaghareyeva uḷuṅkamattaṃ uṇhayāguṃ labhiṃsu. Therassa ca kucchivāto atthi. So cintesi – ‘ayaṃ yāgu mayhaṃ sappāyā, yāva na sītalā hoti tāva naṃ pivāmī’ti. So manussehi ummāratthāya āhaṭe dārukkhandhe nisīditvā taṃ pivi. Itaro taṃ jigucchi – ‘aticchāto vatāyaṃ mahallako amhākaṃ lajjitabbakaṃ akāsī’ti. Thero gāme caritvā vihāraṃ gantvā daharabhikkhuṃ āha – ‘atthi te, āvuso, imasmiṃ sāsane patiṭṭhā’ti? ‘Āma, bhante, sotāpanno aha’nti. ‘Tena hāvuso, uparimaggatthāya vāyāmaṃ mā akāsi, khīṇāsavo tayā upavadito’ti. So taṃ khamāpesi. Tenassa taṃ pākatikaṃ ahosi”. Tasmā yo aññopi ariyaṃ upavadati, tena gantvā sace attanā vuḍḍhataro hoti, “ahaṃ āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me khamāhī”ti khamāpetabbo. Sace navakataro hoti[P 1.0166], vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “ahaṃ bhante tumhe idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me khamathā”ti khamāpetabbo. Sace so nakkhamati disāpakkanto vā hoti, ye tasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū vasanti tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā sace attanā vuḍḍhataro hoti ṭhitakeneva, sace navakataro ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “ahaṃ, bhante, asukaṃ nāma āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, khamatu me so āyasmā”ti evaṃ vadantena khamāpetabbo. Sace so parinibbuto hoti, parinibbutamañcaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yāva sivathikaṃ gantvāpi khamāpetabbo. Evaṃ kate saggāvaraṇañca maggāvaraṇañca na hoti, pākatikameva hoti.

It is said that in a certain village, an elder and a young bhikkhu were walking for alms. At the very first house, they received a ladleful of hot gruel. The elder had a wind ailment in his stomach. He thought: ‘This gruel is suitable for me. I will drink it before it gets cold.’ So, sitting on a log brought by people for a threshold, he drank it. The other was disgusted with him, thinking: ‘This old man is truly greedy! He has done something shameful for us.’ The elder, after walking through the village and going to the monastery, said to the young bhikkhu: ‘Friend, do you have a footing in this Dispensation?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer.’ ‘In that case, friend, do not strive for the higher paths; you have accused a Taintless One.’ The young bhikkhu asked the elder for forgiveness. By that, his kamma became as it was originally. Therefore, whoever else accuses a noble one should go to him. If the noble one is senior to oneself, forgiveness should be asked thus: ‘Venerable sir, I said such-and-such to you; please forgive me.’ If he is junior, one should pay homage, sit on one's heels, raise the joined palms and ask for forgiveness thus: ‘Venerable sir, I said such-and-such to you; please forgive me.’ If he does not forgive, or has gone to another region, one should go to the bhikkhus who reside in that monastery. If one is senior to them, one should ask for forgiveness while standing. If one is junior, one should sit on one's heels, raise the joined palms, and ask for forgiveness, saying: ‘Venerable sirs, I said such-and-such to the venerable one named so-and-so; may that venerable one forgive me.’ If he has attained parinibbāna, one should go to the place of the couch where he attained parinibbāna, even going as far as the charnel ground, and ask for forgiveness. When this is done, it is not an obstruction to heaven and not an obstruction to the path; it becomes just as it was originally.

Micchādiṭṭhikāti viparītadassanā. Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānāti micchādiṭṭhivasena samādinnanānāvidhakammā, ye ca micchādiṭṭhimūlakesu kāyakammādīsu aññepi [M 1.0135] samādapenti. Tattha vacīduccaritaggahaṇeneva ariyūpavāde, manoduccaritaggahaṇena ca micchādiṭṭhiyā saṅgahitāyapi imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puna vacanaṃ mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Mahāsāvajjo hi ariyūpavādo ānantariyasadiso. Yathāha – “seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya; evaṃsampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto, evaṃ niraye”ti (ma. ni. 1.149).

`Micchādiṭṭhikā` means those with perverted seeing. `Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā` means those who have undertaken various kinds of kamma through wrong view, and also those who cause others to undertake bodily actions and so on which are rooted in wrong view. Therein, it should be known that although accusation of noble ones is included by the mention of verbal misconduct, and wrong view is included by the mention of mental misconduct, the repeated mention of these two is for the purpose of showing their state of being greatly blameworthy. For accusation of a noble one is greatly blameworthy, similar to an action with immediate result. As it is said: “Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain Arahantship in this very life; I say, Sāriputta, that this is an infallible outcome: that without having abandoned that speech, without having abandoned that mind, without having relinquished that view, one is placed in hell just as something is brought and set down.”

Micchādiṭṭhito [V 1.0125] ca mahāsāvajjataraṃ nāma aññaṃ natthi. Yathāha – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, evaṃ mahāsāvajjataraṃ, yathayidaṃ, micchādiṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhiparamāni, bhikkhave, vajjānī”ti (a. ni. 1.310).

And there is nothing more greatly blameworthy than wrong view. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, I do not see even one other thing so much more blameworthy as this, that is, wrong view. Bhikkhus, faults have wrong view as their utmost.”

Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattakkhandhaggahaṇe. Athavā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassupacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cuticittato uddhaṃ. Apāyanti evamādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanaṃ. Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasammatā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ [P 1.0167] vā āyassa abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati; dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammunā nibbattā gatīti duggati. Vivasā nipatanti ettha dukkaṭakārinoti vinipāto; vinassantā vā ettha nipatanti sambhijjamānaṅgapaccaṅgāti vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

“Upon the breakup of the body” means the abandoning of the clung-to aggregates. “After death” refers to the taking up of newly arisen aggregates immediately after that. Alternatively, “upon the breakup of the body” means the cutting off of the life faculty. “After death” means subsequent to the death-consciousness. “The plane of misery” and so on are all synonyms for hell. Indeed, hell is called apāya because it is devoid of aya (merit), which is considered the cause of heaven and liberation, or because of the absence of the source of happiness. It is a duggati because it is a destination and resort for suffering; or it is a destination produced by a corrupt action due to an abundance of hatred. It is a vinipāta because evildoers fall there helplessly; or because they fall there being destroyed, with their major and minor limbs shattered. It is niraya because there is no gain perceived as enjoyable there.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti. Tiracchānayoni hi apāyo, sugatiyā apetattā; na duggati, mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayaṃ dīpeti. So hi apāyo ceva duggati ca sugatito apetattā, dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā; na tu vinipāto asurasadisaṃ avinipatitattā. Petamahiddhikānañhi vimānānipi nibbattanti. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ dīpeti. So hi yathāvuttenatthena apāyo ceva duggati ca sabbasamussayehi ca vinipatitattā vinipātoti vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena avīci-ādianekappakāraṃ nirayameva dīpeti. Upapannāti upagatā, tattha abhinibbattāti adhippāyo. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

Alternatively, by the term apāya, the animal realm is indicated. Indeed, the animal realm is an apāya because it is devoid of a good destination; but it is not a duggati, because of the existence of those of great power, such as nāga kings. By the term duggati, the realm of ghosts is indicated. Indeed, that realm is both an apāya and a duggati, because it is devoid of a good destination and because it is a destination for suffering; but it is not a vinipāta, because it is not a place of ruin like that of the asuras. Indeed, mansions even arise for ghosts of great power. By the term vinipāta, the host of asuras is indicated. Indeed, that host is called an apāya and a duggati for the reason already stated, and it is called a vinipāta because it is a fall from all prosperity. By the term niraya, only hell itself, of many kinds such as Avīci, is indicated. Upapannā means they have arrived, they are reborn there; this is the meaning. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been said.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0136] pana viseso – ettha sugatiggahaṇena manussagatipi saṅgayhati. Saggaggahaṇena devagatiyeva. Tattha sundarā gatīti sugati. Rūpādivisayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo. So sabbopi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti ayaṃ vacanattho. Vijjāti dibbacakkhuñāṇavijjā. Avijjāti sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhipaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ayameva hettha viseso – yathā pubbenivāsakathāyaṃ “pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇamukhatuṇḍakena pubbenivutthakkhandhapaacchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā”ti vuttaṃ; evamidha “cutūpapātañāṇamukhatuṇḍakena cutūpapātapaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā”ti vattabbanti.

This, however, is the distinction: herein, by the term sugati, the human destination is also included. By the term sagga, only the divine destination is included. Therein, sugati means a beautiful destination. Sagga means exceedingly excellent with respect to objects such as form. All of that is called loka in the sense of perishing and crumbling—this is the meaning of the word. Vijjā is the knowledge of the divine eye. Avijjā is the ignorance that conceals the passing away and reappearance of beings. The rest is just as has been explained. This is the distinction herein: just as in the discourse on past abodes it was said, “with the beak that is the knowledge of recollection of past abodes, having broken the eggshell that is ignorance, which conceals the aggregates previously lived in”; so too here it should be said, “with the beak that is the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings, having broken the eggshell that is ignorance, which conceals passing away and reappearance.”

Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the knowledge of the divine eye is concluded.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathā

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints

14. So [V 1.0126] evaṃ samāhite citteti idha vipassanāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti arahattamaggañāṇatthāya. Arahattamaggo hi āsavavināsanato āsavānaṃ khayoti vuccati. Tatra cetaṃ ñāṇaṃ tappariyāpannattāti[P 1.0168]. Cittaṃ abhininnāmesinti vipassanācittaṃ abhinīhariṃ. So idaṃ dukkhanti evamādīsu “ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ jāniṃ paṭivijjhiṃ. Tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti, tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati taṃ tesaṃ appavattiṃ nibbānaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti, tassa ca sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ jāniṃ paṭivijjhinti evamattho veditabbo.

14. “Thus, with the mind so concentrated”—here, the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for insight should be understood. “For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints” means for the sake of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship. Indeed, the path to Arahantship is called “the destruction of the taints” because it destroys the taints; and this knowledge is included therein because it pertains to it. “I inclined the mind” means “I directed the insight-consciousness.” Regarding “This is suffering” and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: “Suffering is this much, no more than this.” In this way, by penetrating its own characteristic, I fully knew, understood, and penetrated as it really is the entire truth of suffering; and the craving that brings that suffering into existence as “This is the origin of suffering”; and Nibbāna, the state where, having been reached, both of these cease—their non-arising—as “This is the cessation of suffering”; and the Noble Path that leads to that cessation as “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” Thus the meaning should be understood.

Evaṃ sarūpato saccāni dassetvā idāni kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento “ime āsavā”tiādimāha. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passatoti tassa mayhaṃ evaṃ jānantassa evaṃ passantassa saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ katheti. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccitthāti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Maggakkhaṇe hi cittaṃ vimuccati, phalakkhaṇe vimuttaṃ hoti. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇanti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ [M 1.0137] dasseti. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ. Tena hi ñāṇena bhagavā paccavekkhanto “khīṇā jātī”tiādīni abbhaññāsiṃ. Katamā pana bhagavato jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ abbhaññāsīti? Vuccate – na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā, pubbeva khīṇattā; na anāgatā, anāgate vāyāmābhāvato; na paccuppannā, vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā; taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā “kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotī”ti jānanto abbhaññāsiṃ.

Having thus shown the truths in their own nature, now, wishing to show them indirectly by way of the defilements, he says, “These are the taints,” and so on. “For me, thus knowing, thus seeing”—this speaks of the supramundane path that has reached its culmination together with insight. “From the taint of sensual desire”—with this, he indicates the moment of fruition. Indeed, at the moment of the path the mind is being freed; at the moment of fruition it has been freed. With “When freed, the knowledge arose in me: ‘I am freed,’” he indicates the reviewing knowledge. With “Destroyed is birth,” and so on, he indicates its basis. Indeed, with that knowledge, the Blessed One, reviewing, fully knew, “Destroyed is birth,” and so on. But which birth of the Blessed One was destroyed, and how did he fully know it? It is said: his past birth was not destroyed, for it had already been destroyed; nor his future birth, because there is no striving in the future; nor his present birth, because it still exists. But that birth—differentiated into one, four, or five aggregates in the one-, four-, or five-aggregate planes of existence—which would have arisen due to the non-development of the path, that birth is destroyed by reaching a state of non-arising due to the development of the path. He fully knew this, having reviewed the defilements abandoned through the development of the path and knowing: “In the absence of defilements, even existing kamma does not produce a future linking.”

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ, puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso. Tasmā bhagavā attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto “vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti abbhaññāsiṃ. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayavasena [V 1.0127] soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho[P 1.0169]. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi etaṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā bhagavā attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto “kataṃ karaṇīya”nti abbhaññāsiṃ. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti abbhaññāsiṃ.

‘The holy life has been lived’ means it has been dwelt, fully dwelt, done, practiced, and finished. ‘Holy life’ means the holy life of the path. Indeed, the seven trainees along with the virtuous worldling are said to be dwelling the holy life, whereas one whose taints are destroyed is one who has dwelt it. Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own dwelling of the holy life, fully knew, ‘The holy life has been lived.’ ‘What had to be done has been done’ means that the sixteenfold duty regarding the four truths—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing with the four paths—has been completed. Indeed, virtuous worldlings and others are doing this duty, whereas one whose taints are destroyed is one who has done what had to be done. Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing what he had to do, fully knew, ‘What had to be done has been done.’ ‘There is nothing further for this state of being’ means ‘Now, there is no further duty for me to develop the path for the sake of this state—that is, for the state of these sixteen duties or for the destruction of the defilements.’ Thus, he fully knew.

Idāni evaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇapariggahitaṃ taṃ āsavānaṃ khayañāṇādhigamaṃ brāhmaṇassa dassento ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha vijjāti arahattamaggañāṇavijjā. Avijjāti catusaccapaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa tatiyā abhinibbhidā ahosīti ettha ayaṃ kho mama brāhmaṇa āsavānaṃ khayañāṇamukhatuṇḍakena catusaccapaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā tatiyā abhinibbhidā tatiyā nikkhanti tatiyā ariyajāti ahosi, kukkuṭacchāpakasseva mukhatuṇḍakena vā pādanakhasikhāya vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā tamhā aṇḍakosamhā abhinibbhidā nikkhanti kukkuṭanikāye paccājātīti.

Now, showing the brahmin that attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, which is encompassed by the reviewing knowledge, he says, ‘This, indeed, O brahmin,’ and so on. Therein, ‘knowledge’ means the knowledge that is the path of Arahantship. ‘Ignorance’ means the ignorance that conceals the four truths. The rest is as previously explained. This, however, is the distinction: regarding ‘This, O brahmin, was my third breakthrough,’ the meaning should be understood thus: ‘O brahmin, just as for a chick there is a breakthrough and emergence from the eggshell, a rebirth into the flock of chickens, after shattering the eggshell with the tip of its beak or the tip of its claw; so too, for me, having shattered the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the four truths with the beak-tip that is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, this was the third breakthrough, the third emergence, the third noble birth.’

Ettāvatā [M 1.0138] kiṃ dassetīti? So hi brāhmaṇa kukkuṭacchāpako aṇḍakosaṃ

By this much, what does he show? Indeed, O brahmin, that chick, the eggshell...

Padāletvā tato nikkhamanto sakimeva jāyati, ahaṃ pana pubbe-nivutthakkhandhapaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ bhinditvā paṭhamaṃ tāva pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇavijjāya jāto, tato sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhipaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā dutiyaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇavijjāya jāto, puna catusaccapaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā tatiyaṃ āsavānaṃ khayañāṇavijjāya jāto; evaṃ tīhi vijjāhi tikkhattuṃ jāto. Sā ca me jāti ariyā suparisuddhāti idaṃ dassesi. Evaṃ dassento ca pubbenivāsañāṇena atītaṃsañāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhunā paccuppannānāgataṃsañāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayena sakalalokiyalokuttaraguṇanti evaṃ tīhi vijjāhi sabbepi sabbaññuguṇe pakāsetvā attano ariyāya jātiyā jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ brāhmaṇassa dassesīti.

...having shattered it and emerging from it, is born only once. But I, having first shattered the eggshell of ignorance that covered the aggregates of past existences, was born for the first time through the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. Then, having shattered the eggshell of ignorance that concealed the passing away and rebirth of beings, I was born for the second time through the knowledge of the divine eye. Again, having shattered the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the four truths, I was born for the third time through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. Thus, with the three knowledges, I was born three times. And this birth of mine is noble and exceedingly pure—this he showed. And in showing this, through the knowledge of past lives, he revealed knowledge of the past portion; through the divine eye, knowledge of the present and future portions; and through the destruction of the taints, all worldly and supramundane qualities. Thus, with the three knowledges, having revealed all the qualities of an omniscient one, he showed the brahmin his state of being the eldest and foremost through his own noble birth.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints is finished.

Desanānumodanakathā

A Talk on Rejoicing in the Discourse

15. Evaṃ [P 1.0170] vutte verañjo brāhmaṇoti evaṃ bhagavatā lokānukampakena brāhmaṇaṃ anukampamānena vinigūhitabbepi attano ariyāya jātiyā jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāve vijjattayapakāsikāya [V 1.0128] dhammadesanāya vutte pītivipphāraparipuṇṇagattacitto verañjo brāhmaṇo taṃ bhagavato ariyāya jātiyā jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ viditvā “īdisaṃ nāmāhaṃ sabbalokajeṭṭhaseṭṭhaṃ sabbaguṇasamannāgataṃ sabbaññuṃ ‘aññesaṃ abhivādanādikammaṃ na karotī’ti avacaṃ – ‘dhīratthu vatare aññāṇa’”nti attānaṃ garahitvā “ayaṃ dāni loke ariyāya jātiyā purejātaṭṭhena jeṭṭho, sabbaguṇehi appaṭisamaṭṭhena seṭṭho”ti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “jeṭṭho bhavaṃ gotamo seṭṭho bhavaṃ gotamo”ti. Evañca pana vatvā puna taṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ abbhanumodamāno “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādimāha.

15. When this was said by the Blessed One—who is compassionate towards the world, and who, wishing to show compassion to the brahmin, spoke with a Dhamma discourse that reveals the three kinds of knowledge about his own state of being the eldest and foremost by noble birth, even though it should have been especially concealed—the brahmin Verañja, his body and mind filled with the suffusion of rapture, having understood that state of the Blessed One's being the eldest and foremost by noble birth, reproached himself, thinking: “To such a person—the eldest and foremost in all the world of beings, endowed with all virtues, the All-Knowing—I said, ‘He does not perform the act of paying homage, etc., to others.’ Oh, fie upon this ignorance!” Having come to the conclusion, “Now, in this world of beings, he is the eldest by noble birth, in the sense of being born first, and the foremost by all virtues, in the sense of being incomparable,” he said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama is the eldest, Master Gotama is the foremost!” And having spoken thus, again greatly rejoicing in that Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One, he said, “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!” and so on.

Tatthāyaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. “Abhikkantā, bhante, ratti; nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho”tiādīsu [M 1.0139] (a. ni. 8.20) hi khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ me puggalo khamati, imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

Therein, this word 'abhikkanta' is seen in the meanings of passing away, beautiful, very beautiful form, and greatly rejoicing. It is seen in the sense of passing away in such passages as: “Venerable sir, the night has passed; the first watch is over; the community of monks has been seated for a long time.” It is seen in the sense of beautiful in such passages as: “This person is agreeable to me; he is more excellent and more refined than these four persons.”

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. –

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with power and glory, with a surpassing complexion, illuminating all directions?”

Ādīsu (vi. va. 857) abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ, bhante”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.250) abbhanumodane. Idhāpi abbhanumodaneyeva. Yasmā ca abbhanumodane, tasmā “sādhu sādhu, bho gotamā”ti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

In these and similar passages, it is seen in the sense of a very beautiful form. In phrases such as “Excellent, venerable sir!” it is seen in the sense of greatly rejoicing. Here too, it is only in the sense of greatly rejoicing. And because it is in the sense of greatly rejoicing, it should be understood that it means, “Excellent, excellent, Master Gotama!”

“Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho”ti.

“In fear, anger, praise, haste, in curiosity and wonder, in joy, sorrow, and in faith, a wise person should make a repetition.”

Iminā ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo.

And by this grammatical rule, it should be understood that here this word is spoken twice by way of faith and by way of praise.

Atha vā abhikkantanti atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhi ettha adhippāyo – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā, abhikkantaṃ yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādo”ti. Bhagavatoyeva vā vacanaṃ dve [P 1.0171] dve atthe sandhāya thometi [V 1.0129] – bhoto gotamassa vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato, tathā saddhājananato paññājananato, sātthato sabyañjanato, uttānapadato gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato paññāvadātato, apātharamaṇīyato vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato vīmaṃsiyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ.

Alternatively, 'abhikkanta' means 'most desirable,' 'most pleasing,' 'most beautiful.' Therein, with one word 'abhikkanta' he praises the discourse, and with one he praises his own faith. For this is the intention here: “Excellent, Master Gotama, is this Dhamma discourse of Master Gotama; excellent is this faith of mine that has arisen on account of Master Gotama's Dhamma discourse.” Or, he praises the speech of the Blessed One himself by referring to pairs of meanings: the speech of Master Gotama is excellent because it destroys faults and excellent because it causes the attainment of virtues; likewise, because it generates faith and generates wisdom; because it is complete with meaning and complete with phrasing; because it has clear words and profound meaning; because it is pleasant to the ear and reaches the heart; because it does not exalt oneself and does not disparage others; because it is cool with compassion and pure with wisdom; because it is delightful upon first hearing and can withstand scrutiny; because it is pleasant when being heard and beneficial when being investigated—it should be connected with these and similar meanings.

Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti uparimukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādipaṭicchāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā esa maggoti [M 1.0140] vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasī aḍḍharatta-ghanavanasaṇḍa-meghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tamasi. Ayaṃ tāva anuttānapadattho. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patiṭṭhitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena; yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānā pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena; yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ ācikkhantena; yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāre nimuggassa me buddhādiratanattayarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotaṃ dhārentena, mayhaṃ bhotā gotamena etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

After that, with four similes, he praises the discourse itself. Therein, 'overturned' means placed face down, or having come to be face down. 'Would set upright' means would make it face up. 'Concealed' means covered by grass, leaves, and so on. 'Would reveal' means would uncover. 'To one who is lost' means to one who is confused about directions. 'Would point out the path' means taking by the hand and saying, “This is the path.” 'In darkness' means in the four-factored darkness of the fourteenth day of the waning moon, midnight, a dense forest grove, and a layer of clouds. This, first, is the meaning of the unclear words. This, however, is the application of the meaning: Just as someone might set upright what is overturned, so by raising me—who was turned away from the True Dhamma and established in false dhamma—from that false dhamma; just as one might reveal what is concealed, so by revealing the Dispensation that was concealed by the thicket of wrong view since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; just as one might point out the path to one who is lost, so by pointing out the path to heaven and liberation to me, who was proceeding on a wrong path, a false path; just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so by holding up the lamp of the discourse that destroys the darkness of delusion which conceals those forms, for me who was sunken in the darkness of delusion and could not see the forms of the Triple Gem, the Buddha and so on. Because the Dhamma has been made clear to me by Master Gotama in these ways, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways.

Desanānumodanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Talk on Rejoicing in the Discourse is concluded.

Pasannākārakathā

The Exposition on the Expression of Faith

Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto “esāha”ntiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇanti gacchāmi; bhavaṃ me gotamo saraṇaṃ, parāyaṇaṃ, aghassa tātā, hitassa ca vidhātāti iminā adhippāyena bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ gacchāmi bhajāmi sevāmi payirupāsāmi[P 1.0172], evaṃ vā jānāmi bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho; tasmā “gacchāmī”ti imassa jānāmi bujjhāmīti ayampi attho vutto. Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ettha pana adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca catūsu apāyesu apatamāne [V 1.0130] dhāretīti dhammo; so atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34) vitthāro. Na kevalañca ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca, api ca kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi. Vuttampi hetaṃ chattamāṇavakavimāne –

Having praised the teaching thus, with a mind confident in the Triple Gem on account of this teaching, and wishing to make an expression of faith, he spoke the words beginning with 'esāhaṃ'. Therein, 'esāhaṃ' is 'eso ahaṃ'. 'I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge' means 'I go to the venerable Gotama as refuge'; that is, 'The venerable Gotama is my refuge, my final resort, the protector from evil, and the provider of benefit.' With this intention, I go to, resort to, serve, and attend upon the venerable Gotama; or, thus I know, I understand. Indeed, for those verbal roots that have the meaning of 'going', they also have the meaning of 'understanding'. Therefore, for this word 'gacchāmi', this meaning 'I know, I understand' is also stated. Now, in the phrase 'and the Dhamma and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha', the Dhamma is so called because it holds beings who have attained the path, realized cessation, and are practicing as instructed, preventing them from falling into the four woeful states; in essence, it is the Noble Path and Nibbāna. For this was said: 'Bhikkhus, inasmuch as there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them'—the detailed explanation should be understood. And it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Dhamma of the scriptures along with the noble fruits. This too was said in the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna:

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ, dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ, dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 887);

“The Dhamma of dispassion from lust, unshaken and sorrowless, the unconditioned and unopposed Dhamma; this sweet, proficient, well-expounded Dhamma—approach this Dhamma for the purpose of refuge.”

Ettha hi rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā [M 1.0141] sabbadhammakkhandhāti. Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena saṃhatoti saṅgho, so atthato aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūho. Vuttañhetaṃ tasmiṃyeva vimāne –

Here, by 'dispassion from lust', the Path is described. By 'unshaken and sorrowless', the Fruit is described. By 'the unconditioned Dhamma', Nibbāna is described. By 'unopposed, this sweet, proficient, well-expounded', all the aggregates of the Dhamma, divided into the three Piṭakas, are described. The Saṅgha is so called because it is united by a commonality of view and virtue; in essence, it is the community of the eight noble individuals. And this was said in that very same celestial mansion:

“Yattha ca dinnamahapphalamāhu, catūsu sucīsu purisayugesu;

Aṭṭha ca puggaladhammadasā te, saṅghamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 888);

“They declare that what is given to the four pure pairs of persons is of great fruit; those eight individuals are seers of the Dhamma. Approach this Saṅgha for the purpose of refuge.”

Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho bhikkhusaṅgho. Ettāvatā ca brāhmaṇo tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi.

The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is the Bhikkhusaṅgha. And with this, the brahmin declared his taking of the three refuges.

Pasannākārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Expression of Faith is concluded.

Saraṇagamanakathā

The Discourse on Going for Refuge

Idāni tesveva tīsu saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo saraṇaṃ gacchati,

Now, for the sake of skill in these very three goings for refuge, one should understand: the refuge, the act of going for refuge, the one who goes for refuge,

Saraṇagamanappabhedo, saraṇagamanaphalaṃ, saṃkileso, bhedoti ayaṃ vidhi vedi tabbo. So pana idha vuccamāno atibhāriyaṃ vinayanidānaṃ karotīti na vutto. Atthikehi pana papañcasūdaniyaṃ vā majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanato (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.56) sumaṅgalavilāsiniyaṃ vā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.250) saraṇavaṇṇanato gahetabboti.

the classification of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, its defilement, and its breaking—this method should be understood. However, it is not mentioned here because to do so would make the Vinaya foundation overly burdensome. Yet, those who are interested should take it from either the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, in its explanation of the Bhayabheravasutta, or from the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya, in its explanation of the refuges.

Saraṇagamanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Going for Refuge is concluded.

Upāsakattapaṭivedanākathā

The Discourse on the Declaration of Lay Followership

Upāsakaṃ [V 1.0131] maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretūti maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo “upāsako aya”nti evaṃ dhāretūti attho. Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ panettha ko upāsako, kasmā [P 1.0173] upāsakoti vuccati, kimassa sīlaṃ, ko ājīvo, kā vipatti, kā sampattīti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Taṃ atibhāriyakaraṇato idha na vibhattaṃ, atthikehi pana papañcasūdaniyaṃ majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.56) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ajjataggeti ettha ayaṃ aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. “Ajjatagge, samma dovārika, āvarāmi dvāraṃ nigaṇṭhānaṃ nigaṇṭhīna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.70) hi ādimhi dissati. “Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyya (kathā. 441), ucchaggaṃ veḷagga”ntiādīsu koṭiyaṃ. “Ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā (saṃ. ni. 5.374) anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetu”ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 318) koṭṭhāse. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.34) seṭṭhe. Idha panāyaṃ ādimhi daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Ajjatanti ajjabhāvanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ajjadagge icceva vā [M 1.0142] pāṭho, dakāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ, yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇagataṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu jānātu, ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyyuṃ, neva buddhaṃ “na buddho”ti vā, dhammaṃ “na dhammo”ti vā, saṅghaṃ “na saṅgho”ti vā vadeyyanti. Ettha ca brāhmaṇo pāṇupetaṃ saraṇagatanti puna saraṇagamanaṃ vadanto attasanniyyātanaṃ pakāsetīti veditabbo.

“May the venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower.” The meaning is: “May the venerable Gotama remember me thus: ‘This is a lay follower.’” Here, for the sake of skill in the procedure for a lay follower, one should understand the following miscellaneous points: Who is a lay follower? Why is one called a lay follower? What is their virtue? What is their livelihood? What is their downfall? What is their success? Because elaborating on this would make it too burdensome, it has not been detailed here. However, those who are interested should refer to the method explained in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya. Regarding “from this day forward” (ajjatagge), here the word agga is seen in the senses of beginning, extremity, portion, and excellence. For example: in the sense of ‘beginning’, as in: “From this day forward, dear gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs”; in the sense of ‘extremity’, as in: “With the tip of one’s finger, one may touch the tip of another’s finger,” or “the tip of a sugarcane,” “the tip of a bamboo”; in the sense of a ‘portion’, as in: “I allow, monks, sharing by a dwelling’s portion or a monastic ground's portion,” and “a sour fruit portion, a sweet fruit portion, or a bitter fruit portion”; in the sense of ‘excellence’, as in: “Monks, as far as beings—whether footless, two-footed… the Tathāgata is declared foremost among them.” Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of ‘beginning’. Therefore, “from this day forward” means “having made today the beginning.” Ajjataṃ means “the state of today.” Alternatively, the reading may be ajjadagge, where the letter ‘d’ is a euphonic link, meaning “having made today the beginning.” Pāṇupetaṃ means “endowed with life”—that is, as long as my life lasts. May the venerable Gotama remember me, know me, as one who has gone for refuge to the three refuges, having no other teacher. For even if they were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, ‘He is not the Buddha,’ or of the Dhamma, ‘It is not the Dhamma,’ or of the Saṅgha, ‘It is not the Saṅgha.’ Here, it should be understood that when the brahmin says, “gone for refuge for as long as life lasts,” in repeating the going for refuge, he is declaring his surrender of self.

Evaṃ attānaṃ niyyātetvā bhagavantaṃ saparisaṃ upaṭṭhātukāmo āha – “adhivāsetu ca me bhavaṃ gotamo verañjāyaṃ vassāvāsaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – upāsakañca maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu, adhivāsetu ca me verañjāyaṃ vassāvāsaṃ, tayo māse verañjaṃ upanissāya mama anuggahatthaṃ vāsaṃ sampaṭicchatūti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvenāti athassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhagavā kāyaṅgaṃ vā vācaṅgaṃ vā acopetvā abbhantareyeva khantiṃ cāretvā tuṇhībhāvena adhivāsesi; brāhmaṇassa anuggahatthaṃ manasāva sampaṭicchīti [P 1.0174] vuttaṃ hoti.

Having thus surrendered himself, and wishing to attend upon the Blessed One together with his assembly, he said: “May the venerable Gotama consent to spend the rains-residence in Verañjā together with the community of monks.” What is meant is: “May the venerable Gotama consider me a lay follower, and may he consent to my invitation to spend the rains-residence in Verañjā; for three months, relying on Verañjā, may he accept this residence for my benefit.” The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. That is, having heard his words, the Blessed One, without moving any part of his body or speech, but inwardly establishing acceptance, consented by silence. It is said that he accepted with his mind alone for the brahmin's benefit.

Atha kho verañjo brāhmaṇo bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvāti atha verañjo brāhmaṇo sace me [V 1.0132] samaṇo gotamo nādhivāseyya, kāyena vā vācāya vā paṭikkhipeyya. Yasmā pana appaṭikkhipitvā abbhantare khantiṃ dhāresi, tasmā me manasāva adhivāsesīti evaṃ ākārasallakkhaṇakusalatāya bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā, attano nisinnāsanato vuṭṭhāya catūsu disāsu bhagavantaṃ sakkaccaṃ vanditvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā āgatakālato pabhuti jātimahallakabrāhmaṇānaṃ abhivādanādīni na karotīti vigarahitvāpi idāni viññātabuddhaguṇo kāyena vācāya manasā ca anekakkhattuṃ vandantopi atittoyeva hutvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā yāva dassanavisayo tāva paṭimukhoyeva apakkamitvā dassanavisayaṃ vijahanaṭṭhāne vanditvā pakkāmi.

Then the brahmin Verañja, recognizing the Blessed One's consent, thought: “If the ascetic Gotama were not to consent, he would refuse with body or speech. But since he did not refuse and inwardly established acceptance, he has consented with his mind.” Thus, being skilled in discerning such signs, he understood the Blessed One's consent. Rising from his seat, he reverently paid homage to the Blessed One in the four directions and circumambulated him three times to the right. Although he had been criticized because, from the time of his arrival, he did not perform the customary greetings to the senior brahmins of high birth, now, having understood the Buddha's virtues, he paid homage repeatedly with body, speech, and mind, yet was still as if not satisfied. Raising his joined palms, made radiant by the meeting of his ten fingernails, he placed them on his head. As long as the Blessed One remained in sight, he backed away while still facing him. At the point where he would lose sight of him, he paid homage once more and departed.

Upāsakattapaṭivedanākathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Declaration of Lay Followership is concluded.

Dubbhikkhakathā

The Discourse on Famine

16. Tena kho pana samayena verañjā dubbhikkhā hotīti yasmiṃ samaye verañjena brāhmaṇena bhagavā verañjaṃ upanissāya vassāvāsaṃ yācito[M 1.0143], tena samayena verañjā dubbhikkhā hoti. Dubbhikkhāti dullabhabhikkhā; sā pana dullabhabhikkhatā yattha manussā assaddhā honti appasannā, tattha susassakālepi atisamagghepi pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇe hoti. Verañjāyaṃ pana yasmā na tathā ahosi, apica kho dusassatāya chātakadosena ahosi tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento dvīhitikātiādimāha. Tattha dvīhitikāti dvidhā pavattaīhitikā. Īhitaṃ nāma iriyā dvidhā pavattā – cittairiyā, cittaīhā. “Ettha lacchāma nu kho kiñci bhikkhamānā na lacchāmā”ti, “jīvituṃ vā sakkhissāma nu kho no”ti ayamettha adhippāyo.

16. At that time, Verañjā was suffering from famine. That is, at the time when the brahmin of Verañjā invited the Blessed One to spend the rains retreat near Verañjā, at that time Verañjā was suffering from famine. 'Famine' means almsfood is difficult to obtain. Moreover, this difficulty in obtaining almsfood occurs where people are faithless and without confidence, even during a good harvest season when early and late crops are very cheap. In Verañjā, however, it was not so; rather, it was due to a poor harvest and the fault of starvation. Therefore, to show this meaning, the text says 'dvīhitikā,' etc. Therein, 'dvīhitikā' means having a striving that proceeds in two ways. 'Īhita' means deportment. The mental deportment and mental striving proceeds in two ways as follows: 'Begging here, will we get anything, or will we not get anything?' and 'Will we be able to live, or not?' This is the meaning here.

Atha vā dvīhitikāti dujjīvikā, īhitaṃ īhā iriyanaṃ pavattanaṃ jīvitantiādīni padāni ekatthāni. Tasmā dukkhena īhitaṃ ettha pavattatīti dvīhitikāti ayamettha [P 1.0175] padattho. Setaṭṭhikāti setakāni aṭṭhīni etthāti setaṭṭhikā. Divasampi yācitvā kiñci aladdhā matānaṃ kapaṇamanussānaṃ ahicchattakavaṇṇehi aṭṭhīhi tatra tatra parikiṇṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Setaṭṭikātipi pāṭho. Tassattho – setā aṭṭi etthāti setaṭṭikā. Aṭṭīti āturatā byādhi rogo. Tattha ca sassānaṃ gabbhaggahaṇakāle setakarogena upahatameva pacchinnakhīraṃ aggahitataṇḍulaṃ paṇḍarapaṇḍaraṃ sālisīsaṃ vā yavagodhūmasīsaṃ vā nikkhamati, tasmā “setaṭṭikā”ti vuccati.

Alternatively, dvīhitikā means a difficult livelihood. The words īhita, īhā, iriyana, pavattana, jīvita, and so on, have the same meaning. Therefore, the meaning of the word here is this: 'living proceeds with difficulty here,' thus it is dvīhitikā. Setaṭṭhikā means 'where there are white bones.' It is said that the place is scattered here and there with the bones, which are the color of a mushroom, of poor, destitute people who have died after begging for a whole day and getting nothing. There is also the reading setaṭṭikā. Its meaning is: 'where there is a white disease.' Aṭṭi means affliction, sickness, disease.
