And there, at the time the grain is forming, being afflicted by a 'whitening disease,' the heads of rice, or barley and wheat, emerge very white, with the milk-flow cut off and the grain not having formed. Therefore, it is called setaṭṭikā.

Vappakāle [V 1.0133] suṭṭhu abhisaṅkharitvāpi vuttasassaṃ tattha salākā eva sampajjatīti salākāvuttā; salākāya vā tattha jīvitaṃ pavattentīti salākāvuttā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Tattha kira dhaññavikkayakānaṃ santikaṃ kayakesu gatesu dubbalamanusse abhibhavitvā balavamanussāva dhaññaṃ kiṇitvā gacchanti. Dubbalamanussā alabhamānā mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Dhaññavikkayakā “sabbesaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmā”ti dhaññakaraṇaṭṭhāne dhaññamāpakaṃ nisīdāpetvā ekapasse vaṇṇajjhakkhaṃ nisīdāpesuṃ. Dhaññatthikā vaṇṇajjhakkhassa santikaṃ gacchanti. So āgatapaṭipāṭiyā mūlaṃ gahetvā “itthannāmassa ettakaṃ dātabba”nti salākaṃ likhitvā deti, te taṃ gahetvā dhaññamāpakassa santikaṃ gantvā dinnapaṭipāṭiyā dhaññaṃ gaṇhanti. Evaṃ salākāya tattha jīvitaṃ pavattentīti salākāvuttā.

Even though well-prepared at sowing time, the sown crop there becomes mere stalks, thus it is called salākāvuttā ('sown for stalks'). Or, because they carry on their life there by means of a tally stick (salākā), it is called salākāvuttā ('living by tally stick'). What is meant by this? It is said that there, when buyers go to the grain sellers, the strong people overpower the weak, buy the grain, and leave. The weak people, unable to obtain any, make a great outcry. The grain sellers, thinking, 'We will provide for everyone,' had a grain measurer sit at the grain distribution place and a clerk sit to one side. Those who wanted grain would go to the clerk. He, taking the payment in order of arrival, would write on a tally stick, 'This much should be given to so-and-so,' and give it to them. Taking it, they would go to the grain measurer and receive the grain in the order of the tally sticks given. Thus, because they carry on their life there by means of a tally stick, it is called salākāvuttā.

Na [M 1.0144] sukarā uñchena paggahena yāpetunti paggahena yo uñcho, tena yāpetuṃ na sukarā. Pattaṃ gahetvā yaṃ ariyā uñchaṃ karonti, bhikkhācariyaṃ caranti, tena uñchena yāpetuṃ na sukarāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tadā kira tattha sattaṭṭhagāme piṇḍāya caritvā ekadivasampi yāpanamattaṃ na labhanti.

'It is not easy to sustain oneself by gleaning with an outstretched bowl.' This means: the gleaning which is done with an outstretched bowl—it is not easy to sustain oneself by that. It is said that it is not easy to sustain oneself by that gleaning which the noble ones do, taking a bowl and wandering for alms. It is said that at that time, having wandered for alms in seven or eight villages there, they did not get enough even for one day's sustenance.

Tena kho pana samayena uttarāpathakā assavāṇijā…pe… assosi kho bhagavā udukkhalasaddanti – tenāti yasmiṃ samaye bhagavā verañjaṃ upanissāya vassāvāsaṃ upagato tena samayena. Uttarāpathavāsikā uttarāpathato vā āgatattā evaṃ laddhavohārā assavāṇijā uttarāpathe assānaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhāne [P 1.0176] pañca assasatāni gahetvā diguṇaṃ tiguṇaṃ lābhaṃ patthayamānā desantaraṃ gacchantā tehi attano vikkāyikabhaṇḍabhūtehi pañcamattehi assasatehi verañjaṃ vassāvāsaṃ upagatā honti. Kasmā? Na hi sakkā tasmiṃ dese vassike cattāro māse addhānaṃ paṭipajjituṃ. Upagacchantā ca bahinagare udakena anajjhottharaṇīye ṭhāne attano ca vāsāgārāni assānañca mandiraṃ kārāpetvā vatiyā parikkhipiṃsu. Tāni tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānāni “assamaṇḍalikāyo”ti paññāyiṃsu. Tenāha – “tehi assamaṇḍalikāsu bhikkhūnaṃ patthapatthapulakaṃ paññattaṃ hotī”ti. Patthapatthapulakanti ekamekassa bhikkhuno patthapatthapamāṇaṃ pulakaṃ. Pattho nāma nāḷimattaṃ hoti, ekassa purisassa alaṃ yāpanāya. Vuttampi hetaṃ – “patthodano nālamayaṃ duvinna”nti (jā. 2.21.192). Pulakaṃ nāma nitthusaṃ katvā ussedetvā gahitayavataṇḍulā vuccanti. Yadi hi sathusā honti, pāṇakā vijjhanti, addhānakkhamā na honti. Tasmā te vāṇijā addhānakkhamaṃ katvā yavataṇḍulamādāya addhānaṃ paṭipajjanti [V 1.0134] “yattha assānaṃ khādanīyaṃ tiṇaṃ dullabhaṃ bhavissati, tatthetaṃ assabhattaṃ bhavissatī”ti.

'At that time, horse traders from the northern region… the Blessed One heard the sound of a mortar.' 'At that time' means at the time when the Blessed One had gone to spend the rains retreat near Verañjā. Horse traders, who were residents of the northern region or were so-called because they had come from the northern region, took five hundred horses from the horse-breeding grounds in the northern region. Desiring double or triple profit and traveling to another country with those five hundred horses which were their merchandise for sale, they arrived at Verañjā to spend the rains retreat. Why? Because it is not possible to travel the road in that region during the four months of the rainy season. And upon arriving, outside the city in a place that is not flooded by water, they had their own dwellings and a stable for the horses built, and enclosed them with a fence. Those dwelling places of theirs became known as 'horse-enclosures.' Therefore, he said: 'From them, in the horse-enclosures, a pattha-measure of coarse grain for each was provided to the monks.' 'A pattha-measure of coarse grain for each' means a pattha-measure of coarse grain for each monk. A pattha is a measure of one nāḷi; it is enough to sustain one person. For this is also said: 'A pattha of rice is not enough for two.' Pulaka is said to be barley grains that have been taken after being husked and steamed. For if they have husks, insects pierce them, and they do not last for a long journey. Therefore, those traders, making the barley grains last for a long journey, take them and travel the road, thinking, 'Wherever fodder for the horses—grass—is scarce, this will be the horses' meal.'

Kasmā pana tehi taṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paññattanti? Vuccate – “na hi te dakkhiṇāpathamanussā viya assaddhā appasannā, te pana saddhā pasannā buddhamāmakā, dhammamāmakā, saṅghamāmakā; te pubbaṇhasamayaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena nagaraṃ pavisantā dve tayo divase addasaṃsu sattaṭṭha bhikkhū sunivatthe supārute [M 1.0145] iriyāpathasampanne sakalampi nagaraṃ piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci alabhamāne. Disvāna nesaṃ etadahosi – “ayyā imaṃ nagaraṃ upanissāya vassaṃ upagatā; chātakañca vattati, na ca kiñci labhanti, ativiya kilamanti. Mayañcamha āgantukā, na sakkoma nesaṃ devasikaṃ yāguñca bhattañca paṭiyādetuṃ. Amhākaṃ pana assā sāyañca pāto ca dvikkhattuṃ bhattaṃ labhanti. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ ekamekassa assassa pātarāsabhattato ekamekassa bhikkhuno patthapatthapulakaṃ dadeyyāma. Evaṃ ayyā ca na kilamissanti[P 1.0177], assā ca yāpessantī”ti. Te bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā etamatthaṃ ārocetvā “bhante, tumhe patthapatthapulakaṃ paṭiggahetvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā katvā paribhuñjathā”ti yācitvā devasikaṃ patthapatthapulakaṃ paññapesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “tehi assamaṇḍalikāsu bhikkhūnaṃ patthapatthapulakaṃ paññattaṃ hotī”ti.

But why was this allowance established by them for the monks? It is said: 'They were not faithless and unconfident like the people of the southern region. Rather, they were faithful, confident, and considered the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha as their own. One morning, while entering the city for some business, they saw, over two or three days, seven or eight monks with under-robes well-fastened, with upper-robes well-draped, and endowed with proper deportment, who had wandered the entire city for alms-food but received nothing. Seeing this, they thought: ‘These venerable ones, relying on this city, have entered the rains-retreat. A famine is occurring, yet they receive nothing and are extremely weary. We are visitors and cannot prepare daily gruel and meals for them. But our horses receive food twice, in the evening and in the morning. What if we were to give each monk a pattha-measure of barley grains from each horse’s morning meal? In this way, the venerable ones will not be weary, and the horses will be able to sustain themselves.’ They went to the monks, explained the matter, and requested: ‘Venerable sirs, please accept a pattha-measure of barley grains, prepare it as you see fit, and consume it.’ Thus, they established a daily allowance of a pattha-measure of barley grains. Therefore, it is said: ‘By them, a pattha-measure of barley grains was allowed for the monks in the horse enclosures.’”

Paññattanti niccabhattasaṅkhepena ṭhapitaṃ. Idāni bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvātiādīsu pubbaṇhasamayanti divasassa pubbabhāgasamayaṃ, pubbaṇhasamayeti attho. Pubbaṇhe vā samayaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ, pubbaṇhe ekaṃ khaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ labbhati. Nivāsetvāti paridahitvā, vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasenetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi te tato pubbe anivatthā ahesuṃ. Pattacīvaramādāyāti pattaṃ hatthehi cīvaraṃ kāyena ādiyitvā sampaṭicchādetvā, dhāretvāti attho. Yena vā tena vā hi pakārena gaṇhantā ādāyaicceva vuccanti, yathā “samādāyeva pakkamatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.21). Piṇḍaṃ alabhamānāti sakalampi verañjaṃ caritvā tiṭṭhatu piṇḍo, antamaso “aticchathā”ti vācampi alabhamānā.

‘Established’ means it was set up by way of being counted as a regular meal. Now, in phrases such as ‘the monks in the morning, having dressed…’, the term ‘in the morning’ means the time of the early part of the day; that is the meaning of ‘in the morning time’. Alternatively, ‘a time in the morning’ means for a certain period in the morning; it is said to mean ‘for a moment in the morning’. Thus, the accusative case is used here in the sense of continuous duration. ‘Having dressed’ means having put on; this should be understood in the sense of adjusting the dwelling-robe in the monastery, for indeed, they were not undressed before that. ‘Having taken bowl and robe’ means having taken the bowl with the hands and the robe with the body, having covered oneself, that is, having carried them. For indeed, those who take in any way whatsoever are simply said to be ‘having taken’, as in ‘he departs having taken it’. ‘Not receiving alms-food’ means that having wandered through the whole of Verañjā, let alone alms-food, they did not receive even the words, ‘Please accept this.’”

Patthapatthapulakaṃ ārāmaṃ āharitvāti gatagataṭṭhāne laddhaṃ ekamekaṃ patthapatthapulakaṃ gahetvā ārāmaṃ netvā. Udukkhale koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā paribhuñjantīti therānaṃ koci kappiyakārako natthi, yo nesaṃ taṃ gahetvā yāguṃ vā bhattaṃ vā paceyya. Sāmampi pacanaṃ samaṇasāruppaṃ na hoti na ca vaṭṭati. Te evaṃ no sallahukavuttitā ca bhavissati, sāmapākaparimocanañcāti aṭṭha aṭṭha [V 1.0135] janā vā dasa dasa janā vā ekato hutvā udukkhale koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā sakaṃ sakaṃ paṭivīsaṃ udakena temetvā paribhuñjanti. Evaṃ paribhuñjitvā appossukkā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti[M 1.0146]. Bhagavato pana te assavāṇijā patthapulakañca denti, tadupiyañca sappimadhusakkaraṃ. Taṃ āyasmā ānando āharitvā silāyaṃ pisati. Puññavatā paṇḍitapurisena kataṃ manāpameva hoti. Atha naṃ pisitvā sappiādīhi sammā yojetvā bhagavato [P 1.0178] upanāmesi. Athettha devatā dibbojaṃ pakkhipanti. Taṃ bhagavā paribhuñjati. Paribhuñjitvā phalasamāpattiyā kālaṃ atināmeti. Na tato paṭṭhāya piṇḍāya carati.

‘Having brought a pattha-measure of barley grains to the monastery’ means having taken each pattha-measure of barley grains obtained in every place they went and carried it to the monastery. ‘Having pounded and pounded it in a mortar, they consumed it’ means that the elders had no suitable lay attendant who might take it and cook gruel or a meal for them. Moreover, cooking for themselves is not suitable for ascetics, nor is it allowable. Thinking, ‘In this way, our livelihood will be light, and we will be freed from the fault of cooking ourselves,’ they gathered in groups of eight or ten, pounded and pounded the barley in a mortar, moistened their own portions with water, and consumed them. Having consumed it thus, being unconcerned, they practiced the ascetic’s duties. But to the Blessed One, those horse traders gave a pattha-measure of barley and also ghee, honey, and sugar suitable for it. The Venerable Ānanda brought this and ground it on a stone slab. What is done by a meritorious, wise person is indeed pleasing. Then, having ground it, he mixed it well with ghee and so on and offered it to the Blessed One. Then deities placed divine nutritive essence into it. The Blessed One consumed it. Having consumed it, he passed the time in the attainment of fruition. From that time onwards, he did not go on alms-round.

Kiṃ panānandatthero tadā bhagavato upaṭṭhāko hotīti? Hoti, no ca kho upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ laddhā. Bhagavato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsativassantare nibaddhupaṭṭhāko nāma natthi. Kadāci nāgasamālatthero bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhāsi, kadāci nāgitatthero, kadāci meghiyatthero, kadāci upavāṇatthero, kadāci sāgatatthero, kadāci sunakkhatto licchaviputto. Te attano ruciyā upaṭṭhahitvā yadā icchanti tadā pakkamanti. Ānandatthero tesu tesu upaṭṭhahantesu appossukko hoti, pakkantesu sayameva vattapaṭipattiṃ karoti. Bhagavāpi kiñcāpi me ñātiseṭṭho upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ na tāva labhati, atha kho evarūpesu ṭhānesu ayameva patirūpoti adhivāsesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “āyasmā panānando patthapulakaṃ silāyaṃ pisitvā bhagavato upanāmesi, taṃ bhagavā paribhuñjatī”ti.

‘But was the Venerable Elder Ānanda the Blessed One’s attendant at that time?’ He was, but not one who had obtained the position of attendant. For indeed, within the first twenty years of the Blessed One's enlightenment, there was no one called a permanent attendant. Sometimes the Elder Nāgasamāla attended upon the Blessed One, sometimes the Elder Nāgita, sometimes the Elder Meghiya, sometimes the Elder Upavāṇa, sometimes the Elder Sāgata, and sometimes Sunakkhatta the Licchavi-son. They attended according to their own wish, and when they desired, they departed. While they were attending, the Elder Ānanda was unconcerned; when they had departed, he himself performed the duties and obligations. The Blessed One also, thinking, ‘Although my most excellent relative has not yet obtained the position of attendant, nevertheless in such situations he alone is suitable,’ consented. Therefore it was said: ‘The Venerable Ānanda, having ground the barley grains on a stone slab, offered them to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One consumed them.’”

Nanu ca manussā dubbhikkhakāle ativiya ussāhajātā puññāni karonti, attanā abhuñjitvāpi bhikkhūnaṃ dātabbaṃ maññanti. Te tadā kasmā kaṭacchubhikkhampi na adaṃsu? Ayañca verañjo brāhmaṇo mahatā ussāhena bhagavantaṃ vassāvāsaṃ yāci, so kasmā bhagavato atthibhāvampi na jānātīti? Vuccate – mārāvaṭṭanāya. Verañjañhi brāhmaṇaṃ bhagavato santikā pakkantamattameva sakalañca nagaraṃ samantā ca yojanamattaṃ yattha sakkā purebhattaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā paccāgantuṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ māro āvaṭṭetvā mohetvā sabbesaṃ asallakkhaṇabhāvaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Tasmā na koci antamaso sāmīcikammampi kattabbaṃ maññittha.

Is it not so that in a time of famine, people become exceedingly energetic and perform meritorious deeds, thinking it right to give to the monks even if they themselves do not eat? Why then did they not give even a ladleful of alms? And this brahmin of Verañjā, with great effort, invited the Blessed One for the rains-residence; why did he not even know of the Blessed One's existence? It is said: because of Māra's bewilderment. For just as the brahmin of Verañjā had departed from the presence of the Blessed One, Māra bewildered and deluded the entire city and the surrounding area for a yojana—wherever it was possible to go for alms in the forenoon and return—causing a state of unmindfulness in all, and then he departed. Therefore, no one thought that even a respectful gesture ought to be performed.

Kiṃ [M 1.0147] pana bhagavāpi mārāvaṭṭanaṃ ajānitvāva tattha vassaṃ upagatoti? No ajānitvā. Atha kasmā campā-sāvatthi-rājagahādīnaṃ aññatarasmiṃ na upagatoti? Tiṭṭhantu campā-sāvatthi-rājagahādīni, sacepi bhagavā tasmiṃ saṃvacchare [P 1.0179] uttarakuruṃ vā tidasapuraṃ vā gantvā vassaṃ upagaccheyya, tampi māro āvaṭṭeyya. So kira taṃ saṃvaccharaṃ ativiya āghātena [V 1.0136] pariyuṭṭhitacitto ahosi. Idha pana bhagavā imaṃ atirekakāraṇaṃ addasa – “assavāṇijā bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissantī”ti. Tasmā verañjāyameva vassaṃ upagacchi.

What then, did the Blessed One enter upon the rains-residence there without knowing of Māra's bewilderment? Not without knowing. Then why did he not enter upon it in one of the cities such as Campā, Sāvatthī, or Rājagaha? Let Campā, Sāvatthī, and Rājagaha be. Even if the Blessed One, in that year, had gone to Uttarakuru or to the city of the Tidasas and entered upon the rains-residence, Māra would have bewildered that place too. It is said that in that year, his mind was overcome by exceedingly fierce enmity. But here, the Blessed One saw this additional reason: 'The horse merchants will provide support for the monks.' Therefore, he entered upon the rains-residence in Verañjā itself.

Kiṃ pana māro vāṇijake āvaṭṭetuṃ na sakkotīti? No na sakkoti, te pana āvaṭṭitapariyosāne āgamiṃsu. Paṭinivattitvā kasmā na āvaṭṭetīti? Avisahatāya. Na hi so tathāgatassa abhihaṭabhikkhāya nibaddhadānassa appitavattassa antarāyaṃ kātuṃ visahati. Catunnañhi na sakkā antarāyo kātuṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Tathāgatassa abhihaṭabhikkhāsaṅkhepena vā nibaddhadānassa appitavattasaṅkhepena vā pariccattānaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ. Buddhānaṃ jīvitassa na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ. Asītiyā anubyañjanānaṃ byāmappabhāya vā na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ. Candimasūriyadevabrahmānampi hi pabhā tathāgatassa anubyañjanabyāmappabhāppadesaṃ patvā vihatānubhāvā honti. Buddhānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇassa na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātunti imesaṃ catunnaṃ na sakkā kenaci antarāyo kātuṃ. Tasmā mārena akatantarāyaṃ bhikkhaṃ bhagavā sasāvakasaṅgho tadā paribhuñjatīti veditabbo.

What then, is Māra not able to bewilder the merchants? It is not that he is not able; he is indeed able. However, they arrived at the end of the period of bewilderment. Having returned, why did he not bewilder them again? Because of not daring. For he does not dare to create an obstacle to the alms brought forth for the Tathāgata, to a constant donation, or to a dedicated offering. Indeed, an obstacle cannot be created by anyone for four things. For which four? No one can create an obstacle for the four requisites that have been given up for the Tathāgata, whether categorized as alms brought forth, as a constant donation, or as a dedicated offering. No one can create an obstacle to the life of the Buddhas. No one can create an obstacle to the eighty minor characteristics or the fathom-long radiance. Indeed, even the radiance of the moon, sun, devas, and brahmās, upon reaching the region of the Tathāgata's minor characteristics and fathom-long radiance, becomes devoid of power. No one can create an obstacle to the omniscience of the Buddhas. An obstacle cannot be created by anyone for these four things. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One, together with the community of his disciples, at that time partook of alms for which no obstacle was made by Māra.

Evaṃ paribhuñjanto ca ekadivasaṃ assosi kho bhagavā udukkhalasaddanti bhagavā patthapatthapulakaṃ koṭṭentānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ musalasaṅghaṭṭajanitaṃ udukkhalasaddaṃ suṇi. Tato paraṃ jānantāpi tathāgatāti evamādi yaṃ parato “kinnu kho so, ānanda, udukkhalasaddo”ti pucchi, tassa parihāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – tathāgatā nāma jānantāpi sace tādisaṃ pucchākāraṇaṃ hoti, pucchanti. Sace pana tādisaṃ pucchākāraṇaṃ natthi, jānantāpi [P 1.0180] na pucchanti. Yasmā pana buddhānaṃ ajānanaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā ajānantāpīti na vuttaṃ. Kālaṃ viditvā pucchantīti sace tassā pucchāya so kālo hoti, evaṃ taṃ kālaṃ viditvā pucchanti; sace na hoti[M 1.0148], evampi kālaṃ viditvāva na pucchanti. Evaṃ pucchantāpi ca atthasaṃhitaṃ tathāgatā pucchanti, yaṃ atthanissitaṃ kāraṇanissitaṃ, tadeva pucchanti, no anatthasaṃhitaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā anatthasaṃhite setughāto tathāgatānaṃ. Setu vuccati maggo, maggeneva tādisassa vacanassa ghāto, samucchedoti vuttaṃ hoti.

And while partaking thus, one day the Blessed One heard the sound of a mortar. The Blessed One heard the sound of a small mortar, produced by the striking of pestles, of the monks pounding coarse grain measure by measure. After that, the words beginning with 'Tathāgatas, though knowing...' were spoken for the purpose of showing the answer to the question he then asked: 'What, Ānanda, is that sound of a small mortar?' Herein, this is the summary explanation: Tathāgatas, though knowing, ask if there is such a reason for asking. But if there is no such reason for asking, though knowing, they do not ask. And because for Buddhas there is no such thing as not knowing, it was not said 'though not knowing.' 'Knowing the time, they ask' means: if it is the right time for that question, then knowing that time, they ask; if it is not, even so, it is only after knowing the time that they do not ask. And even when asking, Tathāgatas ask what is connected with benefit. They ask only that which is based on benefit, based on a cause; they do not ask what is not connected with benefit. Why? Because in what is not connected with benefit, there is for the Tathāgatas the destruction of the bridge. The path is called the bridge; by the path itself there is the destruction, the complete cutting off, of such speech. This is what is meant.

Idāni atthasaṃhitanti ettha yaṃ atthasannissitaṃ vacanaṃ tathāgatā pucchanti, taṃ dassento “dvīhākārehī”ti ādimāha. Tattha ākārehīti kāraṇehi. Dhammaṃ vā desessāmāti aṭṭhuppattiyuttaṃ suttaṃ vā pubbacaritakāraṇayuttaṃ jātakaṃ vā kathayissāma. Sāvakānaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ [V 1.0137] paññapessāmāti sāvakānaṃ vā tāya pucchāya vītikkamaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā garukaṃ vā lahukaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāma āṇaṃ ṭhapessāmāti.

Now, herein, regarding 'connected with benefit': showing which speech based on benefit the Tathāgatas ask, he spoke the words beginning with 'for two reasons'. Therein, 'reasons' means 'causes'. 'Or, we will teach the Dhamma' means: we will relate a sutta connected with the occasion of its arising, or a Jātaka connected with a cause from past conduct. 'Or, we will lay down a training rule for the disciples' means: for the disciples, having made a transgression evident through that question, we will lay down a heavy or a light training rule; we will establish a command. It is for these reasons that they ask.

Atha kho bhagavā…pe… etamatthaṃ ārocesīti ettha natthi kiñci vattabbaṃ. Pubbe vuttameva hi bhikkhūnaṃ patthapatthapulakapaṭilābhaṃ sallahukavuttitaṃ sāmapākaparimocanañca ārocento etamatthaṃ ārocesīti vuccati. “Sādhu sādhu, ānandā”ti idaṃ pana bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sampahaṃsento āha. Sādhukāraṃ pana datvā dvīsu ākāresu ekaṃ gahetvā dhammaṃ desento āha – “tumhehi, ānanda, sappurisehi vijitaṃ, pacchimā janatā sālimaṃsodanaṃ atimaññissatī”ti. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – tumhehi, ānanda, sappurisehi evaṃ dubbhikkhe dullabhapiṇḍe imāya sallahukavuttitāya iminā ca sallekhena vijitaṃ. Kiṃ vijitanti? Dubbhikkhaṃ vijitaṃ, lobho vijito, icchācāro vijito. Kathaṃ? “Ayaṃ verañjā dubbhikkhā, samantato pana anantarā gāmanigamā phalabhāranamitasassā subhikkhā sulabhapiṇḍā. Evaṃ santepi bhagavā idheva amhe niggaṇhitvā vasatī”ti ekabhikkhussapi cintā vā vighāto vā natthi. Evaṃ tāva dubbhikkhaṃ vijitaṃ abhibhūtaṃ attano vase vattitaṃ.

Regarding the passage, 'Then the Blessed One… and so on… explained this matter,' there is nothing to be said. For it has already been said that when he was informing of the monks' obtaining of a measure of horse-gram each, their light way of living, and their release from the fault of cooking for themselves, he is said to have 'explained this matter.' The Blessed One said, 'Good, good, Ānanda,' wishing to greatly delight the Venerable Ānanda. And having given his approval, taking one of two reasons, he taught the Dhamma, saying: 'By you good persons, Ānanda, it has been conquered; the future generation will look down upon fine rice with meat.' Herein, this is the intended meaning: By you good persons, Ānanda, in this way during a famine when alms are difficult to obtain, it has been conquered by this light way of living and by this austerity. What has been conquered? The famine has been conquered, greed has been conquered, wrongful desire has been conquered. How? 'This Verañjā has a scarcity of food, but the surrounding, adjacent villages and towns have crops bent with the weight of their fruit, have an abundance of food, and have easily obtainable alms. Even so, the Blessed One is restraining us and dwelling right here'—for not even a single monk is there such a thought or vexation. Thus, firstly, the famine has been conquered, overwhelmed, and brought under one's own control.

Kathaṃ lobho vijito? “Ayaṃ verañjā dubbhikkhā, samantato pana anantarā gāmanigamā phalabhāranamitasassā subhikkhā sulabhapiṇḍā[P 1.0181]. Handa mayaṃ tattha gantvā paribhuñjissāmā”ti lobhavasena ekabhikkhunāpi ratticchedo vā “pacchimikāya tattha vassaṃ upagacchāmā”ti vassacchedo vā na kato. Evaṃ lobho vijito.

How was greed conquered? 'This Verañjā has a scarcity of food, but the surrounding, adjacent villages and towns... (and so on)... Come, let us go there and partake.' Out of greed, not even a single monk broke his stay for a night, nor did any break the Rains-residence with the thought, 'Let us enter the Rains-residence there in the latter period.' Thus, greed was conquered.

Kathaṃ [M 1.0149] icchācāro vijito? Ayaṃ verañjā dubbhikkhā, ime ca manussā amhe dve tayo māse vasantepi na kismiñci maññanti. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ guṇavāṇijjaṃ katvā “asuko bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī…pe… asuko chaḷabhiññoti evaṃ manussānaṃ aññamaññaṃ pakāsetvā kucchiṃ paṭijaggitvā pacchā sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhaheyyāmā”ti ekabhikkhunāpi evarūpā icchā na uppāditā. Evaṃ icchācāro vijito abhibhūto attano vase vattitoti.

How was wrongful desire conquered? 'This Verañjā has a scarcity of food, and these people do not regard us in any way, even though we have been dwelling for two or three months. What if we were to engage in the trade of virtues, revealing to the people about one another, "Such-and-such a monk is an obtainer of the first jhāna... such-and-such a monk has the six supernormal knowledges," and having thus looked after our bellies, we could later establish ourselves in virtue?'—such a base desire was not produced by even a single monk. Thus, wrongful desire was conquered, overwhelmed, and brought under one's own control.

Anāgate pana pacchimā janatā vihāre nisinnā appakasireneva labhitvāpi “kiṃ idaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ atikilinnaṃ aloṇaṃ atiloṇaṃ anambilaṃ accambilaṃ, ko iminā attho”ti ādinā nayena sālimaṃsodanaṃ atimaññissati, oññātaṃ avaññātaṃ karissati. Atha vā janapado [V 1.0138] nāma na sabbakālaṃ dubbhikkho hoti. Ekadā dubbhikkho hoti, ekadā subhikkho hoti. Svāyaṃ yadā subhikkho bhavissati, tadā tumhākaṃ sappurisānaṃ imāya paṭipattiyā pasannā manussā bhikkhūnaṃ yāgukhajjakādippabhedena anekappakāraṃ sālivikatiṃ maṃsodanañca dātabbaṃ maññissanti. Taṃ tumhe nissāya uppannaṃ sakkāraṃ tumhākaṃ sabrahmacārīsaṅkhātā pacchimā janatā tumhākaṃ antare nisīditvā anubhavamānāva atimaññissati, tappaccayaṃ mānañca omānañca karissati. Kathaṃ? Kasmā ettakaṃ pakkaṃ, kiṃ tumhākaṃ bhājanāni natthi, yattha attano santakaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapeyyāthāti.

But in the future, the later generation of monks, sitting in the monastery, even having obtained it with little difficulty, will look down upon fine rice with meat, by the method beginning with, 'What is this? It is undercooked, too soft, unsalted, too salty, not sour, too sour—what is the use of this?' They will treat it with contempt and disdain. Furthermore, a country is not always in famine. Sometimes there is famine, and sometimes there is abundance. When that country has abundance, then people, pleased by this practice of you good persons, will think that various kinds of special preparations of fine rice and rice with meat, distinguished as gruel, hard food, and so on, should be given to the monks. That honor which has arisen on account of you, the later generation, known as your companions in the holy life, sitting in your midst and partaking of it, will look down upon it. On account of that, they will produce conceit and contempt. How so? 'Why was so much cooked? Do you not have your own bowls wherein you could put your own portion and keep it?'

Dubbhikkhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Famine is concluded.

Mahāmoggallānassasīhanādakathā

The Account of Mahāmoggallāna's Lion's Roar

17. Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallānotiādīsu āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ, garugāravasappatissādhivacanametaṃ. Mahāmoggallānoti mahā ca so guṇamahantatāya moggallāno ca gottenāti mahāmoggallāno. Etadavocāti etaṃ avoca. Idāni vattabbaṃ “etarahi bhante”tiādivacanaṃ dasseti. Kasmā avoca? Thero kira pabbajitvā sattame divase sāvakapāramiñāṇassa [P 1.0182] matthakaṃ patto, satthārāpi mahiddhikatāya etadagge ṭhapito. So taṃ attano mahiddhikataṃ nissāya cintesi – “ayaṃ verañjā dubbhikkhā, bhikkhū ca kilamanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ pathaviṃ parivattetvā bhikkhū pappaṭakojaṃ bhojeyya”nti. Athassa [M 1.0150] etadahosi – “sace panāhaṃ bhagavato santike viharanto bhagavantaṃ ayācitvā evaṃ kareyyaṃ, na metaṃ assa patirūpaṃ; yugaggāho viya bhagavatā saddhiṃ kato bhaveyyā”ti. Tasmā yācitukāmo āgantvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca.

17. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—here, "Venerable" is a term of affection, a respectful and reverential expression. "Mahāmoggallāna" means he was great due to the greatness of his virtues, and Moggallāna was his clan name—thus, Mahāmoggallāna. "He said this" means he spoke this. Now, this indicates the words to be spoken, beginning with "now, venerable sir." Why did he speak thus? It is said that the Elder, seven days after his ordination, attained the pinnacle of a disciple's knowledge of the perfections and was placed by the Teacher at the forefront for his great psychic power. Relying on his own great psychic power, he thought: "This Verañjā is experiencing famine, and the monks are suffering. What if I were to overturn the earth and have the monks eat the earth-essence?" Then it occurred to him: "But if I were to do this while dwelling near the Blessed One without first asking him, it would not be fitting for me; it would be like seizing the yoke with the Blessed One." Therefore, desiring to ask, he came to the Blessed One and said this.

Heṭṭhimatalaṃ sampannanti pathaviyā kira heṭṭhimatale pathavimaṇḍo pathavojo pathavi-pappaṭako atthi, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Tattha sampannanti madhuraṃ, sādurasanti attho. Yatheva hi “tatrassa rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo cā”ti (ma. ni. 2.48) ettha madhuraphaloti attho; evamidhāpi sampannanti madhuraṃ sādurasanti veditabbaṃ. Seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ anīḷakanti idaṃ panassa madhuratāya opammanidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Khuddamadhunti khuddakamakkhikāhi katamadhu. Anīḷakanti nimmakkhikaṃ nimmakkhikaṇḍakaṃ parisuddhaṃ. Etaṃ kira madhu sabbamadhūhi aggañca seṭṭhañca surasañca ojavantañca. Tenāha – “seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ anīḷakaṃ evamassāda”nti.

Regarding 'The lower level is consummate': it is said that in the lower level of the earth there exists the earth-disk, the earth-essence, and the earth-crust. It is with reference to this that he speaks. Therein, 'consummate' means sweet and of pleasant taste. Just as in the phrase, "There, that tree has consummate fruit and is laden with fruit" (MN 2.48), the meaning is "having sweet fruit"; so too here, 'consummate' should be understood as sweet and of pleasant taste. The phrase "like honey from small bees, free from the comb" is spoken to illustrate its sweetness by way of simile. "Honey from small bees" refers to honey made by small bees. "Free from the comb" means without bees or bee larvae, perfectly pure. This honey is said to be the foremost, the best, the most delightful, and the most nutritious among all honeys. Hence it is said: "Just like honey from small bees, free from the comb, so is its taste."

Sādhāhaṃ[V 1.0139], bhanteti sādhu ahaṃ, bhante. Ettha sādhūti āyācanavacanametaṃ. Pathaviparivattanaṃ āyācanto hi thero bhagavantaṃ evamāha. Parivatteyyanti ukkujjeyyaṃ, heṭṭhimatalaṃ uparimaṃ kareyyaṃ. Kasmā? Evañhi kate sukhena bhikkhū pappaṭakojaṃ pathavimaṇḍaṃ paribhuñjissantīti. Atha bhagavā ananuññātukāmopi theraṃ sīhanādaṃ nadāpetuṃ pucchi – “ye pana te, moggallāna, pathavinissitā pāṇā te kathaṃ karissasī”ti. Ye pathavinissitā gāmanigamādīsu pāṇā, te pathaviyā parivattiyamānāya ākāse [P 1.0183] saṇṭhātuṃ asakkonte kathaṃ karissasi, kattha ṭhapessasīti? Atha thero bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitabhāvānurūpaṃ attano iddhānubhāvaṃ pakāsento “ekāhaṃ, bhante”tiādimāha. Tassattho – ekaṃ ahaṃ bhante hatthaṃ yathā ayaṃ mahāpathavī evaṃ abhinimminissāmi, pathavisadisaṃ karissāmi. Evaṃ katvā ye pathavinissitā pāṇā te ekasmiṃ hatthatale ṭhite pāṇe tato dutiyahatthatale saṅkāmento viya tattha saṅkāmessāmīti.

"Very well, I, Venerable Sir." Here, "very well" is a word of request. The Elder, requesting the turning of the earth, addressed the Blessed One thus. "I would turn it over" means I would turn it upside down, I would make the lower surface the upper. Why? Because if this is done, the monks could comfortably partake of the earth-crust and earth-essence. Then the Blessed One, though unwilling to grant permission, asked the Elder a question in order to let him utter a lion's roar: "But those beings, Moggallāna, who depend on the earth, what will you do with them?" That is: those beings dependent on the earth in villages, towns, and so on—when the earth is being turned over, being unable to remain in the sky—what will you do with them, where will you place them? Then the Elder, displaying his psychic power in accordance with his being placed by the Blessed One at the forefront, said, "One hand, Venerable Sir," and so on. The meaning is: "I, Venerable Sir, will create one hand to be just like this great earth; I will make it similar to the earth. Having done so, I will transfer the beings dependent on the earth there, just as one might transfer beings situated on one palm to a second palm."

Athassa bhagavā āyācanaṃ paṭikkhipanto “alaṃ moggallānā”tiādimāha. Tattha alanti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Vipallāsampi sattā paṭilabheyyunti viparītaggāhampi sattā sampāpuṇeyyuṃ. Kathaṃ? Ayaṃ nu kho pathavī[M 1.0151], udāhu na ayanti. Atha vā amhākaṃ nu kho ayaṃ gāmo, udāhu aññesa”nti. Evaṃ nigamajanapadakhettārāmādīsu. Na vā esa vipallāso, acinteyyo hi iddhimato iddhivisayo. Evaṃ pana vipallāsaṃ paṭilabheyyuṃ – idaṃ dubbhikkhaṃ nāma na idāniyeva hoti, anāgatepi bhavissati. Tadā bhikkhū tādisaṃ iddhimantaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ kuto labhissanti? Te sotāpanna-sakadāgāmi-anāgāmi-sukkhavipassaka-jhānalābhi-paṭisambhidāppattakhīṇāsavāpi samānā iddhibalābhāvā parakulāni piṇḍāya upasaṅkamissanti. Tatra manussānaṃ evaṃ bhavissati – “buddhakāle bhikkhū sikkhāsu paripūrakārino ahesuṃ. Te guṇe nibbattetvā dubbhikkhakāle pathaviṃ parivattetvā pappaṭakojaṃ paribhuñjiṃsu. Idāni pana sikkhāya paripūrakārino natthi. Yadi siyuṃ, tatheva kareyyuṃ. Na amhākaṃ yaṃ kiñci pakkaṃ vā āmaṃ vā khādituṃ dadeyyu”nti. Evaṃ tesuyeva ariyapuggalesu “natthi ariyapuggalā”ti imaṃ vipallāsaṃ paṭilabheyyuṃ. Vipallāsavasena ca ariye garahantā upavadantā apāyupagā bhaveyyuṃ. Tasmā mā te rucci pathaviṃ parivattetunti.

Then the Blessed One, refusing his request, said, "Enough, Moggallāna," and so on. Herein, "enough" is a term of refusal. "Beings might even grasp a distortion" means beings might arrive at a wrong view. How? "Is this the earth, or is it not?" Or, "Is this our village, or is it someone else’s?" And so on for towns, countries, fields, and parks. Or perhaps this is not the distortion, for the sphere of psychic power of one who possesses it is inconceivable. Rather, they might grasp a distortion in this way: This famine is not just happening now; it will occur in the future too. At that time, where will monks find such a fellow practitioner endowed with psychic powers? Though they may be stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, or arahants who are dry-insight meditators, who have attained jhāna, or who have reached the analytical knowledges—lacking this psychic power—they will have to approach other families for alms. There, it will occur to people: 'In the Buddha’s time, monks were perfect in their training. They developed special qualities and, during the famine, overturned the earth and partook of the earth-essence. But now, there are none who are perfect in the training. If there were, they would do the same; they would not allow us to give them anything to eat, whether cooked or raw.' Thus, regarding these very noble individuals, people might grasp the distortion that "there are no noble individuals." And by way of this distortion, by blaming and disparaging the noble ones, they would be bound for a state of woe. Therefore, let it not please you to overturn the earth.

Atha thero imaṃ yācanaṃ alabhamāno aññaṃ yācanto “sādhu, bhante”tiādimāha. Tampissa bhagavā paṭikkhipanto “alaṃ [P 1.0184] moggallānā”tiādimāha. Tattha kiñcāpi na vuttaṃ “vipallāsampi sattā paṭilabheyyu”nti, atha kho pubbe vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ; atthopi cassa vuttasadisameva veditabbo. Yadi pana bhagavā anujāneyya, thero kiṃ kareyyāti? Mahāsamuddaṃ ekena [V 1.0140] padavītihārena atikkamitabbaṃ mātikāmattaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā naḷerupucimandato uttarakuruabhimukhaṃ maggaṃ nīharitvā uttarakuruṃ gamanāgamanasampanne ṭhāne katvā dasseyya, yathā bhikkhū gocaragāmaṃ viya yathāsukhaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā nikkhameyyunti.

Then the Elder, not obtaining this request, made another request, saying, “Very well, venerable sir,” and so on. The Blessed One, rejecting that request of his as well, said, “Enough, Moggallāna,” and so on. Therein, although it was not said, “Beings might even attain a perversion,” it should nevertheless be understood in the same way as previously stated; and its meaning should be known as just like what was said. But if the Blessed One were to consent, what would the Elder do? He would, having resolved the great ocean to be a mere water channel to be crossed with a single footstep, bring forth a path from the Naḷeru-pucimanda tree facing Uttarakuru, and having made Uttarakuru a place complete with paths for going and coming, show it, so that the monks, like going to an alms-resort village, might enter for alms-food according to their comfort and then depart.

Niṭṭhitā mahāmoggallānassa sīhanādakathā.

The Discourse on the Lion's Roar of Mahāmoggallāna is concluded.

Vinayapaññattiyācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Request for the Vinaya Regulation.

18. Idāni āyasmā upāli vinayapaññattiyā mūlato pabhuti nidānaṃ dassetuṃ sāriputtattherassa sikkhāpadapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vitakkuppādaṃ dassento [M 1.0152] “atha kho āyasmato sāriputtassā”tiādimāha. Tattha rahogatassāti rahasi gatassa. Paṭisallīnassāti sallīnassa ekībhāvaṃ gatassa. Katamesānanti atītesu vipassīādīsu buddhesu katamesaṃ. Ciraṃ assa ṭhiti, cirā vā assa ṭhitīti ciraṭṭhitikaṃ. Sesamettha uttānapadatthameva.

18. Now, the Venerable Upāli, in order to show the source of the Vinaya regulation beginning from its root, wishing to show the arising of a thought connected with the training rule in the Elder Sāriputta, said, “Then, to the Venerable Sāriputta…” and so on. Therein, rahogatassa means: gone to a secluded place. Paṭisallīnassa means: being well absorbed in a single object, or having gone to a state of solitude. Katamesānaṃ means: among the past Buddhas such as Vipassī, of which ones? Ciraṭṭhitikaṃ is so called because: its stability is long (ciraṃ assa ṭhiti), or its stability is long (cirā assa ṭhiti). The rest here has only an obvious word-meaning.

Kiṃ pana thero imaṃ attano parivitakkaṃ sayaṃ vinicchinituṃ na sakkotīti? Vuccate – sakkoti ca na sakkoti ca. Ayañhi imesaṃ nāma buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ na ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ahosi, imesaṃ ciraṭṭhitikanti ettakaṃ sakkoti vinicchinituṃ. Iminā pana kāraṇena na ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ahosi, iminā ciraṭṭhitikanti etaṃ na sakkoti. Mahāpadumatthero panāha – “etampi soḷasavidhāya paññāya matthakaṃ pattassa aggasāvakassa na bhāriyaṃ, sammāsambuddhena pana saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne vasantassa sayaṃ vinicchayakaraṇaṃ tulaṃ chaḍḍetvā hatthena tulanasadisaṃ hotīti bhagavantaṃyeva upasaṅkamitvā pucchī”ti. Athassa bhagavā taṃ vissajjento “bhagavato ca sāriputta vipassissā”tiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthameva.

But is the Elder not able to decide this thought of his by himself? It is said: He is able, and he is not able. For he is able to decide this much: “The Dispensation of these certain Buddhas was not long-lasting, and the Dispensation of these was long-lasting.” But this he is not able to decide: “For this reason it was not long-lasting, and for this reason it was long-lasting.” However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: “Even this is not a heavy burden for the chief disciple who has reached the pinnacle of the sixteen-fold wisdom. But for one dwelling in the same place with a Perfectly Enlightened One, making a decision by oneself is like weighing with the hand after discarding the scales; thus, he approached the Blessed One himself and asked.” Then the Blessed One, explaining it to him, said, “Of the Blessed One Vipassī, Sāriputta…” and so on. That has only an obvious meaning.

19. Puna thero kāraṇaṃ pucchanto ko nu kho, bhante, hetūtiādimāha. Tattha ko nu kho bhanteti kāraṇapucchā[P 1.0185], tassa katamo nu kho bhanteti attho. Hetu paccayoti ubhayametaṃ kāraṇādhivacanaṃ; kāraṇañhi yasmā tena tassa phalaṃ hinoti pavattati, tasmā hetūti vuccati. Yasmā taṃ paṭicca eti pavattati, tasmā paccayoti vuccati. Evaṃ atthato ekampi vohāravasena ca vacanasiliṭṭhatāya ca tatra tatra etaṃ ubhayampi vuccati. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

19. Again, the Elder, asking for the reason, said, “What indeed, venerable sir, is the cause?” and so on. Therein, “What indeed, venerable sir?” is a question about the reason; its meaning is, “Which one indeed, venerable sir?” Hetu (cause) and paccaya (condition)—both of these are designations for a reason. For, because of a reason (kāraṇa), its fruit is impelled and proceeds (hinoti pavattati); therefore, it is called hetu. Because depending on it, the fruit comes and proceeds (eti pavattati); therefore, it is called paccaya. Thus, although being one in meaning, both of these are used here and there by way of convention and for the smoothness of the words. The rest here has only an obvious meaning.

Idāni [V 1.0141] taṃ hetuñca paccayañca dassetuṃ “bhagavā ca sāriputta vipassī”tiādimāha. Tattha kilāsuno ahesunti na ālasiyakilāsuno, na hi buddhānaṃ ālasiyaṃ vā osannavīriyatā vā atthi. Buddhā hi ekassa vā dvinnaṃ vā sakalacakkavāḷassa vā dhammaṃ desentā samakeneva ussāhena dhammaṃ desenti, na parisāya appabhāvaṃ disvā osannavīriyā honti, nāpi mahantabhāvaṃ disvā ussannavīriyā. Yathā hi sīho migarājā sattannaṃ divasānaṃ accayena gocarāya pakkanto khuddake vā mahante vā [M 1.0153] pāṇe ekasadiseneva vegena dhāvati. Taṃ kissa hetu? “Mā me javo parihāyī”ti. Evaṃ buddhā appakāya vā mahatiyā vā parisāya samakeneva ussāhena dhammaṃ desenti. Taṃ kissa hetu? “Mā no dhammagarutā parihāyī”ti. Dhammagaruno hi buddhā dhammagāravāti.

Now, to show that cause and that condition, he said, “The Blessed One Vipassī, Sāriputta…” and so on. Therein, kilāsuno ahesuṃ (“they were weary”) means they were not weary from laziness; for Buddhas have no laziness or slackened energy. Indeed, Buddhas, when teaching the Dhamma to one, or to two, or to a whole cosmos, teach the Dhamma with equal exertion. They do not become of slackened energy upon seeing a small assembly, nor do they become of heightened energy upon seeing a large one. Just as a lion, the king of beasts, after seven days have passed, having set out for its feeding ground, runs with the very same speed at small or large creatures. For what reason? So that he may think, “May my swiftness not decline.” In the same way, Buddhas teach the Dhamma to a small or a large assembly with equal exertion. For what reason? So that they may think, “May our respect for the Dhamma not decline.” For Buddhas have gravity towards the Dhamma, reverence for the Dhamma.

Yathā pana amhākaṃ bhagavā mahāsamuddaṃ pūrayamāno viya vitthārena dhammaṃ desesi, evaṃ te na desesuṃ. Kasmā? Sattānaṃ apparajakkhatāya. Tesaṃ kira kāle dīghāyukā sattā apparajakkhā ahesuṃ. Te catusaccapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ ekagāthampi sutvā dhammaṃ abhisamenti, tasmā na vitthārena dhammaṃ desesuṃ. Teneva kāraṇena appakañca nesaṃ ahosi suttaṃ…pe… vedallanti. Tattha suttādīnaṃ nānattaṃ paṭhamasaṅgītivaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva.

But just as our Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail, as if filling the great ocean, in that way they did not teach. Why? Because of beings having little dust. It is said that in their time, long-lived beings had little dust. Having heard even a single verse connected with the Four Truths, they would penetrate the Dhamma; therefore, they did not teach the Dhamma in detail. For that very reason, their Sutta… and so on… Vedalla was also scant. Therein, the diversity of the Suttas and so on was already spoken of in the Explanation of the First Council.

Apaññattaṃ sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadanti sāvakānaṃ niddosatāya dosānurūpato paññapetabbaṃ sattāpattikkhandhavasena āṇāsikkhāpadaṃ apaññattaṃ. Anuddiṭṭhaṃ [P 1.0186] pātimokkhanti anvaddhamāsaṃ āṇāpātimokkhaṃ anuddiṭṭhaṃ ahosi. Ovādapātimokkhameva te uddisiṃsu; tampi ca no anvaddhamāsaṃ. Tathā hi vipassī bhagavā channaṃ channaṃ vassānaṃ sakiṃ sakiṃ ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisi; tañca kho sāmaṃyeva. Sāvakā panassa attano attano vasanaṭṭhānesu na uddisiṃsu. Sakalajambudīpe ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne bandhumatiyā rājadhāniyā kheme migadāye vipassissa bhagavato vasanaṭṭhāne sabbopi bhikkhusaṅgho uposathaṃ akāsi. Tañca kho saṅghuposathameva; na gaṇuposathaṃ, na puggaluposathaṃ, na pārisuddhiuposathaṃ, na adhiṭṭhānuposathaṃ.

‘The training rule was not laid down for the disciples’ means that the disciplinary training rule, which should be laid down in accordance with a fault by way of the seven groups of offenses, was not laid down for the disciples because of their state of being without fault. ‘The Pātimokkha was not recited’ means that the disciplinary Pātimokkha was not recited every half-month. They recited only the advisory Pātimokkha, and that too not every half-month. To elaborate, the Blessed One Vipassī recited the advisory Pātimokkha only once every six years, and that too by himself. His disciples, however, did not recite it in their own respective dwelling places. In the entire Jambudīpa, the entire community of bhikkhus performed the Uposatha in only one place: in the Migadāya named Khema in the royal city of Bandhumatī, the dwelling place of the Blessed One Vipassī. And that was only the Saṅgha Uposatha; they did not perform the Gaṇa Uposatha, the Puggala Uposatha, the Pārisuddhi Uposatha, or the Adhiṭṭhāna Uposatha.

Tadā kira jambudīpe caturāsītivihārasahassāni honti. Ekamekasmiṃ vihāre abbokiṇṇāni dasapi vīsatipi bhikkhusahassāni vasanti, bhiyyopi vasanti. Uposathārocikā devatā tattha tattha gantvā ārocenti – “mārisā, ekaṃ vassaṃ atikkantaṃ, dve tīṇi cattāri pañca vassāni atikkantāni, idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ vassaṃ, āgāminiyā puṇṇamāsiyā buddhadassanatthaṃ uposathakaraṇatthañca gantabbaṃ! Sampatto vo sannipātakālo”ti. Tato [V 1.0142] sānubhāvā bhikkhū attano attano ānubhāvena gacchanti, itare devatānubhāvena. Kathaṃ? Te kira bhikkhū pācīnasamuddante vā pacchimauttaradakkhiṇasamuddante vā ṭhitā gamiyavattaṃ pūretvā pattacīvaramādāya “gacchāmā”ti cittaṃ uppādenti; saha cittuppādā uposathaggaṃ gatāva [M 1.0154] honti. Te vipassiṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ abhivādetvā nisīdanti. Bhagavāpi sannisinnāya parisāya imaṃ ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisati.

At that time, it is said, there were eighty-four thousand monasteries in Jambudīpa. In each and every monastery, ten thousand or twenty thousand bhikkhus, unmixed with those of dissimilar character, dwelt, and even more. The deities who announce the Uposatha would go to those various monasteries and proclaim: ‘Sirs, one year has passed, two, three, four, five years have passed; this is the sixth year. On the coming full-moon day, it is time to go for the purpose of seeing the Buddha and for performing the Uposatha! Your time for assembly has arrived!’ Because of that announcement, the bhikkhus with psychic power go by their own power; the others go by the power of the deities. How? It is said that those bhikkhus, standing at the shore of the eastern, western, northern, or southern ocean, having fulfilled the duties of a bhikkhu who is to travel and taking their bowl and robes, produce the thought, ‘Let us go.’ Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, they have arrived at the Uposatha hall. They pay homage to Vipassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and sit down. The Blessed One also recites this advisory Pātimokkha to the assembly seated in unison.

“Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā;

Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā;

Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī;

Na samaṇo hoti paraṃ viheṭhayanto.

Patient endurance, which is forbearance, is the supreme ascetic practice. The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme. One who harms another is certainly not ‘one who has gone forth’; one who oppresses another is not a contemplative.

“Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā;

Sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ.

The non-doing of all evil, the accomplishment of the wholesome, the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

“Anupavādo [P 1.0187] anupaghāto, pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro;

Mattaññutā ca bhattasmiṃ, pantañca sayanāsanaṃ;

Adhicitte ca āyogo, etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti. (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183-185);

Not reviling, not harming, and restraint in the Pātimokkha; and knowing the measure in food, a remote lodging, and application to the higher mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Eteneva upāyena itaresampi buddhānaṃ pātimokkhuddeso veditabbo. Sabbabuddhānañhi imā tissova ovādapātimokkhagāthāyo honti. Tā dīghāyukabuddhānaṃ yāva sāsanapariyantā uddesamāgacchanti; appāyukabuddhānaṃ paṭhamabodhiyaṃyeva. Sikkhāpadapaññattikālato pana pabhuti āṇāpātimokkhameva uddisīyati. Tañca kho bhikkhū eva uddisanti, na buddhā. Tasmā amhākampi bhagavā paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsativassamattameva idaṃ ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisi. Athekadivasaṃ pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde nisinno bhikkhū āmantesi – “na dānāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ito paraṃ uposathaṃ karissāmi pātimokkhaṃ uddisissāmi, tumheva dāni bhikkhave ito paraṃ uposathaṃ kareyyātha, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyātha. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso yaṃ tathāgato aparisuddhāya parisāya uposathaṃ kareyya, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyā”ti (cūḷava. 386). Tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhū āṇāpātimokkhaṃ uddisanti. Idaṃ āṇāpātimokkhaṃ tesaṃ anuddiṭṭhaṃ ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “anuddiṭṭhaṃ pātimokkha”nti.

By this very method, the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the other Buddhas should be understood. Indeed, for all Buddhas, there are only these three advisory Pātimokkha verses. For the long-lived Buddhas, they come to be recited until the end of the Dispensation; for the short-lived Buddhas, only at the first awakening. However, from the time the training rules were laid down, only the disciplinary Pātimokkha is recited. And that, only the bhikkhus recite, not the Buddhas. Therefore, our Blessed One also recited this advisory Pātimokkha for only about twenty years during the period of his first awakening. Then one day, while seated in the Pubbārāma, in the mansion of Migāra's mother, he addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, from this day onwards, I will not perform the Uposatha; I will not recite the Pātimokkha. Bhikkhus, from this day onwards, you yourselves should perform the Uposatha; you should recite the Pātimokkha. Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is not the occasion, that a Tathāgata should perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly.' (Cūḷava. 386). From then on, the bhikkhus recite the disciplinary Pātimokkha. This disciplinary Pātimokkha was not recited by them. Therefore, it was said: 'The Pātimokkha was not recited.'

Tesaṃ [V 1.0143] buddhānanti tesaṃ vipassīādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ. Antaradhānenāti khandhantaradhānena; parinibbānenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Buddhānubuddhānanti ye tesaṃ buddhānaṃ anubuddhā sammukhasāvakā tesañca khandhantaradhānena. Ye te pacchimā sāvakāti [M 1.0155] ye tesaṃ sammukhasāvakānaṃ santike pabbajitā pacchimā sāvakā. Nānānāmāti “buddharakkhito, dhammarakkhito”tiādi nāmavasena vividhanāmā. Nānāgottāti “gotamo, moggallāno”tiādi gottavasena vividhagottā. Nānājaccāti “khattiyo, brāhmaṇo”tiādijātivasena nānājaccā. Nānākulā pabbajitāti khattiyakulādivase neva uccanīcauḷāruḷārabhogādikulavasena vā vividhakulā nikkhamma pabbajitā.

'Of those Buddhas' means of those three Buddhas: Vipassī and the others. 'By disappearance' means by the disappearance of the aggregates; that is to say, by final Nibbāna. 'Of the Buddhas and those awakened after them' refers to the disappearance of the aggregates of those direct disciples who were awakened in succession to those Buddhas. 'Those later disciples' means those later disciples who had gone forth in the presence of those direct disciples. 'Of various names' means having various names, by way of names such as 'Buddharakkhita' and 'Dhammarakkhita'. 'Of various clans' means having various clans, by way of clans such as 'Gotama' and 'Moggallāna'. 'Of various births' means having various births, by way of births such as 'khattiya' and 'brāhmaṇa'. 'Gone forth from various families' means having gone forth from various families, either by way of families such as the khattiya family, or by way of families such as high, low, or those with exceedingly great wealth.

Te taṃ brahmacariyanti te pacchimā sāvakā [P 1.0188] yasmā ekanāmā ekagottā ekajātikā ekakulā pabbajitā “amhākaṃ sāsanaṃ tanti paveṇī”ti attano bhāraṃ katvā brahmacariyaṃ rakkhanti, ciraṃ pariyattidhammaṃ pariharanti. Ime ca tādisā na honti. Tasmā aññamaññaṃ viheṭhentā vilomaṃ gaṇhantā “asuko thero jānissati, asuko thero jānissatī”ti sithilaṃ karontā taṃ brahmacariyaṃ khippaññeva antaradhāpesuṃ, saṅgahaṃ āropetvā na rakkhiṃsu. Seyyathāpīti tassatthassa opammanidassanaṃ. Vikiratīti vikkhipati. Vidhamatīti ṭhānantaraṃ neti. Viddhaṃsetīti ṭhitaṭṭhānato apaneti. Yathā taṃ suttena asaṅgahitattāti yathā suttena asaṅgahitattā aganthitattā abaddhattā evaṃ vikirati yathā suttena asaṅgahitāni vikiriyanti, evaṃ vikiratīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evameva khoti opammasampaṭipādanaṃ. Antaradhāpesunti vaggasaṅgaha-paṇṇāsasaṅgahādīhi asaṅgaṇhantā yaṃ yaṃ attano ruccati, taṃ tadeva gahetvā sesaṃ vināsesuṃ adassanaṃ nayiṃsu.

Regarding 'they... that holy life...': When later disciples go forth from the same name, same clan, same birth, and same family, they think, 'Our Dispensation is a lineage, a tradition,' and taking it as their own responsibility, they guard the holy life and maintain the scriptural teaching for a long time. But these disciples were not like that. Therefore, harming one another, taking up what is contrary, and thinking, 'Such-and-such an elder will know, such-and-such an elder will know,' they acted laxly and quickly caused that holy life to disappear; they did not protect it by submitting it to a compilation. 'Just as' indicates a simile for that meaning. 'It scatters' (vikirati) means it disperses (vikkhipati). 'It blows away' (vidhamati) means it leads to another place. 'It demolishes' (viddhaṃseti) means it removes from its established place. 'As it was not held together by a thread' means: just as, because of not being gathered, not being strung, and not being bound by a thread, it scatters; just as things not gathered by a thread are scattered, so it scatters—this is what is meant. 'In the same way' serves to connect the simile with its subject. 'They caused it to disappear' means: not compiling it by means of collections of chapters, collections of fifties, and so on, they took only what pleased them and destroyed the rest, causing it to disappear.

Akilāsuno ca te bhagavanto ahesuṃ sāvake cetasā ceto paricca ovaditunti apica sāriputta te buddhā attano cetasā sāvakānaṃ ceto paricca paricchinditvā ovadituṃ akilāsuno ahesuṃ, paracittaṃ ñatvā anusāsaniṃ na bhāriyato na papañcato addasaṃsu. Bhūtapubbaṃ sāriputtātiādi tesaṃ akilāsubhāvappakāsanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhiṃsanaketi bhayānake bhayajananake. Evaṃ vitakkethāti nekkhammavitakkādayo tayo vitakke vitakketha. Mā evaṃ vitakkayitthāti kāmavitakkādayo tayo akusalavitakke mā vitakkayittha. Evaṃ manasi karothāti “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā asubha”nti manasi karotha. Mā evaṃ manasā [M 1.0156] katthāti “niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā subha”nti mā manasi akarittha. Idaṃ pajahathāti akusalaṃ pajahatha. Idaṃ upasampajja viharathāti kusalaṃ upasampajja paṭilabhitvā nipphādetvā viharatha.

'And those Blessed Ones were tireless in advising disciples, having encompassed mind with mind' means: moreover, Sāriputta, those Buddhas were tireless in advising their disciples by encompassing and defining the disciples' minds with their own mind. Knowing the minds of others, they did not regard the instruction as burdensome or as a proliferation. 'Once upon a time, Sāriputta,' and so forth—this was said to illustrate their tireless nature. 'Terrifying' means frightening, fear-producing. 'Think thus' means: 'Cultivate the three thoughts beginning with the thought of renunciation.' 'Do not think thus' means: 'Do not cultivate the three unwholesome thoughts beginning with the thought of sensuality.' 'Reflect thus' means: 'Reflect on "impermanence, suffering, not-self, unattractiveness."' 'Do not reflect thus' means: 'Do not reflect on "permanence, pleasure, self, attractiveness."' 'Abandon this' means: 'Abandon the unwholesome.' 'Having undertaken this, dwell' means: 'Having undertaken, obtained, and accomplished the wholesome, dwell.'

Anupādāya [P 1.0189][V 1.0144] āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsūti aggahetvā vimucciṃsu. Tesañhi cittāni yehi āsavehi vimucciṃsu, na te tāni gahetvā vimucciṃsu. Anuppādanirodhena pana nirujjhamānā aggahetvā vimucciṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsū”ti. Sabbepi te arahattaṃ patvā sūriyarasmisamphuṭṭhamiva padumavanaṃ vikasitacittā ahesuṃ. Tatra sudaṃ sāriputta bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hotīti tatrāti purimavacanāpekkhaṃ; sudanti padapūraṇamatte nipāto; sāriputtāti ālapanaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha atthayojanā – tatrāti yaṃ vuttaṃ “aññatarasmiṃ bhiṃsanake vanasaṇḍe”ti, tatra yo so bhiṃsanakoti vanasaṇḍo vutto, tassa bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti, bhiṃsanakiriyāya hotīti attho. Kiṃ hoti? Idaṃ hoti – yo koci avītarāgo…pe… lomāni haṃsantīti.

'Their minds were liberated from the taints without clinging' means: they were liberated without grasping. Indeed, concerning the taints from which their minds were liberated, those taints did not liberate those minds by grasping them. Rather, as the taints were ceasing with the cessation of non-arising, the minds were liberated without grasping. Therefore it is said: 'Their minds were liberated from the taints without clinging.' All of them, having attained arahantship, had minds that had blossomed like a lotus grove touched by the sun's rays. 'There, Sāriputta, it is in the terrifying quality of the terrifying forest grove': here, 'there' (tatra) refers to the previous statement; 'sudaṃ' is merely a particle to fill out the line; 'Sāriputta' is a vocative. Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning: 'there' (tatra) refers to what was said, 'in a certain terrifying forest grove.' There, with regard to that forest grove which was called 'terrifying,' 'it is in the terrifying quality' (bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti) of that terrifying forest grove; the meaning is, 'it is by the action of terrifying' (bhiṃsanakiriyāya hoti). What happens? This happens: 'Whoever is not free from lust... their hairs stand on end.'

Atha vā tatrāti sāmiatthe bhummaṃ. Suiti nipāto; “kiṃ su nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.469) viya. Idanti adhippetamatthaṃ paccakkhaṃ viya katvā dassanavacanaṃ. Suidanti sudaṃ, sandhivasena ikāralopo veditabbo. “Cakkhundriyaṃ, itthindriyaṃ, anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ (vibha. 219), “kiṃ sūdha vitta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.73, 246; su. ni. 183) viya. Ayaṃ panettha atthayojanā – tassa sāriputta bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ idaṃsu hoti. Bhiṃsanakatasminti bhiṃsanakabhāveti attho. Ekassa takārassa lopo daṭṭhabbo. Bhiṃsanakattasmintiyeva vā pāṭho. “Bhiṃsanakatāya” iti vā vattabbe liṅgavipallāso kato. Nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ, tasmā evaṃ sambandho veditabbo – bhiṃsanakabhāve idaṃsu hoti, bhiṃsanakabhāvanimittaṃ bhiṃsanakabhāvahetu bhiṃsanakabhāvapaccayā idaṃsu hoti. Yo koci avītarāgo taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati, yebhuyyena lomāni haṃsantīti bahutarāni lomāni haṃsanti uddhaṃ mukhāni sūcisadisāni kaṇṭakasadisāni ca hutvā tiṭṭhanti, appāni na haṃsanti. Bahutarānaṃ vā sattānaṃ haṃsanti. Appakānaṃ atisūrapurisānaṃ na haṃsanti.

Alternatively, 'there' (tatra) is a locative in the sense of relation. 'Su' is a particle, as in 'What, sirs, are those ascetics and brahmins called?' and so forth. 'This' (idaṃ) is a word that shows the intended meaning as if it were directly perceived. 'Su idaṃ' becomes 'sudaṃ'; the elision of the vowel 'i' should be understood as due to sandhi, as in 'the faculty of the eye, the faculty of femininity, the faculty of "I shall know the unknown,"' and 'What, indeed, is wealth here?' and so forth. Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning: Sāriputta, because of the terrifying nature of that terrifying forest grove, this happens. 'Because of the terrifying nature' (bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ) means 'in the state of being terrifying' (bhiṃsanakabhāve). The elision of one 't' should be noted. Alternatively, the reading could be 'bhiṃsanakattasmiṃ.' Or, if it were to be said as 'bhiṃsanakatāya,' a change of gender would be involved. And this locative case is in the sense of a reason (nimitta); therefore, the connection should be understood thus: 'Because of the state of being terrifying, this happens'; that is, 'as a sign of the state of being terrifying, as a cause of the state of being terrifying, as a condition for the state of being terrifying, this happens.' 'Whoever, not free from lust, enters that forest grove—for the most part, their hairs stand on end' means that most of their hairs stand on end—they stand with their tips pointing upwards, having become like needles and thorns—while a few do not. Or, the hairs of most beings stand on end, but they do not for a few exceptionally courageous men.

Idāni [P 1.0190][M 1.0157] ayaṃ kho, sāriputta, hetūtiādi nigamanaṃ. Yañcettha antarantarā na vuttaṃ, taṃ uttānatthameva. Tasmā pāḷikkameneva veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ na ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ahosīti, taṃ purisayugavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Vassagaṇanāya hi vipassissa bhagavato asītivassasahassāni āyu, sammukhasāvakānampissa tattakameva. Evamassa yvāyaṃ sabbapacchimako sāvako, tena saha ghaṭetvā satasahassaṃ saṭṭhimattāni ca vassasahassāni brahmacariyaṃ [V 1.0145] aṭṭhāsi. Purisayugavasena pana yugaparamparāya āgantvā dveyeva purisayugāni aṭṭhāsi. Tasmā na ciraṭṭhitikanti vuttaṃ. Sikhissa pana bhagavato sattativassasahassāni āyu. Sammukhasāvakānampissa tattakameva. Vessabhussa bhagavato saṭṭhivassasahassāni āyu. Sammukhasāvakānampissa tattakameva. Evaṃ tesampi ye sabbapacchimakā sāvakā tehi saha ghaṭetvā satasahassato uddhaṃ cattālīsamattāni vīsatimattāni ca vassasahassāni brahmacariyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Purisayugavasena pana yugaparamparāya āgantvā dve dveyeva purisayugāni aṭṭhāsi. Tasmā na ciraṭṭhitikanti vuttaṃ.

Now, Sāriputta, the passage beginning 'this is the cause' is the conclusion. And whatever was not stated here in between should be understood as having an obvious meaning. Therefore, it should be known simply by the sequence of the Pāli text. As for what was said—'it did not last long'—that should be understood as being spoken in terms of generations of individuals. For, by the calculation of years, the Blessed One Vipassī's lifespan was eighty thousand years, and that of his direct disciples was just as long. Thus, including his very last disciple, the holy life endured for one hundred and sixty thousand years. But in terms of generations of individuals, without proceeding through a succession of generations, it endured for only two generations of individuals. Therefore, it was said, 'it did not last long.' Now, the Blessed One Sikhī's lifespan was seventy thousand years, and that of his direct disciples was just as long. The Blessed One Vessabhū's lifespan was sixty thousand years, and that of his direct disciples was just as long. Thus, for them too, including their very last disciples, the holy life endured for one hundred and forty thousand and one hundred and twenty thousand years respectively. But in terms of generations of individuals, without proceeding through a succession of generations, it endured for only two generations each. Therefore, it was said, 'it did not last long.'

20. Evaṃ āyasmā sāriputto tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ brahmacariyassa na ciraṭṭhitikāraṇaṃ sutvā itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ brahmacariyassa ciraṭṭhitikāraṇaṃ sotukāmo puna bhagavantaṃ “ko pana bhante hetū”ti ādinā nayena pucchi. Bhagavāpissa byākāsi. Taṃ sabbaṃ vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbaṃ. Ciraṭṭhitikabhāvepi cettha tesaṃ buddhānaṃ āyuparimāṇatopi purisayugatopi ubhayathā ciraṭṭhitikatā veditabbā. Kakusandhassa hi bhagavato cattālīsavassasahassāni āyu, koṇāgamanassa bhagavato tiṃsavassasahassāni, kassapassa bhagavato vīsativassasahassāni; sammukhasāvakānampi nesaṃ tattakameva. Bahūni ca nesaṃ sāvakayugāni paramparāya brahmacariyaṃ pavattesuṃ. Evaṃ tesaṃ āyuparimāṇatopi sāvakayugatopi ubhayathā brahmacariyaṃ ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ahosi.

20. Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta, having heard the reason for the non-long-lastingness of the holy life of three Buddhas, and wishing to hear the reason for the long-lastingness of the holy life of the other three, again asked the Blessed One in the manner beginning with, 'But what, Venerable Sir, is the reason?' The Blessed One also explained it to him. All of that should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated. And here, in the case of being long-lasting, the long-lastingness of those Buddhas should be understood in two ways: both in terms of the measure of their lifespan and in terms of the generations of individuals. For the Blessed One Kakusandha's lifespan was forty thousand years, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana's was thirty thousand years, and the Blessed One Kassapa's was twenty thousand years; and the lifespan of their direct disciples was just as long. And many generations of their disciples caused the holy life to continue in succession. Thus, for them, in both ways—in terms of the measure of their lifespan and in terms of the generations of disciples—the holy life was long-lasting.

Amhākaṃ pana bhagavato kassapassa bhagavato upaḍḍhāyukappamāṇe dasavassasahassāyukakāle [P 1.0191] uppajjitabbaṃ siyā. Taṃ asambhuṇantena pañcavassasahassāyukakāle, ekavassasahassāyukakāle, pañcavassasatāyukakālepi vā uppajjitabbaṃ siyā. Yasmā panassa buddhattakārake dhamme esantassa pariyesantassa ñāṇaṃ paripācentassa gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpentassa vassasatāyukakāle [M 1.0158] ñāṇaṃ paripākamagamāsi. Tasmā atiparittāyukakāle uppanno. Tenassa sāvakaparamparāvasena ciraṭṭhitikampi brahmacariyaṃ āyuparimāṇavasena vassagaṇanāya naciraṭṭhitikamevāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

As for our Blessed One, he should have arisen at the time of a ten-thousand-year lifespan, which is the measure of half the lifespan of the Blessed One Kassapa. Not reaching that time, he might have arisen at the time of a five-thousand-year lifespan, or a one-thousand-year lifespan, or even a five-hundred-year lifespan. However, it was because while he was seeking and searching for the qualities that make a Buddha, while maturing his knowledge and causing the embryo of that knowledge to be conceived, his knowledge reached full maturity at the time of a hundred-year lifespan. Therefore, he arose in a time of an extremely short lifespan. For that reason, it is fitting to say that although his holy life is long-lasting by way of the succession of disciples, in terms of the measure of lifespan, by the calculation of years, it is indeed not long-lasting.

21. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputtoti ko anusandhi? Evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ brahmacariyassa ciraṭṭhitikāraṇaṃ sutvā sikkhāpadapaññattiyeva ciraṭṭhitikabhāvahetūti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā bhagavatopi brahmacariyassa ciraṭṭhitikabhāvaṃ icchanto āyasmā sāriputto bhagavantaṃ sikkhāpadapaññattiṃ yāci. Tassā yācanavidhidassanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ – atha kho āyasmā sāriputto uṭṭhāyāsanā [V 1.0146] …pe… ciraṭṭhitikanti. Tattha addhaniyanti addhānakkhamaṃ; dīghakālikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

21. Regarding 'Then the Venerable Sāriputta,' what is the connection? Thus, having heard the reason for the long-lastingness of the holy life of the three Buddhas, and having come to the conclusion that 'the laying down of training rules is itself the cause for being long-lasting,' the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing for the long-lastingness of the Blessed One's holy life as well, requested the Blessed One for the laying down of training rules. To show the method of that request, this was said: 'Then the Venerable Sāriputta, rising from his seat... that it might be long-lasting.' Therein, 'addhaniya' means 'able to endure for a long time'; it means 'long-lasting.' The remainder has an obvious meaning.

Athassa bhagavā “na tāvāyaṃ sikkhāpadapaññattikālo”ti pakāsento “āgamehi tvaṃ sāriputtā”tiādimāha. Tattha āgamehi tvanti tiṭṭha tāva tvaṃ; adhivāsehi tāva tvanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ādaratthavasenevettha dvikkhattuṃ vuttaṃ. Etena bhagavā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sāvakānaṃ visayabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “buddhavisayova sikkhāpadapaññattī”ti āvikaronto “tathāgato vā”tiādimāha. Ettha ca tatthāti sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanāpekkhaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – yaṃ vuttaṃ “sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeyyā”ti, tattha tassā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā tathāgatoyeva kālaṃ jānissatīti. Evaṃ vatvā akālaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “na tāva sāriputtā”tiādimāha.

Then the Blessed One, indicating, 'This is not yet the time for the laying down of a training rule,' said the words beginning, 'Wait, Sāriputta.' Herein, 'Wait, you' means 'You just wait'; it means 'You just be patient.' It was said twice here out of regard. By this, the Blessed One, rejecting that the laying down of a training rule is the domain of disciples and making it manifest that 'the laying down of a training rule is the domain of a Buddha alone,' said the words beginning, 'The Tathāgata will know.' And here, the word 'therein' (tattha) is a locative term with reference to the request for the laying down of a training rule. In that context, this is the construction: regarding what was said, 'May he lay down a training rule,' in the matter of that laying down of a training rule, the Tathāgata alone will know the time. Having said this, in order to show that it was not yet the time, he said the words beginning, 'Not yet, Sāriputta.'

Tattha āsavā tiṭṭhanti etesūti āsavaṭṭhānīyā. Yesu diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikā dukkhāsavā kilesāsavā ca parūpavādavippaṭisāravadhabandhanādayo ceva apāyadukkhavisesabhūtā ca āsavā tiṭṭhantiyeva, yasmā nesaṃ [P 1.0192] te kāraṇaṃ hontīti attho. Te āsavaṭṭhānīyā vītikkamadhammā yāva na saṅghe pātubhavanti, na tāva satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetīti ayamettha yojanā. Yadi hi paññapeyya, parūpavādā parūpārambhā garahadosā na parimucceyya.

Herein, they are called 'grounds for taints' (āsavaṭṭhānīyā) because 'the taints (āsavā) abide (tiṭṭhanti) in these (etesu).' The meaning is: because those transgressions are their cause, the taints—namely the taints of suffering in this life and in future lives, and the taints of defilement, as well as those such as blame by others, remorse, punishment, and bondage, and the taints that are the specific sufferings of the woeful states—surely abide in them. Herein, this is the construction: as long as those grounds for taints, those states of transgression, do not appear in the Saṅgha, for so long the Teacher does not lay down a training rule for the disciples. For if he were to lay it down, he would not be free from blame from others, from fault-finding by others, and from the fault of censure.

Kathaṃ? Paññapentena hi “yo pana bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”tiādi sabbaṃ paññapetabbaṃ bhaveyya. Adisvāva vītikkamadosaṃ imaṃ paññattiṃ ñatvā [M 1.0159] pare evaṃ upavādañca upārambhañca garahañca pavatteyyuṃ – “kathañhi nāma samaṇo gotamo bhikkhusaṅgho me anvāyiko vacanakaroti ettāvatā sikkhāpadehi paliveṭhessati, pārājikaṃ paññapessati? Nanu ime kulaputtā mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ mahantañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ hatthagatāni ca rajjānipi pahāya pabbajitā, ghāsacchādanaparamatāya santuṭṭhā, sikkhāya tibbagāravā, kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhā viharanti. Tesu nāma ko lokāmisabhūtaṃ methunaṃ vā paṭisevissati, parabhaṇḍaṃ vā harissati, parassa vā iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ atimadhuraṃ jīvitaṃ upacchindissati, abhūtaguṇakathāya vā jīvitaṃ kappessati! Nanu pārājike apaññattepi pabbajjāsaṅkhepenevetaṃ pākaṭaṃ kata”nti. Tathāgatassa ca thāmañca balañca sattā na jāneyyuṃ. Paññattampi sikkhāpadaṃ kuppeyya, na yathāṭhāne tiṭṭheyya. Seyyathāpi nāma akusalo vejjo kañci anuppannagaṇḍaṃ purisaṃ pakkosāpetvā “ehi bho purisa, imasmiṃ te sarīrappadese mahāgaṇḍo uppajjitvā anayabyasanaṃ [V 1.0147] pāpessati, paṭikacceva naṃ tikicchāpehī”ti vatvā “sādhācariya, tvaṃyeva naṃ tikicchassū”ti vutto tassa arogaṃ sarīrappadesaṃ phāletvā lohitaṃ nīharitvā ālepanabandhanadhovanādīhi taṃ padesaṃ sañchaviṃ katvā taṃ purisaṃ vadeyya – “mahārogo te mayā tikicchito, dehi me deyyadhamma”nti. So taṃ “kimayaṃ bālavejjo vadati? Kataro kira me iminā rogo tikicchito? Nanu me ayaṃ dukkhañca janeti, lohitakkhayañca maṃ pāpetī”ti evaṃ upavadeyya ceva upārambheyya [P 1.0193] ca garaheyya ca, na cassa guṇaṃ jāneyya. Evameva yadi anuppanne vītikkamadose satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeyya, parūpavādādīhi ca na parimucceyya, na cassa thāmaṃ vā balaṃ vā sattā jāneyyuṃ, paññattampi sikkhāpadaṃ kuppeyya, na yathāṭhāne tiṭṭheyya. Tasmā vuttaṃ – “na tāva sāriputta satthā sāvakānaṃ…pe… pātubhavantī”ti.

How so? For in laying down a rule, one would have to lay down all of them, such as, “Whatever monk should engage in sexual intercourse,” and so on. Without having seen any fault of transgression, others, upon knowing of this regulation, would thus give rise to reproach, fault-finding, and censure, saying: “How indeed, thinking, ‘The community of monks is my follower, one who does my bidding,’ will the ascetic Gotama bind them with so many training rules and lay down a Pārājika offense? Have not these sons of good family gone forth, having abandoned a great mass of wealth, a large circle of relatives, and even kingdoms that had come into their hands? They dwell content with the barest provision of food and robes, with profound reverence for the training, and unconcerned for body and life. Among them, who indeed would engage in sexual intercourse, which is worldly bait, or take the property of another, or cut short the dear, beloved, and exceedingly sweet life of another, or make a living by falsely claiming a superior human state? Surely, even without a Pārājika offense being laid down, this is made evident by the summary of the going forth itself.” And beings would not know the Tathāgata’s strength and power. The training rule, even if laid down, would be unstable and would not stand in its proper place. It is like an unskilled physician who, having summoned a man with no boil, might say, “Come, good sir, a great boil will arise on this part of your body and bring you to ruin and disaster. Have it treated beforehand.” And when told, “Very well, master, you yourself treat it,” he might cut open the healthy part of the man’s body, draw blood, and after treating that area with ointments, bandages, washes, and so on, making the skin whole, he might say to the man, “Your great disease has been treated by me; give me my fee.” That man would thus reproach, find fault, and censure him, saying, “What is this foolish physician saying? What disease of mine has he treated? Has he not just caused me pain and made me lose blood?” And he would not know his skill. In the very same way, if the Teacher were to lay down a training rule for his disciples when a fault of transgression has not yet arisen, he would not be free from the reproach of others and so on, nor would beings know his strength or power, and the training rule, even if laid down, would be unstable and would not stand in its proper place. Therefore, it was said: “Not yet, Sāriputta, does the Teacher lay down a training rule for the disciples… until states that are grounds for the taints appear in the Saṅgha.”

Evaṃ akālaṃ dassetvā puna kālaṃ dassetuṃ “yato ca kho sāriputtā”tiādimāha. Tattha yatoti yadā; yasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vā hettha saṅkhepattho – yasmiṃ samaye “āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā”ti saṅkhyaṃ gatā vītikkamadosā saṅghe pātubhavanti, tadā satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti, uddisati pātimokkhaṃ. Kasmā? Tesaṃyeva “āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā”ti saṅkhyaṃ [M 1.0160] gatānaṃ vītikkamadosānaṃ paṭighātāya. Evaṃ paññapento yathā nāma kusalo vejjo uppannaṃ gaṇḍaṃ phālanalepanabandhanadhovanādīhi tikicchanto rogaṃ vūpasametvā sañchaviṃ katvā na tveva upavādādiraho hoti, sake ca ācariyake viditānubhāvo hutvā sakkāraṃ pāpuṇāti; evaṃ na ca upavādādiraho hoti, sake ca sabbaññuvisaye viditānubhāvo hutvā sakkāraṃ pāpuṇāti. Tañcassa sikkhāpadaṃ akuppaṃ hoti, yathāṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti.

Having thus shown the untimely occasion, to show the timely occasion he then said the words beginning, “But when, Sāriputta…” Therein, 'yato' means ‘when’; that is to say, ‘at which time.’ The rest should be understood in accordance with what has already been said. Or, the summary meaning here is this: at the time when faults of transgression, which have come to be designated as “states that are grounds for the taints,” appear in the Saṅgha, the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples and recites the Pātimokkha. Why? For the counteracting of those very faults of transgression designated as “states that are grounds for the taints.” In laying down the rule in this way, it is like a skilled physician who, treating an existing boil with incision, ointment, bandaging, washing, and so on, pacifies the disease and restores the skin. He is not liable to reproach and the like, and with his influence being known in his own craft, he obtains honor. In the same way, the Teacher is not liable to reproach and the like, and with his influence being known in his own domain of omniscience, he obtains honor. And that training rule of his is unshakeable; it stands in its proper place.

Evaṃ āsavaṭṭhānīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppattiṃ sikkhāpadapaññattiyā akālaṃ uppattiñca kālanti vatvā idāni tesaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppattikālañca uppattikālañca dassetuṃ “na tāva sāriputta idhekacce”tiādimāha. Tattha uttānatthāni padāni pāḷivaseneva veditabbāni. Ayaṃ pana anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – rattiyo jānantīti rattaññū, attano pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bahukā rattiyo jānanti, cirapabbajitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rattaññūhi mahattaṃ rattaññumahattaṃ; cirapabbajitehi mahantabhāvanti attho. Tatra rattaññumahattaṃ patte saṅghe [P 1.0194] upasenaṃ vaṅgantaputtaṃ ārabbha sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti veditabbaṃ. So hāyasmā ūnadasavasse bhikkhū upasampādente disvā ekavasso saddhivihārikaṃ upasampādesi. Atha bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi – “na, bhikkhave[V 1.0148], ūnadasavassena upasampādetabbo. Yo upasampādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 75). Evaṃ paññatte sikkhāpade puna bhikkhū “dasavassāmha dasavassāmhā”ti bālā abyattā upasampādenti. Atha bhagavā aparampi sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpesi – “na, bhikkhave, bālena abyattena upasampādetabbo. Yo upasampādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena dasavassena vā atirekadasavassena vā upasampādetu”nti (mahāva. 76) rattaññumahattaṃ pattakāle dve sikkhāpadāni paññattāni.
