Thus, having stated that the non-arising of states that are grounds for the taints is the untimely occasion for laying down a training rule, and that their arising is the timely occasion, he now says, “Not yet, Sāriputta, here some…” and so on, in order to show the time of their non-arising and the time of their arising. Therein, the words with plain meaning should be understood according to the Pāli itself. This, however, is the explanation of the words that are not plain: They are rattaññū because ‘they know the nights’ (rattiyo jānanti); that is to say, they know many nights starting from the day of their own going forth; this means they are long-ordained. ‘Greatness through seniority’ (rattaññumahattaṃ) is greatness by means of the rattaññū; the meaning is the state of being great on account of the long-ordained. Therein, it should be understood that when the Saṅgha had attained greatness through seniority, a training rule was laid down concerning Upasena Vaṅgantaputta. For that venerable one, seeing monks with less than ten vassas giving ordination, being of one vassa himself, gave ordination to his co-resident. Then the Blessed One laid down the training rule: “Monks, one with less than ten vassas should not give ordination. Whoever should give ordination, it is an offense of wrong-doing.” When this training rule was laid down, monks who were foolish and incompetent again gave ordination, saying, “We are of ten vassas, we are of ten vassas.” Then the Blessed One laid down another training rule: “Monks, a foolish and incompetent one should not give ordination. Whoever should give ordination, it is an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, a competent, capable monk of ten vassas or more than ten vassas to give ordination.” Thus, at the time when greatness through seniority was attained, two training rules were laid down.

Vepullamahattanti vipulabhāvena mahattaṃ. Saṅgho hi yāva na theranavamajjhimānaṃ vasena vepullamahattaṃ patto hoti, tāva senāsanāni pahonti. Sāsane ekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā na uppajjanti. Vepullamahattaṃ pana patte te uppajjanti. Atha satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti. Tattha vepullamahattaṃ patte saṅghe paññattasikkhāpadāni “yo pana bhikkhu anupasampannena uttari dirattatirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya, pācittiyaṃ” [M 1.0161] (pāci. 51); “yā pana bhikkhunī anuvassaṃ vuṭṭhāpeyya, pācittiyaṃ” (pāci. 1171); “yā pana bhikkhunī ekaṃ vassaṃ dve vuṭṭhāpeyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 1175) iminā nayena veditabbāni.

'Greatness through extensiveness' (vepullamahattaṃ) means greatness by way of being extensive. For as long as the Saṅgha has not attained greatness through extensiveness by way of elders, new monks, and middling monks, lodgings are sufficient. In the Dispensation, certain states that are grounds for the taints do not arise. But when greatness through extensiveness is reached, they arise. Then the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples. Herein, the training rules established when the Saṅgha reached greatness through extensiveness should be understood in this way: 'Whatever bhikkhu should arrange to lie down together with an unordained person for more than two or three nights, it is an offense of expiation'; 'Whatever bhikkhunī should give ordination every year, it is an offense of expiation'; 'Whatever bhikkhunī should give ordination to two in one year, it is an offense of expiation'.

Lābhaggamahattanti lābhassa aggamahattaṃ; yo lābhassa aggo uttamo mahantabhāvo, taṃ patto hotīti attho. Lābhena vā aggamahattampi, lābhena seṭṭhattañca mahantattañca pattoti attho. Saṅgho hi yāva na lābhaggamahattaṃ patto hoti, tāva na lābhaṃ paṭicca āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā uppajjanti. Patte pana uppajjanti, atha satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti [P 1.0195] – “yo pana bhikkhu acelakassa vā paribbājakassa vā paribbājikāya vā sahatthā khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā dadeyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 270). Idañhi lābhaggamahattaṃ patte saṅghe sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ.

‘Greatness through the supreme attainment of gain’ (lābhaggamahattaṃ) means the supreme greatness of gain; the meaning is that one has attained that state of greatness which is the highest, the most excellent, of gain. Or, it means supreme greatness by way of gain; the meaning is that one has attained excellence and greatness through gain. For as long as the Saṅgha has not attained greatness through the supreme attainment of gain, states that are grounds for the taints do not arise in dependence on gain. But once it is attained, they arise, and then the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples: ‘Whatever bhikkhu should give, with his own hand, solid food or soft food to a naked ascetic, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, it is an offense of expiation’. Indeed, this training rule was established when the Saṅgha had attained greatness through the supreme attainment of gain.

Bāhusaccamahattanti bāhusaccassa mahantabhāvaṃ. Saṅgho hi yāva na bāhusaccamahattaṃ patto hoti, tāva na āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā uppajjanti. Bāhusaccamahattaṃ patte pana yasmā ekampi nikāyaṃ, dvepi…pe… pañcapi nikāye uggahetvā ayoniso ummujjamānā puggalā rasena rasaṃ saṃsanditvā uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ dīpenti. Atha satthā “yo pana bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi…pe… samaṇuddesopi ce evaṃ vadeyyā”tiādinā (pāci. 418) nayena sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetīti.

'Greatness of vast learning' (bāhusaccamahattaṃ) means the state of greatness of vast learning. For as long as the Saṅgha has not reached the greatness of vast learning, states that are grounds for the taints do not arise. But when the greatness of vast learning is reached, because individuals who, having learned even one collection, two collections... up to five collections, emerge improperly, mixing flavor with flavor, they expound the Teacher's Dispensation as being outside the Dhamma and outside the Vinaya. Then the Teacher lays down a training rule in the way beginning, 'Whatever bhikkhu should speak thus: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One…"... even if a novice should speak thus...'

Evaṃ [V 1.0149] bhagavā āsavaṭṭhānīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppattikālañca uppattikālañca dassetvā tasmiṃ samaye sabbasopi tesaṃ abhāvaṃ dassento “nirabbudo hi sāriputtā”tiādimāha. Tattha nirabbudoti abbudavirahito; abbudā vuccanti corā, niccoroti attho. Corāti ca imasmiṃ atthe dussīlāva adhippetā. Te hi assamaṇāva hutvā samaṇapaṭiññatāya paresaṃ paccaye corenti. Tasmā nirabbudoti niccoro, niddussīloti vuttaṃ hoti. Nirādīnavoti nirupaddavo nirupasaggo; dussīlādīnavarahitoyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Apagatakāḷakoti kāḷakā vuccanti dussīlāyeva; te hi suvaṇṇavaṇṇāpi samānā kāḷakadhammayogā kāḷakātveva veditabbā. Tesaṃ abhāvā apagatakāḷako[M 1.0162]. Apahatakāḷakotipi pāṭho. Suddhoti apagatakāḷakattāyeva suddho pariyodāto pabhassaro. Sāre patiṭṭhitoti sāro vuccanti sīla-samādhi-paññāvimutti-vimuttiñāṇadassanaguṇā, tasmiṃ sāre patiṭṭhitattā sāre patiṭṭhito.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown both the time of non-arising and the time of arising of states that are grounds for the taints, and wishing to show their complete absence at that time, spoke the words beginning, 'Truly, Sāriputta, it is free from tumors...' Herein, 'free from tumors' (nirabbudo) means devoid of tumors; 'tumors' are called thieves, so the meaning is 'free from thieves.' And in this context, by 'thieves' are meant the immoral ones. For they, not being true ascetics, by their claim to be ascetics, steal the requisites of others. Therefore, 'free from tumors' means free from thieves, free from the immoral; thus it is said. 'Free from danger' (nirādīnavo) means free from affliction, free from peril; it is said to mean devoid of the danger of immorality. 'One from whom the black ones have departed' (apagatakāḷako): the immoral are called 'black ones' (kāḷakā); for they, even though they may be of golden complexion, due to their association with black states, should be known as 'black ones.' Due to the absence of these, one is 'one from whom the black ones have departed.' There is also the reading 'one who has struck off the black ones' (apahatakāḷako). 'Pure' (suddho): precisely because of being one from whom the black ones have departed, one is pure, thoroughly cleansed, and radiant. 'Established in the core' (sāre patiṭṭhito): the qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are called the 'core' (sāro). Because of being established in that core, one is 'established in the core.'

Evaṃ sāre patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ vatvā puna so cassa sāre patiṭṭhitabhāvo evaṃ veditabboti dassento imesañhi sāriputtāti ādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – yānimāni verañjāyaṃ [P 1.0196] vassāvāsaṃ upagatāni pañca bhikkhusatāni, imesaṃ yo guṇavasena pacchimako sabbaparittaguṇo bhikkhu, so sotāpanno. Sotāpannoti sotaṃ āpanno; sototi ca maggassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sotāpannoti tena samannāgatassa puggalassa. Yathāha –

Thus, having spoken of the state of being established in the core, and then wishing to show that this state of being established in its core should be understood in this way, he spoke the words beginning, 'For of these, Sāriputta...' Herein, this is the brief explanation: Of these five hundred monks who have undertaken the rains-residence in Verañjā, the monk who is the last one by way of virtue, the one with the least virtue of all, is a stream-enterer. 'Stream-enterer' (sotāpanno) means one who has entered the stream (sotaṃ āpanno). And 'stream' (sota) is a designation for the path. 'Stream-enterer' (sotāpanno) is a designation for a person endowed with that path. As it is said:

“Soto sototi hidaṃ, sāriputta, vuccati; katamo nu kho, sāriputta, sototi? Ayameva hi, bhante, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti. “Sotāpanno sotāpannoti hidaṃ, sāriputta, vuccati; katamo nu kho, sāriputta, sotāpanno”ti? “Yo hi, bhante, iminā ariyena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena samannāgato, ayaṃ vuccati – sotāpanno. Soyamāyasmā evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1001). Idha pana maggena phalassa nāmaṃ dinnaṃ. Tasmā phalaṭṭho “sotāpanno”ti veditabbo.

‘“Stream, stream,” it is said, Sāriputta. But what, Sāriputta, is the stream?’ ‘Indeed, venerable sir, it is this Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view… right concentration.’ ‘“Stream-enterer, stream-enterer,” it is said, Sāriputta. But who, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?’ ‘Whoever, venerable sir, is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer. This venerable one of such a name and such a clan.’ Here, however, the path has given its name to the fruit. Therefore, one established in the fruit should be understood as a 'stream-enterer.'

Avinipātadhammoti vinipātetīti vinipāto; nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo, na attānaṃ apāyesu vinipātanasabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Ye dhammā apāyagamanīyā, tesaṃ parikkhayā. Vinipatanaṃ vā vinipāto, nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo, apāyesu vinipātanasabhāvo assa natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sammattaniyāmena maggena [V 1.0150] niyatattā niyato. Sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ parā gati assāti sambodhiparāyaṇo. Upari maggattayaṃ avassaṃ sampāpakoti attho. Kasmā? Paṭiladdhapaṭhamamaggattāti.

'Not of a nature to fall away' (avinipātadhammo): 'falling away' (vinipāto) is so called because it causes one to fall away. 'Not of a nature to fall away' means that for him there is no state that is a falling away; it is said to mean that he does not have a nature of causing himself to fall away into the lower realms. Why? Because of the destruction of those states that lead to the lower realms. Or, 'falling away' (vinipāto) is the act of falling away. 'Not of a nature to fall away' means that for him there is no state that is a falling away; it is said to mean that for him there is no nature of falling away into the lower realms. He is 'fixed' (niyato) because of being fixed by the path that is the principle of rightness. He is 'bound for supreme awakening' (sambodhiparāyaṇo) because for him supreme awakening is the ultimate destination, the supreme goal. The meaning is that he is one who will certainly attain the three higher paths. Why? Because of having attained the first path.

Vinayapaññattiyācanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Request for the Promulgation of the Vinaya is concluded.

Buddhāciṇṇakathā

The Discourse on the Established Practices of the Buddhas

22. Evaṃ dhammasenāpatiṃ saññāpetvā verañjāyaṃ taṃ vassāvāsaṃ vītināmetvā vutthavasso mahāpavāraṇāya pavāretvā atha kho bhagavā [M 1.0163] āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi. Āmantesīti ālapi abhāsi sambodhesi. Kinti? Āciṇṇaṃ kho panetanti evamādi. Āciṇṇanti caritaṃ vattaṃ anudhammatā. Taṃ kho panetaṃ āciṇṇaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – buddhāciṇṇaṃ, sāvakāciṇṇanti. Katamaṃ buddhāciṇṇaṃ? Idaṃ tāva ekaṃ – yehi nimantitā vassaṃ vasanti, na te anapaloketvā anāpucchitvā janapadacārikaṃ pakkamanti. Sāvakā pana apaloketvā vā anapaloketvā vā yathāsukhaṃ pakkamanti.

22. Having thus informed the General of the Dhamma, and having spent that rains-residence at Verañjā, having completed the rains and performed the great Pavāraṇā, the Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Ānanda. 'Addressed' means he called, he spoke, he made well aware. How so? Beginning with, 'This, indeed, is the established practice.' 'Established practice' means conduct, custom, conformity with the Dhamma. Now, this established practice is of two kinds: the established practice of the Buddhas and the established practice of the disciples. What is the established practice of the Buddhas? This, firstly, is one: those by whom they were invited to spend the rains, they do not depart on a journey through the country without informing them or taking their leave. The disciples, however, depart as they please, whether having informed or not.

Aparampi buddhāciṇṇaṃ – vutthavassā pavāretvā janasaṅgahatthāya janapadacārikaṃ pakkamantiyeva. Janapadacārikaṃ carantā ca mahāmaṇḍalaṃ majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ antimamaṇḍalanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maṇḍalānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ maṇḍale [P 1.0197] caranti. Tattha mahāmaṇḍalaṃ navayojanasatikaṃ, majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ chayojanasatikaṃ, antimamaṇḍalaṃ tiyojanasatikaṃ. Yadā mahāmaṇḍale cārikaṃ caritukāmā honti, tadā mahāpavāraṇāya pavāretvā pāṭipadadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivārā nikkhamitvā gāmanigamādīsu mahājanaṃ āmisapaṭiggahena anuggaṇhantā dhammadānena cassa vivaṭṭupanissitaṃ kusalaṃ vaḍḍhentā navahi māsehi janapadacārikaṃ pariyosāpenti. Sace pana antovasse bhikkhūnaṃ samathavipassanā taruṇā honti, mahāpavāraṇāya appavāretvā pavāraṇāsaṅgahaṃ datvā kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ pavāretvā māgasirassa paṭhamadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivārā nikkhamitvā vuttanayeneva majjhimamaṇḍale aṭṭhahi māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpenti. Sace pana nesaṃ vutthavassānaṃ aparipākindriyā veneyyasattā honti, tesaṃ indriyaparipākaṃ āgamentā māgasiramāsampi tattheva vasitvā phussamāsassa paṭhamadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivārā nikkhamitvā vuttanayeneva antimamaṇḍale sattahi māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpenti. Tesu ca maṇḍalesu yattha katthaci vicarantāpi te te satte kilesehi viyojentā [V 1.0151] sotāpattiphalādīhi payojentā veneyyavaseneva nānāvaṇṇāni pupphāni ocinantā viya caranti.

Another established practice of the Buddhas is this: having completed the rains and performed the Pavāraṇā, they would indeed set out on a journey through the country for the sake of supporting the populace. And while journeying through the country, they would travel in one of these three regions: the great region, the middle region, or the border region. Therein, the great region is nine hundred yojanas, the middle region is six hundred yojanas, and the border region is three hundred yojanas. When they wish to journey in the great region, having performed the great Pavāraṇā, on the first day of the following month, accompanied by a large retinue of the Saṅgha of monks, they set out. Supporting the great populace by accepting material offerings and, through the gift of the Dhamma, increasing their wholesome karma which is a support for turning away from the round of rebirths, they complete their journey through the country in nine months. If, however, during the rains, the monks’ calm and insight are still immature, without performing the great Pavāraṇā, but having granted a concession for the Pavāraṇā, they perform the Pavāraṇā on the full-moon day of Kattika. Then, on the first day of Māgasira, accompanied by a large retinue of the Saṅgha of monks, they set out and, in the aforementioned manner, complete their journey through the middle region in eight months. If, however, for those who have completed the rains, the faculties of the beings to be trained are unripe, awaiting the ripening of their faculties, they reside right there for the month of Māgasira as well. Then, on the first day of the month of Phussa, accompanied by a large retinue of the Saṅgha of monks, they set out and, in the aforementioned manner, complete their journey through the border region in seven months. And, while wandering in any place whatsoever in those regions, they travel disentangling those various beings from defilements and connecting them with the fruits beginning with stream-entry, according to the capacity of those to be trained, like one gathering flowers of various colors.

Aparampi buddhānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ – devasikaṃ paccūsasamaye santaṃ sukhaṃ nibbānārammaṇaṃ katvā phalasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ, phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahitvā devasikaṃ mahākaruṇāsamāpattiyā samāpajjanaṃ, tato vuṭṭhahitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷe bodhaneyyasattasamavalokanaṃ.

Another established practice of the Buddhas is this: daily at dawn, entering into the fruition attainment, having made the peaceful, blissful Nibbāna its object; having arisen from the fruition attainment, daily entering into the attainment of great compassion; and having arisen from that, thoroughly surveying the beings in the ten-thousandfold world-system who are ready to be awakened.

Aparampi [M 1.0164] buddhānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ – āgantukehi saddhiṃ paṭhamataraṃ paṭisanthārakaraṇaṃ, aṭṭhuppattivasena dhammadesanā, otiṇṇe dose sikkhāpadapaññāpananti idaṃ buddhāciṇṇaṃ.

Another established practice of the Buddhas is this: first of all, exchanging friendly greetings with newcomers; teaching the Dhamma by way of an occasion that has arisen; and when an offense has occurred, laying down a training rule. This is the established practice of the Buddhas.

Katamaṃ sāvakāciṇṇaṃ? Buddhassa bhagavato kāle dvikkhattuṃ sannipāto pure vassūpanāyikāya ca kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇatthaṃ, vutthavassānañca adhigataguṇārocanatthaṃ upari kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇatthañca[P 1.0198]. Idaṃ sāvakāciṇṇaṃ. Idha pana buddhāciṇṇaṃ dassento āha – “āciṇṇaṃ kho panetaṃ, ānanda, tathāgatāna”nti.

What is the established practice of the disciples? During the time of the Blessed Buddha, there is an assembly twice: before the day of entering the rains-residence for the purpose of receiving a meditation subject, and for those who have completed the rains-residence, for the purpose of announcing the qualities they have attained and for receiving a higher meditation subject. This is the established practice of the disciples. Here, however, wishing to show the established practice of the Buddhas, he said: 'This, Ānanda, is the established practice of the Tathāgatas.'

Āyāmāti āgaccha yāma. Apalokessāmāti cārikaṃ caraṇatthāya āpucchissāma. Evanti sampaṭicchanatthe nipāto. Bhanteti gāravādhivacanametaṃ; satthuno paṭivacanadānantipi vaṭṭati. Bhagavato paccassosīti bhagavato vacanaṃ paṭiassosi, abhimukho hutvā suṇi sampaṭicchi. Evanti iminā vacanena paṭiggahesīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Āyāma' means 'come, let us go.' 'Apalokessāma' means 'for the purpose of journeying on tour, we will ask leave.' 'Evaṃ' is a particle in the sense of acceptance. 'Bhante' is a term of respect; it is also fitting to say it is a reply given to the Teacher. 'He responded to the Blessed One' means he hearkened to the Blessed One's word; facing him, he listened and accepted. It is said that he accepted with this word 'evaṃ'.

Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvāti idha pubbaṇhasamayanti vā sāyanhasamayanti vā na vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santepi bhagavā katabhattakicco majjhanhikaṃ vītināmetvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ pacchāsamaṇaṃ katvā nagaradvārato paṭṭhāya nagaravīthiyo suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāhi raṃsīhi samujjotayamāno yena verañjassa brāhmaṇassa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Gharadvāre ṭhitamattameva cassa bhagavantaṃ disvā parijano ārocesi. Brāhmaṇo satiṃ paṭilabhitvā saṃvegajāto sahasā vuṭṭhāya mahārahaṃ āsanaṃ paññapetvā bhagavantaṃ paccuggamma “ito, bhagavā, upasaṅkamatū”ti āha. Bhagavā upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Atha kho verañjo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ upanisīditukāmo attanā ṭhitapadesato yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Ito paraṃ uttānatthameva.

In the passage, 'Then the Blessed One, having dressed,' it is not stated whether it was morning time or evening time. Even so, the Blessed One, having completed his meal duties and passed the midday, having taken the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, starting from the city gate and illuminating the city streets with Buddha-rays that were golden like a stream of gold, approached the residence of the brahmin Verañja. As soon as the Blessed One stood at the house door, the brahmin's household saw him and informed the brahmin. The brahmin, regaining his mindfulness and becoming spiritually stirred, rose up in haste, prepared an excellent seat, went out to meet the Blessed One, and said, 'May the Blessed One approach here.' The Blessed One approached and sat down on the prepared seat. Then the brahmin Verañja, wishing to sit down near the Blessed One, approached the Blessed One from the place where he was standing. From this point onward, the meaning is plain.

Yaṃ pana brāhmaṇo āha – “apica yo deyyadhammo, so na dinno”ti. Tatrāyamadhippāyo [V 1.0152] – mayā nimantitānaṃ vassaṃvutthānaṃ tumhākaṃ temāsaṃ divase divase pāto yāgukhajjakaṃ, majjhanhike khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ, sāyanhe anekavidha pānavikati gandhapupphādīhi pūjāsakkāroti evamādiko yo deyyadhammo dātabbo assa, so na dinnoti. Tañca kho no asantanti ettha pana liṅgavipallāso veditabbo. So ca kho deyyadhammo amhākaṃ no asantoti ayañhettha attho. Atha [M 1.0165] vā yaṃ dānavatthuṃ mayaṃ tumhākaṃ dadeyyāma, tañca kho no asantanti evamettha attho veditabbo.

As for what the brahmin said: 'Furthermore, whatever gift should have been given, that was not given'—in that statement, this is the intended meaning: 'For you who were invited by me and have completed the rains-residence, for three months, day by day, in the morning, gruel and hard food; at midday, hard and soft food; in the evening, offerings and respects with many kinds of special drinks, perfumes, flowers, and so forth—whatever gift of this kind should have been given, that was not given.' As for the passage, 'And that was not non-existent for us,' a change of gender should be understood here. Indeed, the meaning here is this: 'And that gift was not non-existent for us.' Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'Whatever alms-object we would have given to you, that too was not non-existent for us.'

Nopi adātukamyatāti adātukāmatāpi [P 1.0199] no natthi, yathā pahūtavittūpakaraṇānaṃ maccharīnaṃ. Taṃ kutettha labbhā bahukiccā gharāvāsāti tatrāyaṃ yojanā – yasmā bahukiccā gharāvāsā, tasmā ettha santepi deyyadhamme dātukamyatāya ca taṃ kuto labbhā kuto taṃ sakkā laddhuṃ, yaṃ mayaṃ tumhākaṃ deyyadhammaṃ dadeyyāmāti gharāvāsaṃ garahanto āha. So kira mārena āvaṭṭitabhāvaṃ na jānāti, “gharāvāsapalibodhena me satisammoso jāto”ti maññi, tasmā evamāha. Apica – taṃ kutettha labbhāti imasmiṃ temāsabbhantare yamahaṃ tumhākaṃ dadeyyaṃ, taṃ kuto labbhā? Bahukiccā hi gharāvāsāti evamettha yojanā veditabbā.

'Nor is there unwillingness to give' means: we also have no unwillingness to give, as there is in misers who have abundant wealth and possessions. As for 'How could that be obtained here, for household lives are full of duties?', in that statement, this is the construction: because household lives are full of duties, therefore, herein, even though there are gifts to be given and there is the willingness to give, from where could that reason be obtained, from where would it be possible to obtain that reason, for which we would give you the gift? Thus, censuring household life, he spoke. It seems he did not know that he had been overcome by Māra; he thought, 'Due to the obstruction of household life, a lapse of mindfulness has occurred in me.' Therefore, he spoke thus. Furthermore, as for 'How could that be obtained here?': within these three months, whatever I would give to you, from where could that be obtained? For household lives are indeed full of duties—thus the construction should be understood here.

Atha brāhmaṇo “yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ me tīhi māsehi dātabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ ekadivaseneva dadeyya”nti cintetvā adhivāsetu me bhavaṃ gotamotiādimāha. Tattha svātanāyāti yaṃ me tumhesu sakkāraṃ karoto sve bhavissati puññañceva pītipāmojjañca, tadatthāya. Atha tathāgato “sace ahaṃ nādhivāseyyaṃ, ‘ayaṃ temāsaṃ kiñci aladdhā kupito maññe, tena me yāciyamāno ekabhattampi na paṭiggaṇhāti, natthi imasmiṃ adhivāsanakhanti, asabbaññū aya’nti evaṃ brāhmaṇo ca verañjāvāsino ca garahitvā bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasaveyyuṃ, taṃ tesaṃ mā ahosī”ti tesaṃ anukampāya adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

Then the brahmin thought, 'What if I were to give all at once in a single day that which should have been given by me over three months? That would be excellent.' Having thought thus, he said, 'May the Venerable Gotama consent to me,' and so on. Therein, 'for tomorrow' means for the sake of the merit and the joy and gladness that will be mine tomorrow when I make an offering to you. Then the Tathāgata reflected, 'If I do not consent, thinking, "This one, having received nothing for three months, is angry, I suppose. For that reason, though requested by me, he does not accept even a single meal. There is no patient acceptance in this one; this one is not omniscient," the brahmin and the inhabitants of Verañjā would censure me and generate much demerit. May that not be for them.' Out of compassion for them, the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Adhivāsetvā ca atha kho bhagavā verañjaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ “alaṃ gharāvāsapalibodhacintāyā”ti saññāpetvā taṅkhaṇānurūpāya dhammiyā kathāya diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ sandassetvā kusale dhamme samādapetvā gaṇhāpetvā tattha ca naṃ samuttejetvā saussāhaṃ katvā tāya saussāhatāya aññehi ca vijjamānaguṇehi sampahaṃsetvā dhammaratanavassaṃ vassetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Pakkante ca pana bhagavati verañjo brāhmaṇo puttadāraṃ āmantesi – “mayaṃ, bhaṇe, bhagavantaṃ temāsaṃ nimantetvā ekadivasaṃ ekabhattampi nādamha. Handa, dāni tathā dānaṃ paṭiyādetha yathā temāsikopi deyyadhammo sve ekadivaseneva [M 1.0166] dātuṃ sakkā hotī”ti. Tato paṇītaṃ [P 1.0200] dānaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā [V 1.0153] yaṃ divasaṃ bhagavā nimantito, tassā rattiyā accayena āsanaṭṭhānaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā mahārahāni āsanāni paññapetvā gandhadhūmavāsakusumavicitraṃ mahāpūjaṃ sajjetvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocāpesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho verañjo brāhmaṇo tassā rattiyā accayena…pe… niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta”nti.

And having consented, the Blessed One then, having made the brahmin of Verañjā understand, 'Enough with thinking about the obstruction of household life,' and having clearly shown him the benefit pertaining to the present life and the future life with a Dhamma talk suitable for the occasion, having made him undertake and accept wholesome states, and having incited him therein, made him zealous, and gladdened him with that zeal and with other existing virtues, caused the rain of the Dhamma jewel to fall, and then rose from his seat and departed. And when the Blessed One had departed, the brahmin of Verañjā addressed his children and wife: 'My dears, having invited the Blessed One for three months, we did not give even a single meal on a single day. Come now, prepare the gift in such a way that the offering for the three months can be given tomorrow in a single day.' Then, having had an excellent gift prepared, after that night had passed—the day on which the Blessed One was invited—he had the seating place adorned, had seats worthy of great ones prepared, arranged a great offering made variegated with perfumes, incense, scents, and flowers, and had the time announced to the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: 'Then, the brahmin of Verañjā, after that night had passed… and so on… the meal is ready.'

23. Bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto tattha agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā…pe… nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti. Atha kho verañjo brāhmaṇo buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghanti buddhappamukhanti buddhapariṇāyakaṃ; buddhaṃ saṅghattheraṃ katvā nisinnanti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṇītenāti uttamena. Sahatthāti sahatthena. Santappetvāti suṭṭhu tappetvā, paripuṇṇaṃ suhitaṃ yāvadatthaṃ katvā. Sampavāretvāti suṭṭhu pavāretvā ‘ala’nti hatthasaññāya mukhasaññāya vacībhedena ca paṭikkhipāpetvā. Bhuttāvinti bhuttavantaṃ. Onītapattapāṇinti pattato onītapāṇiṃ; apanītahatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ticīvarena acchādesīti ticīvaraṃ bhagavato adāsi. Idaṃ pana vohāravacanamattaṃ hoti “ticīvarena acchādesī”ti, tasmiñca ticīvare ekameko sāṭako sahassaṃ agghati. Iti brāhmaṇo bhagavato tisahassagghanakaṃ ticīvaramadāsi uttamaṃ kāsikavatthasadisaṃ. Ekamekañca bhikkhuṃ ekamekena dussayugenāti ekamekena dussayugaḷena. Tatra ekasāṭako pañcasatāni agghati. Evaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pañcasatasahassagghanakāni dussāni adāsi. Brāhmaṇo ettakampi datvā atuṭṭho puna sattaṭṭhasahassagghanake anekarattakambale ca paṭṭuṇṇapattapaṭe ca phāletvā phāletvā āyogaaṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanaparissāvanādīnaṃ atthāya adāsi. Satapākasahassapākānañca bhesajjatelānaṃ tumbāni pūretvā ekamekassa bhikkhuno abbhañjanatthāya sahassagghanakaṃ telamadāsi. Kiṃ bahunā, catūsu paccayesu na koci parikkhāro samaṇaparibhogo [P 1.0201] adinno nāma ahosi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana cīvaramattameva vuttaṃ.

23. The Blessed One, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, went there. Thus it is said: 'Then the Blessed One... sat down together with the community of bhikkhus.' In the phrase 'the community of bhikkhus with the Buddha as their chief,' the term 'Buddha as chief' means having the Buddha as the leader; this means they were seated with the Buddha acting as the elder of the Sangha. 'With the finest' means with the best. 'With his own hands' means with his own hand. 'Having satisfied' means having thoroughly satisfied them, having made them content, sufficient, and well-provided, as much as they desired. 'Having invited them to decline' means having properly caused them to decline, that is, having caused them to refuse by hand gesture, facial gesture, and by verbal expression, saying 'enough.' 'Having eaten' means having finished eating. 'Having withdrawn his hand from the bowl' means having a hand removed from the bowl; that is to say, having a withdrawn hand. 'He clothed him with the triple robe' means he gave the triple robe to the Blessed One. This, however, 'he clothed him with the triple robe,' is merely a conventional expression. In that triple robe, each single cloth was worth a thousand. Thus, the brahmin gave the Blessed One a triple robe worth three thousand, which was excellent and like cloth from the Kāsi country. 'And to each bhikkhu, a pair of cloths' means with each pair of cloths. Therein, one cloth was worth five hundred. Thus, to the five hundred bhikkhus, he gave cloths worth five hundred thousand. The brahmin, having given even this much, was still unsatisfied and again gave many red blankets worth seven or eight thousand, and cloths from Paṭṭuṇṇa and Cīna, having torn them up, for the purpose of making items such as carrying-bands, shoulder-straps, waistbands, and water strainers. And having filled leather bottles with medicinal oils prepared a hundred times and a thousand times, he gave to each bhikkhu oil worth a thousand for the purpose of anointing. What more is there to say? Among the four requisites, there was no requisite for monastic use that was not given. In the Pāḷi text, however, only the robes are mentioned.

Evaṃ mahāyāgaṃ yajitvā saputtadāraṃ vanditvā nisinnaṃ atha kho bhagavā verañjaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ temāsaṃ mārāvaṭṭanena dhammasavanāmatarasaparibhogaparihīnaṃ ekadivaseneva dhammāmatavassaṃ vassetvā puripuṇṇasaṅkappaṃ kurumāno dhammiyā [M 1.0167] kathāya sandassetvā…pe… uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Brāhmaṇopi saputtadāro bhagavantañca bhikkhusaṅghañca vanditvā “punapi, bhante, amhākaṃ anuggahaṃ kareyyāthā”ti evamādīni vadanto anubandhitvā assūni pavattayamāno nivatti.

Thus, having performed a great offering, the brahmin Verañja, together with his sons and wife, paid homage and sat down. Then the Blessed One, seeing that the brahmin Verañja had for three months been deprived of the enjoyment of the nectar-like taste of hearing the Dhamma due to Māra's obstruction, caused the rain of the nectar of the Dhamma to fall in a single day, thereby making his resolve complete. Having instructed him with a talk on the Dhamma... he rose from his seat and departed. The brahmin too, together with his sons and wife, having paid homage to the Blessed One and the community of bhikkhus, followed after them, saying such things as, 'Venerable sir, may you show us favor again,' and, with tears flowing, turned back.

Atha kho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvāti yathājjhāsayaṃ yathārucitaṃ vāsaṃ vasitvā verañjāya nikkhamitvā mahāmaṇḍale cārikāya caraṇakāle gantabbaṃ buddhavīthi pahāya dubbhikkhadosena [V 1.0154] kilantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ujunāva maggena gahetvā gantukāmo soreyyādīni anupagamma payāgapatiṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tattha gaṅgaṃ nadiṃ uttaritvā yena bārāṇasī tadavasari. Tena avasari tadavasari. Tatrāpi yathājjhāsayaṃ viharitvā vesāliṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “anupagamma soreyyaṃ…pe… vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāya”nti.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Verañjā as long as he liked—that is, having dwelled there according to his inclination and liking—departed from Verañjā. When it was time to wander on the great circuit, wishing to go, he avoided the Buddha’s Highway that should be traveled. Taking the community of bhikkhus, who were weary due to the hardship of the famine, by a direct path, he proceeded without passing through Soreyya and other towns to the landing place at Payāga. There, he crossed the river Gaṅgā and went down to Bārāṇasī by that route. Thus, `avasari` becomes `tadavasari`. Having stayed there also as long as he liked, he went to Vesālī. Thus it is said: 'Without passing through Soreyya... he dwells in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, at the Hall with the Gabled Roof.'

Buddhāciṇṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The account of the Buddhas' established practice is completed.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verañja Section is concluded.

Tatridaṃ samantapāsādikāya samantapāsādikattasmiṃ –

Therein, regarding the Samantapāsādikā's quality of being 'All-around Pleasing', this is said:

Ācariyaparamparato, nidānavatthuppabhedadīpanato;

Parasamayavivajjanato, sakasamayavisuddhito ceva.

By way of the lineage of teachers, and by illuminating the varieties of origins and subject matters; by way of avoiding other doctrines, and by the purity of its own doctrine;

Byañjanaparisodhanato, padatthato pāḷiyojanakkamato;

Sikkhāpadanicchayato, vibhaṅganayabhedadassanato.

By way of the purification of the phrasing, the meaning of the words, and the method of construing the Pāḷi; by way of the determination of the training rules, and by showing the different methods of the Vibhaṅga analysis.

Sampassataṃ na dissati, kiñci apāsādikaṃ yato ettha;

Viññūnamayaṃ tasmā, samantapāsādikātveva.

Since, for the wise who are observing, nothing unpleasing is seen herein, therefore this is indeed the 'Samantapāsādikā' (All-around Pleasing).

Saṃvaṇṇanā [P 1.0202] pavattā, vinayassa vineyyadamanakusalena;

Vuttassa lokanāthena, lokamanukampamānenāti.

This commentary on the Vinaya—which was spoken by the Lord of the World, who is skilled in taming those to be tamed and has compassion for the world—has been set forth.

Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verañja Section is concluded.

1. Pārājikakaṇḍaṃ

1. The Chapter on the Pārājikas

1. Paṭhamapārājikaṃ

1. The First Pārājika

Sudinnabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Sudinna Recitation Section

24. Ito [M 1.0168][V 1.0155] paraṃ tena kho pana samayena vesāliyā avidūretiādi yebhuyyena uttānatthaṃ. Tasmā anupadavaṇṇanaṃ pahāya yattha yattha vattabbaṃ atthi, taṃ tadeva vaṇṇayissāma. Kalandagāmoti kalandakā vuccanti kāḷakā, tesaṃ vasena laddhanāmo gāmo. Kalandaputtoti gāmavasena laddhanāmassa rājasammatassa cattālīsakoṭivibhavassa kalandaseṭṭhino putto. Yasmā pana tasmiṃ gāme aññepi kalandanāmakā manussā atthi, tasmā kalandaputtoti vatvā puna seṭṭhiputtoti vuttaṃ. Sambahulehīti bahukehi. Sahāyakehīti sukhadukkhāni saha āyanti upagacchantīti sahāyā, sahāyā eva sahāyakā, tehi sahāyakehi. Saddhinti ekato. Kenacideva karaṇīyenāti kenacideva bhaṇḍappayojanauddhārasāraṇādinā kiccena; kattikanakkhattakīḷākiccenātipi vadanti. Bhagavā hi kattikajuṇhapakkhe vesāliṃ sampāpuṇi. Kattikanakkhattakīḷā cettha uḷārā hoti. Tadatthaṃ gatoti veditabbo.

24. From this point onwards, the passage beginning 'At that time, not far from Vesālī,' is for the most part of manifest meaning. Therefore, abandoning a word-by-word commentary, we shall explain only what needs to be explained, wherever it may be. Regarding 'Kalandagāma' (Kalanda village): squirrels (kāḷakā) are called kalandakā; it is a village that received its name on account of them. Regarding 'Kalandaputta' (son of Kalanda): he was the son of the merchant Kalanda, who was named after the village, was acclaimed as a noble, and possessed a fortune of forty crores. However, since there were also other people in that village named Kalanda, after saying 'Kalandaputta,' it was again said 'seṭṭhiputta' (the merchant’s son). 'Sambahulehi' means 'by many.' 'Sahāyakehi' (by companions): because they approach joys and sorrows together (saha āyanti), they are called sahāyā (companions); sahāyā are indeed sahāyakā; thus, 'by those companions.' 'Saddhiṃ' means 'together.' 'Kenacideva karaṇīyena' (for some business): for some commercial reason, such as engaging in business with goods, collecting debts, or reminding of payments. They also say it was for the purpose of the joyful play of the Kattika constellation festival. Indeed, the Blessed One arrived in Vesālī during the waxing moon of the month of Kattika. And the Kattika constellation festival is magnificent there. It should be understood that he went for that purpose.

Addasa khoti kathaṃ addasa? So kira nagarato bhuttapātarāsaṃ suddhuttarāsaṅgaṃ mālāgandhavilepanahatthaṃ buddhadassanatthaṃ dhammasavanatthañca nikkhamantaṃ mahājanaṃ disvā “kva gacchathā”ti pucchi. “Buddhadassanatthaṃ dhammasavanatthañcā”ti. Tena hi “ahampi gacchāmī”ti gantvā catubbidhāya parisāya parivutaṃ brahmassarena dhammaṃ desentaṃ bhagavantaṃ addasa. Tena vuttaṃ – “addasa kho…pe… desenta”nti. Disvānassāti disvāna assa. Etadahosīti pubbe katapuññatāya codiyamānassa bhabbakulaputtassa etaṃ ahosi. Kiṃ ahosi? Yaṃnūnāhampi dhammaṃ suṇeyyanti[V 1.0156]. Tattha yannūnāti parivitakkadassanametaṃ. Evaṃ kirassa parivitakko uppanno “yamayaṃ parisā ekaggacittā dhammaṃ suṇāti, aho vatāhampi taṃ suṇeyya”nti.

Regarding 'Addasa kho' (he saw): How did he see? It is said that he, having had his morning meal, saw a great crowd of people leaving the city, wearing clean upper robes, with flowers, perfumes, and fragrant ointments in hand, for the purpose of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma. Having seen them, he asked, 'Where are you going?' They replied, 'To see the Buddha and to hear the Dhamma.' Then, saying, 'In that case, I too shall go,' he went and saw the Blessed One, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, teaching the Dhamma with a voice like Brahmā's. Therefore it was said, 'He saw... teaching.' 'Disvānassa' means 'disvāna assa' (having seen, for him). 'Etadahosi' (this occurred to him): This thought occurred to this worthy son of a good family, who was being urged on by his previously performed merit. What occurred to him? 'If only I too could listen to the Dhamma!' Herein, 'yannūna' is a particle that indicates consideration. It is said that this consideration arose in him: 'This assembly listens to the Dhamma with a concentrated mind. Oh, how wonderful it would be if I too could listen to it!'

Atha [P 1.0203] kho sudinno kalandaputto yena sā parisāti idha kasmā “yena bhagavā”ti avatvā “yena sā parisā”ti vuttanti ce. Bhagavantañhi parivāretvā uḷāruḷārajanā mahatī parisā nisinnā, tatra na sakkā iminā pacchā āgatena bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā nisīdituṃ. Parisāya pana ekasmiṃ padese sakkāti so taṃ parisaṃyeva upasaṅkamanto. Tena vuttaṃ [M 1.0169] – “atha kho sudinno kalandaputto yena sā parisā”ti. Ekamantaṃ nisinnassa kho sudinnassa kalandaputtassa etadahosīti na nisinnamattasseva ahosi, atha kho bhagavato sittayūpasaṃhitaṃ thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā; taṃ panassa yasmā ekamantaṃ nisinnasseva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekamantaṃ nisinnassa kho sudinnassa kalandaputtassa etadahosī”ti. Kiṃ ahosīti? Yathā yathā khotiādi.

Regarding 'Then Sudinna Kalandaputta went to where that assembly was': if one were to ask why it was said 'to where that assembly was' instead of 'to where the Blessed One was,' the answer is this: A great assembly of very eminent people was seated surrounding the Blessed One, and it was not possible for this latecomer to approach the Blessed One and sit down. However, it was possible to sit down in a certain place within the assembly. Therefore, he approached that very assembly. For this reason it was said, 'Then Sudinna Kalandaputta went to where that assembly was.' Regarding 'As Sudinna Kalandaputta sat to one side, this occurred to him': this thought did not occur to him merely upon sitting down. Rather, it occurred after hearing a brief Dhamma talk from the Blessed One connected with the three trainings. However, because that thought occurred to him only after he was seated to one side, it was said, 'As Sudinna Kalandaputta sat to one side, this occurred to him.' What occurred to him? The thought beginning, 'In whatever way...'

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepakathā – ahaṃ kho yena yena ākārena bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, tena tena me upaparikkhato evaṃ hoti yadetaṃ sittayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ caritabbaṃ, ekadivasampi ca kilesamalena amalīnaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ. Saṅkhalikhitaṃ likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ na sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ kese ca massuñca ohāretvā kasāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā paridahitvā agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyanti. Ettha ca yasmā agārassa hitaṃ kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ agāriyanti vuccati, tañca pabbajjāya natthi; tasmā pabbajjā “anagāriyā”ti ñātabbā. Taṃ anagāriyaṃ pabbajjaṃ. Pabbajeyyanti paribbajeyyaṃ.

Herein is the summary: In whatever way I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, upon my careful examination, it becomes thus: This noble practice of the three trainings should be lived perfectly and completely, so as to reach the final consciousness, having made it unbroken even for a single day. And it should be lived perfectly pure, so as to reach the final consciousness, having made it unstained by the stain of defilements even for a single day. It should be lived like a polished conch, similar to a scraped conch, comparable to a washed conch. It is not easy for one who lives at home, dwelling in the midst of a house, to live this noble practice perfectly and completely...pe... to live it. If only I, having shaved off my hair and beard, and having put on the ochre-colored robes—so-called because they are dyed with astringent liquid, and which are suitable for those who live the noble practice—were to go forth from the household life into the homeless life! And here, because the work beneficial to the household, such as farming and trade, is called 'agāriyaṃ' (household work), and that does not exist in the going forth, therefore the going forth should be known as 'anagāriyā' (the state without household work). That is, into the going forth which is the homeless life. 'Pabbajeyyaṃ' (I would go forth) means 'paribbajeyyaṃ' (I would wander forth).

25. Aciravuṭṭhitāya parisāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti sudinno avuṭṭhitāya parisāya na bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. Kasmā? Tatrassa [P 1.0204] bahū ñātisālohitā mittāmaccā santi, te “‘tvaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ekaputtako, na labbhā tayā pabbajitu’nti bāhāyampi gahetvā ākaḍḍheyyuṃ, tato pabbajjāya antarāyo bhavissatī”ti saheva parisāya uṭṭhahitvā thokaṃ gantvā puna kenaci sarīrakiccalesena nivattitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sudinno kalandaputto aciravuṭṭhitāya parisāya…pe… pabbājetu maṃ bhagavā”ti.

25. Regarding 'When the assembly had not long been risen, he approached the Blessed One': Sudinna did not ask the Blessed One for the going forth while the assembly had not yet risen. Why? Because he had many relatives, kinsmen, friends, and companions there. They might say, 'You are the only son of your parents; it is not permissible for you to go forth,' and might even seize him by the arm and pull him away. Thinking, 'From that, there would be an obstacle to my going forth,' he did not ask. Rising together with the assembly and going a short distance, he then returned on the pretext of some minor bodily need, approached the Blessed One, and asked for the going forth. Therefore it was said, 'Then Sudinna Kalandaputta, when the assembly had not long been risen...pe... let the Blessed One grant me the going forth.'

Bhagavā [V 1.0157] pana yasmā rāhulakumārassa pabbajitato pabhuti mātāpitūhi ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ na pabbājeti, tasmā naṃ pucchi – “anuññātosi pana tvaṃ sudinna mātāpitūhi…pe… pabbajjāyā”ti.

However, because the Blessed One, from the time of Prince Rāhula's going forth onwards, does not give the going forth to a son who has not been permitted by his parents, he therefore asked him: 'Sudinna, have you been permitted by your parents...pe... for the going forth?'

26. Ito [M 1.0170] paraṃ pāṭhānusāreneva gantvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvāti ettha evamattho veditabbo – dhuranikkhepeneva taṃ karaṇīyaṃ niṭṭhāpetvāti; na hi pabbajjāya tibbacchandassa bhaṇḍappayojanauddhārasāraṇādīsu vā nakkhattakīḷāyaṃ vā cittaṃ namati. Amma tātāti ettha pana ammāti mātaraṃ ālapati; tātāti pitaraṃ. Tvaṃ khosīti tvaṃ kho asi. Ekaputtakoti ekova puttako; añño te jeṭṭho vā kaniṭṭho vā natthi. Ettha ca “ekaputto”ti vattabbe anukampāvasena “ekaputtako”ti vuttaṃ. Piyoti pītijananako. Manāpoti manavaḍḍhanako. Sukhedhitoti sukhena edhito; sukhasaṃvaḍḍhitoti attho. Sukhaparihatoti sukhena parihato; jātakālato pabhuti dhātīhi aṅkato aṅkaṃ haritvā dhāriyamāno assakarathakādīhi bālakīḷanakehi kīḷamāno sādurasabhojanaṃ bhojiyamāno sukhena parihato.

26. From this point onwards, following the text, the meaning of 'having settled that matter' should be understood thus: 'having finished that matter only by laying down the burden.' For indeed, the mind of one with a strong desire for the going forth does not incline towards matters such as managing goods and requisites, or towards playing at festivals. In 'Amma, tāta,' 'amma' addresses the mother; 'tāta' addresses the father. 'Tvaṃ khosi' is 'tvaṃ kho asi.' 'Ekaputtako' means 'the one and only beloved son'; you have no other, whether elder or younger. And here, though 'ekaputto' could have been said, 'ekaputtako' is used out of compassion. 'Piyo' means 'one who generates delight.' 'Manāpo' means 'one who increases affection.' 'Sukhedhito' means 'brought up with ease'; the meaning is 'reared with ease.' 'Sukhaparihato' means 'attended to with ease'; from the time of birth, being carried and held by nurses from lap to lap, being made to play with children's toys such as toy horses and chariots, and being fed delicious food, he was attended to with ease.

Na tvaṃ, tāta sudinna, kiñci dukkhassa jānāsīti tvaṃ tāta sudinna kiñci appamattakampi kalabhāgaṃ dukkhassa na jānāsi; atha vā kiñci dukkhena nānubhosīti attho. Karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, anubhavanatthe ca jānanā; atha vā kiñci dukkhaṃ nassarasīti attho. Upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, saraṇatthe ca jānanā. Vikappadvayepi purimapadassa uttarapadena samānavibhattilopo daṭṭhabbo. Taṃ sabbaṃ saddasatthānusārena ñātabbaṃ. Maraṇenapi mayaṃ te akāmakā vinā bhavissāmāti [P 1.0205] sacepi tava amhesu jīvamānesu maraṇaṃ bhaveyya, tena te maraṇenapi mayaṃ akāmakā anicchakā na attano ruciyā, vinā bhavissāma; tayā viyogaṃ vā pāpuṇissāmāti attho. Kiṃ pana mayaṃ tanti evaṃ sante kiṃ pana kiṃ nāma taṃ kāraṇaṃ yena mayaṃ taṃ jīvantaṃ anujānissāma; atha vā kiṃ pana mayaṃ tanti kena pana kāraṇena mayaṃ taṃ jīvantaṃ anujānissāmāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'You do not know any suffering, dear Sudinna' means: Dear Sudinna, you do not know even a small measure, a mere fraction, of suffering. Alternatively, the meaning is: you have not experienced any sense-object through suffering. The genitive case is in the sense of the instrumental, and 'knowing' is in the sense of 'experiencing.' Alternatively, the meaning is: you do not remember any suffering. The genitive case is in the sense of the accusative, and 'knowing' is in the sense of 'remembering.' In both alternatives, the elision of the identical case ending of the preceding word with the following word should be understood. All this should be known in accordance with the grammatical texts. 'Even by death, we would be unwillingly separated from you' means: If death should occur to you while we are living, then even by that death of yours, we, being unwilling and not desiring it—not by our own wish—will be separated; we will attain separation from you. 'What then of us?' means: This being so, what then is that reason for which we would permit you while you are living? Alternatively, 'What then of us?' means: For what reason would we permit you while you are living? We will certainly not permit it. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

27. Tatthevāti yattha naṃ ṭhitaṃ mātāpitaro nānujāniṃsu, tattheva ṭhāne. Anantarahitāyāti kenaci attharaṇena anatthatāya.

27. 'In that very place' means: in the very place where his parents did not give him permission as he stood there. 'On the uncovered ground' means: unspread with any kind of covering.

28. Paricārehīti gandhabbanaṭanāṭakādīni paccupaṭṭhāpetvā tattha sahāyakehi saddhiṃ yathāsukhaṃ indriyāni cārehi sañcārehi; ito cito ca upanehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā paricārehīti [V 1.0158] gandhabbanaṭanāṭakādīni paccupaṭṭhāpetvā [M 1.0171] tattha sahāyakehi saddhiṃ laḷa, upalaḷa, rama, kīḷassūtipi vuttaṃ hoti. Kāme paribhuñjantoti attano puttadārehi saddhiṃ bhoge bhuñjanto. Puññāni karontoti buddhañca dhammañca saṅghañca ārabbha dānappadānādīni sugatimaggasodhakāni kusalakammāni karonto. Tuṇhī ahosīti kathānuppabandhavicchedanatthaṃ nirālāpasallāpo ahosi. Athassa mātāpitaro tikkhattuṃ vatvā paṭivacanampi alabhamānā sahāyake pakkosāpetvā “esa vo sahāyako pabbajitukāmo, nivāretha na”nti āhaṃsu. Tepi taṃ upasaṅkamitvā tikkhattuṃ avocuṃ, tesampi tuṇhī ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sudinnassa kalandaputtassa sahāyakā…pe… tuṇhī ahosī”ti.

28. 'Entertain yourself' means: having caused singers, dancers, acrobats, and others to be present, let your faculties roam and wander about among those sense-objects with your companions as you please; bring them near, to this and that sense-object—this is what is said. Alternatively, 'entertain yourself' means: having caused singers, dancers, acrobats, and others to be present, be playful, be very playful, enjoy yourself, and play there with your companions—this is also what is said. 'Enjoying sensual pleasures' means: enjoying pleasures with one's own children and wife. 'Making merit' means: with reference to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, performing wholesome actions that cleanse the path to a good destination, such as the giving of excellent gifts. 'He was silent' means: for the purpose of cutting off the continuity of conversation, he was without initial speech or responsive speech. Then his parents, having spoken three times and not receiving even a reply, had his companions summoned and said, 'This friend of yours desires to go forth; prevent him.' They too, having approached him, spoke three times, and to them also he was silent. Therefore it was said: 'Then the companions of Sudinna the Kalandaputta... he was silent.'

29. Athassa sahāyakānaṃ etadahosi – “sace ayaṃ pabbajjaṃ alabhamāno marissati na koci guṇo bhavissati. Pabbajitaṃ pana naṃ mātāpitaropi kālena kālaṃ passissanti. Mayampi passissāma. Pabbajjāpi ca nāmesā bhāriyā, divase divase mattikāpattaṃ gahetvā piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ. Ekaseyyaṃ ekabhattaṃ brahmacariyaṃ atidukkaraṃ. Ayañca sukhumālo nāgarikajātiyo, so taṃ carituṃ asakkonto puna idheva āgamissati. Handassa [P 1.0206] mātāpitaro anujānāpessāmā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Mātāpitaropi naṃ anujāniṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sudinnassa kalandaputtassa sahāyakā yena sudinnassa kalandaputtassa mātāpitaro…pe… anuññātosi mātāpitūhi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjāyā”ti.

29. Then this thought occurred to his companions: 'If this one should die without obtaining the going forth, there will be no benefit. But when he has gone forth, his parents will see him from time to time, and we too will see him. Moreover, this so-called going forth is a heavy burden; day by day one must take a clay bowl and wander for alms. The holy life—sleeping alone, eating one meal—is extremely difficult to practice. And this one is delicate, of city-dweller stock; being unable to practice it, he will come back right here again. Come, let us cause his parents to give permission.' They did so, and his parents also gave him permission. Therefore it was said: 'Then the companions of Sudinna the Kalandaputta went to the parents of Sudinna the Kalandaputta... you have been permitted by your parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness.'

30. Haṭṭhoti tuṭṭho. Udaggoti pītivasena abbhunnatakāyacitto. Katipāhanti katipayāni divasāni. Balaṃ gāhetvāti sappāyabhojanāni bhuñjanto, ucchādananhāpanādīhi ca kāyaṃ pariharanto, kāyabalaṃ janetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā assumukhaṃ ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… pabbājetu maṃ bhante bhagavāti. Bhagavā samīpe ṭhitaṃ aññataraṃ piṇḍacārikaṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “tena hi bhikkhu sudinnaṃ pabbājehi ceva upasampādehi cā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissuṇitvā sudinnaṃ kalandaputtaṃ jinadattiyaṃ saddhivihārikaṃ laddhā pabbājesi ceva upasampādesi ca. Tena vuttaṃ – “alattha kho [M 1.0172] sudinno kalandaputto bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampada”nti.

30. 'Joyful' means: delighted. 'Elated' means: with body and mind greatly uplifted by the power of joy. 'For some days' means: for a few days. 'Having regained strength' means: eating suitable food and attending to his body with such things as rubbing with scented powder and bathing, and having thus generated bodily strength, he paid respects to his parents, left behind his circle of relatives with tearful faces, and approached the Blessed One... saying, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One let me go forth.' The Blessed One addressed a certain monk, an alms-goer, who was standing nearby: 'Well then, monk, let Sudinna go forth and give him the higher ordination.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' that monk replied, having consented to the Blessed One. Having received Sudinna, the son of Kalanda—a gift from the Jina—as his co-resident pupil, he let him go forth and gave him the higher ordination. Therefore it was said: 'Sudinna, the son of Kalanda, obtained the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he obtained the higher ordination.'

Ettha pana ṭhatvā sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca kathitā. Mayaṃ pana yathāṭhitapāḷivaseneva khandhake kathayissāma. Na kevalañcetaṃ, aññampi yaṃ khandhake vā parivāre vā kathetabbaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyehi vibhaṅgekathitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ tattha tattheva kathayissāma. Evañhi kathiyamāne [V 1.0159] pāḷikkameneva vaṇṇanā katā hoti. Tato tena tena vinicchayena atthikānaṃ pāḷikkameneva imaṃ vinayasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ oloketvā so so vinicchayo suviññeyyo bhavissatīti.

Here, however, in all the commentaries, both the going forth and the higher ordination have been discussed. But we shall explain it in the Khandhaka only in accordance with the Pāḷi text as it stands. And not only this, but whatever else that should be discussed in the Khandhaka or the Parivāra has been explained by the commentary teachers in the Vibhaṅga, all of that we shall explain right in those respective places. For when it is explained in this way, the explanation will have been made only in accordance with the sequence of the Pāḷi. Then, for those who are desirous of these various decisions, each particular decision will be easily understood by consulting this Vinaya commentary only in accordance with the sequence of the Pāḷi.

Acirūpasampannoti aciraṃ upasampanno hutvā; upasampadato nacirakāleyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Evarūpeti evaṃvidhe evaṃjātike. Dhutaguṇeti kilesaniddhunanake guṇe. Samādāya vattatīti samādiyitvā gaṇhitvā vattati carati viharati. Āraññiko hotīti gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā āraññikadhutaṅgavasena araññavāsiko hoti. Piṇḍapātikoti atirekalābhapaṭikkhepena cuddasa bhattāni paṭikkhipitvā [P 1.0207] piṇḍapātikadhutaṅgavasena piṇḍapātiko hoti. Paṃsukūlikoti gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā paṃsukūlikadhutaṅgavasena paṃsukūliko hoti. Sapadānacārikoti loluppacāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā sapadānacārikadhutaṅgavasena sapadānacāriko hoti; gharapaṭipāṭiyā bhikkhāya pavisati. Vajjigāmanti vajjīnaṃ gāmaṃ vajjīsu vā gāmaṃ.

Acirūpasampanno means: having been ordained not long ago; that is to say, in not a long time since the higher ordination. Evarūpe means: of such a kind, of such a sort. Dhutaguṇe means: qualities that shake off the defilements. Samādāya vattati means: having undertaken and taken up, he exists, he practices, he dwells. Āraññiko hoti means: having rejected a dwelling at the edge of a village, by means of the forest-dweller's ascetic practice, he is a forest-dweller. Piṇḍapātiko means: by rejecting extra gains, having rejected the fourteen meals, by means of the alms-food-eater's ascetic practice, he is an alms-food-eater. Paṃsukūliko means: having rejected a householder's robe, by means of the rag-robe-wearer's ascetic practice, he is a rag-robe-wearer. Sapadānacāriko means: having rejected greedy wandering, by means of the house-to-house-goer's ascetic practice, he is a house-to-house-goer; he enters for alms according to the sequence of houses. Vajjigāmaṃ means: a village of the Vajjis, or a village in the Vajjian country.

Aḍḍhā mahaddhanātiādīsu upabhogaparibhogūpakaraṇamahantatāya aḍḍhā; ye hi tesaṃ upabhogā yāni ca upabhogūpakaraṇāni, tāni mahantāni bahulāni sārakānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nidhetvā ṭhapitadhanamahantatāya mahaddhanā. Mahābhogāti divasaparibbayasaṅkhātabhogamahantatāya mahābhogā. Aññehi upabhogehi jātarūparajatasseva pahūtatāya pahūtajātarūparajatā. Alaṅkārabhūtassa vittūpakaraṇassa pītipāmojjakaraṇassa pahūtatāya pahūtavittūpakaraṇā. Vohāravasena parivattentassa dhanadhaññassa pahūtatāya pahūtadhanadhaññāti veditabbā.

In texts such as aḍḍhā mahaddhanā, aḍḍhā means wealthy due to the greatness of the requisites for use and enjoyment; for their things for enjoyment and their requisites for enjoyment are great, many, and excellent—this is what is meant. Mahaddhanā means of great wealth due to the greatness of wealth that has been buried and stored away. Mahābhogā means of great possessions due to the greatness of possessions known as daily expenditure. Pahūtajātarūparajatā means having abundant gold and silver due to the abundance of just gold and silver over other possessions. Pahūtavittūpakaraṇā means having abundant pleasing requisites due to the abundance of pleasing requisites that are ornaments and cause joy and delight. Pahūtadhanadhaññā should be understood as having abundant wealth and grain due to the abundance of wealth and grain that is exchanged by way of trade.

Senāsanaṃ [M 1.0173] saṃsāmetvāti senāsanaṃ paṭisāmetvā; yathā na vinassati tathā naṃ suṭṭhu ṭhapetvāti attho. Saṭṭhimatte thālipāketi gaṇanaparicchedato saṭṭhithālipāke. Ekameko cettha thālipāko dasannaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhāti. Taṃ sabbampi channaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ bhattaṃ hoti. Bhattābhihāraṃ abhihariṃsūti ettha abhiharīyatīti abhihāro. Kiṃ abhiharīyati? Bhattaṃ. Bhattameva abhihāro bhattābhihāro, taṃ bhattābhihāraṃ. Abhihariṃsūti abhimukhā hariṃsu. Tassa santikaṃ gahetvā āgamaṃsūti attho. Etassa kiṃ pamāṇanti? Saṭṭhi thālipākā. Tena vuttaṃ – “saṭṭhimatte thālipāke bhattābhihāraṃ abhihariṃsū”ti. Bhikkhūnaṃ vissajjetvāti sayaṃ ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikattā sapadānacāraṃ caritukāmo bhikkhūnaṃ paribhogatthāya pariccajitvā datvā. Ayaṃ hi āyasmā “bhikkhū ca lābhaṃ lacchanti ahañca piṇḍakena na kilamissāmī”ti etadatthameva āgato. Tasmā attano āgamanānurūpaṃ [P 1.0208] karonto bhikkhūnaṃ vissajjetvā sayaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā means: having set the lodging in order; the meaning is, having placed it well in such a way that it will not be destroyed. Saṭṭhimatte thālipāke means: sixty cooking pots, by way of numerical division. And here, each single cooking pot holds food for ten bhikkhus. All of that is food for six hundred bhikkhus. In bhattābhihāraṃ abhihariṃsū: abhihāro is so called because it is brought forward. What is brought forward? Food. Food itself is the offering, a food-offering. Abhihariṃsu means: facing him, they brought it. The meaning is: they took it and came into his presence. What is the measure of this? Sixty cooking pots. Therefore it was said: 'they brought a food-offering of sixty cooking pots.' Bhikkhūnaṃ vissajjetvā means: because he himself was a practitioner of the highest form of the alms-food-eater's practice and wished to go on the uninterrupted alms-round, he relinquished and gave it for the bhikkhus' consumption. For this venerable one had come for this very purpose: 'The bhikkhus will receive a gain, and I will not become weary from the alms-food.' Therefore, doing what was suitable for his arrival, having relinquished it to the bhikkhus, he himself entered for alms-food.

31. Ñātidāsīti [V 1.0160] ñātakānaṃ dāsī. Ābhidosikanti pārivāsikaṃ ekarattātikkantaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – pūtibhāvadosena abhibhūtoti abhidoso, abhidosova ābhidosiko, ekarattātikkantassa vā nāmasaññā esā, yadidaṃ ābhidosikoti, taṃ ābhidosikaṃ. Kummāsanti yavakummāsaṃ. Chaḍḍetukāmā hotīti yasmā antamaso dāsakammakarānampi gorūpānampi aparibhogāraho, tasmā taṃ kacavaraṃ viya bahi chaḍḍetukāmā hoti. Sacetanti sace etaṃ. Bhaginīti ariyavohārena ñātidāsiṃ ālapati. Chaḍḍanīyadhammanti chaḍḍetabbasabhāvaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “bhagini, etaṃ sace bahi chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ nissaṭṭhapariggahaṃ, taṃ idha me patte ākirā”ti.

31. Ñātidāsī means: a female slave of his relatives. Ābhidosikaṃ means: stale, having passed one night, having become putrid. Herein, this is the word-meaning: abhidoso is so called because it is overcome by the fault of putridity; abhidoso itself is ābhidosiko. Or, this designation ābhidosiko is a name for something that has passed one night. Kummāsaṃ means: barley-meal. Chaḍḍetukāmā hoti means: because it is unfit for consumption even by the lowest slaves and workers, and even by cattle, therefore she wishes to discard it outside like rubbish. Sacetanti is to be parsed as sace etaṃ. With bhaginī, he addresses the relative's female slave with the noble form of address. Chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ means: having the nature of being fit to be discarded. This is what is said: 'Sister, if that thing is to be discarded outside, an abandoned possession, then pour it here into my bowl.'

Kiṃ pana evaṃ vattuṃ labbhati, viññatti vā payuttavācā vā na hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Nissaṭṭhapariggahattā. Yañhi chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ nissaṭṭhapariggahaṃ, yattha sāmikā anālayā honti, taṃ sabbaṃ “detha āharatha idha ākirathā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Tathā hi aggaariyavaṃsiko āyasmā raṭṭhapālopi “chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ kummāsaṃ idha me patte ākirā”ti (ma. ni. 2.299) avaca. Tasmā yaṃ evarūpaṃ chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ aññaṃ vā apariggahitaṃ vanamūlaphalabhesajjādikaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ yathāsukhaṃ āharāpetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ, na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ. Hatthānanti [M 1.0174] bhikkhāggahaṇatthaṃ pattaṃ upanāmayato maṇibandhato pabhuti dvinnampi hatthānaṃ. Pādānanti nivāsanantato paṭṭhāya dvinnampi pādānaṃ. Sarassāti “sacetaṃ bhaginī”ti vācaṃ nicchārayato sarassa ca. Nimittaṃ aggahesīti gihikāle sallakkhitapubbaṃ ākāraṃ aggahesi sañjāni sallakkhesi. Sudinno hi bhagavato dvādasame vasse pabbajito vīsatime vasse ñātikulaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho sayaṃ pabbajjāya aṭṭhavassiko hutvā; tena naṃ sā ñātidāsī disvāva na sañjāni, nimittaṃ pana aggahesīti.

But is it permissible to speak thus? Is this not an intimation or a purposeful speech? It is not. Why? Because of the state of having relinquished possession. For whatever thing is of a discardable nature, has its possession relinquished, and regarding which the owners have no attachment, it is proper to say of all that, 'Give, bring, pour it here.' Indeed, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, the foremost among those who practice the noble lineage, also said, 'Pour the discardable barley-meal here into my bowl.' Therefore, whatever thing of such a discardable nature there is, or any other unpossessed thing such as forest roots, fruits, and medicines, all that may be caused to be brought as one pleases and consumed; one should not feel remorse. 'Of the hands' means: of both hands from the wrist onwards as he was presenting the bowl to receive alms. 'Of the feet' means: of both feet starting from the edge of the lower robe. 'Of the voice' means: of the voice as he was uttering the words, 'If this, sister...' 'She grasped the sign' means: she grasped, clearly knew, and noted the characteristic that had been previously marked during his lay life. For Sudinna had gone forth in the twelfth year of the Blessed One. In the twentieth year, being himself eight years in the state of having gone forth, he entered his relatives' home for alms. Because of that, the female slave of the relatives did not recognize him immediately upon seeing him, but she grasped the sign.

Sudinnassa mātaraṃ etadavocāti atigarunā pabbajjūpagatena sāmiputtena [P 1.0209] saddhiṃ “tvaṃ nu kho me, bhante, ayyo sudinno”tiādivacanaṃ vattuṃ avisahantī vegena gharaṃ pavisitvā sudinnassa mātaraṃ etaṃ avoca. Yaggheti ārocanatthe nipāto. Sace je saccanti ettha jeti ālapane nipāto. Evañhi tasmiṃ dese dāsijanaṃ ālapanti, tasmā “tvaṃ, bhoti dāsi, sace saccaṃ bhaṇasī”ti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'She said this to Sudinna's mother' means: Not daring to utter words such as, 'Venerable sir, are you my master Sudinna?' to her master's son—who was greatly respected even as a layman and had now undertaken the life of a renunciant—she quickly entered the house and said this to Sudinna's mother. `Yagghe` is a particle that occurs in the sense of announcing. In `sace je saccaṃ`, `je` is a particle that occurs in the sense of addressing. For in that region, they address a female slave thus. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: 'You, good female slave, if you speak the truth.'

32. Aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlanti tasmiṃ kira dese dānapatīnaṃ gharesu sālā honti, āsanāni cettha paññattāni honti, upaṭṭhāpitaṃ udakakañjiyaṃ; tattha pabbajitā piṇḍāya caritvā [V 1.0161] nisīditvā bhuñjanti. Sace icchanti, dānapatīnampi santakaṃ gaṇhanti. Tasmā tampi aññatarassa kulassa īdisāya sālāya aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlanti veditabbaṃ. Na hi pabbajitā kapaṇamanussā viya asāruppe ṭhāne nisīditvā bhuñjantīti.

32. 'At the foot of a certain wall': It is said that in that region, in the compounds of donors' houses, there are halls. In these halls, seats are prepared, and drinking water, water for use, and rice-gruel are set out. There, renunciants, having wandered for alms, sit down and eat. If they wish, they also take what belongs to the donors. Therefore, that 'foot of a wall' should be understood as the foot of a certain wall of such a hall belonging to some family. For renunciants do not sit and eat in unsuitable places like destitute people.

Atthi nāma tātāti ettha atthīti vijjamānatthe; nāmāti pucchanatthe maññanatthe ca nipāto. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – “atthi nu kho, tāta sudinna, amhākaṃ dhanaṃ, na mayaṃ niddhanāti vattabbā, yesaṃ no tvaṃ īdise ṭhāne nisīditvā ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasi”; tathā “atthi nu kho, tāta sudinna, amhākaṃ jīvitaṃ, na mayaṃ matāti vattabbā, yesaṃ no tvaṃ īdise ṭhāne nisīditvā ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasi”; tathā “atthi maññe, tāta sudinna, tava abbhantare sāsanaṃ nissāya paṭiladdho [M 1.0175] samaṇaguṇo, yaṃ tvaṃ subhojanarasasaṃvaḍḍhitopi imaṃ jigucchaneyyaṃ ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ amatamiva nibbikāro paribhuñjissasī”ti.

In 'Atthi nāma tāta': `atthi` is in the sense of 'it exists'; `nāma` is a particle in the sense of questioning and also in the sense of supposing. For this is what is said: 'Dear Sudinna, is it not so that we, whose son you are who sits in such a place and consumes stale barley-meal, have wealth? We should not be called destitute.' Likewise: 'Dear Sudinna, is it not so that we, whose son you are who sits in such a place and consumes stale barley-meal, are still alive? We should not be called dead.' Furthermore (in the sense of supposing): 'Dear Sudinna, I suppose there must be the quality of a recluse within you, attained by relying on the Teaching, that you, though raised on the taste of fine food, consume this repulsive, stale barley-meal without any change in composure, as if it were ambrosia.'

So pana gahapati dukkhābhitunnatāya etamatthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā vattumasakkonto “atthi nāma, tāta sudinna, ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasī”ti ettakameva avoca. Akkharacintakā panettha imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vadanti – anokappanāmarisanatthavasena etaṃ atthināmasadde upapade “paribhuñjissasī”ti anāgatavacanaṃ kataṃ. Tassāyamattho – atthi nāma…pe… paribhuñjissasi, idaṃ paccakkhampi ahaṃ na saddahāmi [P 1.0210] na marisayāmīti. Tatāyaṃ ābhidosikoti tato tava gehato ayaṃ ābhidosiko kummāso laddhoti attho. Tatoyantipi pāṭho. Tadāyantipi paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Yena sakapitu nivesananti yena sakassa pitu attano pitu nivesananti attho; thero pitari pemeneva subbaco hutvā agamāsi. Adhivāsesīti thero ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikopi samāno “sace ekabhattampi na gahessāmi, ativiya nesaṃ domanassaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñātīnaṃ anukampāya adhivāsesi.

But that householder, being afflicted by sorrow and unable to state this meaning completely, said only this much: 'Is it really so, dear Sudinna, that you will consume stale barley-meal?' The grammarians state this characteristic here: when the proximate word `atthināma` is present, this future tense word `paribhuñjissasi` is used by way of the meaning of disbelief and intolerance. This is its meaning: 'Is it really so... that you will consume...? Even though this is directly perceived, I cannot believe it, I cannot tolerate it.' `Tatāyaṃ ābhidosiko` means: 'This stale barley-meal was obtained from that home of yours.' There is also the reading `tatoyanti`. They also recite `tadāyanti`; that is not good. `Yena sakapitu nivesanaṃ` means: 'where his own father's house is.' The elder, only because of affection for his father, being easy to persuade, went. `Adhivāsesi` means: Although the elder was an observer of the strict alms-food practice, thinking, 'If I do not accept even a single meal, their displeasure will be very great,' he consented out of compassion for his relatives.

33. Opuñjāpetvāti upalimpāpetvā. Ekaṃ hiraññassāti ettha hiraññanti kahāpaṇo veditabbo. Purisoti nātidīgho nātirasso majjhimappamāṇo veditabbo. Tirokaraṇīyanti karaṇatthe bhummaṃ; sāṇipākārena parikkhipitvāti attho. Atha vā tiro karonti etenāti tirokaraṇīyaṃ, taṃ parikkhipitvā; samantato katvāti attho. Tena hīti yasmā ajja sudinno āgamissati tena kāraṇena. Hi iti padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Tenāti ayampi vā uyyojanatthe nipātoyeva.

33. `Opuñjāpetvā` means: having caused to be smeared. In `ekaṃ hiraññassa`, `hirañña` should be understood as a `kahāpaṇa`. `Puriso` should be understood as a man of medium proportions, neither too tall nor too short. `Tirokaraṇīyaṃ`: this word is in the locative case in the sense of an instrument; the meaning is 'having enclosed with a cloth screen'. Alternatively, it is called `tirokaraṇīyaṃ` because 'with it they make a screen'; the meaning is 'having enclosed it', 'having made it all around'. `Tena hi` means: for the reason that Sudinna will come today. `Hi` is a particle that occurs merely as a sentence-filler. Alternatively, this word `tena` is also a particle that occurs in the sense of urging.

34. Pubbaṇhasamayanti [V 1.0162] ettha kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ kālārocanaṃ na vuttaṃ, atha kho ārociteyeva kāle agamāsīti veditabbo. Idaṃ te tātāti dve puñje dassento āha. Mātūti janettiyā. Mattikanti mātito āgataṃ; idaṃ te mātāmahiyā mātu imaṃ gehaṃ āgacchantiyā dinnadhananti attho. Itthikāya itthidhananti hīḷento āha[M 1.0176]. Itthikāya nāma itthiparibhogānaṃyeva nhānacuṇṇādīnaṃ atthāya laddhaṃ dhanaṃ kittakaṃ bhaveyya. Tassāpi tāva parimāṇaṃ passa. Atha vā idaṃ te tāta sudinna mātu dhanaṃ, tañca kho mattikaṃ, na mayā dinnaṃ, tava mātuyeva santakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ panetaṃ na kasiyā na vaṇijjāya sambhūtaṃ, apica kho itthikāya itthidhanaṃ. Yaṃ itthikāya ñātikulato sāmikakulaṃ gacchantiyā laddhabbaṃ nhānacuṇṇādīnaṃ atthāya itthidhanaṃ, taṃ tāva ettakanti evamettha [P 1.0211] attho daṭṭhabbo.

34. Regarding the phrase "at the time of forenoon," although an announcement of the time is not stated in the Pāḷi, it should be understood that he went only after the time was announced. Showing the two piles, he said, "This is for you, my dear." "From your mother" means from the birth mother. "Maternal" means what came from the mother; the meaning is, "This was wealth given to your mother by your maternal grandmother when she came to this house." Speaking disparagingly, he said, "A woman's wealth for a woman." How much wealth could there be, obtained for a woman's use—such as for bathing powder and the like? Just look at its amount. Alternatively, it means, "This, dear Sudinna, is your mother's wealth, and it is indeed maternal wealth, not given by me—it belongs solely to your mother." Furthermore, this wealth was not produced through farming or trade, but rather it was a woman's wealth for a woman. The meaning here should be understood thus: "Whatever woman's wealth is to be received by a woman going from her relatives' family to her husband's family, for the purpose of things like bathing powder, is this much."

Aññaṃ pettikaṃ aññaṃ pitāmahanti yaṃ pana te pitu ca pitāmahānañca santakaṃ, taṃ aññaṃyeva. Nihitañca payuttañca ativiya bahu; ettha ca pitāmahanti taddhitalopaṃ katvā veditabbaṃ. Petāmahanti vā pāṭho. Labbhā tāta sudinna hīnāyāvattitvāti tāta, sudinna, uttamaṃ ariyaddhajaṃ pabbajitaliṅgaṃ pahāya hīnāya gihibhāvāya āvattitvā labbhā bhogā bhuñjituṃ, nālabbhā bhuñjituṃ, na tvaṃ rājabhīto pabbajito, na iṇāyikehi palibuddho hutvāti. Tāta na ussahāmīti ettha pana tātāti vacanaṃ gehasitapemena āha, na samaṇatejena. Na ussahāmīti na sakkomi. Na visahāmīti nappahomi, na samatthomhi.

“Paternal wealth is one thing, ancestral wealth another” means that whatever belonged to your father and your grandfathers is something else entirely. Both what is buried and what is invested is exceedingly abundant. And here, in the word “pitāmahaṃ,” it should be understood that the taddhita suffix has been elided. Alternatively, the reading is “petāmahaṃ.” As for the phrase, “It is possible, dear Sudinna, to revert to the inferior state”: “Dear Sudinna, having abandoned the supreme noble banner, the mark of a renunciant, and having reverted to the inferior state of a householder, it is possible to enjoy these riches. It is not that they are impossible to enjoy. You did not go forth out of fear of the king, nor did you go forth because you were harassed by creditors.” Furthermore, in “My dear, I am not able,” the word “my dear” was spoken with affection based on the household life, not with the power of a renunciant. “I am not able” means “I cannot.” “I cannot bear it” means “I am not able, I am not capable.”

“Vadeyyāma kho taṃ gahapatī”ti idaṃ pana vacanaṃ samaṇatejenāha. Nātikaḍḍheyyāsīti yaṃ te mayi pemaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ, taṃ kodhavasena na atikaḍḍheyyāsi; sace na kujjheyyāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato seṭṭhi “putto me saṅgahaṃ maññe kattukāmo”ti udaggacitto āha – “vadehi tāta sudinnā”ti. Tenahīti uyyojanatthe vibhattipatirūpako nipāto. Tatonidānanti taṃnidānaṃ taṃhetukanti paccattavacanassa to-ādeso veditabbo; samāse cassa lopābhāvo. Bhayaṃ vāti “kinti me bhoge neva rājāno hareyyu”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ rājādibhayaṃ; cittutrāsoti attho. Chambhitattanti rājūhi vā corehi vā “dhanaṃ dehī”ti kammakāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa kāyiñjanaṃ kāyakampo hadayamaṃsacalanaṃ. Lomahaṃsoti uppanne bhaye lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ uddhaggabhāvo. Ārakkhoti anto ca bahi ca rattiñca divā ca ārakkhaṇaṃ.

“We would speak to you, householder”—this statement, however, was made with the power of a renunciant. “You should not pull away” means: you should not pull away the affection you have established for me through the power of anger; this is said as, “if you would not be angry.” Then the merchant, with an uplifted mind, thinking, “I think my son wishes to do me a favor,” said, “Speak, dear Sudinna.” “Tena hi” is a particle that resembles an inflected word, used in the sense of urging. Regarding “tatonidānaṃ”: meaning “having that as its cause, having that as its reason,” the substitution of ‘to’ for the nominative case ending should be understood; and in a compound, there is no elision of it. “Fear, or…” refers to the fear of kings and others, stated in the manner of “How might kings not seize my wealth?” and so on; the meaning is mental terror. “Trembling” means, when being compelled by kings or thieves with the demand, “Give us your wealth!”, there is bodily agitation, bodily trembling, and a fluttering of the heart muscle. “Horripilation” means, when fear arises, the bristling of the hairs, their ends standing up. “Protection” means guarding inside and outside, by night and by day.

35. Tena hi vadhūti seṭṭhi gahapati dhanaṃ dassetvā puttaṃ attanā gihibhāvatthāya palobhetuṃ asakkonto “mātugāmasadisaṃ dāni purisānaṃ [M 1.0177] bandhanaṃ natthī”ti maññitvā tassa purāṇadutiyikaṃ [V 1.0163] āmantesi – “tena hi vadhū”ti. Purāṇadutiyikanti purāṇaṃ dutiyikaṃ pubbe gihikāle dutiyikaṃ, gehasitasukhupabhogasahāyikaṃ bhūtapubbabhariyanti attho. Tena hīti yena kāraṇena mātugāmasadisaṃ bandhanaṃ natthi. Pādesu gahetvāti [P 1.0212] pāde gahetvā; upayogatthe bhummavacanaṃ, pādesu vā taṃ gahetvā. “Kīdisā nāma tā ayyaputta accharāyo”ti kasmā evamāha? Tadā kira sambahule khattiyakumārepi brāhmaṇakumārepi seṭṭhiputtepi mahāsampattiyo pahāya pabbajante disvā pabbajjāguṇaṃ ajānantā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti – “kasmā ete pabbajantī”ti. Athaññe vadanti – “devaccharānaṃ devanāṭakānaṃ kāraṇā”ti. Sā kathā vitthārikā ahosi. Taṃ gahetvā ayaṃ evamāhāti. Thero taṃ paṭikkhipanto na kho ahaṃ bhaginīti āha. Samudācaratīti voharati vadeti. Tattheva mucchitā papatāti naṃ bhaginivādena samudācarantaṃ disvā “anatthiko dāni mayā ayaṃ yo maṃ pajāpatiṃ samānaṃ attanā saddhiṃ ekamātukucchiyā sayitadārikaṃ viya maññatī”ti samuppannabalavasokā hutvā tasmiṃyeva padese mucchitā papatā; patitāti attho.
