35. “Very well then, daughter-in-law”—the merchant-householder, having shown the wealth and being unable himself to entice his son to return to the household life, thought, “Now, for men, there is no bond like a woman,” and addressed his former wife, saying, “Very well then, daughter-in-law.” “Former companion” means: a former second one; in the past, during the time as a householder, a second one; a companion in enjoying the subtle pleasures of the household life; a former wife. This is the meaning. “Very well then” means: for the reason that there is no bond like a woman. “Taking hold of the feet” means taking the feet; the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative, or, taking him at the feet. Why did she say, “What kind of celestial nymphs are those, noble sir?” It is said that at that time, seeing many Khattiya youths, Brahmin youths, and merchants' sons renounce great fortunes and go forth, those who did not know the virtue of renunciation started a discussion, asking, “Why do these men go forth?” Then others would say, “For the sake of celestial nymphs and celestial dancers.” That talk had become widespread. Taking that up, she spoke thus. The Elder, rejecting this, said, “Indeed not, sister.” “Addresses” means speaks to, calls. “Right there she fainted and fell”—seeing him address her with the term “sister,” she thought, “This one now has no need of me, who, though I am his wife, considers me like a little girl who lay in the same mother's womb with him.” With powerful sorrow having arisen, she fainted and fell in that very spot; the meaning is, she collapsed.

Mā no viheṭhayitthāti mā amhe dhanaṃ dassetvā mātugāmañca uyyojetvā viheṭhayittha; vihesā hesā pabbajitānanti. Tena hi tāta sudinna bījakampi dehīti ettha tena hīti abhiratiyaṃ uyyojeti. Sace tvaṃ abhirato brahmacariyaṃ carasi, caritvā ākāse nisīditvā parinibbāyitā hohi, amhākaṃ pana kulavaṃsabījakaṃ ekaṃ puttaṃ dehi. Mā no aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ licchavayo atiharāpesunti mayañhi licchavīnaṃ gaṇarājūnaṃ rajje vasāma, te te pituno accayena imaṃ sāpateyyaṃ evaṃ mahantaṃ amhākaṃ vibhavaṃ aputtakaṃ kuladhanarakkhakena puttena virahitaṃ attano rājantepuraṃ atiharāpeyyunti, taṃ te mā atiharāpesuṃ, mā atiharāpentūti.

“Do not harass us” means: do not harass us by showing wealth and by sending a woman; for this is a harassment for renunciants. In “Very well then… give us at least a seed,” the phrase “very well then” urges him towards delight. “If you, delighting, practice the holy life, then having practiced it, sit in the sky and attain Parinibbāna. But for us, give one son, a seed for the family lineage.” “Lest the Licchavis have our heirless property confiscated” means: for we live in the kingdom of the confederate kings called the Licchavis. After your father's passing, they might have this property, this great wealth of ours—being heirless, devoid of a son to protect the family wealth—brought into their own royal palace. Therefore, may they not have it brought in; may they not bring it in.

Etaṃ kho me, amma, sakkā kātunti kasmā evamāha? So kira cintesi – “etesaṃ sāpateyyassa ahameva sāmī, añño natthi. Te maṃ sāpateyyarakkhaṇatthāya niccaṃ anubandhissanti; tenāhaṃ na lacchāmi appossukko samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ, puttakaṃ pana labhitvā oramissanti, tato [M 1.0178] ahaṃ yathāsukhaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti imaṃ nayaṃ passanto [P 1.0213] evamāhāti.

“Mother, this is possible for me”—why did he say this? It is said that he thought: “I alone am the owner of these parents' property; there is no other. They will constantly follow me for the sake of protecting the property; therefore, I will not get to practice the ascetic's duty without concern. But having obtained a son, they will refrain from following, and then I will be able to practice the ascetic's duty as I please.” Seeing this line of reasoning, he spoke thus.

36. Pupphanti utukāle uppannalohitassa nāmaṃ. Mātugāmassa hi utukāle gabbhapatiṭṭhānaṭṭhāne lohitavaṇṇā piḷakā saṇṭhahitvā satta divasāni vaḍḍhitvā bhijjanti, tato lohitaṃ [V 1.0164] paggharati, tassetaṃ nāmaṃ “puppha”nti. Taṃ pana yāva balavaṃ hoti bahu paggharati, tāva dinnāpi paṭisandhi na tiṭṭhati, doseneva saddhiṃ paggharati; dose pana paggharite suddhe vatthumhi dinnā paṭisandhi khippaṃ patiṭṭhāti. Pupphaṃsā uppajjīti pupphaṃ assā uppajji; akāralopena sandhi purāṇadutiyikāya bāhāyaṃ gahetvāti purāṇadutiyikāya yā bāhā, tatra naṃ gahetvāti attho.

36. "Pupphanti" is the name for the blood that arises at the time of the season. For a woman, at the time of her season, in the place where the embryo is established, reddish boils form, grow for seven days, and then burst. From that, blood flows. This is its name: "puppha" (flower). As long as that is strong and flows profusely, even if rebirth-linking is given, it does not become established; it flows out together with the impurity. But when the impurity has flowed out and the womb is pure, the given rebirth-linking is quickly established. "Pupphaṃsā uppajji" means "a flower arose for her"; the sandhi is by elision of the letter 'a'. "Having taken the former wife by the arm" means having taken her by the arm of the former wife.

Apaññatte sikkhāpadeti paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpade aṭṭhapite. Bhagavato kira paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsati vassāni bhikkhū cittaṃ ārādhayiṃsu, na evarūpaṃ ajjhācāramakaṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyeva idaṃ suttamāha – “ārādhayiṃsu vata me, bhikkhave, bhikkhū ekaṃ samayaṃ citta”nti (ma. ni. 1.225). Atha bhagavā ajjhācāraṃ apassanto pārājikaṃ vā saṅghādisesaṃ vā na paññapesi. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pana vatthusmiṃ avasese pañca khuddakāpattikkhandhe eva paññapesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “apaññatte sikkhāpade”ti.

Regarding "when the training rule was not laid down": this means when the first Pārājika training rule was not established. It is said that for twenty years during the Blessed One's first enlightenment, the monks pleased his mind; they did not commit such a coarse transgression. With reference to that, he spoke this discourse: "Indeed, monks, at one time the monks pleased my mind." Then the Blessed One, not seeing a transgression, did not lay down a Pārājika or a Saṅghādisesa rule. But on this and that matter, he laid down only the remaining five groups of minor offenses. Therefore, it was said, "when the training rule was not laid down."

Anādīnavadassoti yaṃ bhagavā idāni sikkhāpadaṃ paññapento ādīnavaṃ dassessati, taṃ apassanto anavajjasaññī hutvā. Sace hi “ayaṃ idaṃ na karaṇīyanti vā mūlacchejjāya vā saṃvattatī”ti jāneyya, saddhāpabbajito kulaputto tatonidānaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇantopi na kareyya. Ettha pana ādīnavaṃ apassanto niddosasaññī ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “anādīnavadasso”ti. Purāṇadutiyikāyāti bhummavacanaṃ. Abhiviññāpesīti pavattesi; pavattanāpi hi kāyaviññatticopanato “viññāpanā”ti vuccati. Tikkhattuṃ abhiviññāpanañcesa gabbhasaṇṭhānasanniṭṭhānatthamakāsīti veditabbo.

Regarding "not seeing the danger": this means not seeing that danger which the Blessed One, while now laying down the training rule, will point out, and thus having the perception of it being faultless. For if he had known, "This should not be done," or "This leads to the cutting of the root," a clansman gone forth out of faith, even while facing the destruction of his life on that account, would not have done it. But here, not seeing the danger, he had the perception of it being without fault. Therefore, it was said, "not seeing the danger." The word `purāṇadutiyikāya` is in the locative case. `Abhiviññāpesi` means he caused it to occur; for causing to occur is also called "making known" because of the movement that is bodily intimation. And it should be understood that he performed this making known three times for the purpose of confirming the establishment of the embryo.

Sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhīti sā ca teneva ajjhācārena gabbhaṃ gaṇhi, na aññathā. Kiṃ pana aññathāpi gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hotīti[P 1.0214]? Hoti. Kathaṃ? Kāyasaṃsaggena[M 1.0179], coḷaggahaṇena, asucipānena, nābhiparāmasanena, rūpadassanena, saddena, gandhena. Itthiyo hi ekaccā utusamaye chandarāgarattā purisānaṃ hatthaggāha-veṇiggāha-aṅgapaccaṅgaparāmasanaṃ sādiyantiyopi gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti. Evaṃ kāyasaṃsaggena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti.

Regarding "She conceived by that": this means that she conceived by that very transgression, and not otherwise. But can conception occur in other ways? It can. How? By bodily contact, by taking a cloth, by drinking semen, by touching the navel, by seeing a form, by sound, and by smell. For some women, at the time of their season, being impassioned with sensual desire, conceive even while delighting in a man's taking of their hand, taking of their braided hair, or touching of their major and minor limbs. Thus, conception occurs by bodily contact.

Udāyittherassa pana purāṇadutiyikā bhikkhunī taṃ asuciṃ ekadesaṃ mukhena aggahesi, ekadesaṃ coḷakeneva saddhiṃ aṅgajāte pakkhipi. Sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhi. Evaṃ coḷaggahaṇena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti.

But the former wife of the Elder Udāyi, a bhikkhunī, took a part of that semen with her mouth, and a part she placed in her sexual organ together with a cloth. She conceived by that. Thus, conception occurs by the taking of a cloth.

Migasiṅgatāpasassa [V 1.0165] mātā migī utusamaye tāpasassa passāvaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā sasambhavaṃ passāvaṃ pivi. Sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā migasiṅgaṃ vijāyi. Evaṃ asucipānena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti.

The mother of the ascetic Migasiṅga, a doe, at the time of her season, came to the ascetic's place of urination and drank the urine that was together with semen. Having conceived by that, she gave birth to Migasiṅga. Thus, conception occurs by drinking semen.

Sāmassa pana bodhisattassa mātāpitūnaṃ cakkhuparihāniṃ ñatvā sakko puttaṃ dātukāmo dukūlapaṇḍitaṃ āha – “vaṭṭati tumhākaṃ methunadhammo”ti? “Anatthikā mayaṃ etena, isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitāmhā”ti. “Tena hi imissā utusamaye aṅguṭṭhena nābhiṃ parāmaseyyāthā”ti. So tathā akāsi. Sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā sāmaṃ tāpasadārakaṃ vijāyi. Evaṃ nābhiparāmasanena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti. Eteneva nayena maṇḍabyassa ca caṇḍapajjotassa ca vatthu veditabbaṃ.

But Sakka, having known of the future decline of the eyesight of the Bodhisatta Sāma’s parents and wishing to give them a son, said to Dukūlapaṇḍita, "Is the practice of sexual intercourse allowable for you?" "We have no need of this; we have gone forth into the ascetic life." "If so, at the time of this one's season, you should touch her navel with your thumb." He did so. She, having conceived by that, gave birth to the ascetic boy Sāma. Thus, conception occurs by touching the navel. By this same method, the stories of Maṇḍabya and Caṇḍapajjota should be known.

Kathaṃ rūpadassanena hoti? Idhekaccā itthī utusamaye purisasaṃsaggaṃ alabhamānā chandarāgavasena antogehagatāva purisaṃ upanijjhāyati rājorodhā viya, sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti. Evaṃ rūpadassanena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti.

How does conception occur by seeing a form? Here, a certain woman, at the time of her season, not obtaining contact with a man, by the power of sensual desire, while inside the house, gazes intently at a man, like a royal consort; she conceives by that. Thus, conception occurs by seeing a form.

Balākāsu pana puriso nāma natthi, tā utusamaye meghasaddaṃ sutvā gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti. Kukkuṭiyopi kadāci ekassa kukkuṭassa saddaṃ sutvā bahukāpi gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti. Tathā gāvī usabhassa. Evaṃ saddena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti.

But among cranes, there is no such thing as a male; at the time of their season, having heard the sound of a cloud, they conceive. Hens also, sometimes, having heard the sound of one rooster, even many of them conceive. Likewise, cows having heard the sound of a bull. Thus, conception occurs by sound.

Gāvī eva ca kadāci usabhagandhena gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti. Evaṃ gandhena gabbhaggahaṇaṃ hoti.

And cows themselves sometimes conceive by the smell of a bull. Thus, conception occurs by smell.

Idha [M 1.0180] panāyaṃ ajjhācārena gabbhaṃ gaṇhi. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā honti, mātā ca utunī hoti, gandhabbo ca paccupaṭṭhito hoti, evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sannipātā gabbhassāvakkanti hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.408).

But here, this one conceived by transgression. With reference to this it was said: "The mother and father are united, the mother is in her season, and the being to be reborn (gandhabba) is present; thus, by the coming together of these three, the descent of the embryo occurs."

Bhummā [P 1.0215] devā saddamanussāvesunti yasmā natthi loke raho nāma pāpakammaṃ pakubbato. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ hissa taṃ pāpaṃ attanā jānāti, tato ārakkhadevatā, athaññāpi paracittaviduniyo devatā. Tasmāssa paracittavidū sakalavanasaṇḍanissitā bhummā devā taṃ ajjhācāraṃ disvā saddaṃ anussāvesuṃ. Yathā aññepi devā suṇanti, tathā nicchāresuṃ. Kinti[V 1.0166]? Nirabbudo vata, bho…pe… ādīnavo uppāditoti. Tassattho verañjakaṇḍe vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Regarding "The earth-dwelling deities caused a cry to be heard": this is because in this world there is no such thing as a secret place for one who commits an evil deed. Indeed, first of all, that evil-doer knows that evil deed himself; after that, his guardian deity knows; and then other deities who can know the minds of others also know. Therefore, the earth-dwelling deities who dwell in the entire forest thicket and know the minds of others, having seen that transgression, caused a cry to be heard. They uttered it in such a way that other deities would also hear. How so? "Oh, a calamity... a danger has been produced!" The meaning of this should be understood in the way explained in the Verañja section.

Bhummānaṃ devānaṃ saddaṃ sutvā cātumahārājikāti ettha pana bhummānaṃ devānaṃ saddaṃ ākāsaṭṭhadevatā assosuṃ; ākāsaṭṭhānaṃ cātumahārājikāti ayamanukkamo veditabbo. Brahmakāyikāti asaññasatte ca arūpāvacare ca ṭhapetvā sabbepi brahmāno assosuṃ; sutvā ca saddamanussāvesunti veditabbo. Itiha tena khaṇenāti evaṃ tena sudinnassa ajjhācārakkhaṇena. Tena muhuttenāti ajjhācāramuhutteneva. Yāva brahmalokāti yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā. Abbhuggacchīti abhiuggacchi abbhuṭṭhāsi ekakolāhalamahosīti.

Regarding the passage, "Having heard the sound of the earth-dwelling deities, the Cātumahārājika deities..."—here, the sky-dwelling deities heard the sound of the earth-dwelling deities; the Cātumahārājika deities heard the sound of the sky-dwelling deities. This is the sequence that should be understood. As for the Brahmakāyika deities—excepting the non-percipient beings and those in the formless realms—all the Brahmās heard; and it should be understood that having heard, they caused the sound to be heard by others. As for "Thus at that moment," it means thus, at that moment of Sudinna's transgression. As for "in that instant," it means in the very instant of the transgression. As for "up to the Brahmā-world," it means up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā-world. As for "it went up," it means it went up over, it rose up over, and there was a single great commotion.

Puttaṃ vijāyīti suvaṇṇabimbasadisaṃ pacchimabhavikasattaṃ janesi. Bījakoti nāmamakaṃsūti na aññaṃ nāmaṃ kātumadaṃsu, “bījakampi dehī”ti mātāmahiyā vuttabhāvassa pākaṭattā “bījako tvevassa nāmaṃ hotū”ti “bījako”ti nāmamakaṃsu. Puttassa pana nāmavaseneva ca mātāpitūnampissa nāmamakaṃsu. Te aparena samayenāti bījakañca bījakamātarañca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bījakassa kira sattaṭṭhavassakāle tassa mātā bhikkhunīsu so ca bhikkhūsu pabbajitvā kalyāṇamitte upanissāya arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “ubho agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitvā arahattaṃ sacchākaṃsū”ti.

"She gave birth to a son" means she gave birth to a being in his last existence, who was like a golden image. "They gave him the name Bījaka" means they did not allow another name to be given, because it was well-known that his maternal grandmother had said, "Give Bījaka also." Thus, saying, "Let his name be just Bījaka," they gave him the name "Bījaka." Moreover, by the power of the son's name, his parents were also named. As for "They, at a later time," this was said referring to Bījaka and Bījaka's mother. It is said that when Bījaka was seven or eight years old, his mother went forth among the bhikkhunīs and he among the bhikkhus. Relying on good friends, they became established in arahantship. Therefore it was said: "Both, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, realized arahantship."

37. Evaṃ mātāputtānaṃ pabbajjā saphalā ahosi. Pitā pana vippaṭisārābhibhūto vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmato sudinnassaahudeva kukkucca”ntiādi. Tattha ahudevāti [P 1.0216][M 1.0181] ahu eva, dakāro padasandhikaro. Ahosiyevāti attho. Kukkuccanti ajjhācārahetuko pacchānutāpo. Vippaṭisārotipi tasseva nāmaṃ. So hi viññūhi akattabbatāya kucchitakiriyabhāvato kukkuccaṃ. Kataṃ ajjhācāraṃ nivattetuṃ asamatthatāya taṃ paṭicca virūpaṃ saraṇabhāvato vippaṭisāroti vuccati. Alābhā vata meti mayhaṃ vata alābhā; ye jhānādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ alābhā nāma, te mayhaṃ, na aññassāti adhippāyo. Na vata me lābhāti yepi me paṭiladdhā pabbajjasaraṇagamanasikkhāsamādānaguṇā, tepi neva mayhaṃ lābhā ajjhācāramalīnattā. Dulladdhaṃ vata meti idaṃ sāsanaṃ laddhampi me dulladdhaṃ. Na vata me suladdhanti yathā aññesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ, evaṃ na vata me suladdhaṃ. Kasmā? Yamahaṃ evaṃ svākkhātedhammavinaye…pe… brahmacariyaṃ caritunti. Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Kiso ahosīti khādituṃ vā bhuñjituṃ vā asakkonto tanuko ahosi appamaṃsalohito[V 1.0167]. Uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātoti sañjātuppaṇḍuppaṇḍukabhāvo paṇḍupalāsappaṭibhāgo. Dhamanisanthatagattoti pariyādinnamaṃsalohitattā sirājāleneva santharitagatto. Antomanoti anusocanavasena abbhantareyeva ṭhitacitto. Hadayavatthuṃ nissāya pavattanavasena pana sabbepi antomanāyeva. Līnamanoti uddese paripucchāya kammaṭṭhāne adhisīle adhicitte adhipaññāya vattapaṭipattipūraṇe ca nikkhittadhuro avipphāriko aññadatthu kosajjavaseneva līno saṅkucito mano assāti līnamano. Dukkhīti cetodukkhena dukkhī. Dummanoti dosena duṭṭhamano, virūpamano vā domanassābhibhūtatāya. Pajjhāyīti vippaṭisāravasena vahacchinno viya gadrabho taṃ taṃ cintayi.

37. Thus, the going forth of the mother and son was fruitful. The father, however, remained overwhelmed by remorse. Therefore it was said: "Then, for the Venerable Sudinna there was indeed remorse," and so on. Here, "ahudeva" means "ahu eva" (there was indeed); the letter 'd' is a euphonic consonant. The meaning is "there was indeed." "Remorse" (kukkucca) is regret that has the transgression as its cause. "Vippaṭisāra" is another name for it. It is called "kukkucca" by the wise because it is a blameworthy action due to what should not have been done. It is called "vippaṭisāra" because, due to the inability to undo the committed transgression, it is a distorted way of remembering it. "Alas, what a loss for me" means, "Alas, for me there are losses." The intended meaning is: those non-gains of qualities such as jhāna are for me, not for another. "Indeed, no gain for me" means that even the qualities I have obtained—the going forth, taking refuge, and undertaking the training rules—are no gain for me, because they are stained by the transgression. "Alas, poorly obtained by me" means this dispensation, though obtained by me, is poorly obtained. "Indeed, not well-obtained by me" means it is not well-obtained by me as it is for other sons of good family. Why? Because I, having gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, was unable to practice the holy life in its fullness and purity for as long as life lasts. "The holy life" (brahmacariya) means the holy life of the path, which is comprised of the threefold training. "He became emaciated" means, being unable to chew or eat, he became thin, with little flesh and blood. "He became extremely pale" means he acquired an extremely pale complexion, having the appearance of a withered leaf. "His body was covered with veins" means because his flesh and blood were consumed, his body was covered as if by a net of veins. "His mind was turned inward" means his mind was fixed only inside due to constant grieving. (However, in the sense that the mind arises dependent on the heart-base, all beings have minds turned inward.) "His mind was sluggish" means his mind was sluggish and contracted due to laziness; he had laid down his duty and was not energetic in recitation, questioning, the meditation subject, the higher virtue, the higher mind, the higher wisdom, or in fulfilling duties and observances. "Suffering" means he was suffering with mental pain. "Dejected" means his mind was corrupted by aversion, or his mind was distorted due to being overwhelmed by displeasure. "He brooded" means, due to remorse, he pondered this and that, like a donkey with a broken back.

38. Sahāyakā bhikkhūti taṃ evaṃbhūtaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikāpapañcena vītināmentaṃ disvā yassa vissāsikā kathāphāsukā bhikkhū te naṃ etadavocuṃ. Pīṇindriyoti pasādapatiṭṭhānokāsassa sampuṇṇattā paripuṇṇacakkhuādiindriyo. So dāni tvanti ettha dānīti nipāto, so pana tvanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kaccino tvanti kacci nu tvaṃ[P 1.0217]. Anabhiratoti ukkaṇṭhito; gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānoti attho. Tasmā tameva anabhiratiṃ paṭikkhipanto āha – “na kho ahaṃ, āvuso, anabhirato”ti. Adhikusalānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya abhiratova ahanti[M 1.0182]. Atthi me pāpakammaṃ katanti mayā kataṃ ekaṃ pāpakammaṃ atthi upalabbhati saṃvijjati, niccakālaṃ abhimukhaṃ viya me tiṭṭhati. Atha naṃ pakāsento “purāṇadutiyikāyā”tiādimāha.

38. As for "the companion monks": seeing him in such a state, passing his time with the proliferation of socializing in groups, those monks who were his trusted and pleasant-to-talk-to companions said this to him. As for "with plump faculties," it means he had complete faculties, such as the eye, because the physical basis for the sensitive matter was full. In the phrase "so dāni tvaṃ" (that you now), "dāni" is a particle; it means "but you." "Kaccino tvaṃ" means "kacci nu tvaṃ" (Could it be that you...?). "Not delighting" means dissatisfied, discontented; the meaning is "desiring the household life." Therefore, rejecting that very lack of delight, he said, "Indeed, friends, I am not one who does not delight." But in fact, he was not delighting in the cultivation of higher wholesome states. As for "There is an evil deed done by me," it means: "There is an evil deed done by me; it exists, it is found, it is present; it stands before me always as if face-to-face." Then, revealing it, he said, "With my former wife..." and so on.

Alañhi te, āvuso sudinna, kukkuccāyāti āvuso sudinna, tuyhetaṃ pāpakammaṃ alaṃ samatthaṃ kukkuccāya; paṭibalaṃ kukkuccaṃ uppādetunti vuttaṃ hoti. Yaṃ tvanti ādimhi yena pāpena tvaṃ na sakkhissasi brahmacariyaṃ carituṃ, taṃ te pāpaṃ alaṃ kukkuccāyāti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Atha naṃ anusāsantā “nanu āvuso bhagavatā”tiādimāhaṃsu. Tattha nanūti anumatiggahaṇatthe nipāto. Anekapariyāyenāti anekakāraṇena. Virāgāyāti virāgatthāya. No sarāgāyāti no rāgena rajjanatthāya. Bhagavatā hi “imaṃ me dhammaṃ sutvā sattā sabbabhavabhogesu virajjissanti, no rajjissantī” etadatthāya dhammo desitoti adhippāyo. Esa nayo sabbapadesu. Idaṃ panettha pariyāyavacanamattaṃ. Visaṃyogāyāti kilesehi visaṃyujjanatthāya. No saṃyogāyāti na saṃyujjanatthāya. Anupādānāyāti aggahaṇatthāya. No saupādānāyāti na saṅgahaṇatthāya.

“Alañhi te, āvuso sudinna, kukkuccāya” means: Friend Sudinna, this evil deed of yours is sufficient for remorse; it is capable of producing remorse. In the phrase beginning with “Yaṃ tvaṃ,” the connection should be understood thus: “By which evil deed you will not be able to practice the holy life, that evil deed of yours is sufficient for remorse.” Then, instructing him, they said, “Nanu āvuso bhagavatā,” and so on. Therein, ‘nanu’ is a particle in the sense of accepting another’s view. “Anekapariyāyena” means “for many reasons.” “Virāgāya” means “for the purpose of dispassion.” “No sarāgāya” means “not for the purpose of becoming impassioned with lust.” For the Blessed One taught the Dhamma for this purpose: “Having heard this Dhamma of mine, beings will become dispassionate towards all existences and enjoyments; they will not become impassioned.” This is the intention. This is the method in all phrases. Here, this is merely a synonymous expression. “Visaṃyogāya” means “for the purpose of disjunction from the defilements.” “No saṃyogāya” means “not for the purpose of conjunction.” “Anupādānāya” means “for the purpose of non-grasping.” “No saupādānāya” means “not for the purpose of grasping.”

Tattha [V 1.0168] nāma tvanti tasmiṃ nāma tvaṃ. Sarāgāya cetessasīti saha rāgena vattamānāya methunadhammāya cetessasi kappessasi pakappessasi; etadatthaṃ vāyamissasīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Puna rāgavirāgādīni nava padāni nibbattitalokuttaranibbānameva sandhāya vuttāni. Tasmā rāgavirāgāyāti vā madanimmadanāyāti vā vuttepi “nibbānatthāyā”ti evameva attho daṭṭhabbo. Nibbānañhi yasmā taṃ āgamma ārabbha paṭicca rāgo virajjati na hoti, tasmā rāgavirāgoti vuccati. Yasmā pana taṃ āgamma mānamada-purisamadādayo madā nimmadā amadā honti vinassanti, tasmā madanimmadananti vuccati. Yasmā [P 1.0218] ca taṃ āgamma sabbāpi kāmapipāsā vinayaṃ abbhatthaṃ yāti, tasmā pipāsavinayoti vuccati. Yasmā pana taṃ āgamma pañca kāmaguṇālayā samugghātaṃ gacchanti, tasmā ālayasamugghātoti vuccati. Yasmā ca taṃ āgamma tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ upacchijjati, tasmā vaṭṭupacchedoti vuccati. Yasmā pana taṃ āgamma sabbaso taṇhā khayaṃ gacchati virajjati nirujjhati ca, tasmā taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodhoti vuccati. Yasmā [M 1.0183] panetaṃ catasso yoniyo, pañca gatiyo, satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, nava ca sattāvāse, aparāparabhāvāya vinanato ābandhanato saṃsibbanato vānanti laddhavohārāya taṇhāya nikkhantaṃ nissaṭaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ, tasmā nibbānanti vuccatīti.

“Tattha nāma tvaṃ” means: In that Dhamma, will you indeed strive? “Sarāgāya cetessasi” means: Will you indeed strive, will you indeed undertake, will you indeed endeavor for the sake of the sexual act which is accompanied by lust? The meaning is: Will you indeed exert yourself for this purpose? This is the method everywhere. Again, the nine terms beginning with ‘rāgavirāga’ were spoken with reference only to the supramundane Nibbāna that has been brought about. Therefore, even when ‘rāgavirāgāya’ or ‘madanimmadanāya’ is said, the meaning should be understood as just this: ‘for the sake of Nibbāna.’ For, since by resorting to, taking as object, and depending on it, lust fades away and is no more, it is called ‘the fading away of lust.’ And since by resorting to it, intoxications such as the intoxication of conceit and the intoxication of manhood become unintoxicated, without intoxication, and are destroyed, it is called ‘the subduing of intoxication.’ And since by resorting to it, all thirst for sensual pleasures goes to destruction and disappearance, it is called ‘the removal of thirst.’ And since by resorting to it, the attachments to the five strands of sensual pleasure are uprooted, it is called ‘the uprooting of attachments.’ And since by resorting to it, the round of the three realms is cut off, it is called ‘the cutting off of the round.’ And since by resorting to it, craving in every way goes to destruction, fades away, and ceases, it is called ‘the destruction of craving,’ ‘dispassion,’ and ‘cessation.’ And since this is a departure, a release, a disjunction from craving—which has received the designation ‘vāna’ because it weaves, binds, and sews for the sake of repeated existence—therefore, it is called ‘Nibbāna.’”

Kāmānaṃ pahānaṃ akkhātanti vatthukāmānaṃ, kilesakāmānañca pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmasaññānaṃ pariññāti sabbāsampi kāmasaññānaṃ ñātatīraṇapahānavasena tividhā pariññā akkhātā. Kāmapipāsānanti kāmesu pātabyatānaṃ kāme vā pātumicchānaṃ. Kāmavitakkānanti kāmupasañhitānaṃvitakkānaṃ. Kāmapariḷāhānanti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasena uppannapariḷāhānaṃ antodāhānaṃ. Imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu kilesakkhayakaro lokuttaramaggova kathito. Sabbapaṭhamesu pana tīsu ṭhānesu lokiyalokuttaramissako maggo kathitoti veditabbo.

“Is not the abandoning of sensual pleasures declared?” means: The abandoning of both object-sensual pleasures and defilement-sensual pleasures is stated. “Is not the full understanding of sensual perceptions declared?” means: The threefold full understanding of all sensual perceptions—by way of knowing, judging, and abandoning—is declared. “Is not the removal of thirst for sensual pleasures declared?” means: the removal of the cravings of those who would partake in sensual pleasures, or the desires to partake in them. “Is not the uprooting of sensual thoughts declared?” means: the uprooting of thoughts connected with sensual pleasure. “Is not the calming of the fever of sensual pleasures declared?” means: the calming of the fevers and internal burnings that have arisen through the power of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. In these five instances, only the supramundane path that brings about the destruction of defilements is taught. However, in the very first three instances, it should be understood that a mixed path of mundane and supramundane is taught.

Netaṃ āvusoti na etaṃ āvuso, tava pāpakammaṃ appasannānañca pasādāya evarūpānaṃ pasādatthāya na hoti. Atha khvetanti atha kho etaṃ. Atha kho tantipi pāṭho. Aññathattāyāti pasādaññathābhāvāya vippaṭisārāya hoti. Ye maggena anāgatasaddhā, tesaṃ vippaṭisāraṃ karoti – “īdisepi nāma dhammavinaye mayaṃ pasannā, yatthevaṃ duppaṭipannā bhikkhū”ti. Ye pana maggenāgatasaddhā, tesaṃ sineru viya vātehi acalo pasādo īdisehi vatthūhi ito vā dāruṇatarehi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekaccānaṃ aññathattāyā”ti.

“Netaṃ āvuso” means: Friend, this evil deed of yours is not for the confidence of the unconvinced, nor for the purpose of inspiring confidence in such persons. “Atha khvetaṃ” means: But rather, this is. There is also the reading “Atha kho taṃ.” “Aññathattāya” means: it is for the alteration of confidence, that is, for regret. It causes regret for those whose faith has not come by way of the path, thus: “Indeed, we had confidence in such a Dhamma and Discipline where monks are so ill-behaved!” But for those whose faith has come by way of the path, their confidence is unshakable by such incidents or by others more dreadful than this, like Mount Sineru by the winds. Therefore, it was said: “for the alteration of some.”

39. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesunti bhagavato etaṃ atthaṃ ācikkhiṃsu paṭivedayiṃsu. Ārocayamānā [V 1.0169] ca neva piyakamyatāya na bhedapurekkhāratāya[P 1.0219], na tassāyasmato avaṇṇapakāsanatthāya, na kalisāsanāropanatthāya, nāpi “idaṃ sutvā bhagavā imassa sāsane patiṭṭhaṃ na dassati, nikkaḍḍhāpessati na”nti maññamānā ārocesuṃ. Atha kho “imaṃ sāsane uppannaṃ abbudaṃ ñatvā bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessati, velaṃ mariyādaṃ āṇaṃ ṭhapessatī”ti ārocesuṃ.

39. “They reported this matter to the Blessed One” means: They told, they made known this matter to the Blessed One. And in reporting, they did not do so out of a desire to be dear, nor with the intention of causing a schism, nor for the purpose of publicizing that venerable one’s fault, nor for the purpose of casting blame spoken out of anger, nor did they report it thinking, “Having heard this, the Blessed One will not give this one a standing in the Dispensation; he will have him expelled.” But rather, they reported it thinking, “Having known this tumor that has arisen in the Dispensation, the Blessed One will lay down a training rule; he will establish a boundary, a limit, a command.”

Etasmiṃ nidāne etasmiṃ pakaraṇeti ettha sudinnassa ajjhācāravītikkamo sikkhāpadapaññattiyā kāraṇattā nidānañceva pakaraṇañcāti vuttoti veditabbo. Kāraṇañhi yasmā nideti attano phalaṃ “gaṇhātha na”nti [M 1.0184] dassentaṃ viya appeti, pakaroti ca naṃ kattuṃ ārabhati, karotiyeva vā; tasmā nidānañceva pakaraṇañcāti vuccati. Vigarahi buddho bhagavāti buddho bhagavā vigarahi nindi; yathā taṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇārahānaṃ vaṇṇañca avaṇṇañca bhaṇantesu aggapuggalo. Na hi bhagavato sīlavītikkamakaraṃ puggalaṃ disvā “ayaṃ jātiyā vā gottena vā kolaputtiyena vā ganthena vā dhutaṅgena vā ñāto yasassī īdisaṃ puggalaṃ rakkhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, nāpi pesalaṃ guṇavantaṃ disvā tassa guṇaṃ paṭicchādetuṃ cittaṃ uppajjati. Atha kho garahitabbaṃ garahati eva, pasaṃsitabbañca pasaṃsati eva, ayañca garahitabbo; tasmā taṃ tādilakkhaṇe ṭhito avikampamānena cittena vigarahi buddho bhagavā “ananucchavika”ntiādīhi vacanehi.

‘In this origin, in this case’—here, Sudinna’s transgression of overwhelming conduct is to be understood as being called both the ‘origin’ and the ‘case’ because it was the cause for the laying down of the training rule. For a cause, because it points to its own fruit, it presents it as if showing it and saying, ‘Take this;’ and it produces it, begins to make it, or indeed, simply makes it. Therefore, it is called both the ‘origin’ and the ‘case’. ‘The Buddha, the Blessed One, reprimanded’ means the Buddha, the Blessed One, reprimanded, censured; He is the foremost person among those who speak praise and blame of those deserving praise and blame. For when the Blessed One sees a person who commits a breach of virtue, the thought does not arise, ‘This person is well-known and renowned through birth, clan, good family, learning, or ascetic practices; it is right to protect such a person.’ Nor does the thought arise to conceal the virtue of a person who is beloved and virtuous. Rather, He reprimands one who should be reprimanded and praises one who should be praised, and this one was to be reprimanded. Therefore, the Buddha, the Blessed One, established in the characteristic of one who is such, with an unshaken mind, reprimanded him with words such as ‘unsuitable’.

Tatthāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – yadidaṃ tayā, moghapurisa, tucchamanussa kammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ samaṇakaraṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ maggaphalanibbānasāsanānaṃ vā na anucchavikaṃ, tesaṃ chaviṃ chāyaṃ sundarabhāvaṃ na anveti nānugacchati, atha kho ārakāva tehi dhammehi. Ananucchavikattā eva ca ananulomikaṃ, tesaṃ na anulometi; atha kho vilomaṃ paccanīkabhāve ṭhitaṃ. Ananulomikattā eva ca appatirūpaṃ, patirūpaṃ sadisaṃ paṭibhāgaṃ na hoti, atha kho asadisaṃ appaṭibhāgameva. Appatirūpattā eva ca assāmaṇakaṃ, samaṇānaṃ [P 1.0220] kammaṃ na hoti. Assāmaṇakattā akappiyaṃ. Yañhi samaṇakammaṃ na hoti, taṃ tesaṃ na kappati. Akappiyattā akaraṇīyaṃ. Na hi samaṇā yaṃ na kappati, taṃ karonti. Tañcetaṃ tayā kataṃ, tasmā ananucchavikaṃ te, moghapurisa, kataṃ…pe… akaraṇīyanti. Kathañhi nāmāti kena nāma kāraṇena, kiṃ nāma kāraṇaṃ passantoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato kāraṇābhāvaṃ dassento parato “nanu mayā moghapurisā”tiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ vuttatthameva.

Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning: This deed done by you, foolish man, empty man, is not suitable for the qualities that make one a monk, or for the path, fruition, Nibbāna, or the teachings. It does not follow along with their complexion, their radiance, their beautiful nature; rather, it is far from those qualities. And because it is unsuitable, it is non-conforming; it does not conform to them. Rather, it is contrary, standing in opposition. And because it is non-conforming, it is improper; it is not proper, similar, or comparable. Rather, it is dissimilar and incomparable. And because it is improper, it is not befitting a monk; it is not the action of monks. Because it is not befitting a monk, it is unallowable. For what is not the action of a monk is not allowable for them. Because it is unallowable, it is not to be done. For monks do not do what is not allowable. And this is what has been done by you. Therefore, foolish man, what was done by you was unsuitable... not to be done. ‘How indeed?’ means: ‘For what reason? Seeing what cause?’ is what is said. Then, showing the absence of a cause, He subsequently said, ‘Foolish man, did I not...’ and so on. All of that has the same meaning as what has already been said.

Idāni [V 1.0170] yasmā yaṃ tena pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ vipaccamānaṃ ativiya dukkhavipākaṃ hoti, tasmāssa taṃ vipākaṃ dassetuṃ katāparādhaṃ viya puttaṃ anukampakā mātāpitaro dayālukena cittena sudinnaṃ paribhāsanto “varaṃ te moghapurisā”tiādimāha. Tattha āsu sīghaṃ etassa visaṃ āgacchatīti āsīviso. Ghoraṃ caṇḍamassa visanti ghoraviso, tassa āsīvisassa ghoravisassa. “Pakkhitta”nti etassa “vara”nti iminā sambandho[M 1.0185]. Īdisassa āsīvisassa ghoravisassa mukhe aṅgajātaṃ varaṃ pakkhittaṃ; sace pakkhittaṃ bhaveyya, varaṃ siyā; sundaraṃ sādhu suṭṭhu siyāti attho. Na tvevāti na tu eva varaṃ na sundarameva na sādhumeva na suṭṭhumeva. Esa nayo sabbattha. Kaṇhasappassāti kāḷasappassa. Aṅgārakāsuyāti aṅgārapuṇṇakūpe, aṅgārarāsimhi vā. Ādittāyāti padittāya gahitaaggivaṇṇāya. Sampajjalitāyāti samantato pajjalitāya acciyo muccantiyā. Sajotibhūtāyāti sappabhāya. Samantato uṭṭhitāhi jālāhi ekappabhāsamudayabhūtāyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, because the evil deed done by him has an extremely painful result when it ripens, therefore, to show him that result, He, with a compassionate mind, rebuked Sudinna, saying, ‘Better for you, foolish man...’ and so on, just as compassionate parents rebuke a son who has done wrong. Therein, ‘āsīviso’ is so called because its venom (visa) comes (āgacchati) swiftly (āsu). ‘Ghoraviso’ is so called because its venom (visa) is fierce (ghoraṃ). Of that swift-venomed, fierce-venomed serpent. The word ‘pakkhittaṃ’ (inserted) is connected with the word ‘varaṃ’ (better). It would be better for the male organ to be inserted into the mouth of such a swift-venomed, fierce-venomed serpent; if it were inserted, it would be better. The meaning is that it would be more beautiful, good, and excellent. ‘Na tveva’ means: it would not, however, be better, not beautiful, not good, not excellent. This is the method in all cases. ‘Kaṇhasappassa’ means: of a black serpent. ‘Aṅgārakāsuyā’ means: in a pit full of embers, or in a heap of embers. ‘Ādittāya’ means: blazing, having taken on the color of fire. ‘Sampajjalitāya’ means: burning all around, emitting flames. ‘Sajotibhūtāya’ means: radiant. It is said to have become a single mass of light from the flames that have risen all around.

Taṃ kissa hetūti yaṃ mayā vuttaṃ “vara”nti taṃ kissa hetu, katarena kāraṇenāti ce? Maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyyāti yo tattha aṅgajātaṃ pakkhipeyya, so maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Itonidānañca kho…pe… upapajjeyyāti yaṃ idaṃ mātugāmassa aṅgajāte aṅgajātapakkhipanaṃ, itonidānaṃ tassa kārako puggalo nirayaṃ upapajjeyya; evaṃ kammassa mahāsāvajjataṃ passanto taṃ garahi, na tassa dukkhāgamaṃ icchamāno. Tattha nāma tvanti tasmiṃ nāma evarūpe kamme evaṃ [P 1.0221] mahāsāvajje samānepi tvaṃ. Yaṃ tvanti ettha yanti hīḷanatthe nipāto. Tvanti taṃ-saddassa vevacanaṃ; dvīhipi yaṃ vā taṃ vā hīḷitamavaññātanti vuttaṃ hoti. Asaddhammanti asataṃ nīcajanānaṃ dhammaṃ; tehi sevitabbanti attho. Gāmadhammanti gāmānaṃ dhammaṃ; gāmavāsikamanussānaṃ dhammanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vasaladhammanti pāpadhamme vasanti paggharantīti vasalā, tesaṃ vasalānaṃ hīnapurisānaṃ dhammaṃ, vasalaṃ vā kilesapaggharaṇakaṃ dhammaṃ. Duṭṭhullanti duṭṭhu ca kilesadūsitaṃ thūlañca asukhumaṃ, anipuṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Odakantikanti udakakiccaṃ antikaṃ avasānaṃ assāti odakantiko, taṃ odakantikaṃ. Rahassanti rahobhavaṃ, paṭicchanne okāse uppajjanakaṃ. Ayañhi dhammo jigucchanīyattā na sakkā āvi aññesaṃ dassanavisaye kātuṃ, tena vuttaṃ – “rahassa”nti. Dvayaṃdvayasamāpattinti dvīhi dvīhi samāpajjitabbaṃ, dvayaṃ dvayaṃ samāpattintipi pāṭho. Dayaṃ dayaṃ samāpattintipi paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Samāpajjissasīti etaṃ “tattha nāma tva”nti ettha vuttanāmasaddena yojetabbaṃ “samāpajjissasi nāmā”ti.

As for 'For what reason is that?', if it is asked, 'For what reason, by what cause, was that which I said, “better,” spoken?' As for 'He might meet death', whoever would insert the genital organ there might meet death or suffering equivalent to death. As for 'From this cause... he might be reborn', this is the act of inserting the genital organ into a woman’s genital organ—from this cause, the person who performs it might be reborn in hell. Seeing the great faultiness of such an act, he rebuked him, not wishing suffering upon him. As for 'And yet, you', it means you, even though the act is of such a nature, so greatly faulty. As for ‘yaṃ tvaṃ’, herein yaṃ is a particle of contempt. Tvaṃ is a synonym for taṃ. By both, it is said that something is despised or scorned. As for ‘unrighteous conduct’, it is the conduct of the ignoble, of lowly people; it means that which should be practiced by them. As for ‘village conduct’, it is the conduct of villagers; it is said to be the conduct of village-dwelling people. As for ‘outcast conduct’, because they exude evil practices, they are called 'outcasts'; it is the conduct of those outcasts, of base men, or it is a defiling practice that exudes defilements. As for ‘shameful’, it is both bad, being corrupted by defilements, and coarse, being unsubtle and unrefined—this is what is meant. As for ‘water-ending’, it is that which has the 'water-duty' as its end or conclusion. As for ‘secret’, it means occurring in a secluded place, arising in a concealed location. For this practice, due to its disgusting nature, cannot be done openly in the sight of others. Hence, it is called ‘secret’. As for ‘paired attainment’, it is to be entered into two by two. There is also a reading ‘dvayaṃ dvayaṃ samāpattiṃ’. Some read it as ‘dayaṃ dayaṃ samāpattiṃ’, but that is not good. As for ‘You will engage’, this should be connected with the word ‘nāma’ mentioned earlier in ‘tattha nāma tvaṃ’, thus ‘samāpajjissasi nāma’ (you will indeed engage!).

Bahūnaṃ [V 1.0171] kho…pe… ādikattā pubbaṅgamoti sāsanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Imasmiṃ sāsane tvaṃ bahūnaṃ puggalānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādikattā, sabbapaṭhamaṃ [M 1.0186] karaṇato; pubbaṅgamo sabbapaṭhamaṃ etaṃ maggaṃ paṭipannattā; dvāraṃdado, upāyadassakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Imañhi lesaṃ laddhā tava anusikkhamānā bahū puggalā nānappakārake makkaṭiyā methunapaṭisevanādike akusaladhamme karissantīti ayamettha adhippāyo.

As for 'Indeed, for many... the initiator, the foremost', this is spoken with reference to the Dispensation. In this Dispensation, you are the initiator of unwholesome states for many persons because you were the very first to do it; you are the foremost because you were the very first to have entered upon this path; you are the door-giver, the one who shows the method—this is what is said. Indeed, having obtained this pretext, many persons, training in imitation of you, will perform various kinds of unwholesome acts, such as engaging in sexual intercourse with a female monkey and so on—this is the intended meaning here.

Anekapariyāyenāti imehi “ananucchavika”ntiādinā nayena vuttehi, bahūhi kāraṇehi. Dubbharatāya…pe… kosajjassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvāti dubbharatādīnaṃ vatthubhūtassa asaṃvarassa avaṇṇaṃ nindaṃ garahaṃ bhāsitvāti attho. Yasmā hi asaṃvare ṭhitassa puggalassa attā dubbharatañceva dupposatañca āpajjati, tasmā asaṃvaro “dubbharatā, dupposatā”ti ca vuccati. Yasmā pana asaṃvare [P 1.0222] ṭhitassa attā catūsu paccayesu mahicchataṃ sineruppamāṇepi ca paccaye laddhā asantuṭṭhitaṃ āpajjati, tasmā asaṃvaro “mahicchatā, asantuṭṭhitā”ti ca vuccati. Yasmā ca asaṃvare ṭhitassa attā gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya ceva kilesasaṅgaṇikāya ca saṃvattati, kosajjānugato ca hoti aṭṭhakusītavatthupāripūriyā saṃvattati, tasmā asaṃvaro “saṅgaṇikā, ceva kosajjañcā”ti vuccati.

‘In many ways’ means by these reasons stated in the manner of ‘improper’ and so on, by many causes. ‘Having spoken dispraise of being difficult to support... and of laziness’ means having spoken dispraise, blame, or criticism of unrestraint, which is the basis of being difficult to support and so on—this is the meaning. For when a person remains unrestrained, their self becomes difficult to support and difficult to nourish. Therefore, unrestraint is called ‘being difficult to support’ and ‘being difficult to nourish’. Moreover, because a person who remains unrestrained develops great desire for the four requisites and becomes dissatisfied even when obtaining requisites as vast as Mount Sineru, unrestraint is called ‘great desire’ and ‘dissatisfaction’. And because a person who remains unrestrained inclines toward group socializing and associating with defilements, follows laziness, and leads to the fulfillment of the eight grounds for laziness, unrestraint is called ‘association’ and ‘laziness’.

Subharatāya…pe… vīriyārambhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvāti subharatādīnaṃ vatthubhūtassa saṃvarassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvāti attho. Yasmā hi asaṃvaraṃ pahāya saṃvare ṭhitassa attā subharo hoti suposo, catūsu ca paccayesu appicchataṃ nittaṇhabhāvaṃ āpajjati, ekamekasmiñca paccaye yathālābha-yathābala-yathāsāruppavasena tippabhedāya santuṭṭhiyā saṃvattati, tasmā saṃvaro “subharatā ceva suposatā ca appiccho ca santuṭṭho cā”ti vuccati.

As for 'Praise of being easy to support... and of the undertaking of energy', the meaning is: having spoken the praise of restraint, which is the ground for being easy to support and so on. For, because the self of a person who, having abandoned unrestraint, is established in restraint becomes easy to support and easy to nourish, attains fewness of wishes and a state of no craving regarding the four requisites, and in each and every requisite, conduces to threefold contentment—distinguished as contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, and contentment according to what is suitable—therefore restraint is called 'being easy to support,' 'being easy to nourish,' 'having few wishes,' and 'being content'.

Yasmā pana asaṃvaraṃ pahāya saṃvare ṭhitassa attā kilesasallekhanatāya ceva niddhunanatāya ca saṃvattati, tasmā saṃvaro “sallekho ca dhuto cā”ti vuccati.

Moreover, because the self of one who, having abandoned unrestraint, is established in restraint conduces both to the effacing of defilements and to the shaking off of defilements, therefore restraint is called 'effacing' and 'shaking off'.

Yasmā ca asaṃvaraṃ pahāya saṃvare ṭhitassa attā kāyavācānaṃ appāsādikaṃ appasādanīyaṃ asantaṃ asāruppaṃ kāyavacīduccaritaṃ cittassa appāsādikaṃ [M 1.0187] appasādanīyaṃ asantaṃ asāruppaṃ akusalavitakkattayañca anupagamma tabbiparītassa kāyavacīsucaritassa ceva kusalavitakkattayassa ca pāsādikassa pasādanīyassa santassa sāruppassa pāripūriyā saṃvattati, tasmā saṃvaro “pāsādiko”ti vuccati.

And because the self of one who, having abandoned unrestraint, is established in restraint, does not approach bodily and verbal misconduct that is uninspiring, unpleasing, unpeaceful, and unsuitable, nor the threefold unwholesome thoughts that are uninspiring, unpleasing, unpeaceful, and unsuitable, but conduces to the complete fulfillment of their opposites—bodily and verbal good conduct and the threefold wholesome thoughts that are inspiring, pleasing, peaceful, and suitable—therefore restraint is called 'inspiring'.

Yasmā [V 1.0172] pana asaṃvaraṃ pahāya saṃvare ṭhitassa attā sabbakilesāpacayabhūtāya, vivaṭṭāya, aṭṭhavīriyārambhavatthupāripūriyā ca saṃvattati, tasmā saṃvaro “apacayo ceva vīriyārambho cā”ti vuccatīti.

Moreover, because the self of one who, having abandoned unrestraint, is established in restraint conduces to the destruction of all defilements, to the Unbinding, and to the fulfillment of the eight grounds for arousing energy, therefore restraint is called 'destruction' and 'arousing of energy'.

Bhikkhūnaṃ tadanucchavikaṃ tadanulomikanti tattha sannipatitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yaṃ idāni sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessati, tassa anucchavikañceva anulomikañca. Yo vā ayaṃ subharatādīhi saṃvaro vutto, tassa anucchavikañceva anulomikañca saṃvarappahānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ [P 1.0223] asuttantavinibaddhaṃ pāḷivinimuttaṃ okkantikadhammadesanaṃ katvāti attho. Bhagavā kira īdisesu ṭhānesu pañcavaṇṇakusumamālaṃ karonto viya, ratanadāmaṃ sajjento viya, ca ye paṭikkhipanādhippāyā asaṃvarābhiratā te samparāyikena vaṭṭabhayena tajjento anekappakāraṃ ādīnavaṃ dassento, ye sikkhākāmā saṃvare ṭhitā te appekacce arahatte patiṭṭhapento appekacce anāgāmi-sakadāgāmi-sotāpattiphalesu upanissayavirahitepi saggamagge patiṭṭhapento dīghanikāyappamāṇampi majjhimanikāyappamāṇampi dhammadesanaṃ karoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “bhikkhūnaṃ tadanucchavikaṃ tadanulomikaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā”ti.

For the bhikkhus, what is suitable and conforming—that is, for the bhikkhus assembled there, whatever training rule He is now about to lay down, it is both suitable and conforming to it. Or, the restraint spoken of by Subharata and others—that is both suitable and conforming to it, connected with the five restraints and the five abandonments, not bound by the Suttanta, free from the Pāḷi, having given a Dhamma discourse that is to be penetrated by wisdom—this is the meaning. Indeed, in such instances, the Blessed One, as if making a garland of five-colored flowers, and as if arranging a jeweled festoon, by threatening those who have the intention to reject and delight in non-restraint with the danger of future suffering in the round of existence, showing dangers of many kinds; and by establishing some who desire the training and are established in restraint in Arahantship, establishing some in the fruits of non-return, once-return, and stream-entry, and establishing even those devoid of the strong supporting condition on the path to heaven, delivers a Dhamma discourse the length of the Dīgha Nikāya or the length of the Majjhima Nikāya. Referring to that, it was said: 'Having delivered to the bhikkhus a Dhamma talk that is suitable and conforming to it.'

Tena hīti tena sudinnassa ajjhācārena kāraṇabhūtena. Sikkhāpadanti ettha sikkhitabbāti sikkhā, pajjate imināti padaṃ, sikkhāya padaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ; sikkhāya adhigamupāyoti attho. Atha vā mūlaṃ nissayo patiṭṭhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Methunaviratiyā methunasaṃvarassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Methunasaṃvaro hi tadaññesaṃ sikkhāsaṅkhātānaṃ sīlavipassanājhānamaggadhammānaṃ vuttatthavasena padattā idha “sikkhāpada”nti adhippeto. Ayañca attho sikkhāpadavibhaṅge vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Apica tassatthassa dīpakaṃ vacanampi “sikkhāpada”nti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “sikkhāpadanti yo tattha nāmakāyo padakāyo niruttikāyo byañjanakāyo”ti. Atha vā yathā “anabhijjhā dhammapada”nti vutte anabhijjhā eko dhammakoṭṭhāsoti attho [M 1.0188] hoti, evamidhāpi “sikkhāpada”nti sikkhākoṭṭhāso sikkhāya eko padesotipi attho veditabbo.

Therefore, it was because of that transgression of Sudinna which had become the cause. ‘Training rule’—here, because it is to be trained in, it is ‘training’ (sikkhā); because one attains by means of it, it is a ‘means’ (pada). Thus, ‘training rule’ (sikkhāpada) is the means for training; the meaning is that it is the means for the attainment of the training. Alternatively, it is said to be the root, the support, the foundation. This is a designation for abstinence from sexual intercourse, for restraint regarding sexual intercourse. Indeed, restraint regarding sexual intercourse is here intended as a ‘training rule’ because, in the sense already explained, it is the basis for other things called ‘trainings’—namely, virtue, insight, jhāna, and the path-dhammas. And this meaning should be understood in the way stated in the Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga. Moreover, the statement that clarifies that meaning should also be known as a ‘training rule.’ And this has been said: ‘“Training rule” is whatever collection of nouns, collection of verses, collection of expressions, collection of syllables there is.’ Alternatively, just as when it is said, ‘non-covetousness is a Dhamma-portion,’ the meaning is that non-covetousness is one portion of the Dhamma, so too here, ‘training rule’ should be understood to mean a portion of the training, one part of the training.

Dasa atthavase paṭiccāti dasa kāraṇavase sikkhāpadapaññattihetu adhigamanīye hitavisese paṭicca āgamma ārabbha, dasannaṃ hitavisesānaṃ nipphattiṃ sampassamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idāni te dasa atthavase dassento “saṅghasuṭṭhutāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha saṅghasuṭṭhutā nāma saṅghassa suṭṭhubhāvo, “suṭṭhu devā”ti āgataṭṭhāne viya “suṭṭhu, bhante”ti vacanasampaṭicchanabhāvo[V 1.0173]. Yo ca tathāgatassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchati[P 1.0224], tassa taṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hoti, tasmā saṅghassa “suṭṭhu, bhante”ti mama vacanasampaṭicchanatthaṃ paññapessāmi, asampaṭicchane ādīnavaṃ sampaṭicchane ca ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā, na balakkārena abhibhavitvāti etamatthaṃ āvikaronto āha – “saṅghasuṭṭhutāyā”ti. Saṅghaphāsutāyāti saṅghassa phāsubhāvāya; sahajīvitāya sukhavihāratthāyāti attho.

‘Depending on ten purposes’ means this was said: seeing well the accomplishment of ten special benefits, having depended on them as special reasons to be attained for the sake of laying down the training rule. Now, showing those ten purposes, he said, 'For the excellence of the Saṅgha,' and so on. Here, 'excellence of the Saṅgha' means the Saṅgha's state of excellence; like in the passage where 'Well, O gods' occurs, it is the state of accepting the words, saying, 'Very well, venerable sir.' And for whoever accepts the Tathāgata's word, that leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, revealing this meaning—that having shown the danger in not accepting and the benefit in accepting, he would lay it down, not by overpowering with force, for the purpose of the Saṅgha's acceptance of his word, saying, 'Very well, venerable sir'—he said, 'For the excellence of the Saṅgha.' 'For the comfort of the Saṅgha' means for the Saṅgha's state of comfort; the meaning is, for the sake of living together in ease, for dwelling in happiness.

Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyāti dummaṅkū nāma dussīlapuggalā; ye maṅkutaṃ āpādiyamānāpi dukkhena āpajjanti, vītikkamaṃ karontā vā katvā vā na lajjanti, tesaṃ niggahatthāya; te hi sikkhāpade asati “kiṃ tumhehi diṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ sutaṃ – kiṃ amhehi kataṃ; katarasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ katamaṃ āpattiṃ āropetvā amhe niggaṇhathā”ti saṅghaṃ viheṭhessanti, sikkhāpade pana sati te saṅgho sikkhāpadaṃ dassetvā dhammena vinayena satthusāsanena niggahessati. Tena vuttaṃ – “dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”ti.

‘For the subjugation of unruly persons’—unruly persons are persons of bad virtue; who, even when being put to shame, are put to shame only with difficulty, and who, while transgressing or having transgressed, are not ashamed—for the subjugation of them. For if there is no training rule, they will harass the Saṅgha, saying, 'What was seen by you? What was heard? What was done by us? Having charged us with what offense regarding what matter do you subjugate us?' But when there is a training rule, the Saṅgha, having shown them the training rule, will subjugate them by the Dhamma, by the Vinaya, by the Teacher's instruction. Therefore it was said: 'For the subjugation of unruly persons.'

Pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāyāti pesalānaṃ piyasīlānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya. Piyasīlā hi bhikkhū kattabbākattabbaṃ sāvajjānavajjaṃ velaṃ mariyādaṃ ajānantā sikkhattayapāripūriyā ghaṭamānā kilamanti, sandiṭṭhamānā ubbāḷhā honti. Kattabbākattabbaṃ pana sāvajjānavajjaṃ velaṃ mariyādaṃ ñatvā sikkhattayapāripūriyā ghaṭamānā na kilamanti, sandiṭṭhamānā na ubbāḷhā honti. Tena nesaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanā phāsuvihārāya saṃvattati. Yo vā dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggaho, sveva etesaṃ phāsuvihāro. Dussīlapuggale nissāya hi uposatho na tiṭṭhati[M 1.0189], pavāraṇā na tiṭṭhati, saṅghakammāni nappavattanti, sāmaggī na hoti, bhikkhū anekaggā uddesaparipucchākammaṭṭhānādīni anuyuñjituṃ na sakkonti. Dussīlesu pana niggahitesu sabbopi ayaṃ upaddavo na hoti. Tato pesalā bhikkhū phāsu viharanti. Evaṃ “pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsu vihārāyā”ti ettha dvidhā attho [P 1.0225] veditabbo.

‘For the comfortable dwelling of amiable monks’ means for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of amiable monks, those of amiable virtue. For bhikkhus of amiable virtue, not knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameable and blameless, the boundary, and the limit, become weary when striving for the fulfillment of the threefold training; being in doubt, they are troubled. But knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameable and blameless, the boundary, and the limit, they do not become weary when striving for the fulfillment of the threefold training; being in doubt, they are not troubled. Therefore, the laying down of the training rule conduces to their comfortable dwelling. Or, the very subjugation of the unruly persons is their comfortable dwelling. For, on account of persons of bad virtue, the Uposatha is not established, the Pavāraṇā is not established, the Saṅgha acts do not proceed, there is no harmony, and the bhikkhus, with unconcentrated minds, are unable to apply themselves to recitation, questioning, meditation subjects, and so on. But when those of bad virtue have been subjugated, all this trouble does not exist. Then the amiable bhikkhus dwell in comfort. Thus, the meaning of 'for the comfortable dwelling of amiable monks' should be understood in two ways.

Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāyāti diṭṭhadhammikā āsavā nāma asaṃvare ṭhitena tasmiññeva attabhāve pattabbā pāṇippahāra-daṇḍappahāra-hatthaccheda-pādaccheda-akitti-ayasavippaṭisārādayo dukkhavisesā. Iti imesaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya pidhānāya āgamanamaggathakanāyāti attho.

For the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life: 'Taints pertaining to the present life' are the special kinds of suffering to be met with in this very existence by one who abides in non-restraint, such as striking with the hand, striking with a stick, cutting off the hand, cutting off the foot, ill-repute, disgrace, remorse, and so on. Thus, the meaning is: for the restraint, for the closing, for the blocking of the path of arising for these taints pertaining to the present life.

Samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyāti samparāyikā āsavā nāma asaṃvare ṭhitena katapāpakammamūlakā samparāye narakādīsu pattabbā dukkhavisesā, tesaṃ paṭighātatthāya [V 1.0174] paṭippassambhanatthāya vūpasamatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

For the destruction of the taints pertaining to the future life: 'Taints pertaining to the future life' are the special kinds of suffering, rooted in evil deeds done by one who abides in non-restraint, to be met with in the future life in hell and other such states. It is said for the purpose of destroying them, for the purpose of calming them, for the purpose of pacifying them.

Appasannānaṃ pasādāyāti sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hi sati sikkhāpadapaññattiṃ ñatvā vā yathāpaññattaṃ paṭipajjamāne bhikkhū disvā vā yepi appasannā paṇḍitamanussā, te “yāni vata loke mahājanassa rajjana-dussana-muyhanaṭṭhānāni, tehi ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā ārakā viratā viharanti, dukkaraṃ vata karonti, bhāriyaṃ vata karontī”ti pasādaṃ āpajjanti, vinayapiṭake potthakaṃ disvā micchādiṭṭhika-tivedī brāhmaṇo viya. Tena vuttaṃ – “appasannānaṃ pasādāyā”ti.

To inspire confidence in those who are not yet confident: For when a training rule is established, upon knowing the established training rule or seeing monks practicing as prescribed, even those wise people who are not yet confident think: "Indeed, these ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, dwell far from and abstain from what in the world are grounds for the great mass of people's attachment, aversion, and delusion. Truly, they do what is difficult; truly, they undertake what is weighty." Thus, they gain confidence, like the brahmin with wrong views, a knower of the three Vedas, who saw the book of the Vinaya Piṭaka. Therefore, it is said: "To inspire confidence in those who are not yet confident."

Pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāyāti yepi sāsane pasannā kulaputtā tepi sikkhāpadapaññattiṃ ñatvā yathāpaññattaṃ paṭipajjamāne bhikkhū vā disvā “aho ayyā dukkarakārino, ye yāvajīvaṃ ekabhattaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vinayasaṃvaraṃ anupālentī”ti bhiyyo bhiyyo pasīdanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāyā”ti.

For the increase of those who are confident: Those sons of good family who are confident in the Dispensation, upon knowing the enactment of the training rule or seeing the monks practicing as prescribed, think: "Ah, the venerable ones are doers of the difficult, who for as long as life lasts maintain the practice of eating one meal, the holy life, and the restraint of the Vinaya!"—and they become more and more confident. Therefore, it is said: "For the increase of those who are confident."

Saddhammaṭṭhitiyāti tividho saddhammo – pariyattisaddhammo, paṭipattisaddhammo, adhigamasaddhammoti. Tattha piṭakattayasaṅgahitaṃ sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ “pariyattisaddhammo” nāma. Terasa dhutaguṇā, cuddasa khandhakavattāni, dveasīti mahāvattāni, sīlasamādhivipassanāti [M 1.0190] ayaṃ “paṭipattisaddhammo” nāma. Cattāro ariyamaggā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni nibbānañcāti ayaṃ “adhigamasaddhammo” nāma. So sabbopi yasmā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sati bhikkhū sikkhāpadañca tassa vibhaṅgañca tadatthajotanatthaṃ aññañca buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, yathāpaññattañca paṭipajjamānā paṭipattiṃ pūretvā paṭipattiyā adhigantabbaṃ [P 1.0226] lokuttaradhammaṃ adhigacchanti, tasmā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā ciraṭṭhitiko hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “saddhammaṭṭhitiyā”ti.

For the stability of the true Dhamma: The true Dhamma is threefold: the true Dhamma of learning, the true Dhamma of practice, and the true Dhamma of realization. Herein, all the Buddha's words contained in the three Piṭakas are called 'the true Dhamma of learning.' The thirteen ascetic qualities, the fourteen duties of the Khandhakas, the eighty-two great duties, and morality, concentration, and insight—this is called 'the true Dhamma of practice.' The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is called 'the true Dhamma of realization.' Because, when the training rules are laid down, the monks learn the training rule, its analysis, and other words of the Buddha to illuminate its meaning; and practicing as prescribed, they fulfill the practice and, through practice, attain the supramundane Dhamma that is to be realized. Therefore, because of the laying down of the training rules, the true Dhamma becomes long-lasting. Thus, it is said: "For the stability of the true Dhamma."

Vinayānuggahāyāti sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hi sati saṃvaravinayo ca pahānavinayo ca samathavinayo ca paññattivinayo cāti catubbidhopi vinayo anuggahito hoti upatthambhito sūpatthambhito. Tena vuttaṃ – “vinayānuggahāyā”ti.

For the support of the Vinaya: For when a training rule is laid down, all four kinds of Vinaya—the Vinaya of restraint, the Vinaya of abandoning, the Vinaya of calming, and the Vinaya of prescription—are supported, upheld, and well-supported. Therefore, it is said, "For the support of the Vinaya."

Sabbāneva cetāni padāni “sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmī”ti iminā vacanena saddhiṃ yojetabbāni[V 1.0175]. Tatrāyaṃ paṭhamapacchimapadayojanā – “saṅghasuṭṭhutāya sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmi, vinayānuggahāya sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmī”ti.

All these phrases should be connected with the statement, "I will lay down a training rule." Here, this is the connection of the first and last phrases: "For the excellence of the Sangha, I will lay down a training rule; for the support of the Vinaya, I will lay down a training rule."

Api cettha yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghaphāsu taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyāti evaṃ saṅkhalikanayaṃ; yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu taṃ saṅghaphāsu, yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu taṃ dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyāti evañca ekekapadamūlikaṃ dasakkhattuṃ yojanaṃ katvā yaṃ vuttaṃ parivāre (pari. 334) –

Furthermore, herein, 'Whatever is for the excellence of the Sangha is for the ease of the Sangha; whatever is for the ease of the Sangha is for the subduing of unruly persons'—this is the chain method. And, having made the connection rooted in each single term ten times in this way—'Whatever is for the excellence of the Sangha is for the ease of the Sangha; whatever is for the excellence of the Sangha is for the subduing of unruly persons'—as is stated in the Parivāra:

“Atthasataṃ dhammasataṃ, dve ca niruttisatāni;

Cattāri ñāṇasatāni, atthavase pakaraṇe”ti.

"A hundred meanings, a hundred principles, and two hundred expressions; four hundred knowledges in the treatise on the basis of meaning."

Taṃ sabbaṃ veditabbaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ yasmā parivāreyeva āvi bhavissati, tasmā idha na vaṇṇitanti.

All that should be understood. But since this will become clear in the Parivāra itself, it is not described here.

Evaṃ sikkhāpadapaññattiyā ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā tasmiṃ sikkhāpade bhikkhūhi kattabbakiccaṃ dīpento “evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti āha. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Bhikkhave, imaṃ pana mayā iti sandassitānisaṃsaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ evaṃ pātimokkhuddese uddiseyyātha ca pariyāpuṇeyyātha ca dhāreyyātha ca aññesañca vāceyyāthāti. Atirekānayanattho [M 1.0191] hi ettha ca saddo, tenāyamattho ānīto hotīti.

Having thus shown the benefits of laying down the training rule, and indicating the duty to be performed by the bhikkhus with regard to that training rule, he said, “And thus, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule.” What is meant by this? “Bhikkhus, this training rule, whose benefits I have thus shown, you should recite thus in the Pātimokkha recitation, and you should learn it, and you should remember it, and you should have others recite it.” For here, the particle ‘ca’ has the meaning of bringing in something additional; hence this meaning is brought in.

Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ “imaṃ sikkhāpada”nti taṃ dassento “yo pana bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyya, pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso”ti āha. Evaṃ mūlacchejjavasena daḷhaṃ katvā paṭhamapārājike paññatte aparampi anupaññattatthāya makkaṭīvatthu udapādi. Tassuppattidīpanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ – evañcidaṃ bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ hotīti. Tassattho – bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ evaṃ paññattaṃ hoti ca, idañca aññaṃ vatthu udapādīti.

Now, showing what was meant by “this training rule,” he said, “Whatever bhikkhu should engage in sexual intercourse is defeated, no longer in communion.” Thus, having firmly established the first Pārājika by way of cutting off at the root, another incident arose for the purpose of a subsequent enactment: the story of the female monkey. To explain its origin, this was said: “And in this way this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.” Its meaning is: This training rule was thus laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus, and this other incident also arose.

Paṭhamapaññattikathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the first enactment is concluded.

Sudinnabhāṇavāraṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Sudinna recitation section is concluded.

Makkaṭīvatthukathā

The Story of the Female Monkey

40. Idāni [P 1.0227][V 1.0176] yaṃ taṃ aññaṃ vatthu uppannaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “tena kho pana samayenā”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – makkaṭiṃ āmisenāti mahāvane bhikkhūnaṃ khantimettādiguṇānubhāvena nirāsaṅkacittā bahū migamorakukkuṭamakkaṭādayo tiracchānā padhānāgāraṭṭhānesu vicaranti. Tatra ekaṃ makkaṭiṃ āmisena yāgubhattakhajjakādinā upalāpetvā, saṅgaṇhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassāti bhummavacanaṃ. Paṭisevatīti pacurapaṭisevano hoti; pacuratthe hi vattamānavacanaṃ. So bhikkhūti so methunadhammapaṭisevanako bhikkhu. Senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantāti te bhikkhū āgantukā buddhadassanāya āgatā pātova āgantukabhattāni labhitvā katabhattakiccā bhikkhūnaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānāni passissāmāti vicariṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantā”ti. Yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamīti tiracchānagatā nāma ekabhikkhunā saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ katvā aññesupi tādisaññeva cittaṃ uppādenti. Tasmā sā makkaṭī yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ca attano vissāsikabhikkhusseva tesampi taṃ vikāraṃ dassesi.

40. Now, to show that other story which arose, the reciter of the canon said, 'Now at that time...' and so on. Herein, this is the explanation of the non-obvious words. 'A female monkey with food': In the great forest, due to the power of the monks' virtues such as patience and loving-kindness, many animals—deer, peacocks, chickens, monkeys, and the like—roam about in the places of the meditation halls without a mind of doubt. There, it is said that having enticed one female monkey with food such as gruel, rice, and hard food, he won her over. 'Tassā' is a word in the locative case. 'He engages' means he is one who frequently engages, for the present tense is used in the sense of frequency. 'That monk' means that monk who engages in the act of sexual intercourse. 'Wandering on a tour of the lodgings': Those monks were visiting monks who had come to see the Buddha. Having received the visitors' meal early in the morning and having finished their meal duties, they wandered about, thinking, 'We will see the dwelling places of the monks.' Therefore, it was said, 'wandering on a tour of the lodgings.' 'She approached where those monks were': Animals, having established familiarity with one monk, generate a similar state of mind towards other monks as well. Therefore, that female monkey approached where those monks were; and having approached, she showed that perverse behavior to them also, just as she would to the monk with whom she was familiar.

Cheppanti naṅguṭṭhaṃ. Oḍḍīti abhimukhaṃ ṭhapesi. Nimittampi akāsīti yena niyāmena yāya kiriyāya methunādhippāyaṃ te jānanti taṃ akāsīti attho[M 1.0192]. So bhikkhūti yassāyaṃ vihāro. Ekamantaṃ nilīyiṃsūti ekasmiṃ okāse paṭicchannā acchiṃsu.

'Cheppaṃ' means tail. 'Oḍḍi' means she placed it facing them. 'And she made a sign' means: she made that sign by which method, by which action, they would know her intention for sexual intercourse. 'That monk' means the monk whose monastery this is. 'They hid on one side' means they stayed concealed in one place.

41. Saccaṃ, āvusoti sahoḍḍhaggahito coro viya paccakkhaṃ disvā coditattā “kiṃ vā mayā kata”ntiādīni vattuṃ asakkonto “saccaṃ, āvuso”ti āha. Nanu, āvuso, tatheva taṃ hotīti āvuso yathā manussitthiyā, nanu tiracchānagatitthiyāpi taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ tatheva hoti. Manussitthiyāpi hi dassanampi gahaṇampi āmasanampi phusanampi ghaṭṭanampi duṭṭhullameva. Tiracchānagatitthiyāpi taṃ sabbaṃ duṭṭhullameva. Ko ettha viseso? Alesaṭṭhāne tvaṃ lesaṃ oḍḍesīti.

41. 'It is true, friend.' Like a thief caught with the stolen goods, being unable to say, 'What have I done?' and so on, because he was accused after being seen directly, he said, 'It is true, friend.' 'Friend, is it not just so? Friend, just as it is for a human woman, is not that training rule the same for an animal female? For with a human woman, seeing, taking hold of, stroking, touching, and rubbing against are indeed a grave offense. With an animal female also, all of that is indeed a grave offense. What is the difference here? You are raising a pretext in a place where there is no pretext.'

42. Antamaso tiracchānagatāyapi pārājiko hoti asaṃvāsoti tiracchānagatāyapi methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā pārājiko yeva hotīti daḷhataraṃ sikkhāpadamakāsi. Duvidhañhi [P 1.0228] sikkhāpadaṃ – lokavajjaṃ, paṇṇattivajjañca. Tattha yassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajjaṃ nāma. Sesaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ. Tattha lokavajje anupaññatti uppajjamānā rundhantī dvāraṃ pidahantī sotaṃ pacchindamānā gāḷhataraṃ karontī uppajjati, aññatra adhimānā, aññatra supinantāti ayaṃ pana vītikkamābhāvā abbohārikattā ca vuttā. Paṇṇattivajje akate vītikkame uppajjamānā sithilaṃ karontī mocentī dvāraṃ dadamānā aparāparampi anāpattiṃ kurumānā uppajjati, gaṇabhojanaparamparabhojanādīsu anupaññattiyo viya. “Antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapī”ti evarūpā pana kate vītikkame uppannattā paññattigatikāva hoti. Idaṃ pana paṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ yasmā lokavajjaṃ, na paṇṇattivajjaṃ; tasmā ayamanupaññatti rundhantī [V 1.0177] dvāraṃ pidahantī sotaṃ pacchindamānā gāḷhataraṃ karontī uppajji.

42. 'Even with an animal, one is defeated, not in communion' means that having engaged in the act of sexual intercourse even with an animal, one is indeed defeated; thus He made the training rule stricter. For a training rule is twofold: an offense in the world (lokavajja) and an offense by enactment (paṇṇattivajja). Therein, that for which the mind, in the case of it being intentional, is only unwholesome, is called an offense in the world. The remainder is an offense by enactment. Therein, in the case of an offense in the world, a supplementary enactment, when it arises, arises obstructing, closing the door, cutting off the stream, and making it stricter. But this exemption, 'except through conceit, except in a dream,' is stated because of the absence of transgression and because it is not a legal issue. In the case of an offense by enactment, when no transgression has been committed, a supplementary enactment arises making it looser, releasing, giving an opening, and making for non-offense again and again, like the supplementary enactments in the cases of group meals, consecutive meals, and so on. But an enactment of this sort, such as 'even for a momentary one,' because it arose after the transgression was committed, is of the nature of the original enactment. But since this first training rule is an offense in the world, not an offense by enactment, therefore this supplementary enactment arose obstructing, closing the door, cutting off the stream, and making it stricter.

Evaṃ dvepi vatthūni sampiṇḍetvā mūlacchejjavasena daḷhataraṃ katvā paṭhamapārājike paññatte aparampi anupaññattatthāya vajjiputtakavatthu udapādi. Tassuppattidassanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ – “evañcidaṃ bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ hotī”ti[M 1.0193]. Tassattho – bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ evaṃ paññattaṃ hoti ca idañca aññampi vatthu udapādīti.

Thus, having combined both stories and made it stricter by way of cutting off at the root, when the first Pārājika was laid down, another story, that of the Vajjian-son monk, arose for the purpose of a supplementary enactment. To show its origin, this was said: 'Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.' Its meaning is: This training rule was laid down thus by the Blessed One for the monks, and this other story also arose.

Makkaṭīvatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Story of the Female Monkey is concluded.

Santhatabhāṇavāro

The Chapter on Spreading.

Vajjiputtakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Vajjiputtaka Monk.

43-44. Idāni yaṃ taṃ aññampi vatthu uppannaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “tena kho pana samayenā”tiādimāha. Tatrāpi ayamanuttānapadavaṇṇanā – vesālikāti vesālivāsino. Vajjiputtakāti vajjiraṭṭhe vesāliyaṃ kulānaṃ puttā. Sāsane kira yo yo upaddavo ādīnavo abbudamuppajji, sabbaṃ taṃ vajjiputtake nissāya. Tathā hi devadattopi vajjiputtake pakkhe labhitvā saṅghaṃ bhindi. Vajjiputtakā eva ca vassasataparinibbute bhagavati uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ dīpesuṃ. Imepi tesaṃ yeva ekacce evaṃ paññattepi sikkhāpade [P 1.0229] yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjiṃsu…pe… methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseviṃsūti.

43. Now, to show another story that arose, the reciter of the canon began the passage, 'Now at that time...' Here, too, this is the explanation of non-obvious terms: `Vesālikā` means the inhabitants of Vesālī. `Vajjiputtakā` means the sons of families in Vesālī, in the Vajji country. It is said that whatever trouble, danger, or corruption arose in the Dispensation, all of it arose on account of the Vajjiputtaka monks. Thus, Devadatta, having gained the Vajjiputtaka monks as his faction, split the Saṅgha. And it was the Vajjiputtaka monks themselves who, one hundred years after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, proclaimed a non-Dhamma and a non-Vinaya in the Teacher's Dispensation. These monks here were some of those very ones who, although this training rule had been laid down thus, ate as they pleased, slept as they pleased, and bathed as they pleased. And so, having eaten, slept, and bathed as they pleased, and having applied their minds improperly, without renouncing the training and without revealing their weakness, they engaged in the sexual act.

Ñātibyasanenapīti ettha asanaṃ byasanaṃ vikkhepo viddhaṃsanaṃ vināsoti sabbametaṃ ekatthaṃ. Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ, tena ñātibyasanena, rājadaṇḍabyādhimaraṇavippavāsanimittena [V 1.0178] ñātivināsenāti attho. Esa nayo dutiyapadepi. Tatiyapade pana ārogyavināsako rogo eva rogabyasanaṃ. So hi ārogyaṃ byasati vikkhipati vināsetīti byasanaṃ. Rogova byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ, tena rogabyasanena. Phuṭṭhāti adhipannā abhibhūtā samannāgatāti attho.

In the phrase Ñātibyasanenapīti: Here, the words asanaṃ, byasanaṃ, vikkhepo, viddhaṃsanaṃ, and vināso all have the same meaning. The destruction of relatives (ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ) is ñātibyasanaṃ. By that destruction of relatives (tena ñātibyasanena) means by the loss of relatives which has as its cause royal punishment, disease, death, or separation. This same method applies to the second term as well. In the third term, however, disease, which destroys health, is itself rogabyasanaṃ. For it destroys (byasati), scatters (vikkhipati), and ruins (vināseti) health; therefore, it is called byasanaṃ. Disease itself is destruction (byasanaṃ), hence rogabyasanaṃ. By that disease which destroys health (tena rogabyasanena). Phuṭṭhāti means overcome, overwhelmed, or afflicted.

Na mayaṃ, bhante ānanda, buddhagarahinoti bhante ānanda, mayaṃ na buddhaṃ garahāma, na buddhassa dosaṃ dema. Na dhammagarahino, na saṅghagarahino. Attagarahino mayanti attānameva mayaṃ garahāma, attano dosaṃ dema. Alakkhikāti nissirikā. Appapuññāti parittapuññā. Vipassakā kusalānaṃ dhammānanti ye aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu vibhattā kusalā dhammā, tesaṃ vipassakā; tato tato ārammaṇato vuṭṭhāya teva dhamme vipassamānāti [M 1.0194] attho. Pubbarattāpararattanti rattiyā pubbaṃ pubbarattaṃ, rattiyā aparaṃ apararattaṃ, paṭhamayāmañca pacchimayāmañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bodhipakkhikānanti bodhissa pakkhe bhavānaṃ, arahattamaggañāṇassa upakārakānanti attho. Bhāvanānuyoganti vaḍḍhanānuyogaṃ. Anuyuttā vihareyyāmāti gihipalibodhaṃ āvāsapalibodhañca pahāya vivittesu senāsanesu yuttapayuttā anaññakiccā vihareyyāma.

Na mayaṃ, bhante ānanda, buddhagarahinoti means: 'Venerable Ānanda, we do not blame the Buddha; we do not find fault with the Buddha. We do not blame the Dhamma; we do not blame the Saṅgha.' Attagarahino mayanti means: 'We blame only ourselves; we find fault with ourselves.' Alakkhikāti means without splendor. Appapuññāti means of little merit. Vipassakā kusalānaṃ dhammānanti means: discerners of those wholesome states which are analyzed among the thirty-eight meditation objects; the meaning is that, having arisen from this or that meditation object, we would contemplate those very states. Pubbarattāpararattanti means: the earlier part of the night is pubbarattaṃ, and the later part of the night is apararattaṃ; this means the first watch and the last watch. Bodhipakkhikānanti means: of those things that are on the side of enlightenment; the meaning is, of the factors that are beneficial for the path-knowledge of Arahantship. Bhāvanānuyoganti means: devotion to development. Anuyuttā vihareyyāmāti means: having abandoned the obstruction of the lay life and the obstruction of the monastery, we would dwell in secluded lodgings, diligent and striving, with no other task.

Evamāvusoti thero etesaṃ āsayaṃ ajānanto idaṃ nesaṃ mahāgajjitaṃ sutvā “sace ime īdisā bhavissanti, sādhū”ti maññamāno “evamāvuso”ti sampaṭicchi. Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāsoti ubhayampetaṃ kāraṇapaṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tattha tadāyattavuttibhāvena phalaṃ tiṭṭhati. Yasmā cassa taṃ okāso hoti tadāyattavuttibhāvena, tasmā “ṭhānañca avakāso cā”ti vuccati, taṃ paṭikkhipanto āha – “aṭṭhānametaṃ, ānanda[P 1.0230], anavakāso”ti. Etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vā okāso vā natthi. Yaṃ tathāgatoti yena tathāgato vajjīnaṃ vā…pe… samūhaneyya, taṃ kāraṇaṃ natthīti attho. Yadi hi bhagavā etesaṃ “labheyyāma upasampada”nti yācantānaṃ upasampadaṃ dadeyya, evaṃ sante “pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso”ti paññattaṃ samūhaneyya. Yasmā panetaṃ na samūhanati, tasmā “aṭṭhānameta”ntiādimāha.

Evamāvusoti: the elder, not knowing their disposition, heard this great roar of theirs and, thinking, 'If these monks are indeed like this, it is good,' he agreed, saying, 'So be it, friends.' Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāsoti: both of these are terms that reject a cause. For, because the result stands in the cause by being dependent on it, the cause is called a 'place' (ṭhāna). And because that cause is an 'opportunity' (avakāsa) for the result by being dependent on it, it is also called an 'opportunity'.
