Rejecting that, he said, 'This is not the place, Ānanda, this is not the opportunity.' This means: 'This place or this opportunity does not exist.' Yaṃ tathāgatoti means: that cause by which the Tathāgata would abolish the Pārājika training rule laid down on account of the Vajjis or the Vajjiputtakas—that cause does not exist. For if the Blessed One were to grant ordination to these who are asking, 'May we receive ordination,' this being so, he would be abolishing the rule laid down as 'He is defeated, he is not in communion.' But because he does not abolish this, therefore he said, 'This is not the place,' and so on.

So āgato na upasampādetabboti “yadi hi evaṃ āgato upasampadaṃ labheyya, sāsane agāravo bhaveyya. Sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ pana ṭhito sagāravo ca bhavissati, attatthañca karissatī”ti ñatvā anukampamāno bhagavā āha – “so āgato na upasampādetabbo”ti. So āgato upasampādetabboti evaṃ āgato bhikkhubhāve ṭhatvā avipannasīlatāya sāsane sagāravo [V 1.0179] bhavissati, so sati upanissaye nacirasseva uttamatthaṃ pāpuṇissatīti ñatvā upasampādetabboti āha.

So āgato na upasampādetabboti: The Blessed One, knowing out of compassion that 'If one who has returned in this way (without disrobing) were to receive ordination, there would be disrespect in the Dispensation. But if he remains at the stage of a novice, he will be respectful and will also work for his own welfare,' said, 'One who has returned thus should not be ordained.' So āgato upasampādetabboti: He said, 'He should be ordained,' knowing that 'One who has returned in this way (after disrobing), having been established in the state of a monk, will be respectful in the Dispensation due to his unbroken virtue, and if he has the supporting condition, he will before long attain the supreme goal.'

Evaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā āgatesu anupasampādetabbañca upasampādetabbañca dassetvā tīṇipi vatthūni samodhānetvā paripuṇṇaṃ katvā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetukāmo “evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti vatvā “yo pana bhikkhu…pe… asaṃvāso”ti paripuṇṇaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi.

Thus, having shown, among those who returned after engaging in the sexual act, both the one who should not be ordained and the one who should be ordained, and having connected the three stories, wishing to lay down the training rule, he said, 'And so, monks, you should recite this training rule in this way,' and laid down the complete training rule: 'Whatever monk... not in communion.'

Vajjiputtakavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of the Vajjiputtaka Monks is concluded.

Catubbidhavinayakathā

Discourse on the Fourfold Vinaya

45. Idānissa [M 1.0195] atthaṃ vibhajanto “yo panāti, yo yādiso”tiādimāha. Tasmiṃ pana sikkhāpade ca sikkhāpadavibhaṅge ca sakale ca vinayavinicchaye kosallaṃ patthayantena catubbidho vinayo jānitabbo –

Now, analyzing its meaning, he stated the beginning, 'Yo panāti means yo yādiso'. Furthermore, by one who aspires to skill in that training rule, in the analysis of the training rule, and in the entire Vinaya decision, the fourfold Vinaya should be known:

Catubbidhañhi vinayaṃ, mahātherā mahiddhikā;

Nīharitvā pakāsesuṃ, dhammasaṅgāhakā purā.

45. For in ancient times, the compilers of the Dhamma, the great elders of great power, extracted and made manifest the fourfold Vinaya.

Katamaṃ catubbidhaṃ? Suttaṃ, suttānulomaṃ, ācariyavādaṃ, attanomatinti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “āhaccapadena rasena ācariyavaṃsena adhippāyā”ti, ettha hi āhaccapadanti suttaṃ adhippetaṃ, rasoti suttānulomaṃ, ācariyavaṃsoti ācariyavādo, adhippāyoti attanomati.

What is the fourfold? The Sutta, Suttānuloma, the Teachers' Doctrine, and one's own opinion. With reference to this it was said: 'By the authoritative word, by the essence, by the lineage of teachers, and by one's own inclination.' Herein, by 'authoritative word' is meant the Sutta; by 'essence' is meant Suttānuloma; by 'lineage of teachers' is meant the Teachers' Doctrine; and by 'one's own inclination' is meant one's own opinion.

Tattha suttaṃnāma sakale vinayapiṭake pāḷi.

Therein, what is called 'Sutta' is the Pāḷi in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.

Suttānulomaṃ nāma cattāro mahāpadesā; ye bhagavatā evaṃ vuttā – “yaṃ, bhikkhave[P 1.0231], mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ ce akappiyaṃ anulometi; kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ ce kappiyaṃ anulometi; akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave[V 1.0180], mayā ‘idaṃ kappatī’ti ananuññātaṃ, taṃ ce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati; taṃ vo na kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ kappatī’ti ananuññātaṃ, taṃ ce kappiyaṃ anulometi, akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati; taṃ vo kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305).

What is called Suttānuloma are the four great references, which were spoken thus by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, whatever has not been rejected by me, saying, "This is not allowable," if that conforms to what is not allowable and obstructs what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. Bhikkhus, whatever has not been rejected by me, saying, "This is not allowable," if that conforms to what is allowable and obstructs what is not allowable, that is allowable for you. Bhikkhus, whatever has not been permitted by me, saying, "This is allowable," if that conforms to what is not allowable and obstructs what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. Bhikkhus, whatever has not been permitted by me, saying, "This is allowable," if that conforms to what is allowable and obstructs what is not allowable, that is allowable for you.'

Ācariyavādo nāma dhammasaṅgāhakehi pañcahi arahantasatehi ṭhapitā pāḷivinimuttā okkantavinicchayappavattā aṭṭhakathātanti.

What is called the Teachers' Doctrine is the textual tradition of the commentary, established by the five hundred Arahants who were compilers of the Dhamma, which is independent of the Pāḷi and proceeds from decisions arrived at through insight.

Attanomati nāma sutta-suttānuloma-ācariyavāde muñcitvā anumānena attano anubuddhiyā nayaggāhena upaṭṭhitākārakathanaṃ.

What is called one's own opinion is, having set aside the Sutta, Suttānuloma, and the Teachers' Doctrine, the stating of a matter as it appears to oneself by means of inference, one's own consequential understanding, and the grasping of a method.

Apica suttantābhidhammavinayaṭṭhakathāsu āgato sabbopi theravādo “attanomati” nāma. Taṃ pana attanomatiṃ gahetvā kathentena na daḷhaggāhaṃ [M 1.0196] gahetvā voharitabbaṃ. Kāraṇaṃ sallakkhetvā atthena pāḷiṃ, pāḷiyā ca atthaṃ saṃsanditvā kathetabbaṃ. Attanomati ācariyavāde otāretabbā. Sace tattha otarati ceva sameti ca, gahetabbā. Sace neva otarati na sameti, na gahetabbā. Ayañhi attanomati nāma sabbadubbalā. Attanomatito ācariyavādo balavataro.

Moreover, every Theravāda doctrine that comes in the commentaries to the Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya is called 'one's own opinion'. However, one who speaks having adopted that 'one's own opinion' should not speak holding it with a firm grasp. Having marked the reason, and having compared the meaning with the Pāḷi and the Pāḷi with the meaning, one should speak. 'One's own opinion' should be tested against the Teachers' Doctrine. If it is consistent and agrees with it, it should be accepted. If it is neither consistent nor agrees, it should not be accepted. For this 'one's own opinion' is the weakest of all. Stronger than 'one's own opinion' is the Teachers' Doctrine.

Ācariyavādopi suttānulome otāretabbo. Tattha otaranto samentoyeva gahetabbo, itaro na gahetabbo. Ācariyavādato hi suttānulomaṃ balavataraṃ.

The Teachers' Doctrine should also be tested against Suttānuloma. Only that which is consistent and agrees with it should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. For Suttānuloma is stronger than the Teachers' Doctrine.

Suttānulomampi sutte otāretabbaṃ. Tattha otarantaṃ samentameva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Suttānulomato hi suttameva balavataraṃ. Suttañhi appaṭivattiyaṃ kārakasaṅghasadisaṃ buddhānaṃ ṭhitakālasadisaṃ. Tasmā yadā dve bhikkhū sākacchanti, sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paravādī suttānulomaṃ. Tehi aññamaññaṃ khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvā suttānulomaṃ sutte otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce, na gahetabbaṃ; suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro ācariyavādaṃ. Tehipi aññamaññaṃ khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvā ācariyavādo sutte otāretabbo. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbo. Anotaranto asamento ca gārayhācariyavādo na gahetabbo; suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Suttānuloma should also be tested against the Sutta. Only that which is consistent and agrees with it should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. For the Sutta itself is stronger than Suttānuloma. Indeed, the Sutta is irrefutable, like the compiling Saṅgha, like the very time of the Buddhas' presence. Therefore, when two bhikkhus are discussing, and the proponent of one view speaks having taken the Sutta, while the proponent of the other view speaks having taken Suttānuloma, they, without casting blame or reproach on each other, should test Suttānuloma against the Sutta. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand on the Sutta alone. Or, if one speaks having taken the Sutta, and the other speaks having taken the Teachers' Doctrine, they too, without casting blame or reproach on each other, should test the Teachers' Doctrine against the Sutta. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. A blameworthy Teachers' Doctrine that is not consistent and does not agree should not be accepted; one should stand on the Sutta alone.

Athāyaṃ suttaṃ [P 1.0232] gahetvā katheti, paro attanomatiṃ. Tehipi aññamaññaṃ khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā [V 1.0181] akatvā attanomati sutte otāretabbā. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbā. No ce, na gahetabbā. Suttasmiṃ yeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if one speaks having taken the Sutta, and the other speaks having taken one's own opinion, they too, without casting blame or reproach on each other, should test one's own opinion against the Sutta. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted. One should stand on the Sutta alone.

Atha panāyaṃ suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttaṃ. Suttaṃ suttānulome otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, tisso saṅgītiyo ārūḷhaṃ pāḷiāgataṃ paññāyati, gahetabbaṃ. No ce tathā paññāyati na otarati na sameti, bāhirakasuttaṃ vā hoti siloko vā aññaṃ vā gārayhasuttaṃ guḷhavessantaraguḷhavinayavedallādīnaṃ aññatarato āgataṃ, na gahetabbaṃ. Suttānulomasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

But if one speaks having taken Suttānuloma, and the other speaks having taken the Sutta, the Sutta should be tested against Suttānuloma. If it is consistent and agrees, and is recognized as having been included in the three councils and come down in the Pāḷi, it should be accepted. If it is not so recognized, is not consistent, and does not agree, and it is an external sutta, or a verse, or some other blameworthy sutta that has come from one of the Guḷhavessantara, Guḷhavinaya, Vedalla, and so on, it should not be accepted. One should stand on Suttānuloma alone.

Athāyaṃ [M 1.0197] suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro ācariyavādaṃ. Ācariyavādo suttānulome otāretabbo. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbo. No ce, na gahetabbo. Suttānulomeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if one speaks having taken Suttānuloma, and the other speaks having taken the Teachers' Doctrine, the Teachers' Doctrine should be tested against Suttānuloma. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted. One should stand on Suttānuloma alone.

Athāyaṃ suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro attanomatiṃ. Attanomati suttānulome otāretabbā. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbā. No ce, na gahetabbā. Suttānulomeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if one speaks having taken Suttānuloma, and the other speaks having taken one's own opinion, one's own opinion should be tested against Suttānuloma. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted. One should stand on Suttānuloma alone.

Atha panāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttaṃ. Suttaṃ ācariyavāde otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbaṃ. Itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Ācariyavādeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

But if one speaks having taken the Teachers' Doctrine, and the other speaks having taken the Sutta, the Sutta should be tested against the Teachers' Doctrine. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. The other, a blameworthy sutta, should not be accepted. One should stand on the Teachers' Doctrine alone.

Athāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttānulomaṃ. Suttānulomaṃ ācariyavāde otāretabbaṃ. Otarantaṃ samentameva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Ācariyavādeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if one speaks having taken the Teachers' Doctrine, and the other speaks having taken Suttānuloma, Suttānuloma should be tested against the Teachers' Doctrine. Only that which is consistent and agrees should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. One should stand on the Teachers' Doctrine alone.

Athāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro attanomatiṃ. Attanomati ācariyavāde otāretabbā. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbā. No ce, na gahetabbā. Ācariyavādeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if one speaks having taken the Teachers' Doctrine, and the other speaks having taken one's own opinion, one's own opinion should be tested against the Teachers' Doctrine. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted. One should stand on the Teachers' Doctrine alone.

Atha panāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttaṃ. Suttaṃ attanomatiyaṃ otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbaṃ. Itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Attanomatiyameva ṭhātabbaṃ.

But if one speaks having taken one's own opinion, and the other speaks having taken the Sutta, the Sutta should be tested against one's own opinion. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted. The other, a blameworthy sutta, should not be accepted. One should stand on one's own opinion alone.

Athāyaṃ [V 1.0182] attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttānulomaṃ. Suttānulomaṃ attanomatiyaṃ otāretabbaṃ. Otarantaṃ samentameva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Attanomatiyameva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if one speaks having taken one's own opinion, and the other speaks having taken Suttānuloma, Suttānuloma should be tested against one's own opinion. Only that which is consistent and agrees should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. One should stand on one's own opinion alone.

Athāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro ācariyavādaṃ. Ācariyavādo attanomatiyaṃ otāretabbo. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbo; itaro gārayhācariyavādo na gahetabbo. Attanomatiyameva ṭhātabbaṃ. Attano gahaṇameva [P 1.0233] baliyaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sabbaṭṭhānesu ca khepo vā garahā vā na kātabbāti.

Or, if one speaks having taken one's own opinion, and the other speaks having taken the Teachers' Doctrine, the Teachers' Doctrine should be tested against one's own opinion. If it is consistent and agrees, it should be accepted; the other, a blameworthy Teachers' Doctrine, should not be accepted. One should stand on one's own opinion alone. One's own position should be made strong. And in all cases, neither rejection of the view nor blame of the person should be made.

Atha [M 1.0198] panāyaṃ “kappiya”nti gahetvā katheti, paro “akappiya”nti. Sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbaṃ. Sace kappiyaṃ hoti, kappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Sace akappiyaṃ, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ.

But if one speaks having taken the position 'it is allowable,' and the other, 'it is not allowable,' it should be tested against the Sutta and Suttānuloma. If it is allowable, one should stand on what is allowable. If it is not allowable, one should stand on what is not allowable.

Athāyaṃ tassa kappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dasseti, paro kāraṇaṃ na vindati. Kappiyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha paro tassa akappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dasseti, anena attano gahaṇanti katvā daḷhaṃ ādāya na ṭhātabbaṃ. “Sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā akappiyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissati, paṭikkhittabhāvoyeva sādhu, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Vinayañhi patvā kappiyākappiyavicāraṇamāgamma rundhitabbaṃ, gāḷhaṃ kattabbaṃ, sotaṃ pacchinditabbaṃ, garukabhāveyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Or, if this one demonstrates much reasoning and judgment from the Sutta to establish its allowability, and the other finds no reasoning, one should stand firm in what is allowable. Or, if the other demonstrates much reasoning and judgment from the Sutta to establish its unallowability, this one should not, having considered it 'my view,' stand firm by taking it rigidly. Having accepted it with 'Good,' one should stand firm in what is unallowable. Or, if a semblance of reasoning is seen for both, the state of being rejected is indeed good; one should stand firm in what is unallowable. For, having come to the Vinaya and undertaken the investigation of what is allowable and unallowable, the view of allowability should be obstructed, firmness in the unallowable should be established, the stream of that view should be cut off, and one must stand firm in the graver position, that is, the unallowable.

Atha panāyaṃ “akappiya”nti gahetvā katheti, paro “kappiya”nti. Sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbaṃ. Sace kappiyaṃ hoti, kappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Sace akappiyaṃ, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ.

Then again, if this one speaks having taken the position 'it is unallowable,' and the other, 'it is allowable,' it should be compared with the Sutta and that which is in conformity with the Sutta. If it is allowable, one should stand firm in what is allowable. If it is unallowable, one should stand firm in what is unallowable.

Athāyaṃ bahūhi suttavinicchayakāraṇehi akappiyabhāvaṃ dasseti, paro kāraṇaṃ na vindati, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha paro bahūhi suttavinicchayakāraṇehi kappiyabhāvaṃ dasseti, ayaṃ kāraṇaṃ na vindati, kappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissati, attano gahaṇaṃ na vissajjetabbaṃ. Yathā cāyaṃ kappiyākappiye akappiyakappiye ca vinicchayo vutto; evaṃ anāpattiāpattivāde āpattānāpattivāde ca, lahukagarukāpattivāde garukalahukāpattivāde cāpi [V 1.0183] vinicchayo veditabbo. Nāmamattaṃyeva hi ettha nānaṃ, yojanānaye nānaṃ natthi, tasmā na vitthāritaṃ.

Or, if this one demonstrates the unallowable nature through many reasons of scriptural judgment, and the other finds no reason, one should stand firm in the unallowable. Or, if the other demonstrates the allowable nature through many reasons of scriptural judgment, and this one finds no reason, one should stand firm in the allowable. Or, if a semblance of reasoning is seen for both, one should not abandon one’s own position. And just as this judgment concerning what is allowable and unallowable has been stated, so too should the judgment be understood in disputes of non-offense and offense, and of light and grave offenses. For here the difference is merely in name; there is no difference in the method of application, therefore it has not been elaborated.

Evaṃ kappiyākappiyādivinicchaye uppanne yo sutta-suttānulomaācariyavādaattanomatīsu atirekakāraṇaṃ labhati, tassa vāde ṭhātabbaṃ. Sabbaso pana kāraṇaṃ vinicchayaṃ alabhantena suttaṃ na jahitabbaṃ, suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbanti. Evaṃ tasmiṃ sikkhāpade ca sikkhāpadavibhaṅge ca sakale ca vinayavinicchaye kosallaṃ patthayantena ayaṃ catubbidho vinayo jānitabbo.

Thus, when a judgment concerning what is allowable, unallowable, and so forth arises, one should stand by the position of whoever finds a superior reason among the Sutta, that which is in conformity with the Sutta, the Teachers' doctrine, and one's own opinion. However, one who finds no reason or judgment at all should not abandon the Sutta, but should stand by the Sutta itself. In this way, one who aspires to skill in that training rule, in the analysis of the training rule, and in the entire judgment of the Vinaya, should know this fourfold Vinaya.

Imañca [M 1.0199][P 1.0234] pana catubbidhaṃ vinayaṃ ñatvāpi vinayadharena puggalena tilakkhaṇasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ. Tīṇi hi vinayadharassa lakkhaṇāni icchitabbāni. Katamāni tīṇi? “Suttañcassa svāgataṃ hoti suppavatti suvinicchitaṃ suttato anubyañjanato”ti idamekaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. “Vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti asaṃhīro”ti idaṃ dutiyaṃ. “Ācariyaparamparā kho panassa suggahitā hoti sumanasikatā sūpadhāritā”ti idaṃ tatiyaṃ.

Furthermore, even after knowing this fourfold Vinaya, a person who is a Vinaya-holder should be endowed with three characteristics. For three characteristics of a Vinaya-holder are to be desired. What are the three? 'The Sutta is well-mastered by him, fluent, and well-decided according to the text and its analysis'—this is the first characteristic. 'And he is established in the Vinaya, unshakeable'—this is the second characteristic. 'And the lineage of teachers is well-grasped by him, well-considered, and well-retained'—this is the third characteristic.

Tattha suttaṃ nāma sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ. Tañcassa svāgataṃ hotīti suṭṭhu āgataṃ. Suppavattīti suṭṭhu pavattaṃ paguṇaṃ vācuggataṃ suvinicchitaṃ. Suttato anubyañjanatoti pāḷito ca paripucchato ca aṭṭhakathāto ca suvinicchitaṃ hoti, kaṅkhacchedaṃ katvā uggahitaṃ.

Herein, 'Sutta' means the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. That it is 'well-mastered by him' means it has been well-mastered. 'Fluent' means it is well-practiced, skillful, memorized, and well-decided. 'Well-decided according to the text and its analysis' means it has been well-decided by means of the Pāḷi, repeated questioning, and the commentary; it has been learned after having cut off all doubt.

Vinaye kho pana ṭhito hotīti vinaye lajjībhāvena patiṭṭhito hoti. Alajjī hi bahussutopi samāno lābhagarutāya tantiṃ visaṃvādetvā uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ dīpetvā sāsane mahantaṃ upaddavaṃ karoti. Saṅghabhedampi saṅgharājimpi uppādeti. Lajjī pana kukkuccako sikkhākāmo jīvitahetupi tantiṃ avisaṃvādetvā dhammameva vinayameva ca dīpeti, satthusāsanaṃ garuṃ katvā ṭhapeti. Tathā hi pubbe mahātherā tikkhattuṃ vācaṃ nicchāresuṃ – “anāgate lajjī rakkhissati, lajjī rakkhissati, lajjī rakkhissatī”ti. Evaṃ yo lajjī, so vinayaṃ avijahanto avokkamanto lajjībhāvena vinaye ṭhito hoti suppatiṭṭhitoti. Asaṃhīroti saṃhīro nāma yo pāḷiyaṃ vā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vā heṭṭhato vā uparito vā padapaṭipāṭiyā vā pucchiyamāno vitthunati vipphandati santiṭṭhituṃ na sakkoti; yaṃ yaṃ parena vuccati taṃ taṃ anujānāti; sakavādaṃ chaḍḍetvā paravādaṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana pāḷiyaṃ vā aṭṭhakathāya vā heṭṭhupariyena vā padapaṭipāṭiyā [P 1.0235] vā pucchiyamāno na vitthunati na vipphandati, ekekalomaṃ saṇḍāsena gaṇhanto viya “evaṃ mayaṃ vadāma; evaṃ no ācariyā vadantī”ti [V 1.0184] vissajjeti; yamhi pāḷi ca pāḷivinicchayo ca suvaṇṇabhājane pakkhittasīhavasā viya parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ agacchanto tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ vuccati “asaṃhīro”ti.

'One who is established in the Vinaya' means one is established in the practice of the Vinaya through the state of being conscientious. For a shameless person, even if very learned, due to esteeming gain, may distort the textual lineage, presenting the Teacher's Dispensation as non-Dhamma or non-Vinaya, and thus create great danger in the Dispensation. He may even cause schism in the Saṅgha or disputes in the Saṅgha. But a conscientious person, being scrupulous and desirous of the training, would not distort the textual lineage even for the sake of his life. He illuminates only the Dhamma and only the Vinaya, holding the Teacher's Dispensation in high esteem. Indeed, the great elders of the past uttered the words three times: 'In the future, the conscientious one will protect, the conscientious one will protect, the conscientious one will protect!' Thus, whoever is conscientious, not abandoning or transgressing the Vinaya, is established, well-established in the Vinaya through the state of being conscientious. 'Unshakeable' means: one who is 'shakeable' is a person who, when questioned about the Pāḷi or the Aṭṭhakathā, from the lower part or the upper part, or by the sequence of words, fumbles, trembles, and is not able to stand firm; whatever is said by another, he approves of it; abandoning his own doctrine, he takes up the doctrine of another. But one who, when questioned about the Pāḷi or the Aṭṭhakathā, from the lower or upper part, or by the sequence of words, does not fumble, does not tremble; like one plucking out each single hair with tweezers, he is able to answer, 'Thus we say; thus our teachers say.' In whom the Pāḷi and the decision on the Pāḷi stand without going to exhaustion or complete consumption, like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel; this one is called 'unshakeable'.

Ācariyaparamparā kho panassa suggahitā hotīti theraparamparā vaṃsaparamparā cassa suṭṭhu gahitā hoti. Sumanasikatāti suṭṭhu manasikatā; āvajjitamatte ujjalitapadīpo viya hoti. Sūpadhāritāti suṭṭhu [M 1.0200] upadhāritā pubbāparānusandhito atthato kāraṇato ca upadhāritā; attano matiṃ pahāya ācariyasuddhiyā vattā hoti “mayhaṃ ācariyo asukācariyassa santike uggaṇhi, so asukassā”ti evaṃ sabbaṃ ācariyaparamparaṃ theravādaṅgaṃ āharitvā yāva upālitthero sammāsambuddhassa santike uggaṇhīti pāpetvā ṭhapeti. Tatopi āharitvā upālitthero sammāsambuddhassa santike uggaṇhi, dāsakatthero attano upajjhāyassa upālittherassa, soṇakatthero attano upajjhāyassa dāsakattherassa, siggavatthero attano upajjhāyassa soṇakattherassa, moggaliputtatissatthero attano upajjhāyassa siggavattherassa caṇḍavajjittherassa cāti. Evaṃ sabbaṃ ācariyaparamparaṃ theravādaṅgaṃ āharitvā attano ācariyaṃ pāpetvā ṭhapeti. Evaṃ uggahitā hi ācariyaparamparā suggahitā hoti. Evaṃ asakkontena pana avassaṃ dve tayo parivaṭṭā uggahetabbā. Sabbapacchimena hi nayena yathā ācariyo ca ācariyācariyo ca pāḷiñca paripucchañca vadanti, tathā ñātuṃ vaṭṭati.

By 'his lineage of teachers is well-grasped' is meant that his lineage of elders and ancestral lineage is well-grasped. By 'well-considered' is meant 'thoroughly attended to'; just upon adverting to it, it is like a lit lamp. By 'well-retained' is meant 'well-borne in mind', borne in mind with connection between the preceding and subsequent, by meaning, and by reason; abandoning his own opinion, he is one who speaks with the purity of the teachers, saying: 'My teacher learned in the presence of such-and-such a teacher, and he in the presence of such-and-such.' Thus, bringing forth the entire lineage of teachers, the doctrine of the elders, he establishes it, having made it reach up to the Elder Upāli who learned in the presence of the Sammāsambuddha. Bringing it forth from there also: the Elder Upāli learned in the presence of the Sammāsambuddha; the Elder Dāsaka in the presence of his preceptor, the Elder Upāli; the Elder Soṇaka in the presence of his preceptor, the Elder Dāsaka; the Elder Siggava in the presence of his preceptor, the Elder Soṇaka; the Elder Moggaliputtatissa in the presence of his preceptors, the Elder Siggava and the Elder Caṇḍavajji. Thus, bringing forth the entire lineage of teachers, the doctrine of the elders, he establishes it, having made it reach his own teacher. Indeed, a lineage of teachers learned in this way is well-grasped. But by one who is unable to do so, two or three successions must certainly be learned. Indeed, by the very last method, it is proper to know just as the teacher and the teacher's teacher speak the Pāḷi and the commentary.

Imehi ca pana tīhi lakkhaṇehi samannāgatena vinayadharena vatthuvinicchayatthaṃ sannipatite saṅghe otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ codakena ca cuditakena ca vutte vattabbe sahasā avinicchinitvāva cha ṭhānāni oloketabbāni. Katamāni cha? Vatthu oloketabbaṃ, mātikā oloketabbā, padabhājanīyaṃ oloketabbaṃ, tikaparicchedo oloketabbo, antarāpatti oloketabbā, anāpatti oloketabbāti.

And further, by a Vinaya-holder endowed with these three characteristics, when the Saṅgha has assembled for the purpose of deciding a case, when the case has come up, and when what should be said has been said by both the accuser and the accused, without deciding hastily, six points should be examined. What are the six? The origin story of the rule should be examined, the matrix should be examined, the word-analysis should be examined, the threefold classification should be examined, an intermediate offense should be examined, and a non-offense should be examined.

Vatthuṃ olokentopi [P 1.0236] hi “tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabbaṃ, na tveva naggena āgantabbaṃ; yo āgaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 517) evaṃ ekaccaṃ āpattiṃ passati. So taṃ suttaṃ ānetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati.

Indeed, when examining the origin story, he sees a certain offense, such as: 'One should come having covered oneself with grass or with leaves; one should certainly not come naked. Whichever monk should come naked, it is an offense of wrong conduct.' He, having brought that text, will settle that legal case.

Mātikaṃ olokentopi “sampajānamusāvāde pācittiya”ntiādinā (pāci. 2) nayena [V 1.0185] pañcannaṃ āpattīnaṃ aññataraṃ āpattiṃ passati, so taṃ suttaṃ ānetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati.

When examining the matrix, by the method beginning with 'In the case of a deliberate lie, it is a pācittiya offense,' he sees one or another of the five offenses. He, having brought that text, will settle that legal case.

Padabhājanīyaṃ [M 1.0201] olokentopi “akkhayite sarīre methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati, āpatti pārājikassa. Yebhuyyena khayite sarīre methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati, āpatti thullaccayassā”tiādinā (pārā. 59 ādayo, atthato samānaṃ) nayena sattannaṃ āpattīnaṃ aññataraṃ āpattiṃ passati, so padabhājanīyato suttaṃ ānetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati.

When examining the word-analysis, by the method beginning with 'If one engages in sexual intercourse with a body not yet eaten, it is a pārājika offense. If one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that has been mostly eaten, it is a thullaccaya offense,' he sees one or another of the seven offenses. He, having brought the text from the word-analysis, will settle that legal case.

Tikaparicchedaṃ olokentopi tikasaṅghādisesaṃ vā tikapācittiyaṃ vā tikadukkaṭaṃ vā aññataraṃ vā āpattiṃ tikaparicchede passati, so tato suttaṃ ānetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati.

When examining the threefold classification, he sees in the threefold classification a threefold saṅghādisesa offense, or a threefold pācittiya offense, or a threefold dukkaṭa offense, or some other offense. He, having brought the text from there, will settle that legal case.

Antarāpattiṃ olokentopi “paṭilātaṃ ukkhipati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pāci. 355) evaṃ yā sikkhāpadantaresu antarāpatti hoti taṃ passati, so taṃ suttaṃ ānetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati.

When examining an intermediate offense, he sees that which is an intermediate offense occurring between the training rules, such as: 'If one lifts up a firebrand that has fallen down, it is a dukkaṭa offense.' He, having brought that text, will settle that legal case.

Anāpattiṃ olokentopi “anāpatti bhikkhu asādiyantassa, atheyyacittassa, na maraṇādhippāyassa, anullapanādhippāyassa, na mocanādhippāyassa, asañcicca, assatiyā, ajānantassā”ti (pārā. 72 ādayo) evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sikkhāpade niddiṭṭhaṃ anāpattiṃ passati, so taṃ suttaṃ ānetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati.

When examining non-offenses, he sees the non-offense pointed out in each and every training rule, thus: 'There is no offense for a bhikkhu who does not consent, who has no thieving intention, who does not intend death, who does not intend to boast, who does not intend to release, unintentionally, unmindfully, unknowingly.' He, having brought that text, will settle that legal case.

Yo hi bhikkhu catubbidhavinayakovido tilakkhaṇasampanno imāni cha ṭhānāni oloketvā adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamessati, tassa vinicchayo appaṭivattiyo, buddhena sayaṃ nisīditvā vinicchitasadiso hoti. Taṃ cevaṃ vinicchayakusalaṃ bhikkhuṃ koci katasikkhāpadavītikkamo bhikkhu upasaṅkamitvā attano kukkuccaṃ puccheyya; tena sādhukaṃ sallakkhetvā sace anāpatti hoti, “anāpattī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace pana āpatti hoti, “āpattī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sā desanāgāminī ce, “desanāgāminī”ti vattabbaṃ. Vuṭṭhānagāminī ce, “vuṭṭhānagāminī”ti vattabbaṃ. Athassa pārājikacchāyā [P 1.0237] dissati, “pārājikāpattī”ti na tāva vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Methunadhammavītikkamo hi uttarimanussadhammavītikkamo ca oḷāriko. Adinnādānamanussaviggahavītikkamā pana sukhumā cittalahukā. Te sukhumeneva āpajjati[V 1.0186], sukhumena rakkhati, tasmā visesena taṃvatthukaṃ kukkuccaṃ pucchiyamāno “āpattī”ti avatvā sacassa ācariyo dharati, tato tena so bhikkhu “amhākaṃ ācariyaṃ [M 1.0202] pucchā”ti pesetabbo. Sace so puna āgantvā “tumhākaṃ ācariyo suttato nayato oloketvā ‘satekiccho’ti maṃ āhā”ti vadati, tato anena so “sādhu suṭṭhu yaṃ ācariyo bhaṇati taṃ karohī”ti vattabbo. Atha panassa ācariyo natthi, saddhiṃ uggahitatthero pana atthi, tassa santikaṃ pesetabbo – “amhehi saha uggahitatthero gaṇapāmokkho, taṃ gantvā pucchā”ti. Tenāpi “satekiccho”ti vinicchite “sādhu suṭṭhu tassa vacanaṃ karohī”ti vattabbo. Atha saddhiṃ uggahitattheropi natthi, antevāsiko paṇḍito atthi, tassa santikaṃ pesetabbo – “asukadaharaṃ gantvā pucchā”ti. Tenāpi “satekiccho”ti vinicchite “sādhu suṭṭhu tassa vacanaṃ karohī”ti vattabbo. Atha daharassāpi pārājikacchāyāva upaṭṭhāti, tenāpi “pārājikosī”ti na vattabbo. Dullabho hi buddhuppādo, tato dullabhatarā [M 1.0203] pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca. Evaṃ pana vattabbo – “vivittaṃ okāsaṃ sammajjitvā divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā sīlāni sodhetvā dvattiṃsākāraṃ tāva manasi karohī”ti. Sace tassa arogaṃ sīlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭayati, saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, upacārappanāppattaṃ viya cittampi ekaggaṃ hoti, divasaṃ atikkantampi na jānāti. So divasātikkame upaṭṭhānaṃ āgato evaṃ vattabbo – “kīdisā te cittappavattī”ti. Ārocitāya cittappavattiyā vattabbo – “pabbajjā nāma cittavisuddhatthāya, appamatto samaṇadhammaṃ karohī”ti.

Indeed, a bhikkhu who is skilled in the fourfold discipline, endowed with the three characteristics, and who examines these six factors will settle a legal case. His judgment is irreversible, comparable to one decided by the Buddha himself while seated in person. If such a bhikkhu skilled in judgment is approached by another bhikkhu who has violated a training rule and asks about his scruple, the skilled bhikkhu should carefully consider it. If there is no offense, he should say, 'There is no offense.' If, however, there is an offense, he should say, 'There is an offense.' If it is one leading to confession, he should say, 'It leads to confession.' If it is one leading to rehabilitation, he should say, 'It leads to rehabilitation.' But if the shadow of a pārājika offense appears to him, he should not yet say, 'It is a pārājika offense.' Why? Because the transgression of sexual intercourse and the transgression of claiming a superhuman state are gross, whereas the transgressions of theft and of killing a human being are subtle and involve a quickness of mind. One falls into them subtly and guards against them subtly. Therefore, when questioned about a scruple concerning such a matter, without saying 'It is an offense,' if his teacher is living, that bhikkhu should be sent away with the words, 'Go and ask our teacher.' If he returns and says, 'After examining the text and the method, your teacher told me, "It is remediable,"' then he should be told, 'Good, do well what the teacher says.' But if he has no teacher, yet there is an elder with whom he has studied, he should be sent to him, saying, 'The elder with whom we have studied is the head of the group; go and ask him.' When it has been decided by him also that 'it is remediable,' he should be told, 'Good, do well what he says.' If there is no such elder either, but there is a learned resident pupil, he should be sent to him, saying, 'Go and ask such-and-such a young bhikkhu.' When it has been decided by him also that 'it is remediable,' he should be told, 'Good, do well what he says.' But if even to the young bhikkhu the shadow of a pārājika appears, he too should not say, 'You are a pārājika offender.' For the arising of a Buddha is rare, and rarer still are the going forth and higher ordination. Instead, he should be told this: 'Sweep a secluded place, sit for the day's abiding, purify your virtues, and for now, attend to the thirty-two parts of the body.' If his virtue is sound, the meditation subject succeeds, the formations become manifest, and his mind becomes one-pointed as if reaching access or absorption concentration; he may not even notice the passing of the day. When he comes for attendance at the end of the day, he should be asked, 'What was the process of your mind?' When the process of his mind is reported, he should be told, 'The going forth is for the sake of purifying the mind. Be diligent and practice the duties of a recluse.'

Yassa pana sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti, tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ghaṭayati, patodābhitunnaṃ viya cittaṃ vikampati, vippaṭisāragginā ḍayhati, tattapāsāṇe nisinno viya taṅkhaṇaññeva vuṭṭhāti. So [P 1.0238] āgato “kā te cittappavattī”ti pucchitabbo. Ārocitāya cittappavattiyā “natthi loke raho nāma pāpakammaṃ pakubbato. Sabbapaṭhamañhi pāpaṃ karonto attanā jānāti, athassa ārakkhadevatā paracittavidū samaṇabrāhmaṇā aññā ca devatā jānanti, tvaṃyeva dāni tava sotthiṃ pariyesāhī”ti vattabbo.

But for one whose virtue is broken, the meditation subject does not succeed; his mind trembles as if struck by a goad, he is burned by the fire of remorse, and he rises up at that very moment as if sitting on a hot stone slab. When he comes, he should be asked, 'What was the process of your mind?' When the process of his mind is reported, he should be told, 'For one who does an evil deed, there is no such thing as a secret place in the world. Indeed, first of all, the one doing evil knows it himself. Then his guardian deity, recluses and brahmins who know the minds of others, and other deities know it. Now you yourself must seek your own welfare.'

Niṭṭhitā catubbidhavinayakathā

The fourfold discourse on the Vinaya is concluded.

Vinayadharassa ca lakkhaṇādikathā.

And the discourse on the characteristics and so on of a Vinaya-holder.

Bhikkhupadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Analysis of the Term 'Bhikkhu'.

Idāni [V 1.0187] sikkhāpadavibhaṅgassa atthaṃ vaṇṇayissāma. Yaṃ vuttaṃ yo panāti yo yādisotiādi. Ettha yo panāti vibhajitabbapadaṃ; yo yādisotiādīni tassa vibhajanapadāni. Ettha ca yasmā panāti nipātamattaṃ; yoti atthapadaṃ; tañca aniyamena puggalaṃ dīpeti, tasmā tassa atthaṃ dassento aniyamena puggaladīpakaṃ yo saddameva āha. Tasmā ettha evamattho veditabbo – yo panāti yo yokocīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yasmā pana yo yokoci nāma, so avassaṃ liṅga-yutta-jāti-nāma-gotta-sīla-vihāra-gocaravayesu ekenākārena paññāyati, tasmā taṃ tathā ñāpetuṃ taṃ pabhedaṃ pakāsento “yādiso”tiādimāha. Tattha yādisoti liṅgavasena yādiso vā tādiso vā hotu; dīgho vā rasso vā kāḷo vā odāto vā maṅguracchavi vā kiso vā thūlo vāti attho. Yathāyuttoti yogavasena yena vā tena vā yutto hotu; navakammayutto vā uddesayutto vā vāsadhurayutto vāti attho. Yathājaccoti jātivasena yaṃjacco vā taṃjacco vā hotu; khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vāti attho. Yathānāmoti nāmavasena yathānāmo vā tathānāmo vā hotu; buddharakkhito vā dhammarakkhito vā saṅgharakkhito vāti attho. Yathāgottoti gottavasena yathāgotto vā tathāgotto vā yena vā tena vā gottena hotu; kaccāyano vā vāsiṭṭho vā kosiyo vāti attho. Yathāsīloti sīlesu yathāsīlo vā tathāsīlo vā hotu; navakammasīlo vā uddesasīlo vā vāsadhurasīlo vāti attho. Yathāvihārīti vihāresupi yathāvihārī vā tathāvihārī vā hotu; navakammavihārī vā uddesavihārī vā vāsadhuravihārī vāti attho. Yathāgocaroti gocaresupi yathāgocaro vā tathāgocaro vā hotu; navakammagocaro [P 1.0239] vā uddesagocaro vā vāsadhuragocaro vāti attho. Thero vāti ādīsu vayovuḍḍhādīsu yo vā so vā hotu; paripuṇṇadasavassatāya thero vā ūnapañcavassatāya navo vā atirekapañcavassatāya [M 1.0204] majjhimo vāti attho. Atha kho sabbova imasmiṃ atthe eso vuccati “yo panā”ti.

Now we shall explain the meaning of the analysis of the training rule. What was said was 'yo pana,' 'yo yādiso,' and so on. Here, 'yo pana' is the term to be analyzed; 'yo yādiso' and so forth are the terms for its analysis. And here, since 'pana' is merely a particle and 'yo' is the term with meaning—and it indicates a person indefinitely—therefore, to show its meaning, He spoke only the word 'yo,' which indicates a person indefinitely. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'yo pana' means 'whoever.' Since 'whoever' is invariably recognized by one characteristic among appearance, engagement, birth, name, clan, habit, abiding, resort, or age, therefore, to make that person known in such a way, He spoke 'yādiso,' etc., to show that distinction. Therein, 'yādiso' means, by way of appearance: whatever kind he may be, whether tall or short, dark or fair, of a dusky complexion, thin or stout. 'Yathāyutto' means, by way of engagement: with whatever he may be engaged, whether engaged in new construction work, in recitation, or in the duty of insight practice. 'Yathājacco' means, by way of birth: of whatever birth he may be, whether a Khattiya, a Brahmin, a Vessa, or a Sudda. 'Yathānāmo' means, by way of name: of whatever name he may be, whether Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, or Saṅgharakkhita. 'Yathāgotto' means, by way of clan: of whatever clan he may be, whether Kaccāyana, Vāsiṭṭha, or Kosiya. 'Yathāsīlo' means, by way of habit: of whatever habit he may be, whether his habit is new construction work, recitation, or the duty of insight practice. 'Yathāvihārī' means, by way of abiding: in whatever way he may abide, whether abiding in new construction work, in recitation, or in the duty of insight practice. 'Yathāgocaro' means, by way of resort: whatever his resort may be, whether his resort is new construction work, recitation, or the duty of insight practice. In 'thero vā,' etc., among those senior in age and so on: whoever he may be, whether an elder due to having completed ten years, a junior monk due to having less than five years, or a monk of middle standing due to having more than five years. Indeed, in this context, every one of these is called 'yo pana'.

Bhikkhuniddese bhikkhatīti bhikkhako; labhanto vā alabhanto vā ariyāya yācanāya yācatīti attho. Buddhādīhi ajjhupagataṃ bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagato nāma. Yo hi koci appaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, so kasigorakkhādīhi jīvikakappanaṃ hitvā liṅgasampaṭicchaneneva bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu. Parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā vā vihāramajjhe kājabhattaṃ bhuñjamānopi [V 1.0188] bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu; piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjāya ussāhajātattā vā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu. Agghaphassavaṇṇabhedena bhinnaṃ paṭaṃ dhāretīti bhinnapaṭadharo. Tattha satthakacchedanena agghabhedo veditabbo. Sahassagghanakopi hi paṭo satthakena khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinno bhinnaggho hoti. Purimagghato upaḍḍhampi na agghati. Suttasaṃsibbanena phassabhedo veditabbo. Sukhasamphassopi hi paṭo suttehi saṃsibbito bhinnaphasso hoti. Kharasamphassataṃ pāpuṇāti. Sūcimalādīhi vaṇṇabhedo veditabbo. Suparisuddhopi hi paṭo sūcikammato paṭṭhāya sūcimalena, hatthasedamalajallikāhi, avasāne rajanakappakaraṇehi ca bhinnavaṇṇo hoti; pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahati. Evaṃ tīhākārehi bhinnapaṭadhāraṇato bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu. Gihivatthavisabhāgānaṃ vā kāsāvānaṃ dhāraṇamatteneva bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu.

In the explanation of a bhikkhu: 'He begs' (bhikkhati), therefore he is a beggar (bhikkhako); this means he begs with the noble way of asking, whether he receives anything or not. Because he has undertaken the alms-round (bhikkhācariya) that was undertaken by the Buddha and others, he is called 'one who has undertaken the alms-round.' For whoever, having abandoned a small or great mass of wealth, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, and, having given up a livelihood from farming, cattle-herding, and so on, has undertaken the alms-round merely by accepting the outward sign of a monk, is a bhikkhu. Or, because his livelihood is dependent on others, even while eating food brought on carrying-poles within the monastery, he has undertaken the alms-round, and is therefore a bhikkhu. Or, because zeal for the going forth has arisen in him through relying on eating morsels of alms-food, he has undertaken the alms-round, and is therefore a bhikkhu. 'He wears a broken cloth' (bhinna-paṭa), therefore he is a bhinnapaṭadharo (wearer of a broken cloth). Here, the breaking of value should be understood as cutting with a small knife. For even a cloth worth a thousand, when cut into pieces with a small knife, becomes broken in value; it is not worth even half its former value. The breaking of texture should be understood as stitching with thread. For even a cloth with a pleasant texture, when stitched with threads, becomes broken in texture; it becomes rough to the touch. The breaking of color should be understood as being from needle-stains and so on. For even a very clean cloth, from the time of sewing onwards, becomes broken in color from needle-stains, from sweat and grime from the hands, and finally from dyeing and the making of the allowable mark; it loses its original color. Thus, from wearing a cloth broken in these three ways, he is a bhinnapaṭadharo, and therefore a bhikkhu. Or, merely by wearing saffron robes, which are different from the clothes of householders, he is a bhinnapaṭadharo, and therefore a bhikkhu.

Samaññāyāti paññattiyā vohārenāti attho. Samaññāya eva hi ekacco “bhikkhū”ti paññāyati. Tathā hi nimantanādimhi bhikkhūsu gaṇiyamānesu sāmaṇerepi gahetvā “sataṃ bhikkhū sahassaṃ bhikkhū”ti vadanti. Paṭiññāyāti attano paṭijānanena paṭiññāyapi hi ekacco “bhikkhū”ti paññāyati. Tassa “ko etthāti? Ahaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhū”ti (a. ni. 10.96) evamādīsu sambhavo daṭṭhabbo[P 1.0240]. Ayaṃ pana ānandattherena vuttā dhammikā paṭiññā. Rattibhāge pana dussīlāpi paṭipathaṃ āgacchantā “ko etthā”ti vutte adhammikāya paṭiññāya abhūtāya “mayaṃ bhikkhū”ti vadanti.

By designation: this means by concept or by convention. For by designation alone, someone is recognized as a 'bhikkhu.' For instance, when bhikkhus are being counted for an invitation and the like, even novices are included when they say, 'a hundred bhikkhus, a thousand bhikkhus.' By avowal: this means by one's own acknowledgement. For by avowal also, someone is recognized as a 'bhikkhu.' The occurrence of this should be seen in such instances as: 'Who is here?' 'I, friend, am a bhikkhu.' This, however, spoken by the Elder Ānanda, is a righteous avowal. But at night, even immoral ones, when coming along a path and asked, 'Who is here?', make an unrighteous and false avowal, saying, 'We are bhikkhus.'

Ehi [M 1.0205] bhikkhūti ehi bhikkhu nāma bhagavato “ehi bhikkhū”ti vacanamattena bhikkhubhāvaṃ ehibhikkhūpasampadaṃ patto. Bhagavā hi ehibhikkhubhāvāya upanissayasampannaṃ puggalaṃ disvā rattapaṃsukūlantarato suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ dakkhiṇahatthaṃ nīharitvā brahmaghosaṃ nicchārento “ehi, bhikkhu, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti vadati. Tassa saheva bhagavato vacanena gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyati, pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca ruhati. Bhaṇḍu kāsāyavasano hoti. Ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ aṃse ṭhapetvā vāmaṃsakūṭe āsattanīluppalavaṇṇamattikāpatto –

The 'ehi-bhikkhu' is a person who has attained the state of a bhikkhu, the ehi-bhikkhu higher ordination, merely by the Blessed One’s utterance, “Come, bhikkhu.” For the Blessed One, having seen a person endowed with the supporting conditions for the state of an ehi-bhikkhu, extends his golden-hued right hand from within his reddish rag-robe, and uttering a voice like that of Brahmā, says, “Come, bhikkhu, live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.” Simultaneously with the Blessed One's words, the layperson's appearance vanishes, and both the going forth and the higher ordination arise. He becomes shaven-headed and clad in ochre robes. Having put on one robe, draped another, and placed a third on his shoulder, he has an earthen bowl the color of a blue lotus attached to his left shoulder-tip.

“Ticīvarañca patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti.

“The three robes and the bowl, the small adze, needle, and the belt; together with the water strainer, these eight are the requisites of a bhikkhu devoted to the practice.”

Evaṃ [V 1.0189] vuttehi aṭṭhahi parikkhārehi sarīre paṭimukkehiyeva saṭṭhivassikatthero viya iriyāpathasampanno buddhācariyako buddhupajjhāyako sammāsambuddhaṃ vandamānoyeva tiṭṭhati. Bhagavā hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kāle ehibhikkhūpasampadāya eva upasampādeti. Evaṃ upasampannāni ca sahassupari ekacattālīsuttarāni tīṇi bhikkhusatāni ahesuṃ; seyyathidaṃ – pañca pañcavaggiyattherā, yaso kulaputto, tassa parivārā catupaṇṇāsa sahāyakā, tiṃsa bhaddavaggiyā, sahassapurāṇajaṭilā, saddhiṃ dvīhi aggasāvakehi aḍḍhateyyasatā paribbājakā, eko aṅgulimālattheroti. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Thus, with these eight requisites just mentioned placed upon his body, like an elder of sixty vassas, accomplished in deportment, having the Buddha as his teacher and the Buddha as his preceptor, he stands venerating the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For the Blessed One, during the first period of his awakening, ordained solely by means of the ehi-bhikkhu higher ordination. And there were one thousand three hundred and forty-one bhikkhus thus ordained; namely: the five elders of the group of five, Yasa the clansman, his retinue of fifty-four companions, the thirty Bhaddavaggiyas, the thousand former matted-hair ascetics, two hundred and fifty wanderers along with the two chief disciples, and the one elder Aṅgulimāla. For this was stated in the commentary:

“Tīṇi sataṃ sahassañca, cattālīsaṃ punāpare;

Eko ca thero sappañño, sabbe te ehibhikkhukā”ti.

“One thousand, three hundred, and forty, and furthermore one other wise elder—all of them were ehi-bhikkhus.”

Na kevalañca ete eva, aññepi bahū santi. Seyyathidaṃ – tisataparivāro selo brāhmaṇo, sahassaparivāro mahākappino, dasasahassā [P 1.0241] kapilavatthuvāsino kulaputtā, soḷasasahassā pārāyanikabrāhmaṇāti evamādayo. Te pana vinayapiṭake pāḷiyaṃ na niddiṭṭhattā na vuttā. Ime tattha niddiṭṭhattā vuttāti.

And not only these, there are many others. Namely: the brahmin Sela with a retinue of three hundred; Mahākappina with a retinue of a thousand; ten thousand clansmen residing in Kapilavatthu; sixteen thousand Pārāyanika brahmins, and so forth. However, because they are not indicated in the Pāḷi of the Vinaya Piṭaka, they were not mentioned. These are mentioned because they are indicated therein.

“Sattavīsa sahassāni, tīṇiyeva satāni ca;

Etepi sabbe saṅkhātā, sabbe te ehibhikkhukā”ti.

“Twenty-seven thousand, and three hundred as well; all these too are counted, all of them were ehi-bhikkhus.”

Tīhi [M 1.0206] saraṇagamanehi upasampannoti “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”tiādinā nayena tikkhattuṃ vācaṃ bhinditvā vuttehi tīhi saraṇagamanehi upasampanno. Ayañhi upasampadā nāma aṭṭhavidhā – ehibhikkhūpasampadā, saraṇagamanūpasampadā, ovādapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā, pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā, garudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā, dūtenūpasampadā, aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā, ñatticatutthakammūpasampadāti. Tattha ehibhikkhūpasampadā, saraṇagamanūpasampadā ca vuttā eva.

“One ordained by the three goings for refuge” means one who is ordained by the three goings for refuge, which are uttered by distinctly pronouncing the words three times in the manner of “I go to the Buddha for refuge,” etc. For this higher ordination is of eight kinds: the ehi-bhikkhu higher ordination, the higher ordination by going for refuge, the higher ordination by acceptance of exhortation, the higher ordination by answering a question, the higher ordination by acceptance of the weighty principles, the higher ordination by a messenger, the higher ordination by eight utterances, and the higher ordination by an act of motion and three announcements. Among these, the ehi-bhikkhu higher ordination and the higher ordination by going for refuge have already been spoken of.

Ovādapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā nāma “tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘tibbaṃ me hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati theresu navesu majjhimesu cā’ti. Evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabbaṃ. Tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘yaṃ kiñci dhammaṃ sossāmi kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbacetasā samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ sossāmī’ti. Evaṃ hi te, kassapa, sikkhitabbaṃ. Tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ [V 1.0190] – ‘sātasahagatā ca me kāyagatāsati na vijahissatī’ti. Evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabba”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) iminā ovādapaṭiggahaṇena mahākassapattherassa anuññātaupasampadā.

The higher ordination by acceptance of exhortation is the higher ordination permitted to the Elder Mahākassapa through his acceptance of this exhortation: “Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Keen shame and fear of wrongdoing shall be present in me towards elders, new monks, and those of middle standing.’ Thus, Kassapa, should you train. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Whatever teaching connected with the wholesome I shall hear, all of it I shall listen to, making it essential, bearing it in mind, applying my whole mind, with ear inclined.’ Thus, Kassapa, should you train. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘And mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by delight will not forsake me.’ Thus, Kassapa, should you train.”

Pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā nāma sopākassa anuññātaupasampadā. Bhagavā kira pubbārāme anucaṅkamantaṃ sopākasāmaṇeraṃ “‘uddhumātakasaññā’ti vā, sopāka, ‘rūpasaññā’ti vā ime dhammā nānatthā nānābyañjanā[P 1.0242], udāhu ekatthā, byañjanameva nāna”nti dasa asubhanissite pañhe pucchi. So te byākāsi. Bhagavā tassa sādhukāraṃ datvā “kativassosi tvaṃ, sopākā”ti pucchi. “Sattavassohaṃ, bhagavā”ti. “Sopāka, tvaṃ mama sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā pañhe byākāsī”ti āraddhacitto upasampadaṃ anujāni. Ayaṃ pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā.

The higher ordination by answering a question is the higher ordination permitted to Sopāka. It is said that the Blessed One, at the Pubbārāma, asked the novice Sopāka, who was walking in meditation behind him, ten questions based on the unlovely: “Sopāka, are these things, ‘the perception of a bloated corpse’ and ‘the perception of form,’ different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning, with only the phrasing being different?” He answered them. The Blessed One gave him his approval and asked, “How old are you, Sopāka?” “I am seven years old, Blessed One.” “Sopāka, you have answered the questions by comparing them with my omniscient knowledge.” And with a pleased mind, he permitted the higher ordination. This is the higher ordination by answering a question.

Garudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadā nāma mahāpajāpatiyā aṭṭhagarudhammassa paṭiggahaṇena anuññātaupasampadā.

The higher ordination by acceptance of the weighty principles is the higher ordination permitted to Mahāpajāpatī on account of her acceptance of the eight weighty principles.

Dūtenūpasampadā nāma aḍḍhakāsiyā gaṇikāya anuññātaupasampadā.

The higher ordination by a messenger is the higher ordination permitted to the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī.

Aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā nāma bhikkhuniyā bhikkhunisaṅghato ñatticatutthena bhikkhusaṅghato ñatticatutthenāti imehi dvīhi kammehi upasampadā.

The higher ordination by eight utterances is the higher ordination of a bhikkhunī by means of these two acts: by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha with a motion and three announcements, and by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with a motion and three announcements.

Ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā [M 1.0207] nāma bhikkhūnaṃ etarahi upasampadā. Imāsu aṭṭhasu upasampadāsu “yā sā, bhikkhave, mayā tīhi saraṇagamanehi upasampadā anuññātā, taṃ ajjatagge paṭikkhipāmi. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ñatticatutthena kammena upasampādetu”nti (mahāva. 69) evaṃ anuññātāya imāya upasampadāya upasampannoti vuttaṃ hoti.

The higher ordination by an act of motion and three announcements is the higher ordination for bhikkhus at the present time. Among these eight kinds of higher ordination, it is said that one is ordained by this higher ordination which was permitted thus: “Bhikkhus, that higher ordination by the three goings for refuge that was permitted by me, I reject it from this day forward. I permit, bhikkhus, to ordain by an act of motion and three announcements” (Mahāvagga 69).

Bhadroti apāpako. Kalyāṇaputhujjanādayo hi yāva arahā, tāva bhadrena sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanena ca samannāgatattā “bhadro bhikkhū”ti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Sāroti tehiyeva sīlasārādīhi samannāgatattā nīlasamannāgamena nīlo paṭo viya “sāro bhikkhū”ti veditabbo. Vigatakilesapheggubhāvato vā khīṇāsavova “sāro”ti veditabbo. Sekhoti puthujjanakalyāṇakena saddhiṃ satta [V 1.0191] ariyā tisso sikkhā sikkhantīti sekhā. Tesu yo koci “sekho bhikkhū”ti veditabbo. Na sikkhatīti asekho. Sekkhadhamme atikkamma aggaphale ṭhito, tato uttari sikkhitabbābhāvato khīṇāsavo “asekho”ti vuccati. Samaggena saṅghenāti sabbantimena pariyāyena pañcavaggakaraṇīye kamme yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattā, tesaṃ āgatattā chandārahānaṃ chandassa āhaṭattā, sammukhībhūtānañca appaṭikkosanato ekasmiṃ kamme samaggabhāvaṃ upagatena. Ñatticatutthenāti [P 1.0243] tīhi anussāvanāhi ekāya ca ñattiyā kātabbena. Kammenāti dhammikena vinayakammena. Akuppenāti vatthu-ñatti-anussāvana-sīmā-parisasampattisampannattā akopetabbataṃ appaṭikkositabbatañca upagatena. Ṭhānārahenāti kāraṇārahena satthusāsanārahena. Upasampanno nāma uparibhāvaṃ samāpanno, pattoti attho. Bhikkhubhāvo hi uparibhāvo, tañcesa yathāvuttena kammena samāpannattā “upasampanno”ti vuccati. Ettha ca ñatticatutthakammaṃ ekameva āgataṃ. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā cattāri saṅghakammāni nīharitvā vitthārato kathetabbānīti sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Tāni ca “apalokanakammaṃ ñattikammaṃ ñattidutiyakammaṃ ñatticatutthakamma”nti paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā vitthārena khandhakato parivārāvasāne kammavibhaṅgato ca pāḷiṃ āharitvā kathitāni. Tāni mayaṃ parivārāvasāne kammavibhaṅgeyeva vaṇṇayissāma. Evañhi sati paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā ca [M 1.0208] na bhāriyā bhavissati; yathāṭhitāya ca pāḷiyā vaṇṇanā suviññeyyā bhavissati. Tāni ca ṭhānāni asuññāni bhavissanti; tasmā anupadavaṇṇanameva karoma.

‘Bhadra’ means one without evil. Indeed, from the virtuous ordinary person up to the Arahant, because they are endowed with good virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are reckoned as ‘a good bhikkhu.’ ‘Sāra’ (essence) means that because they are endowed with those very essences of virtue and so on, like a blue cloth is called blue due to being endowed with blue color, they should be known as ‘an essential bhikkhu.’ Or, because of the state of being without the sapwood of defilements, only one whose cankers are destroyed should be known as ‘essential.’ ‘Sekha’ (trainee) means that together with the virtuous ordinary person, the seven noble ones are trainees because they train in the three trainings. Among them, any one should be known as ‘a trainee bhikkhu.’ ‘Asekha’ (non-trainee) means one who does not train. Having transcended the things to be trained in and being established in the highest fruit, because there is nothing further to be trained in, one whose cankers are destroyed is called ‘a non-trainee.’ ‘By a united Saṅgha’ means by a Saṅgha that has reached a state of harmony in a single act—in an act to be done by a chapter of five, by the very last method—because as many bhikkhus as are competent for the act have come, the consent of those worthy of giving consent has been brought, and because of the non-protest of those who are present. ‘By a motion and three announcements’ means by that which is to be done with three announcements and one motion. ‘By an act’ means by a lawful Vinaya act. ‘Irrevocable’ means by an act that has reached a state of being unshakeable and not to be protested against, because it is endowed with the completeness of the object, motion, announcements, boundary, and assembly. ‘Worthy of the position’ means worthy of the cause, worthy of the Teacher's Dispensation. ‘One who is ordained’ means one who has attained the higher state; the meaning is ‘attained.’ Indeed, the state of a bhikkhu is the higher state, and because this person has attained it by the afore-mentioned act, he is called ‘ordained.’ And here, only the act of a motion and three announcements has come up. But, it is said in all the ancient commentaries that, standing in this place, the four Saṅgha acts should be brought out and spoken of in detail. And those—the act of seeking leave, the act of a motion, the act of a motion and one announcement, and the act of a motion and three announcements—having been set down in order, have been explained in detail by bringing the Pāḷi from the Khandhaka and from the Kammavibhaṅga at the end of the Parivāra. We will explain them only in the Kammavibhaṅga at the end of the Parivāra. For if this is so, the commentary on the first Pārājika will not be burdensome, and the explanation of the Pāḷi as it stands will be easily understood. And those places will not be empty; therefore, we will do only the word-by-word commentary.

Tatrāti tesu “bhikkhako”tiādinā nayena vuttesu bhikkhūsu. Yvāyaṃ bhikkhūti yo ayaṃ bhikkhu. Samaggena saṅghena…pe… upasampannoti aṭṭhasu upasampadāsu ñatticatuttheneva kammena upasampanno. Ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippeto bhikkhūti ayaṃ imasmiṃ “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā pārājiko hotī”ti atthe “bhikkhū”ti adhippeto. Itare pana “bhikkhako”ti ādayo atthuddhāravasena vuttā. Tesu ca “bhikkhako”ti ādayo niruttivasena vuttā, “samaññāya bhikkhu, paṭiññāya bhikkhū”ti ime dve abhilāpavasena vuttā, “ehi bhikkhū”ti buddhena upajjhāyena paṭiladdhaupasampadāvasena vutto. Saraṇagamanabhikkhu anuppannāya kammavācāya upasampadāvasena vutto, “bhadro”tiādayo guṇavasena vuttāti veditabbā.

‘Therein’ refers to those bhikkhus spoken of in the way beginning with ‘a beggar-bhikkhu.’ ‘This bhikkhu who…’ means this bhikkhu. ‘By a united Saṅgha… ordained’ means: among the eight kinds of higher ordination, one who has received higher ordination only by the act of a motion and three announcements. ‘This is the bhikkhu intended in this meaning’ means: this one is intended as ‘bhikkhu’ in this meaning, namely, ‘Having engaged in sexual intercourse, one is defeated.’ But the others, beginning with ‘a beggar-bhikkhu,’ are stated by way of extracting the meaning. And among them, those beginning with ‘a beggar-bhikkhu’ are stated by way of etymology; ‘a bhikkhu by convention’ and ‘a bhikkhu by acknowledgement’—these two are stated by way of designation; the ‘Come, bhikkhu’ is stated by way of the higher ordination received with the Buddha as preceptor. The bhikkhu by going for refuge is stated by way of a higher ordination that existed before the formal act (kammavācā) had arisen; those beginning with ‘a good bhikkhu’ are stated by way of qualities. Thus it should be known.

Bhikkhupadabhājanīyaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Analysis of the Term ‘Bhikkhu’ is concluded.

Sikkhāsājīvapadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Terms ‘Training’ and ‘Livelihood’

Idāni [V 1.0192] “bhikkhūna”nti idaṃ padaṃ visesatthābhāvato avibhajitvāva yaṃ sikkhañca sājīvañca samāpannattā bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno hoti, taṃ dassento sikkhātiādimāha. Tattha sikkhitabbāti sikkhā. Tissoti gaṇanaparicchedo[P 1.0244]. Adhisīlasikkhāti adhikaṃ uttamaṃ sīlanti adhisīlaṃ; adhisīlañca taṃ sikkhitabbato sikkhā cāti adhisīlasikkhā. Esa nayo adhicitta-adhipaññāsikkhāsu.

Now, without analyzing the word ‘bhikkhūnaṃ’ as it has no special meaning, he said ‘sikkhā,’ etc., in order to show the training and the livelihood with which one must be endowed to become ‘one endowed with the training and livelihood of bhikkhus.’ Therein, ‘sikkhā’ (trainings) are so called because they are to be trained in. The word ‘tisso’ (three) is a numerical demarcation. ‘Adhisīlasikkhā’ (higher virtue training) means: ‘higher virtue’ (adhisīlaṃ) is higher (adhikaṃ), supreme (uttamaṃ) virtue (sīlaṃ); and because that is both higher virtue and is to be trained in, it is a training, thus it is ‘higher virtue training.’ This is the method for the higher mind training and the higher wisdom training.

Katamaṃ panettha sīlaṃ, katamaṃ adhisīlaṃ, katamaṃ cittaṃ, katamaṃ adhicittaṃ, katamā paññā, katamā adhipaññāti? Vuccate – pañcaṅgadasaṅgasīlaṃ tāva sīlameva. Tañhi buddhe uppannepi anuppannepi loke pavattati. Uppanne buddhe tasmiṃ sīle buddhāpi sāvakāpi mahājanaṃ samādapenti. Anuppanne buddhe paccekabuddhā ca kammavādino ca dhammikā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cakkavattī ca mahārājāno mahābodhisattā ca samādapenti. Sāmampi paṇḍitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā samādiyanti. Te taṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paripūretvā devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhonti. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ pana “adhisīla”nti vuccati, tañhi sūriyo viya pajjotānaṃ sineru viya pabbatānaṃ sabbalokiyasīlānaṃ [M 1.0209] adhikañceva uttamañca, buddhuppādeyeva ca pavattati, na vinā buddhuppādā. Na hi taṃ paññattiṃ uddharitvā añño satto ṭhapetuṃ sakkoti, buddhāyeva pana sabbaso kāyavacīdvāraajjhācārasotaṃ chinditvā tassa tassa vītikkamassa anucchavikaṃ taṃ sīlasaṃvaraṃ paññapenti. Pātimokkhasaṃvaratopi ca maggaphalasampayuttameva sīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ, taṃ pana idha anadhippetaṃ. Na hi taṃ samāpanno bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati.

What is virtue here, what is higher virtue, what is mind, what is higher mind, what is wisdom, what is higher wisdom? It is said: First, the five-fold and ten-fold virtue is simply virtue. That indeed prevails in the world whether a Buddha has arisen or not. When a Buddha has arisen, both the Buddhas and their disciples cause the multitude to undertake that virtue. When no Buddha has arisen, Paccekabuddhas, those who assert the doctrine of kamma, righteous ascetics and brahmins, wheel-turning monarchs and great kings, and great bodhisattas cause them to undertake it. Wise ascetics and brahmins also undertake it themselves. Having fulfilled that wholesome quality, they experience prosperity among gods and humans. The virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint, however, is called 'higher virtue.' For that is like the sun among lights, like Mount Sineru among mountains—superior and excellent among all worldly virtues. It prevails only when a Buddha has arisen, not without the arising of a Buddha. For no other being is able to bring forth and establish that prescription. Indeed, the Buddhas alone, having completely cut off the stream of misconduct through the doors of body and speech, prescribe that restraint of virtue appropriate for each and every transgression. Furthermore, the virtue associated with the path and fruition is higher virtue even beyond Pātimokkha-restraint, but that is not intended here. For a bhikkhu who has attained it does not engage in sexual intercourse.

Kāmāvacarāni pana aṭṭha kusalacittāni, lokiyaaṭṭhasamāpatticittāni ca ekajjhaṃ katvā cittamevāti veditabbāni. Buddhuppādānuppāde cassa pavatti, samādapanaṃ samādānañca sīle vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vipassanāpādakaṃ aṭṭhasamāpatticittaṃ pana “adhicitta”nti vuccati. Tañhi adhisīlaṃ viya sīlānaṃ sabbalokiyacittānaṃ adhikañceva uttamañca, buddhuppādeyeva ca hoti, na vinā buddhuppādā. Tatopi ca maggaphalacittameva adhicittaṃ, taṃ pana idha anadhippetaṃ. Na hi taṃ samāpanno bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati.

However, the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses and the eight mundane attainment-consciousnesses, taken together, should be known as merely 'consciousness'. Its occurrence, causing others to undertake it, and undertaking it oneself—whether a Buddha has arisen or not—should be understood in the very same way as was stated for virtue. However, the eight attainment-consciousnesses that are the basis for insight are called 'higher consciousness'. For that, just as higher virtue is superior and excellent among virtues, is likewise superior and excellent among all mundane consciousnesses. It arises only when a Buddha has arisen, not without the arising of a Buddha. And even beyond that, the consciousness of the path and fruition is higher consciousness, but that is not intended here. For a bhikkhu who has attained it does not engage in sexual intercourse.

“Atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭha”nti (dha. sa. 1371; vibha. 793; ma. ni. 3.92) -ādinayappavattaṃ pana kammassakatañāṇaṃ paññā, sā hi buddhe uppannepi [P 1.0245] anuppannepi loke [V 1.0193] pavattati. Uppanne buddhe tassā paññāya buddhāpi buddhasāvakāpi mahājanaṃ samādapenti. Anuppanne buddhe paccekabuddhā ca kammavādino ca dhammikā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cakkavattī ca mahārājāno mahābodhisattā ca samādapenti. Sāmampi paṇḍitā sattā samādiyanti. Tathā hi aṅkuro dasavassasahassāni mahādānaṃ adāsi. Velāmo, vessantaro, aññe ca bahū paṇḍitamanussā mahādānāni adaṃsu. Te taṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paripūretvā devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu. Tilakkhaṇākāraparicchedakaṃ pana vipassanāñāṇaṃ “adhipaññā”ti vuccati. Sā hi adhisīla-adhicittāni viya sīlacittānaṃ sabbalokiyapaññānaṃ adhikā ceva uttamā ca, na ca vinā buddhuppādā loke pavattati. Tatopi ca maggaphalapaññāva adhipaññā, sā pana idha anadhippetā. Na hi taṃ samāpanno bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevatīti.

However, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, which proceeds according to the method beginning with 'There is the fruit of what is given, there is the fruit of what is sacrificed,' is 'wisdom'. For this wisdom prevails in the world whether a Buddha has arisen or not. When a Buddha has arisen, both the Buddhas and their disciples cause the multitude to undertake this wisdom. When no Buddha has arisen, Paccekabuddhas, those who assert the doctrine of kamma, righteous ascetics and brahmins, wheel-turning monarchs and great kings, and great bodhisattas cause them to undertake it. Wise beings also undertake it themselves. Indeed, Aṅkura gave great alms for ten thousand years. Velāma, Vessantara, and many other wise people gave great alms. Having fulfilled that wholesome quality, they experienced prosperity among gods and humans. However, the insight-knowledge that discerns the characteristics of the three marks is called 'higher wisdom'. For that wisdom, just as higher virtue and higher consciousness are superior and excellent in relation to virtue and consciousness, is likewise superior and excellent among all mundane wisdoms, and it does not prevail in the world without the arising of a Buddha. And even beyond that, the wisdom of the path and fruition is higher wisdom, but that is not intended here. For a bhikkhu who has attained it does not engage in sexual intercourse.

Tatrāti tāsu tīsu sikkhāsu. Yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhāti yā ayaṃ pātimokkhasīlasaṅkhātā adhisīlasikkhā. Etaṃ sājīvaṃ nāmāti etaṃ sabbampi [M 1.0210] bhagavatā vinaye ṭhapitaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ, yasmā ettha nānādesajātigottādibhedabhinnā bhikkhū saha jīvanti ekajīvikā sabhāgajīvikā sabhāgavuttino honti, tasmā “sājīva”nti vuccati. Tasmiṃ sikkhatīti taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ cittassa adhikaraṇaṃ katvā “yathāsikkhāpadaṃ nu kho sikkhāmi na sikkhāmī”ti cittena olokento sikkhati. Na kevalañcāyametasmiṃ sājīvasaṅkhāte sikkhāpadeyeva sikkhati, sikkhāyapi sikkhati, “etaṃ sājīvaṃ nāmā”ti imassa pana anantarassa padassa vasena “tasmiṃ sikkhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi taṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ, atha kho ayamettha attho daṭṭhabbo – tassā ca sikkhāya sikkhaṃ paripūrento sikkhati, tasmiñca sikkhāpade avītikkamanto sikkhatīti. Tena vuccati sājīvasamāpannoti idampi anantarassa sājīvapadasseva vasena vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana so sikkhampi samāpanno, tasmā sikkhāsamāpannotipi atthato veditabbo. Evañhi sati “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti etassa padassa padabhājanampi paripuṇṇaṃ [P 1.0246] hoti.

Therein (tatrā): that is, among those three trainings. 'This training in higher virtue' (yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā): that is, the training in higher virtue designated as the virtue of the Pātimokkha. 'This is called a shared livelihood' (etaṃ sājīvaṃ nāma): this refers to this entire training rule established by the Blessed One in the Vinaya. Because herein, bhikkhus divided by various distinctions of country, birth, clan, and so on, live together—having a single livelihood, a common livelihood, a common mode of conduct—therefore it is called 'shared livelihood' (sājīva). 'One trains in it' (tasmiṃ sikkhati): having made that training rule the foundation for the mind, one trains while observing with the mind, "Do I train in accordance with the training rule, or do I not?" And this one does not train merely in this training rule called 'shared livelihood'; one trains in the training as well. However, it is said 'one trains in it' by the power of the immediately preceding phrase, 'this is called a shared livelihood'. Although it was stated thus, nevertheless, this meaning should be understood here: one trains by fulfilling the training in that training, and one trains by not transgressing that training rule. Therefore it is said, 'one who has attained the shared livelihood' (sājīvasamāpanno). This too is stated by the power of the immediately preceding word 'sājīva'. However, because that one has also attained the training, he should therefore be understood in meaning as 'one who has attained the training' (sikkhāsamāpanno). This being so, the word-analysis of the phrase 'one who has attained the training and shared livelihood' (sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno) also becomes complete.

Sikkhāsājīvapadabhājanīyaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Word-Analysis of 'Training and Shared Livelihood' is concluded.

Sikkhāpaccakkhānavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Analysis of Renouncing the Training

Sikkhaṃ [V 1.0194] appaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvāti sikkhañca appaṭikkhipitvā dubbalabhāvañca appakāsetvā. Yasmā ca dubbalye āvikatepi sikkhā appaccakkhātāva hoti, sikkhāya pana paccakkhātāya dubbalyaṃ āvikatameva hoti. Tasmā “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti iminā padena na koci visesattho labbhati. Yathā pana “dirattatirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeyyā”ti vutte dirattavacanena na koci visesattho labbhati, kevalaṃ lokavohāravasena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya mukhārūḷhatāya etaṃ vuttaṃ. Evamidampi vohāravasena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya mukhārūḷhatāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Without renouncing the training, without revealing weakness” means not having rejected the training and not having shown one’s state of weakness. For even when weakness is revealed, the training is still not renounced; but when the training is renounced, weakness is indeed revealed. Therefore, no special meaning is obtained by this phrase “without revealing weakness.” Just as when it is said, “He may cohabitate for two or three nights,” no special meaning is obtained by the word “two nights”; it is said merely by way of worldly convention, for the elegance of the expression and for ease of speech. In the same way, this too should be understood as being said by way of convention, for the elegance of the expression and for ease of speech.

Yasmā vā bhagavā sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, tasmā “sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāyā”ti iminā atthaṃ sampādetvā “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti iminā byañjanaṃ sampādeti. Parivārakapadavirahitañhi ekameva atthapadaṃ vuccamānaṃ parivāravirahito rājā viya, vatthālaṅkāravirahito viya ca puriso na sobhati; parivārakena pana atthānulomena sahāyapadena saddhiṃ taṃ sobhatīti.

Alternatively, because the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma with meaning and with expression, therefore with “without renouncing the training” he fulfills the meaning, and with “without revealing weakness” he fulfills the expression. For a single word of meaning, when spoken without accompanying words, does not shine, like a king without a retinue or a person without clothing and ornaments; but with an accompanying word that is suitable to the meaning, it shines.

Yasmā [M 1.0211] vā sikkhāpaccakkhānassa ekaccaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ attho hoti, tasmā taṃ sandhāya “sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāyā”tipadassa atthaṃ vivaranto “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti āha.

Alternatively, because a certain revealing of weakness is a meaning of “renunciation of the training,” therefore, with reference to that, wishing to explain the meaning of the phrase “without renouncing the training,” he said “without revealing weakness.”

Tattha siyā yasmā na sabbaṃ dubbalyāvikammaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ, tasmā “dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti paṭhamaṃ vatvā tassa atthaniyamanatthaṃ “sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāyā”ti vattabbanti, tañca na; kasmā? Atthānukkamābhāvato. “Sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti hi vuttattā yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno, taṃ appaccakkhāyāti vuccamāno anukkameneva attho vutto hoti, na aññathā. Tasmā idameva paṭhamaṃ vuttanti.

Herein, there might be this objection: since not every revealing of weakness is a renunciation of the training, therefore, having first said “without revealing weakness,” should it not be said “without renouncing the training” for the purpose of defining its meaning? But that is not so. Why? Because of the absence of a sequence of meaning. For, since it has been said, “one who has undertaken the training and livelihood,” when it is said “without renouncing that training which one has undertaken,” the meaning is spoken in sequence, not otherwise. Therefore, this very phrase was said first.

Apica anupaṭipāṭiyāpi ettha attho veditabbo. Kathaṃ? “Sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti ettha yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno taṃ appaccakkhāya yañca sājīvaṃ samāpanno tattha dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvāti.

Moreover, the meaning here should also be understood sequentially. How? In the phrase “one who has undertaken the training and livelihood,” it should be understood as: not having renounced the training one has undertaken, and not having revealed weakness in the livelihood one has undertaken.

Idāni [V 1.0195] sikkhāpaccakkhānadubbalyāvikammānaṃ visesāvisesaṃ [P 1.0247] sikkhāpaccakkhānalakkhaṇañca dassento “atthi bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha atthi bhikkhavetiādīni dve mātikāpadāni; tāni vibhajanto “kathañca bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – kathanti kena ākārena. Dubbalyāvikammañcāti dubbalyassa āvikammañca. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Ukkaṇṭhitoti anabhiratiyā imasmiṃ sāsane kicchajīvikappatto. Atha vā ajja yāmi, sve yāmi, ito yāmi, ettha yāmīti uddhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ katvā viharamāno, vikkhitto anekaggoti vuttaṃ hoti. Anabhiratoti sāsane abhirativirahito.

Now, wishing to show the distinction and non-distinction between renouncing the training and revealing weakness, and the characteristic of renouncing the training, he said, “There is, monks…” etc. Herein, “There is, monks…” and so on are two matrix terms. Analyzing them, he said, “And how, monks…” etc. Therein, this is the explanation of terms whose meaning is not obvious: “How” means in what manner. “And the revealing of weakness” means the revealing of weakness. “Here” means in this Dispensation. “Discontented” means, due to discontent, having arrived at a difficult livelihood in this Dispensation. Alternatively, it means one who dwells with his neck craned, thinking, “I will go today, I will go tomorrow, I will go from here, I will go there”; it means he is scattered and not one-pointed. “Without delight” means devoid of delight in the Dispensation.

Sāmaññā cavitukāmoti samaṇabhāvato apagantukāmo. Bhikkhubhāvanti bhikkhubhāvena. Karaṇatthe upayogavacanaṃ. “Kaṇṭhe āsattena aṭṭīyeyyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 162) pana yathālakkhaṇaṃ karaṇavacaneneva vuttaṃ. Aṭṭīyamānoti aṭṭaṃ pīḷitaṃ dukkhitaṃ viya attānaṃ ācaramāno; tena vā bhikkhubhāvena aṭṭo kariyamāno pīḷiyamānoti attho. Harāyamānoti lajjamāno. Jigucchamānoti asuciṃ viya taṃ jigucchanto. Gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānotiādīni uttānatthāniyeva. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ buddhaṃ paccakkheyyanti ettha yaṃnūnāti parivitakkadassane nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “sacāhaṃ buddhaṃ paccakkheyyaṃ, sādhu vata me siyā”ti. Vadati viññāpetīti [M 1.0212] imamatthaṃ etehi vā aññehi vā byañjanehi vacībhedaṃ katvā vadati ceva, yassa ca vadati, taṃ viññāpeti jānāpeti. Evampīti uparimatthasampiṇḍanatto pikāro. Evampi dubbalyāvikammañceva hoti sikkhā ca appaccakkhātā, aññathāpi.
