“Desiring to fall away from the ascetic life” means wishing to depart from the state of an ascetic. “The state of a bhikkhu” means by the state of a bhikkhu; it is an accusative word in the instrumental sense. In phrases like “He would be troubled by what is stuck in the throat,” etc., however, it is stated with an instrumental word according to its characteristic. “Being troubled” means acting as if one is oppressed and afflicted; or it means being oppressed and tormented by that state of a bhikkhu. “Being ashamed” means feeling shame. “Being disgusted” means being disgusted with it as if it were something impure. “Longing for the household life,” and so on, have obvious meanings. In “What if I were to renounce the Buddha?”, “what if” is a particle that shows deliberation. This is what is meant: “If I were to renounce the Buddha, it would surely be good for me.” “He speaks, he makes it known” means he speaks this meaning with these or other expressions, making a verbal utterance, and he makes it known to whomever he speaks. In “In this way also,” the particle “pi” is for the purpose of combining with the subsequent meaning. In this way also, there is both a revealing of weakness and the training is not renounced; and in other ways as well.

Idāni taṃ aññathāpi dubbalyāvikammaṃ sikkhāya ca appaccakkhānaṃ dassento “atha vā panā”tiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ atthato uttānameva. Padato panettha ādito paṭṭhāya “buddhaṃ paccakkheyyaṃ, dhammaṃ, saṅghaṃ, sikkhaṃ, vinayaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ, uddesaṃ, upajjhāyaṃ, ācariyaṃ, saddhivihārikaṃ, antevāsikaṃ, samānupajjhāyakaṃ, samānācariyakaṃ, sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkheyya”nti imāni cuddasa padāni [P 1.0248] paccakkhānākārena vuttāni.

Now, showing that revealing of weakness and the non-renunciation of the training in other ways as well, he said, “Or else…” etc. All of that is clear in meaning. As for the words, from the beginning: “I would renounce the Buddha,” “the Dhamma,” “the Saṅgha,” “the training,” “the Vinaya,” “the Pātimokkha,” “the recitation,” “the preceptor,” “the teacher,” “the co-resident,” “the pupil,” “one with the same preceptor,” “one with the same teacher,” “a fellow monk in the holy life”—these fourteen terms are stated in the manner of renunciation.

Gihī assantiādīni “gihī, upāsako, ārāmiko, sāmaṇero, titthiyo, titthiyasāvako, assamaṇo, asakyaputtiyo assa”nti imāni aṭṭha padāni “assa”nti iminā bhāvavikappākārena vuttāni. Evaṃ “yaṃnūnāha”nti iminā paṭisaṃyuttāni dvāvīsati padāni.

“I would be a householder,” etc.—“I would be a householder,” “a lay follower,” “a monastery attendant,” “a novice,” “a sectarian,” “a sectarian disciple,” “a non-ascetic,” “a non-Sākyan son”—these eight terms are stated with the word “I would be” (`assaṃ`) in the manner of considering various alternative states of being. Thus, connected with this phrase “What if I...”, there are twenty-two terms.

46. Yathā [V 1.0196] ca etāni, evaṃ “yadi panāhaṃ, apāhaṃ, handāhaṃ, hoti me”ti imesu ekamekena paṭisaṃyuttāni dvāvīsatīti sabbāneva satañca dasa ca padāni honti.

46. And just as there are these twenty-two terms, so too with each of these phrases—‘If I...’ (`yadi panāhaṃ`), ‘I go away...’ (`apāhaṃ`), ‘Come now, I...’ (`handāhaṃ`), and ‘It would be for me...’ (`hoti me`)—there are twenty-two connected terms. Thus, there are one hundred and ten terms in all.

47. Tato paraṃ saritabbavatthudassananayena pavattāni “mātaraṃ sarāmī”tiādīni sattarasa padāni. Tattha khettanti sālikhettādiṃ. Vatthunti tiṇapaṇṇasākaphalāphalasamuṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ. Sippanti kumbhakārapesakārasippādikaṃ.

47. After that, there are seventeen terms that proceed by way of showing things that should be recollected, such as 'I remember my mother.' Therein, 'field' refers to a rice field and so on. 'Ground' refers to a place where grass, leaves, vegetables, minor fruits, and major fruits arise. 'Craft' refers to the craft of a potter, the craft of a weaver, and so on.

48. Tato paraṃ sakiñcanasapalibodhabhāvadassanavasena pavattāni “mātā me atthi, sā mayā posetabbā”tiādīni nava padāni.

48. After that, there are nine terms that proceed by way of showing the state of being with concerns and obstacles, such as 'I have a mother; she must be supported by me.'

49. Tato paraṃ sanissayasappatiṭṭhabhāvadassanavasena pavattāni “mātā me atthi, sā maṃ posessatī”tiādīni soḷasa padāni.

49. After that, there are sixteen terms that proceed by way of showing the state of having support and a foundation, such as 'I have a mother; she will support me.'

50. Tato paraṃ ekabhattaekaseyyabrahmacariyānaṃ dukkarabhāvadassanavasena pavattāni “dukkara”ntiādīni aṭṭha padāni.

50. After that, there are eight terms, such as 'difficult,' that proceed by way of showing the difficulty of the practices of eating one meal, sleeping alone, and the holy life.

Tattha [M 1.0213] dukkaranti ekabhattādīnaṃ karaṇe dukkarataṃ dasseti. Na sukaranti sukarabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Evaṃ duccaraṃ na sucaranti ettha. Na ussahāmīti tattha ussāhābhāvaṃ asakkuṇeyyataṃ dasseti. Na visahāmīti asayhataṃ dasseti. Na ramāmīti ratiyā abhāvaṃ dasseti. Nābhiramāmīti abhiratiyā abhāvaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ imāni ca paññāsa, purimāni ca dasuttarasatanti saṭṭhisataṃ padāni dubbalyāvikammavāre vuttānīti veditabbāni.

Therein, 'difficult' shows the difficulty in the performance of the practice of one meal and so on. 'Not easy' rejects the state of being easy. The same applies to 'difficult to practice' and 'not easy to practice.' 'I am not able' shows a lack of striving or inability. 'I cannot bear it' shows unbearableness. 'I do not delight' shows the absence of delight. 'I do not greatly delight' shows the absence of great delight. Thus, these fifty terms and the previous one hundred and ten—so one hundred and sixty terms—should be understood as spoken in the section on the declaration of weakness.

51. Sikkhāpaccakkhānavārepi “kathañca bhikkhave”ti ādi sabbaṃ atthato uttānameva. Padato panetthāpi “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi, dhammaṃ, saṅghaṃ, sikkhaṃ, vinayaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ, uddesaṃ, upajjhāyaṃ, ācariyaṃ, saddhivihārikaṃ, antevāsikaṃ, samānupajjhāyakaṃ, samānācariyakaṃ, sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkhāmī”ti imāni cuddasa padāni sikkhāpaccakkhānavacanasambandhena pavattāni. Sabbapadesu ca “vadati viññāpetī”ti vacanassa ayamattho – vacībhedaṃ katvā vadati, yassa ca vadati taṃ teneva vacībhedena “ayaṃ sāsanaṃ jahitukāmo sāsanato [P 1.0249] muccitukāmo bhikkhubhāvaṃ cajitukāmo imaṃ vākyabhedaṃ karotī”ti viññāpeti sāveti jānāpeti.

51. In the section on renouncing the training as well, the meaning of everything beginning with 'And how, O bhikkhus...' is clear. However, regarding the terms here, these fourteen terms—'I renounce the Buddha,' 'the Dhamma,' 'the Saṅgha,' 'the training,' 'the Vinaya,' 'the Pātimokkha,' 'the recitation,' 'the preceptor,' 'the teacher,' 'the co-resident,' 'the pupil,' 'one with the same preceptor,' 'one with the same teacher,' 'a fellow practitioner of the holy life'—have proceeded in connection with the words for renouncing the training. And in all these terms, this is the meaning of the phrase 'he speaks, he makes known': having made a verbal utterance, he speaks; and to the one to whom he speaks, by that very verbal utterance he makes known, causes to hear, and causes to know that 'This person, desiring to abandon the Dispensation, desiring to be free from the Dispensation, desiring to give up the state of a bhikkhu, makes this distinct statement.'

Sace [V 1.0197] panāyaṃ “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattukāmo padapaccābhaṭṭhaṃ katvā “paccakkhāmi buddha”nti vā vadeyya. Milakkhabhāsāsu vā aññatarabhāsāya tamatthaṃ vadeyya. “Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattukāmo uppaṭipāṭiyā “dhammaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vā “sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vā vadeyya, seyyathāpi uttarimanussadhammavibhaṅge “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjāmī”ti vattukāmo “dutiyaṃ jhāna”nti vadati, sace yassa vadati so “ayaṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ cajitukāmo etamatthaṃ vadatī”ti ettakamattampi jānāti, viraddhaṃ nāma natthi; khettameva otiṇṇaṃ, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Sakkattā vā brahmattā vā cutasatto viya cutova hoti sāsanā.

But if this one, desiring to say, 'I renounce the Buddha,' having reversed the words, should say, 'Renounce I the Buddha'; or if in one of the barbarian languages he should state that meaning; or if, desiring to say, 'I renounce the Buddha,' he should say out of order, 'I renounce the Dhamma' or 'I renounce a fellow practitioner of the holy life'—just as in the analysis of the rule on superhuman states, one desiring to say, 'I attain the first jhāna,' says, 'the second jhāna'—if the one to whom he speaks knows even this much, that 'This person, desiring to give up the state of a bhikkhu, is saying this with that meaning,' then there is no failure; the field is indeed reached, and the training is indeed renounced. Like a being fallen from the state of Sakka or Brahmā, he has indeed fallen from the Dispensation.

Sace pana “buddhaṃ paccakkhi”nti vā, “buddhaṃ paccakkhissāmī”ti vā, “buddhaṃ paccakkheyya”nti vāti atītānāgataparikappavacanehi vadati, dūtaṃ vā pahiṇāti, sāsanaṃ vā peseti, akkharaṃ vā chindati, hatthamuddāya vā tamatthaṃ āroceti, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Uttarimanussadhammārocanaṃ pana hatthamuddāyapi sīsaṃ eti. Sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ manussajātikasattassa santike cittasampayuttaṃ vacībhedaṃ [M 1.0214] karontasseva sīsaṃ eti. Vacībhedaṃ katvā viññāpentopi ca yadi “ayameva jānātū”ti ekaṃ niyametvā āroceti, tañca soyeva jānāti, paccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Atha so na jānāti, añño samīpe ṭhito jānāti, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Atha dvinnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne dvinnampi niyametvā “etesaṃ ārocemī”ti vadati, tesu ekasmiṃ jānantepi dvīsu jānantesupi paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Evaṃ sambahulesupi veditabbaṃ.

But if one speaks with words of the past, future, or optative—such as 'I have renounced the Buddha,' or 'I will renounce the Buddha,' or 'I should renounce the Buddha'—or if one sends a messenger, or sends a written message, or carves a letter, or communicates that meaning by a hand gesture, the training is not renounced. The declaration of a superhuman state, however, is accomplished even by a hand gesture. The renunciation of the training is accomplished only for one who, in the presence of a being of human birth, makes a verbal utterance associated with intention. And even when making a verbal utterance to inform, if one, having specified a single person with 'Let this one alone know,' so informs, and that very person understands, the training is renounced. But if that person does not understand, and another standing nearby understands, the training is not renounced. If, in a place where two are standing, having specified both with 'I will inform them,' one speaks, then whether one of them understands or both understand, the training is indeed renounced. The same should be understood in the case of many people.

Sace pana anabhiratiyā pīḷito sabhāge bhikkhū parisaṅkamāno “yo koci jānātū”ti uccasaddaṃ karonto “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vadati, tañca avidūre ṭhito navakammiko vā añño vā samayaññū puriso sutvā “ukkaṇṭhito ayaṃ samaṇo gihibhāvaṃ [P 1.0250] pattheti, sāsanato cuto”ti jānāti, paccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Taṅkhaṇaññeva pana apubbaṃ acarimaṃ dujjānaṃ, sace āvajjanasamaye jānāti; yathā pakatiyā loke manussā vacanaṃ sutvā jānanti, paccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Atha aparabhāge “kiṃ iminā vutta”nti kaṅkhanto cirena jānāti, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Idañhi sikkhāpaccakkhānañca upari abhūtārocanaduṭṭhullavācā-attakāmaduṭṭhadosabhūtā-rocanasikkhāpadāni ca ekaparicchedāni. Āvajjanasamaye ñāte eva sīsaṃ enti, “kiṃ ayaṃ bhaṇatī”ti kaṅkhatā [V 1.0198] cirena ñāte sīsaṃ na enti. Yathā cāyaṃ “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti pade vinicchaye vutto; evaṃ sabbapadesu veditabbo.

But if, oppressed by discontent and being suspicious of bhikkhus of like disposition, one makes a loud sound, thinking, 'Let anyone at all know!' and says, 'I renounce the Buddha'; and if a bhikkhu in charge of new works or another man who knows the doctrine, standing not far away, hears this and knows, 'This discontented recluse desires the lay life; he has fallen from the Dispensation,' the training is indeed renounced. However, it is difficult to know if this occurs at that very moment, neither before nor after. If one knows at the time of adverting—just as people in the world normally understand upon hearing speech—the training is renounced. But if, later, being doubtful and thinking, 'What was said by him?' one understands after a long time, the training is not renounced. For this renunciation of the training and the training rules mentioned hereafter—concerning unfounded accusation, gross speech, self-interest, corrupt ill will, and true accusation—are of the same defining limit. They are accomplished only when known at the time of adverting; they are not accomplished when known after a long time by one who was doubtful, thinking, 'What is he saying?' And just as this decision was stated for the term 'I renounce the Buddha,' so it should be understood for all the terms.

Yasmā ca yadā sikkhā paccakkhātā hoti, tadā “yaṃnūnāhaṃ buddhaṃ paccakkheyya”ntiādīni avadatāpi dubbalyaṃ āvikatameva hoti; tasmā sabbesaṃ padānaṃ avasāne vuttaṃ – “evampi, bhikkhave, dubbalyāvikammañceva hoti sikkhā ca paccakkhātā”ti.

And since, when the training is renounced, weakness is clearly revealed even by one not saying such things as, 'Would that I might renounce the Buddha,' etc., therefore at the end of all these phrases it is said: 'Even so, monks, it is a manifestation of weakness, and the training is renounced.'

Tato paraṃ gihīti maṃ dhārehīti ettha sacepi “gihī bhavissāmī”ti vā “gihī homī”ti vā “gihī jātomhī”ti vā “gihimhī”ti vā vadati, appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Sace pana “ajja paṭṭhāya gihīti maṃ dhārehī”ti vā “jānāhī”ti vā “sañjānāhī”ti vā “manasi karohī”ti vā vadati, ariyakena vā vadati milakkhakena vā; evametasmiṃ atthe vutte [M 1.0215] yassa vadati, sace so jānāti, paccakkhātā hoti sikkhā. Esa nayo sesesupi “upāsako”tiādīsu sattasu padesu. Evaṃ imāni ca aṭṭha, purimāni ca cuddasāti dvāvīsati padāni honti.

After this, regarding the phrase 'Consider me a layperson,' even if one says, 'I will be a layperson,' or 'I am a layperson,' or 'I have become a layperson,' or 'I am a layperson,' the training is not renounced. But if one says, 'From today onward, consider me a layperson,' or 'Know me as such,' or 'Recognize me as such,' or 'Bear it in mind,' and one says this whether in the noble language or in a barbarian language; when this meaning is expressed, if the one to whom it is said understands, the training is renounced. This is the method also in the remaining seven phrases, such as 'a lay follower,' etc. Thus, these eight and the previous fourteen make twenty-two phrases.

52. Ito paraṃ purimāneva cuddasa padāni “alaṃ me, kinnu me, na mamattho, sumuttāha”nti imehi catūhi yojetvā vuttāni chappaññāsa honti. Tattha alanti hotu, pariyattanti attho. Kiṃnu meti kiṃ mayhaṃ kiccaṃ, kiṃ karaṇīyaṃ, kiṃ sādhetabbanti attho. Na mamatthoti natthi mama attho. Sumuttāhanti sumutto ahaṃ. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Evaṃ imāni ca chappaññāsa purimāni ca dvāvīsatīti aṭṭhasattati padāni sarūpeneva [P 1.0251] vuttāni.

52. After this, the previous fourteen phrases themselves, when combined with these four—'Enough for me,' 'What is it to me?,' 'It is of no use to me,' 'I am well freed'—become fifty-six. Therein, 'enough' means 'let it be,' the meaning is 'sufficient.' 'What is it to me?' means 'What business is it of mine? What is to be done by me? What is to be accomplished by me?' 'It is of no use to me' means 'There is no benefit for me.' 'I am well freed' means 'I am well freed.' The rest here is by the method already stated. Thus, these fifty-six and the previous twenty-two, making seventy-eight phrases, are stated in their very form.

53. Yasmā pana tesaṃ vevacanehipi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti, tasmā “yāni vā panaññānipī”tiādimāha. Tattha yāni vā panaññānipīti pāḷiyaṃ “buddha”ntiādīni āgatapadāni ṭhapetvā yāni aññāni atthi. Buddhavevacanāni vāti buddhassa vā pariyāyanāmāni…pe… asakyaputtiyassa vā. Tattha vaṇṇapaṭṭhāne āgataṃ nāmasahassaṃ upāligāthāsu (ma. ni. 2.76) nāmasataṃ aññāni ca guṇato labbhamānāni nāmāni “buddhavevacanānī”ti veditabbāni. Sabbānipi dhammassa nāmāni dhammavevacanānīti veditabbāni. Esa nayo sabbattha.

53. But since renunciation of the training also occurs through their synonyms, he therefore stated the passage beginning, 'or whatever others.' Therein, 'or whatever others' means whatever other phrases there are, setting aside the phrases such as 'Buddha' that have come in the Pāḷi. 'Or synonyms of the Buddha' means alternative names of the Buddha… or of the non-Sakyan son. In this context, the thousand names that come in the Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna, the hundred names in the Upāligāthās, and other names obtainable from his qualities should be known as 'synonyms of the Buddha.' All names of the Dhamma should be known as 'synonyms of the Dhamma.' This is the method in all cases.

Ayaṃ panettha yojanā – buddhaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevavacanena paccakkhānaṃ yathārutameva. “Sammāsambuddhaṃ [V 1.0199] paccakkhāmi, anantabuddhiṃ, anomabuddhiṃ, bodhipaññāṇaṃ, dhīraṃ, vigatamohaṃ, pabhinnakhīlaṃ, vijitavijayaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evamādibuddhavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ.

This is the application here: The renunciation 'I renounce the Buddha' is not a renunciation by a synonym; it is just as it was stated. Renunciation of the training by a synonym of the Buddha is thus: 'I renounce the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the one of infinite wisdom, the one of superior wisdom, the one marked by the wisdom of awakening, the resolute one, the one free from delusion, the one who has destroyed the mental stake, the one who has conquered the conqueror,' and so on.

Dhammaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ, yathārutameva. “Svākkhātaṃ dhammaṃ paccakkhāmi, sandiṭṭhikaṃ, akālikaṃ, ehipassikaṃ, opaneyyikaṃ, paccattaṃ veditabbaṃ viññūhi dhammaṃ paccakkhāmi. Asaṅkhataṃ dhammaṃ paccakkhāmi; virāgaṃ, nirodhaṃ, amataṃ dhammaṃ paccakkhāmi, dīghanikāyaṃ paccakkhāmi, brahmajālaṃ majjhimanikāyaṃ, mūlapariyāyaṃ, saṃyuttanikāyaṃ, oghataraṇaṃ, aṅguttaranikāyaṃ, cittapariyādānaṃ, khuddakanikāyaṃ, jātakaṃ, abhidhammaṃ, kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, akusalaṃ dhammaṃ, abyākataṃ dhammaṃ, satipaṭṭhānaṃ, sammappadhānaṃ, iddhipādaṃ, indriyaṃ, balaṃ, bojjhaṅgaṃ, maggaṃ, phalaṃ, nibbānaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassesu ekadhammakkhandhassapi [M 1.0216] nāmaṃ dhammavevacanameva. Evaṃ dhammavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

The renunciation 'I renounce the Dhamma' is not a renunciation by a synonym; it is just as it was stated. Renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of the Dhamma, such as: 'I renounce the well-proclaimed Dhamma, the directly visible, the timeless, the one inviting inspection, the one leading onward, to be known individually by the wise. I renounce the unconditioned Dhamma; I renounce the Dhamma that is dispassion, cessation, the deathless. I renounce the Dīgha Nikāya, the Brahmajāla, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Mūlapariyāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Oghataraṇa, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Cittapariyādāna, the Khuddaka Nikāya, the Jātaka, the Abhidhamma, the wholesome Dhamma, the unwholesome Dhamma, the indeterminate Dhamma, the establishments of mindfulness, the right exertions, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the fruit, Nibbāna.' The name of even one of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma is a synonym of 'Dhamma.' Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of the Dhamma.

Saṅghaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Suppaṭipannaṃ saṅghaṃ paccakkhāmi, ujuppaṭipannaṃ, ñāyappaṭipannaṃ, sāmīcippaṭipannaṃ saṅghaṃ, catupurisayugaṃ saṅghaṃ, aṭṭhapurisapuggalaṃ saṅghaṃ, āhuneyyaṃ saṅghaṃ, pāhuneyyaṃ, dakkhiṇeyyaṃ, añjalikaraṇīyaṃ, anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ saṅghaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ saṅghavevacanena [P 1.0252] sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

The renunciation 'I renounce the Saṅgha' is not a renunciation by a synonym. Renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of the Saṅgha, such as: 'I renounce the Saṅgha who have practiced well, who have practiced uprightly, who have practiced methodically, who have practiced properly; the Saṅgha of the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons; the Saṅgha worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit.' Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of the Saṅgha.

Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Bhikkhusikkhaṃ paccakkhāmi, bhikkhunīsikkhaṃ, adhisīlasikkhaṃ, adhicittasikkhaṃ, adhipaññāsikkhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ sikkhāvevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

The renunciation 'I renounce the training' is not a renunciation by a synonym. Renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of 'training', such as: 'I renounce the bhikkhu training, the bhikkhunī training, the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, the training in higher wisdom.' Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of 'training'.

Vinayaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Bhikkhuvinayaṃ paccakkhāmi, bhikkhunīvinayaṃ, paṭhamaṃ pārājikaṃ, dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthaṃ pārājikaṃ, saṅghādisesaṃ, thullaccayaṃ, pācittiyaṃ, pāṭidesanīyaṃ, dukkaṭaṃ, dubbhāsitaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evamādivinayavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

The renunciation 'I renounce the Vinaya' is not a renunciation by a synonym. Renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of 'Vinaya', such as: 'I renounce the bhikkhu Vinaya, the bhikkhunī Vinaya, the first pārājika, the second, third, and fourth pārājika, the saṅghādisesa, the thullaccaya, the pācittiya, the pāṭidesanīya, the dukkaṭa, the dubbhāsita,' and so on. Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of 'Vinaya'.

Pātimokkhaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Bhikkhupātimokkhaṃ bhikkhunīpātimokkhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ pātimokkhavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

The renunciation 'I renounce the Pātimokkha' is not a renunciation by a synonym. Renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of 'Pātimokkha', such as: 'I renounce the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.' Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by a synonym of 'Pātimokkha'.

Uddesaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Bhikkhupātimokkhuddesaṃ, bhikkhunīpātimokkhuddesaṃ[V 1.0200], paṭhamaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ, dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ, sammāsambuddhuddesaṃ, anantabuddhiuddesaṃ, anomabuddhiuddesaṃ, bodhipaññāṇuddesaṃ, dhīruddesaṃ, vigatamohuddesaṃ, pabhinnakhīluddesaṃ, vijitavijayuddesaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evamādiuddesavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce the recitation,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of the recitation, such as, 'I renounce the recitation of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, the recitation of the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, the first recitation of the Pātimokkha, the second, the third, the fourth, the fifth recitation of the Pātimokkha, the recitation of the Perfectly Enlightened One... the recitation of the Victorious Conqueror,' and so forth, a renunciation of the training occurs.

Upajjhāyaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Yo maṃ pabbājesi, yo maṃ upasampādesi, yassa mūlenāhaṃ pabbajito, yassa mūlenāhaṃ upasampanno, yassamūlikā mayhaṃ pabbajjā, yassamūlikā mayhaṃ upasampadā tāhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ upajjhāyavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce the preceptor,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of the preceptor, such as, 'I renounce him who gave me the going forth, him who gave me the full ordination, him by whose root I went forth, him by whose root I was fully ordained, him who is the root of my going forth, him who is the root of my full ordination,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Ācariyaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Yo maṃ pabbājesi, yo maṃ anussāvesi, yāhaṃ nissāya vasāmi, yāhaṃ uddisāpemi, yāhaṃ [M 1.0217] paripucchāmi, yo maṃ uddisati, yo maṃ paripucchāpeti tāhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ ācariyavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce the teacher,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of the teacher, such as, 'I renounce him who gave me the going forth, him who instructed me, him on whom I live in dependence, him whom I cause to recite, him whom I question, him who recites to me, him who causes me to question,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Saddhivihārikaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Yāhaṃ pabbājesiṃ, yāhaṃ upasampādesiṃ, mayhaṃ mūlena yo pabbajito, mayhaṃ mūlena yo upasampanno, mayhaṃmūlikā yassa pabbajjā, mayhaṃ mūlikā yassa upasampadā tāhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ saddhivihārikavevacanena [P 1.0253] sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce the co-resident,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of the co-resident, such as, 'I renounce him to whom I gave the going forth, him to whom I gave the full ordination, him who went forth by my root, him who was fully ordained by my root, him whose going forth has me as its root, him whose full ordination has me as its root,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Antevāsikaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Yāhaṃ pabbājesiṃ, yāhaṃ anussāvesiṃ, yo maṃ nissāya vasati, yo maṃ uddisāpeti, yo maṃ paripucchati, yassāhaṃ uddisāmi, yāhaṃ paripucchāpemi taṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ antevāsikavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce the pupil,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of the pupil, such as, 'I renounce him to whom I gave the going forth, him whom I instructed, him who lives in dependence on me, him who causes me to recite, him who questions me, him to whom I recite, him whom I cause to question,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Samānupajjhāyakaṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Mayhaṃ upajjhāyo yaṃ pabbājesi, yaṃ upasampādesi, yo tassa mūlena pabbajito, yo tassa mūlena upasampanno, yassa tammūlikā pabbajjā, yassa tammūlikā upasampadā taṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ samānupajjhāyakavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce one with a common preceptor,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of one with a common preceptor, such as, 'I renounce him to whom my preceptor gave the going forth, him to whom he gave the full ordination, him who went forth by his root, him who was fully ordained by his root, him whose going forth is based on that root, him whose full ordination is based on that root,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Samānācariyakaṃ [V 1.0201] paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Mayhaṃ ācariyo yaṃ pabbājesi, yaṃ anussāvesi, yo taṃ nissāya vasati, yo taṃ uddisāpeti paripucchati, yassa me ācariyo uddisati, yaṃ paripucchāpeti taṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ samānācariyakavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce one with a common teacher,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of one with a common teacher, such as, 'I renounce him to whom my teacher gave the going forth, him whom my teacher instructed, him who lives in dependence on him, him who causes him to recite and questions him, him to whom my teacher recites, him whom my teacher causes to question,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Sabrahmacāriṃ paccakkhāmīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Yenāhaṃ saddhiṃ adhisīlaṃ sikkhāmi, adhicittaṃ adhipaññaṃ sikkhāmi taṃ paccakkhāmī”ti evaṃ sabrahmacārivevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'I renounce the fellow practitioner in the holy life,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of the fellow practitioner in the holy life, such as, 'I renounce him with whom I train in the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Gihīti maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Āgārikoti maṃ dhārehi, kassako, vāṇijo, gorakkho, okallako, moḷibaddho, kāmaguṇikoti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ gihivevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as a layman,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of a layman, such as, 'Regard me as a house-dweller, a farmer, a merchant, a cowherd, a destitute person, one with a topknot, or one who indulges in sensual pleasures,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Upāsakoti [M 1.0218] maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Dvevāciko upāsakoti maṃ dhārehi, tevāciko upāsako, buddhaṃ saraṇagamaniko, dhammaṃ saṅghaṃ saraṇagamaniko, pañcasikkhāpadiko dasasikkhāpadiko upāsakoti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ upāsakavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as a lay follower,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of a lay follower, such as, 'Regard me as a lay follower of the two-fold formula, a lay follower of the three-fold formula, one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, a lay follower who undertakes the five training rules, or a lay follower who undertakes the ten training rules,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Ārāmikoti maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Kappiyakārakoti maṃ dhārehi, veyyāvaccakaro, appaharitakārako, yāgubhājako, phalabhājako, khajjakabhājakoti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ ārāmikavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as a monastery attendant,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of a monastery attendant, such as, 'Regard me as one who makes things allowable, one who performs services, one who clears away green growth, one who distributes gruel, one who distributes fruit, or one who distributes hard food,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Sāmaṇeroti maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Kumārakoti maṃ dhārehi, cellako, ceṭako, moḷigallo, samaṇuddeso’ti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ sāmaṇeravecanena [P 1.0254] sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as a novice,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of a novice, such as, 'Regard me as a young boy novice, a junior novice, an intermediate novice, a senior novice, or a recluse-in-training,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Titthiyoti maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Nigaṇṭhoti maṃ dhārehi, ājīvako, tāpaso, paribbājako, paṇḍaraṅgoti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ titthiyavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as a sectarian,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of a sectarian, such as, 'Regard me as a Nigaṇṭha, an Ājīvaka, an ascetic, a wanderer, or a white-robed ascetic,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Titthiyasāvakoti [V 1.0202] maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Nigaṇṭhasāvakoti maṃ dhārehi” ājīvaka tāpasa paribbājaka paṇḍaraṅgasāvakoti maṃ dhārehīti evaṃ titthiyasāvakavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as a sectarian's disciple,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of a sectarian's disciple, such as, 'Regard me as a disciple of a Nigaṇṭha, a disciple of an Ājīvaka, a disciple of an ascetic, a disciple of a wanderer, or a disciple of a white-robed ascetic,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Assamaṇoti maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Dussīloti maṃ dhārehi, pāpadhammo, asucisaṅkassarasamācāro, paṭicchannakammanto, assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño, abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño, antopūti, avassuto, kasambujāto, koṇṭho’ti maṃ dhārehī”ti evaṃ assamaṇavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

By the phrase 'Regard me as not a recluse,' there is no renunciation by way of a synonym. However, by a designation of one who is not a recluse, such as, 'Regard me as one who is immoral, of evil nature, of impure and suspect conduct, of concealed deeds, a non-recluse who claims to be a recluse, an unchaste person who claims to be chaste, one who is rotten within, one who is corrupt, one who is like rubbish, or a defective person,' a renunciation of the training occurs.

Asakyaputtiyoti maṃ dhārehīti na vevacanena paccakkhānaṃ. “Na sammāsambuddhaputtoti maṃ dhārehi, na anantabuddhiputto, na anomabuddhiputto, na bodhipaññāṇaputto, na dhīraputto, na vigatamohaputto, na pabhinnakhīlaputto[M 1.0219], na vijitavijayaputtoti maṃ dhārehī”ti evamādiasakyaputtiyavevacanena sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hoti.

Renunciation is not by the expression, 'Regard me as not a son of the Sakyan.' A renunciation of the training occurs by means of expressions synonymous with 'not a son of the Sakyan,' such as, 'Regard me as not a son of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, not a son of infinite wisdom, not a son of peerless wisdom, not a son of the wisdom of awakening, not a son of the steadfast, not a son of one free from delusion, not a son of one who has broken through the obstructions, not a son of one who has conquered victory.'

Tehi ākārehi tehi liṅgehi tehi nimittehīti tehi “buddhavevacanāni vā”tiādinā nayena vuttehi buddhādīnaṃ vevacanehi. Vevacanāni hi sikkhāpaccakkhānassa kāraṇattā ākārāni, buddhādīnaṃ saṇṭhānadīpanattā sikkhāpaccakkhānasaṇṭhānattā eva vā liṅgāni, sikkhāpaccakkhānassa sañjānanahetuto manussānaṃ tilakādīni viya nimittānīti vuccanti. Evaṃ kho bhikkhaveti ito paraṃ aññassa sikkhāpaccakkhānakāraṇassa abhāvato niyamento āha. Ayañhettha attho, evameva dubbalyāvikammañceva hoti sikkhāpaccakkhānañca, na ito paraṃ kāraṇamatthīti.

By those modes, by those signs, by those indications—that is, by those expressions of the Buddha and others, spoken of in the manner of 'or the expressions of the Buddha,' and so on. Indeed, the expressions are called 'modes' because they are the cause of the renunciation of the training; they are called 'signs' because they indicate the nature of the Buddha and others, or because they are the very nature of the renunciation of the training; and they are called 'indications' because they are the reason for recognizing the renunciation of the training, just like moles and other marks on humans. 'Thus, O bhikkhus'—he stated this, thereby delimiting, because beyond this there is no other cause for the renunciation of the training. And this is the meaning here: in this very way, there is both the act of declaring weakness and the renunciation of the training, and there is no cause beyond this.

54. Evaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānalakkhaṇaṃ dassetvā appaccakkhāne asammohatthaṃ tasseva ca sikkhāpaccakkhānalakkhaṇassa puggalādivasena vipattidassanatthaṃ “kathañca, bhikkhave, appaccakkhātā”tiādimāha. Tattha yehi ākārehītiādi vuttanayameva. Ummattakoti yakkhummattako vā pittummattako vā yo koci viparītasañño, so sace paccakkhāti, appaccakkhātā [P 1.0255] hoti sikkhā. Ummattakassāti tādisasseva ummattakassa; tādisassa hi santike sace pakatatto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāti, ummattako na jānāti, appaccakkhātāva hoti sikkhā. Khittacittoti yakkhummattako vuccati. Purimapade pana ummattakasāmaññena vuttaṃ “yakkhummattako vā pittummattako vā”ti. Ubhinnampi viseso anāpattivāre āvi bhavissati[V 1.0203]. Evaṃ khittacitto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāti, appaccakkhātāva hoti. Tassa santike paccakkhātāpi tamhi ajānante appaccakkhātāva hoti.

54. Having thus shown the characteristic of the renunciation of the training, for the purpose of non-bewilderment regarding non-renunciation, and for the purpose of showing the failure of that very characteristic of the renunciation of the training with respect to individuals and so on, he said, 'And how, O bhikkhus, is it not renounced?' and so on. Therein, 'by which modes,' etc., is in the same manner as has been stated. 'One who is insane' means one insane due to possession by a yakkha, or one insane due to a bile disorder, or anyone with distorted perception; if such a person renounces, the training is not renounced. 'Of one who is insane' means of such an insane person; for if a person of normal mind renounces the training in the presence of such a one, and the insane person does not understand, the training is indeed not renounced. 'One with a deranged mind' is said of one who is insane due to possession by a yakkha. But in the previous passage, 'insane' was spoken of generally as 'one insane due to possession by a yakkha or one insane due to a bile disorder.' The distinction between both will become clear in the chapter on non-offenses. Thus, if one with a deranged mind renounces the training, it is not renounced. Even if it is renounced in his presence, if he does not understand, it is indeed not renounced.

Vedanāṭṭoti balavatiyā dukkhavedanāya phuṭṭho mucchāpareto; tena vilapantena paccakkhātāpi appaccakkhātāva hoti. Tassa santike paccakkhātāpi tamhi ajānante appaccakkhātā hoti.

'One afflicted by feeling' means one who is afflicted by a strong, painful feeling and is overcome by fainting; even if renounced by such a person while lamenting, it is not renounced. Even if it is renounced in his presence, if he does not understand, it is not renounced.

Devatāya santiketi bhummadevataṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva akaniṭṭhadevatāya santike paccakkhātāpi appaccakkhātāva hoti. Tiracchānagatassāti nāgamāṇavakassa vā supaṇṇamāṇavakassa vā kinnara-hatthi-makkaṭādīnaṃ vā yassa kassaci santike paccakkhātāpi appaccakkhātāva hoti[M 1.0220]. Tatra ummattakādīnaṃ santike ajānanabhāvena appaccakkhātāti āha. Devatāya santike atikhippaṃ jānanabhāvena. Devatā nāma mahāpaññā tihetukapaṭisandhikā atikhippaṃ jānanti, cittañca nāmetaṃ lahuparivattaṃ. Tasmā cittalahukassa puggalassa cittavaseneva “mā atikhippaṃ vināso ahosī”ti devatāya santike sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ paṭikkhipi.

'In the presence of a deity' means that even if renounced in the presence of a deity—from an earth deity up to an Akaniṭṭha deity—it is not renounced. 'Of an animal' means that even if renounced in the presence of a nāga youth, a supaṇṇa youth, or any kinnara, elephant, monkey, and so on, it is not renounced. There, in the case of the insane and others, he said it is not renounced because of their state of not knowing. In the presence of a deity, it is because of their extremely swift knowing. Deities, it is said, are of great wisdom, possessing a three-rooted rebirth-linking, and they know very quickly. And this mind is swift to change. Therefore, out of compassion for a person with a swift mind, thinking, 'May there not be swift destruction merely by the power of the mind,' he disallowed the renunciation of the training in the presence of a deity.

Manussesu pana niyamo natthi. Yassa kassaci sabhāgassa vā visabhāgassa vā gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā viññussa santike paccakkhātā paccakkhātāva hoti. Sace pana so na jānāti, appaccakkhātāva hotīti etamatthaṃ dassento “ariyakenā”tiādimāha. Tattha ariyakaṃ nāma ariyavohāro, māgadhabhāsā. Milakkhakaṃ nāma yo koci anariyako andhadamiḷādi. So ca na paṭivijānātīti bhāsantare vā anabhiññatāya, buddhasamaye vā akovidatāya “idaṃ nāma atthaṃ esa bhaṇatī”ti nappaṭivijānāti. Davāyāti sahasā aññaṃ bhaṇitukāmo sahasā “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti bhaṇati. Ravāyāti ravābhaññena, “aññaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti aññaṃ bhaṇanto. Purimena [P 1.0256] ko visesoti ce? Purimaṃ paṇḍitassāpi sahasāvasena aññabhaṇanaṃ. Idaṃ pana mandattā momūhattā apakataññuttā pakkhalantassa “aññaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti aññabhaṇanaṃ.

But among humans, there is no fixed rule. If renounced in the presence of any discerning person—whether a man of similar nature or a woman of dissimilar nature, a householder or one gone forth—it is indeed renounced. But if that person does not understand, it is not renounced. To show this meaning, he said, 'by the noble language,' and so on. Therein, 'noble language' means the speech of the noble ones, the Magadhan language. 'Barbarian language' means any non-noble language, such as that of the Andhakas, Damiḷas, and so on. And 'if he does not understand' means that, either due to not knowing another language or due to not being skilled in the conventions of the Buddha's dispensation, he does not understand, thinking, 'This is the meaning of what this person is saying.' 'In jest' means that, desiring to say something else, one hastily says, 'I renounce the Buddha.' 'By a slip of the tongue' means speaking erroneously; intending to say one thing, one says something else. If it is asked, 'What is the difference from the former?' The former is the speaking of something else even by a wise person due to haste. This latter, however, is the speaking of something else by one who stumbles due to dullness, delusion, and lack of practical knowledge, thinking, 'I will say something else.'

Asāvetukāmo sāvetīti imassa sikkhāpadassa pāḷiṃ vāceti paripucchati uggaṇhāti sajjhāyaṃ karoti vaṇṇeti, ayaṃ vuccati “asāvetukāmo sāvetī”ti. Sāvetukāmo na sāvetīti dubbalabhāvaṃ āvikatvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhanto vacībhedaṃ na karoti, ayaṃ vuccati “sāvetukāmo [V 1.0204] na sāvetī”ti. Aviññussa sāvetīti mahallakassa vā potthakarūpasadisassa, garumedhassa vā samaye akovidassa, gāmadārakānaṃ vā aviññutaṃ pattānaṃ sāveti. Viññussa na sāvetīti paṇḍitassa ñātuṃ samatthassa na sāveti. Sabbaso vā panāti “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādīsu yena yena pariyāyena sikkhā paccakkhātā hoti, tato ekampi vacībhedaṃ katvā na sāveti. Evaṃ khoti appaccakkhānalakkhaṇaṃ niyameti. Ayaṃ hettha attho – “evameva sikkhā appaccakkhātā hoti, na aññena kāraṇenā”ti.

'One not wishing to announce, announces' refers to one who teaches the Pāḷi of this training rule, asks questions about it, learns it, recites it, or expounds upon it; this is called 'one not wishing to announce, announces.' 'One wishing to announce, does not announce' refers to one who, having declared his weakness, does not make a verbal utterance while renouncing the training; this is called 'one wishing to announce, does not announce.' 'He announces to one who does not understand' means he announces in the presence of an old man who is like a painted figure, or one of dull intellect who is unskilled in the doctrine, or village children who have not yet reached the state of understanding. 'He does not announce to one who understands' means he does not announce in the presence of a wise person who is capable of understanding. 'Or in every way' means that, among the ways such as 'I renounce the Buddha,' by whichever method the training is renounced, he does not announce by making even one verbal utterance from that method. 'Thus indeed'—by this, he delimits the characteristic of non-renunciation. This is the meaning here: 'In this very way the training is not renounced, and not for any other reason.'

Sikkhāpaccakkhānavibhaṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The analysis of the renunciation of the training is concluded.

Mūlapaññattivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Root Enactment

55. Idāni [M 1.0221] “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”tiādīnaṃ atthadassanatthaṃ “methunadhammo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha methunadhammo nāmāti idaṃ niddisitabbassa methunadhammassa uddesapadaṃ. Asaddhammoti asataṃ nīcajanānaṃ dhammo. Gāmadhammoti gāmavāsīnaṃ sevanadhammo. Vasaladhammoti vasalānaṃ dhammo; kilesavassanato vā sayameva vasalo dhammoti vasaladhammo. Duṭṭhullanti duṭṭhuñca kilesehi duṭṭhattā, thūlañca anipuṇabhāvatoti duṭṭhullaṃ. Ito paṭṭhāya ca tīsu padesu “yo so”ti idaṃ parivattetvā “yaṃ ta”nti katvā yojetabbaṃ – “yaṃ taṃ duṭṭhullaṃ, yaṃ taṃ odakantikaṃ, yaṃ taṃ rahassa”nti. Ettha ca yasmā tassa kammassa parivārabhūtaṃ dassanampi gahaṇampi āmasanampi phusanampi ghaṭṭanampi duṭṭhullaṃ, tasmāpi taṃ kammaṃ duṭṭhullaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ duṭṭhullaṃ so methunadhammo. Udakaṃ assa ante suddhatthaṃ ādīyatīti udakantaṃ, udakantameva odakantikaṃ; yaṃ taṃ odakantikaṃ[P 1.0257], so methunadhammo. Raho paṭicchanne okāse kattabbatāya rahassaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ rahassaṃ, so methunadhammoti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

55. Now, to show the meaning of the phrases beginning with “should engage in sexual intercourse,” the Blessed One said the Pāḷi analysis beginning with “Sexual practice is called…” Therein, this phrase “Sexual practice is called” is the introductory term for the sexual practice which is to be explained in detail. “Unrighteous practice” is the practice of ignoble, base people. “Village practice” is the practice to be engaged in by villagers. “Outcaste practice” is the practice of outcastes; or, because it sheds defilements, it is itself a shedding practice, hence it is “outcaste practice.” “Obscene” means it is both corrupt because it is corrupted by defilements, and coarse because of its unrefined nature, thus it is “obscene.” And from this point onward, in the three phrases, this phrase “yo so” should be changed to “yaṃ taṃ” and connected thus: “that which is obscene, that which is water-at-the-end, that which is secret.” And herein, because the attendant acts of that deed—seeing, taking, touching, contacting, and rubbing—are also obscene, that deed itself is also obscene. That which is the obscene practice, that is the sexual practice. Because water is taken at its end for purification, it is “water-at-the-end” (udakanta); “water-at-the-end” itself is odakantika. That which is odakantika, that is the sexual practice. Because it is to be done in a secret, concealed place, it is “secret” (rahassa). That which is the secret practice, that is the sexual practice. Thus the connection should be understood.

Dvayena dvayena samāpajjitabbato dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti. Tattha yojanā – “yā sā dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti so methunadhammo nāmā”ti. Idha pana taṃ sabbaṃ ekajjhaṃ nigamento āha “eso methunadhammo nāmā”ti. Kiṃ kāraṇā vuccati methunadhammoti? Ubhinnaṃ rattānaṃ sārattānaṃ avassutānaṃ pariyuṭṭhitānaṃ ubhinnaṃ sadisānaṃ dhammoti, taṃ kāraṇā vuccati methunadhammoti.

Because it is to be attained by a pair, it is 'the mutual attainment of a pair' (dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti). Therein, the connection is: ‘That which is the mutual attainment of a pair, that is called the sexual practice.’ But here, wishing to conclude all that together, the Blessed One said, ‘This is called the sexual practice.’ For what reason is it called the sexual practice? It is the practice of two similar beings who are impassioned, strongly impassioned, moistened, and obsessed; for that reason, it is called the sexual practice.

Paṭisevati nāmāti idaṃ “paṭiseveyyā”ti ettha yenākārena paṭiseveyyāti vuccati, tassākārassa dassanatthaṃ mātikāpadaṃ. Yo nittena nimittantiādīsu yo bhikkhu itthiyā nimittena [V 1.0205] attano nimittaṃ, itthiyā aṅgajātena attano aṅgajātaṃ sabbantimena pamāṇena ekatilabījamattampi vātena asamphuṭṭhe allokāse paveseti, eso paṭisevati nāma; ettakena sīlabhedaṃ pāpuṇāti, pārājiko hoti.

The phrase 'engages, it is called' is the head-word for showing the manner in which it is said one 'should engage.' Whatever bhikkhu inserts his own sign into a woman's sign, or his own genital organ into a woman's genital organ, even to the very last measure of a single sesame seed, into a moist place untouched by the wind, this one is called 'one who engages.' By this much, he attains the breaking of virtue and is defeated.

Ettha ca itthinimitte cattāri passāni, vemajjhañcāti pañca ṭhānāni labbhanti. Purisanimitte cattāri passāni, majjhaṃ, uparicāti cha. Tasmā itthinimitte heṭṭhā pavesentopi pārājiko hoti. Uparito pavesentopi, ubhohi passehi [M 1.0222] pavesentopi cattāri ṭhānāni muñcitvā majjhena pavesentopi pārājiko hoti. Purisanimittaṃ pana heṭṭhābhāgena chupantaṃ pavesentopi pārājiko hoti. Uparibhāgena chupantaṃ pavesentopi, ubhohi passehi chupantaṃ pavesentopi, majjheneva chupantaṃ pavesentopi samañchitaṅguliṃ viya majjhimapabbapiṭṭhiyā saṅkocetvā uparibhāgena chupantaṃ pavesentopi pārājiko hoti. Tattha tulādaṇḍasadisaṃ pavesentassāpi cattāri passāni, majjhañcāti pañca ṭhānāni; saṅkocetvā pavesentassāpi cattāri passāni, uparibhāgamajjhañcāti pañca ṭhānāni – evaṃ sabbānipi purisanimitte dasa ṭhānāni honti.

And herein, in the female sign, four sides and the center are obtained—thus five places. In the male sign, four sides, the middle tip, and the upper part are obtained—thus six places. Therefore, regarding the female sign, one who inserts from below is defeated. One who inserts from above, one who inserts from both sides, or one who, leaving aside the four sides, inserts through the middle, is also defeated. As for the male sign, one who inserts it while it is touching with its lower part is defeated. One who inserts it while it is touching with its upper part, one who inserts it while it is touching with both sides, one who inserts it while it is touching only with the middle, or one who, having contracted it, inserts it while it is touching with its upper part—like inserting a bent finger with the back of its middle joint—is also defeated. Therein, for one who inserts it straight like a balance-rod, there are four sides and the middle—thus five places. For one who inserts it having contracted it, there are four sides and the middle of the upper part—thus five places. In this way, there are altogether ten places in the male sign.

Nimitte jātaṃ anaṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ cammakhīlaṃ vā piḷakaṃ vā paveseti, āpatti pārājikassa. Naṭṭhakāyappasādaṃ matacammaṃ vā sukkhapiḷakaṃ vā paveseti, āpatti [P 1.0258] dukkaṭassa. Methunassādena lomaṃ vā aṅguli-aṅguṭṭhabījādīni vā pavesentassāpi dukkaṭameva. Ayañca methunakathā nāma yasmā duṭṭhullā kathā asabbhikathā, tasmā etaṃ vā aññaṃ vā vinaye īdisaṃ ṭhānaṃ kathentena paṭikkūlamanasikārañca samaṇasaññañca hirottappañca paccupaṭṭhapetvā sammāsambuddhe gāravaṃ uppādetvā asamakāruṇikassa lokanāthassa karuṇāguṇaṃ āvajjetvā kathetabbaṃ. So hi nāma bhagavā sabbaso kāmehi vinivattamānasopi sattānuddayāya lokānukampāya sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca sikkhāpadapaññāpanatthāya īdisaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. “Aho satthu karuṇāguṇo”ti evaṃ lokanāthassa karuṇāguṇaṃ āvajjetvā kathetabbaṃ.

If one inserts a skin-peg or a boil with undestroyed bodily sensitivity that has grown on the sign, it is a pārājika offense. If one inserts dead skin or a dry boil with destroyed bodily sensitivity, it is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who inserts a hair, or a finger, toe, thumb, big toe, testicle, and so on with the savor of sexual intercourse, it is only a dukkaṭa offense. And because this talk on sexual intercourse is coarse talk, ignoble talk, therefore, when recounting this or another such case in the Vinaya, one should speak only after having established attention to the repulsive, the perception of being a monk, and shame and moral dread; after having generated reverence for the Perfectly Enlightened One; and after having reflected on the quality of compassion of the Lord of the World, who is of incomparable compassion. For that Blessed One, though his mind was completely turned away from all sensual pleasures, still spoke on such a topic for the welfare of beings, for the benefit of the world, out of compassion for beings, for the purpose of laying down the training rule. Reflecting, 'Oh, the Teacher's quality of compassion!', one should speak, having reflected on the quality of compassion of the Lord of the World.

Apica yadi bhagavā sabbākārena īdisaṃ kathaṃ na katheyya, ko jāneyya “ettakesu

Furthermore, if the Blessed One had not spoken on such a topic in every way, who would be able to know, 'In so many

Ṭhānesu pārājikaṃ, ettakesu thullaccayaṃ, ettakesu dukkaṭa”nti. Tasmā suṇantenapi kathentenapi bījakena mukhaṃ apidhāya dantavidaṃsakaṃ hasamānena na nisīditabbaṃ. “Sammāsambuddhenāpi īdisaṃ kathita”nti paccavekkhitvā gabbhitena hirottappasampannena satthupaṭibhāgena hutvā kathetabbanti.

places it is a pārājika offense, in so many places a thullaccaya offense, and in so many places a dukkaṭa offense.' Therefore, whether listening or speaking, one should not sit laughing and showing one's teeth without covering one's mouth with a small fan. Reflecting, 'Even the Perfectly Enlightened One spoke on such a topic,' one should speak with gravity, endowed with shame and moral dread, being a counterpart to the Teacher.

Mūlapaññattaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Root Enactment is concluded.

Anupaññattivāre [V 1.0206] – antamasoti sabbantimena paricchedena. Tiracchānagatāyapīti paṭisandhivasena tiracchānesu gatāyapi. Pageva manussitthiyāti paṭhamataraṃ manussajātikāya itthiyā. Pārājikavatthubhūtā eva cettha tiracchānagatitthī tiracchānagatāti gahetabbā, na sabbā. Tatrāyaṃ paricchedo –

In the section on the Supplementary Enactment—‘even down to’ means by the very last limit. ‘Even an animal female’ means even one gone to the animal realm by way of rebirth-linking. ‘How much more so a human female’ means a female of the human species from the very first. And here, only an animal female who has become a basis for a pārājika offense should be taken as an ‘animal female,’ not every one. Therein, this is the distinction:

Apadānaṃ ahi macchā, dvipadānañca kukkuṭī;

Catuppadānaṃ majjārī, vatthu pārājikassimāti.

Of the footless, the female snake and the female fish; of bipeds, the hen; and of quadrupeds, the female cat—these are the grounds for a pārājika offense.

Tattha [P 1.0259] ahiggahaṇena sabbāpi ajagaragonasādibhedā dīghajāti saṅgahitā. Tasmā dīghajātīsu yattha tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ sakkā tilaphalamattampi pavesetuṃ, sā pārājikavatthu. Avasesā dukkaṭavatthūti veditabbā. Macchaggahaṇena sabbāpi macchakacchapamaṇḍūkādibhedā odakajāti saṅgahitā. Tatrāpi dīghajātiyaṃ vuttanayeneva pārājikavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – pataṅgamukhamaṇḍūkā nāma honti tesaṃ mukhasaṇṭhānaṃ mahantaṃ, chiddaṃ appakaṃ, tattha pavesanaṃ nappahoti; mukhasaṇṭhānaṃ pana vaṇasaṅkhepaṃ gacchati, tasmā taṃ thullaccayavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Kukkuṭiggahaṇena sabbāpi kākakapotādibhedā pakkhijāti saṅgahitā. Tatrāpi vuttanayeneva pārājikavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca veditabbaṃ. Majjāriggahaṇena sabbāpi rukkhasunakha-muṅgusa-godhādibhedā catuppadajāti saṅgahitā. Tatrāpi vuttanayeneva pārājikavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca veditabbaṃ.

Herein, by the term ‘snake’ are included all long-bodied species such as pythons and vipers. Thus, among long-bodied species, wherever it is possible to insert even the size of a sesame seed into one of the three paths, that is a ground for a pārājika. The remainder should be understood as grounds for a dukkaṭa offense. By the term ‘fish’ are included all kinds of aquatic creatures such as fish, turtles, and frogs. There too, the ground for a pārājika and the ground for a dukkaṭa offense should be understood according to the method stated for long-bodied creatures. However, there is this distinction: there are frogs called 'grasshopper-mouthed'; the shape of their mouths is large, but the opening is small, so insertion is not possible. The shape of the mouth, however, amounts to a contracted wound; therefore, that should be understood as a ground for a thullaccaya offense. By the term ‘hen’ are included all kinds of winged creatures such as crows and pigeons. There too, the ground for a pārājika and the ground for a dukkaṭa offense should be understood according to the method stated above. By the term ‘cat’ are included all kinds of four-footed creatures such as squirrels, dogs, mongooses, and monitor lizards. There too, the ground for a pārājika and the ground for a dukkaṭa offense should be understood according to the method stated above.

Pārājikoti parājito, parājayaṃ āpanno. Ayañhi pārājikasaddo sikkhāpadāpattipuggalesu vattati. Tattha “aṭṭhānametaṃ, ānanda, anavakāso yaṃ tathāgato vajjīnaṃ vā vajjiputtakānaṃ vā kāraṇā sāvakānaṃ pārājikaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ samūhaneyyā”ti (pārā. 43) evaṃ sikkhāpade vattamāno veditabbo. “Āpattiṃ tvaṃ, bhikkhu, āpanno pārājika”nti (pārā. 67) evaṃ āpattiyaṃ. “Na mayaṃ pārājikā, yo avahaṭo so pārājiko”ti (pārā. 155) evaṃ puggale vattamāno veditabbo. “Pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃseyyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 384) pana dhamme vattatīti vadanti. Yasmā pana tattha dhammoti katthaci āpatti[M 1.0224], katthaci sikkhāpadameva adhippetaṃ, tasmā so visuṃ na vattabbo. Tattha sikkhāpadaṃ yo taṃ atikkamati, taṃ parājeti, tasmā “pārājika”nti vuccati. Āpatti pana yo naṃ ajjhāpajjati, taṃ parājeti, tasmā “pārājikā”ti [V 1.0207] vuccati. Puggalo yasmā [P 1.0260] parājito parājayamāpanno, tasmā “pārājiko”ti vuccati. Etameva hi atthaṃ sandhāya parivārepi –

Pārājika means: defeated, having attained defeat. For this term “pārājika” applies to the training rule, the offense, and the person. Therein, “It is impossible, Ānanda, it cannot happen that the Tathāgata would revoke a training rule entailing pārājika for the disciples because of the Vajjians or the Vajjian princes”—thus it should be understood as applying to the training rule. “You, monk, have committed a pārājika offense”—thus it applies to the offense. “We are not pārājika; the one who was carried off is pārājika”—thus it should be understood as applying to the person. In phrases such as, “He should not charge with a pārājika matter,” some say it applies to 'dhamma' (matter/principle). However, since in that context 'dhamma' is intended sometimes as the offense and sometimes as the training rule itself, it should not be stated as a separate category. Therein, the training rule defeats whoever transgresses it; therefore, it is called “pārājika.” The offense, in turn, defeats whoever commits it; therefore, it is called “pārājikā.” The person is called “pārājiko” because he is defeated and has attained defeat. It is with reference to this very meaning that in the Parivāra it is also said:

“Pārājikanti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ suṇohi yathātathaṃ;

Cuto paraddho bhaṭṭho ca, saddhammā hi niraṅkato;

Saṃvāsopi tahiṃ natthi, tenetaṃ iti vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ. (pari. 339);

“‘Pārājika’—that which is so called, listen to it as it truly is: ‘Fallen, failed, and dropped, he is removed from the good Dhamma; there is also no communion with him, for that reason it is so called,’ it is said.”

Ayañhettha attho – “taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamanto āpattiñca āpanno puggalo cuto hotīti sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuccatīti yena kāraṇena assamaṇo hoti asakyaputtiyo paribhaṭṭho chinno parājito sāsanato, tena vuccati. Kinti? “Pārājiko hotī”ti.

This is the meaning here: ‘A person who transgresses that training rule and commits the offense is fallen’—all this should be connected. The phrase ‘for that reason it is so called’ means: for the reason that he is not a recluse, not a son of the Sakyan, has fallen away from, is cut off from, and is defeated from the Dispensation—for that reason it is said. How is it said? It is said, ‘He is a pārājika.’”

Saha vasanti etthāti saṃvāso, taṃ dassetuṃ “saṃvāso nāmā”ti vatvā “ekakamma”ntiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saddhiṃ yojanāya vaṇṇanā – catubbidhampi saṅghakammaṃ sīmāparicchinnehi pakatattehi bhikkhūhi ekato kattabbattā ekakammaṃ nāma. Tathā pañcavidhopi pātimokkhuddeso ekato uddisitabbattā ekuddeso nāma. Paññattaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ sabbehipi lajjīpuggalehi samaṃ sikkhitabbabhāvato samasikkhatā nāma. Ettha yasmā sabbepi lajjino etesu kammādīsu saha vasanti, na ekopi tato bahiddhā sandissati, tasmā tāni sabbānipi gahetvā “eso saṃvāso nāmā”ti āha. So ca vuttappakāro saṃvāso tena puggalena saddhiṃ natthi, tena kāraṇena so pārājiko puggalo asaṃvāsoti vuccatīti.

‘They live together here’ (saha vasanti etthā), thus it is ‘communion’ (saṃvāso). To show this, after saying ‘Communion, namely…,’ he said ‘a single act,’ etc. Here is the explanation together with the word-connection: The four kinds of Sangha acts must be performed together by monks who are of normal status and within a single boundary; hence, it is called a ‘single act.’ Similarly, the five kinds of recitation of the Pātimokkha must be recited together; hence, it is called a ‘single recitation.’ The laid-down training rule, however, must be trained in equally by all conscientious persons; hence, it is called ‘equal training.’ Here, since all conscientious ones live together in these acts, etc., and not even one is found outside of them, therefore, having taken all of these together, he said, ‘This is called communion.’ And that communion of the kind described does not exist with that person; for that reason, that pārājika person is said to be ‘one without communion’ (asaṃvāso).

56. Evaṃ uddiṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ padānukkamena vibhajitvā idāni yaṃ taṃ “paṭiseveyyā”ti ettha yenākārena paṭiseveyyāti vuccati, tassākārassa dassanatthaṃ “paṭisevati nāmā”ti idaṃ mātikāpadaṃ ṭhapetvā “nimittena nimittaṃ aṅgajātena aṅgajāta”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā na kevalaṃ itthiyā [M 1.0225] eva nimittaṃ pārājikavatthu, na ca manussitthiyā eva, suvaṇṇarajatādimayānañca itthīnampi nimittaṃ vatthumeva na hoti; tasmā yaṃ yaṃ vatthu hoti, taṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “tisso itthiyo”tiādinā nayena yesaṃ nimittāni vatthūni honti, te satte vatvā “manussitthiyā tayo magge”tiādinā nayena tāni vatthūni āha.

56. Having thus analyzed the training rule that was set forth term by term, now, regarding the phrase ‘should engage,’ in order to show the manner in which one is said to ‘engage,’ this mātikā-heading ‘engages, namely…’ was established, and it was said, ‘sign with sign, organ with organ.’ Therein, since the sign of a woman is not the only ground for a pārājika, nor is it only that of a human woman, and the signs of women made of gold, silver, and so on are not grounds at all; therefore, to show which things are grounds, having first stated, by the method beginning ‘three women,’ the beings whose signs are grounds, he then stated those grounds by the method beginning ‘the three paths of a human woman.’”

Tattha tisso itthiyo, tayo ubhatobyañjanakā, tayo paṇḍakā, tayo purisāti pārājikavatthūnaṃ [V 1.0208] nimittānaṃ nissayā dvādasa sattā honti. Tesu itthipurisā pākaṭā eva[P 1.0261]. Paṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakabhedo pabbajjākhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ pākaṭo bhavissati.

Herein, there are three women, three hermaphrodites, three eunuchs, and three men; thus, there are twelve beings who are the supports for the signs that are grounds for a pārājika. Among them, women and men are obvious. The distinction between eunuchs and hermaphrodites will become clear in the commentary on the Ordination Section.

Manussitthiyā tayo magge methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantassāti ettha ca manussitthiyā tīsu maggesūti attho veditabbo. Evaṃ sabbattha. Sabbe eva cete manussitthiyā tayo maggā, amanussitthiyā tayo, tiracchānagatitthiyā tayoti nava; manussaubhatobyañjanakādīnaṃ nava; manussapaṇḍakādīnaṃ dve dve katvā cha; tathā manussapurisādīnanti samatiṃsa maggā honti. Etesu nimittasaṅkhātesu yattha katthaci attano aṅgajātaṃ tilaphalamattampi pavesetvā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto pārājikaṃ āpajjati.

As for the phrase 'engaging in sexual intercourse in the three passages of a human woman,' the meaning should be understood as 'in the three passages of a human woman.' Thus it is in all cases. And all these passages are: the three passages of a human woman, three of a non-human woman, and three of a female animal, making nine; nine for human hermaphrodites and the like; for human eunuchs and the like, taking two each, makes six; similarly for human men and the like, six—thus there are thirty passages. Among these, which are known as orifices, in any one whatsoever, a monk who inserts his own sexual organ even to the extent of a sesame seed and engages in sexual intercourse falls into a Pārājika offense.

Paṭhamacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the First Tetrad

57. Āpajjanto pana yasmā sevanacitteneva āpajjati, na vinā tena; tasmā taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ dassento bhagavā “bhikkhussa sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhite”tiādimāha. Tattha bhikkhussāti methunasevanakassa bhikkhussa. Sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhiteti bhummatthe paccattavacanaṃ, sevanacitte paccupaṭṭhiteti attho. Vaccamaggaṃ aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassāti yena maggena vaccaṃ nikkhamati taṃ maggaṃ attano aṅgajātaṃ purisanimittaṃ tilaphalamattampi pavesentassa. Āpatti pārājikassāti āpatti pārājikā assa hotīti attho. Atha vā āpattīti āpajjanaṃ hoti. Pārājikassāti pārājikadhammassa. Esa nayo sabbattha.

57. Now, since one who falls into an offense does so only with the mind of engaging, and not without it, therefore, to show that characteristic, the Blessed One said, 'When the mind of engaging is present for a monk,' and so on. Therein, 'of a monk' means of a monk who engages in sexual intercourse. In the phrase 'the mind of engaging is present,' this is a nominative used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is 'when the mind of engaging is present.' 'Of one inserting the sexual organ into the passage for excrement' means of one who inserts his own sexual organ, the male sign, even to the extent of a sesame seed, into that passage through which excrement exits. 'The offense of Pārājika' means 'a Pārājika offense occurs for him.' Alternatively, 'offense' means 'the falling into'; 'of Pārājika' means 'of the Pārājika rule.' This is the method in all cases.

58. Evaṃ sevanacitteneva pavesentassa āpattiṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā taṃ pavesanaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ attūpakkameneva, parūpakkamenāpi hoti[M 1.0226]. Tatrāpi ca sādiyantasseva āpatti paṭisevanacittasamaṅgissa, na itarassa. Tasmā ye saddhāpabbajitā kulaputtā sammāpaṭipannakā parūpakkamena pavesanepi sati na sādiyanti, tesaṃ rakkhaṇatthaṃ “bhikkhupaccatthikā manussitthi”ntiādimāha.

58. Having thus shown the offense for one who inserts with only the mind of engaging, now, because that which is called insertion occurs not only by one's own effort but also by another's effort—and even in that case, an offense occurs only for one who consents, being endowed with the mind of engaging, not for another—therefore, for the protection of those sons of good family who have gone forth in faith, are of right conduct, and do not consent even when there is insertion by another's effort, He said, 'Hostile monks, a human woman,' and so on.

Tattha paṭipakkhaṃ atthayanti icchantīti paccatthikā, bhikkhū eva paccatthikā bhikkhupaccatthikā; visabhāgānaṃ veribhikkhūnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Manussitthiṃ bhikkhussa santike ānetvāti issāpakatā taṃ bhikkhuṃ nāsetukāmā āmisena vā upalāpetvā mittasanthavavasena vā “idaṃ amhākaṃ kiccaṃ karohī”ti vatvā kañci manussitthiṃ [P 1.0262] rattibhāge tassa bhikkhussa vasanokāsaṃ [V 1.0209] ānetvā. Vaccamaggena aṅgajātaṃ abhinisīdentīti taṃ bhikkhuṃ hatthapādasīsādīsu suggahitaṃ nipparipphandaṃ gahetvā itthiyā vaccamaggena tassa bhikkhuno aṅgajātaṃ abhinisīdenti; sampayojentīti attho.

Therein, 'adversaries' (paccatthikā) are so called because they desire an opponent. Monks themselves are the adversaries, hence 'monk-adversaries' (bhikkhupaccatthikā); this is a designation for hostile monks of a different faction. As for 'having brought a human woman near a monk': being overcome by jealousy and wishing to destroy that monk, either having enticed him with material things or by means of feigning friendship, saying, 'Please do this task for us,' they bring some human woman during the night to that monk's dwelling place. As for 'they press down upon the sexual organ with the passage for excrement': having seized that monk firmly by the hands, feet, head, and so on, so that he is motionless, they make the woman press down upon that monk's sexual organ with her passage for excrement; the meaning is, they cause them to be joined together.

So cetiādīsu so ce bhikkhu vaccamaggabbhantaraṃ attano aṅgajātassa pavesanaṃ sādiyati adhivāseti tasmiṃ khaṇe sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Paviṭṭhaṃ sādiyati adhivāseti, paviṭṭhakāle sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Ṭhitaṃ sādiyati adhivāseti, ṭhānappattakāle sukkavissaṭṭhisamaye sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Uddharaṇaṃ sādiyati adhivāseti, nīharaṇakāle paṭisevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ catūsu ṭhānesu sādiyanto “mama verisamaṇehi idaṃ kata”nti vattuṃ na labhati, pārājikāpattimeva āpajjati. Yathā ca imāni cattāri sādiyanto āpajjati; evaṃ purimaṃ ekaṃ asādiyitvā tīṇi sādiyantopi, dve asādiyitvā dve sādiyantopi, tīṇi asādiyitvā ekaṃ sādiyantopi āpajjatiyeva. Sabbaso pana asādiyanto āsīvisamukhaṃ viya aṅgārakāsuṃ viya ca paviṭṭhaṃ aṅgajātaṃ maññamāno nāpajjati. Tena vuttaṃ – “pavesanaṃ na sādiyati…pe… uddharaṇaṃ na sādiyati, anāpattī”ti. Imañhi evarūpaṃ āraddhavipassakaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhaṃ ekādasahi aggīhi sampajjalitāni ca sabbāyatanāni ukkhittāsike viya ca vadhake pañca kāmaguṇe passantaṃ puggalaṃ rakkhanto bhagavā paccatthikānañcassa manorathavighātaṃ [M 1.0227] karonto imaṃ “pavesanaṃ na sādiyatī”tiādikaṃ catukkaṃ nīharitvā ṭhapesīti.

In the text beginning 'If he,' if that monk consents to or acquiesces in the insertion of his own sexual organ into the passage for excrement, and at that moment arouses the mind of engaging; if he consents to or acquiesces in it having been inserted, and at the time of it having been inserted arouses the mind of engaging; if he consents to or acquiesces in its remaining, and at the time of its reaching its position, at the time of emitting semen, arouses the mind of engaging; if he consents to or acquiesces in the withdrawal, and at the time of withdrawal arouses the mind of engaging—thus, by consenting in these four instances, he does not get to say, 'This was done to me by hostile ascetics,' but falls only into a Pārājika offense. And just as he falls into an offense by consenting to these four, so too he certainly falls into an offense by not consenting to the first one but consenting to the three; or by not consenting to two but consenting to two; or by not consenting to three but consenting to one. However, one who does not consent at all, regarding the inserted sexual organ as if it had entered the mouth of a venomous snake or a pit of embers, does not fall into an offense. Therefore it was said: 'He does not consent to the insertion... (etc.)... he does not consent to the withdrawal, there is no offense.' Indeed, the Blessed One, protecting such a person—one who has undertaken insight meditation, is unconcerned with body and life, who sees all sense bases as blazing with the eleven fires and the five strands of sensual pleasure as executioners with raised swords—and also thwarting the desire of his adversaries, extracted and established this tetrad beginning with 'he does not consent to the insertion.'

Paṭhamacatukkakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the First Tetrad is concluded.

Ekūnasattatidvisatacatukkakathā

The Discourse on the Two Hundred and Sixty-Nine Sets of Four.

59-60. Evaṃ paṭhamacatukkaṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā bhikkhupaccatthikā itthiṃ ānetvā na kevalaṃ vaccamaggeneva abhinisīdenti, atha kho passāvamaggenapi mukhenapi. Itthiṃ ānetvāpi ca keci jāgarantiṃ ānenti, keci suttaṃ, keci mattaṃ, keci ummattaṃ, keci pamattaṃ aññavihitaṃ vikkhittacittanti [P 1.0263] attho. Keci mataṃ akkhāyitaṃ, soṇasiṅgālādīhi akkhāyitanimittanti attho. Keci mataṃ yebhuyyena akkhāyitaṃ, yebhuyyena akkhāyitā nāma yassā nimitte vaccamagge passāvamagge mukhe vā bahutaro okāso akkhāyito hoti. Keci mataṃ yebhuyyena khāyitaṃ, yebhuyyena khāyitā nāma yassā vaccamaggādike nimitte bahuṃ khāyitaṃ [V 1.0210] hoti, appaṃ akkhāyitaṃ. Na kevalañca manussitthimeva ānenti, atha kho amanussitthimpi tiracchānagatitthimpi. Na kevalañca vuttappakāraṃ itthimeva, ubhatobyañjanakampi paṇḍakampi purisampi ānenti. Tasmā tesaṃ vasena aññānipi catukkāni dassento “bhikkhupaccatthikā manussitthiṃ jāgaranti”ntiādimāha.

Having thus presented the first set of four, now, because the monks' adversaries bring a woman and make her sit upon not only the excretory passage, but also the urinary passage and the mouth. And having brought a woman, some bring one who is awake, some one who is asleep, some one who is intoxicated, some one who is insane, or some one who is heedless, meaning one whose mind is distracted. Some bring one dead and unconsumed—meaning one whose sexual organ is unconsumed by dogs, jackals, and so on. Some bring one dead and mostly unconsumed—'mostly unconsumed' refers to one in whose sexual organ, whether the excretory passage, urinary passage, or mouth, the greater part is unconsumed. Some bring one dead and mostly consumed—'mostly consumed' refers to one in whose sexual organ, such as the excretory passage, much is consumed and little is unconsumed. And not only do they bring human women, but they also bring non-human women and female animals. And not only do they bring women of the kind described, but they also bring hermaphrodites, eunuchs, and men. Therefore, on account of these cases, he shows other sets of four, beginning with, 'The monks' adversaries bring a human woman who is awake...'

Tattha pāḷiyā asammohatthaṃ vuttacatukkāni evaṃ saṅkhyāto veditabbāni – manussitthiyā tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vasena tīṇi suddhikacatukkāni, tīṇi jāgarantīcatukkāni, tīṇi suttacatukkāni, tīṇi mattacatukkāni, tīṇi ummattacatukkāni, tīṇi pamattacatukkāni, tīṇi mataakkhāyitacatukkāni, tīṇi yebhuyyena akkhāyitacatukkāni, tīṇi yebhuyyena khāyitacatukkānīti sattavīsati catukkāni. Tathā amanussitthiyā; tathā tiracchānagatitthiyāti itthivāre ekāsīti catukkāni. Yathā ca itthivāre evaṃ ubhatobyañjanakavāre. Paṇḍakapurisavāresu pana dvinnaṃ maggānaṃ vasena catupaṇṇāsa catupaṇṇāsa honti. Evaṃ sabbānipi dvesatāni, sattati ca catukkāni honti, tāni uttānatthāniyeva.

Here, to avoid confusion in the Pāli text, the groups of four should be understood by number as follows: For a human woman, based on the three passages, there are three purity groups of four, three wakeful groups of four, three sleeping groups of four, three intoxicated groups of four, three insane groups of four, three heedless groups of four, three dead and unconsumed groups of four, three mostly unconsumed groups of four, and three mostly consumed groups of four—totaling twenty-seven groups of four. Similarly, for a non-human woman; likewise for a female animal—thus, in the section on women, there are eighty-one groups of four. Just as in the section on women, so too in the section on hermaphrodites. However, in the sections on eunuchs and men, due to the two passages, there are fifty-four groups of four each. Thus, all together, there are two hundred and seventy groups of four, and their meanings are straightforward.

Sabbavāresu [M 1.0228] panettha “mataṃ yebhuyyena akkhāyitaṃ khāyita”nti etasmiṃ ṭhāne ayaṃ vinicchayo – tambapaṇṇidīpe kira dve vinayadharā samānācariyakā therā ahesuṃ – upatissatthero ca, phussadevatthero ca. Te mahābhaye uppanne vinayapiṭakaṃ pariharantā rakkhiṃsu. Tesu upatissatthero byattataro. Tassāpi dve antevāsikā ahesuṃ – mahāpadumatthero ca mahāsumatthero ca. Tesu mahāsumatthero nakkhattuṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ assosi, mahāpadumatthero tena saddhiṃ navakkhattuṃ, visuñca ekakova navakkhattunti aṭṭhārasakkhattuṃ assosi; ayameva tesu byattataro[P 1.0264]. Tesu mahāsumatthero navakkhattuṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ sutvā ācariyaṃ muñcitvā aparagaṅgaṃ agamāsi. Tato mahāpadumatthero āha – “sūro vata, re, esa vinayadharo yo dharamānakaṃyeva ācariyaṃ muñcitvā aññattha vasitabbaṃ maññati. Nanu ācariye dharamāne vinayapiṭakañca aṭṭhakathā ca anekakkhattuṃ gahetvāpi na vissajjetabbaṃ, niccakālaṃ sotabbaṃ, anusaṃvaccharaṃ sajjhāyitabba”nti.

Moreover, in all these sections, regarding the point of 'dead, mostly unconsumed, and consumed,' this is the decision: In the island of Tambapaṇṇi, there were two Vinaya-holding elders who were fellow students—the elder Upatissa and the elder Phussadeva. When a great peril arose, they preserved and protected the Vinaya Piṭaka. Among them, the elder Upatissa was the more skilled. He also had two pupils—the elder Mahāpaduma and the elder Mahāsuma. Among them, the elder Mahāsuma heard the Vinaya Piṭaka nine times, while the elder Mahāpaduma heard it nine times together with him and separately nine times alone—thus eighteen times in total. He was indeed the more skilled of the two. The elder Mahāsuma, having heard the Vinaya Piṭaka nine times, left his teacher and went to the region beyond the Ganges. Then the elder Mahāpaduma said, "What a bold Vinaya-holder this is, who, while his teacher is still alive, abandons him and thinks to dwell elsewhere. Surely, as long as the teacher lives, even after learning the Vinaya Piṭaka and its commentaries many times, one should not depart. One should listen constantly and recite it every year."

Evaṃ vinayagarukānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kāle ekadivasaṃ upatissatthero mahāpadumattherappamukhānaṃ pañcannaṃ antevāsikasatānaṃ paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpade imaṃ padesaṃ vaṇṇento nisinno hoti. Taṃ antevāsikā pucchiṃsu – “bhante, yebhuyyena akkhāyite pārājikaṃ, yebhuyyena khāyite thullaccayaṃ, upaḍḍhakkhāyite kena bhavitabba”nti? Thero āha – “āvuso, buddhā nāma pārājikaṃ [V 1.0211] paññapentā na sāvasesaṃ katvā paññapenti, anavasesaṃyeva katvā sabbaṃ pariyādiyitvā sotaṃ chinditvā pārājikavatthusmiṃ pārājikameva paññapenti. Idañhi sikkhāpadaṃ lokavajjaṃ, na paṇṇattivajjaṃ. Tasmā yadi upaḍḍhakkhāyite pārājikaṃ bhaveyya, paññapeyya sammāsambuddho. Pārājikacchāyā panettha na dissati, thullaccayameva dissatī”ti.

Thus, in the time of monks who revered the Vinaya, one day the elder Upatissa was seated explaining this portion of the first Pārājika training rule to five hundred disciples, headed by the elder Mahāpaduma. Then the disciples asked: "Venerable sir, when mostly unconsumed, it is a Pārājika; when mostly consumed, it is a Thullaccaya. But when half-consumed, what should it be?" The elder replied: "Friends, the Buddhas, when laying down a Pārājika rule, do not do so leaving a remainder. They lay it down only without a remainder, having completely exhausted the matter and cut off the stream; in a matter for a Pārājika offense, they lay down only a Pārājika. For this training rule is a worldly fault, not a fault by enactment. Therefore, if half-consumed were to be a Pārājika, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One would have declared it so. Here, not even the shadow of a Pārājika is seen—only a Thullaccaya is seen."

Apica matasarīre pārājikaṃ paññapento bhagavā yebhuyyena akkhāyite ṭhapesi “tato paraṃ pārājikaṃ natthī”ti dassetuṃ. Thullaccayaṃ paññapento yebhuyyena khāyite ṭhapesi “tato paraṃ thullaccayaṃ natthī”ti dassetuntipi veditabbaṃ. Khāyitākhāyitañca nāmetaṃ matasarīrasmiṃyeva veditabbaṃ, na jīvamāne. Jīvamāne hi nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇepi chavimaṃse vā nhārumhi [M 1.0229] vā sati pārājikameva hoti. Yadipi nimittaṃ sabbaso khāyitaṃ chavicammaṃ natthi, nimittasaṇṭhānaṃ paññāyati, pavesanaṃ jāyati, pārājikameva. Nimittasaṇṭhānaṃ pana anavasesetvā sabbasmiṃ nimitte chinditvā samantato tacchetvā uppāṭite vaṇasaṅkhepavasena thullaccayaṃ. Nimittato patitāya maṃsapesiyā upakkamantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Matasarīre pana yadipi sabbaṃ sarīraṃ khāyitaṃ hoti, yadipi akkhāyitaṃ, tayo pana maggā akkhāyitā, tesu upakkamantassa [P 1.0265] pārājikaṃ. Yebhuyyena akkhāyite pārājikameva. Upaḍḍhakkhāyite ca yebhuyyena khāyite ca thullaccayaṃ.

Moreover, the Blessed One, when prescribing the pārājika offense concerning a dead body, established it in the case of a body that is mostly unconsumed, in order to show that 'beyond that, there is no pārājika offense.' It should also be understood that when prescribing the thullaccaya offense, He established it in the case of a body that is mostly consumed, in order to show that 'beyond that, there is no thullaccaya offense.' And this, namely 'consumed' and 'unconsumed,' should be understood only with regard to a dead body, not a living one. For in the case of a living being, if there is skin and flesh, or sinew, even of the size of the back of a fingernail, it is indeed a pārājika offense. Even if the sexual organ is entirely consumed and there is no skin, if the shape of the sexual organ is discernible and penetration can occur, it is indeed a pārājika offense. However, if, having left no remainder of the shape of the sexual organ, the entire sexual organ has been cut off, scraped all around, and torn out, for one who makes an effort by way of insertion into the wound, there is a thullaccaya offense. For one who makes an effort with a piece of flesh that has fallen from the sexual organ, there is a dukkaṭa offense. However, in the case of a dead body, even if the entire body is consumed, or even if it is unconsumed, if the three orifices are unconsumed, for one who makes an effort in them, there is a pārājika offense. In an orifice that is mostly unconsumed, it is indeed a pārājika offense. In an orifice that is half-consumed and in one that is mostly consumed, there is a thullaccaya offense.
