Manussānaṃ jīvamānakasarīre akkhināsakaṇṇacchiddavatthikosesu satthakādīhi katavaṇe vā methunarāgena tilaphalamattampi aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassa thullaccayameva. Avasesasarīre upakacchakādīsu dukkaṭaṃ. Mate allasarīre pārājikakkhette pārājikaṃ, thullaccayakkhette thullaccayaṃ, dukkaṭakkhette dukkaṭaṃ. Yadā pana sarīraṃ uddhumātakaṃ hoti kuthitaṃ nīlamakkhikasamākiṇṇaṃ kimikulasamākulaṃ navahi vaṇamukhehi paggaḷitapubbakuṇapabhāvena upagantumpi asakkuṇeyyaṃ, tadā pārājikavatthuñca thullaccayavatthuñca vijahati; tādise sarīre yattha katthaci upakkamato dukkaṭameva. Tiracchānagatānaṃ hatthi-assa-goṇa-gadrabha-oṭṭhamahiṃsādīnaṃ nāsāya thullaccayaṃ. Vatthikose thullaccayameva. Sabbesampi tiracchānagatānaṃ akkhikaṇṇavaṇesu dukkaṭaṃ, avasesasarīrepi dukkaṭameva. Matānaṃ allasarīre pārājikakkhette pārājikaṃ, thullaccayakkhette thullaccayaṃ, dukkaṭakkhette dukkaṭaṃ.

In the living body of a human, for one who, with sexual lust, inserts the sexual organ even to the extent of a sesame seed into the eye sockets, nostrils, ear holes, scrotum, or in a wound made by a small knife and so on, there is indeed a thullaccaya offense. For inserting it into the rest of the body, such as the armpits, there is a dukkaṭa offense. In a dead, moist body, in a region for a pārājika offense, there is a pārājika offense; in a region for a thullaccaya offense, there is a thullaccaya offense; in a region for a dukkaṭa offense, there is a dukkaṭa offense. But when the body is bloated, putrid, swarming with bluebottles, infested with families of worms, with pus flowing from the nine wound-orifices, and is unapproachable due to its state as a foul corpse, then it leaves behind the grounds for a pārājika offense and the grounds for a thullaccaya offense; for making an effort anywhere whatsoever in such a body, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. Among animals—such as elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and so on—for one who inserts into the nose, there is a thullaccaya offense. For one who inserts into the scrotum, there is indeed a thullaccaya offense. For all animals, in the eyes, ears, and wounds, there is a dukkaṭa offense; in the rest of the body also, there is indeed a dukkaṭa offense. In the moist body of dead animals, in a region for a pārājika offense, there is a pārājika offense; in a region for a thullaccaya offense, there is a thullaccaya offense; in a region for a dukkaṭa offense, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

Kuthitakuṇape pana pubbe vuttanayeneva sabbattha dukkaṭaṃ. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena vā methunarāgena vā jīvamānakapurisassa vatthikosaṃ appavesento nimittena nimittaṃ chupati, dukkaṭaṃ. Methunarāgena [V 1.0212] itthiyā appavesento nimittena nimittaṃ chupati, thullaccayaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “itthinimittaṃ methunarāgena mukhena chupati thullaccaya”nti vuttaṃ. Cammakkhandhake “chabbaggiyā bhikkhū aciravatiyā nadiyā gāvīnaṃ tarantīnaṃ visāṇesupi gaṇhanti, kaṇṇesupi gaṇhanti, gīvāyapi gaṇhanti, cheppāyapi gaṇhanti, piṭṭhimpi abhiruhanti, rattacittāpi aṅgajātaṃ chupantī”ti (mahāva. 252) imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā avisesena vuttaṃ – “na ca, bhikkhave, rattacittena aṅgajātaṃ chupitabbaṃ, yo chupeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti [M 1.0230] (mahāva. 252). Taṃ sabbampi saṃsanditvā yathā na virujjhati tathā gahetabbaṃ. Kathañca [P 1.0266] na virujjhati? Yaṃ tāva mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “methunarāgena mukhena chupatī”ti. Tatra kira nimittamukhaṃ mukhanti adhippetaṃ. “Methunarāgenā”ti ca vuttattāpi ayameva tattha adhippāyoti veditabbo. Na hi itthinimitte pakatimukhena methunupakkamo hoti. Khandhakepi ye piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhantā methunarāgena aṅgajātena aṅgajātaṃ chupiṃsu, te sandhāya thullaccayaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Itarathā hi dukkaṭaṃ siyā. Keci panāhu “khandhakepi mukheneva chupanaṃ sandhāya oḷārikattā kammassa thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyampi taṃ sandhāyabhāsitaṃ gahetvāva methunarāgena mukhena chupati thullaccayanti vutta”nti. Tasmā suṭṭhu sallakkhetvā ubhosu vinicchayesu yo yuttataro so gahetabbo. Vinayaññū pana purimaṃ pasaṃsanti. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena pana pakatimukhena vā nimittamukhena vā itthinimittaṃ chupantassa saṅghādiseso. Tiracchānagatitthiyā passāvamaggaṃ nimittamukhena chupantassa vuttanayeneva thullaccayaṃ. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena dukkaṭanti.

However, in a putrid corpse, by the same method as stated before, there is a dukkaṭa offense in all places. If, with lust for bodily contact or with sexual lust, without inserting into the scrotum of a living man, one touches sexual organ with sexual organ, there is a dukkaṭa offense. If, with sexual lust, without inserting into a woman, one touches sexual organ with sexual organ, there is a thullaccaya offense. However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'If one touches a woman's sexual organ with the mouth with sexual lust, it is a thullaccaya offense.' In the Cammakkhandhaka, regarding the incident where 'the group-of-six monks, while cows were crossing the Aciravatī river, grabbed their horns, ears, necks, and tails, mounted their backs, and with lustful minds, touched the sexual organ,' it was stated generally: 'Monks, one should not touch the sexual organ with a lustful mind. Whoever should touch it, there is an offense of thullaccaya.' All of this should be collated and understood in such a way that it is not contradictory. And how is it not contradictory? Firstly, regarding what is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, 'touches with the mouth with sexual lust,' it is said that 'mouth' is intended to mean the tip of the sexual organ. And because it is said 'with sexual lust,' it should be known that this very meaning is intended there. For an attempt at intercourse with a woman's sexual organ does not happen with the ordinary mouth. Also in the Khandhaka, it should be understood that the thullaccaya offense was stated with reference to those who, while mounting the backs of the cows, touched sexual organ with sexual organ with sexual lust. Otherwise, it would be a dukkaṭa offense. Some teachers, however, say: 'Also in the Khandhaka, the thullaccaya offense was stated with reference to touching with the mouth itself, due to the grossness of the act. In the Aṭṭhakathā as well, taking that which was spoken with reference to this, it was said: "touching with the mouth with sexual lust is a thullaccaya offense."' Therefore, having carefully considered, of the two decisions, the one that is more suitable should be taken. However, those who know the Vinaya praise the former decision. However, for one who touches a woman's sexual organ with the ordinary mouth or with the tip of the sexual organ with lust for bodily contact, there is a saṅghādisesa offense. For one who touches the urinary passage of a female animal with the tip of the sexual organ with sexual lust, by the method already stated, there is a thullaccaya offense. Touching it with lust for bodily contact is a dukkaṭa offense.

Ekūnasattatidvisatacatukkakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Two Hundred and Sixty-Nine Quatrains is concluded.

Santhatacatukkabhedakathā

The Discourse on the Analysis of the Quatrain on Felt Rugs

61-62. Evaṃ bhagavā paṭipannakassa bhikkhuno rakkhaṇatthaṃ sattatidvisatacatukkāni nīharitvā “idāni ye anāgate pāpabhikkhū ‘santhataṃ imaṃ na kiñci upādinnakaṃ upādinnakena phusati, ko ettha doso’ti sañcicca lesaṃ oḍḍessanti, tesaṃ sāsane patiṭṭhā eva na bhavissatī”ti disvā tesu sattatidvisatacatukkesu ekamekaṃ catukkaṃ catūhi santhatādibhedehi bhinditvā dassento bhikkhupaccatthikā manussitthiṃ bhikkhussa santike ānetvā vaccamaggena passāvamaggena mukhena aṅgajātaṃ abhinisīdenti santhatāya asanthatassātiādimāha.

Thus the Blessed One, for the protection of the monk who practices insight meditation, having brought forth the two hundred and seventy fourfold groups, and having foreseen, 'Now, in the future, whatever evil monks, thinking, "This is covered; no appropriated matter touches appropriated matter. What is the fault herein?", will intentionally set up a pretext,' and 'For them, there will be no footing at all in the Dispensation,' divided each one of those two hundred and seventy fourfold groups by the four divisions beginning with 'covered,' and showing this, spoke the passage beginning with 'bhikkhupaccatthikā... asanthatassa'.

Tattha santhatāya asanthatassātiādīsu santhatāya itthiyā vaccamaggena passāvamaggena mukhena [V 1.0213] asanthatassa bhikkhussa aṅgajātaṃ abhinisīdentīti iminā [M 1.0231] nayena yojanā veditabbā. Tattha santhatā nāma yassā tīsu [P 1.0267] maggesu yo koci maggo paliveṭhetvā vā anto vā pavesetvā yena kenaci vatthena vā paṇṇena vā vākapaṭṭena vā cammena vā tipusīsādīnaṃ paṭṭena vā paṭicchanno. Santhato nāma yassa aṅgajātaṃ tesaṃyeva vatthādīnaṃ yena kenaci paṭicchannaṃ. Tattha upādinnakena vā anupādinnakaṃ ghaṭṭiyatu, anupādinnakena vā upādinnakaṃ, anupādinnakena vā anupādinnakaṃ, upādinnakena vā upādinnakaṃ, sace yattake paviṭṭhe pārājikaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ, tattakaṃ pavisati, sabbattha sādiyantassa pārājikakkhette pārājikaṃ; thullaccayakkhette thullaccayaṃ, dukkaṭakkhette dukkaṭameva hoti. Sace itthinimittaṃ khāṇuṃ katvā santhataṃ, khāṇuṃ ghaṭṭentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Sace purisanimittaṃ khāṇuṃ katvā santhataṃ, khāṇuṃ pavesentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Sace ubhayaṃ khāṇuṃ katvā santhataṃ, khāṇunā khāṇuṃ ghaṭṭentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Sace itthinimitte veḷunaḷapabbādīnaṃ kiñci pakkhittaṃ, tassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ cepi phusanto tilaphalamattaṃ paveseti, pārājikaṃ. Uparibhāgaṃ cepi ubhosu passesu ekapassaṃ cepi phusanto paveseti, pārājikaṃ. Cattāripi passāni aphusanto pavesetvā tassa talaṃ cepi phusati, pārājikaṃ. Yadi pana passesu vā tale vā aphusanto ākāsagatameva katvā pavesetvā nīharati, dukkaṭaṃ. Bahiddhā khāṇuke phusati dukkaṭameva. Yathā ca itthinimitte vuttaṃ, evaṃ sabbattha lakkhaṇaṃ veditabbanti.

Therein, in the phrases beginning with 'of a covered one, for an uncovered one,' the application should be known by this method: they cause the genital organ of an uncovered monk to be sat upon by the passage for excrement, the passage for urine, or the mouth of a covered woman. Therein, a woman is called 'covered' (santhatā) if any one of her three passages is covered, either by wrapping around or inserting inside, with any kind of cloth, leaf, strip of bark, leather, or a plate of tin, lead, or the like. A monk is called 'covered' (santhato) if his genital organ is covered by any of those same things, such as cloth. Therein, whether appropriated matter touches unappropriated matter, or unappropriated matter touches appropriated matter, or unappropriated matter touches unappropriated matter, or appropriated matter touches appropriated matter, if it penetrates to the extent about which it was said, 'When this much has been inserted, it is a Pārājika,' then for one who consents, it is a Pārājika in the sphere of Pārājika, a Thullaccaya in the sphere of Thullaccaya, and a Dukkaṭa in the sphere of Dukkaṭa in all cases. If the female sign is made into a stump and is covered, for one who touches the stump, it is a Dukkaṭa. If the male sign is made into a stump and is covered, for one who inserts into the stump, it is a Dukkaṭa. If both are made into stumps and are covered, for one who touches a stump with a stump, it is a Dukkaṭa. If something like a bamboo joint or a reed joint is placed in the female sign, if one inserts to the measure of a sesame seed while touching even its lower part, it is a Pārājika. If one inserts while touching even the upper part, or even one of the two sides, it is a Pārājika. Having inserted without touching any of the four sides, if one touches even its base, it is a Pārājika. But if one, without touching the sides or the base, having made it pass only through the space, inserts and then withdraws it, it is a Dukkaṭa. If one touches the stump on the outside, it is a Dukkaṭa indeed. And just as it was stated in the case of the female sign, so should the characteristic be understood in all cases.

Santhatacatukkabhedakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Division of the Covered Fourfold Group is concluded.

Bhikkhupaccatthikacatukkabhedavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Fourfold Division Concerning the Monk's Adversary

63-64. Evaṃ santhatacatukkabhedaṃ vatvā idāni yasmā na kevalaṃ manussitthiādike bhikkhussa eva santike ānenti. Atha kho bhikkhumpi tāsaṃ santike ānenti, tasmā tappabhedaṃ dassento “bhikkhupaccatthikā bhikkhuṃ manussitthiyā santike”ti ādinā nayena sabbāni tāni catukkāni punapi nīharitvā dassesi. Tesu vinicchayo vuttanayeneva veditabboti.

Having thus spoken on the fourfold division concerning the covered, now, because they do not only bring human women and so on near a monk, but indeed they also bring a monk near them, therefore, to show that distinction, he again brought forth and showed all those fourfold sets by the method beginning with 'the monk's adversaries (bring) a monk near a human woman,' and so on. In these, the determination should be understood by the method already stated.

Bhikkhupaccatthikavasena catukkabhedavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the fourfold division regarding the monk's adversary is concluded.

Rājapaccatthikādicatukkabhedakathā

The Discourse on the Fourfold Division Beginning with the King's Adversaries

65. Yasmā [M 1.0232][P 1.0268][V 1.0214] pana na bhikkhupaccatthikā eva evaṃ karonti, rājapaccatthikādayopi karonti. Tasmā tampi pabhedaṃ dassento “rājapaccatthikā”tiādimāha. Tattha rājāno eva paccatthikā rājapaccatthikā. Te ca sayaṃ ānentāpi aññehi āṇāpentāpi ānentiyevāti veditabbā. Corā eva paccatthikā corapaccatthikā. Dhuttāti methunupasaṃhitakhiḍḍāpasutā nāgarikakerāṭiyapurisā, itthidhuttasurādhuttādayo vā; dhuttā eva paccatthikā dhuttapaccatthikā. Gandhanti hadayaṃ vuccati, taṃ uppāṭentīti uppalagandhā, uppalagandhā eva paccatthikā uppalagandhapaccatthikā. Ete kira na kasivaṇijjādīhi jīvanti, panthaghātagāmaghātādīni katvā puttadāraṃ posenti. Te kammasiddhiṃ patthayamānā devatānaṃ āyācetvā tāsaṃ balikammatthaṃ manussānaṃ hadayaṃ uppāṭenti. Sabbakāle ca manussā dullabhā. Bhikkhū pana araññe viharantā sulabhā honti. Te sīlavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā “sīlavato vadho nāma bhāriyo hotī”ti maññamānā tassa sīlavināsanatthaṃ manussitthiādike vā ānenti; taṃ vā tattha nenti. Ayamettha viseso. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Bhikkhupaccatthikavāre vuttanayeneva ca imesu catūsupi vāresu catukkāni veditabbāni. Pāḷiyaṃ pana saṃkhittena vuttāni.

65. Furthermore, because not only the monk's adversaries act in this way, but the king's adversaries and others also do so, therefore, to show that distinction as well, he said what begins with 'the king's adversaries.' Therein, kings themselves are the adversaries; these are the 'king's adversaries.' And they, whether bringing someone themselves or commanding others to do so, should be understood as 'those who bring.' Thieves themselves are the adversaries; these are the 'thief's adversaries.' 'Rogues' refers to city-dwelling, crafty men devoted to amusements connected with sexual intercourse, or womanizers, drunkards, and so on; rogues themselves are the adversaries; these are the 'rogue's adversaries.' 'Gandha' is said to be the heart; because they tear it out, they are called 'uppalagandhā.' The uppalagandhā themselves are the adversaries; these are the 'uppalagandha's adversaries.' It is said that these do not make a living by farming, trade, and so on, but support their wives and children by committing highway robbery, village raiding, and the like. They, desiring success in their deeds, pray to deities and, for the purpose of making an offering to them, tear out the hearts of humans. And at all times, humans are difficult to obtain, but monks dwelling in the forest are easy to obtain. They, having seized a virtuous monk and thinking, 'The killing of a virtuous one is indeed a grave matter,' bring human women and so on for the purpose of destroying his virtue, or they take him there. This is the distinction herein. The rest should be understood by the method already stated. And the fourfold sets in these four sections should also be understood by the very method stated in the section on the monk's adversary. In the Pāḷi text, however, they are stated concisely.

Sabbākārena catukkabhedakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the fourfold division in all aspects is concluded.

Āpattānāpattivāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Offenses and Non-Offenses

66. Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ “manussitthiyā tayo magge methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantassā”tiādi, ettha asammohatthaṃ “maggena magga”ntiādimāha. Tattha maggena magganti itthiyā tīsu maggesu aññatarena maggena attano aṅgajātaṃ paveseti atha vā sambhinnesu dvīsu maggesu passāvamaggena vaccamaggaṃ vaccamaggena vā passāvamaggaṃ paveseti. Maggena amagganti passāvādimaggena pavesetvā tassa sāmantā vaṇena nīharati. Amaggena magganti maggasāmantena vaṇena [P 1.0269] pavesetvā maggena nīharati. Amaggena amagganti dvīsu sambhinnavaṇesu ekena vaṇena pavesetvā dutiyena nīharati. Imassa [M 1.0233] suttassa anulomavasena sabbattha vaṇasaṅkhepe thullaccayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

66. Now, regarding what was said, “For one engaging in sexual intercourse with a human woman through the three passages,” etc., to avoid confusion in this matter, He said, “a passage with a passage,” etc. Therein, “a passage with a passage” means one inserts one’s own sexual organ into any one of a woman’s three passages; or, in the case of two conjoined passages, one inserts it into the anal passage through the urinary passage, or into the urinary passage through the anal passage. “A passage with a non-passage” means one inserts it through a passage such as the urinary one and withdraws it through a wound in its vicinity. “A non-passage with a passage” means one inserts it through a wound in the vicinity of a passage and withdraws it through the passage. “A non-passage with a non-passage” means, in the case of two conjoined wounds, one inserts it through one wound and withdraws it through the second. In accordance with this rule, a grave offense should be understood in all cases summarized as involving a wound.

Idāni yaṃ parato vakkhati “anāpatti ajānantassa asādiyantassā”ti, tattha asammohatthaṃ [V 1.0215] “bhikkhu suttabhikkhumhī”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yo paṭibuddho sādiyati so “suttamhi mayi eso vippaṭipajji, nāhaṃ jānāmī”ti na muccati. Ubho nāsetabbāti cettha dvepi liṅganāsanena nāsetabbā. Tatra dūsakassa paṭiññākaraṇaṃ natthi, dūsito pucchitvā paṭiññāya nāsetabbo. Sace na sādiyati, na nāsetabbo. Esa nayo sāmaṇeravārepi.

Now, regarding what will be said later, “There is no offense for one who is unaware, for one who does not consent,” to avoid confusion in this matter, He said, “A monk, in a sleeping monk…” etc. Therein, this is the intended meaning: he who, being awake, consents, is not freed from the offense by saying, “This one transgressed against me while I was sleeping; I did not know.” And in the phrase, “Both should be destroyed,” both are to be destroyed by the destruction of their characteristic [i.e., disrobed]. Therein, there is no making the defiler confess; the one who was defiled, having been questioned, is to be destroyed upon his confession. If he does not consent, he is not to be destroyed. This is the same method in the section on novices as well.

Evaṃ tattha tattha taṃ taṃ āpattiñca anāpattiñca dassetvā idāni anāpattimeva dassento “anāpatti ajānantassā”tiādimāha. Tattha ajānanto nāma yo mahāniddaṃ okkanto parena kataṃ upakkamampi na jānāti vesāliyaṃ mahāvane divāvihāragato bhikkhu viya. Evarūpassa anāpatti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “‘nāhaṃ bhagavā jānāmī’ti; ‘anāpatti, bhikkhu, ajānantassā’”ti (pārā. 75). Asādiyanto nāma yo jānitvāpi na sādiyati, tattheva sahasā vuṭṭhitabhikkhu viya. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “‘nāhaṃ bhagavā sādiyi’nti. ‘Anāpatti, bhikkhu, asādiyantassā”ti.

Having thus shown the respective offenses and non-offenses in various cases, now, showing only the non-offense, He says, “There is no offense for one who does not know,” etc. Therein, “one who does not know” is he who, having entered a deep sleep, does not know even the attempt made by another, like the monk who had gone for the day’s abiding in the Great Forest at Vesālī. For one of such a nature, there is no offense. And this was also said: “‘I did not know, Blessed One.’ ‘There is no offense, monk, for one who does not know.’” “One who does not consent” is he who, even knowing, does not consent, like the monk who suddenly arose in that very place. And this was also said: “‘I did not consent, Blessed One.’ ‘There is no offense, monk, for one who does not consent.’”

Ummattako nāma pittummattako. Duvidhañhi pittaṃ – baddhapittaṃ, abaddhapittañcāti. Tattha abaddhapittaṃ lohitaṃ viya sabbaṅgagataṃ, tamhi kupite sattānaṃ kaṇḍukacchusarīrakampādīni honti. Tāni bhesajjakiriyāya vūpasamanti. Baddhapittaṃ pana pittakosake ṭhitaṃ. Tamhi kupite sattā ummattakā honti vipallatthasaññā hirottappaṃ chaḍḍetvā asāruppācāraṃ caranti. Lahukagarukāni sikkhāpadāni maddantāpi na jānanti. Bhesajjakiriyāyapi atekicchā honti. Evarūpassa ummattakassa anāpatti.

A madman is one maddened by bile. For bile is of two kinds: bound bile and unbound bile. Therein, unbound bile, like blood, pervades the entire body. When it is agitated, beings experience such things as itching, scabies, and bodily tremors. These are pacified by medical treatment. Bound bile, however, is situated in the bile sac. When it is agitated, beings become mad, have perverted perception, and, having abandoned moral shame and moral dread, engage in unsuitable conduct. Even while transgressing minor and major training rules, they do not know. They are also incurable by medical treatment. For such a madman, there is no offense.

Khittacitto nāma vissaṭṭhacitto yakkhummattako vuccati. Yakkhā kira bheravāni vā ārammaṇāni dassetvā mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetvā [P 1.0270] hadayarūpaṃ vā maddantā satte vikkhittacitte vipallatthasaññe karonti. Evarūpassa khittacittassa anāpatti. Tesaṃ pana ubhinnaṃ ayaṃ viseso – pittummattako niccameva ummattako hoti, pakatisaññaṃ na labhati. Yakkhummattako [M 1.0234] antarantarā pakatisaññaṃ paṭilabhatīti. Idha pana pittummattako vā hotu yakkhummattako vā, yo sabbaso muṭṭhassati kiñci na jānāti, aggimpi suvaṇṇampi gūthampi candanampi ekasadisaṃ maddantova vicarati, evarūpassa anāpatti. Antarantarā saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā ñatvā karontassa pana āpattiyeva.

One with a deranged mind, that is, one with a scattered mind, is called one maddened by a yakkha. Yakkhas, it is said, make beings have scattered minds and perverted perception either by showing them frightful objects or by inserting a hand through the mouth and crushing the heart-materiality. For such a one with a deranged mind, there is no offense. But this is the difference between the two: one maddened by bile is always mad and does not regain normal perception; one maddened by a yakkha intermittently regains normal perception. Here, however, whether one is maddened by bile or maddened by a yakkha, for one who is completely unmindful, knows nothing, and wanders about trampling on fire, gold, excrement, and sandalwood as if they were all the same—for such a one, there is no offense. But for one who acts after having intermittently regained perception and with knowledge, there is indeed an offense.

Vedanāṭṭo [V 1.0216] nāma yo adhimattāya dukkhavedanāya āturo kiñci na jānāti, evarūpassa anāpatti.

One overcome by pain is one who, afflicted by intense painful feeling, knows nothing. For such a one, there is no offense.

Ādikammiko nāma yo tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kamme ādibhūto. Idha pana sudinnatthero ādikammiko, tassa anāpatti. Avasesānaṃ makkaṭīsamaṇavajjiputtakādīnaṃ āpattiyevāti.

The first-doer is he who is the originator of a particular action. Here, in this training rule, the Elder Sudinna was the first-doer; for him, there is no offense. For the remaining ones, such as the monk who consorted with the she-monkey, the Vajjian-puttaka monks, and others, there is indeed an offense.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the word-analysis is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

A Discourse on Miscellaneous Matters

Imasmiṃ pana sikkhāpade kosallatthaṃ idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃveditabbaṃ –

Furthermore, in this training rule, for the sake of proficiency, this miscellaneous discourse should be understood:

“Samuṭṭhānañca kiriyā, atho saññā sacittakaṃ;

Lokavajjañca kammañca, kusalaṃ vedanāya cā”ti.

Origin and action, and also perception, that with consciousness; worldly fault and kamma, and the wholesome, along with feeling.

Tattha “samuṭṭhāna”nti sabbasaṅgāhakavasena cha sikkhāpadasamuṭṭhānāni. Tāni parivāre āvi bhavissanti. Samāsato pana sikkhāpadaṃ nāma – atthi chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, atthi catusamuṭṭhānaṃ, atthi tisamuṭṭhānaṃ, atthi kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ, atthi eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ, atthi dhuranikkhepādisamuṭṭhānanti.

Therein, ‘origin’ means that, by way of a comprehensive inclusion, there are six origins of training rules. These will become clear in the Parivāra. In brief, however, as for a training rule, there is that of six origins, there is that of Kathina-origin, there is that of eḷaka-wool-origin, there is that of laying-down-the-yoke-origin, and so on.

Tatrāpi kiñci kiriyato samuṭṭhāti, kiñci akiriyato samuṭṭhāti, kiñci kiriyākiriyato samuṭṭhāti, kiñci siyā kiriyato, siyā akiriyato samuṭṭhāti, kiñci siyā kiriyato siyā kiriyākiriyato samuṭṭhāti.

Therein also, some arise from action, some arise from non-action, some arise from action and non-action. Some may arise from action or may arise from non-action. Some may arise from action or may arise from action and non-action.

Tatrāpi atthi saññāvimokkhaṃ, atthi nosaññāvimokkhaṃ. Tattha yaṃ cittaṅgaṃ labhatiyeva, taṃ saññāvimokkhaṃ; itaraṃ nosaññāvimokkhaṃ.

Therein also, there is that which is an exemption through perception, and there is that which is not an exemption through perception. Therein, that which necessarily involves the mental factor is an exemption through perception; the other is not an exemption through perception.

Puna [M 1.0235] atthi sacittakaṃ, atthi acittakaṃ. Yaṃ saheva cittena āpajjati, taṃ sacittakaṃ; yaṃ vināpi cittena āpajjati, taṃ acittakaṃ[P 1.0271]. Taṃ sabbampi lokavajjaṃ paṇṇattivajjanti duvidhaṃ. Tesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vuttameva.

Again, there is that which is with consciousness, and there is that which is without consciousness. That which one incurs only together with consciousness is ‘with consciousness’; that which one incurs even without consciousness is ‘without consciousness’. All of that is twofold: fault in the world and fault by designation. Their characteristics have indeed been stated.

Kammakusalavedanāvasenāpi [V 1.0217] cettha atthi sikkhāpadaṃ kāyakammaṃ, atthi vacīkammaṃ. Tattha yaṃ kāyadvārikaṃ, taṃ kāyakammaṃ; yaṃ vacīdvārikaṃ, taṃ vacīkammanti veditabbaṃ. Atthi pana sikkhāpadaṃ kusalaṃ, atthi akusalaṃ, atthi abyākataṃ. Dvattiṃseva hi āpattisamauṭṭhāpakacittāni – aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalāni, dvādasa akusalāni, dasa kāmāvacarakiriyacittāni, kusalato ca kiriyato ca dve abhiññācittānīti. Tesu yaṃ kusalacittena āpajjati, taṃ kusalaṃ; itarehi itaraṃ. Atthi ca sikkhāpadaṃ tivedanaṃ, atthi dvivedanaṃ, atthi ekavedanaṃ. Tattha yaṃ āpajjanto tīsu vedanāsu aññataravedanāsamaṅgī hutvā āpajjati, taṃ tivedanaṃ; yaṃ āpajjanto sukhasamaṅgī vā upekkhāsamaṅgī vā āpajjati, taṃ dvivedanaṃ; yaṃ āpajjanto dukkhavedanāsamaṅgīyeva āpajjati, taṃ ekavedananti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ –

And also herein, by way of kamma, the wholesome, and feeling: there is a training rule that is bodily kamma, and there is one that is verbal kamma. Therein, what is of the body-door is bodily kamma; what is of the speech-door is verbal kamma—so it should be understood. Furthermore, there is a training rule that is wholesome, there is one that is unwholesome, and there is one that is indeterminate. For there are indeed thirty-two consciousnesses that originate an offense: eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, twelve unwholesome ones, ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses, and two supernormal-knowledge consciousnesses from the wholesome and the functional. Among these, that which one incurs with a wholesome consciousness is 'wholesome'; that which is incurred through the others is 'the other'. And there is a training rule with three feelings, one with two feelings, and one with one feeling. Therein, that which one incurs while endowed with any one of the three feelings is 'with three feelings'. That which one incurs while endowed with either pleasant feeling or equanimous feeling is 'with two feelings'. That which one incurs while endowed only with painful feeling is 'with one feeling'—so it should be understood. Thus:

“Samuṭṭhānañca kiriyā, atho saññā sacittakaṃ;

Lokavajjañca kammañca, kusalaṃ vedanāya cā”ti.

“Origin and action, and also perception, that with consciousness; worldly fault and kamma, and the wholesome, along with feeling.”

Imaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ viditvā tesu samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samuṭṭhānato ekasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Aṅgavasena dukasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kāyacittato samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyasamuṭṭhānañca karontoyeva hi etaṃ āpajjati. Methunapaṭisaṃyuttāya kāmasaññāya abhāvena muccanato saññāvimokkhaṃ. “Anāpatti ajānantassa asādiyantassā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Methunacitteneva naṃ āpajjati, na vinā cittenāti sacittakaṃ. Rāgavaseneva āpajjitabbato lokavajjaṃ. Kāyadvāreneva samuṭṭhānato kāyakammaṃ. Cittaṃ panettha aṅgamattaṃ hoti, na tassa vasena kammabhāvo labbhati. Lobhacittena āpajjitabbato akusalacittaṃ. Sukhasamaṅgī vā upekkhāsamaṅgī vā taṃ āpajjatīti dvivedananti veditabbaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ āpattiyaṃ yujjati. Sikkhāpadasīsena pana sabbaaṭṭhakathāsudesanā ārūḷhā, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

Having understood this miscellaneous discourse, among these origins and so on, this training rule, from the perspective of origin, is of one origin. By way of factors, it is of two origins; it arises from body and mind. And it is of action-origin, for one incurs this only by performing the act. It is an exemption through perception, because one is exempted by the absence of sensual perception connected with sexual intercourse. For it has been said: 'There is no offense for one who does not know and does not consent.' One incurs it only with a mind for sexual intercourse, not without the mind; thus, it is 'with consciousness'. Because it is to be incurred only through the power of lust, it is a 'fault in the world'. Because it arises only through the body-door, it is 'bodily kamma'. Herein, the mind is merely a factor; the state of being kamma is not obtained by way of it. Because it is to be incurred with a mind of greed, it is 'unwholesome consciousness'. One incurs it while endowed with pleasure or endowed with equanimity; thus, it should be understood as 'with two feelings'. And all this is applicable to the offense. However, the discourse in all the commentaries is established under the heading of the training rule; therefore, it was stated thus.

Pakiṇṇakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Miscellaneous Matters is concluded.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Decided Cases

Makkaṭī [M 1.0236][P 1.0272] vajjiputtā ca…pe… vuḍḍhapabbajito migoti idaṃ kiṃ? Imā vinītavatthūnaṃ bhagavatā sayaṃ vinicchitānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ uddānagāthā nāma. Tāni vatthūni “sukhaṃ vinayadharā [V 1.0218] uggaṇhissantī”ti dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi ṭhapitāni. Vatthugāthā pana dharamāneyeva bhagavati upālittherena ṭhapitā “iminā lakkhaṇena āyatiṃ vinayadharā vinayaṃ vinicchinissantī”ti. Tasmā ettha vuttalakkhaṇaṃ sādhukaṃ sallakkhetvā paṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Dutiyādīnañca vinītavatthūsu vuttalakkhaṇena dutiyādīni. Vinītavatthūni hi sippikānaṃ paṭicchannakarūpāni viya vinayadharānaṃ paṭicchannakavatthūni hontīti.

“The she-monkey, the Vajjian-prince… (and so on) …the old renunciate Miga.” What is this? These are the summary verses for those various cases decided by the Blessed One himself; they are called the summary verses of the decided cases. These cases were established by the elders of the Dhamma council with the thought that “those who uphold the Vinaya may learn them with ease.” The case verses, however, were established by the Elder Upāli while the Blessed One was still living, with the thought that “by this characteristic, future upholders of the Vinaya will decide upon the Vinaya.” Therefore, having carefully noted the characteristic stated herein, the first training rule should be decided. And the second and subsequent training rules should be decided by the characteristic stated in the decided cases for the second and subsequent rules. For the decided cases are like the hidden forms of craftsmen; they are the hidden cases for the upholders of the Vinaya.

67. Tattha purimāni dve vatthūni anupaññattiyaṃyeva vuttatthāni. Tatiye vatthumhi gihiliṅgenāti gihivesena odātavattho hutvā. Catutthe natthi kiñci vattabbaṃ. Tato paresu sattasu vatthūsu kusacīranti kuse ganthetvā katacīraṃ. Vākacīraṃ nāma tāpasānaṃ vakkalaṃ. Phalakacīraṃ nāma phalakasaṇṭhānāni phalakāni sibbitvā katacīraṃ. Kesakambaloti kesehi tante vāyitvā katakambalo. Vālakambaloti camaravālehi vāyitvā katakambalo. Ulūkapakkhikanti ulūkasakuṇassa pakkhehi katanivāsanaṃ. Ajinakkhipanti salomaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinamigacammaṃ. Dvādasame vatthumhi sārattoti kāyasaṃsaggarāgena sāratto; taṃ rāgaṃ ñatvā bhagavā “āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti āha.

67. Herein, the meaning of the first two cases has already been stated in the supplementary regulation. In the third case, 'in the guise of a householder' means having worn white clothes in the manner of a householder. Regarding the fourth, there is nothing to be said. In the seven cases that follow, 'a kusa-grass garment' means a garment made by weaving kusa grass. 'A bark garment' is the bark-cloth of ascetics. 'A wooden-plank garment' means a garment made by sewing together small pieces shaped like planks. 'A hair blanket' means a blanket woven with human hair on a loom. 'A tail-hair blanket' means a blanket woven with the tail-hairs of a camara animal. 'An owl's wing garment' means a lower garment made from the wings of an owl. 'An ajina-hide garment' means the hide of an ajina deer, complete with its hair and hooves. In the twelfth case, 'impassioned' means being impassioned with the lust for bodily contact; knowing that lust, the Blessed One said, 'It is a Saṅghādisesa offense.'

68. Terasame vatthumhi uppalavaṇṇāti sā therī sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhidhītā satasahassakappe abhinīhārasampannā. Tassā pakatiyāpi atidassanīyā nīluppalavaṇṇā kāyacchavi, abbhantare pana [P 1.0273] kilesasantāpassa abhāvena ativiya virocati. Sā tāyeva vaṇṇapokkharatāya “uppalavaṇṇā”ti nāmaṃ labhi. Paṭibaddhacittoti gihikālato paṭṭhāya rattacitto; so kira tassā ñātidārako hoti. Atha khoti anantaratthe nipāto; mañcake nisinnānantaramevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Divā bāhirato āgantvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nisinnānañhi paṭhamaṃ andhakāraṃ hoti. So yāvassā taṃ andhakāraṃ na nassati, tāvadeva [M 1.0237] evamakāsīti attho. Dūsesīti padhaṃsesi. Therī pana anavajjā attano samaṇasaññaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā asādiyantī nisīdi asaddhammādhippāyena parāmaṭṭhā aggikkhandha-silāthambha-khadirasārakhāṇukā viya. Sopi attano manorathaṃ pūretvā gato. Tassā theriyā dassanapathaṃ vijahantasseva ayaṃ mahāpathavī sinerupabbataṃ dhāretuṃ samatthāpi taṃ pāpapurisaṃ byāmamattakaḷevaraṃ dhāretuṃ asakkontī viya bhijjitvā vivaramadāsi. So taṅkhaṇaññeva avīcijālānaṃ indhanabhāvaṃ agamāsi. Bhagavā taṃ sutvā “anāpatti, bhikkhave, asādiyantiyā”ti vatvā theriṃ sandhāya dhammapade imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

68. In the thirteenth case, Uppalavaṇṇā: that elder nun was a treasurer's daughter in Sāvatthī, who had made an aspiration one hundred thousand eons ago. By nature, her skin's complexion was exceedingly beautiful, like the color of a blue lotus, and due to the absence of the inner heat of defilements, it shone all the more. Because of this excellent complexion, she received the name 'Uppalavaṇṇā.' 'With mind attached' means that from her time as a layperson, he was infatuated with her; it is said he was a young relative of hers. The particle 'atha kho' indicates immediacy; meaning this happened just after she sat on the couch. For when one comes from outside during the day and closes the door, it is dark at first. The meaning is that he did this while that darkness had not yet dispersed for her. 'He violated her' means he ruined her. The elder nun, however, was blameless. Establishing her perception as a monastic, she sat without consenting, like a mass of fire, a stone pillar, or a stake of acacia heartwood when touched with wrongful intent. He too, having fulfilled his heart's desire, departed. Just as he was leaving the elder nun's range of sight, this great earth—though capable of supporting Mount Sineru—as if unable to support that evil man's fathom-long body, split apart and gave an opening. At that very moment, he became fuel for the flames of Avīci. The Blessed One, having heard of this, said, 'Bhikkhus, there is no offense for one who does not consent,' and with reference to the elder nun, he spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

“Vāri [V 1.0219] pokkharapatteva, āraggeriva sāsapo;

Yo na limpati kāmesu, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 401);

“Like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl, one who is not smeared by sensual pleasures—that one I call a brāhmaṇa.”

69. Cuddasame vatthumhi itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhūtanti rattibhāge niddaṃ okkantassa purisasaṇṭhānaṃ massudāṭhikādi sabbaṃ antarahitaṃ itthisaṇṭhānaṃ uppannaṃ. Tameva upajjhaṃ tameva upasampadanti pubbe gahitaupajjhāyameva pubbe kataupasampadameva anujānāmi. Puna upajjhā na gahetabbā; upasampadā na kātabbāti attho. Tāniyeva [P 1.0274] vassānīti bhikkhuupasampadato pabhuti yāva vassagaṇanā, taṃyeva vassagaṇanaṃ anujānāmi. Na ito paṭṭhāya vassagaṇanā kātabbāti attho. Bhikkhunīhi saṅgamitunti bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ saṅgamituṃ saṅgantuṃ samaṅgī bhavituṃ anujānāmīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – appatirūpaṃ dānissā bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe vasituṃ, bhikkhunupassayaṃ gantvā bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ vasatūti. Yā āpattiyo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi sādhāraṇāti yā desanāgāminiyo vā vuṭṭhānagāminiyo vā āpattiyo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ sādhāraṇā. Tā āpattiyo bhikkhunīnaṃ santike vuṭṭhātunti tā sabbāpi bhikkhunīhi kātabbaṃ vinayakammaṃ katvā bhikkhunīnaṃ santike vuṭṭhātuṃ anujānāmīti attho. Tāhi āpattīhi anāpattīti yā pana bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi asādhāraṇā sukkavissaṭṭhi-ādikā āpattiyo, tāhi anāpatti. Liṅgaparivattanena tā āpattiyo vuṭṭhitāva honti. Puna pakatiliṅge uppannepi tāhi āpattīhi tassa anāpattiyevāti ayaṃ tāvettha pāḷivinicchayo.

69. In the fourteenth case, 'the female characteristic appeared' means that during the night, while he had fallen asleep, the entire male form—beard, mustache, and so on—disappeared, and the female form arose. 'The same preceptor, the same ordination' means: I allow the very preceptor taken before and the very ordination performed before. The meaning is that a preceptor is not to be taken again, and an ordination is not to be performed again. 'The same number of rains-residences' means: whatever the count of rains-residences is from the time of his bhikkhu ordination, I allow that very same count. The meaning is that the count of rains-residences is not to be made starting from this time. 'To associate with bhikkhunīs' means: I allow her to move in with, associate with, and be in communion with the bhikkhunīs. This is what is said: It is now unsuitable for her to live in the midst of the bhikkhus; let her go to a bhikkhunī monastery and live with the bhikkhunīs. 'Whatever offenses are common to bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs' means: whatever offenses leading to confession or leading to rehabilitation are common to bhikkhus with bhikkhunīs. 'Those offenses are to be cleared in the presence of the bhikkhunīs' means: I allow her to be cleared of all those offenses in the presence of the bhikkhunīs, after having done the Vinaya procedure that should be done by the bhikkhunīs. 'There is no offense regarding those offenses' means: as for those offenses not common to bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, such as the emission of semen and so on, for those there is no offense. By the change of gender, those offenses are already cleared. Even if the original gender arises again, for that person there is still no offense regarding those offenses. This, for now, is the decision on the Pāḷi herein.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0238] pana pāḷimutto okkantikavinicchayo – imesu tāva dvīsu liṅgesu purisaliṅgaṃ uttamaṃ, itthiliṅgaṃ hīnaṃ; tasmā purisaliṅgaṃ balavaakusalena antaradhāyati. Itthiliṅgaṃ dubbalakusalena patiṭṭhāti. Itthiliṅgaṃ pana antaradhāyantaṃ dubbalaakusalena antaradhāyati. Purisaliṅgaṃ balavakusalena patiṭṭhāti. Evaṃ ubhayampi akusalena antaradhāyati, kusalena paṭilabbhati.

Now, this is the extra-canonical incidental decision: among these two genders, the male gender is superior, the female gender is inferior. Therefore, the male gender disappears due to strong unwholesome karma, and the female gender is established due to weak wholesome karma. The female gender, however, disappears due to weak unwholesome karma, and the male gender is established due to strong wholesome karma. Thus, in both transformations, a gender disappears due to unwholesome karma, and is attained through wholesome karma.

Tattha sace dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ekato sajjhāyaṃ vā dhammasākacchaṃ vā katvā ekāgāre nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkantānaṃ ekassa itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhavati, ubhinnampi sahaseyyāpatti hoti. So ce paṭibujjhitvā attano taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā dukkhī dummano rattibhāgeyeva itarassa āroceyya, tena samassāsetabbo – “hotu, mā cintayittha. Vaṭṭasseveso doso. Sammāsambuddhena dvāraṃ dinnaṃ, bhikkhu vā hotu bhikkhunī vā, anāvaṭo dhammo [P 1.0275] avārito saggamaggo”ti. Samassāsetvā ca evaṃ vattabbaṃ – “tumhehi bhikkhunupassayaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Atthi [V 1.0220] vo kāci sandiṭṭhā bhikkhuniyo”ti. Sacassā honti tādisā bhikkhuniyo atthīti, no ce honti natthīti vatvā so bhikkhu vattabbo – “mama saṅgahaṃ karotha; idāni maṃ paṭhamaṃ bhikkhunupassayaṃ nethā”ti. Tena bhikkhunā taṃ gahetvā tassā vā sandiṭṭhānaṃ attano vā sandiṭṭhānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ santikaṃ gantabbaṃ. Gacchantena ca na ekakena gantabbaṃ. Catūhi pañcahi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ jotikañca kattaradaṇḍañca gahetvā saṃvidahanaṃ parimocetvā “mayaṃ asukaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ gacchāmā”ti gantabbaṃ. Sace bahigāme dūre vihāro hoti, antarāmagge gāmantara-nadīpāra-rattivippavāsa-gaṇaohīyanāpattīhi anāpatti. Bhikkhunupassayaṃ gantvā tā bhikkhuniyo vattabbā – “asukaṃ nāma bhikkhuṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āma, ayyā”ti. “Tassa itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, saṅgahaṃ dānissa karothā”ti. Tā ce “sādhu, ayyā, idāni mayampi sajjhāyissāma, dhammaṃ sossāma, gacchatha tumhe”ti vatvā saṅgahaṃ karonti, ārādhikā ca honti saṅgāhikā lajjiniyo, tā kopetvā aññattha na gantabbaṃ. Gacchati ce, gāmantara-nadīpāra-rattivippavāsa-gaṇaohīyanāpattīhi na muccati. Sace pana lajjiniyo honti, na saṅgāhikāyo; aññattha gantuṃ labbhati. Sacepi alajjiniyo honti, saṅgahaṃ pana karonti; tāpi pariccajitvā aññattha gantuṃ labbhati. Sace lajjiniyo ca saṅgāhikā [M 1.0239] ca, ñātikā na honti, āsannagāme pana aññā ñātikāyo honti paṭijagganikā, tāsampi santikaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Gantvā sace bhikkhubhāvepi nissayapaṭipanno, patirūpāya bhikkhuniyā santike nissayo gahetabbo. Mātikā vā vinayo vā uggahito suggahito, puna uggaṇhanakāraṇaṃ natthi. Sace bhikkhubhāve parisāvacaro, tassa santikeyeva upasampannā sūpasampannā. Aññassa [P 1.0276] santike nissayo gahetabbo. Pubbe taṃ nissāya vasantehipi aññassa santikeyeva nissayo gahetabbo. Paripuṇṇavassasāmaṇerenāpi aññassa santikeyeva upajjhā gahetabbā.

In this case, if two monks, having recited together or discussed the Dhamma together, lie down in the same dwelling and fall asleep, and the female gender appears in one of them, both incur the offense of lying down together. If, upon waking, he sees his own transformation and is distressed and unhappy, he should inform the other during the night. The other should console him, saying: “Let it be, do not worry. This is merely a fault of saṃsāra. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has provided an opening; whether a monk or a nun, the Dhamma is unclosed, the path to heaven unbarred.” After consoling him, he should say: “It is proper for you to go to the nuns’ residence. Are there any nuns known to you?” If there are such nuns for her, she should say there are; if not, she should say there are none. Then the former monk should say: “Please give me your support; now take me first to the nuns’ residence.” That monk should take her and go to the presence of those nuns known to her or to the presence of nuns known to himself. And when going, he should not go alone. Taking a light and a staff, he should go with four or five monks, and avoiding any prearrangement, he should announce, “We are going to such-and-such a place.” If the monastery is far outside the village, there is no offense for crossing between villages, crossing a river, staying away overnight, or falling behind the group along the way. Upon arriving at the nuns’ residence, those nuns should be asked: “Do you know such-and-such a monk?” If they reply, “Yes, venerable sirs,” he should say: “The female gender has appeared in him. Please give her your support now.” If they say, “Good, venerable sirs, now we too will study and listen to the Dhamma; you may go,” and they provide support, and are agreeable, supportive, and modest, then she should not go elsewhere, offending them. If she goes, she is not freed from the offenses of crossing between villages, crossing a river, staying away overnight, or falling behind the group. But if they are modest yet not supportive, she may go elsewhere. Even if they are shameless but still provide support, she may abandon them and go elsewhere. If they are modest and supportive but are not relatives, yet there are other relatives in a nearby village who can care for her, it is said that she may go to them. Having gone, if even in the state of a monk he was under dependence, dependence should be taken in the presence of a suitable nun. If the Mātikā or Vinaya has been learned and well-learned, there is no reason to learn it again. If, in the state of a monk, he was an expert of the assembly, those ordained in his presence are well-ordained. Dependence should be taken in the presence of another. Even by those who previously lived in dependence on him, dependence must be taken in the presence of another. Even by a novice who has completed twenty years of age, a preceptor must be taken in the presence of another.

Yaṃ panassa bhikkhubhāve adhiṭṭhitaṃ ticīvarañca patto ca, taṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahati, puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Saṅkaccikā ca udakasāṭikā ca gahetabbā. Yaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ vā atirekapatto vā vinayakammaṃ katvā ṭhapito hoti, taṃ sabbampi vinayakammaṃ vijahati, puna kātabbaṃ. Paṭiggahitatelamadhuphāṇitādīnipi paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahanti. Sace paṭiggahaṇato sattame divase liṅgaṃ parivattati, puna paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana bhikkhukāle aññassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ, taṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahati. Yaṃ ubhinnaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ avibhajitvā ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ pakatatto rakkhati. Yaṃ pana vibhattaṃ etasseva santakaṃ, taṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati. Vuttampi cetaṃ parivāre –

Moreover, whatever one has determined in the state as a monk—the three robes and the bowl—that determination is relinquished; it must be determined anew. A breast-cloth and a bathing cloth must be taken. Whatever extra robe or extra bowl was set aside after performing a formal act of Vinaya, all that formal act of Vinaya is relinquished; it must be done again. The acceptance of oil, honey, molasses, and the like is also relinquished. If the gender changes on the seventh day from its acceptance, it must be accepted again, whereupon it is allowable for seven days. However, whatever was accepted as belonging to another monk during one's time as a monk, that acceptance is not relinquished. Whatever was set aside as common property without being divided, the one who remains in their original state protects it. But whatever was divided as one's own property, that acceptance is relinquished. And this is also stated in the Parivāra—

“Telaṃ [V 1.0221] madhuṃ phāṇitañcāpi sappiṃ;

Sāmaṃ gahetvāna nikkhipeyya;

Avītivatte sattāhe;

Sati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 480);

“Oil, honey, molasses, and ghee; having taken them oneself, one should put them away. If seven days have not passed, and there is a cause, for one who consumes them, there is an offense. This is a question considered by the skilled.”

Idañhi liṅgaparivattanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma liṅgaparivattanena, kālaṃkiriyāya, sikkhāpaccakkhānena, hīnāyāvattanena, anupasampannassa dānena, anapekkhavissajjanena, acchinditvā gahaṇena ca vijahati. Tasmā sacepi harītakakhaṇḍampi paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitamatthi, sabbamassa paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati. Bhikkhuvihāre pana yaṃkiñcissā santakaṃ paṭiggahetvā vā appaṭiggahetvā [M 1.0240] vā ṭhapitaṃ, sabbassa sāva issarā, āharāpetvā gahetabbaṃ. Yaṃ panettha thāvaraṃ tassā santakaṃ senāsanaṃ vā uparopakā vā, te yassicchati tassa dātabbā. Terasasu sammutīsu [P 1.0277] yā bhikkhukāle laddhā sammuti, sabbā sā paṭippassambhati. Purimikāya senāsanaggāho paṭippassambhati. Sace pacchimikāya senāsane gahite liṅgaṃ parivattati, bhikkhunisaṅgho cassā uppannaṃ lābhaṃ dātukāmo hoti, apaloketvā dātabbo. Sace bhikkhunīhi sādhāraṇāya paṭicchannāya āpattiyā parivasantassa liṅgaṃ parivattati, pakkhamānattameva dātabbaṃ. Sace mānattaṃ carantassa parivattati, puna pakkhamānattameva dātabbaṃ. Sace ciṇṇamānattassa parivattati, bhikkhunīhi abbhānakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace akusalavipāke parikkhīṇe pakkhamānattakāle punadeva liṅgaṃ parivattati, chārattaṃ mānattameva dātabbaṃ. Sace ciṇṇe pakkhamānatte parivattati, bhikkhūhi abbhānakammaṃ kātabbanti.

Indeed, this was said with reference to the change of gender. Acceptance, it should be known, is relinquished by a change of gender, by death, by renouncing the training, by reverting to a lower state, by giving to one not fully ordained, by discarding without concern, and by taking after seizing it. Therefore, even if a piece of myrobalan fruit has been accepted and set aside, all his acceptance is relinquished. However, in the monks' monastery, whatever belonging of hers was set aside—whether accepted or not accepted—she alone is the owner of all of it; it should be caused to be brought and taken. Whatever fixed property of hers is here, such as a dwelling or young trees that have been planted, those should be given to whomever she wishes. Among the thirteen authorizations, whatever authorization was obtained during the time as a monk, all of that is annulled. The taking of a dwelling in the first period is annulled. If, after a dwelling has been taken in the later period, the gender changes, and the community of nuns wishes to give her the gain that has arisen, it should be given after informing them. If the gender changes while one is undergoing parivāsa for a concealed offense common to the nuns, only pakkhamānatta should be given. If the gender changes while one is undergoing mānatta, pakkhamānatta should be given again. If the gender changes for one who has completed mānatta, the act of rehabilitation should be performed by the nuns. If, when the unwholesome result has been exhausted, during the period of pakkhamānatta, the gender changes back again, only a six-night mānatta should be given. If it changes after pakkhamānatta has been completed, the act of rehabilitation should be performed by the monks.

Anantare bhikkhuniyā liṅgaparivattanavatthumhi idha vuttanayeneva sabbo vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – sacepi bhikkhunikāle āpannā sañcarittāpatti paṭicchannā hoti, parivāsadānaṃ natthi, chārattaṃ mānattameva dātabbaṃ. Sace pakkhamānattaṃ carantiyā liṅgaṃ parivattati, na tenattho, chārattaṃ mānattameva dātabbaṃ. Sace ciṇṇamānattāya parivattati, puna mānattaṃ adatvā bhikkhūhi abbhetabbo. Atha bhikkhūhi mānatte adinne puna liṅgaṃ parivattati, bhikkhunīhi pakkhamānattameva dātabbaṃ. Atha chārattaṃ mānattaṃ carantassa puna parivattati, pakkhamānattameva dātabbaṃ. Ciṇṇamānattassa pana liṅgaparivatte jāte bhikkhunīhi abbhānakammaṃ kātabbaṃ[V 1.0222]. Puna parivatte ca liṅge bhikkhunibhāve ṭhitāyapi yā āpattiyo pubbe paṭippassaddhā, tā suppaṭippassaddhā evāti.

In the immediately following case of a nun's change of gender, every decision should be understood in the same way as stated here. However, this is the distinction: even if a sañcaritta offense committed during the time as a nun was concealed, there is no giving of parivāsa; only a six-night mānatta should be given. If the gender changes while she is undergoing pakkhamānatta, that is of no use; only a six-night mānatta should be given. If the gender changes for one who has completed mānatta, she should be rehabilitated by the monks without giving mānatta again. Then, if the gender changes again before mānatta has been given by the monks, only pakkhamānatta should be given by the nuns. Then, if the gender changes again while he is undergoing a six-night mānatta, only pakkhamānatta should be given. But if a change of gender occurs for one who has completed mānatta, the act of rehabilitation should be performed by the nuns. And when the gender has changed again, for her who is established in the state of a nun, those offenses that were previously annulled are indeed well-annulled.

70. Ito parāni “mātuyā methunaṃ dhamma”ntiādīni cattāri vatthūni uttānatthāniyeva.

70. The four cases following this, beginning with “sexual intercourse with one’s mother,” are of straightforward meaning.

71. Mudupiṭṭhikavatthumhi so kira bhikkhu naṭapubbako. Tassa sippakosallatthaṃ parikammakatā [P 1.0278] piṭṭhi mudukā ahosi. Tasmā evaṃ kātuṃ asakkhi.

71. In the case of the soft-backed one, that monk, it is said, was formerly an acrobat. For the sake of skill in his art, his back, having been prepared, became soft. Therefore, he was able to do so.

Lambīvatthumhi [M 1.0241] tassa bhikkhussa aṅgajātaṃ dīghaṃ hoti lambati, tasmā lambīti vutto.

In the case of Lambī, that monk’s sexual organ was long and hung down; therefore, he was called Lambī.

Ito parāni dve vaṇavatthūni uttānāneva. Lepacittavatthumhi lepacittaṃ nāma cittakammarūpaṃ.

The two cases concerning a wound following this are straightforward. In the case of the painted figure, a lepacitta is a painted image made with artistry.

Dārudhītalikavatthumhi dārudhītalikā nāma kaṭṭharūpaṃ. Yathā ca imesu dvīsu evaṃ aññesupi dantarūpa-potthakarūpa-loharūpādīsu anupādinnakesu itthirūpesu nimitte methunarāgena upakkamantassa asuci muccatu vā mā vā, dukkaṭameva. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena upakkamantassāpi tatheva dukkaṭaṃ. Mocanarāgena pana upakkamantassa mutte saṅghādiseso, amutte thullaccayanti.

In the case of the wooden doll, a dārudhītalikā is a figure made of wood. And just as in these two cases, so too with other unanimated female figures—such as those of ivory, plaster, metal, and so on—for one who strives with lust for sexual intercourse at the sexual organ, whether seminal fluid is emitted or not, it is an offense of wrong-doing. For one who strives with lust for bodily contact, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing. But for one who strives with lust for emission, if there is emission, it is a saṅghādisesa offense; if there is no emission, it is a thullaccaya offense.

72. Sundaravatthumhi ayaṃ sundaro nāma rājagahe kuladārako saddhāya pabbajito; attabhāvassa abhirūpatāya “sundaro”ti nāmaṃ labhi. Taṃ rathikāya gacchantaṃ disvā samuppannachandarāgā sā itthī imaṃ vippakāraṃ akāsi. Thero pana anāgāmī. Tasmā so na sādiyi. Aññesaṃ pana avisayo eso.

72. In the case of Sundara, this Sundara was a young man of good family in Rājagaha who had gone forth out of faith. Due to the beauty of his person, he received the name 'Sundara.' Seeing him going along the street, a woman, with lust and passion arisen, committed this transgression. But the Elder was a non-returner. Therefore, he did not consent. However, this is not within the domain of others.

Ito paresu catūsu vatthūsu te bhikkhū jaḷā dummedhā mātugāmassa vacanaṃ gahetvā tathā katvā pacchā kukkuccāyiṃsu.

In the four cases following this, those monks, being sluggish and unwise, acted according to the words of a woman and afterwards felt remorse.

73. Akkhāyitādīni tīṇi vatthūni uttānatthāneva. Dvīsu chinnasīsavatthūsu ayaṃ vinicchayo – vaṭṭakate mukhe vivaṭe aṅgajātaṃ pavesento sace heṭṭhā vā upari vā ubhayapassehi vā chupantaṃ paveseti, pārājikaṃ. Catūhipi passehi achupantaṃ pavesetvā abbhantare tālukaṃ chupati, pārājikameva. Cattāri passāni tālukañca achupanto ākāsagatameva [V 1.0223] katvā paveseti ca nīharati ca, dukkaṭaṃ. Yadi pana dantā suphusitā, antomukhe okāso natthi, dantā ca bahi oṭṭhamaṃsena paṭicchannā, tattha vātena asamphuṭṭhaṃ allokāsaṃ tilaphalamattampi pavesentassa pārājikameva. Uppāṭite pana oṭṭhamaṃse dantesuyeva upakkamantassa thullaccayaṃ. Yopi danto bahi nikkhamitvā tiṭṭhati[P 1.0279], na sakkā oṭṭhehi pidahituṃ. Tattha upakkamantepi bahi nikkhantajivhāya upakkamantepi thullaccayameva. Jīvamānakasarīrepi bahi nikkhantajivhāya thullaccayameva. Yadi pana bahijivhāya paliveṭhetvā antomukhaṃ paveseti, pārājikameva. Uparigīvāya [M 1.0242] chinnasīsassapi adhobhāgena aṅgajātaṃ pavesetvā tālukaṃ chupantassa pārājikameva.

73. The three cases beginning with that of being eaten are of clear meaning. Regarding the two cases of severed heads, this is the judgment: If, when the mouth is made round and is open, one inserts the genital organ, and if it enters while touching below, above, or on either side, it is a pārājika offense. If one inserts it without touching the four sides but touches the palate inside, it is indeed a pārājika offense. If one inserts and withdraws it without touching the four sides or the palate, having made it as if situated in empty space, it is an offense of wrong-doing. But if the teeth are tightly closed, there is no space inside the mouth, and the teeth are covered on the outside by the flesh of the lips, then for one inserting even a sesame-seed's amount into that moist place untouched by wind, it is indeed a pārājika offense. But when the lip-flesh has been pulled away, for one who makes an attempt on the teeth alone, it is a thullaccaya offense. And if a tooth protrudes outside and cannot be covered by the lips, for one making an attempt there, or for one making an attempt on a tongue that has come out, it is indeed a thullaccaya offense. Even in a living body, for one making an attempt on a tongue that has come out, it is indeed a thullaccaya offense. But if, having wrapped it with the tongue that is outside, one inserts it into the mouth, it is indeed a pārājika offense. Even in the case of a head severed above the neck, for one who, having inserted the genital organ through the lower part, touches the palate, it is indeed a pārājika offense.

Aṭṭhikavatthumhi susānaṃ gacchantassāpi dukkaṭaṃ. Aṭṭhikāni saṅkaḍḍhantassāpi, nimitte methunarāgena upakkamantassāpi, kāyasaṃsaggarāgena upakkamantassāpi, muccatu vā mā vā, dukkaṭameva. Mocanarāgena pana upakkamantassa muccante saṅghādiseso, amuccante thullaccayameva.

In the case of bones, even for one going to a charnel ground, it is an offense of wrong-doing. For one collecting the bones, and for one making an attempt on the sign with lust for sexual intercourse—whether emission occurs or not—it is only an offense of wrong-doing.

Nāgīvatthumhi nāgamāṇavikā vā hotu kinnarīādīnaṃ vā aññatarā, sabbattha pārājikaṃ.

In the case of a nāgī, whether it be a nāga maiden or one of the beings beginning with kinnarīs, in all cases it is a pārājika offense.

Yakkhīvatthumhi sabbāpi devatā yakkhīyeva.

In the case of a yakkhī, all female deities are indeed yakkhīs.

Petīvatthumhi nijjhāmataṇhikādipetiyo allīyitumpi na sakkā. Vimānapetiyo pana atthi; yāsaṃ kāḷapakkhe akusalaṃ vipaccati, juṇhapakkhe devatā viya sampattiṃ anubhonti. Evarūpāya petiyā vā yakkhiyā vā sace dassana-gahaṇa-āmasana-phusana-ghaṭṭanāni paññāyanti, pārājikaṃ. Athāpi dassanaṃ natthi, itarāni paññāyanti, pārājikameva. Atha dassanagahaṇāni na paññāyanti, āmasanaphusanaghaṭṭanehi paññāyamānehi taṃ puggalaṃ visaññaṃ katvā attano manorathaṃ pūretvā gacchati, ayaṃ avisayo nāma. Tasmā ettha avisayattā anāpatti. Paṇḍakavatthu pākaṭameva.

In the case of a petī, petas such as the Nijjhāmataṇhikā cannot even be clung to. But there are Vimānapetīs, for whom the unwholesome ripens during the dark fortnight, while during the bright fortnight, they enjoy prosperity like deities. With such a petī or a yakkhī, if seeing, seizing, touching, pressing, or rubbing are apparent, it is a pārājika offense. Even if there is no seeing, but the other actions are apparent, it is indeed a pārājika offense. If seeing and seizing are not apparent, but by means of apparent touching, pressing, and rubbing, having made that person unconscious, one then departs, this is called 'not the domain.' Therefore, here, because of it not being the domain, there is no offense. The case of a paṇḍaka is obvious.

Upahatindriyavatthumhi upahatindriyoti upahatakāyappasādo khāṇukaṇṭakamiva sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā na vedayati. Avedayantassāpi sevanacittavasena āpatti.

In the case of one with an impaired faculty, 'with an impaired faculty' means one whose bodily sensitivity is impaired; like a tree stump or a thorn, one does not feel pleasure or pain. Even for one who does not feel it, an offense is incurred by the power of the mind set on indulging.

Chupitamattavatthusmiṃ [V 1.0224] yo “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevissāmī”ti mātugāmaṃ [P 1.0280] gaṇhitvā methune virajjitvā vippaṭisārī hoti, dukkaṭamevassa hoti. Methunadhammassa hi pubbapayogā hatthaggāhādayo yāva sīsaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva dukkaṭe tiṭṭhanti. Sīse patte pārājikaṃ hoti. Paṭhamapārājikassa hi dukkaṭameva sāmantaṃ. Itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ thullaccayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu methunadhamme virajjitvā kāyasaṃsaggaṃ sādiyīti veditabbo. Tenāha bhagavā – “āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti.

In the case of mere contact, if a monk, having taken hold of a woman with the thought, 'I will engage in the act of sexual intercourse,' then becomes dispassionate towards sexual intercourse and is remorseful, for him it is only an offense of wrong-doing. Indeed, the preliminary acts of the act of sexual intercourse—such as taking the hand—remain as offenses of wrong-doing as long as the culmination is not reached. When the culmination is reached, it becomes a pārājika offense. Indeed, for the first pārājika offense, that which is adjacent is only an offense of wrong-doing. For the other three, it is a thullaccaya offense. But this monk should be understood as one who, having become dispassionate towards the act of sexual intercourse, consented to bodily contact. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'It is a saṅghādisesa offense.'

74. Bhaddiyavatthusmiṃ [M 1.0243] bhaddiyaṃ nāma taṃ nagaraṃ. Jātiyāvanaṃ nāma jātipupphagumbānaṃ ussannatāya evaṃ laddhanāmaṃ; taṃ tassa nagarassa upacāre vanaṃ hoti. So tattha nipanno tena vātupatthambhena mahāniddaṃ okkami. Ekarasaṃ bhavaṅgameva vattati. Kilinnaṃ passitvāti asucikiliṭṭhaṃ passitvā.

74. In the case of Bhaddiya, that city was named Bhaddiya. The Jātiyāvana was a grove so named because of the abundance of jasmine flower bushes; that grove was in the vicinity of the city. He, lying down there, fell into a deep sleep due to a wind affliction. Only the life-continuum, of a single function, proceeded. 'Seeing it soiled' means seeing it stained with impurity.

75. Ito parāni sādiyanapaṭisaṃyuttāni cattāri vatthūni, ajānanavatthu cāti pañca uttānatthāneva.

75. After this, the four cases connected with consenting and the case of not knowing—thus five cases—are of clear meaning.

76. Dvīsu asādiyanavatthūsu sahasā vuṭṭhāsīti āsīvisena daṭṭho viya agginā daḍḍho viya ca turitaṃ vuṭṭhāsi. Akkamitvā pavattesīti appamatto bhikkhu āraddhavipassako upaṭṭhitassati khippaṃ vuṭṭhahantova akkamitvā bhūmiyaṃ vaṭṭento parivaṭṭento viheṭhento pātesi. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi evarūpesu ṭhānesu cittaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ. Ayañca tesaṃ aññataro saṅgāmasīsayodho bhikkhu.

76. In the two cases of not consenting, 'he arose hastily' means that like one bitten by a venomous snake or like one burned by fire, he got up quickly. 'Having kicked it, he made it roll away' means that a non-negligent monk, one who has undertaken insight meditation, with mindfulness established, while getting up quickly, having kicked it, making it roll on the ground, making it roll over and over, tormenting it, made it fall. Indeed, by a virtuous worldling, in such situations the mind must be guarded. And this monk was one of them, a warrior chief on the battlefield.

77. Dvāraṃ vivaritvā nipannavatthumhi divā paṭisallīyantenāti divā nipajjantena. Dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā paṭisallīyitunti dvāraṃ pidahitvā nipajjituṃ. Ettha ca kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “ayaṃ nāma āpattī”ti na vuttā. Vivaritvā nipannadosena pana uppanne vatthusmiṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, divā paṭisallīyantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā paṭisallīyitu”nti vuttattā asaṃvaritvā paṭisallīyantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhagavato hi adhippāyaṃ ñatvā upālittherādīhi aṭṭhakathā ṭhapitā. “Atthāpatti divā āpajjati no ratti”nti (pari. 323) imināpi cetaṃ siddhaṃ.

77. In the case of lying down having opened the door, 'by one secluding oneself by day' means by one lying down by day. 'To seclude oneself having closed the door' means to lie down having shut the door. And here, although in the Pāḷi it was not said, 'This is such-and-such an offense,' when a case arose from the fault of lying down with the door open, it was said, 'I allow, monks, one secluding oneself by day to seclude oneself having closed the door.' Therefore, an offense of wrong-doing was stated for one who secludes oneself without closing it. Indeed, having known the Blessed One’s intention, the commentary was established by the Elder Upāli and others. And by this, 'An offense is incurred by day, not by night' (Pvr. 323), this is established.

Kīdisaṃ [P 1.0281] pana dvāraṃ saṃvaritabbaṃ, kīdisaṃ na saṃvaritabbaṃ? Rukkhapadaraveḷupadarakilañjapaṇṇādīnaṃ [V 1.0225] yena kenaci kavāṭaṃ katvā heṭṭhā udukkhale upari uttarapāsake ca pavesetvā kataṃ parivattakadvārameva saṃvaritabbaṃ. Aññaṃ gorūpānaṃ vajesu viya rukkhasūcikaṇṭakadvāraṃ, gāmathakanakaṃ cakkalakayuttadvāraṃ, phalakesu vā kiṭikāsu vā dve tīṇi cakkalakāni yojetvā kataṃ saṃsaraṇakiṭikadvāraṃ, āpaṇesu viya kataṃ ugghāṭanakiṭikadvāraṃ, dvīsu tīsu ṭhānesu veṇusalākā gopphetvā paṇṇakuṭīsu kataṃ salākahatthakadvāraṃ, dussasāṇidvāranti evarūpaṃ dvāraṃ na saṃvaritabbaṃ. Pattahatthassa kavāṭappaṇāmane pana [M 1.0244] ekaṃ dussasāṇidvārameva anāpattikaraṃ, avasesāni paṇāmentassa āpatti. Divā paṭisallīyantassa pana parivattakadvārameva āpattikaraṃ, sesāni saṃvaritvā vā asaṃvaritvā vā nipannassa āpatti natthi. Saṃvaritvā pana nipajjitabbaṃ, etaṃ vattaṃ.

Furthermore, what kind of door should be closed, and what kind should not be closed? A revolving door—made from planks of wood, strips of bamboo, mats, leaves, or the like, with a door-leaf fitted below into a pivot-socket and above into an upper ring—is the one that should be closed. Other types of doors should not be closed, such as: a door of wooden spikes or thorns like those in cattle pens; a village gate-closer fitted with a wheel; a sliding lattice-door made of planks or lattices fitted with two or three wheels; a lift-off lattice-door like those in shops; a door for a leaf hut made of a bundle of slats woven together; or a cloth-curtain door. For a monk holding a bowl, when pushing the door-leaf, only pushing a cloth-curtain door does not constitute an offense; pushing the others is an offense. For one secluding himself during the day, only a revolving door, if left open, constitutes an offense. For the other types, there is no offense for one lying down whether they are closed or not. However, one should lie down after closing it; this is the proper conduct.

Parivattakadvāraṃ pana kittakena saṃvutaṃ hoti? Sūcighaṭikādīsu dinnāsu saṃvutameva hoti. Apica kho sūcimattepi dinne vaṭṭati. Ghaṭikamattepi dinne vaṭṭati. Dvārabāhaṃ phusitvā pihitamattepi vaṭṭati. Īsakaṃ aphusitepi vaṭṭati. Sabbantimena vidhinā yāvatā sīsaṃ nappavisati tāvatā aphusitepi vaṭṭatīti. Sace bahūnaṃ vaḷañjanaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, bhikkhuṃ vā sāmaṇeraṃ vā “dvāraṃ, āvuso, jaggāhī”ti vatvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Atha bhikkhū cīvarakammaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci karontā nisinnā honti, “ete dvāraṃ jaggissantī”ti ābhogaṃ katvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “upāsakampi āpucchitvā vā, ‘esa jaggissatī’ti ābhogaṃ katvā vā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kevalaṃ bhikkhuniṃ vā mātugāmaṃ vā āpucchituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha dvārassa [P 1.0282] udukkhalaṃ vā uttarapāsako vā bhinno vā hoti aṭṭhapito vā, saṃvarituṃ na sakkoti, navakammatthaṃ vā pana iṭṭhakapuñjo vā mattikādīnaṃ vā rāsi antodvāre kato hoti, aṭṭaṃ vā bandhanti, yathā saṃvarituṃ na sakkoti; evarūpe antarāye sati asaṃvaritvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Yadi pana kavāṭaṃ natthi, laddhakappameva. Upari sayantena nisseṇiṃ āropetvā nipajjitabbaṃ. Sace nisseṇimatthake thakanakaṃ hoti, thaketvāpi nipajjitabbaṃ. Gabbhe nipajjantena gabbhadvāraṃ vā pamukhadvāraṃ vā yaṃkiñci saṃvaritvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace ekakuṭṭake gehe dvīsu passesu dvārāni katvā vaḷañjanti, dvepi dvārāni jaggitabbāni.

Furthermore, to what extent is a revolving door considered closed? It is considered properly closed when the bolt and latch are engaged. Moreover, it is allowable if only the bolt is inserted. It is allowable if only the latch is inserted. It is allowable if it is merely closed to the point of touching the doorpost. It is allowable even if it is slightly ajar. By the final method, it is allowable even if it is ajar, so long as a head cannot pass through. If it is a place used by many, it is allowable to lie down after saying to a monk or a novice, “Friend, please watch the door.” Or if monks are sitting doing robe work or some other task, it is allowable to lie down after making the mental note, “These monks will watch the door.” In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is said: “It is allowable to lie down after asking a layman, or after making the mental note, ‘He will watch.’ It is only a bhikkhunī or a woman whom it is not allowable to ask.” Now, if the door’s pivot-socket or upper ring is broken or not fixed, and one is unable to close it; or if for the purpose of new construction work a pile of bricks or a heap of clay and so on is placed inside the doorway; or if they are constructing a scaffold in such a way that one is unable to close it—when such an obstacle is present, it is allowable to lie down without closing it. If, however, there is no door-leaf, it is simply permissible. One sleeping on an upper floor should lie down after raising the ladder. If there is a closing-device at the top of the ladder, one should lie down after closing it as well. One sleeping in an inner room may lie down after closing any door, whether it is the inner room’s door or the entrance door. If, in a dwelling with a single surrounding wall, they make and use doors on two sides, both doors must be watched.

Tibhūmakepi pāsāde dvāraṃ jaggitabbameva. Sace bhikkhācārā paṭikkamma lohapāsādasadisaṃ pāsādaṃ bahū bhikkhū divāvihāratthaṃ pavisanti, saṅghattherena dvārapālassa “dvāraṃ jaggāhī”ti vatvā vā “dvārajagganaṃ etassa bhāro”ti ābhogaṃ katvā vā pavisitvā nipajjitabbaṃ[V 1.0226]. Yāva saṅghanavakena evameva kattabbaṃ. Pure pavisantānaṃ “dvārajagganaṃ nāma pacchimānaṃ bhāro”ti evaṃ ābhogaṃ kātumpi vaṭṭati. Anāpucchā vā ābhogaṃ vā akatvā antogabbhe vā asaṃvutadvāre bahi vā nipajjantānaṃ āpatti. Gabbhe vā bahi vā nipajjanakālepi “dvārajagganaṃ nāma mahādvāre dvārapālassa bhāro”ti [M 1.0245] ābhogaṃ katvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Lohapāsādādīsu ākāsatale nipajjantenāpi dvāraṃ saṃvaritabbameva.

Even in a three-storied mansion, the door must be watched. If, after returning from the alms-round, many monks enter a mansion like the Lohapāsāda for their day-dwelling, the Saṅghatthera should enter and lie down after either telling the doorkeeper, “Watch the door,” or making the mental note, “Watching the door is his responsibility.” This should be done in the same way by all, down to the most junior monk of the Saṅgha. It is also allowable for those who enter first to make the mental note, “Guarding the door is the responsibility of those who come last.” When the door is unclosed, for those who lie down either inside an inner room or outside, without having asked or made a mental note, there is an offense. Even when lying down inside a room or outside, it is indeed permissible to lie down after making the mental note, “Guarding the door at the main entrance is the doorkeeper’s responsibility.” In places like the Lohapāsāda, even for one lying down on an open-air terrace, the door must be closed.

Ayañhettha saṅkhepo – idaṃ divāpaṭisallīyanaṃ yena kenaci parikkhitte sadvārabandhe ṭhāne kathitaṃ. Tasmā abbhokāse vā rukkhamūle vā maṇḍape vā yattha katthaci sadvārabandhe nipajjantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvāva nipajjitabbaṃ. Sace mahāpariveṇaṃ hoti, mahābodhiyaṅgaṇalohapāsādaṅgaṇasadisaṃ bahūnaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, yattha dvāraṃ saṃvutampi saṃvutaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, dvāraṃ alabhantā pākāraṃ āruhitvāpi vicaranti, tattha saṃvaraṇakiccaṃ natthi. Rattiṃ dvāraṃ [P 1.0283] vivaritvā nipanno aruṇe uggate uṭṭhahati, anāpatti. Sace pabujjhitvā puna supati, āpatti. Yo pana “aruṇe uggate vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti paricchinditvāva dvāraṃ asaṃvaritvā rattiṃ nipajjati, yathāparicchedameva ca na vuṭṭhāti, tassa āpattiyeva. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “evaṃ nipajjanto anādariyadukkaṭāpi na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ.

Here is the summary in this matter: This sleeping in the daytime has been spoken of in the context of a place enclosed by some kind of barrier and having a fitted door. Therefore, when lying down in a place with a fitted door—be it in the open air, at the foot of a tree, in a pavilion, or anywhere else—one must lie down only after closing the door. If it is a large monastery compound, like the precincts of the Mahābodhi Tree or the Lohapāsāda, a place of arrival for many people, where the door, even if closed, does not stay closed, and where those who cannot find the door open climb over the surrounding wall to move about—in such a place, there is no duty to close it. If one lies down at night with the door open and gets up when dawn has arisen, there is no offense. If, after waking, one sleeps again, there is an offense. As for one who lies down at night without closing the door, having determined, “I will get up when dawn has arisen,” and then does not get up according to that determination, for him there is indeed an offense. In the Mahāpaccarī Commentary, however, it is said: “One who lies down in this manner is not free from an offense of disrespect.”

Yo pana bahudeva rattiṃ jaggitvā addhānaṃ vā gantvā divā kilantarūpo mañce nisinno pāde bhūmito amocetvāva niddāvasena nipajjati, tassa anāpatti. Sace okkantaniddo ajānantopi pāde mañcakaṃ āropeti, āpattiyeva. Nisīditvā apassāya supantassa anāpatti. Yopi ca “niddaṃ vinodessāmī”ti caṅkamanto patitvā sahasāva vuṭṭhāti, tassāpi anāpatti. Yo pana patitvā tattheva sayati, na vuṭṭhāti, tassa āpatti.

Now, for whichever monk who, having kept watch for much of the night or having traveled a long distance, sits on a bed exhausted during the day and lies down by the power of sleep without having lifted his feet from the ground, for him there is no offense. If, being overcome by sleep, he unknowingly places his feet on the small bed, there is indeed an offense. For one who, having sat down, sleeps while leaning against something, there is no offense. And also for whichever monk who, thinking, 'I will dispel sleepiness,' falls while walking up and down but immediately gets up, for him also there is no offense. But for whichever monk who, having fallen, lies right there and does not get up, for him there is an offense.

Ko muccati, ko na muccatīti? Mahāpaccariyaṃ tāva “ekabhaṅgena nipannakoyeva muccati. Pāde pana bhūmito mocetvā nipanno yakkhagahitakopi visaññībhūtopi na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “bandhitvā nipajjāpitova muccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yo caṅkamanto muccitvā patito tattheva supati, tassāpi avisayattā āpatti na dissati. Ācariyā pana evaṃ na kathayanti. Tasmā āpattiyevāti mahāpadumattherena vuttaṃ. Dve pana janā āpattito muccantiyeva, yo ca yakkhagahitako, yo ca bandhitvā nipajjāpito”ti.

Who is released, and who is not released? First, in the Mahāpaccariya, it is said: 'Only one who lies down on one side is released. But one who lies down after lifting his feet from the ground, even if seized by a yakkha or having become unconscious, is not released.' In the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'Only one who is bound and made to lie down is released.' But in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'For a monk who, while walking up and down, faints and falls, and sleeps right there, for him also, because it is outside the scope, an offense is not apparent. The teachers, however, do not say so. Therefore, it is indeed an offense,' so it was said by the Elder Mahāpaduma. But two persons are indeed released from the offense: one who is seized by a yakkha, and one who is bound and made to lie down.

78. Bhārukacchakavatthumhi [V 1.0227][M 1.0246] anāpatti supinantenāti yasmā supinante avisayattā evaṃ hoti, tasmā upālitthero bhagavatā avinicchitapubbampi imaṃ vatthuṃ nayaggāhena vinicchini. Bhagavāpi ca sutvā “sukathitaṃ, bhikkhave, upālinā; apade padaṃ karonto viya, ākāse padaṃ dassento viya upāli imaṃ pañhaṃ kathesī”ti vatvā theraṃ etadagge ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upālī”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 228). Ito parāni [P 1.0284] supabbādīni vatthūni uttānatthāneva.

78. In the case of the Bhārukaccha incident, the phrase 'no offense in a dream' means that because in a dream it happens thus due to it being outside the scope, therefore the Elder Upāli decided this case by taking a legal precedent, even though it had not been previously decided by the Blessed One. And the Blessed One, having heard it, said: 'Well spoken, monks, by Upāli! Like one making a track in a trackless place, like one showing a track in the sky, Upāli has explained this question.' Having said this, he placed the elder in the foremost position: 'Monks, the foremost among my monk disciples who are upholders of the Vinaya is this Upāli.' (A. Ni. 1.219, 228). The cases after this, beginning with Supabbā, are of plain meaning.

80. Bhikkhunīsampayojanādīsu te licchavikumārakā khiḍḍāpasutā attano anācārena evaṃ akaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya ca licchavīnaṃ vināso eva udapādi.

80. In the cases beginning with the association with bhikkhunīs, those Licchavi princes, being devoted to play, acted thus out of their own misconduct. And from that time onwards, the very destruction of the Licchavis arose.

82. Vuḍḍhapabbajitavatthumhi dassanaṃ agamāsīti anukampāya “taṃ dakkhissāmī”ti gehaṃ agamāsi. Athassa sā attano ca dārakānañca nānappakārehi anāthabhāvaṃ saṃvaṇṇesi. Anapekkhañca naṃ ñatvā kupitā “ehi vibbhamāhī”ti balakkārena aggahesi. So attānaṃ mocetuṃ paṭikkamanto jarādubbalatāya uttāno paripati. Tato sā attano manaṃ akāsi. So pana bhikkhu anāgāmī samucchinnakāmarāgo tasmā na sādiyīti.

82. In the story of the elderly ordained one, the phrase 'he went to see' means: out of compassion, thinking, 'I will see her,' he went to the house. Then she described to him in various ways the helplessness of herself and her children. And knowing him to be unconcerned, she became angry and, saying, 'Come, disrobe!', seized him by force. He, while stepping back to free himself, fell flat on his back due to old age and weakness. Then she did her will. But that monk was a non-returner, one who had completely cut off sensual passion; therefore, he did not consent.

83. Migapotakavatthu uttānatthamevāti.

83. The story of the fawn is of plain meaning.

Vinītavatthu niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Vinītavatthu is concluded.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya,

Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first Pārājika is concluded.

Tatridaṃ samantapāsādikāya samantapāsādikattasmiṃ –
