Herein, this is regarding the Samantapāsādikā's quality of being 'Samantapāsādikā' (Universally Inspiring):

Ācariyaparamparato, nidānavatthuppabhedadīpanato;

Parasamayavivajjanato, sakasamayavisuddhito ceva.

By reason of the succession of teachers, by the elucidation of the varieties of introductory stories; by the avoidance of other doctrines, and by the purity of its own doctrine.

Byañjanaparisodhanato, padatthato pāḷiyojanakkamato;

Sikkhāpadanicchayato, vibhaṅganayabhedadassanato.

By the purification of the phrasing, by the meaning of the words, by the sequential method of construing the Pāḷi; by the determination of the training rules, and by showing the distinctions in the method of the Vibhaṅga.

Sampassataṃ [V 1.0228][M 1.0247] na dissati, kiñci apāsādikaṃ yato ettha;

Viññūnamayaṃ tasmā, samantapāsādikātveva.

Because herein, for the discerning wise, nothing uninspiring is seen; therefore, this is indeed 'Samantapāsādikā' (Universally Inspiring).

Saṃvaṇṇanā pavattā, vinayassa vineyyadamanakusalena;

Vuttassa lokanāthena, lokamanukampamānenāti.

This commentary on the Vinaya—spoken by the Lord of the World, who is skilled in taming the trainable and has compassion for the world—is set forth.

Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first Pārājika is concluded.

2. Dutiyapārājikaṃ

The Second Pārājika

Dutiyaṃ [P 2.0285] adutiyena, yaṃ jinena pakāsitaṃ;

Pārājikaṃ tassa dāni, patto saṃvaṇṇanākkamo.

2. The second Pārājika, which was proclaimed by the unequalled Conqueror; now the turn for its exposition has come.

Yasmā tasmā suviññeyyaṃ, yaṃ pubbe ca pakāsitaṃ;

Taṃ sabbaṃ vajjayitvāna, hoti saṃvaṇṇanā ayaṃ.

Therefore, having omitted all that is easily understood and what was previously explained, this exposition proceeds.

Dhaniyavatthuvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Story of Dhaniya

84. Tena samayena buddho bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbateti tattha rājagaheti evaṃnāmake nagare, tañhi mandhātu-mahāgovindādīhi pariggahitattā “rājagaha”nti vuccati. Aññepettha pakāre vaṇṇayanti. Kiṃ tehi! Nāmametaṃ tassa nagarassa. Taṃ panetaṃ buddhakāle ca cakkavattikāle ca nagaraṃ hoti. Sesakāle suññaṃ hoti yakkhapariggahitaṃ, tesaṃ vasantavanaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ gocaragāmaṃ dassetvā nivāsanaṭṭhānamāha – gijjhakūṭe pabbateti. So ca gijjhā tassa kūṭesu vasiṃsu, gijjhasadisāni vā tassa kūṭāni; tasmā gijjhakūṭoti vuccatīti veditabbo.

At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, on Mount Vulture Peak. There, in the city named Rājagaha—for it was taken possession of by Mandhātu, Mahāgovinda, and others, hence it is called 'Rājagaha.' Others describe other reasons here. What is the use of them! This is the name of that city. Moreover, this was a capital city in the time of a Buddha and in the time of a universal monarch. At other times, it was empty, possessed by yakkhas, remaining as their pleasure-grove for the spring season. Having thus shown the village for alms-round, the dwelling place is stated: 'on Mount Vulture Peak.' And vultures dwelt on its peaks, or its peaks were like vultures; therefore, it is called Vulture Peak. This should be understood.

Sambahulāti vinayapariyāyena tayo janā sambahulāti vuccanti, tato paraṃ saṅgho. Suttantapariyāyena tayo tayo eva, tato paṭṭhāya sambahulā. Idha pana te suttantapariyāyena sambahulāti [P 2.0286] veditabbā. Sandiṭṭhāti nātivissāsikā na daḷhamittā; tattha tattha saṅgamma diṭṭhattā hi te sandiṭṭhāti vuccanti. Sambhattāti ativissāsikā daḷhamittā; te [M 1.0248] hi suṭṭhu bhattā [V 1.0229] bhajamānā ekasambhogaparibhogāti katvā “sambhattā”ti vuccanti. Isigilipasseti isigili nāma pabbato, tassa passe. Pubbe kira pañcasatamattā paccekabuddhā kāsikosalādīsu janapadesu piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ tasmiṃ pabbate sannipatitvā samāpattiyā vītināmenti. Manussā te pavisanteva passanti na nikkhamante. Tato āhaṃsu – “ayaṃ pabbato ime isayo gilatī”ti. Tadupādāya tassa “isigili”tveva samaññā udapādi, tassa passe pabbatapāde.

'Several' (sambahulā): according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called 'several'; beyond that is the Saṅgha. According to the Sutta method, three are just three; from that point onward, they are called 'several.' Here, however, they should be understood as 'several' according to the Sutta method. 'Acquaintances' (sandiṭṭhā): not very intimate, not firm friends; for because they meet here and there and are seen, they are called 'acquaintances.' 'Companions' (sambhattā): very intimate, firm friends; for they are devotedly associated, sharing the same material requisites and the Dhamma, hence they are called 'companions.' 'On the slopes of Isigili' (Isigilipasse): Isigili is the name of a mountain, on its slope. Formerly, it is said, about five hundred Paccekabuddhas, having wandered for alms in the Kāsi and Kosala countries, would gather on that mountain after their meal and spend time in meditative attainments. People saw them entering but not leaving. Then they said, 'This mountain swallows these seers.' Based on that, the designation 'Isigili' arose for it; on its slope, at the foot of that mountain.

Tiṇakuṭiyo karitvāti tiṇacchadanā sadvārabandhā kuṭiyo katvā. Vassaṃ upagacchantena hi nālakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannenāpi pañcannaṃ chadanānaṃ aññatarena channeyeva sadvārabandhe senāsane upagantabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabbaṃ. Yo upagaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 204). Tasmā vassakāle sace senāsanaṃ labhati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce labhati, hatthakammaṃ pariyesitvāpi kātabbaṃ. Hatthakammaṃ alabhantena sāmampi kātabbaṃ. Na tveva asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabbaṃ. Ayamanudhammatā. Tasmā te bhikkhū tiṇakuṭiyo karitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīni paricchinditvā katikavattāni ca khandhakavattāni ca adhiṭṭhāya tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhamānā vassaṃ upagacchiṃsu.

'Having made grass huts' means having made huts with grass roofing and with fixed doors. For one undertaking the rains-residence, even one following the Nālaka practice, must undertake it in a dwelling covered by one of the five kinds of roofing and with a fixed door. For it was said: 'Monks, the rains-residence should not be undertaken without a dwelling. Whoever should undertake it, commits an offense of wrong-doing.' Therefore, during the rains season, if a dwelling is obtained, this is good; if it is not obtained, it should be made even after seeking out manual labor. One who does not obtain manual labor may make it oneself. But one must certainly not undertake the rains-residence without a dwelling. This is in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, those monks, having made grass huts, having defined the places for night and day, and having undertaken the agreement-duties and the Khandhaka-duties, entered the rains while training in the three trainings.

Āyasmāpi dhaniyoti na kevalaṃ te therāva imassa sikkhāpadassa ādikammiko āyasmā dhaniyopi. Kumbhakāraputtoti kumbhakārassa putto; tassa hi nāmaṃ dhaniyo, pitā kumbhakāro, tena vuttaṃ – “dhaniyo kumbhakāraputto”ti. Vassaṃ upagacchīti tehi therehi saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāneyeva tiṇakuṭikaṃ karitvā vassaṃ upagacchi. Vassaṃvutthāti purimikāya upagatā mahāpavāraṇāya pavāritā pāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya “vutthavassā”ti vuccanti. Evaṃ [P 2.0287] vassaṃvutthā hutvā.

'Venerable Dhaniya too' means not only those elders, but also Venerable Dhaniya, the originator of this training rule. 'The potter’s son' means the son of a potter; for his name was Dhaniya, and his father was a potter, therefore it was said, 'Dhaniya the potter’s son.' 'He entered the rains' means that together with those elders, having made a grass hut in the very same place, he entered the rains. 'Having spent the rains' means that those who entered the earlier rains-residence and performed the Pavāraṇā on the great Pavāraṇā day are called 'those who have spent the rains' from the day following it. Thus, having spent the rains.

Tiṇakuṭiyo bhinditvāti na daṇḍamuggarādīhi cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ katvā, vattasīsena pana tiṇañca dāruvalli-ādīni ca oropetvāti attho. Yena hi vihārapaccante kuṭi katā hoti, tena sace āvāsikā bhikkhū honti, te āpucchitabbā. “Sace imaṃ kuṭiṃ paṭijaggitvā koci vasituṃ ussahati, tassa dethā”ti vatvā pakkamitabbaṃ. Yena araññe vā katā hoti[M 1.0249], paṭijagganakaṃ vā na labhati, tena “aññesampi paribhogaṃ bhavissatī”ti paṭisāmetvā gantabbaṃ. Te pana bhikkhū araññe kuṭiyo katvā paṭijagganakaṃ alabhantā tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca paṭisāmetvā saṅgopetvāti attho. Yathā ca ṭhapitaṃ taṃ upacikāhi na khajjati[V 1.0230], anovassakañca hoti, tathā ṭhapetvā “idaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgantvā vasitukāmānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ upakārāya bhavissatī”ti gamiyavattaṃ pūretvā.

'Having dismantled the grass huts' means not by smashing them into powder with sticks, mallets, and so on, but rather, the meaning is that, in accordance with proper conduct, they took down the grass, wood, vines, and so on. For if a monk has built a hut on the outskirts of a monastery, and if there are resident monks, they should be asked. Having said, 'If anyone is able to look after this hut and live here, please give it to them,' he should depart. If a monk has built one in the forest, or if he cannot find a caretaker, he should put it in order, thinking, 'It will be for the use of others as well,' and then depart. But those monks, having built huts in the forest and not finding a caretaker, put the grass and wood in order and secured it well; this is the meaning. And having placed it in such a way that it would not be eaten by termites and would not be soaked by rain, they fulfilled the duty of one who is departing, thinking, 'This will be for the benefit of fellow practitioners who come to this place wishing to stay.'

Janapadacārikaṃ pakkamiṃsūti attano attano cittānukūlaṃ janapadaṃ agamaṃsu. Āyasmā pana dhaniyo kumbhakāraputto tattheva vassaṃ vasītiādi uttānatthameva. Yāvatatiyakanti yāvatatiyavāraṃ. Anavayoti anuavayo, sandhivasena ukāralopo. Anu anu avayo, yaṃ yaṃ kumbhakārehi kattabbaṃ nāma atthi, sabbattha anūno paripuṇṇasippoti attho. Saketi attano santake. Ācariyaketi ācariyakamme. Kumbhakārakammeti kumbhakārānaṃ kamme; kumbhakārehi kattabbakammeti attho. Etena sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sarūpato dassitaṃ hoti. Pariyodātasippoti parisuddhasippo. Anavayattepi sati aññehi asadisasippoti vuttaṃ hoti.

'They set out on a journey through the country' means they went to a region that suited their own inclinations. 'But the Venerable Dhaniya, the potter’s son, stayed right there for the rains,' and so forth, is clear in meaning. 'Up to the third time' means up to the third time. 'Without deficiency' (anavayo) is divided as 'anu-avayo', with the elision of the vowel 'u' due to sandhi. 'Anu anu avayo' means that in every single task, there is no deficiency; whatever work is to be done by potters, in all of it he was not deficient, a craftsman of complete skill. This is the meaning. 'His own' (sake) means belonging to himself. 'In the master's work' (ācariyake) means in the work of a master. 'In the potter's work' (kumbhakārakamme) means in the work of potters; that is, in the work to be done by potters. This is the meaning. By this, his own master-craftsmanship is shown in its true form. 'Of purified skill' (pariyodātasippo) means of purified skill. Even while being without deficiency, it is said that his skill was unlike that of others.

Sabbamattikāmayanti piṭṭhasaṅghāṭakakavāṭasūcighaṭikavātapānakavāṭamattaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ bhittichadaniṭṭhakathambhādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ gehasambhāraṃ mattikāmayameva katvāti attho. Tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca gomayañca saṅkaḍḍhitvā taṃ kuṭikaṃ pacīti taṃ sabbamattikāmayaṃ katvā pāṇikāya ghaṃsitvā sukkhāpetvā telatambamattikāya parimajjitvā anto ca bahi ca tiṇādīhi pūretvā yathā pakkā supakkā hoti, evaṃ paci. Evaṃ pakkā ca pana sā ahosi kuṭikā[P 2.0288]. Abhirūpāti surūpā. Pāsādikāti pasādajanikā. Lohitikāti lohitavaṇṇā. Kiṅkaṇikasaddoti kiṅkaṇikajālassa saddo. Yathā kira nānāratanehi katassa kiṅkaṇikajālassa saddo hoti, evaṃ tassā kuṭikāya vātapānantarikādīhi paviṭṭhena vātena samāhatāya saddo ahosi. Etenassā anto ca bahi ca supakkabhāvo dassito hoti. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kiṅkaṇikā”ti kaṃsabhājanaṃ, tasmā yathā abhihatassa kaṃsabhājanassa saddo, evamassā vātappahatāya saddo ahosī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Made entirely of clay' means: having set aside only the door-frame, door-leaf, bolt, hinge, and window-leaf, having made all the remaining components of the dwelling—such as the walls, roofing tiles, and pillars—entirely of clay. This is the meaning. 'He baked that hut by collecting grass, wood, and cow dung' means: having made it entirely of clay, he smoothed it with a trowel, let it dry, polished it with red clay mixed with oil, and filled it both inside and out with grass and other materials; he then baked it in such a way that it would be well-baked. And that hut, thus baked, became beautiful. 'Beautiful' (abhirūpā) means of good form. 'Pleasing' (pāsādikā) means inspiring serenity. 'Reddish' (lohitikā) means of a red color. 'The sound of a small bell' (kiṅkaṇikasaddo) means the sound of a net of small bells. Just as there is the sound of a net of small bells made of various gems, so too there was a sound from that hut when it was struck by the wind that entered through the window openings and so on. By this, it is shown that it was well-baked both inside and out. However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, 'kiṅkaṇikā' is a bronze vessel. Therefore, it is said: 'Just as there is the sound of a bronze vessel when struck, so too was the sound of this hut when struck by the wind.'

85. Kiṃ [M 1.0250] etaṃ, bhikkhaveti ettha jānantova bhagavā kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchi. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesunti sabbamattikāmayāya kuṭikāya karaṇabhāvaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Kathañhi nāma so, bhikkhave…pe… kuṭikaṃ karissatīti idaṃ atītatthe anāgatavacanaṃ; akāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ saddasatthato pariyesitabbaṃ. Na hi nāma, bhikkhave, tassa moghapurisassa pāṇesu anuddayā anukampā avihesā bhavissatīti ettha anuddayāti anurakkhaṇā; etena mettāpubbabhāgaṃ dasseti. Anukampāti paradukkhena cittakampanā. Avihesāti avihiṃsanā; etehi karuṇāpubbabhāgaṃ dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “bhikkhave[V 1.0231], tassa moghapurisassa pathavīkhaṇanacikkhallamaddanaaggidānesu bahū khuddānukhuddake pāṇe byābādhentassa vināsentassa tesu pāṇesu mettākaruṇānaṃ pubbabhāgamattāpi anuddayā anukampā avihesā na hi nāma bhavissati appamattakāpi nāma na bhavissatī”ti. Mā pacchimā janatā pāṇesu pātabyataṃ āpajjīti pacchimo janasamūho pāṇesu pātabyabhāvaṃ mā āpajji. “Buddhakālepi bhikkhūhi evaṃ kataṃ, īdisesu ṭhānesu pāṇātipātaṃ karontānaṃ natthi doso”ti maññitvā imassa diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjamānā pacchimā janatā mā pāṇesu pātabye ghaṃsitabbe evaṃ maññīti vuttaṃ hoti.

85. 'What is this, bhikkhus?' Here, the Blessed One, although knowing, asked for the purpose of raising the topic of conversation. 'They informed the Blessed One of this matter' means they informed the Blessed One from the very beginning about the fact of the making of the hut made entirely of clay. 'How indeed, bhikkhus... could he build a hut?' This is a future tense expression used in a past sense; it means 'how indeed did he do it?'. Its grammatical rule should be sought from the grammatical texts. 'Surely, bhikkhus, for that foolish man could there be any sympathy, pity, or non-injury for living beings?' Here, 'sympathy' (anuddayā) means protection; by this, the preliminary stage of loving-kindness is shown. 'Pity' (anukampā) means the trembling of the heart at the suffering of others. 'Non-injury' (avihesā) means non-harming; by these, the preliminary stage of compassion is shown. This is what is said: 'Bhikkhus, for that foolish man, while harming and destroying many small and tiny living beings in the course of digging the earth, kneading the mud, and applying fire, could there indeed be toward those beings even a measure of the preliminary stage of loving-kindness and compassion, such as sympathy, pity, or non-injury? Could there indeed be even a small amount?' 'Lest the future generation should fall into destructiveness towards living beings' means: lest the future generation of people should fall into a state of destructiveness towards living beings. It is said: Lest the future generation, thinking, 'Even in the Buddha's time, bhikkhus did thus; in such situations, there is no fault for those who commit the destruction of life,' and thereby following the view of this one, should think that living beings may be destroyed and crushed.

Evaṃ [P 2.0289] dhaniyaṃ garahitvā na ca, bhikkhave, sabbamattikāmayā kuṭikā kātabbāti āyatiṃ tādisāya kuṭikāya karaṇaṃ paṭikkhipi; paṭikkhipitvā ca “yo kareyya āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti sabbamattikāmayakuṭikākaraṇe āpattiṃ ṭhapesi. Tasmā yopi pathavīkhaṇanādinā pāṇesu pātabyataṃ anāpajjanto tādisaṃ kuṭikaṃ karoti, sopi dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Pathavīkhaṇanādīhi pana pāṇesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanto yaṃ yaṃ vatthuṃ vītikkamati, tattha tattha vuttameva āpattiṃ āpajjati. Dhaniyattherassa ādikammikattā anāpatti. Sesānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ atikkamitvā karontānampi kataṃ labhitvā tattha vasantānampi dukkaṭameva. Dabbasambhāramissakā pana yathā vā tathā vā missā hotu, vaṭṭati. Suddhamattikāmayāva na vaṭṭati. Sāpi iṭṭhakāhi giñjakāvasathasaṅkhepena katā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ bhanteti kho…pe… taṃ kuṭiṃ bhindiṃsūti bhagavato vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā kaṭṭhehi ca pāsāṇehi ca taṃ kuṭikaṃ vikirantā bhindiṃsu.

Having thus rebuked Dhaniya, he said, 'And, bhikkhus, a hut made entirely of clay is not to be made,' thus prohibiting the making of such a hut in the future. And having prohibited it, he laid down an offense for making a hut made entirely of clay, saying, 'Whoever should make one, there is an offense of wrongdoing.' Therefore, whichever bhikkhu makes such a hut without falling into destructiveness towards living beings through digging the earth and so on, he too incurs an offense of wrongdoing. Furthermore, one who, while falling into destructiveness towards living beings through digging the earth and so on, transgresses any rule, incurs the very offense stated for each respective transgression. For Elder Dhaniya, because he was the originator of the deed, there is no offense. For the others—for those who make one by transgressing the training rule, and also for those who, having received one already made, dwell therein—there is an offense of wrongdoing. However, a hut mixed with material components, however it may be mixed, is allowable. Only one made purely of clay is not allowable. Even that, if made with bricks in the manner of a brick house, is allowable. 'Having said, "So be it, venerable sir,"... they broke that hut' means: having accepted the Blessed One's word, they broke that hut, scattering it with pieces of wood and with stones.

Atha [M 1.0251] kho āyasmā dhaniyotiādimhi ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – dhaniyo ekapasse divāvihāraṃ nisinno tena saddena āgantvā te bhikkhū “kissa me tumhe, āvuso, kuṭiṃ bhindathā”ti pucchitvā “bhagavā bhedāpetī”ti sutvā subbacatāya sampaṭicchi.

Regarding the passage beginning 'Then the Venerable Dhaniya,' this is the summary meaning: Dhaniya, who was seated for his day-sojourn to one side, came on account of that sound and asked those bhikkhus, 'Friends, why are you breaking my hut?' Having heard, 'The Blessed One has ordered it to be broken,' he accepted it due to his quality of being easy to admonish.

Kasmā pana bhagavā iminā atimahantena ussāhena attano vasanatthaṃ kataṃ kuṭikaṃ bhedāpesi, nanu etassettha vayakammampi atthīti? Kiñcāpi atthi, atha kho naṃ bhagavā akappiyāti bhindāpesi, titthiyadhajoti bhindāpesi. Ayamettha vinicchayo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana aññānipi kāraṇāni vuttāni – sattānuddayāya, pattacīvaraguttatthāya, senāsanabāhullapaasedhanāyātiādīni. Tasmā idānipi yo bhikkhu bahussuto vinayaññū aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ akappiyaṃ parikkhāraṃ gahetvā vicarantaṃ disvā taṃ chindāpeyya vā bhindāpeyya vā anupavajjo[V 1.0232], so neva codetabbo na sāretabbo; na taṃ labbhā vattuṃ “mama parikkhāro tayā nāsito, taṃ me dehī”ti.

Why then did the Blessed One, with such great effort, have the hut built for his own dwelling destroyed? Is there not also the expense involved here? Although there is, the Blessed One had it destroyed because it was unallowable; he had it destroyed because it was a banner of the sectarians. This is the determination here. But in the Commentary, other reasons are also stated—for the sake of compassion for beings, for the security of the bowl and robes, for the prohibition of a proliferation of lodgings, and so on. Therefore, even now, if a learned bhikkhu who knows the Vinaya sees another bhikkhu going about with an unallowable requisite and has it cut or broken, he is blameless. He should neither be accused nor reproached. It is not allowable to say to him, 'My requisite has been destroyed by you; give it to me.'

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayo

A Determination on Matters Outside the Pāḷi Canon

Tatrāyaṃ [P 2.0290] pāḷimuttako kappiyākappiyaparikkhāravinicchayo – keci tālapaṇṇacchattaṃ anto vā bahi vā pañcavaṇṇena suttena sibbantā vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ karonti, taṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekavaṇṇena pana nīlena vā pītakena vā yena kenaci suttena anto vā bahi vā sibbituṃ chattadaṇḍaggāhakaṃ salākapañjaraṃ vā vinandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Tañca kho thirakaraṇatthaṃ, na vaṇṇamaṭṭhatthāya. Chattapaṇṇakesu makaradantakaṃ vā aḍḍhacandakaṃ vā chindituṃ na vaṭṭati. Chattadaṇḍe gehathambhesu viya ghaṭako vā vāḷarūpakaṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Sacepi sabbattha āraggena lekhā dinnā hoti, sāpi na vaṭṭati. Ghaṭakampi vāḷarūpampi bhinditvā dhāretabbaṃ. Lekhāpi ghaṃsitvā vā apanetabbā, suttakena vā daṇḍo veṭhetabbo. Daṇḍabunde pana ahicchattakasaṇṭhānaṃ vaṭṭati. Vātappahārena acalanatthaṃ chattamaṇḍalikaṃ rajjukehi gāhetvā daṇḍe bandhanti, tasmiṃ bandhanaṭṭhāne valayamiva ukkiritvā lekhaṃ ṭhapenti, sā vaṭṭati.

Herein is the determination concerning allowable and unallowable requisites, which is outside the Pāḷi Canon: Some bhikkhus, sewing a palm-leaf umbrella either inside or outside with five-colored thread, make it ornamental; that is not allowable. However, it is allowable to sew it either inside or outside with a single-colored thread—whether blue, yellow, or any other whatsoever—or to bind the cage of ribs that holds the umbrella shaft. And this is for the purpose of making it firm, not for the purpose of ornamentation. On the umbrella leaves, it is not allowable to cut a makara-tooth pattern or a half-moon pattern. On the umbrella shaft, like on house pillars, a small pot or a beast-figure is not allowable. Even if lines are made all over with a stylus, that too is not allowable. The small pot and the beast-figure should be broken off before it is used. The lines should be rubbed off or removed, or the shaft should be wrapped with thread. But on the base of the shaft, a mushroom shape is allowable. To prevent it from moving due to the striking of the wind, they take the small inner circle of the umbrella with small cords and tie it to the shaft. At that binding place, they carve a line like a bracelet and leave it; that is allowable.

Cīvaramaṇḍanatthāya nānāsuttakehi satapadīsadisaṃ sibbantā āgantukapaṭṭaṃ ṭhapenti, aññampi yaṃkiñci sūcikammavikāraṃ karonti, paṭṭamukhe vā pariyante [M 1.0252] vā veṇiṃ vā saṅkhalikaṃ vā, evamādi sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati, pakatisūcikammameva vaṭṭati. Gaṇṭhikapaṭṭakañca pāsakapaṭṭañca aṭṭhakoṇampi soḷasakoṇampi karonti, tattha agghiyagayamuggarādīni dassenti, kakkaṭakkhīni ukkiranti, sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati, catukoṇameva vaṭṭati. Koṇasuttapiḷakā ca cīvare ratte duviññeyyarūpā vaṭṭanti. Kañjikapiṭṭhakhaliādīsu cīvaraṃ pakkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati. Cīvarakammakāle pana hatthamalasūcimalādīnaṃ dhovanatthaṃ kiliṭṭhakāle ca dhovanatthaṃ vaṭṭati. Gandhaṃ vā lākhaṃ vā telaṃ [P 2.0291] vā rajane pakkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati.

For the purpose of adorning a robe, they affix a patch, sewing with threads of various colors to resemble a centipede. They also do any other kind of fancy needlework, such as a braid-like stitch or a chain-like stitch at the edge of the patch or at the border. All such things are not allowable; only ordinary needlework is allowable. They make a patch for a knot and a patch for a loop, eight-cornered or even sixteen-cornered. Thereon they show things like a cetiya-shape, a goad-shape, a club-shape, and so on; they carve out crab's-eye patterns. All of this is not allowable; only a four-cornered patch is allowable. And the thread-knots at the corners, being of a form that is difficult to discern on a dyed robe, are allowable. It is not allowable to put a robe into rice-gruel, flour-paste, dregs, and so on. But during the time of robe-making, it is allowable for washing off dirt from the hands, dirt from the needle, and the like, and for washing the robe when it is soiled. It is not allowable to put perfume, lac, or oil into the dye.

Cīvaraṃ rajitvā saṅkhena vā maṇinā vā yena kenaci na ghaṭṭetabbaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ jāṇukāni nihantvā hatthehi gahetvā doṇiyampi na ghaṃsitabbaṃ. Doṇiyaṃ vā phalake vā ṭhapetvā ante gāhāpetvā hatthehi paharituṃ pana vaṭṭati; tampi muṭṭhinā na kātabbaṃ. Porāṇakattherā pana doṇiyampi na ṭhapesuṃ. Eko gahetvā tiṭṭhati; aparo hatthe katvā hatthena paharati. Cīvarassa kaṇṇasuttakaṃ na vaṭṭati, rajitakāle chinditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṇṇasuttaka”nti [V 1.0233] (mahāva. 344) evaṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ anuvāte pāsakaṃ katvā bandhitabbaṃ rajanakāle lagganatthāya. Gaṇṭhikepi sobhākaraṇatthaṃ lekhā vā piḷakā vā na vaṭṭati, nāsetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

After dyeing a robe, it should not be polished with a conch, a gem, or any other object. Placing the knees on the ground and taking it with the hands, it should not be beaten even in a trough. However, it is allowable to place it in a trough or on a board, have someone hold the ends, and beat it with the hands; even that should not be done with a fist. But the ancient elders did not place it even in a trough. One holds it and stands; another places it over one hand and beats it with the other hand. A corner-thread on a robe is not allowable; it should be cut off at the time of dyeing. But that corner-thread which was allowed thus, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a corner-thread,' should be made into a loop and tied in a place with airflow for the purpose of hanging it at the time of dyeing. On a knot, for the purpose of beautification, a line or a knob is not allowable; it should be destroyed before the robe is used.

Patte vā thālake vā āraggena lekhaṃ karonti, anto vā bahi vā na vaṭṭati. Pattaṃ bhamaṃ āropetvā majjitvā pacanti – “maṇivaṇṇaṃ karissāmā”ti, na vaṭṭati; telavaṇṇo pana vaṭṭati. Pattamaṇḍale bhittikammaṃ na vaṭṭati, makaradantakaṃ pana vaṭṭati.

On a bowl or a plate, they make lines with a stylus; either inside or outside, this is not allowable. They fire a bowl after putting it on a lathe and polishing it, thinking, 'We will make it jewel-colored'; this is not allowable. But an oil-colored one is allowable. On the base-ring of the bowl, plaster-work is not allowable, but a makara-tooth pattern is allowable.

Dhamakaraṇachattakassa upari vā heṭṭhā vā dhamakaraṇakucchiyaṃ vā lekhā na vaṭṭati, chattamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ panassa lekhā vaṭṭati.

On the top or the bottom of the umbrella-like part of a water-strainer, or in the 'belly' of the water-strainer, a line is not allowable. But on the rim of its umbrella-like opening, a line is allowable.

Kāyabandhanassa sobhanatthaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ diguṇaṃ suttaṃ koṭṭenti, kakkaṭacchīni uṭṭhapenti, na vaṭṭati. Ubhosu pana antesu dasāmukhassa thirabhāvāya diguṇaṃ koṭṭetuṃ vaṭṭati. Dasāmukhe pana ghaṭakaṃ vā makaramukhaṃ vā deḍḍubhasīsaṃ vā yaṃkiñci vikārarūpaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tattha tattha acchīni dassetvā mālākammalatākammādīni vā katvā koṭṭitakāyabandhanampi na vaṭṭati. Ujukameva pana macchakaṇṭakaṃ vā khajjuripattakaṃ vā maṭṭhapaṭṭikaṃ vā katvā koṭṭituṃ [P 2.0292] vaṭṭati. Kāyabandhanassa dasā ekā vaṭṭati, dve tīṇi cattāripi vaṭṭanti; tato [M 1.0253] paraṃ na vaṭṭanti. Rajjukakāyabandhanaṃ ekameva vaṭṭati. Pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Dasā pana pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānāpi vaṭṭati. Bahurajjuke ekato katvā ekena nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ bahurajjukanti na vattabbaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati.

For the purpose of beautifying a waistband, they weave a doubled thread here and there and make raised crab's-eye patterns; this is not allowable. But at both ends, for the firmness of the fringe-end, it is allowable to weave it doubled. On the fringe-end, however, it is not allowable to make a small pot shape, a makara-face, a water-snake's head, or any other fancy shape. A waistband woven showing 'eyes' here and there, or having made flower-work, creeper-work, and the like, is also not allowable. But it is allowable to weave it making it just straight, or like a fish-bone, a date-palm leaf, or a smooth band. For a waistband, one fringe is allowable; two, three, or even four are allowable. More than that are not allowable. A rope-waistband of only a single strand is allowable. But one with the shape of a chisel-handle is not allowable, not even a single one. A fringe, however, with the shape of a chisel-handle is allowable. One made by gathering many small cords together and wrapping them continuously with a single cord should not be called a 'many-corded' one; that is allowable.

Kāyabandhanavidhe aṭṭhamaṅgalādikaṃ yaṃkiñci vikārarūpaṃ na vaṭṭati, paricchedalekhāmattaṃ vaṭṭati. Vidhakassa ubhosu antesu thirakaraṇatthāya ghaṭakaṃ karonti, ayampi vaṭṭati.

On a belt buckle or belt knob, any altered form such as the eight auspicious signs is not allowable; only a mere demarcation line is allowable. To make both ends of the buckle or knob firm, they make a small pot-shaped knob, and this is also allowable.

Añjaniyaṃ itthipurisacatuppadasakuṇarūpaṃ vā mālākamma-latākammamakaradantaka-gomuttakaaḍḍhacandakādibhedaṃ vā vikārarūpaṃ na vaṭṭati. Ghaṃsitvā vā chinditvā vā yathā vā na paññāyati, tathā suttena veṭhetvā vaḷañjetabbā. Ujukameva pana caturaṃsā vā aṭṭhaṃsā vā soḷasaṃsā vā añjanī vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhato pissā dve vā tisso vā vaṭṭalekhāyo vaṭṭanti. Gīvāyampissā pidhānakabandhanatthaṃ ekā vaṭṭalekhā vaṭṭati.

On a collyrium pot, an altered form in the shape of a woman, man, four-footed animal, or bird, or with variations such as garland-work, creeper-work, makara-tooth patterns, cow-urine patterns, half-moon shapes, and so on, is not allowable. It should be used only after rubbing it off, cutting it off, or wrapping it with thread in such a way that the design is not apparent. However, a collyrium pot that is simply straight, or is square, octagonal, or sixteen-sided, is allowable. At its base, two or three circular lines are allowable. On its neck, one circular line for the purpose of tying the lid is allowable.

Añjanisalākāyapi [V 1.0234] vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭati. Añjanitthavikāyampi yaṃkiñci nānāvaṇṇena suttena vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭati. Eseva nayo kuñcikākosakepi. Kuñcikāya vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭati, tathā sipāṭikāyaṃ. Ekavaṇṇasuttena panettha yena kenaci sibbituṃ vaṭṭati.

For a collyrium stick, smoothed and polished decorative work is not allowable. For a collyrium pot bag, any smoothed and polished decorative work with multicolored thread is not allowable. The same rule applies to a key pouch. On a key, smoothed and polished decorative work is not allowable; likewise for a pouch. In these cases, it is allowable to stitch with any single-colored thread.

Ārakaṇṭakepi vaṭṭamaṇikaṃ vā aññaṃ vā vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Gīvāyaṃ pana paricchedalekhā vaṭṭati. Pipphalikepi maṇikaṃ vā piḷakaṃ vā yaṃkiñci uṭṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Daṇḍake pana paricchedalekhā vaṭṭati. Nakhacchedanaṃ valitakaṃyeva karonti, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭati. Uttarāraṇiyaṃ vā adharāraṇiyaṃ vā araṇidhanuke vā [P 2.0293] uparipellanadaṇḍake vā mālākammādikaṃ yaṃkiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, pellanadaṇḍakassa pana vemajjhe maṇḍalaṃ hoti, tattha paricchedalekhāmattaṃ vaṭṭati. Sūcisaṇḍāsaṃ karonti, yena sūciṃ ḍaṃsāpetvā ghaṃsanti, tattha makaramukhādikaṃ yaṃkiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, sūciḍaṃsanatthaṃ pana mukhamattaṃ hoti, taṃ vaṭṭati.

For an awl, a round bead-shape or any other smoothed and polished form is not allowable. However, a demarcation line on its neck is allowable. For a small knife, it is not allowable to create a bead-shape, a raised bump, or any such feature. However, a demarcation line on the handle is allowable. A nail-cutter they make only curved; therefore, that is allowable. For the upper fire-stick, the lower fire-stick, the fire-bow, or the upper pressing-stick, any smoothed and polished form such as garland-work is not allowable. However, in the middle of the pressing-stick there is a round hole; there, a mere demarcation line is allowable. They make needle-pincers with which they grip a needle to polish it; on these, any smoothed and polished form such as a makara-face is not allowable. However, a mere mouth-shape for the purpose of gripping the needle is present, and that is allowable.

Dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsiyampi yaṃkiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, ujukameva kappiyalohena ubhosu vā passesu caturaṃsaṃ vā aṭṭhaṃsaṃ vā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Kattaradaṇḍepi yaṃkiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā ekā vā dve vā vaṭṭalekhā upari ahicchattakamakuḷamattañca vaṭṭati.

For a tooth-stick cutter, any smoothed and polished decorative work is not allowable; it is allowable only for it to be straight and to bind it on both sides, or on one side, with a square or octagonal piece of allowable metal. On a walking stick, any smoothed and polished decorative work is not allowable. At the bottom, one or two circular lines are allowable, and at the top, a mere mushroom-bud shape is allowable.

Telabhājanesu [M 1.0254] visāṇe vā nāḷiyaṃ vā alābuke vā āmaṇḍasārake vā ṭhapetvā itthirūpaṃ purisarūpañca avasesaṃ sabbampi vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭati.

Among oil containers—whether a horn, a tube, a gourd, or a container made from castor-oil fruit pulp—all remaining smoothed and polished decorative work is allowable, with the exception of the forms of women and men.

Mañcapīṭhe bhisibimbohane bhūmattharaṇe pādapuñchane caṅkamanabhisiyā sammuñjaniyaṃ kacavarachaḍḍanake rajanadoṇikāya pānīyauḷuṅke pānīyaghaṭe pādakathalikāya phalakapīṭhake valayādhārake daṇḍādhārakepattapidhāne tālavaṇṭe vījaneti – etesu sabbaṃ mālākammādivaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭati. Senāsane pana dvārakavāṭavātapānakavāṭādīsu sabbaratanamayampi vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭati.

On a bed, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a floor-covering, a foot-wiper, a mat for a walking path, a broom, a refuse basket, a dye-trough, a water-strainer, a water-pot, a foot-scrubber, a plank-seat, a ring-stand for a bowl, a staff-stand for a bowl, a bowl-lid, a palm-leaf fan, or a square fan—on these, all smoothed and polished decorative work such as garland-work is allowable. Furthermore, in a dwelling, on door-panels, window-panels, and so on, smoothed and polished decorative work is allowable, even if made entirely of gems.

Senāsane kiñci paṭisedhetabbaṃ natthi, aññatra viruddhasenāsanā. Viruddhasenāsanaṃ nāma aññesaṃ sīmāya rājavallabhehi katasenāsanaṃ vuccati, tasmā ye tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ karonti, te vattabbā – “mā amhākaṃ sīmāya senāsanaṃ karothā”ti. Anādiyitvā karontiyeva, punapi vattabbā – “mā evaṃ akattha, mā amhākaṃ uposathapavāraṇānaṃ antarāyamakattha, mā sāmaggiṃ [V 1.0235] bhindittha, tumhākaṃ senāsanaṃ katampi kataṭṭhāne na ṭhassatī”ti. Sace balakkārena karontiyeva, yadā tesaṃ lajjiparisā ussannā hoti, sakkā [P 2.0294] ca hoti laddhuṃ dhammiko vinicchayo, tadā tesaṃ pesetabbaṃ – “tumhākaṃ āvāsaṃ harathā”ti. Sace yāva tatiyaṃ pesite haranti, sādhu; no ce haranti, ṭhapetvā bodhiñca cetiyañca avasesasenāsanāni bhinditabbāni, no ca kho aparibhogaṃ karontehi, paṭipāṭiyā pana chadana-gopānasī-iṭṭhakādīni apanetvā tesaṃ pesetabbaṃ – “tumhākaṃ dabbasambhāre harathā”ti. Sace haranti, sādhu; no ce haranti, atha tesu dabbasambhāresu himavassavātātapādīhi pūtibhūtesu vā corehi vā haṭesu agginā vā daḍḍhesu sīmasāmikā bhikkhū anupavajjā, na labbhā codetuṃ “tumhehi amhākaṃ dabbasambhārā nāsitā”ti vā “tumhākaṃ gīvā”ti vā. Yaṃ pana sīmasāmikehi bhikkhūhi kataṃ, taṃ sukatameva hotīti.

In a dwelling, there is nothing that needs to be forbidden, except for a hostile dwelling. A 'hostile dwelling' is the name for a dwelling built by those favored by the king within the boundary of others. Therefore, those who build such a dwelling should be told: “Do not build a dwelling within our boundary.” If they disregard this and build anyway, they should be told again: “Do not do this. Do not create an obstacle for our Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies. Do not break the harmony. Your dwelling, even if built, will not remain in the place it was built.” If they persist in building by force, then when their conscientious faction becomes numerous and it is possible to obtain a righteous decision, a message should be sent to them: “Remove your dwelling.” If, after the message is sent up to the third time, they remove it, that is good. If they do not remove it, then, setting aside the Bodhi tree and the cetiya, the remaining dwellings should be dismantled. However, this should not be done by rendering them unusable. Rather, the roofing, rafters, bricks, and so on should be removed in order, and a message should be sent to them: “Take away your building materials.” If they take them, that is good. If they do not take them, then if those building materials become rotten due to snow, rain, wind, and sun, or are taken by thieves, or are burned by fire, the monks who are masters of the boundary are blameless. They cannot be accused by saying, “You have destroyed our building materials,” or, “It is your liability.” Whatever is done by the monks who are masters of the boundary is well done.

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayo niṭṭhito.

The Determination of Cases Beyond the Pāḷi is concluded.

86. Evaṃ bhinnāya pana kuṭikāya dhaniyassa parivitakkañca puna kuṭikaraṇatthāya ussāhañca dassetuṃ “atha kho āyasmato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha [M 1.0255] dārugahe gaṇakoti rañño dārubhaṇḍāgāre dārugopako. Devagahadārūnīti devena gahitadārūni. Rājapaṭiggahitabhūtāni dārūnīti attho. Nagarapaṭisaṅkhārikānīti nagarassa paṭisaṅkhārūpakaraṇāni. Āpadatthāya nikkhittānīti aggidāhena vā purāṇabhāvena vā paṭirājūparundhanādinā vā gopuraṭṭālakarājantepurahatthisālādīnaṃ vipatti āpadāti vuccati. Tadatthaṃ nikkhittānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chedāpetvāti attano kuṭiyā pamāṇaṃ sallakkhetvā kiñci agge kiñci majjhe kiñci mūle khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karonto chedāpesi.

86. Thus, when the hut was broken, to show Dhaniya’s reflection and his renewed effort to rebuild the hut, the passage beginning, 'Then the Venerable…' was spoken. Here, 'dārugahe gaṇako' means the guardian of the timber in the king’s timber storehouse. 'Devagahadārūni' means timber taken by the king. The meaning is that it was timber that had been royally appropriated. 'Nagarapaṭisaṅkhārikāni' refers to materials for the repair of the city. 'Āpadatthāya nikkhittāni' means set aside for emergencies—such misfortunes as destruction by fire, dilapidation, siege by rival kings, or damage to city gates, watchtowers, royal palaces, elephant stables, and so on, are called 'emergencies.' It means they were set aside for that purpose. 'Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chedāpetvāti' means, having assessed the dimensions of his own hut, he had it cut into various pieces—some at the top, some in the middle, and some at the base.

87. Vassakāroti tassa brāhmaṇassa nāmaṃ. Magadhamahāmattoti magadharaṭṭhe mahāmatto, mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgato, magadharañño vā mahāmatto; mahāamaccoti vuttaṃ hoti. Anusaññāyamānoti tattha tattha gantvā paccavekkhamāno. Bhaṇeti issarānaṃ nīcaṭṭhānikapurisālapanaṃ. Bandhaṃ āṇāpesīti brāhmaṇo pakatiyāpi [P 2.0295] tasmiṃ issāpakatova. So rañño “āṇāpehī”ti vacanaṃ sutvā yasmā “pakkosāpehī”ti rañño na vuttaṃ, tasmā “naṃ hatthesu ca pādesu ca bandhaṃ katvā āṇāpessāmī”ti bandhaṃ āṇāpesi. Addasa kho āyasmā dhaniyoti kathaṃ addasa? So kira attanā lesena dārūnaṃ haṭabhāvaṃ ñatvā “nissaṃsayaṃ esa dārūnaṃ kāraṇā rājakulato vadhaṃ vā bandhaṃ vā pāpuṇissati, tadā naṃ ahameva mocessāmī”ti [V 1.0236] niccakālaṃ tassa pavattiṃ suṇantoyeva vicarati. Tasmā takhaṇaññeva gantvā addasa. Tena vuttaṃ – “addasa kho āyasmā dhaniyo”ti. Dārūnaṃ kiccāti dārūnaṃ kāraṇā. Purāhaṃ haññāmīti ahaṃ purā haññāmi; yāva ahaṃ na haññāmi, tāva tvaṃ eyyāsīti attho.

87. 'Vassakāra' is the name of that brahmin. 'Magadhamahāmatta' means a great minister in the Magadha kingdom, endowed with a great measure of authority, or a great minister of the king of Magadha; it is said to mean a great minister. 'Anusaññāyamāno' means going here and there and inspecting. 'Bhaṇe' is an address used by superiors to a person of lower rank. 'He ordered him to be bound' means that the brahmin, being by nature jealous of him, upon hearing the king’s word, 'Give the order,' and because the king did not say, 'Have him summoned,' thought, 'I will have him bound hand and foot and then give the order,' and so he ordered him to be bound. 'The Venerable Dhaniya saw'—how did he see? It is said that he, having understood through his own subtle hint that the timber had been taken, thought, 'Without a doubt, on account of this timber, he will receive execution or imprisonment from the royal court; then I myself will free him.' Thus, he went about constantly listening for news of him. Therefore, he went and saw him at that very moment. For that reason, it is said: 'The Venerable Dhaniya saw.' 'Dārūnaṃ kiccā' means on account of the timber. 'Purāhaṃ haññāmi' means 'Before I am killed'; the meaning is, 'You should come before I am killed.'

88. Iṅgha, bhante, sarāpehīti ettha iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Paṭhamābhisittoti abhisitto hutvā paṭhamaṃ. Evarūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti “dinnaññeva samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ paribhuñjantū”ti imaṃ evarūpiṃ vācaṃ abhisitto hutvā paṭhamameva yaṃ tvaṃ abhāsi, taṃ sayameva bhāsitvā idāni sarasi, na sarasīti vuttaṃ hoti. Rājāno kira abhisittamattāyeva dhammabheriṃ carāpenti – “dinnaññeva samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ paribhuñjantū”ti taṃ sandhāya esa vadati. Tesaṃ mayā sandhāya bhāsitanti [M 1.0256] tesaṃ appamattakepi kukkuccāyantānaṃ samitabāhitapāpānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhodakaharaṇaṃ sandhāya mayā etaṃ bhāsitaṃ; na tumhādisānanti adhippāyo. Tañca kho araññe apariggahitanti tañca tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ yaṃ araññe apariggahitaṃ hoti; etaṃ sandhāya mayā bhāsitanti dīpeti.

88. In the phrase 'Pray, sir, remind him,' the word 'iṅgha' is a particle used in the sense of urging. 'First anointed' means first, after having been anointed. 'He spoke such a speech' means: it is said, 'That very speech of this kind—"Let ascetics and brahmins use the grass, wood, and water that has been given"—which you yourself spoke right at the beginning after being anointed, do you now remember it, or do you not remember it?' It is said that kings, just after being anointed, have the drum of the Teaching sounded thus: 'Let ascetics and brahmins use the grass, wood, and water that has been given.' He speaks with reference to that. 'It was spoken by me with reference to them' means: the intention is, 'This was spoken by me with reference to the taking of grass, wood, and water by those ascetics and brahmins who are scrupulous even about minor things, who have pacified and banished evil; it was not spoken with reference to those like you.' The phrase 'And that, in the forest, unclaimed' clarifies: 'It was spoken by me with reference to that grass, wood, and water which is unclaimed in the forest.'

Lomena tvaṃ muttosīti ettha lomamiva lomaṃ, kiṃ pana taṃ? Pabbajjāliṅgaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā nāma dhuttā “maṃsaṃ khādissāmā”ti mahagghalomaṃ eḷakaṃ gaṇheyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ añño viññupuriso disvā “imassa eḷakassa maṃsaṃ kahāpaṇamattaṃ [P 2.0296] agghati. Lomāni pana lomavāre lomavāre aneke kahāpaṇe agghantī”ti dve alomake eḷake datvā gaṇheyya. Evaṃ so eḷako viññupurisamāgamma lomena mucceyya. Evameva tvaṃ imassa kammassa katattā vadhabandhanāraho. Yasmā pana arahaddhajo sabbhi avajjharūpo, tvañca sāsane pabbajitattā yaṃ pabbajjāliṅgabhūtaṃ arahaddhajaṃ dhāresi. Tasmā tvaṃ iminā pabbajjāliṅgalomena eḷako viya viññupurisamāgamma muttosīti.

In the phrase 'You are freed by the fleece,' 'fleece' means 'like a fleece.' But what is that? The sign of the going forth. What is meant by this? Just as rogues, thinking, 'We will eat meat,' might seize a sheep with valuable fleece. Another wise person, seeing it, might think, 'This sheep's meat is worth about one kahāpaṇa, but its fleece, at each shearing, is worth many kahāpaṇas,' and giving two sheep without fleece, might take it. Thus that sheep, on account of the wise person, would be freed by its fleece. In the very same way, you, because you have done this deed, are deserving of execution and imprisonment. But because the banner of the Arahants is inviolable to the good, and you, having gone forth in the Dispensation, wear that banner of the Arahants which is the sign of the going forth, therefore, by this 'fleece' of the sign of the going forth, you are freed, just as the sheep was on account of the wise person.

Manussā ujjhāyantīti rañño parisati bhāsamānassa sammukhā ca parammukhā ca sutvā tattha tattha manussā ujjhāyanti, avajjhāyanti, avajānantā taṃ jhāyanti olokenti lāmakato vā cintentīti attho. Khiyyantīti tassa avaṇṇaṃ kathenti pakāsenti. Vipācentīti vitthārikaṃ karonti, sabbattha pattharanti; ayañca attho saddasatthānusārena veditabbo. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā – “alajjino ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā”tiādīni cintentā ujjhāyanti. “Natthi imesaṃ sāmañña”ntiādīni bhaṇantā khiyyanti. “Apagatā ime sāmaññā”tiādīni tattha tattha vitthārentā vipācentīti. Etena nayena imesaṃ padānaṃ ito [V 1.0237] parampi tattha tattha āgatapadānurūpena yojanā veditabbā. Brahmacārinoti seṭṭhacārino. Sāmaññanti samaṇabhāvo. Brahmaññanti seṭṭhabhāvo. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

'People complained' means that, having heard the king speaking in his assembly, both in his presence and in his absence, people here and there complained, looked down upon him, and, regarding him with contempt, they watched him or thought of him as base—this is the meaning. 'They disparaged' means they spoke his dispraise, making it known. 'They spread it about' means they made it widespread, they spread it everywhere; and this meaning should be understood according to the grammatical texts. Herein, this is the application: thinking such things as, 'These Sakyan ascetics are shameless,' they complained. Saying such things as, 'There is no asceticism in them,' they disparaged. Spreading such things as, 'They are devoid of asceticism,' here and there, they spread it about. By this method, the application of these terms should be understood from here on, according to the terms that appear in various places. 'Brahmacārino' means those of excellent conduct. 'Sāmañña' means the state of an ascetic. 'Brahmañña' means the state of excellence. The rest has a plain meaning.

Rañño dārūnītiādimhi “adinnaṃ ādiyissatī”ti ayaṃ ujjhāyanattho. Yaṃ panetaṃ adinnaṃ ādiyi, taṃ dassetuṃ “rañño dārūnī”ti vuttaṃ. Iti vacanabhede asammuyhantehi attho veditabbo. Purāṇavohāriko [M 1.0257] mahāmattoti bhikkhubhāvato purāṇe gihikāle vinicchayavohāre niyuttattā “vohāriko”ti saṅkhaṃ gato mahāamacco.

In the phrase beginning with 'the king's timber,' the meaning of the reproach is this: 'He will take what is not given.' Now, to show that he took what was not given, the phrase 'the king's timber' was said. Thus, the meaning should be understood by those who are not confused by the difference in grammatical number. 'The great minister who was a former legal official' means a great minister who, in his former time as a layman before becoming a monk, was appointed to legal judgments and thus came to be known as 'a legal official.'

Atha kho bhagavā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavocāti bhagavā sāmaṃyeva lokavohārampi jānāti, atītabuddhānaṃ paññattimpi jānāti – “pubbepi buddhā ettakena pārājikaṃ paññapenti, ettakena thullaccayaṃ, ettakena dukkaṭa”nti. Evaṃ santepi sace aññehi lokavohāraviññūhi [P 2.0297] saddhiṃ asaṃsanditvā pādamattena pārājikaṃ paññapeyya, tenassa siyuṃ vattāro “sīlasaṃvaro nāma ekabhikkhussapi appameyyo asaṅkhyeyyo mahāpathavī-samudda-ākāsāni viya ativitthiṇṇo, kathañhi nāma bhagavā pādamattakena nāsesī”ti! Tato tathāgatassa ñāṇabalaṃ ajānantā sikkhāpadaṃ kopeyyuṃ, paññattampi sikkhāpadaṃ yathāṭhāne na tiṭṭheyya. Lokavohāraviññūhi pana saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā paññatte so upavādo na hoti. Aññadatthu evaṃ vattāro honti – “imehi nāma agārikāpi pādamattena coraṃ hanantipi bandhantipi pabbājentipi. Kasmā bhagavā pabbajitaṃ na nāsessati; yena parasantakaṃ tiṇasalākamattampi na gahetabba”nti! Tathāgatassa ca ñāṇabalaṃ jānissanti. Paññattampi ca sikkhāpadaṃ akuppaṃ bhavissati, yathāṭhāne ṭhassati. Tasmā lokavohāraviññūhi saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā paññapetukāmo sabbāvantaṃ parisaṃ anuvilokento atha kho bhagavā avidūre nisinnaṃ disvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca “kittakena kho bhikkhu rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro coraṃ gahetvā hanati vā bandhati vā pabbājeti vā”ti.

Then the Blessed One addressed that monk. The Blessed One himself knows worldly conventions and he knows the regulations laid down by past Buddhas: 'Past Buddhas also prescribed a pārājika offense for such an amount, a thullaccaya offense for such an amount, and a dukkaṭa offense for such an amount.' Even so, if, without consulting others who understand worldly conventions, he were to prescribe a pārājika offense for a mere pāda, there would be those who would say of him, 'Indeed, virtuous restraint for even a single monk is immeasurable, incalculable, and vast like the great earth, the ocean, and the sky. How could the Blessed One destroy it for a mere pāda?' Then, not knowing the Tathāgata's power of knowledge, they would violate the training rule, and the prescribed training rule would not stand in its proper place. But when it is prescribed after consulting with those who understand worldly conventions, that reproach does not occur. On the contrary, there are those who say this: 'Even these householders kill, bind, or banish a thief for a mere pāda. Why would the Blessed One not ruin a monastic, by whom not even so much as a blade of grass belonging to another should be taken?' And they will come to know the Tathāgata's power of knowledge. The prescribed training rule will also become unshakeable and will stand in its proper place. Therefore, wishing to prescribe it after consulting with those who understand worldly conventions, and while surveying the entire assembly, the Blessed One saw that monk sitting not far away and said this to him: 'Monk, for what amount does King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having caught a thief, execute, bind, or banish him?'

Tattha māgadhoti magadhānaṃ issaro. Seniyoti senāya sampanno. Bimbisāroti tassa nāmaṃ. Pabbājeti vāti raṭṭhato nikkhāmeti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Pañcamāsako pādoti tadā rājagahe vīsatimāsako kahāpaṇo hoti, tasmā pañcamāsako pādo. Etena lakkhaṇena sabbajanapadesu kahāpaṇassa catuttho bhāgo “pādo”ti veditabbo. So ca kho porāṇassa nīlakahāpaṇassa vasena, na itaresaṃ rudradāmakādīnaṃ. Tena hi pādena atītabuddhāpi pārājikaṃ paññapesuṃ, anāgatāpi paññapessanti. Sabbabuddhānañhi pārājikavatthumhi vā pārājike vā nānattaṃ [V 1.0238] natthi. Imāneva cattāri pārājikavatthūni[M 1.0258]. Imāneva cattāri pārājikāni. Ito ūnaṃ vā atirekaṃ vā natthi. Tasmā bhagavāpi dhaniyaṃ [P 2.0298] vigarahitvā pādeneva dutiyapārājikaṃ paññapento “yo pana bhikkhu adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhāta”ntiādimāha.

Therein, 'Māgadha' means ruler of the Magadhans. 'Seniya' means endowed with an army. 'Bimbisāra' is his name. 'Or banishes' means he makes him leave the country. The rest here is clear in meaning. 'A pāda is five māsakas': at that time in Rājagaha, a kahāpaṇa was twenty māsakas; therefore, five māsakas is a pāda. By this standard, in all regions, the fourth part of a kahāpaṇa should be understood as a 'pāda'. And that should be understood by way of the ancient pure kahāpaṇa, not of others such as the rudradāmakas. For indeed, by that pāda past Buddhas also prescribed the pārājika offense, and future Buddhas will also prescribe it. For among all Buddhas, there is no difference in the grounds for a pārājika offense or in the pārājika offense itself. These alone are the four grounds for a pārājika offense. These alone are the four pārājika offenses. There is nothing less or more than these. Therefore, the Blessed One also, having rebuked Dhaniya and wishing to prescribe the second pārājika offense with a pāda only, said the words beginning, 'Whatever monk, what is not given, reckoned as theft...'

Evaṃ mūlacchejjavasena daḷhaṃ katvā dutiyapārājike paññatte aparampi anupaññattatthāya rajakabhaṇḍikavatthu udapādi, tassuppattidīpanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ – “evañcidaṃ bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ hotī”ti. Tassattho ca anupaññattisambandho ca paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ ito paresu sabbasikkhāpadesu. Yaṃ yaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ vajjetvā uparūpari apubbameva vaṇṇayissāma. Yadi hi yaṃ yaṃ vuttanayaṃ, taṃ taṃ punapi vaṇṇayissāma, kadā vaṇṇanāya antaṃ gamissāma! Tasmā yaṃ yaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ sādhukaṃ upasallakkhetvā tattha tattha attho ca yojanā ca veditabbā. Apubbaṃ pana yaṃkiñci anuttānatthaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ mayameva vaṇṇayissāma.

Thus, after the second pārājika was firmly established by way of cutting off at the root, another incident, the story of the washerman's bundle, arose for the purpose of a supplementary regulation. To explain its origin, this was said by the compilers of the canon: 'And so this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.' Its meaning and its connection to the supplementary regulation should be understood in the same way as stated in the commentary on the first pārājika. And as it is here, so it is in all subsequent training rules. Whatever has been explained before, leaving all of that aside, we will commentate only on what is new hereafter. For if we were to commentate again on whatever has already been explained, when would we reach the end of the commentary! Therefore, whatever has been explained before, all of that should be carefully noted, and in each case the meaning and the application should be understood. But whatever is new and has a meaning that is not obvious, all of that we ourselves will explain.

Dhaniyavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Dhaniya is concluded.

90. Rajakattharaṇaṃ gantvāti rajakatitthaṃ gantvā; tañhi yasmā tattha rajakā vatthāni attharanti, tasmā rajakattharaṇanti vuccati. Rajakabhaṇḍikanti rajakānaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ; rajakā sāyanhasamaye nagaraṃ pavisantā bahūni vatthāni ekekaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhanti. Tato ekaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ tesaṃ pamādena apassantānaṃ avaharitvā thenetvāti attho.

90. 'Having gone to the washerman's spreading-place' means having gone to the washerman's ford. Indeed, because the washermen spread out cloths there, it is called the 'washerman's spreading-place.' 'The washerman's bundle' means the bundle of the washermen. In the evening, when entering the city, washermen tie many cloths into separate bundles. The meaning is: having carried away and stolen one bundle from among those, while they were not looking due to their negligence.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Analysis of Terms

92. Gāmo nāmāti evamādi “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti ettha vuttassa gāmassa ca araññassa ca pabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmiṃ gāme ekā eva kuṭi, ekaṃ gehaṃ seyyathāpi malayajanapade; ayaṃ ekakuṭiko gāmo nāma. Etena nayena aparepi veditabbā. Amanusso nāma yo sabbaso vā manussānaṃ abhāvena yakkhapariggahabhūto; yato vā manussā kenaci kāraṇena punapi āgantukāmā eva apakkantā. Parikkhitto nāma iṭṭhakapākāraṃ ādiṃ katvā antamaso kaṇṭakasākhāhipi parikkhitto. Gonisādiniviṭṭho nāma vīthisannivesādivasena anivisitvā yathā gāvo tattha tattha dve tayo nisīdanti, evaṃ [P 2.0299] tattha tattha [V 1.0239][M 1.0259] dve tīṇi gharāni katvā niviṭṭho. Satthoti jaṅghasatthasakaṭasatthādīsu yo koci. Imasmiñca sikkhāpade nigamopi nagarampi gāmaggahaṇeneva gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

92. 'A village is...' and so on, is said to show the distinctions of 'a village' and 'a wilderness' mentioned in that context. Therein, a village where there is only one hut, one house—as in the Malay country—is called a 'one-hut village.' By this method, the others should also be understood. A 'non-human' village is one that is either entirely without humans and has become possessed by yakkhas, or one from which humans have departed for some reason, intending to return again. An 'enclosed' village is one enclosed by anything from a brick wall down to thorny branches. A village 'settled like resting cattle' is one not established by way of streets and so on, but with two or three houses built here and there, just as two or three cows sit here and there. 'A caravan' is any of the various kinds, such as a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. And in this training rule, it should be understood that a market town and a city are also included by the taking up of the word 'village.'

Gāmūpacārotiādi araññaparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Indakhīle ṭhitassāti yassa gāmassa anurādhapurasseva dve indakhīlā, tassa abbhantarime indakhīle ṭhitassa; tassa hi bāhiro indakhīlo ābhidhammikanayena araññasaṅkhepaṃ gacchati. Yassa pana eko, tassa gāmadvārabāhānaṃ vemajjhe ṭhitassa. Yatrāpi hi indakhīlo natthi, tatra gāmadvārabāhānaṃ vemajjhameva “indakhīlo”ti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ – “gāmadvārabāhānaṃ vemajjhe ṭhitassā”ti. Majjhimassāti thāmamajjhimassa, no pamāṇamajjhimassa, neva appathāmassa, na mahāthāmassa; majjhimathāmassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Leḍḍupātoti yathā mātugāmo kāke uḍḍāpento ujukameva hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā leḍḍuṃ khipati, yathā ca udakukkhepe udakaṃ khipanti, evaṃ akhipitvā yathā taruṇamanussā attano balaṃ dassentā bāhaṃ pasāretvā leḍḍuṃ khipanti, evaṃ khittassa leḍḍussa patanaṭṭhānaṃ. Patito pana luṭhitvā yattha gacchati, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

The passage beginning 'The vicinity of the village' was stated to show the demarcation of the wilderness. As for 'of one standing at the indakhīla': for a village which, like Anurādhapura, has two indakhīlas, it refers to one standing at the inner indakhīla; for indeed, its outer indakhīla, according to the Abhidhammic method, is included in the category of wilderness. For a village that has only one, however, it refers to one standing at the midpoint between the village gateposts. Indeed, even where there is no indakhīla, the very midpoint between the village gateposts is called the 'indakhīla.' Hence it was said: 'of one standing at the midpoint between the village gateposts.' As for 'of a medium one': this refers to one of medium strength, not of medium size; neither of weak strength nor of great strength. It means one of medium strength. As for 'a clod's fall': it is the place where a clod lands when thrown not as a woman throws a clod when scaring away crows, raising her hand straight up, nor as they throw water in an udakukkhepa ritual, but as young men throw a clod, extending their arm to display their strength. However, the place to which it goes after having fallen and rolled is not to be taken.

Aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupātoti ettha pana nibbakosassa udakapātaṭṭhāne ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa suppapāto vā musalapāto vā gharūpacāro nāma. Tasmiṃ gharūpacāre ṭhitassa leḍḍupāto gāmūpacāroti kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyampi tādisameva. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “gharaṃ nāma, gharūpacāro nāma, gāmo nāma, gāmūpacāro nāmā”ti mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā nibbakosassa udakapātaṭṭhānabbhantaraṃ gharaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana dvāre ṭhito mātugāmo bhājanadhovanaudakaṃ chaḍḍeti, tassa patanaṭṭhānañca mātugāmeneva antogehe ṭhitena pakatiyā bahi khittassa suppassa [P 2.0300] vā sammuñjaniyā vā patanaṭṭhānañca, gharassa purato dvīsu koṇesu sambandhitvā majjhe rukkhasūcidvāraṃ ṭhapetvā gorūpānaṃ pavesananivāraṇatthaṃ kataparikkhepo ca ayaṃ sabbopi gharūpacāro nāma. Tasmiṃ gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupātabbhantaraṃ gāmo nāma. Tato aññassa leḍḍupātassa abbhantaraṃ gāmūpacāro [M 1.0260] nāmāti vuttaṃ. Idamettha pamāṇaṃ. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbattha yo yo aṭṭhakathāvādo vā theravādo vā pacchā vuccati so pamāṇato daṭṭhabbo.

In the context of the rule, 'For an unenclosed village, the fall of a clod from a man of medium strength standing in the house-vicinity': here, however, the place where a winnowing basket falls or a pestle falls for a man of medium strength standing at the place where water drips from the eaves is called the house-vicinity. The place where a clod falls for one standing within this house-vicinity is called the village-vicinity, as stated in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā. In the Mahāpaccarī also, it is just the same. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, after setting down the matrix—'what is called a house, what is called the house-vicinity, what is called a village, what is called the village-vicinity'—it is stated: the area within the place where water drips from the eaves is called a house. But the place where a woman standing at the door discards water used for washing dishes, and the place where a winnowing basket or a broom, thrown outside in the ordinary way by a woman standing inside the house, falls, and the enclosure made to prevent the entry of cattle by connecting the two corners in front of the house and placing a wooden-pin gate in the middle—all this is called the house-vicinity. The area within the fall of a clod from a man of medium strength standing in that house-vicinity is called a village. The area within the fall of another clod from there is called the village-vicinity. This is the authority here. And as it is here, so everywhere: whichever commentary-view or elder-view is stated later should be regarded as the authority.

Yañcetaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pāḷiyā viruddhamiva dissati. Pāḷiyañhi – “gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana taṃ leḍḍupātaṃ gāmasaṅkhepaṃ katvā tato paraṃ gāmūpacāro vuttoti? Vuccate – saccameva pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ[V 1.0240], adhippāyo panettha veditabbo. So ca aṭṭhakathācariyānameva vidito. Tasmā yathā “gharūpacāre ṭhitassā”ti ettha gharūpacāralakkhaṇaṃ pāḷiyaṃ avuttampi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttavasena gahitaṃ. Evaṃ sesampi gahetabbaṃ.

And this which is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā appears to contradict the Pāḷi. For in the Pāḷi, only this much is said: 'the fall of a clod from a man of medium strength standing within the house-vicinity.' In the commentary, however, that fall of a clod is made into the village-boundary, and beyond that the village-vicinity is stated. The answer is: what is stated in the Pāḷi is indeed true, but the intended meaning here should be understood. And that is known only to the commentary teachers. Therefore, just as in the phrase 'of one standing within the house-vicinity,' the characteristic of the house-vicinity, though unstated in the Pāḷi, is taken according to what is stated in the commentary, so too should the rest be taken.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – idha gāmo nāma duvidho hoti – parikkhitto ca aparikkhitto ca. Tatra parikkhittassa parikkhepoyeva paricchedo. Tasmā tassa visuṃ paricchedaṃ avatvā “gāmūpacāro nāma parikkhittassa gāmassa indakhīle ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Aparikkhittassa pana gāmassa gāmaparicchedo vattabbo. Tasmā tassa gāmaparicchedadassanatthaṃ “aparikkhittassa gāmassa gharūpacāre ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti vuttaṃ. Gāmaparicchede ca dassite gāmūpacāralakkhaṇaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva sakkā ñātunti puna “tattha ṭhitassa majjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto”ti na vuttaṃ. Yo pana gharūpacāre ṭhitassa leḍḍupātaṃyeva “gāmūpacāro”ti vadati, tassa gharūpacāro gāmoti āpajjati. Tato gharaṃ, gharūpacāro, gāmo[P 2.0301], gāmūpacāroti esa vibhāgo saṅkarīyati. Asaṅkarato cettha vinicchayo veditabbo vikāle gāmappavesanādīsu. Tasmā pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca saṃsanditvā vuttanayenevettha gāmo ca gāmūpacāro ca veditabbo. Yopi ca gāmo pubbe mahā hutvā pacchā kulesu naṭṭhesu appako hoti, so gharūpacārato leḍḍupāteneva paricchinditabbo. Purimaparicchedo panassa parikkhittassāpi aparikkhittassāpi appamāṇamevāti.

Therein, this is the method: here, a village is of two kinds: enclosed and unenclosed. Therein, for an enclosed village, the enclosure itself is the boundary. Therefore, without stating its boundary separately, it is said in the Pāḷi: 'The village-vicinity, for an enclosed village, is the fall of a clod from a man of medium strength standing at the boundary-post.' For an unenclosed village, however, the village boundary should be stated. Therefore, to show its village boundary, it is said: 'The village, for an unenclosed village, is the fall of a clod from a man of medium strength standing in the house-vicinity.' And when the village boundary has been shown, the characteristic of the village-vicinity can be known by the method previously stated; thus, it is not said again: 'The village-vicinity is the fall of a clod from a man of medium strength standing there.' But as for one who says that the village-vicinity is simply the fall of a clod from one standing in the house-vicinity, for him it follows that the house-vicinity is the village. Consequently, this division—house, house-vicinity, village, village-vicinity—becomes confused. And the decision here should be understood without confusion in cases such as entering a village at the wrong time. Therefore, by comparing the Pāḷi and the commentary, the village and the village-vicinity should be understood here according to the stated method. Furthermore, if a village that was formerly large later becomes small when the families have perished, it should be demarcated only by the fall of a clod from the house-vicinity. Its former boundary, however, for both an enclosed and an unenclosed village, is not the measure.

Araññaṃ nāma ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcāti imaṃ yathāvuttalakkhaṇaṃ gāmañca gāmūpacārañca ṭhapetvā imasmiṃ adinnādānasikkhāpade avasesaṃ “araññaṃ” [M 1.0261] nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Abhidhamme pana “araññanti nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) vuttaṃ. Āraññakasikkhāpade “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) vuttaṃ. Taṃ indakhīlato paṭṭhāya āropitena ācariyadhanunā pañcadhanusatappamāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ bhagavatā “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti etassa atthaṃ vibhajantena “gharaṃ, gharūpacāro, gāmo, gāmūpacāro arañña”nti pāpabhikkhūnaṃ lesokāsanisedhanatthaṃ pañca koṭṭhāsā dassitā. Tasmā ghare vā gharūpacāre vā gāme vā gāmūpacāre vā araññe vā pādagghanakato paṭṭhāya sassāmikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharantassa pārājikamevāti veditabbaṃ.

The term 'wilderness' means that which remains when excluding the village and the village-vicinity. It should be understood that in this training rule on taking what is not given, whatever remains after excluding this village and village-vicinity with their aforementioned characteristics is called 'wilderness'. In the Abhidhamma, however, it is said: 'Wilderness is all that area having gone out beyond the boundary-post.' In the training rule on forest-dwelling, it is said: 'A forest dwelling is a lodging at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths.' This should be understood as a measure of five hundred bow-lengths, by a master-bowman's bow with the string drawn, starting from the boundary-post. Thus, the Blessed One, when analyzing the meaning of 'from a village or from a wilderness,' showed five divisions—house, house-vicinity, village, village-vicinity, and wilderness—for the purpose of preventing an opportunity for a pretext for corrupt monks. Therefore, it should be understood that for one who misappropriates an article with an owner, starting from one worth a pāda, whether in a house, a house-vicinity, a village, a village-vicinity, or a wilderness, it is indeed a pārājika offense.

Idāni [V 1.0241] “adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyeyyā”tiādīnaṃ atthadassanatthaṃ “adinnaṃ nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha adinnanti dantaponasikkhāpade attano santakampi appaṭiggahitakaṃ kappiyaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ vuccati. Idha pana yaṃkiñci parapariggahitaṃ sassāmikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ, tadetaṃ tehi sāmikehi kāyena vā vācāya vā na dinnanti adinnaṃ. Attano hatthato vā yathāṭhitaṭṭhānato vā na nissaṭṭhanti anissaṭṭhaṃ. Yathāṭhāne ṭhitampi anapekkhatāya na pariccattanti apariccattaṃ. Ārakkhasaṃvidhānena rakkhitattā rakkhitaṃ. Mañjūsādīsu pakkhipitvā gopitattā gopitaṃ. “Mama ida”nti taṇhāmamattena mamāyitattā mamāyitaṃ. Tāhi apariccāgarakkhaṇagopanāhi [P 2.0302] tehi bhaṇḍasāmikehi parehi pariggahitanti parapariggahitaṃ. Etaṃ adinnaṃ nāma.

Now, to show the meaning of 'one might take what is not given, designated as theft,' and so on, he said, 'What is not given is...' and so on. Therein, in the training rule on tooth-wood, 'not given' is said of one's own allowable consumable that has not been formally received. Here, however, 'not given' is said of any article whatsoever that is possessed by another and has an owner. This is 'not given' because it has not been given by those owners, either by body or by speech. It is 'not released' because it has not been released from their hand or from the place where it was. It is 'not relinquished' because, even while remaining in its place, it has not been relinquished through lack of concern. It is 'guarded' because it is protected by the arrangement of a guard. It is 'secured' because it is made safe by being placed in chests and so on. It is 'cherished' because it is treated as 'mine' with the 'my-making' of craving, as in 'This is mine.' Because it is possessed by others, who are the owners of the article, through that non-relinquishing, guarding, and securing, it is 'possessed by another.' This is what is called 'not given'.

Theyyasaṅkhātanti ettha thenoti coro, thenassa bhāvo theyyaṃ; avaharaṇacittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Saṅkhā, saṅkhāta”nti atthato ekaṃ; koṭṭhāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 880) viya. Theyyañca taṃ saṅkhātañcāti theyyasaṅkhātaṃ, theyyacittasaṅkhāto eko cittakoṭṭhāsoti attho. Karaṇatthe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, tasmā theyyasaṅkhātenāti atthato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yo ca theyyasaṅkhātena ādiyati, so yasmā theyyacitto hoti, tasmā byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā atthameva dassetuṃ theyyacitto avaharaṇacittoti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase 'designated as theft' (theyyasaṅkhāta), a thena is a thief; the state of a thief is theyya (theft). This is a designation for the mind of misappropriation. 'Saṅkhā' and 'saṅkhāta' are one in meaning; this is a designation for a component, as in 'for perceptions are the source of the components of proliferation,' and so on. It is 'designated as theft' because it is both theft (theyya) and a designation (saṅkhāta). The meaning is: a single component of consciousness designated as a thieving mind. And this is a nominative word in the sense of the instrumental; therefore, it should be seen in meaning as 'with that which is designated as theft.' And since one who takes with that which is designated as theft has a thieving mind, it should be understood that, therefore, without adhering to the letter, but to show the meaning alone, its word-analysis is given thus: 'a thieving mind is a mind of misappropriation.'

Ādiyeyya [M 1.0262], hareyya, avahareyya, iriyāpathaṃ vikopeyya, ṭhānā cāveyya, saṅketaṃ vītināmeyyāti ettha pana paṭhamapadaṃ abhiyogavasena vuttaṃ, dutiyapadaṃ aññesaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ harantassa gacchato vasena, tatiyapadaṃ upanikkhittabhaṇḍavasena, catutthaṃ saviññāṇakavasena, pañcamaṃ thale nikkhittādivasena, chaṭṭhaṃ parikappavasena vā suṅkaghātavasena vā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yojanā panettha ekabhaṇḍavasenapi nānābhaṇḍavasenapi hoti. Ekabhaṇḍavasena ca saviññāṇakeneva labbhati, nānābhaṇḍavasena saviññāṇakāviññāṇakamissakena.

Furthermore, regarding 'one might take, one might carry, one might misappropriate, one might disturb the posture, one might move from its place, one might transgress a boundary': here, the first term is stated with reference to laying a claim; the second term, with reference to one who goes along carrying another's article; the third term, with reference to a deposited article; the fourth, with reference to an animate object; the fifth, with reference to an article placed on dry land, and so on; the sixth, it should be understood, is stated with reference to a pre-arranged place or with reference to a customs post. The application here occurs with reference to a single article and with reference to various articles. With reference to a single article, it applies only to an animate one; with reference to various articles, it applies to a mixture of animate and inanimate ones.

Tattha nānābhaṇḍavasena tāva evaṃ veditabbaṃ – ādiyeyyāti ārāmaṃ abhiyuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Sāmiko “na mayhaṃ bhavissatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, āpatti pārājikassa.

Therein, it should first be understood thus with reference to various articles: 'One might take' means one lays claim to a park; there is an offense of wrong-doing. One causes doubt in the owner; there is a grave offense. The owner gives up his effort, thinking, 'It will not be mine'; there is a pārājika offense.

Hareyyāti [V 1.0242] aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ haranto sīse bhāraṃ theyyacitto āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Khandhaṃ oropeti, āpatti pārājikassa.

'One might carry' means: while carrying another's goods, if, with a thievish mind, one touches the load on one's head, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If one makes it move, there is a grave offense. If one lowers it to one's shoulder, there is a pārājika offense.

Avahareyyāti upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ “dehi me bhaṇḍa”nti vuccamāno “nāhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti bhaṇati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Sāmiko “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, āpatti pārājikassa[P 2.0303].

'One might misappropriate' means: regarding deposited goods, when told, 'Give me my goods,' if one says, 'I did not take it,' there is an offense of wrong-doing. If one causes doubt in the owner, there is a grave offense. If the owner, thinking, 'He will not give it back to me,' abandons responsibility, there is a pārājika offense.

Iriyāpathaṃ vikopeyyāti “sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ nessāmī”ti paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ saṅkāmeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Dutiyaṃ pādaṃ saṅkāmeti, āpatti pārājikassa.

'One might disturb the posture' means: thinking, 'I will lead away the one carrying the goods, along with the goods,' if one moves the first foot, there is a grave offense. If one moves the second foot, there is a pārājika offense.

Ṭhānā cāveyyāti thalaṭṭhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacitto āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Ṭhānā cāveti, āpatti pārājikassa.

'One might move from its place' means: with a thievish mind, one touches goods placed on land; there is an offense of wrong-doing. If one makes it move, there is a grave offense. If one moves it from its place, there is a pārājika offense.

Saṅketaṃ vītināmeyyāti parikappitaṭṭhānaṃ paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti, āpatti pārājikassa. Atha vā paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ suṅkaghātaṃ atikkāmeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti, āpatti pārājikassāti – ayamettha nānābhaṇḍavasena yojanā.

'One might transgress the boundary' means: if one crosses a pre-arranged place with the first foot, there is a grave offense. If one crosses with the second foot, there is a pārājika offense. Alternatively, if one crosses a customs post with the first foot, there is a grave offense. If one crosses with the second foot, there is a pārājika offense. This here is the application with reference to various articles.

Ekabhaṇḍavasena [M 1.0263] pana sassāmikaṃ dāsaṃ vā tiracchānaṃ vā yathāvuttena abhiyogādinā nayena ādiyati vā harati vā avaharati vā iriyāpathaṃ vā vikopeti, ṭhānā vā cāveti, paricchedaṃ vā atikkāmeti – ayamettha ekabhaṇḍavasena yojanā.

However, with reference to a single article: if one takes, or carries away, or misappropriates, or disturbs the deportment of, or moves from its place, or transgresses the boundary of a slave or an animal that has an owner, by the method of laying a claim and so on, as has been described—this here is the application with reference to a single article.

Pañcavīsatiavahārakathā

The Discourse on the Twenty-five Kinds of Misappropriation

Apica imāni cha padāni vaṇṇentena pañca pañcake samodhānetvā pañcavīsati avahārā dassetabbā. Evaṃ vaṇṇayatā hi idaṃ adinnādānapārājikaṃ suvaṇṇitaṃ hoti. Imasmiñca ṭhāne sabbaaṭṭhakathā ākulā luḷitā duviññeyyavinicchayā. Tathā hi sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu yāni tāni pāḷiyaṃ “pañcahākārehi adinnaṃ ādiyantassa āpatti pārājikassa, parapariggahitañca hotī”tiādinā nayena avahāraṅgāni vuttāni, tānipi gahetvā katthaci ekaṃ pañcakaṃ dassitaṃ, katthaci “chahākārehī”ti āgatehi saddhiṃ dve pañcakāni [V 1.0243] dassitāni. Etāni ca pañcakāni na honti. Yattha hi ekekena padena avahāro sijjhati, taṃ pañcakaṃ nāma vuccati. Ettha pana sabbehipi padehi ekoyeva avahāro. Yāni ca tattha labbhamānāniyeva pañcakāni dassitāni, tesampi na sabbesaṃ attho pakāsito. Evamimasmiṃ ṭhāne sabbaaṭṭhakathā ākulā luḷitā duviññeyyavinicchayā. Tasmā pañca pañcakesamodhānetvā dassiyamānā ime pañcavīsati avahārā sādhukaṃ sallakkhetabbā.

Furthermore, when explaining these six terms, twenty-five kinds of misappropriation should be shown by combining five pentads. For by explaining in this way, this pārājika offense for taking what is not given becomes well-explained. And in this matter, all the commentaries are confused, agitated, and their decisions are difficult to understand. Indeed, in all the commentaries, those factors of misappropriation spoken of in the Pāli by the method beginning, “For one who takes what is not given in five ways, there is an offense of pārājika…,” are taken, and in some places one pentad is shown; in other places, two pentads are shown along with the terms that come as “in six ways.” But these are not pentads. For a “pentad” is so called when a misappropriation is accomplished by each single term. Here, however, by all the terms together there is only one misappropriation. And of those pentads that are indeed found and shown there, the meaning of not all of them has been made clear. Thus, in this matter, all the commentaries are confused, agitated, and their decisions are difficult to understand. Therefore, these twenty-five kinds of misappropriation, which are being shown by combining five pentads, should be carefully noted.

Pañca pañcakāni nāma – nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ, ekabhaṇḍapañcakaṃ, sāhatthikapañcakaṃ, pubbapayogapañcakaṃ[P 2.0304], theyyāvahārapañcakanti. Tattha nānābhaṇḍapañcakañca ekabhaṇḍapañcakañca “ādiyeyya, hareyya, avahareyya, iriyāpathaṃ vikopeyya, ṭhānā cāveyyā”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ vasena labbhanti. Tāni pubbe yojetvā dassitanayeneva veditabbāni. Yaṃ panetaṃ “saṅketaṃ vītināmeyyā”ti chaṭṭhaṃ padaṃ, taṃ parikappāvahārassa ca nissaggiyāvahārassa ca sādhāraṇaṃ. Tasmā taṃ tatiyapañcamesu pañcakesu labbhamānapadavasena yojetabbaṃ. Vuttaṃ nānābhaṇḍapañcakañca ekabhaṇḍapañcakañca.

The five pentads are named: the pentad of various goods, the pentad of a single item of goods, the pentad concerning one's own hand, the pentad concerning prior effort, and the pentad of theft. Among these, the pentad of various goods and the pentad of a single item of goods are derived by means of these terms: “he would take… he would move from its place.” They are to be understood by the method of application shown previously. As for this sixth term, “he would transgress an agreement,” it is common to both misappropriation by scheming and misappropriation by casting down. Therefore, it should be applied in the third and fifth pentads, by way of the terms found therein. The pentad of various goods and the pentad of a single item of goods have been discussed.

Katamaṃ sāhatthikapañcakaṃ? Pañca avahārā – sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, atthasādhako, dhuranikkhepoti. Tattha sāhatthiko nāma parassa bhaṇḍaṃ sahatthā avaharati. Āṇattiko nāma “asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ [M 1.0264] avaharā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpeti.
