Nissaggiyo nāma antosuṅkaghāte ṭhito bahisuṅkaghātaṃ pāteti, āpatti pārājikassāti, iminā ca saddhiṃ “saṅketaṃ vītināmeyyā”ti idaṃ padayojanaṃ labhati. Atthasādhako nāma “asukaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā avaharā”ti āṇāpeti. Tattha sace paro anantarāyiko hutvā taṃ avaharati, āṇāpako āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājiko hoti, avahārako pana avahaṭakāle. Ayaṃ atthasādhako. Dhuranikkhepo pana upanikkhittabhaṇḍavasena veditabbo. Idaṃ sāhatthikapañcakaṃ.

What is the pentad concerning one's own hand? There are five kinds of misappropriation: by one's own hand, by command, by casting down, by accomplishing the purpose, and by casting off the burden. Therein, “by one's own hand” is when one misappropriates another's goods with one's own hand. “By command” is when one instructs another, “Misappropriate the goods of so-and-so.” “By casting down” is when, standing inside a customs post, one causes something to fall outside the customs post, there is an offense of pārājika; and with this, the application of the term “he would transgress an agreement” is found. “By accomplishing the purpose” is when one instructs, “Whenever you are able, misappropriate the goods called so-and-so.” In that case, if the other person, being without obstacle, misappropriates it, the instructor becomes guilty of a pārājika offense at the very moment of giving the instruction, whereas the one who misappropriates becomes guilty at the time of the misappropriation. This is “by accomplishing the purpose.” “Casting off the burden” is to be understood by way of deposited goods. This is the pentad concerning one's own hand.

Katamaṃ pubbapayogapañcakaṃ? Aparepi pañca avahārā – pubbapayogo, sahapayogo, saṃvidāvahāro, saṅketakammaṃ, nimittakammanti. Tattha āṇattivasena pubbapayogo veditabbo. Ṭhānā cāvanavasena sahapayogo. Itare pana tayo pāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 118-120) āgatanayeneva veditabbāti. Idaṃ pubbapayogapañcakaṃ.

What is the pentad concerning prior effort? There are five other kinds of misappropriation: prior effort, simultaneous effort, misappropriation by agreement, action by sign, and action by hint. Therein, prior effort is to be understood by way of command. Simultaneous effort is to be understood by way of moving from a place. The other three, however, are to be understood according to the method that has come in the Pāli. This is the pentad concerning prior effort.

Katamaṃ theyyāvahārapañcakaṃ? Aparepi pañca avahārā – theyyāvahāro, pasayhāvahāro, parikappāvahāro[V 1.0244], paṭicchannāvahāro, kusāvahāroti. Te pañcapi “aññataro bhikkhu saṅghassa cīvare bhājiyamāne theyyacitto kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā cīvaraṃ aggahesī”ti (pārā. 138) etasmiṃ kusasaṅkāmanavatthusmiṃ vaṇṇayissāma. Idaṃ theyyāvahārapañcakaṃ. Evamimāni pañca pañcakāni samodhānetvā ime pañcavīsati avahārā veditabbā.

What is the pentad of theft? There are five other kinds of misappropriation: misappropriation by stealth, misappropriation by force, misappropriation by scheming, misappropriation by concealment, and misappropriation by a grass-blade marker. These five we will explain in the context of the case of moving the grass-blade marker: “a certain monk, with thieving intent, while robes were being distributed to the Sangha, moved a grass-blade marker and took a robe.” This is the pentad of theft. Thus, having combined these five pentads, these twenty-five misappropriations should be understood.

Imesu ca pana pañcasu pañcakesu kusalena vinayadharena otiṇṇaṃ vatthuṃ sahasā avinicchinitvāva [P 2.0305] pañca ṭhānāni oloketabbāni. Yāni sandhāya porāṇā āhu –

Furthermore, in these five pentads, a skilled Vinaya-expert should not decide a case that has arisen hastily, but should examine five points. Concerning which, the ancients have said:

“Vatthuṃ kālañca desañca, agghaṃ paribhogapañcamaṃ;

Tulayitvā pañca ṭhānāni, dhāreyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇo”ti.

“The object, the time, the place, the value, and use as the fifth; having weighed these five points, the discerning one should determine the matter.”

Tattha vatthunti bhaṇḍaṃ; avahārakena hi “mayā idaṃ nāma avahaṭa”nti vuttepi āpattiṃ anāropetvāva taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sassāmikaṃ vā assāmikaṃ vāti upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Sassāmikepi sāmikānaṃ sālayabhāvo vā nirālayabhāvo vā upaparikkhitabbo. Sace tesaṃ sālayakāle avahaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā āpatti kātabbā. Sace nirālayakāle[M 1.0265], na pārājikena kāretabbo. Bhaṇḍasāmikesu pana bhaṇḍaṃ āharāpentesu bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbaṃ. Ayamettha sāmīci.

Herein, ‘object’ means the article. For even when the misappropriator says, “I misappropriated such and such an item,” without yet imposing an offense, that article should be investigated as to whether it has an owner or is ownerless. Even if it has an owner, it should be investigated whether the owners had attachment to it or had no attachment. If it was misappropriated at a time when they had attachment, having had the article valued, the offense should be determined. If it was at a time of non-attachment, he should not be made to incur a pārājika offense. However, if the owners of the article have it brought back, the article should be given. This is the proper conduct in this matter.

Imassa panatthassa dīpanatthamidaṃ vatthu – bhātiyarājakāle kira mahācetiyapūjāya dakkhiṇadisato eko bhikkhu sattahatthaṃ paṇḍukāsāvaṃ aṃse karitvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ pāvisi; taṅkhaṇameva ca rājāpi cetiyavandanatthaṃ āgato. Tattha ussāraṇāya vattamānāya mahājanasammaddo ahosi. Atha so bhikkhu janasammaddapīḷito aṃsato patantaṃ kāsāvaṃ adisvāva nikkhanto; nikkhamitvā ca kāsāvaṃ apassanto “ko īdise janasammadde kāsāvaṃ lacchati, na dāni taṃ mayha”nti dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā gato. Athañño bhikkhu pacchā āgacchanto taṃ kāsāvaṃ disvā theyyacittena gahetvā puna vippaṭisārī hutvā “assamaṇo dānimhi, vibbhamissāmī”ti citte uppannepi “vinayadhare pucchitvā ñassāmī”ti cintesi.

Furthermore, to illustrate this matter, here is a case: It is said that during the reign of King Bhātiya, at a festival for the Great Cetiya, a certain monk from the southern direction entered the cetiya courtyard, having placed a seven-cubit pale ochre robe on his shoulder. At that very moment, the king also arrived to pay homage to the cetiya. As the way was being cleared, a great throng of people arose. Then that monk, being pressed by the throng of people, left without seeing the robe fall from his shoulder. And having left, not seeing the robe, he thought, “Who could get the robe in such a throng? It is no longer mine,” and having thus abandoned responsibility for it, he went on his way. Then another monk, coming along behind, saw that robe and, with thieving intent, took it. He then became remorseful, and although the thought arose, “Now I am no longer a monk; I will disrobe,” he reflected, “I will ask the Vinaya-experts and find out.”

Tena ca samayena cūḷasumanatthero nāma sabbapariyattidharo vinayācariyapāmokkho mahāvihāre paṭivasati. So bhikkhu theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā okāsaṃ kāretvā attano kukkuccaṃ pucchi. Thero tena bhaṭṭhe [P 2.0306] janakāye pacchā āgantvā gahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “atthi dāni ettha okāso”ti cintetvā āha – “sace kāsāvasāmikaṃ bhikkhuṃ āneyyāsi, sakkā [V 1.0245] bhaveyya tava patiṭṭhā kātu”nti. “Kathāhaṃ, bhante, taṃ dakkhissāmī”ti? “Tahiṃ tahiṃ gantvā olokehī”ti. So pañcapi mahāvihāre oloketvā neva addakkhi. Tato naṃ thero pucchi – “katarāya disāya bahū bhikkhū āgacchantī”ti? “Dakkhiṇadisāya, bhante”ti. “Tena hi kāsāvaṃ dīghato ca tiriyañca minitvā ṭhapehi. Ṭhapetvā dakkhiṇadisāya vihārapaṭipāṭiyā vicinitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ ānehī”ti. So tathā katvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā therassa santikaṃ ānesi. Thero pucchi – “tavedaṃ kāsāva”nti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kuhiṃ te pātita”nti? So sabbaṃ ācikkhi. Thero pana tena kataṃ dhuranikkhepaṃ sutvā itaraṃ pucchi – “tayā idaṃ kuhiṃ disvā gahita”nti? Sopi sabbaṃ ārocesi. Tato naṃ thero āha – “sace te suddhacittena gahitaṃ abhavissa, anāpattiyeva te assa. Theyyacittena pana gahitattā dukkaṭaṃ āpannosi. Taṃ desetvā anāpattiko hohi. Idañca kāsāvaṃ attano [M 1.0266] santakaṃ katvā etasseva bhikkhuno dehī”ti. So bhikkhu amateneva abhisitto paramassāsappatto ahosīti. Evaṃ vatthu oloketabbaṃ.

And at that time, an elder named Cūḷasumana, a master of all the scriptures and foremost among the Vinaya teachers, was residing in the Great Monastery. That monk approached the elder, paid homage, requested an opportunity, and asked about his scruple. The elder, knowing that the monk had come along afterwards and taken the robe after it had been dropped in the crowd, thought, “There is now an opportunity here,” and said: “If you can bring the monk who owns the robe, it might be possible to establish a standing-ground for you.” “Venerable sir, how will I see him?” “Go and look in various places.” He looked through all five great monasteries but did not see him. Then the elder asked him: “From which direction are many monks coming?” “From the southern direction, venerable sir.” “In that case, measure the robe’s length and width and set it aside. Having done so, search for that monk along the rows of monasteries in the southern direction and bring him here.” He did as instructed, and upon seeing that monk, brought him to the elder’s presence. The elder asked: “Is this your robe?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Where did you drop it?” He explained everything. Then the elder, having heard about the abandonment of effort made by that monk, asked the other: “Where did you see this and take it?” He too related everything. Then the elder said to him: “If you had taken it with a pure mind, it would have been no offense for you. But because you took it with thieving intent, you have committed a dukkaṭa offense. Having confessed that, become free of offense. And this robe, having made it your own property, give to this very monk.” That monk, as if sprinkled with the deathless, attained the highest consolation. Thus should the object be examined.

Kāloti avahārakālo. Tadeva hi bhaṇḍaṃ kadāci samagghaṃ hoti, kadāci mahagghaṃ. Tasmā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ kāle avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva kāle yo tassa aggho hoti, tena agghena āpatti kāretabbā. Evaṃ kālo oloketabbo.

‘Time’ means the time of misappropriation. For that very same article is sometimes of low value and sometimes of high value. Therefore, at whatever time that article was misappropriated, the offense should be determined according to whatever its value is at that very time. Thus should the time be examined.

Desoti avahāradeso. Tañhi bhaṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ dese avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva dese yo tassa aggho hoti, tena agghena āpatti kāretabbā. Bhaṇḍuṭṭhānadese hi bhaṇḍaṃ samagghaṃ hoti, aññattha mahagghaṃ.

‘Place’ means the place of misappropriation. For at whatever place that article was misappropriated, the offense should be determined according to whatever its value is in that very place. For in the place where an article originates, it is of low value, but elsewhere it is of high value.

Imassāpi ca atthassa dīpanatthamidaṃ vatthu – antarasamudde kira eko bhikkhu susaṇṭhānaṃ nāḷikeraṃ labhitvā bhamaṃ āropetvā saṅkhathālakasadisaṃ manoramaṃ pānīyathālakaṃ katvā tattheva ṭhapetvā cetiyagiriṃ agamāsi. Athañño bhikkhu antarasamuddaṃ gantvā tasmiṃ vihāre paṭivasanto taṃ thālakaṃ disvā theyyacittena gahetvā cetiyagirimeva āgato. Tassa tattha yāguṃ pivantassa taṃ [P 2.0307] thālakaṃ disvā thālakasāmiko bhikkhu āha – “kuto te idaṃ laddha”nti? “Antarasamuddato me ānīta”nti. So taṃ “netaṃ tava santakaṃ, theyyāya te gahita”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ ākaḍḍhi. Tattha ca vinicchayaṃ alabhitvā mahāvihāraṃ agamiṃsu. Tattha bheriṃ paharāpetvā mahācetiyasamīpe sannipātaṃ katvā vinicchayaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Vinayadharattherā avahāraṃ saññāpesuṃ.

And to illustrate the meaning of this, here is a story: It is said that at Antarasamudda, a certain monk, having obtained a well-shaped coconut, placed it on a lathe and made a delightful drinking bowl resembling a conch-shell bowl. Having left it right there, he went to Cetiyagiri. Then another monk, going to Antarasamudda and residing in that monastery, saw the bowl and, with a thievish mind, took it and came to Cetiyagiri itself. While he was there drinking gruel, the monk who owned the bowl saw it and said, “From where did you get this?” “It was brought by me from Antarasamudda.” That monk said to him, “This is not your property; it was taken by you through theft,” and dragged him into the midst of the Sangha. And not being able to get a decision there, they went to the Mahāvihāra. There, having had the drum beaten and having convened an assembly near the Mahācetiya, they began the adjudication. The elders who are masters of the Vinaya made known the manner of the theft.

Tasmiñca [V 1.0246] sannipāte ābhidhammikagodattatthero nāma vinayakusalo hoti. So evamāha – “iminā idaṃ thālakaṃ kuhiṃ avahaṭa”nti? “Antarasamudde avahaṭa”nti. “Tatridaṃ kiṃ agghatī”ti? “Na kiñci agghati. Tatra hi nāḷikeraṃ bhinditvā miñjaṃ khāditvā kapālaṃ chaḍḍenti, dāruatthaṃ pana pharatī”ti. “Imassa bhikkhuno ettha hatthakammaṃ kiṃ agghatī”ti? “Māsakaṃ vā ūnamāsakaṃ vā”ti. “Atthi pana katthaci sammāsambuddhena māsakena vā ūnamāsakena vā pārājikaṃ paññatta”nti. Evaṃ vutte “sādhu! Sādhu! Sukathitaṃ suvinicchita”nti ekasādhukāro ahosi. Tena ca samayena bhātiyarājāpi cetiyavandanatthaṃ nagarato nikkhamanto taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ ida”nti pucchitvā sabbaṃ paṭipāṭiyā sutvā nagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “mayi sante bhikkhūnampi bhikkhūnīnampi [M 1.0267] gihīnampi adhikaraṇaṃ ābhidhammikagodattattherena vinicchitaṃ suvinicchitaṃ, tassa vinicchaye atiṭṭhamānaṃ rājāṇāya ṭhapemī”ti. Evaṃ deso oloketabbo.

And in that assembly, there was one skilled in the Vinaya named Elder Ābhidhammika Godatta. He said thus: 'By this monk, where was this bowl stolen?' 'It was stolen at Antarasamudda.' 'There, what is this worth?' 'It is not worth anything. For there, they break the coconut, eat the kernel, and discard the shell; it serves only the purpose of firewood.' 'What is the value of this monk's handiwork on it?' 'A māsaka or less than a māsaka.' 'But is there anywhere a Pārājika offense laid down by the Perfectly Enlightened One for a māsaka or less than a māsaka?' When this was said, there was a simultaneous cry of approval: 'Excellent! Excellent! Well-spoken, well-adjudicated!' And at that time, King Bhātiya, while coming out from the city for the purpose of venerating the cetiya, heard that sound and, having asked, 'What is this?' and having heard the entire matter in sequence, had a drum circulated in the city, proclaiming: 'While I am present, any legal question of monks, nuns, or laypeople, when adjudicated by Elder Ābhidhammika Godatta, is well-adjudicated. One who does not abide by his adjudication, I will enforce by royal command.' Thus, the region should be considered.

Agghoti bhaṇḍaggho. Navabhaṇḍassa hi yo aggho hoti, so pacchā parihāyati; yathā navadhoto patto aṭṭha vā dasa vā agghati, so pacchā bhinno vā chiddo vā āṇigaṇṭhikāhato vā appaggho hoti tasmā na sabbadā bhaṇḍaṃ pakatiaggheneva kātabbanti. Evaṃ aggho oloketabbo.

'Value' means the value of the goods. Indeed, whatever value new goods have, that later diminishes. For example, a newly polished bowl is worth eight or ten, but later, being broken, or having a hole, or having been repaired with a peg and knot, it becomes of little value. Therefore, goods should not always be assessed at their original value. Thus, the value should be considered.

Paribhogoti bhaṇḍaparibhogo. Paribhogenāpi hi vāsiādibhaṇḍassa aggho parihāyati. Tasmā evaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ, sace koci kassaci pādagghanakaṃ vāsiṃ harati, tatra vāsisāmiko pucchitabbo [P 2.0308] – “tayā ayaṃ vāsi kittakena kītā”ti? “Pādena, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ pana te kiṇitvāva ṭhapitā, udāhu taṃ vaḷañjesī”ti? Sace vadati “ekadivasaṃ me dantakaṭṭhaṃ vā rajanachalliṃ vā pattapacanakadāruṃ vā chinnaṃ, ghaṃsitvā vā nisitā”ti. Athassā porāṇo aggho bhaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Yathā ca vāsiyā evaṃ añjaniyā vā añjanisalākāya vā kuñcikāya vā palālena vā thusehi vā iṭṭhakacuṇṇena vā ekavāraṃ ghaṃsitvā dhovanamattenāpi aggho bhassati. Tipumaṇḍalassa makaradantacchedanenāpi parimajjitamattenāpi, udakasāṭikāya sakiṃ nivāsanapārupanenāpi paribhogasīsena aṃse vā sīse vā ṭhapanamattenāpi, taṇḍulādīnaṃ papphoṭanenāpi tato ekaṃ vā dve vā apanayanenāpi, antamaso ekaṃ pāsāṇasakkharaṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍitamattenāpi, sappitelādīnaṃ bhājanantarapaavattanenāpi, antamaso tato makkhikaṃ vā kipillikaṃ vā uddharitvā chaḍḍitamattenāpi, guḷapiṇḍakassa madhurabhāvajānanatthaṃ nakhena vijjhitvā aṇumattaṃ gahitamattenāpi aggho bhassati. Tasmā [V 1.0247] yaṃkiñci pādagghanakaṃ vuttanayeneva sāmikehi paribhogena ūnaṃ kataṃ hoti, na taṃ avahaṭo bhikkhu pārājikena kātabbo. Evaṃ paribhogo oloketabbo. Evaṃ imāni tulayitvā pañca ṭhānāni dhāreyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇo, āpattiṃ vā anāpattiṃ vā garukaṃ vā lahukaṃ vā āpattiṃ yathāṭhāne ṭhapeyyāti.

'Use' means the use of goods. Indeed, even through use, the value of goods such as an adze diminishes. Therefore, it should be examined thus: if someone steals someone's adze worth a pāda, the owner of the adze should be asked: 'For how much was this adze bought by you?' 'For a pāda, venerable sir.' 'But was it just bought and put away by you, or did you use it?' If he says: 'One day a tooth-stick was cut by me, or bark for dye, or firewood for firing a bowl was cut, or it was sharpened by rubbing,' then it should be understood that its former value is lost. And just as with the adze, so too with a collyrium pot, a collyrium applicator stick, or a key, even by rubbing and washing it once with straw, husks, or brick powder, the value is lost. For a tin bowl-stand, even by merely cutting a makara-tooth pattern on it or by polishing it; for a water-strainer cloth, even by wearing or draping it once, or as a form of use, by merely placing it on the shoulder or head; for rice and so on, even by winnowing it or by removing one or two grains from it, or at the least, by merely picking out and discarding one stone or pebble; for ghee, oil, and so on, even by transferring it to another vessel, or at the least, by merely picking out and discarding a fly or an ant from it; for a lump of jaggery, even by merely taking a minute amount after piercing it with a fingernail to know its sweetness, the value is lost. Therefore, regarding any item worth a pāda that has been diminished in value by the owners through use in the manner described, a monk who has stolen it should not be made liable for a Pārājika offense. Thus, use should be considered. Thus, a discerning person, having weighed these five points, should grasp the meaning and should place an offense or no-offense, a grave offense or a light offense, in its proper place.

Niṭṭhito “ādiyeyya…pe… saṅketaṃ vītināmeyyā”ti.

The section from 'he would take...' up to '...he would transgress the agreed limit' is concluded.

Imesaṃ padānaṃ vinicchayo.

The adjudication of these terms is concluded.

Idāni [M 1.0268] yadidaṃ “yathārūpe adinnādāne”tiādīni vibhajantena “yathārūpaṃ nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathārūpanti yathājātikaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā pādato paṭṭhāya hoti, tasmā “pādaṃ vā pādārahaṃ vā atirekapādaṃ vā”ti āha. Tattha pādena kahāpaṇassa catutthabhāgaṃ akappiyabhaṇḍameva dasseti. Pādārahena [P 2.0309] pādagghanakaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ. Atirekapādena ubhayampi. Ettāvatā sabbākārena dutiyapārājikappahonakavatthu dassitaṃ hoti.

Now, when analyzing 'in such and such a kind of taking what is not given,' etc., it was said, 'what is "such and such a kind"?' etc. Therein, 'of such a kind' means of such a nature. And since that is from a pāda upwards, therefore it was said, 'a pāda, or what is worth a pāda, or more than a pāda.' Therein, by 'pāda,' he indicates only unallowable goods that are the fourth part of a kahāpaṇa. By 'what is worth a pāda,' he indicates allowable goods worth a pāda. By 'more than a pāda,' he indicates both. By this much, the object sufficient for the second Pārājika has been shown in all its aspects.

Pathabyā rājāti sakalapathaviyā rājā dīpacakkavattī asokasadiso, yo vā panaññopi ekadīpe rājā, sīhaḷarājasadiso. Padesarājāti ekadīpassa padesissaro, bimbisāra-pasenadi-ādayo viya. Maṇḍalikā nāma ye dīpapadesepi ekamekaṃ maṇḍalaṃ bhuñjanti. Antarabhogikā nāma dvinnaṃ rājūnaṃ antarā katipayagāmasāmikā. Akkhadassāti dhammavinicchanakā, te dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīditvā aparādhānurūpaṃ corānaṃ hatthapādacchejjādiṃ anusāsanti. Ye pana ṭhānantarappattā amaccā vā rājakumārā vā katāparādhā honti, te rañño ārocenti, garukaṃ ṭhānaṃ sayaṃ na vinicchinanti. Mahāmattāti ṭhānantarappattā mahāamaccā; tepi tattha tattha gāme vā nigame vā nisīditvā rājakiccaṃ karonti. Ye vā panāti aññepi ye rājakulanissitā vā sakissariyanissitā vā hutvā chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsanti, sabbepi te imasmiṃ atthe “rājāno”ti dasseti.

A 'king of the earth' means a king of the entire earth, a universal monarch of a continent like Asoka, or any other king on a single continent, like the king of Sīhaḷa. A 'regional king' means the ruler of a part of a continent, like Bimbisāra and Pasenadi. Those called 'maṇḍalikas' are those who rule over a single district even within a part of a continent. Those called 'antarabhogikas' are lords of a few villages situated between the territories of two kings. 'Akkhadassas' means adjudicators of the law; they, sitting in the court of justice, decree punishments for thieves, such as the cutting of hands and feet, according to their offense. However, when ministers who have attained high office or princes have committed an offense, they report them to the king; they do not decide on serious matters themselves. 'Mahāmattas' means great ministers who have attained high office; they too, sitting in various villages or towns, carry out the king's business. As for 'or others,' it is shown that any others who, relying on the royal family or on their own authority, decree cutting and breaking—all of them in this context are 'kings'.

Haneyyunti potheyyuñceva chindeyyuñca. Pabbājeyyunti nīhareyyuṃ. Corosīti evamādīni ca vatvā paribhāseyyuṃ; tenevāha – “paribhāso eso”ti. Purimaṃ upādāyāti methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā pārājikaṃ āpattiṃ āpannaṃ puggalaṃ upādāya. Sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayattā uttānapadatthattā ca pākaṭamevāti.

'They should strike' means they should both beat and cut. 'They should banish' means they should expel. And having said, 'You are a thief!' and so on, they should revile; for that very reason, it was said, 'This is reviling.' 'With reference to the preceding' means with reference to a person who has fallen into a pārājika offense by having engaged in sexual intercourse. The rest is indeed clear, both because of the method already stated before and because of the plain meaning of the words.

93. Evaṃ [V 1.0248] uddiṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ padānukkamena vibhajitvā idāni yaṃ taṃ ādiyeyyātiādīhi chahi padehi saṅkhepato ādānaṃ dassetvā saṅkhepatoeva “pādaṃ vā pādārahaṃ vā atirekapādaṃ vā”ti ādātabbabhaṇḍaṃ dassitaṃ, taṃ yattha yattha ṭhitaṃ, yathā yathā ādānaṃ gacchati, anāgate [M 1.0269] pāpabhikkhūnaṃ lesokāsanirundhanatthaṃ tathā tathā vitthārato dassetuṃ “bhūmaṭṭhaṃ [P 2.0310] thalaṭṭha”ntiādinā nayena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā “bhūmaṭṭhaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhittaṃ hotī”tiādinā nayena tassa vibhaṅgaṃ āha.

93. Having thus analyzed the stated training rule term by term, and now, after briefly indicating the taking with the six terms beginning with 'one might take,' and having briefly indicated the items to be taken as 'a pāda, what is worth a pāda, or more than a pāda'—in order to show in detail where that item is situated and how the taking occurs, for the purpose of blocking the opportunity for excuses for evil monks in the future, a matrix is established with the method beginning 'Situated on the ground, situated on land...,' and its analysis is stated with the method beginning 'An item situated on the ground means an item that has been placed on the ground...'

Pañcavīsatiavahārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion of the twenty-five legal cases is concluded.

Bhūmaṭṭhakathā

The Explanation concerning [Things] Situated in the Ground

94. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanāya saddhiṃ vinicchayakathā. Nikhātanti bhūmiyaṃ khaṇitvā ṭhapitaṃ. Paṭicchannanti paṃsuiṭṭhakādīhi paṭicchannaṃ. Bhūmaṭṭhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ…pe… gacchati vā, āpatti dukkaṭassāti taṃ evaṃ nikhaṇitvā vā paṭicchādetvā vā ṭhapitattā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yo bhikkhu kenacideva upāyena ñatvā “āharissāmī”ti theyyacitto hutvā rattibhāge uṭṭhāya gacchati, so bhaṇḍaṭṭhānaṃ appatvāpi sabbakāyavacīvikāresu dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Kathaṃ? So hi tassa āharaṇatthāya uṭṭhahanto yaṃ yaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ phandāpeti, sabbattha dukkaṭameva. Nivāsanapārupanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, hatthavāre hatthavāre dukkaṭaṃ. “Mahantaṃ nidhānaṃ na sakkā ekena āharituṃ, dutiyaṃ pariyesissāmī”ti kassaci sahāyassa santikaṃ gantukāmo dvāraṃ vivarati, padavāre ca hatthavāre ca dukkaṭaṃ. Dvārapidahane pana aññasmiṃ vā gamanassa anupakāre anāpatti. Tassa nipannokāsaṃ gantvā “itthannāmā”ti pakkosati, tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “ehi gacchāmā”ti vadati, vācāya vācāya dukkaṭaṃ. So tassa vacanena uṭṭhahati, tassāpi dukkaṭaṃ. Uṭṭhahitvā tassa santikaṃ gantukāmo nivāsanapārupanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, dvāraṃ vivaritvā tassa samīpaṃ gacchati, hatthavārapadavāresu sabbattha dukkaṭaṃ. So taṃ pucchati “asuko ca asuko ca kuhiṃ, asukañca asukañca pakkosāhī”ti, vācāya vācāya dukkaṭaṃ. Sabbe samāgate disvā “mayā asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne evarūpo nidhi upaladdho, gacchāma taṃ gahetvā puññāni ca karissāma, sukhañca jīvissāmā”ti vadati, vācāya vācāya dukkaṭameva.

Herein, this is the discourse giving a decision, together with the explanation of unclear terms. 'Buried' means having dug in the ground, it is placed. 'Concealed' means concealed by means of dust, bricks, and so on. Regarding 'An item situated in the ground… or he goes, there is an offense of dukkaṭa': Because it was placed by having been dug in or by having been concealed, an item is situated in the ground. Whatever monk, knowing of it by some means, with a thievish thought, thinking, 'I will take it,' rises in the night and goes, that monk, even without having reached the item's location, incurs a dukkaṭa offense in all actions of body and speech. How so? Indeed, as he rises for the purpose of taking it, whatever major and minor limbs he causes to move, in every case there is a dukkaṭa. He arranges his lower and upper robes; for every movement of the hand, there is a dukkaṭa. Thinking, 'The treasure is large; it is not possible for one person to bring it; I will search for a second person,' he, desiring to go to a certain companion, opens a door; for every movement of the foot and for every movement of the hand, there is a dukkaṭa. However, in closing the door or in another action not helpful to the going, there is no offense. Going to the place where that person is lying down, he calls out, 'So-and-so!' Having explained the matter, he says, 'Come, let us go'; for every word, there is a dukkaṭa. If that person rises because of his words, for him also there is a dukkaṭa. Having risen, desiring to go to his presence, he arranges his lower and upper robes, opens the door, and goes near him; in all movements of the hand and foot, there is a dukkaṭa. He asks him, 'Where are so-and-so and so-and-so? Call so-and-so and so-and-so'; for every word, there is a dukkaṭa. Seeing that all have assembled, he says, 'By me, such a treasure has been found in a place named so-and-so. Let us go, and having taken it, we shall both perform meritorious deeds and live in comfort'; for every word, there is a dukkaṭa.

Evaṃ laddhasahāyo kudālaṃ pariyesati. Sace panassa attano kudālo atthi, “taṃ āharissāmī”ti gacchanto ca gaṇhanto ca āharanto ca sabbattha hatthavārapadavāresu dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati[V 1.0249]. Sace natthi, aññaṃ [M 1.0270] bhikkhuṃ vā gahaṭṭhaṃ vā gantvā yācati, yācanto ca sace “kudālaṃ me dehi, kudālena me attho[P 2.0311], kiñci kātabbamatthi, taṃ katvā paccāharissāmī”ti musā abhaṇanto yācati, vācāya vācāya dukkaṭaṃ. Sace “mātikā sodhetabbā atthi, vihāre bhūmikammaṃ kātabbaṃ atthī”ti musāpi bhaṇati, yaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ musā, tattha tattha pācittiyaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana saccepi alikepi dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ, taṃ pamādalikhitanti veditabbaṃ. Na hi adinnādānassa pubbapayoge pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭaṃ nāma atthi. Sace pana kudālassa daṇḍo natthi, “daṇḍaṃ karissāmī”ti vāsiṃ vā pharasuṃ vā niseti, tadatthāya gacchati, gantvā sukkhakaṭṭhaṃ chindati tacchati ākoṭeti, sabbattha hatthavārapadavāresu dukkaṭaṃ. Allarukkhaṃ chindati, pācittiyaṃ. Tato paraṃ sabbapayogesu dukkaṭaṃ. Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mahāpaccariyañca tattha jātakakaṭṭhalatāchedanatthaṃ vāsipharasuṃ pariyesantānampi dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Sace pana tesaṃ evaṃ hoti “vāsipharasukudāle yācantā āsaṅkitā bhavissāma, lohaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā karomā”ti. Tato araññaṃ gantvā lohabījatthaṃ pathaviṃ khaṇanti, akappiyapathaviṃ khaṇantānaṃ dukkaṭehi saddhiṃ pācittiyānīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭā na muccati. Kappiyapathaviṃ khaṇantānaṃ dukkaṭāniyeva. Bījaṃ pana gahetvā tato paraṃ sabbakiriyāsu payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ.

94. Thus, having found a companion, he searches for a spade. If, however, he has his own spade, then in going to fetch it, in taking it, and in bringing it, in all movements of the hand and foot, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense. If he does not have one, he goes to another monk or a householder and asks for one. And in asking, if he asks without speaking a falsehood, saying, 'Give me a spade, I have a need for a spade, there is something to be done, having done it I will bring it back,' for every word, there is a dukkaṭa. If he also speaks a falsehood, saying, 'There is a water channel to be cleared' or 'There is earthwork to be done in the monastery,' then for whichever words are false, in each case there is a pācittiya. In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said there is only a dukkaṭa for both truth and falsehood; that should be known as written through negligence. For indeed, in the preliminary effort of taking what is not given, there is no such thing as a dukkaṭa in a case where a pācittiya applies. If, however, the spade has no handle, thinking, 'I will make a handle,' he sharpens an adze or an axe, goes for that purpose, and having gone, cuts dry wood, carves it, and hammers it in; in all movements of the hand and foot, there is a dukkaṭa. If he cuts a living tree, it is a pācittiya. Thereafter, in all efforts, it is a dukkaṭa. However, in the Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā and the Mahāpaccariya, it is said that for those searching for an adze or axe for the purpose of cutting the wood and creepers that have grown there, there is also a dukkaṭa. If, however, it occurs to them thus: 'Asking for adzes, axes, or spades, we will be suspected; let us produce the metal and make them,' then, having gone to the forest, they dig the earth for iron ore. For those digging unsuitable earth, there are pācittiyas along with dukkaṭas, it is said in the Mahāpaccariya. And just as here, so everywhere: in a case where a pācittiya applies, one is not freed from the dukkaṭa. For those digging suitable earth, there are only dukkaṭas. However, having taken the ore, thereafter in all activities, for every effort, there is a dukkaṭa.

Piṭakapariyesanepi hatthavārapadavāresu vuttanayeneva dukkaṭaṃ. Musāvāde pācittiyaṃ. Piṭakaṃ kātukāmatāya vallicchedane pācittiyanti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Gacchati vā āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ pariyiṭṭhasahāyakudālapiṭako nidhiṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana gacchanto “imaṃ nidhiṃ laddhā buddhapūjaṃ vā dhammapūjaṃ vā saṅghabhattaṃ vā karissāmī”ti kusalaṃ uppādeti, kusalacittena gamane anāpatti. Kasmā? “Theyyacitto dutiyaṃ [P 2.0312] vā…pe… gacchati vā, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttattā. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha atheyyacittassa anāpatti. Maggato okkamma nidhānaṭṭhānaṃ gamanatthāya maggaṃ karonto bhūtagāmaṃ chindati, pācittiyaṃ. Sukkhakaṭṭhaṃ chindati, dukkaṭaṃ.

Also in searching for a basket, for movements of the hand and foot, there is a dukkaṭa according to the method stated. For false speech, there is a pācittiya. For cutting a creeper with the desire to make a basket, there is a pācittiya. All this should be understood according to the preceding method. Regarding '...or he goes, there is an offense of dukkaṭa': Thus, he who has searched for a companion, a spade, and a basket goes to the treasure site; for every single step, there is a dukkaṭa. If, however, while going he gives rise to a wholesome thought, thinking, 'Having obtained this treasure, I will make an offering to the Buddha, or an offering to the Dhamma, or provide a meal for the Saṅgha,' in going with a wholesome mind, there is no offense. Why? Because it was said, 'With a thievish mind... or he goes, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.' And just as here, so everywhere: for one without a thievish mind, there is no offense. Deviating from the path, while making a path for the purpose of going to the treasure site, if he cuts a living plant, it is a pācittiya. If he cuts dry wood, it is a dukkaṭa.

Tatthajātakanti ciranihitāya kumbhiyā upari jātakaṃ. Kaṭṭhaṃ vā lataṃ vāti na kevalaṃ kaṭṭhalatameva, yaṃkiñci allaṃ vā sukkhaṃ vā tiṇarukkhalatādiṃ chindantassa sahapayogattā dukkaṭameva hoti.

'Grown there' means grown on top of a pot that was placed there long ago. Regarding 'wood or a creeper': it is not that there is an offense only for one who cuts just wood or a creeper, but for one who cuts anything whatsoever—wet or dry—such as grass, trees, creepers, and so on, because it is a conjoined effort, there is only a dukkaṭa offense.

Aṭṭhavidhaṃ [M 1.0271] hetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ nāma imasmiṃ ṭhāne samodhānetvā therehi dassitaṃ – pubbapayogadukkaṭaṃ[V 1.0250], sahapayogadukkaṭaṃ, anāmāsadukkaṭaṃ, durupaciṇṇadukkaṭaṃ, vinayadukkaṭaṃ, ñātadukkaṭaṃ, ñattidukkaṭaṃ, paṭissavadukkaṭanti. Tattha “theyyacitto dutiyaṃ vā kudālaṃ vā piṭakaṃ vā pariyesati gacchati vā, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti idaṃ pubbapayogadukkaṭaṃ nāma. Ettha hi dukkaṭaṭṭhāne dukkaṭaṃ, pācittiyaṭṭhāne pācittiyameva hoti. “Tatthajātakaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ vā lataṃ vā chindati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti idaṃ sahapayogadukkaṭaṃ nāma. Ettha pana pācittiyavatthu ca dukkaṭavatthu ca dukkaṭaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati. Kasmā? Avahārassa sahapayogattāti. Yaṃ pana dasavidhaṃ ratanaṃ, sattavidhaṃ dhaññaṃ, sabbañca āvudhabhaṇḍādiṃ āmasantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ anāmāsadukkaṭaṃ nāma. Yaṃ kadalināḷikerādīnaṃ tatthajātakaphalāni āmasantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ durupaciṇṇadukkaṭaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana piṇḍāya carantassa patte raje patite pattaṃ appaṭiggahetvā adhovitvā vā tattha bhikkhaṃ gaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ vinayadukkaṭaṃ nāma. “Sutvā na vadanti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 419) idaṃ ñātadukkaṭaṃ nāma. Yaṃ ekādasasu samanubhāsanāsu “ñattiyā dukkaṭa”nti (pārā. 414) vuttaṃ, idaṃ ñattidukkaṭaṃ nāma. “Tassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno purimikā ca na paññāyati, paṭissave ca āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 207) idaṃ paṭissavadukkaṭaṃ nāma. Idaṃ pana sahapayogadukkaṭaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “yaṃkiñci allaṃ vā sukkhaṃ vā tiṇarukkhalatādiṃ chindantassa sahapayogattā dukkaṭameva hotī”ti.

There are eight kinds of offenses of wrong-doing named here, as shown by the Elders by combining them in this context: the dukkaṭa of prior application, the dukkaṭa of concurrent application, the dukkaṭa concerning what is not to be touched, the dukkaṭa of improper practice, the dukkaṭa of the Vinaya, the dukkaṭa of knowing, the dukkaṭa of the motion, and the dukkaṭa of acknowledgment. Among these, 'One with the intention to steal searches for or goes after a companion, a spade, or a basket—one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.' This is called the dukkaṭa of prior application. Here, in a case of an offense of wrong-doing, it is an offense of wrong-doing; in a case of an offense entailing expiation, it is only an offense entailing expiation. 'Cutting wood or vines that grow there—one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.' This is called the dukkaṭa of concurrent application. Here, however, both the basis for an offense entailing expiation and the basis for an offense of wrong-doing stand only in the place of an offense of wrong-doing. Why? Because of the concurrent application of theft. That which is called an offense of wrong-doing for touching the ten kinds of gems, the seven kinds of grains, or any weapons and goods, etc.—this is called the dukkaṭa concerning what is not to be touched. That which is called an offense of wrong-doing for touching fruits growing there, such as those from a banana or coconut palm—this is called the dukkaṭa of improper practice. That which is called an offense of wrong-doing for a bhikkhu walking for alms who, when dust has fallen into his bowl, receives almsfood in it without having the bowl re-accepted or without washing it—this is called the dukkaṭa of the Vinaya. 'Having heard, they do not speak—one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.' This is called the dukkaṭa of knowing. That which is called 'a dukkaṭa by the motion' in the eleven formal acts of inquiry—this is called the dukkaṭa of the motion. 'Bhikkhus, for that bhikkhu, the prior offense is not discerned, but in the acknowledgment, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' This is called the dukkaṭa of acknowledgment. This, however, is the dukkaṭa of concurrent application. Therefore, it is said: 'Whatever fresh or dry grass, trees, or vines one cuts—because of the concurrent application, it is only an offense of wrong-doing.'

Sace panassa tatthajātake tiṇarukkhalatādimhi chinnepi [P 2.0313] lajjidhammo okkamati, saṃvaro uppajjati, chedanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ desetvā muccati. Atha dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā saussāhova paṃsuṃ khaṇati, chedanadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, khaṇanadukkaṭe patiṭṭhāti. Akappiyapathaviṃ khaṇantopi hi idha sahapayogattā dukkaṭameva āpajjati. Sace panassa sabbadisāsu khaṇitvā kumbhimūlaṃ pattassāpi lajjidhammo okkamati, khaṇanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ desetvā muccati.

If, however, even when grass, trees, or creepers that have grown there are cut, a sense of shame arises in him and restraint is established, he is freed after confessing the offense of wrong-doing due to the cutting. Then, without abandoning the task and with vigor, he digs the earth. The offense of wrong-doing due to cutting subsides, and he is established in the offense of wrong-doing due to digging. Indeed, even when digging unallowable earth, here, due to the concurrent application, he incurs only an offense of wrong-doing. If, however, even after digging in all directions and reaching the base of the pot, a sense of shame arises in him, he is freed after confessing the offense of wrong-doing due to digging.

Byūhati vāti atha pana saussāhova paṃsuṃ viyūhati, ekapasse rāsiṃ karoti, khaṇanadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, viyūhanadukkaṭe patiṭṭhāti. Tañca paṃsuṃ tattha tattha puñjaṃ karonto payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Sace pana rāsiṃ katvāpi dhuranikkhepaṃ karoti, lajjidhammaṃ āpajjati[M 1.0272], viyūhanadukkaṭaṃ desetvā muccati. Uddharati vāti atha pana saussāhova paṃsuṃ uddharitvā bahi pāteti, viyūhanadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, uddharaṇadukkaṭe patiṭṭhāti. Paṃsuṃ pana kudālena vā hatthehi vā pacchiyā vā tahiṃ tahiṃ pātento payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Sace pana sabbaṃ paṃsuṃ nīharitvā kumbhiṃ thalaṭṭhaṃ katvāpi lajjidhammaṃ [V 1.0251] āpajjati, uddharaṇadukkaṭaṃ desetvā muccati. Atha pana saussāhova kumbhiṃ āmasati, uddharaṇadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, āmasanadukkaṭe patiṭṭhāti. Āmasitvāpi ca lajjidhammaṃ āpajjanto āmasanadukkaṭaṃ desetvā muccati. Atha saussāhova kumbhiṃ phandāpeti, āmasanadukkaṭaṃ paṭippassambhati, “phandāpeti, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vuttathullaccaye patiṭṭhāti.

Or he clears away. Then with vigor, he clears away the dust, making a pile on one side. The offense of wrong-doing due to digging subsides, and he is established in the offense of wrong-doing due to clearing away. And while making piles of that dust here and there, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing with each effort. But if, after making a pile, he abandons the task and a sense of shame arises in him, he is freed after confessing the offense of wrong-doing due to clearing away. Or he lifts it out. Then with vigor, he lifts out the dust and throws it outside. The offense of wrong-doing due to clearing away subsides, and he is established in the offense of wrong-doing due to lifting out. But while throwing the dust here and there with a spade, with his hands, or with a basket, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing with each effort. If, however, after removing all the dust and making the pot stand on high ground, a sense of shame arises in him, he is freed after confessing the offense of wrong-doing due to lifting out. Then with vigor, he touches the pot. The offense of wrong-doing due to lifting out subsides, and he is established in the offense of wrong-doing due to touching. And even after touching it, if a sense of shame arises in him, he is freed after confessing the offense of wrong-doing due to touching. Then with vigor, he makes the pot shake. The offense of wrong-doing due to touching subsides, and he is established in the grave offense spoken of as, 'If he makes it shake, he incurs a grave offense.'

Tatrāyaṃ dukkaṭathullaccayānaṃ dvinnampi vacanattho – paṭhamaṃ tāvettha duṭṭhu kataṃ satthārā vuttakiccaṃ virādhetvā katanti dukkaṭaṃ. Atha vā duṭṭhaṃ kataṃ, virūpā sā kiriyā bhikkhukiriyānaṃ majjhe na sobhatīti evampi dukkaṭaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Herein, this is the verbal analysis of both dukkaṭa and thullaccaya: First, in this context, dukkaṭa is so called because it is 'badly done,' that is, done having contravened the duty declared by the Teacher. Alternatively, it is a bad action; that action is unseemly and does not shine among the actions of bhikkhus. For this reason also it is called dukkaṭa. And this has been said:

“Dukkaṭaṃ iti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ suṇohi yathātathaṃ;

Aparaddhaṃ viraddhañca, khalitaṃ yañca dukkaṭaṃ.

“What is called a dukkaṭa, listen to it as it truly is; an error, a transgression, and a fault—that is a dukkaṭa.

“Yaṃ manusso kare pāpaṃ, āvi vā yadi vā raho;

Dukkaṭanti pavedenti, tenetaṃ iti vuccatī”ti. (pari. 339);

Whatever evil a person does, openly or in secret, they call it a dukkaṭa; therefore, it is so called.”

Itaraṃ [P 2.0314] pana thūlattā, accayattā ca thullaccayaṃ. “Samparāye ca duggati” (saṃ. ni. 1.49), “yaṃ hoti kaṭukapphala”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 66; netti. 91) viya cettha saṃyogabhāvo veditabbo. Ekassa santike desetabbesu hi accayesu tena samo thūlo accayo natthi. Tasmā vuttaṃ “thūlattā accayattā ca thullaccaya”nti. Vuttañcetaṃ –

The other, however, is a thullaccaya because of its grossness and because of its being an offense. And, as in such phrases as “and in the future life, a bad destination” and “which has a bitter fruit,” here too the nature of it being a compound should be understood. Indeed, among the offenses that should be confessed in the presence of a single bhikkhu, there is no gross offense equal to it. Therefore, it was said, “because of its grossness and because of its being an offense, it is a thullaccaya.” And this has been said:

“Thullaccayanti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ suṇohi yathātathaṃ;

Ekassa mūle yo deseti, yo ca taṃ paṭiggaṇhati;

Accayo tena samo natthi, tenetaṃ iti vuccatī”ti. (pari. 339);

“What is called a thullaccaya, listen to it as it truly is; he who confesses it at the feet of one, and he who accepts it—there is no offense equal to that; therefore, it is so called.”

Phandāpentassa [M 1.0273] ca payoge payoge thullaccayaṃ. Phandāpetvāpi ca lajjidhammaṃ okkanto thullaccayaṃ desetvā muccati. Sahapayogato paṭṭhāyeva cettha purimā purimā āpatti paṭippassambhati. Sahapayogaṃ pana akatvā lajjidhammaṃ okkantena yā pubbapayoge dukkaṭapācittiyā āpannā, sabbā tā desetabbā. Sahapayoge ca tatthajātakacchedane bahukānipi dukkaṭāni paṃsukhaṇanaṃ patvā paṭippassambhanti. Ekaṃ khaṇanadukkaṭameva hoti. Khaṇane [V 1.0252] bahukānipi viyūhanaṃ, viyūhane bahukānipi uddharaṇaṃ, uddharaṇe bahukānipi āmasanaṃ, āmasane bahukānipi phandāpanaṃ patvā paṭippassambhanti. Paṃsukhaṇanādīsu ca lajjidhamme uppanne bahukāpi āpattiyo hontu, ekameva desetvā muccatīti kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Purimāpattipaṭippassaddhi ca nāmesā “ñattiyā dukkaṭaṃ, dvīhi kammavācāhi thullaccayā paṭippassambhantī”ti (pārā. 414) evaṃ anusāvanāsuttesuyeva āgatā. Idha pana dutiyapārājike aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahetabbāti.

And for one causing it to shake, for each and every attempt, there is a thullaccaya. And having caused it to shake, one who enters a state of shame is freed by confessing the thullaccaya. And here, from the concurrent application onwards, each preceding offense subsides. However, by one who, without making a concurrent application, enters a state of shame, whatever offenses of wrong-doing and offenses entailing expiation were incurred in the preliminary application, all of them must be confessed. And in the concurrent application, even many offenses of wrong-doing from cutting what has grown there subside upon reaching the digging of the earth. There is only one offense of wrong-doing for digging. In digging, many offenses subside upon reaching scattering; in scattering, many offenses subside upon reaching lifting; in lifting, many offenses subside upon reaching touching; and in touching, many offenses subside upon reaching the act of causing it to shake. And in digging the earth and so on, when a state of shame has arisen, even if there are many offenses, let them be; by confessing only one, he is freed—thus it is said in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā. This so-called subsiding of a previous offense has come only in the formal procedural texts thus: “For the motion, an offense of wrong-doing; for the two formal acts, grave offenses subside.” Here, however, in this second Pārājika, it should be taken according to the authority of the commentary teachers.

Ṭhānā cāveti, āpatti pārājikassāti yo pana phandāpetvāpi lajjidhammaṃ anokkamitvāva taṃ kumbhiṃ ṭhānato antamaso kesaggamattampi cāveti, pārājikameva āpajjatīti attho. Ṭhānā cāvanañcettha chahi ākārehi veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Kumbhiṃ mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhanto iminā antena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kesaggamattampi [P 2.0315] pārimantena atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Tatheva gahetvā parato pellento pārimantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kesaggamattampi iminā antena atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Vāmato vā dakkhiṇato vā apanāmento vāmantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kesaggamattampi dakkhiṇantena atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Dakkhiṇantena vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kesaggamattampi vāmantena atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Uddhaṃ ukkhipanto kesaggamattampi bhūmito moceti, pārājikaṃ. Khaṇitvā heṭṭhato osīdento bundena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kesaggamattampi mukhavaṭṭiyā atikkāmeti, pārājikanti evaṃ ekaṭṭhāne ṭhitāya kumbhiyā. Yadi pana kumbhimukhavaṭṭiyā pāsaṃ katvā lohakhāṇuṃ vā khadirasārādikhāṇuṃ vā pathaviyaṃ ākoṭetvā tattha saṅkhalikāya bandhitvā ṭhapenti, ekissā disāya ekāya saṅkhalikāya baddhāya dve ṭhānāni labbhanti, dvīsu tīsu catūsu disāsu catūhi saṅkhalikāhi baddhāya pañca ṭhānāni labbhanti.

“He moves it from its place, there is an offense of Pārājika” means: whatever monk, having caused it to shake but without entering into a state of shame, moves that pot from its place even as much as a hair's breadth, he incurs a Pārājika offense. This is the meaning. And here, the moving from its place should be understood in six ways. How? Taking the pot by its rim and pulling it towards himself, if he causes the far edge to pass even a hair's breadth beyond the spot originally touched by the near edge, it is a Pārājika. Taking it in the same way and pushing it away, if he causes the near edge to pass even a hair's breadth beyond the spot originally touched by the far edge, it is a Pārājika. Or moving it away to the left or to the right, if he causes the right edge to pass even a hair's breadth beyond the spot originally touched by the left edge, it is a Pārājika. Or if he causes the left edge to pass even a hair's breadth beyond the spot originally touched by the right edge, it is a Pārājika. Lifting it upwards, if he frees it from the ground even a hair's breadth, it is a Pārājika. Having dug and sinking it downwards, if he causes the rim to pass even a hair's breadth beyond the spot originally touched by the base, it is a Pārājika. Thus it is for a pot standing in one place. But if, having made a loop on the pot's rim and having driven an iron stake or a stake of acacia heartwood, etc., into the ground, they place it, having tied it there with a chain, then for a pot tied with one chain in one direction, two positions are obtained; for a pot tied with four chains in two, three, or four directions, five positions are obtained.

Tattha [M 1.0274] ekakhāṇuke baddhakumbhiyā paṭhamaṃ khāṇukaṃ vā uddharati, saṅkhalikaṃ vā chindati, thullaccayaṃ. Tato kumbhiṃ yathāvuttanayena kesaggamattampi ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Atha paṭhamaṃ kumbhiṃ uddharati, thullaccayaṃ. Tato khāṇukaṃ kesaggamattampi ṭhānā cāveti, saṅkhalikaṃ vā chindati, pārājikaṃ. Etena upāyena dvīsu tīsu catūsu khāṇukesu baddhakumbhiyāpi pacchime ṭhānācāvane pārājikaṃ. Sesesu thullaccayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, for a pot tied to a single stake, if he first pulls out the stake or cuts the chain, it is a thullaccaya. Thereafter, if he moves the pot from its place even a hair's breadth in the aforesaid manner, it is a Pārājika. Or, if he first lifts the pot, it is a thullaccaya. Thereafter, if he moves the stake from its place even a hair's breadth or cuts the chain, it is a Pārājika. By this method, also for a pot tied to two, three, or four stakes, for moving the last one from its place, there is a Pārājika. For the remaining ones, it should be understood as a thullaccaya.

Sace khāṇu natthi, saṅkhalikāya agge valayaṃ katvā tatthajātake mūle pavesitaṃ hoti, paṭhamaṃ kumbhiṃ uddharitvā pacchā mūlaṃ chetvā valayaṃ nīharati, pārājikaṃ. Atha mūlaṃ acchetvā valayaṃ [V 1.0253] ito cito ca sāreti, rakkhati. Sace pana mūlato anīharitvāpi hatthena gahetvā ākāsagataṃ karoti, pārājikaṃ. Ayamettha viseso. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

If there is no stake, and a ring made at the end of a chain has been inserted into a root that has grown there, if he first lifts the pot, and afterwards, having cut the root, takes out the ring, it is a Pārājika. Or, without cutting the root, if he moves the ring here and there, he is protected. But if, without taking it out from the root, he takes it with his hand and makes it go into the air, it is a Pārājika. This is the special case here. The rest is just as has been said.

Keci [P 2.0316] pana nimittatthāya kumbhimatthake nigrodharukkhādīni ropenti, mūlāni kumbhiṃ vinandhitvā ṭhitāni honti, “mūlāni chinditvā kumbhiṃ gahessāmī”ti chindantassa payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Chinditvā okāsaṃ katvā kumbhiṃ kesaggamattampi ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Mūlāni chindatova luṭhitvā kumbhī ninnaṭṭhānaṃ gatā, rakkhati tāva. Gataṭṭhānato uddharati, pārājikaṃ. Sace chinnesu mūlesu ekamūlamattena kumbhī tiṭṭhati, so ca taṃ “imasmiṃ mūle chinne patissatī”ti chindati, chinnamatte pārājikaṃ. Sace pana ekamūleneva pāse baddhasūkaro viya ṭhitā hoti, aññaṃ kiñci lagganakaṃ natthi, tasmimpi mūle chinnamatte pārājikaṃ. Sace kumbhimatthake mahāpāsāṇo ṭhapito hoti, taṃ daṇḍena ukkhipitvā apanetukāmo kumbhimatthake jātarukkhaṃ chindati, dukkaṭaṃ. Tassā samīpe jātakaṃ chetvā āharati, atatthajātakattā taṃ chindato pācittiyaṃ.

But some, for the sake of a sign, plant banyan trees and so on on top of the pot; the roots entwine the pot and are established. For one who cuts them thinking, 'Having cut the roots, I will take the pot,' for each attempt there is an offense of wrong-doing. Having cut them and made an opening, if he moves the pot from its place even a hair's breadth, it is a Pārājika offense. If, while he is cutting the roots, the pot rolls and goes to a lower place, he is still protected for the time being. If he lifts it from the place it has gone to, it is a Pārājika offense. If, when the roots have been cut, the pot stands by means of just one root, and he cuts it knowing, 'When this root is cut, it will fall,' it is a Pārājika offense at the very moment of being cut. But if it stands by just one root like a pig caught in a snare, and there is nothing else holding it, then also, at the very moment that root is cut, it is a Pārājika offense. If a large stone has been placed on top of the pot, and wishing to remove it by lifting it with a stick, he cuts a tree that has grown on the pot, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he cuts and brings a tree that has grown near it, because it has not grown there, for him who cuts it, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

Attano bhājananti sace pana kumbhiṃ uddharituṃ asakkonto kumbhigatabhaṇḍaggahaṇatthaṃ attano bhājanaṃ pavesetvā antokumbhiyaṃ pañcamāsakaṃ vā atirekapañcamāsakaṃ vā agghanakaṃ theyyacitto āmasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Paricchedo cettha pārājikaniyamanatthaṃ vutto. Theyyacittena pana ūnapañcamāsakampi āmasanto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatiyeva.

‘One's own vessel’: But if, being unable to lift the pot, for the purpose of taking the goods that are in the pot, one inserts one's own vessel and, inside the pot, with a thievish mind, touches goods worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, there is an offense of wrong-doing. And here, the limit has been stated for the purpose of defining the Pārājika offense. But indeed, one who touches even goods worth less than five māsakas with a thievish mind certainly incurs an offense of wrong-doing.

Phandāpetīti [M 1.0275] ettha yāva ekābaddhaṃ katvā attano bhājanaṃ paveseti, tāva phandāpetīti vuccati. Api ca ito cito ca apabyūhantopi phandāpetiyeva, so thullaccayaṃ āpajjati. Yadā pana ekābaddhabhāvo chinno, kumbhigataṃ kumbhiyameva, bhājanagatampi bhājaneyeva hoti, tadā attano bhājanagataṃ nāma hoti. Evaṃ katvā kumbhito anīhatepi ca bhājane pārājikaṃ āpajjati.

Regarding 'shakes it': As long as one makes it a single connected mass and causes it to enter one's own vessel, it is called 'shaking it.' Moreover, even one who moves it to and fro is indeed 'shaking it'; he incurs a grave offense. But when the state of being a single connected mass is severed, what is in the pot is in the pot itself, and what has entered the vessel is in the vessel itself; then it is called 'what has entered one's own vessel.' Having done so, even if the vessel has not yet been removed from the pot, one incurs an offense entailing expulsion.

Muṭṭhiṃ vā chindatīti ettha yathā aṅgulantarehi nikkhantakahāpaṇā kumbhigate kahāpaṇe na samphusanti, evaṃ muṭṭhiṃ karonto muṭṭhiṃ chindati nāma; sopi pārājikaṃ āpajjati.

Regarding 'Or cuts a fist': Just as kahāpaṇas that have come out from between the fingers do not touch the kahāpaṇas in the pot, so a monk who makes a fist in such a way is called 'one who cuts a fist'; he also incurs an offense entailing expulsion.

Suttārūḷhanti sutte ārūḷhaṃ; suttena āvutassāpi suttamayassāpi etaṃ adhivacanaṃ[P 2.0317]. Pāmaṅgādīnihi sovaṇṇamayānipi honti rūpiyamayānipi suttamayānipi, muttāvaliādayopi ettheva [V 1.0254] saṅgahaṃ gatā. Veṭhananti sīsaveṭhanapaṭo vuccati. Etesu yaṃkiñci theyyacitto āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Phandāpeti, thullaccayaṃ. Pāmaṅgādīni koṭiyaṃ gahetvā ākāsaṭṭhaṃ akaronto uccāreti, thullaccayaṃ.

‘Mounted on a thread’ means mounted on a thread; this is a designation for that which is strung with a thread and also for that which is made of thread. For items such as pāmaṅga can be made of gold, silver, or thread; strings of pearls and the like are also included here. ‘Wrapped around’ refers to a head-wrapping cloth. If, with intent to steal, one touches any of these, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If one shakes it, it is a grave offense. If one takes a pāmaṅga or similar item by the end and lifts it without making it stand free in the air, it is a grave offense.

Ghaṃsanto nīharatīti ettha pana paripuṇṇāya kumbhiyā upari samatittikaṃ kumbhiṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ vā ekaṃ koṭiṃ bunde ekaṃ koṭiṃ mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ vā ghaṃsantassa nīharato thullaccayaṃ. Kumbhimukhā mocentassa pārājikaṃ. Yaṃ pana upaḍḍhakumbhiyaṃ vā rittakumbhiyaṃ vā ṭhapitaṃ, tassa attano phuṭṭhokāsova ṭhānaṃ, na sakalā kumbhī, tasmā taṃ ghaṃsantassāpi nīharato patiṭṭhitokāsato kesaggamatte mutte pārājikameva. Kumbhiyā pana paripuṇṇāya vā ūnāya vā ujukameva uddharantassa heṭṭhimakoṭiyā patiṭṭhitokāsā muttamatteva pārājikaṃ. Antokumbhiyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ yaṃkiñci pārājikappahonakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sakalakumbhiyaṃ cārentassa, pāmaṅgādiñca ghaṃsitvā nīharantassa yāva mukhavaṭṭiṃ nātikkamati, tāva thullaccayameva. Tassa hi sabbāpi kumbhī ṭhānanti saṅkhepamahāpaccariyādīsu vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ṭhapitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ, na sakalā kumbhī. Tasmā yathāṭhitaṭṭhānato kesaggamattampi mocentassa pārājikamevā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pamāṇaṃ. Itaraṃ pana ākāsagataṃ akarontassa cīvaravaṃse ṭhapitacīvaraveṭhanakanayena vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Vinayavinicchaye hi āgate garuke ṭhātabbaṃ, esā vinayadhammatā. Apica “attano bhājanagataṃ [M 1.0276] vā karoti, muṭṭhiṃ vā chindatī”ti vacanato petaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathā antokumbhiyaṃ ṭhitassa na sabbā kumbhī ṭhānanti.

Regarding 'scraping, one removes': In the case of goods placed on top of a pot that is full to the brim, or goods placed with one end at the bottom and the other at the mouth-rim, for one who removes them by scraping, it is a grave offense. For one who releases it from the mouth of the pot, it is an offense entailing expulsion. But as for what is placed in a half-full or an empty pot, its place is only the area it has touched, not the entire pot. Therefore, for one removing it even while scraping, when it is freed by a hair's breadth from its established place, it is an offense entailing expulsion. But for one lifting straight up from a full or less-than-full pot, as soon as the lower end is freed from its established place, it is an offense entailing expulsion. For one moving any item worth a Pārājika offense around the entire pot, or for one scraping out a pāmaṅga or the like and removing it, as long as it does not pass the mouth-rim, it is only a grave offense. For in that case, the entire pot is its place—so it is said in the Saṅkhepamahāpaccariya and other texts. In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'Only the place where it was put is the place, not the entire pot. Therefore, for one who dislodges it even a hair's breadth from where it was placed, it is an offense entailing expulsion.' That is the authority. The other view, which is explained in the manner of a roll of robes placed on a robe-line without being suspended in the air, should not be accepted. For when a point of Vinaya needs to be decided, one should stand on the weighty opinion; this is the nature of the Vinaya. Furthermore, this should be understood from the text, '...makes it enter one's own vessel, or cuts a fist,' that for something placed inside a pot, the entire pot is not its place.

Sappiādīsu yaṃkiñci pivato ekapayogena pītamatte [P 2.0318] pārājikanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyādīsu pana ayaṃ vibhāgo dassito – “mukhaṃ anapanetvā ākaḍḍhantassa pivato sace paragalagataṃ pādaṃ na agghati, mukhagatena saddhiṃ agghati, rakkhati tāva. Kaṇṭhena pana paricchinnakāleyeva pārājikaṃ hoti. Sacepi oṭṭhehi paricchindanto oṭṭhe pidahati, pārājikameva. Uppaladaṇḍaveḷunāḷinaḷanāḷiādīhi pivantassāpi sace paragalagatameva pādaṃ agghati, pārājikaṃ. Sace saha mukhagatena agghati, na tāva pārājikaṃ hoti. Uppaladaṇḍādigatena saddhiṃ ekābaddhabhāvaṃ kopetvā oṭṭhehi paricchinnamatte pārājikaṃ. Sace uppaladaṇḍādigatena saddhiṃ agghati, uppaladaṇḍādīnaṃ bunde aṅguliyāpi pihitamatte pārājikaṃ. Pādagghanake paragalaṃ appaviṭṭhe uppaladaṇḍādīsu ca mukhe ca atirekapādārahampi ekābaddhaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, rakkhatiyevā”ti. Taṃ sabbampi yasmā “attano bhājanagataṃ vā karoti[V 1.0255], muṭṭhiṃ vā chindatī”ti imaṃ nayaṃ bhajati, tasmā sudassitameva. Esa tāva ekābaddhe nayo.

Regarding ghee and other such items, in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā it is said that for one who drinks any of them, an offense entailing expulsion occurs as soon as it is drunk in a single effort. In the Mahāpaccariya and other texts, however, this distinction is shown: 'For one drinking by drawing it in without removing the mouth, if what has reached the other side of the throat is not worth a pāda, but is worth a pāda together with what is in the mouth, one is protected for the time being. But at the very moment it is cut off by the throat, it is an offense entailing expulsion. Even if, while cutting it off with the lips, one closes the lips, it is an offense entailing expulsion. For one drinking with a lotus stalk, bamboo tube, reed tube, or the like, if what has reached the other side of the throat is itself worth a pāda, it is an offense entailing expulsion. If it is worth a pāda together with what is in the mouth, it is not yet an offense entailing expulsion. Having broken the state of being a single connected mass with what is in the lotus stalk or other tube, as soon as it is cut off by the lips, it is an offense entailing expulsion. If it is worth a pāda together with what is in the lotus stalk or other tube, as soon as the bottom of the tube is blocked even with a finger, it is an offense entailing expulsion. When an amount worth a pāda has not yet entered the other side of the throat, and even more than a pāda's worth remains as a single connected mass in the lotus stalk and in the mouth, one is still protected.' Since all of this conforms to the method, '...makes it enter one's own vessel, or cuts a fist,' it is therefore well-shown. This, for now, is the method regarding a single connected mass.

Sace pana hatthena vā pattena vā thālakādinā vā kenaci bhājanena gahetvā pivati, yamhi payoge pādagghanakaṃ pūreti, tamhi gate pārājikaṃ. Atha mahagghaṃ hoti, sippikāyapi ekapayogeneva pādagghanakaṃ gahetuṃ sakkā hoti, ekuddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ. Bhājanaṃ pana nimujjāpetvā gaṇhantassa yāva ekābaddhaṃ hoti, tāva rakkhati. Mukhavaṭṭiparicchedena vā uddhārena vā pārājikaṃ. Yadā pana sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā acchaṃ telasadisameva madhuphāṇitaṃ vā kumbhiṃ āviñchetvā attano bhājane paveseti, tadā tesaṃ acchatāya ekābaddhatā natthīti pādagghanake mukhavaṭṭito gaḷitamatte pārājikaṃ.

If, however, one drinks by taking it with the hand, or a bowl, or a plate, or some other vessel, an offense entailing expulsion occurs upon the completion of the effort in which one fills an amount worth a pāda. Now, if the substance is very valuable, so that it is possible to take an amount worth a pāda in a single effort, the offense entailing expulsion occurs in that single act of lifting out. But for one who takes by submerging a vessel, one is protected as long as it remains a single, unbroken mass. The offense entailing expulsion occurs either by the demarcation of the mouth-rim or by the lifting out. When, however, one pours ghee, or oil, or clear honey or molasses which is just like oil, by tilting a pot and causing it to enter one's own vessel, then, because of their clarity, there is no state of being a single, unbroken mass. Thus, when an amount worth a pāda is involved, the offense entailing expulsion occurs as soon as it has dripped from the mouth-rim.

Pacitvā ṭhapitaṃ pana madhuphāṇitaṃ sileso viya cikkanaṃ ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanayoggaṃ hoti, uppanne kukkucce ekābaddhameva hutvā paṭinīharituṃ [P 2.0319] sakkoti, etaṃ mukhavaṭṭiyā nikkhamitvā bhājane paviṭṭhampi bāhirena saddhiṃ ekābaddhattā rakkhati, mukhavaṭṭito chinnamatte pana pārājikaṃ. Yopi theyyacittena [M 1.0277] parassa kumbhiyā pādagghanakaṃ sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā avassapivanakaṃ yaṃkiñci dukūlasāṭakaṃ vā cammakhaṇḍādīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ pakkhipati, hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ.

But honey or molasses that has been cooked and set aside becomes sticky like lac, suitable for being pulled and stretched. When remorse arises, it can be taken back only if it remains connected as one. Even if it emerges from the rim of the mouth and enters a vessel, because it remains connected as one with what is outside, one is protected. But at the moment it is severed from the rim of the mouth, it is an offense entailing expulsion. Also, if a monk with a thieving mind puts into another's pot any item such as a fine cloth or a piece of leather that will certainly absorb ghee or oil worth a pāda, it is an offense entailing expulsion at the moment it is released from the hand.

Rittakumbhiyā “idāni telaṃ ākirissantī”ti ñatvā yaṃkiñci bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacitto pakkhipati, taṃ ce tattha tele ākiṇṇe pañcamāsakaagghanakaṃ pivati, pītamatte pārājikanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana tattheva sukkhataḷāke sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇavinicchayena virujjhati, avahāralakkhaṇañcettha na paññāyati, tasmā na gahetabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyādīsu pana tassa uddhāre pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ.

In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā it is said: If a monk with a thieving mind, knowing, 'Now they will pour oil into it,' places any item into an empty pot, and if that item, when oil has been poured in there, absorbs oil worth five māsakas, it is an offense entailing expulsion at the moment of absorption. But that statement is contradicted by the decision in that very commentary concerning the straightening of a dry water-channel in a dry lake; and the characteristic of theft is not apparent here. Therefore, it should not be accepted. But in the Mahāpaccarī and other commentaries, it is said that an offense entailing expulsion occurs upon its removal; that is proper.

Parassa rittakumbhiyā saṅgopanatthāya bhaṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā tattha tele ākiṇṇe “sace ayaṃ jānissati, maṃ palibujjhissatī”ti bhīto pādagghanakaṃ telaṃ pītaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacittena uddharati, pārājikaṃ. Suddhacittena uddharati, pare āharāpente bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ nāma yaṃ parassa naṭṭhaṃ, tassa mūlaṃ vā tadeva vā bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbanti attho. No ce deti, sāmikassa dhuranikkhepe pārājikaṃ. Sace parassa kumbhiyā añño sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā ākirati, tatra cāyaṃ theyyacittena telapivanakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ pakkhipati, vuttanayeneva pārājikaṃ. Attano rittakumbhiyā [V 1.0256] parassa sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā ākiraṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā theyyacittena bhaṇḍaṃ nikkhipati, pubbe vuttanayeneva uddhāre pārājikaṃ. Suddhacitto nikkhipitvā pacchā theyyacittena uddharati, pārājikameva. Suddhacittova uddharati, neva avahāro, na gīvā; mahāpaccariyaṃ pana anāpattimattameva vuttaṃ. “‘Kissa mama kumbhiyaṃ telaṃ ākirasī’ti kupito attano bhaṇḍaṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍeti, no bhaṇḍadeyya”nti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Theyyacittena mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā kumbhiṃ āviñchati [P 2.0320] telaṃ gaḷetukāmo, pādagghanake gaḷite pārājikaṃ. Theyyacitteneva jajjaraṃ karoti “savitvā gamissatī”ti pādagghanake savitvā gate pārājikaṃ. Theyyacitteneva chiddaṃ karoti omaṭṭhaṃ vā ummaṭṭhaṃ vā vemaṭṭhaṃ vā, idaṃ pana sammohaṭṭhānaṃ; tasmā suṭṭhu sallekkhetabbaṃ. Ayañhettha vinicchayo – omaṭṭhaṃ nāma adhomukhachiddaṃ; ummaṭṭhaṃ nāma uddhaṃmukhachiddaṃ; vemaṭṭhaṃ nāma uḷuṅkasseva ujugatachiddaṃ. Tatra omaṭṭhassa bahi paṭṭhāya katassa abbhantarantato pādagghanake tele gaḷite bahi anikkhantepi pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā tato gaḷitamattameva bahigataṃ nāma [M 1.0278] hoti, na kumbhigatasaṅkhyaṃ labhati. Anto paṭṭhāya katassa bāhirantato pādagghanake gaḷite pārājikaṃ. Ummaṭṭhassa yathā tathā vā katassa bāhirantato pādagghanake gaḷite pārājikaṃ. Tañhi yāva bāhirantato na gaḷati, tāva kumbhigatameva hoti. “Vemaṭṭhassa ca kapālamajjhato gaḷitavasena kāretabbo”ti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana anto ca bahi ca paṭṭhāya majjhe ṭhapetvā katachidde taḷākassa ca mariyādabhedena sameti. Anto paṭṭhāya kate pana bāhirantena, bahi paṭṭhāya kate abbhantarantena kāretabboti idamettha yuttaṃ. Yo pana “vaṭṭitvā gacchissatī”ti theyyacittena kumbhiyā ādhārakaṃ vā upatthambhanaleḍḍuke vā apaneti, vaṭṭitvā gatāya pārājikaṃ. Telākiraṇabhāvaṃ pana ñatvā rittakumbhiyā jajjarabhāve vā chiddesu vā katesu pacchā nikkhantatelappamāṇena bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ hoti. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana katthaci pārājikantipi likhitaṃ, taṃ pamādalikhitaṃ.

Having placed an item in another's empty pot for safekeeping, when oil is poured in there, if, being afraid and thinking, 'If this person finds out, he will trouble me,' he removes with a thieving mind the item which has absorbed oil worth a quarter, it is a pārājika offense. If he removes it with a pure mind, when the owners demand restitution, it is a case of `bhaṇḍadeyya` (restitution for the item). `Bhaṇḍadeyya` means that the value of what is lost to another, or that very item, should be given; this is the meaning. If he does not give it, it is a pārājika offense due to the owner's abandonment of their claim. If another person pours ghee or oil into someone's pot, and this monk, with a thieving mind, puts in an item that will absorb the oil, it is a pārājika offense in the way already stated. Knowing that another will pour their ghee or oil into his own empty pot, if he places an item there with a thieving mind, it is a pārājika offense upon its removal, in the way previously stated. If he places it with a pure mind and later removes it with a thieving mind, it is indeed a pārājika offense. If he removes it with a pure mind, it is neither theft nor a debt (`gīvā`); but in the Mahāpaccarī, only 'no offense' is mentioned. In the Kurundī it is said: 'If, being angry and saying, “Why do you pour oil into my pot?” he removes his own item and throws it away, it is not a case of `bhaṇḍadeyya`.' If, with a thieving mind, wishing for the oil to drip out, he takes hold of the pot's rim and tilts it, when oil worth a quarter has dripped out, it is a pārājika offense. If, with a thieving mind, he makes it worn out, thinking, 'It will seep out and be gone,' when oil worth a quarter has seeped out and gone, it is a pārājika offense. If, with a thieving mind, he makes a hole—whether downward-facing (`omaṭṭha`), upward-facing (`ummaṭṭha`), or straight-through (`vemaṭṭha`)—this, however, is a place of confusion; therefore, it should be carefully considered. Herein, this is the decision: `omaṭṭha` means a downward-facing hole; `ummaṭṭha` means an upward-facing hole; `vemaṭṭha` means a straight-through hole like that of a water-sprinkler. Therein, in the case of an `omaṭṭha` hole made starting from the outside, when oil worth a quarter has dripped from the inner end, even if it has not exited to the outside, it is a pārājika offense. Why? Because the mere dripping from there is called 'gone outside'; it does not obtain the count of 'being in the pot'. In the case of a hole made starting from the inside, when a quarter's worth has dripped from the outer end, it is a pārājika offense. In the case of an `ummaṭṭha` hole, however it is made, when a quarter's worth has dripped from the outer end, it is a pārājika offense. For as long as it does not drip from the outer end, it is still considered to be in the pot. And for a `vemaṭṭha` hole, it is said in the commentaries: 'The offense should be judged by way of its dripping from the middle of the pot's wall.' But that corresponds with the breaking of a lake's boundary in the case of a hole made by starting from both inside and outside and stopping in the middle. But in the case of a hole made starting from the inside, the offense should be judged by the outer end, and in the case of one made starting from the outside, by the inner end. This is what is proper here. But if a monk, with a thieving mind, thinking, 'It will roll away,' removes the pot's stand or the supporting pebbles, it is a pārājika offense when it has rolled away. But if, knowing that oil will be poured, one makes an empty pot worn out or makes holes in it, it later becomes a case of `bhaṇḍadeyya` according to the amount of oil that has come out. However, in some commentaries, it is also written as a pārājika offense; that was written through negligence.

Paripuṇṇāya kumbhiyā upari kathalaṃ vā pāsāṇaṃ vā “patitvā bhindissati, tato telaṃ paggharissatī”ti theyyacittena dubbandhaṃ vā karoti, duṭṭhapitaṃ vā ṭhapeti, avassapatanakaṃ tathā karontassa katamatte pārājikaṃ. Rittakumbhiyā upari karoti, taṃ pacchā puṇṇakāle patitvā bhindati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu bhaṇḍassa natthikāle [P 2.0321] katapayogattā āditova pārājikaṃ na hoti. Bhaṇḍavināsadvārassa pana katattā bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ hoti. Āharāpentesu adadato sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepena pārājikaṃ.

If, on top of a full pot, a monk with a thieving mind makes a potsherd or a stone badly tied or places it badly, thinking, 'It will fall and break it, and from that the oil will flow out,' if it is something that will certainly fall, it is a pārājika offense for the one doing so at the very moment of doing it. If he does this on top of an empty pot, and that item later falls and breaks it when it is full, it is a case of `bhaṇḍadeyya` (restitution for the item). For in such cases, because the effort was made at a time when the goods were not present, it is not a pārājika offense from the outset. But because a means for the destruction of the goods was made, it is a case of `bhaṇḍadeyya`. If, when the owners demand restitution, he does not give it, it is a pārājika offense due to the owners' abandonment of their claim.

Theyyacittena mātikaṃ ujukaṃ karoti “vaṭṭitvā vā gamissati, velaṃ vā uttarāpessatī”ti[V 1.0257]; vaṭṭitvā vā gacchatu, velaṃ vā uttaratu, ujukaraṇakāle pārājikaṃ. Īdisā hi payogā pubbapayogāvahāre saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Sukkhamātikāya ujukatāya pacchā udake āgate vaṭṭitvā vā gacchatu, velaṃ vā uttaratu, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Kasmā? Ṭhānā cāvanapayogassa abhāvā. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ nāvaṭṭhe āvi bhavissati.

If, with a thieving intent, one straightens a water channel, thinking, ‘It will either roll away or cause the bank to be overflowed,’ then whether it rolls away or overflows the bank, it is a pārājika offense at the moment of straightening. Indeed, such efforts are included in the category of preliminary acts of theft. If a dry water channel is straightened, and later water arrives, whether it rolls away or overflows the bank, it is a case of `bhaṇḍadeyya`. Why? Because there is no effort of displacing it from its place. Its characteristic will become evident in the section on boats.

Tattheva bhindati vātiādīsu aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva vuttaṃ – “bhindati vāti muggarena pothetvā bhindati. Chaḍḍeti vāti udakaṃ vā vālikaṃ vā ākiritvā uttarāpeti. Jhāpeti vāti dārūni āharitvā jhāpeti. Aparibhogaṃ [M 1.0279] vā karotīti akhāditabbaṃ vā apātabbaṃ vā karoti; uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā visaṃ vā ucchiṭṭhaṃ vā kuṇapaṃ vā pātesi, āpatti dukkaṭassāti ṭhānācāvanassa natthitāya dukkaṭaṃ, buddhavisayo nāmeso. Kiñcāpi dukkaṭaṃ, āharāpente pana bhaṇḍadeyya”nti. Tattha purimadvayaṃ na sameti. Tañhi kumbhijajjarakaraṇena ca mātikāujukaraṇena ca saddhiṃ ekalakkhaṇaṃ. Pacchimaṃ pana dvayaṃ ṭhānā acāventenāpi sakkā kātuṃ. Tasmā ettha evaṃ vinicchayaṃ vadanti – “aṭṭhakathāyaṃ kira ‘ṭhānā cāvanassa natthitāya dukkaṭa’nti idaṃ pacchimadvayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ṭhānā cāvanaṃ akarontoyeva hi theyyacittena vā vināsetukāmatāya vā jhāpeyyapi, aparibhogampi kareyya. Purimadvaye pana vuttanayena bhindantassa vā chaḍḍentassa vā ṭhānā cāvanaṃ atthi, tasmā tathā karontassa vināsetukāmatāya bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena pārājika”nti. Pāḷiyaṃ “dukkaṭa”nti vuttattā ayuttanti ce? Na; aññathā gahetabbatthato. Pāḷiyañhi theyyacittapakkhe “bhindati vāti [P 2.0322] udakena sambhindati, chaḍḍeti vāti tattha vamati vā passāvaṃ vā chaḍḍetī”ti evameke vadanti.

In those very passages beginning with ‘breaks’ and so forth, it is first stated in the commentary: ‘“Breaks” means one breaks by striking with a mallet. “Discards” means one causes it to overflow by pouring in water or sand. “Burns” means one burns by bringing firewood. Or “makes it unusable” means one makes it unfit to eat or unfit to drink; if one drops feces, urine, poison, leftovers, or a corpse into it, it is an offense of wrong-doing. It is a wrong-doing because there is no displacement from its place; this is indeed the domain of the Buddha. Although it is a wrong-doing, if the owners make one provide a replacement, it is a debt for the goods.’ Therein, the first pair does not fit. For it has the same characteristic as making a pot fragile and making a water channel straight. But the latter pair can be done even without displacing it from its place. Therefore, herein they state the judgment thus: ‘In the commentary, it is said that this statement, “it is a wrong-doing because there is no displacement from its place,” was stated with reference to the latter pair. Indeed, without displacing it from its place, one could burn it or make it unusable, either with a thieving intent or with the intention to destroy. But in the first pair, for one who breaks or discards in the manner stated, there is displacement from its place. Therefore, for one who acts thus, with the intention to destroy, it is a debt for the goods; with a thieving intent, it is a pārājika offense.’ If one were to say, ‘This is incorrect because “wrong-doing” is stated in the Pāḷi,’ it is not so; because the meaning should be taken in another way. For in the Pāḷi, in the case of a thieving intent, some say thus: ‘“Breaks” means one mixes it with water; “discards” means one vomits or discards urine into it.’

Ayaṃ panettha sāro – vinītavatthumhi tiṇajjhāpako viya ṭhānā acāvetukāmova kevalaṃ bhindati, bhinnattā pana telādīni nikkhamanti, yaṃ vā panettha patthinnaṃ, taṃ ekābaddhameva tiṭṭhati. Achaḍḍetukāmoyeva ca kevalaṃ tattha udakavālikādīni ākirati, ākiṇṇattā pana telaṃ chaḍḍīyati. Tasmā vohāravasena “bhindati vā chaḍḍeti vā”ti vuccatīti. Evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho gahetabbo. Nāsetukāmatāpakkhe pana itarathāpi yujjati. Evañhi kathiyamāne pāḷi ca aṭṭhakathā ca pubbāparena saṃsanditvā kathitā honti. Ettāvatāpi ca santosaṃ akatvā ācariye payirupāsitvā vinicchayo veditabboti.

Herein, this is the essential meaning: like the monk who burned a pile of grass in the Vinītavatthu, one merely breaks, not intending to displace it from its place. But because it is broken, oil and so forth come out, or whatever herein is thick remains as a single mass. And merely not intending to discard, one pours water, sand, and so forth into it; but because it has been poured into, the oil is discarded. Therefore, by way of conventional speech, it is said, ‘breaks or discards.’ Thus, the meaning of these terms should be understood. But in the case of the intention to destroy, it is also suitable otherwise. For when explained thus, both the Pāḷi and the commentary are explained in harmony with what precedes and follows. And even with this much, without being content, one should understand the judgment by attending upon the teachers.

Bhūmaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Things Situated on the Ground is concluded.

Thalaṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on Things Situated on Land

95. Thalaṭṭhe [V 1.0258] thale nikkhittanti bhūmitale vā pāsāṇatalapabbatatalādīsu vā yattha katthaci paṭicchanne vā appaṭicchanne vā ṭhapitaṃ thalaṭṭhanti [M 1.0280] veditabbaṃ. Taṃ sace rāsikataṃ hoti, antokumbhiyaṃ bhājanagatakaraṇamuṭṭhicchedanavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Sace ekābaddhaṃ silesaniyyāsādi pakkamadhuphāṇitavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Sace garukaṃ hoti bhārabaddhaṃ lohapiṇḍi-guḷapiṇḍi-telamadhughaṭādi vā, kumbhiyaṃ ṭhānācāvanavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Saṅkhalikabaddhassa ca ṭhānabhedo sallakkhetabbo. Pattharitvā ṭhapitaṃ pana pāvārattharaṇasāṭakādiṃ ujukaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhati, pārimante orimantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ atikkante pārājikaṃ. Evaṃ sabbadisāsu sallakkhetabbaṃ. Veṭhetvā uddharati, kesaggamattaṃ ākāsagataṃ karontassa pārājikaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

95. Regarding things situated on land, the legal determination should be understood thus: that which is placed on the ground—whether on the surface of the earth, or in places such as the surface of a rock or the surface of a mountain, or anywhere else, whether in a covered or an uncovered place—should be known as 'situated on land.' If those goods are made into a pile, it should be decided by the legal determination for an item inside a pot, which is the determination concerning making it enter one's own container and cutting off a handful. If it is a single bonded mass, such as sticky tree sap, it should be decided by the legal determination for cooked honey and molasses. If it is a heavy item, bound as a load, or a lump of iron, a lump of jaggery, a pot of oil, a pot of honey, and so on, it should be decided by the legal determination for an item in a pot, which is the determination concerning dislodging it from its place.
