And for goods bound with an iron chain, the division of its place should be noted. Furthermore, regarding something spread out and placed, such as a cloak, a ground-covering, or a cloth, if one, having grasped it straight, pulls it, it is a pārājika offense when the far end passes over the space touched by the near end. This should be noted in all directions. If one rolls it up and lifts it, it is a pārājika offense for one who makes even a hair's breadth of it airborne. The remainder is just as has been stated.

Thalaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Things Situated on Land is concluded.

Ākāsaṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on Things Situated in the Air

96. Ākāsaṭṭhe [P 2.0323] morassa chahi ākārehi ṭhānaparicchedo veditabbo – purato mukhatuṇḍakena, pacchato kalāpaggena, ubhayapassesu pakkhapariyantehi, adho pādanakhasikhāya, uddhaṃ sikhaggenāti. Bhikkhu “sassāmikaṃ ākāsaṭṭhaṃ moraṃ gahessāmī”ti purato vā tiṭṭhati, hatthaṃ vā pasāreti, moro ākāseyeva pakkhe cāreti, vātaṃ gāhāpetvā gamanaṃ upacchinditvā tiṭṭhati. Tassa bhikkhuno dukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ aphandento hatthena āmasati, dukkaṭameva. Ṭhānā acāvento phandāpeti, thullaccayaṃ. Hatthena pana gahetvā vā aggahetvā vā mukhatuṇḍakena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ kalāpaggaṃ, kalāpaggena vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ mukhatuṇḍakaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Tathā vāmapakkhapariyantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ dakkhiṇapakkhapariyantaṃ, dakkhiṇapakkhapariyantena vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ vāmapakkhapariyantaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Tathā pādanakhasikhāya phuṭṭhokāsaṃ sikhaggaṃ, sikhaggena vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ pādanakhasikhaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ.

96. Regarding things situated in the air, the demarcation of the place of a peacock should be known by six aspects: in front, by the tip of its beak; behind, by the tip of its tail; on both sides, by the tips of its wings; below, by the tip of its claws; and above, by the tip of its crest. If a bhikkhu, thinking, ‘I will seize this peacock that has an owner and is situated in the air,’ either stands in front of it or stretches out his hand, and the peacock moves its wings while remaining in the air, or stops its movement by catching the wind and stays still, for that bhikkhu there is a dukkaṭa offense. If he touches it without making it flutter, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If he makes it flutter without dislodging it from its place, it is a thullaccaya offense. But, whether having grasped it with the hand or not, if he makes the tip of the tail pass over the space touched by the tip of the beak, or the tip of the beak pass over the space touched by the tip of the tail, it is a pārājika offense. Likewise, if he makes the tip of the right wing pass over the space touched by the tip of the left wing, or the tip of the left wing pass over the space touched by the tip of the right wing, it is a pārājika offense. Likewise, if he makes the tip of the crest pass over the space touched by the tip of the claws, or the tip of the claws pass over the space touched by the tip of the crest, it is a pārājika offense.

Ākāsena gacchanto moro sīsādīsu yasmiṃ aṅge nilīyati, taṃ tassa ṭhānaṃ. Tasmā taṃ hatthe nilīnaṃ ito cito ca karontopi phandāpetiyeva, yadi pana itarena hatthena gahetvā ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ[M 1.0281]. Itaraṃ hatthaṃ upaneti, moro sayameva uḍḍetvā tattha nilīyati, anāpatti[V 1.0259]. Aṅge nilīnabhāvaṃ ñatvā theyyacittena ekaṃ padavāraṃ gacchati, thullaccayaṃ. Dutiye pārājikaṃ.

For a peacock going through the air, on whichever limb, such as its head, it alights, that is its place. Therefore, one who moves it from here to there while it is alighted on the hand only makes it flutter. But if, having grasped it with the other hand, one dislodges it from its place, it is a pārājika offense. If one brings the other hand near, and the peacock of its own accord flies up and alights there, there is no offense. Having known that it is alighted on a limb, if, with a mind set on theft, one takes a single footstep, it is a thullaccaya offense. On the second, it is a pārājika offense.

Bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitamoro dvinnaṃ vā pādānaṃ kalāpassa ca vasena tīṇi ṭhānāni labhati. Taṃ ukkhipantassa yāva ekampi ṭhānaṃ pathaviṃ phusati, tāva thullaccayaṃ. Kesaggamattampi pathaviyā mocitamatte pārājikaṃ. Pañjare ṭhitaṃ saha pañjarena uddharati, pārājikaṃ. Yadi pana pādaṃ na agghati, sabbattha agghavasena kātabbaṃ. Antovatthumhi carantaṃ moraṃ theyyacittena padasā bahivatthuṃ nīharanto dvāraparicchedaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Vaje ṭhitabalībaddassa hi vajo viya antovatthu tassa ṭhānaṃ. Hatthena pana gahetvā antovatthusmimpi ākāsagataṃ karontassa pārājikameva. Antogāme carantampi gāmaparikkhepaṃ atikkāmentassa pārājikaṃ[P 2.0324]. Sayameva nikkhamitvā gāmūpacāre vā vatthūpacāre vā carantaṃ pana theyyacitto kaṭṭhena vā kathalāya vā utrāsetvā aṭavimukhaṃ karoti, moro uḍḍetvā antogāme vā antovatthumhi vā chadanapiṭṭhe vā nilīyati, rakkhati. Sace pana aṭavimukhe uḍḍeti vā gacchati vā “aṭaviṃ pavesetvā gahessāmī”ti parikappe asati pathavito kesaggamattampi uḍḍitamatte vā dutiyapadavāre vā pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā gāmato nikkhantassa ṭhitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ hoti. Kapiñjarādīsupi ayameva vinicchayo.

A peacock standing on the ground has three places by means of its two feet and its tail. For one who is lifting it, as long as even one place is still touching the earth, it is a grave offense. At the very moment it is freed from the earth by even a hair's breadth, it is an offense of defeat. If one lifts a peacock situated in a cage together with the cage, it is an offense of defeat. But if it is not worth a quarter, in all cases the decision should be made according to its value. If a bhikkhu, with a mind set on theft, leads a peacock that is moving about inside a dwelling out to the area outside the dwelling by foot, it is an offense of defeat when he makes it cross the demarcation of the door. Indeed, just as for a bull standing in a pen, the pen is its place, so too the inside of the dwelling is its place. But for one who, having grasped it by hand, makes it become airborne even inside the dwelling, it is an offense of defeat indeed. Also for one who makes a peacock that is moving about inside a village cross the village boundary, it is an offense of defeat. But regarding a peacock that has gone out of its own accord and is moving about in the village precincts or the dwelling precincts, if a bhikkhu with a mind set on theft frightens it with a stick or a potsherd and makes it face the forest, and the peacock flies up and alights inside the village, inside the dwelling, or on a rooftop, he is protected. But if it flies or goes facing the forest, when there is no intention such as, 'Having made it enter the forest, I will seize it,' it is an offense of defeat at the very moment it has flown even a hair's breadth from the ground, or at the second footstep. Why? Because for a peacock that has gone out from the village, the very place where it stands becomes its place. For partridges and other such birds, this is the very same legal determination.

Sāṭakaṃ vāti vātavegukkhittaṃ pathavitale pattharitvā ṭhapitamiva ākāsena gacchantaṃ khalibaddhaṃ sāṭakaṃ abhimukhāgataṃ hatthena ekasmiṃ ante gaṇhāti, ito cito ca ṭhānaṃ avikopentoyeva gamanupacchede dukkaṭaṃ. Ṭhānācāvanaṃ akaronto cāleti, phandāpane thullaccayaṃ. Ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Ṭhānaparicchedo cassa morasseva chahi ākārehi veditabbo.

As for a cloth: if a cloth stiffened with starch, tossed up by the force of the wind and going through the air as if it were spread out and placed on the surface of the ground, is coming towards oneself, and one grasps it at one end with the hand, it is a minor offense for interrupting its movement while not at all disturbing its place from here or there. If one makes it shake without causing it to be dislodged from its place, it is a grave offense for causing it to flutter. If one dislodges it from its place, it is an offense of defeat. And the demarcation of its place should be known by six aspects, just like that of the peacock.

Abaddhasāṭako pana ekasmiṃ ante gahitamatteva dutiyenantena patitvā bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāti, tassa dve ṭhānāni honti – hattho ceva bhūmi ca. Taṃ yathāgahitameva paṭhamaṃ gahitokāsappadesato cāleti, thullaccayaṃ. Pacchā bhūmito dutiyahatthena vā pādena vā ukkhipati, pārājikaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ [M 1.0282] vā bhūmito uddharati, thullaccayaṃ. Pacchā gahitokāsappadesato cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Gahaṇaṃ vā amuñcanto ujukameva hatthaṃ onāmetvā bhūmigataṃ katvā teneva hatthena ukkhipati, pārājikaṃ. Veṭhanepi ayameva vinicchayo.

But as for an unstiffened cloth, at the very moment one end is grasped, it falls by its other end and becomes established on the ground. For it, there are two places: the hand and the ground. If one moves it from the region of space where it was first grasped, just as it was grasped, it is a grave offense. If afterwards one lifts it from the ground with the other hand or with a foot, it is an offense of defeat. Alternatively, if one first lifts it from the ground, it is a grave offense; if afterwards one dislodges it from the region of space where it was grasped, it is an offense of defeat. Alternatively, without releasing one's grasp, having lowered the hand straight down, if one lifts with that same hand the part of the cloth that is on the ground, it is an offense of defeat. For a head-wrap also, this is the very same legal determination.

Hiraññaṃ [V 1.0260] vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā chijjamānanti manussānaṃ alaṅkarontānaṃ gīveyyakādipiḷandhanaṃ vā suvaṇṇasalākaṃ chindantānaṃ suvaṇṇakārānaṃ suvaṇṇakhaṇḍaṃ vā chijjamānaṃ patati, tañce bhikkhu ākāsena āgacchantaṃ theyyacitto hatthena gaṇhāti, gahaṇameva ṭhānaṃ. Gahitappadesato [P 2.0325] hatthaṃ apaneti, pārājikaṃ. Cīvare patitaṃ hatthena ukkhipati, pārājikaṃ. Anuddharitvāva yāti, dutiye padavāre pārājikaṃ. Patte patitepi eseva nayo. Sīse vā mukhe vā pāde vā patiṭṭhitaṃ hatthena gaṇhāti, pārājikaṃ. Aggahetvāva yāti, dutiye padavāre pārājikaṃ. Yattha katthaci patati, tassa patitokāsova ṭhānaṃ, na sabbaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ pattacīvaraṃ vāti.

Regarding silver or gold being cut: for instance, an ornament such as a necklace of people who are adorning themselves, or a piece of gold of goldsmiths who are cutting a gold bar, is being cut and falls. If a bhikkhu with thievish intent takes it with his hand as it comes through the air, the place of grasping itself is the 'place' from which it is stolen. If he moves his hand from the place where it was grasped, it is an offense of defeat. If it has fallen on a robe and he lifts it with his hand, it is an offense of defeat. If he goes without lifting it, it is an offense of defeat at the second footstep. The same principle applies if it has fallen into a bowl. If it is established on his head, face, or foot, and he takes it with his hand, it is an offense of defeat. If he goes without taking it, it is an offense of defeat at the second footstep. Wherever it falls, the place where it has fallen is the 'place', not the entire major and minor limbs, bowl, or robe.

Ākāsaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Things Situated in the Air is concluded.

Vehāsaṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on Things Situated Above Ground

97. Vehāsaṭṭhe mañcapīṭhādīsu ṭhapitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āmāsaṃ vā hotu anāmāsaṃ vā, theyyacittena āmasantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Mañcapīṭhesu ṭhapitabhaṇḍesu panettha thalaṭṭhe vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – sace khaliyā baddhasāṭako mañce vā pīṭhe vā patthaṭo majjhena mañcatalaṃ na phusati, mañcapādeva phusati, tesaṃ vasena ṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pādānaṃ upari phuṭṭhokāsameva hi atikkamitamattena tattha pārājikaṃ hoti. Saha mañcapīṭhehi harantassa pana mañcapīṭhapādānaṃ patiṭṭhitokāsavasena ṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

97. Regarding an item situated above ground: for an item placed on a bed, bench, or the like, whether it is permissible to be touched or not, for one who touches it with thievish intent, there is a minor offense. Here, for items placed on beds or benches, the judgment should be understood according to the method stated for items 'on the ground'. This, however, is the distinction: if a cloth stiffened with starch is spread on a bed or bench and its middle does not touch the bed's surface but only the bed's legs, the 'place' should be determined by means of those legs. For, just by causing it to pass beyond the place of contact on top of the legs, an offense of defeat is incurred. But for one who carries it away together with the bed or bench, the 'place' should be determined by means of the established place of the bed's or bench's legs.

Cīvaravaṃse vāti cīvaraṭhapanatthāya bandhitvā ṭhapite vaṃse vā kaṭṭhadaṇḍake vā. Tattha saṃharitvā pārato antaṃ orato bhogaṃ katvā ṭhapitacīvarassa patiṭṭhitokāsena phuṭṭhokāsova ṭhānaṃ, na sabbo cīvaravaṃso. Tasmā theyyacittena taṃ bhoge gahetvā ākaḍḍhantassa pārato vaṃse patiṭṭhitokāsaṃ orato cīvarena vaṃsassa phuṭṭhappadesaṃ atikkāmentassa [M 1.0283] ekadvaṅgulamattākaḍḍhaneneva pārājikaṃ. Ante gahetvā ākaḍḍhantassāpi eseva nayo. Tattheva pana cīvaravaṃse vāmato vā dakkhiṇato vā sārentassa vāmantena dakkhiṇantaṭṭhānaṃ dakkhiṇantena vā vāmantaṭṭhānaṃ atikkantamatte dasadvādasaṅgulamattasāraṇeneva pārājikaṃ. Uddhaṃ ukkhipantassa kesaggamattukkhipanena pārājikaṃ. Cīvaravaṃsaṃ [P 2.0326] phusantaṃ vā aphusantaṃ vā rajjukena bandhitvā ṭhapitacīvaraṃ mocentassa thullaccayaṃ, mutte pārājikaṃ. Muttamattameva hi taṃ “ṭhānā cuta”nti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Vaṃse veṭhetvā ṭhapitaṃ nibbeṭhentassa thullaccayaṃ, nibbeṭhitamatte pārājikaṃ. Valayaṃ katvā ṭhapite valayaṃ chindati vā moceti vā ekaṃ vā vaṃsakoṭiṃ mocetvā nīharati, thullaccayaṃ[V 1.0261]. Chinnamatte muttamatte nīhaṭamatte ca pārājikaṃ. Tathā akatvāva cīvaravaṃse ito cito ca sāreti, rakkhati tāva. Valayassa hi sabbopi cīvaravaṃso ṭhānaṃ. Kasmā? Tattha saṃsaraṇadhammatāya. Yadā pana naṃ hatthena gahetvā ākāsagataṃ karoti, pārājikaṃ. Pasāretvā ṭhapitassa patiṭṭhitokāsena phuṭṭhokāsova ṭhānaṃ. Tattha saṃharitvā ṭhapite vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo. Yaṃ pana ekenantena bhūmiṃ phusitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, tassa cīvaravaṃse ca bhūmiyañca patiṭṭhitokāsavasena dve ṭhānāni. Tattha bhūmiyaṃ ekenantena patiṭṭhite abaddhasāṭake vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Cīvararajjuyāpi ayameva vinicchayo.

Regarding 'on a robe-pole': that is, on a bamboo or wooden staff set up for the purpose of placing robes. There, for a robe that is placed folded, with one end on the far side and a coil on the near side, the 'place' is the place of contact where it is established, not the entire robe-pole. Therefore, for one with thievish intent who takes it by the folded part and pulls, causing the point of contact of the robe on the near side to pass the established place on the pole on the far side, a pārājika offense is incurred by pulling it just one or two finger-breadths. The same principle applies to one who takes it by the end and pulls. But on that same robe-pole, for one who shifts it from the left or from the right, just by the left end passing the 'place' of the right end, or the right end passing the 'place' of the left end, a pārājika offense is incurred by shifting it a measure of ten or twelve finger-breadths. For one who lifts it upwards, a pārājika offense is incurred by lifting it even a hair's breadth. For one who unties a robe that was placed tied with a small rope, whether it is touching the robe-pole or not, there is a thullaccaya offense; when it is freed, it is a pārājika. For, just by being freed, it is reckoned as 'dislodged from its place'. For one who unwraps a robe that was placed wrapped around the pole, there is a thullaccaya; just by being unwrapped, it is a pārājika. When it is placed made into a loop, if one cuts or unties the loop, or unties one end of the pole and takes it out, there is a thullaccaya. Just by being cut, untied, or taken out, it is a pārājika. Without doing so, if one just shifts it here and there on the robe-pole, it is still guarded. For, in the case of a loop, the entire robe-pole is the 'place'. Why? Because of its nature of being able to slide about there. But when one takes it with the hand and makes it go into the air, it is a pārājika. For a robe placed spread out, the 'place' is the place of contact where it is established. There, for one placed folded, the judgment should be understood by the method stated. But for a robe that stands touching the ground with one end, it has two 'places' by means of the established places on the robe-pole and on the ground. There, for an unstiffened cloth established on the ground by one end, the judgment should be understood by the method already stated. For a robe-rope, too, this is the very same judgment.

Aṅkusake laggetvā ṭhapitabhaṇḍaṃ pana bhesajjaghaṭo vā bhesajjatthavikā vā sace bhittiṃ vā bhūmiṃ vā aphusitvā ṭhapitaṃ lagganakaṃ ghaṃsantassa nīharato aṅkusakoṭito nikkhantamatte pārājikaṃ. Lagganakaṃ baddhaṃ hoti, bundena ukkhipitvā ākāsagataṃ karontassa aṅkusakoṭito anikkhantepi pārājikaṃ. Bhittinissitaṃ hoti, paṭhamaṃ aṅkusakoṭito nīharati, thullaccayaṃ. Pacchā bhittiṃ moceti, pārājikaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ bhittiṃ mocetvā pacchā aṅkusato nīharantassāpi eseva nayo. Sace pana bhāriyaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ nīharituṃ asakkonto sayaṃ bhittinissitaṃ katvā aṅkusato nīharati, puna bhittiṃ amocetvāpi aṅkusato nīhaṭamatteyeva pārājikaṃ. Attanā kataṭṭhānañhi ṭhānaṃ na hoti. Bhūmiṃ phusitvā ṭhitassa pana dve eva ṭhānāni. Tattha vuttoyeva vinicchayo[P 2.0327]. Yaṃ [M 1.0284] pana sikkāya pakkhipitvā laggitaṃ hoti, taṃ sikkāto nīharantassāpi saha sikkāya aṅkusato nīharantassāpi pārājikaṃ. Bhittibhūmisannissitavasena cettha ṭhānabhedopi veditabbo.

But for an item, such as a medicine pot or a medicine bag, placed hooked on a hook, if it is placed without touching a wall or the ground, for one who removes it while rubbing the hanging strap, it is a pārājika offense just as it leaves the tip of the hook. If the hanging strap is taut, for one who lifts it by the base and makes it go into the air, it is a pārājika offense even if it has not left the tip of the hook. If it is leaning against a wall, and one first removes it from the tip of the hook, it is a thullaccaya offense. Afterwards, if one detaches it from the wall, it is a pārājika offense. The same principle applies to one who first detaches it from the wall and afterwards removes it from the hook. But if, being unable to remove a heavy item, one makes it lean against the wall oneself and then removes it from the hook, it is a pārājika offense just by being removed from the hook, even without detaching it from the wall again. For a 'place' made by oneself is not a 'place'. But for an item placed touching the ground, there are two 'places'. The judgment there has already been stated. For an item that is placed in a carrying-net and hooked, it is a pārājika offense for one who removes it from the net, and also for one who removes it from the hook together with the net. And here, the distinction of 'places' should also be understood by means of it leaning against a wall or the ground.

Bhittikhīloti ujukaṃ katvā bhittiyaṃ ākoṭito vā tatthajātako eva vā; nāgadanto pana vaṅko ākoṭito eva. Tesu laggetvā ṭhapitaṃ aṅkusake vuttanayeneva vinicchinitabbaṃ. Dvīsu tīsu pana paṭipāṭiyā ṭhitesu āropetvā ṭhapitaṃ kuntaṃ vā bhindivālaṃ vā agge vā bunde vā gahetvā ākaḍḍhati, ekamekassa phuṭṭhokāsamatte atikkante pārājikaṃ. Phuṭṭhokāsamattameva hi tesaṃ ṭhānaṃ hoti, na sabbe khīlā vā nāgadantā vā. Bhittiabhimukho ṭhatvā majjhe gahetvā ākaḍḍhati, orimantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ pārimantena atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ. Parato pellentassāpi eseva nayo. Hatthena gahetvā ujukaṃ ukkhipanto kesaggamattampi ākāsagataṃ karoti, pārājikaṃ. Bhittiṃ nissāya ṭhapitaṃ bhittiṃ ghaṃsanto ākaḍḍhati, aggena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ bundaṃ, bundena vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ aggaṃ atikkāmentassa pārājikaṃ[V 1.0262]. Bhittiabhimukho ṭhatvā ākaḍḍhanto ekenantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ aparantaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Ujukaṃ ukkhipanto kesaggamattaṃ ākāsagataṃ karoti, pārājikaṃ.

A wall peg is a peg made straight and driven into a wall, or one that has grown there naturally; but an elephant-tusk peg is crooked and is only one that is driven in. Regarding an item placed by hanging on these, the legal determination should be made in the same way as stated for the case of a hook. In the case of two or three pegs situated in a row, if one pulls a spear or a javelin that has been placed across them, grasping it by the tip or the butt, a pārājika offense is committed when it has passed the point of contact of any single peg. Indeed, for the spear or javelin, only the point of contact is the 'place', not all the pegs or elephant-tusk pegs. If one stands facing the wall, grasps it in the middle, and pulls, a pārājika offense is committed as soon as the near end passes the point of contact of the far end. This same rule also applies to one pushing it from the other side. Grasping it with the hand and lifting it straight up, if one makes even a hair's breadth go into the air, it is a pārājika offense. Regarding an item placed leaning against a wall, if one pulls it while it is rubbing against the wall, it is a pārājika offense for one who causes the butt to pass the point of contact of the tip, or the tip to pass the point of contact of the butt. Standing facing the wall and pulling, if one causes one end to pass the point of contact of the other end, it is a pārājika offense. Lifting it straight up, if one makes a hair's breadth go into the air, it is a pārājika offense.

Rukkhe vā laggitanti tālarukkhādīsu āropetvā laggite aṅkusakādīsu vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo. Tatthajātakaṃ pana tālapiṇḍiṃ cālentassa thullaccayaṃ. Yasmiṃ phale pārājikavatthu pūrati, tasmiṃ bandhanā muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Piṇḍiṃ chindati, pārājikaṃ. Aggena paṇṇantaraṃ āropetvā ṭhapitā dve ṭhānāni labhati – ṭhapitaṭṭhānañca vaṇṭaṭṭhānañca; tattha vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo. Yo pana “chinnamattā patamānā saddaṃ kareyyā”ti bhayena sayaṃ aggena paṇṇantaraṃ āropetvā chindati, chinnamatte pārājikaṃ[P 2.0328]. Attanā kataṭṭhānañhi ṭhānaṃ na hoti. Etena upāyena sabbarukkhānaṃ pupphaphalesu vinicchayo veditabbo.

Regarding 'hung on a tree', this refers to an item placed and hung on palm trees and the like; the legal determination should be understood in the way stated for hooks and so on. But, for one who shakes a cluster of palm fruit that has grown there, there is a thullaccaya offense. In the case of whatever fruit meets the value for a pārājika offense, as soon as that fruit is released from its stem, it is a pārājika offense. If one cuts the cluster, it is a pārājika offense. A cluster placed by lifting it by its tip into the space between leaves obtains two 'places': the place where it is set and the place of the stem. There, the legal determination should be understood in the way stated. But if someone, out of fear that 'as soon as it is cut, while falling, it might make a sound', lifts it himself by its tip into the space between leaves and then cuts it, the pārājika offense occurs at the very moment of cutting. For a 'place' made by oneself is not a 'place'. By this method, the legal determination regarding the flowers and fruits of all trees should be understood.

Pattādhārakepīti ettha rukkhādhārako vā hotu valayādhārako vā daṇḍādhārako vā yaṃkiñci pattaṭṭhapanakaṃ pacchikāpi hotu pattādhārako tveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tattha ṭhapitapattassa pattena phuṭṭhokāso eva [M 1.0285] ṭhānaṃ. Tattha rukkhādhārake pañcahākārehi ṭhānaparicchedo hoti. Tattha ṭhitaṃ pattaṃ mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā catūsu disāsu yato kutoci kaḍḍhanto ekenantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ aparantaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Uddhaṃ kesaggamattaṃ ukkhipato pārājikaṃ. Sahādhārakena harantassāpi eseva nayoti.

Herein, regarding 'on a bowl-stand': whether it be a wooden stand, a ring-stand, or a stick-stand, or any kind of bowl-rest, even a small basket, it is counted simply as a 'bowl-stand'. Therein, for a bowl placed on it, the 'place' is only the area touched by the bowl. In the case of a wooden stand, the determination of the 'place' is in five ways. Grasping the bowl situated there by the rim and pulling it from any direction whatsoever in the four directions, if one causes one end to pass the point of contact of the other end, it is a pārājika offense. For one who lifts it upwards even a hair's breadth, it is a pārājika offense. This same rule also applies to one who carries it away together with the stand.

Vehāsaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of 'Things Above Ground' is concluded.

Udakaṭṭhakathā

The Explanation of Things Placed in Water

98. Udakaṭṭhe – udake nikkhittaṃ hotīti rājabhayādibhītehi udakena avinassanadhammesu tambalohabhājanādīsu suppaṭicchannaṃ katvā pokkharaṇīādīsu asandanake udake nikkhittaṃ. Tassa patiṭṭhitokāsoyeva ṭhānaṃ, na sabbaṃ udakaṃ. Gacchati vā āpatti dukkaṭassāti agambhīre udake padasā gacchantassa padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Gambhīre hatthehi vā pādehi vā payogaṃ karontassa hatthavārehi vā padavārehi vā payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Eseva nayo kumbhigahaṇatthaṃ nimujjanummujjanesu. Sace pana antarā kiñci udakasappaṃ vā vāḷamacchaṃ vā disvā bhīto palāyati, anāpatti. Āmasanādīsu bhūmigatāya kumbhiyā vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo[V 1.0263]. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā kaḍḍhati, idha kaddame osāreti. Evaṃ chahākārehi ṭhānaparicchedo hoti.

98. Regarding things placed in water—'placed in water' means that, by those fearing dangers from kings and so forth, items not subject to destruction by water, such as copper and iron vessels, are well-concealed and placed in non-flowing water, such as in a pond. For such an item, only the place where it is established is the 'location,' not the entire body of water. If one goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing. For one going by foot in shallow water, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each step. In deep water, for one making an effort with hands or feet, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each effort with the hands or with the feet. This same principle applies to diving and surfacing for the purpose of taking a pot. If, however, in the interim, one sees a water snake or a fierce fish, becomes frightened, and flees, there is no offense. Regarding touching and so forth, the determination should be understood according to the method stated for a pot placed on the ground. This, however, is the distinction: there, one digs the ground and pulls; here, one clears away the mud. Thus, the determination of the 'place' is in six ways.

Uppalādīsu yasmiṃ pupphe vatthuṃ pūreti, tasmiṃ chinnamatte pārājikaṃ. Uppalajātikānañcettha yāva ekasmimpi passe vāko na chijjati, tāva rakkhati. Padumajātikānaṃ pana daṇḍe chinne abbhantare suttaṃ acchinnampi na rakkhati. Sāmikehi chinditvā ṭhapitāni uppalādīni honti, yaṃ vatthuṃ pūreti, tasmiṃ uddhaṭe [P 2.0329] pārājikaṃ. Hatthakabaddhāni honti, yasmiṃ hatthake vatthu pūrati, tasmiṃ uddhaṭe pārājikaṃ. Bhārabaddhāni honti, taṃ bhāraṃ channaṃ ākārānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhānā cāventassa bhūmaṭṭhakumbhiyaṃ vuttanayena pārājikaṃ. Dīghanāḷāni uppalādīni honti, pupphesu vā nāḷesu vā [M 1.0286] veṇiṃ katvā udakapiṭṭhe rajjukesu tiṇāni santharitvā ṭhapenti vā bandhanti vā, tesaṃ dīghato pupphaggena ca nāḷantena ca tiriyaṃ pariyantehi heṭṭhā patiṭṭhitokāsena uddhaṃ upari ṭhitassa piṭṭhiyāti chahākārehi ṭhānā cāvanaparicchedo veditabbo.

Regarding blue water lilies and so forth, when a flower fulfills the value of the object, the pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment it is cut. For those of the uppala (blue water lily) variety, as long as the fiber on even one side is not severed, it protects from the offense. For those of the paduma (lotus) variety, however, once the stem is cut, the inner thread, even if unsevered, does not protect. There are blue water lilies and so forth that have been cut and placed by their owners; when one of them fulfills the value of the object, the pārājika offense is incurred when it is removed from the water. There are those bound into a handful; when a handful fulfills the value of the object, the pārājika offense is incurred when it is removed from the water. There are those bound into a load; for one who moves that load from its place by any of the six means, the pārājika offense is incurred according to the method stated for the pot placed on the ground. There are blue water lilies and so forth with long stems; having plaited the flowers or the stems, they are placed or tied on the surface of the water upon small ropes over which grass has been spread. For these, the determination of moving from the location is to be understood by six aspects: by length, from the tip of the flower and the end of the stem; by width, from the edges; below, by the place where it is established; and above, by the surface of that which is situated on top.

Yopi udakapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapitapupphakalāpaṃ udakaṃ cāletvā vīciṃ uṭṭhāpetvā kesaggamattampi yathāṭhitaṭṭhānato cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Atha pana parikappeti “ettha gataṃ gahessāmī”ti, rakkhati tāva; gataṭṭhāne pana uddharato pārājikaṃ. Udakato accuggatassa pupphassa sakalamudakaṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ uppāṭetvā ujukaṃ uddharantassa nāḷante kesaggamattaṃ udakato atikkante pārājikaṃ. Pupphe gahetvā apanāmetvā ākaḍḍhanto uppāṭeti, na udakaṃ ṭhānaṃ, uppāṭitamatte pārājikaṃ. Kalāpabaddhāni pupphāni udakaṭṭhāne vā rukkhe vā gacche vā bandhitvā ṭhapenti, bandhanaṃ amocetvā ito cito ca karontassa thullaccayaṃ, bandhane muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ bandhanaṃ mocetvā pacchā harati, ettha chahākārehi ṭhānaparicchedoti idaṃ ubhayaṃ mahāpaccariyādīsu vuttaṃ. Paduminiyaṃ pupphāni saha paduminiṃyā gaṇhitukāmassa pupphanāḷehi ca pattanāḷehi ca phuṭṭhaudakavasena uddhañceva tiriyañca ṭhānaparicchedo veditabbo. Taṃ panassa paduminiṃ anuppāṭetvā pupphāni vā pattāni vā attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhantassa thullaccayaṃ. Uppāṭitamatte pārājikaṃ.

Furthermore, if a monk, having stirred the water and raised a wave, moves a bunch of flowers placed on the water's surface even a hair's breadth from its established position, it is a pārājika offense. If, however, he forms the intention, 'I will take it when it has gone to that place,' he is protected for that long; but for one who removes it at the place it has reached, it is a pārājika offense. For a flower that has emerged from the water, the entire water is its location. For one who uproots it and lifts it straight up, when the end of the stem passes beyond the water by a hair's breadth, it is a pārājika offense. If one grasps the flower, bends it aside, and uproots it while pulling, the water is not the location; at the moment it is uprooted, it is a pārājika offense. They tie flowers bound in bunches to a place in the water, to a tree, or to a bush. For one who moves them here and there without untying the binding, it is a thullaccaya offense. At the moment the binding is untied, it is a pārājika offense. First, one unties the binding and afterwards takes it; here, the determination of the location is by six aspects—this twofold statement is said in the Mahāpaccarī and other texts. For one who desires to take flowers from a lotus bush together with the lotus bush itself, the determination of the location, both vertically and horizontally, is to be understood by way of the water touched by the flower stalks and the leaf stalks. For that monk, pulling the flowers or leaves towards himself without uprooting the lotus bush is a thullaccaya offense. At the moment it is uprooted, it is a pārājika offense.

Pupphapattanāḷe ṭhānato acāvetvāpi paṭhamaṃ paduminiṃ uppāṭentassa thullaccayaṃ. Pacchā pupphapattanāḷesu ṭhānā cāvitesu pārājikaṃ. Uppāṭitāya paduminiyā pupphaṃ gaṇhanto pana bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā [P 2.0330] kāretabbo. Bahi ṭhapite rāsikatakalāpabaddhabhārabaddhapupphepi eseva nayo. Bhisaṃ [V 1.0264] vā muḷālaṃ vā yena vatthu pūrati, taṃ uppāṭentassa pārājikaṃ. Kaddame phuṭṭhokāsavasena cettha ṭhānaṃ paricchinditabbaṃ. Tāni uppāṭentassa sukhumampi mūlaṃ acchinnaṃ hoti, rakkhati tāva. Bhisapabbe jātaṃ pattaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā hoti, tampi rakkhatīti mahāaṭṭhakathāyameva vuttaṃ. Bhisagaṇṭhimhi pana kaṇṭako hoti yobbanappattānaṃ mukhapiḷakā viya, ayaṃ adīghattā na rakkhati. Sesaṃ uppalādīsu vuttanayameva.

For one who first uproots the lotus bush, even without having moved the flower and leaf stalks from their location, it is a grave offense. Afterwards, when the flower and leaf stalks are moved from their location, it is a pārājika offense. However, one who takes a flower from an already uprooted lotus bush should be made to pay compensation after having the value of the item assessed. This same principle applies to flowers placed outside, whether made into a heap, bound in a bunch, or bound as a load. For one who uproots a lotus stalk or a lotus root by which the value of the object is fulfilled, it is a pārājika offense. And here, the location is to be determined by way of the area it touches in the mud. For one uprooting them, as long as even a subtle root remains unsevered, it protects. It is said in the Great Commentary itself that if there is a leaf or flower that has grown on a joint of the lotus stalk, that too protects. On the joint of the lotus stalk, however, there is a thorn, like a pimple on the face of a youth; this, due to its not being long, does not protect. The remainder is according to the method stated for blue water lilies and so forth.

Macchakacchapānaṃ [M 1.0287] sassāmikānaṃ vāpiādīsu sakalamudakaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Tasmā yo paṭijagganaṭṭhāne sassāmikaṃ macchaṃ baḷisena vā jālena vā kumanena vā hatthena vā gaṇhāti, tassa yena macchena vatthu pūrati, tasmiṃ kesaggamattampi udakato uddhaṭamatte pārājikaṃ. Koci maccho gayhamāno ito cito ca dhāvati, ākāsaṃ vā uppatati, tīre vā patati, ākāse vā ṭhitaṃ tīre vā patitaṃ gaṇhatopi pārājikameva. Kacchapampi bahi gocaratthaṃ gataṃ gaṇhato eseva nayo. Udakaṭṭhaṃ pana udakā mocayato pārājikaṃ.

For fish and turtles that have an owner, in ponds and so forth, the entire body of water is the location. Therefore, for a monk who takes a fish that has an owner from a guarded place by means of a hook, a net, a trap, or by hand, the pārājika offense is incurred at the mere moment that the fish by which the value of the object is fulfilled is lifted even a hair's breadth from the water. If some fish, while being caught, darts here and there, leaps into the air, or falls onto the shore, taking it while it is in the air or after it has fallen on the shore is still a pārājika offense. This same principle applies to taking a turtle that has gone outside for the purpose of grazing. However, for one who removes from the water that which is situated in the water, it is a pārājika offense.

Tesu tesu pana janapadesu sabbasādhāraṇassa mahātaḷākassa niddhamanatumbaṃ nissāya sabbasādhāraṇameva kunnadīsadisaṃ udakavāhakaṃ khaṇanti. Tato khuddakamātikāyo nīharitvā mātikākoṭiyaṃ attano attano vaḷañjanatthāya āvāṭe khaṇanti. Tesaṃ pana yadā udakena attho hoti, tadā āvāṭe khuddakamātikāyo udakavāhakañca sodhetvā niddhamanatumbaṃ ugghāṭenti. Tato udakena saddhiṃ macchā nikkhamitvā anupubbena āvāṭe patvā vasanti. Tattha taḷāke ca udakavāhakesu ca macche gaṇhante na vārenti. Khuddakāsu pana attano attano mātikāsu [P 2.0331] udakaāvāṭesu ca paviṭṭhamacche gaṇhituṃ na denti, vārenti; tattha yo taḷāke vā niddhamanatumbe vā udakavāhake vā macche gaṇhāti, avahārena so na kāretabbo. Khuddakamātikāsu pana āvāṭesu vā paviṭṭhaṃ gaṇhanto gahitassa agghavasena kāretabbo. Sace tato gayhamāno maccho ākāse vā uppatati, tīre vā patati, taṃ ākāsaṭṭhaṃ vā tīraṭṭhaṃ vā udakavinimuttaṃ gaṇhato avahāro natthi. Kasmā? Yasmā attano pariggahaṭṭhāne ṭhitasseva te sāmikā. Evarūpā hi tattha katikā. Kacchapepi eseva nayo.

Now, in various regions, relying on the outlet-pipe of a large public reservoir, they dig a large, public water-channel resembling a small river. From that, having led out small channels, they dig pits at the end of the channels for their own respective use. Now, when they have need of water, they, having cleaned the pits, the small channels, and the large water-channel, open the outlet-pipe. From that pipe, fish, emerging together with the water, gradually arrive at the pits and dwell there. There, they do not prevent those who catch fish in the reservoir or in the large water-channels. However, they do not give permission to catch fish that have entered their own respective small channels or water-pits; they prevent it. In this case, whoever catches fish in the reservoir, the outlet-pipe, or the large water-channel is not to be charged with theft. But one who catches a fish that has entered the small channels or pits is to be charged according to the value of what was caught. If a fish, while being caught from there, leaps into the air or falls onto the bank, for one who takes that fish—whether it is in the air or on the bank, freed from the water—there is no theft. Why? Because they are owners only of that which is situated in their own appropriated place. Indeed, such is the convention there. This same principle applies to turtles.

Sace pana maccho gayhamāno āvāṭato khuddakamātikaṃ āruhati, tattha naṃ gaṇhatopi avahāroyeva. Khuddakamātikāto pana udakavāhakaṃ, tato ca taḷākaṃ ārūḷhaṃ gaṇhato avahāro natthi. Yo āvāṭato bhattasitthehi palobhetvā mātikaṃ āropetvā gaṇhāti, avahārova. Tato pana palobhetvā udakavāhakaṃ āropetvā gaṇhantassa avahāro natthi. Keci pana [V 1.0265] kutocideva sabbasādhāraṇaṭṭhānato [M 1.0288] macche ānetvā pacchimavatthubhāge udakāvāṭe khipitvā posetvā divase divase dve tīṇi uttaribhaṅgatthāya mārenti. Evarūpaṃ macchaṃ udake vā ākāse vā tīre vā yattha katthaci ṭhitaṃ gaṇhato avahāro eva. Kacchapepi eseva nayo.

Furthermore, if a fish, while being caught, ascends from the pit to the small channel, for one who catches it there, it is indeed a theft. However, for one who catches a fish that has ascended from the small channel to the large water-channel, and from there to the reservoir, there is no theft. Whoever, having lured a fish from the pit with balls of rice, makes it ascend to the channel and catches it, it is indeed a theft. However, for one who, having lured it from there, makes it ascend to the large water-channel and catches it, there is no theft. Now, some people, having brought fish from some public place, release them into a water-pit in the rear part of their property, raise them, and day by day kill two or three for the purpose of a side-dish. For one who catches such a fish, whether it is situated in the water, in the air, or on the bank—anywhere whatsoever—it is indeed a theft. This same principle applies to turtles.

Nidāghakāle pana nadiyā sote pacchinne katthaci ninnaṭṭhāne udakaṃ tiṭṭhati, tattha manussā macchānaṃ vināsāya madanaphalavasādīni pakkhipitvā gacchanti, macchā tāni khādantā maritvā uttānā udake plavantā tiṭṭhanti. Yo tattha gantvā “yāva sāmikā nāgacchanti, tāvime macche gaṇhissāmī”ti gaṇhāti, agghavasena kāretabbo. Paṃsukūlasaññāya gaṇhato avahāro natthi, āharāpente pana bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Macchavisaṃ pakkhipitvā gatamanussā bhājanāni āharitvā pūretvā gacchanti, yāva “punapi āgacchissāmā”ti sālayā honti, tāva te sassāmikamacchāva. Yadā pana te “alaṃ amhāka”nti nirālayā pakkamanti, tato paṭṭhāya theyyacittena gaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Paṃsukūlasaññissa anāpatti. Yathā ca macchakacchapesu, evaṃ sabbāyapi [P 2.0332] odakajātiyā vinicchayo veditabboti.

Now, in the hot season, when the river's current is cut off, water remains in some low-lying place. There, people, for the destruction of the fish, put in emetic nut, poison, and so on, and go away. The fish, eating those things, die and remain floating on their backs in the water. Whoever, going there and thinking, 'As long as the owners have not yet come, I will take these fish,' takes them, is to be charged according to their value. For one who takes them with the perception of being discarded, there is no theft; however, if the owners make him return them, the goods are to be paid for. The people who went away after putting in the fish-poison bring vessels, fill them, and go. As long as they have the attachment, thinking, 'We will come again,' for so long those fish indeed have an owner. But when they depart without attachment, thinking, 'Enough for us,' from then on, for one who takes them with a thieving thought, there is a dukkaṭa offense. For one with the perception of them being discarded, there is no offense. And just as the legal decision regarding fish and turtles is to be known, so too is the legal decision to be known for all species of aquatic creatures.

Udakaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Water is concluded.

Nāvaṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on Boats

99. Nāvaṭṭhe – paṭhamaṃ tāva nāvaṃ dassento “nāvā nāma yāya taratī”ti āha. Tasmā idha antamaso rajanadoṇikāpi veṇukalāpakopi “nāvā”tveva veditabbo. Sīmāsammannane pana dhuvanāvā anto khaṇitvā vā phalakehi bandhitvā vā katā sabbantimena paricchedena tiṇṇaṃ vāhanikā eva vaṭṭati. Idha pana ekassapi vāhanikā “nāvā” tveva vuccati. Nāvāya nikkhittanti yaṃkiñci indriyabaddhaṃ vā anindriyabaddhaṃ vā; tassa avahāralakkhaṇaṃ thalaṭṭhe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Nāvaṃ avaharissāmītiādimhi ca dutiyapariyesanagamanaāmasanaphandāpanāni vuttanayāneva. Bandhanaṃ mocetīti ettha pana yā bandhane muttamatte ṭhānā na cavati, tassā bandhanaṃ yāva [M 1.0289] na muttaṃ hoti, tāva dukkaṭaṃ. Mutte pana thullaccayampi pārājikampi hoti, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ tāva pāḷivaṇṇanā.

99. Regarding property on a boat—first, when showing what a boat is, it was said, “A boat is that by which one crosses.” Therefore, here, at the very least, even a dyeing trough or a small bundle of bamboo should be understood simply as a “boat.” In the consecration of a boundary, however, a permanent boat—whether made by hollowing out a log or by binding planks together—that is, at the very minimum, capable of carrying three persons is suitable. But here, even one that can carry only one person is called a “boat.” “Placed in a boat” refers to any property whatsoever, whether animate or inanimate. The characteristic of its theft should be understood in the same way as explained for property on dry land. And in the phrase beginning, “I will steal the boat,” the acts of searching for a companion, going, touching, and shaking are just as previously explained. Here, in the phrase, “He unties the mooring,” if a boat does not move from its place merely upon its mooring being untied, then as long as its mooring is not yet untied, it is a dukkaṭa offense. But once it is untied, it can become a thullaccaya offense or a pārājika offense; this will become clear later. The rest is just as previously explained. This, for now, is the explanation of the Pāḷi.

Ayaṃ panettha pāḷimuttakavinicchayo – caṇḍasote bandhitvā ṭhapitanāvāya ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ bandhanameva[V 1.0266], tasmiṃ muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Tattha yutti pubbe vuttā eva. Vippanaṭṭhā nāvā pana yaṃ yaṃ udakappadesaṃ pharitvā ṭhitā hoti, svāssā ṭhānaṃ. Tasmā taṃ uddhaṃ vā uccārentassa, adho vā opilāpentassa, catūsu vā disāsu phuṭṭhokāsaṃ atikkāmentassa atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ. Niccale udake abandhanaṃ attano dhammatāya ṭhitanāvaṃ purato vā pacchato vā vāmadakkhiṇapassato vā kaḍḍhantassa ekenantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ aparena udake patiṭṭhitantena atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ. Uddhaṃ kesaggamattaṃ udakato mocite adho nāvātalena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ mukhavaṭṭiṃ atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ. Tīre bandhitvā niccale [P 2.0333] udake ṭhapitanāvāya bandhanañca ṭhitokāso cāti dve ṭhānāni. Taṃ paṭhamaṃ bandhanā moceti, thullaccayaṃ. Pacchā channaṃ ākārānaṃ aññatarena ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ ṭhānā cāvetvā pacchā bandhanamocanepi eseva nayo. Thale ussādetvā ukkujjitvā ṭhapitanāvāya phuṭṭhokāsova ṭhānaṃ. Tassā pañcahākārehi ṭhānaparicchedo veditabbo.

This, herein, is the legal decision independent of the Pāḷi text: For a boat tied and placed in a fierce current, the mooring itself is its one place; just upon it being untied, a pārājika offense is incurred. The reasoning for this has already been stated. But as for a boat that is adrift, whatever water-region it occupies is its place. Therefore, for one who lifts it upwards, or makes it sink downwards, or makes it pass beyond the space it touches in the four directions, a pārājika offense is incurred just upon it passing beyond. For a boat standing by its own nature, unmoored, in still water, if one pulls it from the front, back, left, or right, a pārājika offense is incurred at the moment one end passes beyond the space previously occupied by the other end. If it is lifted upwards out of the water by a hair’s breadth, or if, when sinking it downwards, the rim of its opening passes beyond the space touched by the bottom of the boat, a pārājika offense is incurred. For a boat tied to the shore and placed in still water, there are two places: the mooring and the occupied space. If one first unties it from the mooring, it is a thullaccaya offense. Afterwards, if one moves it from its place by any of the six methods, it is a pārājika offense. This same method applies if one first moves it from its place and afterwards unties the mooring. For a boat hauled onto land and placed upright, the space it touches is its place. The determination of its place should be understood by five methods.

Nikkujjitvā ṭhapitanāvāya pana mukhavaṭṭiyā phuṭṭhokāsova ṭhānaṃ, tassāpi pañcahākārehi ṭhānaparicchedaṃ ñatvā yato kutoci phuṭṭhokāsaṃ uddhañca kesaggamattaṃ atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ. Thale pana ussādetvā dvinnaṃ dārughaṭikānaṃ upari ṭhapitanāvāya dārughaṭikānaṃ phuṭṭhokāsoyeva ṭhānaṃ, tasmā tattha mañcapādamatthakesuyeva patthaṭabaddhasāṭake nāgadantesu ṭhapitabhindivāle ca vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo.

But for a boat placed upside down, the space touched by its rim is its place. Having understood the determination of its place by five methods, it should be known that a pārājika offense is incurred at the moment it passes beyond the space it touched from any direction, or upwards by a hair's breadth. But for a boat hauled onto land and placed on top of two small wooden blocks, the space touched by the wooden blocks is its place. Therefore, in that case, the legal decision should be understood by the method already stated for a cloth spread out and fastened on the tops of bed-legs, and for a javelin placed on elephant-tusk pegs.

Yottabaddhāya pana nāvāya saṭṭhisattatibyāmappamāṇaṃ yottaṃ amocetvāva ākaḍḍhitvā

But for a boat tied with a rope, having pulled it without untying the rope of sixty or seventy fathoms in length,

Pathavilaggaṃ katvā saha yottena thale ṭhapitāya nāvāya [M 1.0290] na phuṭṭhokāsamattameva ṭhānaṃ. Atha kho yottakoṭito paṭṭhāya yāva nāvāya pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitokāsassa pacchimanto tāva dīghato, tiriyaṃ pana nāvāya ca yottassa ca pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitapariyantappamāṇaṃ ṭhānanti veditabbaṃ. Taṃ dīghato vā tiriyato vā kaḍḍhantassa ekenantena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ aparena pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitantena atikkantamatte, uddhaṃ kesaggamattaṃ saha yottena pathavito mocite pārājikaṃ. Yo pana titthe ṭhitanāvaṃ āruhitvā theyyacitto arittena vā phiyena vā pājeti, pārājikaṃ. Sace pana chattaṃ vā paṇāmetvā cīvaraṃ vā pādehi akkamitvā hatthehi ukkhipitvā laṅkārasadisaṃ katvā vātaṃ gaṇhāpeti, balavā ca vāto āgamma nāvaṃ harati, vāteneva sā haṭā hoti; puggalassa natthi avahāro. Payogo atthi, so pana ṭhānā cāvanapayogo [P 2.0334] na hoti. Yadi pana taṃ nāvaṃ evaṃ gacchantiṃ pakatigamanaṃ upacchinditvā aññaṃ disābhāgaṃ neti, pārājikaṃ. Sayameva yaṃkiñci [V 1.0267] gāmatitthaṃ sampattaṃ ṭhānā acāventova vikkiṇitvā gacchati, neva atthi avahāro. Bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hotīti.

...and having made it lie on the ground, for a boat placed on land together with its rope, its place is not merely the space it touches. Rather, its place lengthwise should be known as extending from the end of the rope up to the rear limit of the space where the boat is established on the ground. But as for its width, the extent of the final limit where both the boat and the rope are established on the ground should be known as its place. For one who pulls it lengthwise or widthwise, a pārājika offense is incurred at the moment one end passes beyond the space it had occupied, while the other end remains established on the ground, or when it is lifted from the ground upwards by a hair's breadth, together with the rope. But if a monk, having boarded a boat stationed at a landing, with the intention to steal, propels it with a pole or an oar, it is a pārājika offense. If, however, having angled an umbrella, or having stepped on a robe with his feet and lifted it with his hands to make it like a sail, he makes it catch the wind, and a strong wind comes and carries the boat, that boat is carried by the wind alone; there is no theft on the part of the person. There is an effort, but that effort is not one that causes it to move from its place. But if, while that boat is thus moving, he interrupts its natural course and directs it to another direction, it is a pārājika offense. If a boat reaches some village landing by itself, and without moving it from its place, he sells it and goes away, there is no theft. But the price of the goods must be paid.

Nāvaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation on property on a boat is concluded.

Yānaṭṭhakathā

The Explanation on Vehicles

100. Yānaṭṭhe – yānaṃ tāva dassento “yānaṃ nāma vayha”ntiādimāha. Tattha upari maṇḍapasadisaṃ padaracchannaṃ sabbapaliguṇṭhimaṃ vā chādetvā kataṃ vayhaṃ. Ubhosu passesu suvaṇṇarajatādimayā gopānasiyo datvā garuḷapakkhakanayena katā sandamānikā. Ratho ca sakaṭañca pākaṭameva. Tesu yattha katthaci saviññāṇakaṃ vā aviññāṇakaṃ vā rāsiādivasena ṭhapitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacittena ṭhānā cāventassa nāvaṭṭhe ca thalaṭṭhe ca vuttanayeneva pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ.

100. Regarding property on a vehicle—first, while explaining what a vehicle is, it is said, “A vehicle is called a vayha,” and so on. Therein, a vehicle covered above with boards like a pavilion, or one made by covering it so as to be completely wrapped all around, is called a vayha. A vehicle made by affixing rafters of gold, silver, and so forth on both sides in the manner of a Garuḷa's wing is called a sandamānikā. A chariot and a cart are self-evident. Among these vehicles, for a monk who, with thievish intent, displaces from its place any goods whatsoever—be they animate or inanimate—that have been placed as a heap or the like, a pārājika offense should be understood by the method already stated for property on a boat and property on land.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – yānaṭṭhaṃ taṇḍulādibhaṇḍaṃ piṭakena gaṇhato piṭake anukkhittepi piṭakaṃ apaharitvā taṇḍulādīnaṃ ekābaddhabhāve vikopite pārājikaṃ. Thalaṭṭhādīsupi ayaṃ nayo labbhati. Yānaṃ [M 1.0291] avaharissāmītiādimhi dutiyapariyesanādīni vuttanayāneva. Ṭhānā cāvetīti ettha pana dukayuttassa yānassa dvinnaṃ goṇānaṃ aṭṭha pādā, dve ca cakkānīti dasa ṭhānāni. Taṃ theyyacittassa dhure nisīditvā pājayato goṇānaṃ pāduddhāre thullaccayaṃ. Cakkānaṃ pana pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitappadesato kesaggamatte atikkante pārājikaṃ. Sace pana goṇā “nāyaṃ amhākaṃ sāmiko”ti ñatvā dhuraṃ chaḍḍetvā ākaḍḍhantā tiṭṭhanti vā phandanti vā, rakkhati tāva. Goṇe puna ujukaṃ paṭipādetvā dhuraṃ āropetvā daḷhaṃ yojetvā pācanena vijjhitvā pājentassa vuttanayeneva tesaṃ pāduddhāre thullaccayaṃ. Cakkātikkame pārājikaṃ.

However, this is the distinction: for a monk who takes goods such as rice that are on a vehicle by means of a basket, even if the basket is not lifted, if he strikes the basket and thereby destroys the state of the rice and other goods being a single connected mass, it is a pārājika offense. This method is also applicable to goods on land and so forth. In the case of intending, “I will steal the vehicle,” and so on, the second search and other matters are just as previously stated. However, in this matter of “displaces from its place,” for a vehicle yoked with two oxen, there are ten points of contact: the eight feet of the two oxen and the two wheels. For a monk with thievish intent who, sitting on the yoke-pole, drives it, there is a thullaccaya offense at the lifting of the oxen's feet. However, for the wheels, when they have passed by a hair's breadth from the place where they were established on the ground, it is a pārājika offense. If, however, the oxen, knowing, “This is not our master,” cast off the yoke and, pulling back, stand still or struggle, he is guarded from pārājika for the time being. For a monk who, having again straightened the oxen, made them take up the yoke, yoked them firmly, and drives them by prodding with a goad, by the method already stated, there is a thullaccaya offense at the lifting of their feet. When the wheels pass beyond their original spot, it is a pārājika offense.

Sacepi sakaddame magge ekaṃ cakkaṃ kaddame laggaṃ hoti, dutiyaṃ cakkaṃ goṇā parivattentā pavattenti, ekassa ṭhitattā na tāva avahāro hoti[P 2.0335]. Goṇe pana puna ujukaṃ paṭipādetvā pājentassa ṭhitacakke kesaggamattaṃ phuṭṭhokāsaṃ atikkante pārājikaṃ. Catuyuttakassa pana aṭṭhārasa ṭhānāni, aṭṭhayuttakassa catuttiṃsāti – etenupāyena yuttayānassa ṭhānabhedo veditabbo.

If, on a muddy road, one wheel becomes stuck in the mud, and the oxen cause the second wheel to turn and roll, the theft has not yet occurred because one wheel is stationary. But for the monk who, having again straightened the oxen, drives them, when the stationary wheel passes by even a hair's breadth the place it was touching, it is a pārājika offense. For a vehicle yoked with four oxen, there are eighteen points of contact; for one yoked with eight, there are thirty-four. By this method, the distinction of points of contact for a yoked vehicle should be understood.

Yaṃ pana ayuttakaṃ dhure ekāya pacchato ca dvīhi upatthambhinīhi upatthambhetvā ṭhapitaṃ, tassa tiṇṇaṃ upatthambhinīnaṃ cakkānañca vasena pañca ṭhānāni. Sace dhure upatthambhinī heṭṭhābhāge [V 1.0268] kappakatā hoti, cha ṭhānāni. Pacchato pana anupatthambhetvā dhure upatthambhitasseva upatthambhinīvasena tīṇi vā cattāri vā ṭhānāni. Dhurena phalakassa vā dārukassa vā upari ṭhapitassa tīṇi ṭhānāni. Tathā pathaviyaṃ ṭhapitassa. Taṃ dhuraṃkaḍḍhitvā vā ukkhipitvā vā purato ca pacchato ca ṭhānā cāventassa thullaccayaṃ. Cakkānaṃ patiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne kesaggamattaṃ atikkante pārājikaṃ. Cakkāni apanetvā dvīhi akkhasīsehi dārūnaṃ upari ṭhapitassa dve ṭhānāni. Taṃ kaḍḍhanto vā ukkhipanto vā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitassa dhurena ca catūhi ca akkhuddhīhi patiṭṭhitavasena pañca ṭhānāni. Taṃ dhure gahetvā kaḍḍhato uddhīnaṃ pacchimantehi purimante atikkante pārājikaṃ. Uddhīsu gahetvā kaḍḍhato uddhīnaṃ purimantehi pacchimante atikkante pārājikaṃ. Passe gahetvā kaḍḍhato uddhīnaṃyeva tiriyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānassa atikkamena pārājikaṃ. Majjhe gahetvā ukkhipato kesaggamattaṃ pathavito [M 1.0292] mutte pārājikaṃ. Atha uddhikhāṇukā na honti, samameva bāhaṃ katvā majjhe vijjhitvā akkhasīsāni pavesitāni honti, taṃ heṭṭhimatalassa samantā sabbaṃ pathaviṃ phusitvā tiṭṭhati. Tattha catūsu disāsu uddhañca phuṭṭhaṭṭhānātikkamavasena pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ nābhiyā ṭhapitacakkassa ekameva ṭhānaṃ, tassa pañcahākārehi paricchedo. Nemipassena ca nābhiyā ca phusitvā ṭhitassa dve ṭhānāni. Nemiyā uṭṭhitabhāgaṃ pādena akkamitvā bhūmiyaṃ phusāpetvā aresu [P 2.0336] vā nemiyā vā gahetvā ukkhipantassa attanā kataṭṭhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ na hoti, tasmā tasmiṃ ṭhitepi avasesaṭṭhāne atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ.

As for an unyoked vehicle that is set up propped by one support-pole at the yoke-pole and by two at the rear, for that vehicle, by means of the three support-poles and the wheels, there are five points of contact. If the support-pole at the yoke-pole is forked in its lower part, there are six points of contact. However, for a vehicle not propped at the rear but propped only at the yoke-pole, by means of the support-pole, there are three or four points of contact. For a cart placed with its yoke-pole on top of a plank or a small log, there are three points of contact. Likewise for one placed on the ground. For one who displaces it from its place by dragging or lifting that yoke-pole, both forwards and backwards, it is a thullaccaya offense. When the wheels pass by a hair's breadth beyond their established resting place, it is a pārājika offense. For a vehicle whose wheels have been removed and which is placed on top of pieces of wood by its two axle-ends, there are two points of contact. If one, while dragging or lifting it, causes it to pass beyond the space it touched, it is a pārājika offense. For one placed on the ground, established by means of its yoke-pole and four linchpins, there are five points of contact. If one takes hold of the yoke-pole and drags it, it is a pārājika offense when the rear ends of the linchpins pass the position of the front end. If one takes hold of the linchpins and drags it, it is a pārājika offense when the front ends of the linchpins pass the position of the rear end. If one takes hold of the side and drags it, it is a pārājika offense due to the sideways passing of the linchpins' established resting place. If one takes hold of the middle and lifts it, it is a pārājika offense when it is freed from the ground by a hair's breadth. If there are no linchpin-stakes, but having made the chassis even, the axle-ends are inserted by piercing the middle, then it stands touching the entire ground all around its lower surface. In that case, a pārājika offense should be understood by means of its passing beyond the place it touched in the four directions and upwards. For a wheel placed on the ground by its hub, there is only one point of contact; its demarcation is of five kinds. For one standing touching the ground with the side of its rim and its hub, there are two points of contact. For one who, having stepped on the raised part of the rim and made it touch the ground, then lifts it by grasping the spokes or the rim, the place made by oneself is not a point of contact. Therefore, even while it is in that position, when the remaining point of contact is passed, it is a pārājika offense.

Bhittiṃ nissāya ṭhapitacakkassāpi dve ṭhānāni. Tattha paṭhamaṃ bhittito mocentassa thullaccayaṃ. Pacchā pathavito kesaggamattuddhāre pārājikaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ bhūmito mocentassa pana sace bhittiyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ na kuppati, eseva nayo. Atha aresu gahetvā heṭṭhā kaḍḍhantassa bhittiṃ phusitvā ṭhitokāsassa uparimo anto heṭṭhimaṃ atikkamati, pārājikaṃ. Maggappaṭipanne yāne yānasāmiko kenacideva karaṇīyena orohitvā maggā okkanto hoti, athañño bhikkhu paṭipathaṃ āgacchanto ārakkhasuññaṃ passitvā, “yānaṃ avaharissāmī”ti ārohati, tassa payogaṃ vināyeva goṇā gahetvā pakkantā, avahāro natthi. Sesaṃ nāvāyaṃ vuttasadisanti.

For a wheel placed leaning against a wall, there are also two points of contact. In that case, for a monk who first frees it from the wall, it is a thullaccaya offense. Afterwards, when he lifts it a hair's breadth from the ground, it is a pārājika offense. However, for a monk who first frees it from the ground, if the place where it was established against the wall is not disturbed, this same method applies. Or, for a monk who, grasping the spokes, pulls it downwards, if the upper end of the place that was touching the wall passes the lower end, it is a pārājika offense. When a vehicle is proceeding on a road, and the vehicle's owner, having dismounted for some business, has gone off the road, then another monk, coming along the road towards it, sees the unguarded vehicle and, thinking, “I will steal the vehicle,” mounts it. If, without any effort from that monk, the oxen take the vehicle and depart, there is no theft. The remainder is similar to what was said in the case of the boat.

Yānaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on Vehicles is concluded.

Bhāraṭṭhakathā

The Exposition on the Burden

101. Ito [V 1.0269] paraṃ bhāroyeva bhāraṭṭhaṃ. So sīsabhārādivasena catudhā dassito. Tattha sīsabhārādīsu asammohatthaṃ sīsādīnaṃ paricchedo veditabbo. Tattha sīsassa tāva purimagale galavāṭako, piṭṭhigale kesañci kesante āvaṭṭo hoti, galasseva ubhosu passesu kesañci kesā oruyha jāyanti, ye kaṇṇacūḷikāti vuccanti, tesaṃ adhobhāgo cāti ayaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedo, tato upari sīsaṃ. Etthantare ṭhitabhāro sīsabhāro nāma.

101. Hereafter, the matter of the burden itself is the Exposition on the Burden. It is shown in four ways, such as the head-burden and so forth. Therein, for the purpose of non-bewilderment regarding the head-burden and so forth, the delimitation of the head and so forth should be understood. Therein, regarding the head, first, at the front of the neck is the throat-hollow; at the back of the neck, for some, there is a whorl at the end of the hair; on both sides of the neck itself, for some, hairs grow downwards, which are called 'ear-locks' (kaṇṇacūḷikā). The lower part of these is the lower delimitation, and above that is the head. A burden placed within this space is called a head-burden.

Ubhosu [M 1.0293] passesu kaṇṇacūḷikāhi paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, kapparehi paṭṭhāya upari, piṭṭhigalāvattato ca galavāṭakato ca paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, piṭṭhivemajjhāvattato ca uraparicchedamajjhe hadayaāvāṭato ca paṭṭhāya upari khandho. Etthantare ṭhitabhāro khandhabhāro nāma.

Downward beginning from the ear-locks on both sides, upward beginning from the elbows, downward beginning from the whorl at the back of the neck and from the throat-hollow, and upward beginning from the whorl at the middle of the back and from the heart-hollow in the middle of the chest-delimitation, is the shoulder. A burden placed within this space is called a shoulder-burden.

Piṭṭhivemajjhāvattato pana hadayaāvāṭato ca paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā yāva pādanakhasikhā, ayaṃ kaṭiparicchedo. Etthantare samantato sarīre ṭhitabhāro kaṭibhāro nāma.

However, downward beginning from the whorl at the middle of the back and from the heart-hollow, as far as the tips of the toenails, this is the delimitation of the waist. A burden placed all around the body within this space is called a waist-burden.

Kapparato paṭṭhāya pana heṭṭhā yāva hatthanakhasikhā, ayaṃ olambakaparicchedo. Etthantare ṭhitabhāro olambako nāma.

However, downward beginning from the elbow, as far as the tips of the fingernails, this is the delimitation of the dangling object. A burden placed within this space is called a dangling object.

Idāni sīse bhārantiādīsu ayaṃ apubbavinicchayo [P 2.0337] – yo bhikkhu “idaṃ gahetvā ettha yāhī”ti sāmikehi anāṇatto sayameva “mayhaṃ idaṃ nāma detha, ahaṃ vo bhaṇḍaṃ vahāmī”ti tesaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sīsena ādāya gacchanto theyyacittena taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Yathāvuttasīsaparicchedaṃ anatikkāmentova ito cito ca ghaṃsanto sāretipi paccāsāretipi, thullaccayaṃ. Khandhaṃ oropitamatte kiñcāpi sāmikānaṃ “vahatū”ti cittaṃ atthi, tehi pana anāṇattattā pārājikaṃ. Khandhaṃ pana anoropetvāpi sīsato kesaggamattaṃ mocentassa pārājikaṃ. Yamakabhārassa pana eko bhāro sīse patiṭṭhāti, eko piṭṭhiyaṃ, tattha dvinnaṃ ṭhānānaṃ vasena vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana suddhasīsabhārādīnaṃyeva vasena desanā āraddhā. Yo cāyaṃ sīsabhāre vutto, khandhabhārādīsupi ayameva vinicchayo.

Now, in 'a burden on the head,' and so forth, this is the sequential decision: If a bhikkhu, not being instructed by the owners, 'Take this and go there,' says on his own accord, 'Give me such-and-such, I will carry your goods,' and, taking their goods on his head and going along, touches those goods with a mind bent on theft, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If, without transgressing the aforesaid delimitation of the head, scraping it here and there, he moves it forward or moves it back, it is a grave offense. At the moment of lowering it to the shoulder, although the owners may have the thought, 'Let him carry it,' yet because he was not instructed by them, it is an offense of defeat. However, even without lowering it to the shoulder, for one who releases it from the head by a hair's breadth, it is an offense of defeat. In the case of a double burden, however, one burden rests on the head and one on the back; there, the decision should be understood according to the two positions. This teaching, however, has been expounded solely by way of pure head-burdens and so forth. And this decision which was stated for the head-burden is the very same decision for shoulder-burdens and so forth.

Hatthe bhāranti ettha pana hatthena gahitattā olambako “hatthe bhāro”ti vutto.

However, here in 'a burden in the hand,' because it is grasped by the hand, the dangling object is called 'a burden in the hand.'

So paṭhamaṃyeva bhūmito vā gahito hotu, suddhacittena sīsādīhi vā, “hatthe bhāro” tveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati[V 1.0270]. Taṃ theyyacittena tādisaṃ gahanaṭṭhānaṃ disvā bhūmiyaṃ vā gacchādīsu vā nikkhipantassa hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Bhūmito gaṇhātīti ettha pana tesaṃ bhārānaṃ yaṃkiñci pātarāsādikāraṇā suddhacittena bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā puna theyyacittena kesaggamattaṃ uddharantassa pārājikanti.

Whether it was first taken from the ground, or with a pure mind from the head and so forth, it is reckoned only as 'a burden in the hand.' For one who, with a mind bent on theft, having seen such a place of concealment, puts it down on the ground or in a bush and so forth, at the very moment it is released from his hand, it is an offense of defeat. However, here in 'takes from the ground,' the decision should be understood thus: having put down any of those burdens on the ground with a pure mind for some reason such as for breakfast, for one who then, with a mind bent on theft, lifts it by a hair's breadth, it is an offense of defeat.

Bhāraṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Burden is concluded.

Ārāmaṭṭhakathā

The Exposition on Goods Situated in a Monastery Park

102. Ārāmaṭṭhepi [M 1.0294] – ārāmaṃ tāva dassento “ārāmo nāma pupphārāmo phalārāmo”ti āha. Tesu vassikādīnaṃ pupphanako pupphārāmo. Ambaphalādīnaṃ phalanako phalārāmo. Ārāme catūhi ṭhānehi nikkhittassa vinicchayo bhūmaṭṭhādīsu vuttanayo eva.

102. Regarding goods situated in a monastery park: first, while showing what a monastery park is, it was said: 'A monastery park, by name, is a flower park or a fruit park.' Among these, a flower park is a place where flowers such as vassikā bloom. A fruit park is a place where fruits such as mangoes grow. The legal decision concerning goods placed in a monastery park in the four locations is according to the method already stated in the section on goods placed on the ground and so forth.

Tatthajātake pana mūlanti usīrahiriverādikaṃ yaṃkiñci mūlaṃ, taṃ uppāṭetvā vā uppāṭitaṃ vā gaṇhantassa yena mūlena vatthu pūrati, tasmiṃ gahite [P 2.0338] pārājikaṃ. Kandopi mūleneva saṅgahito. Uppāṭentassa cettha appamattakepi acchinne thullaccayameva. Tattha vinicchayo bhise vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tacanti bhesajjatthāya vā rajanatthāya vā upayogagamanūpagaṃ yaṃkiñci rukkhattacaṃ; taṃ uppāṭetvā vā uppāṭitaṃ vā gaṇhantassa mūle vuttanayena pārājikaṃ. Pupphanti vassikamallikādikaṃ yaṃkiñci pupphaṃ, taṃ ocinitvā vā ocinitaṃ vā gaṇhantassa uppalapadumesu vuttanayena pārājikaṃ. Pupphānampi hi vaṇṭaṃ vā bandhanaṃ vā acchinnaṃ rakkhati. Vaṇṭabbhantare pana kesañci sūcikā hoti, sā na rakkhati. Phalanti ambaphalatālaphalādikaṃ yaṃkiñci, taṃ rukkhato gaṇhantassa vinicchayo rukkhe laggitakathāyaṃ vutto. Apanetvā ṭhapitaṃ bhūmaṭṭhādisaṅgahitameva.

However, regarding goods grown in that park: 'root' means any kind of root, such as vetiver or fragrant root. For a bhikkhu who takes it after uprooting it, or who takes what has been uprooted, when a root by which the value of a stolen article is completed is taken, it is an offense of defeat. A tuber is also included under 'root.' And here, for one who is uprooting it, as long as even a small part is not severed, it is only a grave offense. The legal decision therein should be understood according to the method stated for the lotus root. 'Bark' means any tree bark suitable for use as medicine or for dyeing. For one who takes it after stripping it, or who takes what has been stripped, it is an offense of defeat according to the method stated for a root. 'Flower' means any kind of flower, such as vassikā or jasmine. For one who takes it after picking it, or who takes what has been picked, it is an offense of defeat according to the method stated for blue and white lotuses. Indeed, for flowers too, an unsevered stalk or binding-place protects it. However, inside the stalk of some flowers, there is a filament; that does not protect. 'Fruit' means any kind of fruit, such as a mango or a palmyra fruit. The legal decision for one who takes it from a tree has been stated in the discourse on things attached to a tree. What has been removed and placed elsewhere is included under goods placed on the ground and so forth.

Ārāmaṃ abhiyuñjatīti parasantakaṃ “mama santako aya”nti musā bhaṇitvā abhiyuñjati, adinnādānassa payogattā dukkaṭaṃ. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādetīti vinicchayakusalatāya balavanissitādibhāvena vā ārāmasāmikassa saṃsayaṃ janeti. Kathaṃ? Tañhi tathā vinicchayappasutaṃ disvā sāmiko cinteti – “sakkhissāmi nu kho ahaṃ imaṃ ārāmaṃ attano kātuṃ, na sakkhissāmi nu kho”ti. Evaṃ tassa vimati uppajjamānā tena uppāditā hoti, tasmā thullaccayaṃ āpajjati.

'He lays claim to a monastery park' means: regarding another's property, having spoken falsely, 'This is my property,' he strives to get it. Because it is a preliminary act of taking what is not given, it is an offense of wrong-doing. 'He causes doubt to arise in the owner' means: either because of skill in judgment or because of being one who relies on the powerful, he generates suspicion in the monastery park's owner. How? Indeed, seeing him so engaged in litigation, the owner thinks: 'Will I be able to make this monastery park my own, or will I not be able?' Thus, when doubt arises in him, it has been caused by that person; therefore, he commits a grave offense.

Dhuraṃ [V 1.0271] nikkhipatīti yadā pana sāmiko “ayaṃ thaddho kakkhaḷo jīvitabrahmacariyantarāyampi me kareyya, alaṃ dāni mayhaṃ iminā ārāmenā”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, abhiyuñjako pārājikaṃ āpajjati. Sace sayampi katadhuranikkhepo hoti, atha ca pana sāmikena dhure nikkhittepi abhiyuñjako dhuraṃ anikkhipitvāva “imaṃ suṭṭhu pīḷetvā mama āṇāpavattiṃ dassetvā kiṅkārappaṭissāvibhāve [M 1.0295] naṃ ṭhapetvā dassāmī”ti dātabbabhāve saussāho hoti, rakkhati tāva. Athāpi abhiyuñjako “acchinditvā [P 2.0339] na dāni naṃ imassa dassāmī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, sāmiko pana na dhuraṃ nikkhipati, pakkhaṃ pariyesati, kālaṃ āgameti, “lajjiparisaṃ tāva labhāmi, pacchā jānissāmī”ti puna gahaṇeyeva saussāho hoti, rakkhatiyeva. Yadā pana sopi “na dassāmī”ti, sāmikopi “na lacchāmī”ti – evaṃ ubhopi dhuraṃ nikkhipanti, tadā abhiyuñjakassa pārājikaṃ. Atha pana abhiyuñjitvā vinicchayaṃ kurumāno aniṭṭhite vinicchaye sāmikenapi dhuranikkhepe akate attano assāmikabhāvaṃ jānantoyeva tato kiñci pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā gaṇhāti, bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo.

'He relinquishes the burden': When the owner thinks, 'This person is stubborn and harsh; he might even cause danger to my life and my holy life. Enough of this monastery for me now,' and relinquishes the burden, if the claimant himself has also relinquished the burden, the claimant commits a pārājika offense. Furthermore, even though the owner has relinquished the burden, if the claimant, without relinquishing the burden, is zealous in the matter of giving it back, thinking, 'After thoroughly oppressing him, demonstrating my authority, and establishing him in a state of subservience, I will give it back to him,' then for the time being, it is protected. Then again, if the claimant relinquishes the burden, thinking, 'Having seized it, I will not give it back to him now,' but the owner does not relinquish the burden—he seeks allies or awaits a suitable time, thinking, 'I have not yet found a conscientious assembly; I will see about it later'—and is thus still zealous about retaking it, it is still protected. But when he, the claimant, thinks, 'I will not give it back,' and the owner too thinks, 'I will not get it back'—thus both relinquish the burden—then there is a pārājika offense for the claimant. Furthermore, if, having laid claim and while the legal decision is being made, before the decision is concluded and before the owner has relinquished the burden, he, knowing his own non-ownership, takes any flower or fruit from there, he should be made to pay the value of the goods.

Dhammaṃ carantoti bhikkhusaṅghe vā rājakule vā vinicchayaṃ karonto. Sāmikaṃ parājetīti vinicchayikānaṃ ukkocaṃ datvā kūṭasakkhiṃ otāretvā ārāmasāmikaṃ jinātīti attho. Āpatti pārājikassāti na kevalaṃ tasseva, sañcicca tassa atthasādhane pavattānaṃ kūṭavinicchayikānampi kūṭasakkhīnampi sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Ettha ca sāmikassa dhuranikkhepavaseneva parājayo veditabbo. Anikkhittadhuro hi aparājitova hoti. Dhammaṃ caranto parajjatīti sacepi dhammena vinayena satthusāsanena vinicchayassa pavattattā sayaṃ parājayaṃ pāpuṇāti; evampi musāvādena sāmikānaṃ pīḷākaraṇapaccayā thullaccayaṃ āpajjatīti.

'While the case proceeds according to law' means: while a legal decision is being made in the community of bhikkhus or in a royal court. 'He defeats the owner' means: having given a bribe to the judges and having introduced a false witness, he defeats the monastery's owner. 'It is a pārājika offense' means: it is not a pārājika offense for him alone, but for all—for the corrupt judges and the false witnesses who, with intention, were engaged in accomplishing his purpose. And here, the defeat of the owner should be understood as being by way of his relinquishing the burden. Indeed, one who has not relinquished the burden is not one who is defeated. 'Abiding by the law, he is defeated' means: even if, because the legal decision proceeds according to Dhamma, Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction, he himself attains defeat; even so, because of the act of harassing the owners with false speech, he commits a thullaccaya offense.

Ārāmaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on monastery property is concluded.

Vihāraṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on Monastery Property

103. Vihāraṭṭhepi – catūhi ṭhānehi nikkhittaṃ vuttanayameva. Abhiyogepi cettha cātuddisaṃ saṅghaṃ uddissa bhikkhūnaṃ dinnaṃ vihāraṃ vā pariveṇaṃ vā āvāsaṃ vā mahantampi khuddakampi abhiyuñjato abhiyogo na ruhati. Acchinditvā gaṇhitumpi na sakkoti. Kasmā? Sabbesaṃ dhuranikkhepābhāvato. Na hettha sabbe cātuddisā bhikkhū dhuranikkhepaṃ karontīti[V 1.0272]. Dīghabhāṇakādibhedassa pana gaṇassa ekapuggalassa vā santakaṃ abhiyuñjitvā gaṇhanto sakkoti [M 1.0296] te dhuraṃ nikkhipāpetuṃ. Tasmā tattha ārāme vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabboti.

103. Regarding monastery property, too, property laid down in four ways is as has been stated. And here, even in a legal claim, if someone makes a claim against a monastery, a precinct, or a dwelling, whether large or small, that has been given to the bhikkhus and dedicated to the Sangha of the four directions, the claim is not valid. Nor can one seize it by force. Why? Because of the non-relinquishing of the burden by all. For here, not all bhikkhus of the four directions relinquish the burden. However, one who makes a claim and takes property belonging to a group with divisions such as the Dīgha-bhāṇakas, or to a single individual, is able to make them relinquish the burden. Therefore, in that case, the decision should be understood according to the method stated for a monastery.

Vihāraṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Monastery Property is concluded.

Khettaṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on Field Property

104. Khettaṭṭhepi [P 2.0340] – khettaṃ tāva dassento “khettaṃ nāma yattha pubbaṇṇaṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā jāyatī”ti āha. Tattha pubbaṇṇanti sāliādīni satta dhaññāni; aparaṇṇanti muggamāsādīni; ucchukhettādikampi ettheva saṅgahitaṃ. Idhāpi catūhi ṭhānehi nikkhittaṃ vuttanayameva. Tatthajātake pana sālisīsādīni nirumbhitvā vā ekamekaṃ hattheneva chinditvā vā asitena lāyitvā vā bahūni ekato uppāṭetvā vā gaṇhantassa yasmiṃ bīje vā sīse vā muṭṭhiyaṃ vā muggamāsādiphale vā vatthu pūrati, tasmiṃ bandhanā mocitamatte pārājikaṃ. Acchijjamāno pana daṇḍako vā vāko vā taco vā appamattakopi rakkhati.

104. Regarding field property, too, first, explaining what a field is, it is said: 'A field is where early grain or later grain grows.' Therein, 'early grain' means the seven grains such as Sāli rice; 'later grain' means beans such as mung beans and black gram; sugarcane fields and the like are also included here. Here too, property laid down in four ways is just as has been stated. However, concerning what is grown there, for one who takes rice heads and the like—either by pulling them up without cutting, or by cutting them one by one with the hand only, or by reaping with a sickle, or by pulling out many at once—in whichever seed, or head, or handful, or fruit such as mung bean or black gram the object of theft is complete, a pārājika offense is committed at the very moment it is freed from its connection. However, an uncut stalk, or fiber, or bark, even a small amount, protects from the offense being complete.

Vīhināḷaṃ dīghampi hoti, yāva antonāḷato vīhisīsadaṇḍako na nikkhamati, tāva rakkhati. Kesaggamattampi nāḷato daṇḍakassa heṭṭhimatale nikkhante bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Asitena lāyitvā gaṇhato pana muṭṭhigatesu heṭṭhā chinnesupi sace sīsāni jaṭitāni, rakkhanti tāva. Vijaṭetvā pana kesaggamattampi ukkhipato sace vatthu pūrati, pārājikaṃ. Sāmikehi pana lāyitvā ṭhapitaṃ sabhusaṃ vā abhusaṃ vā katvā gaṇhato yena vatthu pūrati, tasmiṃ gahite pārājikaṃ. Sace parikappeti “idaṃ madditvā papphoṭetvā sārameva gaṇhissāmī”ti rakkhati tāva. Maddanapapphoṭanesu ṭhānā cāventassāpi pārājikaṃ natthi, pacchā bhājanagate katamatte pārājikaṃ. Abhiyogo panettha vuttanayo eva.

A rice stalk can be long; as long as the stalk of the rice head does not emerge from within the sheath, it protects. If even a hair's breadth of the stalk emerges from the sheath at its lower surface, it should be treated according to the value of the goods. However, for one who takes by reaping with a sickle, even if the stalks in the handful are cut below, if the heads are entangled, they still protect. But having disentangled them, if for one who lifts even a hair's breadth the object of theft is complete, it is a pārājika offense. Furthermore, if one takes rice that has been reaped and set down by the owners, whether with husk or without husk, when one has taken the amount by which the object of theft is completed, it is a pārājika offense. If one intends, 'I will take only the kernel after crushing, shaking, and winnowing this,' it remains protected for that long. There is no pārājika offense even for one who displaces it from its place during crushing and shaking; afterwards, at the very moment of having placed it in a container, it is a pārājika offense. The legal claim here is just as has been stated.

Khīlasaṅkamanādīsu pathavī nāma anagghā. Tasmā sace ekeneva khīlena ito kesaggamattampi pathavippadesaṃ sāmikānaṃ passantānaṃ vā apassantānaṃ vā attano santakaṃ karoti, tasmiṃ khīle nāmaṃ chinditvā vā acchinditvā vā saṅkāmitamatte tassa ca, ye cassa ekacchandā, sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Sace pana [M 1.0297] dvīhi khīlehi gahetabbaṃ hoti, paṭhame khīle thullaccayaṃ; dutiye pārājikaṃ. Sace tīhi gahetabbaṃ hoti, paṭhame dukkaṭaṃ, dutiye thullaccayaṃ, tatiye pārājikaṃ. Evaṃ bahukesupi avasāne dve ṭhapetvā purimehi dukkaṭaṃ, avasāne [P 2.0341][V 1.0273] dvinnaṃ ekena thullaccayaṃ, itarena pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tañca kho sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepena. Evaṃ sabbattha.

In cases of moving boundary stakes and so on, the earth is of inestimable value. Therefore, if with just one stake one makes a plot of land from this side, even a hair's breadth, one's own property—whether the owners are seeing it or not—then at the very moment of having moved that stake, whether having carved a name on it or not, it is a pārājika offense for that person and for all who are of the same intention. However, if the land is to be taken with two stakes, on moving the first stake there is a thullaccaya offense; on the second, a pārājika offense. If it is to be taken with three, on the first there is a dukkaṭa offense, on the second a thullaccaya, and on the third a pārājika.
