Similarly, even with many stakes, leaving the last two, for the preceding ones there is a dukkaṭa offense; of the last two, for one there is a thullaccaya, and for the other a pārājika offense is to be understood. And this is to be understood in relation to the owners' relinquishing of responsibility. Thus it is in all cases.

Rajjuṃ vāti “mama santakaṃ ida”nti ñāpetukāmo rajjuṃ vā pasāreti, yaṭṭhiṃ vā pāteti, dukkaṭaṃ. “Idāni dvīhi payogehi attano santakaṃ karissāmī”ti tesaṃ paṭhame thullaccayaṃ, dutiye pārājikaṃ.

Regarding a rope, if one, wishing to make it known, 'This is my property,' stretches out a rope or throws down a stick, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If one intends, 'Now I will make it my own with two efforts,' for the first of these there is a thullaccaya offense, and for the second, a pārājika offense.

Vatiṃ vāti parassa khettaṃ parikkhepavasena attano kātukāmo dārūni nikhaṇati, payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Ekasmiṃ anāgate thullaccayaṃ, tasmiṃ āgate pārājikaṃ. Sace tattakena asakkonto sākhāparivāreneva attano kātuṃ sakkoti, sākhāpātanepi eseva nayo. Evaṃ yena yena parikkhipitvā attano kātuṃ sakkoti, tattha tattha paṭhamapayogehi dukkaṭaṃ. Avasāne dvinnaṃ ekena thullaccayaṃ, itarena pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding a fence, if one, wishing to make another's field one's own by means of enclosing it, plants wooden posts, for each effort there is a dukkaṭa offense. Before the final one is in place, there is a thullaccaya offense; when it is in place, a pārājika offense. If, being unable to do so with that much, one can make it one's own only with an enclosure of branches, this same method applies to the felling of branches. Thus, by whatever means one is able to enclose and make it one's own, for the initial efforts there is a dukkaṭa offense. At the end, of the last two, for one there is a thullaccaya, and for the other a pārājika offense is to be understood.

Mariyādaṃ vāti parassa khettaṃ “mama ida”nti ñāpetukāmo attano khettamariyādaṃ

Regarding a boundary, if one, wishing to make it known 'This is mine' concerning another's field, alters the boundary of one's own field,

Kedārapāḷiṃ yathā parassa khettaṃ atikkamati, evaṃ saṅkāmeti, paṃsumattikādīhi vā vaḍḍhetvā vitthataṃ karoti, akataṃ vā pana patiṭṭhāpeti, purimapayogehi dukkaṭaṃ. Dvinnaṃ pacchimānaṃ ekena thullaccayaṃ, itarena pārājikanti.

by moving the paddy-ridge in such a way that it encroaches upon another's field, or by making it wider by adding soil, clay, and the like, or by establishing one where none was made before—for the initial efforts, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Of the last two, for one there is a thullaccaya offense, and for the other, a pārājika offense.

Khettaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Field-Located Items is concluded.

Vatthuṭṭhakathā

Commentary on Site-Located Items

105. Vatthuṭṭhepi – vatthuṃ tāva dassento vatthu nāma “ārāmavatthu vihāravatthū”ti āha. Tattha bījaṃ vā uparopake vā aropetvāva kevalaṃ bhūmiṃ sodhetvā tiṇṇaṃ pākārānaṃ yena kenaci parikkhipitvā vā aparikkhipitvā vā pupphārāmādīnaṃ atthāya ṭhapito bhūmibhāgo ārāmavatthu nāma. Eteneva nayena ekavihārapariveṇaāvāsānaṃ atthāya ṭhapito bhūmibhāgo vihāravatthu nāma. Yopi pubbe ārāmo [M 1.0298] ca vihāro ca hutvā pacchā vinassitvā bhūmimatto ṭhito, ārāmavihārakiccaṃ na karoti, sopi ārāmavihāravatthusaṅgaheneva saṅgahito. Vinicchayo panettha khettaṭṭhe vuttasadisoyevāti.

105. Regarding site-located items: first, showing what a site is, he said, 'A site is called "a monastery site" or "a dwelling site."' Therein, a portion of land that, without yet having planted seeds or saplings, has been merely cleared and set aside for the purpose of flower gardens and the like, whether enclosed by any of the three kinds of walls or not enclosed, is called a 'monastery site.' By this same method, a portion of land set aside for the purpose of a single monastery, a single precinct, or a single dwelling is called a 'dwelling site.' Moreover, a place which, having formerly been a monastery and a dwelling, was later destroyed and remains as mere land, not performing the function of a monastery or dwelling, that too is included under the category of 'monastery site' and 'dwelling site.' The judgment here is just like that stated in the section on field-located items.

Vatthuṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Site-Located Items is concluded.

106. Gāmaṭṭhe [V 1.0274] yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ vuttameva.

106. Regarding village-located items, what was to be said has already been said.

Araññaṭṭhakathā

Commentary on Wilderness-Located Items

107. Araññaṭṭhe [P 2.0342] – araññaṃ tāva dassento “araññaṃ nāma yaṃ manussānaṃ pariggahitaṃ hoti, taṃ arañña”nti āha. Tattha yasmā araññaṃ nāma manussānaṃ pariggahitampi atthi, apariggahitampi; idha pana yaṃ pariggahitaṃ sārakkhaṃ, yato na vinā mūlena kaṭṭhalatādīni gahetuṃ labbhanti, taṃ adhippetaṃ. Tasmā “yaṃ manussānaṃ pariggahitaṃ hotī”ti vatvā puna “arañña”nti vuttaṃ. Tena imamatthaṃ dasseti – “na pariggahitabhāvo araññassa lakkhaṇaṃ. Yaṃ pana attano araññalakkhaṇena araññaṃ manussānañca pariggahitaṃ, taṃ imasmiṃ atthe arañña”nti. Tattha vinicchayo ārāmaṭṭhādīsu vuttasadiso.

107. Regarding wilderness-located items: first, showing what wilderness is, he said, 'Wilderness is that which is possessed by humans; that is wilderness.' Therein, since there is wilderness that is possessed by humans and that which is not possessed, in this context, however, what is intended is that which is possessed and guarded, from which one cannot take wood, vines, and so forth without payment. Therefore, having said, 'that which is possessed by humans,' it is again said, 'wilderness.' By that, he shows this meaning: 'The state of being possessed is not the characteristic of wilderness. But that which is wilderness by its own characteristic of wilderness, and is also possessed by humans, that is "wilderness" in this context.' The judgment there is similar to that stated for monastery-located items and so on.

Tatthajātakesu panettha ekasmimpi mahaggharukkhe chinnamatte pārājikaṃ. Lataṃ vāti ettha ca vettopi latāpi latā eva; tattha yo vetto vā latā vā dīghā hoti, mahārukkhe ca gacche ca vinivijjhitvā vā veṭhetvā vā gatā, sā mūle chinnāpi avahāraṃ na janeti agge chinnāpi, yadā pana aggepi mūlepi chinnā hoti, tadā avahāraṃ janeti. Sace pana veṭhetvā ṭhitā hoti, veṭhetvā ṭhitā pana rukkhato mocitamattā avahāraṃ janeti.

Here, among things grown in that place, upon the mere cutting of even a single valuable tree, it is a pārājika offense. In the phrase 'or a creeper,' both rattan and a creeper are just 'creeper.' Therein, whichever rattan or creeper is long and has gone piercing or entwining a large tree and a bush, it does not constitute a theft even when cut at the base, nor when cut at the top. But when it is cut at both the top and the base, it constitutes a theft. However, if it is standing entwined, it constitutes a theft only upon being freed from the tree.

Tiṇaṃ vāti ettha tiṇaṃ vā hotu paṇṇaṃ vā, sabbaṃ tiṇaggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ; taṃ gehacchadanādīnamatthāya parehi chinnaṃ vā attanā chinditvā vā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Na kevalañca tiṇapaṇṇameva, aññampi yaṃkiñci vākachalli ādi, yattha sāmikā sālayā, taṃ gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Tacchetvā ṭhapito addhagatopi rukkho na gahetabbo. Yo pana agge ca mūle ca chinno hoti, sākhāpissa pūtikā [M 1.0299] jātā, challiyopi gaḷitā, “ayaṃ sāmikehi chaḍḍito”ti gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Lakkhaṇacchinnassāpi yadā lakkhaṇaṃ challiyā pariyonaddhaṃ hoti, tadā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Gehādīnaṃ atthāya rukkhe chinditvā yadā tāni katāni ajjhāvutthāni ca honti, dārūnipi araññe vassena ca ātapena ca vinassanti, īdisānipi disvā “chaḍḍitānī”ti gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Yasmā araññasāmikā etesaṃ anissarā. Yehi araññasāmikānaṃ deyyadhammaṃ datvā [P 2.0343] chinnāni, te eva issarā, tehi ca tāni chaḍḍitāni, nirālayā tattha jātāti.

Herein, in the phrase 'or grass,' whether it be grass or a leaf, all is included by the term 'grass.' One who takes that—whether cut by others or having cut it oneself—for the purpose of roofing a house and so on, is to be charged according to the value of the goods. And not only grass and leaves, but also anything else such as bark fiber, bark, and so forth, for which the owners have attachment; one who takes it is to be charged according to the value of the goods. A tree that has been trimmed and set aside, even one that is old, should not be taken. But a tree that is cut at the top and at the base, its branches have become rotten, and its bark has fallen off—it is permissible to take it, thinking, 'This has been abandoned by the owners.' Even in the case of a tree marked for cutting, when the mark becomes covered over by the bark, it is then permissible to take it. When, after cutting trees for the purpose of houses and so on, those structures are built and inhabited, and the timber in the forest is being destroyed by rain and sun, upon seeing even such timber, it is permissible to take it, thinking, 'It has been abandoned.' Why? Because the owners of the forest are not the masters of these things. Those by whom the trees were cut, having given the due payment to the forest owners, they alone are the masters. And by them, those things have been abandoned; they have become unattached to them.

Yopi [V 1.0275] bhikkhu paṭhamaṃyeva araññapālānaṃ deyyadhammaṃ datvā araññaṃ pavisitvā yathārucite rukkhe gāhāpeti, tassa tesaṃ ārakkhaṭṭhānaṃ agantvāpi yathārucitena maggena gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Athāpi pavisanto adatvā “nikkhamanto dassāmī”ti rukkhe gāhāpetvā nikkhamanto tesaṃ dātabbaṃ datvā gacchati, vaṭṭati eva. Athāpi ābhogaṃ katvā gacchati “dehī”ti vutte “dassāmī”ti, “dehī”ti vutte dātabbameva. Sace koci attano dhanaṃ datvā “bhikkhussa gantuṃ dethā”ti vadati, laddhakappameva, gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana koci issarajātiko dhanaṃ adatvāva “bhikkhūnaṃ bhāgaṃ mā gaṇhathā”ti vāreti, araññapālā ca “mayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tāpasānañca bhāgaṃ agaṇhantā kuto lacchāma, detha, bhante”ti vadanti, dātabbameva.

Moreover, a monk who, having first given the due payment to the forest guards, enters the forest and has trees taken as he desires, it is permissible for him to go by a path of his choosing, even without going to their guard post. Or, entering without giving, thinking, 'I will give when leaving,' he has trees taken, and upon leaving, gives what is to be given and departs—it is indeed permissible. Or, he goes having formed the intention, 'When told, "Give," I will give'; when told, 'Give,' it must be given. If someone, giving their own money, says, 'Allow the monk to go,' it is a permitted allowance; it is permissible to go. But if some person of authority, without giving money, forbids them, saying, 'Do not take the monks' share,' and the forest guards say, 'If we do not take the share from monks and ascetics, from where will we get anything? Give, venerable sirs,' then it must be given.

Yo pana araññapālesu niddāyantesu vā kīḷāpasutesu vā katthaci pakkantesu vā āgantvā “kuhiṃ araññapālā”ti pakkositvāpi adisvā gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Yopi ārakkhaṭṭhānaṃ patvā kammaṭṭhānādīni manasikaronto vā aññavihito vā assatiyā atikkamati, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Yassāpi taṃ ṭhānaṃ pattassa coro vā hatthī vā vāḷamigo vā mahāmegho vā vuṭṭhahati, so ca tamhā upaddavā muccitukamyatāya sahasā taṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamati, rakkhati tāva, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. Idaṃ pana araññe ārakkhaṭṭhānaṃ nāma suṅkaghātatopi garukataraṃ. Suṅkaghātassa hi paricchedaṃ anokkamitvā dūratova pariharanto dukkaṭameva āpajjati. Idaṃ pana theyyacittena pariharantassa ākāsena gacchatopi pārājikameva. Tasmā ettha appamattena bhavitabbanti.

But a monk who, arriving when the forest guards are sleeping or engaged in play, or have gone off somewhere, calls out, 'Where are the forest guards?' and then leaves without seeing them, payment for the goods is due. And one who, having reached the guard post, passes by out of mindlessness, whether reflecting on meditation subjects or being otherwise occupied, payment for the goods is indeed due. And for one who has reached that place, should a thief, an elephant, a beast of prey, or a great storm cloud arise, and he, out of a desire to be freed from that danger, hastily passes beyond that place, he protects himself for the time being, but payment for the goods is due. Moreover, this guard post in the forest is more serious than a customs post. For one who avoids a customs post from afar, without entering its boundary, incurs only a dukkaṭa offense. But for one who avoids this post with a thievish mind, even if going through the sky, it is a pārājika offense. Therefore, one must be diligent in this matter.

Araññaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Forest Commentary is concluded.

Udakakathā

The Discourse on Water

108. Udake [M 1.0300] pana – bhājanagatanti udakadullabhakāle udakamaṇikādīsu bhājanesu saṅgopetvā ṭhapitaṃ; taṃ yasmiṃ bhājane ṭhapitaṃ hoti, taṃ bhājanaṃ āviñchitvā vā chiddaṃ katvā vā tattha pokkharaṇītaḷākesu ca attano bhājanaṃ pavesetvā [P 2.0344] gaṇhantassa sappitelesu vuttanayena vinicchayo veditabbo.

108. Now, concerning water—regarding water in a vessel: at a time when water is scarce, it is stored securely in containers such as water pots. For one who takes it by either tilting the vessel in which it is placed, or by making a hole in it, or by inserting one's own vessel into those containers or into square ponds and reservoirs, the decision is to be understood in the manner stated concerning ghee and oil.

Mariyādacchedane pana tattha jātakabhūtagāmena saddhimpi mariyādaṃ chindantassa adinnādānapayogattā dukkaṭaṃ. Tañca pana pahāre pahāre hoti. Antoṭhatvā bahimukho chindanto bahi antena kāretabbo. Bahi ṭhatvā antomukho chindanto [V 1.0276] antoantena kāretabbo. Anto ca bahi ca chinditvā majjhe ṭhapetvā taṃ chindanto majjhena kāretabbo. Mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā gāvo pakkosati, gāmadārakehi vā pakkosāpeti, tā āgantvā khurehi mariyādaṃ chindanti, teneva chinnā hoti. Mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā gāvo udake paveseti, gāmadārakehi vā pavesāpeti, tāhi uṭṭhāpitavīciyo mariyādaṃ bhinditvā gacchanti. Gāmadārake vā “udake kīḷathā”ti vadati, kīḷante vā utrāseti, tehi uṭṭhāpitavīciyopi mariyādaṃ chinditvā gacchanti. Antoudake jātarukkhaṃ chindati, aññena vā chindāpeti, tenapi patantena uṭṭhāpitavīciyo mariyādaṃ chinditvā gacchanti, teneva chinnā hoti. Mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā taḷākarakkhaṇatthāya taḷākato nibbahanaudakaṃ vā niddhamanatumbaṃ vā pidahati, aññato gacchantaṃ vā udakaṃ yathā ettha pavisati, evaṃ pāḷiṃ vā bandhati, mātikaṃ vā ujukaṃ karoti, tassa uparibhāge ṭhitaṃ attano taḷākaṃ vā bhindati, ussannaṃ udakaṃ mariyādaṃ gahetvā gacchati, teneva chinnā hoti. Sabbattha nikkhantaudakagghānurūpena avahārena kāretabbo.

Now, concerning the cutting of an embankment: for one who cuts the embankment along with the living plants growing on it, there is a dukkaṭa offense because of the effort of taking what is not given. And this occurs with every strike. One who, standing inside and facing outward, cuts, is to be charged according to the outer edge. One who, standing outside and facing inward, cuts, is to be charged according to the inner edge. One who, having cut on the inside and the outside, leaves the middle and then cuts that, is to be charged according to the middle. Having weakened the embankment, if he calls cows, or has village children call them, and they come and break the embankment with their hooves, it is considered to have been broken by him. Having weakened the embankment, if he makes cows enter the water, or has village children make them enter, the waves raised by them break the embankment and pass through. Or if he tells village children, 'Play in the water,' or frightens them while they are playing, the waves raised by them also break the embankment and pass through. If he cuts a tree growing in the water, or has another cut it, the waves raised by it as it falls also break the embankment and pass through; it is considered to have been broken by him. Having weakened the embankment, if, in order to protect the reservoir, he blocks the reservoir's water outlet or drain pipe; or if he builds an embankment or straightens a channel so that water going elsewhere enters here; or if he breaks his own reservoir situated above it, and the abundant water carries away the embankment, it is considered to have been broken by him. In all cases, he is to be charged with theft corresponding to the value of the water that has gone out.

Niddhamanapanāḷiṃ ugghāṭetvā nīharantassāpi eseva nayo. Sace pana tena mariyādāya dubbalāya katāya attano dhammatāya āgantvā vā anāṇattehi gāmadārakehi āropitā vā gāviyo khurehi mariyādaṃ bhindanti, attanoyeva dhammatāya anāṇattehi vā gāmadārakehi udake pavesitā vīciyo uṭṭhāpenti, gāmadārakā vā sayameva pavisitvā kīḷantā uṭṭhāpenti antoudake vā rukkho aññena chijjamāno [M 1.0301] patitvā uṭṭhāpeti, uṭṭhāpitā vīciyo mariyādaṃ chindanti, sacepi mariyādaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā sukkhataḷākassa udakanibbahanaṭṭhānaṃ [P 2.0345] vā udakaniddhamanatumbaṃ vā pidahati, aññato gamanamagge vā pāḷiṃ bandhati, sukkhamātikaṃ vā ujukaṃ karoti, pacchā deve vuṭṭhe udakaṃ āgantvā mariyādaṃ bhindati, sabbattha bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ.

For one who opens the drain-pipe and lets water out, this is the very same method. But if, after the embankment has been made weak by him, cows break the embankment with their hooves, having come by their own nature or having been driven onto it by uninstructed village children; or if cows, having entered the water by their own nature or having been made to enter by uninstructed village children, raise waves; or if village children, having entered by themselves and playing, raise waves; or if a tree, being cut by another, falls into the water and raises waves, and these raised waves break the embankment; and if, having weakened the embankment, he blocks the water outlet or drain-pipe of a dry reservoir, or builds an embankment on a path going elsewhere, or straightens a dry channel, and afterwards, when it rains, the water comes and breaks the embankment—in all cases, restitution for the goods is to be made.

Yo pana nidāghe sukkhavāpiyā mariyādaṃ yāva talaṃ pāpetvā chindati, pacchā deve vuṭṭhe āgatāgataṃ udakaṃ palāyati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Yattakaṃ tappaccayā sassaṃ uppajjati, tato pādamattagghanakampi adento sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepena assamaṇo hoti.

Now, whoever in the hot season cuts the embankment of a dry reservoir down to its base, so that afterwards, when it rains, all the water that comes flows away, restitution for the goods is to be made. Whatever crop could have been produced on account of that water, if he does not give to the owners compensation worth even a quarter of it, by this abandonment of duty, he is not a monk.

Yaṃ pana sabbasādhāraṇaṃ taḷākaṃ hoti; taḷāke udakassa sabbepi manussā issarā. Heṭṭhato panassa sassāni karonti, sassapālanatthaṃ taḷākato mahāmātikā nikkhamitvā khettamajjhena yāti, sāpi sadā sandanakāle sabbasādhāraṇā. Tato pana khuddakamātikā nīharitvā [V 1.0277] attano attano kedāresu udakaṃ pavesenti. Taṃ aññesaṃ gahetuṃ na denti. Nidāghasamayeva udake mandībhūte vārena udakaṃ denti, yo udakavāre sampatte na labhati, tassa sassāni milāyanti; tasmā aññesaṃ vāre añño gahetuṃ na labhati. Tattha yo bhikkhu paresaṃ khuddakamātikāto vā kedārato vā udakaṃ theyyacittena attano vā parassa vā mātikaṃ vā kedāraṃ vā paveseti, aṭavimukhaṃ vā vāheti, avahāro vassa hoti.

Now, as for a reservoir that is common to all, all people are masters of the water in the reservoir. But below it, they cultivate crops. For the purpose of nourishing the crops, a large main channel goes out from the reservoir and runs through the middle of the fields; that too, at the time of flowing, is common to all. Then, having led out small channels from it, they make water enter their own respective fields. They do not allow others to take that water. In the hot season itself, when the water becomes scarce, they distribute water by turns. Whoever does not get water when his turn arrives, his crops wither; therefore, another does not get to take it during the turn of others. In this situation, if a monk with intent to steal makes water from another's small channel or field enter his own or another's channel or field, or makes it flow towards the forest, it is theft for him.

Yopi “cirena me udakavāro bhavissati, idañca sassaṃ milāyatī”ti paresaṃ kedāre

And whoever, thinking, “It will be a long time before my water turn comes, and this crop is withering,” in others’ fields—

Pavisantassa udakassa pavisanamaggaṃ pidahitvā attano kedāraṃ paveseti, avahāro eva. Sace pana taḷākato aniggate paresaṃ mātikāmukhaṃ asampatteva udake sukkhamātikaṃyeva yathā āgacchantaṃ udakaṃ aññesaṃ kedāre appavisitvā attanoyeva kedāraṃ pavisati, evaṃ tattha tattha bandhati. Anikkhante baddhā subaddhā, nikkhante baddhā, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Taḷākaṃ gantvā sayameva niddhamanapanāḷiṃ ugghāṭetvā attano kedāraṃ pavesentassāpi natthi [P 2.0346] avahāro. Kasmā? Taḷākaṃ nissāya khettassa katattā. Kurundiyādīsu pana “avahāro”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ [M 1.0302] “vatthuṃ kālañca desañcā”ti iminā lakkhaṇena na sameti. Tasmā mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva yuttanti.

…having blocked the entry path of the entering water, makes it enter his own field, it is indeed theft. But if, before the water has gone out from the reservoir and before it has reached the mouth of others' channels, he dams up the dry channel itself here and there in such a way that the incoming water, without entering the fields of others, enters only his own field; if it is dammed before the water has gone out, it is well-dammed; if it is dammed after it has gone out, restitution for the goods is to be made. Even for one who goes to the reservoir and himself opens the drain-pipe to make water enter his own field, there is no theft. Why? Because the field was made in dependence on the reservoir. But in the Kurundī and other commentaries, it is said, 'It is theft.' That does not agree with this characteristic of 'object, time, and place.' Therefore, what is said in the Great Commentary is indeed proper.

Udakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Water is concluded.

Dantaponakathā

The Explanation of Tooth-sticks

109. Dantapoṇaṃ ārāmaṭṭhakavinicchayena vinicchinitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yo saṅghassa vetanabhato hutvā devasikaṃ vā pakkhamāsavārena vā dantakaṭṭhaṃ āharati, so taṃ āharitvā chinditvāpi yāva bhikkhusaṅghaṃ na sampaṭicchāpeti, tāva tasseva hoti. Tasmā taṃ theyyacittena gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Tatthajātakaṃ pana garubhaṇḍaṃ, tampi bhikkhusaṅghena rakkhitagopitaṃ gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Eseva nayo gaṇapuggalagihimanussasantakepi chinnake acchinnake ca. Tesaṃ ārāmuyyānabhūmīsu jātaṃ sāmaṇerā vārena bhikkhusaṅghassa dantakaṭṭhaṃ āharantā ācariyupajjhāyānampi āharanti, taṃ yāva chinditvā saṅghaṃ na paṭicchāpenti, tāva sabbaṃ tesaṃyeva hoti. Tasmā tampi theyyacittena gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Yadā pana te chinditvā saṅghassa paṭicchāpetvā dantakaṭṭhamāḷake nikkhipanti, “yathāsukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho paribhuñjatū”ti; tato paṭṭhāya avahāro natthi, vattaṃ pana jānitabbaṃ. Yo hi devasikaṃ saṅghamajjhe osarati, tena divase divase ekameva dantakaṭṭhaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Yo pana [V 1.0278] devasikaṃ na osarati, padhānaghare vasitvā dhammasavane vā uposathagge vā dissati, tena pamāṇaṃ sallakkhetvā cattāri pañcadantakaṭṭhāni attano vasanaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā khāditabbāni. Tesu khīṇesu sace punapi dantakaṭṭhamāḷake bahūni hontiyeva, punapi āharitvā khāditabbāni. Yadi pana pamāṇaṃ asallakkhetvā āharati, tesu akkhīṇesuyeva māḷake khīyanti, tato keci therā “yehi gahitāni, te paṭiāharantū”ti vadeyyuṃ, keci “khādantu, puna sāmaṇerā āharissantī”ti, tasmā vivādapariharaṇatthaṃ [P 2.0347] pamāṇaṃ sallakkhetabbaṃ. Gahaṇe pana doso natthi. Maggaṃ gacchantenāpi ekaṃ vā dve vā thavikāya pakkhipitvā gantabbanti.

109. The matter of a tooth-stick should be decided according to the method for deciding on property established in a monastery. Herein, this is the distinction: If someone, being a paid servant of the Saṅgha, brings a tooth-stick daily or by the turn of a fortnight or a month, that tooth-stick remains his own property until he has brought it, cut it, and handed it over to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Therefore, one who takes it with the intention to steal should be made to pay according to the value of the goods. Furthermore, a tooth-stick that has grown there is property of consequence; if one takes even that, which has been guarded and protected by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, one should be made to pay according to the value of the goods. This same method applies to what is owned by a group, an individual, or a householder, whether it is cut or uncut, and also to what has grown in their monastery grounds or garden grounds. When novices, taking turns, bring tooth-sticks for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they also bring them for their teachers and preceptors. Until they have cut them and handed them over to the Saṅgha, all of it remains their own property. Therefore, if one takes that too with the intention to steal, one should be made to pay according to the value of the goods. But when they, having cut and handed them over to the Saṅgha, place them on the tooth-stick stand, thinking, 'Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus use them at their convenience,' from that point on there is no misappropriation. However, the proper conduct should be known. Indeed, whoever enters the midst of the Saṅgha daily should take only one tooth-stick each day. But whoever does not enter daily, but lives in a meditation hall and is seen at a Dhamma-hearing or in the Uposatha hall, he, having considered the amount, may take four or five tooth-sticks, keep them at his dwelling place, and chew them. When those are exhausted, if there are still many on the tooth-stick stand, he may bring more and chew them. But if he brings them without considering the amount, and the tooth-sticks on the stand run out while his own are not yet exhausted, then some elders might say, 'Let those by whom they were taken bring them back,' while others might say, 'Let them chew; the novices will bring more.' Therefore, to avoid dispute, the amount should be considered. However, there is no fault in the taking. Even one going on a journey may put one or two in a bag and go.

Dantaponakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Tooth-sticks is concluded.

Vanappatikathā

The Explanation of Forest Trees

110. Vanassa [M 1.0303] patīti vanappati; vanajeṭṭhakarukkhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana sabbopi manussehi pariggahitarukkho adhippeto ambalabujapanasādiko. Yattha vā pana maricavalliādīni āropenti, so chijjamāno sace ekāyapi challiyā vā vākena vā sakalikāya vā pheggunā vā sambaddhova hutvā bhūmiyaṃ patati, rakkhati tāva.

110. “Lord of the forest” (vanassa pati), thus it is a “vanappati”; this is a designation for the chief tree of the forest. Here, however, any tree taken possession of by humans is intended, such as the mango, labuja, jackfruit, and so on. Furthermore, also intended is a tree on which they plant pepper vines and the like. If that tree, while being cut, falls to the ground but remains connected by even a single piece of bark, or bast, or a splinter, or sapwood, it is protected for that long.

Yo pana chinnopi vallīhi vā sāmantarukkhasākhāhi vā sambaddho sandhāritattā ujukameva tiṭṭhati, patanto vā bhūmiṃ na pāpuṇāti, natthi tattha parihāro, avahāro eva hoti. Yopi kakacena chinno acchinno viya hutvā tatheva tiṭṭhati, tasmimpi eseva nayo.

But as for a tree which, though cut, stands upright because it is connected to and supported by vines or the branches of a nearby tree, or which, in falling, does not reach the ground, there is no avoidance in that case; it is indeed a misappropriation. This same method also applies to a tree which, having been cut with a saw, stands just as it was, as if uncut.

Yo pana rukkhaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā pacchā cāletvā pāteti, aññena vā cālāpeti; aññaṃ vāssa santike rukkhaṃ chinditvā ajjhottharati, parena vā ajjhottharāpeti; makkaṭe vā paripātetvā tattha āropeti, aññena vā āropāpeti; vagguliyo vā tattha āropeti, parena vā āropāpeti; tā taṃ rukkhaṃ pātenti, tasseva avahāro.

But if someone, having weakened a tree, afterwards shakes it and fells it, or has another shake it; or cuts another tree near it and makes it fall upon the first, or has another make it fall upon it; or, having chased monkeys, makes them climb onto it, or has another make them climb; or makes bats climb onto it, or has another make them climb; and if they fell that tree, it is a misappropriation on his part.

Sace pana tena rukkhe dubbale kate añño anāṇatto eva taṃ cāletvā pāteti,

But if, when the tree has been weakened by him, another person, uncommanded, shakes it and fells it,

Rukkhena vā ajjhottharati, attano dhammatāya makkaṭā vā vagguliyo vā ārohanti, paro vā anāṇatto āropeti, sayaṃ vā esa vātamukhaṃ sodheti, balavavāto āgantvā rukkhaṃ pāteti; sabbattha bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Vātamukhasodhanaṃ panettha asampatte vāte sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇādīhi [V 1.0279] sameti, no aññathā. Rukkhaṃ āvijjhitvā satthena vā ākoṭeti, aggiṃ vā deti, maṇḍukakaṇṭakaṃ vā visaṃ vā ākoṭeti, yena so marati, sabbattha bhaṇḍadeyyamevāti.

or makes another tree fall upon it; or monkeys or bats climb on it of their own accord; or another person, uncommanded, makes them climb on it; or if he himself clears the path of the wind, and a strong wind comes and fells the tree—in all cases, there is payment for the goods. Herein, clearing the path of the wind is comparable to actions such as straightening a dry water-channel before the wind has arrived, but not otherwise. If, having gone around a tree, one strikes it with a weapon, or applies fire, or inserts a shark's thorn or poison, by which it dies—in all cases, there is indeed payment for the goods.

Vanappatikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Forest Trees is finished.

Haraṇakakathā

The Explanation on Taking Away

111. Haraṇake [M 1.0304][P 2.0348] – aññassa haraṇakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacitto āmasatīti paraṃ sīsabhārādīhi bhaṇḍaṃ ādāya gacchantaṃ disvā “etaṃ harissāmī”ti vegena gantvā āmasati, ettāvatā assa dukkaṭaṃ. Phandāpetīti ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanaṃ karoti, sāmiko na muñcati, tenassa thullaccayaṃ. Ṭhānā cāvetīti ākaḍḍhitvā sāmikassa hatthato moceti, tenassa pārājikaṃ. Sace pana taṃ bhaṇḍasāmiko uṭṭhahitvā pothetvā puna taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ mocāpetvā gaṇheyya, bhikkhu paṭhamaggahaṇeneva pārājiko. Sīsato vā kaṇṇato vā gīvato vā hatthato vā alaṅkāraṃ chinditvā vā mocetvā vā gaṇhantassa sīsādīhi mocitamatte pārājikaṃ. Hatthe pana valayaṃ vā kaṭakaṃ vā anīharitvā aggabāhaṃ ghaṃsantova aparāparaṃ vā sāreti, ākāsagataṃ vā karoti, rakkhati tāva. Rukkhamūlacīvaravaṃsesu valayamiva na pārājikaṃ janeti. Kasmā? Saviññāṇakattā. Saviññāṇakakoṭṭhāsagatañhi yāva tato na nīhaṭaṃ, tāva tattheva hoti. Eseva nayo aṅgulimuddikapādakaṭakakaṭūpagapiḷandhanesu.

111. Regarding things taken away: if one with a thievish intention touches another's goods—that is, seeing someone going along carrying goods on their head and so forth, and thinking, “I will take this,” one goes with speed and touches it—by that much, for him there is a dukkaṭa offense. If one makes it move—that is, one performs a pulling towards or a pulling from side to side, but the owner does not let go—because of that, for him there is a thullaccaya offense. If one displaces it from its place—that is, having pulled it, one frees it from the owner's hand—because of that, for him there is a pārājika offense. If, however, the owner of the goods, having gotten up and struck him, then causes the goods to be released and takes them back, the monk is guilty of a pārājika offense by the very first act of taking. For one who takes an ornament from the head, or from the ear, or from the neck, or from the hand, having either cut it or removed it, there is a pārājika offense at the very moment it is freed from the head and so forth. But in the case of a bracelet or an armlet on the hand, if without taking it off one only rubs the upper arm, or moves it back and forth, or makes it go into the air, it is protected for the time being. It does not generate a pārājika offense, unlike a ring on a tree root or a robe-rack bamboo. Why? Because its base is a conscious being. Indeed, as long as an item that is on a conscious part of the body has not been taken from there, it remains right there. This is the same method for finger-rings, anklets, and waist-ornaments.

Yo pana parassa nivatthasāṭakaṃ acchindati, paro ca salajjitāya sahasā na muñcati, ekenantena coro kaḍḍhati, ekenantena paro, rakkhati tāva. Parassa hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Athāpi taṃ kaḍḍhantassa chijjitvā ekadeso hatthagato hoti, so ca pādaṃ agghati pārājikameva. Sahabhaṇḍahārakanti “sabhaṇḍahārakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ nessāmī”ti cintetvā “ito yāhī”ti bhaṇḍahārakaṃ tajjeti, so bhīto corena adhippetadisābhimukho hutvā ekaṃ pādaṃ saṅkāmeti, corassa thullaccayaṃ; dutiye pārājikaṃ. Pātāpetīti athāpi coro bhaṇḍahārakassa hatthe āvudhaṃ disvā sāsaṅko hutvā pātāpetvā gahetukāmo ekamantaṃ paṭikkamma santajjetvā pātāpeti, parassa hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ.

Furthermore, if a monk snatches another's worn robe, and the other person, out of shame, does not suddenly let go, the thief pulls on one end, and the other person pulls on the other end; for the time being, it is protected. At the very moment it is released from the other's hand, it is a pārājika offense. And if, while pulling it, a piece tears off and comes into his hand, and that piece is worth a pāda, it is a pārājika offense indeed. Regarding “the goods together with the carrier”: if, thinking, “I will take the goods together with their carrier,” one threatens the goods-carrier, saying, “Go this way,” and that person, being frightened, faces the direction desired by the thief and moves one footstep, for the thief there is a thullaccaya offense; on the second footstep, it is a pārājika offense. As for “causing to drop”: if the thief, seeing a weapon in the goods-carrier's hand, becomes apprehensive and, desiring to take the goods by causing them to be dropped, withdraws to one side, threatens him, and causes him to drop them, it is a pārājika offense at the very moment they are released from the other's hand.

Pātāpeti, āpatti dukkaṭassātiādi pana parikappavasena [P 2.0349] vuttaṃ. Yo hi bhaṇḍaṃ pātāpetvā “yaṃ mama ruccati, taṃ gahessāmī”ti parikappetvā pātāpeti, tassa pātāpane ca āmasane [V 1.0280] ca dukkaṭaṃ, phandāpane thullaccayaṃ. Pādagghanakassa ṭhānā cāvane pārājikaṃ. Taṃ pacchā paṭipātiyamānassa muñcatopi natthiyeva samaṇabhāvo. Yopi bhaṇḍahārakaṃ [M 1.0305] atikkamantaṃ disvā anubandhanto “tiṭṭha, tiṭṭha, bhaṇḍaṃ pātehī”ti vatvā pātāpeti, tassāpi tena hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ.

However, the statement beginning with “He causes to drop, the offense is a dukkaṭa” was spoken in connection with a pre-determined item. For the monk who, having pre-determined, “Having caused the goods to be dropped, I will take what pleases me,” causes them to be dropped, for him there is a dukkaṭa offense for causing them to be dropped and for touching them, and a thullaccaya offense for causing them to move. For displacing from its place an item worth a pāda, there is a pārājika offense. Even for one who releases it afterwards when it is being made to be dropped back, his status as a monk is simply gone. And also for the monk who, seeing a goods-carrier going past, follows him and, saying, “Stop, stop, drop the goods,” causes him to drop them—for him too, at the very moment they are released from that person's hand, there is a pārājika offense.

Yo pana “tiṭṭha tiṭṭhā”ti vadati, “pātehī”ti na vadati; itaro ca taṃ oloketvā “sace esa maṃ pāpuṇeyya, ghāteyyāpi ma” nti sālayova hutvā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahanaṭṭhāne pakkhipitvā “puna nivattitvā gahessāmī”ti pakkamati, pātanapaccayā pārājikaṃ natthi. Āgantvā pana theyyacittena gaṇhato uddhāre pārājikaṃ. Atha panassa evaṃ hoti – “mayā pātāpenteneva idaṃ mama santakaṃ kata”nti tato naṃ sakasaññāya gaṇhāti; gahaṇe rakkhati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. “Dehī”ti vutte adentassa sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepe pārājikaṃ. “So imaṃ chaḍḍetvā gato, anajjhāvutthakaṃ dāni ida”nti paṃsukūlasaññāya gaṇhatopi eseva nayo. Atha pana sāmiko “tiṭṭha tiṭṭhā”ti vuttamatteneva olokento taṃ disvā “na dāni idaṃ mayha”nti dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā nirālayo chaḍḍetvā palāyati, taṃ theyyacittena gaṇhato uddhāre dukkaṭaṃ. Āharāpente dātabbaṃ, adentassa pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Tassa payogena chaḍḍitattāti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññesu pana vicāraṇā eva natthi. Purimanayeneva sakasaññāya vā paṃsukūlasaññāya vā gaṇhantepi ayameva vinicchayoti.

Furthermore, if a monk says, 'Stop, stop,' but does not say, 'Drop it'; and the other person, looking at him, thinks, 'If this one should catch up to me, he might even kill me,' and, still having attachment to the goods, places those goods in a thicket and departs, thinking, 'I will come back again and take them,' there is no pārājika offense on account of the dropping. However, for one who comes back and takes it with a thievish intention, at the moment of lifting, there is a pārājika offense. But if this thought occurs to him: 'By my very act of causing it to be dropped, this was made my property,' and he then takes it with the perception that it is his own, he is protected from a pārājika offense at the time of taking, but the goods are to be returned. When told, 'Give it back,' for the one who does not give it back, there is a pārājika offense at the moment the owners relinquish responsibility. For one who takes it with the perception of it being discarded rags, thinking, 'He abandoned this and left; now this is unowned,' this is the same method. But if the owner, merely on being told, 'Stop, stop,' while looking, sees that monk and, relinquishing responsibility by thinking, 'Now this is not mine,' abandons it without attachment and then flees—for one who takes it with a thievish intention, at the moment of lifting, there is a dukkaṭa offense. If made to bring it back by the owners, it should be given; for one who does not give it, there is a pārājika offense. Why? Because it was abandoned due to his effort. Thus it is said in the Great Commentary. But in other commentaries, there is no such investigation. By the previously stated method, even for one who takes it with the perception of it being his own property or with the perception of it being discarded rags, this very same is the decision.

Haraṇakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Taking Away is concluded.

Upanidhikathā

The Discourse on Deposits

112. Upanidhimhi – nāhaṃ gaṇhāmīti sampajānamusāvādepi adinnādānassa payogattā dukkaṭaṃ. “Kiṃ tumhe bhaṇatha? Nevidaṃ mayhaṃ anurūpaṃ, na tumhāka”ntiādīni vadantassāpi dukkaṭameva. “Raho mayā etassa hatthe ṭhapitaṃ, na [P 2.0350] añño koci jānāti, ‘dassati nu kho me no’”ti sāmiko vimatiṃ uppādeti, bhikkhussa thullaccayaṃ. Tassa pharusādibhāvaṃ disvā sāmiko “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, tatra sacāyaṃ bhikkhu “kilametvā naṃ dassāmī”ti dāne saussāho, rakkhati tāva. Sacepi so dāne nirussāho, bhaṇḍassāmiko pana gahaṇe saussāho[M 1.0306], rakkhateva. Yadi pana so dāne nirussāho bhaṇḍasāmikopi “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, evaṃ ubhinnaṃ dhuranikkhepena bhikkhuno pārājikaṃ[V 1.0281]. Yadipi mukhena “dassāmī”ti vadati, cittena pana adātukāmo, evampi sāmikassa dhuranikkhepe pārājikaṃ. Taṃ pana upanidhi nāma saṅgopanatthāya attano hatthe parehi ṭhapitabhaṇḍaṃ, aguttadesato ṭhānā cāvetvā guttaṭṭhāne ṭhapanatthāya harato anāpatti. Theyyacittenapi ṭhānā cāventassa avahāro natthi. Kasmā? Attano hatthe nikkhittattā, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. Theyyacittena paribhuñjatopi eseva nayo. Tāvakālikaggahaṇepi tatheva. Dhammaṃ carantotiādi vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ tāva pāḷivaṇṇanā.

112. Regarding a deposit: even in the case of a deliberate falsehood, saying, “I did not receive it,” because it is a preliminary act of theft, it is a dukkaṭa offense. For a monk who says such things as, “What are you saying? This is not suitable for me, nor for you,” it is also a dukkaṭa offense. If the owner gives rise to doubt, thinking, “It was placed in his hand by me in private, no one else knows, ‘Will he give it back to me or not?’” for the monk, it is a thullaccaya offense. Seeing his harshness and so on, the owner gives up the responsibility, thinking, “He will not give it to me.” Therein, if this monk is diligent in giving, thinking, “I will give it to him after making him weary,” he is protected for the time being. Even if that monk is not diligent in giving, but the owner of the goods is diligent in reclaiming them, he is still protected. But if that monk is not diligent in giving, and the owner of the goods also gives up the responsibility, thinking, “He will not give it to me,” thus, through the giving up of responsibility by both, for the monk it is a pārājika offense. Even if he says with his mouth, “I will give it,” but with his mind is unwilling to give, even so, upon the owner's giving up of responsibility, it is a pārājika offense. Now, that which is called a deposit is goods placed in one's own hand by others for the purpose of safekeeping. For one who carries it from an unsafe place for the purpose of placing it in a safe place, there is no offense. Even for one who displaces it from its place with a thieving mind, there is no act of removal. Why? Because of it having been placed in his own hand; however, the goods are to be returned. For one who uses it with a thieving mind, this is the same rule. Even in the case of taking it temporarily, it is likewise. The phrase “practicing the Dhamma,” and so on, is as has been explained. This, for now, is the explanation of the Pāḷi.

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayo panettha pattacatukkādivasena evaṃ vutto – eko kira bhikkhu parassa mahagghe patte lobhaṃ uppādetvā taṃ haritukāmo ṭhapitaṭṭhānamassa suṭṭhu sallakkhetvā attanopi pattaṃ tasseva santike ṭhapesi. So paccūsasamaye āgantvā dhammaṃ vācāpetvā niddāyamānaṃ mahātheramāha – “vandāmi, bhante”ti. “Ko eso”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, āgantukabhikkhu, kālassevamhi gantukāmo, asukasmiñca me ṭhāne īdisena nāma aṃsabaddhakena īdisāya pattatthavikāya patto ṭhapito. Sādhāhaṃ, bhante, taṃ labheyya”nti thero pavisitvā taṃ gaṇhi. Uddhāreyeva corassa pārājikaṃ. Sace āgantvā “kosi tvaṃ avelāya āgato”ti [P 2.0351] vutto bhīto palāyati, pārājikaṃ patvāva palāyati. Therassa pana suddhacittattā anāpatti. Thero “taṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti aññaṃ gaṇhi, eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana aññaṃ tādisameva gaṇhante yujjati, manussaviggahe āṇattasadisavatthusmiṃ viya. Kurundiyaṃ pana “padavārena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ atādisameva gaṇhante yujjati.

Herein, the determination of cases outside the Pāḷi is explained thus by way of the fourfold case of the bowl, and so on. It is said that a certain monk, having aroused greed for another’s valuable bowl and wishing to steal it, carefully noted the place where it was kept and also placed his own bowl near that very one. Then, at dawn, he came, had the Dhamma recited, and said to the great elder who was dozing, “I pay respects, venerable sir.” “Who is this?” “I, venerable sir, am a visiting monk. I wish to go early. In such-and-such a place, my bowl with such-and-such a shoulder strap and such-and-such a bowl-bag has been placed. Good, venerable sir, may I get it?” The elder, having entered, took that bowl. At the very lifting, for the thief, it is a pārājika offense. If, having come, being spoken to thus, “Who are you, having come at an untimely hour?” he flees out of fear, he flees only after having committed the pārājika offense. But for the elder, because of his pure mind, there is no offense. The elder, thinking, “I will take that one,” took another; this is the same rule. This, however, is applicable when he takes another one that is just like it, like the case of an object similar to the one ordered in the training rule concerning killing a human being. But in the Kurundī, it is said, “He is to be dealt with by way of footsteps.” That is applicable when he takes one that is not like it.

Taṃ maññamāno attano pattaṃ gaṇhitvā adāsi, corassa sāmikena dinnattā pārājikaṃ natthi, asuddhacittena pana gahitattā dukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ maññamāno corasseva pattaṃ gaṇhitvā adāsi, idhāpi corassa attano santakattā pārājikaṃ natthi, asuddhacittena pana gahitattā dukkaṭameva. Sabbattha therassa anāpatti.

If, thinking it to be the one indicated, he took his own bowl and gave it, for the thief, because it was given by its owner, there is no pārājika offense; however, because it was taken with an impure mind, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If, thinking it to be the one indicated, he took the thief's own bowl and gave it, here too, for the thief, because it is his own property, there is no pārājika offense; however, because it was taken with an impure mind, it is a dukkaṭa offense indeed. In all cases, for the elder, there is no offense.

Aparo [M 1.0307] “pattaṃ coressāmī”ti tatheva niddāyamānaṃ theraṃ vandi. “Ko aya”nti ca vutte ‘ahaṃ, bhante, gilānabhikkhu, ekaṃ tāva me pattaṃ detha, gāmadvāraṃ gantvā bhesajjaṃ āharissāmī”ti. Thero “idha gilāno natthi, coro ayaṃ bhavissatī”ti sallakkhetvā “imaṃ haratū”ti attano veribhikkhussa pattaṃ nīharitvā adāsi, dvinnampi uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ. “Veribhikkhussa patto”ti saññāya aññassa pattaṃ uddharantepi eseva nayo. Sace pana “verissāya”nti saññāya corasseva pattaṃ uddharitvā deti, vuttanayeneva therassa pārājikaṃ, corassa [V 1.0282] dukkaṭaṃ. Atha “verissāya”nti maññamāno attano pattaṃ deti, vuttanayeneva ubhinnampi dukkaṭaṃ.

Another monk, thinking, “I will steal a bowl,” in the same way paid respects to the dozing elder. And when asked, “Who is this?” he replied, “Venerable sir, I am a sick monk. Please give me one bowl for now; I will go to the village gate and bring medicine.” The elder, having noted, “There is no sick monk here; this one must be a thief,” and thinking, “Let him take this one,” took out and gave the bowl of his enemy monk. For both, at the very lifting, it is a pārājika offense. Even when, with the perception “It is the enemy monk's bowl,” he takes out another's bowl, this is the same rule. But if, with the perception “This is the enemy's,” he takes out and gives the thief's own bowl, then according to the rule stated, for the elder it is a pārājika offense, and for the thief, a dukkaṭa offense. Then, if thinking “This is the enemy's,” he gives his own bowl, according to the rule stated, for both it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Eko mahāthero upaṭṭhākaṃ daharabhikkhuṃ “pattacīvaraṃ gaṇha, asukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ gantvā piṇḍāya carissāmā”ti āha. Daharo gahetvā therassa pacchato pacchato gacchanto theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā sace sīse bhāraṃ khandhe karoti, pārājikaṃ natthi. Kasmā? Āṇattiyā gahitattā. Sace pana maggato okkamma aṭaviṃ pavisati, padavārena kāretabbo. Atha nivattitvā vihārābhimukho palāyitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā gacchati, upacārātikkame pārājikaṃ. Athāpi mahātherassa nivāsanaparivattanaṭṭhānato gāmābhimukho palāyati, gāmūpacārātikkame pārājikaṃ. Yadi pana ubhopi piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjitvā vā [P 2.0352] gahetvā vā nikkhamanti, thero ca punapi taṃ vadati – “pattacīvaraṃ gaṇha, vihāraṃ gamissāmā”ti. Tatra ce so purimanayeneva theyyacittena sīse bhāraṃ khandhe karoti, rakkhati tāva. Aṭaviṃ pavisati, padavārena kāretabbo. Nivattitvā gāmābhimukho eva palāyati, gāmūpacārātikkame pārājikaṃ. Purato vihārābhimukho palāyitvā vihāre aṭṭhatvā anisīditvā avūpasanteneva theyyacittena gacchati, upacārātikkame pārājikaṃ. Yo pana anāṇatto gaṇhāti, tassa sīse bhāraṃ khandhe karaṇādīsupi pārājikaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

A certain great elder said to his attendant, a young bhikkhu, “Take the bowl and robe; we will go to such-and-such a village for alms.” The young bhikkhu, taking them and following behind the elder, conceived a thought of theft. If he places the burden on his head or shoulder, there is no pārājika offense. Why? Because it was taken by command. However, if he leaves the path and enters the forest, he is to be dealt with by the footstep-reckoning. If he turns back and flees toward the monastery, entering the monastery and then proceeding, it is a pārājika offense upon exceeding the boundary. Alternatively, if he flees toward the village from the place where the great elder changes his lower robe, it is a pārājika offense upon exceeding the village boundary. But if both have gone for alms, eaten, or taken food, and then depart, and the elder again tells him, “Take the bowl and robe, we will return to the monastery,” and if, in that case, the young bhikkhu, with the same previous thought of theft, proceeds with the thought of theft still unallayed, it is a pārājika offense upon exceeding the boundary. But for one who takes something without being commanded, placing the burden on his head or shoulder or similar actions is a pārājika offense. The rest is the same as the preceding.

Yo pana “asukaṃ nāma vihāraṃ gantvā cīvaraṃ dhovitvā rajitvā vā ehī”ti vutto “sādhū”ti gahetvā gacchati, tassapi antarāmagge theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā sīse bhāraṃ khandhe karaṇādīsu pārājikaṃ natthi. Maggā okkamane padavārena kāretabbo. Taṃ vihāraṃ gantvā tattheva vasanto [M 1.0308] theyyacittena paribhuñjanto jīrāpeti, corā vā tassa taṃ haranti, avahāro natthi, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. Tato nikkhamitvā āgacchatopi eseva nayo.

As for one who is told, “Go to such-and-such a monastery, wash or dye the robe, and then come back,” and who, saying “Very well,” takes it and goes—even if he generates a thought of theft along the way, there is no pārājika offense for placing the burden on his head, carrying it on his shoulder, or for similar actions. If he deviates from the path, he is to be dealt with by the footstep-reckoning. If, upon reaching that monastery, he stays there and uses the robe with a thieving intent until it wears out, or if thieves steal it from him, there is no offense of removal, but it becomes an item to be restored. The same principle applies when he departs from there and returns.

Yo pana anāṇatto therena nimitte vā kate sayameva vā kiliṭṭhaṃ sallakkhetvā “detha, bhante, cīvaraṃ; asukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ gantvā rajitvā āharissāmī”ti gahetvā gacchati; tassa antarāmagge theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā sīse bhāraṃ khandhe karaṇādīsu pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Anāṇattiyā gahitattā. Maggā okkamatopi paṭinivattitvā tameva vihāraṃ āgantvā vihārasīmaṃ atikkamatopi vuttanayeneva pārājikaṃ. Tattha gantvā rajitvā paccāgacchatopi theyyacitte uppanne eseva nayo. Sace pana yattha gato, tattha vā antarāmagge vihāre vā tameva vihāraṃ paccāgantvā tassa ekapasse vā upacārasīmaṃ anatikkamitvā vasanto theyyacittena [V 1.0283] paribhuñjanto jīrāpeti, corā vā tassa taṃ haranti, yathā vā tathā vā nassati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Upacārasīmaṃ atikkamato pana pārājikaṃ.

But as for a bhikkhu who, without being commanded, yet when a sign is made by the elder or when he himself has noticed a soiled robe, takes it, saying, “Venerable sir, give me the robe; I will go to such-and-such a village, dye it, and bring it back,” and sets out—if along the way he generates a thought of theft and carries the burden on his head or shoulder, and so on, it is a pārājika offense. Why? Because it was taken without command. For one who deviates from the path, or turns back and returns to that same monastery and crosses the monastery boundary, it is a pārājika offense in the manner stated. The same principle applies if, having gone there, dyed it, and while returning, a thought of theft arises. But if, where he has gone, or in a monastery along the way, or having returned to that same monastery and staying in its vicinity without crossing the boundary of the precincts, he uses it with a thought of theft and wears it out, or thieves steal it from him, or it is lost in one way or another, it is an item to be restored. For one who crosses the boundary of the precincts, however, it is a pārājika offense.

Yo pana therena nimitte kayiramāne “detha, bhante, ahaṃ rajitvā [P 2.0353] āharissāmī”ti vatvā “kattha gantvā, bhante, rajāmī”ti pucchati. Thero ca naṃ “yattha icchasi, tattha gantvā rajāhī”ti vadati, ayaṃ “vissaṭṭhadūto” nāma. Theyyacittena palāyantopi na avahārena kāretabbo. Theyyacittena pana palāyatopi paribhogena vā aññathā vā nāsayatopi bhaṇḍadeyyameva hoti. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe kiñci parikkhāraṃ pahiṇati – “asukavihāre asukabhikkhussa dehī”ti, tassa theyyacitte uppanne sabbaṭṭhānesu “asukaṃ nāma vihāraṃ gantvā cīvaraṃ dhovitvā rajitvā vā ehī”ti ettha vuttasadiso vinicchayo.

But as for one who, while the elder is making a sign, says, “Venerable sir, give it to me; I will dye it and bring it back,” and then asks, “Venerable sir, where should I go to dye it?” and the elder replies, “Go wherever you wish and dye it there,” this one is called a “dismissed messenger.” Even if he flees with a thought of theft, he is not to be dealt with for removal. But for one who flees with a thought of theft and destroys it through use or in some other way, it only becomes an item to be restored. If a bhikkhu sends some requisite by the hand of another bhikkhu, saying, “Give this to such-and-such a bhikkhu in such-and-such a monastery,” and a thought of theft arises in the messenger, the decision in all instances is similar to what was stated in the case of “Go to such-and-such a monastery, wash or dye the robe, and then come back.”

Aparo bhikkhuṃ pahiṇitukāmo nimittaṃ karoti – “ko nu kho gahetvā gamissatī”ti, tatra ce eko – “detha, bhante, ahaṃ gahetvā gamissāmī”ti gahetvā gacchati, tassa theyyacitte uppanne sabbaṭṭhānesu “detha, bhante, cīvaraṃ, asukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ gantvā rajitvā āharissāmī”ti ettha vuttasadiso vinicchayo. Therena cīvaratthāya vatthaṃ labhitvā upaṭṭhākakule ṭhapitaṃ hoti. Athassa antevāsiko vatthaṃ haritukāmo tatra gantvā “taṃ kira vatthaṃ dethā”ti therena pesito viya vadati; tassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā upāsakena ṭhapitaṃ upāsikā vā, upāsikāya ṭhapitaṃ [M 1.0309] upāsako vā añño vā, koci nīharitvā deti, uddhāreyevassa pārājikaṃ. Sace pana therassa upaṭṭhākehi “imaṃ therassa dassāmā”ti attano vatthaṃ ṭhapitaṃ hoti. Athassa antevāsiko taṃ haritukāmo tattha gantvā “therassa kira vatthaṃ dātukāmattha, taṃ dethā”ti vadati. Te cassa saddahitvā “mayaṃ, bhante, bhojetvā dassāmāti ṭhapayimha, handa gaṇhāhī”ti denti. Sāmikehi dinnattā pārājikaṃ natthi, asuddhacittena pana gahitattā dukkaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍadeyyañca hoti.

Another bhikkhu, wishing to send someone, makes a sign, thinking, “Who, I wonder, will take it and go?” If, in that case, one says, “Venerable sir, give it; I will take it and go,” and takes it and goes, should a thought of theft arise in him, the decision in all instances is similar to what was stated in the case of “Venerable sir, give me the robe; I will go to such-and-such a village, dye it, and bring it back.” Cloth for a robe, obtained by an elder, is placed in the household of a supporter. Then his resident pupil, wishing to take the cloth, goes there and says, as if sent by the elder, “It is said, ‘Give that cloth.’” If, trusting his words, a female supporter gives what a male supporter had placed, or a male supporter gives what a female supporter had placed, or anyone else brings it out and gives it, it is a pārājika for him by the very act of removal. But if the elder’s supporters, thinking, “We will give this to the elder,” have placed their own cloth there, and his resident pupil, wishing to take it, goes there and says, “I hear that you wish to give cloth to the elder; give it,” and they, trusting him, say, “Venerable sir, we placed it aside, thinking to give it after offering a meal; here, take it,” and give it—since it was given by the owners, there is no pārājika; but because it was taken with an impure mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing, and it becomes an item to be restored.

Bhikkhu bhikkhussa vatvā gāmaṃ gacchati, “itthannāmo mama vassāvāsikaṃ dassati, taṃ gahetvā ṭhapeyyāsī”ti. “Sādhū”ti so bhikkhu tena dinnaṃ mahagghasāṭakaṃ attanā laddhena appagghasāṭakena saddhiṃ ṭhapetvā tena āgatena attano mahagghasāṭakassa laddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā vā añatvā vā “dehi me vassāvāsika”nti vutto “tava thūlasāṭako laddho, mayhaṃ pana sāṭako mahaggho, dvepi asukasmiṃ nāma okāse ṭhapitā, pavisitvā [P 2.0354] gaṇhāhī”ti vadati. Tena pavisitvā thūlasāṭake gahite itarassa itaraṃ gaṇhato uddhāre pārājikaṃ. Athāpi tassa sāṭake [V 1.0284] attano nāmaṃ attano ca sāṭake tassa nāmaṃ likhitvā “gaccha nāmaṃ vācetvā gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, tatrāpi eseva nayo. Yo pana attanā ca tena ca laddhasāṭake ekato ṭhapetvā taṃ evaṃ vadati – “tayā ca mayā ca laddhasāṭakā dvepi antogabbhe ṭhapitā, gaccha yaṃ icchasi, taṃ vicinitvā gaṇhāhī”ti. So ca lajjāya āvāsikena laddhaṃ thūlasāṭakameva gaṇheyya, tatrāvāsikassa vicinitvā gahitāvasesaṃ itaraṃ gaṇhato anāpatti. Āgantuko bhikkhu āvāsikānaṃ cīvarakammaṃ karontānaṃ samīpe pattacīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā “ete saṅgopessantī”ti maññamāno nhāyituṃ vā aññatra vā gacchati. Sace naṃ āvāsikā saṅgopenti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce, naṭṭhe gīvā na hoti. Sacepi so “idaṃ, bhante, ṭhapethā”ti vatvā gacchati, itare ca sakiccappasutattā na jānanti, eseva nayo. Athāpi te “idaṃ, bhante, ṭhapethā”ti vuttā “mayaṃ byāvaṭā”ti paṭikkhipanti, itaro ca “avassaṃ ṭhapessantī”ti anādiyitvā gacchati, eseva nayo. Sace pana tena yācitā vā ayācitā vā “mayaṃ ṭhapessāma, tvaṃ gacchā”ti vadanti; taṃ saṅgopitabbaṃ. No ce saṅgopenti, naṭṭhe gīvā. Kasmā? Sampaṭicchitattā.

A bhikkhu, going to a village, tells another bhikkhu, “So-and-so will give me my rains-residence robe; please take it and keep it.” “Very well,” says that bhikkhu. Having placed the valuable robe given by that person together with a cheap robe he himself had obtained, when the first bhikkhu returns and, whether knowing or not knowing that the valuable robe for him had been received, says, “Give me my rains-residence robe,” the other replies, “A coarse robe was received for you, but my robe is valuable. Both are placed in such-and-such a place; go in and take it.” When the former has entered and taken the coarse robe, for the other bhikkhu who then takes the other, valuable robe, it is a pārājika offense at the point of removal. Or if, having written his own name on the other's robe and the other's name on his own robe, he says, “Go, read the name and take it,” the same principle applies there too. But as for one who, having placed the robes obtained by himself and by the other together, says to him thus: “The two robes obtained by you and me are both placed inside the room; go and choose whichever you wish and take it.” And if the visitor, out of modesty, should take only the coarse cloth obtained by the resident, then for the resident bhikkhu who takes the other, remaining item after it has been chosen and taken, there is no offense. A visiting bhikkhu, while resident bhikkhus are making robes, places his bowl and robe nearby, thinking, “These will look after them,” and goes to bathe or elsewhere. If the resident bhikkhus look after them, that is good. If not, and they are lost, there is no liability. Even if he says, “Venerable sirs, please keep this,” and leaves, but the others, being preoccupied with their own duties, do not notice, the same principle applies. Or if, when told, “Venerable sirs, please keep this,” they refuse, saying, “We are busy,” and the other, disregarding their refusal and thinking, “They will surely keep it,” leaves, the same principle applies. But if, whether asked by him or not, they say, “We will keep it; you go,” then it must be looked after. If they do not look after it, and it is lost, there is liability. Why? Because they accepted.

Yo [M 1.0310] bhikkhu bhaṇḍāgāriko hutvā paccūsasamaye eva bhikkhūnaṃ pattacīvarāni heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ oropetvā dvāraṃ apidahitvā tesampi anārocetvāva dūre bhikkhācāraṃ gacchati; tāni ce corā haranti, tasseva gīvā. Yo pana bhikkhūhi “oropetha, bhante, pattacīvarāni; kālo salākaggahaṇassā”ti vutto “samāgatatthā”ti pucchitvā “āma, samāgatamhā”ti vutte pattacīvarāni nīharitvā nikkhipitvā bhaṇḍāgāradvāraṃ bandhitvā “tumhe pattacīvarāni gahetvā heṭṭhāpāsādadvāraṃ paṭijaggitvā gaccheyyāthā”ti vatvā gacchati. Tatra ceko alasajātiko bhikkhu bhikkhūsu gatesu pacchā akkhīni puñchanto uṭṭhahitvā [P 2.0355] udakaṭṭhānaṃ mukhadhovanatthaṃ gacchati, taṃ khaṇaṃ disvā corā tassa pattacīvaraṃ haranti, suhaṭaṃ. Bhaṇḍāgārikassa gīvā na hoti.

The bhikkhu who, being the storekeeper, early in the morning, having lowered the bhikkhus’ bowls and robes to the lower floor of the building, goes far away for alms without closing the door and without even informing them; if thieves steal those items, the liability is his alone. But as for one who, when told by the bhikkhus, “Venerable sir, please lower the bowls and robes; it is time for the taking of lots,” asks, “Have you all assembled?” and when they reply, “Yes, we have assembled,” he brings out the bowls and robes, places them down, locks the storeroom door, and says, “You take the bowls and robes and, after guarding the door of the lower floor, you may go,” and then leaves. Then, if a lazy bhikkhu, after the other bhikkhus have left, gets up later wiping his eyes and goes to the place with water to wash his face—seeing that opportunity, thieves steal his bowl and robe; it is considered well taken. The storekeeper is not liable.

Sacepi koci bhaṇḍāgārikassa anārocetvāva bhaṇḍāgāre attano parikkhāraṃ ṭhapeti, tasmimpi naṭṭhe bhaṇḍāgārikassa gīvā na hoti. Sace pana bhaṇḍāgāriko taṃ disvā “aṭṭhāne ṭhapita”nti gahetvā ṭhapeti, naṭṭhe tassa gīvā. Sacepi ṭhapitabhikkhunā “mayā, bhante, īdiso nāma parikkhāro ṭhapito, upadhāreyyāthā”ti vutto “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, dunnikkhittaṃ vā maññamāno aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeti, tasseva gīvā. “Nāhaṃ jānāmī”ti paṭikkhipantassa pana natthi gīvā. Yopi tassa passantasseva ṭhapeti, bhaṇḍāgārikañca na sampaṭicchāpeti[V 1.0285], naṭṭhaṃ sunaṭṭhameva. Sace taṃ bhaṇḍāgāriko aññatra ṭhapeti, naṭṭhe gīvā. Sace bhaṇḍāgāraṃ suguttaṃ, sabbo saṅghassa ca cetiyassa ca parikkhāro tattheva ṭhapīyati, bhaṇḍāgāriko ca bālo abyatto dvāraṃ vivaritvā dhammakathaṃ vā sotuṃ, aññaṃ vā kiñci kātuṃ katthaci gacchati, taṃ khaṇaṃ disvā yattakaṃ corā haranti, sabbaṃ tassa gīvā. Bhaṇḍāgārato nikkhamitvā bahi caṅkamantassa vā dvāraṃ vivaritvā sarīraṃ utuṃ gāhāpentassa vā tattheva samaṇadhammānuyogena nisinnassa vā tattheva nisīditvā kenaci kammena byāvaṭassa vā uccārapassāvapīḷitassāpi tato tattheva upacāre vijjamāne bahi gacchato vā aññena vā kenaci ākārena pamattassa sato dvāraṃ vivaritvā vā vivaṭameva pavisitvā vā sandhiṃ chinditvā vā yattakaṃ tassa pamādapaccayā corā haranti, sabbaṃ tasseva gīvā. Uṇhasamaye pana vātapānaṃ vivaritvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Uccārapīḷitassa pana [M 1.0311] tasmiṃ upacāre asati aññattha gacchantassa gilānapakkhe ṭhitattā avisayo; tasmā gīvā na hoti.

If a certain one, without informing the storekeeper, places his own requisites in the storehouse, should they be lost, there is no liability for the storekeeper. If, however, the storekeeper sees them and, thinking, 'They are placed in an unsuitable spot,' takes and places them elsewhere, should they be lost, the liability is his. If, when told by the bhikkhu who placed the item, 'Venerable sir, I have placed such-and-such a requisite here; please take note of it,' the storekeeper accepts with 'Very well,' or if, thinking it is poorly placed, he moves it to another spot, the liability is his alone. But for one who refuses, saying, 'I do not know of it,' there is no liability. And as for one who places something while the storekeeper is watching but does not have him accept responsibility, if it is lost, it is simply lost. If the storekeeper moves it elsewhere, should it be lost, the liability is his. If the storehouse is well-guarded, and all the requisites of the Saṅgha and the shrine are kept there, but the storekeeper is foolish and incompetent, opens the door, and goes somewhere to listen to a Dhamma talk or to do something else—whatever thieves take upon seeing that opportunity, the liability for all of it is his. If, on account of his negligence—such as leaving the storehouse and walking in meditation outside, or opening the door to air his body, or sitting right there engaged in the duties of a recluse, or sitting right there occupied with some work, or, though afflicted by the need to urinate or defecate, going outside even when there is a suitable place in the vicinity, or being negligent in any other way—thieves enter by opening the door, or through one already open, or by breaking through a joint, and take whatever they do, the liability for all of it is his alone. However, they say that during the hot season, it is permissible to open a window and lie down. As for one afflicted by the need to relieve himself, if there is no suitable place in the vicinity and he must go elsewhere, since he is considered to be in the category of the sick, it is beyond his responsibility; thus, there is no liability.

Yo pana anto uṇhapīḷito dvāraṃ suguttaṃ katvā bahi nikkhamati, corā ca naṃ gahetvā “dvāraṃ vivarā”ti vadanti, yāva tatiyaṃ na vivaritabbaṃ. Yadi pana te corā “sace na vivarasi, tañca māressāma, dvārañca bhinditvā parikkhāraṃ [P 2.0356] harissāmā”ti pharasuādīni ukkhipanti. “Mayi ca mate saṅghassa ca senāsane vinaṭṭhe guṇo natthī”ti vivarituṃ vaṭṭati. Idhāpi avisayattā gīvā natthīti vadanti. Sace koci āgantuko kuñcikaṃ vā deti, dvāraṃ vā vivarati, yattakaṃ corā haranti, sabbaṃ tassa gīvā. Saṅghena bhaṇḍāgāraguttatthāya sūciyantakañca kuñcikamuddikā ca yojetvā dinnā hoti, bhaṇḍāgāriko ghaṭikamattaṃ datvā nipajjati, corā vivaritvā parikkhāraṃ haranti, tasseva gīvā. Sūciyantakañca kuñcikamuddikañca yojetvā nipannaṃ panetaṃ sace corā āgantvā “vivarā”ti vadanti, tattha purimanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Evaṃ guttaṃ katvā nipanne pana sace bhittiṃ vā chadanaṃ vā bhinditvā umaṅgena vā pavisitvā haranti, na tassa gīvā. Sace bhaṇḍāgāre aññepi therā vasanti, vivaṭe dvāre attano attano parikkhāraṃ gahetvā gacchanti, bhaṇḍāgāriko tesu gatesu dvāraṃ na jaggati, sace tattha kiñci avaharīyati, bhaṇḍāgārikassa issaratāya bhaṇḍāgārikasseva gīvā. Therehi pana sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tattha sāmīci.

Furthermore, if one who is inside, oppressed by heat, goes out after securing the door well, and thieves seize him and say, 'Open the door,' he should not open it until the third time. If, however, those thieves raise axes and other weapons, saying, 'If you do not open it, we will kill you, and we will break the door and take the requisites,' it is permissible to open it, thinking, 'There is no benefit if I am killed and the Saṅgha's lodging is destroyed.' Here too, they say there is no liability because it is beyond his capability. If some visiting monk gives a key or opens the door, whatever the thieves take, the entire liability is his. If the Saṅgha has provided a bolt mechanism, a key, and a lock to be fitted for safeguarding the storeroom, and the storekeeper, having applied only the latch, lies down, and thieves open it and take the requisites, the liability is his alone. But if, after securing it with the bolt mechanism, key, and lock, he is lying down, and thieves come and say, 'Open it,' he should proceed in the same manner as before. If, however, after guarding it in this way and lying down, thieves break through the wall or the roof, or enter through a tunnel and take things, there is no liability for him. If other elders are also staying in the storeroom, and when the door is open they take their own requisites and leave, and the storekeeper does not guard the door after they have gone, should anything be stolen there, because of the storekeeper’s authority, the liability is the storekeeper's alone. However, the elders should be his assistants. This is the proper conduct in that case.

Yadi bhaṇḍāgāriko “tumhe bahi ṭhatvāva tumhākaṃ parikkhāraṃ gaṇhatha, mā pavisitthā”ti vadati, tesañca eko lolamahāthero sāmaṇerehi ceva upaṭṭhākehi ca saddhiṃ bhaṇḍāgāraṃ [V 1.0286] pavisitvā nisīdati ceva nipajjati ca, yattakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ nassati, sabbaṃ tassa gīvā. Bhaṇḍāgārikena pana avasesattherehi ca sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ. Atha bhaṇḍāgārikova lolasāmaṇere ca upaṭṭhāke ca gahetvā bhaṇḍāgāre nisīdati ceva nipajjati ca, yaṃ tattha nassati, sabbaṃ tasseva gīvā. Tasmā bhaṇḍāgārikeneva tattha vasitabbaṃ. Avasesehi appeva rukkhamūle vasitabbaṃ, na ca bhaṇḍāgāreti.

If the storekeeper says, 'You must stay outside and take your requisites; do not enter,' and one fickle senior monk among them enters the storeroom along with novices and attendants, and sits down and lies down, whatever goods are lost, the entire liability is his. However, the storekeeper and the remaining elders should be his assistants. Furthermore, if the storekeeper himself, taking fickle novices and attendants, sits down and lies down in the storeroom, whatever is lost there, the entire liability is his alone. Therefore, the storekeeper alone should stay there. The remaining monks should preferably stay at the foot of a tree, but not in the storeroom.

Ye [M 1.0312] pana attano attano sabhāgabhikkhūnaṃ vasanagabbhesu parikkhāraṃ ṭhapenti, parikkhāre naṭṭhe yehi ṭhapito, tesaṃyeva gīvā. Itarehi pana sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ. Yadi pana saṅgho bhaṇḍāgārikassa vihāreyeva yāgubhattaṃ dāpeti, so ca bhikkhācāratthāya gāmaṃ gacchati, naṭṭhaṃ tasseva [P 2.0357] gīvā. Bhikkhācāraṃ pavisantehi atirekacīvararakkhaṇatthāya ṭhapitavihāravārikassāpi yāgubhattaṃ vā nivāpaṃ vā labhamānasseva bhikkhācāraṃ gacchato yaṃ tattha nassati, sabbaṃ gīvā. Na kevalañca ettakameva, bhaṇḍāgārikassa viya yaṃ tassa pamādappaccayā nassati, sabbaṃ gīvā.

Furthermore, for those who place the requisites of their like-minded fellow monks in their own living quarters, if the requisites are lost, the liability belongs only to those who placed them there. However, the other monks should be their assistants. Furthermore, if the Saṅgha has the storekeeper provided with rice-gruel and food in the monastery itself, and he goes to the village for the alms-round, the liability for what is lost is his alone. In the case of a monk on monastery duty, appointed to guard the extra robes of those going for the alms-round, if he, while receiving rice-gruel or a ration, goes for the alms-round, whatever is lost there, the entire liability is his. And not only this much; like the storekeeper, whatever is lost due to his negligence, the entire liability is his.

Sace vihāro mahā hoti, aññaṃ padesaṃ rakkhituṃ gacchantassa aññasmiṃ padese nikkhittaṃ haranti, avisayattā gīvā na hoti. Īdise pana vihāre vemajjhe sabbesaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhāne parikkhāre ṭhapetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Vihāravārikā vā dve tayo ṭhapetabbā. Sace tesaṃ appamattānaṃ ito cito ca rakkhataṃyeva kiñci nassati, gīvā na hoti. Vihāravārike bandhitvā haritabhaṇḍampi corānaṃ paṭipathaṃ gatesu aññena maggena haritabhaṇḍampi na tesaṃ gīvā. Sace vihāravārikānaṃ vihāre dātabbaṃ yāgubhattaṃ vā nivāpo vā na hoti, tehi pattabbalābhato atirekā dve tisso yāgusalākā, tesaṃ pahonakabhattasalākā ca ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Nibaddhaṃ katvā pana na ṭhapetabbā, manussā hi vippaṭisārino honti, “vihāravārikāyeva amhākaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjantī”ti. Tasmā parivattetvā ṭhapetabbā. Sace tesaṃ sabhāgā salākabhattāni āharitvā denti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce denti, vāraṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpetabbāni. Sace vihāravāriko dve tisso yāgusalākā, cattāri pañca salākabhattāni ca labhamānova bhikkhācāraṃ gacchati, bhaṇḍāgārikassa viya sabbaṃ naṭṭhaṃ gīvā hoti. Sace saṅghassa vihārapālānaṃ dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ vā nivāpo vā natthi, bhikkhū vihāravāraṃ gahetvā attano attano nissitake jaggenti, sampattavāraṃ aggahetuṃ na labhanti, yathā aññe bhikkhū karonti, tatheva kātabbaṃ. Bhikkhūhi pana asahāyakassa vā attadutiyassa vā yassa sabhāgo bhikkhu bhattaṃ ānetvā dātā natthi, evarūpassa vāro na pāpetabbo.

If the monastery is large, when a guard goes to watch another area, and thieves take items left in a different area, there is no liability, as it is beyond his capability. In such a monastery, one should stay in a central place where all gather, having placed the requisites there. Or, two or three monastery attendants should be appointed. If, while they are being vigilant and guarding here and there, something is lost, there is no liability. Even if goods are taken after binding the monastery attendants, or if goods are taken by another route while the attendants have gone to intercept the thieves, there is no liability for them. If there is no rice-gruel or ration to be given to the monastery attendants in the monastery, it is permissible for them to set aside two or three extra rice-gruel tickets beyond what they are entitled to receive, and sufficient meal tickets. However, these should not be set aside permanently, as people may become resentful, thinking, 'Only the monastery attendants are eating our food.' Therefore, they should be set aside on a rotational basis. If their like-minded fellow monks bring and give them the ticket-meals, that is good; if they do not, they should have them brought out by assigning turns. If a monastery attendant, while receiving two or three rice-gruel tickets and four or five meal tickets, still goes on the alms-round, just like the storekeeper, the entire liability for whatever is lost is his. If the Saṅgha has no meal or ration to give to the monastery guards, and the monks, taking turns to guard the monastery, have their own dependents keep watch, they cannot refuse their turn when it comes. It should be done just as the other monks do. However, the monks should not assign a turn to one who is without a companion, or who has only himself as a companion, or for whom there is no like-minded monk to bring and give him food.

Yampi [M 1.0313][V 1.0287] pākavattatthāya vihāre ṭhapenti, taṃ gahetvā upajīvantena ṭhātabbaṃ. Yo taṃ na upajīvati[P 2.0358], so vāraṃ na gāhāpetabbo. Phalāphalatthāyapi vihāre bhikkhuṃ ṭhapenti, jaggitvā gopetvā phalavārena bhājetvā khādanti. Yo tāni khādati, tena ṭhātabbaṃ. Anupajīvanto na gāhāpetabbo. Senāsanamañcapīṭhapaccattharaṇarakkhaṇatthāyapi ṭhapenti, āvāse vasantena ṭhātabbaṃ. Abbhokāsiko pana rukkhamūliko vā na gāhāpetabbo.

Whatever is placed in the monastery for the purpose of the cooking turn, a monk who subsists on it should take his turn in guarding it. Whoever does not subsist on it should not be made to take a turn. A monk may also be appointed in the monastery for the purpose of guarding fruits, both small and large; having watched over and protected them, they divide and eat them according to the fruit-turn. Whoever eats those fruits, he should take his turn. One who does not subsist on them should not be made to take a turn. A monk may also be appointed for the purpose of protecting lodgings, beds, stools, and coverings; one who dwells in the residence should take his turn. However, a monk who dwells in the open air or at the foot of a tree should not be made to take a turn.

Eko navako hoti, bahussuto pana bahūnaṃ dhammaṃ vāceti, paripucchaṃ deti, pāḷiṃ vaṇṇeti, dhammakathaṃ katheti, saṅghassa bhāraṃ nittharati, ayaṃ lābhaṃ paribhuñjantopi āvāse vasantopi vāraṃ na gāhetabbo. “Purisaviseso nāma ñātabbo”ti vadanti.

A certain junior monk, however, may be very learned; he teaches the Dhamma to many, gives answers to questions, explains the Pāḷi, gives Dhamma talks, and carries the burden of the Saṅgha. This monk, even while enjoying gains and dwelling in the residence, should not be made to take a turn. The teachers say, 'A person of distinction should be recognized.'

Uposathāgārapaṭimāgharajaggakassa pana diguṇaṃ yāgubhattaṃ devasikaṃ taṇḍulanāḷi saṃvacchare ticīvaraṃ, dasavīsagghanakaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍañca dātabbaṃ. Sace pana tassa taṃ labhamānasseva pamādena tattha kiñci nassati, sabbaṃ gīvā. Bandhitvā balakkārena acchinnaṃ pana na gīvā. Tattha cetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā santakena cetiyassa santakaṃ rakkhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Cetiyassa santakena saṅghassa santakaṃ rakkhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana cetiyassa santakena saddhiṃ saṅghassa santakaṃ ṭhapitaṃ hoti, taṃ cetiyasantake rakkhāpite rakkhitameva hotīti evaṃ vaṭṭati. Pakkhavārena uposathāgārādīni rakkhatopi pamādavasena naṭṭhaṃ gīvāyevāti.

To the guardian of the Uposatha hall and the image house, a double portion of gruel and rice, a daily nāḷi of rice, the three robes annually, and allowable goods worth ten or twenty should be given. However, if, while he is receiving these, any property there is lost through his negligence, it is all his liability. But what is taken by force after he has been bound is not his liability. In this matter, it is allowable to have the property of a cetiya guarded by means of the property of the cetiya or of the Saṅgha. It is not allowable to have the property of the Saṅgha guarded by means of the property of a cetiya. However, if property of the Saṅgha has been placed together with property of a cetiya, when the cetiya's property is guarded, that is considered guarded as well; thus, this is allowable. Even for one who guards the Uposatha hall and other such places on a fortnightly turn, what is lost through negligence is indeed his liability.

Upanidhikathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion on deposits is concluded.

Suṅkaghātakathā

The discussion on evading customs duty.

113. Suṅkaṃ tato hanantīti suṅkaghātaṃ; suṅkaṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi yasmā tato suṅkārahaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ suṅkaṃ adatvā nīharantā rañño suṅkaṃ hananti vināsenti, tasmā suṅkaghātanti vuttaṃ. Tatra pavisitvāti tatra pabbatakhaṇḍādīsu raññā paricchedaṃ katvā ṭhapite suṅkaṭṭhāne pavisitvā. Rājaggaṃ bhaṇḍanti rājārahaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ; yato rañño pañcamāsakaṃ [M 1.0314] vā atirekapañcamāsakaṃ vā agghanakaṃ suṅkaṃ dātabbaṃ hoti, taṃ bhaṇḍanti attho. Rājakantipi [P 2.0359] pāṭho, ayamevattho. Theyyacittoti “ito rañño suṅkaṃ na dassāmī”ti theyyacittaṃ uppādetvā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Ṭhapitaṭṭhānato gahetvā thavikāya vā pakkhipati, paṭicchannaṭṭhāne vā [V 1.0288] ūrunā saddhiṃ bandhati, thullaccayaṃ. Suṅkaṭṭhānena paricchinnattā ṭhānācāvanaṃ na hoti. Suṅkaṭṭhānaparicchedaṃ dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ.

113. Because 'they evade the customs duty there' (suṅkaṃ tato hananti), it is called a 'customs evasion point' (suṅkaghāta); this is a designation for a customs post. For, because those who carry away goods liable to customs duty from there without paying the customs duty evade or destroy the king's customs duty, it is therefore called a 'customs evasion point'. 'Having entered there' means having entered a customs post established by the king in a mountain pass or other such place after he has demarcated it. 'Goods for the king's share' means goods due to the king; the meaning is, goods on which a customs duty worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas is to be given to the king. There is also the reading 'rājakanti', but the meaning is the same. 'With a thieving mind' means that, having generated the thieving thought, 'I will not give the king the customs duty from this,' one touches those goods; this is a dukkaṭa offense. If one takes them from the place where they were put and places them in a bag, or binds them to one's thigh in a concealed place, it is a thullaccaya offense. Because it is demarcated by the customs post, the offense of moving from its place does not occur. When one makes one's second foot cross the boundary of the customs post, it is a pārājika offense.

Bahisuṅkaghātaṃ pātetīti rājapurisānaṃ aññavihitabhāvaṃ passitvā anto ṭhitova bahi patanatthāya khipati. Tañce avassaṃ patanakaṃ, hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ. Tañce rukkhe vā khāṇumhi vā paṭihataṃ balavavātavegukkhittaṃ vā hutvā puna antoyeva patati, rakkhati. Puna gaṇhitvā khipati, pubbe vuttanayeneva pārājikaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ patitvā vaṭṭantaṃ puna anto pavisati, pārājikameva. Kurundīsaṅkhepaṭṭhakathāsu pana “sace bahi patitaṃ ṭhatvā vaṭṭantaṃ pavisati, pārājikaṃ. Sace atiṭṭhamānaṃyeva vaṭṭitvā pavisati rakkhatī”ti vuttaṃ.

'He makes it fall outside the customs post' means that, seeing the king's men are distracted, while standing inside he throws it for the purpose of it falling outside. If it is certain to fall, it is a pārājika offense the moment it is released from his hand. If it is deflected by a tree or a stump, or is thrown up by the force of a strong wind and falls back inside, he is safe.
