If he picks it up and throws it again, it is a pārājika offense according to the method previously stated. If, having fallen to the ground, it rolls and re-enters, it is indeed a pārājika offense. However, in the Kurundī and Saṅkhepa commentaries it is said: 'If, having fallen outside, it stops and then rolls and enters, it is a pārājika offense. If it rolls and enters without having stopped, he is safe.'

Anto ṭhatvā hatthena vā pādena vā yaṭṭhiyā vā vaṭṭeti, aññena vā vaṭṭāpeti, sace aṭṭhatvā vaṭṭamānaṃ gataṃ, pārājikaṃ. Anto ṭhatvā bahi gacchantaṃ rakkhati, “vaṭṭitvā gamissatī”ti vā “añño naṃ vaṭṭessatī”ti vā anto ṭhapitaṃ pacchā sayaṃ vā vaṭṭamānaṃ aññena vā vaṭṭitaṃ bahi gacchati, rakkhatiyeva. Suddhacittena ṭhapite pana tathā gacchante vattabbameva natthi. Dve puṭake ekābaddhe katvā suṅkaṭṭhānasīmantare ṭhapeti, kiñcāpi bahipuṭake suṅkaṃ pādaṃ agghati, tena saddhiṃ ekābaddhatāya pana anto puṭako rakkhati. Sace pana parivattetvā abbhantarimaṃ bahi ṭhapeti, pārājikaṃ. Kājepi ekabaddhaṃ katvā ṭhapite eseva nayo. Sace pana abandhitvā kājakoṭiyaṃ ṭhapitamattameva hoti, pārājikaṃ.

Standing inside, if one rolls it with one's hand, foot, or a stick, or has another roll it, and if it goes out while rolling without having stopped, it is a pārājika offense. If an object is placed inside with the thought, 'It will go out by rolling,' or, 'Another will roll it,' and it later goes outside, either rolling by itself or being rolled by another, he is indeed safe. If it was placed with a pure mind and goes out in such a way, there is nothing to be said. If one makes two bundles into one and places them on the boundary of the customs post, even if the customs duty on the outer bundle is worth a pāda, the inner bundle is protected by being bound together with it. But if one turns them around and places the inner one outside, it is a pārājika offense. This is the same principle when they are bound together and placed on a carrying pole. However, if, without being bound, it is merely placed on the end of the carrying pole, it is a pārājika offense.

Gacchante yāne vā assapiṭṭhiādīsu vā ṭhapeti “bahi nīharissatī”ti nīhaṭepi avahāro natthi, bhaṇḍadeyyampi na hoti. Kasmā? “Atra paviṭṭhassa [P 2.0360] suṅkaṃ gaṇhantū”ti vuttattā idañca suṅkaṭṭhānassa bahi ṭhitaṃ, na ca tena nītaṃ, tasmā neva bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ na pārājikaṃ.

If one places an item on a moving vehicle, or on the back of a horse or the like, thinking, 'It will carry it outside,' even when it has been carried out, there is no theft, nor is there liability for the goods. Why? Because it has been said, 'Let them collect the customs duty for what has entered here.' And this item was situated outside the customs post, and it was not carried out by him. Therefore, there is neither liability for the goods nor a pārājika offense.

Ṭhitayānādīsu ṭhapite vinā tassa payogaṃ gatesu theyyacittepi sati nevatthi avahāro. Yadi pana ṭhapetvā yānādīni pājento atikkāmeti[M 1.0315], hatthisuttādīsu vā kataparicayattā purato ṭhatvā “ehi, re”ti pakkosati, sīmātikkame pārājikaṃ. Eḷakalomasikkhāpade imasmiṃ ṭhāne aññaṃ harāpeti, anāpatti, idha pārājikaṃ. Tatra aññassa yāne vā bhaṇḍe vā ajānantassa pakkhipitvā tiyojanaṃ atikkāmeti, nissaggiyāni hontīti pācittiyaṃ. Idha anāpatti.

When goods are placed on stationary vehicles and the like, should they move without his effort, even if there is a thieving mind, there is no theft. But if, having placed the goods, one drives the vehicles and so forth and makes them go beyond, or due to being practiced in the art of elephant training and so forth, stands in front and calls, “Hey, come!”, upon crossing the boundary, it is a pārājika offense. In the training rule concerning ram's wool, if in this situation one causes another to carry it, there is no offense; here, it is a pārājika offense. There, if one places something in another’s vehicle or goods without their knowledge and it crosses three yojanas, they become items for forfeiture, and it is a pācittiya offense. Here, there is no offense.

Suṅkaṭṭhāne [V 1.0289] suṅkaṃ datvāva gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Eko ābhogaṃ katvā gacchati “sace ‘suṅkaṃ dehī’ti vakkhanti, dassāmi; no ce vakkhanti, gamissāmī”ti. Taṃ disvā eko suṅkiko “eso bhikkhu gacchati, gaṇhatha naṃ suṅka”nti vadati, aparo “kuto pabbajitassa suṅkaṃ, gacchatū”ti vadati, laddhakappaṃ hoti, gantabbaṃ. “Bhikkhūnaṃ suṅkaṃ adatvā gantuṃ na vaṭṭati, gaṇha upāsakā”ti vutte pana “bhikkhussa suṅkaṃ gaṇhantehi pattacīvaraṃ gahetabbaṃ bhavissati, kiṃ tena, gacchatū”ti vuttepi laddhakappameva. Sacepi suṅkikā niddāyanti vā, jūtaṃ vā kīḷanti, yattha katthaci vā gatā, ayañca “kuhiṃ suṅkikā”ti pakkositvāpi na passati, laddhakappameva. Sacepi suṅkaṭṭhānaṃ patvā aññavihito, kiñci cintento vā sajjhāyanto vā manasikāraṃ anuyuñjanto vā corahatthisīhabyagghādīhi sahasā vuṭṭhāya samanubaddho vā, mahāmeghaṃ uṭṭhitaṃ disvā purato sālaṃ pavisitukāmo vā hutvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamati, laddhakappameva.

At a customs post, it is proper to go only after giving the toll. A certain monk goes having made the intention: “If they say, ‘Give the toll,’ I will give it; if they do not say, I will go.” Seeing him, one toll-collector says, “That monk is going, take the toll from him,” but another says, “From where would a renunciate have a toll? Let him go.” It becomes permissible; he should go. But if it is said, “It is not proper for monks to go without giving the toll. Lay follower, take it!”, and even when it is then said, “By those taking the toll from a monk, the bowl and robes will have to be taken. What is the use of that? Let him go,” it is indeed permissible. Even if the toll-collectors are sleeping, or playing at dice, or have gone somewhere or other, and this monk, even after calling out, “Where are the toll-collectors?”, does not see them, it is indeed permissible. Even if, having reached the customs post, he is distracted, or thinking of something, or reciting, or applying his mind to a meditation subject, or is pursued by suddenly arisen thieves, elephants, lions, tigers, and so forth, or, having seen a great cloud arise, becomes desirous of entering a hall in front and passes that place, it is indeed permissible.

Suṅkaṃ pariharatīti ettha upacāraṃ okkamitvā kiñcāpi pariharati, avahāroyevāti

Herein, regarding 'evading the toll': even if one evades it after having entered the vicinity, it is theft indeed.

Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃpana “‘pariharantaṃ rājapurisā viheṭhentī’ti kevalaṃ ādīnavaṃ dassetvā upacāraṃ [P 2.0361] okkamitvā pariharato dukkaṭaṃ, anokkamitvā pariharato anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ pāḷiyā sameti. Ettha dvīhi leḍḍupātehi upacāro paricchinditabboti.

This was stated in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā. But in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā it is stated: “By showing merely the danger with the words, ‘The king's men harass one who evades,’ for one who evades after having entered the vicinity, there is a dukkaṭa offense; for one who evades without having entered, there is no offense.” This agrees with the Pāḷi. Herein, the vicinity is to be determined by two clod-throws.

Suṅkaghātakathā niṭṭhitā.

The section on evading the toll is concluded.

Pāṇakathā

The Section on Living Beings

114. Ito parasmiṃ ekaṃsena avahārappahonakapāṇaṃ dassento “manussapāṇo”ti āha. Tampi bhujissaṃ harantassa avahāro natthi. Yopi [M 1.0316] bhujisso mātarā vā pitarā vā āṭhapito hoti, attanā vā attano upari katvā paññāsaṃ vā saṭṭhiṃ vā aggahesi, tampi harantassa avahāro natthi; dhanaṃ pana gataṭṭhāne vaḍḍhati. Antojātaka-dhanakkīta-karamarānītappabhedaṃ pana dāsaṃyeva harantassa avahāro hoti. Tameva hi sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ – “pāṇo nāma manussapāṇo vuccatī”ti. Ettha ca gehadāsiyā kucchimhi dāsassa jāto antojātako, dhanena kīto dhanakkīto, paradesato paharitvā ānetvā dāsabyaṃ upagamito karamarānītoti veditabbo. Evarūpaṃ pāṇaṃ “harissāmī”ti āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Hatthe vā pāde vā gahetvā ukkhipanto phandāpeti, thullaccayaṃ. Ukkhipitvā palāyitukāmo kesaggamattampi ṭhitaṭṭhānato atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Kesesu vā hatthesu vā gahetvā kaḍḍhati, padavārena kāretabbo.

114. Following this, showing a living being that can certainly be stolen, he says, 'a human being.' Even for one carrying away a free person, there is no theft. If a free person has been pledged by his mother or father, or if he himself, having incurred a debt, has received fifty or sixty, for one carrying him away also, there is no theft; but the wealth increases in the place he has gone. However, for one carrying away only a slave—of the kinds born in the house, bought with money, or brought as a captive of war—there is theft. Indeed, it is with reference to this very slave that this was said: 'By "living being" is meant a "human being".' And here, one born in the womb of a female house-slave to a male slave is an 'antojātaka'; one bought with money is a 'dhanakkīta'; one brought from a foreign country, captured, and made into a slave should be known as a 'karamarānīta'. If one touches such a living being with the thought, 'I will steal him,' it is a dukkaṭa offense. If, seizing him by the hand or foot, one lifts him and makes him struggle, it is a thullaccaya offense. If, having lifted him up, desiring to flee, one moves him even a hair's breadth from the place where he stood, it is a pārājika offense. If one seizes him by the hair or hands and drags him, the offense is to be determined by the step.

Padasā [V 1.0290] nessāmīti tajjento vā paharanto vā “ito gacchāhī”ti vadati, tena vuttadisābhāgaṃ gacchantassa dutiyapadavārena pārājikaṃ. Yepi tena saddhiṃ ekacchandā honti, sabbesaṃ ekakkhaṇe pārājikaṃ. Bhikkhu dāsaṃ disvā sukhadukkhaṃ pucchitvā vā apucchitvā vā “gaccha, palāyitvā sukhaṃ jīvā”ti vadati, so ce palāyati, dutiyapadavāre pārājikaṃ. Taṃ attano samīpaṃ āgataṃ añño “palāyā”ti vadati, sace bhikkhusataṃ paṭipāṭiyā attano samīpamāgataṃ vadati, sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Yo pana vegasā palāyantaṃyeva “palāya, yāva taṃ [P 2.0362] sāmikā na gaṇhantī”ti bhaṇati, anāpatti pārājikassa. Sace pana saṇikaṃ gacchantaṃ bhaṇati, so ca tassa vacanena sīghaṃ gacchati, pārājikaṃ. Palāyitvā aññaṃ gāmaṃ vā desaṃ vā gataṃ disvā tatopi palāpentassa pārājikameva.

If, with the thought 'I will lead him away by steps,' one, threatening or striking, says, 'Go from here,' a pārājika offense is incurred at the second step of the one going in the direction told by him. Those who are of the same intention with him all incur a pārājika offense at the same moment. If a bhikkhu, having seen a slave, whether having asked about his well-being or not, says, 'Go, flee and live happily,' and if he flees, a pārājika offense is incurred at the second step. If another says 'Flee' to him who has come near, and if a hundred bhikkhus in succession say this to him as he comes near each of them, it is a pārājika offense for all. But for one who says to a slave already fleeing with speed, 'Flee, as long as your masters do not catch you,' there is no pārājika offense. But if one says this to one going slowly, and he goes quickly because of that word, it is a pārājika offense. Having seen one who has fled and gone to another village or country, for one who makes him flee from there also, it is indeed a pārājika offense.

Adinnādānaṃ nāma pariyāyena muccati. Yo hi evaṃ vadati – “tvaṃ idha kiṃ karosi,

One is freed from the offense of taking what is not given by means of indirect speech. For if one says thus: 'What are you doing here?'

Kiṃ te palāyituṃ na vaṭṭatīti vā, kiṃ katthaci gantvā sukhaṃ jīvituṃ na vaṭṭatīti vā, dāsadāsiyo palāyitvā amukaṃ nāma padesaṃ gantvā sukhaṃ jīvantī”ti vā, so ca tassa vacanaṃ sutvā palāyati, avahāro natthi. Yopi “mayaṃ amukaṃ nāma padesaṃ gacchāma, tatrāgatā sukhaṃ jīvanti, amhehi ca saddhiṃ gacchantānaṃ antarāmaggepi pātheyyādīhi kilamatho natthī”ti vatvā sukhaṃ attanā saddhiṃ āgacchantaṃ gahetvā gacchati [M 1.0317] maggagamanavasena, na theyyacittena; nevatthi avahāro. Antarāmagge ca coresu uṭṭhitesu “are! Corā uṭṭhitā, vegena palāya, ehi yāhī”ti vadantassāpi corantarāya mocanatthāya vuttattā avahāraṃ na vadantīti.

Or, 'Is it not proper for you to flee?' Or, 'Is it not proper to go somewhere and live happily?' Or, 'Male and female slaves flee, go to such-and-such a place, and live happily.' And if he, having heard these words, flees, there is no theft. And if one, saying, 'We are going to such-and-such a place; those who arrive there live happily, and for those going with us, there is no fatigue from lack of provisions and so on even on the way,' takes one who comes along happily with him and goes for the sake of the journey, not with a thievish mind, there is no theft. And on the way, when robbers have arisen, even for one who says, 'Hey! Robbers have arisen, flee with speed, come, go!'—because it was said for the purpose of freeing them from the danger of robbers, they do not call it theft.

Pāṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Section on Living Beings is concluded.

Apadakathā

The Section on Footless Creatures

Apadesu ahi nāma sassāmiko ahituṇḍikādīhi gahitasappo; yaṃ kīḷāpentā

Among footless creatures, a snake that has an owner is a snake captured by snake charmers and the like, which they make perform,

Aḍḍhampi pādampi kahāpaṇampi labhanti, muñcantāpi hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā gahetvāva muñcanti. Te kassaci bhikkhuno nisinnokāsaṃ gantvā sappakaraṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā niddāyanti vā, katthaci vā gacchanti, tatra ce so bhikkhu theyyacittena taṃ karaṇḍaṃ āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Phandāpeti, thullaccayaṃ. Ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Sace pana karaṇḍakaṃ ugghāṭetvā sappaṃ gīvāya gaṇhāti, dukkaṭaṃ. Uddharati, thullaccayaṃ. Ujukaṃ katvā uddharantassa karaṇḍatalato sappassa naṅguṭṭhe kesaggamatte mutte pārājikaṃ. Ghaṃsitvā kaḍḍhantassa naṅguṭṭhe mukhavaṭṭito muttamatte pārājikaṃ[V 1.0291]. Karaṇḍamukhaṃ īsakaṃ vivaritvā pahāraṃ vā datvā “ehi, re”ti nāmena pakkositvā nikkhāmeti, pārājikaṃ[P 2.0363]. Tatheva vivaritvā maṇḍūkasaddaṃ vā mūsikasaddaṃ vā lājāvikiraṇaṃ vā katvā nāmena pakkosati, accharaṃ vā paharati, evaṃ nikkhantepi pārājikaṃ. Mukhaṃ avivaritvāpi evaṃ kate chāto sappo sīsena karaṇḍapuṭaṃ āhacca okāsaṃ katvā palāyati, pārājikameva. Sace pana mukhe vivarite sayameva sappo nikkhamitvā palāyati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Athāpi mukhaṃ vivaritvā vā avivaritvā vā kevalaṃ maṇḍūkamūsikasaddaṃ lājāvikiraṇameva ca karoti, na nāmaṃ gahetvā pakkosati, na accharaṃ vā paharati, sappo ca chātattā “maṇḍūkādīni khādissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā palāyati, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Maccho kevalaṃ idha apadaggahaṇena āgato. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ udakaṭṭhe vuttamevāti.

They obtain half a kahāpaṇa, a quarter kahāpaṇa, or a kahāpaṇa; and even when releasing them, they release them only after taking silver or gold. They go to where a certain monk is sitting, place the snake basket, and then either sleep or go somewhere else. If that monk, with thieving intent, touches that basket, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If he causes it to move, it is a thullaccaya offense. If he removes it from its place, it is a pārājika offense. Furthermore, if he opens the basket and grabs the snake by the neck, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If he lifts it out, it is a thullaccaya offense. For one who, having straightened it, is lifting it out, when the snake's tail is freed from the bottom of the basket by a hair's breadth, it is a pārājika offense. For one who is pulling it out by dragging it, when the tail is just freed from the rim of the mouth, it is a pārājika offense. If he slightly opens the basket’s mouth, gives it a tap, calls it by name saying, “Come, you!” and makes it exit, it is a pārājika offense. Similarly, if he opens it, makes frog sounds or mouse sounds or scatters parched grain, calls it by name, or snaps his fingers, and it exits in this way, it is a pārājika offense. Even without opening the mouth, if these things are done and the hungry snake, striking the basket’s lid with its head, makes an opening and flees, it is a pārājika offense indeed. If, however, when the mouth is opened, the snake exits on its own and flees, it is a bhaṇḍadeyya offense. Moreover, whether the mouth is opened or not, if he merely makes frog or mouse sounds or scatters parched grain, and does not call it by name or snap his fingers, and the snake, being hungry, thinking, “I will eat frogs, etc.,” exits and flees, it is a bhaṇḍadeyya offense indeed. A fish is included here merely by the term 'footless'. Whatever should be said about this has already been stated in the section on things situated in water.

Apadakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Section on Footless Creatures is concluded.

Dvipadakathā

The Section on Bipeds

115. Dvipadesu [M 1.0318] – ye avaharituṃ sakkā, te dassento “manussā pakkhajātā”ti āha. Devatā pana avaharituṃ na sakkā. Pakkhā jātā etesanti pakkhajātā. Te lomapakkhā cammapakkhā aṭṭhipakkhāti tividhā. Tattha morakukkuṭādayo lomapakkhā, vagguliādayo cammapakkhā, bhamarādayo aṭṭhipakkhāti veditabbā. Te sabbepi manussā ca pakkhajātā ca kevalaṃ idha dvipadaggahaṇena āgatā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ ākāsaṭṭhe ca pāṇe ca vuttanayamevāti.

115. Among bipeds, showing those that can be stolen, he said, “Humans and winged creatures.” Deities, however, cannot be stolen. They are called 'winged creatures' (pakkhajātā) because wings have grown for them. They are of three kinds: feather-winged, skin-winged, and bone-winged. Among them, peacocks, chickens, and the like are to be known as feather-winged; bats and the like as skin-winged; and bees and the like as bone-winged. All of them—both humans and winged creatures—are included here merely by the term 'biped'. Whatever should be said about this is just according to the method already stated in the sections on things situated in space and on living beings.

Dvipadakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Section on Bipeds is concluded.

Catuppadakathā

The Section on Quadrupeds

116. Catuppadesu – pasukāti pāḷiyaṃ āgatāvasesā sabbā catuppadajātīti veditabbā. Hatthiādayo pākaṭāyeva. Tattha theyyacittena hatthiṃ āmasantassa dukkaṭaṃ, phandāpentassa thullaccayaṃ. Yo pana mahābalo balamadena taruṇaṃ bhiṅkacchāpaṃ nābhimūle sīsena uccāretvā gaṇhanto cattāro pāde, soṇḍaṃ ca bhūmito kesaggamattampi moceti, pārājikaṃ. Hatthī pana koci hatthisālāyaṃ bandhitvā ṭhapito [P 2.0364] hoti, koci abaddhova tiṭṭhati, koci antovatthumhi [V 1.0292] tiṭṭhati, koci rājaṅgaṇe tiṭṭhati, tattha hatthisālāyaṃ gīvāya bandhitvā ṭhapitassa gīvābandhanañca cattāro ca pādāti pañca ṭhānāni honti. Gīvāya ca ekasmiñca pāde ayasaṅkhalikāya baddhassa cha ṭhānāni. Gīvāya ca dvīsu ca pādesu baddhassa satta ṭhānāni. Tesaṃ vasena phandāpanaṭhānācāvanāni veditabbāni. Abaddhassa sakalā hatthisālā ṭhānaṃ. Tato atikkamane, pārājikaṃ. Antovatthumhi ṭhitassa sakalaṃ antovatthumeva ṭhānaṃ. Tassa vatthudvārātikkamane pārājikaṃ. Rājaṅgaṇe ṭhitassa sakalanagaraṃ ṭhānaṃ. Tassa nagaradvārātikkamane pārājikaṃ. Bahinagare ṭhitassa ṭhitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ. Taṃ haranto padavārena kāretabbo. Nipannassa ekameva ṭhānaṃ. Taṃ theyyacittena uṭṭhāpentassa uṭṭhitamatte pārājikaṃ. Assepi ayameva vinicchayo. Sace pana so catūsu pādesu baddho hoti, aṭṭha ṭhānāni veditabbāni. Esa nayo oṭṭhepi.

116. Among quadrupeds—as for `pasu` (animals), it should be understood as all species of quadrupeds remaining from those mentioned in the Pali. Elephants and so forth are evident. In this context, for one who touches an elephant with thieving intent, there is a dukkaṭa offense; for one who makes it move, a thullaccaya offense. However, should any monk who is very strong, through intoxication with his strength, while taking a young elephant calf, lift it with his head at the base of its navel, and release its four feet and trunk from the ground even by a hair's breadth, a pārājika offense is incurred. Furthermore, some elephants are tied and kept in an elephant stable; some stand untied; some stand within the premises; some stand in the royal courtyard. Among these, for one tied by the neck in an elephant stable, there are five locations: the neck-binding and the four feet. For one bound by an iron chain on the neck and on one leg, there are six locations. For one bound on the neck and on two feet, there are seven locations. Based on these, the acts of making it move and displacing it from its location are to be understood. For an untied elephant, the entire elephant stable is its location. Upon taking it beyond that, a pārājika offense is incurred. For one standing within the premises, the entire premises is its location. Upon taking it beyond the entrance of the premises, a pārājika offense is incurred. For one standing in the royal courtyard, the entire city is its location. Upon taking it beyond the city gate, a pārājika offense is incurred. For one standing outside the city, only the place where it stands is its location. For one taking it, the offense is to be determined by the footstep. For one that is lying down, there is only one location. For one who, with thieving intent, makes it stand up, a pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment it has stood up. For a horse, too, this is the very same ruling. If, however, it is bound on four feet, eight locations are to be understood. This is the method for a camel as well.

Goṇopi [M 1.0319] koci gehe bandhitvā ṭhapito hoti. Koci abaddhova tiṭṭhati, koci pana vaje bandhitvā ṭhapito hoti, koci abaddhova tiṭṭhati. Tattha gehe bandhitvā ṭhapitassa cattāro pādā, bandhanañcāti pañca ṭhānāni; abaddhassa sakalaṃ gehaṃ. Vajepi baddhassa pañca ṭhānāni. Abaddhassa sakalo vajo. Taṃ vajadvāraṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Vajaṃ bhinditvā haranto khaṇḍadvāraṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Dvāraṃ vā vivaritvā vajaṃ vā bhinditvā bahi ṭhito nāmena pakkositvā nikkhāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Sākhābhaṅgaṃ dassetvā pakkosantassāpi eseva nayo. Dvāraṃ avivaritvā vajaṃ abhinditvā sākhābhaṅgaṃ cāletvā pakkosati, goṇo chātatāya vajaṃ laṅghetvā nikkhamati, pārājikameva. Sace pana dvāre vivarite vaje vā bhinne sayameva nikkhamati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Dvāraṃ vivaritvā vā avivaritvā vā vajampi bhinditvā vā abhinditvā vā kevalaṃ sākhābhaṅgaṃ [P 2.0365] cāleti, na pakkosati, goṇo chātatāya padasā vā laṅghetvā vā nikkhamati, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Eko majjhe gāme baddho ṭhito, eko nipanno. Ṭhitagoṇassa pañca ṭhānāni honti, nipannassa dve ṭhānāni; tesaṃ vasena phandāpanaṭhānācāvanāni veditabbāni.

As for an ox, some are tied and kept in a house; some stand untied. Furthermore, some are tied and kept in a pen; some stand untied. Among these, for one tied and kept in a house, there are five locations: the four feet and the tether; for an untied one, the entire house is the location. In a pen also, for a tied one there are five locations. For an untied one, the entire pen is the location. If one causes it to cross the pen's gate, a pārājika offense is incurred. One who, having broken the pen, is taking it away, incurs a pārājika offense if he causes it to cross the broken opening. If, having opened the gate or broken the pen, one stands outside, calls it by name, and makes it exit, a pārājika offense is incurred. For one who calls it by showing a broken branch, this is the very same method. If, without opening the gate and without breaking the pen, one shakes a broken branch and calls, and the ox, due to hunger, leaps over the pen and exits, it is a pārājika offense indeed. If, however, the gate having been opened or the pen broken, it exits by itself, it is a bhaṇḍadeyya offense. Whether one has opened the gate or not, or broken the pen or not, if one merely shakes a broken branch and does not call, and the ox, due to hunger, walks out or leaps out, it is a bhaṇḍadeyya offense indeed. One ox stands tied in the middle of the village; another is lying down. For the standing ox, there are five locations; for the lying one, there are two locations. Based on these, the acts of making it move and displacing it from its location are to be understood.

Yo pana nipannaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā tattheva ghāteti, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Suparikkhitte pana dvārayutte gāme ṭhitagoṇassa sakalagāmo ṭhānaṃ. Aparikkhitte ṭhitassa vā carantassa vā pādehi akkantaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ gadrabhapasukāsupi ayameva vinicchayoti.

Furthermore, should one kill it right there while it is lying down, without having made it stand up, it is a bhaṇḍadeyya offense. However, in a well-enclosed village equipped with gates, for a standing ox, the entire village is its location. In an unenclosed village, for one that is standing or for one that is roaming, only the place trodden by its feet is its location. For donkeys and other animals as well, this is the very same ruling.

Catuppadakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of Quadrupeds is concluded.

Bahuppadakathā

The Account of Many-Footed Beings

117. Bahuppadesu [V 1.0293] – sace ekāya satapadiyā vatthu pūrati, taṃ padasā nentassa navanavuti thullaccayāni, ekaṃ pārājikaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

117. Among many-footed beings: if the matter is fulfilled with one centipede, for the monk who leads it by its feet, there are ninety-nine thullaccaya offenses and one pārājika offense. The rest is as has been explained.

Bahuppadakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of Many-Footed Beings is concluded.

Ocarakakathā

The Account of the Informer

118. Ocaratīti [M 1.0320] ocarako, tattha tattha anto anupavisatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ocaritvāti sallakkhetvā, upadhāretvāti attho. Ācikkhatīti parakulesu vā vihārādīsu vā duṭṭhapitaṃ asaṃvihitārakkhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ aññassa corakammaṃ kātuṃ paṭibalassa āroceti. Āpatti ubhinnaṃ pārājikassāti avassaṃ hāriye bhaṇḍe ocarakassa āṇattikkhaṇe itarassa ṭhānācāvaneti evaṃ āpatti ubhinnaṃ pārājikassa. Yo pana “puriso gehe natthi, bhaṇḍaṃ asukasmiṃ nāma padese ṭhapitaṃ asaṃvihitārakkhaṃ, dvāraṃ asaṃvutaṃ, gatamatteneva sakkā harituṃ, natthi nāma koci purisakārūpajīvī, yo taṃ gantvā hareyyā”tiādinā nayena pariyāyakathaṃ karoti, tañca sutvā añño “ahaṃ dāni harissāmī”ti gantvā harati, tassa ṭhānācāvane pārājikaṃ, itarassa pana anāpatti. Pariyāyena hi adinnādānato muccatīti.

118. He is called an `ocaraka` (informer) because he roams about; it is said that he enters inside here and there. 'Having reconnoitered' means having noted and having investigated. 'He informs' means he reports to another who is capable of committing theft about goods that are poorly placed and unguarded in other families' houses or in monasteries and so forth. 'There is a pārājika offense for both' means: in the case of goods that are definitely to be taken, for the informer at the moment of giving the command, and for the other upon displacing it from its location—thus there is a pārājika offense for both. But as for one who speaks in a roundabout way, such as: 'There is no man in the house, the goods are placed in such-and-such a place unguarded, the door is not closed, it is possible to take it just by going; is there no one who lives by manly effort who, having gone, would take it?'—and another, having heard this, thinks, 'I will now take it,' and having gone, takes it; for that one, upon displacing it from its location, there is a pārājika offense, but for the other, there is no offense. For by an indirect method, one is freed from the offense of taking what is not given.

Ocarakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Informer is concluded.

Oṇirakkhakathā

The Account of the Guardian of a Deposit

Oṇiṃ rakkhatīti oṇirakkho. Yo parena attano vasanaṭṭhāne ābhataṃ bhaṇḍaṃ “idaṃ

He who guards a deposit (`oṇi`) is called an `oṇirakkha`. He is one who guards goods brought by another to his own dwelling place, [who is told,] 'this...'

Tāva, bhante, muhuttaṃ oloketha, yāva ahaṃ idaṃ nāma kiccaṃ katvā āgacchāmī”ti vutto [P 2.0366] rakkhati, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tenevāha – “oṇirakkho nāma āhaṭaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gopento”ti. Tattha oṇirakkho yebhuyyena bandhitvā laggetvā ṭhapitabhaṇḍaṃ amocetvāva heṭṭhā pasibbakaṃ vā puṭakaṃ vā chinditvā kiñcimattaṃ gahetvā sibbanādiṃ puna pākatikaṃ karoti, “evaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āmasanādīni karontassa anurupā āpattiyo veditabbāti.

'Venerable sir, for as long as it takes me to do this task and return, for that long, please look after this for a moment.' Having been told thus, he guards it. This is the designation for him. Therefore, it was said: 'An oṇirakkha is one who protects goods that have been deposited.' Therein, the oṇirakkha generally, without untying the goods that have been placed, having been tied and sealed, but having cut open the bag or bundle from underneath, and having taken just a small amount, again makes it appear as it was originally by means of sewing and so forth. For one who performs acts of touching and so forth, thinking, 'I will take it in this way,' the offenses corresponding to the value should be known.

Oṇirakkhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Guardian of a Deposit is concluded.

Saṃvidāvahārakathā

The Discourse on Theft by Agreement

Saṃvidhāya [M 1.0321][V 1.0294] avahāro saṃvidāvahāro; aññamaññasaññattiyā katāvahāroti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃvidahitvāti ekacchandatāya ekajjhāsayatāya sammantayitvāti attho. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – sambahulā bhikkhū “asukaṃ nāma gehaṃ gantvā, chadanaṃ vā bhinditvā, sandhiṃ vā chinditvā bhaṇḍaṃ harissāmā”ti saṃvidahitvā gacchanti. Tesu eko bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati. Tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Parivārepi cetaṃ vuttaṃ –

Theft by agreement is called saṃvidāvahāra; it is said to be theft done through mutual understanding. ‘Having arranged’ means having consulted with one intention and one resolve—this is the meaning. Herein, this is the decision: many monks, having made an arrangement, saying, ‘We will go to such-and-such a house, and having broken the roof or having cut through a joint, we will take the goods,’ then go. Among them, one steals the goods. Upon his removal of it, it is a pārājika offense for all of them. And this is also stated in the Parivāra:

“Caturo janā saṃvidhāya, garubhaṇḍaṃ avāharuṃ;

Tayo pārājikā, eko na pārājiko;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 479);

“Four persons, having conspired, stole heavy goods; three are subject to pārājika, one is not subject to pārājika; this question has been considered by the skilled.”

Tassāyaṃ attho – cattāro janā ācariyantevāsikā chamāsakaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ āharitukāmā jātā. Tattha ācariyo “tvaṃ ekaṃ māsakaṃ hara, tvaṃ ekaṃ, tvaṃ ekaṃ, ahaṃ tayo harissāmī”ti āha. Antevāsikesu pana paṭhamo “tumhe, bhante, tayo haratha, tvaṃ ekaṃ hara, tvaṃ ekaṃ, ahaṃ ekaṃ harissāmī”ti āha. Itarepi dve evameva āhaṃsu. Tattha antevāsikesu ekamekassa ekeko māsako sāhatthiko hoti, tena nesaṃ dukkaṭāpattiyo; pañca āṇattikā, tehi tiṇṇampi pārājikaṃ. Ācariyassa pana tayo sāhatthikā, tehissa thullaccayaṃ. Tayo āṇattikā, tehipi thullaccayameva. Imasmiñhi adinnādānasikkhāpade sāhatthikaṃ vā āṇattikassa, āṇattikaṃ vā sāhatthikassa [P 2.0367] aṅgaṃ na hoti. Sāhatthikaṃ pana sāhatthikeneva kāretabbaṃ, āṇattikaṃ āṇattikeneva. Tena vuttaṃ – “caturo janā saṃvidhāya…pe… pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti.

This is its meaning: four persons, a teacher and his disciples, became desirous of taking heavy goods worth six māsakas. Therein, the teacher said, ‘You take one māsaka, you take one, you take one, and I will take three.’ Among the disciples, however, the first said, ‘Venerable sir, you take three, you take one, you take one, and I will take one.’ The other two also spoke in this very same way. Therein, for each of the disciples, one māsaka is taken by his own hand; because of that, for them there are dukkaṭa offenses. Five māsakas are taken by instruction; because of these, for all three of them it is a pārājika offense. For the teacher, however, three māsakas are taken by his own hand; because of these, for him it is a thullaccaya offense. Three are taken by instruction; because of these also, it is a thullaccaya offense indeed. For in this training rule on taking what is not given, an act by one’s own hand is not a component of an act by instruction, nor is an act by instruction a component of an act by one’s own hand. Rather, an act by one’s own hand must be completed by one’s own hand, and an act by instruction must be completed by instruction. Therefore it was said: ‘Four persons, having conspired… this question has been considered by the skilled.’”

Apica saṃvidāvahāre asammohatthaṃ “ekabhaṇḍaṃ ekaṭṭhānaṃ, ekabhaṇḍaṃ nānāṭhānaṃ; nānābhaṇḍaṃ ekaṭṭhānaṃ, nānābhaṇḍaṃ nānāṭhāna”nti idampi catukkaṃ atthato sallakkhetabbaṃ. Tattha ekabhaṇḍaṃ ekaṭṭhānanti ekakulassa āpaṇaphalake pañcamāsakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ duṭṭhapitaṃ disvā sambahulā bhikkhū ekaṃ āṇāpenti “gacchetaṃ āharā”ti, tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Ekabhaṇḍaṃ [M 1.0322] nānāṭhānanti ekakulassa pañcasu āpaṇaphalakesu ekekamāsakaṃ duṭṭhapitaṃ disvā sambahulā ekaṃ āṇāpenti “gacchete āharā”ti, pañcamassa māsakassa uddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Nānābhaṇḍaṃ ekaṭṭhānanti bahūnaṃ santakaṃ pañcamāsakaṃ vā atirekapañcamāsakaṃ vā agghanakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ [V 1.0295] ekasmiṃ ṭhāne duṭṭhapitaṃ disvā sambahulā ekaṃ āṇāpenti “gacchetaṃ āharā”ti, tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Nānābhaṇḍaṃ nānāṭhānanti pañcannaṃ kulānaṃ pañcasu āpaṇaphalakesu ekekamāsakaṃ duṭṭhapitaṃ disvā sambahulā ekaṃ āṇāpenti “gacchete āharā”ti, pañcamassa māsakassa uddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikanti.

Furthermore, in theft by agreement, for the purpose of non-confusion, this tetrad should also be noted by way of its meaning: ‘one item, one place; one item, various places; various items, one place; various items, various places.’ Therein, ‘one item, one place’ is as follows: having seen goods worth five māsakas belonging to one family carelessly placed on a shop-board, many monks instruct one, saying, ‘Go, bring it.’ Upon its removal, it is a pārājika offense for all. ‘One item, various places’ is as follows: having seen goods worth one māsaka each, belonging to one family, carelessly placed on five shop-boards, many monks instruct one, saying, ‘Go, bring them.’ Upon the removal of the fifth māsaka, it is a pārājika offense for all. ‘Various items, one place’ is as follows: having seen goods worth five māsakas or more, belonging to many people, carelessly placed in one location, many monks instruct one, saying, ‘Go, bring it.’ Upon its removal, it is a pārājika offense for all. ‘Various items, various places’ is as follows: having seen goods worth one māsaka each, belonging to five families, carelessly placed on five shop-boards, many monks instruct one, saying, ‘Go, bring them.’ Upon the removal of the fifth māsaka, it is a pārājika offense for all.

Saṃvidāvahārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Theft by Agreement is concluded.

Saṅketakammakathā

The Discourse on an Act by Agreement

119. Saṅketakammanti sañjānanakammaṃ; kālaparicchedavasena saññāṇakaraṇanti attho. Ettha ca “purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte ajja vā purebhattaṃ avaharatu, sve vā, anāgate vā saṃvacchare, natthi visaṅketo; ubhinnampi ocarake vuttanayeneva pārājikaṃ. Sace pana “ajja purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte sve purebhattaṃ avaharati, “ajjā”ti niyāmitaṃ taṃ saṅketaṃ atikkamma pacchā avahaṭaṃ hoti. Sace “sve purebhattaṃ avaharā”ti vutte ajja purebhattaṃ avaharati[P 2.0368], “sve”ti niyāmitaṃ taṃ saṅketaṃ appatvā pure avahaṭaṃ hoti; evaṃ avaharantassa avahārakasseva pārājikaṃ, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpatti. “Sve purebhatta”nti vutte tadaheva vā sve pacchābhattaṃ vā harantopi taṃ saṅketaṃ pure ca pacchā ca haratīti veditabbo. Esa nayo pacchābhattarattindivesupi. Purimayāma-majjhimayāma-pacchimayāma-kāḷajuṇha-māsa-utu-saṃvaccharādivasenāpi cettha saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā. “Purebhattaṃ harā”ti vutte “purebhattameva harissāmī”ti vāyamantassa pacchābhattaṃ hoti; ettha kathanti? Mahāsumatthero tāva āha – “purebhattapayogova eso, tasmā mūlaṭṭho na muccatī”ti. Mahāpadumatthero panāha – “kālaparicchedaṃ atikkantattā visaṅketaṃ, tasmā mūlaṭṭho muccatī”ti.

119. An act by agreement (saṅketakamma) is an act of recognition; the meaning is the making of a sign by way of defining a period of time. And here, when it is said, “Steal in the forenoon,” whether one steals in the forenoon today, or tomorrow, or in a future year, there is no failed agreement; for both, a pārājika offense is incurred in the same way as stated in the Discourse on the Instigator. But if, when it is said, “Steal today in the forenoon,” one steals tomorrow in the forenoon, that agreement specified as “today” has been transgressed, and the theft is committed afterwards. If, when it is said, “Steal tomorrow in the forenoon,” one steals today in the forenoon, that agreement specified as “tomorrow” has not been reached, and the theft is committed beforehand; when stealing thus, the pārājika offense is for the one who steals only, and there is no offense for the original instigator. When it is said, “Tomorrow in the forenoon,” it should be understood that one who steals on that very day or tomorrow in the afternoon steals both before and after that agreement. This is the method also for the afternoon, night, and day. And here, the state of being an agreement and the state of being a failed agreement should also be understood by way of the first watch, middle watch, last watch, the dark and bright fortnights, month, season, year, and so on. When it is said, “Steal in the forenoon,” while one is striving, thinking, “I will steal only in the forenoon,” it becomes afternoon; what is the case here? The Elder Mahāsuma first said: “This is an undertaking of the forenoon; therefore, the original instigator is not absolved.” But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: “Because the time-limit has been transgressed, it is a failed agreement; therefore, the original instigator is absolved.”

Saṅketakammakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on an Act by Agreement is concluded.

Nimittakammakathā

The Discourse on an Act by a Sign

120. Nimittakammanti [M 1.0323] saññuppādanatthaṃ kassaci nimittassa karaṇaṃ, taṃ “akkhiṃ vā nikhaṇissāmī”tiādinā nayena tidhā vuttaṃ. Aññampi panettha hatthalaṅghana-pāṇippahāraaṅguliphoṭana-gīvunnāmana-ukkāsanādianekappakāraṃ [V 1.0296] saṅgahetabbaṃ. Sesamettha saṅketakamme vuttanayamevāti.

120. An act by a sign (`nimittakamma`) is the making of some sign for the purpose of producing an understanding. This has been spoken of in three ways, by the method beginning with, “I will wink an eye.” And here, many other kinds should also be included, such as raising the hand, clapping the hands, snapping the fingers, raising the neck, clearing the throat, and so on. The rest here is just according to the method stated in the Discourse on an Act by Agreement.

Nimittakammakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on an Act by a Sign is concluded.

Āṇattikathā

The Discourse on Command

121. Idāni etesveva saṅketakammanimittakammesu asammohatthaṃ “bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetī”tiādimāha. Tattha so taṃ maññamāno tanti so avahārako yaṃ āṇāpakena nimittasaññaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, taṃ etanti maññamāno tameva avaharati, ubhinnaṃ pārājikaṃ. So taṃ maññamāno aññanti yaṃ avaharāti vuttaṃ, taṃ etanti maññamāno aññaṃ tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne ṭhapitaṃ avaharati, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpatti. Aññaṃ maññamāno tanti āṇāpakena nimittasaññaṃ katvā vuttabhaṇḍaṃ appagghaṃ, idaṃ aññaṃ tasseva samīpe ṭhapitaṃ sārabhaṇḍanti evaṃ aññaṃ maññamāno tameva avaharati, ubhinnampi pārājikaṃ. Aññaṃ maññamāno aññanti purimanayeneva idaṃ aññaṃ tasseva samīpe ṭhapitaṃ sārabhaṇḍanti [P 2.0369] maññati, tañce aññameva hoti, tasseva pārājikaṃ.

121. Now, for the purpose of non-bewilderment regarding these very acts by agreement and acts by a sign, He said the passage beginning with, “A bhikkhu commands a bhikkhu.” Therein, regarding so taṃ maññamāno taṃ (he, thinking it is that, steals that): if that thieving bhikkhu, thinking, “That which was spoken of by the commander after making an indicative sign is this,” steals that very article, it is a pārājika for both. Regarding so taṃ maññamāno aññaṃ (he, thinking it is that, steals another): thinking, “That which was told, ‘Steal,’ is this,” he steals another article placed in that very spot; there is no offense for the original commander. Regarding aññaṃ maññamāno taṃ (thinking it is another, he steals that): the article spoken of by the commander after making an indicative sign is of little value, but thinking, “This is another, a valuable article placed near that very one,” he steals that very article spoken of; it is a pārājika for both as well. Regarding aññaṃ maññamāno aññaṃ (thinking it is another, he steals another): in the same way as before, he thinks, “This is another, a valuable article placed near that very one,” and if it is indeed another article, it is a pārājika for him (the thief) alone.

Itthannāmassa pāvadātiādīsu eko ācariyo tayo buddharakkhita-dhammarakkhita-saṅgharakkhitanāmakā antevāsikā daṭṭhabbā. Tattha bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetīti ācariyo kiñci bhaṇḍaṃ katthaci sallakkhetvā tassa haraṇatthāya buddharakkhitaṃ āṇāpeti. Itthannāmassa pāvadāti gaccha tvaṃ, buddharakkhita, etamatthaṃ dhammarakkhitassa pāvada. Itthannāmo itthannāmassa pāvadatūti dhammarakkhitopi saṅgharakkhitassa pāvadatu. Itthannāmo itthannāmaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharatūti evaṃ tayā āṇattena dhammarakkhitena āṇatto saṅgharakkhito itthannāmaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharatu, so hi amhesu vīrajātiko paṭibalo imasmiṃ kammeti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ āṇāpentassa ācariyassa tāva dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana sā āṇatti yathādhippāyaṃ [M 1.0324] gacchati, yaṃ parato thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ, āṇattikkhaṇe tadeva hoti. Atha taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avassaṃ hāriyaṃ hoti, yaṃ parato “sabbesaṃ āpatti pārājikassā”ti vuttaṃ, tato imassa taṅkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ hotīti ayaṃ yutti sabbattha veditabbā.

In the phrases beginning with “Tell so-and-so,” one teacher and three disciples named Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita are to be understood. Therein, “a bhikkhu commands a bhikkhu” means: the teacher, having noted some article somewhere, commands Buddharakkhita for the purpose of stealing it. “Tell so-and-so” means: “You go, Buddharakkhita, tell this matter to Dhammarakkhita.” “Let so-and-so tell so-and-so” means: “Let Dhammarakkhita also tell Saṅgharakkhita.” “Let so-and-so steal the article named so-and-so” means: “Thus, let Saṅgharakkhita, who was commanded by Dhammarakkhita who was commanded by you, steal the article named so-and-so, for among us, he is of a courageous nature and is capable in this kind of work.” Regarding “There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)”: for the teacher commanding thus, there is at first a dukkaṭa. But if that command proceeds according to intention, what is later called a grave offense (thullaccaya), that very offense occurs at the moment of command. Or, if that article is one that will definitely be stolen, then because of what is later said, “For all, there is an offense of pārājika,” for this teacher, it becomes a pārājika at that very moment of command. This logic should be understood in all such cases.

So itarassa ārocetīti buddharakkhito dhammarakkhitassa, dhammarakkhito ca saṅgharakkhitassa “amhākaṃ ācariyo evaṃ vadati – ‘itthannāmaṃ kira bhaṇḍaṃ avahara, tvaṃ kira amhesu ca vīrapuriso’”ti [V 1.0297] āroceti, evaṃ tesampi dukkaṭaṃ. Avahārako paṭiggaṇhātīti “sādhu harissāmī”ti saṅgharakkhito sampaṭicchati. Mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti thullaccayassāti saṅgharakkhitena paṭiggahitamatte ācariyassa thullaccayaṃ, mahājano hi tena pāpe niyojitoti. So taṃ bhaṇḍanti so ce saṅgharakkhito taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, sabbesaṃ catunnampi janānaṃ pārājikaṃ. Na kevalañca catunnaṃ, etena upāyena visaṅketaṃ akatvā paramparāya āṇāpentaṃ samaṇasataṃ samaṇasahassaṃ vā hotu, sabbesaṃ pārājikameva.

“He informs the other” means: Buddharakkhita informs Dhammarakkhita, and Dhammarakkhita informs Saṅgharakkhita, saying, “Our teacher says thus: ‘It is said, steal the article named so-and-so. It is said, you among us are a brave man.’” Thus, for them (Buddharakkhita and Dhammarakkhita) also, there is a dukkaṭa. “The thief accepts” means: Saṅgharakkhita accepts, saying, “Good, I will steal it.” “For the original person, there is an offense of thullaccaya” means: at the very moment of acceptance by Saṅgharakkhita, it is a thullaccaya for the teacher, for a great number of people have been incited to evil by him. Regarding “he steals that article”: if that Saṅgharakkhita steals that article, it is a pārājika for all four persons. And not only for the four; by this method, without making a deviation from the instruction, whether it be a hundred samaṇas or a thousand samaṇas commanding in succession, it is a pārājika for all of them.

Dutiyavāre – so aññaṃ āṇāpetīti so ācariyena āṇatto buddharakkhito dhammarakkhitaṃ adisvā vā avattukāmo vā hutvā saṅgharakkhitameva upasaṅkamitvā “amhākaṃ ācariyo evamāha – ‘itthannāmaṃ kira bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā’”ti āṇāpeti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti āṇattiyā tāva buddharakkhitassa dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassāti saṅgharakkhitena sampaṭicchite mūlaṭṭhasseva [P 2.0370] dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. Sace pana so taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āṇāpakassa ca buddharakkhitassa, avahārakassa ca saṅgharakkhitassāti ubhinnampi pārājikaṃ. Mūlaṭṭhassa pana ācariyassa visaṅketattā pārājikena anāpatti. Dhammarakkhitassa ajānanatāya sabbena sabbaṃ anāpatti. Buddharakkhito pana dvinnaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ katvā attanā naṭṭho.

In the second case, regarding “he commands another”: that Buddharakkhita, commanded by the teacher, having not seen Dhammarakkhita or being unwilling to speak to him, approaches only Saṅgharakkhita and commands, “Our teacher said thus: ‘It is said, steal the article named so-and-so.’” Regarding “There is an offense of dukkaṭa”: because of the command, there is at first a dukkaṭa for Buddharakkhita. Regarding “He accepts, there is an offense of dukkaṭa”: it should be understood that when it is accepted by Saṅgharakkhita, there is a dukkaṭa for the original person (the teacher). But if he (Saṅgharakkhita) steals that article, it is a pārājika for both the commander, Buddharakkhita, and the thief, Saṅgharakkhita. But for the original person, the teacher, there is no offense of pārājika due to the deviation from the instruction. For Dhammarakkhita, due to not knowing, there is no offense whatsoever. But Buddharakkhita, having brought about the security of two persons, is himself ruined.

Ito paresu catūsu āṇattivāresu paṭhame tāva so gantvā puna paccāgacchatīti bhaṇḍaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā anto ca bahi ca ārakkhaṃ disvā avaharituṃ asakkonto āgacchati. Yadā sakkosi, tadāti kiṃ ajjeva avahaṭaṃ hoti? Gaccha yadā sakkosi tadā naṃ avaharāti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ puna āṇattiyāpi dukkaṭameva hoti. Sace pana taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avassaṃ hāriyaṃ hoti, atthasādhakacetanā nāma maggānantaraphalasadisā, tasmā [M 1.0325] ayaṃ āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājiko. Sacepi avahārako saṭṭhivassātikkamena taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āṇāpako ca antarāyeva kālaṃ vā karoti, hīnāya vā āvattati; assamaṇova hutvā kālaṃ vā karissati, hīnāya vā āvattissati, avahārakassa pana avahārakkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ.

In the first of the four subsequent cases of command, regarding “he, having gone, returns again”: this means he goes to the place of the article, and seeing guards both inside and outside, being unable to steal, he returns. Regarding “When you are able, then...”: this means the commander says, “Go, when you are able, then steal it.” Regarding “There is an offense of dukkaṭa”: thus, for the repeated command also, there is a dukkaṭa. But if that article is one that will definitely be stolen, the volition that accomplishes the purpose is like the fruit immediately following the path; therefore, this one (the commander) is a pārājika offender at the very moment of command. Even if the thief steals that article after sixty years have passed, and the commander in the meantime either dies or reverts to a lower state, he, having already become a non-samaṇa, will die or will revert to a lower state. But for the thief, the pārājika occurs at the very moment of stealing.

Dutiyavāre – yasmā taṃ saṇikaṃ vā bhaṇanto tassa vā badhiratāya “mā avaharī”ti

In the second instance: because, either by speaking softly or due to his (the other's) deafness, regarding the words 'Do not take it away',

Etaṃ vacanaṃ na sāveti, tasmā mūlaṭṭho na mutto. Tatiyavāre – pana sāvitattā mutto. Catutthavāre [V 1.0298] – tena ca sāvitattā, itarena ca “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā oratattā ubhopi muttāti.

he does not cause this statement to be heard, therefore the original person is not absolved. But in the third instance, because it was caused to be heard, he is absolved. In the fourth instance, both because it was caused to be heard by him, and because the other, having accepted with 'Good,' desisted, both are absolved.

Āṇattikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Command is finished.

Āpattibhedaṃ

The Classification of Offenses

122. Idāni tattha tattha ṭhānā cāvanavasena vuttassa adinnādānassa aṅgaṃ vatthubhedena ca āpattibhedaṃ dassento “pañcahi ākārehī”tiādimāha. Tattha pañcahi ākārehīti pañcahi kāraṇehi; pañcahi aṅgehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – adinnaṃ ādiyantassa “parapariggahitañca hotī”tiādinā nayena vuttehi pañcahākārehi pārājikaṃ hoti, na tato ūnehīti. Tatrime pañca ākārā – parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitasaññitā[P 2.0371], parikkhārassa garukabhāvo, theyyacittaṃ, ṭhānācāvananti. Ito parehi pana dvīhi vārehi lahuke parikkhāre vatthubhedena thullaccayañca dukkaṭañca dassitaṃ.

122. Now, showing the factor of the taking of what is not given—which was spoken of by way of removing from its place in those various instances—and the classification of offenses by the distinction of the object, he said, beginning with, 'by five modes.' Therein, 'by five modes' means by five causes; it is said to mean by five factors. Herein, this is the summary meaning: for one who takes what is not given, it is a Pārājika offense by the five modes spoken of in the method beginning with 'it is possessed by another,' and not by fewer than these. Therein, these are the five modes: (1) being possessed by another, (2) the perception of it as being possessed by another, (3) the requisite being of significant value, (4) the intention to steal, and (5) removing it from its place. Furthermore, in the two sections following this, a Thullaccaya and a Dukkaṭa offense are shown for a minor requisite, with distinctions based on the object.

125. “Chahākārehī”tiādinā nayena vuttavārattaye pana na sakasaññitā, na vissāsaggāhitā, na tāvakālikatā, parikkhārassa garukabhāvo, theyyacittaṃ, ṭhānācāvananti evaṃ cha ākārā veditabbā. Vatthubhedena panetthāpi paṭhamavāre pārājikaṃ. Dutiyatatiyesu thullaccayadukkaṭāni vuttāni. Tato paresu pana tīsu vāresu vijjamānepi vatthubhede vatthussa parehi apariggahitattā dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ. Tatra yadetaṃ “na [M 1.0326] ca parapariggahita”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ anajjhāvutthakaṃ vā hotu chaḍḍitaṃ chinnamūlakaṃ assāmikavatthu, attano santakaṃ vā, ubhayampi “na ca parapariggahita”ntveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Yasmā panettha parapariggahitasaññā ca atthi, theyyacittena ca gahitaṃ, tasmā anāpatti na vuttāti.

125. However, in the three sections spoken of in the method beginning with 'by six modes,' these six modes should be understood: (1) not perceiving it as one's own, (2) not taking it with trust, (3) not taking it temporarily, (4) the requisite being of significant value, (5) the intention to steal, and (6) removing it from its place. Furthermore, herein also, by the distinction of the object, in the first section, a Pārājika is stated. In the second and third, Thullaccaya and Dukkaṭa offenses are stated. However, in the three sections following that, even though there is a distinction of the object, because the object is not possessed by others, only a Dukkaṭa is stated. Therein, that which is stated as 'and not possessed by another,' let that be an object not under anyone's dominion, or discarded, or one on which claim has been relinquished, an ownerless object, or one's own property—both are classified as 'and not possessed by another.' Because herein there is the perception of it as possessed by another and it is taken with the intention to steal, therefore, no-offense is not stated.

Āpattibhedaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Classification of Offenses is concluded.

Anāpattibhedaṃ

The Classification of No-Offenses

131. Evaṃ vatthuvasena ca cittavasena ca āpattibhedaṃ dassetvā idāni anāpattibhedaṃ dassento “anāpatti sasaññissā”tiādimāha. Tattha sasaññissāti sakasaññissa, “mayhaṃ santakaṃ [V 1.0299] idaṃ bhaṇḍa”nti evaṃ sasaññissa parabhaṇḍampi gaṇhato gahaṇe anāpatti, gahitaṃ pana puna dātabbaṃ. Sace sāmikehi “dehī”ti vutto na deti, tesaṃ dhuranikkhepe pārājikaṃ.

131. Having thus shown the classification of offenses by way of the object and by way of the mind, now, showing the classification of no-offenses, he said, beginning with, 'There is no offense for one with the perception of it as one's own.' Therein, 'for one with the perception of it as one's own' means for one with the perception of it as one's own property, thus: 'This item is my property.' For one with such a perception, there is no offense in the act of taking even another's item; however, what has been taken must be given back. If, having been told 'Give it' by the owners, he does not give it, it becomes a Pārājika offense at the point of their abandonment of the burden of seeking its return.

Vissāsaggāheti vissāsaggahaṇepi anāpatti. Vissāsaggāhalakkhaṇaṃ pana iminā suttena jānitabbaṃ – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa vissāsaṃ gahetuṃ – sandiṭṭho ca hoti, sambhatto ca, ālapito ca, jīvati ca, gahite ca attamano”ti (mahāva. 356). Tattha sandiṭṭhoti diṭṭhamattakamitto, sambhattoti daḷhamitto, ālapitoti “mama santakaṃ yaṃ icchasi, taṃ gaṇheyyāsi, āpucchitvā gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ natthī”ti vutto. Jīvatīti anuṭṭhānaseyyāya sayitopi yāva [P 2.0372] jīvitindriyupacchedaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Gahite ca attamanoti gahite tuṭṭhacitto hoti, evarūpassa santakaṃ “gahite me attamano bhavissatī”ti jānantena gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anavasesapariyādānavasena cetāni pañcaṅgāni vuttāni. Vissāsaggāho pana tīhi aṅgehi ruhati – sandiṭṭho, jīvati, gahite attamano; sambhatto, jīvati, gahite attamano; ālapito, jīvati, gahite attamanoti.

Regarding taking with trust: even in taking with trust, there is no offense. However, the characteristic of taking with trust should be known through this discourse: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, to take with trust from one endowed with five factors: (1) he is an acquaintance, (2) he is a close friend, (3) he has given leave, (4) he is alive, and (5) he is pleased when it is taken.' Therein, 'an acquaintance' (sandiṭṭho) means a friend merely by having been seen. 'A close friend' (sambhatto) means a firm friend. 'Has given leave' (ālapito) means one has been told, 'Take whatever of mine you wish; there is no reason to ask before taking.' 'Is alive' (jīvati) means that even if one is lying in a sleep from which one does not rise, one has not yet reached the cutting off of the life faculty. 'Is pleased when it is taken' (gahite ca attamano) means one has a pleased mind when it is taken. It is proper for one who knows, 'He will be pleased in mind when I take it,' to take the property of such a person. These five factors are stated by way of a complete enumeration. However, taking with trust is established by three factors: (1) an acquaintance, is alive, and is pleased when it is taken; (2) a close friend, is alive, and is pleased when it is taken; or (3) has given leave, is alive, and is pleased when it is taken.

Yo pana na jīvati, na ca gahite attamano hoti; tassa santakaṃ vissāsaggāhena gahitampi puna dātabbaṃ. Dadamānena ca matakadhanaṃ tāva ye tassa dhane issarā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā, tesaṃ dātabbaṃ. Anattamanassa santakaṃ tasseva dātabbaṃ. Yo pana paṭhamaṃyeva “suṭṭhu kataṃ tayā mama santakaṃ gaṇhantenā”ti vacībhedena vā cittuppādamattena vā anumoditvā pacchā [M 1.0327] kenaci kāraṇena kupito, paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yopi adātukāmo cittena pana adhivāseti, na kiñci vadati, sopi puna paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yo pana “mayā tumhākaṃ santakaṃ gahitaṃ vā paribhuttaṃ vā”ti vutte “gahitaṃ vā hotu paribhuttaṃ vā, mayā pana taṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena ṭhapitaṃ, pākatikaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadati. Ayaṃ paccāharāpetuṃ labhati.

As for one who is not alive, or is not pleased when it is taken, what belongs to him, even if taken with trust, must be given back. And when giving it back, the wealth of a deceased person should first be given to those, whether householders or renunciates, who are the masters of his wealth or his heirs. The property of one who is displeased should be given to that very person. However, one who, having first rejoiced either by verbal expression or by a mere arising of thought, saying, 'It was well done by you in taking my property,' later becomes angry for some reason, does not get to have it brought back. Also, one who is unwilling to give but consents with his mind and says nothing, he too does not get to have it brought back. But one who, when it is said, 'Your property was taken or used by me,' says, 'Let it be taken or used, but I had set it aside for some purpose; it is proper to restore it to its original state'—this person gets to have it brought back.

Tāvakāliketi “paṭidassāmi paṭikarissāmī”ti evaṃ gaṇhantassa tāvakālikepi gahaṇe anāpatti. Gahitaṃ pana sace bhaṇḍasāmiko puggalo vā gaṇo vā “tuyhevetaṃ hotū”ti anujānāti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce anujānāti, āharāpente dātabbaṃ. Saṅghasantakaṃ pana paṭidātumeva vaṭṭati.

Regarding taking temporarily: for one who takes something thinking, 'I will give it back; I will replace it,' there is no offense even in this temporary taking. However, regarding what was taken, if the owner of the item, whether an individual or a group, permits it, saying, 'Let this be yours,' this is wholesome. If they do not permit it, it must be given back when they ask for its return. But what belongs to the Sangha, it is proper only to give it back.

Petapariggaheti ettha pana pettivisaye upapannāpi kālaṃ katvā tasmiṃyeva attabhāve nibbattāpi [V 1.0300] cātumahārājikādayo devāpi sabbe “petā” tveva saṅkhyaṃ gatā, tesaṃ pariggahe anāpatti. Sacepi hi sakko devarājā āpaṇaṃ pasāretvā nisinno hoti, dibbacakkhuko ca bhikkhu taṃ ñatvā attano cīvaratthāya satasahassagghanakampi sāṭakaṃ [P 2.0373] tassa “mā gaṇha, mā gaṇhā”ti vadantassāpi gahetvā gacchati, vaṭṭati. Devatā pana uddissa balikammaṃ karontehi rukkhādīsu laggitasāṭake vattabbameva natthi.

Regarding taking what is possessed by petas: Herein, those arisen in the sphere of petas, those who, having died, are reborn in that very same existence, and even devas such as the Cātumahārājikas—all are classified only as 'petas.' In taking what is possessed by them, there is no offense. For even if Sakka, king of the devas, is sitting having spread out a shop, and a bhikkhu with the divine eye, knowing that, takes a cloth worth a hundred thousand for his own robe and goes away, even while Sakka is saying, 'Do not take, do not take!' it is allowable. However, regarding a cloth hung on trees and so on by those making offerings dedicated to deities, there is nothing at all to be said (about its being allowable).

Tiracchānagatapariggaheti tiracchānagatānampi pariggahe anāpatti. Sacepi hi nāgarājā vā supaṇṇamāṇavako vā manussarūpena āpaṇaṃ pasāreti, tato cassa santakaṃ koci bhikkhu purimanayeneva gahetvā gacchati, vaṭṭati. Sīho vā byaggho vā migamahiṃsādayo vadhitvā khādanto jighacchāpīḷito āditova na vāretabbo. Anatthampi hi kareyya. Yadi pana thoke khāyite vāretuṃ sakkoti, vāretvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Senādayopi āmisaṃ gahetvā gacchante pātāpetvā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati.

Regarding taking what belongs to an animal: There is no offense in taking what belongs even to animals. Indeed, if a nāga king or a young supaṇṇa sets up a shop in human form, and a certain monk, having taken something belonging to him from there in the previously mentioned manner, goes away, it is permissible. If a lion, a tiger, or other such animals, being afflicted by hunger, are killing and eating a deer, a buffalo, or the like, they should not be stopped or scared away from the very beginning. Indeed, they might cause harm. However, if one is able to stop them after a little has been eaten, having stopped them, it is permissible to take the rest. It is also permissible to take flesh from hawks and other birds while they are flying away with it, by causing them to drop it.

Paṃsukūlasaññissāti assāmikaṃ “idaṃ paṃsukūla”nti evaṃsaññissāpi gahaṇe anāpatti. Sace pana taṃ sassāmikaṃ hoti, āharāpente dātabbaṃ[M 1.0328]. Ummattakassāti pubbe vuttappakārassa ummattakassāpi anāpatti. Ādikammikassāti idha dhaniyo ādikammiko, tassa anāpatti. Avasesānaṃ pana rajakabhaṇḍikādicorānaṃ chabbaggiyādīnaṃ āpattiyevāti.

For one who perceives it as dust-heap cloth: In the taking by a monk who perceives an ownerless thing thus, 'This is dust-heap cloth,' there is no offense. However, if it has an owner, it should be given back when they ask for its return. For an insane person: For an insane person of the type previously mentioned, there is no offense. For the first offender: Here, Dhaniya is the first offender; for him, there is no offense. However, for the remaining ones, such as the thieves of the washermen's bundles, the group-of-six monks, and others, there is indeed an offense.

Anāpattibhedaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Non-Offenses is concluded.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Word-Analysis is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse

Samuṭṭhānañca kiriyā, atho saññā sacittakaṃ;

Lokavajjañca kammañca, kusalaṃ vedanāya cāti.

Origination and action, then perception and intentionality; worldly fault and action, mental state and feeling.

Imasmiṃ pana pakiṇṇake idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ – sāhatthikaṃ kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti, āṇattikaṃ vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti, sāhatthikāṇattikaṃ kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyāsamuṭṭhānañca, karontoyeva hi etaṃ āpajjati na akaronto. “Adinnaṃ ādiyāmī”ti saññāya abhāvena muccanato saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ[V 1.0301], lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, tuṭṭho vā bhīto vā majjhatto vā taṃ āpajjatīti tivedananti sabbaṃ paṭhamasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, in this miscellaneous discourse, this training rule has three origins: an act by one's own hand originates from body and mind; an act by command originates from speech and mind; an act by one's own hand and by command originates from body, speech, and mind. It also originates from action; indeed, only one who acts incurs this offense, not one who does not act. It is a 'release through perception' because one is absolved due to the absence of the perception, 'I am taking what is not given.' It is intentional, a worldly fault, a bodily action, and a verbal action. It involves an unwholesome mind. One incurs it whether pleased, afraid, or indifferent, thus it involves three feelings. All this should be understood in the manner explained in the first training rule.

Pakiṇṇakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Miscellaneous Discourse is concluded.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Judged Cases

132. Vinītavatthukathāsu [P 2.0374] chabbaggiyavatthu anupaññattiyaṃ vuttameva.

132. In the accounts of the judged cases, the case of the group-of-six monks was already stated in the supplementary regulation.

Dutiyavatthumhi – cittaṃ nāma puthujjanānaṃ rāgādivasena pakatiṃ vijahitvā dhāvati sandhāvati vidhāvati. Sace bhagavā kāyavacīdvārabhedaṃ vināpi cittuppādamattena āpattiṃ paññapeyya, ko sakkuṇeyya anāpattikaṃ attānaṃ kātuṃ! Tenāha – “anāpatti bhikkhu cittuppāde”ti. Cittavasikena pana na bhavitabbaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānabalena cittaṃ nivāretabbamevāti.

In the second case: The mind of ordinary people, abandoning its natural state on account of lust and so on, runs, runs exceedingly, and runs in various ways. If the Blessed One were to lay down an offense merely for the arising of a thought, even without a breach of the body-door or speech-door, who would be able to keep themselves free from offense? Therefore, He said: 'Monk, there is no offense in the arising of a thought.' However, one should not be under the sway of the mind; the mind must certainly be restrained by the power of reflective understanding.

133-4. Āmasana-phandāpana-ṭhānācāvanavatthūni uttānatthāneva. Tato parāni ca theyyacitto bhūmito aggahesīti vatthupariyosānāni.

The cases of touching, causing to tremble, and moving from a place are of clear meaning. The subsequent cases, ending with the case 'with thievish intent, he took from the ground,' are also of clear meaning.

135. Niruttipathavatthusmiṃ 1.329 ādiyīti gaṇhi, “corosi tva”nti parāmasi. Itaro pana “kena avahaṭa”nti vutte “mayā avahaṭa”nti pucchāsabhāgena paṭiññaṃ adāsi. Yadi hi itarena “kena gahitaṃ, kena apanītaṃ, kena ṭhapita”nti vuttaṃ abhavissa, atha ayampi “mayā gahitaṃ, apanītaṃ, ṭhapita”nti vā vadeyya. Mukhaṃ nāma bhuñjanatthāya ca kathanatthāya ca kataṃ, theyyacittaṃ pana vinā avahāro natthi. Tenāha bhagavā – “anāpatti bhikkhu niruttipathe”ti. Vohāravacanamatte anāpattīti attho. Tato paraṃ veṭhanavatthu pariyosānaṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

135. In the case of the path of expression: `ādiyi` means 'he took'; `parāmasi` means 'he accused him, saying, “You are a thief.”' But the other monk, when asked, 'By whom was it taken away?' gave an admission that corresponded with the question, saying, 'It was taken away by me.' For if the other had said, 'By whom was it taken?', 'By whom was it removed?', or 'By whom was it placed?', then this one too would have said, 'It was taken by me,' 'It was removed by me,' or 'It was placed by me.' The mouth, indeed, is made for eating and for speaking, but without a thievish intent, there is no 'taking away.' Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Monk, there is no offense in the path of expression.' The meaning is that there is no offense in a mere conventional utterance. After that, all the cases up to the final case of the wrapping are of clear meaning.

137. Abhinnasarīravatthusmiṃ adhivatthoti sāṭakataṇhāya tasmiṃyeva sarīre nibbatto. Anādiyantoti tassa vacanaṃ agaṇhanto, ādaraṃ vā akaronto. Taṃ sarīraṃ uṭṭhahitvāti peto attano ānubhāvena taṃ sarīraṃ uṭṭhāpesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “taṃ sarīraṃ uṭṭhahitvā”ti. Dvāraṃ thakesīti bhikkhussa susānasamīpeyeva vihāro, tasmā bhīrukajātiko bhikkhu khippameva tattha pavisitvā [V 1.0302] dvāraṃ thakesi. Tattheva paripatīti dvāre thakite peto sāṭake nirālayo hutvā taṃ sarīraṃ pahāya yathākammaṃ gato, tasmā taṃ sarīraṃ tattheva paripati, patitanti vuttaṃ hoti.

137. In the case of the unbroken corpse: `adhivattho` means he was reborn in that very body due to craving for the cloth. `Anādiyanto` means not heeding his words, or not paying attention. 'That corpse rose up' means the peta, by his own power, made that corpse rise up. Therefore it was said, 'that corpse rose up.' 'He bolted the door' means the monk's dwelling was right near the charnel ground; therefore the monk, being of a fearful nature, quickly entered there and bolted the door. 'It fell right there' means that when the door was bolted, the peta, becoming unattached to the cloth, abandoned that body and went according to his kamma. Therefore, that corpse fell right there; this is the meaning of 'it fell.'

Abhinne sarīreti abbhuṇhe allasarīre paṃsukūlaṃ na gahetabbaṃ, gaṇhantassa evarūpā upaddavā honti, dukkaṭañca āpajjati. Bhinne pana [P 2.0375] gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kittāvatā pana bhinnaṃ hoti? Kāka-kulala-soṇa-siṅgālādīhi mukhatuṇḍakena vā dāṭhāya vā īsakaṃ phālitamattenāpi. Yassa pana patato ghaṃsanena chavimattaṃ chinnaṃ hoti, cammaṃ acchinnaṃ, etaṃ abhinnameva; camme pana chinne bhinnaṃ. Yassāpi sajīvakāleyeva pabhinnā gaṇḍakuṭṭhapiḷakā vā vaṇo vā hoti, idampi bhinnaṃ. Tatiyadivasato pabhuti uddhumātakādibhāvena kuṇapabhāvaṃ upagatampi bhinnameva. Sabbena sabbaṃ pana abhinnepi susānagopakehi vā aññehi vā manussehi gāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. No ce aññaṃ labhati, satthakena vā kenaci vā vaṇaṃ katvā gahetabbaṃ. Visabhāgasarīre pana satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā samaṇasaññaṃ uppādetvā sīse vā hatthapādapiṭṭhiyaṃ vā vaṇaṃ katvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Regarding an 'unbroken corpse': Dust-heap cloth should not be taken from a fresh, moist corpse. For one who takes it, dangers of this sort arise, and one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. However, it is permissible to take from a 'broken' one. But to what extent is it considered 'broken'? Even by being slightly split by a crow, hawk, dog, jackal, or the like, with the tip of a beak or a fang. But for a corpse where, from falling and scraping, only the outer skin is broken while the hide is unbroken, that is still 'unbroken'; however, if the hide is broken, it is 'broken.' Also, if a person, even while alive, had burst boils, leprosy, sores, or a wound, this corpse is also considered 'broken.' From the third day onwards, a corpse that has reached a putrid state by becoming bloated and so on is also 'broken.' However, in any case, even if it is completely unbroken, it is permissible to have it taken by charnel-ground keepers or other people. If one cannot find another person, one should make a wound with a small knife or some such instrument and then take it. However, in the case of a corpse of the opposite sex, having established mindfulness and aroused the perception 'I am a monk,' it is permissible to make a wound on the head or on the back of the hands or feet and then take it.

Kusasaṅkāmanavatthukathā

The Discourse on the Case of Transferring the Kusa Grass

138. Tadanantare [M 1.0330] vatthusmiṃ kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā cīvaraṃ aggahesīti pubbe “ādiyeyyā”ti imassa padassa atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ nāmamattena dassitesu theyyāvahāra-pasayhāvahāra-parikappāvahārapaacchannāvahāra-kusāvahāresu kusāvahārena avaharīti attho.

138. In the case immediately following that one, regarding the statement 'having transferred the kusa grass, he took the robe,' the meaning is that he stole by means of 'theft by kusa grass' (kusāvahāra), which is among the types of theft—theft by stealth (theyyāvahāra), theft by force (pasayhāvahāra), theft by scheming (parikappāvahāra), theft by concealment (paṭicchannāvahāra), and theft by kusa grass (kusāvahāra)—that were previously shown by name only in the explanation of the meaning of the word 'ādiyeyya'.

Imesaṃ pana avahārānaṃ evaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ – yo hi koci sassāmikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ rattibhāge vā divasabhāge vā sandhicchedādīni katvā adissamāno avaharati, kūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhi vā vañcetvā gaṇhāti, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro “theyyāvahāro”ti veditabbo.

Furthermore, the distinction among these types of theft should be understood thus: If any monk, unseen, steals goods that have an owner, whether by night or by day, by committing acts such as breaking and entering, or takes them by deceiving with false measures, false coins, and so on, the taking of one who takes in this way is to be known as 'theft by stealth' (theyyāvahāra).

Yo pana pare pasayha balasā abhibhuyya, atha vā pana santajjetvā bhayaṃ dassetvā tesaṃ santakaṃ gaṇhāti, panthaghāta-gāmaghātādīni karontā dāmarikacorā viya kodhavasena paragharavilopaṃ karontā attano pattabalito ca adhikaṃ balakkārena gaṇhantā rāja-rājamahāmattādayo viya; tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro “pasayhāvahāro”ti veditabbo.

Furthermore, if a monk takes the property of others by overpowering and dominating them with force, or else by threatening and showing them danger, like jungle robbers who commit highway robbery, village raids, and so on, or like kings, royal ministers, and others who, through the power of anger, plunder the houses of others and who forcibly take more than the revenue due to them; the taking of one who takes in this way is to be known as 'theft by force' (pasayhāvahāra).

Parikappetvā [V 1.0303] gaṇhato pana avahāro “parikappāvahāro”ti vuccati, so bhaṇḍaparikappa-okāsaparikappavasena duvidho[P 2.0376]. Tatrāyaṃ bhaṇḍaparikappo – idhekacco sāṭakatthiko antogabbhaṃ pavisitvā “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmi; sace suttaṃ, na gaṇhissāmī”ti parikappetvā andhakāre pasibbakaṃ gaṇhāti, sāṭako ce tatra hoti, uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ. Suttaṃ ce hoti, rakkhati. Bahi nīharitvā muñcitvā “sutta”nti ñatvā puna āharitvā yathāṭhāne ṭhapeti, rakkhatiyeva. “Sutta”nti ñatvāpi “yaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ gahetabba”nti gacchati, padavārena kāretabbo. Bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā gaṇhāti, uddhāre pārājikaṃ. “Coro, coro”ti sāmikehi pariyuṭṭhito chaḍḍetvā palāyati, rakkhati. Sāmikā taṃ disvā gaṇhanti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Añño ce koci gaṇhāti, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Atha nivattesu sāmikesu sayameva taṃ disvā “pagevetaṃ mayā nīhaṭaṃ, mama dāni santaka”nti gaṇhāti, rakkhati; bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. “Sace suttaṃ bhavissati, gaṇhissāmi; sace sāṭako, na gaṇhissāmi. Sace [M 1.0331] sappi bhavissati, gaṇhissāmi; sace telaṃ, na gaṇhissāmī”tiādinā nayena parikappetvā gaṇhantassāpi eseva nayo.

The taking by one who schemes is called 'theft by scheming' (parikappāvahāra). It is twofold: scheming about the goods and scheming about the location. Among these, this is scheming about the goods: Here, a certain person, wanting a cloth, enters an inner chamber and schemes, 'If it is a cloth, I will take it; if it is thread, I will not take it.' In the darkness, he takes a bag. If there is a cloth in it, a pārājika offense is incurred upon the very lifting. If it is thread, he is protected. If, having taken it outside and opened it, he realizes it is thread and brings it back and places it in its original spot, he is still protected. If, even after knowing it is thread, he proceeds thinking, 'Whatever is gotten should be taken,' an offense is to be determined by the footstep. If he places it on the ground and then takes it, a pārājika offense is incurred upon lifting. If, being pursued by the owners shouting, 'Thief, thief!', he drops it and flees, he is protected. If the owners see it and take it, that is a good outcome. If someone else takes it, restitution for the goods is required. Then, if the owners have turned back, and he himself, seeing it, takes it thinking, 'This was brought out by me earlier, now it is mine,' he is protected; however, restitution for the goods is required. This same principle applies also to one who takes after scheming in the manner of, 'If it is thread, I will take it; if it is a cloth, I will not take it. If it is ghee, I will take it; if it is oil, I will not take it,' and so on.

Mahāpaccariyādīsu pana “sāṭakatthikopi sāṭakapasibbakameva gahetvā nikkhanto bahi ṭhatvā muñcitvā ‘sāṭako aya’nti disvā gacchanto paduddhāreneva kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha pana “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmī”ti parikappitattā parikappo dissati, disvā haṭattā parikappāvahāro na dissati. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana yaṃ parikappitaṃ taṃ adiṭṭhaṃ parikappitabhāve ṭhitaṃyeva uddharantassa avahāro vutto, tasmā tattha parikappāvahāro dissati. “Taṃ maññamāno taṃ avaharī”ti pāḷiyā ca sametīti. Tattha yvāyaṃ “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmī”tiādinā nayena pavatto parikappo, ayaṃ “bhaṇḍaparikappo” nāma.

However, in the Mahāpaccariya and other commentaries, it is said: 'Even one who wants a cloth, having taken a bag of cloth, gone outside, stood, opened it, and seen "this is a cloth," as he proceeds, an offense is to be determined by the very lifting of the foot.' Here, however, although the scheming is evident because it was schemed, 'If it is a cloth, I will take it,' because it was taken after seeing it, it is not considered 'theft by scheming.' But in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, the taking by one who lifts what was schemed for but is unseen, while it remains in the state of having been schemed for, is called a theft. Therefore, 'theft by scheming' is evident there. And this accords with the Pāḷi text: 'Mistaking it for that, he stole it.' In this context, the scheming that proceeds in the manner of 'If it is a cloth, I will take it,' and so on, is called 'scheming about the goods' (bhaṇḍaparikappa).

Okāsaparikappo pana evaṃ veditabbo – idhekacco lolabhikkhu parapariveṇaṃ vā kulagharaṃ vā araññe kammantasālaṃ vā pavisitvā tattha kathāsallāpena nisinno kiñci lobhaneyyaṃ parikkhāraṃ oloketi, olokento ca pana disvā dvārapamukhaheṭṭhāpāsādapariveṇadvārakoṭṭhakarukkhamūlādivasena paricchedaṃ katvā “sace maṃ etthantare [P 2.0377] passissanti, daṭṭhukāmatāya gahetvā vicaranto viya etesaṃyeva dassāmi; no ce passissanti, harissāmī”ti parikappeti. Tassa taṃ ādāya parikappitaparicchedaṃ atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ. Sace upacārasīmaṃ parikappeti, tadabhimukhova gacchanto kammaṭṭhānādīni manasi karonto vā aññavihito vā asatiyā upacārasīmaṃ atikkamati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Athāpissa taṃ ṭhānaṃ pattassa coro vā hatthī vā vāḷamigo [V 1.0304] vā mahāmegho vā vuṭṭhahati, so ca tamhā upaddavā muccitukamyatāya sahasā taṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamati, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Keci panettha “yasmā mūleva theyyacittena gahitaṃ, tasmā na rakkhati, avahāroyevā”ti vadanti. Ayaṃ tāva mahāaṭṭhakathānayo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “sacepi so antoparicchede hatthiṃ vā assaṃ vā abhiruhitvā taṃ neva pājeti, na pājāpeti; paricchede atikkantepi pārājikaṃ natthi, bhaṇḍadeyyamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tatra yvāyaṃ “sace maṃ etthantare passissanti, daṭṭhukāmatāya gahetvā [M 1.0332] vicaranto viya etesaṃyeva dassāmī”ti pavatto parikappo, ayaṃ “okāsaparikappo” nāma.

Scheming about the location, however, should be understood thus: Here, a certain fickle monk, having entered another's monastery, a family's house, or a workshop in the forest, sits engaged in conversation and observes some desirable requisite. While observing it, having seen it, he marks out a boundary by way of a doorway, the front of a building, the lower story of a mansion, a monastery precinct, a gatehouse, the foot of a tree, and so on, and schemes: 'If they see me within this area, I will act as if I am just looking at it out of curiosity and will give it back to them; if they do not see me, I will take it.' For him, a pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment of crossing the schemed boundary with the item. If he schemes for the boundary of the monastic precinct, and, while walking towards it, he crosses the precinct boundary unmindfully, or while his mind is occupied with meditation subjects or other things, it is a case for restitution of the goods. Or if, while he is at that place, a thief, an elephant, a wild beast, or a great storm arises, and he, desiring to escape from that danger, suddenly crosses that place, it is still only a case for restitution of the goods. Here, some say: 'Because it was taken with a thieving mind from the very beginning, he is not protected; it is simply a theft.' This, for a start, is the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is said: 'If, within the boundary, he mounts an elephant or a horse but neither drives it himself nor has it driven, even upon crossing the boundary, there is no pārājika offense; it is only a case for restitution of the goods.' In this context, the scheming that proceeds in the manner of 'If they see me within this area... I will give it back to them' is called 'scheming about the location' (okāsaparikappa).

Evamimesaṃ dvinnampi parikappānaṃ vasena parikappetvā gaṇhato avahāro “parikappāvahāro”ti veditabbo.

Thus, the taking by one who schemes by way of both of these two kinds of scheming is to be known as 'theft by scheming' (parikappāvahāra).

Paṭicchādetvā pana avaharaṇaṃ paṭicchannāvahāro. So evaṃ veditabbo – yo bhikkhu manussānaṃ uyyānādīsu kīḷantānaṃ vā pavisantānaṃ vā omuñcitvā ṭhapitaṃ alaṅkārabhaṇḍaṃ disvā “sace onamitvā gahessāmi, ‘kiṃ samaṇo gaṇhātī’ti maṃ jānitvā viheṭheyyu”nti paṃsunā vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādeti – “pacchā gaṇhissāmī”ti, tassa ettāvatā uddhāro natthīti na tāva avahāro hoti. Yadā pana te manussā antogāmaṃ pavisitukāmā taṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ vicinantāpi apassitvā “idāni andhakāro, sve jānissāmā”ti sālayā eva gatā honti. Athassa taṃ uddharato uddhāre pārājikaṃ. “Paṭicchannakāleyeva [P 2.0378] taṃ mama santaka”nti sakasaññāya vā “gatā dāni te, chaḍḍitabhaṇḍaṃ ida”nti paṃsukūlasaññāya vā gaṇhantassa pana bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Tesu dutiyadivase āgantvā vicinitvā adisvā dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā gatesupi gahitaṃ bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Kasmā? Yasmā tassa payogena tehi na diṭṭhaṃ, yo pana tathārūpaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ disvā yathāṭhāne ṭhitaṃyeva appaṭicchādetvā theyyacitto pādena akkamitvā kaddame vā vālikāya vā paveseti, tassa pavesitamatteyeva pārājikaṃ.

Furthermore, taking by concealing is 'theft by concealment' (paṭicchannāvahāra).
