It should be understood thus: a monk, seeing an ornament taken off and left behind by people playing in or entering a park or the like, thinks, "If I stoop down and take it, they might recognize me and, thinking, 'What is this monk taking?', harass me," and so covers it with dust or a leaf, thinking, "I will take it later." By this much, there is no 'lifting' for him, so it is not yet a 'taking'. But when those people, wishing to enter the village, search for the item and, not seeing it, depart with lingering attachment, thinking, "It is dark now; we will find out tomorrow," then, for him who lifts it, a pārājika offense is incurred at the moment of lifting. However, for one who takes it with the perception that it is his own, thinking, "At the very time of concealing it, it became my property," or with the perception that it is a discarded item, thinking, "They have now gone; this is an abandoned item," it is a matter for restitution. Even if they, on the second day, come, search, do not see it, and depart, having given up the search, what was taken is still a matter for restitution. Why? Because due to his action, it was not seen by them. Furthermore, if a monk, seeing such an item, does not conceal it but, with thievish intent, while it is still in its original place, steps on it and presses it into mud or sand, for him a pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment of pressing it in.

Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā pana avaharaṇaṃ “kusāvahāro”ti vuccati. Sopi evaṃ veditabbo – yo bhikkhu kusaṃ pātetvā cīvare bhājiyamāne attano koṭṭhāsassa samīpe ṭhitaṃ appagghataraṃ vā mahagghataraṃ vā samasamaṃ vā agghena parassa koṭṭhāsaṃ haritukāmo attano koṭṭhāse patitaṃ kusadaṇḍakaṃ parassa koṭṭhāse pātetukāmo uddharati, rakkhati tāva. Parassa koṭṭhāse pāteti, rakkhateva. Yadā pana tasmiṃ patite parassa koṭṭhāsato parassa kusadaṇḍakaṃ uddharati, uddhaṭamatte pārājiko hoti. Sace paṭhamataraṃ parakoṭṭhāsato kusadaṇḍakaṃ uddharati attano koṭṭhāse [V 1.0305] pātetukāmatāya uddhāre rakkhati[M 1.0333], pātane rakkhati. Attano koṭṭhāsato pana attano kusadaṇḍakaṃ uddharati, uddhāreyeva rakkhati. Taṃ uddharitvā parakoṭṭhāse pātentassa hatthato muttamatte pārājikaṃ.

Furthermore, taking by moving a lot is called 'theft by lot' (kusāvahāra). This too should be understood as follows: when robes are being divided by casting lots, a monk—wishing to take another's share that is near his own, whether it is of lesser, greater, or equal value—lifts the lot-marker that has fallen on his own share, intending to drop it onto the other's share; he is protected for the time being. He drops it onto the other's share; he is still protected. But when, after that lot has fallen, he lifts the other person's lot-marker from the other's share, he becomes guilty of a pārājika offense at the very moment of lifting. If, first, with the intention of dropping it on his own share, he lifts the lot-marker from the other's share, he is protected in the lifting, and he is protected in the dropping. However, if he lifts his own lot-marker from his own share, he is protected in the lifting itself. For the one who, having lifted it, drops it onto the other's share, a pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment it is released from his hand.

Sace pana dvīsupi koṭṭhāsesu patitadaṇḍake adassanaṃ gameti, tato avasesabhikkhūsu gatesu itaro “‘mayhaṃ, bhante, daṇḍako na paññāyatī’ti. ‘Mayhampi, āvuso, na paññāyatī’ti. ‘Katamo pana, bhante, mayhaṃ bhāgo’ti? ‘Ayaṃ tuyhaṃ bhāgo’”ti attano bhāgaṃ dasseti, tasmiṃ vivaditvā vā avivaditvā vā taṃ gaṇhitvā gate itaro tassa bhāgaṃ uddharati, uddhāre pārājikaṃ. Sacepi tena “ahaṃ mama bhāgaṃ tuyhaṃ na demi, tvaṃ pana attano bhāgaṃ ñatvā gaṇhā”ti vutte “nāyaṃ mamā”ti jānantopi tasseva bhāgaṃ gaṇhāti, uddhāre pārājikaṃ. Sace pana itaro “ayaṃ tuyhaṃ bhāgo, ayaṃ mayhaṃ bhāgoti kiṃ iminā vivādenā”ti cintetvā “mayhaṃ vā patto hotu, tumhākaṃ vā, yo varabhāgo taṃ tumhe [P 2.0379] gaṇhathā”ti vadati, dinnakaṃ nāma gahitaṃ hoti, natthettha avahāro. Sacepi so vivādabhīruko bhikkhu “yaṃ tuyhaṃ ruccati, taṃ gaṇhā”ti vutto attano pattaṃ varabhāgaṃ ṭhapetvā lāmakaṃyeva gahetvā gacchati, tato itarassa vicinitāvasesaṃ gaṇhantassāpi avahāro natthevāti.

If, however, he causes the lot-markers that have fallen on both shares to disappear, then after the other bhikkhus have left, one of them says: 'Venerable sir, my lot-marker is not to be found.' 'Friend, mine is not to be found either.' 'But, venerable sir, which is my share?' 'This is your share,' he says, and points out his own share. When that monk, whether disputing or not, takes that share and leaves, the first monk then takes his (the other's) share; upon lifting it, it is a pārājika offense. Even if, when it is said by him, 'I am not giving you my share; you, however, should know your own share and take it,' the other monk, even while knowing 'this is not my share,' takes that very share, it is a pārājika offense upon the [thief's subsequent] lifting [of the remaining share]. But if the other one thinks, 'This is your share, this is my share—what is the use of this dispute?' and says, 'Let it be my allotted share or yours; whichever is the better share, you take it,' then what is taken is considered given, and there is no theft in this case. Even if that bhikkhu, being fearful of dispute, when told, 'Take whichever you prefer,' sets aside the better share that was allotted to him and takes only the inferior one and leaves, then for the other one who takes the remaining portion after the selection, there is no theft whatsoever.

Aṭṭhakathāsupana vuttaṃ – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne kusasaṅkāmanavasena cīvarabhājanīyameva ekaṃ āgataṃ, catunnampi pana paccayānaṃ uppattiñca bhājanīyañca nīharitvā dassetabba”nti evañca vatvā cīvarakkhandhake“paṭiggaṇhātu me, bhante, bhagavā sīveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ; bhikkhusaṅghassa ca gahapaticīvaraṃ anujānātū”ti (mahāva. 337) idaṃ jīvakavatthuṃ ādiṃ katvā uppannacīvarakathā, senāsanakkhandhake “tena kho pana samayena rājagahaṃ dubbhikkhaṃ hoti, manussā na sakkonti saṅghabhattaṃ kātuṃ, icchanti uddesabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ salākabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ uposathikaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ kātu”nti (cūḷava. 325) idaṃ suttamādiṃ katvā piṇḍapātakathā, senāsanakkhandhakeyeva “tena kho pana samayena sattarasavaggiyā bhikkhū aññataraṃ paccantimaṃ mahāvihāraṃ paṭisaṅkharonti – ‘idha mayaṃ vassaṃ vasissāmā’ti. Addasaṃsu kho chabbaggiyā bhikkhū sattarasavaggiye bhikkhū vihāraṃ paṭisaṅkharonte”ti (cūḷava. 316) idaṃ chabbaggiyavatthuṃ ādiṃ katvā āgatasenāsanakathā, tadavasāne ca sappiādibhesajjakathā vitthārena [M 1.0334] kathitā. Mayaṃ pana taṃ sabbaṃ āgatāgataṭṭhāneyeva kathayissāma; evaṃ kathane kāraṇaṃ pubbe vuttameva.

However, in the ancient commentaries it is said: 'In this place, only one case has been presented, namely, the division of robes by means of moving a lot-marker. However, the arising and the distribution of all four requisites should be brought out and shown.' And having said this, the following are related in detail: the discussion on arisen robes, taking as its beginning this story of Jīvaka from the Robe Khandhaka: 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this pair of Sīveyyaka cloths from me; and may he allow householder's robes for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.'; the discussion on almsfood, taking as its beginning this Sutta from the Lodgings Khandhaka: 'Now at that time, Rājagaha was afflicted by a famine. People were not able to prepare a meal for the Saṅgha, but they wished to prepare a meal by designation, by invitation, by lot-ticket, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha-day meal, or a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal.'; the discussion on lodgings that have arrived, taking as its beginning this story of the group of six from the Lodgings Khandhaka itself: 'Now at that time, the group-of-seventeen bhikkhus were repairing a certain large, remote monastery, thinking, "We will spend the rains retreat here." The group-of-six bhikkhus saw the group-of-seventeen bhikkhus repairing the monastery.'; and the remaining discussion on medicines such as ghee. We, however, will relate all of that only in the respective places where it occurs. The reason for relating it in this way has already been stated before.

Kusasaṅkāmanavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion on the story of moving the lot-marker is concluded.

139. Ito [V 1.0306] paraṃ jantāgharavatthu uttānatthameva.

139. Hereafter, the story of the sweat-house is of plain meaning.

140. Pañcasu vighāsavatthūsu te bhikkhū anupasampannena kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paribhuñjiṃsu. Vighāsaṃ pana gaṇhantena khāditāvasesaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Yadi sakkoti khādante [P 2.0380] chaḍḍāpetvā gaṇhituṃ, etampi vaṭṭati. Attaguttatthāya pana parānuddayatāya ca na gahetabbaṃ.

140. In the five cases concerning leftovers, those bhikkhus had a non-ordained person make it suitable and then consumed it. Furthermore, when taking leftovers, what has been discarded after being eaten should be taken. If one is able to take it after causing the creatures that are eating to discard it, this too is allowable. However, for the sake of protecting oneself and out of compassion for other beings, it should not be taken.

141. Odanakhādanīyapūvaucchutimbarūsakabhājanīyavatthūsu aparassa bhāgaṃ dehīti asantaṃ puggalaṃ āha. Amūlakaṃ aggahesīti sāmikesu dentesu evaṃ aggahesi. Anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassāti sāmikehi dinnaṃ aggahesi; tenassa anāpatti vuttā. Āpatti sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyassāti yo panānena sampajānamusāvādo vutto, tasmiṃ pācittiyaṃ āha; parato tekaṭulayāguvatthumhi viya. Gahaṇe pana ayaṃ vinicchayo – saṅghassa santakaṃ sammatena vā āṇattehi vā ārāmikādīhi diyyamānaṃ, gihīnañca santakaṃ sāmikena vā āṇattena vā diyyamānaṃ “aparassa bhāgaṃ dehī”ti vatvā gaṇhato bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Aññena diyyamānaṃ gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Asammatena vā anāṇattena vā diyyamāne “aparampi bhāgaṃ dehī”ti vatvā vā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā vā gaṇhanto pattacatukke viya tassuddhāreyeva bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Itarehi diyyamānaṃ evaṃ gaṇhato bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Sāmikena pana “imassa dehī”ti dāpitaṃ vā sayaṃ dinnaṃ vā sudinnanti ayamettha sabbaaṭṭhakathāvinicchayato sāro.

141. In the cases concerning the distribution of rice, edibles, cakes, sugarcane, and figs, he spoke of a person who was not present, saying, 'Give a portion to another.' He took it without basis; that is, he took it thus while the owners were giving. There is no pārājika offense for the bhikkhu because he took what was given by the owners; for that reason, no-offense was declared for him. There is an offense of Pācittiya for intentional false speech; for the intentional false speech that was spoken by him, a Pācittiya is stated, as in the case of the Tekaṭula gruel story later on. Furthermore, regarding the taking, this is the decision: when taking property belonging to the Sangha being given by an appointed bhikkhu or by those instructed by him, such as monastery attendants, or property belonging to householders being given by the owner or by one instructed by him, after saying, 'Give a portion to another,' it is a matter of restoring the goods. One who takes it when it is being given by another person should be made to pay the value of the goods. When it is being given by one who is not appointed or not instructed, one who takes it after saying, 'Give another portion too,' or after calculating fraudulent years of seniority, should be made to pay the value of the goods at the very moment of its removal, as in the case of the four bowls. For one who takes in this way what is being given by others, it is a matter of restoring the goods. However, what is caused to be given by the owner saying, 'Give to this one,' or what is given by himself, is well-given. This, herein, is the essence from the decisions of all the commentaries.

142-3. Odaniyagharādivatthūsu – odaniyagharaṃ nāma vikkāyikabhattapacanagharaṃ. Sūnagharaṃ nāma vikkāyikamaṃsapacanagharaṃ. Pūvagharaṃ nāma vikkāyikakhajjakapacanagharaṃ. Sesamettha, parikkhāravatthūsu ca pākaṭameva.

In the cases concerning a rice-kitchen and so on: a rice-kitchen (odaniyaghara) is a house where rice is cooked for sale. A butcher's shop (sūnaghara) is a house where meat is cooked for sale. A cake-shop (pūvaghara) is a house where edibles are cooked for sale. The rest here, and in the cases concerning requisites, is indeed clear.

144. Pīṭhavatthusmiṃ [M 1.0335] – so bhikkhu parikappetvā “etaṃ ṭhānaṃ sampattaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti saṅkāmesi. Tenassa saṅkāmane avahāro natthi. Saṅkāmetvā pana parikappitokāsato gahaṇe pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ haranto ca yadi pīṭhake theyyacittaṃ natthi, thavikaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo. Atha [P 2.0381] pīṭhakepi atthi, ubho agghāpetvā kāretabboti. Bhisiādīni tīṇi vatthūni pākaṭāneva.

144. In the case of the bench: that bhikkhu, having premeditated, 'I will take it once it has reached this spot,' moved it. Therefore, for him, there is no theft in the act of moving. However, having moved it, upon taking it from the premeditated place, a Pārājika offense is stated. And, for one carrying it thus, if there is no intention to steal the bench, he should be made to pay the value of the bag. If, however, there is also an intention to steal the bench, he should be made to pay the value of both. The three cases beginning with the cushion are self-evident.

146. Vissāsaggāhādīsu [V 1.0307] tīsu vatthūsu gahaṇe anāpatti, āharāpentesu bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Piṇḍāya paviṭṭhassa paṭiviso antoupacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhitasseva gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yadi pana dāyakā “bahiupacāraṭṭhānampi bhante, bhāgaṃ gaṇhatha, āgantvā paribhuñjissantī”ti vadanti, evaṃ antogāmaṭṭhānampi gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

146. In the three cases beginning with taking on trust, there is no offense in the taking; when one causes it to be brought, it is a matter of restoring the goods. For a bhikkhu who has entered for alms, it is allowable to take a share only for one who is standing within the monastery precincts. However, if the donors say, 'Venerable sirs, please take a share also for those in the place outside the precincts; they will come and consume it,' then it is allowable to take a share also for those in a place within the village. The rest here is of obvious meaning.

148-9. Sattasu ambacorakādivatthūsu paṃsukūlasaññāya gahaṇe anāpatti, āharāpentesu bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena paribhoge pārājikaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – sāmikāpi sālayā, corāpi sālayā, paṃsukūlasaññāya khādantassa bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena gaṇhato uddhāreyeva avahāro, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo. Sāmikā sālayā, corā nirālayā, eseva nayo. Sāmikā nirālayā, corā sālayā; “puna gaṇhissāmā”ti kismiñcideva gahanaṭṭhāne khipitvā gatā, eseva nayo. Ubhopi nirālayā, paṃsukūlasaññāya khādato anāpatti, theyyacittena dukkaṭaṃ.

In the seven cases beginning with the mango thief, in taking with the perception of it being refuse-cloth, there is no offense; when one causes it to be brought, it is a matter of restoring the goods; for consuming it with thieving intent, there is a Pārājika offense. Herein is the decision: if both the owners are attached and the thieves are attached, for one who eats it with the perception of it being refuse-cloth, it is a matter of restoring the goods; for one who takes it with thieving intent, the theft occurs at the very moment of removal, and he should be made to have the goods valued and pay for them. If the owners are attached but the thieves are unattached, this same principle applies. If the owners are unattached but the thieves are attached, and they have thrown it in some dense place and gone, thinking, 'We will take it again,' this same principle applies. If both are unattached, for one who eats it with the perception of it being refuse-cloth, there is no offense; with thieving intent, there is a Dukkaṭa offense.

Saṅghassa ambādīsu pana saṅghārāme jātaṃ vā hotu, ānetvā dinnaṃ vā pañcamāsakaṃ vā atirekapañcamāsakaṃ vā agghanakaṃ avaharantassa pārājikaṃ. Paccante corupaddavena gāmesu vuṭṭhahantesu bhikkhūpi vihāre chaḍḍetvā “puna āvasante janapade āgamissāmā”ti saussāhāva gacchanti. Bhikkhū tādisaṃ vihāraṃ patvā ambapakkādīni “chaḍḍitakānī”ti paṃsukūlasaññāya paribhuñjanti, anāpatti; theyyacittena paribhuñjato avahāro hoti, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo.

However, regarding the Sangha's mangoes and so forth, whether it be grown in the Sangha's monastery or brought and given, for one who steals an item worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, there is a Pārājika offense. In a border region, when villages are being abandoned due to the danger from thieves, bhikkhus also abandon their monasteries and go, being intent on returning, thinking, 'When the country is inhabited again, we will come back.' If bhikkhus, having arrived at such a monastery, consume ripe mangoes and so forth with the perception of them being refuse, thinking, 'These are abandoned things,' there is no offense. For one who consumes it with thieving intent, it is a theft; he should be made to have the goods valued and pay for them.

Mahāpaccariyaṃ [M 1.0336] pana saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyañca avisesena vuttaṃ – “chaḍḍitavihāre pana phalāphalaṃ theyyacittena paribhuñjato pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Āgatānāgatānaṃ santakattā”ti. Gaṇasantake pana puggalike ca saussāhamattameva pamāṇaṃ. Sace pana tato ambapakkādiṃ kulasaṅgahaṇatthāya deti, kuladūsakadukkaṭaṃ. Theyyacittena dento agghena kāretabbo. Saṅghikepi eseva nayo. Senāsanatthāya niyamitaṃ kulasaṅgahaṇatthāya [P 2.0382] dadato dukkaṭaṃ, issaravatāya thullaccayaṃ, theyyacittena pārājikaṃ. No ce vatthu pahoti, agghena kāretabbo. Bahi upacārasīmāya nisīditvā issaravatāya paribhuñjato gīvā. Ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā kālaṃ ghosetvā “mayhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti khāditaṃ sukhāditaṃ. Ghaṇṭiṃ apaharitvā kālameva ghosetvā, ghaṇṭimeva paharitvā kālaṃ aghosetvā, ghaṇṭimpi apaharitvā kālampi aghosetvā aññesaṃ natthibhāvaṃ ñatvā “mayhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti khāditampi sukhāditameva. Pupphārāmavatthudvayaṃ pākaṭameva.

However, in the Mahāpaccari and in the Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā it is stated without distinction: 'However, for one who consumes fruits great and small in an abandoned monastery with thieving intent, there is a Pārājika offense. Why? Because it is the property of those who have come and those who have not yet come.' Furthermore, in the case of property belonging to a group and that which is personal, the mere intention to return is the standard. However, if one gives ripe mangoes and so forth from that for the sake of supporting a family, there is a Dukkaṭa offense of corrupting families. One who gives with thieving intent should be made to pay the value. In the case of Sangha property also, this same principle applies. For giving what is designated for the sake of lodgings for the sake of supporting a family, there is a Dukkaṭa offense; for giving by acting with authority, a Thullaccaya offense; for giving with thieving intent, a Pārājika offense. If the object is not sufficient for Pārājika, one should be made to pay its value. For one sitting outside the monastery precincts and consuming by acting with authority, it is a 'forfeiture of the neck' offense. What is eaten after striking the bell, announcing the time, and thinking, 'It is my turn,' is well-eaten. What is eaten after not striking the bell but only announcing the time; or after striking the bell but not announcing the time; or after neither striking the bell nor announcing the time, but knowing there are no others and thinking, 'It is my turn,' is also well-eaten. The two cases concerning the flower park are self-evident.

150. Vuttavādakavatthuttaye [V 1.0308] vutto vajjemīti tayā vutto hutvā “tava vacanena vadāmī”ti attho. Anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassāti sāmikehi dinnattā anāpatti. Na ca, bhikkhave, “vutto vajjemī”ti vattabboti “ahaṃ tayā vutto hutvā tava vacanena vadāmī”ti evaṃ añño bhikkhu aññena bhikkhunā na vattabboti attho. Paricchedaṃ pana katvā “itthannāmaṃ tava vacanena gaṇhissāmī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Vutto vajjehīti mayā vutto hutvā mama vacanena vadehīti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Imesupi ca dvīsu vatthūsu paricchedaṃ katvā vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Ettāvatā hi upārambhā mutto hotīti.

150. In the three cases concerning 'speaking as instructed', the phrase 'I speak as instructed' means 'having been told by you, I speak by your words.' The phrase 'There is no Pārājika offense for the bhikkhu' means there is no offense because it was given by the owners. And, monks, one should not say, 'I speak as instructed,' meaning that one monk should not say to another monk, 'Having been told by you, I speak by your words.' However, after making a specification, it is permissible to say, 'I will take such-and-such by your words.' The phrase 'You should speak as instructed' means 'having been told by me, you should speak by my words.' The rest is as has been stated. And also in these two cases, it is permissible to speak after making a specification. For by this much, one is freed from censure.

151-2. Maṇivatthuttayassa majjhime vatthusmiṃ – nāhaṃ akallakoti nāhaṃ gilānoti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

In the middle case of the three cases concerning the gem, the phrase 'I am not unfit' means 'I am not ill.' The rest is clear.

153. Sūkaravatthudvaye – kiñcāpi paṭhamassa bhikkhuno chātajjhattaṃ disvā kāruññena mocitattā anāpatti. Sāmikesu pana asampaṭicchantesu bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, tāva mahanto vā matasūkaro āharitvā dātabbo, tadagghanakaṃ vā bhaṇḍaṃ. Sace pāsasāmike kuhiñcipi na passati, pāsasāmantā tadagghanakaṃ sāṭakaṃ vā kāsāvaṃ vā thālakaṃ vā yathā te āgatā [M 1.0337] passanti, īdise ṭhāne ṭhapetvāva gantabbaṃ, theyyacittena pana mocentassa pārājikameva. Ettha ca koci sūkaro pāsaṃ pādena kaḍḍhitvā chinnamatte pāse ṭhānācāvanadhammena ṭhānena ṭhito hoti caṇḍasote baddhanāvā [P 2.0383] viya. Koci attano dhammatāya ṭhito, koci nipanno, koci kūṭapāsena baddho hoti. Kūṭapāso nāma yassa ante dhanukaṃ vā aṅkusako vā añño vā koci daṇḍako baddho hoti, yo tattha tattha rukkhādīsu laggitvā sūkarassa gamanaṃ nivāreti. Tatra pāsaṃ kaḍḍhitvā ṭhitassa ekameva ṭhānaṃ pāsabandhanaṃ, so hi pāse muttamatte vā chinnamatte vā palāyati. Attano dhammatāya ṭhitassa bandhanañca cattāro ca pādāti pañca ṭhānāni. Nipannassa bandhanañca sayanañcāti dve ṭhānāni. Kūṭapāsabaddhassa yattha yattha gacchati, taṃ tadeva ṭhānaṃ. Tasmā taṃ tato tato mocentā dasapi vīsatipi satampi bhikkhū pārājikaṃ āpajjanti. Tattha tattha āgataṃ disvā ekameva dāsaṃ palāpento viya.

153. In the two cases concerning the pig—although for the first monk, seeing the pig afflicted by hunger, there is no offense for having released it out of compassion, if the owners do not accept this, the goods are to be repaid. Either a dead pig of that size must be brought and given, or goods of its value. If the snare's owner is not seen anywhere, one should leave goods of equivalent value—such as a cloth, a saffron robe, or a bowl—near the snare in a place where they would see them upon arriving, and only then depart. But for one who releases it with the intention of theft, it is an offense entailing defeat. And here, one pig, having dragged the snare with its foot, stands in a state of having been displaced from its position when the snare is just broken, like a boat tied in a strong current. Another stands by its own nature, another lies down, and another is bound by a tricky snare. A tricky snare is one to the end of which a small bow, a hook, or some other stick is tied, which, by getting caught on trees and other things here and there, prevents the pig's movement. Among these, for the one that stands having dragged the snare, there is only one place: the binding of the snare; for it runs away as soon as the snare is released or broken. For the one standing by its own nature, there are five places: the binding and the four feet. For the one lying down, there are two places: the binding and its resting place. For the one bound with a tricky snare, wherever it goes, that very place is the location. Therefore, ten, twenty, or even a hundred monks who release it from each of those places all incur an offense entailing defeat. It is like those who cause a single slave to flee, seeing him having arrived at various places.

Purimānaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ catuppadakathāyaṃ vuttanayena phandāpanaṭhānācāvanāni veditabbāni. Sunakhadaṭṭhaṃ sūkaraṃ vissajjāpentassāpi kāruññādhippāyena bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena pārājikaṃ. Pāsaṭṭhānaṃ pana sunakhasamīpaṃ vā asampattaṃ paṭipathaṃ gantvā paṭhamameva palāpentassa avahāro natthi. Yopi baddhasūkarassa ghāsañca pānīyañca datvā balaṃ gāhāpetvā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karoti – “utrasto [V 1.0309] palāyissatī”ti; so ce palāyati, pārājikaṃ. Pāsaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā ukkuṭṭhisaddena palāpentassāpi eseva nayo.

However, for the first three pigs, the acts of causing them to struggle and displacing them from their positions should be understood according to the method stated in the section on quadrupeds. For one who causes a pig bitten by a dog to be released with compassionate intention, the goods are to be repaid; with a thieving intention, it is an offense entailing defeat. However, for one who goes to meet a pig on the path and makes it flee at the very outset, before it has reached the place of the snare or the vicinity of the dog, there is no theft. Also, a monk who, having given food and water to a trapped pig and caused it to gain strength, makes a loud cry, thinking, 'Startled, it will flee'—if it does flee, it is an offense entailing defeat. The same principle applies to one who, after weakening the snare, makes the pig flee with the sound of a loud cry.

Yo pana ghāsañca pānīyañca datvā gacchati, “balaṃ gahetvā palāyissatī”ti; so ce palāyati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Pāsaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā gacchantassāpi eseva nayo. Pāsasantike satthaṃ vā aggiṃ vā ṭhapeti “chinne vā daḍḍhe vā palāyissatī”ti. Sūkaro pāsaṃ cālento chinne vā daḍḍhe vā palāyati, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Pāsaṃ yaṭṭhiyā saha pāteti, pacchā sūkaro taṃ maddanto gacchati[P 2.0384], bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Sūkaro adūhalapāsāṇehi akkanto hoti, taṃ palāpetukāmassa adūhalaṃ kāruññena ukkhipato bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena pārājikaṃ. Sace ukkhittamatte agantvā pacchā gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Ukkhipitvā ṭhapitaṃ adūhalaṃ [M 1.0338] pāteti, pacchā sūkaro taṃ maddanto gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Opāte patitasūkarampi kāruññena uddharato bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena pārājikaṃ. Opātaṃ pūretvā nāseti, pacchā sūkaro taṃ maddanto gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Sūle viddhaṃ kāruññena uddharati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, theyyacittena pārājikaṃ. Sūlaṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍeti, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ.

However, if one gives food and water and then departs, thinking, 'Having gained strength, it will flee,' and if it does flee, it is an offense entailing restitution. The same principle applies to one who departs after weakening the snare. If one places a knife or a fire near the snare, thinking, 'When it is cut or burned, it will flee,' and the pig, shaking the snare, flees when it is cut or burned, it is an offense entailing restitution. If one causes the snare to fall along with its stick, and afterwards the pig tramples it and departs, it is an offense entailing restitution. If a pig is pinned by adūhala stones, for one who desires to make it flee and lifts the adūhala out of compassion, it is an offense entailing restitution; for one who lifts it with a thieving intention, it is an offense entailing defeat. If it does not depart immediately upon the stone being lifted, but departs later, it is an offense entailing restitution. If one causes the lifted and placed adūhala stone to fall, and afterwards the pig tramples it and departs, it is an offense entailing restitution. For one who pulls a pig that has fallen into a pit out of compassion, it is an offense entailing restitution; for one who pulls it out with a thieving intention, it is an offense entailing defeat. If one fills and levels the pit, and afterwards the pig tramples over it and departs, it is an offense entailing restitution. If one pulls out a pig impaled on a stake out of compassion, it is an offense entailing restitution; if one pulls it out with a thieving intention, it is an offense entailing defeat. If one pulls out the stake and discards it, it is an offense entailing restitution.

Vihārabhūmiyaṃ pana pāse vā adūhalaṃ vā oḍḍentā vāretabbā – “migarūpānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṭṭhānametaṃ, mā idha evaṃ karothā”ti. Sace “harāpetha, bhante”ti vadanti, harāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha sayaṃ haranti, sundarameva. Atha neva haranti, na harituṃ denti, rakkhaṃ yācitvā harāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Manussā sassarakkhaṇakāle khettesu pāse ca adūhalapāsāṇādīni ca karonti – “maṃsaṃ khādantā sassāni rakkhissāmā”ti. Vītivatte sassakāle tesu anālayesu pakkantesu tattha baddhaṃ vā patitaṃ vā mocetuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

However, on monastery grounds, those setting snares or adūhala traps should be prevented with the words: 'This is a place of refuge for animals; do not do such things here.' If they say, 'Venerable sirs, please have them removed,' it is permissible to have them removed. If they remove them themselves, that is excellent. But if they neither remove them nor allow them to be removed, it is permissible to request protection and then have them removed. During the crop-guarding season, people set snares and adūhala stones and so on in the fields, thinking, 'While eating meat, we will protect the crops.' When the crop season has passed, and they, having no further concern for those places, have departed, it is permissible to release an animal that is trapped or has fallen there.

Migavatthudvayepi sūkaravatthūsu vuttasadisoyeva vinicchayo.

In both cases concerning deer, the judgment is exactly as stated in the cases concerning pigs.

Macchavatthudvayepi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – kumīnamukhaṃ vivaritvā vā pacchāpuṭakaṃ muñcitvā vā passena chiddaṃ katvā vā kumīnato macche pothetvā palāpentassa pārājikaṃ. Bhattasitthāni dassetvā evaṃ palāpentassāpi pārājikaṃ. Saha kumīnena uddharatopi pārājikaṃ. Kevalaṃ kumīnamukhaṃ vivarati, pacchāpuṭakaṃ muñcati, chiddaṃ vā karoti, macchā pana attano dhammatāya palāyanti, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Evaṃ katvā bhattasitthāni dasseti, macchā gocaratthāya nikkhamitvā palāyanti, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Mukhaṃ avivaritvā pacchāpuṭakaṃ amuñcitvā [V 1.0310] passena chiddaṃ akatvā kevalaṃ bhattasitthāni dasseti, macchā pana chātajjhattā sīsena paharitvā okāsaṃ katvā gocaratthāya nikkhamitvā palāyanti, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Tucchakumīnassa mukhaṃ vā vivarati, pacchāpuṭakaṃ vā muñcati, chiddaṃ vā karoti, āgatāgatā macchā dvāraṃ pattā [P 2.0385] puṭakachiddehi palāyanti, bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Tucchakumīnaṃ gahetvā gumbe khipati, bhaṇḍadeyyamevāti. Yāne bhaṇḍaṃ pīṭhe thavikāya sadisaṃ.

In both cases concerning fish, this is the same principle. This, however, is the distinction: for a monk who, having opened the mouth of the fish trap, or having released its back-pouch, or having made a hole in its side, then strikes the fish from the trap and causes them to flee, it is a Pārājika offense. For one who shows lumps of cooked rice and thus causes them to flee, it is also a Pārājika offense. For one who lifts it up together with the fish trap, it is also a Pārājika offense. If one merely opens the mouth of the fish trap, releases the back-pouch, or makes a hole, but the fish escape by their own nature, it is an offense entailing restitution. Having done so, if one shows lumps of cooked rice, and the fish, having gone out for the purpose of finding food, escape, it is only an offense entailing restitution. If, without opening the mouth, without releasing the back-pouch, and without making a hole in the side, one merely shows lumps of cooked rice, and the fish, oppressed by hunger, strike with their heads to make an opening, go out for the purpose of finding food, and escape, it is only an offense entailing restitution. If one opens the mouth of an empty fish trap, or releases its back-pouch, or makes a hole, and the fish that arrive, upon reaching the opening, escape through the holes in the pouch, it is only an offense entailing restitution. If one takes an empty fish trap and throws it into a thicket, it is only an offense entailing restitution. Goods in a vehicle or on a seat are similar to those in a bag.

Maṃsapesivatthumhi [M 1.0339] – sace ākāse gaṇhāti, gahitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ. Taṃ chahākārehi paricchinditvā ṭhānācāvanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha dārugopālakarajakasāṭakavatthūsu ca ambacorakādivatthūsu vuttanayena vinicchinitabbaṃ.

In the case of a piece of meat: if one takes it in the air, the place where it is taken is indeed the location. The moving from its location should be understood by determining it in six ways. The rest in this case, as in the cases of the wood, the cowherd, the washerman’s cloth, and the mango thief, etc., should be determined according to the stated method.

155. Kumbhivatthusmiṃ – yo sappitelādīni apādagghanakāni gahetvā “na puna evaṃ karissāmī”ti saṃvare ṭhatvā dutiyadivasādīsupi puna citte uppanne evameva dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā paribhuñjanto sabbampi taṃ paribhuñjati, nevatthi pārājikaṃ. Dukkaṭaṃ vā thullaccayaṃ vā āpajjati, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. Ayampi bhikkhu evamevamakāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “anāpatti bhikkhu pārājikassā”ti. Dhuranikkhepaṃ pana akatvā “divase divase paribhuñjissāmī”ti thokaṃ thokampi paribhuñjato yasmiṃ divase pādagghanakaṃ pūrati, tasmiṃ pārājikaṃ.

155. In the case of the pot: if someone takes ghee, oil, or other items worth less than a pāda, having established restraint by thinking, "I will not do this again," but on subsequent days, when the thought arises again, he similarly abandons the undertaking and consumes it, and consumes all of it, there is no Pārājika offense. He incurs either a dukkaṭa or a thullaccaya offense, but it is an offense entailing restitution. This monk acted in the same way. Therefore, it is said, "There is no Pārājika offense for the monk." However, if he does not abandon the undertaking but thinks, "I will consume it little by little each day," even consuming a small amount, on the day when the value of a pāda is reached, on that day he commits a Pārājika offense.

Saṃvidāvahāravatthūni saṃvidāvahāre, muṭṭhivatthūni odaniyagharādivatthūsu dve vighāsavatthūni ambacorakādivatthūsu vuttavinicchayanayena veditabbāni. Dve tiṇavatthūni uttānatthāneva.

The cases concerning taking by mutual agreement are to be understood in relation to taking by mutual agreement; the cases concerning a handful, in cases like the alms-food hall, etc.; the two cases concerning gleanings, in cases like the mango thief, etc., should be understood according to the stated method of determination. The two cases concerning grass are self-evident.

156. Ambabhājāpanādivatthūsu te bhikkhū ekaṃ gāmakāvāsaṃ paricchinnabhikkhukaṃ agamaṃsu. Tattha bhikkhū phalāphalaṃ paribhuñjamānāpi tesu āgatesu “therānaṃ phalāni dethā”ti kappiyakārake na avocuṃ. Atha te bhikkhū “kiṃ saṅghikaṃ amhākaṃ na pāpuṇātī”ti ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā bhājāpetvā tesampi vassaggena bhāgaṃ datvā attanāpi paribhuñjiṃsu. Tena nesaṃ bhagavā “anāpatti, bhikkhave, paribhogatthāyā”ti āha. Tasmā idānipi yattha āvāsikā āgantukānaṃ na denti, phalavāre ca sampatte aññesaṃ atthibhāvaṃ disvā corikāya attanāva khādanti, tattha āgantukehi [P 2.0386] ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā bhājetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

156. In the cases concerning the division of mangoes, etc.: those monks went to a village monastery where the number of monks was limited. There, the resident monks, even while consuming various fruits, did not instruct the attendants when the visiting monks arrived, saying, "Give the fruits to the elders." Then those visiting monks, thinking, "Why does the Sangha's property not reach us?" struck the bell, had the provisions divided, gave a share to the resident monks as well according to their seniority, and themselves partook. Regarding this, the Blessed One said, "Monks, there is no offense for the purpose of consumption." Therefore, even now, where resident monks do not give to visiting monks, and when the fruit season arrives, seeing the presence of others, they themselves eat stealthily—in such cases, it is permissible for the visiting monks to strike the bell, have the provisions divided, and consume them.

Yattha pana āvāsikā rukkhe rakkhitvā phalavāre sampatte bhājetvā khādanti, catūsu paccayesu [V 1.0311] sammā upanenti, anissarā tattha āgantukā. Yepi rukkhā cīvaratthāya niyametvā dinnā, tesupi āgantukā anissarā. Eseva nayo sesapaccayatthāya niyametvā dinnesupi.

However, where resident monks protect the trees and, when the fruit season arrives, divide and eat the fruit, and properly provide the four requisites, visiting monks have no authority there. Even regarding trees designated and given for the purpose of robes, visiting monks have no authority over those either. The same principle applies to those designated and given for other requisites.

Ye [M 1.0340] pana tathā aniyamitā, āvāsikā ca te rakkhitvā gopetvā corikāya paribhuñjanti, na tesu āvāsikānaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbaṃ. Ye phalaparibhogatthāya dinnā, āvāsikāpi ne rakkhitvā gopetvā sammā upanenti, tesuyeva tesaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ niyametvā dinnaṃ theyyacittena paribhuñjanto bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo. Paribhogavaseneva taṃ bhājetvā paribhuñjantassa bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Yaṃ panettha senāsanatthāya niyamitaṃ, taṃ paribhogavaseneva bhājetvā paribhuñjantassa thullaccayañca bhaṇḍadeyyañcā”ti.

But regarding those trees that are not so designated, and which the resident monks guard and protect, consuming them stealthily, one should not abide by the resident monks' agreement concerning them. Regarding those trees that are given for the purpose of fruit consumption, and which the resident monks also guard, protect, and properly present, it is only concerning them that one should abide by their agreement. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said: "One who consumes with a thieving mind what has been designated for the four requisites should be made to pay the value of the item. For one who divides and consumes it merely by way of consumption, it is an offense entailing restitution. But if what is designated herein for lodging is divided and consumed merely by way of consumption, there is both a grave offense and an offense entailing restitution."

Odissa cīvaratthāya dinnaṃ cīvareyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace dubbhikkhaṃ hoti, bhikkhū piṇḍapātena kilamanti, cīvaraṃ pana sulabhaṃ, saṅghasuṭṭhutāya apalokanakammaṃ katvā piṇḍapātepi upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Senāsanena gilānapaccayena vā kilamantesu saṅghasuṭṭhutāya apalokanakammaṃ katvā tadatthāyapi upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Odissa piṇḍapātatthāya gilānapaccayatthāya ca dinnepi eseva nayo. Odissa senāsanatthāya dinnaṃ pana garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, taṃ rakkhitvā gopetvā tadatthameva upanetabbaṃ. Sace pana dubbhikkhaṃ hoti, bhikkhū piṇḍapātena na yāpenti. Ettha rājarogacorabhayādīhi aññattha gacchantānaṃ vihārā palujjanti, tālanāḷikerādike vināsenti, senāsanapaccayaṃ pana nissāya yāpetuṃ sakkā hoti. Evarūpe kāle senāsanaṃ vissajjetvāpi senāsanajagganatthāya paribhogo bhagavatā anuññāto. Tasmā ekaṃ vā dve vā varasenāsanāni ṭhapetvā itarāni lāmakakoṭiyā piṇḍapātatthāya vissajjetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mūlavatthucchedaṃ pana katvā na upanetabbaṃ[P 2.0387].

That which is given specifically for the purpose of robes should be applied only to robes. If there is a famine and the bhikkhus are weary on account of alms-food, but robes are easily obtained, then having performed an act of authorization for the Sangha's well-being, it is allowable to apply it to alms-food as well. If they are weary on account of lodging or requisites for the sick, having performed an act of authorization for the Sangha's well-being, it is allowable to apply it for those purposes also. This same method applies to that which is given specifically for the purpose of alms-food and for the purpose of requisites for the sick. However, that which is given specifically for the purpose of lodging is a weighty item; having protected and guarded it, it should be applied only for that purpose. But if there is a famine and bhikkhus cannot maintain themselves with alms-food, and in that place, due to dangers from kings, disease, thieves, and so on, the monasteries of those going elsewhere are destroyed and they destroy the palm fruits, coconuts, and the like, but it is possible to maintain oneself by relying on the requisites for lodging, in such a time, its use for the purpose of maintaining the lodging is permitted by the Blessed One, even having disposed of the lodging. Therefore, having set aside one or two excellent lodgings, it is allowable to dispose of the others, starting from the inferior ones, for the purpose of alms-food. However, it should not be applied in such a way as to cut off the original object.

Yo pana ārāmo catuppaccayatthāya niyametvā dinno, tattha apalokanakammaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Yena pana paccayena ūnaṃ, tadatthaṃ upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ārāmo jaggitabbo, vetanaṃ datvāpi jaggāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ye pana vetanaṃ labhitvā ārāmeyeva gehaṃ katvā vasantā rakkhanti, te ce āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nāḷikeraṃ vā tālapakkaṃ vā denti, yaṃ tesaṃ saṅghena anuññātaṃ hoti – “divase divase ettakaṃ nāma khādathā”ti tadeva te dātuṃ labhanti; tato uttari tesaṃ dadantānampi gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

As for a park that has been given, having been designated for the purpose of the four requisites, an act of authorization should not be performed there. But for whatever requisite is deficient, it is allowable to apply the park's produce for that purpose. The park should be maintained; it is allowable to have it maintained even by giving wages. But as for those who, having received wages, guard the park while living there, having made a house in the park itself—if they give coconuts or ripe palm fruits to arriving bhikkhus, they are able to give only that which has been permitted to them by the Sangha, saying, 'Each day, eat this much.' Beyond that, it is not allowable to accept it, even if they give it.

Yo [M 1.0341][V 1.0312] pana ārāmaṃ keṇiyā gahetvā saṅghassa catuppaccayatthāya kappiyabhaṇḍameva deti, ayaṃ bahukampi dātuṃ labhati. Cetiyassa padīpatthāya vā khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇatthāya vā dinno ārāmopi paṭijaggitabbo; vetanaṃ datvāpi jaggāpetabbo. Vetanañca panettha cetiyasantakampi saṅghasantakampi dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Etampi ārāmaṃ vetanena tattheva vasitvā rakkhantānañca keṇiyā gahetvā kappiyabhaṇḍadāyakānañca tattha jātakaphaladānaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

But one who, having taken a park by purchase, gives only allowable items to the Sangha for the purpose of the four requisites, this person is able to give even a large amount. A park given for the purpose of lamps for a cetiya or for repairing what is broken and dilapidated should also be maintained; it should be caused to be maintained even by giving wages. And here, it is allowable to give wages from that which belongs to the cetiya and that which belongs to the Sangha. Regarding this park also, the giving of fruit grown there by those who guard it while living right there for wages, and by those who, having taken it by purchase, are donors of allowable items, should be understood in the same way as has been stated.

Ambapālakādivatthūsu – anāpatti, bhikkhave, gopakassa dāneti ettha kataraṃ pana gopakadānaṃ vaṭṭati, kataraṃ na vaṭṭatīti? Mahāsumatthero tāva āha – “yaṃ gopakassa paricchinditvā dinnaṃ hoti – ‘ettakaṃ divase divase gaṇhā’ti tadeva vaṭṭati; tato uttari na vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpadumatthero panāha – “kiṃ gopakānaṃ paṇṇaṃ āropetvā nimittasaññaṃ vā katvā dinnaṃ atthi, etesaṃ hatthe vissaṭṭhakassa ete issarā, tasmā yaṃ te denti taṃ bahukampi vaṭṭatī”ti. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “manussānaṃ ārāmaṃ vā aññaṃ vā phalāphalaṃ dārakā rakkhanti, tehi dinnaṃ vaṭṭati[P 2.0388]. Āharāpetvā pana na gahetabbaṃ. Saṅghike pana cetiyasantake ca keṇiyā gahetvā rakkhantasseva dānaṃ vaṭṭati. Vetanena rakkhantassa attano bhāgamattaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “yaṃ gihīnaṃ ārāmarakkhakā bhikkhūnaṃ denti, etaṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhusaṅghassa pana ārāmagopakā yaṃ attano bhatiyā khaṇḍetvā denti, etaṃ vaṭṭati. Yopi upaḍḍhārāmaṃ vā kecideva rukkhe vā bhatiṃ labhitvā rakkhati, tassāpi attano pattarukkhatoyeva dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Keṇiyā gahetvā rakkhantassa pana sabbampi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Etaṃ pana sabbaṃ byañjanato nānaṃ, atthato ekameva; tasmā adhippāyaṃ ñatvā gahetabbaṃ.

In the stories of the mango-guardian and others—regarding the text, 'There is no offense... in a gift from a guardian,' the question is: which gift from a guardian is allowable, and which is not? The Elder Mahāsuma first said: 'That which is given to the guardian, having been demarcated—"Take this much each day"—only that is allowable. Beyond that is not allowable.' But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: 'Is anything given to the guardians having put it on a leaf or having made a sign? Of that which is relinquished into their hands, they are the masters. Therefore, whatever they give, even if it is much, is allowable.' But in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā it is said: 'Children guard a park or other fruits belonging to people; what is given by them is allowable. But it should not be accepted after having it brought. In the case of Sangha property and cetiya property, the gift of one who guards it having taken it by purchase is allowable. For one who guards for wages, a gift of only his own share is allowable.' And in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'What the park-guardians of laypeople give to bhikkhus, that is allowable. But what the park-guardians of the Bhikkhu Sangha give, having set it apart from their own wages, that is allowable. And for one who guards half a park or only certain trees, having received wages, for him too it is allowable to give only from the trees that have fallen to his share. But for one who guards having taken it by purchase, it is allowable to give even all of it.' All this, however, is different in letter but one and the same in meaning; therefore, having understood the intention, it should be accepted.

Dāruvatthumhi – tāvakāliko ahaṃ bhagavāti tāvakālikacitto ahaṃ bhagavāti vattukāmena vuttaṃ, tāvakālikacittoti “puna āharitvā dassāmī”ti evaṃcitto ahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavā “tāvakālike anāpattī”ti āha.

In the story of the wood: 'I am for a time, Blessed One' was said by one who wished to say, 'I am of a mind for a time, Blessed One.' 'Of a mind for a time' means it was said, 'I am of such a mind: "Having brought it back again, I will give it."' The Blessed One said, 'There is no offense in what is for a time.'

Ayaṃ panettha pāḷimuttakavinicchayo – sace saṅgho saṅghikaṃ kammaṃ kāreti uposathāgāraṃ vā bhojanasālaṃ vā, tato āpucchitvā tāvakālikaṃ haritabbaṃ. Yo pana saṅghiko dabbasambhāro agutto deve vassante [M 1.0342] temeti, ātapena sukkhati, taṃ sabbampi āharitvā attano āvāse kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Saṅgho āharāpento aññena vā dabbasambhārena mūlena vā saññāpetabbo. Na sakkā ce hoti saññāpetuṃ, “saṅghikena, bhante, kataṃ saṅghikaparibhogena vaḷañjathā”ti vattabbaṃ. Senāsanassa pana ayameva bhikkhu issaro. Sacepi pāsāṇatthambho vā rukkhatthambho vā [V 1.0313] kavāṭaṃ vā vātapānaṃ vā nappahoti, saṅghikaṃ tāvakālikaṃ āharitvā pākatikaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Esa nayo aññesupi dabbasambhāresūti.

Herein, this is the legal decision outside the Pāḷi text: If the Sangha has a Sangha work done, such as an Uposatha hall or a dining hall, then having asked permission, it may be taken for a time. But whatever Sangha materials and equipment are unprotected, get wet when it rains, and dry in the sun, it is allowable to bring all of that and place it in one's own dwelling. When the Sangha has it brought back, they should be satisfied with other materials and equipment or with its value. If it is not possible to satisfy them, it should be said: 'Venerable sirs, please use that which was made with Sangha property with the usage appropriate for Sangha property.' But this very bhikkhu is the master of the lodging. Even if a stone pillar, a wooden pillar, a door, or a window is not sufficient, it is allowable to bring Sangha property for a time and make it serviceable. This is the method for other materials and equipment as well.

Udakavatthusmiṃ – yadā [P 2.0389] udakaṃ dullabhaṃ hoti, yojanatopi aḍḍhayojanatopi āharīyati, evarūpe pariggahitaudake avahāro. Yatopi āharimato vā pokkharaṇīādīsu ṭhitato vā kevalaṃ yāgubhattaṃ sampādenti, pānīyaparibhogañca karonti, na aññaṃ mahāparibhogaṃ, tampi theyyacittena gaṇhato avahāro. Yato pana ekaṃ vā dve vā ghaṭe gahetvā āsanaṃ dhovituṃ, bodhirukkhe siñcituṃ udakapūjaṃ kātuṃ, rajanaṃ pacituṃ labbhati, tattha saṅghassa katikavaseneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Atirekaṃ gaṇhanto, mattikādīni vā theyyacittena pakkhipanto bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo.

In the case of water: when water is difficult to obtain and is brought from a yojana or half a yojana away, in the case of such collected water, theft occurs. From water that has been brought from afar or that is in a pond or the like—from which they only prepare gruel and rice and use for drinking and general purposes, and not for other major consumption—taking even that with a thieving intention constitutes theft. However, from a source where it is permissible to take one or two pots to wash a seat, to water Bodhi trees, to make a water offering, or to boil dye, one should act only according to the Saṅgha's agreement. One who takes in excess, or who puts in clay or the like with a thieving intention, should be made to pay compensation after the item has been valued.

Sace āvāsikā katikavattaṃ daḷhaṃ karonti, aññesaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovituṃ vā rajituṃ vā na denti, attanā pana aññesaṃ apassantānaṃ gahetvā sabbaṃ karonti, tesaṃ katikāya na ṭhātabbaṃ. Yattakaṃ te dhovanti, tattakaṃ dhovitabbaṃ. Sace saṅghassa dve tisso pokkharaṇiyo vā udakasoṇḍiyo vā honti, katikā ca katā “ettha nhāyitabbaṃ, ito pānīyaṃ gahetabbaṃ, idha sabbaparibhogo kātabbo”ti. Katikavatteneva sabbaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yattha katikā natthi, tattha sabbaparibhogo vaṭṭatīti.

If the resident bhikkhus make the agreement strict, not allowing others to wash or dye their small belongings, but they themselves, when others are not looking, take the water and do everything, one should not abide by their agreement. As much as they wash, that much may be washed. If the Saṅgha has two or three ponds or water reservoirs, and an agreement has been made, stating: 'Here one should bathe, from here drinking water should be taken, here all general use should be done,' then everything should be done only according to the agreement. Where there is no agreement, all general use is permissible.

Mattikāvatthusmiṃ – yattha mattikā dullabhā hoti, nānappakārā vā vaṇṇamattikā āharitvā ṭhapitā, tattha thokāpi pañcamāsakaṃ agghati, tasmā pārājikaṃ. Saṅghike pana kamme cetiyakamme ca niṭṭhite saṅghaṃ āpucchitvā vā tāvakālikaṃ vā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sudhāyapi cittakammavaṇṇesupi eseva nayo.

In the case of clay: where clay is difficult to obtain, or various kinds of colored clay have been brought and stored, and even a small amount there is worth five māsakas, therefore it is a pārājika offense. However, when Saṅgha work or cetiya work is finished, it is permissible to take it after asking the Saṅgha or for temporary use. This same principle applies to plaster and to colors for decorative work.

Tiṇavatthūsu [M 1.0343] – jhāpitatiṇe ṭhānācāvanassa abhāvā dukkaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. Saṅgho tiṇavatthuṃ jaggitvā saṅghikaṃ āvāsaṃ chādeti, puna kadāci jaggituṃ na sakkoti, athañño eko bhikkhu vattasīsena jaggati, saṅghassevetaṃ. No ce jaggati, saṅgheneko [P 2.0390] bhikkhu vattabbo “jaggitvā dehī”ti. So ce bhāgaṃ icchati, bhāgaṃ datvāpi jaggāpetabbaṃ. Sace bhāgaṃ vaḍḍheti, dātabbameva. Vaḍḍhetiyeva, “gaccha jaggitvā sabbaṃ gahetvā attano santakaṃ senāsanaṃ chādehī”ti vattabbo. Kasmā? Naṭṭhe attho natthi. Dadantehi pana savatthukaṃ na dātabbaṃ[V 1.0314], garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti; tiṇamattaṃ pana dātabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ ce jaggitvā attano senāsanaṃ chādente puna saṅgho jaggituṃ pahoti, “tvaṃ mā jaggi, saṅgho jaggissatī”ti vattabboti.

In the cases of grass: regarding burned grass, due to the absence of displacement from its place, it is a dukkaṭa offense, and restitution for the item is required. The Saṅgha tends a grass plot and roofs a Saṅgha dwelling. If at some time they are unable to tend it, and another bhikkhu tends it as a point of duty, it still belongs to the Saṅgha. If he does not tend it, the Saṅgha should tell one bhikkhu, 'Tend it and give the grass.' If he wants a share, he should be made to tend it even after being given a share. If he increases the share, it must be given. If he increases it yet again, he should be told, 'Go, tend it, take it all, and roof your own lodging.' Why? When it is lost, there is no benefit. However, those giving should not give it together with the land, as the land is a heavy article; only the grass should be given. If, while he is tending it and roofing his own lodging, the Saṅgha again becomes able to tend it, he should be told, 'You, do not tend it; the Saṅgha will tend it.'

Mañcādīni satta vatthūni pākaṭāneva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana anāgatampi pāsāṇatthambhaṃ vā rukkhatthambhaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci pādagghanakaṃ harantassa pārājikameva. Padhānagharādīsu chaḍḍitapatitānaṃ pariveṇādīnaṃ kuṭṭampi pākārampi bhinditvā iṭṭhakādīni avaharantassāpi eseva nayo. Kasmā? Saṅghikaṃ nāma kadāci ajjhāvasanti, kadāci na ajjhāvasanti. Paccante corabhayena janapade vuṭṭhahante chaḍḍitavihārādīsu kiñci parikkhāraṃ harantassāpi eseva nayo. Ye pana tato tāvakālikaṃ haranti, puna āvasitesu ca vihāresu bhikkhū āharāpenti, dātabbaṃ. Sacepi tato āharitvā senāsanaṃ kataṃ hoti, taṃ vā tadagghanakaṃ vā dātabbameva. “Puna āvasissāmā”ti ālayaṃ acchinditvā vuṭṭhitesu janapadesu gaṇasantakaṃ vā puggalikaṃ vā gahitaṃ hoti; te ce anujānanti, paṭikammena kiccaṃ natthi. Saṅghikaṃ pana garubhaṇḍaṃ, tasmā paṭikammaṃ kattabbameva.

The seven cases beginning with the bed are already clear. But even for an item not mentioned in the Pāḷi, for one who carries away a stone pillar, a wooden pillar, or any other thing worth a quarter, it is a pārājika offense. For one who, having broken a wall or an enclosure of abandoned and fallen meditation halls, monastic compounds, or the like, carries away bricks or other such things, this same principle applies. Why? Because a Saṅgha property is sometimes inhabited and sometimes not. When a district in a border region is abandoned due to fear of thieves, for one who carries away any requisite from abandoned monasteries or the like, this same principle applies. But as for those who take items from there temporarily, when the monasteries are re-inhabited and the bhikkhus have them brought back, they should be given back. Even if a lodging has been made from what was brought from there, either that item or its value must be given back. When districts are abandoned without severing the intention to return, thinking, 'We will inhabit it again,' and property belonging to a group or an individual is taken, if they permit it, there is no need for restitution. But Saṅgha property is a heavy article; therefore, restitution must certainly be made.

157. Vihāraparibhogavatthu uttānatthameva.

157. The case concerning the use of a dwelling is clear in meaning.

Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāvakālikaṃ haritunti ettha yo bhikkhu saṅghikaṃ mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā tāvakālikaṃ haritvā attano phāsukaṭṭhāne ekampi dvepi māse saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjati, āgatāgatānaṃ vuḍḍhatarānaṃ deti, nappaṭibāhati[P 2.0391], tassa tasmiṃ naṭṭhepi jiṇṇepi corāvahaṭepi gīvā na hoti. Vasitvā pana gacchantena yathāṭhāne ṭhapetabbaṃ. Yo pana puggalikaparibhogena paribhuñjati, āgatāgatānaṃ vuḍḍhatarānaṃ na [M 1.0344] deti, tasmiṃ naṭṭhe tassa gīvā hoti. Aññaṃ pana āvāsaṃ haritvā paribhuñjantena sace tattha vuḍḍhataro āgantvā vuṭṭhāpeti, “mayā idaṃ asukāvāsato nāma āhaṭaṃ, gacchāmi, naṃ pākatikaṃ karomī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace so bhikkhu “ahaṃ pākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti vadati, tassa bhāraṃ katvāpi gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'I allow, bhikkhus, to take temporarily': a bhikkhu who, having temporarily taken a Saṅgha bed or bench, uses it in his own comfortable place for one or two months in the manner of using Saṅgha property—giving it to more senior bhikkhus who arrive and not refusing—for him there is no liability even if it is lost, worn out, or stolen by thieves. But when leaving after having stayed, it should be placed in its original spot. However, one who uses it in the manner of using personal property and does not give it to more senior bhikkhus who arrive, if it is lost, there is liability for him. Furthermore, by one who takes it to another dwelling and uses it, if a more senior bhikkhu arrives there and displaces him, he should say: 'I brought this from such-and-such a dwelling. I am going; I will return it to its original state.' If that bhikkhu says, 'I will return it to its original state,' it is permissible to go even after entrusting him with that responsibility. This is stated in the summary commentary.

Campāvatthumhi – tekaṭulayāgūti tilataṇḍulamuggehi vā tilataṇḍulamāsehi vā tilataṇḍulakulatthehi vā tilataṇḍulehi saddhiṃ yaṃkiñci ekaṃ aparaṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā tīhi katā, etaṃ kira imehi tīhi catubhāgaudakasambhinne khīre sappimadhusakkarādīhi yojetvā karonti.

In the case of Campā: 'three-ingredient gruel' is gruel made with three ingredients: with sesame, rice, and green gram; or with sesame, rice, and black gram; or with sesame, rice, and horse gram; or by adding any one other pulse together with sesame and rice. It is said that they make this by combining these three ingredients in milk mixed with a quarter part of water, and adding ghee, honey, sugar, and so on.

Rājagahavatthumhi [V 1.0315] – madhugoḷakoti atirasakapūvo vuccati; “madhusīsaka”ntipi vadanti. Sesamettha vatthudvayepi odanabhājanīyavatthusmiṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the story of Rājagaha, an extremely sweet cake is called a 'honey-ball'; they also call it a 'honey-head'. The remainder here in both stories should be understood in the same way as was stated in the story of the division of rice.

158. Ajjukavatthusmiṃ – etadavocāti gilāno hutvā avoca. Āyasmā upāli āyasmato ajjukassa pakkhoti na agatigamanavasena pakkho, api ca kho anāpattisaññitāya lajjīanuggahena vinayānuggahena ca thero pakkhoti veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānameva.

158. In the story of Ajjuka, as for 'he said this,' it means he spoke after becoming ill. As for 'Venerable Upāli was on the side of Venerable Ajjuka,' he was not on his side by way of going to a wrong course; rather, it should be understood that the elder was on his side because of the perception of no offense, out of a desire to support a conscientious person, and out of a desire to support the Vinaya. The remainder here is self-evident.

159. Bārāṇasīvatthusmiṃ – corehi upaddutanti corehi viluttaṃ. Iddhiyā ānetvā pāsāde ṭhapesīti thero kira taṃ kulaṃ sokasallasamappitaṃ āvaṭṭantaṃ vivaṭṭantaṃ disvā tassa kulassa anukampāya pasādānurakkhaṇatthāya dhammānuggahena attano iddhiyā “tesaṃyeva pāsādaṃ dārakānaṃ samīpe hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Dārakā “amhākaṃ pāsādo”ti sañjānitvā abhiruhiṃsu. Tato thero iddhiṃ paṭisaṃhari, pāsādopi [P 2.0392] sakaṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi. Vohāravasena pana vuttaṃ “te dārake iddhiyā ānetvā pāsāde ṭhapesī”ti. Iddhivisayeti īdisāya adhiṭṭhāniddhiyā anāpatti. Vikubbaniddhi pana na vaṭṭati.

159. In the story of Bārāṇasī, 'harassed by thieves' means plundered by thieves. As for 'having brought by psychic power, he placed them in the palace': the elder, seeing that family afflicted by the dart of sorrow, tossing and turning, out of compassion for that family, for the sake of protecting their faith, and through support for the Dhamma, resolved with his own psychic power: “Let their very palace be near the children.” The children, recognizing it as, “This is our palace,” climbed up. Then the elder withdrew his psychic power, and the palace stood in its own place. But it was said by way of convention, “He brought the children by psychic power and placed them in the palace.” In the sphere of psychic power, for such a psychic power of determination, there is no offense. The psychic power of transformation, however, is not allowable.

160-1. Avasāne vatthudvayaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

At the end, the two stories are of self-evident meaning.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second Pārājika is concluded.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 1.0345] anusāsanī –

Therein, this is the instruction:

Dutiyaṃ adutiyena, yaṃ jinena pakāsitaṃ;

Parājitakilesena, pārājikamidaṃ idha.

This second Pārājika was proclaimed here by the Conqueror, who is without a second, by whom defilements have been defeated.

Sikkhāpadaṃ samaṃ tena, aññaṃ kiñci na vijjati;

Anekanayavokiṇṇaṃ, gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ.

No other training rule whatsoever is found equal to it, interspersed as it is with many methods and having profound meaning and decision.

Tasmā vatthumhi otiṇṇe, bhikkhunā vinayaññunā;

Vinayānuggahenettha, karontena vinicchayaṃ.

Therefore, when a case has arisen, by a monk who is a knower of the Vinaya, making a decision herein with support for the Vinaya,

Pāḷiṃ [V 1.0316] aṭṭhakathañceva, sādhippāyamasesato;

Ogayha appamattena, karaṇīyo vinicchayo.

the decision should be made diligently, after having completely penetrated both the Pāḷi and the Commentary, together with their meaning.

Āpattidassanussāho, na kattabbo kudācanaṃ;

Passissāmi anāpatti-miti kayirātha mānasaṃ.

An effort to see an offense should never be made; one should make up one's mind thus: “I will see a non-offense.”

Passitvāpi ca āpattiṃ, avatvāva punappunaṃ;

Vīmaṃsitvātha viññūhi, saṃsanditvā ca taṃ vade.

And even having seen an offense, without yet speaking of it, only after having investigated it again and again and having conferred with the wise, should one then speak of it.

Kappiyepi ca vatthusmiṃ, cittassa lahuvattino;

Vasena sāmaññaguṇā, cavantīdha puthujjanā.

For even in an allowable matter, worldlings here fall away from the quality of a recluse by the power of a fickle mind.

Tasmā paraparikkhāraṃ, āsīvisamivoragaṃ;

Aggiṃ viya ca sampassaṃ, nāmaseyya vicakkhaṇoti.

Therefore, a discerning person, regarding another's requisites as a venomous snake and as a fire, should not handle them.

Pārājikakaṇḍa-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Commentary on the Pārājika Chapter.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

In the Vinaya Piṭaka

Pārājikakaṇḍa-aṭṭhakathā (dutiyo bhāgo)

Commentary on the Pārājika Chapter (Second Part)

3. Tatiyapārājikaṃ

3. The Third Pārājika

Tatiyaṃ [P 2.0393][M 2.0001][V 2.0001] tīhi suddhena, yaṃ buddhena vibhāvitaṃ;

Pārājikaṃ tassa dāni, patto saṃvaṇṇanākkamo.

The sequence of the commentary has now arrived for that third Pārājika, which was made clear by the Buddha, who is pure through the three doors [of body, speech, and mind].

Yasmā tasmā suviññeyyaṃ, yaṃ pubbe ca pakāsitaṃ;

Taṃ vajjayitvā assāpi, hoti saṃvaṇṇanā ayaṃ.

Therefore, since its turn has arrived, avoiding that which is easily understood and that which has been explained before, this is the commentary for this [Pārājika] as well.

Paṭhamapaññattinidānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Origin of the First Promulgation

162. Tena [V 2.0002] samayena buddho bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyanti ettha vesāliyanti evaṃnāmake itthiliṅgavasena pavattavohāre nagare. Tañhi nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ pākāraparikkhepavaḍḍhanena visālībhūtattā “vesālī”ti vuccati. Idampi ca nagaraṃ sabbaññutappatteyeva sammāsambuddhe sabbākārena vepullaṃ pattanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ gocaragāmaṃ dassetvā nivāsaṭṭhāna māha – “mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāya”nti. Tattha mahāvanaṃ nāma sayaṃjātaṃ aropimaṃ saparicchedaṃ mahantaṃ vanaṃ. Kapilavatthusāmantā pana mahāvanaṃ himavantena saha ekābaddhaṃ aparicchedaṃ hutvā mahāsamuddaṃ āhacca ṭhitaṃ. Idaṃ tādisaṃ na hoti, saparicchedaṃ mahantaṃ vananti mahāvanaṃ. Kūṭāgārasālā pana mahāvanaṃ [M 2.0002] nissāya kate ārāme kūṭāgāraṃ anto katvā haṃsavaṭṭakacchadanena katā sabbākārasampannā buddhassa bhagavato gandhakuṭi veditabbā.

162. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, at the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Herein, 'in Vesālī' means in the city with this name, a designation used in the feminine gender. Indeed, that city is called 'Vesālī' because it had become spacious (visālībhūta) through the extension of its surrounding wall three times. And it should be understood that this city reached its full prosperity in every way only when the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One attained omniscience. Having thus shown the alms-round village, the reciter states the dwelling place: 'in the Great Wood, at the Hall with the Peaked Roof.' Therein, the 'Great Wood' is a great forest that is self-arisen, not planted, and has boundaries. The Great Wood, however, near Kapilavatthu, being joined together with the Himālaya, is without boundaries and stands reaching the great ocean. This one is not like that; it is a great forest with boundaries, thus it is the 'Great Wood.' As for the 'Hall with the Peaked Roof,' it should be understood as the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) of the Buddha, the Blessed One, complete in all aspects, built in a monastery established in reliance on the Great Wood, with a gabled hall (kūṭāgāra) placed within, and constructed with a roof covering all around like the spread wing of a haṃsa bird.

Anekapariyāyena asubhakathaṃ kathetīti anekehi kāraṇehi asubhākārasandassanappavattaṃ kāyavicchandaniyakathaṃ katheti. Seyyathidaṃ – “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe. [P 2.0394]… mutta”nti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Bhikkhave, imasmiṃ byāmamatte kaḷevare sabbākārenapi vicinanto na koci kiñci muttaṃ vā maṇiṃ vā veḷuriyaṃ vā agaruṃ vā candanaṃ vā kuṅkumaṃ vā kappūraṃ vā vāsacuṇṇādīni vā aṇumattampi sucibhāvaṃ passati. Atha kho paramaduggandhaṃ jegucchaṃ assirīkadassanaṃ kesalomādinānappakāraṃ asuciṃyeva passati. Tasmā na ettha chando vā rāgo vā karaṇīyo. Yepi hi uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ jātā kesā nāma, tepi asubhā ceva asucino ca paṭikkūlā ca. So ca nesaṃ asubhāsucipaṭikkūlabhāvo vaṇṇatopi saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi āsayatopi okāsatopīti pañcahi kāraṇehi veditabbo. Evaṃ lomādīnanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.182) vuttanayena veditabbo. Iti bhagavā ekamekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse pañcapañcappabhedena anekapariyāyena asubhakathaṃ katheti.

'He speaks the discourse on the non-beautiful in many ways' means: by many reasons, he speaks the discourse that causes the cutting of desire for the body, a discourse that proceeds by showing the non-beautiful aspect. For instance: 'In this body, there are head-hairs, body-hairs... urine.' What is meant by this? 'Bhikkhus, in this fathom-long carcass, one who searches in every way does not see any purity at all, not even a particle, be it a pearl, a gem, beryl, aloe-wood, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, or scented powders and so on. Rather, one sees only what is utterly foul-smelling, disgusting, unsightly, and impure in its various kinds, such as head-hairs and body-hairs. Therefore, neither desire nor lust should be aroused for it. Indeed, even the so-called head-hairs that grow on the head, the highest limb, are non-beautiful, impure, and repulsive. And their state of being non-beautiful, impure, and repulsive is to be understood through five reasons: by way of color, by way of shape, by way of smell, by way of origin, and by way of location. Similarly for body-hairs and so on.' This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be understood in the way stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on the non-beautiful in many ways, with fivefold divisions for each and every part.

Asubhāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti uddhumātakādivasena asubhamātikaṃ nikkhipitvā padabhājanīyena taṃ vibhajanto vaṇṇento saṃvaṇṇento asubhāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Asubhabhāvanāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti yā ayaṃ kesādīsu vā uddhumātakādīsu vā ajjhattabahiddhāvatthūsu asubhākāraṃ gahetvā pavattassa cittassa bhāvanā vaḍḍhanā phātikammaṃ, tassā asubhabhāvanāya ānisaṃsaṃ dassento vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, guṇaṃ parikitteti. Seyyathidaṃ – “asubhabhāvanābhiyutto, bhikkhave[V 2.0003], bhikkhu kesādīsu vā vatthūsu uddhumātakādīsu vā pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ [P 2.0395] paṭilabhati. So taṃ paṭhamajjhānasaṅkhātaṃ cittamañjūsaṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uttamatthaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti.

“He speaks in praise of the non-beautiful” means: having laid down the matrix of the non-beautiful by way of the bloated corpse and so on, while analyzing, describing, and extolling it by means of the Pāda-bhājanīya, he speaks in praise of the non-beautiful. “He speaks in praise of the development of the non-beautiful” means: showing the benefits of that development of the non-beautiful—which is the development, increase, and cultivation of the mind that has arisen by grasping the non-beautiful aspect in internal and external objects, such as head-hairs and so on, or the bloated corpse and so on—he speaks in praise, he proclaims its qualities. For instance: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the development of the non-beautiful, with regard to objects such as head-hairs and so on, or the bloated corpse and so on, attains the first jhāna, which has abandoned the five factors, is endowed with five factors, is good in three ways, and is complete with ten characteristics. Relying on that first jhāna, called the mind-casket, and having developed insight, he reaches the highest goal, Arahantship.”

Tatrimāni [M 2.0003] paṭhamassa jhānassa dasa lakkhaṇāni – pāripanthikato cittavisuddhi, majjhimassa samādhinimittassa paṭipatti, tattha cittapakkhandanaṃ, visuddhassa cittassa ajjhupekkhanaṃ, samathappaṭipannassa ajjhupekkhanaṃ, ekattupaṭṭhānassa ajjhupekkhanaṃ, tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhena tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena āsevanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanāti.

Therein, these are the ten characteristics of the first jhāna: purity of mind from the obstacles; attainment of the moderate sign of concentration; the mind's plunging in there; equanimity towards the purified mind; equanimity towards the mind that has attained serenity; equanimity towards the mind established in oneness; gladdening by way of the non-transgression of the states that have arisen there; gladdening by way of the faculties having a single taste; gladdening by way of bearing energy suitable for that; and gladdening by way of cultivation.

Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – “paṭhamassa jhānassa ko ādi, kiṃ majjhe, kiṃ pariyosānaṃ? Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ. Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, ādissa kati lakkhaṇāni? Ādissa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni – yo tassa paripantho tato cittaṃ visujjhati, visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Yañca paripanthato cittaṃ visujjhati, yañca visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, yañca paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, ādissa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati – ‘paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ ādikalyāṇañceva hoti tilakkhaṇasampannañca’.

Herein, this is the Pāḷi: “Of the first jhāna, what is the beginning, what is the middle, what is the end? Of the first jhāna, the purity of the path is the beginning, the cultivation of equanimity is the middle, gladdening is the end. The purity of the path is the beginning of the first jhāna. Of the beginning, how many characteristics are there? Of the beginning, there are three characteristics: the mind is purified from that which is its obstacle; because it is purified, the mind attains the moderate sign of serenity; because it has been attained, the mind plunges into it. Both that the mind is purified from the obstacle, and that because it is purified the mind attains the moderate sign of serenity, and that because it has been attained the mind plunges into it. The purity of the path is the beginning of the first jhāna; these are the three characteristics of the beginning. Therefore, it is said: ‘The first jhāna is good in the beginning and is endowed with three characteristics.’”

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Majjhassa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni – visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, samathappaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Yañca visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca samathappaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati[P 2.0396], yañca ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati – ‘paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ majjhekalyāṇañceva hoti tilakkhaṇasampannañca’.

“The cultivation of equanimity of the first jhāna is the middle. How many characteristics does the middle have? The middle has three characteristics: one regards with equanimity the purified mind; one regards with equanimity the mind that has attained tranquility; one regards with equanimity the mind established in singularity. And that one regards with equanimity the purified mind, and that one regards with equanimity the mind that has attained tranquility, and that one regards with equanimity the mind established in singularity. The cultivation of equanimity of the first jhāna is the middle; these are the three characteristics of the middle. Therefore, it is said: ‘The first jhāna is good in the middle and is endowed with three characteristics.’”

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, pariyosānassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Pariyosānassa cattāri lakkhaṇāni – tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, āsevanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā. Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, pariyosānassa imāni cattāri lakkhaṇāni[V 2.0004]. Tena vuccati – ‘paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇañceva hoti catulakkhaṇasampannañca. “Evaṃ tividhattagataṃ cittaṃ tividhakalyāṇakaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ [M 2.0004] vitakkasampannañceva hoti vicārasampannañca pītisampannañca sukhasampannañca cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampannañca saddhāsampannañca vīriyasampannañca satisampannañca samādhisampannañca paññāsampannañcā”ti (paṭi. ro. 1.158).

“The gladdening is the culmination of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the culmination have? The culmination has four characteristics: gladdening by way of the non-transgression of the states that have arisen therein; gladdening by way of the faculties having a single taste; gladdening by way of bearing the energy appropriate to that; gladdening by way of repetition. The gladdening is the culmination of the first jhāna; these are the four characteristics of the culmination. Therefore, it is said: ‘The first jhāna is good in its culmination and is endowed with four characteristics.’ Thus, the mind that has reached a threefold state, being threefold good and endowed with ten characteristics, is endowed with initial application, endowed with sustained application, endowed with rapture, endowed with happiness, endowed with the mind's establishment, endowed with faith, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.”

Ādissa ādissa asubhasamāpattiyā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti “evampi itthampī”ti punappunaṃ vavatthānaṃ katvā ādisanto asubhasamāpattiyā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, ānisaṃsaṃ katheti, guṇaṃ parikitteti. Seyyathidaṃ – “asubhasaññāparicitena, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cetasā bahulaṃ viharato methunadhammasamāpattiyā cittaṃ paṭilīyati paṭikuṭati paṭivaṭṭati, na sampasārīyati, upekkhā vā pāṭikulyatā vā saṇṭhāti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kukkuṭapattaṃ vā nhārudaddulaṃ vā aggimhi pakkhittaṃ paṭilīyati paṭikuṭati paṭivaṭṭati, na sampasārīyati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, asubhasaññāparicitena bhikkhuno [P 2.0397] cetasā bahulaṃ viharato methunadhammasamāpattiyā cittaṃ paṭilīyati paṭikuṭati paṭivaṭṭati, na sampasārīyatī”ti (a. ni. 7.49).

“He speaks in praise of the attainment of foulness, pointing it out again and again” means: having defined it again and again, saying, “It is thus, and it is in this way,” and pointing it out, he speaks in praise of the attainment of foulness, declares its benefits, and extols its virtues. For example: “Monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind familiarized with the perception of foulness, the mind recoils from involvement in sexual intercourse, it shrinks back, it turns away, it does not spread out; and either equanimity or loathsomeness is established. Just as, monks, a chicken feather or a strip of sinew, when thrown into a fire, recoils, shrinks back, and turns away, and does not spread out; even so, monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind familiarized with the perception of foulness, the mind recoils from involvement in sexual intercourse, it shrinks back, it turns away, and it does not spread out.”

Icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, addhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyitunti ahaṃ bhikkhave ekaṃ addhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ nilīyituṃ ekova hutvā viharituṃ icchāmīti attho. Namhi kenaci upasaṅkamitabbo aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakenāti yo attanā payuttavācaṃ akatvā mamatthāya saddhesu kulesu paṭiyattaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ nīharitvā mayhaṃ upanāmeti, taṃ piṇḍapātanīhārakaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā namhi aññena kenaci bhikkhunā vā gahaṭṭhena vā upasaṅkamitabboti.

‘I wish, monks, to go into seclusion for half a month.’ The meaning is: Monks, I wish to go into seclusion, to be in solitude, to dwell alone for one half-month. ‘I am not to be approached by anyone, except for the one who brings almsfood.’ This means: apart from the one monk who brings almsfood—that is, one who, without speaking a word related to requisites himself, brings the almsfood prepared in faithful households for my sake and presents it to me—I am not to be approached by any other monk or householder.

Kasmā pana evamāhāti? Atīte kira pañcasatā migaluddakā mahatīhi daṇḍavāgurāhi araññaṃ parikkhipitvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā ekatoyeva yāvajīvaṃ migapakkhighātakammena jīvikaṃ kappetvā niraye upapannā; te tattha paccitvā pubbe katena kenacideva kusalakammena manussesu upapannā kalyāṇūpanissayavasena sabbepi bhagavato santike pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhiṃsu; tesaṃ tato mūlākusalakammato avipakkavipākā aparāparacetanā tasmiṃ addhamāsabbhantare attūpakkamena ca parūpakkamena ca jīvatupacchedāya okāsamakāsi, taṃ bhagavā addasa. Kammavipāko nāma na sakkā kenaci paṭibāhituṃ. Tesu ca bhikkhūsu puthujjanāpi atthi sotāpannasakadāgāmīanāgāmīkhīṇāsavāpi. Tattha khīṇāsavā appaṭisandhikā, itare ariyasāvakā [M 2.0005] niyatagatikā sugatiparāyaṇā, puthujjanānaṃ pana gati aniyatā. Atha bhagavā cintesi [V 2.0005] – “ime attabhāve chandarāgena maraṇabhayabhītā na sakkhissanti gatiṃ visodhetuṃ, handa nesaṃ chandarāgappahānāya asubhakathaṃ kathemi. Taṃ sutvā attabhāve vigatacchandarāgatāya gativisodhanaṃ katvā sagge paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhissanti. Evaṃ nesaṃ mama santike pabbajjā sātthikā [P 2.0398] bhavissatī”ti.

But why did he speak thus? It is said that in the past, five hundred hunters, having encircled a forest with large nets fitted with poles, were joyful and delighted. Having made their living for their entire lives solely by the act of killing beasts and birds, they were reborn in hell. Having been tormented there, due to some wholesome kamma done previously, they were reborn among humans. By the power of a good supporting condition, all of them received the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One. For them, from that root unwholesome kamma, the subsequent volitions whose results had not yet ripened created an opportunity within that half-month for the cutting off of their lives, both by their own undertaking and by the undertaking of others. The Blessed One saw this. The result of kamma, indeed, cannot be prevented by anyone. And among those monks, there were worldlings, and there were also stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants. Therein, the arahants were without rebirth. The other noble disciples had a fixed destiny and were bound for a good destination. For the worldlings, however, the destination was not fixed.
