Then the Blessed One considered: ‘These monks, being attached with desire and lust to their existence and frightened by the fear of death, will not be able to purify their destination. Come, let me give them a discourse on foulness for the abandoning of desire and lust. Having heard it, due to being without desire and lust for their existence, they will purify their destination and take rebirth in a heavenly realm. In this way, their going forth in my presence will be fruitful.’

Tato tesaṃ anuggahāya asubhakathaṃ kathesi kammaṭṭhānasīsena, no maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇanādhippāyena. Kathetvā ca panassa etadahosi – “sace maṃ imaṃ addhamāsaṃ bhikkhū passissanti, ‘ajja eko bhikkhu mato, ajja dve…pe… ajja dasā’ti āgantvā āgantvā ārocessanti. Ayañca kammavipāko na sakkā mayā vā aññena vā paṭibāhituṃ. Svāhaṃ taṃ sutvāpi kiṃ karissāmi? Kiṃ me anatthakena anayabyasanena sutena? Handāhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ adassanaṃ upagacchāmī”ti. Tasmā evamāha – “icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, addhamāsaṃ patisallīyituṃ; namhi kenaci upasaṅkamitabbo aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakenā”ti.

Therefore, to assist them, he gave a discourse on foulness with the meditation subject as the main point; he did not speak with the intention of extolling the virtues of death. And after having spoken, this thought occurred to him: ‘If the monks see me during this half-month, they will come again and again and report, “Today one monk has died, today two… today ten.” And this result of kamma cannot be prevented by me or by anyone else. So, even having heard that, what shall I do? What is the use to me of hearing about this profitless misfortune and disaster? Come, I will go to a place out of the monks’ sight.’ Therefore, he spoke thus: ‘I wish, monks, to go into seclusion for half a month; I am not to be approached by anyone, except for the one who brings almsfood.’

Apare panāhu – “parūpavādavivajjanatthaṃ evaṃ vatvā paṭisallīno”ti. Pare kira bhagavantaṃ upavadissanti – “ayaṃ ‘sabbaññū, ahaṃ saddhammavaracakkavattī’ti paṭijānamāno attanopi sāvake aññamaññaṃ ghātente nivāretuṃ na sakkoti. Kimaññaṃ sakkhissatī”ti? Tattha paṇḍitā vakkhanti – “bhagavā paṭisallānamanuyutto nayimaṃ pavattiṃ jānāti, kocissa ārocayitāpi natthi, sace jāneyya addhā nivāreyyā”ti. Idaṃ pana icchāmattaṃ, paṭhamamevettha kāraṇaṃ. Nāssudhāti ettha “assudhā”ti padapūraṇamatte avadhāraṇatthe vā nipāto; neva koci bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamatīti attho.

But other teachers say: ‘For the purpose of avoiding the censure of others, having spoken thus, he entered seclusion.’ It is said that others would censure the Blessed One: ‘This one, while professing, “I am all-knowing, a supreme wheel-turning monarch of the excellent true Dhamma,” is not able to prevent his own disciples from killing one another. What else will he be able to do?’ Therein, the wise would say: ‘The Blessed One, being devoted to seclusion, does not know of this event. There is no one to inform him either. If he knew, he would surely prevent it.’ But this is merely a matter of opinion; the first reason is the correct one here. In the phrase `nāssudhā`, the word `assudhā` is a particle used merely for filling out the line or for emphasis; the meaning is that no one at all approaches the Blessed One.

Anekehi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīhi kāraṇehi vokāro assāti anekākāravokāro; anekākāravokiṇṇo anekakāraṇasammissoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ko so? Asubhabhāvanānuyogo, taṃ anekākāravokāraṃ asubhabhāvanānuyogaṃ anuyuttā viharantīti yuttapayuttā viharanti. Aṭṭīyantīti sakena kāyena aṭṭā dukkhitā honti[M 2.0006]. Harāyantīti lajjanti. Jigucchantīti sañjātajigucchā honti. Daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanena samannāgato. Maṇḍanakajātikoti maṇḍanakapakatiko. Sīsaṃnhātoti [P 2.0399] sīsena saddhiṃ nhāto. Daharo yuvāti cettha daharavacanena paṭhamayobbanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Paṭhamayobbane hi sattā visesena maṇḍanakajātikā honti. Sīsaṃnhātoti iminā maṇḍanānuyogakālaṃ. Yuvāpi hi kiñci kammaṃ katvā saṃkiliṭṭhasarīro na [V 2.0006] maṇḍanānuyutto hoti; sīsaṃnhāto pana so maṇḍanamevānuyuñjati. Ahikuṇapādīni daṭṭhumpi na icchati. So tasmiṃ khaṇe ahikuṇapena vā kukkurakuṇapena vā manussakuṇapena vā kaṇṭhe āsattena kenacideva paccatthikena ānetvā kaṇṭhe baddhena paṭimukkena yathā aṭṭīyeyya harāyeyya jiguccheyya; evameva te bhikkhū sakena kāyena aṭṭīyantā harāyantā jigucchantā so viya puriso taṃ kuṇapaṃ vigatacchandarāgatāya attano kāyaṃ pariccajitukāmā hutvā satthaṃ ādāya attanāpi attānaṃ jīvitā voropenti. “Tvaṃ maṃ jīvitā voropehi; ahaṃ ta”nti evaṃ aññamaññampi jīvitā voropenti.

Because there is a mixture (`vokāro`) from many causes (`anekehi kāraṇehi`) such as color and shape, it is called `anekākāravokāro` (having a manifold mixture); it is said to be ‘mixed with manifold aspects, commingled with many causes.’ What is that? The practice of meditation on the unattractive. ‘They dwell devoted to it’ means they dwell diligently and ardently. `Aṭṭīyanti` (they are afflicted) means they are afflicted and pained by their own bodies. `Harāyanti` (they are ashamed) means they feel shame. `Jigucchanti` (they are disgusted) means they become filled with revulsion. `Daharo` means young. `Yuvā` means endowed with youth. `Maṇḍanakajātiko` means one whose nature is to adorn oneself. `Sīsaṃnhāto` means having bathed, including the head. Here, in `daharo yuvā`, the word `daharo` indicates the first stage of youth. For in the first stage of youth, beings are especially of a nature to adorn themselves. The phrase `sīsaṃnhāto` indicates the time for indulging in adornment. For even a youth, having done some work and with a soiled body, is not devoted to adornment; but having bathed, including the head, he indulges only in adornment. He does not even wish to see things like a snake’s corpse. Just as at that moment, such a person would be afflicted, ashamed, and disgusted by a snake’s corpse, a dog’s corpse, or a human corpse brought by some enemy and hung on or bound to his neck; in the very same way, those monks—being afflicted, ashamed, and disgusted by their own bodies, and due to their state of being without desire and lust—wishing to abandon their own bodies like that man wishing to abandon the corpse, took up a weapon and deprived themselves of life. And saying, ‘You deprive me of life; I will deprive you,’ they also deprived one another of life.

Migalaṇḍikampi samaṇakuttakanti migalaṇḍikoti tassa nāmaṃ; samaṇakuttakoti samaṇavesadhārako. So kira sikhāmattaṃ ṭhapetvā sīsaṃ muṇḍetvā ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ aṃse katvā vihāraṃyeva upanissāya vighāsādabhāvena jīvati. Tampi migalaṇḍikaṃ samaṇakuttakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadanti. Sādhūti āyācanatthe nipāto. Noti upayogabahuvacanaṃ, sādhu āvuso amhe jīvitā voropehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca ariyā neva pāṇātipātaṃ kariṃsu na samādapesuṃ, na samanuññā ahesuṃ. Puthujjanā pana sabbamakaṃsu. Lohitakanti lohitamakkhitaṃ. Yena vaggumudānadīti vaggumatā lokassa puññasammatā nadī. Sopi kira “taṃ pāpaṃ tattha pavāhessāmī”ti saññāya gato, nadiyā ānubhāvena appamattakampi pāpaṃ pahīnaṃ nāma natthi.

Regarding `Migalaṇḍikampi samaṇakuttakaṃ`: `Migalaṇḍika` is his name; `samaṇakuttaka` means one who bears the guise of an ascetic. It is said that he, having shaved his head leaving only a topknot, wearing one ochre robe and placing one on his shoulder, lives depending on the monastery, sustaining himself by eating leftovers. Approaching that Migalaṇḍika, the sham ascetic, they spoke thus. `Sādhu` is a particle in the sense of entreaty. `No` is an accusative plural form; the meaning is, 'Good sir, please deprive us of life.' And here, the noble ones neither performed the act of killing, nor did they cause others to undertake it, nor did they consent to it. The worldlings, however, did all of it. `Lohitakaṃ` means smeared with blood. `Yena vaggumudānadī` refers to the Vaggumudā river, which is considered meritorious by the world. He too, it is said, went with the perception, 'I will wash away that evil there.' But by the river's power, not even a small amount of evil is what is called 'abandoned'.

163. Ahudeva kukkuccanti tesu kira bhikkhūsu kenacipi kāyavikāro vā [P 2.0400] vacīvikāro vā na kato, sabbe satā sampajānā dakkhiṇena passena nipajjiṃsu. Taṃ anussarato tassa kukkuccaṃ ahosiyeva. Ahu vippaṭisāroti tasseva kukkuccassa sabhāvaniyamanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ[M 2.0007]. Vippaṭisārakukkuccaṃ ahosi, na vinayakukkuccanti. Alābhā vata metiādi kukkuccassa pavattiākāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha alābhā vata meti āyatiṃ dāni mama hitasukhalābhā nāma natthīti anutthunāti. “Na vata me lābhā”tiiminā pana tamevatthaṃ daḷhaṃ karoti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sacepi koci “lābhā te”ti vadeyya, taṃ micchā, na vata me lābhāti. Dulladdhaṃ vata meti kusalānubhāvena laddhampi idaṃ manussattaṃ dulladdhaṃ vata me. Na vata me suladdhantiiminā pana tamevatthaṃ daḷhaṃ karoti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sacepi koci “suladdhaṃ te”ti vadeyya, taṃ micchā; na vata me suladdhanti. Apuññaṃ pasutanti apuññaṃ upacitaṃ janitaṃ vā. Kasmāti ce? Yohaṃ bhikkhū…pe… voropesinti[V 2.0007]. Tassattho – yo ahaṃ sīlavante tāya eva sīlavantatāya kalyāṇadhamme uttamadhamme seṭṭhadhamme bhikkhū jīvitā voropesinti.

163. Regarding `Ahudeva kukkuccaṃ`: It is said that among those monks, no unusual bodily movement or verbal utterance was made by anyone; all, being mindful and clearly comprehending, lay down on their right side. Remembering that, remorse indeed arose for him. `Ahu vippaṭisāro`: this is said to define the nature of that very remorse. It was remorse that is regret; it was not remorse that is a scruple concerning the Vinaya. `Alābhā vata me`, etc., is said to show the way in which the remorse occurred. Therein, `Alābhā vata me` means he laments, 'Alas, for me there is no gain of welfare and happiness, now or in the future.' With `Na vata me lābhā`, he strengthens that same meaning. The intention here is this: even if someone were to say, 'There is gain for you,' that would be false; 'Indeed, for me there is no gain.' `Dulladdhaṃ vata me` means: 'This human state, though gained by the power of merit, is ill-gained by me.' With `Na vata me suladdhaṃ`, he strengthens that same meaning. The intention here is this: even if someone were to say, 'It is well-gained by you,' that would be false; 'Indeed, it is not well-gained by me.' `Apuññaṃ pasutaṃ` means demerit was accumulated or produced. Why? Because 'I who... deprived of life the monks...' The meaning of this is: 'I who deprived of life the monks who were virtuous and, because of that very virtuousness, possessed of wholesome, supreme, and excellent qualities.'

Aññatarā mārakāyikāti nāmavasena apākaṭā ekā bhummadevatā micchādiṭṭhikā mārapakkhikā mārassanuvattikā “evamayaṃ māradheyyaṃ māravisayaṃ nātikkamissatī”ti cintetvā sabbābharaṇavibhūsitā hutvā attano ānubhāvaṃ dassayamānā abhijjamāne udake pathavītale caṅkamamānā viya āgantvā migalaṇḍikaṃ samaṇakuttakaṃ etadavoca. Sādhu sādhūti sampahaṃsanatthe nipāto; tasmā eva dvivacanaṃ [P 2.0401] kataṃ. Atiṇṇe tāresīti saṃsārato atiṇṇe iminā jīvitāvoropanena tāresi parimocesīti. Ayaṃ kira etissā devatāya bālāya dummedhāya laddhi “ye na matā, te saṃsārato na muttā. Ye matā, te muttā”ti. Tasmā saṃsāramocakamilakkhā viya evaṃladdhikā hutvā tampi tattha niyojentī evamāha. Atha kho migalaṇḍiko samaṇakuttako tāva bhusaṃ uppannavippaṭisāropi taṃ devatāya ānubhāvaṃ disvā “ayaṃ devatā evamāha – addhā iminā atthena evameva bhavitabba”nti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā “lābhā kira me”tiādīni parikittayanto. Vihārena vihāraṃ pariveṇena pariveṇaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadetīti taṃ taṃ vihārañca pariveṇañca upasaṅkamitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā anto pavisitvā bhikkhū evaṃ vadati – “ko atiṇṇo, kaṃ tāremī”ti?

A certain deity belonging to Māra’s host—that is, an obscure, unnamed terrestrial deity of wrong view, who sided with Māra and was a follower of Māra—thought, “Thus, this Migalaṇḍika will not transcend Māra’s domain, the realm of Māra.” Having become adorned with all her ornaments and displaying her own power, she approached as if walking on the surface of the earth and on water that does not part, and spoke this to Migalaṇḍika, the sham monk. `Sādhu sādhu` is a particle used for expressing great delight; therefore, the reduplication was made. `Atiṇṇe tāresi` means: you have ferried across, you have liberated, those not yet crossed over from saṃsāra by this act of depriving them of life. This, it seems, was the view of this foolish, unwise deity: “Those who have not died are not yet freed from saṃsāra. Those who have died are freed.” Therefore, like a savage who liberates from saṃsāra, holding such a view and wishing to urge him in that matter, she spoke thus. Then Migalaṇḍika, the sham monk, although having such intense remorse, upon seeing the power of the deity, came to the conclusion, “This deity spoke thus. Surely, by this deed, it must be just so,” and went about proclaiming the words beginning with, “It is a gain for me, it seems!” The phrase `Vihārena vihāraṃ pariveṇena pariveṇaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeti` means: he approached this and that monastery and this and that monastic cell, opened the door, entered inside, and spoke to the monks thus: “Who has not crossed over? Whom shall I ferry across?”

Hotiyeva [M 2.0008] bhayanti maraṇaṃ paṭicca cittutrāso hoti. Hoti chambhitattanti hadayamaṃsaṃ ādiṃ katvā tasmā sarīracalanaṃ hoti; atibhayena thaddhasarīrattantipi eke, thambhitattañhi chambhitattanti vuccati. Lomahaṃsoti uddhaṃṭhitalomatā, khīṇāsavā pana sattasuññatāya sudiṭṭhattā maraṇakasattameva na passanti, tasmā tesaṃ sabbampetaṃ nāhosīti veditabbaṃ. Ekampi bhikkhuṃ dvepi…pe… saṭṭhimpi bhikkhū ekāhena jīvitā voropesīti evaṃ gaṇanavasena sabbānipi tāni pañca bhikkhusatāni jīvitā voropesi.

Fear indeed arises means that on account of death, terror of the mind arises. There is stupefaction means that, beginning with the heart-flesh, trembling of the body occurs; some also say that due to extreme fear, there is the state of having a stiff body. Indeed, the state of being extremely stiff is called stupefaction. Goosebumps means the state of having hair standing on end. However, the destroyers of the cankers, because of having clearly seen the emptiness of a being, do not see a being that dies. Therefore, it should be understood that all of this—fear, stupefaction, and goosebumps—did not occur for them. He deprived one monk... up to sixty monks of their lives in a single day means that thus, by way of counting, he deprived all those five hundred monks of life.

164. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti tesaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ jīvitakkhayapattabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato ekībhāvato vuṭṭhito jānantopi ajānanto viya kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi. Kiṃ nu kho ānanda tanubhūto viya bhikkhusaṅghoti ānanda ito pubbe bahū bhikkhū ekato upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti, uddesaṃ paripucchaṃ gaṇhanti sajjhāyanti, ekapajjoto viya ārāmo dissati, idāni pana addhamāsamattassa accayena [P 2.0402] tanubhūto viya tanuko mando [V 2.0008] appako viraḷaviraḷo viya jāto bhikkhusaṅgho. Kinnu kho kāraṇaṃ, kiṃ disāsu pakkantā bhikkhūti?

164. Having risen from seclusion means: having known that those five hundred monks had reached the state of the destruction of life, and having risen from that solitude, although knowing, as if not knowing, for the purpose of initiating a conversation, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda. Why, Ānanda, does the Saṅgha of monks seem thinned out? means: “Ānanda, previously, many monks would come to the attendance place together; they would take up the Pāli text for learning and the commentary for repeated questioning, and they would recite. The inside of the monastery would appear as if lit by a single flame. But now, with the passing of about half a month, the Saṅgha of monks has become as if thinned out, as if sparse, few, scanty, and scattered. What, I wonder, is the reason? Have the monks departed to the various directions?” Thus he addressed him.

Athāyasmā ānando kammavipākena tesaṃ jīvitakkhayappattiṃ asallakkhento asubhakammaṭṭhānānuyogapaccayā pana sallakkhento “tathā hi pana bhante bhagavā”tiādiṃ vatvā bhikkhūnaṃ arahattappattiyā aññaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācanto “sādhu bhante bhagavā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – sādhu bhante bhagavā aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhatu, yena bhikkhusaṅgho arahatte patiṭṭhaheyya; mahāsamuddaṃ orohaṇatitthāni viya hi aññānipi dasānussatidasakasiṇacatudhātuvavatthānabrahmavihārānāpānasatippabhedāni bahūni nibbānorohaṇakammaṭṭhānāni santi. Tesu bhagavā bhikkhū samassāsetvā aññataraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhatūti adhippāyo.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, not perceiving that their attainment of the destruction of life was due to the result of kamma, but perceiving it was due to the cause of applying themselves to the meditation subject of foulness, said the words beginning with, “Indeed, venerable sir, O Blessed One,” and, wishing to request another meditation subject for the monks’ attainment of Arahantship, spoke the words beginning with, “It would be good, venerable sir, O Blessed One.” The meaning of this is: “Venerable sir, I implore you. May the Blessed One teach another method by which the Saṅgha of monks may be established in Arahantship. For, like the landing places for descending into the great ocean, there are many other meditation subjects that are descents to Nibbāna, such as the ten recollections, the ten kasiṇas, the analysis of the four elements, the divine abidings, and the varieties of mindfulness of breathing. Among those, may the Blessed One, having comforted the monks, teach one or another meditation subject.” This was the Venerable Ānanda’s intention.

Atha bhagavā tathā kātukāmo theraṃ uyyojento “tenahānandā”tiādimāha. Tattha vesāliṃ upanissāyāti vesāliṃ upanissāya samantā gāvutepi addhayojanepi yāvatikā bhikkhū viharanti[M 2.0009], te sabbe sannipātehīti attho. Te sabbe upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ sannipātetvāti attanā gantuṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ sayaṃ gantvā aññattha daharabhikkhū pahiṇitvā muhutteneva anavasese bhikkhū upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ samūhaṃ katvā. Yassa dāni bhante bhagavā kālaṃ maññatīti ettha ayamadhippāyo – bhagavā bhikkhusaṅgho sannipatito esa kālo bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathaṃ kātuṃ, anusāsaniṃ dātuṃ, idāni yassa tumhe kālaṃ jānātha, taṃ kattabbanti.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to do so and urging the Elder, spoke the words beginning with, “Well then, Ānanda.” Therein, relying on Vesālī means: “Relying on Vesālī as the alms-round resort, assemble all the monks, however many there are, who are dwelling all around within a gāvuta or half a yojana.” Having assembled all of them in the attendance hall means: having gone himself to places suitable for him to go and having sent junior monks to other places, in just a moment he gathered the monks without remainder into a group in the attendance hall. Herein, in the passage “Now, venerable sir, it is for the Blessed One to know the time,” this is the intention: “O Blessed One, the Saṅgha of monks is assembled. This is the time to give a Dhamma talk to the monks, to give instruction. Now, for whatever action you know it is time, that should be done.”

Ānāpānassatisamādhikathā

The Discourse on the Concentration of Mindfulness of Breathing

165. Atha kho bhagavā…pe… bhikkhū āmantesi – ayampi kho bhikkhaveti āmantetvā ca pana bhikkhūnaṃ arahattappattiyā pubbe ācikkhitaasubhakammaṭṭhānato aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ [P 2.0403] ācikkhanto “ānāpānassatisamādhī”ti āha.

165. Then the Blessed One… addressed the bhikkhus, saying, “Bhikkhus, this too...” And having addressed them, wishing to teach the bhikkhus another method for the attainment of Arahantship, different from the meditation subject of foulness previously taught, he said, “The concentration of mindfulness of breathing.”

Idāni yasmā bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ santapaṇītakammaṭṭhānadassanatthameva ayaṃ pāḷi vuttā, tasmā aparihāpetvā atthayojanākkamaṃ ettha vaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Tatra “ayampi kho bhikkhave”ti imassa tāva padassa ayaṃ yojanā – bhikkhave na kevalaṃ asubhabhāvanāyeva kilesappahānāya saṃvattati, apica ayampi kho ānāpānassatisamādhi…pe… vūpasametīti.

Now, since this Pāḷi was spoken by the Blessed One for the sole purpose of showing the bhikkhus a peaceful and sublime meditation subject, therefore, I will provide the explanation here without omitting the sequence of the application of the meaning. Therein, this is the application of the phrase, “Bhikkhus, this too...”: “Bhikkhus, it is not that only the development of foulness leads to the abandoning of defilements, but indeed, this concentration of mindfulness of breathing also... pacifies.”

Ayaṃ [V 2.0009] panettha atthavaṇṇanā – ānāpānassatīti assāsapassāsapariggāhikā sati. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

Herein is the explanation of the meaning: mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) is the mindfulness that comprehends the out-breath and the in-breath. For this was said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Ānanti assāso, no passāso. Apānanti passāso, no assāso. Assāsavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ sati, passāsavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ sati. Yo assasati tassupaṭṭhāti, yo passasati tassupaṭṭhātī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.160).

“‘Āna’ (breathing out) is the out-breath (assāsa), not the in-breath (passāsa). ‘Apāna’ (breathing in) is the in-breath (passāsa), not the out-breath (assāsa). The establishment [of mind] by way of the out-breath is mindfulness; the establishment [of mind] by way of the in-breath is mindfulness. For one who breathes out, it is present; for one who breathes in, it is present.”

Samādhīti tāya ānāpānapariggāhikāya satiyā saddhiṃ uppannā cittekaggatā; samādhisīsena cāyaṃ desanā, na satisīsena. Tasmā ānāpānassatiyā yutto samādhi ānāpānassatisamādhi, ānāpānassatiyaṃ vā samādhi ānāpānassatisamādhīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Bhāvitoti uppādito vaḍḍhito ca. Bahulīkatoti punappunaṃ [M 2.0010] kato. Santo ceva paṇīto cāti santo ceva paṇīto ceva, ubhayattha evasaddena niyamo veditabbo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ayañhi yathā asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ kevalaṃ paṭivedhavasena santañca paṇītañca oḷārikārammaṇattā pana paṭikūlārammaṇattā ca ārammaṇavasena neva santaṃ na paṇītaṃ, na evaṃ kenaci pariyāyena asanto vā appaṇīto vā, apica kho ārammaṇasantatāyapi santo vūpasanto nibbuto paṭivedhasaṅkhātaaṅgasantatāyapi ārammaṇappaṇītatāyapi paṇīto atittikaro aṅgappaṇītatāyapīti. Tena vuttaṃ – “santo ceva paṇīto cā”ti.

Concentration (samādhi) is the one-pointedness of mind that arises together with that mindfulness which comprehends the breath. This discourse proceeds with concentration as its head, not mindfulness. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: concentration connected with mindfulness of breathing is ānāpānassatisamādhi; or, concentration that arises in mindfulness of breathing is ānāpānassatisamādhi. ‘Developed’ (bhāvito) means produced and increased. ‘Made much of’ (bahulīkato) means done again and again. ‘Peaceful and sublime’ (santo ceva paṇīto ca): in both ‘peaceful indeed’ and ‘sublime indeed,’ the determination by the word ‘eva’ should be understood. What is meant? Just as the meditation subject of foulness is peaceful and sublime only by way of penetration, but by way of its object—due to the object being gross and repulsive—it is neither peaceful nor sublime; this [concentration of mindfulness of breathing] is not in any way unpeaceful or unsublime. Rather, it is peaceful, calmed, and quenched due to the peacefulness of its object and also due to the peacefulness of its factor known as penetration. It is sublime and does not cause satiety due to the sublimity of its object and also due to the sublimity of its factors. Therefore, it was said: ‘peaceful and sublime.’

Asecanako ca sukho ca vihāroti ettha pana nāssa secananti asecanako anāsittako abbokiṇṇo [P 2.0404] pāṭekko āveṇiko, natthettha parikammena vā upacārena vā santatā ādimanasikārato pabhuti attano sabhāveneva santo ca paṇīto cāti attho. Keci pana asecanakoti anāsittako ojavanto sabhāveneva madhuroti vadanti. Evamayaṃ asecanako ca appitappitakkhaṇe kāyikacetasikasukhappaṭilābhāya saṃvattanato sukho ca vihāroti veditabbo.

Regarding ‘intrinsically delightful and a pleasant abiding’ (asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro): Herein, ‘there is no sprinkling for it’ (nāssa secanaṃ), thus it is asecanako—unsprinkled (anāsittako), unmixed (abbokiṇṇo), separate (pāṭekko), unique (āveṇiko). There is no peacefulness herein by way of preliminary work or access [concentration]; from the initial application of mind onwards, it is peaceful and sublime by its own nature. This is the meaning. Some, however, say asecanako means unsprinkled, nutritious, and naturally sweet. Thus, this should be understood as asecanako and as a pleasant abiding (sukho vihāro) because it leads to the attainment of bodily and mental happiness at every moment of absorption.

Uppannuppanneti avikkhambhite avikkhambhite. Pāpaketi lāmake. Akusale dhammeti akosallasambhūte dhamme. Ṭhānaso antaradhāpetīti khaṇeneva antaradhāpeti vikkhambheti. Vūpasametīti suṭṭhu upasameti, nibbedhabhāgiyattā vā anupubbena ariyamaggavuḍḍhippato samucchindati paṭippassambhetītipi attho.

‘Whatever have arisen’ (uppannuppanne): those that are unsuppressed, unsuppressed. ‘Evil’ (pāpake): base. ‘Unwholesome states’ (akusale dhamme): states arisen from non-skill. ‘It makes them disappear on the spot’ (ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti): it makes them disappear at that very moment, it suppresses them. ‘It pacifies’ (vūpasameti): it pacifies them well; or, because it partakes of penetration, having gradually reached the growth of the noble path, it eradicates and calms them. This is also the meaning.

Seyyathāpīti [V 2.0010] opammanidassanametaṃ. Gimhānaṃ pacchime māseti āsāḷhamāse. Ūhataṃ rajojallanti addhamāse vātātapasukkhāya gomahiṃsādipādappahārasambhinnāya pathaviyā uddhaṃ hataṃ ūhataṃ ākāse samuṭṭhitaṃ rajañca reṇuñca. Mahā akālameghoti sabbaṃ nabhaṃ ajjhottharitvā uṭṭhito āsāḷhajuṇhapakkhe sakalaṃ addhamāsaṃ vassanakamegho. So hi asampatte vassakāle uppannattā akālameghoti idhādhippeto. Ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasametīti khaṇeneva [M 2.0011] adassanaṃ neti, pathaviyaṃ sannisīdāpeti. Evameva khoti opammasampaṭipādanametaṃ. Tato paraṃ vuttanayameva.

“Just as” (seyyathāpi): this indicates a simile. “In the last month of the hot season” (gimhānaṃ pacchime māse): in the month of Āsāḷha. “Stirred up dust and dirt” (ūhataṃ rajojallaṃ): the fine dust (raja) and the coarse dirt (reṇu) raised up and arisen in the sky from the earth that, for eight months, was dried by wind and sun and broken up by the striking of the feet of cattle, buffalo, and so on. “A great untimely cloud” (mahā akālamegho): a rain cloud that arises in the waxing fortnight of Āsāḷha, having covered the entire sky, and rains for a whole half-month. It is considered an “untimely cloud” here because it has arisen before the rainy season has arrived. “It makes them disappear on the spot and pacifies them” (ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasameti): in a single moment, it leads them to where they cannot be seen; it makes them settle down on the ground. “Even so” (evameva kho): this connects the simile with its subject. What follows is in the manner already stated.

Idāni kathaṃ bhāvito ca bhikkhave ānāpānassatisamādhīti ettha kathanti ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanaṃ nānappakārato vitthāretukamyatāpucchā. Bhāvito ca bhikkhave ānāpānassatisamādhīti nānappakārato vitthāretukamyatāya puṭṭhadhammanidassanaṃ[P 2.0405]. Esa nayo dutiyapadepi. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave kenapakārena kenākārena kena vidhinā bhāvito ānāpānassatisamādhi kenapakārena bahulīkato santo ceva…pe… vūpasametīti.

Now, regarding the phrase, “And how, bhikkhus, is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing developed?”: Here, “how” (kathaṃ) is a question asked from the desire to elaborate in various ways on the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing. The phrase “is developed, bhikkhus, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing” indicates the teaching that was asked about in response to the desire to elaborate. This same method applies to the second phrase. Herein is the summary meaning: “Bhikkhus, in what way, in what manner, by what method is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing developed, and in what way is it made much of, so that being peaceful… it pacifies?”

Idāni tamatthaṃ vitthārento “idha bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha idha bhikkhave bhikkhūti bhikkhave imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhettha idhasaddo sabbappakāraānāpānassatisamādhinibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139). Tena vuttaṃ – “imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti.

Now, elaborating on that meaning, he said the passage beginning, “Here, bhikkhus…” Therein, “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu” means “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu in this Dispensation.” For here the word “here” (idha) clarifies the Dispensation that is the support for a person who brings into being all kinds of concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and it denies that other dispensations have that status. For it was said: “Here alone, bhikkhus, is there an ascetic… other doctrines are devoid of ascetics…” Therefore it was said, “a bhikkhu in this Dispensation.”

Araññagato vā…pe… suññāgāragato vāti idamassa ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu anuvisaṭaṃ cittaṃ ānāpānassatisamādhiārammaṇaṃ abhiruhituṃ na icchati. Kūṭagoṇayuttaratho viya uppathameva dhāvati. Tasmā seyyathāpi nāma gopo kūṭadhenuyā sabbaṃ khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhitaṃ kūṭavacchaṃ dametukāmo dhenuto apanetvā ekamante mahantaṃ thambhaṃ nikhaṇitvā tattha yottena bandheyya. Athassa so vaccho ito cito ca vipphanditvā palāyituṃ asakkonto tameva thambhaṃ upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā; evameva imināpi bhikkhunā dīgharattaṃ rūpārammaṇādirasapānavaḍḍhitaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ dametukāmena rūpādiārammaṇato apanetvā araññaṃ vā…pe… suññāgāraṃ vā pavesetvā tattha assāsapassāsathambhe satiyottena bandhitabbaṃ. Evamassa taṃ cittaṃ ito cito ca vipphanditvāpi pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇaṃ alabhamānaṃ [V 2.0011] satiyottaṃ chinditvā palāyituṃ asakkontaṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ upacārappanāvasena upanisīdati ceva upanipajjati ca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

“Whether he has gone to the forest… or to an empty dwelling”—this illustrates the taking up of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. For this bhikkhu’s mind, long diffused among objects such as forms, does not wish to ascend to the object of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. Like a chariot yoked to an unruly ox, it runs only on the wrong path. Therefore, just as a cowherd wishing to tame an unruly calf—one that has grown up by drinking all the milk of an unruly cow—would take it away from the cow, drive a large post into the ground in a secluded spot, and tie it there with a rope; then that calf, struggling this way and that and unable to run away, would sit down or lie down near that very post. Even so, this bhikkhu, wishing to tame his corrupt mind that has for a long time been nurtured by drinking the flavor of objects such as forms, should take it away from objects such as forms and lead it into the forest… or an empty dwelling. There, he should bind it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of in-and-out breathing. Thus, his mind, though struggling this way and that, unable to obtain its formerly frequented object and unable to break the rope of mindfulness and run away, comes to sit down and lie down by that very object through the power of access and absorption concentration. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yathā [P 2.0406][M 2.0012] thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ dammaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha”nti. (visuddhi. 1.217; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.374; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.107; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163);

“Just as a man here wishing to tame a calf would tie it to a post; even so should one firmly bind one’s own mind with mindfulness to the object.”

Evamassetaṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanānurūpaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “idamassa ānāpānassatisamaādhibhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpana”nti.

Thus, this dwelling of his is suitable for development. Therefore, it was said: “This illustrates for him the taking up of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.”

Atha vā yasmā idaṃ kammaṭṭhānappabhede muddhabhūtaṃ sabbaññubuddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ itthipurisahatthiassādisaddasamākulaṃ gāmantaṃ apariccajitvā na sukaraṃ sampādetuṃ, saddakaṇṭakattā jhānassa. Agāmake pana araññe sukaraṃ yogāvacarena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva ca pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ sampāpuṇituṃ, tasmāssa anurūpaṃsenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha.

Alternatively, because this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing—which is the pinnacle among the various kinds of meditation subjects and is the proximate cause for the attainment of special qualities and for a pleasant abiding in this very life for Supremely Enlightened Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—is not easy to accomplish without abandoning a village vicinity crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so on, for sound is a thorn to jhāna. But in a forest without a village, it is easy for a yogī, having taken up this meditation subject, having produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, and having made that very jhāna the basis, to contemplate the formations and fully attain the supreme fruit, Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing a dwelling suitable for him, said, “gone to the forest,” and so forth.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya hi bhagavā, so yathā vatthuvijjācariyo nagarabhūmiṃ passitvā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā “ettha nagaraṃ māpethā”ti upadisati, sotthinā ca nagare niṭṭhite rājakulato mahāsakkāraṃ labhati; evameva yogāvacarassa anurūpasenāsanaṃ upaparikkhitvā ettha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitabbanti upadisati. Tato tattha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuttena yoginā kamena arahatte patte “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā”ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhati. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu “dīpisadiso”ti vuccati. Yathā hi mahādīpirājā araññe tiṇagahanaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pabbatagahanaṃ vā nissāya [P 2.0407] nilīyitvā vanamahiṃsagokaṇṇasūkarādayo mige gaṇhāti; evamevāyaṃ araññādīsu kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto bhikkhu yathākkamena sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiarahattamagge ceva ariyaphalañca gaṇhātīti veditabbo. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Indeed, the Blessed One is like a master of the science of sites. Just as a master of the science of sites, having seen and thoroughly examined a site for a city, instructs, “Construct the city here,” and when the city is completed safely, he receives great honor from the royal family; even so, the Blessed One, having examined a suitable dwelling for a yogī, instructs, “Here the meditation subject should be practiced.” Thereupon, when the yogī who has practiced the meditation subject there gradually attains Arahantship, the Blessed One receives great honor, as the yogī thinks, “Oh, that Blessed One is truly a Perfectly Enlightened One!” This monk, however, is said to be “like a leopard.” For just as a great leopard king, relying on a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, or a thicket of mountains, lies hidden and seizes animals such as wild buffalo, gokaṇṇa deer, and boars; even so, it should be understood that this monk, practicing the meditation subject in forests and so forth, seizes in due order the paths of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and Arahantship, as well as the noble fruits. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yathāpi [V 2.0012] dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhatī mige;

Tathevāyaṃ buddhaputto, yuttayogo vipassako;

Araññaṃ pavisitvāna, gaṇhāti phalamuttama”nti. (mi. pa. 6.1.5);

“Just as a leopard, lying hidden, seizes animals; so too this son of the Buddha, devoted to the practice and discerning, having entered the forest, seizes the supreme fruit.”

Tenassa parakkamajavayoggabhūmiṃ araññasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha.

Therefore, the Blessed One, showing the forest dwelling as the ground suitable for the momentum of his striving, said, “gone to the forest,” and so forth.

Tattha [M 2.0013] araññagato vāti araññanti “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) ca “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 653) ca evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇesu araññesu anurūpaṃ yaṃkiñci pavivekasukhaṃ araññaṃ gato. Rukkhamūlagato vāti rukkhasamīpaṃ gato. Suññāgāragato vāti suññaṃ vivittokāsaṃ gato. Ettha ca ṭhapetvā araññañca rukkhamūlañca avasesasattavidhasenāsanagatopi suññāgāragatoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Evamassa ututtayānukūlaṃ dhātucariyānukūlañca ānāpānassatibhāvanānurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ upadisitvā alīnānuddhaccapakkhikaṃ santamiriyāpathaṃ upadisanto “nisīdatī”ti āha. Athassa nisajjāya daḷhabhāvaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ pavattanasukhataṃ ārammaṇapariggahūpāyañca dassento “pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā”tiādimāha.

Therein, “gone to the forest” means having gone to any forest that affords the pleasure of seclusion, among the forests with the characteristics thus stated: “Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all that is forest,” and “A forest dwelling is a residence that is at a minimum five hundred bow-lengths away.” “Gone to the root of a tree” means having gone near a tree. “Gone to an empty dwelling” means having gone to an empty, secluded place. And here, setting aside the forest and the root of a tree, it is also proper to say “gone to an empty dwelling” of one who has gone to the remaining seven kinds of dwellings. Thus, having instructed him on a dwelling that is suitable for the three seasons, suitable for his physical constitution and temperament, and suitable for the development of mindfulness of breathing, and teaching a peaceful posture that is on the side of non-sluggishness and non-restlessness, He said, “he sits down.” Then, showing the firmness of his sitting, the ease of occurrence of the in-breaths and out-breaths, and the method for grasping the object, He said, “having folded his legs crosswise,” and so forth.

Tattha pallaṅkanti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Ābhujitvāti ābandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimaṃ sarīraṃ [P 2.0408] ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā, aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na paṇamanti. Athassa yā tesaṃ paṇamanappaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā na uppajjanti. Tāsu anuppajjamānāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati. Vuḍḍhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati.

Therein, ‘pallaṅka’ means a cross-legged sitting posture with the thighs bound all around. ‘Ābhujitvā’ means having bound them. ‘Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya’ means setting the upper body straight, making the eighteen vertebrae touch end to end. For one seated thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then, for him, the feelings that would arise moment by moment due to their bending do not arise. When those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed. The meditation subject does not fall away. It attains growth and prosperity.

Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā. Atha vā “parī”ti pariggahaṭṭho; “mukha”nti niyyānaṭṭho; “satī”ti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho; tena vuccati – “parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti. Evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.164-165) vuttanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepo – “pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ katvā”ti. So satova assasatīti so bhikkhu evaṃ nisīditvā evañca satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā taṃ satiṃ avijahanto satoeva assasati, sato passasati, satokārī hotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Having established mindfulness in front’ means having established mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject. Alternatively, ‘pari’ has the meaning of encompassing; ‘mukha’ has the meaning of emergence; ‘sati’ has the meaning of establishment. Therefore it is said: ‘having established mindfulness in front.’ Thus, the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Therein, this is the summary: ‘having made mindfulness that encompasses and leads to emergence.’ ‘He mindfully breathes out’ means that this monk, having sat down thus and having established mindfulness thus, not abandoning that mindfulness, mindfully breathes out, mindfully breathes in; he becomes one who acts with mindfulness—this is what is said.

Idāni [V 2.0013] yehākārehi satokārī hoti, te dassento “dīghaṃ vā assasanto”tiādimāha. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ – “so satova assasati, sato passasatī”ti etasseva vibhaṅge –

Now, showing the modes by which one acts with mindfulness, He said, ‘Breathing out long,’ and so on. For this was stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, in the analysis of this very phrase, ‘Mindful, he breathes out; mindful, he breathes in’:

“Bāttiṃsāya [M 2.0014] ākārehi satokārī hoti. Dīghaṃ assāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena satokārī hoti. Dīghaṃ passāsavasena…pe… paṭinissaggānupassī assāsavasena paṭinissaggānupassī passāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena satokārī hotī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.165).

‘He acts with mindfulness in thirty-two modes. For one who distinctly knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of long out-breathing, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, he acts with mindfulness. By means of long in-breathing… and so on… for one who distinctly knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of contemplating relinquishment while out-breathing, and by means of contemplating relinquishment while in-breathing, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, he acts with mindfulness.’

Tattha dīghaṃ vā assasantoti dīghaṃ vā assāsaṃ pavattento. “Assāso”ti bahi nikkhamanavāto. “Passāso”ti anto pavisanavāto. Suttantaṭṭhakathāsu pana uppaṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ.

Therein, ‘breathing out long’ means producing a long out-breath. ‘Out-breath’ is the outgoing wind. ‘In-breath’ is the incoming wind. In the Sutta commentaries, however, it is given in the reverse order.

Tattha sabbesampi [P 2.0409] gabbhaseyyakānaṃ mātukucchito nikkhamanakāle paṭhamaṃ abbhantaravāto bahi nikkhamati. Pacchā bāhiravāto sukhumaṃ rajaṃ gahetvā abbhantaraṃ pavisanto tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyati. Evaṃ tāva assāsapassāsā veditabbā. Yā pana tesaṃ dīgharassatā, sā addhānavasena veditabbā. Yathā hi okāsaddhānaṃ pharitvā ṭhitaṃ udakaṃ vā vālikā vā “dīghamudakaṃ dīghā vālikā, rassamudakaṃ rassā vālikā”ti vuccati. Evaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi assāsapassāsā hatthisarīre ahisarīre ca tesaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dīghaṃ addhānaṃ saṇikaṃ pūretvā saṇikameva nikkhamanti, tasmā “dīghā”ti vuccanti. Sunakhasasādīnaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ rassaṃ addhānaṃ sīghaṃ pūretvā sīghameva nikkhamanti, tasmā “rassā”ti vuccanti. Manussesu pana keci hatthiahiādayo viya kāladdhānavasena dīghaṃ assasanti ca passasanti ca. Keci sunakhasasādayo viya rassaṃ. Tasmā tesaṃ kālavasena dīghamaddhānaṃ nikkhamantā ca pavisantā ca te dīghā. Ittaramaddhānaṃ nikkhamantā ca pavisantā ca “rassā”ti veditabbā. Tatrāyaṃ bhikkhu navahākārehi dīghaṃ assasanto ca passasanto ca “dīghaṃ assasāmi passasāmī”ti pajānāti. Evaṃ pajānato cassa ekenākārena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā sampajjatīti veditabbā. Yathāha paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

Therein, for all beings lying in the womb, at the time of emerging from the mother's womb, first the internal wind comes out. Afterwards, the external wind, taking up fine dust, enters inside and, striking the palate, ceases. Thus, first, the out-breaths and in-breaths should be understood. As for their length or shortness, that should be understood by way of duration. For just as water or sand spread over a certain area is called ‘long water’ or ‘long sand,’ ‘short water’ or ‘short sand,’ so too, even the very fine out-breaths and in-breaths in the bodies of elephants and snakes, by slowly filling the long duration commensurate with their physical existence and slowly emerging, are therefore called ‘long.’ In dogs, rabbits, and so on, by quickly filling the short duration commensurate with their physical existence and quickly emerging, they are therefore called ‘short.’ Among humans, some, like elephants, snakes, and so on, breathe out and in long by way of time-duration. Some, like dogs, rabbits, and so on, breathe short. Therefore, for them, those breaths that emerge and enter over a long duration of time are ‘long.’ Those that emerge and enter over a shorter duration should be understood as ‘short.’ Therein, this monk, breathing out and in long in nine ways, understands, ‘I breathe out long, I breathe in long.’ For one who understands thus, it should be understood that the development of the foundation of mindfulness which is the contemplation of the body is accomplished in one way. As it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Kathaṃ dīghaṃ assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti [V 2.0014] pajānāti? Dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte [M 2.0015] assasati, dīghaṃ passāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte passasati, dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatipi passasatipi. Dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatopi passasatopi chando [P 2.0410] uppajjati; chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasati, chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ passāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte passasati, chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatipi passasatipi. Chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatopi passasatopi pāmojjaṃ uppajjati; pāmojjavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasati, pāmojjavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ passāsaṃ…pe… dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatipi passasatipi. Pāmojjavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatopi passasatopi dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā cittaṃ vivattati, upekkhā saṇṭhāti. Imehi navahi ākārehi dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā kāyo; upaṭṭhānaṃ sati; anupassanā ñāṇaṃ; kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ, no sati; sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati ca. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena taṃ kāyaṃ anupassati. Tena vuccati – “kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.166).

How, when breathing out long, does one know, 'I am breathing out long'? How, when breathing in long, does one know, 'I am breathing in long'? One breathes out a long out-breath in a long period of time; one breathes in a long in-breath in a long period of time; one breathes out and breathes in a long out-breath and in-breath in a long period of time. When one breathes out and breathes in a long out-breath and in-breath in a long period of time, zeal arises. By the power of zeal, one breathes out a more subtle long out-breath in a long period of time; by the power of zeal, one breathes in a more subtle long in-breath in a long period of time; by the power of zeal, one breathes out and breathes in a more subtle long out-breath and in-breath in a long period of time. When, by the power of zeal, one breathes out and breathes in a more subtle long out-breath and in-breath in a long period of time, joy arises. By the power of joy, one breathes out a more subtle long out-breath in a long period of time; by the power of joy, one breathes in a more subtle long in-breath… and so on… one breathes out and breathes in a long out-breath and in-breath in a long period of time. When, by the power of joy, one breathes out and breathes in a more subtle long out-breath and in-breath in a long period of time, the mind turns away from the long out-breath and in-breath, and equanimity is established. By these nine aspects, the long out-breaths and in-breaths are the body; the establishment is mindfulness; the contemplation is knowledge. The body is the establishment, not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness. With that mindfulness and with that knowledge, one contemplates that body. Therefore, it is said: 'The development of the establishment of mindfulness by way of contemplating the body in the body'.

Eseva nayo rassapadepi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – “yathā ettha ‘dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte’ti vuttaṃ; evamidha ‘rassaṃ assāsaṃ ittarasaṅkhāte assasatī”ti āgataṃ. Tasmā tassa vasena yāva “tena vuccati kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā”ti tāva yojetabbaṃ. Evamayaṃ addhānavasena ittaravasena ca imehākārehi assāsapassāse pajānanto dīghaṃ vā assasanto “dīghaṃ assasāmī”ti pajānāti…pe… rassaṃ vā passasanto “rassaṃ passasāmī”ti pajānātīti veditabbo.

This same method applies also to the section on the short [breath]. This, however, is the distinction: just as it is said here, 'a long out-breath in a long period of time,' so it has come [in the Paṭisambhidāmagga] here, 'one breathes out a short out-breath in a short period of time.' Therefore, by means of that [section on the short breath], it should be applied up to 'Therefore, it is said: "The development of the establishment of mindfulness by way of contemplating the body in the body".' Thus, it should be understood that this bhikkhu, knowing the out-breaths and in-breaths by these aspects—by way of a long period and by way of a short period—when breathing out long, knows, 'I am breathing out long,'… and so on… or when breathing in short, knows, 'I am breathing in short'.

Evaṃ [M 2.0016] pajānato cassa –

And for that bhikkhu who knows thus:

“Dīgho rasso ca assāso;

Passāsopi ca tādiso;

Cattāro vaṇṇā vattanti;

Nāsikaggeva bhikkhuno”ti. (visuddhi. 1.219; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163);

The out-breath is long and short; and the in-breath is likewise. Four aspects occur for the bhikkhu at the very tip of the nose.

Sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī [P 2.0411][V 2.0015] assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatīti sakalassa assāsakāyassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ viditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto “assasissāmī”ti sikkhati. Sakalassa passāsakāyassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ viditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto “passasissāmī”ti sikkhati. Evaṃ viditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto ñāṇasampayuttacittena assasati ceva passasati ca; tasmā “assasissāmi passasissāmī”ti sikkhatīti vuccati. Ekassa hi bhikkhuno cuṇṇavicuṇṇavisaṭe assāsakāye passāsakāye vā ādi pākaṭo hoti, na majjhapariyosānaṃ. So ādimeva pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, majjhapariyosāne kilamati. Ekassa majjhaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, na ādipariyosānaṃ. So majjhameva pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, ādipariyosāne kilamati. Ekassa pariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, na ādimajjhaṃ. So pariyosānaṃyeva pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, ādimajjhe kilamati. Ekassa sabbampi pākaṭaṃ hoti, so sabbampi pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, na katthaci kilamati. Tādisena bhavitabbanti dassento āha – “sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti.

He trains, 'I shall breathe out… and so on… I shall breathe in, experiencing the whole body,' means: making known, making manifest the beginning, middle, and end of the entire out-breath body, he trains, 'I shall breathe out.' Making known, making manifest the beginning, middle, and end of the entire in-breath body, he trains, 'I shall breathe in.' Thus, making it known, making it manifest, he breathes out and breathes in with a mind associated with knowledge. Therefore, it is said, 'He trains, “I shall breathe out, I shall breathe in.”' For one bhikkhu, in the out-breath body or in-breath body that is scattered as if into fine dust, the beginning is manifest, but not the middle and end. He is able to grasp only the beginning; he becomes weary in the middle and end. For another, the middle is manifest, but not the beginning and end. He is able to grasp only the middle; he becomes weary in the beginning and end. For another, the end is manifest, but not the beginning and middle. He is able to grasp only the end; he becomes weary in the beginning and middle. For yet another, the whole—the beginning, middle, and end—is manifest. He is able to grasp the whole and does not become weary at any point. Showing that one should become like such a person, the Blessed One said: 'He trains, “I shall breathe out… and so on… I shall breathe in, experiencing the whole body.”'

Tattha sikkhatīti evaṃ ghaṭati vāyamati. Yo vā tathābhūtassa saṃvaro; ayamettha adhisīlasikkhā. Yo tathābhūtassa samādhi; ayaṃ adhicittasikkhā. Yā tathābhūtassa paññā; ayaṃ adhipaññāsikkhāti. Imā tisso sikkhāyo tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tāya satiyā tena manasikārena sikkhati āsevati bhāveti bahulīkarotīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha yasmā purimanaye kevalaṃ assasitabbaṃ passasitabbameva ca, na aññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ; ito paṭṭhāya pana ñāṇuppādanādīsu yogo karaṇīyo. Tasmā tattha “assasāmīti pajānāti passasāmīti pajānāti”cceva vattamānakālavasena pāḷiṃ vatvā ito paṭṭhāya kattabbassa ñāṇuppādanādino ākārassa dassanatthaṃ “sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī”tiādinā [M 2.0017] nayena anāgatavacanavasena pāḷi āropitāti veditabbā.

Therein, 'he trains' means he strives, he exerts himself. Or, whatever restraint there is for one who is thus, this here is the training in higher virtue. Whatever concentration there is for one who is thus, this is the training in higher mind. Whatever wisdom there is for one who is thus, this is the training in higher wisdom. Thus, the meaning here should be understood as: with that mindfulness, with that attention, one trains in these three trainings in that object, resorts to them, develops them, and makes much of them. Therein, since in the former method merely breathing out and breathing in are to be done, and nothing else is to be done, but from this point onward exertion in the arising of knowledge and so on should be undertaken; therefore, having stated the Pāli in the present tense there, as 'he knows, “I am breathing out,” he knows, “I am breathing in,”' from this point onward, to show the mode of what is to be done, such as the arising of knowledge, the Pāli was set forth by way of the future tense with the method beginning, 'I shall breathe out, experiencing the whole body.' This should be understood.

Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatīti oḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento paṭippassambhento nirodhento vūpasamento [P 2.0412] assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati.

He trains, 'I shall breathe out… and so on… I shall breathe in, calming the bodily formation,' means: calming, tranquilizing, causing to cease, and pacifying the gross bodily formation, he trains, 'I shall breathe out, I shall breathe in.'

Tatrevaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā ca passaddhi ca veditabbā. Imassa hi bhikkhuno pubbe apariggahitakāle kāyo ca cittañca sadarathā honti. Oḷārikānaṃ kāyacittānaṃ oḷārikatte [V 2.0016] avūpasante assāsapassāsāpi oḷārikā honti, balavatarā hutvā pavattanti, nāsikā nappahoti, mukhena assasantopi passasantopi tiṭṭhati. Yadā panassa kāyopi cittampi pariggahitā honti, tadā te santā honti vūpasantā. Tesu vūpasantesu assāsapassāsā sukhumā hutvā pavattanti, “atthi nu kho natthī”ti vicetabbākārappattā honti. Seyyathāpi purisassa dhāvitvā pabbatā vā orohitvā mahābhāraṃ vā sīsato oropetvā ṭhitassa oḷārikā assāsapassāsā honti, nāsikā nappahoti, mukhena assasantopi passasantopi tiṭṭhati. Yadā panesa taṃ parissamaṃ vinodetvā nhatvā ca pivitvā ca allasāṭakaṃ hadaye katvā sītāya chāyāya nipanno hoti, athassa te assāsapassāsā sukhumā honti, “atthi nu kho natthī”ti vicetabbākārappattā. Evameva imassa bhikkhuno pubbe apariggahitakāle kāyo ca…pe… vicetabbākārappattā honti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hissa pubbe apariggahitakāle “oḷārikoḷārike kāyasaṅkhāre passambhemī”ti ābhogasamannāhāramanasikārapaccavekkhaṇā natthi, pariggahitakāle pana atthi. Tenassa apariggahitakālato pariggahitakāle kāyasaṅkhāro sukhumo hoti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, in this way, the grossness and subtlety, and the tranquility, should be understood. Indeed, for this monk, previously, at the time of non-comprehension, both body and mind are agitated. When the gross body and mind are not calmed, due to their grossness, the in-breaths and out-breaths are also gross; they occur having become stronger, the nose is not sufficient, and he remains breathing in and out through the mouth. But when his body and mind are comprehended, then those breaths become peaceful and calmed. When they are calmed, the in-breaths and out-breaths occur having become subtle, and they reach a state where they must be investigated thus: 'Do they exist, or do they not exist?' It is just as when a man has run, or descended from a mountain, or set down a great burden from his head and is standing, his in-breaths and out-breaths are gross, the nose is not sufficient, and he remains breathing in and out through the mouth. But when he has dispelled that fatigue, has bathed and drunk, has placed a wet cloth on his chest, and is lying down in the cool shade, then his in-breaths and out-breaths become subtle, reaching a state where they must be investigated thus: 'Do they exist, or do they not exist?' In the same way, for this monk, previously, at the time of non-comprehension, the body... and so on... they reach a state where they must be investigated. What is the reason for that? Because for him, previously, at the time of non-comprehension, there is no turning the mind towards, application of mind, attention, or reviewing with the thought, 'I will calm the gross bodily formations.' But at the time of comprehension, there is. Therefore, for him, the bodily formation at the time of comprehension is more subtle than at the time of non-comprehension. Hence the ancients said:

“Sāraddhe kāye citte ca, adhimattaṃ pavattati;

Asāraddhamhi kāyamhi, sukhumaṃ sampavattatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.220; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163);

“When the body and mind are agitated, the bodily formation occurs in excess; when the body and mind are unagitated, it proceeds subtly.”

Pariggahepi oḷāriko, paṭhamajjhānūpacāre sukhumo; tasmimpi oḷāriko paṭhamajjhāne sukhumo. Paṭhamajjhāne ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre ca oḷāriko, dutiyajjhāne sukhumo. Dutiyajjhāne ca tatiyajjhānūpacāre ca [M 2.0018] oḷāriko, tatiyajjhāne sukhumo. Tatiyajjhāne ca catutthajjhānūpacāre ca oḷāriko, catutthajjhāne atisukhumo appavattimeva pāpuṇāti. Idaṃ tāva dīghabhāṇakasaṃyuttabhāṇakānaṃ [P 2.0413] mataṃ.

Even at the time of comprehension, it is gross; in the access to the first jhāna, it is subtle. Even in that access, it is gross; in the first jhāna, it is subtle. In the first jhāna and in the access to the second jhāna, it is gross; in the second jhāna, it is subtle. In the second jhāna and in the access to the third jhāna, it is gross; in the third jhāna, it is subtle. In the third jhāna and in the access to the fourth jhāna, it is gross; in the fourth jhāna, it is extremely subtle and reaches non-occurrence itself. This, for now, is the opinion of the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya and the reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Majjhimabhāṇakā pana “paṭhamajjhāne oḷāriko, dutiyajjhānūpacāre sukhumo”ti evaṃ heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato uparūparijjhānūpacārepi sukhumataraṃ icchanti. Sabbesaṃyeva pana matena apariggahitakāle pavattakāyasaṅkhāro pariggahitakāle paṭippassambhati, pariggahitakāle pavattakāyasaṅkhāro paṭhamajjhānūpacāre…pe… catutthajjhānūpacāre pavattakāyasaṅkhāro catutthajjhāne paṭippassambhati. Ayaṃ tāva samathe nayo.

The reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, however, hold: 'In the first jhāna it is gross; in the access to the second jhāna it is subtle.' Thus they hold that in the access concentration of each higher jhāna it is progressively more subtle than in the preceding lower jhāna. But, according to the opinion of all, the bodily formation that occurs at the time of non-comprehension is calmed at the time of comprehension; the bodily formation that occurs at the time of comprehension is calmed in the access to the first jhāna... the bodily formation that occurs in the access to the fourth jhāna is calmed in the fourth jhāna. This, for now, is the method in serenity meditation.

Vipassanāyaṃ [V 2.0017] pana apariggahe pavatto kāyasaṅkhāro oḷāriko, mahābhūtapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, upādārūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, sakalarūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, arūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, rūpārūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, paccayapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, sappaccayanāmarūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya sukhumo. Sopi dubbalavipassanāya oḷāriko, balavavipassanāya sukhumo. Tattha pubbe vuttanayeneva purimassa purimassa pacchimena pacchimena passaddhi veditabbā. Evamettha oḷārikasukhumatā ca passaddhi ca veditabbā.

In insight meditation, however, the bodily formation that occurs without comprehension is gross; with comprehension of the great elements, it is subtle. That too is gross; with comprehension of derived matter, it is subtle. That too is gross; with comprehension of all matter, it is subtle. That too is gross; with comprehension of mentality, it is subtle. That too is gross; with comprehension of matter and mentality, it is subtle. That too is gross; with comprehension of conditions, it is subtle. That too is gross; with comprehension of name-and-form with its conditions, it is subtle. That too is gross; with insight that has characteristics as its object, it is subtle. That too is gross in weak insight, but subtle in strong insight. Therein, in the same way as was stated before, the tranquility of each preceding stage should be understood by means of each succeeding stage. Thus, herein, the grossness and subtlety, and the tranquility, should be understood.

Paṭisambhidāyaṃ panassa saddhiṃ codanāsodhanāhi evamattho vutto – “kathaṃ passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmī”ti sikkhati? Katame kāyasaṅkhārā? Dīghaṃ assāsā kāyikā ete dhammā kāyappaṭibaddhā kāyasaṅkhārā, te kāyasaṅkhāre passambhento nirodhento vūpasamento sikkhati. Dīghaṃ passāsā kāyikā ete dhammā…pe… rassaṃ assāsā…pe… rassaṃ passāsā… sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī assāsā… sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī passāsā kāyikā ete dhammā kāyappaṭibaddhā kāyasaṅkhārā, te kāyasaṅkhāre passambhento nirodhento vūpasamento sikkhati.

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, its meaning is stated thus by the General of the Dhamma, along with questions and clarifications: 'How does one train thus: "Calming the bodily formation, I will breathe out... calming the bodily formation, I will breathe in"?' What are the bodily formations? Long out-breaths are bodily; these phenomena are bound to the body, thus they are bodily formations. One trains by calming, causing to cease, and pacifying these bodily formations. Long in-breaths are bodily; these phenomena... short out-breaths... short in-breaths... experiencing the whole body, out-breaths... experiencing the whole body, in-breaths are bodily; these phenomena are bound to the body, thus they are bodily formations. One trains by calming, causing to cease, and pacifying these bodily formations.

Yathārūpehi kāyasaṅkhārehi yā kāyassa ānamanā vinamanā sannamanā [P 2.0414] paṇamanā iñjanā phandanā calanā kampanā passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti [M 2.0019] sikkhati, passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhati.

One trains thus: 'I will breathe out, calming the gross bodily formation by which there is bending forward, bending sideways, contracting, bending backward, shaking, throbbing, trembling, and quaking of the body.' One trains thus: 'I will breathe in, calming the gross bodily formation.'

Yathārūpehi kāyasaṅkhārehi yā kāyassa na ānamanā na vinamanā na sannamanā na paṇamanā aniñjanā aphandanā acalanā akampanā, santaṃ sukhumaṃ passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti sikkhati, passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhati.

One trains thus: 'I will breathe out, calming the peaceful and subtle bodily formation by which there is no bending forward, no bending sideways, no contracting, no bending backward, no shaking, no throbbing, no trembling, and no quaking of the body.' One trains thus: 'I will breathe in, calming the bodily formation.'

Iti [V 2.0018] kira passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti sikkhati, passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhati. Evaṃ sante vātūpaladdhiyā ca pabhāvanā na hoti, assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā na hoti, ānāpānassatiyā ca pabhāvanā na hoti, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā na na hoti, na ca naṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā samāpajjantipi vuṭṭhahantipi.

One trains, 'I will breathe out, calming the bodily formation'; one trains, 'I will breathe in, calming the bodily formation.' This being so, is there not development of the obtaining of the wind? Is there not development of the in-breaths and out-breaths? Is there not development of mindfulness of breathing? Is there not development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing? And do the wise not attain that attainment, and do they not emerge from it?

Iti kira passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhati. Evaṃ sante vātūpaladdhiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā hoti, tañca naṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā samāpajjantipi vuṭṭhahantipi.

One trains, 'I will breathe out, calming the bodily formation... I will breathe in, calming the bodily formation.' This being so, there is development of the obtaining of the wind, there is development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, there is development of mindfulness of breathing, there is development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; and the wise both attain and emerge from that attainment.

Yathā kathaṃ viya? Seyyathāpi kaṃse ākoṭite paṭhamaṃ oḷārikā saddā pavattanti, oḷārikānaṃ saddānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi oḷārike sadde atha pacchā sukhumakā saddā pavattanti, sukhumakānaṃ saddānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi sukhumake sadde atha pacchā sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpi cittaṃ pavattati; evameva paṭhamaṃ oḷārikā assāsapassāsā pavattanti, oḷārikānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi oḷārike assāsapassāse atha pacchā sukhumakā assāsapassāsā pavattanti, sukhumakānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā [P 2.0415] sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi sukhumake assāsapassāse atha pacchā sukhumaassāsapassāsanimittārammaṇatāpi cittaṃ na vikkhepaṃ gacchati.

How is this to be understood? Just as when a bronze bowl is struck, first coarse sounds arise. Because the sign of the coarse sounds is well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-retained, even when the coarse sound has ceased, then afterwards subtle sounds arise. Because the sign of the subtle sounds is well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-retained, even when the subtle sound has ceased, then afterwards the mind proceeds with the subtle sound-sign as its object. In the same way, first coarse in-breaths and out-breaths arise. Because the sign of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths is well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-retained, even when the coarse in-breath and out-breath has ceased, then afterwards subtle in-breaths and out-breaths arise. Because the sign of the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths is well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-retained, even when the subtle in-breath and out-breath has ceased, then afterwards, with the subtle in-breath and out-breath sign as its object, the mind does not go to distraction.

Evaṃ [M 2.0020] sante vātūpaladdhiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā hoti, tañca naṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā samāpajjantipi vuṭṭhahantipi.

This being so, there is development of the obtaining of the wind, there is development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, there is development of mindfulness of breathing, there is development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; and the wise both attain and emerge from that attainment.

Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti assāsapassāsā kāyo, upaṭṭhānaṃ sati, anupassanā ñāṇaṃ. Kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ no sati, sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati ca, tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena taṃ kāyaṃ anupassati. Tena vuccati – “kāye kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti (paṭi. ma. 1.171).

Regarding 'calming the bodily formation': the in-breaths and out-breaths are the body; establishment is mindfulness; contemplation is knowledge. The body is the place of establishment, not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness itself. With that mindfulness, with that knowledge, one contemplates that body. Therefore it is said: 'Contemplation of the body in the body, the development of the establishment of mindfulness.'

Ayaṃ tāvettha kāyānupassanāvasena vuttassa paṭhamacatukkassa anupubbapadavaṇṇanā.

This, first of all, is the sequential word-by-word explanation of the first tetrad spoken here by way of the contemplation of the body.

Yasmā panettha idameva catukkaṃ ādikammikassa kammaṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ, itarāni pana tīṇi catukkāni ettha pattajjhānassa vedanācittadhammānupassanāvasena vuttāni, tasmā idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā ānāpānassaticatutthajjhānapadaṭṭhānāya vipassanāya saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ [V 2.0019] pāpuṇitukāmena buddhaputtena yaṃ kātabbaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ idheva tāva ādikammikassa kulaputtassa vasena ādito pabhuti evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Catubbidhaṃ tāva sīlaṃ visodhetabbaṃ. Tattha tividhā visodhanā – anāpajjanaṃ, āpannavuṭṭhānaṃ, kilesehi ca appatipīḷanaṃ. Evaṃ visuddhasīlassa hi bhāvanā sampajjati. Yampidaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ bodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ upajjhāyavattaṃ ācariyavattaṃ jantāgharavattaṃ uposathāgāravattaṃ dveasīti khandhakavattāni cuddasavidhaṃ mahāvattanti imesaṃ vasena ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ vuccati, tampi sādhukaṃ paripūretabbaṃ. Yo hi “ahaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhāmi, kiṃ ābhisamācārikena kamma”nti vadeyya, tassa sīlaṃ paripūressatīti netaṃ [P 2.0416] ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ābhisamācārikavatte pana paripūre sīlaṃ paripūrati, sīle paripūre samādhi gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “so vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ābhisamācārikaṃ dhammaṃ aparipūretvā ‘sīlāni paripūressatī’ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (a. ni. 5.21) vitthāretabbaṃ. Tasmā tena yampidaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattādi ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ vuccati, tampi sādhukaṃ paripūretabbaṃ. Tato –

Since, herein, only this tetrad is spoken of by way of a meditation subject for a beginner, while the other three tetrads are spoken of by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and dhammas for one who has attained jhāna herein, therefore, all that should be done by a son of the Buddha who, having developed this meditation subject, wishes to attain Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges through insight that has the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing as its proximate cause, should be understood thus from the very beginning, right here in this first tetrad, by way of the noble son who is a beginner. First, the fourfold virtue should be purified. Therein, purification is threefold: not falling into an offense, rising from an offense that has been fallen into, and not being oppressed by defilements. For one with thus purified virtue, the development of meditation succeeds. And that which is called the virtue of proper conduct—by way of the duties regarding the shrine courtyard, the duties regarding the Bodhi tree courtyard, the duties toward the preceptor, the duties toward the teacher, the duties regarding the bathhouse, the duties regarding the Uposatha hall, the eighty-two duties from the Khandhakas, and the fourteen great duties—this too must be well fulfilled. For if one were to say, 'I guard virtue; what is the use of the practice of proper conduct?', it is impossible that his virtue would be fulfilled. But when the duties of proper conduct are fulfilled, virtue is fulfilled; when virtue is fulfilled, concentration is established. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, it is impossible that a monk who has not fulfilled the practice of proper conduct should fulfill the virtues.' This should be elaborated. Therefore, that which is called the virtue of proper conduct, beginning with the duties regarding the shrine courtyard, must also be well fulfilled. Then:

“Āvāso [M 2.0021] ca kulaṃ lābho, gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ;

Addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho, gantho iddhīti te dasā”ti.

“Dwelling, and supporters; gain; a group; and construction work as the fifth; a journey; relatives; sickness; study; and psychic power—these are the ten.”

Evaṃ vuttesu dasasu palibodhesu yo palibodho atthi, so upacchinditabbo.

Among these ten impediments that have been spoken of, whichever impediment exists, that one should be cut off.

Evaṃ upacchinnapalibodhena kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Tampi duvidhaṃ hoti – sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānañca pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānañca. Tattha sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhikkhusaṅghādīsu mettā maraṇassati ca asubhasaññātipi eke. Kammaṭṭhānikena hi bhikkhunā paṭhamaṃ tāva paricchinditvā sīmaṭṭhakabhikkhusaṅghe mettā bhāvetabbā; tato sīmaṭṭhakadevatāsu, tato gocaragāme issarajane, tato tattha manusse upādāya sabbasattesu. So hi bhikkhusaṅghe mettāya sahavāsīnaṃ muducittataṃ janeti, athassa sukhasaṃvāsatā hoti. Sīmaṭṭhakadevatāsu mettāya mudukatacittāhi devatāhi dhammikāya rakkhāya susaṃvihitārakkho hoti. Gocaragāme issarajane mettāya mudukatacittasantānehi issarehi dhammikāya rakkhāya surakkhitaparikkhāro hoti. Tattha manussesu mettāya pasāditacittehi tehi aparibhūto hutvā vicarati. Sabbasattesu mettāya sabbattha appaṭihatacāro hoti.

Thus, having cut off the impediments, the meditation subject should be taken up. That meditation subject is of two kinds: the all-purpose meditation subject and the regularly-practiced meditation subject. Therein, what is called the all-purpose meditation subject is loving-kindness towards persons beginning with the community of monks, and mindfulness of death. Some also say it is the perception of foulness. Indeed, by a monk practicing meditation, having first demarcated, loving-kindness should be developed towards the community of monks residing within the boundary; then towards the deities within the boundary; then towards the ruling people in the alms-resort village; and then, beginning with the people there, towards all beings. Indeed, through loving-kindness towards the community of monks, he generates gentleness of mind in his co-residents, and then for him there is comfortable association. Through loving-kindness towards the deities within the boundary, he comes to have protection well-arranged with righteous protection by the deities whose minds have been softened. Through loving-kindness towards the ruling people in the alms-resort village, he comes to have his requisites well-protected with righteous protection by the rulers whose mental continuums have been softened. Through loving-kindness towards the people there, he wanders about, not being disrespected by them whose minds have been pleased. Through loving-kindness towards all beings, he becomes one whose movement is unobstructed everywhere.

Maraṇassatiyā pana “avassaṃ maritabba”nti cintento anesanaṃ pahāya uparūparivaḍḍhamānasaṃvego [V 2.0020][P 2.0417] anolīnavuttiko hoti. Asubhasaññāya dibbesupi ārammaṇesu taṇhā nuppajjati. Tenassetaṃ tayaṃ evaṃ bahūpakārattā “sabbattha atthayitabbaṃ icchitabba”nti katvā adhippetassa ca yogānuyogakammassa padaṭṭhānattā “sabbatthakakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati.

Furthermore, through mindfulness of death, by reflecting, 'I must certainly die,' having abandoned improper seeking, one becomes one with ever-increasing spiritual urgency and of un-slackened conduct. Through the perception of foulness, craving does not arise even for divine objects. Therefore, because this triad is thus of great benefit, and because it is to be desired and wished for in all matters, and also because it is a foundation for the intended practice of diligent application, it is called the 'all-purpose meditation subject'.

Aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu pana yaṃ yassa caritānukūlaṃ, taṃ tassa niccaṃ pariharitabbattā yathāvutteneva nayena “pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna”ntipi vuccati. Idha pana idameva ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ “pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana sīlavisodhanakathaṃ palibodhupacchedakathañca icchantena visuddhimaggato gahetabbo.

Furthermore, among the thirty-eight meditation objects, whichever is suitable to a person's temperament, because that object should be constantly maintained by that person, it is also called the 'regularly-practiced meditation subject' by the method already stated. Here, however, this very meditation subject of mindfulness of in-and-out breathing is called the 'regularly-practiced meditation subject.' This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be taken from the Visuddhimagga by one who desires the discourse on the purification of virtue and the discourse on the cutting off of impediments.

Evaṃ visuddhasīlena pana upacchinnapalibodhena ca idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhantena imināva kammaṭṭhānena catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattassa buddhaputtassa santike uggahetabbaṃ. Taṃ alabhantena anāgāmissa, tampi [M 2.0022] alabhantena sakadāgāmissa, tampi alabhantena sotāpannassa, tampi alabhantena ānāpānacatutthajjhānalābhissa, tampi alabhantena pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca asammūḷhassa vinicchayācariyassa santike uggahetabbaṃ. Arahantādayo hi attanā adhigatamaggameva ācikkhanti. Ayaṃ pana gahanapadese mahāhatthipathaṃ nīharanto viya sabbattha asammūḷho sappāyāsappāyaṃ paricchinditvā katheti.

Furthermore, this meditation subject should be taken up by one who is pure in virtue and has cut off the impediments, from a son of the Buddha who, by means of this very meditation subject, having produced the fourth jhāna and developed insight, has attained Arahantship. If not finding such a one, it should be taken up from a son of the Buddha who is a Non-returner who has attained that state through this very meditation subject. If not finding him either, from a son of the Buddha who is a Once-returner who has attained that state through this very meditation subject. If not finding him either, from a son of the Buddha who is a Stream-enterer who has attained that state through this very meditation subject. If not finding him either, from a son of the Buddha who has attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of in-and-out breathing. If not finding him either, it should be taken up from a teacher of decision who is unconfused in the Pāḷi and the Commentary. Indeed, Arahants and others teach only the path they themselves have attained. This one, however, like one clearing a great elephant path in a dense forest, being unconfused in all matters, speaks having distinguished what is suitable and unsuitable.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – tena bhikkhunā sallahukavuttinā vinayācārasampannena vuttappakāramācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vattapaṭipattiyā ārādhitacittassa tassa santike pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Tatrime pañca sandhayo [P 2.0418] – uggaho, paripucchā, upaṭṭhānaṃ, appanā, lakkhaṇanti. Tattha “uggaho” nāma kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanaṃ, “paripucchā” nāma kammaṭṭhānassa paripucchanā, “upaṭṭhānaṃ” nāma kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhānaṃ, “appanā” nāma kammaṭṭhānappanā, “lakkhaṇaṃ” nāma kammaṭṭhānassa lakkhaṇaṃ. “Evaṃlakkhaṇamidaṃ kammaṭṭhāna”nti kammaṭṭhānasabhāvūpadhāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, this is the sequential instruction: that monk, being of light livelihood and accomplished in the conduct of the Vinaya, having approached a teacher of the kind described, should learn from him, whose mind has been pleased by the performance of duties, the meditation subject with its five sections. Therein, these are the five sections: learning, inquiry, manifestation, absorption, and characteristic. Therein, 'learning' is the learning of the meditation subject; 'inquiry' is the repeated questioning about the meditation subject; 'manifestation' is the manifestation of the meditation sign; 'absorption' is the absorption of the meditation subject; 'characteristic' is the characteristic of the meditation subject. It is said that this is the ascertaining of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject, thus: 'This meditation subject has such a characteristic.'

Evaṃ pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhanto attanāpi na kilamati, ācariyampi na viheṭheti; tasmā thokaṃ uddisāpetvā bahukālaṃ sajjhāyitvā evaṃ pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā sace tattha sappāyaṃ hoti, tattheva vasitabbaṃ.
