No ce tattha sappāyaṃ hoti, ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā sace mandapañño yojanaparamaṃ gantvā, sace tikkhapañño dūrampi gantvā aṭṭhārasasenāsanadosavivajjitaṃ, pañcasenāsanaṅgasamannāgataṃ senāsanaṃ upagamma tattha vasantena upacchinnakhuddakapalibodhena [V 2.0021] katabhattakiccena bhattasammadaṃ paṭivinodetvā ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena cittaṃ sampahaṃsetvā ācariyuggahato ekapadampi asammussantena idaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana imaṃ kathāmaggaṃ icchantena visuddhimaggato (visuddhi. 1.55) gahetabbo.

Thus learning the meditation subject with its five sections, one neither tires oneself nor harasses the teacher. Therefore, having had a little recited and having chanted it for a long time, thus having learned the meditation subject with its five sections, if it is suitable there, one should live right there. If it is not suitable there, having taken leave of the teacher, if one is of dull wisdom, one should go at most a yojana; if one is of sharp wisdom, one may go even far. Having approached a lodging that is devoid of the eighteen faults of a lodging and endowed with the five factors of a lodging, while living there, having cut off minor impediments, having completed the meal-duty, having dispelled drowsiness from the meal, having gladdened the mind by repeatedly recollecting the qualities of the Three Jewels, this mindfulness-of-breathing meditation subject should be attended to, without forgetting even one portion of what was learned from the teacher. This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be taken from the Visuddhimagga by one who desires this line of exposition.

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “idaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātabba”nti tatrāyaṃ manasikāravidhi –

Now, as to what was said, 'This mindfulness-of-breathing meditation subject should be attended to,' herein is the method of attending:

“Gaṇanā anubandhanā, phusanā ṭhapanā sallakkhaṇā;

Vivaṭṭanā pārisuddhi, tesañca paṭipassanā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.223; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163);

'Counting, following, contact, establishing, discerning; turning away, purification, and the reviewing of them.'

“Gaṇanā”ti [M 2.0023] gaṇanāyeva. “Anubandhanā”ti anuvahanā. “Phusanā”ti phuṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. “Ṭhapanā”ti appanā. “Sallakkhaṇā”ti [P 2.0419] vipassanā. “Vivaṭṭanā”ti maggo. “Pārisuddhī”ti phalaṃ. “Tesañca paṭipassanā”ti paccavekkhaṇā. Tattha iminā ādikammikakulaputtena paṭhamaṃ gaṇanāya idaṃ kamaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Gaṇentena ca pañcannaṃ heṭṭhā na ṭhapetabbaṃ, dasannaṃ upari na netabbaṃ, antare khaṇḍaṃ na dassetabbaṃ. Pañcannaṃ heṭṭhā ṭhapentassa hi sambādhe okāse cittuppādo vipphandati, sambādhe vaje sanniruddhagogaṇo viya. Dasannaṃ upari nentassa gaṇanānissitova cittuppādo hoti. Antarā khaṇḍaṃ dassentassa “sikhāppattaṃ nu kho me kammaṭṭhānaṃ, no”ti cittaṃ vikampati. Tasmā ete dose vajjetvā gaṇetabbaṃ.

'Counting' is indeed counting. 'Following' is continuous application. 'Contact' is the place of contact. 'Establishing' is absorption. 'Discerning' is insight. 'Turning away' is the path. 'Purification' is the fruit. 'And the reviewing of them' is reflection. Herein, this son of good family who is a beginner should first attend to this meditation subject by means of counting. And when counting, one should not stop below five, nor go beyond ten, nor show a break in between. For one who stops below five, the arising of the mind flutters in a confined space, like a herd of cattle confined in a narrow pen. For one who goes beyond ten, the arising of the mind becomes dependent on counting. For one who shows a break in between, the mind wavers, thinking, 'Has my meditation subject reached its culmination or not?' Therefore, one should count having avoided these faults.

Gaṇentena ca paṭhamaṃ dandhagaṇanāya dhaññamāpakagaṇanāya gaṇetabbaṃ. Dhaññamāpako hi nāḷiṃ pūretvā “eka”nti vatvā okirati. Puna pūrento kiñci kacavaraṃ disvā taṃ chaḍḍento “ekaṃ eka”nti vadati. Esa nayo “dve dve”tiādīsu. Evameva imināpi assāsapassāsesu yo upaṭṭhāti taṃ gahetvā “ekaṃ eka”nti ādiṃkatvā yāva “dasa dasā”ti pavattamānaṃ pavattamānaṃ upalakkhetvāva gaṇetabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ gaṇayato nikkhamantā ca pavisantā ca assāsapassāsā pākaṭā honti.

And when counting, one should first count slowly, with the counting of a grain-measurer. For a grain-measurer fills a measure and, saying 'one,' pours it out. While filling it again, if he sees some rubbish, he discards it and says, 'one, one.' This is the method for 'two, two,' and so on. In the very same way, this one too, among the in-breaths and out-breaths, should grasp whichever becomes manifest and, beginning with 'one, one' up to 'ten, ten,' should count by marking them as they occur again and again. For one who counts in this way, the out-breaths and in-breaths become manifest.

Athānena taṃ dandhagaṇanaṃ dhaññamāpakagaṇanaṃ pahāya sīghagaṇanāya gopālakagaṇanāya gaṇetabbaṃ[V 2.0022]. Cheko hi gopālako sakkharāyo ucchaṅgena gahetvā rajjudaṇḍahattho pātova vajaṃ gantvā gāvo piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā palighatthambhamatthake nisinno dvāraṃ pattaṃ pattaṃyeva gāvaṃ “eko dve”ti sakkharaṃ khipitvā khipitvā gaṇeti. Tiyāmarattiṃ sambādhe okāse dukkhaṃ vutthagogaṇo [P 2.0420] nikkhamanto aññamaññaṃ upanighaṃsanto vegena vegena puñjo puñjo hutvā nikkhamati. So vegena vegena “tīṇi cattāri pañca dasā”ti gaṇetiyeva. Evamimassāpi purimanayena gaṇayato assāsapassāsā pākaṭā hutvā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ punappunaṃ sañcaranti. Tato tena “punappunaṃ sañcarantī”ti ñatvā anto ca bahi ca aggahetvā dvārappattaṃ dvārappattaṃyeva gahetvā “eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañca[M 2.0024], eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañca cha, eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañca cha satta…pe… aṭṭha… nava… dasā”ti sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gaṇetabbameva. Gaṇanāpaṭibaddhe hi kammaṭṭhāne gaṇanābaleneva cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti arittūpatthambhanavasena caṇḍasote nāvāṭhapanamiva.

Then, this one, abandoning that slow counting of the grain-measurer, should count with the fast counting of a cowherd. For a skilled cowherd, taking pebbles in his lap and with a rope and stick in hand, goes to the pen early in the morning, strikes the cows on the back, and sitting on top of the gate-post, counts each cow as it reaches the gate, throwing down a pebble again and again, saying, 'one, two.' The herd of cattle, having stayed with difficulty in a confined space for the three watches of the night, when exiting, rubbing against one another, comes out very quickly in bunches. He counts very quickly, 'three, four, five... ten.' In the same way, for this one too who is counting in the previous manner, the in-breaths and out-breaths, having become manifest, move very quickly, again and again. Then, having known, 'They move again and again,' without grasping them inside or outside, but grasping them only as they reach the 'gate' again and again, one should count very quickly: 'one, two, three, four, five; one, two, three, four, five, six; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven... eight... nine... ten.' For in a meditation subject connected with counting, it is by the power of counting alone that the mind becomes one-pointed, like the steadying of a boat in a swift current by means of a steering-oar.

Tassevaṃ sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gaṇayato kammaṭṭhānaṃ nirantarappavattaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Atha “nirantaraṃ pavattatī”ti ñatvā anto ca bahi ca vātaṃ apariggahetvā purimanayeneva vegena vegena gaṇetabbaṃ. Antopavisanavātena hi saddhiṃ cittaṃ pavesayato abbhantaraṃ vātabbhāhataṃ medapūritaṃ viya hoti, bahinikkhamanavātena saddhiṃ cittaṃ nīharato bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cittaṃ vikkhipati. Phuṭṭhokāse pana satiṃ ṭhapetvā bhāventasseva bhāvanā sampajjati. Tena vuttaṃ – “anto [P 2.0421] ca bahi ca vātaṃ apariggahetvā purimanayeneva vegena vegena gaṇetabba”nti.

For one who counts very quickly in this way, the meditation subject appears as if occurring without interruption. Then, knowing that ‘it is occurring without interruption,’ one should count very quickly in the same manner as before, without grasping the breath inside or outside. For, for one who lets the mind enter together with the in-coming breath, the inside becomes as if struck by wind and filled with fat; for one who leads the mind out together with the out-going breath, the mind becomes scattered among various external objects. But it is only for one who develops meditation by placing mindfulness on the place of contact that the development succeeds. Therefore, it was said: ‘Without grasping the breath inside or outside, one should count very quickly in the same manner as before.’

Kīva ciraṃ panetaṃ gaṇetabbanti? Yāva vinā gaṇanāya assāsapassāsārammaṇe sati santiṭṭhati. Bahi visaṭavitakkavicchedaṃ katvā assāsapassāsārammaṇe sati saṇṭhapanatthaṃyeva hi gaṇanāti.

But for how long should this be counted? For as long as mindfulness remains well established on the object of in-breaths and out-breaths without counting. For counting is only for the purpose of establishing mindfulness on the object of in-breaths and out-breaths, having cut off scattered thoughts on external objects.

Evaṃ gaṇanāya manasikatvā anubandhanāya manasikātabbaṃ. Anubandhanā nāma gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā satiyā nirantaraṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ anugamanaṃ; tañca kho na ādimajjhapariyosānānugamanavasena. Bahinikkhamanavātassa hi nābhi ādi, hadayaṃ majjhaṃ, nāsikaggaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Abbhantarapavisanavātassa nāsikaggaṃ ādi, hadayaṃ majjhaṃ, nābhi pariyosānaṃ. Tañcassa anugacchato vikkhepagataṃ cittaṃ sāraddhāya ceva hoti iñjanāya ca. Yathāha –

Having thus attended by means of counting, one should attend by means of following. Following means, having withdrawn the counting, the uninterrupted following of the in-breaths and out-breaths with mindfulness; and that is not by way of following their beginning, middle, and end. For the out-going breath, the navel is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose is the end. For the in-coming breath, the tip of the nose is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. And for one who follows it thus, the mind goes to distraction and becomes agitated and trembles. As it is said:

“Assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato ajjhattaṃ vikkhepagatena cittena [V 2.0023] kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā ca. Passāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato bahiddhā vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.157).

‘For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath with mindfulness, with a mind that has gone to internal distraction, both body and mind become agitated, shaken, and trembling. For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath with mindfulness, with a mind that has gone to external distraction, both body and mind become agitated, shaken, and trembling.’

Tasmā anubandhanāya manasikarontena na ādimajjhapariyosānavasena manasikātabbaṃ. Apica kho phusanāvasena ca ṭhapanāvasena ca manasikātabbaṃ. Gaṇanānubandhanāvasena [M 2.0025] viya hi phusanāṭhapanāvasena visuṃ manasikāro natthi. Phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva pana gaṇento gaṇanāya ca phusanāya ca manasi karoti. Tattheva gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā te satiyā anubandhanto appanāvasena ca [P 2.0422] cittaṃ ṭhapento “anubandhanāya ca phusanāya ca ṭhapanāya ca manasi karotī”ti vuccati. Svāyamattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttapaṅguḷadovārikopamāhi paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttakakacopamāya ca veditabbo.

Therefore, one who attends by way of following should not attend in terms of beginning, middle, and end. But rather, one should attend by way of contact and by way of establishing. For there is no separate attending by way of contact and establishing as there is by way of counting and following. But while counting at the very point of contact, one attends by way of both counting and contact. Having withdrawn the counting right there, and following them with mindfulness, and establishing the mind by way of absorption, one is said to 'attend by way of following, contact, and establishing.' This meaning should be understood through the similes of the lame man and the gatekeeper mentioned in the commentary, and the simile of the saw mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

Tatrāyaṃ paṅguḷopamā – “seyyathāpi paṅguḷo dolāya kīḷataṃ mātāputtānaṃ dolaṃ khipitvā tattheva dolatthambhamūle nisinno kamena āgacchantassa ca gacchantassa ca dolāphalakassa ubho koṭiyo majjhañca passati, na ca ubhokoṭimajjhānaṃ dassanatthaṃ byāvaṭo hoti. Evamevāyaṃ bhikkhu sativasena upanibandhanatthambhamūle ṭhatvā assāsapassāsadolaṃ khipitvā tattheva nimitte satiyā nisinno kamena āgacchantānañca gacchantānañca phuṭṭhaṭṭhāne assāsapassāsānaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchanto tattha ca cittaṃ ṭhapento passati, na ca tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ byāvaṭo hoti. Ayaṃ paṅguḷopamā.

Herein is the simile of the lame man: 'Just as a lame man, having set the swing in motion for a mother and son playing on it, sits right there at the base of the swing-post and sees both ends and the middle of the swing-plank as it gradually comes and goes, yet is not occupied with seeing both ends and the middle; in the same way, this monk, standing at the base of the tying-post by the power of mindfulness, having set in motion the swing of in-breaths and out-breaths, sits right there with mindfulness at the sign, and sees the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breaths and out-breaths as they gradually come and go at the point of contact, while following them with mindfulness and placing the mind there, yet is not occupied with seeing them. This is the simile of the lame man.'

Ayaṃ pana dovārikopamā – “seyyathāpi dovāriko nagarassa anto ca bahi ca purise ‘ko tvaṃ, kuto vā āgato, kuhiṃ vā gacchasi, kiṃ vā te hatthe’ti na vīmaṃsati, na hi tassa te bhārā. Dvārappattaṃ dvārappattaṃyeva pana vīmaṃsati; evameva imassa bhikkhuno anto paviṭṭhavātā ca bahi nikkhantavātā ca na bhārā honti, dvārappattā dvārappattāyeva bhārāti. Ayaṃ dovārikopamā.

This, however, is the simile of the gatekeeper: 'Just as a gatekeeper of a city does not investigate the people inside or outside—‘Who are you? From where have you come? Where are you going? What is in your hand?’—for indeed, they are not his concern. He investigates only each person who arrives at the gate; in the same way, for this monk, the breaths that have entered within and the breaths that have gone outside are not his concern. Only the breaths that arrive at the gate are his concern. This is the simile of the gatekeeper.'

Kakacopamā pana āditopabhuti evaṃ veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The simile of the saw, however, should be understood from the beginning in this way. For this was stated:

“Nimittaṃ [V 2.0024] assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Ajānato ca tayo dhamme, bhāvanānupalabbhati.

‘The sign and the in-breaths and out-breaths are not the object of a single mind; and for one who does not know the three things, development is not attained.’

“Nimittaṃ assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Jānato ca tayo dhamme, bhāvanā upalabbhatī”ti. (paṭi. ma. 1.159);

‘The sign and the in-breaths and out-breaths are not the object of a single mind; but for one who knows the three things, development is attained.’

Kathaṃ ime tayo dhammā ekacittassa ārammaṇaṃ na honti, na cime tayo dhammā aviditā honti, na ca cittaṃ vikkhepaṃ gacchati, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati[P 2.0423]? Seyyathāpi rukkho same [M 2.0026] bhūmibhāge nikkhitto, tamenaṃ puriso kakacena chindeyya, rukkhe phuṭṭhakakacadantānaṃ vasena purisassa sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, na āgate vā gate vā kakacadante manasi karoti, na āgatā vā gatā vā kakacadantā aviditā honti, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti.

How are these three things not the object of a single mind, and yet these three things are not unknown, and the mind does not go to distraction, and effort is evident, and the application succeeds, and one attains distinction? Just as a log is placed on level ground, and a man might cut it with a saw; the man's mindfulness is established by means of the saw's teeth touching the log. He does not attend to the saw's teeth that are coming or going, yet the saw's teeth that are coming or going are not unknown to him. And effort is evident, and the application succeeds.

Yathā rukkho same bhūmibhāge nikkhitto; evaṃ upanibandhananimittaṃ. Yathā kakacadantā; evaṃ assāsapassāsā. Yathā rukkhe phuṭṭhakakacadantānaṃ vasena purisassa sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, na āgate vā gate vā kakacadante manasi karoti, na āgatā vā gatā vā kakacadantā aviditā honti, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, evameva bhikkhu nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā nisinno hoti, na āgate vā gate vā assāsapassāse manasi karoti, na āgatā vā gatā vā assāsapassāsā aviditā honti, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati.

Just as a log is placed on level ground, so is the binding sign. Just as the saw's teeth, so are the in-breaths and out-breaths. Just as a man's mindfulness is established by means of the saw's teeth touching the log, and he does not attend to the saw's teeth that are coming or going, yet the saw's teeth that are coming or going are not unknown to him, and effort is evident, and the application succeeds; in the very same way, a monk sits, having established mindfulness at the nose-tip or at the sign of the mouth. He does not attend to the in-breaths and out-breaths that are coming or going, yet the in-breaths and out-breaths that are coming or going are not unknown to him, and effort is evident, and the application succeeds, and he attains distinction.

Padhānanti katamaṃ padhānaṃ? Āraddhavīriyassa kāyopi cittampi kammaniyaṃ hoti – idaṃ padhānaṃ. Katamo payogo? Āraddhavīriyassa upakkilesā pahīyanti, vitakkā vūpasammanti – ayaṃ payogo. Katamo viseso? Āraddhavīriyassa saṃyojanā pahīyanti, anusayā byantī honti – ayaṃ viseso. Evaṃ ime tayo dhammā ekacittassa ārammaṇā na honti, na cime tayo dhammā aviditā honti, na ca cittaṃ vikkhepaṃ gacchati, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati.

Regarding 'effort' (padhāna): what is effort? For one with aroused energy, the body and mind become workable—this is effort. What is 'application' (payoga)? For one with aroused energy, the defilements are abandoned and thoughts are stilled—this is application. What is 'distinction' (visesa)? For one with aroused energy, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are brought to an end—this is distinction. In this way, these three things are not the object of a single mind, and yet these three things are not unknown, and the mind does not go to distraction, and effort is evident, and the application succeeds, and distinction is attained.

“Ānāpānassatī [V 2.0025] yassa, paripuṇṇā subhāvitā;

Anupubbaṃ paricitā, yathā buddhena desitā;

So imaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā”ti. (paṭi. ma. 1.160);

For whom mindfulness of breathing is complete and well-developed, practiced in sequence and made familiar, just as it was taught by the Buddha—that one illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

Ayaṃ kakacopamā. Idha panassa āgatāgatavasena amanasikāramattameva payojananti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaroto kassaci nacireneva nimittañca [P 2.0424] uppajjati, avasesajjhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitā appanāsaṅkhātā ṭhapanā ca sampajjati. Kassaci pana gaṇanāvaseneva manasikārakālatopabhuti anukkamato oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodhavasena kāyadarathe vūpasante kāyopi cittampi lahukaṃ hoti, sarīraṃ ākāse laṅghanākārappattaṃ [M 2.0027] viya hoti. Yathā sāraddhakāyassa mañce vā pīṭhe vā nisīdato mañcapīṭhaṃ onamati, vikūjati, paccattharaṇaṃ valiṃ gaṇhāti. Asāraddhakāyassa pana nisīdato neva mañcapīṭhaṃ onamati, na vikūjati, na paccattharaṇaṃ valiṃ gaṇhāti, tūlapicupūritaṃ viya mañcapīṭhaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā asāraddho kāyo lahuko hoti; evameva gaṇanāvasena manasikārakālatopabhuti anukkamato oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodhavasena kāyadarathe vūpasante kāyopi cittampi lahukaṃ hoti, sarīraṃ ākāse laṅghanākārappattaṃ viya hoti.

This is the simile of the saw. Here, it should be understood that the purpose is merely non-attention by way of the incoming and outgoing breaths. For a certain one who attends to this meditation subject, the sign arises before long, and the establishment, called absorption, adorned with the remaining jhāna factors, is accomplished. For a certain one, however, from the time of attending by way of counting, gradually, through the cessation of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths, when the bodily distress has subsided, both body and mind become light; the body becomes as if it has attained a state of levitation in the air. Just as for one with an agitated body sitting on a bed or a chair, the bed or chair bends down, it creaks, and the covering gets creased. But for one with an unagitated body sitting down, the bed or chair neither bends down, nor creaks, nor does the covering get creased; the bed or chair is as if filled with cotton-wool. Why is that? Because an unagitated body is light. In the very same way, from the time of attending by way of counting, gradually, through the cessation of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths, when the bodily distress has subsided, both body and mind become light; the body becomes as if it has attained a state of levitation in the air.

Tassa oḷārike assāsapassāse niruddhe sukhumaassāsapassāsanimittārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ pavattati, tasmimpi niruddhe aparāparaṃ tato sukhumatarasukhumatamanimittārammaṇaṃ pavattatiyeva. Kathaṃ? Yathā puriso mahatiyā lohasalākāya kaṃsatāḷaṃ ākoṭeyya, ekappahārena mahāsaddo uppajjeyya, tassa oḷārikasaddārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ pavatteyya, niruddhe oḷārike sadde atha pacchā sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇaṃ, tasmimpi niruddhe aparāparaṃ tato sukhumatarasukhumatamasaddanimittārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ pavattateva; evanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “seyyathāpi kaṃse ākoṭite”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.171) vitthāro.

When his coarse in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, the mind proceeds with a subtle sign of in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. When that too has ceased, then successively, the mind proceeds with an even subtler and most subtle sign as its object. How? It is as if a man were to strike a bronze gong with a large iron rod; with a single strike a loud sound would arise. His mind would proceed with the coarse sound as its object. When the coarse sound has ceased, then afterwards his mind proceeds with the subtle sound-sign as its object. When that too has ceased, then successively, the mind proceeds with an even subtler and most subtle sound-sign as its object. Thus it should be understood. And this was also said: “Just as when a bronze gong is struck…”; the detailed account should be known.

Yathā hi aññāni kammaṭṭhānāni uparūpari vibhūtāni honti, na tathā idaṃ. Idaṃ pana uparūpari bhāventassa bhāventassa sukhumattaṃ [P 2.0425] gacchati, upaṭṭhānampi na upagacchati. Evaṃ anupaṭṭhahante pana tasmiṃ na tena bhikkhunā uṭṭhāyāsanā cammakhaṇḍaṃ papphoṭetvā gantabbaṃ. Kiṃ kātabbaṃ? “Ācariyaṃ pucchissāmī”ti vā “naṭṭhaṃ dāni me kammaṭṭhāna”nti vā na vuṭṭhātabbaṃ, iriyāpathaṃ [V 2.0026] vikopetvā gacchato hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ navanavameva hoti. Tasmā yathānisinneneva desato āharitabbaṃ.

For while other meditation subjects become progressively clearer, this one does not become so. Rather, as this meditation subject is developed again and again, it goes to subtlety and does not even come into appearance. When it is thus not appearing, that monk should not get up from his seat, shake out his piece of leather, and go away. What should be done? He should not get up thinking, “I will ask the teacher,” or “Now my meditation subject is lost.” For of one who goes away, having broken his posture, the meditation subject becomes entirely new. Therefore, it should be brought back by way of its location while one is seated just as before.

Tatrāyaṃ āharaṇūpāyo. Tena hi bhikkhunā kammaṭṭhānassa anupaṭṭhahanabhāvaṃ ñatvā iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ – “ime assāsapassāsā nāma kattha atthi, kattha natthi, kassa vā atthi, kassa vā natthī”ti. Athevaṃ paṭisañcikkhatā “ime antomātukucchiyaṃ natthi, udake nimuggānaṃ natthi, tathā asaññībhūtānaṃ matānaṃ catutthajjhānasamāpannānaṃ rūpārūpabhavasamaṅgīnaṃ nirodhasamāpannāna”nti [M 2.0028] ñatvā evaṃ attanāva attā paṭicodetabbo – “nanu tvaṃ, paṇḍita, neva mātukucchigato, na udake nimuggo, na asaññībhūto, na mato, na catutthajjhānasamaāpanno, na rūpārūpabhavasamaṅgī, na nirodhasamāpanno, atthiyeva te assāsapassāsā, mandapaññatāya pana pariggahetuṃ na sakkosī”ti. Athānena pakatiphuṭṭhavaseneva cittaṃ ṭhapetvā manasikāro pavattetabbo. Ime hi dīghanāsikassa nāsā puṭaṃ ghaṭṭentā pavattanti, rassanāsikassa uttaroṭṭhaṃ. Tasmānena imaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ ghaṭṭentīti nimittaṃ paṭṭhapetabbaṃ. Imameva hi atthavasaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, muṭṭhassatissa asampajānassa ānāpānassatibhāvanaṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 3.149; saṃ. ni. 5.992). Kiñcāpi hi yaṃkiñci kammaṭṭhānaṃ satassa sampajānasseva sampajjati, ito aññaṃ pana manasikarontassa pākaṭaṃ hoti. Idaṃ pana ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ garukaṃ garukabhāvanaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhaputtānaṃ mahāpurisānameva manasikārabhūmibhūtaṃ, na ceva ittaraṃ, na ca ittarasattasamāsevitaṃ. Yathā yathā manasi karīyati, tathā tathā santañceva [P 2.0426] hoti sukhumañca. Tasmā ettha balavatī sati ca paññā ca icchitabbā.

Herein, this is the method for bringing it back. That bhikkhu, having known the state of the meditation subject's non-appearance, should reflect thus: “These things called in-breaths and out-breaths, where do they exist? Where do they not exist? For whom do they exist, and for whom do they not exist?” Then, having reflected thus, and having known that “These do not exist for one inside a mother's womb, they do not exist for those submerged in water, likewise for those who have become non-percipient, for the dead, for those attained to the fourth jhāna, for those who are endowed with existence in the form and formless realms, and for those attained to cessation,” he should admonish himself with his own self thus: “Surely, you, O wise one, are not one who is in a mother's womb, nor submerged in water, nor one who has become non-percipient, nor dead, nor attained to the fourth jhāna, nor endowed with existence in the form and formless realms, nor attained to cessation. Your in-breaths and out-breaths certainly exist, but due to the dullness of your wisdom, you are unable to grasp them.” Then, having established the mind just by way of the natural point of contact, attention should be set in motion. For these breaths, for one with a long nose, proceed striking the nostril; for one with a short nose, the upper lip. Therefore, by him the sign should be established thus: “They strike this particular place.” It was with reference to this very benefit that it was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, I do not say there is the development of mindfulness of breathing for one who is forgetful and not clearly comprehending.” Although any meditation subject whatsoever is accomplished only for one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, another subject apart from this becomes manifest for one who attends to it. This meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, however, is weighty, a weighty development, the very ground for the attention of great beings—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddha; it is not insignificant, nor is it frequented by insignificant beings. In whatever way it is attended to, in that same way it becomes peaceful and subtle. Therefore, strong mindfulness and wisdom are to be desired here.

Yathā hi maṭṭhasāṭakassa tunnakaraṇakāle sūcipi sukhumā icchitabbā, sūcipāsavedhanampi tato sukhumataraṃ; evameva maṭṭhasāṭakasadisassa imassa kammaṭṭhānassa bhāvanākāle sūcipaṭibhāgā satipi sūcipāsavedhanapaṭibhāgā taṃsampayuttā paññāpi balavatī icchitabbā. Tāhi ca pana satipaññāhi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na te assāsapassāsā aññatra pakatiphuṭṭhokāsā pariyesitabbā.

For just as when sewing a fine cloth, a fine needle is required, and a tool for piercing the needle's eye that is even finer than that; in the very same way, during the time of developing this meditation subject, which is like a fine cloth, strong mindfulness, which is analogous to the needle, and the wisdom associated with it, which is analogous to the tool for piercing the needle's eye, are required. And by a bhikkhu who is endowed with that mindfulness and wisdom, those in-breaths and out-breaths should not be sought elsewhere than at the natural place of contact.

Yathā pana kassako kasiṃ kasitvā balibadde muñcitvā gocarābhimukhe katvā chāyāya nisinno vissameyya, athassa te balibaddā vegena aṭaviṃ paviseyyuṃ. Yo hoti cheko kassako so puna te gahetvā yojetukāmo na tesaṃ anupadaṃ gantvā aṭaviṃ āhiṇḍati. Atha [V 2.0027] kho rasmiñca patodañca gahetvā ujukameva tesaṃ nipātatitthaṃ gantvā nisīdati vā nipajjati vā. Atha te goṇe divasabhāgaṃ caritvā nipātatitthaṃ otaritvā nhatvā ca pivitvā ca paccuttaritvā ṭhite disvā rasmiyā bandhitvā patodena vijjhanto ānetvā yojetvā puna kammaṃ karoti; evameva tena bhikkhunā na te assāsapassāsā aññatra [M 2.0029] pakatiphuṭṭhokāsā pariyesitabbā. Satirasmiṃ pana paññāpatodañca gahetvā pakatiphuṭṭhokāse cittaṃ ṭhapetvā manasikāro pavattetabbo. Evañhissa manasikaroto nacirasseva te upaṭṭhahanti, nipātatitthe viya goṇā. Tato tena satirasmiyā bandhitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne yojetvā paññāpatodena vijjhantena puna kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitabbaṃ; tassevamanuyuñjato nacirasseva nimittaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Taṃ panetaṃ na sabbesaṃ ekasadisaṃ hoti[P 2.0427]; apica kho kassaci sukhasamphassaṃ uppādayamāno tūlapicu viya, kappāsapicu viya, vātadhārā viya ca upaṭṭhātīti ekacce āhu.

Just as a farmer, having plowed the field and released the oxen, having turned them toward the pasture, sits in the shade to rest; then those oxen of his might swiftly enter the forest. A skilled farmer who wants to catch and yoke them again does not wander into the forest following their tracks. But rather, taking the rope and the goad, he goes straight to their watering place and sits or lies down. Then, when the oxen have roamed for a part of the day, gone down to the watering place, bathed and drunk, and come back up, seeing them standing there, he ties them with the rope, prods them with the goad, brings them back, yokes them, and resumes his work. Even so, that bhikkhu should not seek those in-breaths and out-breaths elsewhere than at the naturally touched spot. But, taking the rope of mindfulness and the goad of wisdom, having established the mind at the naturally touched spot, attention should be applied. For to him who attends thus, they will soon appear, like the oxen at the watering place. Then, having tied them with the rope of mindfulness and yoked them in that very place, and prodding them with the goad of wisdom, he should again apply himself to the meditation subject. To him who applies himself thus, the sign will soon appear. This sign, however, is not the same for everyone; but rather, for some, producing a pleasant touch, it appears like a heap of silk-cotton, like a heap of cotton-wool, or like a current of wind—so some say.

Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāvinicchayo – idañhi kassaci tārakarūpaṃ viya, maṇiguḷikā viya, muttāguḷikā viya ca kassaci kharasamphassaṃ hutvā kappāsaṭṭhi viya, sāradārusūci viya ca kassaci dīghapāmaṅgasuttaṃ viya, kusumadāmaṃ viya, dhūmasikhā viya ca kassaci vitthata makkaṭakasuttaṃ viya, valāhakapaṭalaṃ viya, padumapupphaṃ viya, rathacakkaṃ viya, candamaṇḍalaṃ viya, sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ viya ca upaṭṭhāti. Tañca panetaṃ yathā sambahulesu bhikkhūsu suttantaṃ sajjhāyitvā nisinnesu ekena bhikkhunā “tumhākaṃ kīdisaṃ hutvā idaṃ suttaṃ upaṭṭhātī”ti vutte eko “mayhaṃ mahatī pabbateyyā nadī viya hutvā upaṭṭhātī”ti āha. Aparo “mayhaṃ ekā vanarāji viya”. Añño “mayhaṃ sītacchāyo sākhāsampanno phalabhārabharitarukkho viyā”ti. Tesañhi taṃ ekameva suttaṃ saññānānatāya nānato upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ ekameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ saññānānatāya nānato upaṭṭhāti. Saññajañhi etaṃ saññānidānaṃ saññāppabhavaṃ tasmā saññānānatāya nānato upaṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ.

But this is the commentary's determination: Indeed, to some it appears like a star, a jewel-ball, or a pearl-ball; to some, becoming rough to the touch, it appears like a cotton seed or a needle of heartwood; to some, it appears like a long carpenter's thread, a garland of flowers, or a wisp of smoke; to some, it appears like a widespread spider's web, a sheet of cloud, a lotus flower, a chariot wheel, the orb of the moon, or the orb of the sun. And this is like when, among many bhikkhus seated having recited a sutta, one bhikkhu asked, 'To you, sirs, how does this sutta appear?' One said, 'To me, it appears like a great mountain river.' Another said, 'To me, it is like a line of forest.' Yet another said, 'To me, it is like a shady tree, well-branched and laden with fruit.' Indeed, the same sutta appears differently to them due to the diversity of their perceptions. In the same way, a single meditation subject appears differently due to the diversity of perceptions. For this is born of perception, has perception as its cause, and has perception as its origin; therefore, it should be understood that it appears differently due to the diversity of perceptions.

Ettha ca aññameva assāsārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ, aññaṃ passāsārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ nimittārammaṇaṃ yassa hi ime tayo dhammā natthi, tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ neva appanaṃ na upacāraṃ pāpuṇāti. Yassa panime tayo dhammā atthi, tasseva kammaṭṭhānaṃ appanañca upacārañca pāpuṇāti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

And here, the mind with the out-breath as its object is one thing, the mind with the in-breath as its object is another, and the mind with the sign as its object is yet another. For one for whom these three states do not exist, the meditation subject attains neither absorption nor access. But for one for whom these three states exist, for him alone the meditation subject attains both absorption and access. For this has been said:

“Nimittaṃ [P 2.0428][V 2.0028] assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Ajānato ca tayo dhamme, bhāvanānupalabbhati.

The sign, the in-breaths, and the out-breaths are not the objects of a single consciousness; for one who does not know these three states, development is not found.

“Nimittaṃ assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Jānato ca tayo dhamme, bhāvanā upalabbhatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.231);

The sign, the in-breaths, and the out-breaths are not the objects of a single consciousness; for one who knows these three states, development is found.

Evaṃ [M 2.0030] upaṭṭhite pana nimitte tena bhikkhunā ācariyasantikaṃ gantvā ārocetabbaṃ – “mayhaṃ, bhante, evarūpaṃ nāma upaṭṭhātī”ti. Ācariyena pana “etaṃ nimitta”nti vā “na nimitta”nti vā na vattabbaṃ. “Evaṃ hoti, āvuso”ti vatvā pana “punappunaṃ manasi karohī”ti vattabbo. “Nimitta”nti hi vutte vosānaṃ āpajjeyya; “na nimitta”nti vutte nirāso visīdeyya. Tasmā tadubhayampi avatvā manasikāreyeva niyojetabboti. Evaṃ tāva dīghabhāṇakā. Majjhimabhāṇakā panāhu – “nimittamidaṃ, āvuso, kammaṭṭhānaṃ punappunaṃ manasi karohi sappurisāti vattabbo”ti. Athānena nimitteyeva cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Evamassāyaṃ ito pabhuti ṭhapanāvasena bhāvanā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

When such a sign appears, the monk should go to the teacher and report: 'Venerable sir, an object of such and such a nature has appeared to me.' The teacher, however, should not say, 'This is a sign,' or 'This is not a sign.' But having said, 'It happens thus, friend,' he should advise, 'Apply your mind to it again and again.' For if he says, 'This is a sign,' the meditator might stop short; if he says, 'This is not a sign,' he might become hopeless and despondent. Therefore, without saying either, he should be urged only to apply his mind. So say the Dīghabhāṇakas. The Majjhimabhāṇakas, however, say: 'He should be told: “Friend, this is a sign. O good man, apply your mind to the meditation subject again and again.”' Then he should fix his mind on that very sign. From this point onward, his development proceeds by way of stabilization. For this was said by the ancients:

“Nimitte ṭhapayaṃ cittaṃ, nānākāraṃ vibhāvayaṃ;

Dhīro assāsapassāse, sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.232; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163);

Establishing the mind on the sign, and making the various aspects in the in-and-out breaths disappear, the wise one binds his own mind.

Tassevaṃ nimittupaṭṭhānato pabhuti nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāneva honti kilesā sannisinnāva sati upaṭṭhitāyeva, cittaṃ samāhitameva. Idañhi dvīhākārehi cittaṃ samāhitaṃ nāma hohi – upacārabhūmiyaṃ vā nīvaraṇappahānena, paṭilābhabhūmiyaṃ vā aṅgapātubhāvena. Tattha “upacārabhūmī”ti upacārasamādhi; “paṭilābhabhūmī”ti appanāsamādhi. Tesaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ? Upacārasamādhi kusalavīthiyaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati, appanāsamādhi divasabhāge appetvā nisinnassa divasabhāgampi kusalavīthiyaṃ javati, na bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Imesu dvīsu samādhīsu nimittapātubhāvena upacārasamādhinā samāhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti[P 2.0429]. Athānena taṃ nimittaṃ neva vaṇṇato manasikātabbaṃ, na lakkhaṇato paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Apica kho khattiyamahesiyā cakkavattigabbho viya kassakena sāliyavagabbho viya ca appamattena rakkhitabbaṃ; rakkhitaṃ hissa phaladaṃ hoti.

For him, from the time the sign appears, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, the defilements are indeed calmed, mindfulness is indeed established, and the mind is indeed concentrated. For this mind is called 'concentrated' in two ways: either in the access stage through the abandoning of the hindrances, or in the attainment stage through the manifestation of the jhāna factors. Therein, 'access stage' is access concentration; 'attainment stage' is absorption concentration. What is the difference between them? Access concentration, after running in the wholesome cognitive process, descends into the life-continuum. Absorption concentration, for one who is seated having attained it during a part of the day, runs in the wholesome cognitive process even for that entire part of the day and does not descend into the life-continuum. Among these two concentrations, the mind becomes concentrated by means of access concentration through the manifestation of the sign. Then, that sign should not be attended to by him by way of its color, nor should it be reviewed by way of its characteristics. Moreover, it should be guarded with diligence, just as the embryo of a wheel-turning monarch is guarded by a queen of the warrior-caste, and as the embryo of fine rice is guarded by a farmer; for, when guarded, it becomes fruitful for him.

“Nimittaṃ rakkhato laddha, parihāni na vijjati;

Ārakkhamhi asantamhi, laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vinassatī”ti.

For one who guards the sign, there is no loss of what has been gained; when guarding is absent, what has been gained is lost again and again.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 2.0029] rakkhaṇūpāyo – tena bhikkhunā āvāso, gocaro, bhassaṃ, puggalo, bhojanaṃ, utu, iriyāpathoti imāni satta asappāyāni vajjetvā tāneva satta sappāyāni sevantena punappunaṃ taṃ nimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ.

Therein, this is the method of guarding: that monk, having avoided these seven unsuitable things—dwelling, alms-resort, talk, person, food, climate, and posture—and resorting to those same seven suitable things, should attend to that sign again and again.

Evaṃ [M 2.0031] sappāyasevanena nimittaṃ thiraṃ katvā vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ gamayitvā vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā, nimittakusalatā, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sapaggahetabba tasmiṃ samaye cittapaggaṇhanā, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaniggaṇhanā, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye sampahaṃsetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittasampahaṃsanā, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaajjhupekkhanā, asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanā, samāhitapuggalasevanā, tadadhimuttatāti imāni dasa appanākosallāni avijahantena yogo karaṇīyo.

Thus, by resorting to what is suitable, having made the sign stable and caused it to grow and develop, exertion should be made without abandoning these ten skills for absorption: making the basis pure, bringing the faculties to a state of balance, skillfulness in the sign, uplifting the mind at the time it should be uplifted, restraining the mind at the time it should be restrained, gladdening the mind at the time it should be gladdened, looking upon the mind with equanimity at the time it should be looked upon with equanimity, avoiding unconcentrated persons, resorting to concentrated persons, and being inclined towards that.

Tassevaṃ anuyuttassa viharato idāni appanā uppajjissatīti bhavaṅgaṃ vicchinditvā nimittārammaṇaṃ manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati. Tasmiñca niruddhe tadevārammaṇaṃ gahetvā cattāri pañca vā javanāni, yesaṃ paṭhamaṃ parikammaṃ, dutiyaṃ upacāraṃ, tatiyaṃ anulomaṃ, catutthaṃ gotrabhu[P 2.0430], pañcamaṃ appanācittaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ vā parikammañceva upacārañca, dutiyaṃ anulomaṃ, tatiyaṃ gotrabhu, catutthaṃ appanācittanti vuccati. Catutthameva hi pañcamaṃ vā appeti, na chaṭṭhaṃ sattamaṃ vā āsannabhavaṅgapātattā.

For him dwelling thus engaged, when it is the case that 'now absorption will arise,' mind-door adverting arises, having cut off the life-continuum, with the sign as its object. And when that has ceased, taking that same object, four or five impulsions arise, of which the first is called preparation, the second access, the third conformity, the fourth change-of-lineage, and the fifth is absorption-consciousness. Alternatively, the first is called both preparation and access, the second conformity, the third change-of-lineage, and the fourth absorption-consciousness. For it is at the fourth or fifth that it attains absorption, not at the sixth or seventh, because of the nearness of falling into the life-continuum.

Ābhidhammikagodattatthero panāha – “āsevanapaccayena kusalā dhammā balavanto honti; tasmā chaṭṭhaṃ sattamaṃ vā appetī”ti. Taṃ aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittaṃ. Tattha pubbabhāgacittāni kāmāvacarāni honti, appanācittaṃ pana rūpāvacaraṃ. Evamanena pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ, pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ, dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ, tividhakalyāṇaṃ, paṭhamajjhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. So tasmiṃyevārammaṇe vitakkādayo vūpasametvā dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānāni pāpuṇāti. Ettāvatā ca ṭhapanāvasena bhāvanāya pariyosānappatto hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepakathā. Vitthāro pana icchantena visuddhimaggato gahetabbo.

But the Elder Godatta, the Ābhidhammika, said: 'Through the repetition condition, wholesome states become strong; therefore, it attains absorption at the sixth or seventh impulsion.' That has been rejected in the commentaries. Therein, the preliminary consciousnesses are of the sense-sphere, but the absorption-consciousness is of the form-sphere. Thus, by this meditator, the first jhāna is attained—which has abandoned five factors, is possessed of five factors, is endowed with ten characteristics, and has threefold beauty. He, having quieted initial application and so on in that very object, attains the second, third, and fourth jhānas. And to this extent, by way of placement, he has reached the culmination of the development. This here is the brief account. But the detail should be understood from the Visuddhimagga by one who desires it.

Evaṃ pattacatutthajjhāno panettha bhikkhu sallakkhaṇāvivaṭṭanāvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā pārisuddhiṃ pattukāmo tadeva jhānaṃ āvajjanasamāpajjanaadhiṭṭhānavuṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇasaṅkhātehi pañcahākārehi vasippattaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā arūpapubbaṅgamaṃ vā rūpaṃ, rūpapubbaṅgamaṃ vā arūpanti rūpārūpaṃ [V 2.0030] pariggahetvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti. Kathaṃ? So hi jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā jhānaṅgāni pariggahetvā tesaṃ nissayaṃ hadayavatthuṃ taṃ nissayāni ca bhūtāni tesañca nissayaṃ sakalampi [M 2.0032] karajakāyaṃ passati. Tato “jhānaṅgāni arūpaṃ, vatthādīni rūpa”nti rūpārūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

Herein, a monk who has thus attained the fourth jhāna, desiring to attain purity, develops the meditation subject by way of turning away through discernment of characteristics. Having made that same jhāna proficient and mastered in the five ways—namely, adverting, attaining, resolving, emerging, and reviewing—he comprehends materiality preceded by immateriality, or immateriality preceded by materiality—that is, materiality-and-immateriality—and establishes insight. How? For he, having emerged from jhāna, comprehends the jhāna factors and sees the heart-base as their support, the great elements which are the support of that, and the entire physical body which is the support of them. Then he defines materiality-and-immateriality thus: 'The jhāna factors are immateriality; the base and so on are materiality.'

Atha vā samāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā kesādīsu koṭṭhāsesu pathavīdhātuādivasena cattāri bhūtāni taṃnissitarūpāni ca pariggahetvā yathāpariggahitarūpārammaṇaṃ yathāpariggahitarūpavatthudvārārammaṇaṃ vā sasampayuttadhammaṃ [P 2.0431] viññāṇañca passati. Tato “bhūtādīni rūpaṃ sasampayuttadhammaṃ viññāṇaṃ arūpa”nti vavatthapeti.

Alternatively, having emerged from the attainment, one comprehends in the parts of the body beginning with the hair of the head the four great elements—by way of the earth element, etc.—and the derived materiality dependent on them, and then sees consciousness together with its associated states, which has as its object either the materiality as comprehended or the door-basis of materiality as comprehended. Then one defines: 'The great elements and so on are materiality; consciousness with its associated states is immateriality.'

Atha vā samāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā assāsapassāsānaṃ samudayo karajakāyo ca cittañcāti passati. Yathā hi kammāragaggariyā dhamamānāya bhastañca purisassa ca tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicca vāto sañcarati; evameva kāyañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsāti. Tato assāsapassāse ca kāyañca rūpaṃ, cittañca taṃsampayuttadhamme ca arūpanti vavatthapeti.

Alternatively, having emerged from the attainment, he sees that the origin of the in-breaths and out-breaths is the physical body and the mind. For just as when a blacksmith's bellows is being blown, the wind moves in dependence on the bellows and the person's corresponding effort, in the same way, he sees, the in-breaths and out-breaths move in dependence on the body and the mind. Then he defines the in-breaths and out-breaths and the body as materiality, and the mind and its associated states as immateriality.

Evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesati, pariyesanto ca taṃ disvā tīsupi addhāsu nāmarūpassa pavattiṃ ārabbha kaṅkhaṃ vitarati. Vitiṇṇakaṅkho kalāpasammasanavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā udayabbayānupassanāya pubbabhāge uppanne obhāsādayo dasa vipassanupakkilese pahāya upakkilesavimuttaṃ paṭipadāñāṇaṃ “maggo”ti vavatthapetvā udayaṃ pahāya bhaṅgānupassanaṃ patvā nirantaraṃ bhaṅgānupassanena bhayato upaṭṭhitesu sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindanto virajjanto vimuccanto yathākkamaṃ cattāro ariyamagge pāpuṇitvā arahattaphale patiṭṭhāya ekūnavīsatibhedassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa pariyantappatto sadevakassa lokassa aggadakkhiṇeyyo hoti. Ettāvatā cassa gaṇanaṃ ādiṃ katvā vipassanāpariyosānā ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā ca samattā hotīti.

Having thus determined name-and-form, one seeks its condition. And while seeking, having seen it, one overcomes doubt with respect to the occurrence of name-and-form in the three periods of time. Having overcome doubt, by way of the comprehension of groups, one applies the three characteristics. Having abandoned the ten corruptions of insight, such as light, which have arisen in the preliminary stage of the contemplation of rise and fall, and having determined the knowledge of the way that is free from corruptions as 'the path,' one abandons arising and reaches the contemplation of dissolution. Through the uninterrupted contemplation of dissolution, one becomes disenchanted with, dispassionate towards, and liberated from all formations that have appeared as fearful. Having sequentially reached the four noble paths and become established in the fruit of Arahantship, one reaches the culmination of the nineteen kinds of knowledge of reviewing and becomes the foremost one worthy of offerings in the world with its devas. And by this much, for this yogi, the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing, which begins with counting and culminates in insight, is completed.

Ayaṃ sabbākārato paṭhamacatukkavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the first tetrad in all its aspects.

Itaresu pana tīsu catukkesu yasmā visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvanānayo nāma natthi; tasmā anupadavaṇṇanānayeneva nesaṃ attho veditabbo. Pītippaṭisaṃvedīti pītiṃ paṭisaṃviditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati. Tattha dvīhākārehi pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti – ārammaṇato [P 2.0432] ca asammohato ca.

However, in the other three tetrads, since there is no separate method for developing the meditation subject, their meaning should be understood only by the method of word-by-word explanation. 'Experiencing rapture' means one trains thus: 'Making rapture distinctly known, making it manifest, I shall breathe in; I shall breathe out.' Therein, rapture is distinctly known in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion.

Kathaṃ [M 2.0033][V 2.0031] ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjati, tassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇassa paṭisaṃviditattā.

How is rapture distinctly known by way of the object? One attains the two jhānas that are accompanied by rapture. For that one, at the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of jhāna, rapture is distinctly known by way of the object because the object is distinctly known.

Kathaṃ asammohato? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttakapītiṃ khayato vayato sammasati, tassa vipassanākkhaṇe lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

How by way of non-delusion? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and having emerged from them, one comprehends the rapture associated with the jhāna as perishing and vanishing. For that one, at the moment of insight, through the penetration of its characteristic, rapture is distinctly known by way of non-delusion. For this was stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Dīghaṃ assāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Dīghaṃ passāsavasena…pe… rassaṃ assāsavasena… rassaṃ passāsavasena… sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī assāsavasena… sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī passāsavasena… passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assāsavasena… passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Āvajjato sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti jānato… passato… paccavekkhato… cittaṃ adhiṭṭhahato… saddhāya adhimuccato… vīriyaṃ paggaṇhato… satiṃ upaṭṭhāpayato… cittaṃ samādahato… paññāya pajānato… abhiññeyyaṃ abhijānato… pariññeyyaṃ parijānato… pahātabbaṃ pajahato… bhāvetabbaṃ bhāvayato… sacchikātabbaṃ sacchikaroto sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Evaṃ sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.172).

For one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by way of the long in-breath, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is distinctly known. By way of the long out-breath… and so on… by way of the short in-breath… by way of the short out-breath… by way of experiencing the whole body with the in-breath… by way of experiencing the whole body with the out-breath… by way of calming the bodily formation with the in-breath… by way of calming the bodily formation with the out-breath, for one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind, mindfulness is established; with that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is distinctly known. That rapture is distinctly known by one who adverts, by one who knows, by one who sees, by one who reviews, by one who resolves the mind, by one who is resolved through faith, by one who exerts effort, by one who establishes mindfulness, by one who concentrates the mind, by one who understands with wisdom, by one who directly knows what is to be directly known, by one who fully understands what is to be fully understood, by one who abandons what is to be abandoned, by one who develops what is to be developed, by one who realizes what is to be realized. In this way, that rapture is distinctly known.

Eteneva nayena avasesapadānipi atthato veditabbāni. Idaṃ panettha visesamattaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena sukhapaṭisaṃveditā catunnampi vasena cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃveditā veditabbā. “Cittasaṅkhāro”ti vedanādayo dve khandhā. Sukhappaṭisaṃvedipade cettha vipassanābhūmidassanatthaṃ “sukhanti dve sukhāni – kāyikañca sukhaṃ cetasikañcā”ti [P 2.0433] paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāranti oḷārikaṃ oḷārikaṃ cittasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento, nirodhentoti attho. So vitthārato kāyasaṅkhāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Apicettha pītipade pītisīsena vedanā vuttā. Sukhapade sarūpeneva vedanā[M 2.0034]. Dvīsu cittasaṅkhārapadesu “saññā ca vedanā ca cetasikā ete dhammā cittapaṭibaddhā cittasaṅkhārā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.174; ma. ni. 1.463) vacanato [V 2.0032] saññāsampayuttā vedanāti. Evaṃ vedanānupassanānayena idaṃ catukkaṃ bhāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

In this same way, the remaining terms should also be understood as to their meaning. This here is the distinction. The experiencing of happiness should be understood by way of the three jhānas, and the experiencing of the mental formation by way of all four jhānas. 'Mental formation' means the two aggregates, feeling and so on. And here, in the term 'experiencing happiness,' in order to show the ground for insight, it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: '"Happiness" means two kinds of happiness: bodily happiness and mental happiness.' 'Calming the mental formation' means calming, ceasing, the grosser mental formation. This should be understood in detail in the same way as was explained for the bodily formation. Furthermore, here in the term concerning rapture, feeling is mentioned with rapture as its head. In the term concerning happiness, feeling is mentioned in its own form. In the two terms concerning the mental formation, because it is said: 'Perception and feeling are mental; these states are bound to the mind; they are mental formations,' it means feeling associated with perception. Thus, it should be understood that this tetrad was taught by way of the contemplation of feeling.

Tatiyacatukkepi catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena cittapaṭisaṃveditā veditabbā. Abhippamodayaṃ cittanti cittaṃ modento pamodento hāsento pahāsento assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati. Tattha dvīhākārehi abhippamodo hoti – samādhivasena ca vipassanāvasena ca.

In the third tetrad also, the experiencing of the mind should be understood by way of the four jhānas. 'Gladdening the mind' means one trains thus: 'Making the mind glad, making it rejoice, making it pleased, making it delighted, I shall breathe in; I shall breathe out.' Therein, this gladdening occurs in two ways: by way of concentration and by way of insight.

Kathaṃ samādhivasena? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjati, so samāpattikkhaṇe sampayuttāya pītiyā cittaṃ āmodeti pamodeti. Kathaṃ vipassanāvasena? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttakapītiṃ khayato vayato sammasati; evaṃ vipassanākkhaṇe jhānasampayuttakapītiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittaṃ āmodeti pamodeti. Evaṃ paṭipanno “abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti vuccati.

How by way of concentration? One attains the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. At the moment of attainment, one gladdens and delights the mind with the associated rapture. How by way of insight? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and having emerged, one comprehends the rapture associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing. Thus, at the moment of insight, having made the rapture associated with the jhāna the object, one gladdens and delights the mind. One who practices thus is said to be one who trains: 'Gladdening the mind, I shall breathe in; I shall breathe out.'

Samādahaṃ cittanti paṭhamajjhānādivasena ārammaṇe cittaṃ samaṃ ādahanto samaṃ ṭhapento tāni vā pana jhānāni samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttakacittaṃ khayato vayato sammasato vipassanākkhaṇe lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena uppajjati khaṇikacittekaggatā; evaṃ uppannāya khaṇikacittekaggatāya vasenapi ārammaṇe cittaṃ samaṃ ādahanto samaṃ ṭhapento “samādahaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti vuccati.

“Concentrating the mind” means one trains thus: 'Settling the mind evenly on the object by way of the first jhāna and so forth, I shall breathe in; I shall breathe out.' Or alternatively, having attained those jhānas and emerged, for one who contemplates the jhāna-associated mind as subject to destruction and vanishing, at the moment of insight, momentary one-pointedness of mind arises through the penetration of characteristics. And also, by means of the momentary one-pointedness of mind that has thus arisen, one who settles the mind evenly on the object and establishes it evenly is said to train thus: “Concentrating the mind, I shall breathe in; I shall breathe out.”

Vimocayaṃ cittanti paṭhamajjhānena nīvaraṇehi cittaṃ mocento vimocento, dutiyena vitakkavicārehi, tatiyena pītiyā, catutthena sukhadukkhehi cittaṃ mocento vimocento. Tāni vā pana jhānāni samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya [P 2.0434] jhānasampayuttakacittaṃ khayato vayato sammasati. So vipassanākkhaṇe aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāto cittaṃ mocento vimocento, dukkhānupassanāya sukhasaññāto, anattānupassanāya attasaññāto, nibbidānupassanāya nandito, virāgānupassanāya rāgato, nirodhānupassanāya samudayato, paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādānato cittaṃ mocento vimocento assasati ceva passasati ca. Tena vuttaṃ [M 2.0035] – “vimocayaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti. Evaṃ cittānupassanāvasena idaṃ catukkaṃ bhāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

“Releasing the mind” means releasing and thoroughly releasing the mind from the hindrances with the first jhāna; from initial thought and sustained thought with the second; from rapture with the third; and from pleasure and pain with the fourth. Or alternatively, having attained those jhānas and emerged, one contemplates the jhāna-associated mind as subject to destruction and vanishing. That person, at the moment of insight, releases and thoroughly releases the mind from the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence; from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering; from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self; from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment; from lust through the contemplation of dispassion; from arising through the contemplation of cessation; and from grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment—breathing in and breathing out. Therefore it is said: “One trains thus: ‘Releasing the mind, I will breathe in; I will breathe out.’” In this way, it should be understood that this tetrad is spoken by way of the contemplation of the mind.

Catutthacatukke pana aniccānupassīti ettha tāva aniccaṃ veditabbaṃ, aniccatā veditabbā, aniccānupassanā veditabbā[V 2.0033], aniccānupassī veditabbo. Tattha “anicca”nti pañcakkhandhā. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvā. “Aniccatā”ti tesaññeva uppādavayaññathattaṃ hutvā abhāvo vā nibbattānaṃ tenevākārena aṭhatvā khaṇabhaṅgena bhedoti attho. “Aniccānupassanā”ti tassā aniccatāya vasena rūpādīsu “anicca”nti anupassanā; “aniccānupassī”ti tāya anupassanāya samannāgato; tasmā evaṃ bhūto assasanto ca passasanto ca idha “aniccānupassī assasissāmi, passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti veditabbo.

Now, in the fourth tetrad, regarding “contemplating impermanence,” first, the impermanent should be understood, impermanence should be understood, the contemplation of impermanence should be understood, and one who contemplates impermanence should be understood. Therein, “the impermanent” refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because of their state of arising, passing away, and alteration. “Impermanence” means the arising, passing away, and alteration of those very aggregates, or their non-existence after having come to be; the meaning is that for things that have arisen, not remaining in that very same state, it is their breaking up by way of momentary dissolution. “Contemplation of impermanence” is the contemplation of form and so forth as “impermanent” by way of that impermanence. “One who contemplates impermanence” is a person endowed with that contemplation. Therefore, one who has become thus, breathing in and breathing out, should be understood in this context as training thus: “Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe in; contemplating impermanence, I will breathe out.”

Virāgānupassīti ettha pana dve virāgā – khayavirāgo ca accantavirāgo ca. Tattha “khayavirāgo”ti saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgo; “accantavirāgo”ti nibbānaṃ; “virāgānupassanā”ti tadubhayadassanavasena pavattā vipassanā ca maggo ca. Tāya duvidhāyapi anupassanāya samannāgato hutvā assasanto ca passasanto ca “virāgānupassī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti veditabbo. Nirodhānupassīpadepi eseva nayo.

Now, regarding “contemplating dispassion,” there are two kinds of dispassion: dispassion through destruction and ultimate dispassion. Therein, “dispassion through destruction” is the momentary dissolution of formations; “ultimate dispassion” is Nibbāna. “Contemplation of dispassion” is insight and the path that proceed by way of seeing both of these. Being endowed with this twofold contemplation, while breathing in and breathing out, one should be understood to train thus: “Contemplating dispassion, I will breathe in; contemplating dispassion, I will breathe out.” The same method applies to the term “contemplating cessation.”

Paṭinissaggānupassīti etthāpi dve paṭinissaggā – pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ca pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo ca. Paṭinissaggoyeva anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā; vipassanāmaggānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vipassanā hi tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajati, saṅkhatadosadassanena [P 2.0435] ca tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandatīti pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo cāti vuccati. Maggo samucchedavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajati, ārammaṇakaraṇena ca nibbāne pakkhandatīti pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissago cāti vuccati. Ubhayampi pana purimapurimañāṇānaṃ anuanu passanato anupassanāti vuccati. Tāya duvidhāya paṭinissaggānupassanāya samannāgato hutvā assasanto ca passasanto ca paṭinisaggānupassī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatīti veditabbo. Evaṃ bhāvitoti evaṃ soḷasahi ākārehi bhāvito. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Here too, regarding “contemplating relinquishment,” there are two kinds of relinquishment: relinquishment by abandonment and relinquishment by plunging into. Relinquishment itself is contemplation, hence “contemplation of relinquishment”; this is a designation for insight and the paths. For insight, by way of substitution, abandons the defilements together with the aggregates and formations, and by seeing the fault of the conditioned, it plunges into Nibbāna, which is the opposite of that, through inclination towards it—thus it is called both “relinquishment by abandonment” and “relinquishment by plunging into.” The path, by way of cutting off, abandons the defilements together with the aggregates and formations, and by making Nibbāna its object, it plunges into it—thus it is called both “relinquishment by abandonment” and “relinquishment by plunging into.” Furthermore, both are called “contemplation” because of seeing in sequence after the preceding knowledges. Being endowed with this twofold contemplation of relinquishment, while breathing in and breathing out, one should be understood to train thus: “Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in; contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out.” “Developed thus” means developed in these sixteen ways. The remainder is in the manner already stated.

Ānāpānassatisamādhikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Concentration of Mindfulness of Breathing is concluded.

167. Atha [M 2.0036] kho bhagavātiādimhi pana ayaṃ saṅkhepattho. Evaṃ bhagavā ānāpānassatisamādhikathāya bhikkhū samassāsetvā atha yaṃ taṃ tatiyapārājikapaññattiyā nidānañceva [V 2.0034] pakaraṇañca uppannaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aññamaññaṃ jīvitā voropanaṃ, etasmiṃ nidāne etasmiṃ pakaraṇe bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātetvā paṭipucchitvā vigarahitvā ca yasmā tattha attanā attānaṃ jīvitā voropanaṃ migalaṇḍikena ca voropāpanaṃ pārājikavatthu na hoti; tasmā taṃ ṭhapetvā pārājikassa vatthubhūtaṃ aññamaññaṃ jīvitā voropanameva gahetvā pārājikaṃ paññapento “yo pana bhikkhu sañcicca manussaviggaha”ntiādimāha. Ariyapuggalamissakattā panettha “moghapurisā”ti avatvā “te bhikkhū”ti vuttaṃ.

167. Now, regarding the passage beginning “Then the Blessed One,” this is the brief meaning. Thus, the Blessed One, having consoled the bhikkhus with the discourse on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, then, when the cause and the incident for the enactment of the third Pārājika rule had arisen—the bhikkhus depriving one another of life—he had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assemble concerning this cause and this incident, questioned them, and rebuked them. And since therein, neither depriving oneself of life nor causing Migalaṇḍika to deprive them of life constitutes a basis for a Pārājika offense, therefore, setting that aside and taking only the mutual depriving of life, which is the basis for a Pārājika, he, wishing to lay down the Pārājika rule, said: 'Whatever bhikkhu should intentionally deprive a human being of life…' and so on. Herein, because of the mixture of noble individuals, instead of saying 'foolish men,' it is said 'those bhikkhus.'

Evaṃ mūlacchejjavasena daḷhaṃ katvā tatiyapārājike paññatte aparampi anupaññattatthāya maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇanavatthu udapādi, tassuppattidīpanatthaṃ “evañcidaṃ bhagavatā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, when the third Pārājika had been laid down, having been made firm by way of cutting off at the root, a further matter arose for the purpose of a subsequent enactment: the incident of praising the description of death. To show its origin, the text beginning “Thus this by the Blessed One…” was spoken by the compilers of the canon.

168. Tattha paṭibaddhacittāti chandarāgena paṭibaddhacittā; sārattā apekkhavantoti attho. Maraṇavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇemāti jīvite ādīnavaṃ dassetvā maraṇassa [P 2.0436] guṇaṃ vaṇṇema; ānisaṃsaṃ dassemāti. Katakalyāṇotiādīsu ayaṃ padattho – kalyāṇaṃ sucikammaṃ kataṃ tayāti tvaṃ kho asi katakalyāṇo. Tathā kusalaṃ anavajjakammaṃ kataṃ tayāti katakusalo. Maraṇakāle sampatte yā sattānaṃ uppajjati bhayasaṅkhātā bhīrutā, tato tāyanaṃ rakkhaṇakammaṃ kataṃ tayāti katabhīruttāṇo pāpaṃ. Lāmakakammaṃ akataṃ tayāti akatapāpo. Luddaṃ dāruṇaṃ dussīlyakammaṃ akataṃ tayāti akataluddo. Kibbisaṃ sāhasikakammaṃ lobhādikilesussadaṃ akataṃ tayāti akatakibbiso. Kasmā idaṃ vuccati? Yasmā sabbappakārampi kataṃ tayā kalyāṇaṃ, akataṃ tayā pāpaṃ; tena taṃ vadāma – “kiṃ tuyhaṃ iminā rogābhibhūtattā lāmakena pāpakena dukkhabahulattā dujjīvitena”. Mataṃ te jīvitā seyyoti tava maraṇaṃ jīvitā sundarataraṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā ito tvaṃ kālaṅkato katakālo hutvā kālaṃ katvā maritvāti attho. Kāyassa bhedā…pe… upapajjissasi. Evaṃ upapanno ca tattha dibbehi devaloke [M 2.0037] uppannehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi manāpiyarūpādikehi pañcahi vatthukāmakoṭṭhāsehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricarissasi sampayutto samodhānagato hutvā ito cito ca carissasi, vicarissasi abhiramissasi vāti attho.

168. Herein, `paṭibaddhacittā` means a mind bound by desire and lust; the meaning is 'greatly impassioned and full of longing.' `Maraṇavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇemā` means to show the danger in life and then praise the virtue of death; the meaning is 'we show its benefit.' In phrases such as `katakalyāṇo`, this is the meaning of the terms: 'You have done good and pure deeds,' thus you are `katakalyāṇo`. Similarly, 'You have done wholesome and blameless deeds,' thus you are `katakusalo`. At the time of death, from the fear and dread that arise in beings, you have done a protective action, thus you are `katabhīruttāṇo`. 'You have not done an inferior, evil action,' thus you are `akatapāpo`. 'You have not done a cruel, harsh, immoral action,' thus you are `akataluddo`. 'You have not done a faulty, reckless action abounding in defilements such as greed,' thus you are `akatakibbiso`. Why is this said? Because you have done every kind of good and have not done evil; therefore, we say: 'What use is this life to you, being inferior, evil, full of suffering, and because you are overwhelmed by disease?' `Mataṃ te jīvitā seyyo` means 'your death is better than life.' Why? Because when you pass away from here, having fulfilled your time—that is, having died—after the breaking up of the body… you will be reborn. And having thus been reborn there, endowed and furnished with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure that have arisen in the deva world—the five portions of sensual objects such as pleasing forms—you will be associated and brought together with them, and will move about, wander, and delight here and there. This is the meaning.

169. Asappāyānīti ahitāni avuḍḍhikarāni yāni khippameva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti.

169. `Asappāyāni` means that which is unbeneficial, not conducive to growth, and which quickly leads to the destruction of life.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Analysis of Terms

172. Sañciccāti [V 2.0035] ayaṃ “sañcicca manussaviggaha”nti mātikāya vuttassa sañciccapadassa uddhāro. Tattha santi upasaggo, tena saddhiṃ ussukkavacanametaṃ sañciccāti[P 2.0437]; tassa sañcetetvā suṭṭhu cetetvāti attho. Yasmā pana yo sañcicca voropeti, so jānanto sañjānanto hoti, tañcassa voropanaṃ cecca abhivitaritvā vītikkamo hoti. Tasmā byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā atthameva dassetuṃ “jānanto sañjānanto cecca abhivitaritvā vītikkamo”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha jānantoti “pāṇo”ti jānanto. Sañjānantoti “jīvitā voropemī”ti sañjānanto; teneva pāṇajānanākārena saddhiṃ jānantoti attho. Ceccāti vadhakacetanāvasena cetetvā pakappetvā. Abhivitaritvāti upakkamavasena maddanto nirāsaṅkacittaṃ pesetvā. Vītikkamoti evaṃ pavattassa yo vītikkamo ayaṃ sañciccasaddassa sikhāppatto atthoti vuttaṃ hoti.

172. `Sañcicca`: this is an extraction of the word `sañcicca` mentioned in the Mātikā as '`sañcicca manussaviggahaṃ`'. Therein, `saṃ` is a prefix, and together with it, this word `cicca` expresses eagerness; its meaning is 'having intended, having intended well.' Because whoever intentionally deprives of life does so knowing and being fully aware, and that act of depriving of life is a transgression done after intending and carrying it out. Therefore, without paying attention to the letter, but only to show the meaning, its analysis of the term was stated thus: 'knowing, being fully aware, having intended, carrying it out, it is a transgression.' Therein, 'knowing' means knowing 'it is a living being.' 'Being fully aware' means being fully aware 'I am depriving it of life'; the meaning is knowing together with that very mode of knowing it as a living being. 'Having intended' means having intended and planned by way of the volition to kill. 'Carrying it out' means crushing by way of effort, having sent forth a mind without hesitation. 'Transgression' means: whatever transgression there is of one who proceeds thus, this is said to be the ultimate meaning of the word `sañcicca`.

Idāni “manussaviggahaṃ jīvitā voropeyyā”ti ettha vuttaṃ manussattabhāvaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ “manussaviggaho nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha gabbhaseyyakānaṃ vasena sabbasukhumaattabhāvadassanatthaṃ “yaṃ mātukucchismi”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ cittanti paṭisandhicittaṃ. Uppannanti jātaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṃ pātubhūtanti idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. “Mātukucchismiṃ paṭhamaṃ citta”nti vacanena cettha sakalāpi pañcavokārapaṭisandhi dassitā hoti. Tasmā tañca paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ taṃsampayuttā ca tayo arūpakkhandhā tena saha nibbattañca kalalarūpanti ayaṃ sabbapaṭhamo manussaviggaho. Tattha “kalalarūpa”nti itthipurisānaṃ kāyavatthubhāvadasakavasena [M 2.0038] samatiṃsa rūpāni, napuṃsakānaṃ kāyavatthudasakavasena vīsati. Tattha itthipurisānaṃ kalalarūpaṃ jātiuṇṇāya ekena aṃsunā uddhaṭatelabindumattaṃ hoti acchaṃ vippasannaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Now, in order to show the human state of existence mentioned in the phrase 'one might deprive a human being of life,' starting from the beginning, the Blessed One said 'what is called a human being,' and so on. Therein, in order to show the most subtle state of existence by way of those lying in the womb, it was said, 'that which is in the mother's womb.' 'The first mind' means the rebirth-linking consciousness. 'Arisen' means born. 'The first consciousness has appeared' is a synonym for that very thing. And here, by the statement 'the first mind in the mother's womb,' the entire five-aggregate rebirth is shown. Therefore, that first mind, the three immaterial aggregates associated with it, and the `kalala` form arisen together with it—this is the very first human being. Therein, '`kalala` form' means: for females and males, by way of the body-decad, base-decad, and sex-decad, there are thirty material forms; for neuters, by way of the body-decad and base-decad, there are twenty. Therein, for females and males, the `kalala` form is the size of a drop of oil lifted up by a single strand of fine wool; it is clear and very limpid. And this was said in the commentary:

“Tilatelassa yathā bindu, sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ kalalanti pavuccatī”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.235);

“Just as a drop of sesame oil, or the clear surface of ghee, untroubled; of such color and appearance, it is called `kalala`.”

Evaṃ parittakaṃ vatthuṃ ādiṃ katvā pakatiyā vīsavassasatāyukassa sattassa yāva maraṇakālā etthantare anupubbena [P 2.0438] vuḍḍhippatto attabhāvo eso manussaviggaho nāma.

Taking such a minute basis as the beginning, the state of existence of a being whose natural lifespan is one hundred and twenty years, which has attained growth successively in the interval up to the time of death—this is called a human being.

Jīvitā [V 2.0036] voropeyyāti kalalakālepi tāpanamaddanehi vā bhesajjasampadānena vā tato vā uddhampi tadanurūpena upakkamena jīvitā viyojeyyāti attho. Yasmā pana jīvitā voropanaṃ nāma atthato jīvitindriyupacchedanameva hoti, tasmā etassa padabhājane “jīvitindriyaṃ upacchindati uparodheti santatiṃ vikopetī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha jīvitindriyassa paveṇighaṭanaṃ upacchindanto uparodhento ca “jīvitindriyaṃ upacchindati uparodhetī”ti vuccati. Svāyamattho “santatiṃ vikopetī”tipadena dassito. Vikopetīti viyojeti.

`Jīvitā voropeyya` means: one might separate from life even at the `kalala` stage by heating and crushing or by giving medicine, or even after that by a suitable effort. This is the meaning. Because depriving of life, in meaning, is just the cutting off of the life faculty, therefore in the analysis of this term it is said: 'he cuts off the life faculty, he obstructs it, he disrupts the continuity.' Therein, one who is cutting off and obstructing the continuous connection of the life faculty is said to 'cut off the life faculty, obstruct it.' This very meaning is shown by the term 'disrupts the continuity.' `Vikopeti` means 'he separates'.

Tattha duvidhaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ – rūpajīvitindriyaṃ, arūpajīvitindriyañca. Tesu arūpajīvitindriye upakkamo natthi, taṃ voropetuṃ na sakkā. Rūpajīvitindriye pana atthi, taṃ voropetuṃ sakkā. Taṃ pana voropento arūpajīvitindriyampi voropeti. Teneva hi saddhiṃ taṃ nirujjhati tadāyattavuttito. Taṃ pana voropento kiṃ atītaṃ voropeti, anāgataṃ, paccuppannanti? Neva atītaṃ, na anāgataṃ, tesu hi ekaṃ niruddhaṃ ekaṃ anuppannanti ubhapampi asantaṃ, asantattā upakkamo natthi, upakkamassa natthitāya ekampi voropetuṃ na sakkā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Therein, the life faculty is twofold: the material life faculty and the immaterial life faculty. Among these, there is no means of attack against the immaterial life faculty; it cannot be terminated. Against the material life faculty, however, there is a means of attack; it can be terminated. But one who terminates the material life faculty also terminates the immaterial life faculty. For indeed, it ceases together with that very thing, because its existence is dependent on that. Now, in terminating it, does one terminate the past, the future, or the present? Neither the past nor the future. For of these, one has ceased and the other has not yet arisen; thus, both are non-existent. Because they are non-existent, there is no means of attack, and due to the absence of a means of attack, not even one can be terminated. And this has been said:

“Atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvittha, na jīvati; na jīvissati. Anāgate cittakkhaṇe jīvissati, na jīvittha; na jīvati. Paccuppanne cittakkhaṇe jīvati, na jīvittha; na jīvissatī”ti (mahāni. 10).

“In a past mind-moment, one lived; one is not living now and will not live. In a future mind-moment, one will live; one did not live and is not living now. In a present mind-moment, one is living; one did not live and will not live.”

Tasmā [M 2.0039] yattha jīvati tattha upakkamo yuttoti paccuppannaṃ voropeti.

Therefore, where one lives, a means of attack is suitable; thus, one terminates the present.

Paccuppannañca nāmetaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ, santatipaccuppannaṃ, addhāpaccuppannanti tividhaṃ. Tattha “khaṇapaccuppannaṃ” nāma uppādajarābhaṅgasamaṅgi, taṃ voropetuṃ na sakkā. Kasmā? Sayameva nirujjhanato. “Santatipaccuppannaṃ” nāma sattaṭṭhajavanavāramattaṃ sabhāgasantativasena pavattitvā nirujjhanakaṃ, yāva vā uṇhato āgantvā ovarakaṃ pavisitvā nisinnassa andhakāraṃ hoti, sītato vā āgantvā ovarake nisinnassa yāva visabhāgautupātubhāvena purimako utu nappaṭippassambhati, etthantare “santatipaccuppanna”nti vuccati[P 2.0439]. Paṭisandhito pana yāva cuti, etaṃ “addhāpaccuppannaṃ” nāma. Tadubhayampi voropetuṃ sakkā. Kathaṃ? Tasmiñhi upakkame kate laddhupakkamaṃ jīvitanavakaṃ nirujjhamānaṃ dubbalassa parihīnavegassa santānassa paccayo hoti. Tato santatipaccuppannaṃ vā addhāpaccuppannaṃ vā yathāparicchinnaṃ kālaṃ apatvā antarāva nirujjhati[V 2.0037]. Evaṃ tadubhayampi voropetuṃ sakkā, tasmā tadeva sandhāya “santatiṃ vikopetī”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

And this 'present' is threefold: the momentary present, the continuity present, and the duration present. Therein, the 'momentary present' is that which is endowed with arising, aging, and passing away; it cannot be terminated. Why? Because it ceases by itself. The 'continuity present' is that which, having occurred by way of a homogeneous continuity for the duration of about seven or eight impulsion-courses, is about to cease. Or, it is like the interval for one who, having come from the heat, entered a room, and sat down, during which it is still dark; or for one who, having come from the cold and sat down in a room, during which the previous coldness has not yet subsided due to the manifestation of a dissimilar temperature—this interval is called the 'continuity present.' From rebirth-linking up to death, however, is what is called the 'duration present.' Both of these can be terminated. How? Indeed, when an attack is made against it, the life-nonad that has received the attack, while ceasing, becomes a condition for a weak continuity with diminished momentum. Therefore, the continuity present or the duration present ceases in the interim, without reaching its determined time. Thus, both can be terminated. Therefore, it should be understood that the statement, “He disrupts the continuity,” was said with reference to these two.

Imassa panatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ pāṇo veditabbo, pāṇātipāto veditabbo, pāṇātipāti veditabbo, pāṇātipātassa payogo veditabbo. Tattha “pāṇo”ti vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Jīvitindriyañhi atipātento “pāṇaṃ atipātetī”ti vuccati taṃ vuttappakārameva. “Pāṇātipāto”ti yāya cetanāya jīvitindriyupacchedakaṃ payogaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sā vadhakacetanā “pāṇātipāto”ti vuccati. “Pāṇātipātī”ti vuttacetanāsamaṅgi puggalo daṭṭhabbo. “Pāṇātipātassa payogo”ti pāṇātipātassa chapayogā – sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, thāvaro, vijjāmayo, iddhimayoti.
