However, to make the meaning of this clear, 'living being' should be understood, 'the taking of life' should be understood, 'one who takes life' should be understood, and 'the application for taking life' should be understood. Therein, 'living being' is, by conventional designation, a being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty. For one who destroys the life faculty is said to 'take the life of a living being,' and this is just as has been described. 'The taking of life' is the volition of killing by which one initiates an application that cuts off the life faculty; that volition of killing is called 'the taking of life.' 'One who takes life' should be understood as the person endowed with the aforementioned volition. As for 'the application for taking life,' there are six applications for taking life: by one's own hand, by command, by missile, by a fixed device, by magic, and by psychic power.

Tattha “sāhatthiko”ti sayaṃ mārentassa kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā paharaṇaṃ. “Āṇattiko”ti aññaṃ āṇāpentassa “evaṃ vijjhitvā vā paharitvā vā mārehī”ti āṇāpanaṃ. “Nissaggiyo”ti dūre ṭhitaṃ māretukāmassa kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā ususattiyantapāsāṇādīnaṃ nissajjanaṃ. “Thāvaro”ti asañcārimena upakaraṇena māretukāmassa opātaapassenaupanikkhipanaṃ bhesajjasaṃvidhānaṃ. Te cattāropi parato pāḷivaṇṇanāyameva vitthārato āvibhavissanti.

Therein, 'by one's own hand' means striking with one's body or with something connected to one's body, on the part of one who is killing by oneself. 'By command' means the commanding of another, saying, “Kill by piercing or by striking in this way.” 'By missile' means the releasing of arrows, spears, machines, stones, and so on, with one's body or with something connected to one's body, on the part of one who desires to kill someone standing at a distance. 'By a fixed device' means, for one who desires to kill with an immovable instrument, the digging of a pit, the setting of a trap, the placing of a weapon nearby, or the preparing of poison. These four will become clear in detail later in the commentary on the Pāli itself.

Vijjāmayaiddhimayā [M 2.0040] pana pāḷiyaṃ anāgatā. Te evaṃ veditabbā. Saṅkhepato hi māraṇatthaṃ vijjāparijappanaṃ vijjāmayo payogo. Aṭṭhakathāsu [P 2.0440] pana “katamo vijjāmayo payogo? Āthabbaṇikā āthabbaṇaṃ payojenti; nagare vā ruddhe saṅgāme vā paccupaṭṭhite paṭisenāya paccatthikesu paccāmittesu ītiṃ uppādenti, upaddavaṃ uppādenti, rogaṃ uppādenti, pajjarakaṃ uppādenti, sūcikaṃ karonti, visūcikaṃ karonti, pakkhandiyaṃ karonti. Evaṃ āthabbaṇikā āthabbaṇaṃ payojenti. Vijjādhārā vijjaṃ parivattetvā nagare vā ruddhe…pe… pakkhandiyaṃ karontī”ti evaṃ vijjāmayaṃ payogaṃ dassetvā āthabbaṇikehi ca vijjādharehi ca māritānaṃ bahūni vatthūni vuttāni, kiṃ tehi! Idañhettha lakkhaṇaṃ māraṇāya vijjāparijappanaṃ vijjāmayo payogoti.

However, the applications by means of magic and psychic power do not appear in the Pāli. They should be understood thus. In brief, the recitation of spells for the purpose of killing is the application by means of magic. But in the commentaries, having shown the application by means of magic thus: “What is the application by means of magic? Practitioners of the Atharva Veda employ the Atharva spell; when a city is besieged or a battle is imminent, they create affliction, create calamity, create disease, create high fever, cause stabbing pains, cause cholera, and cause dysentery among the opposing army, the hostile, and the enemy. Thus do practitioners of the Atharva Veda employ the Atharva spell. Bearers of spells, having recited the spell repeatedly… cause dysentery,” many stories are told of those killed by practitioners of the Atharva Veda and by bearers of spells. But what is the use of them? For this is the characteristic here: the recitation of spells for the purpose of killing is the application by means of magic.

Kammavipākajāya iddhiyā payojanaṃ iddhimayo payogo. Kammavipākajiddhi ca nāmesā nāgānaṃ nāgiddhi, supaṇṇānaṃ supaṇṇiddhi, yakkhānaṃ yakkhiddhi, devānaṃ deviddhi, rājūnaṃ rājiddhīti [V 2.0038] bahuvidhā. Tattha diṭṭhadaṭṭhaphuṭṭhavisānaṃ nāgānaṃ disvā ḍaṃsitvā phusitvā ca parūpaghātakaraṇe “nāgiddhi” veditabbā. Supaṇṇānaṃ mahāsamuddato dvattibyāmasatappamāṇanāguddharaṇe “supaṇṇiddhi” veditabbā. Yakkhā pana neva āgacchantā na paharantā dissanti, tehi pahaṭasattā pana tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne maranti, tatra tesaṃ “yakkhiddhi” daṭṭhabbā. Vessavaṇassa sotāpannakālato pubbe nayanāvudhena olokitakumbhaṇḍānaṃ maraṇe aññesañca devānaṃ yathāsakaṃ iddhānubhāve “deviddhi” veditabbā. Rañño cakkavattissa saparisassa ākāsagamanādīsu, asokassa heṭṭhā upari ca yojane āṇāpavattanādīsu, piturañño ca sīhaḷanarindassa dāṭhākoṭanena cūḷasumanakuṭumbiyassamaraṇe [P 2.0441] “rājiddhi” daṭṭhabbāti.

The application of power born of kamma-result is the application by means of psychic power. And this power born of kamma-result is of many kinds, namely: for nāgas, it is nāga-power; for supaṇṇas, it is supaṇṇa-power; for yakkhas, it is yakkha-power; for devas, it is deva-power; for kings, it is king-power. Therein, 'nāga-power' should be understood as the act of destroying others by nāgas possessing venom that works by sight, by bite, and by touch. 'Supaṇṇa-power' should be understood as the lifting of nāgas measuring two or three hundred fathoms from the great ocean by supaṇṇas. As for yakkhas, they are not seen when they are coming nor when they are striking; but beings struck by them die on that very spot. Therein, their 'yakkha-power' should be seen. 'Deva-power' should be understood in the case of Vessavaṇa who, before the time he became a stream-enterer, caused the death of kumbhaṇḍas by looking at them with his eye-weapon, and in the majestic power of their respective powers of other devas. 'King-power' should be seen in such cases as the traveling through the sky of a wheel-turning monarch with his retinue; in the exercising of command by Asoka within a yojana below and above; and in the death of the householder Cūḷasumana caused by the striking of the tooth by the Sīhaḷa king, King Piṭu.

Keci pana “puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā iddhimā cetovasippatto aññissā kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ pāpakena manasāanupekkhitā hoti ‘aho vatāyaṃ kucchigato gabbho na sotthinā abhinikkhameyyā’ti. Evampi bhikkhave kulumbassa upaghāto hotī”ti ādikāni suttāni dassetvā bhāvanāmayiddhiyāpi parūpaghātakammaṃ vadanti; saha parūpaghātakaraṇena ca ādittagharūparikhittassa [M 2.0041] udakaghaṭassa bhedanamiva iddhivināsañca icchanti; taṃ tesaṃ icchāmattameva. Kasmā? Yasmā kusalavedanāvitakkaparittattikehi na sameti. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi bhāvanāmayiddhi nāma kusalattike kusalā ceva abyākatā ca, pāṇātipāto akusalo. Vedanāttike adukkhamasukhasampayuttā pāṇātipāto dukkhasampayutto. Vitakkattike avitakkāvicārā, pāṇātipāto savitakkasavicāro. Parittattike mahaggatā, pāṇātipāto parittoti.

Some, however, after citing suttas such as, 'Furthermore, monks, some ascetic or brahmin, possessing power and mastery of mind, might look upon a fetus in another's womb with a malevolent mind, thinking, "Oh, may this fetus in the womb not emerge safely!" In this way too, monks, is the destruction of a family member brought about,' state that the act of destroying others can also be done by the power developed through meditation. And, simultaneously with the act of destroying others, they hold that the power is destroyed, like the breaking of a water pot thrown upon a burning house. But that is merely their own opinion. Why? Because it is not consistent with the wholesome, feeling, thought, and limited triads. How so? This power developed through meditation, in the wholesome triad, is either wholesome or indeterminate, whereas the destruction of life is unwholesome. In the feeling triad, it is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, whereas the destruction of life is associated with painful feeling. In the thought triad, it is without initial and sustained application of thought, whereas the destruction of life has initial and sustained application of thought. In the limited triad, it is exalted, whereas the destruction of life is limited.

Satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyāti ettha haratīti hārakaṃ. Kiṃ harati? Jīvitaṃ. Atha vā haritabbanti hārakaṃ; upanikkhipitabbanti attho. Satthañca taṃ hārakañcāti satthahārakaṃ. Assāti manussaviggahassa. Pariyeseyyāti yathā labhati tathā kareyya; upanikkhipeyyāti attho. Etena thāvarappayogaṃ dasseti. Itarathā hi pariyiṭṭhamatteneva pārājiko bhaveyya; na cetaṃ yuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana sabbaṃ byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā yaṃ ettha thāvarappayogasaṅgahitaṃ satthaṃ, tadeva dassetuṃ “asiṃ vā…pe… rajjuṃ vā”ti padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding the phrase 'or he might seek for him a weapon-bringer' (satthahārakaṃ), here, because it 'takes away' (harati), it is a 'taker' (hāraka). What does it take away? Life. Alternatively, because it is 'to be brought' (haritabba), it is a 'bringer' (hāraka); the meaning is 'to be placed nearby'. It is both a weapon (sattha) and that which takes away or is to be brought (hāraka), thus it is a satthahāraka. 'For him' (assa) means for the human body. 'He might seek' (pariyeseyya) means he should act in such a way that he obtains it; the meaning is that he should place it nearby. By this, a lasting application is shown. For otherwise, he would be defeated merely by the act of searching, and this is not proper. In the Pāli, however, without taking every single word, the analysis of the term (padabhājana) 'a sword or... a rope' is given to show only that weapon which is included in 'lasting application'.

Tattha satthanti vuttāvasesaṃ yaṃkiñci samukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Laguḷapāsāṇavisarajjūnañca jīvitavināsanabhāvato satthasaṅgaho veditabbo. Maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vāti ettha yasmā “kiṃ tuyhiminā [P 2.0442] pāpakena dujjīvitena, yo tvaṃ na labhasi paṇītāni bhojanāni bhuñjitu”ntiādinā [V 2.0039] nayena jīvite ādīnavaṃ dassentopi “tvaṃ khosi upāsaka katakalyāṇo…pe… akataṃ tayā pāpaṃ, mataṃ te jīvitā seyyo, ito tvaṃ kālaṅkato paricarissasi accharāparivuto nandanavane sukhappatto viharissasī”tiādinā nayena maraṇe vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇantopi maraṇavaṇṇameva saṃvaṇṇeti. Tasmā dvidhā bhinditvā padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ – “jīvite ādīnavaṃ dasseti, maraṇe vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇatī”ti.

Therein, 'weapon' should be understood as any remaining thing whatsoever that has a point or edge, other than those already mentioned. And clubs, stones, poison, and ropes should be understood as included under 'weapon' because of their nature of destroying life. Regarding 'or he might praise death', because one who points out the drawbacks of life by saying, 'What use is this evil, wretched life to you, who cannot get to eat fine foods?' and so on, and one who speaks of the virtues of death by saying, 'You, lay follower, have done good... you have done no evil. Death is better for you than life. Having passed away from here, you will move about, attended by celestial nymphs, and will dwell happily in the Nandana Grove,' and so on, are both praising the virtues of death. Therefore, the analysis of the term was given by the Blessed One after dividing it in two: 'he points out the drawbacks in life' and 'he speaks of the virtues in death'.

Maraṇāya vā samādapeyyāti maraṇatthāya upāyaṃ gāhāpeyya. Satthaṃ vā āharāti ādīsu ca yampi na vuttaṃ “sobbhe vā narake vā papāte vā papatā”tiādi, taṃ sabbaṃ parato vuttanayattā atthato vuttamevāti veditabbaṃ. Na hi sakkā sabbaṃ sarūpeneva vattuṃ.

'Or he might incite one to death' means he would cause one to take up a means for the purpose of death. And in cases such as 'Bring a weapon,' whatever was not explicitly stated, such as 'Fall into a pit, a chasm, or off a cliff,' all that should be understood as having been stated in meaning, because of the method stated later. For it is not possible to state everything in its own specific form.

Iti [M 2.0042] cittamanoti iticitto itimano; “mataṃ te jīvitā seyyo”ti ettha vuttamaraṇacitto maraṇamanoti attho. Yasmā panettha mano cittasaddassa atthadīpanatthaṃ vutto, atthato panetaṃ ubhayampi ekameva, tasmā tassa atthato abhedaṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ cittaṃ taṃ mano, yaṃ mano taṃ citta”nti vuttaṃ. Itisaddaṃ pana uddharitvāpi na tāva attho vutto. Cittasaṅkappoti imasmiṃ pade adhikāravasena itisaddo āharitabbo. Idañhi “iticittasaṅkappo”ti evaṃ avuttampi adhikārato vuttameva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hissa tamevaatthaṃ dassento “maraṇasaññī”tiādimāha. Yasmā cettha “saṅkappo”ti nayidaṃ vitakkassa nāmaṃ. Atha kho saṃvidahanamattassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañca saṃvidahanaṃ imasmiṃ atthe saññācetanādhippāyehi saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Tasmā citto nānappakārako saṅkappo assāti cittasaṅkappoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hissa padabhājanampi [P 2.0443] saññācetanādhippāyavasena vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “adhippāyo”ti vitakko veditabbo.

“With such a mind (citta), with such a mind (mano)” means having a mind (citta) for death, a mind (mano) for death, as stated in the phrase “Death is better for you than life.” Since “mano” is used here to clarify the meaning of the word “citta,” and in meaning both are one and the same, to show their non-difference in meaning it is said: “What is citta is mano, what is mano is citta.” However, even having pointed out the word “iti,” its meaning is not yet stated. In the phrase “cittasaṅkappo,” the word “iti” should be supplied by virtue of the context. For this should be understood as having been stated by context, even though it was not explicitly stated as “iticittasaṅkappo.” Indeed, showing that very meaning, He said, “perceiving death,” etc. And here, “saṅkappa” is not a name for “vitakka” (initial thought) alone. Rather, it is a term for mere determination (saṃvidahana). And that determination, in this context, is included by way of perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), and intention (adhippāya). Therefore, the meaning should be seen thus: “He has a varied, manifold intention (saṅkappa),” thus he is one with a “varied intention” (cittasaṅkappa). Indeed, the analysis of this term is also given in terms of perception, volition, and intention. And here, “adhippāya” (intention) should be understood as “vitakka” (initial thought).

Uccāvacehi ākārehīti mahantāmahantehi upāyehi. Tattha maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇane tāva jīvite ādīnavadassanavasena avacākāratā maraṇe vaṇṇabhaṇanavasena uccākāratā veditabbā. Samādapane pana muṭṭhijāṇunipphoṭanādīhi maraṇasamādapanavasena uccākāratā, ekato bhuñjantassa nakhe visaṃ pakkhipitvā maraṇādisamādapanavasena avacākāratā veditabbā.

“By high and low means” means by great and humble, or manifest and unmanifest, methods. Therein, in the context of praising the quality of death, the state of being a humble means is to be understood by way of showing the danger in life, while the state of being a noble means is to be understood by way of speaking of the virtues of death. As for instigation, the state of being a manifest means is to be understood by way of causing one to undertake death through striking with the fist, hitting with the knee, and so on; the state of being an unmanifest means is to be understood by way of causing one to undertake death by putting poison under the fingernail of one eating together with oneself.

Sobbhe vā narake vā papāte vāti ettha sobbho nāma samantato chinnataṭo gambhīro āvāṭo. Narako nāma tattha tattha phalantiyā bhūmiyā sayameva nibbattā mahādarī, yattha hatthīpi patanti, corāpi nilīnā tiṭṭhanti. Papātoti pabbatantare vā thalantare vā ekato chinno [V 2.0040] hoti. Purime upādāyāti methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā adinnañca ādiyitvā pārājikaṃ āpattiṃ āpanne puggale upādāya. Sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca pākaṭamevāti.

Regarding “in a pit, or in a chasm, or on a precipice”: herein, a “pit” (sobbha) is a deep hole with a bank cut away all around. A “chasm” (naraka) is a great ravine that has formed spontaneously in the earth where it has split open in various places, into which even elephants can fall, and where thieves can remain hidden. A “precipice” (papāta) is what is cut off on one side, whether between mountains or between uplands. “With reference to the former” means with reference to those persons who have fallen into a Pārājika offense by having engaged in sexual intercourse and by having taken what was not given. The remainder is clear because it follows the method stated before and because its meaning is plain.

174. Evaṃ uddiṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ padānukkamena vibhajitvā idāni yasmā heṭṭhā padabhājanīyamhi saṅkhepeneva manussaviggahapārājikaṃ dassitaṃ, na vitthārena āpattiṃ āropetvā tanti ṭhapitā. Saṅkhepadassite ca atthe na sabbākāreneva [M 2.0043] bhikkhū nayaṃ gahetuṃ sakkonti, anāgate ca pāpapuggalānampi okāso hoti, tasmā bhikkhūnañca sabbākārena nayaggahaṇatthaṃ anāgate ca pāpapuggalānaṃ okāsapaṭibāhanatthaṃ puna “sāmaṃ adhiṭṭhāyā”tiādinā nayena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārato manussaviggahapārājikaṃ dassento “sāmanti sayaṃ hanatī”tiādimāha.

174. Having thus analyzed the declared training rule according to the sequence of words, now, because the Pārājika concerning a human being was shown below in the word-by-word analysis only in brief—the canonical text was not established by applying the offense in detail. And when the meaning is shown in brief, monks are not able to grasp the method in all its aspects, and in the future, there can be an opportunity for evil persons. Therefore, for the purpose of monks grasping the method in all its aspects and for the purpose of preventing the opportunity for evil persons in the future, showing the Pārājika concerning a human being in detail after again establishing the matrix by the method beginning with “having determined by oneself,” He said, “‘By oneself’ means one kills by oneself,” and so on.

Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanāya saddhiṃ vinicchayakathā – kāyenāti hatthena vā pādena vā muṭṭhinā vā jāṇunā vā yena kenaci aṅgapaccaṅgena. Kāyapaṭibaddhenāti kāyato amocitena asiādinā paharaṇena. Nissaggiyenāti kāyato ca kāyapaṭibaddhato ca mocitena ususattiādinā. Ettāvatā sāhatthiko [P 2.0444] ca nissaggiyo cāti dve payogā vuttā honti.

Herein is the judicial decision, together with the commentary on the unclear words: “By body” means by hand or by foot, by fist or by knee, or by any major or minor limb. “By what is connected to the body” means by a weapon such as a sword that is not released from the body. “By what is thrown” means by a weapon such as an arrow or a spear that is released from the body or from what is connected to the body. By this much, two applications are said to be spoken of: that by one's own hand and that which is thrown.

Tattha ekameko uddissānuddissabhedato duvidho. Tattha uddesike yaṃ uddissa paharati, tasseva maraṇena kammunā bajjhati. “Yo koci maratū”ti evaṃ anuddesike pahārappaccayā yassa kassaci maraṇena kammunā bajjhati. Ubhayathāpi ca paharitamatte vā maratu pacchā vā teneva rogena, paharitamatteyeva kammunā bajjhati. Maraṇādhippāyena ca pahāraṃ datvā tena amatassa puna aññacittena pahāre dinne pacchāpi yadi paṭhamappahāreneva marati, tadā eva kammunā baddho. Atha dutiyappahārena marati, natthi pāṇātipāto. Ubhayehi matepi paṭhamappahāreneva kammunā baddho. Ubhayehi amate nevatthi pāṇātipāto. Esa nayo bahūhipi ekassa pahāre dinne. Tatrāpi hi yassa pahārena marati, tasseva kammunā baddho hotīti.

Therein, each of these is twofold by the distinction of specified and unspecified. Therein, in the specified case, one is bound by the kamma through the death of the very one whom one strikes with intention. In the unspecified case, with the thought, “Let anyone die,” one is bound by the kamma through the death of anyone whatsoever on account of the blow. And in both cases, whether the person dies at the very moment of being struck or later from that same affliction, one is bound by the kamma at the very moment of striking. And having given a blow with the intention to kill, if to that one who did not die from it, a blow is given again with a different intention, and if he dies later only by the first blow, then one is bound by the kamma of that first act. But if he dies by the second blow, there is no taking of life. Even if he dies from both blows, one is bound by the kamma of the first blow alone. If he does not die from both blows, there is no taking of life. This is the method also when blows are given by many to one person. For there too, only the one by whose blow the person dies is bound by the kamma.

Kammāpattibyattibhāvatthañcettha eḷakacatukkampi veditabbaṃ. Yo hi eḷakaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nipannaṃ upadhāreti “rattiṃ āgantvā vadhissāmī”ti. Eḷakassa ca nipannokāse tassa mātā vā pitā vā arahā vā paṇḍukāsāvaṃ pārupitvā nipanno hoti. So rattibhāge āgantvā “eḷakaṃ māremī”ti mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā arahantaṃ vā māreti. “Imaṃ vatthuṃ māremī”ti cetanāya atthibhāvato ghātako ca hoti, anantariyakammañca phusati, pārājikañca āpajjati[V 2.0041]. Añño koci āgantuko nipanno hoti[M 2.0044], “eḷakaṃ māremī”ti taṃ māreti, ghātako ca hoti pārājikañca āpajjati, ānantariyaṃ na phusati. Yakkho vā peto vā nipanno hoti, “eḷakaṃ māremī”ti taṃ māreti ghātakova hoti, na cānantariyaṃ phusati, na ca pārājikaṃ āpajjati, thullaccayaṃ pana hoti. Añño koci nipanno natthi, eḷakova hoti taṃ māreti, ghātako ca hoti, pācittiyañca āpajjati. “Mātāpituarahantānaṃ aññataraṃ [P 2.0445] māremī”ti tesaṃyeva aññataraṃ māreti, ghātako ca hoti, ānantariyañca phusati, pārājikañca āpajjati. “Tesaṃ aññataraṃ māressāmī”ti aññaṃ āgantukaṃ māreti, yakkhaṃ vā petaṃ vā māreti, eḷakaṃ vā māreti, pubbe vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Idha pana cetanā dāruṇā hotīti.

And here, the fourfold case of the goat should also be understood for the purpose of making manifest the distinctions of kamma and offenses. Indeed, a monk observes a goat lying in a certain place, thinking, 'I will come at night and kill it.' And in the place where the goat was lying, his mother or father or an Arahant, having wrapped himself in a pale yellow robe, is lying down. That monk comes in the night and, thinking, 'I will kill the goat,' kills his mother or father or the Arahant. Because of the existence of the intention, 'I will kill this being,' he is a killer, he incurs an immediately resultant kamma, and he falls into a Pārājika offense. If some other visiting person is lying there, and thinking, 'I will kill the goat,' he kills him, he is a killer and falls into a Pārājika offense, but he does not incur an immediately resultant kamma. If a yakkha or a peta is lying there, and thinking, 'I will kill the goat,' he kills it, he is indeed a killer, but he does not incur an immediately resultant kamma, nor does he fall into a Pārājika offense; it is, however, a grave offense. If no one else is lying there and only the goat is, and he kills it, he is a killer and falls into a Pācittiya offense. If, thinking, 'I will kill one among my mother, father, and an Arahant,' he kills one of them, he is a killer, incurs an immediately resultant kamma, and falls into a Pārājika offense. If, thinking, 'I will kill one of them,' he kills another visiting person, or kills a yakkha or a peta, or kills a goat, it should be understood according to the method stated before. Here, however, the intention is fierce, it should be understood.

Aññānipi ettha palālapuñjādivatthūni veditabbāni. Yo hi “lohitakaṃ asiṃ vā sattiṃ vā pucchissāmī”ti palālapuñje pavesento tattha nipannaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā arahantaṃ vā āgantukapurisaṃ vā yakkhaṃ vā petaṃ vā tiracchānagataṃ vā māreti, vohāravasena “ghātako”ti vuccati, vadhakacetanāya pana abhāvato neva kammaṃ phusati, na āpattiṃ āpajjati. Yo pana evaṃ pavesento sarīrasamphassaṃ sallakkhetvā “satto maññe abbhantaragato maratū”ti pavesetvā māreti, tassa tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ anurūpena kammabaddho ca āpatti ca veditabbā. Esa nayo tattha nidahanatthaṃ pavesentassāpi vanappagumbādīsu khipantassāpi.

Here, other cases such as a pile of straw should also be understood. For if someone, thinking, 'I will wipe this blood-stained sword or spear,' thrusts it into a pile of straw and thereby kills a mother, father, Arahant, visiting person, yakkha, peta, or animal lying there, he is called a 'killer' by way of conventional speech. However, due to the absence of an intention to kill, he neither incurs kamma nor falls into an offense. But if someone, while thrusting it in this way, perceives bodily contact and thinks, 'I think it is a being inside; let it die,' and then thrusts it in and kills it, it should be understood that for him there is bondage by kamma and an offense appropriate to those beings. This is the same principle for one who thrusts something in to hide it there, or for one who throws something into a forest thicket and the like.

Yopi “coraṃ māremī”ti coravesena gacchantaṃ pitaraṃ māreti, ānantariyañca phusati, pārājiko ca hoti. Yo pana parasenāya aññañca yodhaṃ pitarañca kammaṃ karonte disvā yodhassa usuṃ khipati, “etaṃ vijjhitvā mama pitaraṃ vijjhissatī”ti yathādhippāyaṃ gate pitughātako hoti. “Yodhe viddhe mama pitā palāyissatī”ti khipati, usu ayathādhippāyaṃ gantvā pitaraṃ māreti, vohāravasena “pitughātako”ti vuccati; ānantariyaṃ pana natthīti.

Furthermore, if someone, thinking, 'I will kill a thief,' kills his father who is going about in the guise of a thief, he incurs an immediately resultant kamma and also commits a pārājika offense. But if one, seeing his father and another warrior fighting in the enemy army, shoots an arrow at the warrior, thinking, 'Having pierced this one, it will then pierce my father,' and it goes as intended, he becomes a parricide. If he shoots thinking, 'When the warrior is struck, my father will flee,' but the arrow goes contrary to his intention and kills his father, he is called a 'parricide' by way of conventional speech; however, there is no immediately resultant kamma.

Adhiṭṭhahitvāti samīpe ṭhatvā. Āṇāpetīti uddissa vā anuddissa vā āṇāpeti. Tattha parasenāya paccupaṭṭhitāya anuddisseva “evaṃ vijjha[M 2.0045], evaṃ pahara, evaṃ ghātehī”ti āṇatte yattake āṇatto ghāteti, tattakā ubhinnaṃ pāṇātipātā. Sace tattha āṇāpakassa mātāpitaro honti, ānantariyampi phusati. Sace āṇattasseva mātāpitaro, sova ānantariyaṃ phusati. Sace [P 2.0446] arahā hoti, ubhopi ānantariyaṃ phusanti. Uddisitvā pana “etaṃ dīghaṃ rassaṃ rattakañcukaṃ nīlakañcukaṃ hatthikkhandhe nisinnaṃ majjhe nisinnaṃ vijjha pahara ghātehī”ti [V 2.0042] āṇatte sace so tameva ghāteti, ubhinnampi pāṇātipāto; ānantariyavatthumhi ca ānantariyaṃ. Sace aññaṃ māreti, āṇāpakassa natthi pāṇātipāto. Etena āṇattiko payogo vutto hoti. Tattha –

“Adhiṭṭhahitvā” means standing nearby. “Āṇāpeti” means he commands, either specifying or not specifying. In this context, when the enemy army is present, if he commands without specifying, 'Shoot like this, strike like this, kill like this,' then for however many the one commanded kills, there are that many acts of killing living beings for both of them. If the commander's parents are among them, he also incurs an immediately resultant kamma. If they are the parents of the one commanded, he alone incurs an immediately resultant kamma. If it is an Arahant, both incur an immediately resultant kamma. But when specifying, commanding: 'Shoot, strike, kill that tall one, that short one, the one wearing a red tunic, the one wearing a blue tunic, the one seated on the elephant's back, the one seated in the middle,' if he kills that very one, it is an act of killing living beings for both; and if the object is one that entails an immediately resultant kamma, an immediately resultant kamma is also incurred. If he kills another, there is no act of killing living beings for the commander. By this, the application by command is explained. Herein—

Vatthuṃ kālañca okāsaṃ, āvudhaṃ iriyāpathaṃ;

Tulayitvā pañca ṭhānāni, dhāreyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇo.

Having weighed the object, the time, the place, the weapon, and the posture—these five factors—the discerning one should grasp the meaning.

Aparo nayo –

Another method—

Vatthu kālo ca okāso, āvudhaṃ iriyāpatho;

Kiriyāvisesoti ime, cha āṇattiniyāmakā.

The object, the time, the place, the weapon, the posture, and the specific action—these six are the determinants of a command.

Tattha “vatthū”ti māretabbo satto. “Kālo”ti pubbaṇhasāyanhādikālo ca yobbanathāvariyādikālo ca. “Okāso”ti gāmo vā vanaṃ vā gehadvāraṃ vā gehamajjhaṃ vā rathikā vā siṅghāṭakaṃ vāti evamādi. “Āvudha”nti asi vā usu vā satti vāti evamādi. “Iriyāpatho”ti māretabbassa gamanaṃ vā nisajjā vāti evamādi. “Kiriyāviseso”ti vijjhanaṃ vā chedanaṃ vā bhedanaṃ vā saṅkhamuṇḍakaṃ vāti evamādi.

Therein, 'the object' means the being to be killed. 'The time' means the time of day, such as morning or evening, and the time of life, such as youth or old age. 'The place' means a village, a forest, a house door, the middle of a house, a street, a crossroads, and so forth. 'The weapon' means a sword, an arrow, a spear, and so forth. 'The posture' means the walking or sitting, and so forth, of the one to be killed. 'The specific action' means piercing, cutting, breaking, making the head bald like a conch shell, and so forth.

Yadi hi vatthuṃ visaṃvādetvā “yaṃ mārehī”ti āṇatto tato aññaṃ māreti, “purato paharitvā mārehī”ti vā āṇatto pacchato vā passato vā aññasmiṃ vā padese paharitvā māreti. Āṇāpakassa natthi kammabandho; āṇattasseva kammabandho. Atha vatthuṃ avisaṃvādetvā yathāṇattiyā māreti, āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇe āṇattassa ca māraṇakkhaṇeti ubhayesampi kammabandho. Vatthuvisesena panettha kammaviseso ca āpattiviseso ca hotīti. Evaṃ tāva vatthumhi saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

For if, there being a discrepancy regarding the object, one who was ordered, 'Kill so-and-so,' kills another; or if, having been ordered, 'Strike and kill him from the front,' he strikes and kills from behind, from the side, or in another place, there is no karmic bondage for the commander; the karmic bondage is for the one commanded only. But if, with no discrepancy regarding the object, he kills according to the command, there is karmic bondage for both: for the commander at the moment of the command, and for the one commanded at the moment of the killing. Herein, according to the distinction of the object, there is also a distinction of kamma and a distinction of offense. Thus, firstly, conformity and non-conformity with the specification regarding the object should be understood.

Kāle [M 2.0046] pana yo “ajja sve”ti aniyametvā “pubbaṇhe mārehī”ti āṇatto [P 2.0447] yadā kadāci pubbaṇhe māreti, natthi visaṅketo. Yo pana “ajja pubbaṇhe”ti vutto majjhanhe vā sāyanhe vā sve vā pubbaṇhe māreti. Visaṅketo hoti, āṇāpakassa natthi kammabandho. Pubbaṇhe māretuṃ vāyamantassa majjhanhe jātepi eseva nayo. Etena nayena sabbakālappabhedesu saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

Regarding time, however: if one is commanded, 'Kill him in the morning,' without the specification 'today' or 'tomorrow,' and he kills him in the morning on some day or other, there is no discrepancy. But if one, having been told, 'Kill him this morning,' kills him at midday, in the evening, or on the next day in the morning, there is a discrepancy; the commander has no karmic bondage. This is the same principle even if it becomes midday while one is striving to kill in the morning. By this method, conformity and non-conformity should be understood in all distinctions of time.

Okāsepi [V 2.0043] yo “etaṃ gāme ṭhitaṃ mārehī”ti aniyametvā āṇatto taṃ yattha katthaci māreti, natthi visaṅketo. Yo pana “gāmeyevā”ti niyametvā āṇatto vane māreti, tathā “vane”ti āṇatto gāme māreti. “Antogehadvāre”ti āṇatto gehamajjhe māreti, visaṅketo. Etena nayena sabbokāsabhedesu saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

Regarding place also: if one is commanded without specification, 'Kill this one who is in the village,' and he kills him anywhere whatsoever, there is no discrepancy. But if one, having been commanded with the specification, 'In the village only,' kills him in the forest; or, similarly, having been commanded, 'In the forest,' kills him in the village; or, having been commanded, 'Within the doorway of the house,' kills him in the middle of the house, there is a discrepancy. By this method, conformity and non-conformity should be understood in all distinctions of place.

Āvudhepi yo “asinā vā usunā vā”ti aniyametvā “āvudhena mārehī”ti āṇatto yena kenaci āvudhena māreti, natthi visaṅketo. Yo pana “asinā”ti vutto usunā, “iminā vā asinā”ti vutto aññena asinā māreti. Etasseva vā asissa “imāya dhārāya mārehī”ti vutto itarāya vā dhārāya talena vā tuṇḍena vā tharunā vā māreti, visaṅketo. Etena nayena sabbaāvudhabhedesu saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

Regarding weapons also: if one is commanded, 'Kill him with a weapon,' without specifying, 'With a sword or with an arrow,' and he kills with any weapon whatsoever, there is no discrepancy. But if one, having been told, 'With a sword,' kills with an arrow; or, having been told, 'With this sword,' kills with another sword; or, of this very sword, having been told, 'Kill with this edge,' he kills with the other edge, or with the flat, or with the point, or with the hilt, there is a discrepancy. By this method, conformity and non-conformity should be understood in all distinctions of weapons.

Iriyāpathe pana yo “etaṃ gacchantaṃ mārehī”ti vadati, āṇatto ca naṃ sace gacchantaṃ māreti, natthi visaṅketo. “Gacchantameva mārehī”ti vutto pana sace nisinnaṃ māreti. “Nisinnameva vā mārehī”ti vutto gacchantaṃ māreti, visaṅketo hoti. Etena nayena sabbairiyāpathabhedesu saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

Furthermore, regarding posture: if one says, 'Kill this person while he is walking,' and the one ordered kills him while he is walking, there is no discrepancy. But if, having been told, 'Kill him only while he is walking,' he kills him while he is sitting; or, having been told, 'Kill him only while he is sitting,' he kills him while he is walking, there is a discrepancy. By this method, conformity and non-conformity should be understood in all distinctions of posture.

Kiriyāvisesepi yo “vijjhitvā mārehī”ti vutto vijjhitvāva māreti, natthi visaṅketo. Yo pana “vijjhitvā mārehī”ti vutto chinditvā māreti, visaṅketo. Etena nayena sabbakiriyāvisesabhedesu saṅketavisaṅketatā veditabbā.

Also regarding the specifics of the action: if one who was told, 'Kill by piercing,' kills by piercing, there is no discrepancy. But if one who was told, 'Kill by piercing,' kills by cutting, there is a discrepancy. By this method, conformity and non-conformity should be understood in all distinctions of specific actions.

Yo pana liṅgavasena “dīghaṃ rassaṃ kāḷaṃ odātaṃ kisaṃ thūlaṃ mārehī”ti aniyametvā āṇāpeti, āṇatto ca yaṃkiñci tādisaṃ [M 2.0047] māreti, natthi [P 2.0448] visaṅketo ubhinnaṃ pārājikaṃ. Atha pana so attānaṃ sandhāya āṇāpeti, āṇatto ca “ayameva īdiso”ti āṇāpakameva māreti, āṇāpakassa dukkaṭaṃ, vadhakassa pārājikaṃ. Āṇāpako attānaṃ sandhāya āṇāpeti, itaro aññaṃ tādisaṃ māreti, āṇāpako muccati, vadhakasseva pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Okāsassa aniyamitattā. Sace pana attānaṃ sandhāya āṇāpentopi okāsaṃ niyameti, “asukasmiṃ nāma rattiṭṭhāne vā divāṭṭhāne vā therāsane vā navāsane vā majjhimāsane vā nisinnaṃ evarūpaṃ nāma mārehī”ti. Tattha ca añño nisinno hoti, sace āṇatto taṃ māreti, neva vadhako muccati na āṇāpako. Kasmā? Okāsassa niyamitattā. Sace pana niyamitokāsato [V 2.0044] aññatra māreti, āṇāpako muccatīti ayaṃ nayo mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ suṭṭhu daḷhaṃ katvā vutto. Tasmā ettha na anādariyaṃ kātabbanti.

Furthermore, if one, by way of characteristics, gives an instruction without specifying, saying, 'Kill a tall one, a short one, a dark one, a fair one, a thin one, or a fat one,' and the one instructed kills any such person, there is no discrepancy; for both, it is a pārājika offense. But if he gives the instruction with reference to himself, and the one instructed, thinking, 'This is such a person,' kills the instructor himself, for the instructor it is a dukkaṭa offense, and for the killer, it is a pārājika. If the instructor gives the instruction with reference to himself, and the other kills another such person, the instructor is exempt; it is a pārājika for the killer only. Why? Because the location was not specified. But if, while giving the instruction with reference to himself, he also specifies the location, saying, 'Kill such a person sitting in such-and-such a place at night, or a place in the day, or on the elder's seat, or the junior's seat, or the middle seat,' and another person is sitting there, if the one instructed kills that person, neither the killer is exempt nor the instructor. Why? Because the location was specified. But if he kills outside the specified location, the instructor is exempt. This principle is stated very firmly in the Great Commentary. Therefore, one should not be heedless in this matter.

Adhiṭṭhāyāti mātikāvasena āṇattikapayogakathā niṭṭhitā.

By way of the mātikā heading 'By determination,' the discussion on the application of a command is concluded.

Idāni ye dūtenāti imassa mātikāpadassa niddesadassanatthaṃ “bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetī”tiādayo cattāro vārā vuttā. Tesu so taṃ maññamānoti so āṇatto yo āṇāpakena “itthannāmo”ti akkhāto, taṃ maññamāno tameva jīvitā voropeti, ubhinnaṃ pārājikaṃ. Taṃ maññamāno aññanti “yaṃ jīvitā voropehī”ti vutto taṃ maññamāno aññaṃ tādisaṃ jīvitā voropeti, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpatti. Aññaṃ maññamāno tanti yo āṇāpakena vutto, tassa balavasahāyaṃ samīpe ṭhitaṃ disvā “imassa balenāyaṃ gajjati, imaṃ tāva jīvitā voropemī”ti paharanto itarameva parivattitvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitaṃ “sahāyo”ti maññamāno jīvitā voropeti, ubhinnaṃ pārājikaṃ. Aññaṃ maññamāno aññanti purimanayeneva “imaṃ tāvassa sahāyaṃ jīvitā voropemī”ti sahāyameva voropeti, tasseva pārājikaṃ.

Now, for the purpose of showing the exposition of the mātikā phrase 'By a messenger,' four sections beginning with 'a bhikkhu instructs a bhikkhu' have been stated. Among these, regarding 'he, thinking of him': the one instructed, who was named by the instructor as 'so-and-so,' thinking it is him, deprives that very person of life; for both, it is a pārājika. Regarding 'thinking of him, but another': having been told, 'Deprive so-and-so of life,' thinking it is him, he deprives another such person of life; for the original instigator, there is no offense. Regarding 'thinking of another, but him': the one who was instructed by the instructor, seeing a strong companion standing nearby, and thinking, 'This one boasts because of this one's strength, I will first deprive this one of life,' while striking, deprives of life the other one—the original target—who had moved and was standing in that place, thinking him to be the companion; for both, it is a pārājika. Regarding 'thinking of another, and another': by the previous method, thinking, 'I will first deprive his companion of life,' he deprives the companion himself of life; for him alone, it is a pārājika.

Dūtaparamparāpadassa niddesavāre itthannāmassa pāvadātiādīsu eko ācariyo tayo buddharakkhitadhammarakkhitasaṅgharakkhitanāmakā antevāsikā [M 2.0048] daṭṭhabbā. Tattha bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetīti ācariyo kañci puggalaṃ [P 2.0449] mārāpetukāmo tamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā buddharakkhitaṃ āṇāpeti. Itthannāmassa pāvadāti gaccha tvaṃ, buddharakkhita, etamatthaṃ dhammarakkhitassa pāvada. Itthannāmo itthannāmassa pāvadatūti dhammarakkhitopi saṅgharakkhitassa pāvadatu. Itthannāmo itthannāmaṃ jīvitā voropetūti evaṃ tayā āṇattena dhammarakkhitena āṇatto saṅgharakkhito itthannāmaṃ puggalaṃ jīvitā voropetu; so hi amhesu vīrajātiko paṭibalo imasmiṃ kammeti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ āṇāpentassa ācariyassa tāva dukkaṭaṃ. So itarassa ārocetīti buddharakkhito dhammarakkhitassa, dhammarakkhito ca saṅgharakkhitassa “amhākaṃ ācariyo evaṃ vadati – ‘itthannāmaṃ kira jīvitā voropehī’ti. Tvaṃ kira amhesu vīrapuriso”ti āroceti; evaṃ tesampi dukkaṭaṃ. Vadhako paṭiggaṇhātīti “sādhu voropessāmī”ti saṅgharakkhito sampaṭicchati. Mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti thullaccayassāti saṅgharakkhitena paṭiggahitamatte ācariyassa thullaccayaṃ. Mahājano hi tena pāpe niyojitoti. So tanti so ce saṅgharakkhito taṃ puggalaṃ jīvitā voropeti, sabbesaṃ catunnampi janānaṃ pārājikaṃ. Na kevalañca [V 2.0045] catunnaṃ, etenūpāyena visaṅketaṃ akatvā paramparāya āṇāpentaṃ samaṇasataṃ samaṇasahassaṃ vā hotu sabbesaṃ pārājikameva.

In the exposition section of the term 'chain of messengers,' regarding phrases such as 'tell so-and-so,' one teacher and three pupils named Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita should be understood. Therein, 'a bhikkhu instructs a bhikkhu' means: the teacher, wishing to have a certain person killed, explains the matter and instructs Buddharakkhita. 'Tell so-and-so' means: 'Go, you, Buddharakkhita, tell this matter to Dhammarakkhita.' 'Let so-and-so tell so-and-so' means: 'Let Dhammarakkhita also tell Saṅgharakkhita.' 'Let so-and-so deprive so-and-so of life' means: 'Thus, let Saṅgharakkhita, instructed by Dhammarakkhita who was instructed by you, deprive the person so-and-so of life; for he is of heroic nature among us and is capable in this deed.' 'The offense is a dukkaṭa' means: for the teacher who instructs in this way, there is at first a dukkaṭa. 'He informs the other' means: Buddharakkhita informs Dhammarakkhita, and Dhammarakkhita informs Saṅgharakkhita, saying, 'Our teacher says thus: "It seems you are to deprive so-and-so of life. It seems you are the hero among us."' Thus, for them too, it is a dukkaṭa. 'The killer accepts' means: Saṅgharakkhita agrees, saying, 'Good, I will deprive him of life.' 'For the original instigator, the offense is a thullaccaya' means: the moment Saṅgharakkhita accepts, for the teacher it is a thullaccaya, for a great number of people have been incited to evil by him. 'If he...' means: if that Saṅgharakkhita deprives that person of life, for all four persons it is a pārājika. And not only for the four; by this method, without any deviation, should a hundred recluses or a thousand recluses give the instruction in succession, for all of them it is a pārājika.

Visakkiyadūtapadaniddese so aññaṃ āṇāpetīti so ācariyena āṇatto buddharakkhito dhammarakkhitaṃ adisvā vā avattukāmo vā hutvā saṅgharakkhitameva upasaṅkamitvā “amhākaṃ ācariyo evamāha – ‘itthannāmaṃ kira jīvitā voropehī”ti visaṅketaṃ karonto āṇāpeti. Visaṅketakaraṇeneva hi esa “visakkiyadūto”ti vuccati. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti āṇattiyā tāva buddharakkhitassa dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭiggaṇhāti āpatti dukkaṭassāti saṅgharakkhitena sampaṭicchite mūlaṭṭhasseva [P 2.0450] dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sante paṭiggahaṇe āpattiyeva na siyā, sañcaritta paṭiggahaṇamaraṇābhinandanesupi ca āpatti hoti, maraṇapaṭiggahaṇe kathaṃ na siyā tasmā paṭiggaṇhantassevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Tenevettha “mūlaṭṭhassā”ti na vuttaṃ. Purimanayepi cetaṃ paṭiggaṇhantassa veditabbameva; okāsābhāvena pana na vuttaṃ. Tasmā yo yo [M 2.0049] paṭiggaṇhāti, tassa tassa tappaccayā āpattiyevāti ayamettha amhākaṃ khanti. Yathā cettha evaṃ adinnādānepīti.

In the explanation of the term 'visakkiyadūta,' 'he orders another' means: that Buddharakkhita, instructed by the teacher, either not seeing Dhammarakkhita or being unwilling to speak, approaches only Saṅgharakkhita and, making a deviation, instructs, 'Our teacher says this: "Deprive so-and-so of life, it is said."' Indeed, because of making a deviation, he is called a 'visakkiyadūta' (a messenger who acts contrary to the instruction). 'There is an offense of wrong-doing' means: because of the instruction, there is, in the first place, a dukkaṭa offense for Buddharakkhita. 'When he accepts, there is an offense of wrong-doing' means: it should be understood that when it is accepted by Saṅgharakkhita, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the one at the root. If this were so, there would be no offense at all in the act of accepting. And yet, an offense does arise even in accepting a commission and in delighting in death; how then could there not be an offense in accepting an instruction for killing? Therefore, this dukkaṭa offense is for the one who accepts. For that very reason, it was not said here 'for the one at the root.' And in the previous method too, this should be understood as being for the one who accepts; however, it was not stated due to the lack of opportunity. Therefore, whoever accepts, for each one of them, an offense arises due to that cause—this is our preferred meaning here. And just as it is here, so too in the case of taking what is not given.

Sace pana so taṃ jīvitā voropeti, āṇāpakassa ca buddharakkhitassa voropakassa ca saṅgharakkhitassāti ubhinnampi pārājikaṃ. Mūlaṭṭhassa pana ācariyassa visaṅketattā pārājikena anāpatti. Dhammarakkhitassa ajānanatāya sabbena sabbaṃ anāpatti. Buddharakkhito pana dvinnaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ katvā attanā naṭṭhoti.

But if he deprives that person of life, then for both the instructor, Buddharakkhita, and the executioner, Saṅgharakkhita, it is a pārājika offense. However, for the teacher at the root, because of the deviation, there is no pārājika offense. For Dhammarakkhita, because of his unawareness, there is no offense whatsoever. But Buddharakkhita, having brought about the well-being of two, is himself ruined.

Gatapaccāgatadūtaniddese – so gantvā puna paccāgacchatīti tassa jīvitā voropetabbassa samīpaṃ gantvā susaṃvihitārakkhattā taṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ asakkonto āgacchati. Yadā sakkosi tadāti kiṃ ajjeva mārito mārito hoti, gaccha yadā sakkosi, tadā naṃ jīvitā voropehīti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ puna āṇattiyāpi dukkaṭameva hoti. Sace pana so avassaṃ jīvitā voropetabbo hoti, atthasādhakacetanā maggānantaraphalasadisā, tasmā ayaṃ āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājiko. Sacepi vadhako saṭṭhivassātikkamena taṃ vadhati, āṇāpako ca antarāva kālaṅkaroti, hīnāya vā āvattati, assamaṇova hutvā kālañca karissati, hīnāya vā āvattissati. Sace āṇāpako gihikāle mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā arahantaṃ vā sandhāya evaṃ āṇāpetvā pabbajati, tasmiṃ pabbajite āṇatto taṃ māreti, āṇāpako gihikāleyeva mātughātako pitughātako arahantaghātako vā hoti, tasmā nevassa pabbajjā[V 2.0046], na upasampadā ruhati. Sacepi māretabbapuggalo āṇattikkhaṇe puthujjano, yadā [P 2.0451] pana naṃ āṇatto māreti tadā arahā hoti, āṇattato vā pahāraṃ labhitvā dukkhamūlikaṃ saddhaṃ nissāya vipassanto arahattaṃ patvā tenevābādhena kālaṃkaroti, āṇāpako āṇattikkhaṇeyeva arahantaghātako. Vadhako pana sabbattha upakkamakaraṇakkhaṇeyeva pārājikoti.

In the explanation of the messenger who has gone and returned: 'He, having gone, returns again' means that having gone near the person who is to be deprived of life, he is unable to deprive him of life because of a well-arranged guard, and so he returns. 'When you are able, then...' means he says, 'Is he to be killed today itself? Go! When you are able to deprive him of life, then do so.' 'There is an offense of wrong-doing' means: thus, for giving the instruction again, there is also just a dukkaṭa offense. But if that person must inevitably be deprived of life, the volition that accomplishes the purpose is like the path with its fruit in the immediate aftermath; therefore, this instructor is pārājika at the very moment of the instruction. Even if the killer kills him after sixty years have passed, and the instructor dies in the interim or reverts to the inferior state, he will die or revert to the inferior state as a non-monk. If an instructor, while a layman, gives such an instruction concerning his mother, father, or an Arahant, and then goes forth, and after he has gone forth the one instructed kills that person, the instructor becomes a matricide, patricide, or killer of an Arahant while still a layman. Therefore, neither his going-forth nor his higher ordination takes root. Even if the person to be killed is a worldling at the moment of the instruction, but when the one instructed kills him, he has become an Arahant; or if, having received a blow from the one instructed, he relies on faith rooted in suffering, practices insight, attains Arahantship, and dies from that very affliction, the instructor becomes a killer of an Arahant at the very moment of the instruction. But the killer, in all cases, becomes pārājika at the very moment of making the attempt.

Idāni ye sabbesuyeva imesu dūtavasena vuttamātikāpadesu saṅketavisaṅketadassanatthaṃ

Now, for the purpose of showing the direct and deviated instructions in all these mātikā-headings that have been spoken by way of a messenger:

Vuttā tayo vārā, tesu paṭhamavāre tāva – yasmā taṃ saṇikaṃ vā bhaṇanto tassa vā badhiratāya “mā ghātehī”ti [M 2.0050] etaṃ vacanaṃ na sāveti, tasmā mūlaṭṭho na mutto. Dutiyavāre – sāvitattā mutto. Tatiyavāre pana tena ca sāvitattā itarena ca “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā oratattā ubhopi muttāti.

Three cases have been stated. Among them, in the first case: because, speaking to him softly or due to his deafness, he does not make the words 'Do not kill' heard, therefore the one at the root is not released. In the second case, because it was made heard, he is released. In the third case, however, because it was made heard by the one and because the other, having accepted with 'Good,' has desisted, both are released.

Dūtakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the messenger is concluded.

175. Araho rahosaññīniddesādīsu arahoti sammukhe. Rahoti parammukhe. Tattha yo upaṭṭhānakāle veribhikkhumhi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ āgantvā purato nisinneyeva andhakāradosena tassa āgatabhāvaṃ ajānanto “aho vata itthannāmo hato assa, corāpi nāma taṃ na hananti, sappo vā na ḍaṃsati, na satthaṃ vā visaṃ vā āharatī”ti tassa maraṇaṃ abhinandanto īdisāni vacanāni ullapati, ayaṃ araho rahosaññī ullapati nāma. Sammukheva tasmiṃ parammukhasaññīti attho. Yo pana taṃ purato nisinnaṃ disvā puna upaṭṭhānaṃ katvā gatehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ gatepi tasmiṃ “idheva so nisinno”ti saññī hutvā purimanayeneva ullapati, ayaṃ raho arahosaññī ullapati nāma. Etenevupāyena araho arahosaññī ca raho rahosaññī ca veditabbo. Catunnampi ca etesaṃ vācāya vācāya dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ.

175. In the explanations of `araho rahosaññī` and so on: `araho` means in the presence; `raho` means in the absence. In this context, should a monk, at a time of attendance, when an enemy monk has come with other monks and is sitting right in front, not know of his arrival due to the fault of darkness and, delighting in his death, utters such words as, 'Oh, if only so-and-so were killed! It seems thieves do not kill him, nor does a snake bite him, nor does he bring a weapon or poison for himself'—this one is called 'one who utters while perceiving one who is present as absent' (`araho rahosaññī`). The meaning is that he perceives one who is right in front as being absent. But should a monk, having seen him sitting in front, still perceive 'He is sitting right here' even after he has departed with the other monks who had attended, and utters in the same way as before—this one is called 'one who utters while perceiving one who is absent as present' (`raho arahosaññī`). By this same method, `araho arahosaññī` (perceiving one present as present) and `raho rahosaññī` (perceiving one absent as absent) should also be understood. And it should be understood that for all four of these, for each and every utterance, there is a `dukkaṭa` offense.

Idāni [P 2.0452] maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇanāya vibhāgadassanatthaṃ vuttesu pañcasu kāyena saṃvaṇṇanādimātikāniddesesu – kāyena vikāraṃ karotīti yathā so jānāti “satthaṃ vā āharitvā visaṃ vā khāditvā rajjuyā vā ubbandhitvā sobbhādīsu vā papatitvā yo marati so kira dhanaṃ vā labhati, yasaṃ vā labhati, saggaṃ vā gacchatīti ayamattho etena vutto”ti tathā hatthamuddādīhi dasseti. Vācāya bhaṇatīti tamevatthaṃ vākyabhedaṃ katvā bhaṇati. Tatiyavāro ubhayavasena vutto. Sabbattha saṃvaṇṇanāya payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Tassa dukkhuppattiyaṃ saṃvaṇṇakassa [V 2.0047] thullaccayaṃ. Yaṃ uddissa saṃvaṇṇanā katā, tasmiṃ mate saṃvaṇṇanakkhaṇeyeva saṃvaṇṇakassa pārājikaṃ. So taṃ na jānāti añño ñatvā “laddho vata me sukhuppattiupāyo”ti tāya saṃvaṇṇanāya marati, anāpatti. Dvinnaṃ uddissa saṃvaṇṇanāya katāya eko ñatvā marati, pārājikaṃ. Dvepi maranti, pārājikañca akusalarāsi ca. Esa nayo sambahulesu. Anuddissa [M 2.0051] maraṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇento āhiṇḍati, yo yo taṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ ñatvā marati, sabbo tena mārito hoti.

Now, for the purpose of showing the classification of the eulogy on the virtue of death, among the five expositions of the mātikā beginning with 'eulogy by body' that have been spoken: 'He makes a gesture with the body' means that he shows with hand gestures and so on, in such a way that that person may know, 'Whoever dies by bringing a weapon, or by eating poison, or by hanging with a rope, or by falling into a pit and so on, it is said that person obtains wealth, or obtains fame, or goes to heaven—this meaning has been conveyed by this one.' 'He speaks with speech' means he speaks that very meaning, varying the words. The third case is spoken of by way of both. In all cases, for every effort in the eulogy, there is a `dukkaṭa` offense. Upon the arising of suffering for that person, for the eulogizer, there is a `thullaccaya` offense. If the one for whom the eulogy was made dies at the very moment of the eulogy, for the eulogizer, there is a `pārājika` offense. If that person does not know it, but another, having known, thinks, 'Indeed, a means for the arising of happiness has been found by me!' and dies because of that eulogy, there is no offense. When a eulogy is made designating two people, and one, having known, dies, there is a `pārājika` offense. If both die, there is both a `pārājika` offense and a mass of demerit. This is the method for many people. If one wanders about eulogizing death without specifying anyone, whoever, having known that eulogy, dies, is considered to have been killed by him.

Dūtena saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “asukaṃ nāma gehaṃ vā gāmaṃ vā gantvā itthannāmassa evaṃ maraṇavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇehī”ti sāsane ārocitamatte dukkaṭaṃ. Yassatthāya pahito tassa dukkhuppattiyā mūlaṭṭhassa thullaccayaṃ, maraṇena pārājikaṃ. Dūto “ñāto dāni ayaṃ saggamaggo”ti tassa anārocetvā attano ñātissa vā sālohitassa vā āroceti, tasmiṃ mate visaṅketo hoti, mūlaṭṭho muccati. Dūto tatheva cintetvā sayaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāya vuttaṃ katvā marati, visaṅketova. Anuddissa pana sāsane ārocite yattakā dūtassa saṃvaṇṇanāya maranti, tattakā pāṇātipātā. Sace mātāpitaro maranti, ānantariyampi hoti.

In the case of eulogy by a messenger: merely upon the message, 'Having gone to such-and-such a house or village, eulogize the virtue of death in this way for so-and-so,' being announced, there is a `dukkaṭa` offense. Due to the arising of suffering for the person for whose sake he was sent, for the one at the root, there is a `thullaccaya` offense; by death, a `pārājika` offense. If the messenger, thinking, 'Now this path to heaven is known!' without informing that person, informs his own relative or kinsman, and when that one dies, it becomes a deviation from the instruction; the one at the root is absolved. If the messenger, thinking in the same way, dies himself after doing what was said in the eulogy, it is also a deviation from the instruction. But when the message is announced without specifying anyone, however many die due to the messenger's eulogy, that many acts of taking life there are. If his parents die, it is also an act with immediate consequence.

176. Lekhāsaṃvaṇṇanāya – lekhaṃ chindatīti paṇṇe vā potthake vā akkharāni likhati – “yo satthaṃ vā āharitvā papāte vā papatitvā aññehi vā aggippavesanaudakappavesanādīhi upāyehi [P 2.0453] marati, so idañcidañca labhatī”ti vā “tassa dhammo hotī”ti vāti. Etthāpi dukkaṭathullaccayā vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Uddissa likhite pana yaṃ uddissa likhitaṃ tasseva maraṇena pārājikaṃ. Bahū uddissa likhite yattakā maranti, tattakā pāṇātipātā. Mātāpitūnaṃ maraṇena ānantariyaṃ. Anuddissa likhitepi eseva nayo. “Bahū marantī”ti vippaṭisāre uppanne taṃ potthakaṃ jhāpetvā vā yathā vā akkharāni na paññāyanti tathā katvā muccati. Sace so parassa potthako hoti, uddissa likhito vā hoti anuddissa likhito vā, gahitaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā muccati. Sace mūlena kīto hoti, potthakassāmikānaṃ potthakaṃ, yesaṃ hatthato mūlaṃ gahitaṃ, tesaṃ mūlaṃ datvā muccati. Sace sambahulā “maraṇavaṇṇaṃ likhissāmā”ti ekajjhāsayā hutvā eko tālarukkhaṃ ārohitvā paṇṇaṃ chindati, eko āharati, eko potthakaṃ karoti, eko likhati, eko sace kaṇṭakalekhā hoti, masiṃ makkheti, masiṃ makkhetvā taṃ potthakaṃ sajjetvā sabbeva [M 2.0052] sabhāyaṃ vā āpaṇe vā yattha vā pana lekhādassanakotūhalakā bahū sannipatanti, tattha ṭhapenti. Taṃ vācetvā sacepi eko marati, sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ. Sace bahukā maranti, vuttasadisova nayo. Vippaṭisāre [V 2.0048] pana uppanne taṃ potthakaṃ sacepi mañjūsāyaṃ gopenti, añño ca taṃ disvā nīharitvā puna bahūnaṃ dasseti, neva muccanti. Tiṭṭhatu mañjūsā, sacepi taṃ potthakaṃ nadiyaṃ vā samudde vā khipanti vā dhovanti vā khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ vā chindanti, aggimhi vā jhāpenti, yāva saṅghaṭṭitepi duddhote vā dujjhāpite vā patte akkharāni paññāyanti, tāva na muccanti. Yathā pana akkharāni na paññāyanti tatheva kate muccantīti.

176. In the case of eulogy by writing: 'He inscribes a writing' means he writes letters on a leaf or in a book, such as: 'Whoever dies by bringing a weapon, or by falling from a precipice, or by other means such as entering fire or entering water, obtains this and that,' or 'his is the true path.' Here too, the dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses should be understood in the way already stated. But when it is written designating someone, by the death of that very person for whom it was written, there is a pārājika offense. When written designating many, however many die, that many acts of taking life there are. By the death of parents, there is an act with immediate consequence. Even when written without designating anyone, this is the same method. When regret arises, thinking, 'Many will die,' he is absolved by burning that book, or by acting in such a way that the letters are not discernible. If that book belongs to another, whether it was written designating someone or written without designating someone, he is absolved by placing it back in the place it was taken from. If it was bought for a price, he is absolved by giving the book to the owners of the book, or by giving the price to those from whose hand the price was taken. If many, having a single intention, think, 'We will write a eulogy on the virtue of death,' and one climbs a palm tree and cuts a leaf, one brings it, one makes the book, one writes, and one applies ink; and having applied the ink and prepared that book, they all place it in an assembly hall, or a market, or wherever many people who are curious to see writings gather. Having read it, if even one person dies, for all of them there is a pārājika offense. If many die, the method is just as has been stated. But when regret arises, even if they secure that book in a chest, and another person, seeing it, takes it out and shows it to many again, they are not absolved. Let alone the chest, even if they throw that book into a river or the sea, or wash it, or cut it into pieces, or burn it in a fire, as long as the letters on the leaf are discernible—even if re-joined, badly washed, or badly burned—they are not absolved. But when it is done in such a way that the letters are not discernible, they are absolved.

Idāni [P 2.0454] thāvarapayogassa vibhāgadassanatthaṃ vuttesu opātādimātikāniddesesu manussaṃ uddissa opātaṃ khanatīti “itthannāmo patitvā marissatī”ti kañci manussaṃ uddisitvā yattha so ekato vicarati, tattha āvāṭaṃ khanati, khanantassa tāva sacepi jātapathaviyā khanati, pāṇātipātassa payogattā payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Yaṃ uddissa khanati, tassa dukkhuppattiyā thullaccayaṃ, maraṇena pārājikaṃ. Aññasmiṃ patitvā mate anāpatti. Sace anuddissa “yo koci marissatī”ti khato hoti, yattakā patitvā maranti, tattakā pāṇātipātā. Ānantariyavatthūsu ca ānantariyaṃ thullaccayapācittiyavatthūsu thullaccayapācittiyāni.

Now, for the purpose of showing the classification of a fixed contrivance, among the expositions of the mātikā beginning with 'pit' that have been spoken: 'He digs a pit designating a person' means that, having designated a certain person, thinking, 'So-and-so will fall and die,' he digs a pit where that person wanders alone. For the one digging, in the first place, even if he digs in natural earth, because it is an effort to take life, for every effort, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Upon the arising of suffering for the person for whom he digs, there is a thullaccaya offense; by death, a pārājika offense. When another falls in and dies, there is no offense. If it is dug without designating anyone, thinking, 'Whoever it may be will die,' then however many fall in and die, that many acts of taking life there are. And in cases that are grounds for an act with immediate consequence, there is an act with immediate consequence; in cases that are grounds for thullaccaya and pācittiya offenses, there are thullaccaya and pācittiya offenses.

Bahū tattha cetanā; katamāya pārājikaṃ hotīti? Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva vuttaṃ – “āvāṭaṃ gambhīrato ca āyāmavitthārato ca khanitvā pamāṇe ṭhapetvā tacchetvā puñchitvā paṃsupacchiṃ uddharantassa sanniṭṭhāpikā atthasādhakacetanā maggānantaraphalasadisā. Sacepi vassasatassa accayena patitvā avassaṃ maraṇakasatto hoti, sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāyameva pārājika”nti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyañca – “imasmiṃ āvāṭe patitvā marissatīti ekasmimpi kuddālappahāre dinne sace koci tattha pakkhalito patitvā marati, pārājikameva. Suttantikattherā pana sanniṭṭhāpakacetanaṃ gaṇhantī”ti vuttaṃ.

There are many intentions therein; by which intention does a pārājika offense occur? First, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'For one who, having dug a pit in terms of depth and in terms of length and breadth, having established it at the desired measurement, having smoothed it, having cleaned it, and is removing the last basket of soil, the final, completing intention that accomplishes the purpose is like the path with its immediate fruit. Even if a being who will certainly die falls in after the passing of a hundred years, the pārājika offense occurs by the completing intention itself.' However, in the Mahāpaccarī and the Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā it is said: 'Thinking, "One will fall into this pit and die," if, when even a single spade-strike is given, someone slips, falls in there, and dies, it is indeed a pārājika offense. The Suttantika elders, however, take the completing intention.'

Eko [M 2.0053] “opātaṃ khanitvā asukaṃ nāma ānetvā idha pātetvā mārehī”ti aññaṃ āṇāpeti, so taṃ pātetvā māreti, ubhinnaṃ pārājikaṃ. Aññaṃ pātetvā māreti, sayaṃ patitvā marati, añño attano dhammatāya patitvā marati, sabbattha visaṅketo hoti, mūlaṭṭho muccati. “Asuko asukaṃ ānetvā idha māressatī”ti khatepi eseva nayo. Maritukāmā idha marissantīti khanati, ekassa maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Bahunnaṃ maraṇe akusalarāsi[P 2.0455], mātāpitūnaṃ maraṇe ānantariyaṃ, thullaccayapācittiyavatthūsu thullaccayapācittiyāni.

One monk commands another, 'Having dug a pit, bring so-and-so, make him fall in here, and kill him.' If that commanded monk makes that specified person fall in and kills him, it is a pārājika offense for both. If he makes another person fall in and kills him, or if he himself falls in and dies, or if another person falls in by his own nature and dies, in all cases it is a deviation from the arrangement; the original instigator is absolved. This same principle also applies in the case of a pit dug thinking, 'So-and-so will bring so-and-so and kill him here.' If one digs thinking, 'Those who wish to die will die here,' on the death of one person, it is a pārājika offense. On the death of many, it is a mass of demerit; on the death of one's mother or father, it is an act with immediate consequence; in cases that are grounds for thullaccaya and pācittiya offenses, there are thullaccaya and pācittiya offenses.

“Ye keci māretukāmā, te idha pātetvā māressantī”ti khanati, tattha pātetvā mārenti[V 2.0049], ekasmiṃ mate pārājikaṃ, bahūsu akusalarāsi, ānantariyādivatthūsu ānantariyādīni. Idheva arahantāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Purimanaye pana “tesaṃ maritukāmatāya patanaṃ natthī”ti te na saṅgayhanti. Dvīsupi nayesu attano dhammatāya patitvā mate visaṅketo. “Ye keci attano verike ettha pātetvā māressantī”ti khanati, tattha ca verikā verike pātetvā mārenti, ekasmiṃ mārite pārājikaṃ, bahūsu akusalarāsi, mātari vā pitari vā arahante vā verikehi ānetvā tattha mārite ānantariyaṃ. Attano dhammatāya patitvā matesu visaṅketo.

If one digs thinking, 'Whoever wishes to kill, they will make others fall in here and kill them,' and they do make others fall in there and kill them: when one dies, it is a pārājika offense; when many die, it is a mass of demerit; in cases that are grounds for acts with immediate result, etc., acts with immediate result, etc., are incurred. In this very method, even Arahants are included. In the former method, however, because 'for them, there is no falling due to a wish to die,' they are not included. In both methods, if one dies having fallen by one's own nature, it is a deviation from the arrangement. If one digs thinking, 'Whoever will make their own enemies fall in here and kill them,' and in that pit, enemies do make enemies fall in and kill them: when one is killed, it is a pārājika offense; when many are killed, it is a mass of demerit. If a mother, or a father, or an Arahant is brought by enemies and killed there, it is an act with immediate result. If they die having fallen by their own nature, it is a deviation from the arrangement.

Yo pana “maritukāmā vā amaritukāmā vā māretukāmā vā amāretukāmā vā ye keci ettha patitā vā pātitā vā marissantī”ti sabbathāpi anuddisseva khanati. Yo yo marati tassa tassa maraṇena yathānurūpaṃ kammañca phusati, āpattiñca āpajjati. Sace gabbhinī patitvā sagabbhā marati, dve pāṇātipātā. Gabbhoyeva vinassati, eko. Gabbho na vinassati, mātā marati, ekoyeva. Corehi anubaddho patitvā marati, opātakhanakasseva pārājikaṃ. Corā tattha pātetvā mārenti, pārājikameva. Tattha patitaṃ bahi nīharitvā mārenti, pārājikameva. Kasmā? Opāte patitappayogena gahitattā. Opātato nikkhamitvā teneva ābādhena marati, pārājikameva. Bahūni vassāni atikkamitvā puna kupitena tenevābādhena marati, pārājikameva. Opāte patanappaccayā uppannarogena gilānasseva añño rogo uppajjati, opātarogo balavataro [M 2.0054] hoti, tena matepi opātakhaṇako na muccati. Sace pacchā uppannarogo balavā hoti, tena mate muccati. Ubhohi mate na muccati. Opāte opapātikamanusso nibbattitvā uttarituṃ asakkonto marati, pārājikameva. Manussaṃ uddissa khate yakkhādīsu patitvā matesu anāpatti. Yakkhādayo [P 2.0456] uddissa khate manussādīsu marantesupi eseva nayo. Yakkhādayo uddissa khanantassa pana khananepi tesaṃ dukkhuppattiyampi dukkaṭameva. Maraṇe vatthuvasena thullaccayaṃ vā pācittiyaṃ vā. Anuddissa khate opāte yakkharūpena vā petarūpena vā patati, tiracchānarūpena marati, patanarūpaṃ pamāṇaṃ, tasmā thullaccayanti upatissatthero. Maraṇarūpaṃ pamāṇaṃ, tasmā pācittiyanti phussadevatthero. Tiracchānarūpena patitvā yakkhapetarūpena matepi eseva nayo.

But if a monk digs, in all ways not specifying anyone, thinking, 'Whether wishing to die or not wishing to die, whether wishing to kill or not wishing to kill, whoever, having fallen or having been made to fall in here, will die,' then for each one who dies, by that death he incurs corresponding kamma and commits an offense. If a pregnant woman falls and dies together with the fetus, there are two acts of taking life. If only the fetus perishes, it is one. If the fetus does not perish but the mother dies, it is only one. If one, being pursued by thieves, falls in and dies, it is a pārājika offense for the pit-digger. If thieves make him fall in there and kill him, it is indeed a pārājika offense. If they take one who has fallen in there outside and kill him, it is indeed a pārājika offense. Why? Because he has been seized by the means of falling into the pit. If, having gotten out of the pit, he dies from that very injury, it is indeed a pārājika offense. If, after many years have passed, he dies from that same injury having become aggravated again, it is indeed a pārājika offense. For one who is sick with a disease that arose due to falling in the pit, another disease arises; if the pit-disease is stronger, even if he dies from that, the pit-digger is not absolved. If the later-arisen disease is strong, if he dies from that, he is absolved. If he dies from both, he is not absolved. If a spontaneously-born human arises in the pit and, being unable to get out, dies, it is indeed a pārājika offense. In a pit dug specifying a human, if yakkhas, etc., fall in and die, there is no offense. This same principle also applies when humans, etc., die in a pit dug specifying yakkhas, etc. However, for one digging specifying yakkhas, etc., for the digging itself and for the arising of suffering in them, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. On their death, according to the being, it is either a thullaccaya or a pācittiya. In a pit dug without specifying, if one falls in with the form of a yakkha or a peta but dies with the form of an animal, the Elder Upatissa said, 'The form at the time of falling is the standard; therefore it is a thullaccaya.' The Elder Phussadeva said, 'The form at the time of death is the standard; therefore it is a pācittiya.' This same principle also applies for one who falls with the form of an animal but dies with the form of a yakkha or peta.

Opātakhanako opātaṃ aññassa vikkiṇāti vā mudhā vā deti, yo yo patitvā marati, tappaccayā tasseva āpatti ca kammabandho ca. Yena laddho so niddoso. Atha sopi “evaṃ [V 2.0050] patitā uttarituṃ asakkontā nassissanti, suuddharā vā na bhavissantī”ti taṃ opātaṃ gambhīrataraṃ vā uttānataraṃ vā dīghataraṃ vā rassataraṃ vā vitthatataraṃ vā sambādhataraṃ vā karoti, ubhinnampi āpatti ca kammabandho ca. Bahū marantīti vippaṭisāre uppanne opātaṃ paṃsunā pūreti, sace koci paṃsumhi patitvā marati, pūretvāpi mūlaṭṭho na muccati. Deve vassante kaddamo hoti, tattha laggitvā matepi. Rukkho vā patanto vāto vā vassodakaṃ vā paṃsuṃ harati, kandamūlatthaṃ vā pathaviṃ khanantā tattha āvāṭaṃ karonti. Tattha sace koci laggitvā vā patitvā vā marati, mūlaṭṭho na muccati. Tasmiṃ pana okāse mahantaṃ taḷākaṃ vā pokkharaṇiṃ vā kāretvā cetiyaṃ vā patiṭṭhāpetvā bodhiṃ vā ropetvā āvāsaṃ vā sakaṭamaggaṃ vā kāretvā muccati. Yadāpi thiraṃ katvā pūrite opāte rukkhādīnaṃ mūlāni mūlehi saṃsibbitāni honti[P 2.0457], jātapathavī jātā, tadāpi muccati. Sacepi nadī āgantvā opātaṃ harati, evampi muccatīti. Ayaṃ tāva opātakathā.

A monk who digs a pit sells it or gives it to another for free. Whoever falls in and dies, because of that, for that very digger there is an offense and karmic bondage. The one by whom it was obtained is blameless. But if he too, thinking, 'Thus, those who have fallen, being unable to get out, will perish, or they will not be easily rescued,' makes that pit deeper or shallower, longer or shorter, wider or narrower, then for both of them there is an offense and karmic bondage. If, when remorse arises thinking, 'Many are dying,' one fills the pit with earth, and if someone falls into the earth and dies, even after it has been filled, the original person is not absolved. When it rains, it becomes mud; even if one gets stuck in it and dies, the original person is not absolved. A falling tree, or the wind, or rainwater may carry away the earth, or those digging the earth for tubers and roots may make a hole there. If someone gets stuck or falls in there and dies, the original person is not absolved. However, in that place, by having a large reservoir or a lotus pond made, or by having a cetiya established, or by having a Bodhi tree planted, or by having a residence or a cart-track made, one is absolved. Also, when the pit has been firmly filled and the roots of trees and so on have become interwoven with other roots, and natural ground has formed, then too one is absolved. Even if a river comes and carries away the pit, in this way too one is absolved. This, for now, is the discourse on pits.

Opātasseva pana anulomesu pāsādīsupi yo tāva pāsaṃ oḍḍeti “ettha bajjhitvā sattā marissantī”ti avassaṃ bajjhanakasattānaṃ vasena [M 2.0055] hatthā muttamatte pārājikānantariyathullaccayapācittiyāni veditabbāni. Uddissa kate yaṃ uddissa oḍḍito, tato aññesaṃ bandhane anāpatti. Pāse mūlena vā mudhā vā dinnepi mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabandho. Sace yena laddho so uggalitaṃ vā pāsaṃ saṇṭhapeti, passena vā gacchante disvā vatiṃ katvā sammukhe paveseti, thaddhataraṃ vā pāsayaṭṭhiṃ ṭhapeti, daḷhataraṃ vā pāsarajjuṃ bandhati, thirataraṃ vā khāṇukaṃ vā ākoṭeti, ubhopi na muccanti. Sace vippaṭisāre uppanne pāsaṃ uggalāpetvā gacchati, taṃ disvā puna aññe saṇṭhapenti, baddhā baddhā maranti, mūlaṭṭho na muccati.

Furthermore, in analogous cases of snares and so on, just as with a pit: whoever sets a snare thinking, 'Here, beings, having been bound, will die,' it should be understood that at the very moment of being released from the hand, the offenses of pārājika, ānantariya, thullaccaya, and pācittiya are incurred, according to the beings who will certainly be bound. When it is done with a specific target, for whomever it was set, there is no offense in the binding of others than that one. Even when the snare is given for a price or for free, the karmic bondage is for the original person alone. If the one by whom it was obtained sets up a loosened snare, or seeing beings passing by the side, makes a fence and directs them into the front of the snare, or places a stiffer snare-stick, or ties a stronger snare-rope, or drives in a firmer stake, both are not absolved. If, when remorse has arisen, one loosens the snare and departs, but seeing it, others set it up again, and beings are bound and die, the original person is not absolved.

Sace pana tena pāsayaṭṭhi sayaṃ akatā hoti, gahitaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā muccati. Tatthajātakayaṭṭhiṃ chinditvā muccati. Sayaṃ katayaṭṭhiṃ pana gopentopi na muccati. Yadi hi taṃ añño gaṇhitvā pāsaṃ saṇṭhapeti, tappaccayā marantesu mūlaṭṭho na muccati. Sace taṃ jhāpetvā alātaṃ katvā chaḍḍeti, tena alātena pahāraṃ laddhā marantesupi na muccati. Sabbaso pana jhāpetvā vā nāsetvā vā muccati, pāsarajjumpi aññehi ca vaṭṭitaṃ gahitaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā muccati. Rajjuke labhitvā sayaṃ vaṭṭitaṃ ubbaṭṭetvā vāke labhitvā vaṭṭitaṃ hīraṃ hīraṃ katvā muccati. Araññato pana sayaṃ vāke āharitvā vaṭṭitaṃ gopentopi na muccati. Sabbaso pana jhāpetvā vā nāsetvā vā muccati.

But if the snare-stick was not made by oneself, one is absolved by placing it back where it was taken. One is absolved by cutting down a stick that grew there. However, regarding a stick made by oneself, one is not absolved even by safeguarding it. For if another person takes it and sets the snare, the original person is not absolved when beings die because of that. If one burns it, makes it into a firebrand, and then discards it, one is not absolved even if beings die from being struck by that firebrand. But one is absolved by completely burning or destroying it. Regarding the snare-rope too, if it was twisted by others, one is absolved by placing it back where it was taken. If one obtained small ropes and untwisted what was twisted by oneself, or obtained bark-strips and, having twisted them, separates them fiber by fiber, one is absolved. But if one brings bark-strips from the forest oneself and twists them, one is not absolved even by safeguarding it. However, one is absolved by completely burning or destroying it.

Adūhalaṃ [V 2.0051] sajjento catūsu pādesu adūhalamañcaṃ ṭhapetvā pāsāṇe āropeti, payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Sabbasajjaṃ katvā hatthato [P 2.0458] muttamatte avassaṃ ajjhottharitabbakasattānaṃ vasena uddissakānuddissakānurūpena pārājikādīni veditabbāni. Adūhale mūlena vā mudhā vā dinnepi mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabaddho. Sace yena laddhaṃ so patitaṃ vā ukkhipati, aññepi pāsāṇe āropetvā garukataraṃ vā karoti, passena vā gacchante disvā vatiṃ katvā adūhale paveseti, ubhopi na muccanti. Sacepi vippaṭisāre uppanne adūhalaṃ pātetvā gacchati, taṃ disvā añño saṇṭhapeti, mūlaṭṭho na muccati. Pāsāṇe pana gahitaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā adūhalapāde ca pāsayaṭṭhiyaṃ vuttanayena gahitaṭṭhāne vā ṭhapetvā jhāpetvā vā muccati.

When preparing a deadfall trap, one places the deadfall platform on four legs and puts stones upon it; for each effort, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Having made all preparations, at the very moment it is released from the hand, depending on the beings who must certainly be crushed, and in accordance with whether they are targeted or not targeted, offenses beginning with pārājika are to be understood. When the deadfall trap is given for a price or for free, the karmic liability is still with the original person. If the one who obtained it lifts it up when it has fallen, or makes it heavier by placing other stones on it, or, seeing beings passing by the side, makes a fence and directs them into the deadfall trap, both are not absolved. Even if, when remorse has arisen, one causes the deadfall trap to fall and departs, and another, seeing it, sets it up again, the original person is not absolved. However, one is absolved by placing the stones back in the place from which they were taken, and, regarding the legs of the deadfall, by either placing them back in their original place or by burning them, in the manner described for the snare-stick.

Sūlaṃ ropentassāpi sabbasajjaṃ katvā hatthato muttamatte sūlamukhe patitvā avassaṃ maraṇakasattānaṃ vasena uddissānuddissānurūpato pārājikādīni [M 2.0056] veditabbāni. Sūle mūlena vā mudhā vā dinnepi mūlaṭṭhasseva kammabaddho. Sace yena laddhaṃ so “ekappahāreneva marissantī”ti tikhiṇataraṃ vā karoti, “dukkhaṃ marissantī”ti kuṇṭhataraṃ vā karoti, “ucca”nti sallakkhetvā nīcataraṃ vā “nīca”nti sallakkhetvā uccataraṃ vā puna ropeti, vaṅkaṃ vā ujukaṃ atiujukaṃ vā īsakaṃ poṇaṃ karoti, ubhopi na muccanti. Sace pana “aṭṭhāne ṭhita”nti aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeti, taṃ ce māraṇatthāya ādito pabhuti pariyesitvā kataṃ hoti, mūlaṭṭho na muccati. Apariyesitvā pana katameva labhitvā ropite mūlaṭṭho muccati. Vippaṭisāre uppanne pāsayaṭṭhiyaṃ vuttanayena gahitaṭṭhāne vā ṭhapetvā jhāpetvā vā muccati.

For one who plants an impaling stake, having made all preparations, at the very moment it is released from the hand, depending on the beings who will certainly die by falling on the point of the stake, and in accordance with whether they are targeted or not targeted, offenses beginning with pārājika are to be understood. Even when the stake is given for a price or for free, the karmic liability is still with the original person. If the one who obtained it, thinking, ‘They will die with a single blow,’ makes it sharper, or thinking, ‘They will die painfully,’ makes it blunter, or, noting ‘it is high,’ plants it lower, or, noting ‘it is low,’ plants it higher again, or makes a crooked one straight, or a very straight one slightly inclined, both are not absolved. If, however, thinking ‘It is in an unsuitable place,’ one places it in another place, and if that stake was sought out and made from the beginning for the purpose of killing, the original person is not absolved. But if one, having obtained an already-made stake without seeking it out, plants it, the original person is absolved. If remorse arises, one is absolved by placing it back in its original place or by burning it, in the manner described for the snare-stick.

177. Apassene satthaṃ vāti ettha apassenaṃ nāma niccaparibhogo mañco vā pīṭhaṃ vā apassenaphalakaṃ vā divāṭṭhāne nisīdantassa apassenakatthambho vā tatthajātakarukkho vā caṅkame apassāya tiṭṭhantassa ālambanarukkho vā ālambanaphalakaṃ vā sabbampetaṃ apassayanīyaṭṭhena apassenaṃ [P 2.0459] nāma; tasmiṃ apassene yathā apassayantaṃ vijjhati vā chindati vā tathā katvā vāsipharasusattiārakaṇṭakādīnaṃ aññataraṃ satthaṃ ṭhapeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Dhuvaparibhogaṭṭhāne nirāsaṅkassa nisīdato vā nipajjato vā apassayantassa vā satthasamphassapaccayā dukkhuppattiyā thullaccayaṃ, maraṇena pārājikaṃ. Taṃ ce aññopi tassa veribhikkhu vihāracārikaṃ caranto disvā “imassa maññe maraṇatthāya idaṃ nikhittaṃ, sādhu suṭṭhu maratū”ti abhinandanto gacchati, dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana sopi tattha “evaṃ kate sukataṃ bhavissatī”ti tikhiṇatarādikaraṇena kiñci kammaṃ karoti, tassāpi pārājikaṃ.
