Sace pana “aṭṭhāne ṭhita”nti uddharitvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeti tadatthameva katvā ṭhapite mūlaṭṭho na muccati. Pākatikaṃ labhitvā ṭhapitaṃ hoti, muccati. Taṃ apanetvā aññaṃ tikhiṇataraṃ ṭhapeti mūlaṭṭho muccateva.

177. Regarding ‘on a support, a weapon,’ here ‘support’ (apassena) refers to something in constant use, such as a couch, a seat, or a leaning-board. For one sitting in a day-place, it could be a supporting pillar or a tree growing in that place. For one standing and leaning on a walking path, it could be a tree to hold on to or a board to hold on to. All of these are called ‘support’ in the sense that they are to be leaned upon. If, on such a support, one places a weapon from among an adze, axe, spear, awl, thorn, or the like, having done so in such a way that it would pierce or cut a person leaning on it, it is a dukkaṭa offense. In a place of constant use, for one who sits, lies down, or leans without suspicion, if suffering arises due to contact with the weapon, it is a thullaccaya offense; if death results, it is a pārājika offense. If another monk, an enemy of that monk, while walking around the monastery, sees it and goes away delighting in the thought, ‘I think this was placed for the purpose of his death. Good, may he die well!’, it is a dukkaṭa offense. But if that monk, thinking, ‘If this is done, it will be well done,’ performs some action such as making it sharper, for him too it is a pārājika offense. If, however, thinking, ‘It is in an unsuitable place,’ one lifts it up and places it in another place, and if it is placed having been made for that same purpose, the original person is not absolved. If a normal weapon is obtained and placed, the original person is absolved. If one removes that weapon and places another, sharper one, the original person is indeed absolved.

Visamakkhanepi yāva maraṇābhinandane dukkaṭaṃ tāva eseva nayo. Sace pana sopi khuddakaṃ visamaṇḍalanti sallakkhetvā mahantataraṃ vā karoti[M 2.0057], mahantaṃ vā “atirekaṃ hotī”ti khuddakaṃ karoti, tanukaṃ vā bahalaṃ; bahalaṃ vā tanukaṃ karoti, agginā tāpetvā heṭṭhā vā upari vā sañcāreti, tassāpi pārājikaṃ. “Idaṃ aṭhāne ṭhita”nti sabbameva tacchetvā puñchitvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeti, attanā bhesajjāni yojetvā kate mūlaṭṭho na muccati[V 2.0052], attanā akate muccati. Sace pana so “idaṃ visaṃ atiparitta”nti aññampi ānetvā pakkhipati, yassa visena marati, tassa pārājikaṃ. Sace ubhinnampi santakena marati, ubhinnampi pārājikaṃ. “Idaṃ visaṃ nibbisa”nti taṃ apanetvā attano visameva ṭhapeti, tasseva pārājikaṃ mūlaṭṭho muccati.

In the case of smearing with poison, this same method applies, up to the dukkaṭa offense for delighting in a death. But if that monk, observing that the area of poison is small, makes it larger; or observing that a large area is excessive, makes it smaller; or makes a thin layer thick, or a thick layer thin; or, having heated it with fire, moves it below or above—for him too, it is a pārājika offense. If, thinking, ‘This is in an unsuitable place,’ one scrapes it all off, wipes it, and places it in another place: if the poison was made by the original person himself having compounded medicines, the original person is not absolved; if it was not made by him, he is absolved. But if that monk, observing, ‘This poison is too little,’ brings another poison and adds it, then for whichever person whose poison causes the death, for that person it is a pārājika offense. If death occurs from the poison belonging to both, it is a pārājika offense for both. If, thinking, ‘This poison is non-poisonous,’ one removes that original poison and places only one’s own poison, for that person alone it is a pārājika offense; the original person is absolved.

Dubbalaṃ vā karotīti [P 2.0460] mañcapīṭhaṃ aṭaniyā heṭṭhābhāge chinditvā vidalehi vā rajjukehi vā yehi vītaṃ hoti, te vā chinditvā appāvasesameva katvā heṭṭhā āvudhaṃ nikkhipati “ettha patitvā marissatī”ti. Apassenaphalakādīnampi caṅkame ālambanarukkhaphalakapariyosānānaṃ parabhāgaṃ chinditvā heṭṭhā āvudhaṃ nikkhipati, sobbhādīsu mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā apassenaphalakaṃ vā ānetvā ṭhapeti, yathā tattha nisinnamatto vā apassitamatto vā patati, sobbhādīsu vā sañcaraṇasetu hoti, taṃ dubbalaṃ karoti; evaṃ karontassa karaṇe dukkaṭaṃ. Itarassa dukkhuppattiyā thullaccayaṃ, maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Bhikkhuṃ ānetvā sobbhādīnaṃ taṭe ṭhapeti “disvā bhayena kampento patitvā marissatī”ti dukkaṭaṃ. So tattheva patati, dukkhuppattiyā thullaccayaṃ, maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Sayaṃ vā pāteti, aññena vā pātāpeti, añño avutto vā attano dhammatāya pāteti, amanusso pāteti, vātappahārena patati, attano dhammatāya patatti, sabbattha maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Kasmā? Tassa payogena sobbhāditaṭe ṭhitattā.

“Or he makes it weak” means: having cut the lower part of the leg of a couch or seat; or having cut the cane strips or ropes with which it is woven, leaving only a little remaining, he places a weapon underneath, thinking, “Falling here, he will die.” Also, for leaning-boards and so on, up to holding-trees and holding-boards on a walking path, he cuts the further part and places a weapon underneath. He brings a couch, seat, or leaning-board and places it over a pit or the like, in such a way that just by sitting on it or just by leaning on it, one falls. Or there is a bridge for passage over a pit or the like, and he makes it weak. For one doing so, at the time of the action, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If suffering arises for the other, it is a grave offense; on death, a pārājika offense. He brings a monk and places him on the edge of a pit or the like, thinking, “Seeing it, trembling with fear, he will fall and die”; this is an offense of wrong-doing. If he falls right there, it is a grave offense if suffering arises, and a pārājika offense on death. Whether he himself makes him fall, or he causes another to make him fall, or another uninstructed makes him fall by his own nature, or a non-human makes him fall, or he falls from a gust of wind, or he falls by his own nature—in all cases, on death, it is a pārājika offense. Why? Because it was due to that one's effort that he was standing on the edge of the pit or the like.

Upanikkhipanaṃ nāma samīpe nikkhipanaṃ. Tattha “yo iminā asinā mato so dhanaṃ vā labhatī”tiādinā nayena maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇetvā “iminā maraṇatthikā marantu, māraṇatthikā mārentū”ti vā vatvā asiṃ upanikkhipati, tassa upanikkhipane dukkaṭaṃ. Maritukāmo vā tena attānaṃ paharatu[M 2.0058], māretukāmo vā aññaṃ paharatu, ubhayathāpi parassa dukkhuppattiyā [V 2.0053] upanikkhepakassa thullaccayaṃ, maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Anuddissa nikkhitte bahūnaṃ maraṇe akusalarāsi. Pārājikādivatthūsu pārājikādīni. Vippaṭisāre uppanne asiṃ gahitaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā muccati. Kiṇitvā gahito hoti, asissāmikānaṃ asiṃ, yesaṃ hatthato mūlaṃ gahitaṃ, tesaṃ mūlaṃ datvā muccati. Sace lohapiṇḍiṃ vā phālaṃ vā kudālaṃ vā gahetvā asi kārāpito hoti, yaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā kārito, tadeva katvā muccati. Sace kudālaṃ gahetvā [P 2.0461] kāritaṃ vināsetvā phālaṃ karoti, phālena pahāraṃ labhitvā marantesupi pāṇātipātato na muccati. Sace pana lohaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā upanikkhipanatthameva kārito hoti, arena ghaṃsitvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ katvā vippakiṇṇe muccati. Sacepi saṃvaṇṇanāpotthako viya bahūhi ekajjhāsayehi kato hoti, potthake vuttanayeneva kammabandhavinicchayo veditabbo. Esa nayo sattibheṇḍīsu. Laguḷe pāsayaṭṭhisadiso vinicchayo. Tathā pāsāṇe. Satthe asisadisova. Visaṃ vāti visaṃ upanikkhipantassa vatthuvasena uddissānuddissānurūpato pārājikādivatthūsu pārājikādīni veditabbāni. Kiṇitvā ṭhapite purimanayena paṭipākatikaṃ katvā muccati. Sayaṃ bhesajjehi yojite avisaṃ katvā muccati. Rajjuyā pāsarajjusadisova vinicchayo.

“Upanikkhipana” means placing nearby. In this case, if a monk places a sword while praising the virtues of death by the method of saying, “Whoever dies by this sword will gain wealth,” and so on, or by saying, “By this, let those who wish to die, die; let those who wish to kill, kill,” for that placing, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Whether one who wishes to die strikes himself with it, or one who wishes to kill strikes another, in either case, due to the arising of suffering for another, for the one who placed it there is a grave offense; upon death, it is an offense of defeat. If it is placed without specifying a target, due to the death of many, there is an accumulation of demerit. In cases involving a pārājika offense and other offenses, the corresponding pārājika and other offenses apply. If remorse arises, one is freed by putting the sword back in the place from which it was taken. If it was obtained by purchase, one is freed by returning the sword to its owners, or by returning the price to those from whom it was taken. If one took an iron lump, a plowshare, or a hoe and had a sword made, one is freed by making it back into the very item that was taken to have it made. If he destroys the sword that was made from a hoe and makes a plowshare, even if people die after being struck by that plowshare, he is not freed from the offense of killing. But if, having produced iron, he has it made for the very purpose of placing it nearby, he is freed by grinding it into fine powder with a file and scattering it. Even if it is made by many with a single intention, like a book of praise, the legal decision on the karmic connection should be understood according to the method stated for the book. This is the method for spears and javelins. For a club, the legal decision is similar to that for a noose-stick. Likewise for a stone. For other weapons, it is just like that for a sword. As for poison, for one who places poison, the pārājika and other offenses should be understood as applying in their respective cases, in accordance with whether a target is specified or unspecified. If poison is bought and placed, one is freed by restoring it to its natural state according to the previous method. If one has compounded it with medicines oneself, one is freed by rendering it non-poisonous. For a rope, the legal decision is just like that for a noose-rope.

Bhesajje – yo bhikkhu veribhikkhussa pajjarake vā visabhāgaroge vā uppanne asappāyānipi sappiādīni sappāyānīti maraṇādhippāyo deti, aññaṃ vā kiñci kandamūlaphalaṃ tassa evaṃ bhesajjadāne dukkaṭaṃ. Parassa dukkhuppattiyaṃ maraṇe ca thullaccayapārājikāni, ānantariyavatthumhi ānantariyanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding medicine: if a monk, when a severe fever or an uncongenial disease has arisen in a hostile monk, gives unsuitable things such as ghee, saying, “These are suitable,” with the intention of causing death, or gives some other root, tuber, or fruit, for giving medicine in this way, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Due to the arising of suffering for another and due to death, there are grave offenses and offenses of defeat. In a case involving an act with immediate retribution, it should be understood as an act with immediate retribution.

178. Rūpūpahāre – upasaṃharatīti paraṃ vā amanāparūpaṃ tassa samīpe ṭhapeti, attanā vā yakkhapetādivesaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati, tassa upasaṃhāramatte dukkaṭaṃ. Parassa taṃ rūpaṃ disvā bhayuppattiyaṃ thullaccayaṃ, maraṇe pārājikaṃ. Sace pana tadeva rūpaṃ ekaccassa manāpaṃ hoti, alābhakena ca sussitvā marati, visaṅketo. Manāpiyepi eseva nayo. Tattha pana visesena [M 2.0059] itthīnaṃ purisarūpaṃ purisānañca itthirūpaṃ manāpaṃ taṃ alaṅkaritvā upasaṃharati, diṭṭhamattakameva karoti, aticiraṃ passitumpi na deti, itaro alābhakena sussitvā marati, pārājikaṃ. Sace uttasitvā marati[P 2.0462], visaṅketo. Atha pana uttasitvā vā alābhakena vāti avicāretvā “kevalaṃ passitvā marissatī”ti upasaṃharati, uttasitvā vā sussitvā vā mate pārājikameva. Etenevūpāyena saddūpahārādayopi veditabbā. Kevalañhettha amanussasaddādayo utrāsajanakā amanāpasaddā, purisānaṃ itthisaddamadhuragandhabbasaddādayo cittassādakarā manāpasaddā. Himavante visarukkhānaṃ mūlādigandhā kuṇapagandhā ca amanāpagandhā, kāḷānusārīmūlagandhādayo manāpagandhā[V 2.0054]. Paṭikūlamūlarasādayo amanāparasā, appaṭikūlamūlarasādayo manāparasā. Visaphassamahākacchuphassādayo amanāpaphoṭṭhabbā, cīnapaṭahaṃsapupphatūlikaphassādayo manāpaphoṭṭhabbāti veditabbā.

178. Regarding the presentation of forms: if one presents an unpleasing form to another, or places it near them, or if one assumes the guise of a yakkha, peta, or other such being and stands there, merely presenting it incurs an offense of wrong-doing. If, upon seeing that form, the other person becomes frightened, it is a grave offense; if death results, it is an offense of defeat. However, if that very form is pleasing to someone, and they wither away and die from not obtaining it, it is a case of uncertainty. The same principle applies to pleasing forms. In that case, specifically, a man's form is pleasing to women, and a woman's form is pleasing to men. If one presents such a form, having adorned it, making it so it is only briefly seen and not allowing it to be seen for very long, and the other person withers away and dies from not obtaining it, it is an offense of defeat. If they die from fright, it is a case of uncertainty. But if one presents it without considering whether they will die from fright or from not obtaining it, thinking only, “They will die merely from seeing it,” and they die either from fright or from withering away, it is indeed an offense of defeat. By this same method, the presentations of sound and so on should also be understood. In this context, non-human sounds and the like are fear-inducing, unpleasant sounds; for men, the sound of a woman's voice, sweet gandhabba sounds, and the like are mind-delighting, pleasant sounds. In the Himalayas, the smells of the roots of poisonous trees and the like, and the stench of a corpse, are unpleasant smells; the fragrance of roots like kāḷānusārī and the like are pleasant smells. The tastes of disgusting roots and the like are unpleasant tastes; the tastes of non-disgusting roots and the like are pleasant tastes. The touch of poison, a large scabies sore, and the like are unpleasant tangibles; the touch of Chinese cloth, goose-flower cotton, and the like are pleasant tangibles. This should be understood.

Dhammūpahāre – dhammoti desanādhammo veditabbo. Desanāvasena vā niraye ca sagge ca vipattisampattibhedaṃ dhammārammaṇameva. Nerayikassāti bhinnasaṃvarassa katapāpassa niraye nibbattanārahassa sattassa pañcavidhabandhanakammakaraṇādinirayakathaṃ katheti. Taṃ ce sutvā so uttasitvā marati, kathikassa pārājikaṃ. Sace pana so sutvāpi attano dhammatāya marati, anāpatti. “Idaṃ sutvā evarūpaṃ pāpaṃ na karissati oramissati viramissatī”ti nirayakathaṃ katheti, taṃ sutvā itaro uttasitvā marati, anāpatti. Saggakathanti devanāṭakādīnaṃ nandanavanādīnañca sampattikathaṃ; taṃ sutvā itaro saggādhimutto sīghaṃ taṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇitukāmo satthāharaṇavisakhādanaāhārupaccheda-assāsapassāsasannirundhanādīhi dukkhaṃ uppādeti, kathikassa thullaccayaṃ, marati pārājikaṃ. Sace pana so sutvāpi yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā attano dhammatāya marati, anāpatti[P 2.0463]. “Imaṃ sutvā puññāni karissatī”ti katheti, taṃ sutvā itaro adhimutto kālaṃkaroti, anāpatti.

Regarding the offering of Dhamma: “Dhamma” should be understood as the Dhamma of teaching. Or, by way of teaching, it is simply the Dhamma as a mental object, distinguishing between misfortune in hell and fortune in heaven. For one destined for hell: this refers to speaking about the fivefold bondage, the infliction of punishments, and so on, to a being whose restraint is broken, who has committed evil, and is fit to be reborn in hell. If, upon hearing this, that person becomes terrified and dies, the speaker incurs an offense of defeat (pārājika). But if, even after hearing it, that person dies by their own nature, there is no offense. If one speaks about hell with the thought, “Having heard this, they will not do such evil, they will desist, they will abstain,” and upon hearing it, the other person becomes terrified and dies, there is no offense. Talk of heaven refers to speaking about the prosperity of divine dancers, the Nandana grove, and so on. If, upon hearing this, the other person becomes intent on heaven and, desiring to quickly attain that prosperity, inflicts suffering upon themselves by means of taking a weapon, eating poison, cutting off food, or restraining the in-and-out breaths, the speaker incurs a grave offense; if the person dies, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika). But if, even after hearing it, that person lives out their lifespan and dies by their own nature, there is no offense. If one speaks with the thought, “Having heard this, they will perform meritorious deeds,” and upon hearing it, the other person, being intent, dies, there is no offense.

179. Ācikkhanāyaṃ – puṭṭho bhaṇatīti “bhante kathaṃ mato dhanaṃ vā labhati sagge vā upapajjatī”ti evaṃ pucchito bhaṇati.

179. Regarding explanation: “When asked, one speaks” means: being asked thus, “Venerable sir, how does one who has died obtain wealth, or how is one reborn in heaven?” one speaks.

Anusāsaniyaṃ – apuṭṭhoti evaṃ apucchito sāmaññeva bhaṇati.

Regarding instruction: “Unasked” means that without being asked thus, one speaks on one's own accord.

Saṅketakammanimittakammāni [M 2.0060] adinnādānakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

The acts of making an appointment and making a sign should be understood in the very way explained in the discussion on taking what is not given.

Evaṃ nānappakārato āpattibhedaṃ dassetvā idāni anāpattibhedaṃ dassento “anāpatti asañciccā”tiādimāha. Tattha asañciccāti “iminā upakkamena imaṃ māremī”ti acetetvā. Evañhi acetetvā katena upakkamena pare matepi anāpatti, vakkhati ca “anāpatti bhikkhu asañciccā”ti. Ajānantassāti “iminā ayaṃ marissatī”ti ajānantassa upakkamena pare matepi anāpatti, vakkhati ca visagatapiṇḍapātavatthusmiṃ “anāpatti bhikkhu ajānantassā”ti. Namaraṇādhippāyassāti maraṇaṃ anicchantassa. Yena hi upakkamena paro marati, tena upakkamena tasmiṃ māritepi namaraṇādhippāyassa anāpatti. Vakkhati [V 2.0055] ca “anāpatti bhikkhu namaraṇādhippāyassā”ti. Ummattakādayo pubbe vuttanayā eva. Idha pana ādikammikā aññamaññaṃ jīvitā voropitabhikkhū, tesaṃ anāpatti. Avasesānaṃ maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇanakādīnaṃ āpattiyevāti.

Having thus shown the various types of offenses, now, to show the types of non-offenses, he said, “There is no offense if unintentional,” and so on. Therein, “unintentional” means without intending thus: “By this effort, I will kill this person.” For indeed, even if another dies by an effort undertaken without such intention, there is no offense. And it will be stated: “There is no offense for a bhikkhu if it is unintentional.” “For one not knowing” means: for one not knowing thus, “By this effort, this person will die.” Even if another dies by the effort of one who does not know, there is no offense. And it will be stated in the case of the poisoned lump of food: “There is no offense for a bhikkhu if he does not know.” “For one without the intention of death” means: for one not desiring death. For indeed, by whatever effort another dies, even if that person is killed by that effort, there is no offense for one who does not have the intention of death. And it will be stated: “There is no offense for a bhikkhu if he has no intention of death.” The insane and so forth are just as previously explained. Here, however, the original perpetrators were the bhikkhus who deprived each other of life; for them, there is no offense. For the remaining ones, such as those who speak in praise of the virtues of death, there is indeed an offense.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Word-Analysis is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu – idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ; kāyacittato ca vācācittato ca kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dukkhavedanaṃ. Sacepi hi sirisayanaṃ ārūḷho rajjasampattisukhaṃ anubhavanto rājā “coro deva ānīto”ti vutte “gacchatha naṃ mārethā”ti hasamānova bhaṇati, domanassacitteneva bhaṇatīti veditabbo. Sukhavokiṇṇattā [P 2.0464] pana anuppabandhābhāvā ca dujjānametaṃ puthujjanehīti.

Regarding the origins and so forth: This training rule has three origins; it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action, is one from which there is exemption through perception, is intentional, is blameworthy in the world, is a bodily action, is a verbal action, involves an unwholesome mind, and has painful feeling. For even if a king, having ascended a glorious couch and enjoying the bliss of royal sovereignty, upon being told, “Your Majesty, a thief has been brought,” says while smiling, “Go, kill him,” it should be understood that he speaks only with a mind of displeasure. However, because it is interspersed with pleasure and because of the lack of a continuous connection, this is difficult for ordinary people to know.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Resolved Cases

180. Vinītavatthukathāsu paṭhamavatthusmiṃ – kāruññenāti te bhikkhū tassa mahantaṃ gelaññadukkhaṃ disvā kāruññaṃ uppādetvā “sīlavā tvaṃ katakusalo, kasmā mīyamāno bhāyasi, nanu sīlavato saggo nāma maraṇamattapaṭibaddhoyevā”ti evaṃ maraṇatthikāva hutvā maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantā maraṇavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇesuṃ. Sopi bhikkhu tesaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāya [M 2.0061] āhārupacchedaṃ katvā antarāva kālamakāsi. Tasmā āpattiṃ āpannā. Vohāravasena pana vuttaṃ “kāruññena maraṇavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇesu”nti. Tasmā idānipi paṇḍitena bhikkhunā gilānassa bhikkhuno evaṃ maraṇavaṇṇo na saṃvaṇṇetabbo. Sace hi tassa saṃvaṇṇanaṃ sutvā āhārūpacchedādinā upakkamena ekajavanavārāvasesepi āyusmiṃ antarā kālaṃkaroti, imināva mārito hoti. Iminā pana nayena anusiṭṭhi dātabbā – “sīlavato nāma anacchariyā maggaphaluppatti, tasmā vihārādīsu āsattiṃ akatvā buddhagataṃ dhammagataṃ saṅghagataṃ kāyagatañca satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā manasikāre appamādo kātabbo”ti. Maraṇavaṇṇe ca saṃvaṇṇitepi yo tāya saṃvaṇṇanāya kañci upakkamaṃ akatvā attano dhammatāya yathāyunā yathānusandhināva marati, tappaccayā saṃvaṇṇako āpattiyā na kāretabboti.

180. In the first of the resolved cases: “Out of compassion” means that those bhikkhus, seeing that bhikkhu's great suffering from illness, gave rise to compassion and, desiring his death yet not knowing that they were desiring his death, praised the virtues of death thus: “You are virtuous, one who has made merit; why do you fear dying? Surely for a virtuous one, heaven is secured by the mere fact of death.” That bhikkhu, because of their praise, cut off his food and died in the interval before his time. Therefore, they incurred an offense. But it was said conventionally, “Out of compassion, they praised the virtues of death.” Therefore, even now, a wise bhikkhu should not praise the virtues of death to a sick bhikkhu in this way. For if, having heard his praise, the sick bhikkhu, through an effort such as cutting off food, dies in the interval even when only one series of thought-moments of life remains, he is considered to have been killed by this very bhikkhu. Instead, instruction should be given in this way: “For a virtuous one, the arising of the path and fruit is not surprising. Therefore, without attachment to the monastery and so forth, having established mindfulness directed towards the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the body, you should be heedful in your contemplation.” And even when the virtues of death have been praised, if a person, without making any effort on account of that praise, dies by his own nature, according to his life-span and according to his continuity, the one who praised should not be charged with an offense on account of that.

Dutiyavatthusmiṃ – na ca bhikkhave appaṭivekkhitvāti ettha kīdisaṃ āsanaṃ paṭivekkhitabbaṃ[V 2.0056], kīdisaṃ na paṭivekkhitabbaṃ? Yaṃ suddhaṃ āsanameva hoti apaccattharaṇakaṃ, yañca āgantvā ṭhitānaṃ passataṃyeva attharīyati, taṃ napaccavekkhitabbaṃ[P 2.0465], nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Yampi manussā sayaṃ hatthena akkamitvā “idha bhante nisīdathā”ti denti, tasmimpi vaṭṭati. Sacepi paṭhamamevāgantvā nisinnā pacchā uddhaṃ vā adho vā saṅkamanti, paccavekkhaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Yampi tanukena vatthena yathā talaṃ dissati, evaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, tasmimpi paccavekkhaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Yaṃ pana paṭikacceva pāvārakojavādīhi atthataṃ hoti, taṃ hatthena parāmasitvā sallakkhetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “ghanasāṭakenāpi atthate yasmiṃ vali na paññāyati, taṃ nappaṭivekkhitabbanti vuttaṃ.

In the second case: Regarding '...and not, O bhikkhus, without having inspected...': what kind of seat should be inspected, and what kind need not be inspected? A seat that is just a bare seat without a covering, and one that is spread while those who have arrived are watching, that need not be inspected; it is permissible to sit on it. Also, a seat which people offer, saying, 'Venerable sirs, sit here,' having pressed down on it themselves with their hand, on that too it is permissible to sit. If those who arrived first and are seated later move up or down for the sake of giving space to those who came later, there is no need for inspection. Also, a seat that is covered with a thin cloth in such a way that the surface below is visible, on that too there is no need for inspection. But a seat that has been spread beforehand with a cloak, a rug, or the like, should be sat upon only after feeling it with the hand and taking note. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said: 'A seat on which, though spread even with a thick cloth, a fold is not apparent, need not be inspected.'

Musalavatthusmiṃ – asañciccoti avadhakacetano viraddhapayogo hi so. Tenāha “asañcicco aha”nti. Udukkhalavatthu uttānameva. Vuḍḍhapabbajitavatthūsupaṭhamavatthusmiṃ “bhikkhusaṅghassa paṭibandhaṃ mā akāsī”ti paṇāmesi. Dutiyavatthusmiṃ – saṅghamajjhepi gaṇamajjhepi “mahallakattherassa putto”ti vuccamāno tena vacanena aṭṭīyamāno “maratu aya”nti paṇāmesi. Tatiyavatthusmiṃ – tassa dukkhuppādanena thullaccayaṃ.

In the case of the pestle: 'Unintentionally' means he was one with no intention to kill, for his effort was misdirected. Therefore, he said, 'I was unintentional.' The case of the mortar is self-evident. In the cases of the old monk: in the first case, he sent him away, saying, 'Do not cause an obstruction for the community of bhikkhus.' In the second case, being called 'the old elder's son' both in the midst of the Sangha and in the midst of a group, and being distressed by that statement, he sent him away thinking, 'Let this one die.' In the third case, for causing him suffering, there is a grave offense.

181. Tato [M 2.0062] parāni tīṇi vatthūni uttānatthāneva. Visagatapiṇḍapātavatthusmiṃ – sārāṇīyadhammapūrako so bhikkhu aggapiṇḍaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvāva bhuñjati. Tena vuttaṃ “aggakārikaṃ adāsī”ti. Aggakārikanti aggakiriyaṃ; paṭhamaṃ laddhapiṇḍapātaṃ aggaggaṃ vā paṇītapaṇītaṃ piṇḍapātanti attho. Yā pana tassa dānasaṅkhātā aggakiriyā, sā na sakkā dātuṃ, piṇḍapātañhi so therāsanato [P 2.0466] paṭṭhāya adāsi. Te bhikkhūti te therāsanato paṭṭhāya paribhuttapiṇḍapātā bhikkhū; te kira sabbepi kālamakaṃsu. Sesamettha uttānameva. Assaddhesu pana micchādiṭṭhikesu kulesu sakkaccaṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ labhitvā anupaparikkhitvā neva attanā paribhuñjitabbaṃ, na paresaṃ dātabbaṃ. Yampi ābhidosikaṃ bhattaṃ vā khajjakaṃ vā tato labhati, tampi na paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Apihitavatthumpi hi sappavicchikādīhi adhisayitaṃ chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ tāni kulāni denti. Gandhahaliddādimakkhitopi tato piṇḍapāto na gahetabbo. Sarīre rogaṭṭhānāni puñchitvā ṭhapitabhattampi hi tāni dātabbaṃ maññantīti.

181. The three subsequent stories are clear in meaning. In the story of the poisoned almsfood: that bhikkhu, a fulfiller of the conditions for cordiality, eats only after having given the first portion of the almsfood to his fellow monks. Therefore it was said, 'He performed the primary act.' 'Primary act' means the foremost action; the meaning is giving the almsfood first received, or giving the choicest, most excellent almsfood. However, that primary act of his, known as giving, could not be given, for he gave the almsfood starting from the elder's seat. 'Those bhikkhus' means those bhikkhus who had consumed the almsfood, starting from the elder's seat; it is said that all of them died. The rest here is clear in meaning. However, in faithless families holding wrong views, having received excellent food prepared with care, one should neither consume it oneself nor give it to others without investigation. Whatever stale food or snacks one receives from them, that too should not be consumed. For those families give things that should be discarded, inhabited by snakes, scorpions, and the like, even uncovered items. Almsfood from them smeared with perfumes, turmeric, and the like should not be accepted. For they think that even food placed after wiping diseased parts of the body is fit to be given.

Vīmaṃsanavatthusmiṃ – vīmaṃsamāno dve vīmaṃsati – “sakkoti nu kho imaṃ māretuṃ no”ti visaṃ vā vīmaṃsati, “mareyya nu kho ayaṃ imaṃ visaṃ khāditvā no”ti puggalaṃ vā. Ubhayathāpi vīmaṃsādhippāyena dinne maratu vā mā vā thullaccayaṃ. “Idaṃ visaṃ etaṃ māretū”ti vā [V 2.0057] “idaṃ visaṃ khāditvā ayaṃ maratū”ti vā evaṃ dinne pana sace marati, pārājikaṃ; no ce, thullaccayaṃ.

In the story of investigation: one who investigates, investigates two things. 'Is this poison capable of killing, or not?'—thus one investigates the poison; or, 'Will this person die after eating this poison, or not?'—thus one investigates the person. In both cases, if it is given with the intention of investigating, whether he dies or does not die, it is a grave offense. However, if it is given thus: 'Let this poison kill him,' or thus: 'Having eaten this poison, let this person die,' then if he dies, it is a pārājika offense; if he does not, it is a grave offense.

182-3. Ito parāni tīṇi silāvatthūni tīṇi iṭṭhakavāsigopānasīvatthūni ca uttānatthāneva. Na kevalañca silādīnaṃyeva vasena ayaṃ āpattānāpattibhedo hoti, daṇḍamuggaranikhādanavemādīnampi vasena hotiyeva, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ anāgatampi āgatanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

182-3. From here, the three subsequent stories about a stone, and the three stories about a brick, an adze, and a rafter, are clear in meaning. And this distinction between offense and non-offense does not arise solely by means of a stone and so on; it also arises by means of a stick, a mallet, a chisel, a shuttle, and so on. Therefore, even what has not been mentioned in the Pāli should be understood by the same method as what has been mentioned.

Aṭṭakavatthūsu – aṭṭakoti vehāsamañco vuccati; yaṃ setakammamālākammalatākammādīnaṃ atthāya bandhanti. Tattha āvuso atraṭṭhito bandhāhīti maraṇādhippāyo yatra ṭhito patitvā khāṇunā vā bhijjeyya, sobbhapapātādīsu vā mareyya[P 2.0467], tādisaṃ ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāha. Ettha ca koci upariṭhānaṃ niyāmeti “ito patitvā marissatī”ti, koci heṭṭhā ṭhānaṃ “idha patitvā marissatī”ti, koci ubhayampi “ito idha patitvā [M 2.0063] marissatī”ti. Tatra yo upari niyamitaṭṭhānā apatitvā aññato patati, heṭṭhā niyamitaṭṭhāne vā apatitvā aññattha patati, ubhayaniyāme vā yaṃkiñci ekaṃ virādhetvā patati, tasmiṃ mate visaṅketattā anāpatti. Vihāracchādanavatthusmimpi eseva nayo.

In the stories of the scaffold: an 'aṭṭaka' is called a scaffold, which they construct for the purpose of whitewashing, flower-pattern work, creeper-work, and so on. Therein, when one says, 'Friend, standing here, you should tie it,' it is said with the intention of causing death, referring to a place where, standing there and falling, one might be pierced by a stump or die in a pit, precipice, or the like. And here, someone specifies the place above, thinking, 'Falling from here, he will die'; someone specifies the place below, thinking, 'Falling here, he will die'; and someone specifies both, thinking, 'Falling from here to here, he will die.' In that case, if one does not fall from the specified place above but falls from another place, or does not fall in the specified place below but falls elsewhere, or in the case of specifying both, falls having missed one or the other, then if that person dies, there is no offense because the designated spot was missed. In the story of roofing the monastery, this is the same method.

Anabhirativatthusmiṃ – so kira bhikkhu kāmavitakkādīnaṃ samudācāraṃ disvā nivāretuṃ asakkonto sāsane anabhirato gihibhāvābhimukho jāto. Tato cintesi – “yāva sīlabhedaṃ na pāpuṇāmi tāva marissāmī”ti. Atha taṃ pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā papāte papatanto aññataraṃ vilīvakāraṃ ottharitvā māresi. Vilīvakāranti veṇukāraṃ. Na ca bhikkhave attānaṃ pātetabbanti na attā pātetabbo. Vibhattibyattayena panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha ca na kevalaṃ na pātetabbaṃ, aññenapi yena kenaci upakkamena antamaso āhārupacchedenapi na māretabbo. Yopi hi gilāno vijjamāne bhesajje ca upaṭṭhākesu ca maritukāmo āhāraṃ upacchindati, dukkaṭameva. Yassa pana mahāābādho cirānubaddho, bhikkhū upaṭṭhahantā kilamanti jigucchanti “kadā nu kho gilānato muccissāmā”ti aṭṭīyanti. Sace so “ayaṃ attabhāvo paṭijaggiyamānopi na tiṭṭhati, bhikkhū ca kilamantī”ti āhāraṃ upacchindati, bhesajjaṃ na sevati vaṭṭati. Yo pana “ayaṃ rogo kharo, āyusaṅkhārā na tiṭṭhanti, ayañca me visesādhigamo hatthappatto viya dissatī”ti upacchindati vaṭṭatiyeva. Agilānassāpi uppannasaṃvegassa “āhārapariyesanaṃ nāma papañco, kammaṭṭhānameva anuyuñjissāmī”ti kammaṭṭhānasīsena [V 2.0058] upacchindantassa vaṭṭati. Visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvā āhāraṃ upacchindati, na vaṭṭati. Sabhāgānañhi [P 2.0468] lajjībhikkhūnaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

In the story of dissatisfaction: It is said that a certain bhikkhu, seeing the arising of sensual thoughts and the like and being unable to restrain them, became dissatisfied with the Teaching and inclined towards the lay life. Then he thought, 'I will die before I break my virtue.' Then, having climbed that mountain and while falling from a precipice, he landed on a certain bamboo-worker and killed him. 'Bamboo-worker' (vilīvakāra) means a worker in bamboo (veṇukāra). And, 'Bhikkhus, one should not cause oneself to fall,' means oneself should not be made to fall. This, however, is said with a change of grammatical case. And here, not only should one not be made to fall, but one should not be killed by any other means whatsoever, not even by cutting off food. For if a sick person, though medicine and attendants are available, wishes to die and cuts off food, it is a dukkaṭa offense. But if someone has a great, chronic illness, and the bhikkhus attending him grow weary, feel revulsion, and are distressed, thinking, 'When, indeed, will we be free from this sick person?'—if that person, thinking, 'This personal existence, even when cared for, does not last, and the bhikkhus are weary,' cuts off food and does not take medicine, it is permissible. Or if one, thinking, 'This disease is harsh, the life-formations do not last, and this special attainment seems to be within my grasp,' cuts off food, it is indeed permissible. Even for one who is not sick but in whom a sense of urgency has arisen, if, thinking, 'The search for food is a proliferation; I will apply myself only to the meditation subject,' one cuts off food with the meditation subject as the main focus, it is permissible. If one declares a special attainment and then cuts off food, it is not permissible. For it is permissible to tell conscientious bhikkhus of a similar disposition.

Silāvatthusmiṃ – davāyāti davena hassena; khiḍḍāyāti attho. Silāti pāsāṇo; na kevalañca pāsāṇo, aññampi yaṃkiñci dārukhaṇḍaṃ vā iṭṭhakākhaṇḍaṃ vā hatthena vā yantena vā pavijjhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Cetiyādīnaṃ atthāya pāsāṇādayo hasantā hasantā pavaṭṭentipi khipantipi ukkhipantipi kammasamayoti vaṭṭati. Aññampi īdisaṃ navakammaṃ vā karontā bhaṇḍakaṃ vā dhovantā rukkhaṃ vā dhovanadaṇḍakaṃ vā ukkhipitvā pavijjhanti, vaṭṭati. Bhattavissaggakālādīsu kāke vā soṇe vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā kathalaṃ vā khipitvā palāpeti, vaṭṭati.

In the story of the stone: 'davāya' means with jesting, with laughter; the meaning is 'for sport'. 'Silā' means a stone. And it is not that it is impermissible only to roll down a stone; it is also impermissible to roll down any other thing whatsoever, be it a piece of wood or a piece of brick, either by hand or by a machine. For the sake of a cetiya and so on, if they roll, throw, or lift stones and so on while laughing and laughing, it is permissible because it is a time for work. While doing other such new work, or while washing their requisites, if they lift and roll down a log or a washing-stick, it is permissible. At the time of meal distribution and so on, if one throws a piece of wood or a potsherd to make crows or dogs flee, it is permissible.

184. Sedanādivatthūni [M 2.0064] sabbāneva uttānatthāni. Ettha ca ahaṃ kukkuccakoti na gilānupaṭṭhānaṃ na kātabbaṃ, hitakāmatāya sabbaṃ gilānassa balābalañca ruciñca sappāyāsappāyañca upalakkhetvā kātabbaṃ.

184. The matters concerning fomentation and so forth are all of clear meaning. And here, it is not that the nursing of the sick should not be done by thinking, 'I am scrupulous.' Out of a desire for the patient's welfare, having observed all the patient's strength and weakness, preferences, and what is suitable and unsuitable, it should be done.

185. Jāragabbhinivatthusmiṃ – pavutthapatikāti pavāsaṃ gatapatikā. Gabbhapātananti yena paribhuttena gabbho patati, tādisaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Dve pajāpatikavatthūni uttānatthāneva. Gabbhamaddanavatthusmiṃ – “madditvā pātehī”ti vutte aññena maddāpetvā pāteti, visaṅketaṃ. “Maddāpetvā pātāpehī”ti vuttepi sayaṃ madditvā pāteti, visaṅketameva. Manussaviggahe pariyāyo nāma natthi. Tasmā “gabbho nāma maddite patatī”ti vutte sā sayaṃ vā maddatu, aññena vā maddāpetvā pātetu, visaṅketo natthi; pārājikameva tāpanavatthusmimpi eseva nayo.

185. In the case of a woman pregnant by a paramour: 'pavutthapatikā' means a woman whose husband has gone to another place. 'Gabbhapātana' means such a medicine by which, when consumed, the fetus is expelled. The two cases concerning the co-wives are of clear meaning. In the case of crushing the fetus: when told, 'Crush it and cause it to be expelled,' if one has another crush it and causes it to be expelled, it is a deviation from the instruction. Even when told, 'Have it crushed and cause it to be expelled,' if one crushes it oneself and causes it to be expelled, it is also a deviation from the instruction. In the case of a human being, there is no such thing as a loophole. Therefore, when it is said, 'A fetus, it is said, is expelled when crushed,' whether she crushes it herself or has another crush it and cause it to be expelled, there is no deviation from the instruction; it is a Pārājika offense indeed. In the case of causing heat also, this is the same principle.

Vañjhitthivatthusmiṃ – vañjhitthī nāma yā gabbhaṃ na gaṇhāti. Gabbhaṃ agaṇhanakaitthī nāma natthi, yassā pana gahitopi gabbho na saṇṭhāti, taṃyeva sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Utusamaye kira sabbitthiyo gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti. Yā panāyaṃ “vañjhā”ti vuccati, tassā kucchiyaṃ nibbattasattānaṃ [P 2.0469] akusalavipāko sampāpuṇāti. Te parittakusalavipākena gahitapaṭisandhikā akusalavipākena adhibhūtā vinassanti. Abhinavapaṭisandhiyaṃyeva hi kammānubhāvena dvīhākārehi gabbho na saṇṭhāti – vātena vā pāṇakehi vā. Vāto sosetvā antaradhāpeti, pāṇakā khāditvā. Tassa pana vātassa pāṇakānaṃ vā paṭighātāya bhesajje kate gabbho saṇṭhaheyya; so bhikkhu taṃ akatvā aññaṃ kharabhesajjaṃ adāsi. Tena sā kālamakāsi. Bhagavā bhesajjassa kaṭattā dukkaṭaṃ paññāpesi.

In the case of a barren woman: a 'barren woman' is a woman who does not conceive. There is no such thing as a woman who cannot conceive; however, it is with reference to her for whom a fetus, though conceived, does not become established that this is said. It is said that during their fertile period, all women conceive. But for this woman who is called 'barren,' the result of unwholesome kamma arrives for the beings who have arisen in her womb. Those beings, having taken rebirth with the result of meager wholesome kamma, are overcome by the result of unwholesome kamma and perish. Indeed, at the very time of new conception, due to the power of kamma, the fetus does not become established for two reasons: either by wind or by small creatures. The wind, having dried it, makes it disappear; the small creatures, having eaten it, make it disappear. However, if medicine were made to counteract that wind or those small creatures, the fetus would become established; but that bhikkhu, not making that, gave another, harsh medicine. Because of that, she died. The Blessed One, because of the medicine having been prepared, laid down a dukkaṭa offense.

Dutiyavatthusmimpi [V 2.0059] eseva nayo. Tasmā āgatāgatassa parajanassa bhesajjaṃ na kātabbaṃ, karonto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Pañcannaṃ pana sahadhammikānaṃ kātabbaṃ bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā sikkhamānāya sāmaṇerassa sāmaṇeriyāti. Samasīlasaddhāpaññānañhi etesaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu yuttānaṃ bhesajjaṃ akātuṃ na labbhati, karontena ca sace tesaṃ atthi, tesaṃ santakaṃ gahetvā yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace natthi, attano santakaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace attanopi natthi, bhikkhācāravattena vā ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato vā pariyesitabbaṃ. Alabhantena gilānassa atthāya akataviññattiyāpi āharitvā kātabbaṃ.

In the second case also, this is the same principle. Therefore, medicine should not be prepared for any other person who comes; one who does so incurs a dukkaṭa offense. However, it should be prepared for the five kinds of co-religionists: a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a probationer, a male novice, and a female novice. Indeed, for these co-religionists who are equal in morality, faith, and wisdom, and who are engaged in the three trainings, it is not allowable not to prepare medicine. And when preparing it, if they have it, their own medicine should be taken, prepared, and given. If they do not have it, one's own should be used to prepare it. If one also does not have it, it should be sought either by the practice of going on alms-round or from the place of relatives or those who have given an invitation. If one does not obtain it, it should be brought and prepared for the sake of the sick person, even by means of an unallowable request.

Aparesampi [M 2.0065] pañcannaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati – mātu, pitu, tadupaṭṭhākānaṃ, attano veyyāvaccakarassa, paṇḍupalāsassāti. Paṇḍupalāso nāma yo pabbajjāpekkho yāva pattacīvaraṃ paṭiyādiyati tāva vihāre vasati. Tesu sace mātāpitaro issarā honti, na paccāsīsanti, akātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana rajjepi ṭhitā paccāsīsanti, akātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Bhesajjaṃ paccāsīsantānaṃ bhesajjaṃ dātabbaṃ, yojetuṃ ajānantānaṃ yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sabbesaṃ atthāya sahadhammikesu vuttanayeneva pariyesitabbaṃ. Sace pana mātaraṃ vihāre ānetvā jaggati, sabbaṃ parikammaṃ anāmasantena kātabbaṃ. Khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ sahatthā dātabbaṃ. Pitā pana yathā sāmaṇero evaṃ sahatthena nhāpanasambāhanādīni [P 2.0470] katvā upaṭṭhātabbo. Ye ca mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti paṭijagganti, tesampi evameva kātabbaṃ. Veyyāvaccakaro nāma yo vetanaṃ gahetvā araññe dārūni vā chindati, aññaṃ vā kiñci kammaṃ karoti, tassa roge uppanne yāva ñātakā na passanti tāva bhesajjaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yo pana bhikkhunissitakova hutvā sabbakammāni karoti, tassa bhesajjaṃ kātabbameva. Paṇḍupalāsepi sāmaṇere viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

It is allowable to prepare it for five other persons as well: one’s mother, father, their attendants, one’s own attendant, and a 'yellow leaf' person. A 'yellow leaf' person is one who, aspiring for ordination, dwells in the monastery for as long as he is preparing his bowl and robes. Among them, if one's parents are powerful and do not expect it, it is allowable not to prepare it. However, if, even while established in kingship, they expect it, it is not allowable not to prepare it. Medicine should be given to those who expect medicine; for those who do not know how to prepare it, it should be prepared and given. For the sake of all of them, it should be sought in the very same way as was stated in the case of co-religionists. However, if one brings one's mother to the monastery and attends to her, all services should be done without touching. Hard and soft food may be given with one's own hand. The father, however, should be attended to just like a novice, by doing things like bathing and massaging with one's own hand. And for those who attend to and care for one's parents, it should be done for them in the very same way. An attendant is one who, having received wages, cuts wood in the forest or does some other work. When illness arises for him, medicine should be prepared for as long as his relatives do not see him. However, for one who, being dependent on a bhikkhu, does all tasks, medicine must certainly be prepared. For a 'yellow leaf' person also, one should act as towards a novice.

Aparesampi dasannaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati – jeṭṭhabhātu, kaniṭṭhabhātu, jeṭṭhabhaginiyā, kaniṭṭhabhaginiyā, cūḷamātuyā, mahāmātuyā, cūḷapituno, mahāpituno, pitucchāya, mātulassāti. Tesaṃ pana sabbesampi karontena tesaṃyeva santakaṃ bhesajjaṃ gahetvā kevalaṃ yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace pana nappahonti, yācanti ca “detha no, bhante, tumhākaṃ paṭidassāmā”ti tāvakālikaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sacepi na yācanti, “amhākaṃ bhesajjaṃ atthi, tāvakālikaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā vā “yadā nesaṃ bhavissati tadā dassantī”ti ābhogaṃ vā katvā dātabbaṃ. Sace paṭidenti, gahetabbaṃ, no ce denti, na codetabbā. Ete dasa ñātake ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ na kātabbaṃ.

It is allowable to prepare it for ten other persons as well: an elder brother, a younger brother, an elder sister, a younger sister, a mother's younger sister, a mother's elder sister, a father's younger brother, a father's elder brother, a father's sister, and a mother's brother. However, when preparing it for all of them, one should take their own medicine and merely prepare and give it. But if they are unable and they request, 'Venerable sir, give it to us; we will give back to you,' it should be given for a time. Even if they do not request, it should be given either after saying, 'We have medicine; take it for a time,' or after forming the thought, 'When they have it, they will give it back.' If they give it back, it should be accepted; if they do not give, they should not be pressed for it. Setting aside these ten relatives, it should not be prepared for others.

Etesaṃ [V 2.0060] puttaparamparāya pana yāva sattamo kulaparivaṭṭo tāva cattāro paccaye āharāpentassa akataviññatti vā bhesajjaṃ karontassa vejjakammaṃ vā kuladūsakāpatti vā na hoti. Sace bhātujāyā bhaginisāmiko vā gilānā honti, ñātakā ce, tesampi vaṭṭati. Aññātakā ce, bhātu ca bhaginiyā ca katvā dātabbaṃ, “tumhākaṃ jagganaṭṭhāne dethā”ti. Atha vā tesaṃ puttānaṃ katvā dātabbaṃ, “tumhākaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ [M 2.0066] dethā”ti. Etenupāyena sabbapadesupi vinicchayo veditabbo.

However, for their descendants, up to the seventh generation of the family lineage, for a monk who causes the four requisites to be brought, there is no [offense of] improper request; for one who makes medicine, there is no [offense of] medical practice; and there is no offense of corrupting a family. If a brother's wife or a sister's husband is sick, and if they are relatives, it is also allowable for them. If they are not relatives, it should be made using the property of the brother and of the sister and given, saying, 'Give this for the purpose of nursing.' Alternatively, having made it the property of their children, it should be given, saying, 'Give this to your parents.' By this method, the decision should be understood in all cases.

Tesaṃ atthāya ca sāmaṇerehi araññato bhesajjaṃ āharāpentena ñātisāmaṇerehi vā āharāpetabbaṃ. Attano atthāya vā āharāpetvā [P 2.0471] dātabbaṃ. Tehipi “upajjhāyassa āharāmā”ti vattasīsena āharitabbaṃ. Upajjhāyassa mātāpitaro gilānā vihāraṃ āgacchanti, upajjhāyo ca disāpakkanto hoti, saddhivihārikena upajjhāyassa santakaṃ bhesajjaṃ dātabbaṃ. No ce atthi, attano bhesajjaṃ upajjhāyassa pariccajitvā dātabbaṃ. Attanopi asante vuttanayena pariyesitvā upajjhāyassa santakaṃ katvā dātabbaṃ. Upajjhāyenapi saddhivihārikassa mātāpitūsu evameva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Esa nayo ācariyantevāsikesupi. Aññopi yo āgantuko vā coro vā yuddhaparājito issaro vā ñātakehi pariccatto kapaṇo vā gamiyamanusso vā gilāno hutvā vihāraṃ pavisati, sabbesaṃ apaccāsīsantena bhesajjaṃ kātabbaṃ.

And for their sake, when causing medicine to be brought from the forest by novices, it should be caused to be brought by relative-novices. Or, having caused it to be brought for one's own sake, it should be given. Even by them, it should be brought with duty as the primary consideration, thinking, 'We will bring it for our preceptor.' If the preceptor's parents are ill and come to the monastery, and the preceptor has departed to another direction, the co-resident disciple should give medicine belonging to the preceptor. If there is none, he should relinquish his own medicine to the preceptor and give it. Even if he himself has none, having searched for it in the manner stated, it should be made the property of the preceptor and be given. The preceptor, too, should act in this same way toward the co-resident disciple's parents. This is the method also for teachers and their pupils. Furthermore, if anyone else—whether a visitor, a thief, a ruler defeated in battle, one abandoned by relatives, a destitute person, or a traveler—enters the monastery ill, medicine should be made for all of them without expecting material gain.

Saddhaṃ kulaṃ hoti catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhāyakaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa mātāpituṭṭhāniyaṃ, tatra ce koci gilāno hoti, tassatthāya vissāsena “bhesajjaṃ katvā bhante dethā”ti vadanti, neva dātabbaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Atha pana kappiyaṃ ñatvā evaṃ pucchanti – “bhante, asukassa nāma rogassa kiṃ bhesajjaṃ karontī”ti? “Idañcidañca gahetvā karontī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Bhante, mayhaṃ mātā gilānā, bhesajjaṃ tāva ācikkhathā”ti evaṃ pucchite pana na ācikkhitabbaṃ. Aññamaññaṃ pana kathā kātabbā – “āvuso, asukassa nāma bhikkhuno imasmiṃ roge kiṃ bhesajjaṃ kariṃsū”ti? “Idañcidañca bhante”ti. Taṃ sutvā itaro mātu bhesajjaṃ karoti, vaṭṭateva.

There is a faithful family that supports the Sangha of bhikkhus with the four requisites, standing in the place of a mother and father. If someone there is sick, and for their sake they say with familiarity, 'Venerable sir, please make and give medicine,' it should neither be given nor made. But if, knowing what is allowable, they ask thus: 'Venerable sir, what medicine do they make for such-and-such an illness?' it is allowable to say, 'They take this and that and make it.' However, if asked directly, 'Venerable sir, my mother is sick—please tell me the medicine,' it should not be told. But a conversation may be held among fellow monks: 'Friend, for such-and-such a bhikkhu with this illness, what medicine did they make?' 'They made this and that, venerable sir.' Hearing that, the other person makes medicine for his mother; this is indeed allowable.

Mahāpadumattheropi kira vasabharañño deviyā roge uppanne ekāya itthiyā āgantvā pucchito “na jānāmī”ti avatvā evameva bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ samullapesi. Taṃ sutvā tassā bhesajjamakaṃsu. Vūpasante ca roge ticīvarena tīhi ca kahāpaṇasatehi saddhiṃ bhesajjacaṅkoṭakaṃ pūretvā [V 2.0061] āharitvā [M 2.0067] therassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā “bhante, pupphapūjaṃ karothā”ti āhaṃsu. Thero “ācariyabhāgo nāmāya”nti kappiyavasena gāhāpetvā pupphapūjaṃ akāsi. Evaṃ tāva bhesajje paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

It is said that when a disease arose in the queen of King Vasabha, the Elder Mahāpaduma, on being asked by a certain woman who came to him, did not say 'I do not know,' but conversed in this very way with the bhikkhus. Hearing that, they made medicine for her. And when the disease had subsided, they filled a medicine basket and, along with the three robes and three hundred kahāpaṇas, brought it, placed it at the Elder's feet, and said, 'Venerable sir, please perform a flower offering.' The Elder, saying, 'This is called the teacher's share,' had it accepted by means of an allowable expression and performed the flower offering. Thus should one act regarding medicine.

Paritte [P 2.0472] pana “gilānassa parittaṃ karotha, bhante”ti vutte na kātabbaṃ, “bhaṇathā”ti vutte pana kātabbaṃ. Sace pissa evaṃ hoti “manussā nāma na jānanti, akayiramāne vippaṭisārino bhavissantī”ti kātabbaṃ; “parittodakaṃ parittasuttaṃ katvā dethā”ti vuttena pana tesaṃyeva udakaṃ hatthena cāletvā suttaṃ parimajjetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace vihārato udakaṃ attano santakaṃ vā suttaṃ deti, dukkaṭaṃ. Manussā udakañca suttañca gahetvā nisīditvā “parittaṃ bhaṇathā”ti vadanti, kātabbaṃ. No ce jānanti, ācikkhitabbaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ nisinnānaṃ pādesu udakaṃ ākiritvā suttañca ṭhapetvā gacchanti “parittaṃ karotha, parittaṃ bhaṇathā”ti na pādā apanetabbā. Manussā hi vippaṭisārino honti. Antogāme gilānassatthāya vihāraṃ pesenti, “parittaṃ bhaṇantū”ti bhaṇitabbaṃ. Antogāme rājagehādīsu roge vā upaddave vā uppanne pakkosāpetvā bhaṇāpenti, āṭānāṭiyasuttādīni bhaṇitabbāni. “Āgantvā gilānassa sikkhāpadāni dentu, dhammaṃ kathentu. Rājantepure vā amaccagehe vā āgantvā sikkhāpadāni dentu, dhammaṃ kathentū”ti pesitepi gantvā sikkhāpadāni dātabbāni, dhammo kathetabbo. “Matānaṃ parivāratthaṃ āgacchantū”ti pakkosanti, na gantabbaṃ. Sīvathikadassane asubhadassane ca maraṇassatiṃ paṭilabhissāmīti kammaṭṭhānasīsena gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ paritte paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Regarding protective chants, however, when it is said, 'Venerable sir, perform a protective chant for the sick,' it should not be done. But when it is said, 'Recite,' it should be done. If, however, one thinks, 'These people do not know the proper way to ask, and if it is not done, they will be regretful,' it should be done. When it is said, 'Having made protective water and a protective thread, please give them,' their own water should be stirred with the hand and their own thread should be rubbed and then given. If one gives water from the monastery or a thread that is one's own property, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If people, having taken water and thread, sit down and say, 'Recite the protective chant,' it should be done. If they do not know how to ask, they should be instructed. If, while the bhikkhus are seated, people pour water at their feet and place a thread there and then leave, saying, 'Perform the protective chant, recite the protective chant,' the feet should not be withdrawn. For people would be regretful. If they send a message to the monastery for the sake of a sick person in the village, saying, 'Let them recite the protective chant,' it should be recited. If, within the village, in places such as the royal palace, a disease or calamity arises and they have monks summoned to recite, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta and others should be recited. Even if a message is sent, saying, 'Let them come and give the training rules to the sick person and teach the Dhamma,' or 'Let them come to the royal inner palace or a minister's house and give the training rules and teach the Dhamma,' one should go and the training rules should be given; the Dhamma should be taught. If they summon monks, saying, 'Let them come to form an entourage for the dead,' one should not go. However, it is allowable to go with the meditation subject as the main purpose, thinking, 'By seeing a charnel ground and seeing the unlovely, I will obtain mindfulness of death.' Thus should one act regarding protective chants.

Piṇḍapāte pana – anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāto kassa dātabbo, kassa na dātabbo? Mātāpitunaṃ tāva dātabbo. Sacepi kahāpaṇagghanako hoti, saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ natthi. Mātāpituupaṭṭhākānaṃ veyyāvaccakarassa paṇḍupalāsassāti [P 2.0473] etesampi dātabbo. Tattha paṇḍupalāsassa thālake pakkhipitvāpi dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ āgārikānaṃ mātāpitunampi na vaṭṭati. Pabbajitaparibhogo hi āgārikānaṃ cetiyaṭṭhāniyo. Apica anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāto nāmesa sampattassa dāmarikacorassāpi issarassāpi dātabbo. Kasmā? Te hi adīyamānepi “na dentī”ti āmasitvā dīyamānepi “ucchiṭṭhakaṃ dentī”ti kujjhanti. Kuddhā jīvitāpi voropenti, sāsanassāpi antarāyaṃ karonti. Rajjaṃ [M 2.0068] patthayamānassa vicarato coranāgassa vatthu cettha kathetabbaṃ. Evaṃ piṇḍapāte paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Regarding almsfood, however: to whom should untouched almsfood be given, and to whom should it not be given? First, it should be given to one's mother and father. Even if it is worth a kahāpaṇa, there is no offense of squandering a faithful offering. It should also be given to those who attend to one’s parents, to one who performs services, and to a candidate for ordination. Among them, it is permissible to give to the candidate for ordination even by placing it in the monks' bowl. Apart from him, it is not permissible to give to other householders, even one's parents, by placing it in the bowl. For what is used by renunciates is in the position of a shrine for householders. Furthermore, this untouched almsfood should be given even to a violent robber or a ruler who has arrived. Why? Because if it is not given, they become angry, thinking, 'They do not give'; and if it is given after being touched, they become angry, thinking, 'They give leftovers.' When angered, they might even take life or create obstacles for the Dispensation. Here, the story of the robber-chief Nāga who was wandering while aspiring for sovereignty should be told. Thus, one should act regarding almsfood.

Paṭisanthāro pana kassa kātabbo, kassa na kātabbo? Paṭisanthāro nāma vihāraṃ sampattassa [V 2.0062] yassa kassaci āgantukassa vā daliddassa vā corassa vā issarassa vā kātabboyeva. Kathaṃ? Āgantukaṃ tāva khīṇaparibbayaṃ vihāraṃ sampattaṃ disvā pānīyaṃ dātabbaṃ, pādamakkhanatelaṃ dātabbaṃ. Kāle āgatassa yāgubhattaṃ, vikāle āgatassa sace taṇḍulā atthi; taṇḍulā dātabbā. Avelāyaṃ sampatto “gacchāhī”ti na vattabbo. Sayanaṭṭhānaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sabbaṃ apaccāsīsanteneva kātabbaṃ. “Manussā nāma catupaccayadāyakā evaṃ saṅgahe kayiramāne punappunaṃ pasīditvā upakāraṃ karissantī”ti cittaṃ na uppādetabbaṃ. Corānaṃ pana saṅghikampi dātabbaṃ.

Regarding hospitality, however, to whom should it be shown, and to whom should it not be shown? Hospitality should indeed be shown to anyone who arrives at the monastery—whether a newcomer, a poor person, a robber, or a ruler. How so? Upon seeing a newcomer with exhausted provisions arrive at the monastery, water for drinking should be given, and oil for anointing the feet. To one who arrives at the proper time, rice gruel and cooked rice should be given; to one who arrives at an improper time, if rice grains are available, rice grains should be given. One who arrives at an untimely hour should not be told, 'Go away.' A place to sleep should be provided. All this should be done without expecting anything in return. One should not entertain the thought, 'People, being donors of the four requisites, will be pleased again and again by such kindness and will render assistance.' To robbers, however, even that which belongs to the Sangha should be given.

Paṭisanthārānisaṃsadīpanatthañca coranāgavatthu, bhātarā saddhiṃ jambudīpagatassa mahānāgarañño vatthu, piturājassa rajje catunnaṃ amaccānaṃ vatthu, abhayacoravatthūti evamādīni bahūni [P 2.0474] vatthūni mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vitthārato vuttāni.

And to illustrate the benefits of hospitality, the story of Coranāga, the story of King Mahānāga who went to Jambudīpa with his elder brother, the story of the four ministers during the reign of his father the king, and the story of the robber Abhaya—these and many other such stories are told in detail in the Great Commentary.

Tatrāyaṃ ekavatthudīpanā – sīhaḷadīpe kira abhayo nāma coro pañcasataparivāro ekasmiṃ ṭhāne khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā samantā tiyojanaṃ ubbāsetvā vasati. Anurādhapuravāsino kadambanadiṃ na uttaranti, cetiyagirimagge janasañcāro upacchinno. Athekadivasaṃ coro “cetiyagiriṃ vilumpissāmī”ti agamāsi. Ārāmikā disvā dīghabhāṇakaabhayattherassa ārocesuṃ. Thero “sappiphāṇitādīni atthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Corānaṃ detha, taṇḍulā atthī”ti? “Atthi, bhante, saṅghassatthāya āhaṭā taṇḍulā ca pattasākañca goraso cā”ti. “Bhattaṃ sampādetvā corānaṃ dethā”ti. Ārāmikā tathā kariṃsu. Corā bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā “kenāyaṃ paṭisanthāro kato”ti pucchiṃsu. “Amhākaṃ ayyena abhayattherenā”ti. Corā therassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā āhaṃsu – “mayaṃ saṅghassa ca cetiyassa [M 2.0069] ca santakaṃ acchinditvā gahessāmāti āgatā, tumhākaṃ pana iminā paṭisanthārenamha pasannā, ajja paṭṭhāya vihāre dhammikā rakkhā amhākaṃ āyattā hotu, nāgarā āgantvā dānaṃ dentu, cetiyaṃ vandantū”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya ca nāgare dānaṃ dātuṃ āgacchante nadītīreyeva paccuggantvā rakkhantā vihāraṃ nenti, vihārepi dānaṃ dentānaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā tiṭṭhanti. Tepi bhikkhūnaṃ bhuttāvasesaṃ corānaṃ denti. Gamanakālepi te corā nadītīraṃ pāpetvā nivattanti.

Here is the explanation of one story: It is said that in the island of Sīhaḷa, a robber named Abhaya with a following of five hundred established a stronghold in one place and lived there, having terrorized the surrounding area for three yojanas. The inhabitants of Anurādhapura did not cross the Kadamba River, and travel on the road to Cetiyagiri was cut off. Then one day, the robber went, thinking, 'I will plunder Cetiyagiri.' The monastery attendants saw him and reported it to the Elder Abhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya. The Elder asked, 'Are there ghee, molasses, and so forth?' 'There are, venerable sir.' 'Give them to the robbers. Are there rice grains?' 'There are, venerable sir—rice grains, cooked greens, and dairy products brought for the Sangha.' 'Prepare a meal and give it to the robbers,' he instructed. The attendants did so. After eating the meal, the robbers asked, 'By whom was this hospitality shown?' 'By our master, the Elder Abhaya.' The robbers went to the Elder, paid homage, and said: 'We came intending to seize and take the property of the Sangha and the cetiya, but we are pleased by this hospitality of yours. From today onwards, let the righteous protection of the monastery be our responsibility. Let the townspeople come and give alms, and let them worship the cetiya.' From then on, when townspeople came to give alms, the robbers would meet them at the riverbank itself and, protecting them, lead them to the monastery. In the monastery too, they stood guard for those giving alms. Those townspeople also gave the leftovers of the monks' meal to the robbers. At the time of their departure, those robbers would escort them to the riverbank and then return.

Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe khīyanakakathā uppannā “thero issaravatāya saṅghassa santakaṃ corānaṃ adāsī”ti. Thero sannipātaṃ kārāpetvā āha – “corā saṅghassa pakativaṭṭañca cetiyasantakañca acchinditvā gaṇhissāmā”ti āgamiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ mayā evaṃ na harissantīti [V 2.0063] ettako nāma paṭisanthāro kato, taṃ sabbampi ekato sampiṇḍetvā agghāpetha. Tena kāraṇena aviluttaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ ekato sampiṇḍetvā agghāpethāti. Tato sabbampi therena dinnakaṃ cetiyaghare ekaṃ varapotthakacittattharaṇaṃ [P 2.0475] na agghati. Tato āhaṃsu – “therena katapaṭisanthāro sukato codetuṃ vā sāretuṃ vā na labbhā, gīvā vā avahāro vā natthī”ti. Evaṃ mahānisaṃso paṭisanthāroti sallakkhetvā kattabbo paṇḍitena bhikkhunāti.

Then one day, a talk of censure arose in the Sangha of monks: 'The Elder, acting with authority, gave the Sangha's property to robbers.' The Elder, having convened an assembly, said: 'The robbers came intending to seize and take the Sangha's cooking provisions and the cetiya's property. Then, so that they would not take them, this much hospitality was shown by me. Gather all of it together and assess its value, considering the goods that were not plundered because of that action.' Then, all that was given by the Elder was not worth even one excellent painted cloth covering for a manuscript in the cetiya-house. Therefore, they said: 'The hospitality shown by the Elder was well done. It is not permissible to accuse or to reproach him; there is no misappropriation or theft.' Thus, having recognized that hospitality has great benefit, it should be performed by a wise monk.

187. Aṅgulipatodakavatthusmiṃ – uttantoti kilamanto. Anassāsakoti nirassāso. Imasmiṃ pana vatthusmiṃ yāya āpattiyā bhavitabbaṃ sā “khuddakesu nidiṭṭhā”ti idha na vuttā.

187. In the story of poking with the finger: `uttanto` means being weary. `Anassāsako` means breathless. Moreover, in this story, whatever offense should be incurred, because it 'is specified among the minor training rules,' it is not stated here.

Tadanantare vatthusmiṃ – ottharitvāti akkamitvā. So kira tehi ākaḍḍhiyamāno patito. Eko tassa udaraṃ abhiruhitvā nisīdi. Sesāpi pannarasa janā pathaviyaṃ ajjhottharitvā adūhalapāsāṇā viya migaṃ māresuṃ. Yasmā pana te kammādhippāyā, na maraṇādhippāyā; tasmā pārājikaṃ na vuttaṃ.

In the story immediately following: `ottharitvā` means having overwhelmed. It is said that he, while being dragged by them, fell. One person climbed onto his abdomen and sat down. The remaining fifteen people also, having overwhelmed him on the ground, killed him as one kills a deer with a pressing-stone. However, because they had the intention of performing a formal monastic act, and not the intention to kill, a pārājika offense was not stated.

Bhūtavejjakavatthusmiṃ – yakkhaṃ māresīti bhūtavijjākapāṭhakā yakkhagahitaṃ mocetukāmā yakkhaṃ āvāhetvā muñcāti vadanti. No ce muñcati, piṭṭhena vā mattikāya vā rūpaṃ katvā hatthapādādīni chindanti, yaṃ yaṃ tassa chijjati taṃ taṃ yakkhassa chinnameva hoti. Sīse chinne yakkhopi marati[M 2.0070]. Evaṃ sopi māresi; tasmā thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Na kevalañca yakkhameva, yopi hi sakkaṃ devarājaṃ māreyya, sopi thullaccayameva āpajjati.

In the Story of the Spirit-Healer: Practitioners versed in the lore of spirit-healing, wishing to free one who is possessed by a yakkha, summon the yakkha and say, 'Release him!' If it does not release him, they make an image with flour or with clay and cut off its hands, feet, and so on. Whatever part of that image is cut, that very part of the yakkha is indeed cut. When the head is cut, the yakkha also dies. In this way, that monk also killed it; therefore, a grave offense is stated. And it is not only a yakkha; for indeed, whoever were to kill Sakka, the king of the devas, he too would incur a grave offense.

Vāḷayakkhavatthusmiṃ – vāḷayakkhavihāranti yasmiṃ vihāre vāḷo caṇḍo yakkho vasati, taṃ vihāraṃ. Yo hi evarūpaṃ vihāraṃ ajānanto kevalaṃ vasanatthāya peseti, anāpatti. Yo maraṇādhippāyo peseti, so itarassa maraṇena pārājikaṃ, amaraṇena thullaccayaṃ āpajjati. Yathā ca vāḷayakkhavihāraṃ; evaṃ yattha vāḷasīhabyagghādimigā vā ajagarakaṇhasappādayo dīghajātikā vā vasanti, taṃ vāḷavihāraṃ pesentassāpi āpattānāpattibhedo [P 2.0476] veditabbo. Ayaṃ pāḷimuttakanayo. Yathā ca bhikkhuṃ vāḷayakkhavihāraṃ pesentassa; evaṃ vāḷayakkhampi bhikkhusantikaṃ pesentassa āpattānāpattibhedo veditabbo. Eseva nayo vāḷakantārādivatthūsupi. Kevalañhettha yasmiṃ kantāre vāḷamigā vā dīghajātikā vā atthi, so vāḷakantāro. Yasmiṃ corā atthi, so corakantāroti evaṃ padatthamattameva nānaṃ. Manussaviggahapārājikañca nāmetaṃ saṇhaṃ, pariyāyakathāya na muccati; tasmā yo vadeyya “asukasmiṃ nāma okāse coro nisinno[V 2.0064], yo tassa sīsaṃ chinditvā āharati, so rājato sakkāravisesaṃ labhatī”ti. Tassa cetaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā koci naṃ gantvā māreti, ayaṃ pārājiko hotīti.

In the Story of the Fierce Yakkha: A 'monastery with a fierce yakkha' is a monastery where a fierce, harsh yakkha dwells. Indeed, if one, not knowing of such a monastery, sends another there merely for the purpose of dwelling, there is no offense. If one sends another with the intention of causing death, he incurs a pārājika offense on account of the other's death, and a thullaccaya offense on account of his non-death. And just as with a monastery with a fierce yakkha, so too, wherever fierce beasts such as lions, tigers, and so on, or long-bodied creatures such as pythons, black snakes, and so on, dwell, for one who sends another to that monastery of fierce creatures, the distinction between offense and no offense should be understood. This is the method independent of the Pāḷi canon. And just as for one who sends a monk to a monastery with a fierce yakkha, so too for one who sends a fierce yakkha to a monk, the distinction between offense and no offense should be understood. This same method applies also in the stories of wildernesses with fierce creatures and so on. Herein, it is only that in whatever wilderness there are fierce beasts or long-bodied creatures, that is a 'wilderness of fierce creatures.' In whatever wilderness there are robbers, that is a 'wilderness of robbers'—thus, only the meaning of the terms is different. And this pārājika offense concerning a human being is subtle; one is not absolved by means of indirect speech. Therefore, if one were to say, 'In such and such a place, a robber is sitting. Whoever cuts off his head and brings it will receive special honors from the king,' and upon hearing this statement, someone goes and kills him, this one incurs a pārājika offense.

188. Taṃ maññamānoti ādīsu so kira bhikkhu attano veribhikkhuṃ māretukāmo cintesi – “imaṃ me divā mārentassa na sukaraṃ bhaveyya sotthinā gantuṃ, rattiṃ naṃ māressāmī”ti sallakkhetvā rattiṃ āgamma bahūnaṃ sayitaṭṭhāne taṃ maññamāno tameva jīvitā voropesi. Aparo taṃ maññamāno aññaṃ, aparo aññaṃ tasseva sahāyaṃ maññamāno taṃ, aparo aññaṃ tasseva sahāyaṃ maññamāno aññaṃ tassa sahāyameva jīvitā voropesi. Sabbesampi pārājikameva.

188. In the passages beginning with 'thinking it was him': It is said that a certain monk, wishing to kill his enemy monk, thought: 'If I kill him during the day, it would not be easy for me to get away safely; I will kill him at night.' Having thus marked the way, he came at night to the sleeping place of many monks and, thinking it was that monk, he deprived that very monk of life. Another, thinking it was the target, deprived another of life. Another, thinking someone else was the target's companion, deprived the target of life. Another, thinking someone else was the target's companion, deprived another, who was indeed his companion, of life. For all of them, it is a pārājika offense.

Amanussagahitavatthūsu paṭhame vatthusmiṃ “yakkhaṃ palāpessāmī”ti pahāraṃ adāsi, itaro “na dānāyaṃ virajjhituṃ samattho, māressāmi na”nti[M 2.0071]. Ettha ca namaraṇādhippāyassa anāpatti vuttāti. Na ettakeneva amanussagahitassa pahāro dātabbo, tālapaṇṇaṃ pana parittasuttaṃ vā hatthe vā pāde vā bandhitabbaṃ, ratanasuttādīni parittāni bhaṇitabbāni, “mā sīlavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ viheṭhehī”ti dhammakathā kātabbāti. Saggakathādīni uttānatthāni. Yañhettha vattabbaṃ taṃ vuttameva.

In the stories of those possessed by non-humans, in the first story, one monk gave a blow, thinking, 'I will make the yakkha flee.' The other monk gave a blow, thinking, 'Now this possessing yakkha is not able to resist; I will kill it.' And here it is stated that there is no offense for one who does not have the intention to kill. Bearing this in mind, a blow should not be given to one possessed by a non-human just for this reason. Rather, a palm leaf or a protective thread should be tied to the hand or foot, protective discourses such as the Ratanasutta should be recited, and a Dhamma talk should be given, saying, 'Do not harm a virtuous monk.' The stories of heaven and so on are of plain meaning. Whatever needed to be said here has already been said.

189. Rukkhacchedanavatthu aṭṭabandhanavatthusadisaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yo rukkhena otthatopi na marati[P 2.0477], sakkā ca hoti ekena passena rukkhaṃ chetvā pathaviṃ vā khanitvā nikkhamituṃ, hatthe cassa vāsi vā kuṭhārī vā atthi, tena api jīvitaṃ pariccajitabbaṃ, na ca rukkho vā chinditabbo, na pathavī vā khaṇitabbā. Kasmā? Evaṃ karonto hi pācittiyaṃ āpajjati, buddhassa āṇaṃ bhañjati, na jīvitapariyantaṃ sīlaṃ karoti. Tasmā api jīvitaṃ pariccajitabbaṃ, na ca sīlanti pariggahetvā na evaṃ kātabbaṃ. Aññassa pana bhikkhuno rukkhaṃ vā chinditvā pathaviṃ vā khanitvā taṃ nīharituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace udukkhalayantakena rukkhaṃ pavaṭṭetvā nīharitabbo hoti, taṃyeva rukkhaṃ chinditvā udukkhalaṃ gahetabbanti mahāsumatthero āha. Aññampi chinditvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti mahāpadumatthero. Sobbhādīsu patitassāpi nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā uttāraṇe eseva nayo. Attanā bhūtagāmaṃ chinditvā nisseṇī na kātabbā, aññesaṃ katvā uddharituṃ vaṭṭatīti.

189. The Story of Cutting a Tree is similar to the Story of the Scaffold-Binding. This, however, is the distinction: if a monk is crushed by a tree but does not die, and it is possible for him to get out by cutting the tree on one side or by digging the earth, and he has an adze or a small axe in his hand, by him, life should be given up, but the tree should not be cut, nor should the earth be dug. Why? Because in doing so, he incurs a pācittiya offense, he breaks the Buddha's command, and he does not maintain the precept up to the end of his life. Therefore, having determined, 'Life should be given up, but the precept should not be given up,' he should not act in this way. However, it is permissible for another monk to cut the tree or dig the earth to get him out. If it is possible to get him out by rolling the tree with a lever-device, the Elder Mahāsuma said that that very tree should be cut to make the lever. The Elder Mahāpaduma said that it is permissible to cut another tree to get it. This same method applies to lifting out one who has fallen into pits and so on by constructing a ladder. He himself should not make a ladder by cutting living plants, but it is permissible for others to make one to lift him out.

190. Dāyālimpanavatthūsu – dāyaṃ ālimpesunti vane aggiṃ adaṃsu. Ettha pana uddissānuddissavasena pārājikānantariyathullaccayapācittivatthūnaṃ anurūpato pārājikādīni akusalarāsibhāvo [V 2.0065] ca pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. “Allatiṇavanappagumbādayo ḍayhantū”ti ālimpentassa ca pācittiyaṃ. “Dabbūpakaraṇāni vinassantū”ti ālimpentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Khiḍḍādhippāyenāpi dukkaṭanti saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yaṃkiñci allasukkhaṃ saindriyānindriyaṃ ḍayhatū”ti ālimpentassa vatthuvasena pārājikathullaccayapācittiyadukkaṭāni veditabbāni.

190. In the Stories of Setting Fire to a Forest-Preserve: 'They set fire to the forest-preserve' means they set fire in the forest. Here, however, by way of specified and unspecified cases, the pārājika offenses and so on, and the state of being a mass of demerit, should be understood in conformity with the cases of pārājika, ānantariya, thullaccaya, and pācittiya, in the manner previously stated. For one who sets fire thinking, 'Let the wet grass, forest shrubs, and so on burn,' it is a pācittiya offense. For one who sets fire thinking, 'Let the wood materials and equipment be destroyed,' it is a dukkaṭa offense. It is a dukkaṭa offense even if done with the intention of play—this is stated in the Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā. For one who sets fire thinking, 'Let whatever, wet or dry, with faculties or without faculties, burn,' the offenses of pārājika, thullaccaya, pācittiya, and dukkaṭa should be known according to the object.

Paṭaggidānaṃ pana parittakaraṇañca bhagavatā anuññātaṃ, tasmā araññe vanakammikehi vā dinnaṃ sayaṃ vā uṭṭhitaṃ aggiṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “tiṇakuṭiyo mā [M 2.0072] vinassantū”ti tassa aggino paṭiaggiṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati, yena saddhiṃ āgacchanto aggi ekato hutvā nirupādāno nibbāti. Parittampi [P 2.0478] kātuṃ vaṭṭati tiṇakuṭikānaṃ samantā bhūmitacchanaṃ parikhākhaṇanaṃ vā, yathā āgato aggi upādānaṃ alabhitvā nibbāti. Etañca sabbaṃ uṭṭhiteyeva aggismiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Anuṭṭhite anupasampannehi kappiyavohārena kāretabbaṃ. Udakena pana nibbāpentehi appāṇakameva udakaṃ āsiñcitabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the giving of a counter-fire and the making of a protective barrier have been permitted by the Blessed One. Therefore, in the forest, upon seeing an approaching fire—whether set by forest workers or arisen spontaneously—it is permissible, thinking, 'May the grass huts not be destroyed,' to set a counter-fire to that fire, by which the approaching fire, having joined with it, is extinguished for lack of fuel. It is also permissible to make a protective barrier, such as scraping the ground or digging a trench around the grass huts, so that the approaching fire, not obtaining fuel, is extinguished. And all this is permissible to do only when the fire has already arisen. When it has not yet arisen, it should be caused to be done by those not fully ordained by means of a permissible expression. Furthermore, by those extinguishing with water, only water that is without living beings should be poured.

191. Āghātanavatthusmiṃ – yathā ekappahāravacane; evaṃ “dvīhi pahārehī”ti ādivacanesupi pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Dvīhī”ti vutte ca ekena pahārena māritepi khettameva otiṇṇattā pārājikaṃ, tīhi mārite pana visaṅketaṃ. Iti yathāparicchede vā paricchedabbhantare vā avisaṅketaṃ, paricchedātikkame pana sabbattha visaṅketaṃ hoti, āṇāpako muccati, vadhakasseva doso. Yathā ca pahāresu; evaṃ purisesupi “eko māretū”ti vutte ekeneva mārite pārājikaṃ, dvīhi mārite visaṅketaṃ. “Dve mārentū”ti vutte ekena vā dvīhi vā mārite pārājikaṃ, tīhi mārite visaṅketanti veditabbaṃ. Eko saṅgāme vegena dhāvato purisassa sīsaṃ asinā chindati, asīsakaṃ kabandhaṃ dhāvati, tamañño paharitvā pātesi, kassa pārājikanti vutte upaḍḍhā therā “gamanūpacchedakassā”ti āhaṃsu. Ābhidhammikagodattatthero “sīsacchedakassā”ti. Evarūpānipi vatthūni imassa vatthussa atthadīpane vattabbānīti.

191. In the case of the slaughterhouse: just as a pārājika should be understood in the expression 'with a single blow,' so too should a pārājika be understood in expressions such as 'with two blows.' And when 'with two blows' is said, even if the person is killed with one blow, it is a pārājika because the field of the offense has been entered; but if killed with three, it is a deviation from the instruction. Thus, whether killed at the specified limit or within the specified limit, it is not a deviation from the instruction. But in exceeding the limit, it is in all cases a deviation from the instruction; the one who gives the order is released, and the fault is the killer's alone. And just as with blows, so too with persons: when it is said, 'Let one person kill,' if he is killed by one person only, it is a pārājika; if killed by two, it is a deviation from the instruction. When it is said, 'Let two persons kill,' if he is killed by one or by two, it is a pārājika; if killed by three, it should be understood as a deviation from the instruction. One monk, in battle, cuts off the head of a man running with speed with a sword. The headless trunk runs on. Another monk strikes it and causes it to fall. When it is asked, 'Whose is the pārājika?' half the elders said, 'It belongs to the one who cut off the movement.' The Elder Godatta, the Abhidhamma master, said, 'It belongs to the one who cut off the head.' Indeed, such cases are to be stated in the explanation of the meaning of this case.

192. Takkavatthusmiṃ – aniyametvā “takkaṃ pāyethā”ti vutte yaṃ vā taṃ vā takkaṃ pāyetvā mārite pārājikaṃ. Niyametvā pana “gotakkaṃ mahiṃsatakkaṃ ajikātakka”nti vā, “sītaṃ uṇhaṃ dhūpitaṃ adhūpita”nti vā vutte yaṃ vuttaṃ, tato aññaṃ pāyetvā mārite visaṅketaṃ.

192. In the case of buttermilk: when, without specifying, it is said, 'Have him drink buttermilk,' if he is killed by being made to drink just any buttermilk, it is a pārājika. But when, having specified, it is said, 'Have him drink cow's buttermilk,' 'buffalo's buttermilk,' or 'goat's buttermilk,' or 'cool,' 'hot,' 'fumigated,' or 'unfumigated,' if he is killed by being made to drink a kind other than what was specified, it is a deviation from the instruction.

Loṇasovīrakavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0066] – loṇasovīrakaṃ nāma sabbarasābhisaṅkhataṃ ekaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Taṃ kira karontā [P 2.0479] harītakāmalakavibhītakakasāve sabbadhaññāni sabbaaparaṇṇāni sattannampi dhaññānaṃ odanaṃ kadaliphalādīni sabbaphalāni vettaketakakhajjūrikaḷīrādayo sabbakaḷīre macchamaṃsakhaṇḍāni anekāni ca madhuphāṇitasindhavaloṇanikaṭukādīni bhesajjāni pakkhipitvā [M 2.0073] kumbhimukhaṃ limpitvā ekaṃ vā dve vā tīṇi vā saṃvaccharāni ṭhapenti, taṃ paripaccitvā jamburasavaṇṇaṃ hoti. Vātakāsakuṭṭhapaṇḍubhagandarādīnaṃ siniddhabhojanaṃ bhuttānañca uttarapānaṃ bhattajīraṇakabhesajjaṃ tādisaṃ natthi. Taṃ panetaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pacchābhattampi vaṭṭati, gilānānaṃ pākatikameva, agilānānaṃ pana udakasambhinnaṃ pānaparibhogenāti.
