In the case of loṇasovīraka: loṇasovīraka is a type of medicine prepared with all flavors. It is said that those who make it, having put in the astringent fruits harītakā, āmalaka, and vibhītaka, all grains, all pulses, cooked rice of the seven grains, all fruits such as bananas, all shoots such as rattan, ketaka, and date palm shoots, pieces of fish and meat, and many medicines such as honey, molasses, rock salt, and the three pungent spices, and having sealed the mouth of the pot, keep it for one, two, or three years. When it is fully fermented, it becomes the color of jambu juice. For those with wind-disease, cough, leprosy, jaundice, fistula, and so on, and for those who have eaten rich food, it is an excellent post-meal drink. There is no digestive medicine like it. Furthermore, this is allowable for monks even after the meal. For the sick, it is allowable as it is. But for those who are not sick, it is allowable when mixed with water, for consumption as a beverage.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Pārājika is concluded.

4. Catutthapārājikaṃ

4. The Fourth Pārājika

Catusaccavidū [P 2.0480] satthā, catutthaṃ yaṃ pakāsayi;

Pārājikaṃ tassa dāni, patto saṃvaṇṇanākkamo.

The Teacher, who has known the Four Truths, proclaimed the fourth Pārājika training rule. The sequential commentary for that Pārājika has now arrived.

Yasmā tasmā suviññeyyaṃ, yaṃ pubbe ca pakāsitaṃ;

Taṃ vajjayitvā assāpi, hoti saṃvaṇṇanā ayaṃ.

Therefore, avoiding that which is easily understood and that which has been explained before, this is the commentary for this Fourth Pārājika as well.

Vaggumudātīriyabhikkhuvatthuvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Story of the Monks of the Vaggumudā Riverbank

193. Tena samayena buddho bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati…pe… gihīnaṃ kammantaṃ adhiṭṭhemāti gihīnaṃ khettesu ceva ārāmādīsu ca kattabbakiccaṃ adhiṭṭhāma; “evaṃ kātabbaṃ, evaṃ na kātabba”nti ācikkhāma ceva anusāsāma cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dūteyyanti dūtakammaṃ. Uttarimanussadhammassāti manusse uttiṇṇadhammassa; manusse atikkamitvā brahmattaṃ vā nibbānaṃ vā pāpanakadhammassāti attho. Uttarimanussānaṃ vā seṭṭhapurisānaṃ jhāyīnañca ariyānañca dhammassa. Asuko bhikkhūtiādīsu attanā evaṃ mantayitvā pacchā gihīnaṃ bhāsantā “buddharakkhito nāma bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī, dhammarakkhito dutiyassā”ti evaṃ nāmavaseneva vaṇṇaṃ bhāsiṃsūti veditabbo. Tattha esoyeva kho āvuso seyyoti kammantādhiṭṭhānaṃ dūteyyaharaṇañca bahusapattaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ na ca samaṇasāruppaṃ. Tato pana ubhayatopi [V 2.0067] eso eva seyyo pāsaṃsataro sundarataro yo amhākaṃ gihīnaṃ aññamaññassa uttarimanussadhammassa vaṇṇo bhāsito. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Iriyāpathaṃ saṇṭhapetvā nisinnaṃ vā caṅkamantaṃ vā pucchantānaṃ vā apucchantānaṃ vā gihīnaṃ “ayaṃ [M 2.0074] asuko nāma bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī”ti evamādinā nayena yo amhākaṃ aññena aññassa uttarimanussadhammassa [P 2.0481] vaṇṇo bhāsito bhavissati, eso eva seyyoti. Anāgatasambandhe pana asati na etehi so tasmiṃ khaṇe bhāsitova yasmā na yujjati, tasmā anāgatasambandhaṃ katvā “yo evaṃ bhāsito bhavissati, so eva seyyo”ti evamettha attho veditabbo. Lakkhaṇaṃ pana saddasatthato pariyesitabbaṃ.

193. At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī… (and so on). The phrase ‘we will manage the work of householders’ means: we will manage the duties to be done in the fields and parks, and so on, of householders; it means, ‘we will both instruct them, saying, “This should be done, this should not be done,” and we will advise them.’ ‘Messenger’s duty’ means the work of a messenger. ‘Of a superhuman state’ means: of a state that transcends humans; the meaning is, of a state that causes one to attain the state of a Brahmā or Nibbāna, having surpassed humans. Or, it is the state of superhuman beings, of excellent persons, of those who attain jhāna, and of noble ones. Regarding ‘such and such a monk,’ and so on, it should be understood that having deliberated thus among themselves, they later spoke praise to the householders only by way of name, saying, ‘The monk named Buddharakkhita is an attainer of the first jhāna; Dhammarakkhita, of the second.’ Therein, ‘This indeed, friends, is better,’ means: managing work and carrying out a messenger’s duty has many enemies, involves great undertakings, and is not befitting a recluse. But better, more praiseworthy, and more beautiful than both of those is this: the praise of one another’s superhuman state that will be spoken by us to the householders. What is meant? Having composed one’s posture, whether sitting or walking, to householders who ask or do not ask, the praise of one another’s superhuman state that will be spoken by us by one monk about another, in the manner beginning with, ‘This monk named so-and-so is an attainer of the first jhāna,’ this indeed is better. However, if there is no connection to the future tense, it is not suitable, because that praise had not yet been spoken by them at that moment of deliberation. Therefore, making a connection to the future tense, the meaning here should be understood thus: ‘Whatever praise will be spoken in this way, that indeed is better.’ The grammatical form, however, should be sought from the science of grammar.

194. Vaṇṇavā ahesunti aññoyeva nesaṃ abhinavo sarīravaṇṇo uppajji, tena vaṇṇena vaṇṇavanto ahesuṃ. Pīṇindriyāti pañcahi pasādehi abhiniviṭṭhokāsassa paripuṇṇattā manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ amilātabhāvena pīṇindriyā. Pasannamukhavaṇṇāti kiñcāpi avisesena vaṇṇavanto sarīravaṇṇato pana nesaṃ mukhavaṇṇo adhikataraṃ pasanno; accho anāvilo parisuddhoti attho. Vippasannachavivaṇṇāti yena ca te mahākaṇikārapupphādisadisena vaṇṇena vaṇṇavanto, tādiso aññesampi manussānaṃ vaṇṇo atthi. Yathā pana imesaṃ; evaṃ na tesaṃ chavivaṇṇo vippasanno. Tena vuttaṃ – “vippasannachavivaṇṇā”ti. Itiha te bhikkhū neva uddesaṃ na paripucchaṃ na kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjantā. Atha kho kuhakatāya abhūtaguṇasaṃvaṇṇanāya laddhāni paṇītabhojanāni bhuñjitvā yathāsukhaṃ niddārāmataṃ saṅgaṇikārāmatañca anuyuñjantā imaṃ sarīrasobhaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, yathā taṃ bālā bhantamigappaṭibhāgāti.

194. ‘They were of good complexion’ means a completely different, new bodily complexion arose for them; with that complexion, they became possessed of good complexion. ‘With plump faculties’ means: because of the fullness of the place where the five sensitivities are established, and because of the unfaded nature of the faculties with the mind as the sixth, they had plump faculties. ‘With serene facial complexions’ means: although they were generally of good complexion, their facial complexion was exceedingly more serene than their bodily complexion; the meaning is clear, untroubled, and utterly pure. ‘With an especially clear skin-complexion’ means: they were of good complexion with a color similar to a great kaṇikāra flower and so on. Other humans also have such a complexion. However, the skin-complexion of those others is not especially clear in the way that the skin-complexion of these monks is. For that reason, it was said, ‘with an especially clear skin-complexion.’ Thus, those monks attained this bodily splendor not by engaging in learning the texts, not by inquiry, and not by engaging in the meditation subject. Rather, having eaten the fine foods obtained through deceit and through praising one another for non-existent virtues, they engaged in delighting in sleep and delighting in company as they pleased, and so attained this bodily splendor, just as foolish people, who are like startled deer, do.

Vaggumudātīriyāti vaggumudātīravāsino. Kacci bhikkhave khamanīyanti bhikkhave kacci tumhākaṃ idaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ khamanīyaṃ sakkā khamituṃ sahituṃ pariharituṃ na kiñci dukkhaṃ uppādetīti. Kacci yāpanīyanti kacci sabbakiccesu yāpetuṃ gametuṃ sakkā, na kiñci antarāyaṃ dassetīti. Kucchi parikantoti kucchi parikantito varaṃ bhaveyya; “parikatto”tipi pāṭho yujjati. Evaṃ [P 2.0482] vaggumudātīriye anekapariyāyena vigarahitvā idāni yasmā tehi katakammaṃ corakammaṃ hoti, tasmā āyatiṃ aññesampi evarūpassa kammassa akaraṇatthaṃ atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi.

‘The monks of the Vaggumudā’ means the monks dwelling on the bank of the Vaggumudā river. ‘Monks, is it bearable?’ means: ‘Monks, is this four-wheeled, nine-gated body-machine of yours bearable? Is it possible to endure, to tolerate, to manage it? Does it not produce any suffering?’ ‘Is it sustainable?’ means: ‘Is it possible to carry on, to proceed in all duties? Does it not show any obstacle?’ ‘The belly should be cut around’ means: it would be better if the belly were cut all around; the reading ‘parikatto’ is also suitable. Having thus rebuked the monks of the Vaggumudā in many ways, now, because the deed done by them is the deed of a thief, therefore, for the purpose of preventing other monks also from doing such a deed in the future, the Blessed One then addressed the monks.

195. Āmantetvā [M 2.0075] ca pana “pañcime bhikkhave mahācorā”tiādimāha. Tattha santo saṃvijjamānāti atthi ceva upalabbhanti cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idhāti imasmiṃ sattaloke. Evaṃ hotīti [V 2.0068] evaṃ pubbabhāge icchā uppajjati. Kudāssu nāmāhanti ettha suiti nipāto; kudā nāmāti attho. So aparena samayenāti so pubbabhāge evaṃ cintetvā anukkamena parisaṃ vaḍḍhento panthadūhanakammaṃ paccantimagāmavilopanti evamādīni katvā vepullappattapariso hutvā gāmepi agāme, janapadepi ajanapade karonto hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācento.

195. And having addressed them, he spoke the teaching beginning with, ‘Monks, these five are great thieves.’ Therein, ‘existing and present’ means they exist and they are found. ‘Here’ means in this world of beings. ‘Thus it is’ means: thus, in the preliminary stage, desire arises. In ‘When indeed will I,’ the word ‘su’ is a particle; the meaning is ‘when indeed.’ ‘He, at a later time’ means: he, having thought thus in the preliminary stage, gradually increasing his retinue, having done such things as highway robbery and the plundering of border villages, becomes one whose retinue has reached a great size, and while making villages into non-villages and districts into non-districts, he kills and causes others to kill, cuts and causes others to cut, torments and causes others to torment.

Iti bāhirakamahācoraṃ dassetvā tena sadise sāsane pañca mahācore dassetuṃ “evameva kho”tiādimāha. Tattha pāpabhikkhunoti aññesu ṭhānesu mūlacchinno pārājikappatto “pāpabhikkhū”ti vuccati. Idha pana pārājikaṃ anāpanno icchācāre ṭhito khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni madditvā vicaranto “pāpabhikkhū”ti adhippeto. Tassāpi bāhirakacorassa viya pubbabhāge evaṃ hoti – “kudāssu nāmāhaṃ…pe… parikkhārāna”nti. Tattha sakkatoti sakkārappatto. Garukatoti garukārappatto. Mānitoti manasā piyāyito. Pūjitoti catupaccayābhihārapūjāya pūjito. Apacitoti apacitippatto. Tattha yassa cattāro paccaye sakkaritvā suṭṭhu abhisaṅkhate paṇītapaṇīte katvā denti, so sakkato. Yasmiṃ garubhāvaṃ paccupetvā denti, so garukato. Yaṃ manasā piyāyanti, so mānito. Yassa sabbampetaṃ karonti, so pūjito. Yassa abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammādivasena [P 2.0483] paramanipaccakāraṃ karonti, so apacito. Imassa ca pana sabbampi imaṃ lokāmisaṃ patthayamānassa evaṃ hoti.

Having thus shown the external great thief, to show five great thieves in the Sāsana who are similar to him, he spoke the words beginning with, ‘Even so, indeed…’. Therein, as for ‘an evil monk,’ in other places a monk whose root is cut off, who has committed a pārājika offense, is called an ‘evil monk.’ Here, however, an ‘evil monk’ is intended to be one who has not committed a pārājika offense but, abiding in evil conduct, wanders about having transgressed the minor and lesser training rules. For him, too, like for the external thief, in the preliminary stage it occurs thus: ‘When, indeed, shall I… requisites?’ Therein, ‘honored’ means having attained honor. ‘Respected’ means having attained respect. ‘Esteemed’ means being cherished in mind. ‘Worshipped’ means being worshipped with the offering of the four requisites. ‘Revered’ means having attained reverence. Therein, one to whom they give the four requisites, having prepared them with care, well-concocted, and made excellent, is ‘honored.’ One to whom they give, having established a sense of gravity, is ‘respected.’ One whom they cherish in mind is ‘esteemed.’ One to whom they do all of this is ‘worshipped.’ One for whom they perform the highest degree of humility by means of salutation, rising, respectful greeting with joined palms, and so on, is ‘revered.’ And for this one who desires all this worldly gain, it occurs thus.

So aparena samayenāti so pubbabhāge evaṃ cintetvā anukkamena sikkhāya atibbagārave uddhate unnaḷe capale mukhare vikiṇṇavāce muṭṭhassatī asampajāne pākatindriye ācariyupajjhāyehi pariccattake lābhagaruke pāpabhikkhū saṅgaṇhitvā iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanādīni kuhakavattāni sikkhāpetvā “ayaṃ thero asukasmiṃ nāma senāsane vassaṃ upagamma vattapaṭipattiṃ pūrayamāno vassaṃ vasitvā niggato”ti lokasammatasenāsanasaṃvaṇṇanādīhi [M 2.0076] upāyehi lokaṃ paripācetuṃ paṭibalehi jātakādīsu kataparicayehi sarasampannehi pāpabhikkhūhi saṃvaṇṇiyamānaguṇo hutvā satena vā sahassena vā parivuto…pe… bhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ. Ayaṃ bhikkhave paṭhamo mahācoroti ayaṃ sandhicchedādicorako viya na ekaṃ kulaṃ na dve, atha kho mahājanaṃ vañcetvā catupaccayagahaṇato “paṭhamo mahācoro”ti veditabbo. Ye pana suttantikā vā ābhidhammikā vā vinayadharā vā bhikkhū bhikkhācāre asampajjamāne pāḷiṃ vācentā aṭṭhakathaṃ kathentā anumodanāya dhammakathāya iriyāpathasampattiyā ca lokaṃ pasādentā janapadacārikaṃ [V 2.0069] caranti sakkatā garukatā mānitā pūjitā apacitā, te “tantipaveṇighaṭanakā sāsanajotakā”ti veditabbā.

Regarding ‘Then, after some time’: he, having reflected thus in the preliminary stage, gradually gathers evil monks who lack great respect for the training, are agitated, haughty, fickle, harsh-tongued, of scattered speech, of lost mindfulness, not clearly comprehending, with unrestrained faculties, abandoned by their teachers and preceptors, and greedy for gain. Having taught them deceitful practices beginning with the proper establishment of deportment, and having become one whose virtues are praised by evil monks—who are capable of persuading the world by means of praising dwellings esteemed by the world and so on, who are practiced in the Jātakas and so on, and who are endowed with a good voice—he wanders surrounded by a hundred or a thousand… (and becomes a) recipient of… requisites. Regarding ‘This, monks, is the first great thief’: this one, unlike a thief who breaks into houses, does not deceive one family or two; rather, because he takes the four requisites after deceiving a great multitude, he should be known as the ‘first great thief.’ But those monks who are experts in the Suttas, Abhidhamma, or Vinaya, who, when the alms-round is not successful, inspire confidence in the world by reciting the Pāḷi, explaining the commentary, with a Dhamma talk of appreciation, and with accomplishment in deportment, and wander the countryside being honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, and revered—they should be known as ‘those who connect the lineage of the texts, the illuminators of the Sāsana.’

Tathāgatappaveditanti tathāgatena paṭividdhaṃ paccakkhakataṃ jānāpitaṃ vā. Attano dahatīti parisamajjhe pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca saṃsanditvā madhurena sarena pasādanīyaṃ suttantaṃ kathetvā dhammakathāvasena acchariyabbhutajātena viññūjanena “aho, bhante, pāḷi ca aṭṭhakathā ca suparisuddhā, kassa santike uggaṇhitthā”ti pucchito “ko amhādise uggahāpetuṃ samattho”ti ācariyaṃ anuddisitvā attanā [P 2.0484] paṭividdhaṃ sayambhuñāṇādhigataṃ dhammavinayaṃ pavedeti. Ayaṃ tathāgatena satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkheyyāni pāramiyo pūretvā kicchena kasirena paṭividdhadhammatthenako dutiyo mahācoro.

‘Proclaimed by the Tathāgata’ means penetrated, directly experienced, or made known by the Tathāgata. ‘He claims it as his own’ means that in the midst of an assembly, after collating the Pāḷi and the commentary and delivering an inspiring Sutta with a sweet voice, at the end of the Dhamma talk he is asked by a wise person in whom astonishment and wonder have arisen, ‘Venerable sir, ah, the Pāḷi and the commentary are so very pure! In whose presence did you learn them?’ Without indicating his teacher, he replies, ‘Who is capable of teaching one such as me?’ and makes it known that the Dhamma and Vinaya was penetrated by himself, attained through self-arisen knowledge. This is the second great thief, a thief of the Dhamma that was penetrated with difficulty and hardship by the Tathāgata after he fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more.

Suddhaṃ brahmacārinti khīṇāsavabhikkhuṃ. Parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carantanti nirupakkilesaṃ seṭṭhacariyaṃ carantaṃ; aññampi vā anāgāmiṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva sīlavantaṃ puthujjanaṃ avippaṭisārādivatthukaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carantaṃ. Amūlakena abrahmacariyena anuddhaṃsetīti tasmiṃ puggale avijjamānena antimavatthunā anuvadati codeti; ayaṃ vijjamānaguṇamakkhī ariyaguṇatthenako tatiyo mahācoro.

‘A pure holy-life practitioner’ means a monk whose cankers are destroyed. ‘Practicing the perfectly pure holy life’ means practicing the noble practice that is without defilements; or else, another, from a non-returner down to a virtuous worldling, who is practicing the perfectly pure holy life which has as its basis non-remorse and so on. ‘He assails with a groundless (accusation of) not living the holy life’ means he speaks against or admonishes that person with regard to a final matter that does not exist in him. This is the third great thief, a denigrator of existing virtue, a thief of the qualities of noble ones.

Garubhaṇḍāni garuparikkhārānīti yathā adinnādāne “caturo janā saṃvidhāya garubhaṇḍaṃ avāharu”nti (pari. 479) ettha pañcamāsakagghanakaṃ “garubhaṇḍa”nti vuccati, idha pana na evaṃ. Atha kho “pañcimāni, bhikkhave, avissajjiyāni na vissajjetabbāni saṅghena vā gaṇena vā puggalena vā. Vissajjitānipi avissajjitāni [M 2.0077] honti. Yo vissajjeyya, āpatti thullaccayassa. Katamāni pañca? Ārāmo, ārāmavatthu…pe… dārubhaṇḍaṃ, mattikābhaṇḍa”nti vacanato avissajjitabbattā garubhaṇḍāni. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, avebhaṅgiyāni na vibhajitabbāni saṅghena vā gaṇena vā puggalena vā. Vibhattānipi avibhattāni honti. Yo vibhajeyya, āpatti thullaccayassa. Katamāni pañca? Ārāmo, ārāmavatthu…pe… dārubhaṇḍaṃ, mattikābhaṇḍa”nti (cūḷava. 322) vacanato avebhaṅgiyattā sādhāraṇaparikkhārabhāvena garuparikkhārāni. Ārāmo ārāmavatthūtiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ “pañcimāni, bhikkhave, avissajjiyānī”ti khandhake āgatasuttavaṇṇanāyameva [P 2.0485] bhaṇissāma. Tehi gihī saṅgaṇhātīti tāni datvā datvā gihīṃ saṅgaṇhāti anuggaṇhāti. Upalāpetīti “aho amhākaṃ ayyo”ti evaṃ lapanake anubandhanake sasnehe karoti. Ayaṃ avissajjiyaṃ avebhaṅgiyañca [V 2.0070] garuparikkhāraṃ tathābhāvato thenetvā gihi saṅgaṇhanako catuttho mahācoro. So ca panāyaṃ imaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ kulasaṅgaṇhanatthaṃ vissajjento kuladūsakadukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Pabbājanīyakammāraho ca hoti. Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ abhibhavitvā issaravatāya vissajjento thullaccayaṃ āpajjati. Theyyacittena vissajjento bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabboti.

“Heavy goods, heavy requisites”: As in the section on theft, where it is said, “Four people, having conspired, carried away heavy goods,” an item worth five māsakas is called “heavy goods.” Here, however, it is not so. Rather, it is because of the passage, “Bhikkhus, these five things are inalienable, not to be given away by the Sangha, by a group, or by an individual. Even if given away, they remain not given away. Whoever would give them away commits a grave offense. What are the five? A monastery, monastery grounds… wooden goods, clay goods,” that they are “heavy goods” due to their inalienable nature. And it is because of the passage, “Bhikkhus, these five things are indivisible, not to be divided by the Sangha, by a group, or by an individual. Even if divided, they remain undivided. Whoever would divide them commits a grave offense. What are the five? A monastery, monastery grounds… wooden goods, clay goods,” that they are “heavy requisites” due to their indivisible nature and their status as communal property. Whatever is to be said regarding “a monastery, monastery grounds,” and so on, all that we will state in the commentary on the sutta that comes in the Khandhaka, beginning, “Bhikkhus, these five things are inalienable.” “With these he wins over householders” means that by giving those things, he wins over and supports householders. “He causes them to speak in praise” means he makes them into people who speak praise, saying, “Oh, our venerable sir!”, into followers, and into those who are affectionate. This one, having stolen a heavy requisite that is inalienable and indivisible from that very state, is the fourth great thief who wins over householders. Furthermore, this monk, in giving away this heavy item for the purpose of winning over families, incurs a dukkaṭa offense of corrupting families. And he is deserving of the act of banishment. Giving it away by overpowering the Sangha of bhikkhus, with the attitude of one in authority, he incurs a grave offense. Giving it away with a thievish mind, he should be made to have the item valued and then be dealt with accordingly.

Ayaṃ aggo mahācoroti ayaṃ imesaṃ corānaṃ jeṭṭhacoro; iminā sadiso coro nāma natthi, yo pañcindriyaggahaṇātītaṃ atisaṇhasukhumaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ theneti. Kiṃ pana sakkā lokuttaradhammo hiraññasuvaṇṇādīni viya vañcetvā thenetvā gahetunti? Na sakkā, tenevāha – “yo asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapatī”ti. Ayañhi attani asantaṃ taṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ “atthi mayhaṃ eso”ti ullapati, na pana sakkoti ṭhānā cāvetuṃ, attani vā saṃvijjamānaṃ kātuṃ. Atha kasmā coroti vuttoti? Yasmā taṃ ullapitvā asantasambhāvanāya uppanne paccaye gaṇhāti. Evañhi gaṇhatā te paccayā sukhumena upāyena vañcetvā thenetvā gahitā honti. Tenevāha – “taṃ kissa hetu? Theyyāya vo bhikkhave raṭṭhapiṇḍo bhutto”ti. Ayañhi ettha attho – yaṃ avocumha – “ayaṃ aggo mahācoro, yo asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapatī”ti[M 2.0078]. Taṃ kissa hetūti kena kāraṇena etaṃ avocumhāti ce. “Theyyāya vo bhikkhave raṭṭhapiṇḍo bhutto”ti bhikkhave yasmā so tena raṭṭhapiṇḍo theyyāya theyyacittena bhutto hoti. Ettha hi vokāro “ye hi vo ariyā araññavanapatthānī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.35-36) viya [P 2.0486] padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Tasmā “tumhehi bhutto”ti evamassa attho na daṭṭhabbo.

“This is the chief great thief”: This one is the foremost thief among these thieves. There is no thief equal to this one, who steals the supramundane Dhamma which is beyond the grasp of the five senses, exceedingly subtle and refined. But is it possible for the supramundane Dhamma to be taken by deceiving and stealing, like gold and silver? It is not possible. For that very reason, He said: “One who claims a non-existent, unreal, superhuman state.” For this one merely boasts of that Dhamma which is non-existent in himself, saying, “This exists for me,” but he is not able to move it from its place or to make it exist in himself. Then why is he called a thief? Because, having boasted of it, he accepts the requisites that arise from the honoring of what is non-existent. For when one accepts in this way, those requisites are taken by deceiving and stealing through a subtle method. For that very reason, He said: “For what reason is this? Bhikkhus, the country's alms-food is eaten through theft.” For this is the meaning here: that which we said—“This is the chief great thief, one who claims a non-existent, unreal, superhuman state”—for what reason did we say this? The answer is: “Bhikkhus, the country's alms-food is eaten through theft,” because that country's alms-food is eaten by that person through theft, with a thievish mind. Here, the particle ‘vo’ is merely an expletive for filling out the line, as in passages like “those noble ones who are in the forest and wilderness.” Therefore, its meaning should not be understood as “eaten by you.”

Idāni tamevatthaṃ gāthāhi vibhūtataraṃ karonto “aññathā santa”ntiādimāha. Tattha aññathā santanti aparisuddhakāyasamācārādikena aññenākārena santaṃ. Aññathā yo pavedayeti parisuddhakāyasamācārādikena aññena ākārena yo pavedeyya. “Paramaparisuddho ahaṃ, atthi me abbhantare lokuttaradhammo”ti evaṃ jānāpeyya. Pavedetvā ca pana tāya pavedanāya uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ arahā viya bhuñjati. Nikacca kitavasseva bhuttaṃ theyyena tassa tanti nikaccāti vañcetvā aññathā santaṃ aññathā dassetvā. Agumbaagacchabhūtameva sākhāpalāsapallavādicchādanena gumbamiva gacchamiva ca attānaṃ dassetvā. Kitavassevāti vañcakassa kerāṭikassa gumbagacchasaññāya araññe āgatāgate sakuṇe gahetvā jīvitakappakassa sākuṇikasseva. Bhuttaṃ theyyena tassa tanti tassāpi anarahantasseva sato arahantabhāvaṃ dassetvā laddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjato; yaṃ taṃ bhuttaṃ taṃ yathā sākuṇikakitavassa nikacca [V 2.0071] vañcetvā sakuṇaggahaṇaṃ, evaṃ manusse vañcetvā laddhassa bhojanassa bhuttattā theyyena bhuttaṃ nāma hoti.

Now, making that same meaning even clearer with verses, He said, “Being otherwise,” and so on. Therein, “being otherwise” means being in another way, with impure bodily conduct and so forth. “Who would make known otherwise” means one who would make it known in another way, with pure bodily conduct and so forth. He would make it known thus: “I am supremely pure; there is supramundane Dhamma within me.” And having made this known, he then eats the food that arises from that declaration as if he were an Arahant. Regarding the line, “His meal is eaten deceitfully, like a trickster's, through theft”: “deceitfully” (nikacca) means having deceived, having shown oneself to be otherwise than one truly is. It is like one who, though in fact not a bush or a thicket, presents himself as a bush or a thicket by covering himself with branches, leaves, and new shoots. “Like a trickster's” (kitavassa) means like that of a deceitful, fraudulent fowler who makes his living by catching the birds that come and go in the forest, based on their perception of him as a bush or thicket. “His meal is eaten through theft” means that for such a person, who is not an Arahant but presents the state of an Arahant and eats the food obtained thereby, that which is eaten—just as is the catching of birds by a trickster-fowler who deceives them, so too, because the food obtained by deceiving people is eaten—is called “eaten through theft.”

Imaṃ pana atthavasaṃ ajānantā ye evaṃ bhuñjanti, kāsāvakaṇṭhā…pe… nirayaṃ te upapajjare kāsāvakaṇṭhāti kāsāvena veṭhitakaṇṭhā. Ettakameva ariyaddhajadhāraṇamattaṃ, sesaṃ sāmaññaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Bhavissanti kho panānanda anāgatamaddhānaṃ gotrabhuno kāsāvakaṇṭhā”ti (ma. ni. 3.380) evaṃ vuttadussīlānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pāpadhammāti lāmakadhammā. Asaññatāti kāyādīhi asaññatā. Pāpāti lāmakapuggalā. Pāpehi kammehīti tehi karaṇakāle ādīnavaṃ adisvā katehi paravañcanādīhi pāpakammehi. Nirayaṃ te upapajjareti nirassādaṃ duggatiṃ te upapajjanti; tasmā seyyo ayoguḷoti gāthā. Tassattho – sacāyaṃ dussīlo asaññato icchācāre ṭhito [M 2.0079] kuhanāya lokaṃ vañcako puggalo tattaṃ aggisikhūpamaṃ ayoguḷaṃ bhuñjeyya [P 2.0487] ajjhohareyya, tassa yañcetaṃ raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ bhuñjeyya, yañcetaṃ ayoguḷaṃ, tesu dvīsu ayoguḷova bhutto seyyo sundarataro paṇītataro ca bhaveyya, na hi ayoguḷassa bhuttattā samparāye sabbaññutañāṇenāpi dujjānaparicchedaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavati. Evaṃ paṭiladdhassa pana tassa raṭṭhapiṇḍassa bhuttattā samparāye vuttappakāraṃ dukkhaṃ anubhoti, ayañhi koṭippatto micchājīvoti.

But those who, not knowing this reason, eat in this way, 'with their necks wrapped in the saffron robe'... are reborn in hell. 'With their necks wrapped in the saffron robe' means having their necks wrapped with the saffron robe. For them, there is only this much: the mere bearing of the noble ones' banner; the rest, the true ascetic life, is absent. Thus it is said: 'In the future, Ānanda, there will be those who are ascetics in name only, with their necks wrapped in the saffron robe' (MN 3.380)—this is a designation for the immoral spoken of thus. 'Of evil nature' means of inferior nature. 'Unrestrained' means unrestrained in body and so forth. 'Wicked' refers to wicked persons. 'By evil deeds' means by those evil deeds, such as deceiving others, done without seeing the danger at the time of their commission. 'They are reborn in hell' means they are reborn in a joyless, unfortunate destination. Therefore, there is the verse, 'Better is an iron ball.' Its meaning is this: If this immoral, unrestrained person, established in conduct according to his wishes, a deceiver of the world through cunning, were to eat or swallow a hot iron ball like a flame of fire, then of the two—eating the country's almsfood and eating that iron ball—eating the iron ball would be better, more excellent, and more sublime. For by eating the iron ball, he does not experience in the future life suffering whose measure is difficult to know even with the knowledge of an Omniscient One. But by eating that country's almsfood obtained in this way, he experiences in the future life suffering of the kind described. For this is wrong livelihood that has reached its peak.

Evaṃ pāpakiriyāya anādīnavadassāvīnaṃ ādīnavaṃ dassetvā “atha kho bhagavā vaggumudātīriye bhikkhū anekapariyāyena vigarahitvā dubbharatāya dupposatāya…pe… imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti ca vatvā catutthapārājikaṃ paññapento “yo pana bhikkhu anabhijāna”nti ādimāha.

Thus, having shown the danger to those who do not see the danger of evil action, the Blessed One, after rebuking the monks on the banks of the Vaggumudā in many ways on account of their being difficult to maintain and difficult to support... and having said, '...you should recite this training rule,' wishing to lay down the fourth pārājika, spoke the words beginning with, 'Whatever monk, not knowing...'

Evaṃ mūlacchejjavasena daḷhaṃ katvā catutthapārājike paññatte aparampi anuppaññattatthāya adhimānavatthu udapādi. Tassuppattidīpanatthaṃ etaṃ vuttaṃ – “evañcidaṃ bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ hotī”ti.

Thus, when the fourth pārājika was laid down, having been made firm by way of cutting off at the root, another case, the story of conceit, arose for the purpose of a supplementary ruling. To show its origin, this was said: 'Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.'

Adhimānavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of Conceit

196. Tattha adiṭṭhe diṭṭhasaññinoti arahatte ñāṇacakkhunā adiṭṭheyeva “diṭṭhaṃ amhehi arahatta”nti diṭṭhasaññino hutvā. Esa nayo appattādīsu. Ayaṃ pana viseso – appatteti attano [V 2.0072] santāne uppattivasena appatte. Anadhigateti maggabhāvanāya anadhigate; appaṭiladdhetipi attho. Asacchikateti appaṭividdhe paccavekkhaṇavasena vā appaccakkhakate. Adhimānenāti adhigatamānena; “adhigatā maya”nti evaṃ uppannamānenāti attho, adhikamānena vā thaddhamānenāti attho. Aññaṃ byākariṃsūti arahattaṃ byākariṃsu; “pattaṃ āvuso amhehi arahattaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīya”nti bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tesaṃ maggena appahīnakilesattā kevalaṃ samathavipassanābalena vikkhambhitakilesānaṃ aparena samayena tathārūpapaccayasamāyoge rāgāya cittaṃ namati; rāgatthāya namatīti attho. Esa nayo itaresu.

196. Herein, 'perceiving the unseen as seen' means: regarding arahantship, which is indeed unseen by the eye of knowledge, having the perception, 'We have seen arahantship.' This is the method in the cases of 'unobtained' and so forth. This, however, is the distinction: 'unobtained' means not yet reached in one's own continuity by way of arising. 'Unattained' means not yet known through the development of the path; the meaning is also 'ungained.' 'Unrealized' means not penetrated, or not made directly present by way of reviewing. 'Through conceit' means by the conceit of having attained; that is, by the conceit that has arisen thus, 'We have attained.' Or, the meaning is: by excessive conceit, by rigid conceit. 'They declared something else' means they declared arahantship; they announced to the monks, 'Friends, we have attained arahantship, our task is done.' Because their defilements were not abandoned by the path, being merely suppressed by the power of serenity and insight, at a later time, when a suitable condition presents itself, their minds incline towards lust; that is, they incline for the sake of lust. This is the method in the other cases.

Tañca [P 2.0488] kho etaṃ abbohārikanti tañca kho etaṃ tesaṃ aññabyākaraṇaṃ abbohārikaṃ āpattipaññāpane vohāraṃ na gacchati; āpattiyā aṅgaṃ na hotīti attho.

And that, indeed, is not actionable. That is, that declaration of theirs is not actionable; it does not enter into the legal terminology for laying down an offense; it is not a factor of an offense—this is the meaning.

Kassa [M 2.0080] panāyaṃ adhimāno uppajjati, kassa nuppajjatīti? Ariyasāvakassa tāva nuppajjati so hi maggaphalanibbānapahīnakilesaavasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇena sañjātasomanasso ariyaguṇapaṭivedhe nikkaṅkho. Tasmā sotāpannādīnaṃ “ahaṃ sakadāgāmī”tiādivasena adhimāno nuppajjati. Dussīlassa nuppajjati, so hi ariyaguṇādhigame nirāsova. Sīlavatopi pariccattakammaṭṭhānassa niddārāmatādimanuyuttassa nuppajjati. Suparisuddhasīlassa pana kammaṭṭhāne appamattassa nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā paccayapariggahena vitiṇṇakaṅkhassa tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasantassa āraddhavipassakassa uppajjati, uppanno ca suddhasamathalābhiṃ vā suddhavipassanālābhiṃ vā antarā ṭhapeti, so hi dasapi vīsatipi tiṃsampi vassāni kilesasamudācāraṃ apassitvā “ahaṃ sotāpanno”ti vā “sakadāgāmī”ti vā “anāgāmī”ti vā maññati. Samathavipassanālābhiṃ pana arahatteyeva ṭhapeti. Tassa hi samādhibalena kilesā vikkhambhitā, vipassanābalena saṅkhārā supariggahitā, tasmā saṭṭhimpi vassāni asītimpi vassāni vassasatampi kilesā na samudācaranti, khīṇāsavasseva cittacāro hoti. So evaṃ dīgharattaṃ kilesasamudācāraṃ apassanto antarā aṭhatvāva “arahā aha”nti maññatīti.

For whom, then, does this conceit arise, and for whom does it not arise? For a noble disciple, it does not arise. For he, with joy arisen from reviewing the path, fruit, Nibbāna, abandoned defilements, and remaining defilements, is without doubt in the penetration of the noble qualities. Therefore, for stream-enterers and so on, conceit does not arise by way of thinking, 'I am a once-returner,' and so forth. For an immoral person, it does not arise, for he is without hope of attaining the noble qualities. Even for a virtuous person who has given up the meditation subject and is devoted to delight in sleep and so forth, it does not arise. But for one of completely pure virtue, who is diligent in the meditation subject, who has defined name-and-form, overcome doubt through grasping conditions, applied the three characteristics, and is contemplating formations—for such a practitioner who has undertaken insight, it arises. And having arisen, it establishes one who has attained pure serenity or pure insight midway. For he, not seeing the occurrence of defilements for ten, twenty, or even thirty years, thinks, 'I am a stream-enterer,' or 'a once-returner,' or 'a non-returner.' For one who has attained both serenity and insight, however, it establishes them only in relation to arahantship. For them, defilements are suppressed by the power of concentration, and formations are well-grasped by the power of insight. Therefore, even for sixty, eighty, or a hundred years, defilements do not occur, and their mental process is like that of one whose taints are destroyed. Such a person, not seeing the occurrence of defilements for a long time, without stopping midway, thinks, 'I am an Arahant.'

Savibhaṅgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Training Rule with Analysis

197. Anabhijānanti na abhijānaṃ. Yasmā panāyaṃ anabhijānaṃ samudācarati, svassa santāne [V 2.0073] anuppanno ñāṇena ca asacchikatoti abhūto hoti. Tenassa padabhājane “asantaṃ abhūtaṃ asaṃvijjamāna”nti vatvā “ajānanto apassanto”ti vuttaṃ[P 2.0489].

197. ‘Anabhijānanti’ means ‘na abhijānaṃ’ (not knowing). Furthermore, because one declares a certain superhuman state without knowing it, that state—not having arisen in his continuity and not having been directly realized by knowledge—is therefore non-existent. For that reason, in the word-analysis of this term, after stating, “non-existent, unreal, not present,” it is said, “not knowing, not seeing.”

Uttarimanussadhammanti uttarimanussānaṃ jhāyīnañceva ariyānañca dhammaṃ. Attupanāyikanti attani taṃ upaneti, attānaṃ vā tattha upanetīti attupanāyiko, taṃ attupanāyikaṃ; evaṃ katvā samudācareyyāti sambandho. Padabhājane pana yasmā uttarimanussadhammo nāma jhānaṃ vimokkhaṃ samādhi samāpatti ñāṇadassanaṃ…pe… suññāgāre abhiratīti evaṃ jhānādayo anekadhammā vuttā. Tasmā tesaṃ sabbesaṃ vasena attupanāyikabhāvaṃ [M 2.0081] dassento “te vā kusale dhamme attani upanetī”ti bahuvacananiddesaṃ akāsi. Tattha “ete dhammā mayi sandissantī”ti samudācaranto attani upaneti. “Ahaṃ etesu sandissāmī”ti samudācaranto attānaṃ tesu upanetīti veditabbo.

‘A superhuman state’ means the state of superior human beings, that is, of meditators and noble ones. ‘Applying to oneself’ (attupanāyika) means one applies that state to oneself, or one applies oneself to that state; thus it is called attupanāyika. The connection is: having applied it thus, one should declare it. Furthermore, in the word-analysis, because it is said, “A superhuman state is jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision… delight in an empty dwelling,” many states such as jhāna are thus mentioned. Therefore, showing the state of applying to oneself with regard to all of them, the plural indication was made: “Or one applies those wholesome states to oneself.” Therein, one who declares, “These states are present in me,” applies them to himself. It should be understood that one who declares, “I am present in these states,” applies himself to them.

Alamariyañāṇadassananti ettha lokiyalokuttarā paññā jānanaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, cakkhunā diṭṭhamiva dhammaṃ paccakkhakaraṇato dassanaṭṭhena dassananti ñāṇadassanaṃ. Ariyaṃ visuddhaṃ uttamaṃ ñāṇadassananti ariyañāṇadassanaṃ. Alaṃ pariyattaṃ kilesaviddhaṃsanasamatthaṃ ariyañāṇadassanamettha, jhānādibhede uttarimanussadhamme alaṃ vā ariyañāṇadassanamassāti alamariyañāṇadassano, taṃ alamariyañāṇadassanaṃ uttarimanussadhammanti evaṃ padatthasambandho veditabbo. Tattha yena ñāṇadassanena so alamariyañāṇadassanoti vuccati. Tadeva dassetuṃ “ñāṇanti tisso vijjā, dassananti yaṃ ñāṇaṃ taṃ dassanaṃ; yaṃ dassanaṃ taṃ ñāṇa”nti vijjāsīsena padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahaggatalokuttarā panettha sabbāpi paññā “ñāṇa”nti veditabbā.

Regarding ‘alamariyañāṇadassananti’: Herein, mundane and supramundane wisdom is ‘knowledge’ (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing; because it makes the Dhamma directly perceived as if seen with the eye, it is ‘vision’ (dassana) in the sense of seeing; thus it is ‘knowledge-and-vision’ (ñāṇadassana). Noble, pure, and supreme knowledge-and-vision is ‘noble knowledge-and-vision’ (ariyañāṇadassana). In this superhuman state, which is of different kinds such as jhāna, there is noble knowledge-and-vision that is sufficient, adequate, and capable of destroying the defilements; or, this superhuman state possesses sufficient noble knowledge-and-vision, thus it is called alamariyañāṇadassano. The connection of the meaning of the words should be understood thus: that superhuman state possessing sufficient noble knowledge-and-vision. Therein, it is by that knowledge-and-vision that it is called alamariyañāṇadassano. To show that very thing, the word-analysis is given with the higher knowledges (vijjā) as the heading, saying: “Knowledge means the three higher knowledges; vision means that which is knowledge is vision, that which is vision is knowledge.” Furthermore, herein all exalted and supramundane wisdom should be understood as ‘knowledge’.

Samudācareyyāti vuttappakārametaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ attupanāyikaṃ katvā āroceyya. Itthiyā vātiādi pana ārocetabbapuggalanidassanaṃ. Etesañhi ārocite ārocitaṃ hoti na devamārabrahmānaṃ, nāpi petayakkhatiracchānagatānanti. Iti jānāmi iti passāmīti samudācaraṇākāranidassanametaṃ. Padabhājane panassa “jānāmahaṃ ete dhamme, passāmahaṃ ete dhamme”ti idaṃ tesu jhānādīsu dhammesu jānanapassanānaṃ pavattidīpanaṃ, “atthi ca me ete dhammā”tiādi attupanāyikabhāvadīpanaṃ[P 2.0490].

‘One should declare’: this means one should announce this superhuman state of the kind mentioned, having applied it to oneself. Furthermore, the phrase ‘to a woman, or…’ and so on is an indication of the person to whom it should be declared. For when it is declared to these, it is considered declared; not so when declared to devas, Māra, or Brahmās, nor to petas, yakkhas, or animals. The phrase ‘Thus I know, thus I see’ is an indication of the mode of declaration. Furthermore, in its word-analysis, the statement, “I know these states, I see these states,” is an explanation of the occurrence of knowing and seeing in regard to those states such as jhāna. The phrase, “And these states are in me,” and so on, is an explanation of the state of applying to oneself.

198. Tato aparena samayenāti āpattipaṭijānanasamayadassanametaṃ. Ayaṃ pana ārocitakkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ āpajjati. Āpattiṃ pana āpanno yasmā parena codito vā acodito [V 2.0074] vā paṭijānāti; tasmā “samanuggāhiyamāno vā asamanuggāhiyamāno vā”ti vuttaṃ.

198. ‘Then, at a later time’: this indicates the time for confessing the offense. However, this monk falls into a Pārājika offense at the very moment of declaring it. Furthermore, since one who has committed an offense confesses it whether questioned by another or not questioned, it is therefore said: ‘whether being interrogated or not being interrogated.’

Tattha samanuggāhiyamāne tāva – kiṃ te adhigatanti adhigamapucchā; jhānavimokkhādīsu, sotāpattimaggādīsu vā kiṃ tayā adhigatanti. Kinti te adhigatanti upāyapucchā. Ayañhi etthādhippāyo – kiṃ tayā aniccalakkhaṇaṃ [M 2.0082] dhuraṃ katvā adhigataṃ, dukkhānattalakkhaṇesu aññataraṃ vā? Kiṃ vā samādhivasena abhinivisitvā, udāhu vipassanāvasena? Tathā kiṃ rūpe abhinivisitvā, udāhu arūpe? Kiṃ vā ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā, udāhu bahiddhāti? Kadā te adhigatanti kālapucchā. Pubbaṇhamajjhanhikādīsu katarasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti? Kattha te adhigatanti okāsapucchā. Katarasmiṃ okāse, kiṃ rattiṭṭhāne, divāṭṭhāne, rukkhamūle, maṇḍape, katarasmiṃ vā vihāreti vuttaṃ hoti. Katame te kilesā pahīnāti pahīnakilesapucchā. Kataramaggavajjhā tava kilesā pahīnāti vuttaṃ hoti. Katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhīti paṭiladdhadhammapucchā. Paṭhamamaggādīsu katamesaṃ dhammānaṃ tvaṃ lābhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

In this context, first, when being interrogated: “What have you attained?” is a question about attainment; what have you attained in jhānas, liberations, etc., or in the path of stream-entry, etc.? “How have you attained it?” is a question about the method. For this is the intention here: “Have you attained it by making the characteristic of impermanence the focus, or one of the characteristics of suffering or non-self? Or have you attained it through concentration, or through insight? Likewise, have you attained it by focusing on form, or on the formless? Or have you attained it by focusing internally, or externally?” “When did you attain it?” is a question about time; this means, “At which time, among morning, midday, etc.?” “Where did you attain it?” is a question about place; this means, “In which place, whether at a night-residence, a day-residence, the foot of a tree, a pavilion, or in which monastery?” “Which of your defilements are abandoned?” is a question about abandoned defilements; this means, “Your defilements to be destroyed by which path have been abandoned?” “Of which states are you a gainer?” is a question about attained states; this means, “Among the first path, etc., of which states are you a gainer?”

Tasmā idāni cepi koci bhikkhu uttarimanussadhammādhigamaṃ byākareyya, na so ettāvatāva sakkātabbo. Imesu pana chasu ṭhānesu sodhanatthaṃ vattabbo – “kiṃ te adhigataṃ, kiṃ jhānaṃ, udāhu vimokkhādīsu aññatara”nti? Yo hi yena adhigato dhammo, so tassa pākaṭo hoti. Sace “idaṃ nāma me adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kinti te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “aniccalakkhaṇādīsu kiṃ dhuraṃ katvā aṭṭhatiṃsāya vā ārammaṇesu rūpārūpaajjhattabahiddhādibhedesu [P 2.0491] vā dhammesu kena mukhena abhinivisitvā”ti yo hi yassābhiniveso, so tassa pākaṭo hoti. Sace “ayaṃ nāma me abhiniveso evaṃ mayā adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kadā te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ pubbaṇhe, udāhu majjhanhikādīsu aññatarasmiṃ kāle”ti sabbesañhi attanā adhigatakālo pākaṭo hoti. Sace “asukasmiṃ nāma kāle adhigatanti vadati, tato “kattha te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ divāṭṭhāne, udāhu rattiṭṭhānādīsu aññatarasmiṃ okāse”ti sabbesañhi attanā adhigatokāso pākaṭo hoti. Sace “asukasmiṃ nāma me okāse adhigata”nti vadati, tato “katame te kilesā pahīnā”ti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ paṭhamamaggavajjhā, udāhu dutiyādimaggavajjhā”ti sabbesañhi attanā adhigatamaggena pahīnakilesā pākaṭā honti. Sace “ime nāma me kilesā pahīnā”ti vadati, tato “katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti pucchitabbo[V 2.0075], “kiṃ sotāpattimaggassa, udāhu sakadāgāmimaggādīsu aññatarassā”ti sabbesaṃ hi attanā adhigatadhammā [M 2.0083] pākaṭā honti. Sace “imesaṃ nāmāhaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti vadati, ettāvatāpissa vacanaṃ na saddhātabbaṃ, bahussutā hi uggahaparipucchākusalā bhikkhū imāni cha ṭhānāni sodhetuṃ sakkonti.

Therefore, if any monk should now declare an attainment of a superhuman state, he should not be honored merely on that account. Rather, he should be questioned for the purpose of clarification on these six points: 'What have you attained? Is it a jhāna, or is it one among the liberations, and so forth?' For whatever state has been attained by someone, that is manifest to him. If he says, 'I have attained such-and-such a state,' he should then be asked, 'How did you attain it?'—'By making what primary among the characteristics of impermanence, and so forth, or by applying the mind with what as the lead among the thirty-eight objects, or among the phenomena classified as form, formless, internal, external, and so forth, by applying the mind with what as the lead?' For whatever a person's application of mind is, that is manifest to him. If he says, 'This is my application of mind; this is how I attained it,' he should then be asked, 'When did you attain it?'—'Was it in the forenoon, or at another time such as midday?' For to each person, the time of their own attainment is manifest. If he says, 'I attained it at such-and-such a time,' he should then be asked, 'Where did you attain it?'—'Was it in a daytime dwelling, or in another location such as a nighttime dwelling?' For to each person, the place of their own attainment is manifest. If he says, 'I attained it in such-and-such a place,' he should then be asked, 'Which of your defilements have been abandoned?'—'Are they the defilements to be abandoned by the first path, or those to be abandoned by the second path and so on?' For to each person, the defilements abandoned by the path they have attained are manifest. If he says, 'These are the defilements I have abandoned,' he should then be asked, 'Of which states are you a gainer?'—'Is it of the stream-entry path, or of one among the once-returning path and so on?' For to each person, the states they have attained are manifest. If he says, 'I am a gainer of these states,' even with that much his word should not be believed. For learned monks, skilled in study and questioning, are able to clarify these six points.

Imassa pana bhikkhuno āgamanapaṭipadā sodhetabbā. Yadi āgamanapaṭipadā na sujjhati, “imāya paṭipadāya lokuttaradhammo nāma na labbhatī”ti apanetabbo. Yadi panassa āgamanapaṭipadā sujjhati, “dīgharattaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu appamatto jāgariyamanuyutto catūsu paccayesu alaggo ākāse pāṇisamena cetasā viharatī”ti paññāyati, tassa bhikkhuno byākaraṇaṃ paṭipadāya saddhiṃ saṃsandati. “Seyyathāpi nāma gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakena saddhiṃ saṃsandati sameti; evameva supaññattā tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.296) vuttasadisaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, this monk's practice that is the basis for the attainment should be examined. If that practice is not pure, he should be dismissed with the words, 'By this practice, a supramundane state cannot be obtained.' But if his practice is pure, and it is apparent that 'For a long time, he has been diligent in the three trainings, devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwells with a mind like a hand in the sky,' then that monk's declaration accords with his practice. It becomes like what was said: 'Just as the water of the Ganges flows together and merges with the water of the Yamunā; even so, the path leading to Nibbāna has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One for the disciples. Nibbāna and the path flow together' (Dī. Ni. 2.296).

Apica kho na ettakenāpi sakkāro kātabbo. Kasmā? Ekaccassa hi puthujjanassāpi sato khīṇāsavapaṭipattisadisā paṭipadā hoti, tasmā so bhikkhu tehi tehi upāyehi uttāsetabbo. Khīṇāsavassa nāma asaniyāpi matthake [P 2.0492] patamānāya bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā na hoti. Sacassa bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā uppajjati, “na tvaṃ arahā”ti apanetabbo. Sace pana abhīrū acchambhī anutrāsī hutvā sīho viya nisīdati, ayaṃ bhikkhu sampannaveyyākaraṇo samantā rājarājamahāmattādīhi pesitaṃ sakkāraṃ arahatīti.

Moreover, honor should not be shown even for this much. Why? Because for a certain worldling, even while being a worldling, there can be a practice similar to the practice of one whose cankers are destroyed. Therefore, that monk should be frightened by various means. For one whose cankers are destroyed, there is no fear, consternation, or hair-raising even if a thunderbolt were to fall on his head. If fear, consternation, or hair-raising arise in him, he should be dismissed with the words, ‘You are not an Arahant.’ But if he remains fearless, unperturbed, and unterrified, sitting like a lion, then this monk, having given a complete explanation, is worthy of the honor sent from all around by kings, royal ministers, and the like.

Pāpicchoti yā sā “idhekacco dussīlova samāno sīlavāti maṃ jano jānātūti icchatī”tiādinā (vibha. 851) nayena vuttā pāpicchā tāya samannāgato. Icchāpakatoti tāya pāpikāya icchāya apakato abhibhūto pārājiko hutvā.

‘One of evil wishes’ means one who is endowed with that evil wish which is spoken of by the method beginning, ‘Here, someone, being immoral, wishes, “May people know me as virtuous.”’ ‘Carried away by wishes’ means being carried away and overwhelmed by that evil wish, having committed a pārājika offense.

Visuddhāpekkhoti attano visuddhiṃ apekkhamāno icchamāno patthayamāno. Ayañhi yasmā pārājikaṃ āpanno, tasmā bhikkhubhāve ṭhatvā abhabbo jhānādīni adhigantuṃ, bhikkhubhāvo hissa saggantarāyo ceva hoti maggantarāyo ca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “sāmaññaṃ dupparāmaṭṭhaṃ nirayāyupakaḍḍhatī”ti [M 2.0084] (dha. pa. 311). Aparampi vuttaṃ – “sithilo hi paribbājo, bhiyyo ākirate raja”nti (dha. pa. 313). Iccassa bhikkhubhāvo visuddhi nāma na hoti[V 2.0076]. Yasmā pana gihī vā upāsako vā ārāmiko vā sāmaṇero vā hutvā dānasaraṇasīlasaṃvarādīhi saggamaggaṃ vā jhānavimokkhādīhi mokkhamaggaṃ vā ārādhetuṃ bhabbo hoti, tasmāssa gihiādibhāvo visuddhi nāma hoti, tasmā taṃ visuddhiṃ apekkhanato “visuddhāpekkho”ti vuccati. Teneva cassa padabhājane “gihī vā hotukāmo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘One who seeks a cause for purity’ means one who looks for, desires, and aspires to his own cause for purity. For since this monk has committed a pārājika offense, remaining in the state of a monk, he is incapable of attaining jhāna and the like. Indeed, for him, the state of a monk is an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the path. And this was said: ‘A monastic life wrongly handled drags one to hell’ (Dhp. 311). And further it was said: ‘A lax monastic practice scatters more dust’ (Dhp. 313). Thus, for him, the state of a monk is not what is called a cause for purity. But because, having become a householder, or a lay follower, or a monastery attendant, or a novice, one is capable of accomplishing the path to heaven through giving, taking refuge, observing virtue, restraint, and so on, or the path to liberation through jhāna, liberations, and so on, therefore, for him, the state of a householder and so forth is called a cause for purity. Therefore, because he looks for that cause for purity, he is called ‘one who seeks a cause for purity.’ For this very reason, in the word-analysis for this term, it is said, ‘desiring to become a householder,’ and so on.

Evaṃ vadeyyāti evaṃ bhaṇeyya. Kathaṃ? “Ajānamevaṃ āvuso avacaṃ jānāmi, apassaṃ passāmī”ti. Padabhājane pana “evaṃ vadeyyā”ti idaṃ padaṃ anuddharitvāva yathā vadanto “ajānamevaṃ āvuso avacaṃ jānāmi, apassaṃ passāmī”ti vadati nāmāti vuccati, taṃ ākāraṃ dassetuṃ “nāhaṃ ete dhamme jānāmī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tucchaṃ musā vilapinti ahaṃ vacanatthavirahato tucchaṃ vañcanādhippāyato musā vilapiṃ, abhaṇinti [P 2.0493] vuttaṃ hoti. Padabhājane panassa aññena padabyañjanena atthamattaṃ dassetuṃ “tucchakaṃ mayā bhaṇita”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

“He would speak thus” means “he would say thus.” How? “Friend, not knowing, I said, ‘I know’; not seeing, I said, ‘I see’.” However, in the word analysis, without taking up this phrase “he would speak thus,” in order to show the manner in which one speaking is said to be one who says, “Friend, not knowing, I said ‘I know’; not seeing, I said ‘I see’,” the passage beginning “I do not know these states” is stated. “He utters a vain falsehood” means, “I uttered a vain statement because it was devoid of the meaning of the word; I uttered a falsehood due to the intention to deceive.” This means, “I spoke.” However, in its word analysis, to show merely the meaning with other words and expressions, the passage beginning “An empty thing was spoken by me” is stated.

Purime upādāyāti purimāni tīṇi pārājikāni āpanne puggale upādāya. Sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca pākaṭamevāti.

“With reference to the former ones” means with reference to persons who have fallen into the three former pārājika offenses. The remainder is indeed evident, both because of the method stated previously and because its meaning is clear.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Word Analysis

199. Evaṃ uddiṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ padānukkamena vibhajitvā idāni yasmā heṭṭhā padabhājanīyamhi “jhānaṃ vimokkhaṃ samādhi samāpatti ñāṇadassanaṃ…pe… suññāgāre abhiratī”ti evaṃ saṃkhitteneva uttarimanussadhammo dassito, na vitthārena āpattiṃ āropetvā tanti ṭhapitā. Saṅkhepadassite ca atthe na sabbe sabbākārena nayaṃ gahetuṃ sakkonti, tasmā sabbākārena nayaggahaṇatthaṃ puna tadeva padabhājanaṃ mātikāṭhāne ṭhapetvā vitthārato uttarimanussadhammaṃ dassetvā āpattibhedaṃ dassetukāmo “jhānanti paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, dutiyaṃ jhāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamajjhānādīhi mettājhānādīnipi asubhajjhānādīnipi ānāpānassatisamādhijjhānampi lokiyajjhānampi lokuttarajjhānampi saṅgahitameva. Tasmā “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjintipi…pe… catutthaṃ jjhānaṃ, mettājhānaṃ, upekkhājhānaṃ asubhajjhānaṃ ānāpānassatisamādhijjhānaṃ[M 2.0085], lokiyajjhānaṃ, lokuttarajjhānaṃ samāpajji”ntipi bhaṇanto pārājikova hotīti veditabbo.

199. Thus, having analyzed the training rule that has been set forth in sequence of words, now, because in the word analysis below, the state of a superior human was shown only concisely as “jhāna… delight in an empty dwelling,” and the textual lineage was not established by assigning an offense in detail. And when the meaning is shown concisely, not all are able to grasp the method in all its aspects. Therefore, for the purpose of grasping the method in all its aspects, desiring to show the distinctions of offenses by again placing that same word analysis in the position of a matrix and showing the state of a superior human in detail, he said, “‘Jhāna’ means the first jhāna, the second jhāna,” and so on. Therein, by “the first jhāna,” and so on, the jhānas of loving-kindness, etc., the jhānas of foulness, etc., the jhāna of concentration through mindfulness of breathing, the worldly jhāna, and the supramundane jhāna are indeed included. Therefore, it should be understood that one who says, “I attained the first jhāna… I attained the fourth jhāna… I attained the supramundane jhāna,” becomes one who has committed a pārājika.

Suṭṭhu [V 2.0077] mutto vividhehi vā kilesehi muttoti vimokkho. So panāyaṃ rāgadosamohehi suññattā suññato. Rāgadosamohanimittehi animittattā animitto. Rāgadosamohapaṇidhīnaṃ abhāvato appaṇihitoti vuccati. Cittaṃ samaṃ ādahati ārammaṇe ṭhapetīti samādhi. Ariyehi samāpajjitabbato samāpatti. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Ettha ca vimokkhattikena ca samādhittikena ca ariyamaggova [P 2.0494] vutto. Samāpattittikena pana phalasamāpatti. Tesu yaṃkiñci ekampi padaṃ gahetvā “ahaṃ imassa lābhīmhī”ti bhaṇanto pārājikova hoti.

Vimokkha (liberation) is so called because one is “well-freed” (suṭṭhu mutto), or because one is “freed from various defilements” (vividhehi kilesehi mutto). This liberation is called suññata (void) because of its emptiness of lust, hatred, and delusion. It is called animitta (signless) because of its signlessness from the signs of lust, hatred, and delusion. It is called appaṇihita (desireless) because of the absence of the aspirations of lust, hatred, and delusion. Samādhi (concentration) is so called because it places the mind evenly (samaṃ ādahati), it sets it on an object (ārammaṇe ṭhapeti). Samāpatti (attainment) is so called because it is to be attained by the noble ones (ariyena samāpajjitabbato). The remainder here is by the same method as stated. And here, by the triad of liberation and by the triad of concentration, only the noble path is spoken of. But by the triad of attainment, fruition-attainment is spoken of. Among these, taking even a single word whatsoever and saying, “I am a gainer of this,” one becomes one who has committed a pārājika.

Tisso vijjāti pubbenivāsānussati, dibbacakkhu, āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇanti. Tattha ekissāpi nāmaṃ gahetvā “ahaṃ imissā vijjāya lābhīmhī”ti bhaṇanto pārājiko hoti. Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vijjānaṃ lābhīmhī’ti bhaṇantopi ‘tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ lābhīmhī’ti bhaṇantopi pārājiko vā”ti vuttaṃ. Maggabhāvanāpadabhājane vuttā sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammā maggasampayuttā lokuttarāva idhādhippetā. Tasmā lokuttarānaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ iddhipādānaṃ indriyānaṃ balānaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa lābhīmhīti vadato pārājikanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyādīsu pana “satipaṭṭhānānaṃ lābhīmhī’ti evaṃ ekekakoṭṭhāsavasenāpi ‘kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānassa lābhīmhī’ti evaṃ tattha ekekadhammavasenāpi vadato pārājikamevā”ti vuttaṃ tampi sameti. Kasmā? Maggakkhaṇuppanneyeva sandhāya vuttattā. Phalasacchikiriyāyapi ekekaphalavasena pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“The three knowledges” are: the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. Therein, taking the name of even one and saying, “I am a gainer of this knowledge,” one becomes one who has committed a pārājika. However, in the Concise Commentary it is said: “One who says, ‘I am a gainer of the knowledges,’ and one who says, ‘I am a gainer of the three knowledges,’ also becomes one who has committed a pārājika.” The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment spoken of in the word analysis of the cultivation of the path are intended here as only supramundane and associated with the path. Therefore, it is said in the Great Commentary that for one who says, “I am a gainer of the supramundane foundations of mindfulness… of the noble eightfold path,” it is a pārājika. However, in the Mahāpaccarī and other texts, it is said: “For one who speaks by way of each single group, such as, ‘I am a gainer of the foundations of mindfulness,’ and for one who speaks by way of each single factor therein, such as, ‘I am a gainer of the foundation of mindfulness concerning the contemplation of the body,’ it is indeed a pārājika.” That also is consistent. Why? Because it is stated with reference only to that which arises at the moment of the path. Also, in the realization of fruition, a pārājika should be understood by way of each single fruition.

Rāgassa pahānantiādittike kilesappahānameva vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā maggena vinā natthi, tatiyamaggena hi kāmarāgadosānaṃ pahānaṃ, catutthena mohassa, tasmā “rāgo me pahīno”tiādīni vadatopi pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ.

In the triad beginning with “the abandoning of lust,” only the abandoning of defilements is spoken of. However, since that abandoning does not exist without the path—for by the third path there is the abandoning of sensual lust and aversion, and by the fourth, the abandoning of delusion—therefore, for one who also says, “Lust is abandoned by me,” and so on, a pārājika is spoken of.

Rāgā cittaṃ vinīvaraṇatātiādittike lokuttaracittameva vuttaṃ. Tasmā “rāgā me cittaṃ vinīvaraṇa”ntiādīni vadatopi pārājikameva.

In the triad beginning with “the mind’s freedom from hindrances such as lust,” only the supramundane mind is spoken of. Therefore, for one who also says, “My mind is free from hindrances such as lust,” and so on, it is indeed a pārājika.

Suññāgārapadabhājane [M 2.0086] pana yasmā jhānena aghaṭetvā “suññāgāre abhiramāmī”ti vacanamattena pārājikaṃ nādhippetaṃ, tasmā “paṭhamena jhānena suññāgāre abhiratī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā yo jhānena ghaṭetvā “iminā [P 2.0495] nāma jhānena suññāgāre abhiramāmī”ti vadati, ayameva pārājiko hotīti veditabbo.

However, in the word analysis of “empty dwelling,” because a pārājika is not intended by the mere statement, “I delight in an empty dwelling,” without connecting it with jhāna, therefore, “delight in an empty dwelling with the first jhāna,” and so on, is stated. Therefore, it should be understood that one who, having connected it with jhāna, says, “I delight in an empty dwelling with such-and-such a jhāna”—only this one becomes one who has committed a pārājika.

Yā [V 2.0078] ca “ñāṇa”nti imassa padabhājane ambaṭṭhasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 1.254 ādayo) vuttāsu aṭṭhasu vijjāsu vipassanāñāṇamanomayiddhiiddhividhadibbasotacetopariyañāṇabhedā pañca vijjā na āgatā, tāsu ekā vipassanāva pārājikavatthu na hoti, sesā hontīti veditabbā. Tasmā “vipassanāya lābhīmhī”tipi “vipassanāñāṇassa lābhīmhī”tipi vadato pārājikaṃ natthi. Phussadevatthero pana bhaṇati – “itarāpi catasso vijjā ñāṇena aghaṭitā pārājikavatthū na honti. Tasmā ‘manomayassa lābhīmhi, iddhividhassa, dibbāya sotadhātuyā, cetopariyassa lābhīmhī’ti vadatopi pārājikaṃ natthī”ti. Taṃ tassa antevāsikeheva paṭikkhittaṃ – “ācariyo na ābhidhammiko bhummantaraṃ na jānāti, abhiññā nāma catutthajjhānapādakova mahaggatadhammo, jhāneneva ijjhati. Tasmā manomayassa lābhīmhī’ti vā ‘manomayañāṇassa lābhīmhī’ti vā yathā vā tathā vā vadatu pārājikamevā”ti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi nibbānaṃ pāḷiyā anāgataṃ, atha kho “nibbānaṃ me patta”nti vā “sacchikata”nti vā vadato pārājikameva. Kasmā? Nibbānassa nibbattitalokuttarattā. Tathā “cattāri saccāni paṭivijjhiṃ paṭividdhāni mayā”ti vadatopi pārājikameva. Kasmā? Saccappaṭivedhoti hi maggassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Yasmā pana “tisso paṭisambhidā kāmāvacarakusalato catūsu ñāṇasampayuttesu cittuppādesu uppajjanti, kriyato catūsu ñāṇasampayuttesu cittuppādesu uppajjanti, atthapaṭisambhidā etesu ceva uppajjati, catūsu maggesu catūsu phalesu ca uppajjatī”ti vibhaṅge (vibha. 746) vuttaṃ. Tasmā “dhammapaṭisambhidāya lābhīmhī”ti vā, “nirutti…pe… paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāya [P 2.0496] lābhīmhī”ti vā “lokiyaatthapaṭisambhidāya lābhīmhī”ti vā vuttepi pārājikaṃ natthi. “Paṭisambhidānaṃ lābhīmhī”ti vutte na tāva sīsaṃ otarati. “Lokuttaraatthapaṭisambhidāya lābhīmhī”ti vutte pana pārājikaṃ hoti. Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana atthapaṭisambhidāppattomhīti avisesenāpi vadato [M 2.0087] pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ. Kurundiyampi “na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ettāvatā pārājikaṃ natthi, ettāvatā sīsaṃ na otarati, ettāvatā na pārājika”nti vicāritattā na sakkā aññaṃ pamāṇaṃ kātunti.

And in the analysis of this word 'knowledge' (ñāṇa), of the eight kinds of higher knowledge (vijjā) mentioned in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta and others, five kinds—insight knowledge, mind-made power, psychic power, divine ear, and knowledge of others' minds—are not included. Among these, only insight does not constitute a ground for a pārājika offense, but the others do; this should be understood. Therefore, for one who says, 'I am a gainer of insight,' or 'I am a gainer of insight knowledge,' there is no pārājika offense. However, the Elder Phussadeva says: 'The other four kinds of higher knowledge, when not associated with the word 'knowledge', do not constitute grounds for a pārājika offense. Therefore, even for one who says, 'I am a gainer of mind-made power,' '...of psychic power,' '...of the divine ear element,' or '...of the knowledge of others' minds,' there is no pārājika offense.' This was refuted by his own pupils: 'The teacher is not an expert in the Abhidhamma and does not understand the distinction of planes. Supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) is an exalted state based on the fourth jhāna and is achieved only through jhāna. Therefore, whether one says, 'I am a gainer of mind-made power,' or 'I am a gainer of mind-made knowledge,' or says it in any other way, it is indeed a pārājika offense.' And here, although Nibbāna is not mentioned in the Pāli text, if someone says, 'Nibbāna has been attained by me,' or 'it has been realized,' it is indeed a pārājika offense. Why? Because Nibbāna is a world-transcending state that has been brought into being. Similarly, for one who says, 'I have penetrated the four truths; they have been penetrated by me,' it is also a pārājika offense. Why? Because 'penetration of the truths' is a synonym for the Path. Furthermore, since it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'The three analytical knowledges arise from wholesome sense-sphere consciousness in the four consciousness-moments associated with knowledge, and from functional consciousness...; the analytical knowledge of meaning arises in these, and also in the four paths and four fruits.' Therefore, even when it is said, 'I am a gainer of the analytical knowledge of Dhamma,' or '...of language... (etc.) ...of ready-wit,' or 'I am a gainer of the mundane analytical knowledge of meaning,' there is no pārājika offense. When it is said, 'I am a gainer of the analytical knowledges,' the head does not yet fall. But when it is said, 'I am a gainer of the supramundane analytical knowledge of meaning,' it is a pārājika offense. In the Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said that for one who says, even without specification, 'I have attained the analytical knowledge of meaning,' it is a pārājika offense. In the Kurundī also, it is said, 'He is not released.' But in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, since it has been examined thus: 'To this extent, there is no pārājika offense; to this extent, the head does not fall; to this extent, it is not a pārājika offense,' it is not possible to take another as the authority.

“Nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjāmī”ti vā “lābhīmhāhaṃ tassā”ti vā vadatopi pārājikaṃ natthi. Kasmā? Nirodhasamāpattiyā neva lokiyattā na lokuttarattāti. Sace panassa evaṃ hoti – “nirodhaṃ nāma anāgāmī vā khīṇāsavo vā samāpajjati, tesaṃ maṃ aññataroti jānissatī”ti byākaroti, so ca naṃ tathā jānāti, pārājikanti mahāpaccarisaṅkhepaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Taṃ vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

Even if one says, 'I am attaining the cessation attainment,' or 'I am a gainer of it,' there is no pārājika offense. Why? Because the cessation attainment is neither mundane nor supramundane. But if this thought occurs to him: 'A non-returner or one whose taints are destroyed attains cessation, and they will know me as one of them,' and he declares this, and that person understands him as such, it is a pārājika offense. This is stated in the Mahāpaccarī and Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā. This should be examined and understood.

“Atītabhave [V 2.0079] kassapasammāsambuddhakāle sotāpannomhī”ti vadatopi pārājikaṃ natthi. Atītakkhandhānañhi parāmaṭṭhattā sīsaṃ na otaratīti. Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “atīte aṭṭhasamāpattilābhīmhī”ti vadato pārājikaṃ natthi, kuppadhammattā idha pana “atthi akuppadhammattāti keci vadantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi tattheva “atītattabhāvaṃ sandhāya kathentassa pārājikaṃ na hoti, paccuppannattabhāvaṃ sandhāya kathentasseva hotī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ.

Even if one says, 'In a past existence, during the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Kassapa, I was a stream-enterer,' there is no pārājika offense. For, because of referring to past aggregates, the head does not fall. However, in the Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā it is said that for one who says, 'In the past, I was a gainer of the eight attainments,' there is no pārājika offense due to their perishable nature; but here [in the case of being a stream-enterer], some say there is an offense due to its imperishable nature. That too is refuted right there: 'For one who speaks referring to a past existence, there is no pārājika offense; it is only for one who speaks referring to a present existence that there is a pārājika offense.'

Suddhikavārakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Simple Section

200. Evaṃ jhānādīni dasa mātikāpadāni vitthāretvā idāni uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapanto yaṃ sampajānamusāvādaṃ bhaṇati, tassa aṅgaṃ dassetvā tasseva vitthārassa vasena cakkapeyyālaṃ bandhanto ullapanākārañca āpattibhedañca dassetuṃ “tīhākārehī”tiādimāha. Tattha suddhikavāro vattukāmavāro paccayapaṭisaṃyuttavāroti tayo mahāvārā. Tesu [P 2.0497] suddhikavāre paṭhamajjhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva mohā cittaṃ vinīvaraṇapadaṃ, tāva ekamekasmiṃ pade samāpajjiṃ, samāpajjāmi, samāpanno, lābhīmhi, vasīmhi, sacchikataṃ mayāti imesu chasu padesu ekamekaṃ padaṃ tīhākārehi, catūhi, pañcahi, chahi, sattahākārehīti evaṃ pañcakkhattuṃ yojetvā suddhikanayo nāma vutto. Tato paṭhamañca jhānaṃ, dutiyañca jhānanti evaṃ paṭhamajjhānena saddhiṃ ekamekaṃ [M 2.0088] padaṃ ghaṭentena sabbapadāni ghaṭetvā teneva vitthārena khaṇḍacakkaṃ nāma vuttaṃ. Tañhi puna ānetvā paṭhamajjhānādīhi na yojitaṃ, tasmā “khaṇḍacakka”nti vuccati. Tato dutiyañca jhānaṃ, tatiyañca jhānanti evaṃ dutiyajjhānena saddhiṃ ekamekaṃ padaṃ ghaṭetvā puna ānetvā paṭhamajjhānena saddhiṃ sambandhitvā teneva vitthārena baddhacakkaṃ nāma vuttaṃ. Tato yathā dutiyajjhānena saddhiṃ, evaṃ tatiyajjhānādīhipi saddhiṃ, ekamekaṃ padaṃ ghaṭetvā puna ānetvā dutiyajjhānādīhi saddhiṃ sambandhitvā teneva vitthārena aññānipi ekūnatiṃsa baddhacakkāni vatvā ekamūlakanayo niṭṭhāpito. Pāṭho pana saṅkhepena dassito, so asammuyhantena vitthārato veditabbo.

200. Having thus elaborated the ten matrix terms beginning with jhāna, now, regarding the deliberate falsehood that a monk speaks when boasting of a superior human state, to show its factor, and by way of its elaboration, while constructing the wheel of repetitions and showing the manner of boasting and the classification of offenses, He spoke the words beginning with 'in three ways.' Herein, there are three great sections: the Section on Purity, the Section on the Desire to Speak, and the Section Connected with Conditions. Among them, in the Section on Purity, starting with the first jhāna up to the term 'the mind is without hindrances from delusion,' for each of the six terms—'I attained,' 'I am attaining,' 'I have attained,' 'I am a gainer,' 'I am a master,' 'it has been realized by me'—each term is combined five times, in three ways, four ways, five ways, six ways, and seven ways; this is called the Method of Purity. Then, regarding 'the first jhāna and the second jhāna,' thus, by combining each term with the first jhāna, all the terms are combined, and by that same elaboration, what is called the Fragmented Wheel is stated. For it is not brought back and combined with the first jhāna and so on; therefore, it is called the 'Fragmented Wheel.' Then, regarding 'the second jhāna and the third jhāna,' thus, by combining each term with the second jhāna, and again bringing it back to connect with the first jhāna, by that same elaboration, what is called the Bound Wheel is stated. Then, just as with the second jhāna, so too with the third jhāna and so forth, by combining each term and again bringing it back to connect with the second jhāna and so on, by that same elaboration, twenty-nine other Bound Wheels are stated, and the Single-Root Method is concluded. The text, however, is shown in brief; it should be understood in detail by one who is not confused.

Yathā ca ekamūlako, evaṃ dumūlakādayopi sabbamūlakapariyosānā catunnaṃ satānaṃ upari pañcatiṃsa nayā vuttā. Seyyathidaṃ – dvimūlakā ekūnatiṃsa, timūlakā aṭṭhavīsa, catumūlakā sattavīsa; evaṃ pañcamūlakādayopi ekekaṃ ūnaṃ katvā yāva tiṃsamūlakā, tāva veditabbā. Pāṭhe pana tesaṃ nāmampi saṅkhipitvā “idaṃ sabbamūlaka”nti tiṃsamūlakanayo eko dassito. Yasmā ca suññāgārapadaṃ jhānena aghaṭitaṃ sīsaṃ na otarati, tasmā taṃ anāmasitvā [P 2.0498] mohā cittaṃ [V 2.0080] vinīvaraṇapadapariyosānāyeva sabbattha yojanā dassitāti veditabbā. Evaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīni paṭipāṭiyā vā uppaṭipāṭiyā vā dutiyajjhānādīhi ghaṭetvā vā aghaṭetvā vā samāpajjintiādinā nayena ullapato mokkho natthi, pārājikaṃ āpajjatiyevāti.

And just as the single-root method was taught, so too the methods from the two-root up to the all-root conclusion—four hundred and thirty-five methods—are taught. That is to say: for the two-root, there are twenty-nine methods; for the three-root, twenty-eight; for the four-root, twenty-seven. In this way, from the five-root onwards, they should be understood by reducing one each time, down to the thirty-root. In the text, however, their names are also summarized, and the one thirty-root method is shown as 'this is the all-root.' And because the term 'empty dwelling,' when not connected with jhāna, does not lead to the ultimate offense (Pārājika), it should be understood that, without considering it, the combination is shown everywhere as concluding with the term 'the mind is without hindrances from delusion.' Thus, for one who boasts by associating the first jhāna and so on with the second jhāna and so on—whether in sequence or out of sequence, whether connected or not connected—according to the method beginning with 'I attained,' there is no escape; one certainly incurs a Pārājika offense.

Imassa atthassa dassanavasena vutte ca panetasmiṃ suddhikamahāvāre ayaṃ saṅkhepato atthavaṇṇanā – tīhākārehīti sampajānamusāvādassa aṅgabhūtehi tīhi kāraṇehi. Pubbevassa hotīti pubbabhāgeyeva assa puggalassa evaṃ hoti “musā bhaṇissa”nti. Bhaṇantassa hotīti bhaṇamānassa hoti. Bhaṇitassa hotīti bhaṇite assa hoti, yaṃ vattabbaṃ tasmiṃ vutte hotīti attho. Atha vā bhaṇitassāti vuttavato niṭṭhitavacanassa hotīti. Yo evaṃ pubbabhāgepi jānāti, bhaṇantopi jānāti, pacchāpi jānāti, “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti so “paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajji”nti bhaṇanto pārājikaṃ āpajjatīti ayamettha attho dassito. Kiñcāpi dassito, atha kho ayamettha viseso – pucchā tāva hoti “‘musā bhaṇissa’nti pubbabhāgo atthi, ‘musā mayā bhaṇita’nti pacchābhāgo natthi, vuttamattameva hi koci pamussati, kiṃ tassa pārājikaṃ hoti, na hotī”ti? Sā evaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vissajjitā – pubbabhāge “musā bhaṇissa”nti ca bhaṇantassa [M 2.0089] “musā bhaṇāmī”ti ca jānato pacchābhāge “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti na sakkā na bhavituṃ. Sacepi na hoti pārājikameva. Purimameva hi aṅgadvayaṃ pamāṇaṃ. Yassāpi pubbabhāge “musā bhaṇissa”nti ābhogo natthi, bhaṇanto pana “musā bhaṇāmī”ti jānāti, bhaṇitepi “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti jānāti, so āpattiyā na kāretabbo. Pubbabhāgo hi pamāṇataro. Tasmiṃ asati davā bhaṇitaṃ vā ravā bhaṇitaṃ vā hotī”ti.

Furthermore, regarding this, when spoken in the Suddhikamahāvāra to show its meaning, this is the brief explanation: ‘By three modes’ means by the three causes that are the factors of deliberate falsehood. ‘It is so for him beforehand’ means that even in the prior stage, it is thus for that person: ‘I will speak falsely.’ ‘It is so for him while speaking’ means it is so for him while he is speaking. ‘It is so for him when it has been spoken’ means it is so for him when it has been spoken; the meaning is that when what was to be said has been said, it is so for him. Alternatively, ‘when it has been spoken’ means it is so for one who has spoken, whose speech is completed. One who thus knows in the prior stage, knows while speaking, and also knows afterward, ‘A falsehood has been spoken by me,’ that person, in saying, ‘I attained the first jhāna,’ incurs a Pārājika offense. This is the meaning shown here. Although it has been shown, there is this distinction here. First, a question arises: ‘The prior stage, “I will speak falsely,” exists, but the later stage, “A falsehood has been spoken by me,” does not exist—for someone might simply forget what was just said—does he incur a Pārājika offense or not?’ This is answered in the commentaries thus: For one who knows in the prior stage, ‘I will speak falsely,’ and while speaking, ‘I am speaking falsely,’ it is not possible for the knowledge in the later stage, ‘A falsehood has been spoken by me,’ not to be. Even if it is not, it is still a Pārājika offense. For the first two factors alone are the standard. As for one who has no prior intention, ‘I will speak falsely,’ but while speaking knows, ‘I am speaking falsely,’ and also knows when it has been spoken, ‘A falsehood has been spoken by me,’ he should not be charged with an offense. For the prior stage is the more decisive standard. When that is absent, what is spoken is either spoken hastily or spoken erroneously.

Ettha ca taṃñāṇatā ca ñāṇasamodhānañca pariccajitabbaṃ. Taṃñāṇatā pariccajitabbāti [P 2.0499] yena cittena “musā bhaṇissa”nti jānāti, teneva “musā bhaṇāmī”ti ca “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti ca jānātīti evaṃ ekacitteneva tīsu khaṇesu jānātīti ayaṃ taṃññaṇatā pariccajitabbā, na hi sakkā teneva cittena taṃ cittaṃ jānituṃ yathā na sakkā teneva asinā so asi chinditunti. Purimaṃ purimaṃ pana cittaṃ pacchimassa pacchimassa cittassa tathā uppattiyā paccayo hutvā nirujjhati. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Here, both the concept of 'that-knowing-ness' (taṃñāṇatā) and the 'confluence of knowledges' (ñāṇasamodhāna) should be rejected. That 'that-knowing-ness' should be rejected means this: the idea that one knows in three moments with a single mind—that with the same mind with which one knows, 'I will speak falsely,' with that very mind one also knows, 'I am speaking falsely,' and 'A falsehood has been spoken by me'—this 'that-knowing-ness' should be rejected. For it is not possible to know that mind with that same mind, just as it is not possible to cut that sword with that same sword. Rather, each preceding mind, having become a condition for the arising of each succeeding mind, ceases. Therefore, this is said:

“Pamāṇaṃ pubbabhāgova, tasmiṃ sati na hessati;

Sesadvayanti nattheta, miti vācā tivaṅgikā”ti.

The prior part alone is the standard. It is not the case that if this exists, the remaining two will not be. Thus, speech has three factors.

“Ñāṇasamodhānaṃ [V 2.0081] pariccajitabba”nti etāni tīṇi cittāni ekakkhaṇe uppajjantīti na gahetabbāni. Idañhi cittaṃ nāma –

“The conjunction of knowledge should be abandoned”—these three minds are not to be taken as arising in a single moment. For this, indeed, is what is called mind:

Aniruddhamhi paṭhame, na uppajjati pacchimaṃ;

Nirantaruppajjanato, ekaṃ viya pakāsati.

When the first has not ceased, the subsequent does not arise; because of its uninterrupted arising, it appears as if it were one.

Ito paraṃ pana yvāyaṃ “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji”nti sampajānamusā bhaṇati, yasmā so “natthi me paṭhamaṃ jhāna”nti evaṃdiṭṭhiko hoti, tassa hi atthevāyaṃ laddhi. Tathā “natthi me paṭhamaṃ jhāna”nti evamassa khamati ceva ruccati ca. Evaṃsabhāvameva cassa cittaṃ “natthi me paṭhamaṃ jhāna”nti. Yadā pana musā vattukāmo hoti, tadā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ vā diṭṭhiyā saha khantiṃ vā diṭṭhikhantīhi saddhiṃ ruciṃ vā, diṭṭhikhantirucīhi saddhiṃ bhāvaṃ vā vinidhāya nikkhipitvā paṭicchādetvā abhūtaṃ katvā bhaṇati, tasmā tesampi vasena aṅgabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “catūhākārehī”tiādi vuttaṃ.
