Parivāre ca “aṭṭhaṅgiko [M 2.0090] musāvādo”ti (paṭi. 328) vuttattā tattha adhippetāya saññāya saddhiṃ aññopi idha “aṭṭhahākārehī”ti eko [P 2.0500] nayo yojetabbo.

Furthermore, from this point on, when one knowingly speaks falsely, saying, ‘I attained the first jhāna,’ since one holds the view, ‘I do not have the first jhāna,’ this tenet is indeed present in him. Thus, it is acceptable and pleasing to him that ‘I do not have the first jhāna.’ His mind is naturally of this state: ‘I do not have the first jhāna.’ But when he wishes to speak falsely, he puts aside that view, or the acceptance along with that view, or the liking along with the view and acceptance, or the inclination along with the view, acceptance, and liking, and having set it down and hidden it, he fabricates a falsehood and speaks. Therefore, to show the division of factors based on these as well, it is said, ‘in four ways,’ and so on. And in the Parivāra, since it is stated, ‘False speech has eight factors,’ together with the perception intended there, another method, ‘in eight ways,’ should also be applied here.

Ettha ca vinidhāya diṭṭhinti balavadhammavinidhānavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vinidhāya khantintiādīni tato dubbaladubbalānaṃ vinidhānavasena. Vinidhāya saññanti idaṃ panettha sabbadubbaladhammavinidhānaṃ. Saññāmattampi nāma avinidhāya sampajānamusā bhāsissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yasmā pana “samāpajjissāmī”tiādinā anāgatavacanena pārājikaṃ na hoti, tasmā “samāpajji”ntiādīni atītavattamānapadāneva pāṭhe vuttānīti veditabbāni.

Here, ‘having put aside the view’ is said with reference to putting aside a strong phenomenon. ‘Having put aside acceptance,’ and so on, are said with reference to putting aside progressively weaker phenomena than that. ‘Having put aside perception’ here refers to the putting aside of the weakest phenomenon of all. It is not possible that one would speak a deliberate falsehood without putting aside even a mere perception. However, because a pārājika offense does not occur with future-tense words like ‘I will attain,’ therefore, it should be understood that phrases like ‘I attained,’ and so on, are stated in the text only as past or present tense words.

207. Ito paraṃ sabbampi imasmiṃ suddhikamahāvāre uttānatthameva. Na hettha taṃ atthi – yaṃ iminā vinicchayena na sakkā bhaveyya viññātuṃ, ṭhapetvā kilesappahānapadassa padabhājane “rāgo me catto vanto”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ. Svāyaṃ vuccati – ettha hi cattoti idaṃ sakabhāvapariccajanavasena vuttaṃ. Vantoti idaṃ puna anādiyanabhāvadassanavasena. Muttoti idaṃ santatito vimocanavasena. Pahīnoti idaṃ muttassāpi kvaci anavaṭṭhānadassanavasena. Paṭinissaṭṭhoti idaṃ pubbe ādinnapubbassa paṭinissaggadassanavasena. Ukkheṭitoti idaṃ ariyamaggena uttāsitattā puna anallīyanabhāvadassanavasena. Svāyamattho saddasatthato pariyesitabbo[V 2.0082]. Samukkheṭitoti idaṃ suṭṭhu uttāsetvā aṇusahagatassāpi puna anallīyanabhāvadassanavasena vuttanti.

207. From this point on, everything in this Great Chapter on Purity is clear in meaning. There is nothing here that cannot be understood through this analysis, except for the meaning of the words in the word-analysis of the section on abandoning defilements—such as ‘My lust is given up, thrown up,’ and so on. This is explained as follows: Here, ‘given up’ (catto) is said in the sense of relinquishing its own state. ‘Thrown up’ (vanto) is said in the sense of showing the state of not taking it up again. ‘Freed’ (mutto) is said in the sense of liberation from the continuity. ‘Abandoned’ (pahīno) is said in the sense of showing that even what is freed does not remain anywhere. ‘Relinquished’ (paṭinissaṭṭho) is said in the sense of showing the relinquishing again of what was previously taken up. ‘Eradicated’ (ukkheṭito) is said in the sense of showing that, having been terrified by the noble path, it will not cling again. This meaning should be sought from the grammatical texts. ‘Thoroughly eradicated’ (samukkheṭito) is said in the sense of showing that, having been well-terrified, even that which is accompanied by the subtle will not cling again.

Suddhikavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the Chapter on Purity is concluded.

Vattukāmavārakathā

Discourse on the Section of Desiring to Speak

215. Vattukāmavārepi “tīhākārehī”tiādīnaṃ attho, vārapeyyālappabhedo ca sabbo idha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kevalañhi yaṃ “mayā virajjhitvā aññaṃ vattukāmena aññaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā natthi mayhaṃ āpattī”ti evaṃ okāsagavesakānaṃ pāpapuggalānaṃ okāsanisedhanatthaṃ vutto. Yatheva hi “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattukāmo “dhammaṃ paccakkhāmī”tiādīsu sikkhāpaccakkhānapadesu yaṃ vā taṃ vā vadantopi khette otiṇṇattā sikkhāpaccakkhātakova [M 2.0091] hoti; evaṃ [P 2.0501] paṭhamajjhānādīsu uttarimanussadhammapadesu yaṃkiñci ekaṃ vattukāmo tato aññaṃ yaṃ vā taṃ vā vadantopi khette otiṇṇattā pārājikova hoti. Sace yassa vadati, so tamatthaṃ taṅkhaṇaññeva jānāti. Jānanalakkhaṇañcettha sikkhāpaccakkhāne vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

215. Also in the Section of Desiring to Speak, the meaning of phrases such as ‘in three ways’ and the classification of the abbreviated section should all be understood here in the same manner as has been stated. For this was stated solely to prevent the opportunity for wicked individuals who seek loopholes by saying, ‘Having erred, and desiring to say one thing, I said another; therefore, there is no offense for me.’ Just as one who, desiring to say, ‘I renounce the Buddha,’ says instead ‘I renounce the Dhamma’ or any other such phrase among the statements for renouncing the training, is considered to have indeed renounced the training because of having fallen into that field; so too, one who, desiring to say any one thing among the statements concerning superhuman states such as the first jhāna, says instead any other thing, commits a pārājika offense because of having fallen into that field, if the person to whom he speaks understands that meaning at that very moment. And here, the characteristic of understanding should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on renouncing the training.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ hatthamuddāya sīsaṃ na otarati. Idaṃ abhūtārocanaṃ hatthamuddāyapi otarati. Yo hi hatthavikārādīhipi aṅgapaccaṅgacopanehi abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ viññattipathe ṭhitassa puggalassa āroceti, so ca tamatthaṃ jānāti, pārājikova hoti. Atha pana yassa āroceti, so na jānāti “ki ayaṃ bhaṇatī”ti, saṃsayaṃ vā āpajjati, ciraṃ vīmaṃsitvā vā pacchā jānāti, appaṭivijānanto icceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Evaṃ appaṭivijānantassa vutte thullaccayaṃ hoti. Yo pana jhānādīni attano adhigamavasena vā uggahaparipucchādivasena vā na jānāti, kevalaṃ jhānanti vā vimokkhoti vā vacanamattameva sutaṃ hoti, sopi tena vutte “jhānaṃ kira samāpajjinti esa vadatī”ti yadi ettakamattampi jānāti, jānāticceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tassa vutte pārājikameva. Seso ekassa vā dvinnaṃ vā bahūnaṃ vā niyamitāniyamitavasena viseso sabbo sikkhāpaccakkhānakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabboti.

However, this is the distinction: renouncing the training does not reach its culmination by means of a hand gesture. This false declaration reaches its culmination even by means of a hand gesture. For if someone declares a false superhuman state through movements of the major and minor limbs, such as unusual hand gestures, to a person standing in the path of communication, and that person understands the meaning, he commits a pārājika offense. But if the one to whom it is declared does not understand, thinking, ‘What is this person saying?’, or falls into doubt, or understands only after investigating for a long time, he is reckoned as one who does not understand. When spoken to one who thus does not understand, a thullaccaya offense is incurred. Furthermore, if someone does not know about things like jhāna, either through personal attainment or by way of learning and questioning, but has merely heard the word ‘jhāna’ or ‘vimokkha,’ and if, when spoken to by that monk, he understands even just this much, thinking, ‘This person is saying that he can, it seems, attain jhāna,’ he is reckoned as one who indeed understands. When spoken to such a person, it is indeed a pārājika offense. All the remaining distinctions—whether concerning one, two, or many people, by way of being specified or unspecified—should be understood according to the method explained in the discussion on renouncing the training.

Vattukāmavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Section of Desiring to Speak is concluded.

Paccayapaṭisaṃyuttavārakathā

Discourse on the Section Pertaining to Requisites

220. Paccayapaṭisaṃyuttavārepi [V 2.0083] – sabbaṃ vārapeyyālabhedaṃ pubbe āgatapadānañca atthaṃ vuttanayeneva ñatvā pāḷikkamo tāva evaṃ jānitabbo. Ettha hi “yo te vihāre vasi, yo te cīvaraṃ paribhuñji, yo te piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñji, yo te senāsanaṃ paribhuñji, yo te gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paribhuñjī”ti ime pañca paccattavacanavārā, “yena te vihāro paribhutto”tiādayo pañca karaṇavacanavārā, “yaṃ tvaṃ āgamma vihāraṃ adāsī”tiādayo pañca upayogavacanavārā vuttā[P 2.0502], tesaṃ vasena idha vuttena suññāgārapadena saddhiṃ pubbe vuttesu paṭhamajjhānādīsu sabbapadesu [M 2.0092] vārapeyyālabhedo veditabbo. “Yo te vihāre, yena te vihāro, yaṃ tvaṃ āgamma vihāra”nti evaṃ pariyāyena vuttattā pana “aha”nti ca avuttattā paṭivijānantassa vuttepi idha thullaccayaṃ, apaṭivijānantassa dukkaṭanti ayamettha vinicchayo.

220. Also in the section pertaining to requisites, having understood all the variations of the repeated phrases and the meaning of the terms that have appeared before in the manner stated, the sequence of the Pāḷi text should first be known thus. Here, indeed, the five sections of personal expression—"who stayed in your dwelling," "who used your robe," "who used your almsfood," "who used your lodging," "who used your medicinal requisites for the sick"—and the five sections of instrumental expression—"by whom your dwelling was used," and so on—and the five sections of objective expression—"on account of whom you gave a dwelling," and so on—are stated. Based on these, the variations of the repeated phrases in all the terms stated before, such as the first jhāna, etc., along with the term "empty dwelling" mentioned here, should be understood. However, because it is stated indirectly in such terms as "who in your dwelling," "by whom your dwelling," "on account of whom, the dwelling," and because "I" is unstated, the decision here is as follows: even if spoken to one who understands, here it is a thullaccaya offense; for one who does not understand, it is a dukkaṭa offense. This is the decision here.

Anāpattibhedakathā

Discourse on the Classification of Non-Offenses

Evaṃ vitthāravasena āpattibhedaṃ dassetvā idāni anāpattiṃ dassento “anāpatti adhimānenā”tiādimāha. Tattha adhimānenāti adhigatamānena samudācarantassa anāpatti. Anullapanādhippāyassāti kohaññe icchācāre aṭhatvā anullapanādhippāyassa sabrahmacārīnaṃ santike aññaṃ byākarontassa anāpatti. Ummattakādayo pubbe vuttanayāeva. Idha pana ādikammikā vaggumudātīriyā bhikkhū. Tesaṃ anāpattīti.

Having thus shown the classification of offenses in detail, now, wishing to show the non-offenses, he says, beginning with ‘There is no offense for one with an overestimate.’ Herein, ‘for one with an overestimate’ means there is no offense for one who acts with the estimation of having attained it. ‘For one whose intention is not to boast’ means there is no offense for one who, not being established in deceit or improper conduct and not having the intention to boast, declares something else in the presence of fellow monastics. The insane, etc., are as previously explained. Here, however, the original perpetrators were the monks from the bank of the river Vaggumudā. For them, there is no offense.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Terms is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ – hatthamuddāya ārocentassa kāyacittato, vacībhedena ārocentassa vācācittato, ubhayaṃ karontassa kāyavācācittato samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, tivedanaṃ hasantopi hi somanassiko ullapati bhāyantopi majjhattopīti.

Among the origins, etc., this training rule has three origins: for one who informs by hand gesture, it originates from body and mind; for one who informs by verbal declaration, it originates from speech and mind; for one who does both, it originates from body, speech, and mind. It is an action, involves release from perception, is intentional, blameworthy in the world, a bodily action, a verbal action, arises from an unwholesome mind, and involves threefold feeling. For indeed, being joyful, one boasts even while laughing; one boasts even while afraid; and one boasts even while neutral.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Decided Cases

223. Vinītavatthūsu – adhimānavatthu anupaññattiyaṃ vuttanayameva.

223. Among the Decided Cases: the case of overestimation is just as explained in the Anupaññatti.

Dutiyavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0084] – paṇidhāyāti patthanaṃ katvā. Evaṃ maṃ jano sambhāvessatīti evaṃ araññe vasantaṃ maṃ jano arahatte vā sekkhabhūmiyaṃ vā sambhāvessati, tato lokassa sakkato bhavissāmi garukato mānito pūjitoti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ paṇidhāya “araññe vasissāmī”ti gacchantassa padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Tathā araññe kuṭikaraṇacaṅkamananisīdananivāsanapāvuraṇādīsu sabbakiccesu payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ [P 2.0503] araññe na vasitabbaṃ. Evaṃ vasanto hi sambhāvanaṃ labhatu vā mā vā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Yo pana samādinnadhutaṅgo [M 2.0093] “dhutaṅgaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti vā “gāmante me vasato cittaṃ vikkhipati, araññaṃ sappāya”nti cintetvā vā “addhā araññe tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ aññataraṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vā “araññaṃ pavisitvā arahattaṃ apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī”ti vā “araññavāso nāma bhagavatā pasattho, mayi ca araññe vasante bahū sabrahmacārino gāmantaṃ hitvā āraññakā bhavissantī”ti vā evaṃ anavajjavāsaṃ vasitukāmo hoti, tena vasitabbaṃ.

In the second case: ‘Having aspired’ means having made an aspiration. Thinking, ‘People will esteem me thus’—that is, ‘While dwelling in the forest, people will regard me as an Arahant or as being in the stage of a trainee, and thereby I will be honored, respected, revered, and worshipped by the world.’ Regarding the offense of wrong-doing: for one going with the thought, ‘I will dwell in the forest,’ having aspired in this way, there is an offense of wrong-doing at every single footstep. Likewise, in the forest, in all activities such as building a hut, walking meditation, sitting, dressing, robing, and so on, there is an offense of wrong-doing at every effort. Therefore, one should not dwell in the forest in this way. For one who dwells thus, whether they receive esteem or not, they commit an offense of wrong-doing. However, one who has undertaken an ascetic practice, thinking, ‘I will maintain the ascetic practice;’ or thinking, ‘While I am dwelling near a village my mind is distracted; the forest is suitable;’ or, ‘Surely, in the forest I will attain one of the three kinds of seclusion;’ or, ‘Having entered the forest, I will not leave without attaining Arahantship;’ or, ‘Dwelling in the forest has been praised by the Blessed One, and while I am dwelling in the forest, many of my companions in the holy life will leave the vicinity of the village and become forest-dwellers;’—if one wishes to dwell blamelessly in this way, they should dwell so.

Tatiyavatthusmimpi – “abhikkantādīni saṇṭhapetvā piṇḍāya carissāmī”ti nivāsanapārupanakiccato pabhuti yāva bhojanapariyosānaṃ tāva payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Sambhāvanaṃ labhatu vā mā vā dukkaṭameva. Khandhakavattasekhiyavattaparipūraṇatthaṃ pana sabrahmacārīnaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanatthaṃ vā pāsādikehi abhikkamapaṭikkamādīhi piṇḍāya pavisanto anupavajjo viññūnanti.

In the third case also: thinking, ‘Having composed my deportment—my going forward and so on—I will go for alms,’ from the act of dressing and robing up to the end of the meal, there is an offense of wrong-doing at every effort. Whether one receives esteem or not, it is still an offense of wrong-doing. However, one who enters for alms with pleasing going forward, returning, and so on, for the sake of fulfilling the duties of the Khandhakas and the training rules, or for the sake of companions in the holy life following one's visible example, is blameless in the eyes of the wise.

Catutthapañcamavatthūsu – “yo te vihāre vasī”ti ettha vuttanayeneva “aha”nti avuttattā pārājikaṃ natthi. Attupanāyikameva hi samudācarantassa pārājikaṃ vuttaṃ.

In the fourth and fifth cases: regarding the statement, ‘Whoever stays in your monastery,’ since ‘I’ is not said, there is no Pārājika offense, just as has been explained. For a Pārājika offense is stated only for one who speaks by applying it to oneself.

Paṇidhāya caṅkamītiādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayāneva.

The cases beginning with ‘Having aspired, I walk back and forth,’ and so on, are just as has been explained before.

Saṃyojanavatthusmiṃ – saṃyojanā pahīnātipi “dasa saṃyojanā pahīnā”tipi “ekaṃ saṃyojanaṃ pahīna”ntipi vadato kilesappahānameva ārocitaṃ hoti, tasmā pārājikaṃ.

In the case of the fetters: for one who says, ‘Fetters are abandoned,’ or ‘Ten fetters are abandoned,’ or ‘One fetter is abandoned,’ it is precisely the abandonment of defilements that is announced; therefore, it is a Pārājika offense.

224. Rahovatthūsu – raho ullapatīti “rahogato arahā aha”nti vadati, na manasā cintitameva karoti. Tenettha dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ.

224. In the cases concerning seclusion: ‘Boasting in seclusion’ means that, having gone to a secluded place, one says, ‘I am an Arahant.’ One does not merely think it with the mind. Therefore, in this case, an offense of wrong-doing is stated.

Vihāravatthu [V 2.0085] upaṭṭhānavatthu ca vuttanayameva.

The case of the monastery and the case of the attendance hall are just as has been explained.

225. Na dukkaravatthusmiṃ – tassa bhikkhuno ayaṃ laddhi – “ariyapuggalāva bhagavato sāvakā”ti. Tenāha – “ye kho te bhagavato sāvakā te evaṃ vadeyyu”nti. Yasmā cassa ayamadhippāyo – “sīlavatā [M 2.0094] āraddhavipassakena na dukkaraṃ aññaṃ byākātuṃ, paṭibalo so arahattaṃ pāpuṇitu”nti. Tasmā “anullapanādhippāyo aha”nti āha.

225. In the case of ‘Not Difficult’: that monk has this view: ‘Only noble individuals are the disciples of the Blessed One.’ Therefore he said: ‘Those who are disciples of the Blessed One would speak thus.’ And because this was his intention: ‘For one who is virtuous and has undertaken insight meditation, it is not difficult to declare the further state, that is, the fruit of Arahantship; such a person is capable of attaining Arahantship.’ Therefore, he said, ‘I have no intention of boasting.’

Vīriyavatthusmiṃ [P 2.0504] ārādhanīyoti sakkā ārādhetuṃ sampādetuṃ nibbattetunti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

In the case of effort: ‘Can be won’ means it is possible to win, to accomplish, to bring into being. The rest is just as has been explained.

Maccuvatthusmiṃ so bhikkhu “yassa vippaṭisāro uppajjati, so bhāyeyya. Mayhaṃ pana avippaṭisāravatthukāni parisuddhāni sīlāni, svāhaṃ kiṃ maraṇassa bhāyissāmī”ti etamatthavasaṃ paṭicca “nāhaṃ āvuso maccuno bhāyāmī”ti āha. Tenassa anāpatti.

In the case of death: that monk, based on this reason, said, ‘One in whom remorse arises, he should fear. But as for me, my virtues are pure, without grounds for remorse; why should I fear death?’ It was based on this reasoning that he said, ‘Friend, I do not fear death.’ Therefore, for him there is no offense.

Vippaṭisāravatthusmimpi eseva nayo. Tato parāni tīṇi vatthūni vīriyavatthusadisāneva.

In the case of remorse also, this is the same method. The three cases following that are just like the case of effort.

Vedanāvatthūsupaṭhamasmiṃ tāva so bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhānabalena adhivāsanakhantiyaṃ ṭhatvā “nāvuso sakkā yena vā tena vā adhivāsetu”nti āha. Tenassa anāpatti.

In the cases concerning feelings, in the first case, that monk, established in patient endurance through the power of reflection, said, ‘Friend, it is not possible for just anyone to endure this.’ Therefore, for him there is no offense.

Dutiye pana attupanāyikaṃ akatvā “nāvuso sakkā puthujjanenā”ti pariyāyena vuttattā thullaccayaṃ.

In the second case, however, because it was said indirectly—‘Friend, it is not possible for an ordinary person’—without applying it to oneself, it is a grave offense.

226. Brāhmaṇavatthūsuso kira brāhmaṇo na kevalaṃ “āyantu bhonto arahanto”ti āha. Yaṃ yaṃ panassa vacanaṃ mukhato niggacchati, sabbaṃ “arahantānaṃ āsanāni paññapetha, pādodakaṃ detha, arahanto pāde dhovantū”ti arahantavādapaṭisaṃyuttaṃyeva. Taṃ panassa pasādabhaññaṃ saddhācaritattā attano saddhābalena samussāhitassa vacanaṃ. Tasmā bhagavā “anāpatti, bhikkhave, pasādabhaññe”ti āha. Evaṃ vuccamānena pana bhikkhunā na haṭṭhatuṭṭheneva paccayā paribhuñjitabbā, “arahattasampāpikaṃ paṭipadaṃ paripūressāmī”ti evaṃ yogo karaṇīyoti.

226. In the cases concerning the brahmin: that brahmin, it seems, did not merely say, ‘May the venerable Arahants come!’ Rather, every word that came from his mouth was connected with talk of Arahants, such as, ‘Prepare seats for the Arahants,’ ‘Give water for their feet,’ ‘Let the Arahants wash their feet.’ This statement of his was speech born of confidence, a statement prompted by the power of his own faith, due to his being of faithful temperament. Therefore, the Blessed One said, ‘Monks, there is no offense in speech born of confidence.’ However, a monk who is addressed in this way should not consume the requisites merely with joy and delight; effort should be made with the thought, ‘I will fulfill the practice that leads to Arahantship.’

Aññabyākaraṇavatthūnisaṃyojanavatthusadisāneva. Agāravatthusmiṃ so bhikkhu gihibhāve anatthikatāya [V 2.0086] anapekkhatāya “abhabbo kho āvuso mādiso”ti āha, na ullapanādhippāyena. Tenassa anāpatti.

The cases of declaring gnosis are just like the case of the fetters. In the case of lack of regard: that monk, due to his lack of desire and lack of attachment for the household life, said, ‘Friend, one like me is incapable,’ not with the intention of boasting. Therefore, for him there is no offense.

227. Āvaṭakāmavatthusmiṃ [M 2.0095] so bhikkhu vatthukāmesu ca kilesakāmesu ca lokiyeneva ādīnavadassanena nirapekkho. Tasmā “āvaṭā me āvuso kāmā”ti āha. Tenassa anāpatti. Ettha ca āvaṭāti [P 2.0505] āvāritā nivāritā, paṭikkhittāti attho.

227. In the case of ‘Sensual Pleasures are Shut Out’: that monk was indifferent towards both sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements, through seeing their danger with a purely worldly perspective. Therefore, he said, ‘Friend, for me sensual pleasures are shut out.’ For that reason, there is no offense for him. And herein, ‘shut out’ means obstructed, warded off, rejected.

Abhirativatthusmiṃ so bhikkhu sāsane anukkaṇṭhitabhāvena uddesaparipucchādīsu ca abhiratabhāvena “abhirato ahaṃ āvuso paramāya abhiratiyā”ti āha, na ullapanādhippāyena. Tenassa anāpatti.

In the case of delight: that monk, through not being averse to the teaching and through delighting in recitation, questioning, and so on, said, ‘Friend, I delight with the highest delight,’ not with the intention of boasting. Therefore, there is no offense for him.

Pakkamanavatthusmiṃ yo imamhā āvāsā paṭhamaṃ pakkamissatīti evaṃ āvāsaṃ vā maṇḍapaṃ vā sīmaṃ vā yaṃkiñci ṭhānaṃ paricchinditvā katāya katikāya yo “maṃ arahāti jānantū”ti tamhā ṭhānā paṭhamaṃ pakkamati, pārājiko hoti. Yo pana ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vā kiccena mātāpitūnaṃ vā kenacideva karaṇīyena bhikkhācāratthaṃ vā uddesaparipucchānaṃ vā atthāya aññena vā tādisena karaṇīyena taṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā gacchati, anāpatti. Sacepissa evaṃ gatassa pacchā icchācāro uppajjati “na dānāhaṃ tattha gamissāmi evaṃ maṃ arahāti sambhāvessantī”ti anāpattiyeva.

In the case of departure: if an agreement has been made after defining a dwelling, a pavilion, a boundary, or any other place, whoever departs first from that place thinking, ‘Let them know I am an Arahant,’ commits a pārājika offense. If, however, one departs from and goes beyond that place for a duty for his teachers or preceptors, or for some necessary task for his parents, or for the purpose of going on alms-round, or for the purpose of recitation and questioning, or for some other similar necessary task, there is no offense. And if, for one who has gone thus, a wicked desire later arises, ‘Now I will not go there; thus they will esteem me as an Arahant,’ it is still no offense.

Yopi kenacideva karaṇīyena taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā sajjhāyamanasikārādivasena aññavihito vā hutvā corādīhi vā anubaddho meghaṃ vā uṭṭhitaṃ disvā anovassakaṃ pavisitukāmo taṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamati, anāpatti. Yānena vā iddhiyā vā gacchantopi pārājikaṃ nāpajjati, padagamaneneva āpajjati. Tampi yehi saha katikā katā, tehi saddhiṃ apubbaṃacarimaṃ gacchanto nāpajjati. Evaṃ gacchantā hi sabbepi aññamaññaṃ rakkhanti. Sacepi maṇḍaparukkhamūlādīsu kiñci ṭhānaṃ paricchinditvā “yo ettha nisīdati vā caṅkamati vā, taṃ arahāti jānissāma” pupphāni vā ṭhapetvā “yo imāni gahetvā pūjaṃ karissati, taṃ arahāti jānissāmā”tiādinā nayena katikā katā hoti, tatrāpi icchācāravasena tathā karontassa pārājikameva. Sacepi upāsakena antarāmagge vihāro vā kato hoti, cīvarādīni vā ṭhapitāni honti, “ye arahanto te imasmiṃ vihāre vasantu, cīvarādīni ca gaṇhantū”ti. Tatrāpi icchācāravasena vasantassa vā cīvarādīni vā gaṇhantassa pārājikameva[V 2.0087]. Etaṃ pana adhammikakatikavattaṃ[P 2.0506], tasmā na kātabbaṃ, aññaṃ vā evarūpaṃ “imasmiṃ temāsabbhantare [M 2.0096] sabbeva āraññakā hontu, piṇḍapātikaṅgādiavasesadhutaṅgadharā vā atha vā sabbeva khīṇāsavā hontū”ti evamādi. Nānāverajjakā hi bhikkhū sannipatanti. Tattha keci dubbalā appathāmā evarūpaṃ vattaṃ anupāletuṃ na sakkonti. Tasmā evarūpampi vattaṃ na kātabbaṃ. “Imaṃ temāsaṃ sabbeheva na uddisitabbaṃ, na paripucchitabbaṃ, na pabbājetabbaṃ, mūgabbataṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ, bahi sīmaṭṭhassāpi saṅghalābho dātabbo”ti evamādikaṃ pana na kātabbameva.

If one, having arrived at that place for some necessary task, transgresses it because he is otherwise occupied by way of recitation, reflection, and so on, or because he is pursued by thieves and others, or because, seeing a cloud rising, he desires to enter a place sheltered from the rain, there is no offense. Even one going by vehicle or by psychic power does not commit a pārājika offense; one commits the offense only by going on foot. And even then, one going simultaneously—not before and not after—with those with whom the agreement was made does not commit an offense. For in going thus, all protect one another. Even if an agreement is made after defining a place in a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or elsewhere, in the manner of, ‘Whoever sits or walks here, we will know him to be an Arahant,’ or, having placed flowers, ‘Whoever takes these and makes an offering, we will know him to be an Arahant,’ and so on—even there, for one who acts thus by way of a wicked desire, it is a pārājika offense. And if a monastery has been built by a lay follower on the road between places, or robes and other requisites have been placed there with the instruction, ‘Let the Arahants dwell in this monastery and take the robes and other requisites,’ even there, for a monk who dwells there or takes the robes and other requisites by way of a wicked desire, it is a pārājika offense. This, however, is an unrighteous agreement; therefore, it should not be made. Nor should another such agreement be made, for instance: ‘Within this three-month period, let all be forest-dwellers, or observers of the remaining ascetic practices such as the alms-food-eater’s practice, or let all be Arahants.’ For monks from various different regions assemble, and among them some are weak and lack strength and are unable to observe such a practice. Therefore, such a practice should not be established. And an agreement such as, ‘For these three months, no one should recite, ask questions, or give the going-forth; the vow of silence should be undertaken; and Sangha gains should be given even to one outside the boundary,’ should certainly not be made.

228. Lakkhaṇasaṃyutte yvāyaṃ āyasmā ca lakkhaṇoti lakkhaṇatthero vutto, esa jaṭilasahassassa abbhantare ehibhikkhūpasampadāya upasampanno ādittapariyāyāvasāne arahattappatto eko mahāsāvakoti veditabbo. Yasmā panesa lakkhaṇasampannena sabbākāraparipūrena brahmasamena attabhāvena samannāgato, tasmā lakkhaṇoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Mahāmoggallānatthero pana pabbajitadivasato sattame divase arahattappatto dutiyo aggasāvako.

228. In the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta, this Venerable Lakkhaṇa who is spoken of as Elder Lakkhaṇa should be understood as one of the great disciples who was ordained among the thousand matted-hair ascetics with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination and attained Arahantship at the end of the Ādittapariyāya. And because he was endowed with a physical form possessing the marks of a great man, complete in all aspects, and like that of a Brahmā, he came to be known as 'Lakkhaṇa'. As for the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, he was the second chief disciple, who attained Arahantship on the seventh day from his ordination.

Sitaṃ pātvākāsīti mandahasitaṃ pātuakāsi, pakāsayi dassesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ pana disvā thero sitaṃ pātvākāsīti? Upari pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ ekaṃ petaloke nibbattaṃ sattaṃ disvā, tañca kho dibbena cakkhunā, na pasādacakkhunā. Pasādacakkhussa hi ete attabhāvā na āpāthaṃ āgacchanti. Evarūpaṃ pana attabhāvaṃ disvā kāruññe kātabbe kasmā sitaṃ pātvākāsīti? Attano ca buddhañāṇassa ca sampattisamanussaraṇato. Tañhi disvā thero “adiṭṭhasaccena nāma puggalena paṭilabhitabbā evarūpā attabhāvā mutto ahaṃ, lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me”ti attano ca sampattiṃ anussaritvā “aho buddhassa bhagavato [P 2.0507] ñāṇasampatti, yo ‘kammavipāko, bhikkhave, acinteyyo; na cintetabbo’ti (a. ni. 4.77) desesi, paccakkhaṃ vata katvā buddhā desenti, suppaṭividdhā buddhānaṃ dhammadhātū”ti evaṃ buddhañāṇasampattiñca saritvā sitaṃ pātvākāsīti. Yasmā pana khīṇāsavā nāma na akāraṇā sitaṃ pātukaronti, tasmā taṃ lakkhaṇatthero pucchi – “ko nu kho āvuso moggallāna hetu, ko paccayo sitassa pātukammāyā”ti. Thero pana yasmā yehi ayaṃ upapatti sāmaṃ adiṭṭhā, te dussaddhāpayā honti, tasmā bhagavantaṃ sakkhiṃ katvā byākātukāmatāya “akālo kho, āvuso”tiādimāha[M 2.0097]. Tato bhagavato santike puṭṭho “idhāhaṃ āvuso”tiādinā nayena byākāsi.

“He revealed a smile” means he made a gentle smile apparent; it means he manifested it, he showed it. But what did the elder see that made him smile? He saw a being reborn in the world of ghosts as a chain of bones, as mentioned in the Pāli text above; and he saw this with the divine eye, not the physical eye. For these forms of existence do not come into the range of the physical eye. But upon seeing such a form of existence, when compassion should have been shown, why did he smile? It was from reflecting on the perfection of his own attainment and that of the Buddha's knowledge. For upon seeing it, the elder reflected on his own attainment: 'I am freed from such states of existence, which are to be obtained by a person who has not seen the truths. Indeed, a gain for me! Indeed, well-gained by me!' And reflecting on the perfection of the Buddha's knowledge—'Oh, the perfection of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who taught, “Monks, the result of kamma is unthinkable; it should not be thought about” (AN 4.77). Truly, Buddhas teach having realized it directly; the Dhamma-element is well-penetrated by the Buddhas!'—he smiled. Now, since those whose cankers are destroyed do not reveal a smile without a reason, the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked him: 'What, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, what is the reason for revealing a smile?' The elder, however, because those who have not seen this state of existence for themselves are difficult to convince, wished to explain with the Blessed One as his witness, and so he said, 'This is not the time, friend,' and so on. Then, when questioned in the presence of the Blessed One, he explained in the manner beginning, 'Here, friend...'

Tattha [V 2.0088] aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikanti setaṃ nimmaṃsalohitaṃ aṭṭhisaṅghātaṃ. Gijjhāpi kākāpi kulalāpīti etepi yakkhagijjhā ceva yakkhakākā ca yakkhakulalā ca paccetabbā. Pākatikānaṃ pana gijjhādīnaṃ āpāthampi etaṃ rūpaṃ nāgacchati. Anupatitvā anupatitvāti anubandhitvā anubandhitvā. Vituḍentīti vinivijjhitvā gacchanti. Vitudentīti vā pāṭho, asidhārūpamehi tikhiṇehi lohatuṇḍehi vijjhantīti attho. Sā sudaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ karotīti ettha sudanti nipāto, sā aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā aṭṭassaraṃ āturassaraṃ karotīti attho. Akusalavipākānubhavanatthaṃ kira yojanappamāṇāpi tādisā attabhāvā nibbattanti, pasādussadā ca honti pakkagaṇḍasadisā; tasmā sā aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā balavavedanāturā tādisaṃ saramakāsīti. Evañca pana vatvā puna āyasmā mahāmoggallāno “vaṭṭagāmikasattā nāma evarūpā attabhāvā na muccantī”ti sattesu kāruññaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ dhammasaṃvegaṃ dassento “tassa mayhaṃ āvuso etadahosi; acchariyaṃ vata bho”tiādimāha.

Therein, 'a skeleton' means a white, fleshless, bloodless heap of bones. 'Vultures, crows, and hawks'—these should be understood as demon-vultures, demon-crows, and demon-hawks. This form, however, does not even come into the range of ordinary vultures and the like. 'Following again and again' means pursuing repeatedly. ‘They peck’ means they pierce and fly away. Or the reading may be ‘they pierce,’ meaning they pierce with sharp iron beaks like sword blades. Here, in 'She, it seems, uttered a cry of pain,' the word 'sudaṃ' is a particle; the meaning is that the skeleton-peta uttered a cry of pain, a cry of the afflicted. It is said that such beings arise even a yojana in size to experience the result of unwholesome kamma, and they are repulsive and like a ripe boil. Therefore, that skeleton-peta, afflicted by intense pain, uttered such a cry. And having spoken thus, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, showing the spiritual urgency that arose on account of his compassion for beings—thinking, 'Beings who fare on in the round of existence are not freed from such states of being'—again said, 'To me, friend, this occurred: "It is wonderful, indeed!"' and so on.

Bhikkhū ujjhāyantīti yesaṃ sā petūpapatti appaccakkhā, te ujjhāyanti[P 2.0508]. Bhagavā pana therassānubhāvaṃ pakāsento “cakkhubhūtā vata bhikkhave sāvakā viharantī”tiādimāha. Tattha cakkhu bhūtaṃ jātaṃ uppannaṃ tesanti cakkhubhūtā; bhūtacakkhukā uppannacakkhukā, cakkhuṃ uppādetvā, viharantīti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Yatra hi nāmāti ettha yatrāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tatrāyamatthayojanā; yasmā nāma sāvakopi evarūpaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sakkhiṃ vā karissati, tasmā avocumha – “cakkhubhūtā vata bhikkhave sāvakā viharanti, ñāṇabhūtā vata bhikkhave sāvakā viharantī”ti.

“The monks complained” means those for whom that peta’s arising was not directly perceived complained. But the Blessed One, revealing the elder’s spiritual power, said, "Truly, monks, the disciples dwell as those who have become vision," and so on. Herein, “those who have become vision” means that for them vision has become, has been born, has arisen; they are those with manifest vision, those with arisen vision, meaning they dwell having generated the eye of knowledge. The same method applies to the second term. Here, the word 'yatra' in “where indeed” is an expression of cause. The application of the meaning here is this: since even a disciple would indeed know, see, or witness such a form, therefore we have said, "Truly, monks, the disciples dwell as those who have become vision; truly, monks, the disciples dwell as those who have become knowledge."

Pubbeva me so bhikkhave satto diṭṭhoti bodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutañāṇappaṭivedhena appamāṇesu cakkavāḷesu appamāṇe sattanikāye bhavagatiyoniṭhitinivāse ca paccakkhaṃ karontena mayā pubbeva so satto diṭṭhoti vadati.

He says: 'Monks, that being was seen by me before.' This means: That being was seen by me before at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, as I was directly perceiving—through the penetration of omniscient knowledge—the immeasurable world-systems, the immeasurable hosts of beings, and their states of existence, destinations, origins, stations of consciousness, and abodes.

Goghātakoti [M 2.0098] gāvo vadhitvā vadhitvā aṭṭhito maṃsaṃ mocetvā vikkiṇitvā jīvikakappanakasatto. Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenāti tassa nānācetanāhi āyūhitassa aparāpariyakammassa. Tatra hi yāya cetanāya narake paṭisandhi janitā, tassā vipāke parikkhīṇe avasesakammaṃ vā kammanimittaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ katvā puna petādīsu paṭisandhi nibbattati, tasmā sā paṭisandhi kammasabhāgatāya vā ārammaṇasabhāgatāya vā “tasseva kammassa [V 2.0089] vipākāvaseso”ti vuccati. Ayañca satto evaṃ upapanno. Tenāha – “tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenā”ti. Tassa kira narakā cavanakāle nimmaṃsakatānaṃ gunnaṃ aṭṭhirāsi eva nimittaṃ ahosi. So paṭicchannampi taṃ kammaṃ viññūnaṃ pākaṭaṃ viya karonto aṭṭhisaṅkhalikapeto jāto.

A cow-slaughterer was a being who made a living by repeatedly killing cows, removing the flesh from their bones, and selling it. 'By the remainder of the result of that very kamma' refers to that kamma to be experienced in successive lives, accumulated through his various intentions. For there, when the result of the volition that generated rebirth-linking in hell was exhausted, rebirth-linking arose again among the petas and so on, taking as its object the remaining kamma or a kamma-sign. Therefore, that rebirth-linking is called “the remainder of the result of that very kamma” due to its affinity with the kamma or its affinity with the object. And this being was reborn in this way. Hence He said: “by the remainder of the result of that very kamma.” It is said that, at the time of his passing away from hell, the very heap of bones of cows made fleshless became his sign. Thus, as if making that concealed kamma manifest to the wise, he was born as a skeleton-peta.

229. Maṃsapesivatthusmiṃ [P 2.0509] goghātakoti gomaṃsapesiyo katvā sukkhāpetvā vallūravikkayena anekāni vassāni jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tenassa narakā cavanakāle maṃsapesiyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. So maṃsapesipeto jāto.

229. In the story of the Flesh-Slice Peta: A cow-slaughterer made slices of beef, dried them, and made a living for many years by selling dried meat. Because of that, at the time of his passing away from hell, the very slice of meat became his sign. He was born as a flesh-slice peta.

Maṃsapiṇḍavatthusmiṃ so sākuṇiko sakuṇe gahetvā vikkiṇanakāle nippakkhacamme maṃsapiṇḍamatte katvā vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tenassa narakā cavanakāle maṃsapiṇḍova nimittaṃ ahosi. So maṃsapiṇḍapeto jāto.

In the story of the Lump-of-Flesh Peta: That fowler made a living by catching birds and, at the time of selling, making them into mere lumps of flesh without feathers and skin and selling them. Because of that, at the time of his passing away from hell, the very lump of flesh became his sign. He was born as a lump-of-flesh peta.

Nicchavivatthusmiṃ tassa orabbhikassa eḷake vadhitvā niccamme katvā kappitajīvikassa purimanayeneva niccammaṃ eḷakasarīraṃ nimittamahosi. So nicchavipeto jāto.

In the story of the Skinless Peta: For that sheep-butcher who made his living by killing sheep and making them skinless, in the same way as before, the skinless body of a sheep became his sign. He was born as a skinless peta.

Asilomavatthusmiṃ so sūkariko dīgharattaṃ nivāpapuṭṭhe sūkare asinā vadhitvā vadhitvā dīgharattaṃ jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tenassa ukkhittāsikabhāvova nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā asilomapeto jāto.

In the story of the Sword-Haired Peta: That swine-butcher, for a long time, made a living by repeatedly killing with a sword pigs that had been fattened with fodder. Because of that, the very state of having a raised sword became his sign. Therefore, he was born as a sword-haired peta.

Sattilomavatthusmiṃ so māgaviko ekaṃ migañca sattiñca gahetvā vanaṃ gantvā tassa migassa samīpaṃ āgatāgate mige sattiyā vijjhitvā māresi, tassa sattiyā vijjhanakabhāvoyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā sattilomapeto jāto.

In the story of the Spear-Haired Peta: That hunter, taking a decoy deer and a spear, went into the forest. When other deer came near that decoy, he would pierce and kill them with his spear. The very act of piercing with the spear became his sign. Therefore, he was born as a spear-haired peta.

Usulomavatthusmiṃ [M 2.0099] kāraṇikoti rājāparādhike anekāhi kāraṇāhi pīḷetvā avasāne kaṇḍena vijjhitvā māraṇakapuriso. So kira asukasmiṃ padese viddho maratīti ñatvāva vijjhati. Tassevaṃ jīvikaṃ kappetvā narake uppannassa tato pakkāvasesena idhūpapattikāle usunā vijjhanabhāvoyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā usulomapeto jāto.

In the story of the Arrow-Haired Peta: An executioner is a man who, after torturing those who committed offenses against the king with many kinds of torture, finally kills them by piercing them with an arrow. It is said that he pierces them only after knowing for sure, 'He will die when pierced in such-and-such a spot.' For him, having made his living in this way and having arisen in hell, at the time of his arising here due to the remaining ripened result from that kamma, the very state of piercing with an arrow became his sign. Therefore, he was born as an arrow-haired peta.

Sūcilomavatthusmiṃ sārathīti assadamako. Godamakotipi kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃvuttaṃ. Tassa patodasūciyā vijjhanabhāvoyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā sūcilomapeto jāto.

In the story of the Needle-Haired Peta: A charioteer is a horse-trainer. It is also said in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā that he was a cow-trainer. For him, the very state of piercing with the goad-needle became his sign. Therefore, he was born as a needle-haired peta.

Dutiyasūcilomavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0090] sūcakoti pesuññakārako[P 2.0510]. So kira manusse aññamaññañca bhindi. Rājakule ca “imassa imaṃ nāma atthi, iminā idaṃ nāma kata”nti sūcetvā sūcetvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpesi. Tasmā yathānena sūcetvā manussā bhinnā, tathā sūcīhi bhedanadukkhaṃ paccanubhotuṃ kammameva nimittaṃ katvā sūcilomapeto jāto.

In the second story of the Needle-Haired Peta: A sūcaka is a slanderer. It is said that he caused division among people. And in the royal family, by repeatedly pointing out faults, saying, “This person has such-and-such a matter; by this one, such-and-such was done,” he caused them to reach ruin and disaster. Therefore, just as people were divided by him through his pointing out of faults, so too, making that very kamma the sign, he was born as a needle-haired peta to experience the suffering of being pierced by needles.

Aṇḍabhāritavatthusmiṃ gāmakūṭoti vinicchayāmacco. Tassa kammasabhāgatāya kumbhamattā mahāghaṭappamāṇā aṇḍā ahesuṃ. So hi yasmā raho paṭicchanna ṭhāne lañjaṃ gahetvā kūṭavinicchayena pākaṭaṃ dosaṃ karonto sāmike assāmike akāsi. Tasmāssa rahassaṃ aṅgaṃ pākaṭaṃ nibbattaṃ. Yasmā daṇḍaṃ paṭṭhapento paresaṃ asayhaṃ bhāraṃ āropesi, tasmāssa rahassaṅgaṃ asayhabhāro hutvā nibbattaṃ. Yasmā yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitena samena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ ṭhatvā visamo ahosi, tasmāssa rahassaṅge visamā nisajjā ahosīti.

In the story of the Peta Burdened with Testicles: A village cheat is a judicial minister. Due to the affinity of his kamma, he had testicles the size of pots, the measure of large water jars. Indeed, because, having taken a bribe in a secret, concealed place, he made owners into non-owners by means of a fraudulent judgment, committing a manifest fault. Therefore, his secret organ arose manifestly. Because, when imposing a penalty, he placed an unbearable burden upon others, therefore his secret organ became an unbearable burden. Because, standing in a place where one should be impartial, he was partial, therefore his sitting upon his secret organ became uneven.

Pāradārikavatthusmiṃ so satto parassa rakkhitaṃ gopitaṃ sassāmikaṃ phassaṃ phusanto mīḷhasukhena kāmasukhena cittaṃ ramayitvā kammasabhāgatāya gūthaphassaṃ phusanto dukkhamanubhavituṃ tattha nibbatto. Duṭṭhabrāhmaṇavatthu pākaṭameva.

In the story of the Adulterer: That being, engaging in sexual contact with another's partner who was protected, guarded, and had a master, delighted his mind with sensual pleasure that is like the pleasure of filth. Due to the affinity of his kamma, he was reborn there to experience the suffering of touching filth. The story of the Wicked Brahmin is self-evident.

230. Nicchavitthivatthusmiṃ yasmā mātugāmo nāma attano phasse anissaro, sā ca taṃ sāmikassa santakaṃ phassaṃ thenetvā paresaṃ abhiratiṃ [M 2.0100] uppādesi, tasmā kammasabhāgatāya sukhasamphassā dhaṃsitvā dukkhasamphassaṃ anubhavituṃ nicchavitthī hutvā upapannā.

230. In the story of the Skinless Woman: Because a woman is not the master of her own physical contact, and she, having stolen that contact which is the property of her husband, produced delight for others, therefore, due to the affinity of her kamma, having fallen away from pleasant contact, she arose as a skinless woman to experience painful contact.

Maṅgulitthivatthusmiṃ maṅgulinti [P 2.0511] virūpaṃ duddasikaṃ bībhacchaṃ, sā kira ikkhaṇikākammaṃ yakkhadāsikammaṃ karontī “iminā ca iminā ca evaṃ balikamme kate ayaṃ nāma tumhākaṃ vaḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti mahājanassa gandhapupphādīni vañcanāya gahetvā mahājanaṃ duddiṭṭhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāpesi, tasmā tāya kammasabhāgatāya gandhapupphādīnaṃ thenitattā duggandhā duddassanassa gāhitattā duddasikā virūpā bībhacchā hutvā nibbattā.

In the story of the Maṅgulī Woman: Maṅgulī means deformed, unsightly, and disgusting. It is said that she, performing the work of a spirit-medium and a female spirit-servant, took perfumes, flowers, and so on from the great populace by means of deception, saying, “If offerings are made in this way with this and that, such-and-such prosperity will be yours.” She caused the great populace to adopt bad views and wrong views. Therefore, due to the affinity of that kamma, because she had stolen the perfumes, flowers, and so on, she became foul-smelling; and because she had caused them to adopt a bad view, she was born as one who is unsightly, deformed, and disgusting.

Okilinivatthusmiṃ uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ okirininti sā kira aṅgāracitake nipannā vipphandamānā viparivattamānā paccati, tasmā uppakkā ceva hoti kharena agginā pakkasarīrā; okilinī ca kilinnasarīrā bindubindūni hissā sarīrato paggharanti. Okirinī ca aṅgārasamparikiṇṇā, tassā hi heṭṭhatopi kiṃsukapupphavaṇṇā aṅgārā, ubhayapassesupi[V 2.0091], ākāsatopissā upari aṅgārā patanti, tena vuttaṃ – “uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ okirini”nti. Sā issāpakatā sapattiṃ aṅgārakaṭāhena okirīti tassā kira kaliṅgarañño ekā nāṭakinī aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ samīpe ṭhapetvā gattato udakañca puñchati, pāṇinā ca sedaṃ karoti. Rājāpi tāya saddhiṃ kathañca karoti, parituṭṭhākārañca dasseti. Aggamahesī taṃ asahamānā issāpakatā hutvā acirapakkantassa rañño taṃ aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ gahetvā tassā upari aṅgāre okiri. Sā taṃ kammaṃ katvā tādisaṃyeva vipākaṃ paccanubhavituṃ petaloke nibbattā.

In the story of Okilinī, regarding the words uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ okiriniṃ: It is said that she, lying on a heap of embers, writhing and rolling about, is being cooked. Therefore, she is uppakkā (scorched), her body cooked by the fierce fire; and she is okilinī (wet-bodied), as drops ooze from her body; and she is okirinī (strewn upon), as she is completely covered with embers. Indeed, beneath her are embers the color of Kiṃsuka flowers, as well as on both sides, and from the sky embers fall upon her. Therefore it was said: “scorched, wet-bodied, and strewn upon.” It is said that a certain female dancer of the king of Kaliṅga, having placed a pan of embers nearby, was wiping water from the king's body and fanning him with her hand. The king also conversed with her and showed signs of being very pleased. The chief queen, unable to bear this and overcome by jealousy, took that pan of embers when the king had not been gone for long and poured the embers over that dancer. Having done that kamma, she was reborn in the peta-world to experience a result of that very same kind.

Coraghātakavatthusmiṃ [P 2.0512] so rañño āṇāya dīgharattaṃ corānaṃ sīsāni chinditvā petaloke nibbattanto asīsakaṃ kabandhaṃ hutvā nibbatti.

In the story of the Thief-Executioner: He, by the king's command, cut off the heads of thieves for a long time. Being reborn in the peta-world, he was born as a headless trunk.

Bhikkhuvatthusmiṃ pāpabhikkhūti lāmakabhikkhu. So kira lokassa saddhādeyye cattāro paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyavacīdvārehi asaṃ yato bhinnājīvo cittakeḷiṃ kīḷanto vicari. Tato ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ niraye paccitvā petaloke nibbattanto bhikkhusadiseneva attabhāvena nibbatti. Bhikkhunī-sikkhamānā-sāmaṇera-sāmaṇerīvatthūsupi ayameva vinicchayo.

In the story of the Monk: A wicked monk is a base monk. It is said that he, having consumed the four requisites given in faith by the laity, wandered about unrestrained in body and speech, with a corrupt livelihood, playing at frivolous games. Thereafter, having been tormented in hell for one Buddha-interval, upon being reborn in the peta-world, he was born with an individual existence just like that of a monk. This same method of judgment applies also in the stories of the Nun, the Female Probationer, the Male Novice, and the Female Novice.

231. Tapodāvatthusmiṃ [M 2.0101] acchodakoti pasannodako. Sītodakoti sītalaudako. Sātodakoti madhurodako. Setakoti parisuddho nissevālapaṇakakaddamo. Suppatitthoti sundarehi titthehi upapanno. Ramaṇīyoti ratijanako. Cakkamattānīti rathacakkappamāṇāni. Kuthitā sandatīti tatrā santattā hutvā sandati. Yatāyaṃ bhikkhaveti yato ayaṃ bhikkhave. So dahoti so rahado. Kuto panāyaṃ sandatīti? Vebhārapabbatassa kira heṭṭhā bhummaṭṭhakanāgānaṃ pañcayojanasatikaṃ nāgabhavanaṃ devalokasadisaṃ maṇimayena talena ārāmuyyānehi ca samannāgataṃ; tattha nāgānaṃ kīḷanaṭṭhāne so udakadaho, tato ayaṃ tapodā sandati. Dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchatīti rājagahanagaraṃ kira āviñjetvā mahāpetaloko, tattha dvinnaṃ mahālohakumbhinirayānaṃ antarena ayaṃ tapodā āgacchati, tasmā kuthitā sandatīti.

231. In the Tapodā account: Acchodaka means clear water. Sītodaka means cool water. Sātodaka means sweet water. Setaka means pure, without algae, duckweed, or mud. Suppatittha means endowed with beautiful fords. Ramaṇīya means delightful. Cakkamattāni means the size of chariot wheels. Kuthitā sandati means it flows, having become heated and thoroughly heated. The phrase ‘Yatāyaṃ, bhikkhave’ means ‘yato ayaṃ, bhikkhave’ (From where this, O monks...). ‘So daho’ means ‘that lake.’ But from where does this flow? It is said that beneath Mount Vebhāra there is a five-hundred-yojana Nāga abode of the earth-dwelling nāgas, which resembles a deva-world and is endowed with a jeweled floor, parks, and gardens. There, in the nāgas' pleasure ground, is that lake of water; from there this Tapodā flows. Regarding the phrase, ‘It comes through the space between two great hells,’ it is said that encircling the city of Rājagaha there is a great peta-world; there, this Tapodā comes through the space between two great Lohakumbhī hells. Therefore, it flows heated.

Yuddhavatthusmiṃ [P 2.0513] nandī caratīti vijayabherī āhiṇḍati. Rājā āvuso licchavīhīti thero kira attano divāṭṭhāne ca rattiṭṭhāne ca nisīditvā “licchavayo katahatthā katūpāsanā, rājā ca tehi saddhiṃ sampahāraṃ detī”ti āvajjento dibbena cakkhunā rājānaṃ parājitaṃ palāyamānaṃ addasa. Tato bhikkhū āmantetvā “rājā āvuso tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhāko licchavīhi pabhaggo”ti [V 2.0092] āha. Saccaṃ, bhikkhave, moggallāno āhāti parājikakāle āvajjitvā yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ bhaṇanto saccaṃ āha.

In the account of the battle, ‘nandī carati’ means the victory drum goes about. Regarding ‘Rājā, āvuso, licchavīhi,’ it is said that the Elder, sitting in his day-place and night-place, reflected: ‘The Licchavīs have practiced hands and are skilled in archery, and the king is giving battle with them.’ Reflecting thus, he saw with his divine eye the king defeated and fleeing. Then, addressing the bhikkhus, he said: ‘Friends, your supporter, the king, has been routed by the Licchavīs.’ Regarding ‘Saccaṃ, bhikkhave, moggallāno āha,’ speaking of what he had seen after reflecting at the time of the defeat, he spoke the truth.

232. Nāgogāhavatthusmiṃ sappinikāyāti evaṃnāmikāya. Āneñjaṃ samādhinti anejaṃ acalaṃ kāyavācāvipphandavirahitaṃ catutthajjhānasamādhiṃ. Nāgānanti hatthīnaṃ. Ogayha uttarantānanti ogayha ogāhetvā puna uttarantānaṃ. Te kira gambhīraṃ udakaṃ otaritvā tattha nhatvā ca pivitvā ca soṇḍāya udakaṃ gahetvā aññamaññaṃ ālolentā uttaranti, tesaṃ evaṃ ogayha uttarantānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Koñcaṃ karontānanti nadītīre ṭhatvā soṇḍaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā koñcanādaṃ karontānaṃ. Saddaṃ assosinti taṃ [M 2.0102] koñcanādasaddaṃ assosiṃ. Attheso, bhikkhave, samādhi so ca kho aparisuddhoti atthi eso samādhi moggallānassa, so ca kho parisuddho na hoti. Thero kira pabbajitato sattame divase tadahuarahattappatto aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu pañcahākārehi anāciṇṇavasībhāvo [P 2.0514] samādhiparipanthake dhamme na suṭṭhu parisodhetvā āvajjanasamāpajjanādhiṭṭhānavuṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇānaṃ saññāmattakameva katvā catutthajjhānaṃ appetvā nisinno, jhānaṅgehi vuṭṭhāya nāgānaṃ saddaṃ sutvā “antosamāpattiyaṃ assosi”nti evaṃsaññī ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “attheso, bhikkhave, samādhi; so ca kho aparisuddho”ti.

232. In the Nāgogāha account, ‘Sappinikāya’ means of the river so-named. ‘Āneñjaṃ samādhiṃ’ means the imperturbable, unwavering fourth jhāna concentration, which is free from bodily and verbal movement. ‘Nāgānaṃ’ means of elephants. ‘Ogayha uttarantānaṃ’ means of those who, having plunged in, are emerging again. It is said that they, having descended into deep water, and having bathed and drunk there, and having taken water with their trunks and splashed one another, emerge. Thus it is said, ‘of those who, having plunged in, are emerging.’ ‘Koñcaṃ karontānaṃ’ means of those who, standing on the riverbank, having placed their trunks in their mouths, make a sound like a curlew's cry. ‘Saddaṃ assosiṃ’ means ‘I heard that sound like a curlew's cry.’ ‘Attheso, bhikkhave, samādhi; so ca kho aparisuddho’ means ‘There is this concentration of Moggallāna, but it is not pure.’ It is said that the Elder, having attained arahantship on the seventh day from his ordination, had not yet practiced mastery in the five ways regarding the eight attainments. Not having thoroughly purified the mental states that are obstacles to concentration, and having made the adverting, attaining, resolving, emerging, and reviewing a matter of mere perception of their names, he entered the fourth jhāna and was seated. Having emerged from the jhāna factors, he heard the sound of the elephants and perceived, ‘I heard it while within the attainment.’ Therefore, it was said: ‘There is, bhikkhus, this concentration; but it is not pure.’

Sobhitavatthusmiṃ ahaṃ, āvuso, pañca kappasatāni anussarāmīti ekāvajjanena anussarāmīti āha. Itarathā hi anacchariyaṃ ariyasāvakānaṃ paṭipāṭiyā nānāvajjanena tassa tassa atīte nivāsassa anussaraṇanti na bhikkhū ujjhāyeyyuṃ. Yasmā panesa “ekāvajjanena anussarāmī”ti āha, tasmā bhikkhū ujjhāyiṃsu. Atthesā, bhikkhave, sobhitassa, sā ca kho ekāyeva jātīti yaṃ sobhito jātiṃ anussarāmīti āha, atthesā jāti sobhitassa, sā ca kho ekāyeva anantarā na uppaṭipāṭiyā anussaritāti adhippāyo.

In the Sobhita account, regarding ‘Ahaṃ, āvuso, pañca kappasatāni anussarāmi,’ he said, ‘I recollect with a single advertence.’ For otherwise, the recollection by noble disciples of their various past abodes in sequence with various advertences is not amazing, and the bhikkhus would not have complained. But because he said, ‘I recollect with a single advertence,’ the bhikkhus complained. Regarding ‘Atthesā, bhikkhave, sobhitassa, sā ca kho ekāyeva jāti,’ the birth that Sobhita said he recollects does exist for Sobhita, and it is just one, the immediately preceding one; it was not recollected out of sequence. This is the intention.

Kathaṃ panāyaṃ etaṃ anussarīti? Ayaṃ kira pañcannaṃ kappasatānaṃ upari titthāyatane

But how did he recollect this? It is said that, in a life prior to five hundred eons, this one, in a heretical sect,

Pabbajitvā asaññasamāpattiṃ nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññabhave nibbatti. Tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā avasāne manussaloke uppanno sāsane pabbajitvā tisso vijjā sacchākāsi. So pubbenivāsaṃ anussaramāno imasmiṃ attabhāve paṭisandhiṃ disvā tato paraṃ tatiye attabhāve cutimeva addasa. Atha ubhinnamantarā acittakaṃ attabhāvaṃ anussarituṃ [V 2.0093] asakkonto nayato sallakkhesi – “addhāahaṃ asaññabhave nibbatto”ti. Evaṃ sallakkhentena panānena dukkaraṃ kataṃ, satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭi paṭividdhā, ākāse padaṃ dassitaṃ. Tasmā naṃ bhagavā [P 2.0515] imasmiṃyeva vatthusmiṃ etadagge ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantānaṃ yadidaṃ sobhito”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 227).

Having gone forth and produced the attainment of non-percipient beings, he passed away without his jhāna having declined and was reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings. There, having remained for the full extent of his lifespan, at the end he was reborn in the human world. He went forth in the Dispensation and realized the three knowledges. While recollecting his past abodes, he saw his rebirth-linking in this present existence, and before that, he saw only the death-moment in the third existence back. Then, being unable to recollect the mindless existence between the two, he inferred it by reasoning: ‘Surely, I was reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings.’ By inferring thus, he had done what is difficult to do, like piercing the tip of a hair with the tip of a hair that has been split a hundred times, or like showing a footprint in the sky. Therefore, the Blessed One, in this very account, established him as foremost, saying: ‘Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who recollect their past lives, Sobhita is the foremost.’

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vinīta account is concluded.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Conclusion

233. Uddiṭṭhā [M 2.0103] kho āyasmanto cattāro pārājikā dhammāti idaṃ idha uddiṭṭhapārājikaparidīpanameva. Samodhānetvā pana sabbāneva catuvīsati pārājikāni veditabbāni. Katamāni catuvīsati? Pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni tāva bhikkhūnaṃ cattāri, bhikkhunīnaṃ asādhāraṇāni cattārīti aṭṭha. Ekādasa abhabbapuggalā, tesu paṇḍakatiracchānagataubhatobyañjanakā, tayo vatthuvipannā ahetukapaṭisandhikā, tesaṃ saggo avārito maggo pana vārito, abhabbā hi te maggappaṭilābhāya vatthuvipannattāti. Pabbajjāpi nesaṃ paṭikkhittā, tasmā tepi pārājikā. Theyyasaṃvāsako, titthiyapakkantako, mātughātako, pitughātako, arahantaghātako, bhikkhunīdūsako, lohituppādako, saṅghabhedakoti ime aṭṭha attano kiriyāya vipannattā abhabbaṭṭhānaṃ pattāti pārājikāva. Tesu theyyasaṃvāsako, titthiyapakkantako, bhikkhunīdūsakoti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saggo avārito maggo pana vāritova. Itaresaṃ pañcannaṃ ubhayampi vāritaṃ. Te hi anantarabhave narake nibbattanakasattā. Iti ime ca ekādasa, purimā ca aṭṭhāti ekūnavīsati. Te gihiliṅge ruciṃ uppādetvā gihinivāsananivatthāya bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ vīsati. Sā hi ajjhācāravītikkamaṃ akatvāpi ettāvatāva assamaṇīti imāni tāva vīsati pārājikāni.

233. ‘Venerable sirs, the four pārājika offenses have been recited.’ This is merely the explanation of the pārājika offenses mentioned here. However, when combined, all twenty-four pārājika offenses should be understood. What are the twenty-four? First, those found in the Pāli: four for bhikkhus and four unique to bhikkhunīs, making eight. Then, eleven types of incapable persons: among them, paṇḍakas, those in animal form, and hermaphrodites; these three have a defective basis—those with a rootless rebirth-linking. For them, the celestial realm is not barred, but the path is barred, as they are incapable of attaining the path due to their defective basis. Their going-forth is also rejected; thus, they too are like those who have committed a pārājika. A thief in communion, one who has gone over to another sect, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a violator of a bhikkhunī, one who sheds the Buddha’s blood, and a schismatic in the Saṅgha—these eight, due to the corruption of their own actions, have reached a state of incapability and are thus indeed like those who have committed a pārājika. Among them, for the thief in communion, the one who has gone over to another sect, and the violator of a bhikkhunī, the celestial realm is not barred, but the path is indeed barred. For the remaining five, both are barred, as they are beings destined to be reborn in hell in the immediately following existence. Thus, these eleven, together with the previous eight, make nineteen. They, together with a bhikkhunī who, having conceived a liking for the lay state, has dressed in lay attire, make twenty. For even without committing an actual transgression, she is thereby no longer a female ascetic. These, then, are the twenty pārājika offenses.

Aparānipi – lambī, mudupiṭṭhiko, parassa aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gaṇhāti, parassa aṅgajāte abhinisīdatīti imesaṃ catunnaṃ vasena cattāri anulomapārājikānīti vadanti. Etāni hi yasmā ubhinnaṃ rāgavasena sadisabhāvūpagatānaṃ dhammo “methunadhammo”ti vuccati. Tasmā etena pariyāyena methunadhammaṃ [P 2.0516] appaṭisevitvāyeva kevalaṃ maggena maggappavesanavasena āpajjitabbattā methunadhammapārājikassa anulomentīti anulomapārājikānīti vuccanti. Iti imāni ca cattāri [V 2.0094] purimāni ca vīsatīti samodhānetvā sabbāneva catuvīsati pārājikāni veditabbāni.

There are others as well—one with a long sexual organ, one with a soft back, one who takes another's sexual organ into the mouth, and one who sits down on another's sexual organ: by way of these four, they speak of four 'analogous pārājika offenses.' For, because the practice of two people who have come to a similar state through the power of lust is called 'sexual intercourse' (methunadhamma), therefore, by this principle, since the offense is incurred merely by way of inserting one passage into another—without even engaging in actual sexual intercourse—these offenses conform to the pārājika offense of sexual intercourse. Hence, they are called 'analogous pārājika offenses.' Thus, these four together with the previous twenty, when combined, make a total of twenty-four pārājika offenses to be understood.

Na labhati bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsanti uposatha-pavāraṇa-pātimokkhuddesa-saṅghakammappabhedaṃ bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ na labhati. Yathā pure tathā pacchāti yathā pubbe gihikāle anupasampannakāle ca pacchā pārājikaṃ āpannopi tatheva asaṃvāso hoti. Natthi tassa bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ [M 2.0104] uposathapavāraṇapātimokkhuddesasaṅghakammappabhedo saṃvāsoti bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ na labhati. Tatthāyasmante pucchāmīti tesu catūsu pārājikesu āyasmante “kaccittha parisuddhā”ti pucchāmi. Kaccitthāti kacci ettha; etesu catūsu pārājikesu kacci parisuddhāti attho. Atha vā kaccittha parisuddhāti kacci parisuddhā attha, bhavathāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Regarding ‘He does not obtain communion with the bhikkhus’: this means he does not obtain that communion with the bhikkhus which is comprised of the various Saṅgha acts such as the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Regarding ‘As before, so afterwards’: just as previously, during the time he was a householder and the time he was unordained, so also afterwards, having committed a pārājika offense, he is likewise without communion. For him, there is no communion with the bhikkhus comprised of the various Saṅgha acts such as the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and the recitation of the Pātimokkha; thus, he does not obtain communion with the bhikkhus. Regarding ‘Therein I ask the venerable sirs’: in those four pārājika offenses, I ask the venerable sirs, ‘Are you pure in this matter?’ ‘Kaccittha’ means ‘kacci ettha’ (is it so here); the meaning is, ‘In these four pārājika offenses, are you pure?’ Alternatively, ‘kaccittha parisuddhā’ means ‘Are you pure? Do you exist as such?’ The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika Offense is concluded.

2. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ

2. The Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses

1. Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Emission of Semen

Yaṃ [P 3.0517][M 2.0105] pārājikakaṇḍassa, saṅgītaṃ samanantaraṃ;

Tassa terasakassāyamapubbapadavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of new words for that chapter of thirteen rules, which was recited immediately after the Pārājika chapter.

234. Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā seyyasako anabhirato brahmacariyaṃ caratīti ettha āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ. Seyyasakoti tassa bhikkhuno nāmaṃ. Anabhiratoti vikkhittacitto kāmarāgapariḷāhena pariḍayhamāno na pana gihibhāvaṃ patthayamāno. So tena kiso hotīti so seyyasako tena anabhiratabhāvena kiso hoti.

234. At that time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery. Now at that time the Venerable Seyyasaka, being discontented, was living the holy life. Here, ‘venerable’ is a term of endearment. ‘Seyyasaka’ is that bhikkhu's name. ‘Discontented’ means his mind was scattered, burning with the fever of sensual desire, but not, however, desiring the householder's life. ‘He became emaciated because of that’ means that Seyyasaka became emaciated because of that discontent.

Addasā kho āyasmā udāyīti ettha udāyīti tassa therassa nāmaṃ, ayañhi seyyasakassa upajjhāyo lāḷudāyī nāma bhantamigasappaṭibhāgo niddārāmatādimanuyuttānaṃ aññataro lolabhikkhu. Kacci no tvanti kacci nu tvaṃ. Yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjātiādīsu yāvatā atthoti yāvadatthaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāvatā te bhojanena attho yattakaṃ tvaṃ icchasi tattakaṃ bhuñja, yattakaṃ kālaṃ rattiṃ vā divā vā supituṃ icchasi tattakaṃ supa, mattikādīhi kāyaṃ ubbaṭṭetvā cuṇṇādīhi ghaṃsitvā yattakaṃ nhānaṃ icchasi tattakaṃ nhāya, uddesena vā paripucchāya vā vattapaṭipattiyā vā kammaṭṭhānena vā attho natthīti. Yadā te anabhirati uppajjatīti yasmiṃ kāle tava [P 3.0518] kāmarāgavasena ukkaṇṭhitatā vikkhittacittatā uppajjati. Rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃsetīti kāmarāgo cittaṃ dhaṃseti padhaṃseti vikkhipati ceva milāpeti ca. Tadā hatthena upakkamitvā asuciṃ mocehīti tasmiṃ kāle hatthena vāyamitvā asucimocanaṃ karohi, evañhi te cittekaggatā bhavissati. Iti taṃ upajjhāyo anusāsi yathā taṃ bālo bālaṃ mago magaṃ.

Regarding 'The Venerable Udāyī saw...': Here, 'Udāyī' is the name of that elder, for this was Lāḷudāyī, the preceptor of Seyyasaka, who resembled a bewildered deer and was one of those monks devoted to such things as delighting in sleep—a fickle monk. 'Is it not so that you...?' is for 'Is it that you...?'. In the phrases 'eat as much as you need' and so on, 'as much as you need' means as much as is sufficient. This is what is said: 'Eat as much food as you desire; sleep as much as you wish by night or day; having anointed your body with clay and so on, and having scrubbed it with powder and so on, bathe as much as you like; there is no benefit in recitation, questioning, observance of duties, or meditation.' 'When dissatisfaction arises in you' means at the time when weariness and a scattered mind arise in you due to sensual desire. 'Lust disturbs the mind' means sensual desire destroys, utterly destroys, scatters, and causes the mind to wither. 'Then, making an effort with your hand, release the impurity' means at that time, striving with your hand, bring about the release of impurity, for in this way your mind will become unified. Thus, his preceptor instructed him, as a fool instructs a fool, or as a wild animal instructs a wild animal.

235. Tesaṃ muṭṭhassatīnaṃ asampajānānaṃ niddaṃ okkamantānanti satisampajaññaṃ pahāya niddaṃ otarantānaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi niddaṃ okkamantānaṃ abyākato [M 2.0106] bhavaṅgavāro pavattati, satisampajaññavāro gaḷati, tathāpi sayanakāle manasikāro kātabbo. Divā supantena yāva nhātassa [V 2.0095] bhikkhuno kesā na sukkhanti tāva supitvā vuṭṭhahissāmīti saussāhena supitabbaṃ. Rattiṃ supantena ettakaṃ nāma rattibhāgaṃ supitvā candena vā tārakāya vā idaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ pattakāle vuṭṭhahissāmīti saussāhena supitabbaṃ. Buddhānussatiādīsu ca dasasu kammaṭṭhānesu ekaṃ aññaṃ vā cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva niddā okkamitabbā. Evaṃ karonto hi sato sampajāno satiñca sampajaññañca avijahitvāva niddaṃ okkamatīti vuccati. Te pana bhikkhū bālā lolā bhantamigasappaṭibhāgā na evamakaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “tesaṃ muṭṭhassatīnaṃ asampajānānaṃ niddaṃ okkamantāna”nti.

235. Regarding 'For those who are unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, sinking into sleep': this means for those who abandon mindfulness and clear comprehension and descend into sleep. In this context, although for those falling asleep the indeterminate bhavaṅga-process occurs and the process of mindfulness and clear comprehension ceases, nevertheless, attention should be applied at the time of sleeping. One who sleeps by day should sleep with the resolve, 'I will sleep only until the hair of a monk who has bathed dries, then I will rise.' One who sleeps at night should sleep with the resolve, 'I will sleep for such a portion of the night, and when the moon or a star has reached such a place, I will rise.' And one should fall asleep only after taking up one of the ten meditation subjects, such as the recollection of the Buddha, or another meditation subject that is agreeable to the mind. For one who does so is said to fall asleep mindful and clearly comprehending, without having abandoned mindfulness and clear comprehension. But those monks—foolish, fickle, and resembling bewildered deer—did not do so. Therefore, it is said: 'For those who are unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, sinking into sleep.'

Atthi cettha cetanā labbhatīti ettha ca supinante assādacetanā atthi upalabbhati. Atthesā, bhikkhave, cetanā; sā ca kho abbohārikāti bhikkhave esā assādacetanā atthi, sā ca kho avisaye uppannattā abbohārikā, āpattiyā aṅgaṃ na hoti. Iti bhagavā supinante cetanāya abbohārikabhāvaṃ dassetvā “evañca pana bhikkhave imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyātha, sañcetanikā sukkavissaṭṭhi aññatra supinantā saṅghādiseso”ti sānupaññattikaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpesi.

Regarding 'Here there is intention, it is obtained': here in a dream, the intention of savoring is present and can be obtained. Regarding 'This, monks, is intention; but it is non-actionable': Monks, this intention of savoring exists, but because it arises in a sphere beyond one's control, it is non-actionable and is not a factor for an offense. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the non-actionable nature of intention in a dream, established the training rule with its subsequent regulation, saying: 'And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule: Intentional emission of semen, other than in a dream, entails a Saṅghādisesa offense.'

236-237. Tattha saṃvijjati cetanā assāti sañcetanā, sañcetanāva sañcetanikā, sañcetanā vā assā atthīti sañcetanikā. Yasmā pana yassa sañcetanikā [P 3.0519] sukkavissaṭṭhi hoti so jānanto sañjānanto hoti, sā cassa sukkavissaṭṭhi cecca abhivitaritvā vītikkamo hoti, tasmā byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā atthameva dassetuṃ “jānanto sañjānanto cecca abhivitaritvā vītikkamo”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha jānantoti upakkamāmīti jānanto. Sañjānantoti sukkaṃ mocemīti sañjānanto, teneva upakkamajānanākārena saddhiṃ jānantoti attho. Ceccāti mocanassādacetanāvasena cetetvā pakappetvā. Abhivitaritvāti upakkamavasena maddanto nirāsaṅkacittaṃ pesetvā. Vītikkamoti evaṃ pavattassa yo vītikkamo ayaṃ sañcetanikāsaddassa sikhāppatto atthoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, because manifest intention is present for it (saṃvijjati cetanā assā), it is called 'intentional' (sañcetanā). That which is intentional is itself called 'intentional' (sañcetanikā). Or, because intention is present for it (sañcetanā assā atthi), it is called 'intentional' (sañcetanikā). And since, for whomever an intentional emission of semen occurs, that person is one who knows and is fully aware, and that emission of semen is a transgression that occurs by intending and overpowering, therefore, without focusing on the letters and just to show the meaning, its word-analysis is given thus: 'knowing, being fully aware, intending, overpowering, it is a transgression.' Therein, 'knowing' means knowing, 'I am making an effort.' 'Being fully aware' means being fully aware, 'I am releasing semen'; the meaning is knowing together with that very mode of knowing the effort. 'Intending' means having intended and determined through the power of the intention of savoring the release. 'Overpowering' means, by means of the effort, pressing on and sending forth a mind without hesitation. 'Transgression' means that the transgression which occurs for one acting thus—this is said to be the pinnacle meaning of the word 'intentional.'

Idāni [M 2.0107] sukkavissaṭṭhīti ettha yassa sukkassa vissaṭṭhi taṃ tāva saṅkhyāto vaṇṇabhedato ca dassetuṃ “sukkanti dasa sukkānī”tiādimāha. Tattha sukkānaṃ āsayabhedato dhātunānattato ca nīlādivaṇṇabhedo veditabbo.

Now, regarding 'emission of semen'—to explain that semen first in terms of enumeration and then distinctions of color, it is said: 'Semen means the ten kinds of semen,' and so on. Herein, the different colors of semen, such as blue, etc., should be understood as being due to the diversity of their repositories and the variety of elements.

Vissaṭṭhīti vissaggo, atthato panetaṃ ṭhānācāvanaṃ hoti, tenāha – “vissaṭṭhīti ṭhānatocāvanā [V 2.0096] vuccatī”ti. Tattha vatthisīsaṃ kaṭi kāyoti tidhā sukkassa ṭhānaṃ pakappenti, eko kirācariyo “vatthisīsaṃ sukkassa ṭhāna”nti āha. Eko “kaṭī”ti, eko “sakalo kāyo”ti, tesu tatiyassa bhāsitaṃ subhāsitaṃ. Kesalomanakhadantānañhi maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānaṃ uccārapassāvakheḷasiṅghāṇikāthaddhasukkhacammāni ca vajjetvā avaseso chavimaṃsalohitānugato sabbopi kāyo kāyappasādabhāvajīvitindriyābaddhapittānaṃ sambhavassa ca ṭhānameva. Tathā hi rāgapariyuṭṭhānenābhibhūtānaṃ hatthīnaṃ ubhohi kaṇṇacūḷikāhi sambhavo nikkhamati, mahāsenarājā ca rāgapariyuṭṭhito sambhavavegaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto satthena bāhusīsaṃ phāletvā vaṇamukhena nikkhantaṃ sambhavaṃ dassesīti.

‘Vissaṭṭhi’ means emission (vissaggo); in terms of essential meaning, however, it is the dislodging from its place. For that reason, it is said: ‘Vissaṭṭhi is called the dislodging from its place.’ Therein, they conceive the place of semen in three ways: the head of the bladder, the waist, and the body. One teacher, it is said, stated, ‘The head of the bladder is the place of semen.’ Another said, ‘The waist,’ and yet another said, ‘The entire body.’ Among these, the third statement is well-spoken. For apart from the flesh-free areas of the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth, as well as excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and rough and dry skin, the rest of the body—pervaded by skin, flesh, and blood—is indeed the place of the body-sensitivity faculty, the gender faculty, the life faculty, unbound bile, and of semen. Thus, when elephants are overcome by the arising of lust, their emission comes forth from both ear-tips. And King Mahāsena, overwhelmed by the arising of lust and unable to endure the force of emission, split his upper arm with a sword and showed the semen emerging from the wound.

Ettha pana paṭhamassa ācariyassa vāde mocanassādena nimitte upakkamato yattakaṃ ekā khuddakamakkhikā piveyya tattake asucimhi vatthisīsato muñcitvā [P 3.0520] dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte bahi nikkhante vā anikkhante vā saṅghādiseso. Dutiyassa vāde tatheva kaṭito muccitvā dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte, tatiyassa vāde tatheva sakalakāyaṃ saṅkhobhetvā tato muccitvā dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte bahi nikkhante vā anikkhante vā saṅghādiseso. Dakasotorohaṇañcettha adhivāsetvā antarā nivāretuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya vuttaṃ, ṭhānā cutañhi avassaṃ dakasotaṃ otarati. Tasmā ṭhānā cāvanamattenevettha āpatti veditabbā, sā ca kho nimitte upakkamantasseva hatthaparikammapādaparikammagattaparikammakaraṇena sacepi asuci muccati, anāpatti. Ayaṃ sabbācariyasādhāraṇavinicchayo.

Now, in the view of the first teacher, for a monk who makes an effort at the sign with the pleasure of emission, when an amount of impurity that a small fly could drink is released from the head of the bladder and has just descended into the urinary passage—whether it has gone outside or not—there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. In the view of the second teacher, likewise, when it is released from the waist and has just descended into the urinary passage, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. In the view of the third teacher, likewise, when, having agitated the entire body, it is released from there and has just descended into the urinary passage—whether it has gone outside or not—there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. And the descent into the urinary passage is mentioned here because of the inability to suppress and stop it midway. For what has been dislodged from its place inevitably descends into the urinary passage. Therefore, the offense here should be understood as occurring merely by the dislodging from its place. And that offense, indeed, is to be understood only for one who makes an effort at the sign; if impurity is released by means of performing repeated action with the hand, repeated action with the foot, or repeated action with the body, there is no offense. This is the decision common to all the teachers.

Aññatra supinantāti ettha supino eva supinanto, taṃ ṭhapetvā apanetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tañca pana supinaṃ passanto catūhi kāraṇehi passati [M 2.0108] dhātukkhobhato vā anubhūtapubbato vā devatopasaṃhārato vā pubbanimittato vāti.

Regarding ‘Except in a dream’: here, a dream itself is what is meant by ‘supinanta’; it is said to mean setting that aside, removing it. And one who dreams sees a dream for four reasons: due to a disturbance of the elements, or because of past experience, or through presentation by deities, or as a premonition.

Tattha pittādīnaṃ khobhakaraṇapaccayayogena khubhitadhātuko dhātukkhobhato supinaṃ passati, passanto ca nānāvidhaṃ supinaṃ passati – pabbatā patanto viya, ākāsena gacchanto viya, vāḷamigahatthīcorādīhi anubaddho viya hoti. Anubhūtapubbato passanto pubbe anubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ passati. Devatopasaṃhārato passantassa devatā atthakāmatāya vā anatthakāmatāya vā atthāya vā anatthāya vā nānāvidhāni ārammaṇāni upasaṃharanti, so tāsaṃ devatānaṃ ānubhāvena tāni ārammaṇāni passati. Pubbanimittato passanto puññāpuññavasena uppajjitukāmassa atthassa vā anatthassa vā pubbanimittabhūtaṃ supinaṃ passati, bodhisattassamātā [V 2.0097] viya puttapaṭilābhanimittaṃ, bodhisatto viya pañca mahāsupine (a. ni. 5.196), kosalarājā viya soḷasa supineti.

Therein, a person whose elements are disturbed due to conjunction with causes that create a disturbance of bile and the like sees a dream due to that disturbance of the elements. And in seeing it, one sees various kinds of dreams: as if falling from a mountain, as if going through the sky, or as if being pursued by beasts of prey, elephants, thieves, and so on. One who sees a dream due to what has been previously experienced sees an object that was experienced in the past. For one who sees a dream due to presentation by deities, the deities—either from a desire for one's welfare or from a desire for one's harm, or for the sake of one's welfare or harm—present various objects, and that person sees those objects through the power of those deities. One who sees a dream due to a prior sign sees a dream that has become a prior sign of the welfare or harm that is about to arise through the power of merit or demerit, like the Bodhisatta’s mother seeing the sign of obtaining a son, like the Bodhisatta seeing the five great dreams, or like the King of Kosala seeing the sixteen dreams.

Tattha yaṃ dhātukkhobhato anubhūtapubbato ca supinaṃ passati na taṃ saccaṃ hoti. Yaṃ devatopasaṃhārato passati taṃ saccaṃ vā hoti alīkaṃ vā, kuddhā hi devatā upāyena vināsetukāmā viparītampi katvā dassenti. Yaṃ pana pubbanimittato passati [P 3.0521] taṃ ekantasaccameva hoti. Etesañca catunnaṃ mūlakāraṇānaṃ saṃsaggabhedatopi supinabhedo hotiyeva.
