Of these, the dream one sees due to a disturbance of the elements or due to past experience is not true. What one sees through presentation by deities may be true or may be false, for angry deities, wishing to destroy by means of deception, may even show things in a contrary way. However, what one sees due to a prior sign is invariably true. And from the various combinations of these four root causes, there is indeed a variety of dreams.

Tañca panetaṃ catubbidhampi supinaṃ sekkhaputhujjanāva passanti appahīnavipallāsattā, asekkhā pana na passanti pahīnavipallāsattā. Kiṃ panetaṃ passanto sutto passati paṭibuddho, udāhu neva sutto na paṭibuddhoti? Kiñcettha yadi tāva sutto passati abhidhammavirodho āpajjati, bhavaṅgacittena hi supati taṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ rāgādisampayuttaṃ vā na hoti, supinaṃ passantassa ca īdisāni cittāni uppajjanti. Atha paṭibuddho passati vinayavirodho āpajjati, yañhi paṭibuddho passati taṃ sabbohārikacittena passati, sabbohārikacittena ca kate vītikkame anāpatti nāma natthi. Supinaṃ passantena pana katepi vītikkame ekantaṃ anāpatti eva. Atha neva sutto na paṭibuddho passati, ko nāma passati; evañca sati supinassa abhāvova āpajjatīti, na abhāvo. Kasmā[M 2.0109]? Yasmā kapimiddhapareto passati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “kapimiddhapareto kho, mahārāja, supinaṃ passatī”ti. Kapimiddhaparetoti makkaṭaniddāya yutto. Yathā hi makkaṭassa niddā lahuparivattā hoti; evaṃ yā niddā punappunaṃ kusalādicittavokiṇṇattā lahuparivattā, yassā pavattiyaṃ punappunaṃ bhavaṅgato uttaraṇaṃ hoti tāya yutto supinaṃ passati, tenāyaṃ supino kusalopi hoti akusalopi abyākatopi. Tattha supinante cetiyavandanadhammassavanadhammadesanādīni karontassa kusalo, pāṇātipātādīni karontassa akusalo, dvīhi antehi mutto āvajjanatadārammaṇakkhaṇe abyākatoti veditabbo. Svāyaṃ dubbalavatthukattā cetanāya paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asamattho, pavatte pana aññehi kusalākusalehi upatthambhito vipākaṃ deti. Kiñcāpi vipākaṃ deti? Atha kho avisaye uppannattā abbohārikāva supinantacetanā. Tenāha – “ṭhapetvā supinanta”nti.

Furthermore, these four kinds of dreams are seen only by trainees and ordinary people because their perversions are not abandoned; but those beyond training do not see them because their perversions are abandoned. Now, does one who sees this do so while asleep or while awake, or while neither asleep nor awake? In this matter, if one sees it while asleep, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma arises. For one sleeps with the bhavaṅga-consciousness, and that consciousness does not have a form-sign, etc., as its object, nor is it associated with lust, etc.; yet for one who sees a dream, such minds arise. If one sees it while awake, a contradiction with the Vinaya arises. For what one sees while awake, one sees with a consciousness that entails full responsibility, and when a transgression is committed with a consciousness that entails full responsibility, there is no such thing as 'no offense'. But when a transgression is committed by one who is dreaming, it is definitely 'no offense'. If one sees it while neither asleep nor awake, then who sees it? This being the case, the non-existence of dreams would result. But there is no non-existence. Why? Because one who is overcome by 'monkey-sleep' sees. For this has been said: 'Great King, one who is overcome by monkey-sleep sees a dream.' 'Overcome by monkey-sleep' means endowed with the sleep of a monkey. For just as a monkey's sleep is of quick transition, so too, the sleep that is of quick transition due to being repeatedly interspersed with wholesome minds, etc., during the occurrence of which there is repeated emergence from the bhavaṅga—one endowed with that sleep sees a dream. Therefore, this dream can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Therein, for one who performs acts such as venerating a cetiya, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma in a dream, the dream is wholesome. For one who performs acts such as killing living beings, it is unwholesome. When it is free from the two extremes, at the moments of adverting and registering, it should be understood as indeterminate. This volition, because of its weak basis, is incapable of drawing forth rebirth-linking. However, in the course of life, when supported by other wholesome and unwholesome states, it gives a result. Although it gives a result, because it has arisen in an uncontrolled sphere, the volition in a dream does not entail responsibility. Therefore, He said: 'except for what occurs in a dream'.

Saṅghādisesoti imassa āpattinikāyassa nāmaṃ. Tasmā yā aññatra supinantā sañcetanikā sukkavissaṭṭhi[P 3.0522], ayaṃ saṅghādiseso nāma āpattinikāyoti evamettha sambandho veditabbo[V 2.0098]. Vacanattho panettha saṅgho ādimhi ceva sese ca icchitabbo assāti saṅghādiseso. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Imaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjitvā vuṭṭhātukāmassa yaṃ taṃ āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ, tassa ādimhi ceva parivāsadānatthāya ādito sese ca majjhe mānattadānatthāya mūlāya paṭikassanena vā saha mānattadānatthāya avasāne abbhānatthāya saṅgho icchitabbo. Na hettha ekampi kammaṃ vinā saṅghena sakkā kātunti saṅgho ādimhi ceva sese ca icchitabbo assāti saṅghādisesoti. Byañjanaṃ pana anādiyitvā atthameva dassetuṃ “saṅghova tassā āpattiyā parivāsaṃ deti, mūlāya paṭikassati, mānattaṃ deti, abbheti na sambahulā na ekapuggalo, tena vuccati saṅghādiseso”ti idamassa padabhājanaṃ –

'Saṅghādisesa' is the name of this class of offenses. Therefore, the connection here should be understood thus: whatever intentional emission of semen occurs other than in a dream, this is the class of offenses named Saṅghādisesa. As for the etymology here: because the Saṅgha is required for it at the beginning (ādi) and in the remainder (sesa), it is 'Saṅghādisesa'. What is meant? For a monk who has fallen into this offense and desires to be rehabilitated, for that rehabilitation from the offense, the Saṅgha is required: at the beginning for the granting of probation (parivāsa); in the middle, which is the remainder from the beginning, for the granting of penance (mānatta), or for the granting of penance together with reinstatement to the beginning; and at the end for rehabilitation (abbhāna). Not even one formal act here can be performed without the Saṅgha. Therefore, the Saṅgha is required for it at the beginning and in the remainder; hence, it is called Saṅghādisesa. However, disregarding the letter and showing only the meaning, this is its word-analysis: 'The Saṅgha alone grants probation for that offense, reinstates to the beginning, grants penance, and rehabilitates—not many, nor a single individual. Therefore, it is called Saṅghādisesa.'

“Saṅghādisesoti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ suṇohi yathātathaṃ;

Saṅghova deti parivāsaṃ, mūlāya paṭikassati;

Mānattaṃ deti abbheti, tenetaṃ iti vuccatī”ti. (pari. 339) –

'That which is called Saṅghādisesa, listen to it as it truly is: The Saṅgha alone grants probation, reinstates to the beginning, grants penance, and rehabilitates; for that reason, it is so called.'

Parivāre [M 2.0110] vacanakāraṇañca vuttaṃ, tattha parivāsadānādīni samuccayakkhandhake vitthārato āgatāni, tattheva nesaṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karissāma.

The reason for the term has also been stated in the Parivāra. Therein, the granting of probation and so on have come down in detail in the Samuccayakkhandhaka; we shall provide the commentary on them in that very place.

Tasseva āpattinikāyassāti tassa eva āpattisamūhassa. Tattha kiñcāpi ayaṃ ekāva āpatti, rūḷhisaddena pana avayave samūhavohārena vā “nikāyo”ti vutto – “eko vedanākkhandho, eko viññāṇakkhandho”tiādīsu viya.

'Of that same class of offenses' means of that very collection of offenses. Herein, although this is just one offense, it is called a 'class' (nikāya) either by a conventional term or by the application of a collective term to a constituent part, just as in such cases as 'one aggregate of feeling, one aggregate of consciousness,' and so on.

Evaṃ uddiṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ padānukkamena vibhajitvā idāni imaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ āpajjantassa upāyañca kālañca adhippāyañca adhippāyavatthuñca dassetuṃ “ajjhattarūpe mocetī”tiādimāha. Ettha hi ajjhattarūpādīhi catūhi padehi upāyo dassito, ajjhattarūpe vā moceyya bahiddhārūpe vā ubhayattha vā ākāse vā kaṭiṃ kampento, ito paraṃ añño upāyo natthi. Tattha rūpe ghaṭṭetvā mocentopi rūpena ghaṭṭetvā mocentopi rūpe moceticceva veditabbo. Rūpe hi [P 3.0523] sati so moceti na rūpaṃ alabhitvā. Rāgūpatthambhādīhi pana pañcahi kālo dassito. Rāgūpatthambhādikālesu hi aṅgajātaṃ kammaniyaṃ hoti, yassa kammaniyatte sati moceti. Ito paraṃ añño kālo natthi, na hi vinā rāgūpatthambhādīhi pubbaṇhādayo kālabhedā mocane nimittaṃ honti.

Having thus analyzed the training rule that was set forth according to the sequence of its words, now, to show the means, the time, the intention, and the object of intention for one who falls into this emission of semen, He said, 'He emits in relation to an internal form,' and so on. Herein, the means is shown by the four terms beginning with 'internal form': one might emit in relation to an internal form, or an external form, or both, or while shaking the hips in the air; beyond these, there is no other means. Therein, whether one emits by striking against a form or by being struck with a form, it should be understood simply as 'emits in relation to a form.' For when a form is present, one emits; not without obtaining a form. The time, however, is shown by the five factors beginning with 'stiffening due to lust.' For it is at such times as stiffening due to lust, etc., that the sexual organ becomes workable; when it is workable, one emits. Beyond these, there is no other time, for without stiffening due to lust, etc., divisions of time like morning and so on are not the cause for emission.

Ārogyatthāyātiādīhi [V 2.0099] dasahi adhippāyo dassito, evarūpena hi adhippāyabhedena moceti na aññathā. Nīlādīhi pana dasahi navamassa adhippāyassa vatthu dassitaṃ, vīmaṃsanto hi nīlādīsu aññatarassa vasena vīmaṃsati na tehi vinimuttanti.

By the ten terms beginning with 'for the sake of health,' the intention is shown; for one emits through such a distinction of intention, not otherwise. But by the ten terms beginning with 'blue,' the object of the ninth intention is shown. For one who is investigating investigates by way of one or another of the 'blue,' etc.; one does not investigate something separate from them.

238. Ito paraṃ pana imesaṃyeva ajjhattarūpādīnaṃ padānaṃ pakāsanatthaṃ “ajjhattarūpeti ajjhattaṃ upādinne rūpe”tiādi vuttaṃ, tattha ajjhattaṃ upādinne rūpeti attano hatthādibhede rūpe. Bahiddhā upādinneti parassa tādiseyeva. Anupādinneti tāḷacchiddādibhede. Tadubhayeti attano ca parassa ca rūpe, ubhayaghaṭṭanavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Attano rūpena ca anupādinnarūpena ca ekato ghaṭṭanepi labbhati. Ākāse vāyamantassāti kenaci rūpena aghaṭṭetvā ākāseyeva kaṭikampanapayaogena aṅgajātaṃ cālentassa.

238. Furthermore, from this point on, to clarify these very terms beginning with 'internal form,' the passage beginning, 'Internal form means form that is internally clung-to,' is stated. Therein, 'form that is internally clung-to' means form with distinctions such as one's own hands. 'Externally clung-to' means the same in another. 'Not clung-to' means form with distinctions such as a keyhole. 'Both' means the form of oneself and of another; this is stated by way of striking both together. It is also obtained when striking one's own form and non-clung-to form together. 'Of one exerting in space' means of one moving the organ by the application of shaking the hips in space alone, without striking it with any form.

Rāgūpatthambheti [M 2.0111] rāgassa balavabhāve, rāgena vā aṅgajātassa upatthambhe, thaddhabhāve sañjāteti vuttaṃ hoti. Kammaniyaṃ hotīti mocanakammakkhamaṃ ajjhattarūpādīsu upakkamārahaṃ hoti.

'Stiffening by lust' means: when, due to the strength of lust, or by lust, the stiffening—the state of rigidity—of the organ has arisen, so it is said. 'It becomes workable' means it is fit for the action of emission; it becomes worthy of effort in regard to internal forms and so on.

Uccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhūpatthambheti uccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhena aṅgajāte upatthambhe. Uccāliṅgapāṇakā nāma lomasapāṇakā honti, tesaṃ lomehi phuṭṭhaṃ aṅgajātaṃ kaṇḍuṃ gahetvā thaddhaṃ hoti, tattha yasmā tāni lomāni aṅgajātaṃ ḍaṃsantāni viya vijjhanti, tasmā “uccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhenā”ti vuttaṃ, atthato pana uccāliṅgapāṇakalomavedhanenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Stiffening by the bite of an uccāliṅga creature' means when the organ becomes stiff due to the bite of an uccāliṅga creature. Uccāliṅga creatures are hairy insects. The organ, having been touched by their hairs, becomes itchy and stiff. Therein, because those hairs pierce the organ as if they were biting it, it is therefore stated as 'by the bite of an uccāliṅga creature.' But in terms of actual meaning, it is said to be 'due to the piercing by the hairs of the uccāliṅga creatures.'

239. Arogo bhavissāmīti mocetvā arogo bhavissāmi. Sukhaṃ vedanaṃ uppādessāmīti mocanena ca muccanuppattiyā muttapaccayā ca yā sukhā vedanā hoti, taṃ uppādessāmīti attho. Bhesajjaṃ bhavissatīti [P 3.0524] idaṃ me mocitaṃ kiñcideva bhesajjaṃ bhavissati. Dānaṃ dassāmīti mocetvā kīṭakipillikādīnaṃ dānaṃ dassāmi. Puññaṃ bhavissatīti mocetvā kīṭādīnaṃ dentassa puññaṃ bhavissati. Yaññaṃ yajissāmīti mocetvā kīṭādīnaṃ yaññaṃ yajissāmi. Kiñci kiñci mantapadaṃ vatvā dassāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Saggaṃ gamissāmīti mocetvā kīṭādīnaṃ dinnadānena vā puññena vā yaññena vā saggaṃ gamissāmi. Bījaṃ bhavissatīti kulavaṃsaṅkurassa dārakassa bījaṃ bhavissati, “iminā bījena putto nibbattissatī”ti iminā adhippāyena mocetīti attho. Vīmaṃsatthāyāti jānanatthāya. Nīlaṃ bhavissatītiādīsu jānissāmi tāva kiṃ me mocitaṃ nīlaṃ bhavissati pītakādīsu aññataravaṇṇanti [V 2.0100] evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Khiḍḍādhippāyoti khiḍḍāpasuto, tena tena adhippāyena kīḷanto mocetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

239. ‘I will be free from disease’ means: having emitted, I will be free from disease. ‘I will produce a pleasant feeling’ means: I will produce that pleasant feeling which arises from the effort of emission, from the arising of the emission, and from the condition of having emitted. ‘It will be medicine’ means: this semen emitted by me will be some kind of medicine. ‘I will give a gift’ means: having emitted, I will give a gift to insects, ants, and so on. ‘It will be meritorious’ means: having emitted, for one giving to insects and so on, it will be meritorious. ‘I will perform a sacrifice’ means: having emitted, I will perform a sacrifice to insects and so on. It means: having recited some mantra-verse, I will give. ‘I will go to heaven’ means: having emitted, by the gift given to insects and so on, or by the merit, or by the sacrifice, I will go to heaven. ‘It will be a seed’ means: it will be a seed for a child, the sprout of the family lineage. The meaning is that he emits with this intention: ‘By this seed, a son will be born.’ ‘For the purpose of investigation’ means for the purpose of knowing. In ‘Will it be blue?’ and so on, the meaning should be seen thus: ‘I will first find out: will the semen emitted by me be blue? Or will it be some other color among yellow and so on?’ ‘With playful intent’ means: being devoted to play, he emits. It means: he emits while playing with this or that intention.

240. Idāni yadidaṃ “ajjhattarūpe mocetī”tiādi vuttaṃ tattha yathā mocento āpattiṃ āpajjati, tesañca padānaṃ vasena yattako āpattibhedo hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ dassento “ajjhattarūpe ceteti upakkamati muccati āpatti saṅghādisesassā”tiādimāha.

240. Now, regarding what was said, beginning with ‘he emits in regard to internal form,’ therein, showing how one who emits incurs an offense, and whatever distinction of offenses there is by means of those terms—showing all that, He spoke the passage beginning, ‘Regarding internal form, he intends, he makes an effort, it is emitted—an offense of Saṅghādisesa.’

Tattha [M 2.0112] cetetīti mocanassādasampayuttāya cetanāya muccatūti ceteti. Upakkamatīti tadanurūpaṃ vāyāmaṃ karoti. Muccatīti evaṃ cetentassa tadanurūpena vāyāmena vāyamato sukkaṃ ṭhānā cavati. Āpatti saṅghādisesassāti imehi tīhi aṅgehi assa puggalassa saṅghādiseso nāma āpattinikāyo hotīti attho. Esa nayo bahiddhārūpetiādīsupi avasesesu aṭṭhavīsatiyā padesu.

Therein, ‘he intends’ means he intends with a volition associated with the pleasure of emission, thinking, ‘Let it be emitted.’ ‘He makes an effort’ means he makes an effort corresponding to that. ‘It is emitted’ means: for one intending thus and striving with a corresponding effort, the semen moves from its place. ‘An offense of Saṅghādisesa’ means: for this person, due to these three factors, the class of offenses named Saṅghādisesa arises. This is the method also in the remaining twenty-eight instances beginning with ‘regarding external form.’

Ettha pana dve āpattisahassāni nīharitvā dassetabbāni. Kathaṃ? Ajjhattarūpe tāva rāgūpatthambhe ārogyatthāya nīlaṃ mocentassa ekā āpatti, ajjhattarūpeyeva rāgūpatthambhe ārogyatthāya pītādīnaṃ mocanavasena aparā navāti dasa. Yathā ca ārogyatthāya dasa, evaṃ sukhādīnaṃ navannaṃ padānaṃ atthāya ekekapade dasa dasa katvā navuti, iti imā ca navuti purimā ca dasāti rāgūpatthambhe tāva sataṃ. Yathā pana rāgūpatthambhe evaṃ vaccūpatthambhādīsupi catūsu ekekasmiṃ upatthambhe sataṃ [P 3.0525] sataṃ katvā cattāri satāni, iti imāni cattāri purimañca ekanti ajjhattarūpe tāva pañcannaṃ upatthambhānaṃ vasena pañca satāni. Yathā ca ajjhattarūpe pañca, evaṃ bahiddhārūpe pañca, ajjhattabahiddhārūpe pañca, ākāse kaṭiṃ kampentassa pañcāti sabbānipi catunnaṃ pañcakānaṃ vasena dve āpattisahassāni veditabbāni.

Here, however, two thousand offenses should be extracted and shown. How? First, regarding internal form, in the case of strengthening by lust, for one emitting blue for the sake of health, there is one offense. Regarding internal form itself, in the case of strengthening by lust itself, for the sake of health itself, by way of emitting yellow and so on, there are another nine—thus, ten offenses. And just as there are ten for the sake of health, so for the nine terms beginning with ‘happiness,’ by making ten offenses for each term, there are ninety. Thus, these ninety and the previous ten make one hundred offenses in the case of strengthening by lust. And just as there are one hundred in the case of strengthening by lust, so too in the four cases beginning with strengthening by feces, by making one hundred for each strengthening, there are four hundred. Thus, these four hundred and the previous one hundred make five hundred by way of the five strengthenings regarding internal form. And just as there are five hundred regarding internal form, so too five hundred regarding external form, five hundred regarding both internal and external form, and five hundred for one shaking the hips in space. Thus, all together, by way of the four groups of five hundred, two thousand offenses are to be understood.

Idāni ārogyatthāyātiādīsu tāva dasasu padesu paṭipāṭiyā vā uppaṭipāṭiyā vā heṭṭhā vā gahetvā upari gaṇhantassa, upari vā gahetvā heṭṭhā gaṇhantassa, ubhato vā gahetvā majjhe ṭhapentassa, majjhe vā gahetvā ubhato harantassa, sabbamūlaṃ vā katvā gaṇhantassa cetanūpakkamamocane sati visaṅketo nāma natthīti dassetuṃ “ārogyatthañca sukhatthañcā”ti khaṇḍacakkabaddhacakkādibhedavicittaṃ pāḷimāha.

Now, to show that in these ten instances beginning with ‘for the sake of health,’ whether for one who takes them in order or out of order, or takes from below and proceeds upwards, or takes from above and proceeds downwards, or takes from both ends and places in the middle, or takes from the middle and extends to both ends, or takes them all as a whole—when there is intention, effort, and emission, there is no such thing as a deviation, He spoke the Pāli passage, variegated with distinctions such as the ‘broken wheel’ and ‘bound wheel,’ beginning ‘for the sake of health and for the sake of happiness.’

Tattha ārogyatthañca sukhatthañca ārogyatthañca bhesajjatthañcā ti evaṃ ārogyapadaṃ sabbapadehi yojetvā vuttamekaṃ khaṇḍacakkaṃ. Sukhapadādīni sabbapadehi [V 2.0101] yojetvā yāva attano attano atītānantarapadaṃ tāva ānetvā vuttāni nava baddhacakkānīti evaṃ ekekamūlakāni dasa cakkāni honti, tāni dumūlakādīhi saddhiṃ asammohato vitthāretvā veditabbāni. Attho panettha pākaṭoyeva.

Herein, ‘for the sake of health and for the sake of happiness,’ ‘for the sake of health and for the sake of medicine,’ and so forth: in this way, by combining the term ‘health’ with all the terms, one broken wheel is stated. By combining the terms beginning with ‘happiness’ with all the terms, bringing them up to their own respective immediately preceding term, nine bound wheels are stated. Thus, there are ten wheels, each with a single root; these should be understood by expanding upon them in detail without confusion, together with those having double roots and so forth. The meaning here, however, is quite clear.

Yathā [M 2.0113] ca ārogyatthāyātiādīsu dasasu padesu, evaṃ nīlādīsupi “nīlañca pītakañca ceteti upakkamatī”tiādinā nayena dasa cakkāni vuttāni, tānipi asammohato vitthāretvā veditabbāni. Attho panettha pākaṭoyeva.

And just as in the ten terms beginning with ‘for the sake of health,’ so too in the terms beginning with ‘blue,’ ten wheels are stated by the method beginning with, ‘he intends blue and yellow and makes an effort.’ These too should be understood by expanding upon them in detail without confusion. The meaning here is quite clear.

Puna ārogyatthañca nīlañca ārogyatthañca sukhatthañca nīlañca pītakañcāti ekenekaṃ dvīhi dve…pe… dasahi dasāti evaṃ purimapadehi saddhiṃ pacchimapadāni yojetvā ekaṃ missakacakkaṃ vuttaṃ.

Again, ‘for the sake of health and blue,’ ‘for the sake of health and for happiness, and blue and yellow,’ and so forth: thus, by combining the succeeding terms with the preceding terms—one with one, two with two… up to ten with ten—one mixed wheel is stated.

Idāni yasmā “nīlaṃ mocessāmī”ti cetetvā upakkamantassa pītakādīsu muttesupi pītakādivasena cetetvā upakkamantassa itaresu muttesupi nevatthi visaṅketo[P 3.0526], tasmā etampi nayaṃ dassetuṃ “nīlaṃ mocessāmīti ceteti upakkamati pītakaṃ muccatī”tiādinā nayena cakkāni vuttāni. Tato paraṃ sabbapacchimapadaṃ nīlādīhi navahi padehi saddhiṃ yojetvā kucchicakkaṃ nāma vuttaṃ. Tato pītakādīni nava padāni ekena nīlapadeneva saddhiṃ yojetvā piṭṭhicakkaṃ nāma vuttaṃ. Tato lohitakādīni nava padāni ekena pītakapadeneva saddhiṃ yojetvā dutiyaṃ piṭṭhicakkaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ lohitakapadādīhi saddhiṃ itarāni nava nava padāni yojetvā aññānipi aṭṭha cakkāni vuttānīti evaṃ dasagatikaṃ piṭṭhicakkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, because for one who, having intended, ‘I will release the blue,’ makes an effort, there is no mismatch of intention even if yellow and so forth are released; and for one who, having intended by way of yellow and so forth, makes an effort, there is no mismatch of intention even if other colors are released—therefore, to show this method as well, the wheels are stated by the method beginning with, ‘He intends, “I will release the blue,” makes an effort, and yellow is released.’ After that, by combining the very last term with the nine terms beginning with ‘blue,’ what is called the ‘belly wheel’ is stated. Then, by combining the nine terms beginning with ‘yellow’ with only the single term ‘blue,’ what is called the ‘back wheel’ is stated. After that, by combining the nine terms beginning with ‘red’ with only the single term ‘yellow,’ a second ‘back wheel’ is stated. In this way, by combining the other sets of nine terms with the terms beginning with ‘red’ and so on, eight other wheels are also stated. Thus, the ‘back wheel’ with its ten variations should be understood.

Evaṃ khaṇḍacakkādīnaṃ anekesaṃ cakkānaṃ vasena vitthārato garukāpattimeva dassetvā idāni aṅgavaseneva garukāpattiñca lahukāpattiñca anāpattiñca dassetuṃ “ceteti upakkamati muccatī”tiādimāha. Tattha purimanayena ajjhattarūpādīsu rāgādiupatthambhe sati ārogyādīnaṃ atthāya cetentassa upakkamitvā asucimocane tivaṅgasampannā garukāpatti vuttā. Dutiyena nayena cetentassa upakkamantassa ca mocane asati duvaṅgasampannā lahukā thullaccayāpatti. “Ceteti na upakkamati muccatī”tiādīhi chahi nayehi anāpatti.

Thus, having shown in detail only the grave offense by way of the many wheels, such as the broken wheel, now, in order to show the grave offense, the light offense, and non-offense by way of the factors themselves, He said, beginning with, ‘He intends, he makes an effort, it is released.’ Therein, according to the first method, when there is a stiffening due to lust and so forth in regard to internal forms and so forth, for one who intends for the sake of health and so forth, a grave offense endowed with three factors is stated for releasing impurity after having made an effort. According to the second method, for one who both intends and makes an effort, when there is no release, a light offense of thullaccaya, endowed with two factors, is stated. By the six methods beginning with, ‘He intends, does not make an effort, it is released,’ non-offense is stated.

Ayaṃ pana āpattānāpattibhedo saṇho sukhumo, tasmā suṭṭhu sallakkhetabbo[V 2.0102]. Suṭṭhu sallakkhetvā kukkuccaṃ pucchitena āpatti vā anāpatti vā ācikkhitabbā, vinayakammaṃ vā kātabbaṃ. Asallakkhetvā karonto hi roganidānaṃ ajānitvā bhesajjaṃ karonto vejjo viya vighātañca [M 2.0114] āpajjati, na ca taṃ puggalaṃ tikicchituṃ samattho hoti. Tatrāyaṃ sallakkhaṇavidhi – kukkuccena āgato bhikkhu yāvatatiyaṃ pucchitabbo – “katarena payogena katarena rāgena āpannosī”ti. Sace paṭhamaṃ aññaṃ vatvā pacchā aññaṃ vadati na ekamaggena katheti, so vattabbo – “tvaṃ na ekamaggena kathesi pariharasi, na sakkā tava vinayakammaṃ kātuṃ gaccha sotthiṃ gavesā”ti. Sace pana tikkhattumpi ekamaggeneva katheti, yathābhūtaṃ attānaṃ āvikaroti, athassa āpattānāpattigarukalahukāpattivinicchayatthaṃ ekādasannaṃ rāgānaṃ vasena ekādasa payogā samavekkhitabbā.

This distinction between offense and non-offense, however, is subtle and delicate; therefore, it should be carefully examined. Having carefully examined, the Vinaya expert who has been asked about the remorse should declare it an offense or a non-offense, or a disciplinary act should be performed. For one who acts without careful examination, like a physician who administers medicine without knowing the cause of the disease, encounters trouble and is not able to treat that person. Herein, this is the method of examination: a monk who has come with remorse should be questioned up to the third time: ‘By what application, by what lust, have you fallen into an offense?’ If, having said one thing at first, he says another thing later and does not speak in one consistent way, he should be told: ‘You do not speak consistently; you are evading. It is not possible to perform a disciplinary act for you. Go, seek your own well-being.’ But if, even for the third time, he speaks in one consistent way and reveals himself truthfully, then for the purpose of deciding for him about offense, non-offense, grave offense, and light offense, eleven applications should be considered by way of the eleven lusts.

Tatrime [P 3.0527] ekādasa rāgā – mocanassādo, muccanassādo, muttassādo, methunassādo, phassassādo, kaṇḍuvanassādo, dassanassādo, nisajjassādo, vācassādo, gehassitapemaṃ, vanabhaṅgiyanti. Tattha mocetuṃ assādo mocanassādo, muccane assādo muccanassādo, mutte assādo muttassādo, methune assādo methunassādo, phasse assādo phassassādo, kaṇḍuvane assādo kaṇḍuvanassādo, dassane assādo dassanassādo, nisajjāya assādo nisajjassādo, vācāya assādo vācassādo, gehassitaṃ pemaṃ gehassitapemaṃ, vanabhaṅgiyanti yaṃkiñci pupphaphalādi vanato bhañjitvā āhaṭaṃ. Ettha ca navahi padehi sampayuttaassādasīsena rāgo vutto. Ekena padena sarūpeneva, ekena padena vatthunā vutto, vanabhaṅgo hi rāgassa vatthu na rāgoyeva.

Herein are these eleven lusts: delight in causing emission, delight in the state of emission, delight in what has been emitted, delight in sexual intercourse, delight in touch, delight in relieving an itch, delight in seeing, delight in sitting together, delight in conversation, household-based affection, and forest-plunder. Therein, delight in causing to be emitted is ‘delight in causing emission’; delight in the state of emission is ‘delight in the state of emission’; delight when it has been emitted is ‘delight in what has been emitted’; delight in sexual intercourse is ‘delight in sexual intercourse’; delight in touch is ‘delight in touch’; delight in relieving an itch is ‘delight in relieving an itch’; delight in seeing is ‘delight in seeing’; delight in sitting together is ‘delight in sitting together’; delight in conversation is ‘delight in conversation’; household-based affection is ‘household-based affection’; and ‘forest-plunder’ is any object such as flowers, fruit, etc., plucked and brought from the forest. And herein, by nine terms, lust is stated under the heading of associated delight. By one term, it is stated by its very form; by one term, it is stated by its object, for forest-plunder is the object of lust, not lust itself.

Etesaṃ pana rāgānaṃ vasena evaṃ payogā samavekkhitabbā – mocanassāde mocanassādacetanāya cetento ceva assādento ca upakkamati muccati saṅghādiseso. Tatheva cetento ca assādento ca upakkamati na muccati thullaccayaṃ. Sace pana sayanakāle rāgapariyuṭṭhito hutvā ūrunā vā muṭṭhinā vā aṅgajātaṃ gāḷhaṃ pīḷetvā mocanatthāya saussāhova supati, supantassa cassa asuci muccati saṅghādiseso. Sace rāgapariyuṭṭhānaṃ asubhamanasikārena vūpasametvā suddhacitto supati, supantassa muttepi anāpatti.

Now, by way of these lusts, the applications should be considered thus: In the case of ‘delight in causing emission,’ if, with the intention of delighting in causing emission, one both intends and delights, makes an effort, and it is released, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. In the same way, if one both intends and delights, makes an effort, but it is not released, it is a Thullaccaya offense. Furthermore, if at bedtime, having become overcome by lust, one presses the sexual organ firmly with the thigh or with the fist for the purpose of emission and sleeps while still striving, and for him, while sleeping, impurity is released, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. If, having calmed the arising of lust by means of attention to the foul, one sleeps with a pure mind, then even if it is released while one is sleeping, there is no offense.

Muccanassāde [M 2.0115] attano dhammatāya muccamānaṃ assādeti na upakkamati anāpatti. Sace pana muccamānaṃ assādento upakkamati, tena upakkamena mutte saṅghādiseso. Attano dhammatāya [V 2.0103] muccamāne “mā kāsāvaṃ vā senāsanaṃ vā dussī”ti aṅgajātaṃ gahetvā jagganatthāya udakaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati vaṭṭatīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding delight in the process of emission: If one delights in what is being emitted by its own nature but does not make an effort, there is no offense. But if, while delighting in the process of emission, one makes an effort, and it is emitted due to that effort, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. When it is being emitted by its own nature, if, thinking, 'May the robe or the lodging not be spoiled,' one takes hold of the genital organ and goes to a place with water for the purpose of cleaning, it is allowable. Thus it is said in the Mahāpaccariya.

Muttassāde attano dhammatāya mutte ṭhānā cute asucimhi pacchā assādentassa vinā upakkamena muccati, anāpatti. Sace assādetvā puna mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in what has been emitted: If, after impurity has been emitted by its own nature and has moved from its place, one delights in it afterwards, and more is emitted without effort, there is no offense. If, having delighted, one again makes an effort at the organ for the purpose of emission and causes it to be emitted, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Methunassāde methunarāgena mātugāmaṃ gaṇhāti, tena payogena asuci muccati, anāpatti. Methunadhammassa [P 3.0528] payogattā pana tādise gahaṇe dukkaṭaṃ, sīsaṃ patte pārājikaṃ. Sace methunarāgena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in sexual intercourse: If one takes hold of a woman with lust for intercourse, and impurity is emitted due to that act, there is no offense for the emission. However, due to it being an application of the act of intercourse, there is a Dukkaṭa offense for such an act of taking hold; upon reaching its culmination, it is a Pārājika offense. If, impassioned with lust for intercourse, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Phassassāde duvidho phasso – ajjhattiko, bāhiro ca. Ajjhattike tāva attano nimittaṃ thaddhaṃ mudukanti jānissāmīti vā lolabhāvena vā kīḷāpayato asuci muccati, anāpatti. Sace kīḷāpento assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso. Bāhiraphasse pana kāyasaṃsaggarāgena mātugāmassa aṅgamaṅgāni parāmasato ceva āliṅgato ca asuci muccati, anāpatti. Kāyasaṃsaggasaṅghādisesaṃ pana āpajjati. Sace kāyasaṃsaggarāgena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti visaṭṭhipaccayāpi saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in touch: Touch is twofold—internal and external. First, regarding internal touch: if impurity is emitted from one who agitates their own organ, thinking, 'I will know if it is stiff or soft,' or out of wantonness, there is no offense. If, while agitating it, one delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. Regarding external touch: if impurity is emitted from one who strokes or embraces the limbs of a woman with lust for bodily contact, there is no offense for the emission. However, one does fall into the saṅghādisesa offense of bodily contact. If, impassioned with lust for bodily contact, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense also on account of the emission.

Kaṇḍuvanassāde daddukacchupiḷakapāṇakādīnaṃ aññataravasena kaṇḍuvamānaṃ nimittaṃ kaṇḍuvanassāde neva kaṇḍuvato asuci muccati, anāpatti. Kaṇḍuvanassādena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in scratching: If impurity is emitted from one who scratches an itching organ—the itch being due to one or another cause such as ringworm, scabies, pustules, or small creatures—with only the delight of relieving the itch, there is no offense. If, impassioned with the delight of scratching, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense.

Dassanassāde dassanassādena punappunaṃ mātugāmassa anokāsaṃ upanijjhāyato asuci muccati, anāpatti. Mātugāmassa anokāsupanijjhāne pana [M 2.0116] dukkaṭaṃ. Sace dassanassādena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in seeing: If impurity is emitted from one who, with the delight of seeing, repeatedly gazes intently at a woman's private parts, there is no offense for the emission. However, for intently gazing at a woman's private parts, there is a dukkaṭa offense. If, impassioned with the delight of seeing, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense.

Nisajjassāde mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisajjassādarāgena nisinnassa asuci muccati, anāpatti. Raho nisajjapaccayā pana āpannāya āpattiyā kāretabbo. Sace nisajjassādena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in sitting: If impurity is emitted from one sitting in a secluded place with a woman with lust for the delight of sitting, there is no offense for the emission. However, one must be dealt with for the offense incurred on account of sitting in a secluded place. If, impassioned with the delight of sitting, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense.

Vācassāde [V 2.0104] vācassādarāgena mātugāmaṃ methunasannissitāhi vācāhi obhāsantassa asuci muccati, anāpatti. Duṭṭhullavācāsaṅghādisesaṃ pana āpajjati. Sace vācassādena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding delight in speech: If impurity is emitted from one who, with lust for the delight of speech, addresses a woman with words connected to sexual intercourse, there is no offense for the emission. However, one does fall into the saṅghādisesa offense for coarse speech. If, impassioned with the delight of speech, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense.

Gehassitapeme mātaraṃ vā mātupemena bhaginiṃ vā bhaginipemena punappunaṃ parāmasato [P 3.0529] ceva āliṅgato ca asuci muccati, anāpatti. Gehassitapemena pana phusanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ. Sace gehassitapemena ratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso.

Regarding household-based affection: If impurity is emitted from one who repeatedly strokes or embraces his mother with affection for a mother, or his sister with affection for a sister, there is no offense for the emission. However, on account of touching with household-based affection, there is a dukkaṭa offense. If, impassioned with household-based affection, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense.

Vanabhaṅge itthipurisā aññamaññaṃ kiñcideva tambūlagandhapupphavāsādippakāraṃ paṇṇākāraṃ mittasanthavabhāvassa daḷhabhāvatthāya pesenti ayaṃ vanabhaṅgo nāma. Tañce mātugāmo kassaci saṃsaṭṭhavihārikassa kulūpakabhikkhuno peseti, tassa ca “asukāya nāma idaṃ pesita”nti sārattassa punappunaṃ hatthehi taṃ vanabhaṅgaṃ kīḷāpayato asuci muccati, anāpatti. Sace vanabhaṅge sāratto puna assādetvā mocanatthāya nimitte upakkamitvā moceti, saṅghādiseso. Sace upakkamantepi na muccati, thullaccayaṃ.

Regarding a 'forest-plucked' gift (vanabhaṅga): Men and women send to one another some kind of gift—such as betel, perfumes, flowers, or fragrant powders—for the sake of strengthening the state of their friendship; this is called a 'forest-plucked' gift. If a woman sends such a gift to a certain monk who lives in association with and frequents families, and impurity is emitted from him as, being impassioned and thinking, 'This was sent by so-and-so,' he repeatedly plays with that 'forest-plucked' gift in his hands, there is no offense for the emission. If, being impassioned by the 'forest-plucked' gift, one again delights and, for the purpose of emission, makes an effort at the organ and causes it to be emitted, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. If, despite making an effort, it is not emitted, it is a thullaccaya offense.

Evametesaṃ ekādasannaṃ rāgānaṃ vasena ime ekādasa payoge samevekkhitvā āpatti vā anāpatti vā sallakkhetabbā. Sallakkhetvā sace garukā hoti “garukā”ti ācikkhitabbā. Sace lahukā hoti “lahukā”ti ācikkhitabbā. Tadanurūpañca vinayakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Evañhi kataṃ sukataṃ hoti roganidānaṃ ñatvā vejjena katabhesajjamiva, tassa ca puggalassa sotthibhāvāya saṃvattati.

Thus, by way of these eleven kinds of lust, having well considered these eleven applications, one should discern whether it is an offense or not an offense. Having discerned, if it is a serious offense, it should be declared 'serious.' If it is a minor offense, it should be declared 'minor.' And a disciplinary act appropriate to that should be performed. For when done thus, it is well done—like medicine prepared by a physician who knows the cause of the disease—and it conduces to that person's state of well-being.

262. Ceteti na upakkamatītiādīsu mocanassādacetanāya ceteti, na upakkamati, muccati, anāpatti. Mocanassādapīḷito “aho vata [M 2.0117] mucceyyā”ti ceteti, na upakkamati, na muccati, anāpatti. Mocanassādena na ceteti, phassassādena kaṇḍuvanassādena vā upakkamati, muccati, anāpatti. Tatheva na ceteti, upakkamati, na muccati, anāpatti. Kāmavitakkaṃ vitakkento mocanatthāya na ceteti, na upakkamati, muccati, anāpatti. Sace panassa vitakkayatopi na muccati idaṃ āgatameva hoti, “na ceteti, na upakkamati, na muccati, anāpattī”ti.

262. Regarding 'one intends, one does not make an effort,' and so on: If one intends with the intention of delighting in emission, does not make an effort, and it is emitted, there is no offense. If, afflicted by the delight of emission, one intends, 'Oh, that it might be emitted!', does not make an effort, and it is not emitted, there is no offense. If one does not intend with the delight of emission, but makes an effort with the delight of touch or the delight of scratching, and it is emitted, there is no offense. Likewise, if one does not intend, makes an effort, and it is not emitted, there is no offense. While thinking a sensual thought, if one does not intend for the purpose of emission and does not make an effort, and it is emitted, there is no offense. But if, for one who is thinking, it is not emitted, this comes under what is already stated: 'One does not intend, does not make an effort, it is not emitted—no offense.'

Anāpatti [V 2.0105] supinantenāti suttassa supine methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantassa viya kāyasaṃsaggādīni āpajjantassa viya supinanteneva kāraṇena yassa asuci muccati, tassa anāpatti. Supine pana [P 3.0530] uppannāya assādacetanāya sacassa visayo hoti, niccalena bhavitabbaṃ, na hatthena nimittaṃ kīḷāpetabbaṃ, kāsāvapaccattharaṇarakkhaṇatthaṃ pana hatthapuṭena gahetvā jagganatthāya udakaṭṭhānaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati.

There is no offense through a dream: For one who is asleep, if impurity is emitted due to the mere fact of dreaming—as if engaging in sexual intercourse or as if committing bodily contact and so forth in a dream—there is no offense for him. However, if in the dream a volition associated with pleasure arises, and if it is an object within his control, he should remain motionless; the sexual organ should not be played with by hand. But for the purpose of protecting the dyed robe and the bedsheet, it is allowable to take it with the cupped hand and go to a place with water for the purpose of washing.

Namocanādhippāyassāti yassa bhesajjena vā nimittaṃ ālimpantassa uccārādīni vā karontassa namocanādhippāyassa muccati, tassāpi anāpatti. Ummattakassa duvidhassāpi anāpatti. Idha seyyasako ādikammiko, tassa anāpatti ādikammikassāti.

For one with no intention to emit: For one who, while applying medicine to the sexual organ or while performing excretion and so forth, emits impurity without the intention to emit, for him also there is no offense. For an insane person of both kinds who emits impurity, there is no offense. Here, Seyyasaka is the first offender; for him, the first offender, there is no offense.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the word-analysis is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyacittato samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyā, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dvivedanaṃ, sukhamajjhattadvayenāti.

In regard to the origins and so forth, this training rule has the same origin as the first pārājika; it arises from body and mind. It is an action, not released by perception, intentional, a worldly fault, a bodily action, with unwholesome consciousness, and with two feelings, that is, by means of the pair of pleasant and neutral feeling.

263. Vinītavatthūsu supinavatthu anupaññattiyaṃ vuttanayameva. Uccārapassāvavatthūni uttānatthāneva.

263. Among the decided cases, the case of the dream is just according to the method stated in the supplementary regulation. The cases of feces and urine are of plain meaning.

Vitakkavatthusmiṃ kāmavitakkanti gehassitakāmavitakkaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi anāpatti vuttā, atha kho vitakkagatikena na bhavitabbaṃ. Uṇhodakavatthūsu paṭhamaṃ uttānameva. Dutiye so bhikkhu mocetukāmo uṇhodakena nimittaṃ paharitvā paharitvā nhāyi, tenassa āpatti vuttā. Tatiye upakkamassa atthitāya thullaccayaṃ. Bhesajjakaṇḍuvanavatthūni uttānatthāneva.

In the case of thought, 'sensual thought' means sensual thought based on the household life. Although 'no offense' is stated there, nevertheless, one should not be led by thought. In the cases of hot water, the first is of plain meaning. In the second, that monk, being desirous of emitting, bathed, striking the sexual organ again and again with hot water; for that reason, an offense was stated for him. In the third, due to the existence of the effort, a grave offense was stated. The cases of medicine and scratching are of plain meaning.

264. Maggavatthūsu [M 2.0118] paṭhamassa thulaūrukassa maggaṃ gacchantassa sambādhaṭṭhāne ghaṭṭanāya asuci mucci, tassa namocanādhippāyattā anāpatti. Dutiyassa tatheva mucci, mocanādhippāyattā pana saṅghādiseso. Tatiyassa na mucci, upakkamasabbhāvato pana thullaccayaṃ. Tasmā maggaṃ gacchantena uppanne pariḷāhe na gantabbaṃ, gamanaṃ upacchinditvā asubhādimanasikārena cittaṃ vūpasametvā suddhacittena kammaṭṭhānaṃ ādāya gantabbaṃ. Sace ṭhito vinodetuṃ [V 2.0106] na sakkoti, maggā okkamma nisīditvā vinodetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ ādāya suddhacitteneva gantabbaṃ.

264. In the cases concerning a path: for the first monk, one with thick thighs, while going along a path, impurity was emitted due to friction in a narrow place; for him, because of having no intention to emit, there is no offense. For the second monk, it was emitted in the same way, but because of the intention to emit, it is a Saṅghādisesa. For the third monk, it was not emitted, but due to the actual existence of the effort, it is a grave offense. Therefore, for a monk going along a path, when a feverish state arises, he should not continue to go. Having cut off the going, and having calmed the mind with attention to the foul and so forth, he should go, having taken up the meditation subject with a pure mind. If, while standing, he is not able to dispel it, he should withdraw from the path, sit down, dispel it, and go on only with a pure mind, having taken up the meditation subject.

Vatthivatthūsu te bhikkhū vatthiṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā pūretvā pūretvā vissajjentā [P 3.0531] gāmadārakā viya passāvamakaṃsu. Jantāgharavatthusmiṃ udaraṃ tāpentassa mocanādhippāyassāpi amocanādhippāyassāpi mutte anāpattiyeva. Parikammaṃ karontassa nimittacālanavasena asuci mucci, tasmā āpattiṭṭhāne āpatti vuttā.

In the cases concerning the urinary passage: those monks, holding the tip of the urinary passage firmly, filling it up repeatedly and then releasing, urinated like village boys. In the case of the steam-bath house: for one heating the abdomen, when emission occurs—whether with the intention to emit or without the intention to emit—there is indeed no offense for the emission of semen. For one performing a preliminary action, impurity was emitted by means of moving the sexual organ; therefore, in a case where an offense applies, an offense was stated.

265. Ūrughaṭṭāpanavatthūsu yesaṃ āpatti vuttā te aṅgajātampi phusāpesunti veditabbāti evaṃ kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sāmaṇerādivatthūni uttānatthāneva.

265. In the cases of causing contact with the thigh, for those for whom an offense was stated, it should be known that they also caused the sexual organ to be touched. Thus it was stated in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā. The cases concerning the novice and so forth are of plain meaning.

266. Kāyatthambhanavatthusmiṃ kāyaṃ thambhentassāti ciraṃ nisīditvā vā nipajjitvā vā navakammaṃ vā katvā ālasiyavimocanatthaṃ vijambhentassa.

266. In the case of stiffening the body: 'for one stiffening the body' means for one who, having sat or lain down for a long time, or having done new work, stretches for the purpose of being released from laziness.

Upanijjhāyanavatthusmiṃ sacepi paṭasataṃ nivatthā hoti purato vā pacchato vā ṭhatvā “imasmiṃ nāma okāse nimitta”nti upanijjhāyantassa dukkaṭameva. Anivatthānaṃ gāmadārikānaṃ nimittaṃ upanijjhāyantassa pana kimeva vattabbaṃ. Tiracchānagatānampi nimitte eseva nayo. Ito cito ca aviloketvā pana divasampi ekapayogena upanijjhāyantassa ekameva dukkaṭaṃ. Ito cito ca viloketvā punappunaṃ upanijjhāyantassa payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Ummīlananimīlanavasena pana na kāretabbo. Sahasā upanijjhāyitvā puna paṭisaṅkhāya saṃvare tiṭṭhato anāpatti, taṃ saṃvaraṃ pahāya puna upanijjhāyato dukkaṭameva.

In the case of gazing intently: even if a woman is clothed in a hundred garments, for a monk who, having stood in front or behind, gazes intently thinking, 'In such and such a place is the sexual organ,' there is indeed a dukkaṭa offense. What then need be said about one who gazes intently at the sexual organ of unclothed village girls? This is the same method for the sexual organ of female animals too. However, for one who, without looking here and there, gazes intently for a whole day with a single effort, there is only one dukkaṭa offense. For one who, looking here and there, gazes intently again and again, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each effort. However, an offense is not to be reckoned for each effort by means of opening and closing the eyes. For one who, having gazed intently inadvertently, then stands in restraint with reflective wisdom, there is no offense. For one who, having abandoned that restraint, gazes intently again, there is indeed a dukkaṭa offense.

267. Tāḷacchiddādivatthūni [M 2.0119] uttānatthāneva. Nhānavatthūsu ye udakasotaṃ nimittena pahariṃsu tesaṃ āpatti vuttā. Udañjalavatthūsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca udañjalanti udakacikkhallo vuccati. Eteneva upāyena ito parāni sabbāneva udake dhāvanādivatthūni veditabbāni. Ayaṃ pana viseso. Pupphāvaḷiyavatthūsu sacepi namocanādhippāyassa anāpatti, kīḷanapaccayā pana dukkaṭaṃ hotīti.

267. The cases concerning the keyhole and so forth are of plain meaning. In the cases of bathing, for those who struck the stream of water with the sexual organ, an offense was stated. This is the same method in the cases of watery mud as well. And here, 'udañjala' is called watery mud. By this same method, all the subsequent cases from this one, such as running in water and so forth, should be understood. However, this is the distinction: in the cases of the flower-garland, even if there is no offense for one with no intention to emit, there is a dukkaṭa offense due to the condition of playing.

Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the emission of semen is concluded.

2. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Bodily Contact.

269. Tena [P 3.0532][V 2.0107] samayena buddho bhagavāti kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – araññe viharatīti na āveṇike araññe, jetavanavihārasseva paccante ekapasse. Majjhe gabbhoti tassa ca vihārassa majjhe gabbho hoti. Samantā pariyāgāroti samantā panassa maṇḍalamāḷaparikkhepo hoti. So kira majjhe caturassaṃ gabbhaṃ katvā bahi maṇḍalamāḷaparikkhepena kato, yathā sakkā hoti antoyeva āviñchantehi vicarituṃ.

269. The passage beginning with `Tena samayena buddho bhagavā` is the Training Rule on Bodily Contact. Herein, this is the explanation of the terms that are not obvious: `araññe viharati` (he dwells in the forest) means he does not dwell in a separate forest dwelling, but on one side, at the very edge of the Jetavana monastery itself. `majjhe gabbho` (a chamber in the middle) means in the middle of that dwelling there is a chamber. `samantā pariyāgāro` (a surrounding cloister) means around it there is a circular pavilion enclosure. It is said that, having made a square chamber in the middle, it was constructed with a circular pavilion enclosure on the outside, so that it was possible for those walking around to move about entirely within.

Supaññattanti suṭṭha ṭhapitaṃ, yathā yathā yasmiṃ yasmiñca okāse ṭhapitaṃ pāsādikaṃ hoti lokarañjakaṃ tathā tathā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ okāse ṭhapitaṃ, vattasīsena hi soṃ ekakiccampi na karoti. Ekacce vātapāne vivarantoti yesu vivaṭesu andhakāro hoti tāni vivaranto yesu vivaṭesu āloko hoti tāni thakento.

`Supaññattaṃ` (well-laid-out) means well-placed; in whatever manner and in whatever place it is placed, it is inspiring and pleasing to the people, and in that manner and in that place it was placed. For he does not perform even a single duty with the Khandhaka observances as primary. `Ekacce vātapāne vivaranto` (opening some windows) means opening those which, when opened, cause darkness, and closing those which, when opened, cause light.

Evaṃ vutte sā brāhmaṇī taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ etadavocāti evaṃ tena brāhmaṇena pasaṃsitvā vutte sā brāhmaṇī “pasanno ayaṃ brāhmaṇo pabbajitukāmo maññe”ti sallakkhetvā nigūhitabbampi taṃ attano vippakāraṃ pakāsentī kevalaṃ tassa saddhāvighātāpekkhā hutvā etaṃ “kuto tassa uḷārattatā”tiādivacanamavoca. Tattha uḷāro attā assāti uḷārattā, uḷārattano bhāvo uṭṭhārattatā. Kulitthīhītiādīsu kulitthiyo nāma gharassāminiyo. Kuladhītaro nāma purisantaragatā kuladhītaro[M 2.0120]. Kulakumāriyo nāma aniviṭṭhā vuccanti. Kulasuṇhā nāma parakulato ānītā kuladārakānaṃ vadhuyo.

`Evaṃ vutte sā brāhmaṇī taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ etadavoca` (When this was said, that brahmin woman said this to the brahmin) means: when it was said thus after being praised by that brahmin, that brahmin woman, perceiving, “This brahmin is pleased; I think he desires to go forth,” and wishing to reveal that misbehavior of hers, which should have been concealed, being solely intent on destroying his faith, spoke this utterance beginning with, “Whence is his nobility?” Therein, `uḷārattā` means one for whom there is a noble mind; `uḷārattatā` is the state of one with a noble mind. In the passage beginning with `kulitthīhi`: `kulitthiyo` are mistresses of the house. `Kuladhītaro` are daughters of good family who have been approached by another man. `Kulakumāriyo` are said to be unpenetrated maidens of good family. `Kulasuṇhā` are the wives of the sons of the family, brought from another family.

270. Otiṇṇoti yakkhādīhi viya sattā anto uppajjantena rāgena otiṇṇo, kūpādīni viya sattā asamapekkhitvā rajanīye ṭhāne rajjanto sayaṃ vā rāgaṃ otiṇṇo, yasmā pana ubhayathāpi rāgasamaṅgissevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā “otiṇṇo nāma sāratto apekkhavā paṭibaddhacitto”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

270. `Otiṇṇa` means: overcome by lust that arises within, just as beings are possessed by yakkhas and so on; or, having himself descended into lust by becoming attached to a desirable object without proper reflection, just as beings descend into a well and so on. However, since this term, in both senses, is a designation only for one who is endowed with lust, therefore its word-analysis has been stated thus: “`Otiṇṇa` means one who is impassioned, desirous, with a mind that is attached.”

Tattha [P 3.0533] sārattoti kāyasaṃsaggarāgena suṭṭhu ratto. Apekkhavāti kāyasaṃsaggāpekkhāya apekkhavā. Paṭibaddhacittoti kāyasaṃsaggarāgeneva tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ paṭibaddhacitto. Vipariṇatenāti parisuddhabhavaṅgasantatisaṅkhātaṃ pakatiṃ vijahitvā aññathā pavattena, virūpaṃ vā pariṇatena [V 2.0108] virūpaṃ parivattena, yathā parivattamānaṃ virūpaṃ hoti evaṃ parivattitvā ṭhitenāti adhippāyo.

Therein, `sāratto` means strongly impassioned with the lust for bodily contact. `Apekkhavā` means desirous due to the desire for bodily contact. `Paṭibaddhacitto` means with a mind attached to that object by the very lust for bodily contact. `Vipariṇatena` means: by that which proceeds otherwise, having abandoned the natural state known as the utterly pure continuity of the life-continuum (`bhavaṅga`); or, by that which has changed into a deformed state through a deformed alteration. The intended meaning is: by the mind that remains altered, having changed in such a way that as it changes, it becomes deformed.

271. Yasmā panetaṃ rāgādīhi sampayogaṃ nātivattati, tasmā “vipariṇatanti rattampi citta”ntiādinā nayenassa padabhājanaṃ vatvā ante idhādhippetamatthaṃ dassento “apica rattaṃ cittaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetaṃ vipariṇata”nti āha.

271. However, since this (perverted mind) does not transcend association with lust and so on, therefore, having stated its word-analysis by the method beginning with, “`Vipariṇata` means a mind that is impassioned,” at the end, showing the meaning intended here, he said, “Furthermore, an impassioned mind is intended in this sense as `vipariṇata` (perverted).”

Tadahujātāti taṃdivasaṃ jātā jātamattā allamaṃsapesivaṇṇā, evarūpāyapi hi saddhiṃ kāyasaṃsagge saṅghādiseso, methunavītikkame pārājikaṃ, raho nisajjassāde pācittiyañca hoti. Pagevāti paṭhamameva.

`Tadahujātā` means born on that day, just born, the color of a piece of fresh meat. For, even with one of such a form, in the case of bodily contact, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense; in the case of transgressing through sexual intercourse, a Pārājika offense; and in the case of delighting in sitting together in a secluded place, a Pācittiya offense. `Pageva` means at the very first.

Kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyāti hatthaggahaṇādikāyasampayogaṃ kāyamissībhāvaṃ samāpajjeyya, yasmā panetaṃ samāpajjantassa yo so kāyasaṃsaggo nāma so atthato ajjhācāro hoti, rāgavasena abhibhavitvā saññamavelaṃ ācāro, tasmāssa saṅkhepana atthaṃ dassento “ajjhācāro vuccatī”ti padabhājanamāha.

`Kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyya` means one might attain bodily connection, such as holding the hand, the state of being physically mingled. However, since for a monk who attains this, that which is called bodily contact is, in essence, a transgression (`ajjhācāra`)—that is, conduct that, due to lust, overwhelms the boundary of restraint—therefore, showing its meaning in brief, he stated the word-analysis: “It is called `ajjhācāra`.”

Hatthaggāhaṃ vātiādibhedaṃ panassa vitthārena atthadassanaṃ. Tattha hatthādīnaṃ vibhāgadassanatthaṃ “hattho nāma kapparaṃ upādāyā”tiādimāha tattha kapparaṃ upādāyāti dutiyaṃ. Mahāsandhiṃ upādāya. Aññattha pana maṇibandhato [M 2.0121] paṭṭhāya yāva agganakhā hattho idha saddhiṃ aggabāhāya kapparato paṭṭhāya adhippeto.

The passage beginning with `Hatthaggāhaṃ vā` is the showing of its meaning in detail. Therein, for the purpose of showing the division of the hand and so on, he stated the passage beginning with, “`Hattho nāma` means from the elbow onwards.” Therein, “from the elbow onwards” means including the second great joint. However, elsewhere, the hand is intended to be from the wrist up to the tip of the nails. Here, it is intended as from the elbow onwards, together with the forearm.

Suddhakesā vāti suttādīhi amissā suddhā kesāyeva. Veṇīti tīhi kesavaṭṭīhi vinandhitvā katakesakalāpassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Suttamissāti pañcavaṇṇena suttena kese missetvā katā. Mālāmissāti vassikapupphādīhi missetvā tīhi kesavaṭṭīhi vinandhitvā [P 3.0534] katā, avinaddhopi vā kevalaṃ pupphamissako kesakalāpo idha “veṇī”ti veditabbo. Hiraññamissāti kahāpaṇamālāya missetvā katā. Suvaṇṇamissāti suvaṇṇacīrakehi vā pāmaṅgādīhi vā missetvā katā. Muttāmissāti muttāvalīhi missetvā katā. Maṇimissāti suttārūḷhehi maṇīhi missetvā katā. Etāsu hi yaṃkiñci veṇiṃ gaṇhantassa saṅghādisesoyeva. “Ahaṃ missakaveṇiṃ aggahesi”nti vadantassa mokkho natthi. Veṇiggahaṇena cettha kesāpi gahitāva honti, tasmā yo ekampi kesaṃ gaṇhāti tassapi āpattiyeva.

`Suddhakesā` means just pure hair, unmixed with thread and so on. `Veṇī` is the name for a mass of hair made by braiding with three strands of hair. `Suttamissā` is a braid made by mixing the hair with five-colored thread. `Mālāmissā` is a braid made by mixing with jasmine flowers and so on and braiding with three strands of hair; here, even a mass of hair that is merely mixed with flowers, though unbraided, should be known as a `veṇī`. `Hiraññamissā` is a braid made by mixing with a garland of coins. `Suvaṇṇamissā` is a braid made by mixing with gold strips or `pāmaṅga` ornaments and so on. `Muttāmissā` is a braid made by mixing with strings of pearls. `Maṇimissā` is a braid made by mixing with gems strung on a thread. Indeed, for one who takes any of these braids, there is only a Saṅghādisesa offense. There is no release for one who says, “I took a mixed braid.” And here, by the taking of the braid, the hairs themselves are also taken. Therefore, for one who takes even a single hair, there is an offense.

Hatthañca [V 2.0109] veṇiñca ṭhapetvāti idha vuttalakkhaṇaṃ hatthañca sabbappakārañca veṇiṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ sarīraṃ “aṅga”nti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ paricchinnesu hatthādīsu hatthassa gahaṇaṃ hatthaggāho, veṇiyā gahaṇaṃ veṇiggāho, avasesasasarīrassa parāmasanaṃ aññatarassa vā aññatarassa vā aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ, yo taṃ hatthaggāhaṃ vā veṇiggāhaṃ vā aññatarassa vā aññatarassa vā aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ samāpajjeyya, tassa saṅghādiseso nāma āpattinikāyo hotīti. Ayaṃ sikkhāpadassa attho.

'Having set aside the hand and the braid' means: Here, having set aside the hand with the stated characteristics and every kind of braid, the remainder of the body is to be understood as 'a limb.' Thus, among the hand and so forth which have been distinguished, the grasping of the hand is 'hand-grasping'; the grasping of the braid is 'braid-grasping'; the touching of the remaining body is 'the touching of any one or another limb.' Whichever monk should engage in that hand-grasping, or that braid-grasping, or the touching of any one or another limb, for him there is a class of offenses called Saṅghādisesa. This is the meaning of the training rule.

272. Yasmā pana yo ca hatthaggāho yo ca veṇiggāho yañca avasesassa aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ taṃ sabbampi bhedato dvādasavidhaṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ bhedaṃ dassetuṃ “āmasanā parāmasanā”tiādinā nayenassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yañca vuttaṃ “āmasanā nāma āmaṭṭhamattā”ti yañca “chupanaṃ nāma phuṭṭhamatta”nti, imesaṃ ayaṃ viseso – āmasanāti āmajjanā phuṭṭhokāsaṃ anatikkamitvāpi tattheva saṅghaṭṭanā. Ayañhi “āmaṭṭhamattā”ti vuccati. Chupananti asaṅghaṭṭetvā phuṭṭhamattaṃ.

272. Furthermore, because hand-grasping, braid-grasping, and the touching of a remaining limb are, by way of division, of twelve kinds, therefore, to show that division, the word analysis for this is given in the manner of 'touching, stroking,' and so on. Therein, regarding what was said, 'Touching (`āmasanā`) means mere stroking,' and 'Contact (`chupana`) means mere touching,' this is the distinction between them: 'Touching' (`āmasanā`) is rubbing; it is strong impact at the very point of contact, even without moving beyond it. This indeed is called 'mere stroking.' 'Contact' (`chupana`) is mere touching without strong impact.

Yampi [M 2.0122] ummasanāya ca ullaṅghanāya ca niddese “uddhaṃ uccāraṇā”ti ekameva padaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi ayaṃ viseso – paṭhamaṃ attano kāyassa itthiyā kāye uddhaṃ pesanavasena vuttaṃ, dutiyaṃ itthiyā kāyaṃ ukkhipanavasena, sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

And for the explanation of both 'rubbing upwards' (`ummasanā`) and 'raising up' (`ullaṅghanā`), the single term 'moving upwards' (`uddhaṃ uccāraṇā`) is stated. Here too, this is the distinction: the first is stated by way of sending one's own body upwards onto a woman's body; the second is stated by way of lifting up a woman's body. The rest is self-evident.

273. Idāni [P 3.0535] yvāyaṃ otiṇṇo vipariṇatena cittena kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjati, tassa etesaṃ padānaṃ vasena vitthārato āpattibhedaṃ dassento “itthī ca hoti itthisaññī sāratto ca bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā kāyena kāya”ntiādimāha. Tattha bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā kāyena kāyanti so sāratto ca itthisaññī ca bhikkhu attano kāyena. Nanti nipātamattaṃ. Atha vā etaṃ tassā itthiyā hatthādibhedaṃ kāyaṃ. Āmasati parāmasatīti etesu ce ekenāpi ākārena ajjhācarati, āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Tattha sakiṃ āmasato ekā āpatti, punappunaṃ āmasato payoge payoge saṅghādiseso.

273. Now, for that monk who, being overcome and with a perverted mind, engages in bodily contact, in order to show in detail the division of offenses by means of these terms, it is said: 'And it is a woman, and he perceives her as a woman, and he is lustful, and the monk with his body (touches) the woman's body,' and so on. Therein, 'the monk with his body (touches) the woman's body' means: that monk, being lustful and perceiving her as a woman, (touches) with his own body. 'Naṃ' is merely a particle. Or, it refers to this body of that woman, with its parts such as the hand. If he transgresses in any one of these ways, such as touching or stroking, there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa. Therein, for touching once, there is one offense; for touching repeatedly, there is a Saṅghādisesa for each application.

Parāmasantopi sace kāyato amocetvāva ito cito ca attano hatthaṃ vā kāyaṃ vā sañcopeti harati peseti divasampi parāmasato ekāva āpatti. Sace kāyato mocetvā mocetvā parāmasati payoge payoge āpatti.

Also, for one who is stroking, if, without releasing from the body, he moves his own hand or body to and fro, brings it back, or sends it forth, even if he strokes for a whole day, there is only one offense. If he strokes after repeatedly releasing from the body, there is an offense for each application.

Omasantopi [V 2.0110] sace kāyato amocetvāva itthiyā matthakato paṭṭhāya yāva pādapiṭṭhiṃ omasati ekāva āpatti. Sace pana udarādīsu taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā muñcitvā muñcitvā omasati payoge payoge āpatti. Ummasanāyapi pādato paṭṭhāya yāva sīsaṃ ummasantassa eseva nayo.

Also, for one who is stroking downwards, if, without releasing from the body, he strokes from the woman's head down to the top of her foot, there is only one offense. But if, having reached various places such as the chest, he repeatedly releases and then strokes downwards, there is an offense for each application. For stroking upwards as well, this same method applies for one who strokes from the foot up to the head.

Olaṅghanāya mātugāmaṃ kesesu gahetvā nāmetvā cumbanādīsu yaṃ ajjhācāraṃ icchati taṃ katvā muñcato ekāva āpatti. Uṭṭhitaṃ punappunaṃ nāmayato payoge payoge āpatti. Ullaṅghanāyapi kesesu vā hatthesu vā gahetvā vuṭṭhāpayato eseva nayo.

In the case of pulling down: for one who, having grasped a woman by the hair and bent her down, commits whatever transgression he desires, such as kissing, and then releases her, there is only one offense. For repeatedly bending down a woman who has stood up, there is an offense for each application. In the case of raising up as well, this same method applies for one who grasps her by the hair or hands and makes her stand up.

Ākaḍḍhanāya attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhanto yāva na muñcati tāva ekāva āpatti. Muñcitvā muñcitvā ākaḍḍhantassa payoge payoge āpatti. Patikaḍḍhanāyapi parammukhaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ gahetvā paṭippaṇāmayato eseva nayo.

In the case of pulling: for one who is pulling another towards himself, as long as he does not release, there is only one offense. For one who pulls after repeatedly releasing, there is an offense for each application. In the case of pushing away as well, this same method applies for one who grasps another from behind or by the back and pushes them away.

Abhiniggaṇhanāya [M 2.0123] hatthe vā bāhāya vā daḷhaṃ gahetvā yojanampi gacchato ekāva āpatti. Muñcitvā punappunaṃ gaṇhato payoge payoge āpatti. Amuñcitvā punappunaṃ phusato ca āliṅgato ca payoge payoge āpattīti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero [P 3.0536] panāha – “mūlaggahaṇameva pamāṇaṃ, tasmā yāva na muñcati tāva ekā eva āpattī”ti.

In the case of holding firmly: for one who, having grasped tightly by the hand or by the arm, goes even a yojana, there is only one offense. For one who releases and repeatedly grasps, there is an offense for each application. For one who, without releasing, repeatedly touches and embraces, there is an offense for each application—so said the Elder Mahāsumata. But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: 'The initial grasping alone is the standard; therefore, as long as one does not release, there is only one offense.'

Abhinippīḷanāya vatthena vā ābharaṇena vā saddhiṃ pīḷayato aṅgaṃ aphusantassa thullaccayaṃ, phusantassa saṅghādiseso, ekapayogena ekā āpatti, nānāpayogena nānā.

In the case of squeezing: for one who squeezes together with a cloth or an ornament, if he does not touch the limb, there is a thullaccaya offense; if he does touch it, there is a Saṅghādisesa. For one application, there is one offense; for various applications, various offenses.

Gahaṇachupanesu aññaṃ kiñci vikāraṃ akarontopi gahitamattaphuṭṭhamattenāpi āpattiṃ āpajjati.

In cases of grasping and touching, even without causing any other change, one incurs an offense merely by the act of grasping or the act of touching.

Evametesu āmasanādīsu ekenāpi ākārena ajjhācārato itthiyā itthisaññissa saṅghādiseso, vematikassa thullaccayaṃ, paṇḍakapurisatiracchānagatasaññissāpi thullaccayameva. Paṇḍake paṇḍakasaññissa thullaccayaṃ, vematikassa dukkaṭaṃ. Purisatiracchānagataitthisaññissāpi dukkaṭameva. Purise purisasaññissāpi vematikassāpi itthipaṇḍakatiracchānagatasaññissāpi dukkaṭameva. Tiracchānagatepi sabbākārena dukkaṭamevāti. Imā ekamūlakanaye vuttā āpattiyo sallakkhetvā imināva upāyena “dve itthiyo dvinnaṃ itthīna”ntiādivasena vutte dumūlakanayepi [V 2.0111] diguṇā āpattiyo veditabbā. Yathā ca dvīsu itthīsu dve saṅghādisesā; evaṃ sambahulāsu sambahulā veditabbā.

Thus, for one who transgresses in any of these ways, such as touching: with a woman, for one who perceives her as a woman, there is a Saṅghādisesa; for one who is uncertain, a thullaccaya; for one who perceives her as a paṇḍaka, a man, or an animal, it is also a thullaccaya. With a paṇḍaka, for one who perceives him as a paṇḍaka, there is a thullaccaya; for one who is uncertain, a dukkaṭa; for one who perceives him as a man, an animal, or a woman, it is also a dukkaṭa. With a man, for one who perceives him as a man, or is uncertain, or perceives him as a woman, a paṇḍaka, or an animal, it is also a dukkaṭa. With an animal, in all circumstances, it is only a dukkaṭa. Having noted these offenses stated in the single-root method, in the same way, the offenses in the double-root method—spoken of by way of 'two women, of two women,' and so on—should be understood as doubled. And just as for two women there are two Saṅghādisesa offenses, so for many women, many offenses should be understood.

Yo hi ekato ṭhitā sambahulā itthiyo bāhāhi parikkhipitvā gaṇhāti so yattakā itthiyo phuṭṭhā tāsaṃ gaṇanāya saṅghādisese āpajjati, majjhagatānaṃ gaṇanāya thullaccaye. Tā hi tena kāyappaṭibaddhena āmaṭṭhā honti. Yo pana sambahulānaṃ aṅguliyo vā kese vā ekato katvā gaṇhāti, so aṅguliyo ca kese ca agaṇetvā itthiyo gaṇetvā saṅghādisesehi kāretabbo. Yāsañca itthīnaṃ aṅguliyo vā kesā vā majjhagatā honti, tāsaṃ gaṇanāya thullaccaye āpajjati. Tā hi tena kāyappaṭibaddhena āmaṭṭhā honti, sambahulā pana itthiyo kāyappaṭibaddhehi rajjuvatthādīhi parikkhipitvā gaṇhanto sabbāsaṃyeva [M 2.0124] antoparikkhepagatānaṃ gaṇanāya thullaccaye āpajjati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ aphuṭṭhāsu dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā pāḷiyaṃ kāyappaṭibaddhappaṭibaddhena [P 3.0537] āmasanaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā sabbampi kāyappaṭibaddhappaṭibaddhaṃ kāyappaṭibaddheneva saṅgahetvā mahāaṭṭhakathāyañca kurundiyañca vutto purimanayoyevettha yuttataro dissati.

Indeed, a monk who encircles many women standing together with his arms and grasps them incurs Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of women touched, and thullaccaya offenses according to the number of those in the middle. For they are touched by him with what is connected to the body. But a monk who gathers the fingers or hairs of many women together and grasps them should be dealt with by Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the count of the women, not by counting the fingers or hairs. And for those women whose fingers or hairs are in the middle, he incurs thullaccaya offenses according to their number. For they are touched by him with what is connected to the body. However, a monk who encircles many women with things connected to the body, such as ropes or cloth, and grasps them, incurs thullaccaya offenses according to the number of all those within the enclosure. In the Mahāpaccarī, a dukkaṭa offense is stated for those not touched. Therein, since in the Pāḷi there is no such thing as touching with something connected to something connected to the body, therefore, by including all cases of 'what is connected to what is connected to the body' under 'what is connected to the body' itself, the previous method stated in both the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā and the Kurundī appears more suitable here.

Yo hi hatthena hatthaṃ gahetvā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhitāsu itthīsu samasārāgo ekaṃ hatthe gaṇhāti, so gahititthiyā vasena ekaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjati, itarāsaṃ gaṇanāya purimanayeneva thullaccaye. Sace so taṃ kāyappaṭibaddhe vatthe vā pupphe vā gaṇhāti, sabbāsaṃ gaṇanāya thullaccaye āpajjati. Yatheva hi rajjuvatthādīhi parikkhipantena sabbāpi kāyappaṭibaddhena āmaṭṭhā honti, tathā idhāpi sabbāpi kāyappaṭibaddhena āmaṭṭhā honti. Sace pana tā itthiyo aññamaññaṃ vatthakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā honti, tatra ceso purimanayeneva paṭhamaṃ itthiṃ hatthe gaṇhāti gahitāya vasena saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjati, itarāsaṃ gaṇanāya dukkaṭāni. Sabbāsañhi tāsaṃ tena purimanayeneva kāyapaṭibaddhena kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ āmaṭṭhaṃ hoti. Sace pana sopi taṃ kāyappaṭibaddheyeva gaṇhāti tassā vasena thullaccayaṃ āpajjati, itarāsaṃ gaṇanāya anantaranayeneva dukkaṭāni.

Indeed, if a monk, with equal lust, among women standing in a row holding hands, grasps one of them by the hand, he incurs one Saṅghādisesa offense on account of the woman grasped, and for the others, Thullaccaya offenses according to the previous method. If he grasps her by means of something connected to the body, such as a garment or a flower, he incurs Thullaccaya offenses according to the number of all of them. For just as when one encircles with things such as ropes or cloth, all are touched by what is connected to the body, so too here, all are touched by what is connected to the body. If, however, those women are standing holding one another's garment-hem, and if he, by the same previous method, grasps the first woman by the hand, he incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense on account of the one grasped, and for the others, Dukkaṭa offenses. For in the case of all of them, by that previous method, what is connected to a body has been touched by means of what is connected to a body. But if he also grasps her by what is connected to the body itself, he incurs a Thullaccaya offense on her account, and for the others, Dukkaṭa offenses by the immediately preceding method.

Yo pana ghanavatthanivatthaṃ itthiṃ kāyasaṃsaggarāgena vatthe ghaṭṭeti, thullaccayaṃ. Viraḷavatthanivatthaṃ ghaṭṭeti, tatra ce vatthantarehi itthiyā vā nikkhantalomāni bhikkhuṃ bhikkhuno vā paviṭṭhalomāni itthiṃ phusanti, ubhinnaṃ lomāniyeva vā lomāni phusanti, saṅghādiseso. Upādinnakena [V 2.0112] hi kammajarūpena upādinnakaṃ vā anupādinnakaṃ vā anupādinnakenapi kenaci kesādinā upādinnakaṃ vā anupādinnakaṃ vā phusantopi saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjatiyeva.

But a monk who, with lust for bodily contact, rubs against a woman wearing thick clothing on her clothing, incurs a Thullaccaya offense. If he rubs against a woman wearing thin clothing, and if, through the gaps in the cloth, the woman's protruding hairs touch the monk, or the monk's hairs that have entered touch the woman, or the hairs of both touch the hairs of the other, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. Indeed, by touching with an appropriated, kamma-born form—whether what is touched is appropriated or unappropriated—or even by touching with something unappropriated, such as hair, etc.—whether what is touched is appropriated or unappropriated—one indeed incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Tattha kurundiyaṃ “lomāni gaṇetvā saṅghādiseso”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “lomāni gaṇetvā āpattiyā na kāretabbo, ekameva saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjati. Saṅghikamañce pana apaccattharitvā nipanno lomāni gaṇetvā kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ[P 3.0538], tadeva yuttaṃ. Itthivasena hi ayaṃ āpatti, na koṭṭhāsavasenāti.

Therein, in the Kurundī it is stated: “Saṅghādisesa offenses are to be incurred by counting the hairs.” In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is stated: “One should not be dealt with for the offense by counting the hairs; one incurs only one Saṅghādisesa offense. But a monk who lies down on a Saṅgha couch without spreading a covering should be dealt with by counting the hairs.” That very view is proper. For this offense occurs on account of the woman, not on account of the parts.

Etthāha [M 2.0125] “yo pana ‘kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti kāyaṃ gaṇhāti, ‘kāyaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhāti, so kiṃ āpajjatī”ti. Mahāsumatthero tāva “yathāvatthukamevā”ti vadati. Ayaṃ kirassa laddhi –

Here a certain questioner asks: “But what of a monk who, thinking, ‘I will grasp what is connected to the body,’ grasps the body; or thinking, ‘I will grasp the body,’ grasps what is connected to the body—what offense does he incur?” First, the Elder Mahāsumatta says, “It is according to the actual object.” This, it seems, is his view:

“Vatthu saññā ca rāgo ca, phassappaṭivijānanā;

Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddese, garukaṃ tena kāraye”ti.

“The object, and perception, and lust, and the knowing of contact; in the exposition as pointed out, for that reason, one should be dealt with for the grave offense.”

Ettha “vatthū”ti itthī. “Saññā”ti itthisaññā. “Rāgo”ti kāyasaṃsaggarāgo. “Phassappaṭivijānanā”ti kāyasaṃsaggaphassajānanā. Tasmā yo itthiyā itthisaññī kāyasaṃsaggarāgena “kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ gahessāmī”ti pavattopi kāyaṃ phusati, garukaṃ saṅghādisesaṃyeva āpajjati. Itaropi thullaccayanti mahāpadumatthero panāha –

Herein, “object” is the woman. “Perception” is the perception of a woman. “Lust” is the lust for bodily contact. “The knowing of contact” is the knowing of the touch of bodily contact. Therefore, a monk who, perceiving a woman as a woman, with lust for bodily contact, even though proceeding with the thought, “I will grasp what is connected to the body,” touches the body, incurs the grave Saṅghādisesa offense itself. And the other one incurs a Thullaccaya offense. But the Elder Mahāpaduma says:

“Saññāya virāgitamhi, gahaṇe ca virāgite;

Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddese, garukaṃ tattha na dissatī”ti.

“When the perception is faulty, and the grasping is also faulty, a grave offense is not seen therein, in the exposition as pointed out.”

Assāpāyaṃ laddhi itthiyā itthisaññino hi saṅghādiseso vutto. Iminā ca itthisaññā virāgitā kāyappaṭibaddhe kāyappaṭibaddhasaññā uppāditā, taṃ gaṇhantassa pana thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā ca gahaṇampi virāgitaṃ taṃ aggahetvā itthī gahitā, tasmā ettha itthisaññāya abhāvato saṅghādiseso na dissati, kāyappaṭibaddhassa aggahitattā thullaccayaṃ na dissati, kāyasaṃsaggarāgena phuṭṭhattā pana dukkaṭaṃ. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgena hi imaṃ nāma vatthuṃ phusato anāpattīti natthi, tasmā dukkaṭamevāti.

This is also his view: Indeed, a Saṅghādisesa offense is stated for one who perceives a woman as a woman. And by this monk, the perception of 'woman' was made faulty; in what is connected to the body, the perception of 'what is connected to the body' was produced. But for one who grasps that, a Thullaccaya offense is stated. And by this one, the grasping was also made faulty; not grasping that, the woman was grasped. Therefore, here, due to the absence of the perception of a woman, a Saṅghādisesa offense is not seen; due to not grasping what is connected to the body, a Thullaccaya offense is not seen. However, due to touching with lust for bodily contact, a Dukkaṭa offense is seen. For indeed, there is no such thing as 'no offense' for one who touches any object whatsoever with lust for bodily contact; therefore, it is only a Dukkaṭa offense.

Idañca [V 2.0113] pana vatvā idaṃ catukkamāha. “Sārattaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti sārattaṃ gaṇhi saṅghādiseso, ‘virattaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti virattaṃ gaṇhi dukkaṭaṃ, ‘sārattaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti virattaṃ gaṇhi dukkaṭaṃ, ‘virattaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti sārattaṃ gaṇhi dukkaṭamevā”ti. Kiñcāpi evamāha?
