Atha kho mahāsumattheravādoyevettha “itthi ca hoti itthisaññī sāratto ca bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā kāyena kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ [P 3.0539] āmasati parāmasati…pe… gaṇhāti chupati āpatti thullaccayassā”ti imāya pāḷiyā “yo hi ekato ṭhitā sambahulā itthiyo bāhāhi parikkhipitvā gaṇhāti, so yattakā itthiyo phuṭṭhā tāsaṃ gaṇanāya saṅghādisese āpajjati, majjhagatānaṃ [M 2.0126] gaṇanāya thullaccaye”tiādīhi aṭṭhakathāvinicchayehi ca sameti. Yadi hi saññādivirāgena virāgitaṃ nāma bhaveyya “paṇḍako ca hoti itthisaññī”tiādīsu viya “kāyappaṭibaddhañca hoti kāyasaññī cā”tiādināpi nayena pāḷiyaṃ visesaṃ vadeyya. Yasmā pana so na vutto, tasmā itthiyā itthisaññāya sati itthiṃ āmasantassa saṅghādiseso, kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ āmasantassa thullaccayanti yathāvatthukameva yujjati.

And furthermore, having said this, he stated this tetrad: 'Thinking, “I will take a lustful person,” he takes a lustful person: it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. Thinking, “I will take a non-lustful person,” he takes a non-lustful person: it is a dukkaṭa offense. Thinking, “I will take a lustful person,” he takes a non-lustful person: it is a dukkaṭa offense. Thinking, “I will take a non-lustful person,” he takes a lustful person: it is only a dukkaṭa offense.' Although he said this, nevertheless, the view of the Elder Mahāsumatta is what is consistent here with this Pāḷi passage: 'There is a woman, and he perceives her as a woman... an offense of thullaccaya,' and with the resolutions of the Commentary, such as: 'For one who, standing in one place, embraces many women with his arms and takes hold of them, he falls into Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of women touched, and into thullaccaya offenses according to the number of those in the middle.' For if an act were indeed considered faulty due to an error in perception and so on, then, as in the cases beginning 'There is a paṇḍaka, and he perceives him as a woman,' the Pāḷi would also state a distinction by the method beginning 'There is something connected to the body, and he perceives it as the body.' But since that is not stated, it is therefore appropriate according to the object itself that when there is a woman and the perception of her as a woman, for one who touches the woman, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense, and for one who touches what is connected to her body, it is a thullaccaya offense.

Mahāpaccariyampi cetaṃ vuttaṃ – “nīlaṃ pārupitvā sayitāya kāḷitthiyā kāyaṃ ghaṭṭessāmī’ti kāyaṃ ghaṭṭeti, saṅghādiseso; ‘kāyaṃ ghaṭṭessāmī’ti nīlaṃ ghaṭṭeti, thullaccayaṃ; ‘nīlaṃ ghaṭṭessāmī’ti kāyaṃ ghaṭṭeti, saṅghādiseso; ‘nīlaṃ ghaṭṭessāmī’ti nīlaṃ ghaṭṭeti, thullaccaya”nti. Yopāyaṃ “itthī ca paṇḍako cā”tiādinā nayena vatthumissakanayo vutto, tasmimpi vatthu saññāvimativasena vuttā āpattiyo pāḷiyaṃ asammuyhantena veditabbā.

And this is also stated in the Mahāpaccarī: 'Thinking, “I will touch the body of the dark-skinned woman lying down covered in a blue garment,” he touches the body: it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. Thinking, “I will touch the body,” he touches the blue garment: it is a thullaccaya offense. Thinking, “I will touch the blue garment,” he touches the body: it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. Thinking, “I will touch the blue garment,” he touches the blue garment: it is a thullaccaya offense.' In that method of mixed objects which was stated by the method beginning, 'A woman and a paṇḍaka,' the offenses spoken of according to the object, perception, and doubt should be understood by one who is not confused regarding the Pāḷi.

Kāyenakāyappaṭibaddhavāre pana itthiyā itthisaññissa kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhato thullaccayaṃ, sese sabbattha dukkaṭaṃ. Kāyappaṭibaddhenakāyavārepi eseva nayo. Kāyappaṭibaddhenakaāyappaṭibaddhavāre ca nissaggiyenakāyavārādīsu cassa sabbattha dukkaṭameva.

Furthermore, in the section on touching what is connected to the body with the body, for one who perceives a woman as a woman, taking hold of what is connected to her body is a thullaccaya offense; in all other cases, it is a dukkaṭa offense. In the section on touching the body with what is connected to the body, this is the same method. And in the section on touching what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, and in the sections beginning with touching the body with a disposable item, in all cases it is only a dukkaṭa offense.

“Itthī ca hoti itthisaññī sāratto ca itthī ca naṃ bhikkhussa kāyena kāya”ntiādivāro pana bhikkhumhi mātugāmassa rāgavasena vutto. Tattha itthī ca naṃ bhikkhussa kāyena kāyanti bhikkhumhi sārattā itthī tassa nisinnokāsaṃ vā nipannokāsaṃ vā gantvā attano kāyena taṃ bhikkhussa kāyaṃ āmasati…pe… chupati. Sevanādhippāyo kāyena vāyamati, phassaṃ paṭivijānātīti evaṃ tāya āmaṭṭho vā chupito vā sevanādhippāyo hutvā sace phassappaṭivijānanatthaṃ īsakampi kāyaṃ cāleti phandeti, saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjati.

The section beginning, 'There is a woman, he perceives her as a woman, he is lustful, and a woman touches the monk's body with her body,' is stated on account of a woman's lust for a monk. Therein, 'a woman touches the monk's body with her body' means: a woman who is lustful towards the monk, having gone to the place where he is sitting or lying down, touches or makes contact with that monk's body with her own body. If, having been stroked or touched by her in this way, having the intention for intercourse, he moves or makes his body tremble even a little for the purpose of recognizing the touch, he falls into a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Dve [V 2.0114] itthiyoti ettha dve saṅghādisese āpajjati, itthiyā ca paṇḍake ca saṅghādisesena saha dukkaṭaṃ[P 3.0540]. Etena upāyena yāva “nissaggiyena nissaggiyaṃ āmasati, sevanādhippāyo kāyena vāyamati na ca phassaṃ paṭivijānāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti tāva purimanayeneva āpattibhedo veditabbo.

Here, in the case of 'two women,' he falls into two Saṅghādisesa offenses. In the case of a woman and a paṇḍaka, he falls into a dukkaṭa offense along with a Saṅghādisesa offense. By this method, the classification of offenses should be understood by the preceding method, up to the Pāḷi which states: 'He touches a disposable item with a disposable item; having the intention for intercourse, he makes an effort with the body but does not recognize the touch; it is a dukkaṭa offense.'

Ettha [M 2.0127] ca kāyena vāyamati na ca phassaṃ paṭivijānātīti attanā nissaṭṭhaṃ pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā itthiṃ attano nissaggiyena pupphena vā phalena vā paharantiṃ disvā kāyena vikāraṃ karoti, aṅguliṃ vā cāleti, bhamukaṃ vā ukkhipati, akkhiṃ vā nikhaṇati, aññaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vikāraṃ karoti, ayaṃ vuccati “kāyena vāyamati na ca phassaṃ paṭivijānātī”ti. Ayampi kāyena vāyamitattā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati, dvīsu itthīsu dve, itthīpaṇḍakesupi dve eva dukkaṭe āpajjati.

And here, 'he makes an effort with the body but does not recognize the touch' means this: after he himself has discarded a flower or fruit, seeing a woman striking him with her own disposable flower or fruit, he makes a physical gesture—he moves a finger, or raises an eyebrow, or winks an eye, or makes another such gesture. This is called 'he makes an effort with the body but does not recognize the touch.' This one also, because of having made an effort with the body, falls into a dukkaṭa offense. In the case of two women, he falls into two dukkaṭa offenses; in the case of a woman and a paṇḍaka, he also falls into two dukkaṭa offenses.

279. Evaṃ vatthuvasena vitthārato āpattibhedaṃ dassetvā idāni lakkhaṇavasena saṅkhepato āpattibhedañca anāpattibhedañca dassento “sevanādhippāyo”tiādimāha. Tattha purimanaye itthiyā phuṭṭho samāno sevanādhippāyo kāyena vāyamati, phassaṃ paṭivijānātīti tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso. Dutiye naye nissaggiyena nissaggiyāmasane viya vāyamitvā achupane viya ca phassassa appaṭivijānanato duvaṅgasampattiyā dukkaṭaṃ. Tatiye kāyena avāyamato anāpatti. Yo hi sevanādhippāyopi niccalena kāyena kevalaṃ phassaṃ paṭivijānāti sādiyati anubhoti, tassa cittuppādamatte āpattiyā abhāvato anāpatti. Catutthe pana nissaggiyena nissaggiyāmasane viya phassappaṭivijānanāpi natthi, kevalaṃ cittuppādamattameva, tasmā anāpatti. Mokkhādhippāyassa sabbākāresu anāpattiyeva.

279. Having thus shown in detail the classification of offenses according to the object, now, showing in brief the classification of offenses and non-offenses according to their characteristics, he said what begins with 'having the intention for intercourse.' Therein, in the first method: when touched by a woman, if one has the intention for intercourse, makes an effort with the body, and recognizes the touch—due to the fulfillment of these three factors, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. In the second method, due to making an effort but not recognizing the touch, it is a dukkaṭa offense due to the fulfillment of two factors. In the third method, due to not making an effort with the body, there is no offense. For one who, although having the intention for intercourse, with an unmoving body merely recognizes, consents to, and experiences the touch, for him there is no offense, because there is no offense in the mere arising of a thought. But in the fourth method, there is not even the recognition of touch; there is only the mere arising of a thought. Therefore, there is no offense. For one whose intention is for release, in all circumstances, there is no offense at all.

Ettha pana yo itthiyā gahito taṃ attano sarīrā mocetukāmo paṭippaṇāmeti vā paharati vā ayaṃ kāyena vāyamati phassaṃ paṭivijānāti. Yo āgacchantiṃ disvā tato muñcitukāmo uttāsetvā palāpeti, ayaṃ kāyena vāyamati na ca phassaṃ paṭivijānāti. Yo tādisaṃ dīghajātiṃ kāye ārūḷhaṃ disvā “saṇikaṃ gacchatu ghaṭṭiyamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyā”ti [P 3.0541] na ghaṭṭeti, itthimeva vā aṅgaṃ phusamānaṃ ñatvā “esā ‘anatthiko ayaṃ mayā’ti sayameva pakkamissatī”ti ajānanto viya niccalo hoti, balavitthiyā vā gāḷhaṃ āliṅgitvā gahito daharabhikkhu palāyitukāmopi suṭṭhu gahitattā niccalo hoti, ayaṃ na ca kāyena vāyamati, phassaṃ paṭivijānāti. Yo pana āgacchantiṃ disvā “āgacchatu [V 2.0115] tāva tato naṃ paharitvā vā paṇāmetvā [M 2.0128] vā pakkamissāmī”ti niccalo hoti, ayaṃ mokkhādhippāyo na ca kāyena vāyamati, na ca phassaṃ paṭivijānātīti veditabbo.

Here, a monk who, having been seized by a woman, desires to free himself from her body and pushes her away or strikes her—this one strives with the body and knows the contact. A monk who, seeing a woman approaching, desires to be free from her, frightens her and makes her flee—this one strives with the body but does not know the contact. A monk who, seeing a long-bodied creature such as a snake crawling on his body, thinks, 'Let it go slowly; if struck, it could lead to harm,' and does not strike it; or, knowing that a woman is touching his limb, thinks, 'She will depart on her own, knowing that, “This monk has no need of me,”' and remains motionless as if not knowing; or a young monk who, being seized and tightly embraced by a strong woman, though desiring to escape, remains motionless because of being held very firmly—this one does not strive with the body, but knows the contact. But a monk who, seeing a woman approaching, remains motionless, thinking, 'Let her come first; then I will depart after striking or pushing her'—this one should be understood as having the intention of release, but not striving with the body, nor knowing the contact.

280. Asañciccāti iminā upāyena imaṃ phusissāmīti acetetvā, evañhi acetetvā pattappaṭiggahaṇādīsu mātugāmassa aṅge phuṭṭhepi anāpatti.

280. ‘Unintentionally’ means without intending, “By this means I will touch this woman.” For, thus without intending, even if one touches a woman's limb when receiving a bowl and so on, there is no offense.

Asatiyāti aññavihito hoti mātugāmaṃ phusāmīti sati natthi, evaṃ asatiyā hatthapādapasāraṇādikāle phusantassa anāpatti.

‘Through lack of mindfulness’ means one's mind is directed elsewhere; the mindfulness, “I am touching a woman,” is not present. Thus, for one who touches due to lack of mindfulness at the time of stretching out a hand or foot, etc., there is no offense.

Ajānantassāti dārakavesena ṭhitaṃ dārikaṃ “itthī”ti ajānanto kenacideva karaṇīyena phusati, evaṃ “itthī”ti ajānantassa phusato anāpatti.

‘For one not knowing’ means that one, not knowing that a young girl standing in the guise of a boy is a woman, touches her for some necessary reason. Thus, for one who touches without knowing she is a woman, there is no offense.

Asādiyantassāti kāyasaṃsaggaṃ asādiyantassa, tassa bāhāparamparāya nītabhikkhussa viya anāpatti. Ummattakādayo vuttanayāeva. Idha pana udāyitthero ādikammiko, tassa anāpatti ādikammikassāti.

‘For one not consenting’ means for one not enjoying physical contact. For him, like the monk who was led by a chain of arms, there is no offense. The cases of the insane and others are as has been stated. Here, however, the Elder Udāyi was the original transgressor; for him, as the original transgressor, there is no offense.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the word-analysis is finished.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyacittato samuṭṭhāti, kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dvivedanaṃ, sukhamajjhattadvayenāti.

Regarding the origins and so forth, this training rule has the same origin as the first pārājika rule. It arises from body and mind; it is an action, not exempt due to perception, intentional, blameworthy in the world, a bodily action, with unwholesome consciousness, and associated with two feelings, namely, pleasure and equanimity.

281. Vinītavatthūsu – mātuyā mātupemenāti mātupemena mātuyā kāyaṃ āmasi. Esa nayo dhītubhaginivatthūsu. Tattha yasmā mātā vā hotu dhītā vā itthī nāma sabbāpi brahmacariyassa pāripanthikāva. Tasmā “ayaṃ me mātā ayaṃ dhītā ayaṃ me bhaginī”ti gehassitapemena āmasatopi dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ.

281. In the decided cases: ‘with affection for a mother’ means he touched his mother's body with affection for his mother. This is the same principle in the cases of a daughter and a sister. Therein, because whether it is a mother or a daughter, any woman whatsoever is an obstacle to the holy life. Therefore, even for touching them with household-based affection, thinking, “This is my mother, this is my daughter, this is my sister,” an offense of wrong-doing is stated.

Imaṃ pana bhagavato āṇaṃ anussarantena sacepi nadīsotena vuyhamānaṃ mātaraṃ passati neva hatthena parāmasitabbā. Paṇḍitena pana bhikkhunā nāvā vā phalakaṃ [P 3.0542] vā kadalikkhandho vā dārukkhandho vā upasaṃharitabbo. Tasmiṃ asati kāsāvampi upasaṃharitvā purato ṭhapetabbaṃ, “ettha [M 2.0129][V 2.0116] gaṇhāhī”ti pana na vattabbā. Gahite parikkhāraṃ kaḍḍhāmīti kaḍḍhantena gantabbaṃ. Sace bhāyati purato purato gantvā “mā bhāyī”ti samassāsetabbā. Sace bhāyamānā puttassa sahasā khandhe vā abhiruhati, hatthe vā gaṇhāti, na “apehi mahallike”ti niddhunitabbā, thalaṃ pāpetabbā. Kaddame laggāyapi kūpe patitāyapi eseva nayo.

But a monk recollecting this command of the Blessed One, even if he sees his mother being swept away by a river current, should not touch her by hand. A wise monk, however, should bring near a boat, a plank, a banana trunk, or a log. If these are not available, he should bring his robe near and place it in front of her. But he should not say, “Take hold here.” Once she has taken hold, he should proceed by pulling, with the thought, ‘I am pulling my requisite.’ If she is afraid, he should go in front of her and reassure her, saying, “Do not be afraid.” If, being afraid, she suddenly climbs onto her son's shoulder or grabs his hand, she should not be shaken off with the words, “Go away, old woman.” She should be brought to dry land. This is the same principle if she is stuck in mud or has fallen into a well.

Tatrapi hi yottaṃ vā vatthaṃ vā pakkhipitvā hatthena gahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā uddharitabbā, natveva āmasitabbā. Na kevalañca mātugāmassa sarīrameva anāmāsaṃ, nivāsanapāvuraṇampi ābharaṇabhaṇḍampi tiṇaṇḍupakaṃ vā tāḷapaṇṇamuddikaṃ vā upādāya anāmāsameva, tañca kho nivāsanapārupanaṃ piḷandhanatthāya ṭhapitameva. Sace pana nivāsanaṃ vā pārupanaṃ vā parivattetvā cīvaratthāya pādamūle ṭhapeti vaṭṭati. Ābharaṇabhaṇḍesu pana sīsapasādhanakadantasūciādikappiyabhaṇḍaṃ “imaṃ bhante tumhākaṃ gaṇhathā”ti diyyamānaṃ sipāṭikāsūciādiupakaraṇatthāya gahetabbaṃ. Suvaṇṇarajatamuttādimayaṃ pana anāmāsameva dīyyamānampi na gahetabbaṃ. Na kevalañca etāsaṃ sarīrūpagameva anāmāsaṃ, itthisaṇṭhānena kataṃ kaṭṭharūpampi dantarūpampi ayarūpampi loharūpampi tipurūpampi potthakarūpampi sabbaratanarūpampi antamaso piṭṭhamayarūpampi anāmāsameva. Paribhogatthāya pana “idaṃ tumhākaṃ hotū”ti labhitvā ṭhapetvā sabbaratanamayaṃ avasesaṃ bhinditvā upakaraṇārahaṃ upakaraṇe paribhogārahaṃ paribhoge upanetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Indeed, even in that case, having thrown in a rope or a cloth, and knowing that it has been grasped by hand, she should be pulled out, but she should certainly not be touched. And not only is a woman’s body not to be touched, but also her lower garment, outer garment, ornaments—even down to a grass ring or a palm-leaf ring—are not to be touched. And that is with respect to a lower garment and outer garment that are placed for the purpose of being worn. But if she exchanges her lower or outer garment and places it at his feet for the purpose of a robe, it is allowable to touch it. As for ornaments, allowable items like a head ornament or an ivory pin, if given with the words, “Venerable sirs, take this for yourselves,” may be accepted for the purpose of requisites like a pouch or needle. But things made of gold, silver, pearls, and so on are not to be touched; even if given, they should not be accepted. And not only are things that go on their bodies not to be touched, but also a figure made in the shape of a woman—whether a wooden figure, an ivory figure, an iron figure, a bronze figure, a tin figure, a cloth figure, any jeweled figure, or even down to a figure made of flour—is not to be touched. But if, for the purpose of use, having received it with the words, “Let this be for you,” and having set aside any made entirely of jewels, one may break up the rest; what is suitable for requisites may be applied to requisites, and what is suitable for use may be applied to use.

Yathā ca itthirūpakaṃ; evaṃ sattavidhampi dhaññaṃ anāmāsaṃ. Tasmā khettamajjhena gacchatā tatthajātakampi dhaññaphalaṃ na āmasantena gantabbaṃ. Sace gharadvāre vā antarāmagge vā dhaññaṃ pasāritaṃ hoti passena ca maggo atthi [P 3.0543] na maddantena gantabbaṃ. Gamanamagge asati maggaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gantabbaṃ. Antaraghare dhaññassa upari āsanaṃ paññāpetvā denti nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Keci āsanasālāyaṃ dhaññaṃ ākiranti, sace sakkā hoti harāpetuṃ harāpetabbaṃ, no ce ekamantaṃ dhaññaṃ amaddantena pīṭhakaṃ paññapetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Sace okāso na hoti, manussā dhaññamajjheyeva āsanaṃ paññapetvā denti, nisīditabbaṃ. Tatthajātakāni muggamāsādīni aparaṇṇānipi tālapanasādīni vā phalāni kīḷantena na āmasitabbāni. Manussehi rāsikatesupi eseva nayo. Araññe pana rukkhato patitāni phalāni “anupasampannānaṃ dassāmī”ti gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati.

Just as with a figure of a woman, so too are the seven kinds of grain not to be touched. Therefore, when walking through the middle of a field, one should go without touching the fruit of the grain growing there. If grain is spread out at the door of a house or along the path, and there is a path to the side, one should go without trampling it. If there is no path for walking, one should determine a path and proceed. Inside a house, if they spread a seat over grain and offer it, it is permissible to sit. Some scatter grain in a sitting hall; if it can be removed, it should be removed. If not, one should set up a stool to one side without crushing the grain and then sit. If there is no space, and people prepare a seat right in the middle of the grain and offer it, one should sit. Legumes such as green gram and black gram, or fruits such as palm and jackfruit growing there should not be touched playfully. This same rule applies to those piled up by people. In the forest, however, it is permissible to pick up fruits that have fallen from a tree, thinking, 'I will give them to those who are not fully ordained.'

Muttā[M 2.0130], maṇi, veḷuriyo, saṅkho, silā, pavāḷaṃ, rajataṃ, jātarūpaṃ, lohitaṅko, masāragallanti [V 2.0117] imesu dasasu ratanesu muttā adhotā anividdhā yathājātāva āmasituṃ vaṭṭati. Sesā anāmāsāti vadanti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “muttā dhotāpi adhotāpi anāmāsā bhaṇḍamūlatthāya ca sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati, kuṭṭharogassa bhesajjatthāya pana vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Antamaso jātiphalikaṃ upādāya sabbopi nīlapītādivaṇṇabhedo maṇi dhotaviddhavaṭṭito anāmāso, yathājāto pana ākaramutto pattādibhaṇḍamūlatthaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatīti vutto. Sopi mahāpaccariyaṃ paṭikkhitto, pacitvā kato kācamaṇiyeveko vaṭṭatīti vutto. Veḷuriyepi maṇisadisova vinicchayo.

Pearl, gem, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat's-eye—among these ten precious things, a pearl that is unwashed and unpierced can be touched just as it is by nature. The rest, they say, are not to be touched. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is stated: 'Pearls, whether washed or unwashed, are not to be touched, nor is it permissible to accept them for the value of goods; but it is permissible to accept them as medicine for leprosy.' Furthermore, any gem of varied color such as blue or yellow, up to and including natural crystal, once washed, pierced, and polished, is not to be touched. But an uncut gem, just as it comes from the mine, it is said, is permissible to accept for the value of goods such as a bowl. This too is rejected in the Mahāpaccariya, where it is said that only a single type of glass gem that is fired and made is permissible. For beryl, the ruling is the same as for a gem.

Saṅkho dhamanasaṅkho ca dhotaviddho ca ratanamisso anāmāso. Pānīyasaṅkho dhotopi adhotopi āmāsova sesañca añjanādibhesajjatthāyapi bhaṇḍamūlatthāyapi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Silā dhotaviddhā ratanasaṃyuttā muggavaṇṇāva anāmāsā. Sesā satthakanisānādiatthāya gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Ettha ca ratanasaṃyuttāti suvaṇṇena saddhiṃ yojetvā pacitvā katāti vadanti. Pavāḷaṃ dhotaviddhaṃ anāmāsaṃ. Sesaṃ āmāsaṃ bhaṇḍamūlatthañca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ [P 3.0544] pana “dhotampi adhotampi sabbaṃ anāmāsaṃ, na ca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

A blowing conch that is washed, pierced, and mixed with jewels is not to be touched. A conch for drinking water, whether washed or unwashed, is to be touched; and the remainder is permissible to accept for the purpose of collyrium and other medicines, or for the value of goods. A crystal that is washed, pierced, joined with jewels, and has the color of green gram is not to be touched. The remainder is permissible to take for the purpose of a small knife, whetstone, and the like. Here, 'joined with jewels' means, they say, that which is combined with gold, fired, and made. Coral that is washed and pierced is not to be touched. The rest is to be touched, and it is permissible to accept it for the value of goods. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is stated: 'All coral, whether washed or unwashed, is not to be touched, nor is it permissible to accept it.'

Rajataṃ jātarūpañca katabhaṇḍampi akatabhaṇḍampi sabbena sabbaṃ bījato paṭṭhāya anāmāsañca asampaṭicchiyañca, uttararājaputto kira suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ kāretvā mahāpadumattherassa pesesi. Thero “na kappatī”ti paṭikkhipi. Cetiyaghare suvaṇṇapadumasuvaṇṇabubbuḷakādīni honti, etānipi anāmāsāni. Cetiyagharagopakā pana rūpiyachaḍḍakaṭṭhāne ṭhitā, tasmā tesaṃ keḷāpayituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana taṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Suvaṇṇacetiye kacavarameva harituṃ vaṭṭatīti ettakameva anuññātaṃ. Ārakūṭalohampi jātarūpagatikameva anāmāsanti sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Senāsanaparibhogo pana sabbakappiyo, tasmā jātarūparajatamayā sabbepi senāsanaparikkhārā āmāsā. Bhikkhūnaṃ dhammavinayavaṇṇanaṭṭhāne ratanamaṇḍape [M 2.0131] karonti phalikatthambhe ratanadāmapatimaṇḍite, tattha sabbūpakaraṇāni bhikkhūnaṃ paṭijaggituṃ vaṭṭati.

Silver and gold, whether worked or unworked, are in every way and entirely, from their very origin, not to be touched and not to be received. It is said that Prince Uttara had a golden shrine made and sent it to the Elder Mahāpaduma. The Elder rejected it, saying, 'It is not allowable.' In the shrine house, there are golden lotuses, golden bubbles, and the like; these too are not to be touched. The guardians of the shrine house, however, stand in the position of one who discards money; therefore, it is said that it is allowable for them to move these items. But in the Kurundiya, this is rejected. In a golden shrine, only removing the refuse is allowable; only this much is permitted. Brass and bronze are also like gold and not to be touched, as is stated in all the commentaries. The use of lodgings, however, is entirely allowable. Therefore, all lodging requisites made of gold and silver are to be touched. In the place where the Dhamma and Vinaya are explained to the monks, they make jeweled pavilions with crystal pillars, adorned with garlands of gems. There, it is allowable for the monks to attend to all the furnishings.

Lohitaṅkamasāragallā dhotaviddhā anāmāsā, itare āmāsā, bhaṇḍamūlatthāya vaṭṭantīti vuttā. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “dhotāpi adhotāpi sabbaso anāmāsā na ca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ.

Rubies and cat's-eyes, when washed and pierced, are not to be touched. The others are to be touched, and it is said that they are permissible to accept for the value of goods. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is stated: 'Whether washed or unwashed, they are in every way not to be touched, nor is it permissible to accept them.'

Sabbaṃ āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ anāmāsaṃ, bhaṇḍamūlatthāya dīyyamānampi na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Satthavaṇijjā [V 2.0118] nāma na vaṭṭati. Suddhadhanudaṇḍopi dhanujiyāpi patodopi aṅkusopi antamaso vāsipharasuādīnipi āvudhasaṅkhepena katāni anāmāsāni. Sace kenaci vihāre satti vā tomaro vā ṭhapito hoti, vihāraṃ jaggantena “harantū”ti sāmikānaṃ pesetabbaṃ. Sace na haranti, taṃ acālentena vihāro paṭijaggitabbo. Yuddhabhūmiyaṃ patitaṃ asiṃ vā sattiṃ vā tomaraṃ vā disvā pāsāṇena vā kenaci vā asiṃ bhinditvā satthakatthāya gahetuṃ vaṭṭati, itarānipi viyojetvā [P 3.0545] kiñci satthakatthāya gahetuṃ vaṭṭati kiñci kattaradaṇḍādiatthāya. “Idaṃ gaṇhathā”ti dīyyamānaṃ pana “vināsetvā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ karissāmī”ti sabbampi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati.

All weapons are not to be touched. Even if given for the value of goods, they should not be received, for trading in weapons is not permissible. Even a simple bow-staff, a bowstring, a goad, a hook, or even an adze, axe, and the like—if made in the manner of a weapon—are not to be touched. If someone has placed a spear or a javelin in a monastery, the monk maintaining the monastery should send a message to the owners, saying, 'Take them away.' If they do not take them, the monastery should be maintained without moving them. If one sees a sword, spear, or javelin fallen on a battlefield, it is permissible to break the sword with a stone or something else and take it for the purpose of a small knife. It is also permissible to dismantle the other weapons and take a part for the purpose of a small knife and another part for the purpose of a walking stick and the like. However, if a weapon is offered with the words, 'Take this,' it is permissible to accept it all, thinking, 'I will render it unusable as a weapon and make an allowable requisite.'

Macchajālapakkhijālādīnipi phalakajālikādīni saraparittānānīpi sabbāni anāmāsāni. Paribhogatthāya labbhamānesu pana jālaṃ tāva “āsanassa vā cetiyassa vā upari bandhissāmi, chattaṃ vā veṭhessāmī”ti gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Saraparittānaṃ sabbampi bhaṇḍamūlatthāya sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Parūparodhanivāraṇañhi etaṃ na uparodhakaranti phalakaṃ dantakaṭṭhabhājanaṃ karissāmīti gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Fishing nets, bird nets, and the like; latticed planks and the like; and arrow-guards—all these are not to be touched. However, among those that are obtained for use, it is first allowable to take a net, thinking, 'I will tie it above a seat or a cetiya, or I will wrap an umbrella with it.' It is allowable to accept any arrow-guard for the value of goods. For indeed, this is for preventing oppression by others, not for causing oppression. It is allowable to take a plank, thinking, 'I will make a tooth-stick container.'

Cammavinaddhāni vīṇābheriādīni anāmāsāni. Kurundiyaṃ pana “bherisaṅghāṭopi vīṇāsaṅghāṭopi tucchapokkharampi mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ āropitacammampi vīṇādaṇḍakopi sabbaṃ anāmāsa”nti vuttaṃ. Onahituṃ vā onahāpetuṃ vā vādetuṃ vā vādāpetuṃ vā na labbhatiyeva. Cetiyaṅgaṇe pūjaṃ katvā manussehi chaḍḍitaṃ disvāpi acāletvāva antarantare sammajjitabbaṃ, kacavarachaḍḍanakāle pana kacavaraniyāmeneva haritvā ekamantaṃ nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhaṇḍamūlatthāya sampaṭicchitumpi vaṭṭati. Paribhogatthāya labbhamānesu pana vīṇādoṇikañca bheripokkharañca dantakaṭṭhabhājanaṃ [M 2.0132] karissāma cammaṃ satthakakosakanti evaṃ tassa tassa parikkhārassa upakaraṇatthāya gahetvā tathā tathā kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

Musical instruments such as lutes and drums bound with leather are not to be touched. However, in the Kurundī it is said: 'A large drum with bound leather, a lute with bound leather, an empty drum-body or lute-body, leather attached to the rim, and the neck of a lute—all are not to be touched.' It is not allowable at all to bind it oneself, to have another bind it, to play it oneself, or to have another play it. Even upon seeing such an item discarded by people after making an offering in a cetiya courtyard, one should sweep in between without moving it. However, at the time of discarding rubbish, it is allowable to carry it away and place it in a secluded spot, only with the perception of it as rubbish; so it is said in the Mahāpaccarī. It is also allowable to accept it for the value of the goods. However, among those items obtained for use, it is allowable to take the body of a lute and the body of a drum, thinking, 'We will make a tooth-stick container,' and the leather, thinking, 'We will make a sheath for a small knife,' and thus, having taken them to serve as accessories for those various requisites, to make them accordingly.

Purāṇadutiyikāvatthu uttānameva. Yakkhivatthusmiṃ sacepi paranimmitavasavattideviyā kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjati thullaccayameva. Paṇḍakavatthu ca suttitthivatthu ca pākaṭameva. Matitthivatthusmiṃ pārājikappahonakakāle thullaccayaṃ, tato paraṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Tiracchānagatavatthusmiṃ [P 3.0546] nāgamāṇavikāyapi supaṇṇamāṇavikāyapi kinnariyāpi gāviyāpi dukkaṭameva. Dārudhītalikāvatthusmiṃ [V 2.0119] na kevalaṃ dārunā eva, antamaso cittakammalikhitepi itthirūpe dukkaṭameva.

The story of the former wife is self-evident. In the story of the yakkhiṇī, even if one were to engage in physical contact with a goddess of the Paranimmitavasavattī realm, it is only a thullaccaya offense. The story of the paṇḍaka and the story of the sleeping woman are clear. In the story of the dead woman, at the time when it is sufficient for a pārājika, it is a thullaccaya offense; after that, it is a dukkaṭa offense. In the story of an animal, for one who engages in physical contact with a young nāga female, a young supaṇṇa female, a kinnarī, or a cow, it is only a dukkaṭa offense. In the story of the wooden female figure, for engaging in physical contact with a female figure made solely of wood, there is no dukkaṭa offense; however, for engaging in physical contact with a female figure, even one drawn in elaborate painting, it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense.

282. Sampīḷanavatthu uttānatthameva. Saṅkamavatthusmiṃ ekapadikasaṅkamo vā hotu sakaṭamaggasaṅkamo vā, cālessāmīti payoge katamatteva cāletu vā mā vā, dukkaṭaṃ. Maggavatthu pākaṭameva. Rukkhavatthusmiṃ rukkho mahanto vā hotu mahājambuppamāṇo khuddako vā, taṃ cāletuṃ sakkotu vā mā vā, payogamattena dukkaṭaṃ. Nāvāvatthusmimpi eseva nayo. Rajjavatthusmiṃ yaṃ rajjuṃ āviñchanto ṭhānā cāletuṃ sakkoti, tattha thullaccayaṃ. Yā mahārajju hoti, īsakampi ṭhānā na calati, tattha dukkaṭaṃ. Daṇḍepi eseva nayo. Bhūmiyaṃ patitamahārukkhopi hi daṇḍaggahaṇeneva idha gahito. Pattavatthu pākaṭameva. Vandanavatthusmiṃ itthī pāde sambāhitvā vanditukāmā vāretabbā pādā vā paṭicchādetabbā, niccalena vā bhavitabbaṃ. Niccalassa hi cittena sādiyatopi anāpatti. Avasāne gahaṇavatthupākaṭamevāti.

282. The story of being pressed has a clear meaning. In the story of the bridge, be it a small bridge that can be crossed in a single step or a cart-road bridge, merely upon making the effort with the thought, 'I will shake it,' it is a dukkaṭa offense, whether it shakes or not. The story of the road is clear. In the story of the tree, be the tree large, the size of the great Jambu tree, or small, and whether one is able to shake it or not, it is a dukkaṭa offense by the mere effort. In the story of the boat, this is the same principle. In the story of the rope, when pulling a rope that one is able to move from its place, in that case it is a thullaccaya offense. When it is a large rope that does not move from its place even slightly, in that case it is a dukkaṭa offense. In the case of a staff, this is the same principle. Indeed, even a great tree fallen on the ground is included here by the word 'staff'. The story of the bowl is clear. In the story of veneration, if a woman, wishing to venerate, massages the feet, she should be prevented, or the feet should be covered, or one should remain motionless. Indeed, for one who is motionless, there is no offense even if one acquiesces with the mind. In the end, the story of intending to touch is clear.

Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on physical contact is concluded.

3. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lewd Speech

283. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha ādissāti apadisitvā. Vaṇṇampi bhaṇatītiādīni parato āvi bhavissanti. Chinnikāti chinnaottappā. Dhuttikāti saṭhā. Ahirikāyoti nillajjā[M 2.0133]. Uhasantīti sitaṃ katvā mandahasitaṃ hasanti. Ullapantīti “aho ayyo”tiādinā nayena uccakaraṇiṃ nānāvidhaṃ palobhanakathaṃ kathenti. Ujjagghantīti mahāhasitaṃ hasanti. Uppaṇḍentīti “paṇḍako ayaṃ, nāyaṃ puriso”tiādinā [P 3.0547] nayena parihāsaṃ karonti.

283. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... this is the training rule on lewd speech. Therein, 'ādissa' means having pointed out. The phrases beginning with 'vaṇṇampi bhaṇati' will become clear later on. 'Chinnikā' means those whose fear of wrongdoing is cut off. 'Dhuttikā' means deceitful. 'Ahirikāyo' means shameless. 'Uhasanti' means, having made a smile, they laugh a gentle laugh. 'Ullapanti' means they speak various kinds of enticing words that are elevating, by way of saying, “Oh, noble sir!” and so on. 'Ujjagghanti' means they laugh a great laugh. 'Uppaṇḍenti' means they make a mockery by way of saying, “This one is a eunuch; this one is not a man,” and so on.

285. Sārattoti duṭṭhullavācassādarāgena sāratto. Apekkhavā paṭibaddhacittoti vuttanayameva, kevalaṃ idha vācassādarāgo yojetabbo. Mātugāmaṃ duṭṭhullāhi vācāhīti ettha adhippetaṃ mātugāmaṃ dassento “mātugāmo”tiādimāha. Tattha viññū paṭibalā subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullaṃ ājānitunti yā paṇḍitā sātthakaniratthakakathaṃ asaddhammasaddhammapaṭisaṃyuttakathañca jānituṃ paṭibalā, ayaṃ idha adhippetā. Yā pana mahallikāpi bālā elamūgā ayaṃ idha anadhippetāti dasseti.

285. 'Sāratto' means infatuated by the lust that delights in lewd speech. 'Apekkhavā paṭibaddhacitto' is just as was explained before; only here, the lust that delights in speech should be applied. In the phrase 'to a woman with lewd speech,' wishing to show the intended woman, he said, 'mātugāmo,' and so on. Therein, 'viññū... ājānitun'ti' means: whatever woman is wise and capable of understanding meaningful and meaningless talk, and talk connected with the practice of the unvirtuous and the virtuous—this woman is intended here. But a woman who, though elderly, is a drivelling fool, is not intended here; this is what is shown.

Obhāseyyāti [V 2.0120] avabhāseyya nānāppakārakaṃ asaddhammavacanaṃ vadeyya. Yasmā panevaṃ obhāsantassa yo so obhāso nāma, so atthato ajjhācāro hoti rāgavasena abhibhavitvā saññamavelaṃ ācāro, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “obhāseyyāti ajjhācāro vuccatī”ti āha. Yathā tanti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ, yathā yuvā yuvatinti attho.

'Obhāseyya' means he might speak basely; he might speak various kinds of speech connected with the practice of the unvirtuous. Because for one who speaks basely in this way, that which is called 'base speech' is, in its essential meaning, a transgression—conduct that, by the power of lust, overcomes the boundary of restraint. Therefore, to show that meaning, he said, “'Obhāseyya' is called a transgression.” In the text 'yathā taṃ,' the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle. The meaning is: just as a young man speaks basely to a young woman.

Dve magge ādissātiādi yenākārena obhāsato saṅghādiseso hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha dve maggeti vaccamaggañca passāvamaggañca. Sesaṃ uddese tāva pākaṭameva. Niddese pana thometīti “itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”ti vadati, na tāva sīsaṃ eti. “Tava vaccamaggo ca passāvamaggo ca īdiso tena nāma īdisena itthilakkhaṇena subhalakkhaṇena samannāgatāsī”ti vadati, sīsaṃ eti, saṅghādiseso. Vaṇṇeti pasaṃsatīti imāni pana thomanapadasseva vevacanāni.

'Dve magge ādissa,' and so on, was said to show the manner in which a Saṅghādisesa offense occurs for one who speaks basely. Therein, 'dve magge' means the passage for feces and the passage for urine. The rest, in the summary section, is already clear. In the detailed explanation, however, 'thometi' means he says, “You are endowed with the characteristics of a woman, with beautiful characteristics”; this does not yet reach the peak. If he says, “Your passage for feces and passage for urine are like this; you are endowed with such-and-such a female characteristic, with that so-called beautiful characteristic,” it reaches the peak; it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. 'Vaṇṇeti' and 'pasaṃsati' are synonyms for the word 'thometi'.

Khuṃsetīti vācāpatodena ghaṭṭeti. Vambhetīti apasādeti. Garahatīti dosaṃ deti. Parato pana pāḷiyā āgatehi “animittāsī”tiādīhi [M 2.0134] ekādasahi padehi aghaṭite sīsaṃ na eti, ghaṭitepi tesu sikharaṇīsi sambhinnāsi ubhatobyañjanāsīti imehi tīhi ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso.

'Khuṃseti' means he strikes with the goad of words. 'Vambheti' means he disparages. 'Garahati' means he speaks of a fault. Furthermore, if unconnected with the eleven terms that come later in the Pāḷi, beginning with 'animittāsi,' it does not reach the peak. Even if connected, among those terms, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense only when connected with these three: 'sikharaṇīsi,' 'sambhinnāsi,' and 'ubhatobyañjanāsi.'

Dehi meti yācanāyapi ettakeneva sīsaṃ na eti, “methunaṃ dhammaṃ dehī”ti evaṃ methunadhammena ghaṭite eva saṅghādiseso.

Even in asking, with just 'dehi me,' it does not reach the peak. It is a Saṅghādisesa offense only when connected with the act of sexual intercourse, as in 'methunaṃ dhammaṃ dehi.'

Kadā te mātā pasīdissatītiādīsu āyācanavacanesupi ettakeneva [P 3.0548] sīsaṃ na eti, “kadā te mātā pasīdissati, kadā te methunaṃ dhammaṃ labhissāmī”ti vā “tava mātari pasannāya methunaṃ dhammaṃ labhissāmī”ti vā ādinā pana nayena methunadhammena ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso.

In words of entreaty, such as 'kadā te mātā pasīdissati,' with just this much it does not reach the peak. But it is a Saṅghādisesa offense only when connected with the act of sexual intercourse, by way of saying, “When will your mother be pleased with me? When will I obtain the act of sexual intercourse from you?” or, “When your mother is pleased, I will obtain the act of sexual intercourse,” and so on.

Kathaṃ tvaṃ sāmikassa desītiādīsu pucchāvacanesupi methunadhammanti vutteyeva saṅghādiseso, na itarathā. Evaṃ kira tvaṃ sāmikassa desīti paṭipucchāvacanesupi eseva nayo.

Even in words of questioning, such as 'kathaṃ tvaṃ sāmikassa desi,' it is a Saṅghādisesa offense only when 'methunadhammaṃ' is stated, not otherwise. In words of counter-questioning, such as 'evaṃ kira tvaṃ sāmikassa desi,' this is the same principle.

Ācikkhanāya puṭṭho bhaṇatīti “kathaṃ dadamānā sāmikassa piyā hotī”ti evaṃ puṭṭho ācikkhati. Ettha ca “evaṃ [V 2.0121] dehi evaṃ dadamānā”ti vuttepi sīsaṃ na eti. “Methunadhammaṃ evaṃ dehi evaṃ upanehi evaṃ methunadhammaṃ dadamānā upanayamānā piyā hotī”tiādinā pana nayena methunadhammena ghaṭiteyeva saṅghādiseso. Anusāsanīvacanesupi eseva nayo.

Regarding 'ācikkhanāya puṭṭho bhaṇati': being asked, “How does one who gives become dear to her husband?” he explains. And here, even if it is said, “Give like this; one who gives like this becomes dear,” it does not reach the peak. It is a Saṅghādisesa offense only when connected with the act of sexual intercourse, by way of saying, “Give the act of sexual intercourse like this; offer it like this. One who gives and offers the act of sexual intercourse like this becomes dear,” and so on. In words of instruction, this is the same principle.

Akkosaniddese – animittāsīti nimittarahitāsi, kuñcikapaṇālimattameva tava dakasotanti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the explanation of abuse: 'animittāsi' means you are devoid of the sign; it means it is said, “Your urinary passage is merely the size of a keyhole.”

Nimittamattāsīti tava itthinimittaṃ aparipuṇṇaṃ saññāmattamevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Alohitāti sukkhasotā. Dhuvalohitāti niccalohitā kilinnadakasotā. Dhuvacoḷāti niccapakkhittāṇicoḷā, sadā āṇicoḷakaṃ sevasīti vuttaṃ hoti. Paggharantīti savantī; sadā te muttaṃ savatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sikharaṇīti bahinikkhantaāṇimaṃsā. Itthipaṇḍakāti animittāva vuccati. Vepurisikāti samassudāṭhikā purisarūpā [M 2.0135] itthī. Sambhinnāti sambhinnavaccamaggapassāvamaggā. Ubhatobyañjanāti itthinimittena ca purisanimittena cāti ubhohi byañjanehi samannāgatā.

“Nimittamattāsi” means it is said, “Your female sign is incomplete; it is merely a mark.” “Alohitā” means having a dry passage. “Dhuvalohitā” means having constant blood, having a moist urinary passage. “Dhuvacoḷā” means having a constantly inserted cloth plug; it means it is said, “You always use a cloth plug.” “Paggharantī” means leaking; it means it is said, “Your urine always leaks.” “Sikharaṇī” means having a flesh-plug that protrudes outside. “Itthipaṇḍakā” is said of one who is without the sign. “Vepurisikā” means a woman with a beard and canine teeth, having the form of a man. “Sambhinnā” means one whose passage for feces and passage for urine are joined. “Ubhatobyañjanā” means endowed with both signs, that is, the female sign and the male sign.

Imesu ca pana ekādasasu padesu sikharaṇīsi sambhinnāsi ubhatobyañjanāsīti imāniyeva tīṇi padāni suddhāni sīsaṃ enti. Iti imāni ca tīṇi purimāni ca vaccamaggapassāvamaggamethunadhammapadāni tīṇīti cha padāni suddhāni āpattikarāni. Sesāni animittātiādīni “animitte [P 3.0549] methunadhammaṃ me dehī”ti vā “animittāsi methunadhammaṃ me dehī”ti vā ādinā nayena methunadhammena ghaṭitāneva āpattikarāni hontīti veditabbāni.

And among these eleven terms, only these three terms—“sikharaṇīsi,” “sambhinnāsi,” and “ubhatobyañjanāsi”—by themselves reach the peak. Thus, these three, and the previous three terms—the terms for the passage for feces, the passage for urine, and the act of sexual intercourse—these six terms by themselves incur an offense. The remaining terms, beginning with “animittā,” should be understood to incur an offense only when connected with the act of sexual intercourse, by way of saying, “To the one without a sign, give me the act of sexual intercourse,” or, “You are without a sign; give me the act of sexual intercourse,” and so on.

286. Idāni yvāyaṃ otiṇṇo vipariṇatena cittena obhāsati, tassa vaccamaggapassāvamagge ādissa etesaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanādīnaṃ vasena vitthārato āpattibhedaṃ dassento “itthī ca hoti itthisaññī”tiādimāha. Tesaṃ attho kāyasaṃsagge vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

286. Now, as for that monk who, being overcome by a perverted mind, speaks lewdly, the Teacher, showing in detail the classification of offenses by way of speaking of the attributes and so on, referring to the passage for feces and the passage for urine, spoke the passage beginning with, “She is a woman, and he is percipient of her as a woman.” The meaning of these words should be understood in the same way as was explained in the training rule on bodily contact.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – adhakkhakanti akkhakato paṭṭhāya adho. Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala jāṇumaṇḍalato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ. Ubbhakkhakanti akkhakato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ. Adho jāṇumaṇḍalanti jāṇumaṇḍalato paṭṭhāya adho. Akkhakaṃ pana jāṇumaṇḍalañca ettheva dukkaṭakkhette saṅgahaṃ gacchanti bhikkhuniyā kāyasaṃsagge viya. Na hi buddhā garukāpattiṃ sāvasesaṃ paññapentīti. Kāyappaṭibaddhanti vatthaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā ābharaṇaṃ vā.

However, this is the distinction: “Below the collarbone” means from the collarbone downwards. “Above the kneecap” means from the kneecap upwards. “Above the collarbone” means from the collarbone upwards. “Below the kneecap” means from the kneecap downwards. Furthermore, the collarbone and the kneecap are included right in this field of a dukkaṭa offense, just as in the case of bodily contact with a bhikkhunī. For indeed, the Buddhas do not prescribe a grave offense with a remainder. “Connected to the body” means clothing, or flowers, or ornaments.

287. Atthapurekkhārassāti [V 2.0122] animittātiādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ kathentassa, aṭṭhakathaṃ vā sajjhāyaṃ karontassa.

287. As for “one who gives precedence to the meaning”: this refers to one who is explaining the meaning of words such as “without a sign,” or who is reciting the commentary.

Dhammapurekkhārassāti pāḷiṃ vācentassa vā sajjhāyantassa vā. Evaṃ atthañca dhammañca purakkhatvā bhaṇantassa atthapurekkhārassa ca dhammapurekkhārassa ca anāpatti.

As for “one who gives precedence to the Dhamma”: this refers to one who is teaching or reciting the Pāḷi. Thus, for one who speaks giving precedence to both the meaning and the Dhamma, there is no offense for one who gives precedence to the meaning and for one who gives precedence to the Dhamma.

Anusāsanipurekkhārassāti “idānipi animittāsi ubhattobyañjanāsi appamādaṃ idāni kareyyāsi, yathā āyatimpi evarūpā na hohisī”ti evaṃ anusiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā bhaṇantassa anusāsanipurekkhārassa anāpatti. Yo pana bhikkhunīnaṃ pāḷiṃ vācento pakativācanāmaggaṃ pahāya hasanto hasanto “sikharaṇīsi sambhinnāsi ubhatobyañjanāsī”ti punappunaṃ bhaṇati, tassa [M 2.0136] āpattiyeva. Ummattakassa anāpatti. Idha ādikammiko udāyitthero, tassa anāpatti ādikammikassāti.

As for “one who gives precedence to instruction”: there is no offense for one who gives precedence to instruction, speaking words of instruction thus: “Even now, you are a woman without a sign, you are one with the characteristics of both sexes. You should now practice heedfulness, so that in a future life you will not be such a one.” Furthermore, whatever monk, while teaching the Pāḷi to bhikkhunīs, abandons the normal way of teaching and, laughing again and again, says repeatedly, “You are a sikharaṇī, you are a sambhinnā, you are one with the characteristics of both sexes,” for that monk there is indeed an offense. For one who is insane, there is no offense. Here, the original offender was the Elder Udāyī; for him, there is no offense because he was the original offender.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Padabhājanīya is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyacittato vācācittato kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti, kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ[P 3.0550], sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dvivedananti.

In the section on origins, etc.: this training rule has three origins; it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action, not released by perception, intentional, blameworthy in the world, a bodily action, a verbal action, arising from an unwholesome mind, and accompanied by two feelings.

288. Vinītavatthūsu lohitavatthusmiṃ so bhikkhu itthiyā lohitakaṃ nimittaṃ sandhāyāha – itarā na aññāsi, tasmā dukkaṭaṃ.

288. Among the decided cases, in the case concerning blood: that monk spoke referring to the woman's red organ. The other, the woman, did not understand; therefore, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Kakkasalomanti rassalomehi bahulomaṃ. Ākiṇṇalomanti jaṭitalomaṃ. Kharalomanti thaddhalomaṃ. Dīghalomanti arassalomaṃ. Sabbaṃ itthinimittameva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

“Having rough hair” means having abundant short hair. “Having matted hair” means having tangled hair. “Having coarse hair” means having stiff hair. “Having long hair” means having hair that is not short. All this was said referring only to the female organ.

289. Vāpitaṃ kho teti asaddhammaṃ sandhāyāha, sā asallakkhetvā no ca kho paṭivuttanti āha. Paṭivuttaṃ nāma udakavappe bījehi appatiṭṭhitokāse pāṇakehi vināsitabīje vā okāse puna bījaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā udakena āsittaṃ, thalavappe visamapatitānaṃ vā bījānaṃ samakaraṇatthāya puna aṭṭhadantakena samīkataṃ, tesu aññataraṃ sandhāya esā āha.

289. He said, “It has been sown by you,” referring to the unrighteous practice. She, not perceiving this, said, “No, it has not been re-sown.” “Re-sown” means, in a wet field, seeds that are sprinkled with water after being sown again in a place where seeds have not taken root or in a place where seeds have been destroyed by creatures. In a dry field, it means seeds that are made even again with an eight-toothed harrow for the purpose of leveling seeds that have fallen unevenly. This woman spoke referring to one of these two.

Maggavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0123] maggo saṃsīdatīti aṅgajātamaggaṃ sandhāyāha. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti.

In the case concerning the path, he said, “The path is sinking,” referring to the path that is the sexual organ. The rest is clear.

Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning coarse speech is concluded.

4. Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Service for One's Own Desire

290. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti attakāmasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha kulūpakoti kulapayirupāsanako catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ atthāya kulūpasaṅkamane niccappayutto.

290. “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One…”: the training rule concerning one's own desire. Therein, `kulūpaka` means one who frequents families, a monk who is constantly engaged in approaching families for the sake of the four requisites.

Cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti [M 2.0137] cīvarañca piṇḍapātañca senāsanañca gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārañca. Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti cettha patikaraṇatthena paccayo, yassa kassaci sappāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhisakkassa kammaṃ tena anuññātattāti bhesajjaṃ. Gilānapaccayova bhesajjaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ, yaṃkiñci gilānassa sappāyaṃ bhisakkakammaṃ telamadhuphāṇitādīti vuttaṃ hoti. Parikkhāroti pana “sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhataṃ hotī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.67) parivāro vuccati. “Ratho [P 3.0551] sīsaparikkhāro jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.4) alaṅkāro. “Ye cime pabbajitena jīvitaparikkhārā samudānetabbā”tiādīsu (ro. ni. 1.1.191) sambhāro. Idha pana sambhāropi parivāropi vaṭṭati. Tañhi gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ jīvitassa parivāropi hoti jīvitavināsakābādhuppattiyā antaraṃ adatvā rakkhaṇato, sambhāropi yathā ciraṃ pavattati evamassa kāraṇabhāvato, tasmā parikkhāroti vuccati. Evaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjañca taṃ parikkhāro cāti gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro, taṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

“Robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick” means robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Herein, regarding `gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāra`, `paccaya` (requisite) is used in the sense of a remedy; it is a designation for anything suitable. `Bhesajja` (medicine) is a physician's work; because it is permitted by him, it is called medicine. The requisite for the sick is itself the medicine, hence `gilānapaccayabhesajja`; it is said to be any physician's work suitable for the sick, such as oil, honey, molasses, and so on. As for `parikkhāra` (requisite), in passages such as, “It is well-fortified with the seven city fortifications,” it is called `parivāra` (protection). In passages such as, “The chariot has virtue as its adornment, jhāna for an axle, and energy for its wheels,” it is called `alaṅkāra` (adornment). In passages such as, “These requisites for life are to be acquired by one who has gone forth,” it is called `sambhāra` (support). Here, however, both ‘support’ and ‘protection’ are applicable. For that medicine, a requisite for the sick, is also a `parivāra` (protection) for life, because it protects by not giving an opportunity for the arising of a life-destroying illness. It is also a `sambhāra` (support) for life, because it is a cause for it to continue for a long time. Therefore, it is called `parikkhāra`. Thus, it is medicine that is a requisite for the sick, and that is a requisite (in the sense of protection and support); hence, it is `gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro`. The meaning of `taṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ` should be understood in this way.

Vasalanti hīnaṃ lāmakaṃ. Atha vā vassatīti vasalo, paggharatīti attho, taṃ vasalaṃ, asucipaggharaṇakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Niṭṭhuhitvāti kheḷaṃ pātetvā.

“Vasala” means base, vile. Alternatively, because it flows (`vassati`), it is called `vasala`; the meaning is that it oozes. That `vasala` is said to be that which oozes impurity. “Having spat” means having caused saliva to fall.

Kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmīti ahaṃ kassā aññissā itthiyā kena bhogena vā alaṅkārena vā rūpena vā parihāyāmi, kā nāma mayā uttaritarāti dīpeti.

The phrase `Kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmi` shows this meaning: “To what other woman am I inferior, whether by wealth, or by adornment, or by beauty? What woman is superior to me?”

291. Santiketi upacāre ṭhatvā sāmantā avidūre, padabhājanepi ayamevaattho dīpito[V 2.0124]. Attakāmapāricariyāyāti methunadhammasaṅkhātena kāmena pāricariyā kāmapāricariyā. Attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā attakāmapāricariyā, attanā vā kāmitā icchitāti attakāmā, sayaṃ methunarāgavasena patthitāti attho. Attakāmā ca sā pāricariyā cāti attakāmapāricariyā, tassā attakāmapāricariyāya. Vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyāti guṇaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ pakāseyya.

291. `Santike` means standing in the vicinity, nearby, not far; this very meaning is also shown in the word-analysis. `Attakāmapāricariyāya`: Here, service (`pāricariyā`) by means of sensual pleasure (`kāma`) designated as the act of sexual intercourse is `kāmapāricariyā`. `Kāmapāricariyā` for one's own (`attano`) sake is `attakāmapāricariyā`. Alternatively, `attakāmā` means desired (`kāmitā`) or wished for (`icchitā`) by oneself (`attanā`); the meaning is service that is personally longed for through sexual lust. That service (`pāricariyā`) which is desired by oneself (`attakāmā`) is `attakāmapāricariyā`. For that `attakāmapāricariyā`. `Vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya` means one would speak of its virtue and benefit.

Tatra [M 2.0138] yasmā “attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā”ti imasmiṃ atthavikappe kāmo ceva hetu ca pāricariyā ca attho, sesaṃ byañjanaṃ. “Attakāmā ca sā pāricariyā cāti attakāmapāricariyā”ti imasmiṃ atthavikappe adhippāyo ceva pāricariyā cāti attho, sesaṃ byañjanaṃ. Tasmā byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “attano kāmaṃ attano hetuṃ attano adhippāyaṃ attano pāricariya”nti padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. “Attano kāmaṃ attano hetuṃ attano pāricariya”nti hi vutte jānissanti paṇḍitā “ettāvatā attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā vuttā”ti. “Attano adhippāyaṃ attano pāricariya”nti vuttepi jānissanti “ettāvatā attanā icchitakāmitaṭṭhena attakāmapāricariyā vuttā”ti.

Here, because in the interpretation of meaning for “service through sensual pleasure for one's own sake” (`attano atthāya kāmapāricariyā`), sensual pleasure (`kāma`), the cause (`hetu`), and service (`pāricariyā`) are the meaning, while the rest is mere wording. In the interpretation of meaning for “that service which is desired by oneself is `attakāmapāricariyā`” (`attakāmā ca sā pāricariyā cāti attakāmapāricariyā`), the intention (`adhippāya`) and the service are the meaning, while the rest is mere wording. Therefore, without paying attention to the wording, and only to show the meaning, the word-analysis is given as: “one’s own sensual pleasure, one’s own cause, one’s own intention, one’s own service.” For when it is said, “one’s own sensual pleasure, one’s own cause, one’s own service,” the wise will understand, “by this much, ‘service through sensual pleasure for one's own sake’ has been stated.” And when it is said, “one’s own intention, one’s own service,” they will understand, “by this much, `attakāmapāricariyā` has been stated in the sense of being desired and wished for by oneself.”

Idāni [P 3.0552] tassā attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇabhāsanākāraṃ dassento “etadagga”ntiādimāha. Taṃ uddesatopi niddesatopi uttānatthameva. Ayaṃ panettha padasambandho ca āpattivinicchayo ca – etadaggaṃ…pe… paricareyyāti yā mādisaṃ sīlavantaṃ kalyāṇadhammaṃ brahmacāriṃ etena dhammena paricareyya, tassā evaṃ mādisaṃ paricarantiyā yā ayaṃ pāricariyā nāma, etadaggaṃ pāricariyānanti.

Now, showing the manner of speaking in praise of that service for one's own desire, he said, “This is the foremost,” and so on. Its meaning is plain both in the summary and in the detailed explanation. Herein is the connection of the words and the determination of the offense: “This is the foremost… should serve” means: whichever woman should serve one like me—virtuous, of good character, a celibate—with this act, for her who serves one like me in such a way, this service is the foremost of services.

Methunupasaṃhitena saṅghādisesoti evaṃ attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanto ca methunupasaṃhitena methunadhammapaṭisaṃyutteneva vacanena yo bhāseyya, tassa saṅghādisesoti.

“Connected with sexual intercourse, a Saṅghādisesa”—thus, whoever speaks in praise of service for his own desire, and speaks with words connected with sexual intercourse, indeed connected with the sexual act, for him it is a Saṅghādisesa.

Idhāni yasmā methunupasaṃhiteneva bhāsantassa saṅghādiseso vutto, tasmā “ahampi khattiyo, tvampi khattiyā, arahati khattiyā khattiyassa dātuṃ samajātikattā”ti evamādīhi vacanehi pāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsamānassāpi saṅghādiseso natthi. “Ahampi khattiyo”tiādike pana bahūpi pariyāye vatvā “arahasi tvaṃ mayhaṃ methunadhammaṃ dātu”nti evaṃ methunappaṭisaṃyutteneva bhāsamānassa saṅghādisesoti.

Here, because a Saṅghādisesa offense is declared only for speaking with words connected with sexual intercourse, therefore, for one who praises the service with words such as, “I too am a noble, you too are a noble lady; it is fitting for a noble lady to give to a noble man, being of the same caste,” there is no Saṅghādisesa. But if, after saying many such phrases like, “I too am a noble,” and so on, one speaks with words connected with sexual intercourse, saying, “You ought to give me the sexual act,” then it is a Saṅghādisesa.

Itthī [V 2.0125] ca hotītiādi pubbe vuttanayameva. Idha udāyitthero ādikammiko, tassa anāpatti ādikammikassāti.

“And it is a woman,” etc., is in the same manner as previously stated. Here, the Elder Udāyī was the originator of the offense; for the originator, there is no offense.

Samuṭṭhānādi sabbaṃ duṭṭhullavācāsadisaṃ. Vinītavatthūni uttānatthānevāti.

The origin and so on are all similar to that for lewd speech. The decided cases are of plain meaning.

Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Service for One's Own Desire is concluded.

5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Acting as a Go-between

296. Tena [M 2.0139] samayena buddho bhagavāti sañcarittaṃ. Tattha paṇḍitāti paṇḍiccena samannāgatā gatimantā. Byattāti veyyattiyena samannāgatā, upāyena samannāgatā upāyaññū visāradā. Medhāvinīti medhāya samannāgatā, diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ karoti. Dakkhāti chekā. Analasāti uṭṭhānavīriyasampannā. Channāti anucchavikā.

296. At that time, the Blessed One [was dwelling, and the matter of] acting as a go-between [arose]. Herein, 'wise' means endowed with wisdom, possessing understanding. 'Skilled' means endowed with skill, endowed with means, knowing methods, confident. 'Intelligent' means endowed with intelligence, accomplishes what is seen to be done. 'Clever' means adroit. 'Diligent' means endowed with energy and vigor. 'Channā' means appropriate.

Kismiṃ viyāti kicchaṃ viya kileso viya, hiri viya amhākaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Kumārikāya vattunti “imaṃ tumhe gaṇhathā”ti kumārikāya kāraṇā vattuṃ.

As for 'in what way?': The intention is, 'It is like a difficulty, like a defilement, it is like a matter of shame for us.' To say, 'You take this one,' for the sake of the girl, is like a matter of shame.

Āvāhādīsu āvāhoti dārakassa parakulato dārikāya [P 3.0553] āharaṇaṃ. Vivāhoti attano dārikāya parakulapesanaṃ. Vāreyyanti “detha no dārakassa dārika”nti yācanaṃ, divasanakkhattamuhuttaparicchedakaraṇaṃ vā.

Among terms like 'āvāha,' 'āvāha' means bringing a girl from another family for a boy. 'Vivāha' means sending one's own girl to another family. 'Vāreyya' means requesting, saying, 'Give us a girl for our boy,' or it refers to determining the day, constellation, and auspicious time.

297. Purāṇagaṇakiyāti ekassa gaṇakassa bhariyāya, sā tasmiṃ jīvamāne gaṇakīti paññāyittha, mate pana purāṇagaṇakīti saṅkhaṃ gatā. Tirogāmoti bahigāmo, añño gāmoti adhippāyo. Manussāti udāyissa imaṃ sañcarittakamme yuttapayuttabhāvaṃ jānanakamanussā.

297. As for 'the former accountant's wife': she was the wife of a certain accountant; while he was alive, she was known as 'the accountant's wife,' but after his death, she came to be known as 'the former accountant's wife.' As for 'a village across': an outer village; the meaning is another village. As for 'people': the people who knew of Udāyī's deep involvement in this act of being a go-between.

Suṇisabhogenāti yena bhogena suṇisā bhuñjitabbā hoti randhāpanapacāpanapaavesanādinā, tena bhuñjiṃsu. Tato aparena dāsibhogenāti māsātikkame yena bhogena dāsī bhuñjitabbā hoti khettakammakacavarachaḍḍanaudakāharaṇādinā, tena bhuñjiṃsu. Duggatāti daliddā, yattha vā gatā duggatā hoti tādisaṃ kulaṃ gatā. Māyyo imaṃ kumārikanti mā ayyo imaṃ kumārikaṃ. Āhārūpahāroti āhāro ca upahāro ca gahaṇañca dānañca, na amhehi [V 2.0126] kiñci āhaṭaṃ na upāhaṭaṃ tayā saddhiṃ kayavikkayo vohāro amhākaṃ natthīti dīpenti. Samaṇena bhavitabbaṃ abyāvaṭena, samaṇo assa susamaṇoti samaṇena nāma īdisesu kammesu abyāvaṭena abyāpārena bhavitabbaṃ, evaṃ [M 2.0140] bhavanto hi samaṇo susamaṇo assāti, evaṃ naṃ apasādetvā “gaccha tvaṃ na mayaṃ taṃ jānāmā”ti āhaṃsu.

As for 'with the treatment of a daughter-in-law': they made use of her with the treatment by which a daughter-in-law is to be maintained—such as having rice cooked, having other foods cooked, and serving food. Then, after a month had passed, as for 'with the treatment of a female slave': they made use of her with the treatment by which a female slave is to be maintained—such as doing fieldwork, throwing out rubbish, and fetching water. As for 'wretched': poor; or, having gone to a family where one becomes wretched, she has gone to such a family. As for 'māyyo imaṃ kumārikaṃ': 'Sirs, do not make use of this girl.' As for 'bringing and offering': there is no bringing and offering, no taking and giving. They declared, 'Nothing has been brought by us, nothing offered; we have no transaction of buying and selling with you.' As for 'a monk... a good monk': A monk by name should be unconcerned and have no business in such matters; for, being thus, a monk would be a good monk. Thus rebuking him, they said, 'Go away, you! We do not know you.'

298. Sajjitoti sabbūpakaraṇasampanno maṇḍitapasādhito vā.

298. As for 'prepared': endowed with all necessities, or adorned and prepared.

300. Dhuttāti itthidhuttā. Paricārentāti manāpiyesu rūpādīsu ito cito ca samantā indriyāni cārentā, kīḷantā abhiramantāti vuttaṃ hoti. Abbhutamakaṃsūti yadi karissati tvaṃ ettakaṃ jito, yadi na karissati ahaṃ ettakanti paṇamakaṃsu. Bhikkhūnaṃ pana abbhutaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yo karoti parājitena dātabbanti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ.

300. As for 'rogues': womanizers. As for 'indulging': it means causing the senses to wander here and there all around in pleasing sense-objects such as forms, playing and delighting. As for 'they made a wager': they made a bet, saying, 'If he does it, you have won this much; if he does not do it, I have won this much.' But it is not proper for monks to make a wager. It is said in the Mahāpaccariya: 'Whoever does so, it must be given by the one who is defeated.'

Kathañhi nāma ayyo udāyī taṅkhaṇikanti ettha taṅkhaṇoti acirakālo [P 3.0554] vuccati. Taṅkhaṇikanti acirakālādhikārikaṃ.

Herein, in the phrase '...even for a moment': 'taṅkhaṇa' is said to be a short time. 'Taṅkhaṇika' means pertaining to a short period of time.

301. Sañcarittaṃ samāpajjeyyāti sañcaraṇabhāvaṃ samāpajjeyya. Yasmā pana taṃ samāpajjantena kenaci pesitena katthaci gantabbaṃ hoti, parato ca “itthiyā vā purisamati”nti ādivacanato idha itthipurisā adhippetā, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “itthiyā vā pahito purisassa santike gacchati, purisena vā pahito itthiyā santike gacchatī”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Itthiyā vā purisamatiṃ purisassa vā itthimatinti ettha āroceyyāti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo, tenevassa padabhājane “purisassa matiṃ itthiyā āroceti, itthiyā matiṃ purisassa ārocetī”ti vuttaṃ.

301. As for 'should engage in being a go-between': one would enter the state of being a go-between. Since one who engages in this must go somewhere, having been sent by someone, and further, because of the saying beginning 'a woman's intention to a man,' women and men are intended here. Therefore, to show that meaning, the word analysis for this is stated as: 'Sent by a woman, he goes to a man; or sent by a man, he goes to a woman.' Herein, in the phrase 'a woman's intention to a man, or a man's intention to a woman,' the remainder of the text, 'should report,' is to be understood. For that very reason, in its word analysis, it is stated: 'He reports a man's intention to a woman, or he reports a woman's intention to a man.'

Idāni yadatthaṃ taṃ tesaṃ matiṃ adhippāyaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ chandaṃ ruciṃ āroceti, taṃ dassento “jāyattane vā jārattane vā”tiādimāha. Tattha jāyattaneti jāyābhāve. Jārattaneti jārabhāve. Purisassa hi matiṃ itthiyā ārocento jāyattane āroceti, itthiyā matiṃ purisassa ārocento jārattane āroceti; apica purisasseva matiṃ itthiyā ārocento jāyattane vā āroceti nibaddhabhariyābhāve, jārattane vā micchācārabhāve. Yasmā panetaṃ ārocentena “tvaṃ kirassa jāyā bhavissasī”tiādi vattabbaṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ vattabbatākāraṃ dassetuṃ “jāyattane vāti jāyā bhavissasi, jārattane [M 2.0141] vāti jārī bhavissasī”ti assa padabhājanaṃ [V 2.0127] vuttaṃ. Eteneva ca upāyena itthiyā matiṃ purisassa ārocanepi pati bhavissasi, sāmiko bhavissasi, jāro bhavissasīti vattabbatākāro veditabbo.

Now, showing for what purpose he reports their intention, inclination, disposition, wish, and preference, He said, 'for the state of a wife or for the state of a lover,' and so on. Therein, 'for the state of a wife' means in the state of being a wife. 'For the state of a lover' means in the state of being a lover. For when reporting a man's intention to a woman, he reports it for the state of a wife; when reporting a woman's intention to a man, he reports it for the state of a lover. Furthermore, when reporting a man's intention to a woman, he reports it either for the state of a wife, meaning in the state of a permanent wife, or for the state of a lover, meaning in the state of misconduct. And since the one reporting this must say things like, 'It seems you will become his wife,' therefore, to show that manner of speaking, the word analysis for this is stated: ''For the state of a wife' means 'you will become a wife'; 'for the state of a lover' means 'you will become a lover.'' And by this same method, when reporting a woman's intention to a man, the manner of speaking should be understood as: 'You will become her husband,' 'you will become her master,' 'you will become her lover.'

Antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapīti sabbantimena paricchedena yā ayaṃ taṅkhaṇe muhuttamatte paṭisaṃvasitabbato taṅkhaṇikāti vuccati, muhuttikāti attho. Tassāpi “muhuttikā bhavissasī”ti evaṃ purisamatiṃ ārocentassa saṅghādiseso. Etenevupāyena “muhuttiko bhavissasī”ti evaṃ purisassa itthimatiṃ ārocentopi saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjatīti veditabbo.

As for 'at the very least for a momentary one': by the final limit, she who is called 'taṅkhaṇikā' because she is to be associated with for just a moment, for a short while—the meaning is 'muhuttikā' (a momentary one). For one who reports the man's intention to her, saying, 'You will be a momentary one,' it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. By this same method, it should be understood that one who reports the woman's intention to a man, saying, 'You will be a momentary one,' also incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense.

303. Idāni “itthiyā vā purisamati”nti ettha adhippetā itthiyo pabhedato dassetvā tāsu sañcarittavasena āpattibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “dasa itthiyo”tiādimāha. Tattha māturakkhitāti mātarā rakkhitā. Yathā purisena saṃvāsaṃ na kappeti, evaṃ mātarā rakkhitā, tenassa padabhājanepi vuttaṃ – “mātā rakkhati [P 3.0555] gopeti issariyaṃ kāreti vasaṃ vattetī”ti. Tattha rakkhatīti katthaci gantuṃ na deti. Gopetīti yathā aññe na passanti, evaṃ guttaṭṭhāne ṭhapeti. Issariyaṃ kāretīti serivihāramassā nisedhentī abhibhavitvā pavattati. Vasaṃ vattetīti “idaṃ karohi, idaṃ mā akāsī”ti evaṃ attano vasaṃ tassā upari vatteti. Etenupāyena piturakkhitādayopi ñātabbā. Gottaṃ vā dhammo vā na rakkhati, sagottehi pana sahadhammikehi ca ekaṃ satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajitehi ekagaṇapariyāpannehi ca rakkhitā “gottarakkhitā dhammarakkhitā”ti vuccati, tasmā tesaṃ padānaṃ “sagottā rakkhantī”tiādinā nayena padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

303. Now, in the text 'a woman's (message) to a man,' having shown by way of classification the women who are intended, in order to show the classification of offenses by means of acting as a go-between with them, the text states that which begins with 'ten women.' Therein, 'mother-protected' means protected by the mother. She is protected by her mother in such a way that she cannot arrange cohabitation with a man. Therefore, in its word-analysis it is said: 'The mother guards, protects, exercises authority, and wields control.' Therein, 'guards' means she does not allow her to go anywhere. 'Protects' means she places her in a secure location in such a way that others do not see her. 'Exercises authority' means, forbidding her independent living, she acts having overpowered her. 'Wields control' means she makes her own control prevail over her, thus: 'Do this, do not do that.' By this method, 'protected by the father' and so on should also be understood. A clan or the Dhamma does not protect; rather, a woman protected by those of the same clan, or by fellow practitioners who have gone forth under the same teacher and are included in the same group, is called 'clan-protected' or 'Dhamma-protected'. Therefore, the word-analysis of these terms is given by the method beginning with 'those of the same clan protect her.'

Saha ārakkhenāti sārakkhā. Saha paridaṇḍenāti saparidaṇḍā. Tāsaṃ niddesā pākaṭāva. Imāsu dasasu pacchimānaṃ dvinnameva purisantaraṃ gacchantīnaṃ micchācāro hoti, na itarāsaṃ.

She who exists with protection (`saha ārakkhena`) is `sārakkhā`. She who exists with an imposed penalty (`saha paridaṇḍena`) is `saparidaṇḍā`. Their expositions are indeed clear. Among these ten, for only the last two does sexual misconduct occur when they go to another man, not for the others.

Dhanakkītādīsu appena vā bahunā vā dhanena kītā dhanakkītā. Yasmā pana sā na kītamattā eva saṃvāsatthāya pana kītattā bhariyā, tasmāssa niddese dhanena kiṇitvā vāsetīti vuttaṃ.

Among terms such as `dhanakkītā` (bought with wealth), she who is bought with little or much wealth is a `dhanakkītā`. However, since she is not merely bought, but is a wife because she is bought for the purpose of cohabitation, it is therefore said in its exposition: 'Having bought her with wealth, he cohabits with her.'

Chandena [M 2.0142] attano ruciyā vasatīti chandavāsinī. Yasmā pana sā na attano chandamatteneva [V 2.0128] bhariyā hoti purisena pana sampaṭicchitattā, tasmāssa niddese “piyo piyaṃ vāsetī”ti vuttaṃ.

She who lives by her own will and liking (`chandena attano ruciyā`) is a `chandavāsinī`. However, since she does not become a wife merely by her own will, but because of being accepted by the man, it is therefore said in its exposition: 'A dear one cohabits with a dear one.'

Bhogena vasatīti bhogavāsinī. Udukkhalamusalādigharūpakaraṇaṃ labhitvā bhariyābhāvaṃ gacchantiyā janapaditthiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

She who lives by means of possessions (`bhogena`) is a `bhogavāsinī`. This is a designation for a country woman who, having received household equipment such as a mortar and pestle, attains the state of a wife.

Paṭena vasatīti paṭavāsinī. Nivāsanamattampi pāvuraṇamattampi labhitvā bhariyābhāvaṃ upagacchantiyā dalidditthiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

She who lives by means of cloth (`paṭena`) is a `paṭavāsinī`. This is a designation for a poor woman who, having received merely an undergarment or an upper garment, approaches the state of a wife.

Odapattakinīti ubhinnaṃ ekissā udakapātiyā hatthe otāretvā “idaṃ udakaṃ viya saṃsaṭṭhā abhejjā hothā”ti vatvā pariggahitāya vohāranāmametaṃ, niddesepissa “tāya saha udakapattaṃ āmasitvā taṃ vāsetī”ti evamattho veditabbo.

`Odapattakinī` is a conventional name for a woman who is taken in marriage after the hands of both have been dipped into a single water vessel and it has been said: 'Just as this water is mingled and indivisible, so may you be mingled and indivisible.' In its exposition also, the meaning should be understood thus: 'Having touched the water vessel together with her, he cohabits with her.'

Obhaṭaṃ oropitaṃ cumbaṭamassāti obhaṭacumbaṭā, kaṭṭhahārikādīnaṃ aññatarā, yassā sīsato cumbaṭaṃ oropetvā ghare vāseti, tassā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

`Obhaṭacumbaṭā` is she for whom the head-pad (`cumbaṭa`) has been taken down; she is one among wood-gatherers and the like. This is a designation for a woman from whose head he has had the head-pad taken down and whom he makes to live in his house.

Dāsī cāti attanoyeva dāsī ca hoti bhariyā ca.

`Dāsī ca` (and a slave) means she is his own female slave and also his wife.

Kammakārī nāma gehe bhatiyā kammaṃ [P 3.0556] karoti, tāya saddhiṃ koci gharāvāsaṃ kappeti attano bhariyāya anatthiko hutvā. Ayaṃ vuccati “kammakārī ca bhariyā cā”ti.

A `kammakārī` is a woman who does work in the house for a wage. Some man, having no need for his wife, establishes a household life with her. This one is called `kammakārī ca bhariyā ca` (both a worker and a wife).

Dhajena āhaṭā dhajāhaṭā, ussitaddhajāya senāya gantvā paravisayaṃ vilumpitvā ānītāti vuttaṃ hoti, taṃ koci bhariyaṃ karoti, ayaṃ dhajāhaṭā nāma. Muhuttikā vuttanayāeva, etāsaṃ dasannampi purisantaragamane micchācāro hoti. Purisānaṃ pana vīsatiyāpi etāsu micchācāro hoti, bhikkhuno ca sañcarittaṃ hotīti.

`Dhajāhaṭā` is one brought by a banner; that is to say, she is brought after an army with raised banners has gone and plundered a foreign territory. If some man makes her his wife, she is called `dhajāhaṭā`. The `muhuttikā` (momentary wife) is as has been explained. For all ten of these, going to another man constitutes sexual misconduct. Furthermore, for men, sexual misconduct occurs with all twenty of these women, and for a monk, it constitutes acting as a go-between.

305. Idāni puriso bhikkhuṃ pahiṇatītiādīsu paṭiggaṇhātīti so bhikkhu tassa purisassa “gaccha, bhante, itthannāmaṃ māturakkhitaṃ brūhi, hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā”ti evaṃ vuttavacanaṃ “sādhu upāsakā”ti vā “hotū”ti vā “ārocessāmī”ti vā yena kenaci ākārena vacībhedaṃ katvā vā sīsakampanādīhi vā sampaṭicchati. Vīmaṃsatīti [V 2.0129][M 2.0143] evaṃ paṭiggaṇhitvā tassā itthiyā santikaṃ gantvā taṃ sāsanaṃ āroceti. Paccāharatīti tena ārocite sā itthī “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchatu vā paṭikkhipatu vā lajjāya vā tuṇhī hotu, puna āgantvā tassa purisassa taṃ pavattiṃ āroceti.

305. Now, in the text beginning 'a man sends a monk': 'He accepts' means that the monk accepts the words spoken by that man—such as, 'Go, venerable sir, tell the mother-protected woman of such-and-such a name: "Be, it is said, the wife of the man of such-and-such a name, one bought with wealth"'—either by making a verbal utterance in some way, such as 'Very well, lay follower,' or 'Let it be,' or 'I will announce it,' or by nodding the head and so on. 'He delivers the message' (`vīmaṃsati`) means that, having accepted thus, he goes to that woman and announces that message. 'He reports back' means that, when he has announced it, whether that woman accepts, saying 'Very well,' or rejects it, or remains silent out of modesty, he returns and announces that event to the man.

Ettāvatā imāya paṭiggahaṇārocanapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātāya tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso hoti. Sā pana tassa bhariyā hotu vā mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ. Sace pana so māturakkhitāya santikaṃ pesito taṃ adisvā tassā mātuyā taṃ sāsanaṃ āroceti, bahiddhā vimaṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā visaṅketanti mahāpadumatthero āha. Mahāsumatthero pana mātā vā hotu pitā vā antamaso gehadāsīpi añño vāpi yo koci taṃ kiriyaṃ sampādessati, tassa vuttepi vimaṭṭhaṃ nāma na hoti, tivaṅgasampattikāle āpattiyeva.

By this much, through the accomplishment of these three factors—namely acceptance, announcement, and reporting back—a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. Whether or not she becomes his wife is not the cause. However, if he, having been sent to a mother-protected woman, does not see her and announces the message to her mother, it is called 'handled externally'; therefore, it is a mistaken arrangement (`visaṅketaṃ`), so said the Elder Mahāpaduma. But the Elder Mahāsuma said: Whether it be the mother, the father, or even a household slave or anyone else who can accomplish that task, even if it is told to that person, it is not called 'handled amiss' (`vimaṭṭhaṃ`); the offense is indeed incurred at the time of the accomplishment of the three factors.

Nanu yathā “buddhaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vattukāmo virajjhitvā “dhammaṃ paccakkhāmī”ti vadeyya paccakkhātāvassa sikkhā. Yathā vā “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjāmī”ti vattukāmo virajjhitvā “dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjāmī”ti vadeyya āpannovassa [P 3.0557] pārājikaṃ. Evaṃsampadamidanti āha. Taṃ panetaṃ “paṭiggaṇhāti, antevāsiṃ vīmaṃsāpetvā attanā paccāharati, āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti iminā sameti, tasmā subhāsitaṃ.

Is it not so? Just as one who, wishing to say, 'I renounce the Buddha,' makes a mistake and says, 'I renounce the Dhamma,' has indeed renounced the training; or as one who, wishing to say, 'I am attaining the first jhāna,' makes a mistake and says, 'I am attaining the second jhāna,' has indeed incurred a Pārājika offense. 'This case is of such a kind,' he said. And this view agrees with the canonical text: 'He accepts; having had a resident pupil deliver the message, he himself reports back—this is an offense of Saṅghādisesa.' Therefore, it is well-spoken.

Yathā ca “māturakkhitaṃ brūhī”ti vuttassa gantvā tassā ārocetuṃ samatthānaṃ mātādīnampi vadato visaṅketo natthi, evameva “hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā dhanakkītā”ti vattabbe “hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā chandavāsinī”ti evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttesu chandavāsiniādīsu vacanesu aññataravasena vā avuttesupi “hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā jāyā pajāpati puttamātā gharaṇī gharasāminī bhattarandhikā sussūsikā paricārikā”tievamādīsu saṃvāsaparidīpakesu vacanesu aññataravasena vā vadantassāpi visaṅketo natthi tivaṅgasampattiyā āpattiyeva. “Māturakkhitaṃ brūhī”ti pesitassa pana gantvā aññāsu piturakkhitādīsu aññataraṃ vadantassa visaṅketaṃ. Esa nayo “piturakkhitaṃ brūhī”tiādīsupi.
