Just as for one who, having been told, 'Speak to the woman protected by her mother,' goes and speaks even to her mother or others who are able to inform her, there is no mistake in the message; in the very same way, when it should be said, 'Be, it is said, the wife of so-and-so, bought with wealth,' but instead one says, 'Be, it is said, the wife of so-and-so, living by consent,' or speaks by way of any of the other words mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as 'living by consent,' or even by way of words not mentioned in the Pāḷi that indicate cohabitation, such as, 'Be, it is said, the wife of so-and-so, his spouse, consort, mother of his children, lady of the house, mistress of the house, cook, obedient one, or attendant'—for one who speaks thus, there is also no mistake in the message. With the fulfillment of the three factors, there is indeed an offense. However, for one who was sent with the instruction, 'Speak to the woman protected by her mother,' but who goes and speaks to another among the women protected by their father and so on, there is a mistake in the message. This is the method also in cases such as, 'Speak to the woman protected by her father.'

Kevalañhettha [M 2.0144] ekamūlakadumūlakādivasena “purisassa mātā bhikkhuṃ pahiṇati, māturakkhitāya mātā bhikkhuṃ pahiṇatī”ti evamādīnaṃ mūlaṭṭhānañca vasena peyyālabhedoyeva viseso[V 2.0130]. Sopi pubbe vuttanayattā pāḷianusāreneva sakkā jānitunti nāssa vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ ādaraṃ karimha.

Indeed, the only difference here is the variation in the elided passages, by way of being single-rooted, double-rooted, and so on, and by way of the words at the root, such as, 'The man's mother sends a monk,' 'The mother of the woman protected by her mother sends a monk.' Since that difference can be known just by following the Pāḷi, according to the method previously stated, we have not made an effort to show its analysis.

338. Paṭiggaṇhātītiādīsu pana dvīsu catukkesu paṭhamacatukke ādipadena tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso, majjhe dvīhi duvaṅgasampattiyā thullaccayaṃ, ante ekena ekaṅgasampattiyā dukkaṭaṃ. Dutiyacatukke ādipadena duvaṅgasampattiyā thullaccayaṃ, majjhe dvīhi ekaṅgasampattiyā dukkaṭaṃ, ante ekena aṅgābhāvato anāpatti. Tattha paṭiggaṇhātīti āṇāpakassa sāsanaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti. Vīmaṃsatīti pahitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ āroceti. Paccāharatīti puna āgantvā mūlaṭṭhassa āroceti.

338. Furthermore, in the two sets of four beginning with 'accepts,' in the first set of four, for the first case, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense due to the fulfillment of three factors; for the two in the middle, a Thullaccaya offense due to the fulfillment of two factors; for the one at the end, a Dukkaṭa offense due to the fulfillment of one factor. In the second set of four, for the first case, there is a Thullaccaya offense due to the fulfillment of two factors; for the two in the middle, a Dukkaṭa offense due to the fulfillment of one factor; for the one at the end, there is no offense due to the absence of a factor. Therein, 'accepts' means he accepts the message of the one who gives the order. 'Investigates' means that having gone to the place to which he was sent, he delivers the message. 'Reports back' means that having come back again, he informs the one at the origin.

Na paccāharatīti ārocetvā ettova pakkamati. Paṭiggaṇhāti na vīmaṃsatīti purisena “itthannāmaṃ gantvā brūhī”ti vuccamāno “sādhū”ti tassa sāsanaṃ paṭiggaṇhitvā taṃ pamussitvā vā appamussitvā vā [P 3.0558] aññena karaṇīyena tassā santikaṃ gantvā kiñcideva kathaṃ kathento nisīdati, ettāvatā “paṭiggaṇhāti na vīmaṃsati nāmā”ti vuccati. Atha naṃ sā itthī sayameva vadati “tumhākaṃ kira upaṭṭhāko maṃ gehe kātukāmo”ti evaṃ vatvā ca “ahaṃ tassa bhariyā bhavissāmī”ti vā “na bhavissāmī”ti vā vadati. So tassā vacanaṃ anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā tuṇhībhūtova uṭṭhāyāsanā tassa purisassa santikaṃ āgantvā taṃ pavattiṃ āroceti, ettāvatā “na vīmaṃsati paccāharati nāmā”ti vuccati. Na vīmaṃsati na paccāharatīti kevalaṃ sāsanārocanakāle paṭiggaṇhātiyeva, itaraṃ pana dvayaṃ na karoti.

'He does not report back' means that having delivered the message, he departs from that very place. 'He accepts but does not investigate' means that when told by a man, 'Go and speak to so-and-so woman,' he accepts his message with 'Very well,' and then, whether having forgotten it or not, goes to her presence on some other business and sits down, making some conversation. To this extent, it is called 'he accepts but does not investigate.' Then that woman herself says to him, 'It is said your supporter wishes to take me,' and having said this, she adds, 'I will become his wife,' or 'I will not become his wife.' He, neither delighting in nor rejecting her words, remains silent, rises from his seat, goes to that man, and reports what has occurred. To this extent, it is called 'he does not investigate but reports back.' 'He does not investigate and does not report back' means he merely accepts at the time the message is given, but does not do the other two things.

Na paṭiggaṇhāti vīmaṃsati paccāharatīti koci puriso bhikkhussa ṭhitaṭṭhāne vā nisinnaṭṭhāne vā tathārūpiṃ kathaṃ katheti, bhikkhu tena appahitopi pahito viya hutvā itthiyā santikaṃ gantvā “hohi kira itthannāmassa bhariyā”tiādinā nayena vīmaṃsitvā tassā ruciṃ vā aruciṃ vā puna āgantvā imassa āroceti. Teneva nayena vīmaṃsitvā apaccāharanto [M 2.0145] “na paṭiggaṇhāti vīmaṃsati na paccāharatī”ti vuccati. Teneva nayena gato avīmaṃsitvā tāya samuṭṭhāpitaṃ kathaṃ sutvā paṭhamacatukkassa tatiyapade vuttanayena āgantvā imassa ārocento “na paṭiggaṇhāti na vīmaṃsati paccāharatī”ti vuccati. Catutthapadaṃ pākaṭameva.

'He does not accept, but investigates and reports back' means that some man makes such a conversation with a monk where he is standing or sitting. The monk, though not sent by him, acts as if sent, goes to the woman's presence, and investigates by the method beginning with, 'Be, it is said, the wife of so-and-so.' Having ascertained her liking or disliking, he comes back again and informs this man. One who, in the same way, investigates but does not report back is called 'he does not accept, investigates, but does not report back.' One who, having gone in the same way without investigating, hears the conversation initiated by her and, according to the method stated in the third case of the first set of four, comes and informs this man, is called 'he does not accept, does not investigate, but reports back.' The fourth case is self-evident.

Sambahule bhikkhū āṇāpetītiādinayā pākaṭāyeva. Yathā pana sambahulāpi ekavatthumhi āpajjanti, evaṃ ekassapi sambahulavatthūsu sambahulā āpattiyo veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Puriso bhikkhuṃ [V 2.0131] āṇāpeti “gaccha, bhante, asukasmiṃ nāma pāsāde saṭṭhimattā vā sattatimattā vā itthiyo ṭhitā tā vadehi, hotha kira itthannāmassa bhariyāyo”ti. So sampaṭicchitvā tattha gantvā ārocetvā puna taṃ sāsanaṃ paccāharati. Yattakā itthiyo tattakā āpattiyo āpajjati. Vuttañhetaṃ parivārepi –

The method beginning with 'he commands many bhikkhus' is self-evident. Furthermore, just as many bhikkhus may incur an offense in regard to a single case, so too should it be understood that a single bhikkhu may incur many offenses in regard to many cases. How? A man commands a bhikkhu, saying, 'Go, venerable sir, in such-and-such a palace are sixty or seventy women standing. Tell them, "Be, it is said, the wives of so-and-so."' He, having accepted, goes there, delivers the message, and then brings back that message. He falls into as many offenses as there are women. And this has been said in the Parivāra:

“Padavītihāramattena, vācāya bhaṇitena ca;

Sabbāni garukāni sappaṭikammāni;

Catusaṭṭhi āpattiyo āpajjeyya ekato;

Pañhāmesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 480);

'By the mere taking of a step, and by what is spoken with the voice, one might fall into sixty-four offenses at once—all of them serious and remediable. This is a question considered by the skilled.'

Imaṃ [P 3.0559] kira atthavasaṃ paṭicca ayaṃ pañho vutto. Vacanasiliṭṭhatāya cettha “catusaṭṭhi āpattiyo”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ karonto pana satampi sahassampi āpajjatīti. Yathā ca ekena pesitassa ekassa sambahulāsu itthīsu sambahulā āpattiyo, evaṃ eko puriso sambahule bhikkhū ekissā santikaṃ peseti, sabbesaṃ saṅghādiseso. Eko sambahule bhikkhū sambahulānaṃ itthīnaṃ santikaṃ peseti, itthigaṇanāya saṅghādisesā. Sambahulā purisā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ekissā santikaṃ pesenti, purisagaṇanāya saṅghādisesā. Sambahulā ekaṃ sambahulānaṃ itthīnaṃ santikaṃ pesenti, vatthugaṇanāya saṅghādisesā. Sambahulā sambahule ekissā santikaṃ pesenti, vatthugaṇanāya saṅghādisesā. Sambahulā purisā sambahule bhikkhū sambahulānaṃ itthīnaṃ santikaṃ pesenti, vatthugaṇanāya saṅghādisesā. Esa nayo “ekā itthī ekaṃ bhikkhu”ntiādīsupi. Ettha ca sabhāgavibhāgatā nāma appamāṇaṃ, mātāpitunampi pañcasahadhammikānampi sañcarittakammaṃ karontassa āpattiyeva.

It is said that this question was asked with reference to this particular reason. And here, for the sake of conciseness of speech, it was said, 'sixty-four offenses.' However, one who acts in this way can indeed incur a hundred or even a thousand offenses. And just as for one bhikkhu sent by one man to many women there are many offenses, so too if one man sends many bhikkhus to one woman, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense for all of them. If one man sends many bhikkhus to many women, there are Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of women. If many men send one bhikkhu to one woman, there are Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of men. If many men send one bhikkhu to many women, there are Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of cases. If many men send many bhikkhus to one woman, there are Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of cases. If many men send many bhikkhus to many women, there are Saṅghādisesa offenses according to the number of cases. This same method applies in cases such as 'one woman, one bhikkhu,' and so on. And in this matter, whether the parties are compatible or incompatible is not the measure; for one who performs the act of a go-between even for one's mother and father or for the five kinds of fellow Dhamma-farers, it is indeed an offense.

Puriso [M 2.0146] bhikkhuṃ āṇāpeti gaccha bhanteti catukkaṃ aṅgavasena āpattibheda dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa pacchimapade antevāsī vīmaṃsitvā bahiddhā paccāharatīti āgantvā ācariyassa anārocetvā ettova gantvā tassa purisassa āroceti. Āpatti ubhinnaṃ thullaccayassāti ācariyassa paṭiggahitattā ca vīmaṃsāpitattā ca dvīhaṅgehi thullaccayaṃ, antevāsikassa vīmaṃsitattā ca paccāhaṭattā ca dvīhaṅgehi thullaccayaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

The tetrad beginning, 'A man commands a bhikkhu, “Go, venerable sir,”' was spoken for the purpose of showing the distinctions of offenses by way of their factors. In its last phrase, 'the pupil, having investigated, reports it externally,' means that without returning and informing his teacher, he goes from that very place and informs that man. The offense for both is a grave offense. For the teacher, because of accepting and because of causing the investigation, there is a grave offense due to two factors. For the pupil, because of investigating and because of reporting back, there is a grave offense due to two factors. The rest is evident.

339. Gacchanto sampādetīti paṭiggaṇhāti ceva vīmaṃsati ca. Āgacchanto visaṃvādetīti na paccāharati. Gacchanto visaṃvādetīti na paṭiggaṇhāti. Āgacchanto sampādetīti [V 2.0132] vīmaṃsati ceva paccāharati ca. Evaṃ ubhayattha dvīhaṅgehi thullaccayaṃ. Tatiyapade āpatti, catutthe anāpatti.

339. 'While going, he accomplishes' means he both accepts and investigates. 'While returning, he deceives' means he does not report back. 'While going, he deceives' means he does not accept. 'While returning, he accomplishes' means he both investigates and reports back. Thus, in the first two cases, there is a grave offense due to two factors. In the third phrase, there is an offense; in the fourth, there is no offense.

340. Anāpatti saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā gilānassa vā karaṇīyena gacchati ummattakassa ādikammikassāti ettha bhikkhusaṅghassa uposathāgāraṃ vā kiñci vā vippakataṃ hoti. Tattha kārukānaṃ [P 3.0560] bhattavetanatthāya upāsako vā upāsikāya santikaṃ bhikkhuṃ pahiṇeyya, uṃpāsikā vā upāsakassa, evarūpena saṅghassa karaṇīyena gacchantassa anāpatti. Cetiyakamme kayiramānepi eseva nayo. Gilānassa bhesajjatthāyapi upāsakena vā upāsikāya santikaṃ upāsikāya vā upāsakassa santikaṃ pahitassa gacchato anāpatti. Ummattakaādikammikā vuttanayā eva.

340. Regarding 'There is no offense for one who goes on business for the Saṅgha, or a cetiya, or a sick person; nor for one who is insane or is the first offender': Herein, if the Uposatha hall of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha or some other building is unfinished, and for the purpose of providing food and wages for the workers there, a male lay follower might send a bhikkhu to a female lay follower, or a female lay follower to a male lay follower—for one going on such business for the Saṅgha, there is no offense. This same method applies when work is being done on a cetiya. Also, for the sake of medicine for a sick person, for one who goes having been sent by a male lay follower to a female lay follower, or by a female lay follower to a male lay follower, there is no offense. The cases of the insane person and the first offender are as has been stated.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the analysis of the terms is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, sīsukkhipanādinā kāyavikārena sāsanaṃ gahetvā gantvā hatthamuddāya vīmaṃsitvā puna āgantvā hatthamuddāya eva ārocentassa kāyato samuṭṭhāti. Āsanasālāya nisinnassa “itthannāmā āgamissati, tassā cittaṃ jāneyyāthā”ti kenaci vutte “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ āgataṃ vatvā tassā gatāya puna tasmiṃ purise āgate ārocentassa vācato samuṭṭhāti. Vācāya “sādhū”ti sāsanaṃ gahetvā aññena karaṇīyena tassā gharaṃ gantvā aññattha vā gamanakāle taṃ disvā vacībhedeneva vīmaṃsitvā puna aññeneva [M 2.0147] karaṇīyena tato apakkamma kadācideva taṃ purisaṃ disvā ārocentassāpi vācatova samuṭṭhāti. Paṇṇattiṃ ajānantassa pana khīṇāsavassāpi kāyavācato samuṭṭhāti. Kathaṃ? Sace hissa mātāpitaro kujjhitvā alaṃvacanīyā honti, tañca bhikkhuṃ gharaṃ upagataṃ therapitā vadati “mātā te tāta maṃ mahallakaṃ chaḍḍetvā ñātikulaṃ gatā, gaccha taṃ maṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ pesehī”ti. So ce gantvā taṃ vatvā puna pituno tassā āgamanaṃ vā anāgamanaṃ vā āroceti, saṅghādiseso. Imāni tīṇi acittakasamuṭṭhānāni.

Regarding the origins and so forth, this training rule has six origins. For one who receives a message through a bodily gesture such as raising the head, goes and investigates by means of a hand signal, and then returns and reports back by means of a hand signal, the offense arises from the body. For one who is sitting in a rest house when someone says, 'A woman of such-and-such a name will come; you should ascertain her mind,' and who agrees by saying, 'Good,' speaks to that woman when she has come, and after she has left, reports back when that man returns, the offense arises from speech. For one who accepts a message by saying 'Good' with his speech, goes to her house on some other business, or sees her while on his way elsewhere, investigates only by means of verbal exchange, and then, having departed from there on some other business, at some time sees that man and reports to him, the offense arises from speech alone. However, for one who does not know the regulation, even for a Worthy One whose corruptions are destroyed, it arises from body and speech. How so? If his mother and father, having quarreled, are amenable to being reconciled, and when that bhikkhu has gone to the house, the elder's father says: 'Son, your mother has abandoned me, an old man, and gone to her relatives' home. Go, send her to me to attend to me.' If he goes and speaks to her and then reports back to his father about her coming or not coming, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. These three are origins without intention.

Paṇṇattiṃ pana jānitvā eteheva tīhi nayehi sañcarittaṃ samāpajjato kāyacittato vācācittato kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Imāni tīṇi paṇṇattijānanacittena sacittakasamuṭṭhānāni. Kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, kusalādivasena cettha tīṇi cittāni, sukhādivasena tisso vedanāti.

However, for one who knows the regulation and engages in the act of a go-between by these same three methods, the offense arises from body-and-mind, from speech-and-mind, and from body-speech-and-mind. These three are origins with intention, with a mind that knows the regulation. It is functional, there is no exemption through perception, it is an offense by regulation, it is a bodily action, and a verbal action. Herein, there are three kinds of consciousness by way of wholesome, etc., and three kinds of feeling by way of pleasure, etc.

341. Vinītavatthūsu [V 2.0133] ādito vatthupañcake paṭiggahitamattattā dukkaṭaṃ.

341. In the Decided Cases, in the first pentad of cases, it is a dukkaṭa offense for merely having accepted.

Kalahavatthusmiṃ sammodanīyaṃ akāsīti taṃ saññāpetvā [P 3.0561] puna gehagamanīyaṃ

In the case of the quarrel, 'he exchanged friendly greetings' means he persuaded her that she should go back home again.

Akāsi. Nālaṃvacanīyāti na pariccattāti attho. Yā hi yathā yathā yesu yesu janapadesu pariccattā pariccattāva hoti, bhariyābhāvaṃ atikkamati, ayaṃ “alaṃvacanīyā”ti vuccati. Esā pana na alaṃvacanīyā kenacideva kāraṇena kalahaṃ katvā gatā, tenevettha bhagavā “anāpattī”ti āha. Yasmā pana kāyasaṃsagge yakkhiyā thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā duṭṭhullādīsupi yakkhipetiyo thullaccayavatthumevāti veditabbā. Aṭṭhakathāsu panetaṃ na vicāritaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

He did so. Nālaṃvacanīyā means 'not relinquished.' For indeed, in whatever way and in whatever regions a woman, having been relinquished, is truly relinquished and transcends the state of being a wife, she is called alaṃvacanīyā ('one who is relinquished'). This woman, however, is not an alaṃvacanīyā; she left after quarreling for some reason. Therefore, in this case, the Blessed One said, 'There is no offense.' Furthermore, since a grave offense is stated in the training rule on physical contact with a yakkhiṇī, it should be understood that in the training rules on lewd speech and so on, yakkhiṇīs and petīs are also grounds for a grave offense. However, this matter was not examined in the commentaries. The meaning of the rest is plain everywhere.

Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning acting as a go-between is concluded.

6. Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Hut-Building

342. Tena samayenāti kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha āḷavakāti āḷaviraṭṭhe jātā dārakā āḷavakā nāma, te pabbajitakālepi “āḷavakā”tveva paññāyiṃsu. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “āḷavakā bhikkhū”ti. Saññācikāyoti [M 2.0148] sayaṃ yācitvā gahitūpakaraṇāyo. Kārāpentīti karontipi kārāpentipi, te kira sāsane vipassanādhurañca ganthadhurañcāti dvepi dhurāni chaḍḍetvā navakammameva dhuraṃ katvā paggaṇhiṃsu. Assāmikāyoti anissarāyo, kāretā dāyakena virahitāyoti attho. Attuddesikāyoti attānaṃ uddissa attano atthāya āraddhāyoti attho. Appamāṇikāyoti “ettakena niṭṭhaṃ gacchissantī”ti evaṃ aparicchinnappamāṇāyo, vuddhippamāṇāyo vā mahantappamāṇāyoti attho.

342. ‘At that time’ introduces the training rule on hut-building. Therein, Āḷavakā refers to boys born in the country of Āḷavī, who were known as ‘Āḷavakā’ even after their ordination. It is with reference to them that it was said, ‘the Āḷavaka bhikkhus.’ Saññācikāya means huts for which they obtained the materials by personally requesting them. Kārāpenti means they both build them and have them built. It is said that in the Dispensation, they abandoned both the burdens of insight meditation and study, and took up only the new construction work as their burden. Assāmikā means without a master; that is, without a donor to have it built. Attuddesikā means intended for oneself; that is, undertaken for one's own sake, designating oneself. Appamāṇikā means of an unspecified size; that is, of a size that is not determined, as in ‘it will be finished with this much’; or, of increasing size, meaning of a great size.

Yācanā eva bahulā etesaṃ mandaṃ aññaṃ kammanti yācanabahulā. Evaṃ viññattibahulā veditabbā. Atthato panettha nānākaraṇaṃ natthi, anekakkhattuṃ “purisaṃ detha, purisatthakaraṃ dethā”ti yācantānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha mūlacchejjāya purisaṃ yācituṃ na vaṭṭati, sahāyatthāya kammakaraṇatthāya “purisaṃ dethā”ti yācituṃ vaṭṭati. Purisatthakaranti purisena kātabbaṃ hatthakammaṃ vuccati, taṃ yācituṃ vaṭṭati. Hatthakammaṃ nāma kiñci vatthu na hoti, tasmā [P 3.0562] ṭhapetvā migaluddakamacchabandhakādīnaṃ sakakammaṃ avasesaṃ sabbaṃ kappiyaṃ. “Kiṃ, bhante, āgatattha kena kamma”nti pucchite vā apucchite vā yācituṃ vaṭṭati, viññattipaccayā doso natthi. Tasmā migaluddakādayo sakakammaṃ na yācitabbā, “hatthakammaṃ dethā”ti aniyametvāpi na yācitabbā; evaṃ [V 2.0134] yācitā hi te “sādhu, bhante”ti bhikkhū uyyojetvā migepi māretvā āhareyyuṃ. Niyametvā pana “vihāre kiñci kattabbaṃ atthi, tattha hatthakammaṃ dethā”ti yācitabbā. Phālanaṅgalādīni upakaraṇāni gahetvā kasituṃ vā vapituṃ vā lāyituṃ vā gacchantaṃ sakiccapasutampi kassakaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci hatthakammaṃ yācituṃ vaṭṭateva. Yo pana vighāsādo vā añño vā koci nikkammo niratthakakathaṃ kathento niddāyanto vā viharati, evarūpaṃ ayācitvāpi “ehi re idaṃ vā idaṃ vā karohī”ti yadicchakaṃ kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

For them, requesting is frequent and other work is little, hence they are yācanabahulā (frequent requesters). Similarly, they should be understood as viññattibahulā (frequent intimators). In terms of meaning, there is no difference here; this is a designation for those who repeatedly ask, 'Give a man, give a man's labor.' In this context, it is not allowable to ask for a man by way of a lump-sum payment. It is allowable to ask, 'Give a man,' for the purpose of companionship or for doing work. Purisatthakaraṃ refers to manual labor to be done by a man; it is allowable to ask for that. Manual labor is not a physical object; therefore, setting aside the personal work of deer-hunters, fishermen, and the like, all remaining manual labor is allowable. Whether asked, 'Venerable sirs, why have you come? What work is there?' or not asked, it is allowable to request. There is no offense on account of the intimation. Therefore, deer-hunters and the like should not be asked for their personal work, nor should one ask without specifying, 'Give manual labor.' For if asked in this way, they might say, 'Very well, venerable sirs,' send the bhikkhus away, and then kill even deer and bring them. However, one should ask by specifying, 'There is something to be done in the monastery; give manual labor for that.' It is indeed allowable to ask for some manual labor even from a farmer or another person who is engaged in his own task, who is going to plow, sow, or reap, having taken up a plowshare, plow, and other implements. But as for one who eats leftovers, or some other idle person who spends his time engaging in useless talk or sleeping, it is allowable to have such a person do whatever one wishes without even asking, saying, 'Hey, you! Come and do this or that.'

Hatthakammassa pana sabbakappiyabhāvadīpanatthaṃ imaṃ nayaṃ kathenti. Sace hi bhikkhu pāsādaṃ kāretukāmo hoti, thambhatthāya pāsāṇakoṭṭakānaṃ gharaṃ gantvā vattabbaṃ “hatthakammaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati upāsakā”ti. Kiṃ kātabbaṃ, bhante,ti? Pāsāṇatthambhā uddharitvā dātabbāti. Sace te uddharitvā [M 2.0149] vā denti, uddharitvā nikkhitte attano thambhe vā denti, vaṭṭati. Athāpi vadanti – “amhākaṃ, bhante, hatthakammaṃ kātuṃ khaṇo natthi, aññaṃ uddharāpetha, tassa mūlaṃ dassāmā”ti uddharāpetvā “pāsāṇatthambhe uddhaṭamanussānaṃ mūlaṃ dethā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Etenevupāyena pāsādadārūnaṃ atthāya vaḍḍhakīnaṃ santikaṃ iṭṭhakatthāya iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakīnaṃ chadanatthāya gehacchādakānaṃ cittakammatthāya cittakārānanti yena yena attho hoti, tassa tassa atthāya tesaṃ tesaṃ sippakārakānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā hatthakammaṃ yācituṃ vaṭṭati. Hatthakammayācanavasena ca mūlacchejjāya vā bhattavetanānuppadānena vā laddhampi sabbaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Araññato āharāpentena ca sabbaṃ anajjhāvutthakaṃ āharāpetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, to show the complete allowability of manual labor, they state this method. If a bhikkhu wishes to have a storied building constructed, he should go to the house of stone-cutters for the purpose of pillars and say, 'Lay followers, it is allowable to receive manual labor.' If they ask, 'What is to be done, venerable sir?' he should say, 'Stone pillars are to be quarried and given.' If they quarry and give them, or if they give their own pillars that have been quarried and set aside, it is allowable. And even if they say, 'Venerable sir, we do not have time to do the manual labor; have someone else quarry them, and we will give the payment,' it is allowable, after having them quarried, to say, 'Give the payment to the people who quarried the stone pillars.' By this same method, for the purpose of timber for the storied building, one may go to carpenters; for bricks, to brickmakers; for roofing, to roofers; for painted decorations, to painters. For whatever is needed, one may go to the respective artisans and request manual labor. And by way of requesting manual labor, it is allowable to accept everything obtained, whether through a lump-sum payment or by the provision of food and wages. And when having things brought from the forest, everything that is not owned by others should be brought.

Na kevalañca pāsādaṃ kāretukāmena mañcapīṭhapattaparissāvanadhamakarakacīvarādīni [P 3.0563] kārāpetukāmenāpi dārulohasuttādīni labhitvā te te sippakārake upasaṅkamitvā vuttanayeneva hatthakammaṃ yācitabbaṃ. Hatthakammayācanavasena ca mūlacchejjāya vā bhattavetanānuppadānena vā laddhampi sabbaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Sace pana kātuṃ na icchanti, bhattavetanaṃ paccāsīsanti, akappiyakahāpaṇādi na dātabbaṃ. Bhikkhācāravattena taṇḍulādīni pariyesitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati.

And it is not only a bhikkhu who wishes to have a storied building made who should request manual labor. One who wishes to have beds, chairs, bowls, strainers, water-pots, robes, and so on made should also, after obtaining wood, metal, thread, and other materials, approach the respective artisans and request manual labor in the manner already stated. And by way of requesting manual labor, everything obtained, whether through a lump-sum payment or by the provision of food and wages, should be accepted. If, however, they do not wish to do the work but expect food and wages, unallowable items such as kahāpaṇas should not be given. It is allowable to seek out rice and other provisions by the practice of the alms-round and give those.

Hatthakammavasena pattaṃ kāretvā tatheva pācetvā navapakkassa pattassa puñchanatelatthāya antogāmaṃ paviṭṭhena “bhikkhāya āgato”ti sallakkhetvā yāguyā vā bhatte vā ānīte hatthena patto pidhātabbo. Sace upāsikā “kiṃ, bhante”ti pucchati, “navapakko patto puñchanatelena attho”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace sā “dehi, bhante”ti pattaṃ gahetvā telena puñchitvā yāguyā vā bhattassa vā pūretvā deti, viññatti nāma na hoti, gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

Having had a bowl made by means of manual labor and having had it fired in the same way, when a monk has entered a village for the purpose of obtaining oil to wipe the newly fired bowl, and when gruel or cooked rice is brought by someone perceiving, 'He has come for alms,' the bowl should be covered with the hand. If a laywoman asks, 'What is it, venerable sir?' it should be said, 'The bowl is newly fired; there is a need for wiping-oil.' If she, saying, 'Give it, venerable sir,' takes the bowl, wipes it with oil, and gives it back filled with gruel or cooked rice, this is not what is called soliciting; it is permissible to accept it.

Bhikkhū [V 2.0135] pageva piṇḍāya caritvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā āsanaṃ apassantā tiṭṭhanti. Tatra ce upāsakā bhikkhū ṭhite disvā sayameva āsanāni āharāpenti, nisīditvā gacchantehi āpucchitvā gantabbaṃ. Anāpucchā gatānampi naṭṭhaṃ gīvā na hoti, āpucchitvā gamanaṃ pana vattaṃ. Sace bhikkhūhi “āsanāni āharathā”ti vuttehi āhaṭāni honti, āpucchitvāva gantabbaṃ. Anāpucchā gatānaṃ vattabhedo ca naṭṭhañca gīvāti. Attharaṇakojavādīsupi eseva nayo.

Monks, having gone for alms early, go to the assembly hall and, not seeing a seat, they stand. If laymen there, seeing the monks standing, have seats brought of their own accord, then having sat down, when leaving, they should depart after asking permission. Even for those who have gone without asking permission, a lost seat does not become a liability; however, to depart after asking permission is a duty. If seats are brought by those who were told by the monks, 'Bring seats,' then they must certainly depart after asking permission. For those who have gone without asking permission, there is both a breach of duty and a lost seat becomes a liability. This is the same principle in the case of coverings, rugs, and so on.

Makkhikāyo [M 2.0150] bahukā honti, “makkhikābījaniṃ āharathā”ti vattabbaṃ. Pucimandasākhādīni āharanti, kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paṭiggahetabbāni. Āsanasālāya udakabhājanaṃ rittaṃ hoti, “dhamakaraṇaṃ gaṇhā”ti na vattabbaṃ. Dhamakarakañhi rittabhājane pakkhipanto bhindeyya “nadiṃ vā taḷākaṃ vā gantvā pana udakaṃ āharā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Gehato āharā”ti neva vattuṃ vaṭṭati, na āhaṭaṃ [P 3.0564] paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Āsanasālāyaṃ vā araññake vā bhattakiccaṃ karontehi tatthajātakaṃ anajjhāvutthakaṃ yaṃkiñci uttaribhaṅgārahaṃ pattaṃ vā phalaṃ vā sace kiñci kammaṃ karontaṃ āharāpeti, hatthakammavasena āharāpetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Alajjīhi pana bhikkhūhi vā sāmaṇerehi vā hatthakammaṃ na kāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva purisatthakare nayo.

If there are many flies, it may be said, 'Bring a fly whisk.' If they bring neem branches and so on, having had them made allowable, they should be accepted. If the water vessel in the assembly hall is empty, it should not be said, 'Take the water filter,' for one putting the water filter into an empty vessel might break it. However, it is permissible to say, 'Go to the river or the pond and bring water.' It is not at all permissible to say, 'Bring it from a house,' and what has been brought should not be used. When monks are making their meal in an assembly hall or in a forest dwelling, if they have something brought—whatever unowned thing grown in that place, such as a leaf or fruit suitable for a side-dish—by someone doing some work, it is permissible to have it brought by means of manual labor and to use it. However, manual labor should not be caused to be done by shameless monks or novices. This, for now, is the principle in the matter of what is to be done before the meal.

Goṇaṃ pana aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato āharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, āharāpentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Ñātipavāritaṭṭhānatopi mūlacchejjāya yācituṃ na vaṭṭati, tāvakālikanayena sabbattha vaṭṭati. Evaṃ āharāpitañca goṇaṃ rakkhitvā jaggitvā sāmikā paṭicchāpetabbā. Sacassa pādo vā siṅgaṃ vā bhijjati vā nassati vā sāmikā ce sampaṭicchanti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce sampaṭicchanti, gīvā hoti. Sace “tumhākaṃyeva demā”ti vadanti na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. “Vihārassa demā”ti vutte pana “ārāmikānaṃ ācikkhatha jagganatthāyā”ti vattabbaṃ.

However, it is not permissible to have a bull brought from non-relatives or from those who have not given an invitation; for one who has it brought, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Even from relatives or from those who have given an invitation, it is not permissible to ask for it permanently; by the method of temporary use, it is permissible to ask in all cases. And a bull that has been brought thus, having been guarded and tended to, should be returned to the owners. If its foot or horn is broken or is lost, and if the owners accept it back, this is good. If they do not accept it back, it becomes a liability. If they say, 'We give it only to you,' it should not be accepted. But when it is said, 'We give it to the monastery,' it should be said, 'Inform the monastery attendants for the purpose of tending to it.'

“Sakaṭaṃ dethā”tipi aññātakaappavārite vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, viññattieva hoti dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Ñātipavāritaṭṭhāne pana vaṭṭati, tāvakālikaṃ vaṭṭati kammaṃ katvā puna dātabbaṃ. Sace nemiyādīni bhijjanti pākatikāni katvā dātabbaṃ. Naṭṭhe gīvā hoti. “Tumhākameva demā”ti vutte dārubhaṇḍaṃ nāma sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Esa nayo vāsipharasukuṭhārīkudālanikhādanesu. Valliādīsu ca parapariggahitesu. Garubhaṇḍappahonakesuyeva ca valliādīsu viññatti hoti, na tato oraṃ.

Also, to say 'Give a cart' to non-relatives or the uninvited is not permissible; it is just a solicitation, and one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. However, in the case of relatives or the invited, it is permissible. It is permissible for temporary use; after the work is done, it must be given back. If the wheel-rims and so on are broken, it must be returned after restoring them to their original condition. If it is lost, it becomes a liability. When it is said, 'We give it only to you,' it is permissible to accept what is called 'wooden goods.' This is the principle for an adze, axe, hatchet, hoe, and chisel, and also for vines and so on that are possessed by others. And solicitation for vines and so on occurs only in the case of those that amount to heavy articles, not for anything less than that.

Anajjhāvutthakaṃ [V 2.0136] pana yaṃkiñci āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Rakkhitagopitaṭṭhāneyeva hi viññatti nāma vuccati. Sā dvīsu paccayesu sabbena sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati, senāsanapaccaye pana “āhara dehī”ti viññattimattameva na vaṭṭati[M 2.0151], parikathobhāsanimittakammāni vaṭṭanti. Tattha uposathāgāraṃ vā bhojanasālaṃ vā aññaṃ vā yaṃkiñci senāsanaṃ icchato “imasmiṃ vata okāse evarūpaṃ senāsanaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vā “yutta”nti vā “anurūpa”nti vātiādinā [P 3.0565] nayena vacanaṃ parikathā nāma. “Upāsakā tumhe kuhiṃ vasathā”ti? “Pāsāde, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pana upāsakā pāsādo na vaṭṭatī”ti evamādivacanaṃ obhāso nāma. Manusse disvā rajjuṃ pasāreti, khīle ākoṭāpeti. “Kiṃ idaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “idha āvāsaṃ karissāmā”ti evamādikaraṇaṃ pana nimittakammaṃ nāma. Gilānapaccaye pana viññattipi vaṭṭati, pageva parikathādīni.

However, it is permissible to have anything that is unowned brought. Indeed, it is only called 'solicitation' in the case of a guarded and protected place. That solicitation is not permissible in any way at all for the two requisites of robes and almsfood. But in the case of the requisite of lodging, a mere solicitation like 'bring' or 'give' is not permissible; allusive talk, giving a hint, and making a sign are permissible. Therein, for a monk who desires an Uposatha hall, a dining hall, or any other lodging, a statement made in the manner of, 'Indeed, in this spot it would be proper to build such a lodging,' or 'it would be suitable,' or 'it would be appropriate,' is called 'allusive talk.' Asking, 'Laymen, where do you live?' and when they say, 'In a mansion, venerable sir,' saying, 'But laymen, is a mansion not permissible for monks?'—a statement such as this is called 'giving a hint.' Seeing people, stretching out a measuring-line, having stakes hammered in, and when asked, 'What is this, venerable sir?' saying, 'We will make a dwelling here'—an act such as this is called 'making a sign.' But in the case of the requisite for the sick, even solicitation is permissible, let alone allusive talk and so on.

Manussā upaddutā yācanāya upaddutā viññattiyāti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tāya yācanāya ca viññattiyā ca pīḷitā. Ubbijjantipīti “kiṃ nu āharāpessantī”ti ubbegaṃ iñjanaṃ calanaṃ paṭilabhanti. Uttasantipīti ahiṃ viya disvā sahasā tasitvā ukkamanti. Palāyantipīti dūratova yena vā tena vā palāyanti. Aññenapi gacchantīti yaṃ maggaṃ paṭipannā taṃ pahāya nivattitvā vāmaṃ vā dakkhiṇaṃ vā gahetvā gacchanti, dvārampi thakenti.

'People are troubled by begging, troubled by solicitation' means: they are oppressed by that begging and that solicitation of those monks. 'They become anxious' means: thinking, 'What now will they have us bring?' they experience agitation, trembling, and wavering. 'They are terrified' means: as if having seen a snake, being suddenly startled, they retreat. 'They flee' means: from afar they flee to any place whatsoever. 'They go by another way' means: abandoning the path they have taken, they turn back and, taking a left or a right path, they go; they even shut the door.

344. Bhūtapubbaṃ bhikkhaveti iti bhagavā te bhikkhū garahitvā tadanurūpañca dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā punapi viññattiyā dosaṃ pākaṭaṃ kurumāno iminā “bhūtapubbaṃ bhikkhave”tiādinā nayena tīṇi vatthūni dassesi. Tattha maṇikaṇṭhoti so kira nāgarājā sabbakāmadadaṃ mahagghaṃ maṇiṃ kaṇṭhe pilandhitvā carati, tasmā “maṇikaṇṭho” tveva paññāyittha. Uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ karitvā aṭṭhāsīti so kira tesaṃ dvinnaṃ isīnaṃ kaniṭṭho isi mettāvihārī ahosi, tasmā nāgarājā nadito uttaritvā devavaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā tassa santike nisīditvā sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ katvā taṃ devavaṇṇaṃ pahāya sakavaṇṇameva upagantvā taṃ isiṃ parikkhipitvā pasannākāraṃ karonto uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ karitvā chattaṃ viya dhārayamāno muhuttaṃ ṭhatvā pakkamati, tena vuttaṃ “uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ karitvā aṭṭhāsī”ti. Maṇimassa kaṇṭhe pilandhananti maṇiṃ assa kaṇṭhe pilandhitaṃ, āmukkanti attho. Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsīti tena devavaṇṇena āgantvā tāpasena saddhiṃ sammodamāno ekasmiṃ padese aṭṭhāsi.

344. “Monks, in the past…”: Thus, having rebuked those monks and given a Dhamma talk appropriate to that, the Blessed One, again making clear the fault of solicitation, showed three stories by this method beginning with, “Monks, in the past…”. Therein, Maṇikaṇṭha: It is said that that Nāga king wanders about wearing on his neck a valuable gem that grants all wishes; therefore, he became known as “Maṇikaṇṭha”. He stood with a large hood above his head: It is said that the younger of the two ascetics was one who dwelt in loving-kindness. Therefore, the Nāga king, having emerged from the river and created a divine form, sat near him, engaged in pleasant conversation, then abandoned that divine form, returned to his own form, encircled that ascetic, displayed a pleased demeanor, made a large hood above his head, held it like an umbrella, stood for a moment, and then departed. Therefore it was said, “He stood with a large hood above his head.” The gem fastened on his neck: The gem fastened on his neck, meaning it was worn. He stood to one side: Having come in that divine form and conversing pleasantly with the ascetic, he stood in one place.

Mamannapānanti [M 2.0152] mama annañca pānañca. Vipulanti bahulaṃ. Uḷāranti paṇītaṃ[P 3.0566]. Atiyācakosīti [V 2.0137] ativiya yācako, asi punappunaṃ yācasīti vuttaṃ hoti. Susūti taruṇo, thāmasampanno yobbanappattapuriso. Sakkharā vuccati kāḷasilā, tattha dhoto asi “sakkharadhoto nāmā”ti vuccati, sakkharadhoto pāṇimhi assāti sakkharadhotapāṇi, pāsāṇe dhotanisitakhaggahatthoti attho. Yathā so asihattho puriso tāseyya, evaṃ tāsesi maṃ selaṃ yācamāno, maṇiṃ yācantoti attho.

“My food and drink”: My food and drink. “Abundant”: Much. “Excellent”: Exquisite. “You are an excessive beggar”: You are a great beggar; this means, you beg again and again. Susū: A young man, endowed with strength, who has reached youth. Sakkharā is called black stone; a sword sharpened on it is called sakkharadhoto (“sharpened on stone”). Because he has a sword sharpened on stone in his hand, he is sakkharadhotapāṇi (“one with a sword sharpened on stone in hand”); the meaning is one who has in hand a sharp sword sharpened on a whetstone. Just as that man with a sword in hand would frighten, so you frighten me by asking for the gem, meaning asking for the jewel.

Na taṃ yāceti taṃ na yāceyya. Kataraṃ? Yassa piyaṃ jigīseti yaṃ assa sattassa piyanti jāneyya.

“One should not ask for that”: One should not ask for that thing. Which thing? Regarding ‘that which is dear to another,’ this means that which one might know is dear to that being.

Kimaṅgaṃ pana manussabhūtānanti manussabhūtānaṃ amanāpāti kimevettha vattabbaṃ.

“How much more so for human beings?”: This means, what need is there to speak of it being displeasing for human beings?

345. Sakuṇasaṅghassa saddena ubbāḷhoti so kira sakuṇasaṅgho paṭhamayāmañca pacchimayāmañca nirantaraṃ saddameva karoti, so bhikkhu tena saddena pīḷito hutvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Tenāha – “yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamī”ti.

345. “Disturbed by the noise of the flock of birds”: That flock of birds, it is said, made continuous noise during the first and last watches of the night. That monk, oppressed by that noise, went to the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, he said: “I approached where he was.”

Kuto ca tvaṃ bhikkhu āgacchasīti ettha nisinno so bhikkhu na āgacchati vattamānasamīpe pana evaṃ vattuṃ labbhati. Tenāha – “kuto ca tvaṃ bhikkhu āgacchasī”ti, kuto āgatosīti attho. Tato ahaṃ bhagavā āgacchāmīti etthāpi so eva nayo. Ubbāḷhoti pīḷito, ukkaṇṭhāpito hutvāti attho.

“Monk, from where are you coming?”: Here, that seated monk is not in the process of coming, but it is permissible to speak thus of the recent past. Therefore, He said, “Monk, from where are you coming?”, meaning, “From where have you come?”. “From there, Blessed One, I am coming”: Here too, the same principle applies. Ubbāḷho: Oppressed, meaning having been made dissatisfied.

So sakuṇasaṅgho “bhikkhu pattaṃ yācatī”ti ettha na te sakuṇā bhikkhuno vacanaṃ jānanti, bhagavā pana attano ānubhāvena yathā jānanti tathā akāsi.

Regarding that flock of birds and the passage ‘the monk asks for a feather’: those birds do not understand the monk’s words, but the Blessed One, by his own power, made it so that they understood.

346. Apāhaṃ te na jānāmīti api ahaṃ te jane “ke vā ime, kassa vā ime”ti na jānāmi. Saṅgamma yācantīti samāgantvā vaggavaggā hutvā yācanti. Yācako appiyo hotīti yo yācati so appiyo hoti. Yācaṃ adadamappiyoti yācanti yācitaṃ vuccati, yācitamatthaṃ adadantopi appiyo hoti. Atha vā yācanti yācantassa, adadamappiyoti [M 2.0153] adento appiyo hoti. Mā me videssanā ahūti mā me appiyabhāvo ahu, ahaṃ vā tava, tvaṃ vā mama videsso appiyo mā ahosīti attho.

346. “I do not know you”: I do not know these people, neither who they are nor whose they are. “They come together and ask”: Having come together and formed into various groups, they ask. “A beggar is disliked”: He who asks is disliked. “Not giving what is asked for, one is disliked”: Here, yācaṃ is said for what is solicited; one who does not give the solicited item is also disliked. Alternatively, yācaṃ is for the one asking; one who does not give is disliked. “May there be no aversion for me”: May the state of being disliked not befall me. The meaning is: May I not be disliked by you, nor you by me.

347. Dussaṃharānīti [V 2.0138] kasigorakkhādīhi upāyehi dukkhena saṃharaṇīyāni.

347. “Hard to gather”: Things that are to be gathered with difficulty by means such as ploughing and cattle-herding.

348-9. Saññācikāya pana bhikkhunāti ettha saññācikā nāma sayaṃ pavattitayācanā vuccati, tasmā “saññācikāyā”ti attano [P 3.0567] yācanāyāti vuttaṃ hoti, sayaṃ yācitakehi upakaraṇehīti attho. Yasmā pana sā sayaṃyācitakehi kayiramānā sayaṃ yācitvā kayiramānā hoti, tasmā taṃ atthapariyāyaṃ dassetuṃ “sayaṃ yācitvā purisampī”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

348-9. “By a monk through solicitation”: Here, saññācikā is the name for a request initiated by oneself. Therefore, “by solicitation” means by one’s own request; the meaning is with materials obtained by one’s own asking. And since a hut being made with materials obtained by one’s own asking is one that is made by having solicited oneself, therefore, to show that alternative meaning, the word analysis for this term is given as, “having solicited oneself….”

Ullittāti antolittā. Avalittāti bahilittā. Ullittāvalittāti antarabāhiralittāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Ullittā: Plastered inside. Avalittā: Plastered outside. Ullittāvalittā: This means plastered inside and out.

Kārayamānenāti imassa padabhājane “kārāpentenā”ti ettakameva vattabbaṃ siyā, evañhi byañjanaṃ sameti. Yasmā pana saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karontenāpi idha vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ, tasmā karonto vā hotu kārāpento vā ubhopete “kārayamānenā”ti imināva padena saṅgahitāti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “karonto vā kārāpento vā”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi pana karontena vā kārāpentena vāti vadeyya, byañjanaṃ vilomitaṃ bhaveyya, na hi kārāpento karonto nāma hoti, tasmā atthamattamevettha dassitanti veditabbaṃ.

“By one causing to be made”: In the word analysis of this term, it would have been sufficient to say “by one causing to be made” (kārāpentena), for in that way the wording would accord. However, since one who is himself making a hut by solicitation must also proceed in the manner described here, it was stated “whether making or causing to be made” to show that both the one making and the one causing to be made are included under the single term “by one causing to be made” (kārayamānenā). But if it had said, “by one who is making or by one who is causing to be made,” the wording would be contrary, for one who causes to be made is not called one who is making. Therefore, it should be understood that only the meaning is indicated here.

Attuddesanti “mayhaṃ esā”ti evaṃ attā uddeso assāti attuddesā, taṃ attuddesaṃ. Yasmā pana yassā attā uddeso sā attano atthāya hoti, tasmā atthapariyāyaṃ dassento “attuddesanti attano atthāyā”ti āha. Pamāṇikā kāretabbāti pamāṇayuttā kāretabbā. Tatridaṃ pamāṇanti tassā kuṭiyā idaṃ pamāṇaṃ. Sugatavidatthiyāti sugatavidatthi nāma idāni majjhimassa purisassa tisso [M 2.0154] vidatthiyo vaḍḍhakīhatthena diyaḍḍho hattho hoti. Bāhirimena mānenāti kuṭiyā bahikuṭṭamānena dvādasa vidatthiyo, minantena pana sabbapaṭhamaṃ dinno mahāmattikapariyanto na gahetabbo. Thusapiṇḍapariyantena minitabbaṃ. Thusapiṇḍassaupari setakammaṃ abbohārikaṃ. Sace thusapiṇḍena anatthiko mahāmattikāya eva niṭṭhāpeti, mahāmattikāva paricchedo.

‘With self as the one indicated’ (attuddesaṃ): Because for this hut there is a person indicated as ‘self,’ as in ‘this is mine,’ it is called ‘one with self as the one indicated’ (attuddesā). That (hut) ‘with self as the one indicated.’ Furthermore, since a hut for which there is a person indicated as ‘self’ is for one’s own benefit, therefore, showing the synonymous meaning, he said: ‘“With self as the one indicated” means for one’s own benefit.’ ‘It should be made to measure’ means it should be made endowed with the proper measure. ‘Herein, this is the measure’ means this is the measure of that hut. ‘By the Sugata-span’: A Sugata-span is, at present, three spans of a man of average height; by a carpenter’s cubit, it is one and a half cubits. ‘By the outer measurement’ means by the measurement of the outer wall of the hut, it is twelve spans. When measuring, however, the limit of the great clay plaster applied first of all should not be taken. It should be measured by the limit of the heap of chaff. The whitewashing on top of the heap of chaff is not to be included in the measurement. If, having no need for the heap of chaff, one finishes with only the great clay plaster, the great clay plaster itself is the boundary.

Tiriyanti vitthārato. Sattāti satta sugatavidatthiyo. Antarāti imassa pana ayaṃ niddeso[V 2.0139], “abbhantarimena mānenā”ti, kuṭṭassa bahi antaṃ aggahetvā abbhantarimena antena miniyamāne tiriyaṃ satta [P 3.0568] sugatavidatthiyo pamāṇanti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Across’ (tiriyaṃ) means in width. ‘Seven’ (sattā) means seven Sugata-spans. Furthermore, of this word ‘within’ (antarā), this is the explanation: ‘by the inner measurement.’ This means it is said that when measuring by the inner limit, not taking the outer limit of the wall, the measure is seven Sugata-spans across.

Yo pana lesaṃ oḍḍento yathāvuttappamāṇameva karissāmīti dīghato ekādasa vidatthiyo tiriyaṃ aṭṭha vidatthiyo, dīghato vā terasa vidatthiyo tiriyaṃ cha vidatthiyo kareyya, na vaṭṭati. Ekatobhāgena atikkantampi hi pamāṇaṃ atikkantameva hoti. Tiṭṭhatu vidatthi, kesaggamattampi dīghato vā hāpetvā tiriyaṃ tiriyato vā hāpetvā dīghaṃ vaḍḍhetuṃ na vaṭṭati, ko pana vādo ubhato vaḍḍhane? Vuttañhetaṃ – “āyāmato vā vitthārato vā antamaso kesaggamattampi atikkamitvā karoti vā kārāpeti vā payoge dukkaṭa”ntiādi (pārā. 353). Yathāvuttappamāṇā eva pana vaṭṭati. Yā pana dīghato saṭṭhihatthāpi hoti tiriyaṃ tihatthā vā ūnakacatuhatthā vā yattha pamāṇayutto mañco ito cito ca na parivattati, ayaṃ kuṭīti saṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, tasmā ayampi vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana pacchimakoṭiyā catuhatthavitthārā vuttā, tato heṭṭhā akuṭi. Pamāṇikāpi pana adesitavatthukā vā sārambhā vā aparikkamanā vā na vaṭṭati. Pamāṇikā desitavatthukā anārambhā saparikkamanāva vaṭṭati. Pamāṇato ūnatarampi catuhatthaṃ pañcahatthampi karontena desitavatthukāva kāretabbā. Pamāṇātikkantañca pana karonto lepapariyosāne garukaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati.

Furthermore, should any bhikkhu, setting forth a pretext [and thinking], ‘I will make it exactly of the prescribed measure,’ make it eleven spans in length and eight spans across, or thirteen spans in length and six spans across, it is not allowable. For a measure exceeded even on one side is indeed exceeded. Let alone a span, it is not allowable to increase the width by reducing the length even by a hair's breadth, or to increase the length by reducing the width. What then is to be said of increasing both? For this has been said: ‘If one makes or has made [a hut] exceeding the measure in length or in width by even so much as a hair’s breadth, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the undertaking,’ and so on. Only one of the prescribed measure is allowable. Furthermore, a dwelling that is sixty cubits in length and three or less than four cubits across, wherein a standard-sized bed cannot be turned from here and there, this does not count as a ‘hut’; therefore, this too is allowable. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said that the minimum limit is four cubits in width; below that, it is not a hut. Moreover, even a hut that is of the proper measure is not allowable if it is without a designated site, or is with dangers, or is without surrounding space. Only a hut of the proper measure that has a designated site, is without dangers, and has surrounding space is allowable. One making a hut even smaller than the measure—four or five cubits—should have it made only on a designated site. And furthermore, one who makes a hut exceeding the measure incurs a grave offense at the completion of the plastering.

Tattha lepo ca alepo ca lepokāso ca alepokāso ca veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – lepoti dve lepā – mattikālepo ca sudhālepo ca. Ṭhapetvā pana ime dve lepe avaseso bhasmagomayādibhedo lepo, alepo. Sacepi kalalalepo hoti, alapo eva. Lepokāsoti bhittiyo ceva chadanañca, ṭhapetvā [M 2.0155] pana bhitticchadane avaseso thambhatulāpiṭṭhasaṅghāṭavātapānadhūmacchiddādi alepāraho okāso sabbopi alepokāsoti veditabbo.

Therein, plaster, non-plaster, plasterable space, and non-plasterable space should be understood. To wit: as for plaster, there are two kinds of plaster—clay plaster and lime plaster. Excluding these two kinds of plaster, the remaining kinds, such as those of ash, cow-dung, and so on, are non-plaster. Even if it is mud plaster, it is still non-plaster. Plasterable space means the walls and the roof. Excluding the walls and roof, all the remaining space unsuitable for plastering—such as pillars, beams, door-posts, windows, smoke-vents, and so on—should be understood as non-plasterable space.

Bhikkhū abhinetabbā vatthudesanāyāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne kuṭiṃ kāretukāmo hoti, tattha vatthudesanatthāya bhikkhū netabbā. Tena kuṭikārakenātiādi pana yena vidhinā te bhikkhū abhinetabbā, tassa dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha kuṭivatthuṃ sodhetvāti na visamaṃ araññaṃ bhikkhū gahetvā gantabbaṃ[P 3.0569], kuṭivatthuṃ pana paṭhamameva sodhetvā samatalaṃ sīmamaṇḍalasadisaṃ katvā pacchā saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamitvā yācitvā netabbāti dasseti. Evamassa vacanīyoti saṅgho evaṃ vattabbo assa. Parato pana “dutiyampi yācitabbā”ti bhikkhū sandhāya bahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. No ce sabbo saṅgho ussahatīti sace sabbo saṅgho na icchati, sajjhāyamanasikārādīsu uyyuttā te te [V 2.0140] bhikkhū honti. Sārambhaṃ anārambhanti saupaddavaṃ anupaddavaṃ. Saparikkamanaṃ aparikkamananti saupacāraṃ anupacāraṃ.

‘The bhikkhus should be led for the designation of the site’ means: in whatever place one wishes to have a hut made, bhikkhus should be led there for the purpose of designating the site. Furthermore, the passage beginning with ‘by that hut-maker’ is stated to show the procedure by which those bhikkhus should be led. Therein, ‘having cleared the hut site’ means one should not take the bhikkhus and go to an uneven forest area; rather, it shows that one should first clear the hut site, make it level like a boundary circle, and only afterwards approach the Saṅgha, request them, and lead them there. ‘He should be spoken to thus’ means the Saṅgha should be spoken to thus. Further on, the plural in ‘they should be requested a second time’ is stated with reference to the bhikkhus. ‘If the entire Saṅgha is not willing’ means if the whole Saṅgha does not consent, because those bhikkhus are diligent in recitation, mindfulness, and so on. ‘With dangers, without dangers’ means with peril, without peril. ‘With surrounding space, without surrounding space’ means with an approach-way, without an approach-way.

Pattakallanti patto kālo imassa olokanassāti pattakālaṃ, pattakālameva pattakallaṃ. Idañca vatthuṃolokanatthāya sammutikammaṃ anusāvanānayena oloketvāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Parato pana vatthudesanākammaṃ yathāvuttāya eva ñattiyā ca anusāvanāya ca kātabbaṃ, oloketvā kātuṃ na vaṭṭati.

‘The time is suitable’ (pattakallaṃ): The time (kālo) for this inspection has arrived (patto), thus it is pattakālaṃ (the arrived time); pattakālaṃ itself is pattakallaṃ. And this formal act of authorization for the purpose of inspecting the site is allowable to be done even by making a request according to the method of announcement. Subsequently, however, the formal act of designating the site must be done only with the motion and the announcement as prescribed; it is not allowable to do it by making a request.

353. Kipillikānanti rattakāḷapiṅgalādibhedānaṃ yāsaṃ kāsañci kipillikānaṃ. Kipīllakānantipi pāṭho. Āsayoti nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānaṃ, yathā ca kipillikānaṃ evaṃ upacikādīnampi nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānaṃyeva āsayo veditabbo. Yattha pana te gocaratthāya āgantvā gacchanti, sabbesampi tādiso sañcaraṇappadeso avārito, tasmā tattha apanetvā sodhetvā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Imāni tāva cha ṭhānānisattānuddayāya paṭikkhittāni.

353. ‘Of ants’ (kipillikānaṃ) means of any ants whatsoever of various kinds, such as red, black, tawny, and so on. There is also the reading ‘kipīllakānaṃ.’ ‘Abode’ (āsayo) means a permanent dwelling place. And just as for ants, so too for termites and other such creatures, their permanent dwelling place should be understood as their ‘abode.’ But a place where they come and go for the purpose of foraging—such a thoroughfare for all of them is not prohibited. Therefore, in such a place, it is allowable to build after removing them and clearing it. These six places, then, are prohibited out of compassion for beings.

Hatthīnaṃ vāti hatthīnaṃ pana nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānampi nibaddhagocaraṭṭhānampi na vaṭṭati, sīhādīnaṃ āsayo ca gocarāya pakkamantānaṃ nibaddhagamanamaggo ca na vaṭṭati. Etesaṃ gocarabhūmi na gahitā. Yesaṃ kesañcīti aññesampi vāḷānaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ[M 2.0156]. Imāni satta ṭhānāni sappaṭibhayāni bhikkhūnaṃ ārogyatthāya paṭikkhittāni. Sesāni nānāupaddavehi saupaddavāni. Tattha pubbaṇṇanissitanti pubbaṇṇaṃ nissitaṃ sattannaṃ [P 3.0570] dhaññānaṃ viruhanakakhettasāmantā ṭhitaṃ. Eseva nayo aparaṇṇanissitādīsupi. Ettha pana abbhāghātanti kāraṇāgharaṃ verigharaṃ, corānaṃ māraṇatthāya katanti kurundiādīsu.

“Or for elephants”: for elephants, neither their fixed dwelling places nor their fixed grazing grounds are suitable. For lions and other such animals, neither their lairs nor their regular paths when going out to graze are suitable. Their grazing grounds are not to be taken. “For any other” means for other fierce beasts. These seven places, being dangerous, are prohibited for bhikkhus for the sake of their well-being. The remaining places are prohibited as they are subject to various dangers. Therein, “dependent on the early-ripening grain” means situated near the fields where the seven kinds of grain sprout. The same principle applies to “dependent on the late-ripening grain” and so on. Here, however, “abbhāghāta” means a house of torment, a house of enemies, or a place built for the killing of thieves, as stated in the Kurundī and other commentaries.

Āghātananti dhammagandhikā vuccati. Susānanti mahāsusānaṃ. Saṃsaraṇanti anibbijjhagamanīyo gatapaccāgatamaggo vuccati. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

“Āghātana” is called a place where the limbs of thieves are cut off according to the law. “Susāna” means a great charnel ground. “Saṃsaraṇa” is called a path of coming and going that is to be traversed without passing through. The rest is self-evident.

Na sakkā hoti yathāyuttena sakaṭenāti dvīhi balibaddehi yuttena sakaṭena ekaṃ cakkaṃ nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāne ekaṃ bahi katvā āvijjituṃ na sakkā hoti. Kurundiyaṃ pana “catūhi yuttenā”ti vuttaṃ. Samantā nisseṇiyā anuparigantunti nisseṇiyaṃ ṭhatvā gehaṃ chādentehi na sakkā hoti samantā nisseṇiyā āvijjituṃ. Iti evarūpe sārambhe ca aparikkamane ca ṭhāne [V 2.0141] na kāretabbā. Anārambhe pana saparikkamane kāretabbā, taṃ vuttapaṭipakkhanayena pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva.

“It is not possible with a properly yoked cart” means: it is not possible to turn a cart yoked with two oxen, with one wheel in the place where the eaves-water falls and one wheel outside of it. In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is stated, “yoked with four.” “To go around with a ladder” means: it is not possible for those roofing a house, while standing on a ladder, to move the ladder all around. Thus, a hut should not be built in such a place that involves danger and lacks space for maneuvering. However, it should be built in a place that is without danger and has space for maneuvering; this is indeed stated in the Pāḷi by way of the opposite of what was said.

Puna saññācikā nāmāti evamādi “sārambhe ce bhikkhu vatthusmiṃ aparikkamane saññācikāya kuṭiṃ kāreyyā”ti evaṃ vuttasaṃyācikādīnaṃ atthappakāsanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

The passage beginning “Again, what is meant by ‘by request’…” was stated to clarify the meaning of terms such as ‘by request’ which were mentioned thus: “If a bhikkhu should have a hut built by request on a site involving danger and without space for maneuvering…”

Payoge dukkaṭanti evaṃ adesitavatthukaṃ vā pamāṇātikkantaṃ vā kuṭiṃ kāressāmīti araññato rukkhā haraṇatthāya vāsiṃ vā pharasuṃ vā niseti dukkaṭaṃ, araññaṃ pavisati dukkaṭaṃ, tattha allatiṇāni chindati dukkaṭena saddhiṃ pācittiyaṃ, sukkhāni chindati dukkaṭaṃ. Rukkhesupi eseva nayo. Bhūmiṃ sodheti khaṇati, paṃsuṃ uddharati, cināti; evaṃ yāva pācīraṃ bandhati tāva pubbapayogo nāma hoti. Tasmiṃ pubbapayoge sabbattha pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭena saddhiṃ pācittiyaṃ, dukkaṭaṭṭhāne dukkaṭaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya sahapayogo nāma. Tattha thambhehi kātabbāya thambhaṃ ussāpeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Iṭṭhakāhi cinitabbāya [P 3.0571] iṭṭhakaṃ ācināti, dukkaṭaṃ. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ upakaraṇaṃ yojeti, sabbattha payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Tacchantassa hatthavāre hatthavāre tadatthāya gacchantassa pade pade dukkaṭaṃ. Evaṃ kataṃ pana dārukuṭṭikaṃ vā iṭṭhakakuṭṭikaṃ vā silākuṭṭikaṃ vā antamaso paṇṇasālampi sabhitticchadanaṃ limpissāmīti [M 2.0157] sudhāya vā mattikāya vā limpantassa payoge payoge yāva thullaccayaṃ na hoti, tāva dukkaṭaṃ. Etaṃ pana dukkaṭaṃ mahālepeneva vaṭṭati, setarattavaṇṇakaraṇe vā cittakamme vā anāpatti.

“For each effort, a dukkaṭa”: Thus, intending, “I will make a hut on a site that has not been indicated or one that exceeds the proper size,” if one sharpens a small axe or a large axe for the purpose of bringing wood from the forest, it is a dukkaṭa. Entering the forest is a dukkaṭa. There, cutting wet grass is a pācittiya with a dukkaṭa; cutting dry grass is a dukkaṭa. The same principle applies to trees. Clearing the ground, digging, removing soil, piling it up—thus, up to the point of building the enclosure wall is called the preliminary effort. In that preliminary effort, in every case where a pācittiya is incurred, it is a pācittiya with a dukkaṭa; where a dukkaṭa is incurred, it is a dukkaṭa. From then on, it is called the concurrent effort. Therein, for a hut to be made with posts, when one erects a post, it is a dukkaṭa. For a hut to be built with bricks, when one lays a brick, it is a dukkaṭa. Thus, whatever component one attaches, for each and every effort, it is a dukkaṭa. For one who is planing, for every stroke of the hand, it is a dukkaṭa; for one going for that purpose, for every step, it is a dukkaṭa. Furthermore, having thus made a hut with wooden walls, a hut with brick walls, a hut with stone walls, or even just a leaf-hut, if one plasters it complete with walls and roof, intending, “I will plaster it,” with lime or clay, for the one plastering, for each and every effort, it is a dukkaṭa, for as long as it does not become a thullaccaya. However, this dukkaṭa applies only to the main plastering; for making it white or red, or for painting, there is no offense.

Ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgateti yo sabbapacchimo eko lepapiṇḍo, taṃ ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ asampatte kuṭikamme. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, idāni dvīhi piṇḍehi niṭṭhānaṃ gamissatīti tesu paṭhamapiṇḍadāne thullaccayanti.

“When one lump has not yet come” means: when the work on the hut has not yet reached the one lump of plaster that is the very last of all. This is what is said: when it can be said, “Now, it will reach completion with two lumps,” upon the application of the first of those two lumps, a thullaccaya is incurred.

Tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgateti yaṃ ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate kuṭikamme thullaccayaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ avasānapiṇḍe āgate dinne ṭhapite lepassa ghaṭitattā āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Evaṃ lempantassa ca antolepe vā antolepena saddhiṃ bhittiñca chadanañca ekābaddhaṃ katvā ghaṭite bahilepe vā bahilepena saddhiṃ ghaṭite saṅghādiseso. Sace pana dvārabaddhaṃ vā vātapānaṃ vā aṭṭhapetvāva mattikāya limpati, tasmiñca tassokāsaṃ puna vaḍḍhetvā vā avaḍḍhetvā vā ṭhapite lepo na ghaṭīyati rakkhati tāva, puna limpantassa pana ghaṭitamatte saṅghādiseso. Sace taṃ ṭhapiyamānaṃ [V 2.0142] paṭhamaṃ dinnalepena saddhiṃ nirantarameva hutvā tiṭṭhati, paṭhamameva saṅghādiseso. Upacikāmocanatthaṃ aṭṭhaṅgulamattena appattacchadanaṃ katvā bhittiṃ limpati, anāpatti. Upacikāmocanatthameva heṭṭhā pāsāṇakuṭṭaṃ katvā taṃ alimpitvā upari limpati, lepo na ghaṭiyati nāma, anāpattiyeva.

“When that lump has come”: Regarding that one lump for which a thullaccaya is incurred when the work on the hut has not yet reached it—when that final lump has come, been given, and been placed, because the plaster has been joined, the offense of saṅghādisesa is incurred. Thus, for one plastering, if the inner plaster is joined, or if the inner plaster is made one continuous whole with the wall and the roof and is joined, or if the outer plaster is joined, or if the outer plaster is joined together with them, it is a saṅghādisesa. However, if one plasters with clay without having installed a door-frame or a window, and when that is installed in its place, whether the space is enlarged or not, the plaster does not join, one is protected from an offense for the time being. But for one plastering again, at the very moment of joining, it is a saṅghādisesa. If that which is being installed stands continuously with the plaster applied first, it is a saṅghādisesa from the very beginning. For the purpose of getting rid of termites, if one plasters the wall, leaving a gap of eight finger-breadths so that it does not reach the roof, there is no offense. For the very purpose of getting rid of termites, having made a stone wall below, and without plastering it, one plasters above; the plaster is considered not joined, and there is indeed no offense.

Iṭṭhakakuṭṭikāya iṭṭhakāhiyeva vātapāne [P 3.0572] ca dhūmanettāni ca karoti, lepaghaṭaneneva āpatti. Paṇṇasālaṃ limpati, lepaghaṭaneneva āpatti. Tattha ālokatthāya aṭṭhaṅgulamattaṃ ṭhapetvā limpati, lepo na ghaṭīyati nāma, anāpattiyeva. Sace “vātapānaṃ laddhā ettha ṭhapessāmī”ti karoti, vātapāne ṭhapite lepaghaṭanena āpatti. Sace mattikāya kuṭṭaṃ karoti, chadanalepena saddhiṃ ghaṭane āpatti. Eko ekapiṇḍāvasesaṃ katvā ṭhapeti, añño taṃ disvā “dukkataṃ ida”nti vattasīsena limpati ubhinnampi anāpatti.

In a hut made of brick, if one makes windows and smoke-vents with bricks themselves, an offense is incurred only through the joining of the plaster. If one plasters a leaf-hut, an offense is incurred only through the joining of the plaster. Therein, for the sake of light, if one plasters leaving a space of about eight finger-breadths, the plaster is considered not joined, and there is indeed no offense. If one acts thinking, “Having obtained a window, I will install it here,” when the window is installed, an offense is incurred through the joining of the plaster. If one makes a wall with clay, an offense is incurred upon its joining with the roof plaster. One person leaves it with one lump remaining. Another, seeing that, thinks, “This is badly done,” and plasters it out of a sense of duty. There is no offense for either of them.

354. Bhikkhu kuṭiṃ karotīti evamādīni chattiṃsa catukkāni āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ vuttāni, tattha sārambhāya dukkaṭaṃ, aparikkamanāya dukkaṭaṃ[M 2.0158], pamāṇātikkantāya saṅghādiseso, adesitavatthukāya saṅghādiseso, etesaṃ vasena vomissakāpattiyo veditabbā.

354. “A bhikkhu builds a hut,” and so on—these thirty-six sets of four are stated for the purpose of showing the divisions of offenses. Among them: due to it having an owner, a dukkaṭa offense; due to not clearing the site, a dukkaṭa offense; due to exceeding the measurement, a saṅghādisesa offense; due to the site not being indicated, a saṅghādisesa offense. By means of these, the mixed offenses should be understood.

355. Āpatti dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesena dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānantiādīsu ca dvīhi saṅghādisesehi saddhiṃ dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānantiādinā nayena attho veditabbo.

355. And in phrases such as, “The offense is two saṅghādisesas and two dukkaṭas,” the meaning should be understood according to the method of “two dukkaṭas together with two saṅghādisesas,” and so on.

361. So ce vippakate āgacchatītiādīsu pana ayaṃ atthavinicchayo. Soti samādisitvā pakkantabhikkhu. Vippakateti aniṭṭhite kuṭikamme. Aññassa vā dātabbāti aññassa puggalassa vā saṅghassa vā cajitvā dātabbā. Bhinditvā vā puna kātabbāti kittakena bhinnā hoti, sace thambhā bhūmiyaṃ nikhātā, uddharitabbā. Sace pāsāṇānaṃ upari ṭhapitā, apanetabbā. Iṭṭhakacitāya yāva maṅgaliṭṭhakā tāva kuṭṭā apacinitabbā. Saṅkhepato bhūmisamaṃ katvā vināsitā bhinnā hoti, bhūmito upari caturaṅgulamattepi ṭhite abhinnāva. Sesaṃ sabbacatukkesu pākaṭameva. Na hettha aññaṃ kiñci atthi, yaṃ pāḷianusāreneva dubbiññeyyaṃ siyā.

361. Now, in phrases such as, “If he comes when it is unfinished,” this is the determination of the meaning. “He” refers to a bhikkhu who, having given instructions, has departed. “Unfinished” means the work on the hut is not yet finished. “Or it should be given to another” means it should be relinquished and given to another individual or to the Sangha. “Or it must be rebuilt after breaking it down”—by how much must it be broken to be considered broken? If the posts are embedded in the ground, they should be uprooted. If they are placed on top of stones, they should be removed. For a hut built of bricks, the walls should be dismantled down to the auspicious brick. In short, when it has been destroyed by being leveled to the ground, it is considered broken; if even as much as four finger-widths remain standing above the ground, it is not considered broken. The rest is clear in all the sets of four. There is nothing else here that would be difficult to understand just by following the Pāli text.

363. Attanā vippakatantiādīsu pana attanā āraddhaṃ kuṭiṃ. Attanā pariyosāpetīti [V 2.0143] mahāmattikāya vā thusamattikāya vā yāya kataṃ pariyositabhāvaṃ pāpetukāmo hoti, tāya avasānapiṇḍaṃ dento pariyosāpeti[P 3.0573].

363. Now, in phrases such as, “Unfinished by oneself,” it refers to a hut begun by oneself. As for, “One completes it oneself,” it means: if one wishes to bring to completion a hut made with either coarse clay or clay mixed with chaff, one completes it by applying the final lump of that clay.

Parehi pariyosāpetīti attanova atthāya parehi pariyosāpeti. Attanā vā hi vippakatā hotu parehi vā ubhayehi vā, taṃ ce attano atthāya attanā vā pariyosāpeti, parehi vā pariyosāpeti, attanā ca parehi cāti yuganaddhaṃ vā pariyosāpeti, saṅghādisesoyevāti ayamettha vinicchayo.

“One has others complete it” means one has others complete it for one’s own benefit. Indeed, whether it was left unfinished by oneself, by others, or by both, if one completes that hut for one’s own benefit—whether one completes it oneself, has others complete it, or completes it jointly with others—it is a saṅghādisesa offense. This is the decision here.

Kurundiyaṃpana vuttaṃ – “dve tayo bhikkhū ‘ekato vasissāmā’ti karonti, rakkhati tāva, avibhattattā anāpatti. ‘Idaṃ ṭhānaṃ tava, idaṃ mamā’ti vibhajitvā karonti āpatti. Sāmaṇero ca bhikkhu ca ekato karonti, yāva avibhattā tāva rakkhati. Purimanayena vibhajitvā karonti, bhikkhussa āpattī”ti.

However, in the Kurundī commentary it is said: “If two or three bhikkhus build, thinking, ‘We will live together,’ it protects them from an offense for the time being; due to it not being divided, there is no offense. If they build after dividing it, saying, ‘This place is yours, this is mine,’ there is an offense. If a novice and a bhikkhu build together, it protects them from an offense as long as it is undivided. If they build after dividing it in the former way, there is an offense for the bhikkhu.”

364. Anāpatti [M 2.0159] leṇetiādīsu leṇaṃ mahantampi karontassa anāpatti. Na hettha lepo ghaṭīyati. Guhampi iṭṭhakāguhaṃ vā silāguhaṃ vā dāruguhaṃ vā bhūmiguhaṃ vā mahantampi karontassa anāpatti.

364. In phrases such as, “No offense for a cave (leṇa),” there is no offense for one who makes even a large cave. Plastering is not applicable here. Also, for a cavern (guha)—whether a brick cavern, a stone cavern, a wooden cavern, or an earth cavern—there is no offense for one who makes even a large one.

Tiṇakuṭikāyāti sattabhūmikopi pāsādo tiṇapaṇṇacchadano “tiṇakuṭikā”ti vuccati. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana kukkuṭacchikagehanti chadanaṃ daṇḍakehi jālabaddhaṃ katvā tiṇehi vā paṇṇehi vā chāditakuṭikāva vuttā, tattha anāpatti. Mahantampi tiṇacchadanagehaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, ullittādibhāvo eva hi kuṭiyā lakkhaṇaṃ, so ca chadanameva sandhāya vuttoti veditabbo. Caṅkamanasālāyaṃ tiṇacuṇṇaṃ paripatati “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ogumphetvā ullittāvalittaṃ kātu”ntiādīni (cūḷava. 260) cettha sādhakāni, tasmā ubhato pakkhaṃ vā kūṭabaddhaṃ vā vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā yaṃ “imaṃ etassa gehassa chadana”nti chadanasaṅkhepena kataṃ hoti, tassa bhittilepena saddhiṃ lepe ghaṭite āpatti. Sace pana ullittāvalittacchadanassa gehassa leparakkhaṇatthaṃ upari tiṇena chādenti, ettāvatā tiṇakuṭi nāma na hoti. Kiṃ panettha adesitavatthukappamāṇātikkantapaccayāva anāpatti, udāhu sārambhaaparikkamanapaccayāpīti sabbatthāpi [P 3.0574] anāpatti. Tathā hi tādisaṃ kuṭiṃ sandhāya parivāre vuttaṃ –

Regarding a ‘grass hut’: even a seven-storied mansion with a roof of grass or leaves is called a ‘grass hut.’ However, in the ancient commentaries, it is said to be a ‘chicken-coop dwelling,’ that is, a hut whose roof is made by forming a lattice with sticks and covering it with grass or leaves; for such a hut, there is no offense. It is permissible to build even a large grass-roofed house, for indeed the characteristic of a ‘hut’ (in the sense of this training rule) is its being plastered, and this should be understood as referring only to the roof. The words, “Grass dust is falling in the walking meditation hall... I allow you, bhikkhus, to remove the thatch and plaster it inside and out,” and so on, are evidence here. Therefore, for any roof—whether gabled, hipped, round, or square—that is made with the designation, “This is the roof of this house,” if its plaster is connected with the plaster of the wall, there is an offense. However, if they cover a plastered roof with grass on top to protect the plaster, by that much it does not become a ‘grass hut.’ Is there no offense here only on account of the site not being indicated and the measurement being exceeded, or is there also no offense on account of it having an owner and the site not being cleared? In all cases, there is no offense. For it is said regarding such a hut in the Parivāra:

“Bhikkhu [V 2.0144] saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karoti;

Adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ;

Sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ anāpatti;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 479);

“A bhikkhu builds a hut with resources obtained by request; its site was not indicated, and it exceeds the measurement; it has an owner, and the site was not cleared—[yet there is] no offense. This question was considered by the wise.”

Aññassatthāyāti kuṭilakkhaṇappattampi kuṭiṃ aññassa upajjhāyassa vā ācariyassa vā saṅghassa vā atthāya karontassa anāpatti. Yaṃ pana “āpatti kārukānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭāna”ntiādi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ yathāsamādiṭṭhāya akaraṇapaccayā vuttaṃ.

“For the sake of another”: even for a hut that meets the characteristics [that would incur an offense], there is no offense for one who builds it for the sake of another—whether for a preceptor, a teacher, or the Sangha. However, what is stated in the Pāli text, “There is a dukkaṭa offense for the three builders,” and so on, was said on account of not building according to the instructions given.

Vāsāgāraṃ ṭhapetvā sabbatthāti attano vasanatthāya agāraṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ uposathāgāraṃ vā jantāgharaṃ vā bhojanasālā vā aggisālā vā bhavissatīti kāreti, sabbattha anāpatti. Sacepissa hoti “uposathāgārañca bhavissati, ahañca vasissāmi jantāgharañca bhojanasālā [M 2.0160] ca aggisālā ca bhavissati, ahañca vasissāmī”ti kāritepi ānāpattiyeva. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “anāpattī”ti vatvā “attano vāsāgāratthāya karontasseva āpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Ummattakassa ādikammikānañca āḷavakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anāpatti.

“Everywhere except a dwelling place”: having set aside a dwelling for one’s own residence, if one has another building constructed—thinking it will be an Uposatha hall, a steam-bath house, a dining hall, or a fire hall—there is no offense in any of these cases. Even if one thinks, “It will be an Uposatha hall, and I will also live there; it will be a steam-bath house, and I will also live there; it will be a dining hall, and I will also live there; it will be a fire hall, and I will also live there,” and has it built with this thought, there is still no offense. However, in the Mahāpaccarī commentary, after stating, “There is no offense,” it is said: “An offense is incurred only by one who builds it for the purpose of one’s own dwelling.” There is no offense for one who is insane, nor for the first offenders, the bhikkhus of Āḷavī.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu chasamuṭṭhānaṃ kiriyañca kiriyākiriyañca, idañhi vatthuṃ desāpetvā pamāṇātikkantaṃ karoto kiriyato samuṭṭhāti, vatthuṃ adesāpetvā karoto kiriyākiriyato, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding the origins and other points: this offense has six origins; it arises from action and from action-and-inaction. For when one has the site indicated and then builds exceeding the measurement, the offense arises from action. When one builds without having the site indicated, it arises from action and inaction. It is not an offense from which one is absolved by a change of perception; it is an offense not requiring intention; it is an offense by formulation; it is bodily action and verbal action; it is associated with three kinds of consciousness and three kinds of feeling.

Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kuṭikāra training rule is concluded.

7. Vihārakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Building a Dwelling

365. Tena samayenāti vihārakārasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha kosambiyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Ghositārāmeti ghositassa ārāme. Ghositanāmakena kira seṭṭhinā so kārito, tasmā “ghositārāmo”ti vuccati. Channassāti bodhisattakāle upaṭṭhākachannassa. Vihāravatthuṃ, bhante, jānāhīti vihārassa patiṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ, bhante, jānāhi. Ettha ca vihāroti na sakalavihāro, eko āvāso, tenevāha – “ayyassa vihāraṃ kārāpessāmī”ti.

365. The training rule beginning with Tena samayena is the Vihārakāra training rule. Therein, Kosambiyaṃ means in a city of that name. Ghositārāme means in the monastery of Ghosita. It is said that it was caused to be made by a wealthy man named Ghosita; therefore, it is called ‘Ghositārāma’. Channassa means for Channa, the attendant during the time of the Bodhisatta. Vihāravatthuṃ, bhante, jānāhi means: ‘Venerable sir, know a site for the establishment of a dwelling.’ And here, vihāro does not mean the entire monastery complex, but a single lodging. Therefore, he said, ‘I will have a dwelling built for the noble one.’

Cetiyarukkhanti [P 3.0575][V 2.0145] ettha cittīkataṭṭhena cetiyaṃ, pūjārahānaṃ devaṭṭhānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, “cetiya”nti sammataṃ rukkhaṃ cetiyarukkhaṃ. Gāmena pūjitaṃ gāmassa vā pūjitanti gāmapūjitaṃ. Eseva nayo sesapadesupi. Apicettha janapadoti ekassa rañño rajje ekeko koṭṭhāso. Raṭṭhanti sakalarajjaṃ veditabbaṃ, sakalarajjampi hi kadāci kadāci tassa rukkhassa pūjaṃ karoti, tena vuttaṃ “raṭṭhapūjita”nti. Ekindriyanti kāyindriyaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Jīvasaññinoti sattasaññino.

Cetiyarukkhaṃ: Here, it is a cetiya because it is revered (cittīkataṭṭhena); this is a designation for the abodes of deities worthy of veneration. A tree regarded as a cetiya is a cetiyarukkha. Gāmapūjitaṃ means honored by the village (gāmena pūjitaṃ) or honored of the village (gāmassa vā pūjitaṃ). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Furthermore, here, janapada is a single portion in the kingdom of a single king. Raṭṭhaṃ should be understood as the entire kingdom, for indeed the entire kingdom sometimes makes offerings to that tree; therefore, it is called raṭṭhapūjitaṃ. Ekindriyaṃ is said with reference to the body-faculty. Jīvasaññino means those who perceive it as a being.

366. Mahallakanti sassāmikabhāvena saṃyācikakuṭito mahantabhāvo etassa atthīti mahallako. Yasmā vā vatthuṃ desāpetvā pamāṇātikkamenapi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā pamāṇamahantatāyapi mahallako[M 2.0161], taṃ mahallakaṃ. Yasmā panassa taṃ pamāṇamahattaṃ sassāmikattāva labbhati, tasmā tadatthadassanatthaṃ “mahallako nāma vihāro sassāmiko vuccatī”ti padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ kuṭikārasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ saddhiṃ samuṭṭhānādīhi. Sassāmikabhāvamattameva hi ettha kiriyato samuṭṭhānābhāvo pamāṇaniyamābhāvo ca viseso, pamāṇaniyamābhāvā ca catukkapārihānīti.

366. Mahallakaṃ: It is mahallaka because, due to having an owner, it possesses a state of greatness greater than a solicited hut. Or, because it is permissible to build it even in excess of the standard measure after having the site indicated, it is also mahallaka due to the greatness of its measure. However, since this greatness of measure is obtained only because it has an owner, to show that meaning, the analysis of the term was stated: ‘A dwelling is called mahallaka when it has an owner.’ All the rest, together with the origination and so on, should be understood in the very way stated in the training rule on huts. Indeed, the distinctions here are merely the state of having an owner, the absence of origination from the action, and the absence of a regulation on the measure; and because of the absence of a regulation on the measure, there is a reduction of the fourfold classification.

Vihārakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning building a dwelling is concluded.
