8. Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Malicious Accusation

380. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti duṭṭhadosasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha veḷuvane kalandakanivāpeti veḷuvananti tassa uyyānassa nāmaṃ, taṃ kira veḷuhi ca parikkhittaṃ ahosi aṭṭhārasahatthena ca pākārena gopuraṭṭālakayuttaṃ nīlobhāsaṃ manoramaṃ tena “veḷuvana”nti vuccati, kalandakānañcettha nivāpaṃ adaṃsu tena “kalandakanivāpa”ti vuccati.

380. The phrase 'At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One...' introduces the Training Rule Concerning Malicious Accusation. Therein, regarding the phrase 'in the Bamboo Grove at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place': 'Bamboo Grove' is the name of that park. It is said that it was surrounded by bamboos and by an eighteen-cubit wall, endowed with gates and watchtowers, of a dark blue lustre, and delightful; for that reason, it is called 'Bamboo Grove.' And in this park, they gave food to the squirrels; for that reason, it is called 'Squirrels’ Feeding Place.'

Pubbe kira aññataro rājā tattha uyyānakīḷanatthaṃ āgato, surāmadena matto divāseyyaṃ supi, parijanopissa sutto rājāti pupphaphalādīhi palobhiyamāno ito cito ca pakkami. Atha surāgandhena aññatarasmā susirarukkhā kaṇhasappo nikkhamitvā rañño abhimukho āgacchati, taṃ disvā rukkhadevatā “rañño jīvitaṃ dassāmī”ti kāḷakavesena āgantvā kaṇṇamūle saddamakāsi, rājā paṭibujjhi, kaṇhasappo nivatto, so taṃ disvā “imāya kāḷakāya mama jīvitaṃ dinna”nti kāḷakānaṃ [P 3.0576] tattha nivāpaṃ paṭṭhapesi, abhayaghosanañca ghosāpesi[V 2.0146], tasmā taṃ tatopabhuti kalandakanivāpanti saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ. Kalandakāti hi kāḷakānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ.

It is said that in the past, a certain king came there to enjoy the park. Intoxicated with liquor, he fell asleep during the day. His retinue, thinking, 'The king is asleep,' and being enticed by flowers, fruits, and so on, wandered off here and there. Then, drawn by the scent of liquor, a black serpent came out of a hollow tree and approached the king. Seeing this, a tree-deity thought, 'I will give the king his life,' and approaching in the guise of a squirrel, made a sound at his ear. The king awoke, and the black serpent retreated. Seeing this, the king thought, 'My life has been given by this squirrel,' and he established a feeding place for squirrels there and had a proclamation of safety made. Therefore, from that time on, it came to be known as 'Kalandakanivāpa' (Squirrels' Feeding Place). For 'Kalandaka' is a name for squirrels.

Dabboti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Mallaputtoti mallarājassa putto. Jātiyā sattavassena arahattaṃ sacchikatanti thero kira sattavassikova saṃvegaṃ labhitvā pabbajito khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti veditabbo. Yaṃkiñci sāvakena pattabbaṃ sabbaṃ tena anuppattanti sāvakena pattabbaṃ [M 2.0162] nāma tisso vijjā, catasso paṭisambhidā, cha abhiññā, nava lokuttaradhammāti idaṃ guṇajātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ tena anuppattaṃ hoti. Natthi cassa kiñci uttari karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu, catūhi maggehi, soḷasavidhassa kiccassa katattā idānissa kiñci uttari karaṇīyaṃ natthi. Katassa vā paticayoti tasseva katassa kiccassa puna vaḍḍhanampi natthi, dhotassa viya vatthassa paṭidhovanaṃ pisitassa viya gandhassa paṭipisanaṃ, pupphitassa viya ca pupphassa paṭipupphananti. Rahogatassāti rahasi gatassa. Paṭisallīnassāti tato tato paṭikkamitvā sallīnassa, ekībhāvaṃ gatassāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Dabba' is the name of that elder. 'Mallaputta' means son of a Malla king. Regarding 'realized arahantship at the age of seven by birth,' it should be understood that the elder, it is said, having gained a sense of spiritual urgency when he was only seven years old, went forth and attained arahantship at the very conclusion of the shaving of his head. Regarding 'Whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all that was attained by him,' what is to be attained by a disciple is this collection of qualities: the three knowledges, the four analytical insights, the six higher knowledges, and the nine supramundane states. All of that was attained by him. Regarding 'And there is nothing further for him to do,' because the sixteen-fold task concerning the four truths has been done by means of the four paths, there is now nothing further for him to do. Regarding 'or an accumulation of what has been done,' there is no further augmenting of the task that has already been done, just as there is no rewashing of a cloth that has been washed, no regrinding of perfume that has been ground, and no re-blooming of a flower that has bloomed. 'Having gone to a secluded place' means having gone into solitude. 'Withdrawn' means having retreated from this and that sensory object and become absorbed; it is said to mean having attained a state of solitude.

Atha kho āyasmato dabbassa mallaputtassa etadahosi – “yannūnāhaṃ saṅghassa senāsanañca paññapeyyaṃ bhattāni ca uddiseyya”nti thero kira attano katakiccabhāvaṃ disvā “ahaṃ imaṃ antimasarīraṃ dhāremi, tañca kho vātamukhe ṭhita padīpo viya aniccatāmukhe ṭhitaṃ, nacirasseva nibbāyanadhammaṃ yāva na nibbāyati tāva kinnu kho ahaṃ saṅghassa veyyāvaccaṃ kareyya”nti cintento iti paṭisañcikkhati – “tiroraṭṭhesu bahū kulaputtā bhagavantaṃ adisvāva pabbajanti, te bhagavantaṃ ‘passissāma ceva vandissāma cā’ti dūratopi āgacchanti, tatra yesaṃ senāsanaṃ nappahoti, te silāpaṭṭakepi seyyaṃ kappenti. Pahomi kho panāhaṃ attano ānubhāvena tesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ [P 3.0577] icchāvasena pāsādavihāraaḍḍhayogādīni mañcapīṭhakattharaṇādīni ca senāsenāni nimminitvā dātuṃ. Punadivase cettha ekacce ativiya kilantarūpā honti, te gāravena bhikkhūnaṃ purato ṭhatvā bhattānipi na uddisāpenti, ahaṃ kho pana nesaṃ bhattānipi uddisituṃ pahomī”ti. Iti paṭisañcikkhantassa “atha kho āyasmato dabbassa mallaputtassa etadahosi – ‘yannūnāhaṃ saṅghassa senāsanañca paññapeyyaṃ bhattāni ca uddiseyya”nti.

Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta: 'What if I were to prepare the lodgings for the Saṅgha and assign the meals?' It is said that the elder, seeing that his task was done, thought: 'I bear this final body, and it stands at the mouth of impermanence like a lamp placed in the wind; it is of a nature to be extinguished before long. For as long as it is not extinguished, what service might I perform for the Saṅgha?' Reflecting thus, he considered further: 'In foreign lands, many sons of good family go forth without having seen the Blessed One. They come from afar, thinking, "We will see the Blessed One and pay homage to him." There, for those for whom lodging is not sufficient, they prepare a bed even on a stone slab. But I am able, by my own power, to create and give to those sons of good family, according to their wish, lodgings such as mansions, monasteries, and half-gabled buildings, as well as beds, chairs, and coverings. Furthermore, on the next day, some here are extremely weary. Out of respect, standing before the monks, they do not have meals assigned. But I am able to assign meals for them.' As he was considering thus, this thought occurred to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta: 'What if I were to prepare the lodgings for the Saṅgha and assign the meals?'

Nanu ca imāni dve ṭhānāni bhassārāmatādimanuyuttassa yuttāni, ayañca khīṇāsavo nippapañcārāmo, imassa kasmā imāni paṭibhaṃsūti? Pubbapatthanāya coditattā. Sabbabuddhānaṃ kira [V 2.0147] imaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ pattā sāvakā hontiyeva. Ayañca padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle aññatarasmiṃ kule paccājāto imaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ pattassa bhikkhuno ānubhāvaṃ disvā aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyā bhikkhusatasahassehi [M 2.0163] saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ satta divasāni nimantetvā mahādānaṃ datvā pādamūle nipajjitvā “anāgate tumhādisassa buddhassa uppannakāle ahampi itthannāmo tumhākaṃ sāvako viya senāsanapaññāpako ca bhattuddesako ca assa”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Bhagavā anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ pesetvā addasa, disvā ca ito kappasatasahassassa accayena gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tadā tvaṃ dabbo nāma mallaputto hutvā jātiyā sattavasso nikkhamma pabbajitvā arahattaṃ sacchikarissasi, imañca ṭhānantaraṃ lacchasī”ti byākāsi. So tatopabhuti dānasīlādīni pūrayamāno devamanussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle tena bhagavatā byākatasadisameva arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Athassa rahogatassa “kinnu kho ahaṃ saṅghassa veyyāvaccaṃ kareyya”nti cintayato tāya pubbapatthanāya coditattā imāni dve ṭhānāni paṭibhaṃsūti.

Are not these two positions suitable for one devoted to delighting in talk and so on? And this one is an Arahant who delights in non-proliferation—why did these things occur to him? Because he was urged by a former aspiration. Indeed, for all Buddhas, there are disciples who attain this special office. And this one, in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, was reborn in a certain family. Seeing the power of a monk who had attained this special office, he invited the Blessed One together with six million eight hundred thousand monks for seven days, gave a great offering, and prostrating at his feet, made this aspiration: 'In the future, at the time of the arising of a Buddha like you, may I also, a disciple of yours named so-and-so, be an arranger of lodgings and a distributor of meals.' The Blessed One, directing his knowledge of the future, saw and prophesied: 'After a hundred thousand eons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. At that time, you, as Dabba the son of the Malla, will go forth from home at the age of seven, and having gone forth, you will realize Arahantship and will obtain this special office.' From then on, fulfilling generosity, virtue, and so on, and having experienced divine and human prosperity, in the time of our Blessed One, he realized Arahantship just as prophesied by that Blessed One. Then, as he was in solitude considering, 'What service might I perform for the Saṅgha?', these two positions occurred to him, urged on by that former aspiration.

Athassa etadahosi – “ahaṃ kho anissarosmi attani, satthārā saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne vasāmi, sace maṃ bhagavā anujānissati[P 3.0578], imāni dve ṭhānāni samādiyissāmī”ti bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā dabbo mallaputto…pe… bhattāni ca uddisitu”nti. Atha naṃ bhagavā “sādhu sādhu dabbā”ti sampahaṃsetvā yasmā arahati evarūpo agatigamanaparibāhiro bhikkhu imāni dve ṭhānāni vicāretuṃ, tasmā “tena hi tvaṃ dabba saṅghassa senāsanañca paññapehi bhattāni ca uddisā”ti āha. Bhagavato paccassosīti bhagavato vacanaṃ patiassosi abhimukho assosi, sampaṭicchīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Then this thought occurred to him: 'I am not my own master; I live in the same place as the Teacher. If the Blessed One permits me, I will undertake these two duties.' Thus he went to the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: 'Then the venerable Dabba Mallaputta… and to distribute the meals.' Then the Blessed One, having greatly encouraged him, saying, 'Good, good, Dabba!', said: 'Because such a monk, who is free from the wrong courses, is worthy to manage these two duties, therefore, well then, Dabba, you arrange the lodgings for the Saṅgha and distribute the meals.' 'He assented to the Blessed One' means he listened attentively to the Blessed One’s words, listened facing him, and accepted them; this is what is meant.

Paṭhamaṃ dabbo yācitabboti kasmā bhagavā yācāpeti? Garahamocanatthaṃ. Passati hi bhagavā “anāgate dabbassa imaṃ ṭhānaṃ nissāya mettiyabhumajakānaṃ vasena mahāupaddavo uppajjissati, tatra keci garahissanti ‘ayaṃ tuṇhībhūto attano kammaṃ akatvā kasmā īdisaṃ ṭhānaṃ vicāretī’ti. Tato aññe vakkhanti ‘ko imassa doso eteheva yācitvā ṭhapito’ti evaṃ garahato muccissatī”ti. Evaṃ garahamocanatthaṃ yācāpetvāpi puna yasmā asammate bhikkhusmiṃ saṅghamajjhe kiñci kathayamāne khiyyanadhammo uppajjati “ayaṃ kasmā saṅghamajjhe uccāsaddaṃ karoti, issariyaṃ dassetī”ti. Sammate pana kathente [M 2.0164] “māyasmanto kiñci avacuttha, sammato ayaṃ, kathetu yathāsukha”nti vattāro bhavanti. Asammatañca abhūtena abbhācikkhantassa lahukā āpatti hoti dukkaṭamattā. Sammataṃ pana abbhācikkhato garukatarā [V 2.0148] pācittiyāpatti hoti. Atha sammato bhikkhu āpattiyā garukabhāvena verīhipi duppadhaṃsiyataro hoti, tasmā taṃ āyasmantaṃ sammannāpetuṃ “byattena bhikkhunā”tiādimāha. Kiṃ pana dve sammutiyo ekassa dātuṃ vaṭṭantīti? Na kevalaṃ dve, sace pahoti, terasāpi dātuṃ vaṭṭanti. Appahontānaṃ pana ekāpi dvinnaṃ vā tiṇṇaṃ vā dātuṃ vaṭṭati.

First, why does the Blessed One have the Saṅgha ask Dabba? For the purpose of freedom from blame. For the Blessed One sees: 'In the future, on account of this position of Dabba's, a great trouble will arise through the Mettiya and Bhummajaka monks. There, some will find fault, saying, "Why does this one, remaining silent and not doing his own work, administer such a position?" Then others will say, "What is his fault? He was appointed after being asked by these very monks." In this way, he will be freed from blame.' Even after having him asked for the purpose of freedom from blame, there is another reason: because when an unappointed monk says something in the midst of the Saṅgha, a cause for scorn arises: "Why does this one speak loudly in the midst of the Saṅgha? Is he showing off his authority?" But when an appointed monk speaks, they say: "Venerable sirs, do not say anything. This one is appointed; let him speak as he pleases." Furthermore, for one who falsely accuses an unappointed monk, there is a light offense, merely a dukkaṭa. But for one who falsely accuses an appointed monk, there is a more serious pācittiya offense. Thus, an appointed monk is harder to assail even by his enemies due to the gravity of the offense. Therefore, in order to have that venerable one appointed, he said, 'by a competent monk,' and so on. But is it permissible to give two appointments to one person? Not only two—if one is capable, it is permissible to give even thirteen. But for those who are not capable, it is not permissible to give even one appointment to two or three.

382. Sabhāgānanti guṇasabhāgānaṃ, na mittasanthavasabhāgānaṃ. Tenevāha “ye te bhikkhū suttantikā tesaṃ ekajjha”ntiādi[P 3.0579]. Yāvatikā hi suttantikā honti, te uccinitvā ekato tesaṃ anurūpameva senāsanaṃ paññapeti; evaṃ sesānaṃ. Kāyadaḷhībahulāti kāyassa daḷhībhāvakaraṇabahulā, kāyaposanabahulāti attho. Imāyapime āyasmanto ratiyāti imāya saggamaggassa tiracchānabhūtāya tiracchānakathāratiyā. Acchissantīti viharissanti.

382. “Of those who are compatible” means of those who are compatible in virtue, not of those who are compatible through friendship or intimacy. Therefore, he said: “Those monks who are experts in the Suttas, for them together,” and so on. For however many experts in the Suttas there are, having selected them, he arranges suitable lodging for them together; likewise for the rest. “Much given to bodily sturdiness” means much given to making the body sturdy, that is, much given to nourishing the body. “These venerable ones with this delight” means with this delight in worldly talk, which is an obstruction to heaven and the path. “They will sit” means they will dwell.

Tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvā tenevālokenāti tejokasiṇacatutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya abhiññāñāṇena aṅgulijalanaṃ adhiṭṭhāya teneva tejodhātusamāpattijanitena aṅgulijālālokenāti attho. Ayaṃ pana therassa ānubhāvo nacirasseva sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi, taṃ sutvā iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ daṭṭhukāmā apisu bhikkhū sañcicca vikāle āgacchanti. Te sañcicca dūre apadisantīti jānantāva dūre apadisanti. Kathaṃ? “Amhākaṃ āvuso dabba gijjhakūṭe”ti iminā nayena.

“Having entered upon the fire element, by that very light” means: having entered upon the fourth jhāna of the fire kasiṇa, and having emerged from it, with the knowledge of supernormal power he resolved upon the flaming of his finger; by the very light of the finger-flame produced by that attainment of the fire element—this is the meaning. And this power of the elder soon became manifest throughout all of Jambudīpa. Hearing of it, monks wishing to see the marvel of psychic power would come deliberately, even at the wrong time. “They deliberately point to a distant place” means that, knowing full well it is far, they point to a distant place. How? In this way: “Friend Dabba, our lodging is on Vulture Peak.”

Aṅguliyā jalamānāya purato purato gacchatīti sace eko bhikkhu hoti, sayameva gacchati. Sace bahū honti, bahū attabhāve nimmināti. Sabbe attanā sadisā eva senāsanaṃ paññapenti.

“With a flaming finger, he goes before them” means: if there is one monk, he goes by himself. If there are many, he creates many bodies. All of them, identical to himself, arrange the lodging.

Ayaṃ mañcotiādīsu pana there “ayaṃ mañco”ti vadante nimmitāpi attano attano gatagataṭṭhāne “ayaṃ mañco”ti vadanti; evaṃ sabbapadesu. Ayañhi nimmitānaṃ dhammatā –

Furthermore, in instances such as “This is a bed,” when the Elder says, “This is a bed,” the created beings also say, “This is a bed,” in their own respective places where they have gone. Thus it is in all phrases. For this is the nature of created beings:

“Ekasmiṃ [M 2.0165] bhāsamānasmiṃ, sabbe bhāsanti nimmitā;

Ekasmiṃ tuṇhimāsīne, sabbe tuṇhī bhavanti te”ti.

“When one speaks, all the created beings speak; when one sits in silence, all of them become silent.”

Yasmiṃ pana vihāre mañcapīṭhādīni na paripūranti, tasmiṃ attano ānubhāvena pūrenti. Tena nimmitānaṃ avatthukavacanaṃ na hoti.

Furthermore, in a monastery where beds, chairs, and so forth are not sufficient, they provide them by their own power. Therefore, the speech of the created beings is not baseless.

Senāsanaṃ [V 2.0149] paññapetvā punadeva veḷuvanaṃ paccāgacchatīti tehi saddhiṃ janapadakathaṃ kathento na nisīdati, attano vasanaṭṭhānameva paccāgacchati.

“Having prepared the lodging, he returned again to the Bamboo Grove” means: he does not sit down engaging in conversation with them about the region, but returns only to his own dwelling place.

383. Mettiyabhūmajakāti mettiyo ceva bhūmajako ca, chabbaggiyānaṃ aggapurisā ete. Lāmakāni ca bhattānīti senāsanāni [P 3.0580] tāva navakānaṃ lāmakāni pāpuṇantīti anacchariyametaṃ. Bhattāni pana salākāyo pacchiyaṃ vā cīvarabhoge vā pakkhipitvā āloḷetvā ekamekaṃ uddharitvā paññāpenti, tānipi tesaṃ mandapuñatāya lāmakāni sabbapacchimāneva pāpuṇanti. Yampi ekacārikabhattaṃ hoti, tampi etesaṃ pattadivase lāmakaṃ vā hoti, ete vā disvāva paṇītaṃ adatvā lāmakameva denti.

383. “Mettiya and Bhūmajaka” refers to Mettiya and Bhūmajaka; these were the chief persons of the group-of-six monks. And “inferior meals”: Firstly, that inferior lodgings reach the junior monks is not surprising. As for the meals, however, they are assigned by putting tickets into a basket or a fold of a robe, mixing them up, and drawing them out one by one. Even these meals, due to their lack of merit, reach them as inferior and the very last of all. And whatever meal for a single wanderer there is, even that is inferior on the day it is their turn to receive it; or, upon seeing them, people do not give fine food but give only the inferior kind.

Abhisaṅkhārikanti nānāsambhārehi abhisaṅkharitvā kataṃ susajjitaṃ, susampāditanti attho. Kaṇājakanti sakuṇḍakabhattaṃ. Bilaṅgadutiyanti kañjikadutiyaṃ.

“Specially prepared” (abhisaṅkhārikaṃ) means: made by preparing with various ingredients, well-arranged, well-accomplished; this is the meaning. “Food with broken grains” (kaṇājakaṃ) means rice together with broken grains. “With sour gruel as a second item” (bilaṅgadutiyaṃ) means having sour gruel as the second item.

Kalyāṇabhattikoti kalyāṇaṃ sundaraṃ ativiya paṇītaṃ bhattamassāti kalyāṇabhattiko, paṇītadāyakattā bhatteneva paññāto. Catukkabhattaṃ detīti cattāri bhattāni deti, taddhitavohārena pana “catukkabhatta”nti vuttaṃ. Upatiṭṭhitvā parivisatīti sabbakammante vissajjetvā mahantaṃ pūjāsakkāraṃ katvā samīpe ṭhatvā parivisati. Odanena pucchantīti odanahatthā upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ bhante odanaṃ demā”ti pucchanti, evaṃ karaṇattheyeva karaṇavacanaṃ hoti. Esa nayo sūpādīsu.

“One with fine meals” (kalyāṇabhattiko) means: because he has a meal that is good, beautiful, and exceedingly fine, he is a “kalyāṇabhattiko”; he is known by his meals for being a giver of fine food. “He gives a meal for four” (catukkabhattaṃ deti) means he gives meals for four monks; but by taddhita usage, it is called “catukkabhattaṃ”. “Having attended, he serves” (upatiṭṭhitvā parivisati) means: having set aside all work and having made great offerings and veneration, he stands nearby and serves. “They ask with rice” (odanena pucchanti) means: approaching with rice in hand, they ask, “Venerable sir, shall we give rice?” Thus, the word in the instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument. This same method applies to curries and so forth.

Svātanāyāti sve bhavo bhattaparibhogo svātano tassatthāya, svātanāya sve kattabbassa bhattaparibhogassatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Uddiṭṭhaṃ hotīti pāpetvā dinnaṃ hoti. Mettiyabhūmajakānaṃ kho gahapatīti idaṃ thero asamannāharitvā āha. Evaṃbalavatī hi tesaṃ [M 2.0166] mandapuññatā, yaṃ sativepullappattānampi asamannāhāro hoti. Ye jeti ettha jeti dāsiṃ ālapati.

“For tomorrow” (svātanāya) means: the meal consumption that will be tomorrow is “svātana”; for its sake is “svātanāya”. It means for the sake of the meal consumption to be done tomorrow. “It has been designated” (uddiṭṭhaṃ hoti) means it has been caused to arrive in turn and given. The Elder said, “Indeed, householder, for Mettiya and Bhūmajaka,” without paying attention. So powerful, indeed, is their lack of merit that even for those who have attained fullness of mindfulness, a lack of attention occurs. In the phrase “Ye je,” the word “je” is used to address a female slave.

Hiyyo kho āvuso amhākanti rattiṃ sammantayamānā atītaṃ divasabhāgaṃ sandhāya “hiyyo”ti vadanti. Na cittarūpanti na cittānurūpaṃ, yathā pubbe yattakaṃ icchanti, tattakaṃ supanti, na evaṃ supiṃsu, appakameva supiṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Yesterday, friends, for us…” means: conferring at night, they say “yesterday” referring to the part of the day that has passed. “Not as we would have liked” (na cittarūpaṃ) means not in accordance with their minds; they did not sleep as they used to before, when they would sleep as much as they wished. It means they slept only a little.

Bahārāmakoṭṭhaketi [V 2.0150] veḷuvanavihārassa bahidvārakoṭṭhake. Pattakkhandhāti patitakkhandhā khandhaṭṭhikaṃ nāmetvā nisinnā. Pajjhāyantāti padhūpāyantā.

“At the outer monastery gatehouse” (bahārāmakoṭṭhake) means at the outer gatehouse of the Veḷuvana Monastery. “With drooping shoulders” (pattakkhandhā) means with fallen shoulders, sitting with their necks bent. “Brooding” (pajjhāyantā) means fuming with anger.

Yato nivātaṃ [P 3.0581] tato savātanti yattha nivātaṃ appakopi vāto natthi, tattha mahāvāto uṭṭhitoti adhippāyo. Udakaṃ maññe ādittanti udakaṃ viya ādittaṃ.

“From where it is sheltered, from there comes the wind” (yato nivātaṃ tato savātaṃ) means: where it is sheltered and there is not even a slight wind, there a great wind has arisen; this is the intention. “The water, I think, is on fire” (udakaṃ maññe ādittaṃ) means it is as if the water is on fire.

384. Sarasi tvaṃ dabba evarūpaṃ kattāti tvaṃ dabba evarūpaṃ kattā sarasi. Atha vā sarasi tvaṃ dabba evarūpaṃ yathāyaṃ bhikkhunī āha, kattā dhāsi evarūpaṃ, yathāyaṃ bhikkhunī āhāti evaṃ yojetvāpettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ye pana “katvā”ti paṭhanti tesaṃ ujukameva.

384. “Do you, Dabba, remember having done such a thing?” (Sarasi tvaṃ dabba evarūpaṃ kattā) means: “Do you, Dabba, remember being the doer of such a thing?” Or else, the meaning here should be understood by construing it thus: “Do you, Dabba, remember such a thing as this bhikkhunī has said? And were you the doer of such a thing as this bhikkhunī has said?” As for those who read it as “katvā” (having done), for them the meaning is straightforward.

Yathā maṃ bhante bhagavā jānātīti thero kiṃ dasseti. Bhagavā bhante sabbaññū, ahañca khīṇāsavo, natthi mayhaṃ vatthupaṭisevanā, taṃ maṃ bhagavā jānāti, tatrāhaṃ kiṃ vakkhāmi, yathā maṃ bhagavā jānāti tathevāhaṃ daṭṭhabboti.

By the words, “Venerable sir, as the Blessed One knows me,” what does the Elder show? He shows this: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One is all-knowing, and I am one whose taints are destroyed. There is no indulgence in the act for me. The Blessed One knows that about me. In that case, what shall I say? I should be regarded exactly as the Blessed One knows me.”

Na kho dabba dabbā evaṃ nibbeṭhentīti ettha na kho dabba paṇḍitā yathā tvaṃ parappaccayena nibbeṭhesi, evaṃ nibbeṭhenti; api ca kho yadeva sāmaṃ ñātaṃ tena nibbeṭhentīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sace tayā kataṃ katanti iminā kiṃ dasseti? Na hi sakkā parisabalena vā pakkhupatthambhena vā akārako kārako kātuṃ, kārako vā akārako kātuṃ, tasmā yaṃ sayaṃ kataṃ vā akataṃ vā tadeva vattabbanti dasseti. Kasmā pana bhagavā jānantopi “ahaṃ jānāmi, khīṇāsavo tvaṃ; natthi tuyhaṃ doso, ayaṃ bhikkhunī [M 2.0167] musāvādinī”ti nāvocāti? Parānuddayatāya. Sace hi bhagavā yaṃ yaṃ jānāti taṃ taṃ vadeyya, aññena pārājikaṃ āpannena puṭṭhena “ahaṃ jānāmi tvaṃ pārājiko”ti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, tato so puggalo “ayaṃ pubbe dabbaṃ mallaputtaṃ suddhaṃ katvā idāni maṃ asuddhaṃ karoti; kassa dāni kiṃ vadāmi, yatra satthāpi sāvakesu chandāgatiṃ gacchati; kuto imassa sabbaññubhāvo”ti āghātaṃ bandhitvā apāyūpago bhaveyya, tasmā bhagavā imāya parānuddayatāya jānantopi nāvoca.

In the passage, 'Dabba, the wise do not resolve the matter in this way,' the meaning should be understood thus: Dabba, the wise do not resolve the matter by relying on another's testimony as you do; rather, they resolve the matter only by what is known by themselves. By 'If it was done by you, say it was done,' what does he show? He shows this: It is not possible, by the power of an assembly or by the support of a faction, to make a non-doer into a doer, or a doer into a non-doer. Therefore, one should state only what was actually done or not done by oneself. But why did the Blessed One, though knowing, not say, 'I know, you are one whose taints are destroyed; there is no fault in you, this bhikkhunī is a liar'? Out of compassion for others. For if the Blessed One were to say whatever he knows, then when asked by another who has committed a Pārājika offense, he would have to say, 'I know you have committed a Pārājika.' Then that person, thinking, 'This one, having previously declared Dabba Mallaputta pure, now declares me impure. To whom can I now speak, in a teaching where even the Teacher goes astray through favoritism among his disciples? Where is his omniscience?'—having formed a grudge, he would go to a state of loss. Therefore, because of this compassion for others, the Blessed One, though knowing, did not speak.

Kiñca bhiyyo upavādaparivajjanatopi nāvoca. Yadi hi bhagavā evaṃ [P 3.0582] vadeyya, evaṃ upavādo bhaveyya “dabbassa mallaputtassa vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, sammāsambuddhaṃ pana sakkhiṃ labhitvā vuṭṭhito”ti. Idañca vuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ maññamānā “buddhakālepi sakkhinā suddhi vā asuddhi [V 2.0151] vā hoti mayaṃ jānāma, ayaṃ puggalo asuddho”ti evaṃ pāpabhikkhū lajjimpi vināseyyunti. Apica anāgatepi bhikkhū otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ codetvā sāretvā “sace tayā kataṃ, ‘kata’nti vadehī”ti lajjīnaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā kammaṃ karissantīti vinayalakkhaṇe tantiṃ ṭhapento “ahaṃ jānāmī”ti avatvāva “sace tayā kataṃ, ‘kata’nti vadehī”ti āha.

Furthermore, He did not speak in order to avoid accusation. For if the Blessed One were to speak thus, this accusation would arise: “The emergence from an offense of Dabba, the son of the Malla, is a weighty matter, but he has emerged having obtained the Perfectly Enlightened One as a witness.” And, considering this to be a characteristic of emerging from an offense, evil monks might thus destroy even a conscientious person, thinking, “Even in the Buddha’s time, purity or impurity occurs by means of a witness; we know that this person is impure.” Moreover, in the future, when a matter has come before the Saṅgha, monks, having accused and reminded a conscientious person, will take their admission, saying, “If it was done by you, say, ‘It was done,’” and then perform the formal act. Thus, establishing the textual tradition in the characteristic of Vinaya discipline, without saying, “I know,” He said, “If it was done by you, say, ‘It was done.’”

Nābhijānāmi supinantenapi methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitāti supinantenapi methunaṃ dhammaṃ na abhijānāmi, na paṭisevitā ahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā paṭisevitā hutvā supinantenapi methunaṃ dhammaṃ na jānāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ye pana “paṭisevitvā”ti paṭhanti tesaṃ ujukameva. Pageva jāgaroti jāgaranto pana paṭhamaṃyeva na jānāmīti.

Regarding the phrase, “I do not recall having engaged in the sexual act, even in a dream,” the meaning is: “Even in a dream, I do not know the sexual act; I have not engaged in it.” Alternatively, the meaning is said to be: 'Having engaged in it, even in a dream I do not know the sexual act.' For those, however, who read 'paṭisevitvā' (having engaged in), their reading is straightforward. As for “how much more so when awake,” it means, “while awake, I do not know it from the very beginning.”

Tena hi bhikkhave mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsethāti yasmā dabbassa ca imissā ca vacanaṃ na ghaṭīyati tasmā mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsethāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Regarding the phrase, “Therefore, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā”: because the statement of Dabba and that of this nun are not consistent, it was therefore said, “Expel the nun Mettiyā.”

Tattha tisso nāsanā – liṅganāsanā, saṃvāsanāsanā, daṇḍakammanāsanāti. Tāsu “dūsako nāsetabbo”ti (pārā. 66) ayaṃ “liṅganāsanā”. Āpattiyā adassane vā appaṭikamme vā pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge vā ukkhepanīyakammaṃ karonti, ayaṃ “saṃvāsanāsanā”. “Cara [M 2.0168] pire vinassā”ti (pāci. 429) daṇḍakammaṃ karonti, ayaṃ “daṇḍakammanāsanā”. Idha pana liṅganāsanaṃ sandhāyāha – “mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsethā”ti.

Here, there are three kinds of expulsion: expulsion of the outward sign, expulsion from communion, and expulsion by penal act. Among these, “The corrupt one should be expelled” is ‘expulsion of the outward sign.’ When they perform an act of suspension for not seeing an offense, not making amends, or not relinquishing a wrong view, this is ‘expulsion from communion.’ When they perform a penal act, saying, “Go, wretch, perish!” this is ‘expulsion by penal act.’ Here, however, referring to the expulsion of the outward sign, He said, “Expel the nun Mettiyā.”

Ime ca bhikkhū anuyuñjathāti iminā imaṃ dīpeti “ayaṃ bhikkhunī attano dhammatāya akārikā addhā aññehi uyyojitā, tasmā yehi uyyojitā ime bhikkhū anuyuñjatha gavesatha jānāthā”ti.

By the phrase, “And investigate these monks,” He indicates this: “This nun, by her own nature, is not one to make such an accusation; surely she has been incited by others. Therefore, investigate, search for, and come to know these monks by whom she was incited.”

Kiṃ pana bhagavatā mettiyā bhikkhunī paṭiññāya nāsitā appaṭiññāya nāsitāti, kiñcettha yadi tāva paṭiññāya nāsitā, thero kārako hoti sadoso? Atha appaṭiññāya, thero akārako hoti niddoso.

But was the nun Mettiyā expelled by the Blessed One on the basis of an admission, or without an admission? Regarding this, if she was expelled on the basis of an admission, is the Elder the perpetrator and at fault? Or, if without an admission, is the Elder not the perpetrator and faultless?

Bhātiyarājakālepi mahāvihāravāsīnañca abhayagirivāsīnañca [P 3.0583] therānaṃ imasmiṃyeva pade vivādo ahosi. Abhayagirivāsinopi attano suttaṃ vatvā “tumhākaṃ vāde thero kārako hotī”ti vadanti. Mahāvihāravāsinopi attano suttaṃ vatvā “tumhākaṃ vāde thero kārako hotī”ti [V 2.0152] vadanti. Pañho na chijjati. Rājā sutvā there sannipātetvā dīghakārāyanaṃ nāma brāhmaṇajātiyaṃ amaccaṃ “therānaṃ kathaṃ suṇāhī”ti āṇāpesi. Amacco kira paṇḍito bhāsantarakusalo so āha – “vadantu tāva therā sutta”nti. Tato abhayagiritherā attano suttaṃ vadiṃsu – “tena hi, bhikkhave, mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ sakāya paṭiññāya nāsethā”ti. Amacco “bhante, tumhākaṃ vāde thero kārako hoti sadoso”ti āha. Mahāvihāravāsinopi attano suttaṃ vadiṃsu – “tena hi, bhikkhave, mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsethā”ti. Amacco “bhante, tumhākaṃ vāde thero akārako hoti niddoso”ti āha. Kiṃ panettha yuttaṃ? Yaṃ pacchā vuttaṃ vicāritañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyehi, bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ amūlakena antimavatthunā anuddhaṃseti, saṅghādiseso; bhikkhuniṃ anuddhaṃseti, dukkaṭaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana “musāvāde pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ.

Even in the time of King Bhātiya, a dispute arose between the elders residing at the Mahāvihāra and those at the Abhayagiri on this very phrase. The Abhayagiri residents, reciting their own text, would say, “In your argument, the Elder is the perpetrator.” The Mahāvihāra residents, reciting their own text, would also say, “In your argument, the Elder is the perpetrator.” The issue was not resolved. The king, having heard of this, assembled the elders and commanded a minister of Brahmin caste named Dīghakārāyana, “Listen to the elders’ discussion.” The minister, who was said to be wise and skilled in other languages, said, “Let the elders first recite their text.” Then the Abhayagiri elders recited their text: “Therefore, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā on the basis of her own admission.” The minister said, “Venerable sirs, in your argument, the Elder is the perpetrator and at fault.” The Mahāvihāra residents also recited their text: “Therefore, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā.” The minister said, “Venerable sirs, in your argument, the Elder is not the perpetrator and is faultless.” What is correct here? That which was stated last is correct. This was investigated by the commentary masters: if a monk accuses another monk with a groundless, ultimate matter, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense; if he accuses a nun, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is said, “For false speech, it is a Pācittiya.”

Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā, purimanaye tāva anuddhaṃsanādhippāyattā dukkaṭameva yujjati. Yathā satipi musāvāde bhikkhuno bhikkhusmiṃ saṅghādiseso, satipi ca musāvāde asuddhaṃ suddhadiṭṭhino akkosādhippāyena vadantassa omasavādeneva [M 2.0169] pācittiyaṃ, na sampajānamusāvādena; evaṃ idhāpi anuddhaṃsanādhippāyattā sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyaṃ na yujjati, dukkaṭameva yuttaṃ. Pacchimanayepi musāvādattā pācittiyameva yujjati, vacanappamāṇato hi anuddhaṃsanādhippāyena bhikkhussa bhikkhusmiṃ saṅghādiseso. Akkosādhippāyassa ca omasavādo. Bhikkhussa pana bhikkhuniyā dukkaṭantivacanaṃ natthi, sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyanti vacanamatthi, tasmā pācittiyameva yujjati.

Herein is the investigation. Firstly, in the first method, because the intention is accusation, only a Dukkaṭa offense is suitable. Just as, although it is false speech, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense for a monk towards another monk; and just as, although it is false speech, for one who, viewing an impure person as pure, speaks with the intention to insult, it is a Pācittiya offense only under the rule on contemptuous speech, not under the rule on intentional false speech; so too here, because the intention is accusation, a Pācittiya offense for intentional false speech is not suitable—only a Dukkaṭa is suitable. In the latter method, because it is false speech, only a Pācittiya is suitable. For, according to the authority of the Buddha's word, for a monk with the intention of accusation towards another monk, it is a Saṅghādisesa; and for one with the intention to insult, it is contemptuous speech. However, there is no statement that for a monk towards a nun it is a Dukkaṭa offense, but there is the statement that for intentional false speech, it is a Pācittiya. Therefore, only a Pācittiya is suitable.

Tatra pana idaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ – “anuddhaṃsanādhippāye asati pācittiyaṃ, tasmiṃ sati kena bhavitabba”nti? Tatra yasmā musā bhaṇantassa pācittiye siddhepi amūlakena saṅghādisesena anuddhaṃsane visuṃ pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā anuddhaṃsanādhippāye sati sampajānamusāvāde [P 3.0584] pācittiyassa okāso na dissati, na ca sakkā anuddhaṃsentassa anāpattiyā bhavitunti purimanayovettha parisuddhataro khāyati. Tathā bhikkhunī bhikkhuniṃ amūlakena antimavatthunā anuddhaṃseti saṅghādiseso, bhikkhuṃ anuddhaṃseti dukkaṭaṃ, tatra saṅghādiseso vuṭṭhānagāmī dukkaṭaṃ, desanāgāmī etehi nāsanā natthi. Yasmā pana sā pakatiyāva dussīlā pāpabhikkhunī idāni ca sayameva “dussīlāmhī”ti vadati tasmā naṃ bhagavā asuddhattāyeva nāsesīti.

Furthermore, this should be examined here: 'When there is no intention to accuse, it is a pācittiya offense; when there is such an intention, what offense should it be?' In this regard, because, even when a pācittiya offense is established for one who speaks falsely, a separate pācittiya offense is stated for accusing with a groundless saṅghādisesa offense, therefore, when there is an intention to accuse, no opportunity for the pācittiya offense of intentional false speech is seen. And it is not possible for one who accuses to be without an offense; thus, the former method appears purer here. Similarly, if a bhikkhunī groundlessly accuses another bhikkhunī with the ultimate matter, it is a saṅghādisesa offense; if she accuses a bhikkhu, it is a dukkaṭa offense. Therein, the saṅghādisesa is rehabilitable, and the dukkaṭa is confessable; there is no expulsion on account of these. However, because she was by nature immoral, an evil bhikkhunī, and now she herself says, 'I am immoral,' therefore the Blessed One had her expelled precisely because of her impurity.

Atha [V 2.0153] kho mettiyabhūmajakāti evaṃ “mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsetha, ime ca bhikkhū anuyuñjathā”ti vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭhe bhagavati tehi bhikkhūhi “detha dāni imissā setakānī”ti nāsiyamānaṃ taṃ bhikkhuniṃ disvā te bhikkhū taṃ mocetukāmatāya attano aparādhaṃ āvikariṃsu, etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “atha kho mettiyabhūmajakā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The passage beginning 'Then, Mettiya and Bhūmajaka...' was stated by the compilers of the canon to show this meaning: When the Blessed One, having said, 'Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya and interrogate these bhikkhus,' rose from his seat and entered the vihāra, the bhikkhus of the assembly began to expel that bhikkhunī, saying, 'Now give her the white clothes.' Seeing this, those bhikkhus (Mettiya and Bhūmajaka), desiring to free her, revealed their own offense.

385-6. Duṭṭho dosoti dūsito ceva dūsako ca. Uppanne hi dose puggalo tena dosena dūsito hoti pakatibhāvaṃ jahāpito, tasmā “duṭṭho”ti vuccati. Parañca dūseti vināseti, tasmā “doso”ti vuccati. Iti “duṭṭho doso”ti ekassevetaṃ puggalassa ākāranānattena nidassanaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “duṭṭho dosoti dūsito ceva [M 2.0170] dūsako cā”ti tattha saddalakkhaṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Yasmā pana so “duṭṭho doso”ti saṅkhyaṃ gato paṭighasamaṅgīpuggalo kupitādibhāve ṭhitova hoti, tenassa padabhājane “kupito”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kupitoti kuppabhāvaṃ pakatito cavanabhāvaṃ patto. Anattamanoti na sakamano attano vase aṭṭhitacitto; apica pītisukhehi na attamano na attacittoti anattamano. Anabhiraddhoti na sukhito na vā pasāditoti anabhiraddho. Paṭighena āhataṃ cittamassāti āhatacitto. Cittathaddhabhāvacittakacavarasaṅkhātaṃ paṭighakhīlaṃ [P 3.0585] jātamassāti khilajāto. Appatītoti nappatīto pītisukhādīhi vajjito, na abhisaṭoti attho. Padabhājane pana yesaṃ dhammānaṃ vasena appatīto hoti, te dassetuṃ “tena ca kopenā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

385-6. Duṭṭho doso means both 'the corrupted' and 'the corruptor.' For when anger arises, a person is corrupted by that anger, made to abandon their natural state; hence, they are called duṭṭho (corrupted). They also corrupt and destroy another; hence, it is called doso (anger/corruption). Thus, duṭṭho doso is an indication of one and the same person through a difference in aspect. Therefore it was said: 'Duṭṭho doso means both 'the corrupted' and 'the corruptor.'' Here, the grammatical characteristic should be sought. However, because that person endowed with aversion, who has come to be designated as 'duṭṭho doso,' is indeed established in the state of being angry and so forth, in the word-analysis section, 'kupito (angry),' etc., was stated. Therein, kupito means one who has reached a state of agitation, a state of deviation from one's natural condition. Anattamano means not having one's own mind, one whose mind is not established under one's own control; moreover, not having a mind that is gratified or has attained joy and happiness—thus, anattamano. Anabhiraddho means not happy or not gladdened—thus, anabhiraddho. Āhatacitto means one whose mind is struck by aversion. Khilajāto means one in whom the stake of aversion, known as mental rigidity and mental refuse, has arisen. Appatīto means not approached, devoid of joy, happiness, and so forth; the meaning is 'not pervaded.' However, in the word-analysis section, to show by means of which phenomena one is displeased, 'and by that anger...' etc., was stated.

Tattha tena ca kopenāti yena duṭṭhoti ca kupitoti ca vutto ubhayampi hetaṃ pakatibhāvaṃ jahāpanato ekākāraṃ hoti. Tena ca dosenāti yena “doso”ti vutto. Imehi dvīhi saṅkhārakkhandhameva dasseti.

Therein, 'and by that anger (kopa)' refers to that by which one is called both 'duṭṭho' (corrupted) and 'kupito' (angered). Both of these, because they cause the abandonment of one's natural state, are of a single characteristic. 'And by that corruption (dosa)' refers to that by which one is called 'doso.' By these two, he indicates only the aggregate of formations.

Tāya ca anattamanatāyāti yāya “anattamano”ti vutto. Tāya ca anabhiraddhiyāti yāya “anabhiraddho”ti vutto. Imehi dvīhi vedanākkhandhaṃ dasseti.

'And by that displeasure (anattamanatā)' refers to that by which one is called 'anattamano' (displeased). 'And by that dissatisfaction (anabhiraddhi)' refers to that by which one is called 'anabhiraddho' (dissatisfied). By these two, he indicates the aggregate of feeling.

Amūlakena pārājikenāti ettha nāssa mūlanti amūlakaṃ, taṃ panassa amūlakattaṃ yasmā codakavasena adhippetaṃ, na cuditakavasena. Tasmā tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ padabhājane “amūlakaṃ nāma adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ aparisaṅkita”nti āha. Tena imaṃ dīpeti “yaṃ pārājikaṃ codakena cuditakamhi puggale neva diṭṭhaṃ na sutaṃ na parisaṅkitaṃ idaṃ etesaṃ dassanasavanaparisaṅkāsaṅkhātānaṃ mūlānaṃ [V 2.0154] abhāvato amūlakaṃ nāma, taṃ pana so āpanno vā hotu anāpanno vā etaṃ idha appamāṇanti.

Regarding 'by a groundless pārājika offense,' here, 'it has no basis (mūla),' thus it is 'groundless' (amūlaka). However, its groundlessness is intended from the perspective of the accuser, not from the perspective of the accused. Therefore, to show that meaning, in the word-analysis section, it is said: 'Groundless means unseen, unheard, unsuspected.' By this, he clarifies the following meaning: 'A pārājika offense that the accuser has neither seen in, nor heard about, nor suspected of the accused person—this, due to the absence of those bases called seeing, hearing, and suspecting, is termed 'groundless.' However, whether that person has actually committed the offense or not, that is not the main point here.'

Tattha adiṭṭhaṃ nāma attano pasādacakkhunā vā dibbacakkhunā vā adiṭṭhaṃ. Asutaṃ nāma tatheva kenaci vuccamānaṃ na sutaṃ. Aparisaṅkitaṃ nāma cittena aparisaṅkitaṃ.

Therein, 'unseen' means not seen by one's own physical eye or by the divine eye. 'Unheard' means, in the same way, not having heard it being spoken by someone. 'Unsuspected' means not suspected by the mind.

“Diṭṭhaṃ” [M 2.0171] nāma attanā vā parena vā pasādacakkhunā vā dibbacakkhunā vā diṭṭhaṃ. “Sutaṃ” nāma tatheva sutaṃ. “Parisaṅkita”mpi attanā vā parena vā parisaṅkitaṃ. Tattha attanā diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhameva, parehi diṭṭhaṃ attanā sutaṃ, parehi sutaṃ, parehi parisaṅkitanti idaṃ pana sabbampi attanā sutaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati.

'Seen' means seen by oneself or by others with the physical eye or the divine eye. 'Heard' means heard in the same way. 'Suspected' also means suspected by oneself or by others. Therein, what is seen by oneself is simply 'seen'; what is seen by others is 'heard' by oneself. Furthermore, what is heard by others and what is suspected by others—all of this stands only in the category of what is 'heard' by oneself.

Parisaṅkitaṃ pana tividhaṃ – diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ, sutaparisaṅkitaṃ, mutaparisaṅkitanti. Tattha diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma eko bhikkhu uccārapassāvakammena gāmasamīpe ekaṃ gumbaṃ paviṭṭho, aññatarāpi itthī kenacideva karaṇīyena taṃ gumbaṃ pavisitvā nivattā, nāpi bhikkhu itthiṃ addasa; na itthī bhikkhuṃ, adisvāva ubhopi yathāruciṃ pakkantā, aññataro bhikkhu ubhinnaṃ tato nikkhamanaṃ [P 3.0586] sallakkhetvā “addhā imesaṃ kataṃ vā karissanti vā”ti parisaṅkati, idaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma.

Suspicion, however, is of three kinds: suspicion based on what is seen, suspicion based on what is heard, and suspicion based on what is sensed. Therein, suspicion based on what is seen is as follows: a certain bhikkhu enters a thicket near a village for the purpose of urination or defecation. A certain woman also enters that thicket for some reason and then leaves. The bhikkhu did not see the woman, nor did the woman see the bhikkhu. Without seeing each other, both departed as they pleased. Another bhikkhu, noticing the exit of both of them from there, suspects, 'Surely, these two have done something or will do something.' This is called suspicion based on what is seen.

Sutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma idhekacco andhakāre vā paṭicchanne vā okāse mātugāmena saddhiṃ bhikkhuno tādisaṃ paṭisanthāravacanaṃ suṇāti, samīpe aññaṃ vijjamānampi “atthi natthī”ti na jānāti, so “addhā imesaṃ kataṃ vā karissanti vā”ti parisaṅkati, idaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma.

Suspicion based on what is heard is when a certain person here, in darkness or in a concealed place, hears a bhikkhu exchanging such friendly talk with a woman, and does not know whether another is present nearby or not. He suspects, 'Surely, these two have done something or will do something.' This is called suspicion based on what is heard.

Mutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma sambahulā dhuttā rattibhāge pupphagandhamaṃsasurādīni gahetvā itthīhi saddhiṃ ekaṃ paccantavihāraṃ gantvā maṇḍape vā bhojanasālādīsu vā yathāsukhaṃ kīḷitvā pupphādīni vikiritvā gatā, punadivase bhikkhū taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā “kassidaṃ kamma”nti vicinanti. Tatra ca kenaci bhikkhunā pageva vuṭṭhahitvā vattasīsena maṇḍapaṃ vā bhojanasālaṃ vā paṭijaggantena pupphādīni āmaṭṭhāni honti, kenaci upaṭṭhākakulato ābhatehi pupphādīhi pūjā katā hoti, kenaci bhesajjatthaṃ ariṭṭhaṃ pītaṃ hoti, atha te “kassidaṃ kamma”nti vicinantā [V 2.0155] bhikkhū tesaṃ hatthagandhañca mukhagandhañca ghāyitvā te bhikkhū parisaṅkanti, idaṃ mutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma.

Suspicion based on what is sensed is when many rogues, taking flowers, perfumes, meat, liquor, and so forth, go with women to a remote monastery at night. They enjoy themselves as they please in a pavilion or dining hall and so forth, scatter the flowers and other items, and then leave. The next day, bhikkhus seeing the disarray investigate, 'Whose work is this?' And there, a certain bhikkhu who had risen early and was tending to the pavilion or dining hall as a matter of duty might have handled the flowers and such. Another might have made offerings with flowers brought from a supporter’s family. Another might have drunk ariṭṭha for medicinal purposes. Then, those bhikkhus investigating, 'Whose work is this?' smelling the scent on their hands and the scent on their mouths, suspect those bhikkhus. This is called suspicion based on what is sensed.

Tattha diṭṭhaṃ atthi samūlakaṃ, atthi amūlakaṃ; diṭṭhameva atthi saññāsamūlakaṃ, atthi saññāamūlakaṃ. Esa nayo sutepi. Parisaṅkite pana diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ atthi samūlakaṃ, atthi amūlakaṃ; diṭṭhaparisaṅkitameva atthi saññāsamūlakaṃ[M 2.0172], atthi saññāamūlakaṃ. Esa nayo sutamutaparisaṅkitesu. Tattha diṭṭhaṃ samūlakaṃ nāma pārājikaṃ āpajjantaṃ disvāva “diṭṭho mayā”ti vadati, amūlakaṃ nāma paṭicchannokāsato nikkhamantaṃ disvā vītikkamaṃ adisvā “diṭṭho mayā”ti vadati. Diṭṭhameva saññāsamūlakaṃ nāma disvāva diṭṭhasaññī hutvā codeti, saññāamūlakaṃ nāma pubbe pārājikavītikkamaṃ disvā pacchā adiṭṭhasaññī jāto, so saññāya amūlakaṃ katvā “diṭṭho mayā”ti codeti. Etena nayena sutamutaparisaṅkitānipi vitthārato veditabbāni. Ettha ca sabbappakāreṇāpi samūlakena vā saññāsamūlakena vā codentassa anāpatti, amūlakena vā pana saññāamūlakena vā codentasseva [P 3.0587] āpatti.

Herein, what is seen can be with a basis, and it can be without a basis; what is seen itself can be with a basis in perception, and it can be without a basis in perception. This same method applies to what is heard. But regarding what is suspected, suspicion based on what is seen can be with a basis, and it can be without a basis; suspicion based on what is seen itself can be with a basis in perception, and it can be without a basis in perception. This same method applies to suspicion based on what is heard and what is sensed. Herein, 'what is seen with a basis' means, having seen one committing a pārājika offense, one says, 'He was seen by me.' 'What is seen without a basis' means, having seen one coming out of a concealed place, but not having seen the transgression, one says, 'He was seen by me.' 'What is seen with a basis in perception' means, having seen, and having the perception of having seen, one accuses. 'What is seen without a basis in perception' means, having previously seen a pārājika transgression, one later comes to have the perception of not having seen it; he then, making the accusation baseless through perception, accuses, saying, 'He was seen by me.' By this method, suspicion based on what is heard and what is sensed should also be understood in detail. And here, in all cases, there is no offense for one who accuses with a basis or with a basis in perception, but there is an offense only for one who accuses without a basis or without a basis in perception.

Anuddhaṃseyyāti dhaṃseyya padhaṃseyya abhibhaveyya ajjhotthareyya. Taṃ pana anuddhaṃsanaṃ yasmā attanā codentopi parena codāpentopi karotiyeva, tasmāssa padabhājane “codeti vā codāpeti vā”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Anuddhaṃseyya’ means one would destroy, one would utterly destroy, one would overpower, one would overwhelm. But since this act of destruction is done even when one accuses by oneself or causes another to accuse, therefore in its word-analysis it is stated: 'one accuses or causes to accuse.'

Tattha codetīti “pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpannosī”tiādīhi vacanehi sayaṃ codeti, tassa vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso. Codāpetīti attanā samīpe ṭhatvā aññaṃ bhikkhu āṇāpeti, so tassa vacanena taṃ codeti, codāpakasseva vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso. Atha sopi “mayā diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ atthī”ti codeti, dvinnampi janānaṃ vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso.

Herein, 'one accuses' means one accuses by oneself with words such as, 'You have committed a pārājika offense'; for that person, for every utterance, there is a saṅghādisesa offense. 'One causes to accuse' means, standing nearby oneself, one commands another bhikkhu, and that one accuses him by his word; for the one who causes the accusation only, for every utterance, there is a saṅghādisesa offense. Then, if that commanded one also accuses, saying, 'By me it was seen, it was heard,' for both persons, for every utterance, there is a saṅghādisesa offense.

Codanāppabhedakosallatthaṃ panettha ekavatthuekacodakādicatukkaṃ tāva veditabbaṃ. Tattha eko bhikkhu ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ekena vatthunā codeti, imissā codanāya ekaṃ vatthu eko codako. Sambahulā ekaṃ ekavatthunā codenti, pañcasatā mettiyabhūmajakappamukhā chabbaggiyā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ dabbaṃ mallaputtamiva, imissā codanāya ekaṃ vatthu nānācodakā. Eko bhikkhu ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ sambahulehi vatthūhi codeti, imissā codanāya nānāvatthūni eko codako. Sambahulā sambahule sambahulehi vatthūhi codenti, imissā codanāya nānāvatthūni nānācodakā.

Here, for the purpose of skill in the distinctions of accusations, the tetrad beginning with 'one matter, one accuser' should first be understood. Therein, one bhikkhu accuses one bhikkhu regarding one matter; in this accusation, there is one matter and one accuser. Many accuse one regarding one matter—like the five hundred group-of-six bhikkhus, led by Mettiya, Bhūmajaka, and Kappa, accused the Venerable Dabba the Mallian; in this accusation, there is one matter and many accusers. One bhikkhu accuses one bhikkhu regarding many matters; in this accusation, there are many matters and one accuser. Many accuse many regarding many matters; in this accusation, there are many matters and many accusers.

Codetuṃ [M 2.0173][V 2.0156] pana ko labhati, ko na labhatīti? Dubbalacodakavacanaṃ tāva gahetvā koci na labhati. Dubbalacodako nāma sambahulesu kathāsallāpena nisinnesu eko ekaṃ ārabbha anodissakaṃ katvā pārājikavatthuṃ katheti, añño taṃ sutvā itarassa gantvā āroceti. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tvaṃ kira maṃ idañcidañca vadasī”ti vadati. So “nāhaṃ evarūpaṃ jānāmi, kathāpavattiyaṃ pana mayā anodissakaṃ katvā vuttamatthi, sace ahaṃ tava imaṃ dukkhuppattiṃ jāneyyaṃ, ettakampi na katheyya”nti ayaṃ dubbalacodako. Tassetaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ gahetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ koci codetuṃ na labhati. Etaṃ pana aggahetvā sīlasampanno bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā sīlasampannā ca bhikkhunī bhikkhunīmeva codetuṃ [P 3.0588] labhatīti mahāpadumatthero āha. Mahāsumatthero pana “pañcapi sahadhammikā labhantī”ti āha. Godattatthero pana “na koci na labhatī”ti vatvā “bhikkhussa sutvā codeti, bhikkhuniyā sutvā codeti…pe… titthiyasāvakānaṃ sutvā codetī”ti idaṃ suttamāhari. Tiṇṇampi therānaṃ vāde cuditakasseva paṭiññāya kāretabbo.

But who is allowed to accuse, and who is not? First, taking the statement of a weak accuser, no one is allowed to. A 'weak accuser' is as follows: while many are seated engaged in conversation, one speaks about a pārājika matter concerning another, but without specifying anyone. Another, hearing that, goes and reports it to the person concerned. That person approaches the first and says, 'It is said that you spoke about me in such and such a way.' He replies, 'I know nothing of the kind. But in the course of the conversation, something was said by me without specifying anyone. If I had known this would cause you distress, I would not have said even that much.' This is a weak accuser. No one is allowed to accuse that bhikkhu based on this conversation of his. However, setting this aside, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue is allowed to accuse a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, and a bhikkhunī endowed with virtue is allowed to accuse only a bhikkhunī—so said the Elder Mahāpaduma. The Elder Mahāsuma, however, said, 'The five kinds of co-religionists are allowed to accuse.' The Elder Godatta, on the other hand, said, 'There is no one who is not allowed to accuse,' and brought forth this Sutta passage: 'Having heard from a bhikkhu, one accuses; having heard from a bhikkhunī, one accuses… having heard from the disciples of heretics, one accuses.' In the doctrines of all three elders, the accused should be dealt with only by their own confession.

Ayaṃ pana codanā nāma dūtaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā pesetvā codentassa sīsaṃ na eti, puggalassa pana samīpe ṭhatvāva hatthamuddāya vā vacībhedena vā codentasseva sīsaṃ eti. Sikkhāpaccakkhānameva hi hatthamuddāya sīsaṃ na eti, idaṃ pana anuddhaṃsanaṃ abhūtārocanañca etiyeva. Yo pana dvinnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne ekaṃ niyametvā codeti, so ce jānāti, sīsaṃ eti. Itaro jānāti, sīsaṃ na eti. Dvepi niyametvā codeti, eko vā jānātu dve vā, sīsaṃ etiyeva. Esava nayo sambahulesu. Taṅkhaṇeyeva ca jānanaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ, samayena āvajjitvā ñāte pana ñātameva hoti. Pacchā ce jānāti, sīsaṃ na eti. Sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ abhūtārocanaṃ duṭṭhullavācā-attakāma-duṭṭhadosabhūtārocanasikkhāpadānīti sabbāneva hi imāni ekaparicchedāni.

Furthermore, this so-called accusation does not reach its culmination for one who accuses by sending a messenger, a letter, or a verbal message. However, for one who accuses by standing near the person and using a hand gesture or by distinct speech, it does reach its culmination. Indeed, only the renunciation of the training does not reach its culmination by a hand gesture; but this denigration and the false reporting of a higher human state do indeed reach it. Furthermore, if one, in a place where two are standing, designates one and accuses him, and if that one knows, it reaches its culmination. If the other one knows, it does not reach its culmination. If one designates and accuses both, whether one knows or both know, it does indeed reach its culmination. This is the same method in the case of many. And knowing at that very moment is difficult, but when it is known after reflecting at a later time, it is indeed known. If one knows afterwards, it does not reach its culmination. The renunciation of the training, the false reporting of a higher human state, the training rules on lewd speech, matchmaking, baseless accusation out of ill will, and reporting an actual offense—all these are indeed of one and the same division.

Evaṃ kāyavācāvasena cāyaṃ duvidhāpi codanā. Puna diṭṭhacodanā, sutacodanā, parisaṅkitacodanāti tividhā hoti. Aparāpi catubbidhā hoti – sīlavipatticodanā, ācāravipatticodanā, diṭṭhivipatticodanā, ājīvavipatticodanāti. Tattha garukānaṃ dvinnaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ vasena sīlavipatticodanā [M 2.0174] veditabbā. Avasesānaṃ vasena ācāravipatticodanā, micchādiṭṭhiantaggāhikadiṭṭhivasena diṭṭhivipatticodanā, ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vasena ājīvavipatticodanā veditabbā.

Thus, this accusation is also twofold, by way of body and speech. Again, it becomes threefold: accusation based on what is seen, accusation based on what is heard, and accusation based on suspicion. It also becomes fourfold: accusation regarding a lapse in morality, accusation regarding a lapse in conduct, accusation regarding a lapse in view, and accusation regarding a lapse in livelihood. Therein, accusation regarding a lapse in morality is to be understood by way of the two grave categories of offenses. Accusation regarding a lapse in conduct is to be understood by way of the remaining offenses; accusation regarding a lapse in view, by way of wrong view and extremist views; and accusation regarding a lapse in livelihood is to be understood by way of the six training rules laid down on account of livelihood.

Aparāpi [V 2.0157] catubbidhā hoti – vatthusandassanā, āpattisandassanā, saṃvāsapaṭikkhepo, sāmīcipaṭikkhepoti. Tattha vatthusandassanā nāma “tvaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevittha, adinnaṃ ādiyittha, manussaṃ ghātayittha, abhūtaṃ ārocayitthā”ti evaṃ pavattā. Āpattisandassanā nāma “tvaṃ methunadhammapārājikāpattiṃ āpanno”ti evamādinayappavattā. Saṃvāsapaṭikkhepo nāma “natthi [P 3.0589] tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā saṅghakammaṃ vā”ti evaṃ pavattā; ettāvatā pana sīsaṃ na eti, “assamaṇosi asakyaputtiyosī”tiādivacanehi saddhiṃ ghaṭiteyeva sīsaṃ eti. Sāmīcipaṭikkhepo nāma abhivādana-paccuṭṭhāna-añjalikamma-bījanādikammānaṃ akaraṇaṃ. Taṃ paṭipāṭiyā vandanādīni karoto ekassa akatvā sesānaṃ karaṇakāle veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā ca codanā nāma hoti, āpatti pana sīsaṃ na eti. “Kasmā mama vandanādīni na karosī”ti pucchite pana “assamaṇosi asakyaputtiyosī”tiādivacanehi saddhiṃ ghaṭiteyeva sīsaṃ eti. Yāgubhattādinā pana yaṃ icchati taṃ āpucchati, na tāvatā codanā hoti.

It is also fourfold: pointing out the matter, pointing out the offense, rejection of communion, and rejection of respectful conduct. Therein, pointing out the matter is that which proceeds thus: 'You have engaged in sexual intercourse; you have taken what was not given; you have killed a human being; you have reported a non-existent higher human state.' Pointing out the offense is that which proceeds in a manner beginning with: 'You have fallen into a Pārājika offense related to sexual intercourse.' Rejection of communion is that which proceeds thus: 'There is no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or formal act of the Saṅgha with you.' By this much, however, it does not yet reach its culmination. It reaches its culmination only when connected with words such as: 'You are not an ascetic; you are not a son of the Sakyans.' Rejection of respectful conduct is the non-performance of acts such as paying homage, rising up, making the añjali gesture, fanning, and so on. This is to be understood at a time when one, while performing acts of veneration and so on in sequence, does not do so for one person while doing so for the others. And by this much it is called an accusation, but the offense does not yet reach its culmination. However, when asked, 'Why do you not perform acts of veneration and so on towards me?' it reaches its culmination only when connected with words such as: 'You are not an ascetic; you are not a son of the Sakyans.' Furthermore, if one asks leave of whomever one wishes regarding things like gruel and rice, by that much it is not an accusation.

Aparāpi pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhake “ekaṃ, bhikkhave, adhammikaṃ pātimokkhaṭṭhapanaṃ ekaṃ dhammika”nti ādiṃ “katvā yāva dasa adhammikāni pātimokkhaṭṭhapanāni dasa dhammikānī”ti (cūḷava. 387) evaṃ adhammikā pañcapaññāsa dhammikā pañcapaññāsāti dasuttarasataṃ codanā vuttā. Tā diṭṭhena codentassa dasuttarasataṃ, sutena codentassa dasuttarasataṃ, parisaṅkitena codentassa dasuttarasatanti tiṃsāni tīṇi satāni honti. Tāni kāyena codentassa, vācāya codentassa, kāyavācāhi codentassāti tiguṇāni katāni navutāni nava satāni honti. Tāni attanā codentassāpi parena codāpentassāpi tattakānevāti vīsatiūnāni dve sahassāni honti, puna diṭṭhādibhede samūlakāmūlakavasena anekasahassā codanā hontīti veditabbā.

Furthermore, in the Khandhaka on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha, beginning with 'Bhikkhus, one suspension of the Pātimokkha is unrighteous, one is righteous,' and so on, up to 'ten suspensions of the Pātimokkha are unrighteous, ten are righteous,' in this way one hundred and ten accusations are spoken of: fifty-five unrighteous and fifty-five righteous. For one who accuses based on what is seen, there are one hundred and ten; for one who accuses based on what is heard, one hundred and ten; for one who accuses based on suspicion, one hundred and ten—thus there are three hundred and thirty. These, for one who accuses by body, for one who accuses by speech, and for one who accuses by both body and speech, being made threefold, become nine hundred and ninety. These amount to the same number for one who accuses by oneself and for one who causes another to accuse—thus they become two thousand less twenty (1,980). Furthermore, it should be understood that in the divisions of seen and so on, by way of being with a basis or without a basis, many thousands of accusations come to be.

Imasmiṃ [M 2.0175] pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā aṭṭhakathāya “attādānaṃ ādātukāmena upāli bhikkhunā pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ attādānaṃ ādātabba”nti (cūḷava. 398) ca “codakena upāli bhikkhunā paraṃ codetukāmena pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ paccavekkhitvā paro codetabbo”ti (cūḷava. 399) ca evaṃ upālipañcakādīsu vuttāni bahūni suttāni āharitvā attādānalakkhaṇañca codakavattañca cuditakavattañca saṅghena kātabbakiccañca anuvijjakavattañca sabbaṃ vitthārena kathitaṃ, taṃ mayaṃ yathāāgataṭṭhāneyeva vaṇṇayissāma.

However, at this point in the commentary, by citing many discourses spoken in the Upāli Pañcaka and so on, such as: 'Upāli, a bhikkhu wishing to take up a case himself should take up a case himself when endowed with five factors,' and 'Upāli, a bhikkhu who is an accuser, wishing to accuse another, should accuse the other after internally reflecting on five things,' everything has been explained in detail: the characteristic of taking up a case oneself, the duty of the accuser, the duty of the accused, the task to be done by the Saṅgha, and the duty of the investigator. We shall explain all that in the very place where it occurs.

Vuttappabhedāsu [V 2.0158] pana imāsu codanāsu yāya kāyaci [P 3.0590] codanāya vasena saṅghamajjhe osaṭe vatthusmiṃ cuditakacodakā vattabbā “tumhe amhākaṃ vinicchayena tuṭṭhā bhavissathā”ti. Sace “bhavissāmā”ti vadanti, saṅghena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Atha pana “vinicchinatha tāva, bhante, sace amhākaṃ khamissati, gaṇhissāmā”ti vadanti. “Cetiyaṃ tāva vandathā”tiādīni vatvā dīghasuttaṃ katvā vissajjitabbaṃ. Te ce cirarattaṃ kilantā pakkantaparisā upacchinnapakkhā hutvā puna yācanti, yāvatatiyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā yadā nimmadā honti tadā nesaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Vinicchinantehi ca sace alajjussannā hoti, parisā ubbāhikāya taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Sace bālussannā hoti parisā “tumhākaṃ sabhāge vinayadhare pariyesathā”ti vinayadhare pariyesāpetvā yena dhammena yena vinayena yena satthusāsanena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamati, tathā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ.

Furthermore, among these aforementioned types of accusations, when a matter is brought before the Saṅgha by means of any accusation whatsoever, the accused and the accuser should be asked, 'Will you be satisfied with our decision?' If they say, 'We will be satisfied,' the Saṅgha should accept that legal issue. But if they say, 'Venerable sirs, decide first; if it is agreeable to us, we will accept it,' then, after saying things such as, 'First, pay homage to the shrine,' and making it a long-drawn-out affair, they should be dismissed. If, having become weary after a long time, with the assembly departed and their faction broken, they request again, they should be refused up to the third time. When they are without pride, then their legal issue should be decided. And by those deciding, if the assembly is full of the shameless, that legal issue should be decided by referral to a committee. If the assembly is full of the foolish, having told them, 'Seek out Vinaya-experts of your own kind,' and having had them seek out Vinaya-experts, by whichever Dhamma, by whichever Vinaya, and by whichever Teacher's instruction that legal issue is settled, so should that legal issue be settled.

Tattha ca “dhammo”ti bhūtaṃ vatthu. “Vinayo”ti codanā sāraṇā ca. “Satthusāsana”nti ñattisampadā ca anusāvanasampadā ca. Tasmā codakena vatthusmiṃ ārocite cuditako pucchitabbo “santametaṃ, no”ti. Evaṃ vatthuṃ upaparikkhitvā bhūtena vatthunā codetvā sāretvā ca ñattisampadāya anusāvanasampadāya ca taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Tatra ce alajjī lajjiṃ codeti, so ca alajjī bālo hoti abyatto nāssa nayo dātabbo. Evaṃ pana vattabbo – “kimhi naṃ codesī”ti? Addhā so vakkhati – “kimidaṃ, bhante, kimhi naṃ nāmā”ti. Tvaṃ kimhi nampi na jānāsi, na yuttaṃ tayā evarūpena bālena paraṃ codetunti uyyojetabbo nāssa anuyogo dātabbo. Sace pana so alajjī paṇḍito hoti [M 2.0176] byatto diṭṭhena vā sutena vā ajjhottharitvā sampādetuṃ sakkoti etassa anuyogaṃ datvā lajjisseva paṭiññāya kammaṃ kātabbaṃ.

And therein, 'Dhamma' is the true matter. 'Vinaya' is the accusation and the reminding. 'The Teacher's instruction' is the completeness of the motion and the completeness of the proclamation. Therefore, when the matter has been reported by the accuser, the accused should be asked, 'Is this existent, or not?' Having thus investigated the matter, and having accused and reminded with the true matter, that legal issue should be settled by the completeness of the motion and the completeness of the proclamation. Therein, if a shameless one accuses a scrupulous one, and that shameless one is foolish and unskilled, the procedure should not be given to him. But he should be spoken to thus: 'On what grounds do you accuse him?' Surely he will say, 'Venerable sir, what is this "on what grounds"?' He should be dismissed, having been told, 'You do not even know "on what grounds." It is not proper for a fool such as you to accuse another.' The inquiry should not be given to him. But if that shameless one is wise and skilled, and is able to overwhelm and accomplish the matter by means of what was seen or heard, having given the inquiry to him, the formal act should be carried out on the admission of the scrupulous one.

Sace lajjī alajjiṃ codeti, so ca lajjī bālo hoti abyatto, na sakkoti anuyogaṃ dātuṃ. Tassa nayo dātabbo – “kimhi naṃ codesi sīlavipattiyā vā ācāravipattiādīsu [P 3.0591] vā ekissā”ti. Kasmā pana imasseva evaṃ nayo dātabbo, na itarassa? Nanu na yuttaṃ vinayadharānaṃ agatigamananti? Na yuttameva. Idaṃ pana agatigamanaṃ na hoti, dhammānuggaho nāma eso alajjiniggahatthāya hi lajjipaggahatthāya ca sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ. Tatra alajjī nayaṃ labhitvā ajjhottharanto ehīti, lajjī pana nayaṃ labhitvā diṭṭhe diṭṭhasantānena, sute sutasantānena patiṭṭhāya kathessati, tasmā tassa dhammānuggaho vaṭṭati. Sace pana [V 2.0159] so lajjī paṇḍito hoti byatto, patiṭṭhāya katheti, alajjī ca “etampi natthi, etampi natthī”ti paṭiññaṃ na deti, alajjissa paṭiññāya eva kātabbaṃ.

If a scrupulous one accuses a shameless one, and that scrupulous one is foolish and unskilled, and is not able to conduct the inquiry, the procedure should be given to him: 'On what grounds do you accuse him? Is it for a corruption of virtue, or for one of the corruptions of conduct, and so on?' Why, then, should the procedure be given to this one, but not to the other? Is it not, in fact, improper for Vinaya-experts to follow a wrong course of action? It is indeed improper. However, this is not following a wrong course; this is called upholding the Dhamma. For the training rule was laid down for the sake of restraining the shameless and for the sake of supporting the scrupulous. Therein, the shameless one, having received the procedure, will proceed by overwhelming. But the scrupulous one, having received the procedure, will speak being established in what was seen with a continuity of what was seen, and in what was heard with a continuity of what was heard. Therefore, upholding the Dhamma is proper for him. But if that scrupulous one is wise and skilled, and speaks with a firm basis, and the shameless one does not give an admission, saying, 'This is not so, and this is not so,' the formal act should be carried out only on the admission of the shameless one.

Tadatthadīpanatthañca idaṃ vatthu veditabbaṃ. Tepiṭakacūḷābhayatthero kira lohapāsādassa heṭṭhā bhikkhūnaṃ vinayaṃ kathetvā sāyanhasamaye vuṭṭhāti, tassa vuṭṭhānasamaye dve attapaccatthikā kathaṃ pavattesuṃ. Eko “etampi natthi, etampi natthī”ti paṭiññaṃ na deti. Atha appāvasese paṭhamayāme therassa tasmiṃ puggale “ayaṃ patiṭṭhāya katheti, ayaṃ pana paṭiññaṃ na deti, bahūni ca vatthūni osaṭāni addhā etaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti asuddhaladdhi uppannā. Tato bījanīdaṇḍakena pādakathalikāya saññaṃ datvā “ahaṃ āvuso vinicchinituṃ ananucchaviko aññena vinicchināpehī”ti āha. Kasmā bhanteti? Thero tamatthaṃ ārocesi, cuditakapuggalassa kāye ḍāho uṭṭhito, tato so theraṃ vanditvā “bhante, vinicchinituṃ anurūpena vinayadharena nāma tumhādiseneva bhavituṃ vaṭṭati. Codakena ca īdiseneva bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā setakāni nivāsetvā “ciraṃ kilamitattha mayā”ti khamāpetvā pakkāmi.

And for the purpose of clarifying this meaning, this story should be known. The Elder Tepiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, it is said, having taught the Vinaya to the bhikkhus below the Lohapāsāda, rises in the evening. At the time of his rising, two litigants began a discussion. One does not give an admission, saying, 'This is not so, and this is not so.' Then, when little of the first watch of the night remained, a conviction of his impurity arose in the Elder regarding that person: 'This one speaks with a firm basis, but this one does not give an admission. And many matters have been brought up. Surely this must have been done by him.' Then, having given a sign on the foot-scraper with the handle of his fan, he said, 'Friend, I am not suitable to decide. Have it decided by another.' 'Venerable sir, why?' The Elder explained the reason. A burning arose in the body of the accused person. Then he, having paid homage to the Elder, said, 'Venerable sir, a Vinaya-expert suitable for deciding should indeed be one such as you. And an accuser should indeed be one such as this.' Having said this, and having put on white clothes, he asked for forgiveness, saying, 'You have been troubled by me for a long time,' and departed.

Evaṃ lajjinā codiyamāno alajjī bahūsupi vatthūsu uppannesu paṭiññaṃ na deti, so neva “suddho”ti vattabbo na “asuddho”ti. Jīvamatako nāma āmakapūtiko nāma cesa.

Thus, a shameless one, being accused by a scrupulous one, does not give an admission even when many matters have arisen. He should be spoken of as neither 'pure' nor 'impure.' This one is called 'dead while living' and 'putrid while raw'.

Sace [M 2.0177] panassa aññampi tādisaṃ vatthuṃ uppajjati na vinicchinitabbaṃ[P 3.0592]. Tathā nāsitakova bhavissati. Sace pana alajjīyeva alajjiṃ codeti, so vattabbo “āvuso tava vacanenāyaṃ kiṃ sakkā vattu”nti itarampi tatheva vatvā ubhopi “ekasambhogaparibhogā hutvā jīvathā”ti vatvā uyyojetabbā, sīlatthāya tesaṃ vinicchayo na kātabbo. Pattacīvarapariveṇādiatthāya pana patirūpaṃ sakkhiṃ labhitvā kātabbo.

But if another such matter arises for him, it should not be decided. He will be one who is ruined in just that way. But if a shameless one accuses a shameless one, he, the accuser, should be spoken to thus: 'Friend, by your word, what can be said about this person?' And having said the same to the other one, both should be dismissed after being told, 'You live having communal partaking and communal use.' For the sake of virtue, a decision should not be made for them. But for the sake of matters concerning bowls, robes, monastic cells, and so on, it should be done after obtaining a suitable witness.

Atha lajjī lajjiṃ codeti, vivādo ca nesaṃ kismiñcideva appamattako hoti, saññāpetvā “mā evaṃ karothā”ti accayaṃ desāpetvā uyyojetabbā. Atha panettha cuditakena sahasā viraddhaṃ hoti, ādito paṭṭhāya alajjī nāma natthi. So ca pakkhānurakkhaṇatthāya paṭiññaṃ na deti, “mayaṃ saddahāma, mayaṃ saddahāmā”ti bahū uṭṭhahanti. So tesaṃ paṭiññāya ekavāraṃ dvevāraṃ suddho hotu. Atha pana viraddhakālato paṭṭhāya ṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, vinicchayo na dātabbo.

Now, if a scrupulous monk accuses a scrupulous monk, and their dispute is over something insignificant, they should be made to understand, told, “Do not act thus,” made to confess their transgression, and then dismissed. If, however, in this case, the accused has suddenly erred—though from the beginning he was not what is called a shameless one—and he does not make an acknowledgement for the sake of protecting his faction, while many rise up saying, “We believe, we believe,” then let him be cleared once or twice on their declaration. But if, from the time of the error, he no longer stands in the position of a scrupulous one, a judgment should not be given.

Evaṃ [V 2.0160] yāya kāyaci codanāya vasena saṅghamajjhe osaṭe vatthusmiṃ cuditakacodakesu paṭipattiṃ ñatvā tassāyeva codanāya sampattivipattijānanatthaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānādīnaṃ vasena vinicchayo veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ codanāya ko ādi, kiṃ majjhe, kiṃ pariyosānaṃ? Codanāya “ahaṃ taṃ vattukāmo, karotu me āyasmā okāsa”nti evaṃ okāsakammaṃ ādi, otiṇṇena vatthunā codetvā sāretvā vinicchayo majjhe, āpattiyaṃ vā anāpattiyaṃ vā patiṭṭhāpanena samatho pariyosānaṃ.

Thus, when a matter has been brought up in the midst of the Saṅgha by means of whatever accusation, having known the conduct of the accused and the accuser, the judgment should be known by means of its beginning, middle, and end, for the sake of knowing the success and failure of that very accusation. That is to say: What is the beginning of the accusation? What is the middle? What is the end? The beginning of the accusation is the act of asking for permission, thus: “I wish to speak to you; may the venerable one grant me permission.” The middle is accusing with the matter that has been brought up, reminding, and the judgment. The end is the settlement by means of establishing either an offense or no offense.

Codanāya kati mūlāni, kati vatthūni, kati bhūmiyo? Codanāya dve mūlāni – samūlikā vā amūlikā vā; tīṇi vatthūni – diṭṭhaṃ, sutaṃ, parisaṅkitaṃ; pañca bhūmiyo – kālena vakkhāmi no akālena, bhūtena vakkhāmi no abhūtena, saṇhena vakkhāmi no pharusena, atthasaṃhitena vakkhāmi no anatthasaṃhitena, mettacitto vakkhāmi no dosantaroti. Imāya ca pana codanāya codakena puggalena “parisuddhakāyasamācāro nu khomhī”tiādinā (cūḷava. 399) nayena upālipañcake vuttesu pannarasasu dhammesu patiṭṭhātabbaṃ, cuditakena dvīsu dhammesu patiṭṭhātabbaṃ sacce ca akuppe cāti.

How many roots does an accusation have? How many objects? How many grounds? An accusation has two roots: one with a basis or one without a basis. It has three objects: what is seen, what is heard, and what is suspected. It has five grounds: ‘I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time; I will speak with what is true, not with what is untrue; I will speak with gentle speech, not with harsh speech; I will speak with what is connected to the goal, not with what is unconnected to the goal; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred.’ Furthermore, with this accusation, the person who is the accuser should be established in the fifteen qualities spoken of in the Upāli Pentad by the method beginning, “Am I of pure bodily conduct?” The accused should be established in two qualities: in truth and in imperturbability.

Appeva [M 2.0178] nāma naṃ imamhā brahmacariyā cāveyyanti api [P 3.0593] eva nāma naṃ puggalaṃ imamhā seṭṭhacariyā cāveyyaṃ, “sādhu vatassa sacāhaṃ imaṃ puggalaṃ imamhā brahmacariyā cāveyya”nti iminā adhippāyena anuddhaṃseyyāti vuttaṃhoti. Padabhājane pana “brahmacariyā cāveyya”nti imasseva pariyāyamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “bhikkhubhāvā cāveyya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding ‘Perhaps I might make him fall away from this holy life’: this means, ‘I might be able to make that person fall away from this excellent conduct.’ It means that he would slander him with this intention: ‘It would be good indeed if I could make this person fall away from this holy life.’ But in the Padabhājana, to show a mere synonym for this very phrase ‘make him fall away from the holy life,’ it is said, ‘make him fall away from the state of being a monk,’ and so on.

Khaṇādīni samayavevacanāni. Taṃ khaṇaṃ taṃ layaṃ taṃ muhuttaṃ vītivatteti tasmiṃ khaṇe tasmiṃ laye tasmiṃ muhutte vītivatte. Bhummappattiyā hi idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ.

The words `khaṇa` and so on are synonyms for `samaya` (time). The phrase ‘He passes beyond that moment (`taṃ khaṇaṃ`), that interval (`taṃ layaṃ`), that instant (`taṃ muhuttaṃ`)’ means ‘when that moment (`tasmiṃ khaṇe`), that interval (`tasmiṃ laye`), that instant (`tasmiṃ muhutte`) has passed.’ For this is an accusative expression used in the sense of the locative.

Samanuggāhiyamānaniddese yena vatthunā anuddhaṃsito hotīti catūsu pārājikavatthūsu yena vatthunā codakena cuditako anuddhaṃsito abhibhūto ajjhotthaṭo hoti. Tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ samanuggāhiyamānoti tasmiṃ codakena vuttavatthusmiṃ so codako anuvijjakena “kiṃ te diṭṭhaṃ, kinti te diṭṭha”ntiādinā nayena anuvijjiyamāno vīmaṃsiyamāno upaparikkhiyamāno.

In the exposition on ‘being questioned,’ the phrase ‘by which object... is slandered’ means: among the four Pārājika objects, by which object the accused is slandered, overcome, and overwhelmed by the accuser. ‘Being questioned in that object’ means: in that Pārājika object stated by the accuser, that accuser is being investigated, examined, and scrutinized by an investigator with the method beginning, ‘What was seen by you? How was it seen by you?’ and so on.

Asamanuggāhiyamānaniddese na kenaci vuccamānoti anuvijjakena vā aññena vā kenaci, atha vā diṭṭhādīsu vatthūsu kenaci avuccamāno. Etesañca dvinnaṃ mātikāpadānaṃ parato [V 2.0161] “bhikkhu ca dosaṃ patiṭṭhātī”tiiminā sambandho veditabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – “evaṃ samanuggāhiyamāno vā asamanuggāhiyamāno vā bhikkhu ca dosaṃ patiṭṭhāti paṭicca tiṭṭhati paṭijānāti saṅghādiseso”ti. Idañca amūlakabhāvassa pākaṭakāladassanatthameva vuttaṃ. Āpattiṃ pana anuddhaṃsitakkhaṇeyeva āpajjati.

In the exposition on ‘not being questioned,’ ‘not being spoken to by anyone’ means: not being spoken to by an investigator or by some other person, or else not being spoken to by anyone regarding the objects such as what was seen.
