And the connection of these two mātikā-terms should be known with what follows: ‘and the monk establishes the fault.’ For this is what is said: ‘Thus, whether being questioned or not being questioned, the monk establishes the fault, stands by it, acknowledges it; it is a Saṅghādisesa.’ And this was said only for the purpose of showing the time when the baselessness becomes apparent. The offense, however, is incurred at the very moment of the slander.

Idāni “amūlakañceva taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ hotī”ti ettha yasmā amūlakalakkhaṇaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ, tasmā taṃ avatvā apubbameva dassetuṃ “adhikaraṇaṃ nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā adhikaraṇaṃ adhikaraṇaṭṭhena ekampi vatthuvasena nānā hoti, tenassa taṃ nānattaṃ dassetuṃ “cattāri adhikaraṇāni vivādādhikaraṇa”ntiādimāha. Ko pana so adhikaraṇaṭṭho, yenetaṃ ekaṃ hotīti? Samathehi adhikaraṇīyatā. Tasmā yaṃ adhikicca ārabbha paṭicca sandhāya samathā vattanti, taṃ “adhikaraṇa”nti veditabbaṃ.

Now, in the phrase ‘and that legal issue is baseless,’ because the characteristic of baselessness was stated before, therefore, without stating that, to show only what was not stated before, he said, ‘A legal issue is called…’ and so on. Therein, because a legal issue, while being one in the sense of a legal issue, is diverse by way of its object, therefore, to show its diversity, he said, ‘There are four legal issues…’ and so on. But what is that sense of a legal issue by which it is one? It is the state of being that which is to be settled by the settlement procedures. Therefore, that with reference to which, on account of which, because of which, and concerning which the settlement procedures proceed, that should be known as a ‘legal issue’.

Aṭṭhakathāsu [M 2.0179] pana vuttaṃ – “adhikaraṇanti keci gāhaṃ vadanti, keci cetanaṃ, keci [P 3.0594] akkhantiṃ keci vohāraṃ, keci paṇṇatti”nti. Puna evaṃ vicāritaṃ “yadi gāho adhikaraṇaṃ nāma, eko attādānaṃ gahetvā sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ mantayamāno tattha ādīnavaṃ disvā puna cajati, tassa taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ samathappattaṃ bhavissati. Yadi cetanā adhikaraṇaṃ, “idaṃ attādānaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti uppannā cetanā nirujjhati. Yadi akkhanti adhikaraṇaṃ, akkhantiyā attādānaṃ gahetvāpi aparabhāge vinicchayaṃ alabhamāno vā khamāpito vā cajati. Yadi vohāro adhikaraṇaṃ, kathento āhiṇḍitvā aparabhāge tuṇhī hoti niravo, evamassa taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ samathappattaṃ bhavissati, tasmā paṇṇatti adhikaraṇanti.

But in the commentaries it is said: ‘Some say `adhikaraṇa` is grasping; some say it is intention; some say it is intolerance; some say it is speech; some say it is designation.’ Again, it was considered thus: ‘If grasping were the `adhikaraṇa`, a certain monk, having taken up his own view, while discussing with a like-minded monk, sees the danger therein and gives it up again; for him, that `adhikaraṇa` would become settled. If intention were the `adhikaraṇa`, the intention that arose, “I will take up this view,” ceases; for him, that `adhikaraṇa` would become settled. If intolerance were the `adhikaraṇa`, having taken up a view due to intolerance, but later not obtaining a judgment or being asked for forgiveness, he gives it up; for him, that `adhikaraṇa` would become settled. If speech were the `adhikaraṇa`, having gone about speaking, he later becomes silent and makes no sound; thus, for him, that `adhikaraṇa` would become settled. Therefore, designation is the `adhikaraṇa`.’

Taṃ panetaṃ “methunadhammapārājikāpatti methunadhammapārājikāpattiyā tabbhāgiyā…pe… evaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ āpattādhikaraṇassa tabbhāgiyanti ca vivādādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusalaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”nti ca evamādīhi virujjhati. Na hi te paṇṇattiyā kusalādibhāvaṃ icchanti, na ca “amūlakena pārājikena dhammenā”ti ettha āgato pārājikadhammo paṇṇatti nāma hoti. Kasmā? Accantaakusalattā. Vuttampi hetaṃ – “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”nti (pari. 303).

However, this contradicts such Pali passages as: “An offense of pārājika due to sexual intercourse… related to an offense of pārājika due to sexual intercourse… thus a legal question concerning an offense is related to a legal question concerning an offense,” and “A legal question of dispute may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate.” Indeed, they do not accept that a designation has a wholesome nature, etc. And the pārājika offense that occurs in the phrase “by a groundless pārājika offense” is not what is called a designation. Why? Because it is extremely unwholesome. Indeed, this was also stated: “A legal question concerning an offense may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate.”

Yañcetaṃ “amūlakena pārājikenā”ti ettha amūlakaṃ pārājikaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ, tassevāyaṃ “amūlakañceva taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ hotī”ti paṭiniddeso, na paṇṇattiyā na hi aññaṃ niddisitvā [V 2.0162] aññaṃ paṭiniddisati. Yasmā pana yāya paṇṇattiyā yena abhilāpena codakena so puggalo pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannoti paññatto, pārājikasaṅkhātassa adhikaraṇassa amūlakattā sāpi paññatti amūlikā hoti, adhikaraṇe pavattattā ca adhikaraṇaṃ. Tasmā iminā pariyāyena paṇṇatti “adhikaraṇa”nti yujjeyya, yasmā vā yaṃ amūlakaṃ nāma adhikaraṇaṃ taṃ sabhāvato natthi, paññattimattameva atthi. Tasmāpi paṇṇatti adhikaraṇanti yujjeyya. Tañca kho idheva na sabbattha. Na hi vivādādīnaṃ paṇṇatti adhikaraṇaṃ. Adhikaraṇaṭṭho pana tesaṃ pubbe vuttasamathehi adhikaraṇīyatā. Iti iminā adhikaraṇaṭṭhena idhekacco vivādo vivādo ceva adhikaraṇañcāti vivādādhikaraṇaṃ. Esa nayo sesesu[P 3.0595].

And that groundless pārājika which was pointed out in the phrase “by a groundless pārājika,” of that very thing this is the re-exposition: “That legal question is indeed groundless.” It is not a re-exposition of the designation, for indeed one does not point out one thing and then re-expound another. However, because of the groundlessness of the legal question known as pārājika, that designation by which, through a certain expression, the accuser has designated that person as “having committed a pārājika offense,” also becomes groundless. And because it occurs in a legal question, it is a legal question. Therefore, by this method, it is suitable that a designation is a “legal question.” Or, because that which is called a groundless legal question does not exist in reality—there is only a mere designation—therefore, it is also suitable that a designation is a legal question. And this is suitable only here, not everywhere. Indeed, the designation of disputes, etc., is not a legal question. However, the meaning of ‘legal question’ for them is the state of being fit to be settled by the settlements mentioned previously. Thus, by this meaning of ‘legal question,’ here a certain dispute is both a dispute and a legal question; hence, it is a legal question of dispute. This is the method in the remaining cases.

Tattha [M 2.0180] “idha bhikkhū vivadanti dhammoti vā adhammoti vā”ti evaṃ aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni nissāya uppanno vivādo vivādādhikaraṇaṃ. “Idha bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ anuvadanti sīlavipattiyā vā”ti evaṃ catasso vipattiyo nissāya uppanno anuvādo anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ. “Pañcapi āpattikkhandhā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ, sattapi āpattikkhandhā āpattādhikaraṇa”nti evaṃ āpattiyeva āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. “Yā saṅghassa kiccayatā karaṇīyatā apalokanakammaṃ ñattikammaṃ ñattidutiyakammaṃ ñatticatutthakamma”nti (cūḷava. 215) evaṃ catubbidhaṃ saṅghakiccaṃ kiccādhikaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

Among these, a dispute that has arisen depending on the eighteen grounds for schism, such as when “monks here dispute, ‘This is the Dhamma’ or ‘This is not the Dhamma,’” is a legal question of dispute. An accusation that has arisen depending on the four kinds of failure, such as when “monks here accuse a monk of a failure in virtue,” is a legal question of accusation. Thus, when it is said, “The five groups of offenses are a legal question concerning offenses; the seven groups of offenses are a legal question concerning offenses,” an offense itself is a legal question concerning offenses. Thus, when it is said, “Whatever is the duty of the Sangha, its obligation: an act of proclamation, an act of motion, an act of motion with a second proclamation, an act of motion with a fourth proclamation,” this fourfold business of the Sangha should be known as a legal question concerning duties.

Imasmiṃ panatthe pārājikāpattisaṅkhātaṃ āpattādhikaraṇameva adhippetaṃ. Sesāni atthuddhāravasena vuttāni, ettakā hi adhikaraṇasaddassa atthā. Tesu pārājikameva idha adhippetaṃ. Taṃ diṭṭhādīhi mūlehi amūlakañceva adhikaraṇaṃ hoti. Ayañca bhikkhu dosaṃ patiṭṭhāti, paṭicca tiṭṭhati “tucchakaṃ mayā bhaṇita”ntiādīni vadanto paṭijānāti. Tassa bhikkhuno anuddhaṃsitakkhaṇeyeva saṅghādisesoti ayaṃ tāvassa sapadānukkamaniddesassa sikkhāpadassa attho.

Furthermore, in this context, only the legal question concerning offenses, known as a pārājika offense, is intended. The remaining ones were stated by way of explaining the meaning, for the meanings of the word ‘legal question’ are this many. Among them, only the pārājika is intended here. That legal question is indeed groundless with respect to the roots such as ‘seen,’ etc. And this monk incurs a fault, is established in it, and confesses, saying such things as, “I have spoken empty words.” For that monk, at the very moment of not being admonished, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. This, first of all, is the meaning of this training rule with its word-by-word analysis.

387. Idāni yāni tāni saṅkhepato diṭṭhādīni codanāvatthūni vuttāni, tesaṃ vasena vitthārato āpattiṃ ropetvā dassento “adiṭṭhassa hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha adiṭṭhassa hotīti adiṭṭho assa hoti. Etena codakena adiṭṭho hoti, so puggalo pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjantoti attho. Esa nayo asutassa hotītiādīsupi.

387. Now, those grounds for accusation, such as ‘unseen,’ etc., which were stated briefly—showing how to establish the offense in detail by means of them, he said, “It is on the basis of the unseen,” etc. Therein, “it is on the basis of the unseen” means it is unseen by him. The meaning is: that person, while committing a pārājika offense, is unseen by this accuser. This is the method in “it is on the basis of the unheard,” etc., as well.

Diṭṭho mayāti diṭṭhosi mayāti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo suto mayātiādīsupi. Sesaṃ adiṭṭhamūlake [V 2.0163] uttānatthameva. Diṭṭhamūlake pana tañce codeti “suto mayā”ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ suttādīnaṃ ābhāvena amūlakattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“Seen by me” means it is said, “You were seen by me.” This is the method in “heard by me,” etc., as well. In the case based on the unseen, the remainder has an obvious meaning. However, in the case based on the seen, if one accuses by saying, “Heard by me,” the groundlessness should be understood as due to the absence of the stated grounds, such as ‘heard,’ etc.

Sabbasmiṃyeva ca imasmiṃ codakavāre yathā idhāgatesu “pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosi, assamaṇosi, asakyaputtiyosī”ti imesu vacanesu ekekassa vasena vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso hoti, evaṃ [M 2.0181] aññatra āgatesu “dussīlo, pāpadhammo, asucisaṅkassarasamācāro, paṭicchannakammanto[P 3.0596], assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño, abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño, antopūti, avassuto, kasambujāto”ti imesupi vacanesu ekekassa vasena vācāya vācāya saṅghādiseso hotiyeva.

And in this entire section on the accuser, just as for these words that occur here—“You have committed a pārājika offense,” “You are not an ascetic,” “You are not a son of the Sakyan”—a Saṅghādisesa offense occurs for each and every utterance, so too for these words that occur elsewhere—“You are immoral,” “You are of evil nature,” “You have impure and questionable conduct,” “You have concealed deeds,” “Though not an ascetic, you claim to be an ascetic,” “Though not celibate, you claim to be celibate,” “You are rotten within,” “You are lustful,” “You are like rubbish”—for each and every utterance, a Saṅghādisesa offense certainly occurs.

“Natthi tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā saṅghakammaṃ vā”ti imāni pana suddhāni sīsaṃ na enti, “dussīlosi natthi tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā”ti evaṃ dussīlādipadesu pana “pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosī”tiādipadesu vā yena kenaci saddhiṃ ghaṭitāneva sīsaṃ enti, saṅghādisesakarāni honti.

However, these statements, “With you there is no Uposatha, or Pavāraṇā, or Saṅghakamma,” being on their own, do not reach the culmination. But only when connected with any term whatsoever—either among terms such as “immoral,” as in “You are immoral; there is no Uposatha with you,” or among terms such as “You have committed a pārājika offense”—do they reach the culmination and bring about a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Mahāpadumatthero panāha – “na kevalaṃ idha pāḷiyaṃ anāgatāni ‘dussīlo pāpadhammo’tiādipadāneva sīsaṃ enti, ‘koṇṭhosi mahāsāmaṇerosi, mahāupāsakosi, jeṭṭhabbatikosi, nigaṇṭhosi, ājīvakosi, tāpasosi, paribbājakosi, paṇḍakosi, theyyasaṃvāsakosi, titthiyapakkantakosi, tiracchānagatosi, mātughātakosi, pitughātakosi, arahantaghātakosi, saṅghabhedakosi, lohituppādakosi, bhikkhunīdūsakosi, ubhatobyañjanakaosī’ti imānipi sīsaṃ entiyevā”ti. Mahāpadumattheroyeva ca “diṭṭhe vematikotiādīsu yadaggena vematiko tadaggena no kappeti, yadaggena no kappeti tadaggena nassarati, yadaggena nassarati tadaggena pamuṭṭho hotī”ti vadati.

The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, states: "Not only do the terms not found in the Pāḷi here, such as 'immoral, of bad character,' etc., reach the principal point, but also these: 'You are Koṇṭha,' 'You are a great novice,' 'You are a great lay follower,' 'You are a Jeṭṭhabbatika,' 'You are a Nigaṇṭha,' 'You are an Ājīvaka,' 'You are an ascetic,' 'You are a wanderer,' 'You are a paṇḍaka,' 'You are a thief in communion,' 'You have deserted to the heretics,' 'You are an animal,' 'You are a matricide,' 'You are a patricide,' 'You are a murderer of an arahant,' 'You are a schismatic,' 'You have caused blood to flow from a Buddha,' 'You have violated a bhikkhunī,' 'You are a hermaphrodite'—all these also reach the principal point." And the Elder Mahāpaduma himself says: "In 'one who is doubtful about what is seen,' etc., to the extent that one is doubtful, to that extent one does not accept; to the extent that one does not accept, to that extent one forgets; to the extent that one forgets, to that extent one is oblivious."

Mahāsumatthero pana ekekaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā catunnampi pāṭekkaṃ nayaṃ dasseti. Kathaṃ? Diṭṭhe vematikoti ayaṃ tāva dassane vā vematiko hoti puggale vā, tattha “diṭṭho nukho mayā na diṭṭho”ti evaṃ dassane vematiko hoti. “Ayaṃ nukho mayā diṭṭho añño”ti evaṃ puggale vematiko hoti. Evaṃ dassanaṃ vā no kappeti puggalaṃ vā, dassanaṃ vā nassarati puggalaṃ vā, dassanaṃ vā pamuṭṭho hoti puggalaṃ vā. Ettha ca vematikoti vimatijāto. No kappetīti na saddahati. Nassaratīti asāriyamāno nassarati. Yadā pana taṃ [V 2.0164] “asukasmiṃ nāma bhante ṭhāne asukasmiṃ nāma kāle”ti sārenti tadā sarati. Pamuṭṭhoti [P 3.0597] yo tehi tehi upāyehi sāriyamānopi nassaratiyevāti[M 2.0182]. Etenevupāyena codāpakavāropi veditabbo, kevalañhi tattha “mayā”ti parihīnaṃ, sesaṃ codakavārasadisameva.

The Elder Mahāsumana, however, breaking each one into two, shows the method for each of the four individually. How? Regarding 'one who is doubtful about what was seen,' this one may be doubtful either about the seeing or about the person. Therein, one is doubtful about the seeing, thinking, "Was it seen by me or not?" One is doubtful about the person, thinking, "Is this the one I saw, or is it someone else?" In the same way, one may not accept either the seeing or the person; one may forget either the seeing or the person; or one may be oblivious about either the seeing or the person. And here, 'doubtful' means one in whom doubt has arisen. 'Does not accept' means does not believe. 'Forgets' means one forgets when not being reminded. But when they remind him, "Venerable sir, at such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time," then he remembers. 'Oblivious' refers to one who, even when reminded by these and those means, still forgets. By this same method, the section on the one being accused should also be understood; the only difference there is the omission of 'by me'; the rest is just like the section on the accuser.

389. Tato paraṃ āpattibhedaṃ anāpattibhedañca dassetuṃ “asuddhe suddhadiṭṭhī”tiādikaṃ catukkaṃ ṭhapetvā ekamekaṃ padaṃ catūhi catūhi bhedehi niddiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ pāḷinayeneva sakkā jānituṃ. Kevalaṃ hetthādhippāyabhedo veditabbo. Ayañhi adhippāyo nāma – cāvanādhippāyo, akkosādhippāyo, kammādhippāyo, vuṭṭhānādhippāyo, uposathapavāraṇaṭṭhapanādhippāyo, anuvijjanādhippāyo, dhammakathādhippāyoti anekavidho. Tattha purimesu catūsu adhippāyesu okāsaṃ akārāpentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Okāsaṃ kārāpetvāpi ca sammukhā amūlakena pārājikena anuddhaṃsentassa saṅghādiseso. Amūlakena saṅghādisesena anuddhaṃsentassa pācittiyaṃ. Ācāravipattiyā anuddhaṃsentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Akkosādhippāyena vadantassa pācittiyaṃ. Asammukhā pana sattahipi āpattikkhandhehi vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Asammukhā eva sattavidhampi kammaṃ karontassa dukkaṭameva.

389. After that, to show the classification of offenses and non-offenses, the tetrad beginning with "having the view of purity in what is impure" has been established, and each term is specified with fourfold classifications. All of this can be known by the method of the Pāḷi itself. Only the difference in intention should be understood here. For this intention is of many kinds: the intention for expulsion, the intention for reviling, the intention for formal acts, the intention for rehabilitation, the intention for suspending the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, the intention for investigation, and the intention for preaching the Dhamma. Among these, in the first four intentions, for one who does not request permission, it is a dukkaṭa offense. And if, having requested permission, one admonishes another to their face with a groundless pārājika accusation, it is a saṅghādisesa offense. For one who admonishes with a groundless saṅghādisesa accusation, it is a pācittiya offense. For one who admonishes due to a failure in conduct, it is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who speaks with the intention of reviling, it is a pācittiya offense. However, for one who speaks in another's absence regarding any of the seven classes of offenses, it is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who performs any of the seven kinds of formal acts in another’s absence, it is also a dukkaṭa offense.

Kurundiyaṃ pana “vuṭṭhānādhippāyena ‘tvaṃ imaṃ nāma āpattiṃ āpanno taṃ paṭikarohī’ti vadantassa okāsakiccaṃ natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbattheva pana “uposathapavāraṇaṃ ṭhapentassa okāsakammaṃ natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Ṭhapanakkhettaṃ pana jānitabbaṃ. “Suṇātu me bhante saṅgho ajjuposatho pannaraso yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ saṅgho uposathaṃ kareyya”ti etasmiñhi re-kāre anatikkanteyeva ṭhapetuṃ labbhati. Tato paraṃ pana yya-kāre patte na labbhati. Esa nayo pavāraṇāya. Anuvijjakassāpi osaṭe vatthusmiṃ “atthetaṃ tavā”ti anuvijjanādhippāyena vadantassa okāsakammaṃ natthi.

In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is said: "For one who speaks with the intention of rehabilitation, saying, 'You have committed such-and-such an offense, you should remedy it,' there is no duty to request permission." Furthermore, it is said in all the commentaries: "For one who suspends the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, there is no formal act of requesting permission." However, the proper occasion for suspension should be known. For in the phrase, "Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the Uposatha, the fifteenth. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha (saṅgho uposathaṃ kareyya)," it is permissible to suspend it only before the syllable 're' has been passed. But after that, when the syllable 'yya' is reached, it is not permissible. This is also the method for the Pavāraṇā. Also for an investigator, regarding a matter that has been concluded, for one who speaks with the intention of investigation, saying, "Does this matter concern you?", there is no formal act of requesting permission.

Dhammakathikassāpi dhammāsane nisīditvā “yo idañcidañca karoti, ayaṃ bhikkhu assamaṇo”tiādinā nayena anodissa dhammaṃ kathentassa okāsakammaṃ natthi. Sace pana odissa niyametvā “asuko ca asuko [P 3.0598] ca assamaṇo anupāsako”ti katheti, dhammāsanato orohitvā āpattiṃ desetvā gantabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana tattha tattha “anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā”ti vuttaṃ tassa okāsaṃ akārāpetvāti evamattho veditabbo, na hi koci anokāso nāma atthi, yamokāsaṃ [M 2.0183] kārāpetvā āpattiṃ āpajjati, okāsaṃ pana akārāpetvā āpajjatīti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

Also for a Dhamma-preacher, sitting on the Dhamma-seat and preaching the Dhamma without specifying, by the method of saying, "Whoever does this and that, this monk is not an ascetic," and so on, there is no formal act of requesting permission. But if, having specified and determined, one says, "So-and-so and so-and-so is not an ascetic, not a lay follower," one should descend from the Dhamma-seat, confess the offense, and depart. As for what is said here and there, "anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā" (having caused a non-opportunity), its meaning should be understood as "okāsaṃ akārāpetvā" (without having requested permission). For there is no such thing as a 'non-opportunity' that one could request and thereby incur an offense; rather, one incurs an offense by not having requested permission. The rest is self-evident.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu [V 2.0165] tisamuṭṭhānaṃ – kāyacittato, vācācittato, kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dukkhavedananti.

Regarding origins and so forth, it has three origins, arising from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action, a release by perception, volitional, a worldly offense, a bodily action, a verbal action, with an unwholesome mind, and with painful feeling.

Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Training Rule on Malicious Ill-Will is concluded.

9. Dutiyaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Malicious Ill-Will

391. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti dutiyaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha handa mayaṃ āvuso imaṃ chagalakaṃ dabbaṃ mallaputtaṃ nāma karomāti te kira paṭhamavatthusmiṃ attano manorathaṃ sampādetuṃ asakkontā laddhaniggahā vighātappattā “idāni jānissāmā”ti tādisaṃ vatthuṃ pariyesamānā vicaranti. Athekadivasaṃ disvā tuṭṭhā aññamaññaṃ oloketvā evamāhaṃsu – “handa mayaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ chagalakaṃ dabbaṃ mallaputtaṃ nāma karomā”ti, “dabbo mallaputto nāmāya”nti evamassa nāmaṃ karomāti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo mettiyaṃ nāma bhikkhuninti etthāpi.

391. At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One... this is the Second Training Rule on Malicious Accusation. Therein, regarding the phrase 'Come, friends, let us name this goat Dabba Mallaputta': it is said that those bhikkhus, being unable to fulfill their own desire in the first case, having been rebuked and having become frustrated, wandered about searching for such an incident, thinking, 'Now we shall know!' Then one day, upon seeing it, they were pleased, and looking at one another, they spoke thus: 'Come, friends, let us name this goat Dabba Mallaputta.' This means, 'Let us give it the name Dabba Mallaputta.' This same method applies also in the case of the bhikkhunī named Mettiyā.

Te bhikkhū mettiyabhumajake bhikkhū anuyuñjiṃsūti evaṃ anuyuñjiṃsu –“āvuso, kuhiṃ tumhehi dabbo mallaputto mettiyāya bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ diṭṭho”ti? “Gijjhakūṭapabbatapāde”ti. “Kāya velāya”ti? “Bhikkhācāragamanavelāyā”ti. Āvuso dabba ime evaṃ vadanti – “tvaṃ tadā kuhi”nti? “Veḷuvane bhattāni uddisāmī”ti. “Tava tāya velāya veḷuvane atthibhāvaṃ ko jānātī”ti? “Bhikkhusaṅgho, bhante”ti. Te saṅghaṃ pucchiṃsu – “jānātha tumhe tāya velāya imassa veḷuvane atthibhāva”nti. “Āma, āvuso, jānāma, thero sammutiladdhadivasato [P 3.0599] paṭṭhāya veḷuvaneyevā”ti. Tato mettiyabhumajake āhaṃsu – “āvuso, tumhākaṃ kathā na sameti, kacci no lesaṃ oḍḍetvā vadathā”ti. Evaṃ te tehi bhikkhūhi anuyuñjiyamānā āma āvusoti vatvā etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ.

As for 'Those bhikkhus questioned the Mettiya and Bhūmajaka bhikkhus,' they questioned them thus: 'Friends, where did you see Dabba Mallaputta with the bhikkhunī Mettiyā?' 'At the foot of Gijjhakūṭa mountain.' 'At what time?' 'At the time of going for alms-food.' 'Friend Dabba, these bhikkhus say thus—where were you at that time?' 'I was distributing meals in Veḷuvana.' 'Who knows of your presence in Veḷuvana at that time?' 'The Saṅgha of bhikkhus, venerable sir.' They asked the Saṅgha: 'Do you know of his presence in Veḷuvana at that time?' 'Yes, friends, we know. The Elder has been in Veḷuvana itself since the day he received the authorization.' Then they said to the Mettiya and Bhūmajaka bhikkhus: 'Friends, your story does not cohere. Do you perhaps speak having set up some pretext?' Thus, being questioned by those bhikkhus, they said, 'Yes, friends,' and reported this matter.

Kiṃ [M 2.0184] pana tumhe, āvuso, āyasmantaṃ dabbaṃ mallaputtaṃ aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassāti ettha aññabhāgassa idaṃ, aññabhāgo vā assa atthīti aññabhāgiyaṃ. Adhikaraṇanti ādhāro veditabbo, vatthu adhiṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo hi so “dabbo mallaputto nāmā”ti chagalako vutto, so yvāyaṃ āyasmato dabbassa mallaputtassa bhāgo koṭṭhāso pakkho manussajāti ceva bhikkhubhāvo ca tato aññassa bhāgassa koṭṭhāsassa pakkhassa hoti tiracchānajātiyā [V 2.0166] ceva chagalakabhāvassa ca so vā aññabhāgo assa atthīti tasmā aññabhāgiyasaṅkhyaṃ labhati. Yasmā ca tesaṃ “imaṃ mayaṃ dabbaṃ mallaputtaṃ nāma karomā”ti vadantānaṃ tassā nāmakaraṇasaññāya ādhāro vatthu adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā adhikaraṇanti veditabbo. Tañhi sandhāya “te bhikkhū aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassā”ti āhaṃsu, na vivādādhikaraṇādīsu aññataraṃ. Kasmā? Asambhavato. Na hi te catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ kassaci aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa kañcidesaṃ lesamattaṃ upādiyiṃsu. Na ca catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ leso nāma atthi. Jātilesādayo hi puggalānaṃyeva lesā vuttā, na vivādādhikaraṇādīnaṃ. Idañca “dabbo mallaputto”ti nāmaṃ tassa aññabhāgiyādhikaraṇabhāve ṭhitassa chagalakassa koci deso hoti theraṃ amūlakena pārājikena anuddhaṃsetuṃ lesamatto.

Herein, `aññabhāgiya` means 'this belongs to another part,' or 'it has another part.' `Adhikaraṇa` should be understood as a basis; it is said to mean a ground, a foundation. For that goat which was called 'Dabba Mallaputta' belongs to a different part, portion, and faction—namely that of animal birth and the state of a goat—from that part, portion, and faction of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, which is human birth and the state of a bhikkhu. Or, because it has that other part, it therefore obtains the designation `aññabhāgiya`. And because for those who say, 'Let us name this Dabba Mallaputta,' it is the basis, ground, and foundation for that perception of naming, it should therefore be understood as an `adhikaraṇa`. It is with reference to this that those bhikkhus said, 'of an `adhikaraṇa` that is `aññabhāgiya`,' and not with reference to one of the legal issues such as disputes. Why? Because of its impossibility. For they did not take up even a mere hint or a certain part of any `adhikaraṇa` that is `aññabhāgiya` among the four legal issues. And there is no such thing as a `lesa` (hint, trace) of the four legal issues. For traces such as birth-traces are spoken of only for persons, not for legal issues such as disputes. And this name 'Dabba Mallaputta,' for that goat standing in the state of an `aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa`, becomes a certain part, a mere hint, for accusing the Elder of a groundless Pārājika offense.

Ettha ca dissati apadissati assa ayanti voharīyatīti deso. Jātiādīsu aññatarakoṭṭhāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aññampi vatthuṃ lissati silissati vohāramatteneva īsakaṃ allīyatīti leso. Jātiādīnaṃyeva aññatarakoṭṭhāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tato paraṃ uttānatthameva. Sikkhāpadapaññattiyampi ayamevattho. Padabhājane pana yassa aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa kiñcidesaṃ lesamattaṃ upādāya pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃseyya[P 3.0600], taṃ yasmā aṭṭhuppattivaseneva āvibhūtaṃ, tasmā na vibhattanti veditabbaṃ.

And herein, a `desa` (part) is that which is seen, is pointed out, or is spoken of as 'this is of that.' This is a designation for a certain portion among birth and so on. A `lesa` (trace, hint) is that which clings or adheres to another matter; it sticks slightly merely by convention. This is also a designation for a certain portion among birth and so on. After that, the meaning is plain. In the promulgation of the training rule also, this is the very meaning. But in the word-analysis, regarding the phrase 'whosoever, taking up some part, a mere hint, of an `adhikaraṇa` that is `aññabhāgiya`, should accuse with a Pārājika rule,' that `aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa` should be understood as not being analyzed in detail because it became manifest simply through the arising of the origin story.

393. Yāni pana adhikaraṇanti vacanasāmaññato atthuddhāravasena pavattāni cattāri adhikaraṇāni, tesaṃ aññabhāgiyatā ca tabbhāgiyatā ca yasmā apākaṭā jānitabbā ca vinayadharehi, tasmā vacanasāmaññato laddhaṃ [M 2.0185] adhikaraṇaṃ nissāya taṃ āvikaronto “aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassāti āpattaññabhāgiyaṃ vā hoti adhikaraṇaññabhāgiyaṃ vā”tiādimāha. Yā ca sā avasāne āpattaññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa vasena codanā vuttā, tampi dassetuṃ ayaṃ sabbādhikaraṇānaṃ tabbhāgiyaaññabhāgiyatā samāhaṭāti veditabbā.

393. Now, as for the four legal issues (`adhikaraṇa`) that proceed by way of extracting the meaning from the general term `adhikaraṇa`: because their nature of being `aññabhāgiya` (of another part) and `tabbhāgiya` (of the same part) is not manifest and should be known by experts in the Vinaya, therefore, based on the legal issues obtained from the general term, and in order to make this nature manifest, the text begins, 'As for an `adhikaraṇa` that is `aññabhāgiya`, it can be one that is `āpattaññabhāgiya` (an offense of another part) or one that is `adhikaraṇaññabhāgiya` (a legal issue of another part)...' Furthermore, it should be understood that in order to also show the accusation spoken of at the end by way of an `adhikaraṇa` that is `āpattaññabhāgiya`, this `tabbhāgiya` and `aññabhāgiya` nature of all legal issues has been brought together here.

Tattha ca āpattaññabhāgiyaṃ vāti paṭhamaṃ uddiṭṭhattā “kathañca āpatti āpattiyā aññabhāgiyā hotī”ti niddese ārabhitabbe yasmā āpattādhikaraṇassa tabbhāgiyavicāraṇāyaṃyeva ayamattho āgamissati, tasmā evaṃ anārabhitvā “kathañca adhikaraṇaṃ adhikaraṇassa aññabhāgiya”nti pacchimapadaṃyeva gahetvā niddeso āraddhoti veditabbo.

And therein, because 'or `āpattaññabhāgiya`' was indicated first, the detailed explanation ought to have begun with, 'And how is an offense `aññabhāgiya` in relation to an offense?' However, because this meaning will come up in the investigation of the `tabbhāgiya` nature of an offense-issue itself, it should be understood that the explanation was not started in that way. Instead, having taken up only the latter phrase, 'And how is a legal issue `aññabhāgiya` in relation to a legal issue?', the detailed explanation was begun.

Tattha [V 2.0167] aññabhāgiyavāro uttānatthoyeva. Ekamekañhi adhikaraṇaṃ itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ aññabhāgiyaṃ aññapakkhiyaṃ aññakoṭṭhāsiyaṃ hoti, vatthuvisabhāgattā, tabbhāgiyavāre pana vivādādhikaraṇaṃ vivādādhikaraṇassa tabbhāgiyaṃ tappakkhiyaṃ taṃkoṭṭhāsiyaṃ vatthusabhāgattā, tathā anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇassa. Kathaṃ? Buddhakālato paṭṭhāya hi aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni nissāya uppannavivādo ca idāni uppajjanakavivādo ca vatthusabhāgatāya ekaṃ vivādādhikaraṇameva hoti, tathā buddhakālato paṭṭhāya catasso vipattiyo nissāya uppannaanuvādo ca idāni uppajjanakaanuvādo ca vatthusabhāgatāya ekaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇameva hoti. Yasmā pana āpattādhikaraṇaṃ āpattādhikaraṇassa sabhāgavisabhāgavatthuto sabhāgasarikkhāsarikkhato ca ekaṃsena tabbhāgiyaṃ na hoti, tasmā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ āpattādhikaraṇassa siyā tabbhāgiyaṃ siyā aññabhāgiyanti vuttaṃ. Tattha ādito paṭṭhāya aññabhāgiyassa paṭhamaṃ niddiṭṭhattā idhāpi aññabhāgiyameva paṭhamaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ, tattha aññabhāgiyattañca parato tabbhāgiyattañca vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Herein, the section on matters of a different portion is of clear meaning. For each single legal question is of a different portion, of a different side, of a different group from the other three, due to the dissimilarity of the subject matter. In the section on matters of the same portion, however, a legal question concerning disputes is of the same portion, of the same side, of the same group as another legal question concerning disputes, due to the similarity of the subject matter; similarly, a legal question concerning accusations is of the same portion as another legal question concerning accusations. How so? For a dispute that arose based on the eighteen grounds for schism from the time of the Buddha onwards and a dispute that arises now are a single legal question concerning disputes due to the similarity of the subject matter. Similarly, an accusation that arose based on the four failures from the time of the Buddha onwards and an accusation that arises now are a single legal question concerning accusations due to the similarity of the subject matter. But since a legal question concerning offenses is not in every case of the same portion as another legal question concerning offenses—due to the similarity or dissimilarity of the subject matter and the likeness or unlikeness of the nature—it is said that a legal question concerning offenses may be of the same portion or it may be of a different portion from another legal question concerning offenses. Therein, since that which is of a different portion was explained first from the beginning, here too that which is of a different portion is explained first. Therein, the state of being of a different portion and, subsequently, the state of being of the same portion should be understood in the manner already stated.

Kiccādhikaraṇaṃ [P 3.0601] kiccādhikaraṇassa tabbhāgiyanti ettha pana buddhakālato paṭṭhāya cattāri saṅghakammāni nissāya uppannaṃ adhikaraṇañca idāni cattāri saṅghakammāni nissāya uppajjanakaṃ adhikaraṇañca sabhāgatāya sarikkhatāya ca ekaṃ kiccādhikaraṇameva hoti. Kiṃ pana saṅghakammāni nissāya uppannaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ [M 2.0186] kiccādhikaraṇaṃ, udāhu saṅghakammānamevetaṃ adhivacananti? Saṅghakammānamevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Evaṃ santepi saṅghakammaṃ nāma “idañcidañca evaṃ kattabba”nti yaṃ kammalakkhaṇaṃ manasikaroti taṃ nissāya uppajjanato purimaṃ purimaṃ saṅghakammaṃ nissāya uppajjanato ca saṅghakammāni nissāya uppannaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ kiccādhikaraṇanti vuttaṃ.

As for the statement, 'A legal question concerning duties is of the same portion as another legal question concerning duties': Here, a legal question that arose based on the four Saṅgha acts from the time of the Buddha onwards, and a legal question that now arises based on the four Saṅgha acts, are considered a single legal question concerning duties due to the similarity of their subject matter and the similarity of their nature. But is a legal question that has arisen based on Saṅgha acts a 'legal question concerning duties,' or is this merely a designation for the Saṅgha acts themselves? This is merely a designation for the Saṅgha acts themselves. Even so, because it arises based on that characteristic of an act which one bears in mind as 'this and that should be done thus,' and because it arises based on each preceding Saṅgha act, a legal question that has arisen based on Saṅgha acts is called a 'legal question concerning duties.'

394. Kiñci desaṃ lesamattaṃ upādāyāti ettha pana yasmā desoti vā lesamattoti vā pubbe vuttanayeneva byañjanato nānaṃ atthato ekaṃ, tasmā “leso nāma dasa lesā jātileso nāmaleso”tiādimāha. Tattha jātiyeva jātileso. Esa nayo sesesu.

394. As for the phrase 'taking some part or a mere trace': Here, since 'part' or 'mere trace', according to the method previously stated, are different in letter but one in meaning, therefore it is said: 'A trace means ten traces: the trace of birth, the trace of name,' and so on. Therein, birth itself is the trace of birth. This is the method in the remaining cases.

395. Idāni tameva lesaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ yathā taṃ upādāya anuddhaṃsanā hoti tathā savatthukaṃ katvā dassento “jātileso nāma khattiyo diṭṭho hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha khattiyo diṭṭho hotīti añño koci khattiyajātiyo iminā codakena diṭṭho hoti. Pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjantoti methunadhammādīsu aññataraṃ āpajjanto. Aññaṃ khattiyaṃ passitvā [V 2.0168] codetīti atha so aññaṃ attano veriṃ khattiyajātiyaṃ bhikkhuṃ passitvā taṃ khattiyajātilesaṃ gahetvā evaṃ codeti “khattiyo mayā diṭṭho pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto, tvaṃ khattiyo, pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosī” atha vā “tvaṃ so khattiyo, na añño, pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosi, assamaṇosi asakyaputtiyosi natthi tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā saṅghakammaṃ vā”ti, āpatti vācāya vācāya saṅghādisesassa. Ettha ca tesaṃ khattiyānaṃ aññamaññaṃ asadisassa tassa tassa dīghādino vā diṭṭhādino vā vasena aññabhāgiyatā khattiyajātipaññattiyā ādhāravasena adhikaraṇatā ca veditabbā, etenupāyena sabbapadesu yojanā veditabbā.

395. Now, to explain that very trace in detail, showing it with its basis in such a way that, by taking it up, an accusation occurs, the text says: 'The trace of birth is: a Khattiya is seen...' and so on. Here, 'a Khattiya is seen' means some other person of Khattiya birth was seen by this accuser. 'Committing an offense entailing expulsion' means committing one of the offenses such as sexual intercourse. 'Having seen another Khattiya, he accuses' means that then, having seen another monk of Khattiya birth who is his enemy, he takes that trace of Khattiya birth and accuses him thus: 'A Khattiya was seen by me committing an offense entailing expulsion; you are a Khattiya, you have committed an offense entailing expulsion.' Or else: 'You are that Khattiya, not another; you have committed an offense entailing expulsion; you are not a recluse, not a son of the Sakyans; there is no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or Saṅgha act with you.' There is a Saṅghādisesa offense for every word. And here, the state of being of a different portion should be understood by way of the dissimilarity between those Khattiyas in terms of their respective length, appearance, and so on; and the state of being a legal question should be understood by way of its basis in the designation of Khattiya birth. By this method, the application should be understood in all instances.

400. Pattalesaniddese ca [P 3.0602] sāṭakapattoti lohapattasadiso susaṇṭhāno succhavi siniddho bhamaravaṇṇo mattikāpatto vuccati. Sumbhakapattoti pakatimattikāpatto.

400. And in the explanation of the trace of a bowl, a 'sāṭaka bowl' refers to a clay bowl that resembles a metal bowl, being well-formed, of fine surface, smooth, and the color of a bee. A 'sumbhaka bowl' means an ordinary clay bowl.

406. Yasmā [M 2.0187] pana āpattilesassa ekapadeneva saṅkhepato niddeso vutto, tasmā vitthāratopi taṃ dassetuṃ “bhikkhu saṅghādisesaṃ ajjhāpajjanto diṭṭho hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kasmā panassa tattheva niddesaṃ avatvā idha visuṃ vuttoti? Sesaniddesehi asabhāgattā. Sesaniddesā hi aññaṃ disvā aññassa codanāvasena vuttā. Ayaṃ pana ekameva aññaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjantaṃ disvā aññāya āpattiyā codanāvasena vutto. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ aññabhāgiyaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ hotīti? Āpattiyā. Teneva vuttaṃ – “evampi āpattaññabhāgiyañca hoti leso ca upādinno”ti. Yañhi so saṅghādisesaṃ āpanno taṃ pārājikassa aññabhāgiyaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ. Tassa pana aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa leso nāma yo so sabbakhattiyānaṃ sādhāraṇo khattiyabhāvo viya sabbāpattīnaṃ sādhāraṇo āpattibhāvo. Etenupāyena sesāpattimūlakanayo codāpakavāro ca veditabbo.

406. But since the explanation of the trace of an offense was stated briefly with a single phrase, to show it in detail, it is said: 'A bhikkhu is seen committing a Saṅghādisesa offense...' and so on. Why, then, was its explanation not given there, but stated separately here? Because of its dissimilarity to the other explanations. Indeed, the other explanations are stated by way of accusing one person after seeing another. This one, however, is stated by way of accusing a single person of a different offense after seeing him committing one offense. If so, how does it become a legal question of a different portion? By way of the offense. Therefore it was said: 'Even in this way, the offense is of a different portion, and a trace has been taken up.' For the Saṅghādisesa offense that he committed is a legal question of a different portion relative to a Pārājika offense. The trace of that legal question of a different portion is the nature of an offense that is common to all offenses, just as the nature of being a Khattiya is common to all Khattiyas. By this method, the procedure based on other offenses and the section on the accuser should be understood.

408. Anāpatti tathāsaññī codeti vā codāpeti vāti “pārājikaṃyeva ayaṃ āpanno”ti yo evaṃ tathāsaññī codeti vā codāpeti vā tassa anāpatti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Samuṭṭhānādīnipi paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasadisānevāti.

408. As for 'There is no offense if one, having such a perception, accuses or causes another to accuse': If one, having such a perception, accuses or causes another to accuse, thinking, 'This person has indeed committed a Pārājika offense,' there is no offense for that person. The rest is clear everywhere. The origins and so on are also similar to the first offense of malice.

Dutiyaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule concerning corrupt intention is concluded.

10. Paṭhamasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Causing Division in the Saṅgha

409. Tena [V 2.0169] samayena buddho bhagavāti saṅghabhedasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha atha kho devadattotiādīsu yo ca devadatto, yathā ca pabbajito, yena ca kāraṇena kokālikādayo upasaṅkamitvā “etha mayaṃ āvuso samaṇassa gotamassa saṅghabhedaṃ karissāma cakkabheda”nti āha. Taṃ sabbaṃ saṅghabhedakkhandhake (cūḷava. 343) āgatameva. Pañcavatthuyācanā pana kiñcāpi tattheva āgamissati. Atha kho idhāpi āgatattā yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ vatvāva gamissāma.

409. The training rule on causing division in the Saṅgha begins with the words, 'At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One...' In that, regarding the passage beginning 'Then, Devadatta...' and so on: who Devadatta was, how he went forth, and for what reason he approached Kokālika and others and said, 'Come, friends, let us cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama and a division of the wheel'—all of that has already appeared in the chapter on causing division in the Saṅgha. However, although the request of the five points will also appear there, since it has also appeared here, we will say what should be said about it here and then proceed.

Sādhu bhanteti āyācanā. Bhikkhū yāvajīvaṃ āraññikā assūti āraññikadhutaṅgaṃ samādāya sabbepi bhikkhū yāva jīvanti tāva āraññikā hontu[M 2.0188], araññeyeva vasantu. Yo gāmantaṃ osareyya vajjaṃ naṃ phuseyyāti [P 3.0603] yo ekabhikkhupi araññaṃ pahāya nivāsatthāya gāmantaṃ osareyya, vajjaṃ taṃ phuseyya naṃ bhikkhuṃ doso phusatu, āpattiyā naṃ bhagavā kāretū”ti adhippāyena vadati. Esa nayo sesavatthūsupi.

The words 'Excellent, venerable sir' are the request. As for 'May the monks be forest-dwellers for life': having undertaken the forest-dweller's ascetic practice, may all monks, for as long as they live, be forest-dwellers; may they dwell only in the forest. As for 'Should anyone go down to a village vicinity, may blame touch them': if even a single monk, having abandoned the forest, should go down to a village vicinity for the sake of residence, may blame touch him. This means: may fault touch that monk; may the Blessed One make him deal with an offense. He speaks with this intention. This is the method for the remaining points as well.

410. Janaṃ saññāpessāmāti janaṃ amhākaṃ appicchatādibhāvaṃ jānāpessāma, atha vā paritosessāma pasādessāmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

410. As for 'We will make the people know': this means, 'We will make the people know our state of having few desires and so on,' or alternatively, 'We will gratify them, we will inspire faith in them.' Thus it is said.

Imāni pana pañca vatthūni yācato devadattassa vacanaṃ sutvāva aññāsi bhagavā “saṅghabhedatthiko hutvā ayaṃ yācatī”ti. Yasmā pana tāni anujāniyamānāni bahūnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ maggantarāyāya saṃvattanti, tasmā bhagavā “alaṃ devadattā”ti paṭikkhipitvā “yo icchati āraññiko hotū”tiādimāha.

Furthermore, upon the very hearing of the words of Devadatta requesting these five points, the Blessed One knew: 'This one requests this, being desirous of causing division in the Saṅgha.' And because those points, if they were to be allowed, would lead to an obstruction of the path for many sons of good family, the Blessed One therefore rejected them, saying, 'Enough, Devadatta,' and then said, 'Whoever wishes, let him be a forest-dweller,' and so on.

Ettha pana bhagavato adhippāyaṃ viditvā kulaputtena attano patirūpaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayañhettha bhagavato adhippāyo – “eko bhikkhu mahajjhāsayo hoti mahussāho, sakkoti gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā araññe viharanto dukkhassantaṃ kātuṃ. Eko dubbalo hoti appathāmo araññe na sakkoti, gāmanteyeva sakkoti. Eko mahabbalo samappavattadhātuko adhivāsanakhantisampanno iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu samacitto araññepi gāmantepi sakkotiyeva. Eko neva gāmante na araññe sakkoti padaparamo hoti.

Here, however, having understood the Blessed One's intention, a son of good family should know what is suitable for himself. For this is the Blessed One's intention here: 'One monk is of great aspiration and great energy; having rejected a lodging in a village vicinity, he is able, dwelling in the forest, to make an end of suffering. Another is weak and of little strength; he is not able in the forest, but is able only in a village vicinity. Another is of great strength, with his bodily elements in equilibrium, endowed with enduring patience, and of even mind towards the agreeable and disagreeable; he is able indeed both in the forest and in a village vicinity. Another is able neither in a village vicinity nor in the forest; he has the text as his highest resort.'

Tatra [V 2.0170] yvāyaṃ mahajjhāsayo hoti mahussāho, sakkoti gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā araññe viharanto dukkhassantaṃ kātuṃ, so araññeyeva vasatu, idamassa patirūpaṃ. Saddhivihārikādayopi cassa anusikkhamānā araññe vihātabbameva maññissanti.

Among these, the one who is of great aspiration and great energy, who is able, having rejected a lodging in a village vicinity, to make an end of suffering while dwelling in the forest—let him dwell only in the forest. This is suitable for him. And his pupils and others, training in imitation of him, will think that one should only dwell in the forest.

Yo pana dubbalo hoti appathāmo gāmanteyeva sakkoti dukkhassantaṃ kātuṃ, na araññe so gāmanteyeva vasatu, yvāyaṃ mahabbalo samappavattadhātuko adhivāsanakhantisampanno iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu samacitto araññepi gāmantepi sakkotiyeva, ayampi gāmantasenāsanaṃ pahāya [M 2.0189] araññe viharatu, idamassa patirūpaṃ saddhivihārikāpi hissa anusikkhamānā araññe vihātabbaṃ maññissanti.

But as for the one who is weak and of little strength, who is able to make an end of suffering only in a village vicinity and not in the forest—let him dwell only in the village vicinity. And as for the one who is of great strength, with his bodily elements in equilibrium, endowed with enduring patience, and of even mind towards the agreeable and disagreeable, who is able indeed both in the forest and in a village vicinity—let this one too, having abandoned a lodging in a village vicinity, dwell in the forest. This is suitable for him, and indeed his pupils, training in imitation of him, will think that one should dwell in the forest.

Yo panāyaṃ neva gāmante na araññe sakkoti padaparamo hoti. Ayampi araññeyeva [P 3.0604] vasatu. Ayaṃ hissa dhutaṅgasevanā kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca āyatiṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo bhavissati. Saddhivihārikādayo cassa anusikkhamānā araññe vihātabbaṃ maññissantīti.

But as for this one who is able neither in a village vicinity nor in the forest, who has the text as his highest resort—let this one too dwell only in the forest. For his practice of the ascetic observances and development of the meditation subject will in the future be a strong supporting condition for the paths and fruits. And his pupils and others, training in imitation of him, will think, 'One should dwell in the forest.'

Evaṃ yvāyaṃ dubbalo hoti appathāmo gāmanteyeva viharanto sakkoti dukkhassantaṃ kātuṃ na araññe, imaṃ puggalaṃ sandhāya bhagavā “yo icchati gāmante viharatū”ti āha. Iminā ca puggalena aññesampi dvāraṃ dinnaṃ.

Thus, with reference to this person who is weak and of little strength, who is able to make an end of suffering while dwelling only in a village vicinity and not in the forest, the Blessed One said, 'Let him who wishes dwell in a village vicinity.' And through this person, an opening was given for others as well.

Yadi pana bhagavā devadattassa vādaṃ sampaṭiccheyya, yvāyaṃ puggalo pakatiyā dubbalo hoti appathāmo, yopi daharakāle araññavāsaṃ abhisambhuṇitvā jiṇṇakāle vā vātapittādīhi samuppannadhātukkhobhakāle vā nābhisambhuṇāti, gāmanteyeva pana viharanto sakkoti dukkhassantaṃ kātuṃ, tesaṃ ariyamaggupacchedo bhaveyya, arahattaphalādhigamo na bhaveyya, uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ vilomaṃ aniyyānikaṃ satthu sāsanaṃ bhaveyya, satthā ca tesaṃ asabbaññū assa “sakavādaṃ chaḍḍetvā devadattavāde patiṭṭhito”ti gārayho ca bhaveyya. Tasmā bhagavā evarūpe puggale saṅgaṇhanto devadattassa vādaṃ paṭikkhipi. Etenevūpāyena piṇḍapātikavatthusmimpi paṃsukūlikavatthusmimpi aṭṭha māse rukkhamūlikavatthusmimpi vinicchayo veditabbo. Cattāro pana māse rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhittameva.

Furthermore, if the Blessed One were to accept Devadatta's doctrine, then for that person who is by nature weak and of little strength, and also for the one who, having been able to live in the forest in his youth, is not able to do so in old age or at a time of disturbance of the elements arising from wind, bile, and so on—but who is able to make an end of suffering while dwelling only in a village vicinity—for them there would be a cutting off of the noble path. The attainment of the fruit of arahantship would not occur. The Teacher's dispensation would become one without Dhamma, without Vinaya, contrary, and not leading to release. And the Teacher would be not all-knowing to them and would be blameworthy, accused of having 'abandoned his own doctrine and established himself in Devadatta's doctrine.' Therefore the Blessed One, accommodating such persons, rejected Devadatta's doctrine. By this same method, the decision should be understood in the matter of the alms-food practice, in the matter of the rag-robe practice, and in the matter of the tree-root-dweller practice for eight months. A tree-root lodging for four months, however, is indeed rejected.

Macchamaṃsavatthusmiṃ tikoṭiparisuddhanti tīhi koṭīhi parisuddhaṃ, diṭṭhādīhi aparisuddhīhi virahitanti attho. Tenevāha – “adiṭṭhaṃ, asutaṃ, aparisaṅkita”nti. Tattha “adiṭṭhaṃ” nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gayhamānaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ. “Asutaṃ” nāma bhikkhūnaṃ [V 2.0171] atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gahitanti asutaṃ. “Aparisaṅkitaṃ” pana diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitañca ñatvā tabbipakkhato jānitabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhū passanti manusse jālavāgurādihatthe [M 2.0190] gāmato va nikkhamante araññe vā vicarante, dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya [P 3.0605] paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena diṭṭhena parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nukho atthāya kata”nti idaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ, nāma etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā bhante na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ bhante bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kata”nti vadanti kappati.

In the matter of fish and meat, “purified in three respects” means purified by three aspects, that is, free from the impurities of being seen, and so on; this is the meaning. For that very reason, it is said: “unseen, unheard, unsuspected.” Therein, “unseen” means not having seen game and fish being taken after being killed for the sake of monks. “Unheard” means not having heard, “It has been taken after being killed for the sake of monks.” “Unsuspected,” however, should be understood by knowing suspicion based on sight, suspicion based on hearing, and suspicion free from both of those two, and then by way of their opposite. How so? Here, monks see people with nets, snares, and so on in hand, either leaving the village or wandering in the forest. And on the next day, when those monks have entered that village for alms, people bring them almsfood containing fish and meat. They, on account of what was seen, suspect, “Could it be that this was prepared for the sake of the monks?” This is called “suspicion based on sight”; it is not proper to accept this. That which is not suspected in this way is proper. But if those people, having been asked, “Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?” and having heard the reason, say, “Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the monks; it was prepared by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on,” then it is allowable.

Naheva kho bhikkhū passanti; apica suṇanti, manussā kira jālavāgurādihatthā gāmato vā nikkhamanti, araññe vā vicarantī”ti. Dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ “bhikkhūnaṃ nukho atthāya kata”nti idaṃ “sutaparisaṅkitaṃ” nāma. Etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati, yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kata”nti vadanti kappati.

Monks indeed do not see; however, they hear, “It is said that people with nets, snares, and so on in hand are leaving the village, or are wandering in the forest.” And on the next day, for those monks who have entered that village for alms, the suspicion, “Could it be that this was prepared for the sake of the monks?” is called “suspicion based on hearing.” It is not proper to accept this. That which is not suspected in this way is proper. But if those people, having been asked, “Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?” and having heard the reason, say, “Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the monks; it was prepared by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on,” then it is allowable.

Naheva kho pana bhikkhū passanti, na suṇanti; apica kho tesaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ pattaṃ gahetvā samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā abhiharanti, te parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nukho atthāya kata”nti idaṃ “tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ” nāma. Etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kataṃ pavattamaṃsaṃ vā kappiyameva labhitvā bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya sampādita”nti vadanti kappati. Matānaṃ petakiccatthāya maṅgalādīnaṃ vā atthāya katepi eseva nayo. Yaṃ yañhi bhikkhūnaṃyeva atthāya akataṃ, yattha ca nibbematiko hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ kappati.

Furthermore, monks indeed do not see, nor do they hear; but indeed, when they have entered a village for alms, people take their bowls, prepare almsfood with fish and meat, and bring it to them. They suspect, “Could it be that this was prepared for the sake of the monks?” This is called “suspicion free from both of those two.” It is not proper to accept this. That which is not suspected in this way is proper. But if those people, having been asked, “Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?” and having heard the reason, say, “Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the monks; it was prepared by us for our own sake, or for the sake of royal officials and so on, or it was already existing, allowable meat that was obtained and prepared for the sake of the monks,” then it is allowable. In the case of meat prepared for the sake of funeral rites for the dead or for the sake of auspicious ceremonies and so on, this is the same method. Indeed, whatever meat is not prepared solely for the sake of monks, and about which one is without doubt, all that is allowable.

Sace pana ekasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū uddissa kataṃ hoti, te ca attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ na jānanti, aññe jānanti. Ye jānanti, tesaṃ na vaṭṭati[P 3.0606], itaresaṃ vaṭṭati. Aññe na jānanti, teyeva jānanti, tesaṃyeva na vaṭṭati, aññesaṃ vaṭṭati. Tepi amhākaṃ atthāya katanti jānanti, aññepi etesaṃ atthāya [V 2.0172] katanti jānanti, sabbesampi na vaṭṭati, sabbe [M 2.0191] na jānanti, sabbesampi vaṭṭati. Pañcasu hi sahadhammikesu yassa vā tassa vā atthāya uddissa kataṃ, sabbesaṃ na kappati.

But if in a certain monastery something is prepared having designated the monks, and they do not know the fact that it was prepared for their own sake, but others know, it is not proper for those who know; it is proper for the others. If others do not know, and only they themselves know, it is not proper for them alone; it is proper for others. If they themselves know, “It was prepared for our sake,” and others also know, “It was prepared for their sake,” it is not proper for any of them. If none of them know, it is proper for all of them. For, among the five kinds of co-religionists, if it is prepared having designated it for the sake of one or another, it is not allowable for any of them.

Sace pana koci ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ vadhitvā tassa pattaṃ pūretvā deti, so ca attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ jānaṃyeva gahetvā aññassa bhikkhuno deti, so tassa saddhāya paribhuñjati, kassa āpattīti? Dvinnampi anāpatti. Yañhi uddissa kataṃ tassa abhuttatāya anāpatti, itarassa ajānanatāya. Kappiyamaṃsassa hi paṭiggahaṇe āpatti natthi. Uddissa katañca ajānitvā bhuttassa pacchā ñatvā āpattidesanākiccaṃ nāma natthi, akappiyamaṃsaṃ pana ajānitvā bhuttena pacchā ñatvāpi āpatti desetabbā, uddissa katañhi ñatvā bhuñjatova āpatti. Akappiyamaṃsaṃ ajānitvā bhuñjantassāpi āpattiyeva. Tasmā āpattibhīrukena rūpaṃ sallakkhentenapi pucchitvāva maṃsaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Paribhogakāle pucchitvā paribhuñjissāmīti vā gahetvā pucchitvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Duviññeyyattā. Acchamaṃsaṃ hi sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ hoti, dīpimaṃsādīnipi migamaṃsādisadisāni, tasmā pucchitvā gahaṇameva vattanti vadanti.

But if someone, having killed a living being for a certain monk, fills his bowl and gives it, and that monk, knowing full well that it was prepared for his sake, takes it and gives it to another monk, and that other monk consumes it out of faith in him, whose offense is it? For both, there is no offense. For the one for whom it was designated, there is no offense because of not having eaten it; for the other, there is no offense because of not knowing. Indeed, for accepting allowable meat, there is no offense. For one who has eaten meat that was designated for him without knowing, there is no duty of confessing an offense after finding out later. But for one who has eaten unallowable meat without knowing, the offense must be confessed even after finding out later. Indeed, an offense is incurred only by one who eats designated meat knowing it to be so. For one who eats unallowable meat even without knowing, there is still an offense. Therefore, by a monk who is fearful of offenses, even while observing its appearance, meat should be accepted only after asking. Or, having accepted it thinking, “I will ask at the time of consumption and then consume it,” it should be consumed only after asking. Why? Because it is difficult to discern. Indeed, bear meat resembles pork, and the meat of leopards and so on resembles the meat of deer and so on. Therefore, they say that the proper conduct is only to accept it after asking.

Haṭṭho udaggoti tuṭṭho ceva unnatakāyacitto ca hutvā. So kira “na bhagavā imāni pañca vatthūni anujānāti, idāni sakkhissāmi saṅghabhedaṃ kātu”nti kokālikassa iṅgitākāraṃ dassetvā yathā visaṃ vā khāditvā rajjuyā vā ubbandhitvā satthaṃ vā āharitvā maritukāmo puriso visādīsu aññataraṃ labhitvā tappaccayā āsannampi maraṇadukkhaṃ ajānanto haṭṭho udaggo hoti; evameva saṅghabhedapaccayā āsannampi avīcimhi nibbattitvā paṭisaṃvedanīyaṃ dukkhaṃ ajānanto “laddho dāni me saṅghabhedassa upāyo”ti haṭṭho udaggo sapariso uṭṭhāyāsanā teneva haṭṭhabhāvena bhagavantaṃ [P 3.0607] abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

Haṭṭho udaggo (delighted and elated) means being both pleased and uplifted in body and mind. He, it is said, thinking, “The Blessed One does not permit these five points; now I will be able to cause a schism in the Saṅgha,” showed a sign of his intention to Kokālika. Just as a man who wishes to die—having swallowed poison, or hanged himself with a rope, or taken up a weapon—obtains one of these means and, because of that, is delighted and elated, not knowing the imminent suffering of death; in the very same way, not knowing the imminent suffering to be experienced after being reborn in Avīci due to the schism of the Saṅgha, he thought, “Now the means for schism in the Saṅgha has been found by me!” Delighted and elated, he rose from his seat with his retinue and, with that very same delight, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed.

Te mayaṃ imehi pañcahi vatthūhi samādāya vattāmāti ettha pana “imāni pañca vatthūnī”ti vattabbepi te mayaṃ imehi pañcahi vatthūhi janaṃ saññāpessāmāti abhiṇhaṃ parivitakkavasena vibhattivipallāsaṃ asallakkhetvā abhiṇhaṃ parivitakkānurūpameva “te mayaṃ imehi pañcahi vatthūhī”ti āha, yathā taṃ vikkhittacitto.

Now, in the phrase 'We will live undertaking these five points,' although it should have been said, 'these five points' (imāni pañca vatthūni), due to the power of his constant reflection, 'We will make the people understand by means of these five points,' he did not notice the confusion of case endings. In accordance with that constant reflection, he said, 'by these five points' (imehi pañcahi vatthūhi), just as one with a distracted mind would.

Dhutā [M 2.0192][V 2.0173] sallekhavuttinoti yā paṭipadā kilese dhunāti, tāya samannāgatattā dhutā. Yā ca kilese sallikhati, sā etesaṃ vuttīti sallekhavuttino.

Dhutā sallekhavuttino (those who are austere, whose practice is effacement) means: because they possess the practice that shakes off defilements, they are dhutā (austere). And because their practice (vutti) is that which scrapes away defilements, they are sallekhavuttino (those whose practice is effacement).

Bāhulikoti cīvarādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ bahulabhāvo bāhullaṃ, taṃ bāhullamassa atthi, tasmiṃ vā bāhulle niyutto ṭhitoti bāhuliko. Bāhullāya cetetīti bāhulattāya ceteti kappeti pakappeti. Kathañhi nāma mayhañca sāvakānañca cīvarādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ bahulabhāvo bhaveyyāti evaṃ ussukkamāpannoti adhippāyo. Cakkabhedāyāti āṇābhedāya.

Bāhuliko (one given to abundance): Abundance (bāhullaṃ) is the state of having many requisites, such as robes. He is bāhuliko because he has that abundance, or because he is engaged in and established in that abundance. Bāhullāya ceteti (he strives for abundance) means he strives, arranges, and contrives for the sake of abundance. The intended meaning of those who use this term is that he has become zealous, thinking: “How indeed could there be an abundance of requisites, such as robes, for me and my disciples?” Cakkabhedāya (for the breaking of the wheel) means for the breaking of the sphere of authority.

Dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvāti khandhake vuttanayena “alaṃ, devadatta, mā te rucci saṅghabhedo. Garuko kho, devadatta, saṅghabhedo. Yo kho, devadatta, samaggaṃ saṅghaṃ bhindati, kappaṭṭhikaṃ kibbisaṃ pasavati, kappaṃ nirayamhi paccati, yo ca kho, devadatta, bhinnaṃ saṅghaṃ samaggaṃ karoti, brahmaṃ puññaṃ pasavati, kappaṃ saggamhi modatī”ti (cūḷava. 343) evamādikaṃ anekappakāraṃ devadattassa ca bhikkhūnañca tadanucchavikaṃ tadanulomikaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā.

Dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā (having given a Dhamma talk) means having given a Dhamma talk in various ways according to the method stated in the Khandhaka, such as: “Enough, Devadatta! Let schism in the Saṅgha not be your pleasure. Schism in the Saṅgha is a grave matter, Devadatta. Whoever, Devadatta, divides a united Saṅgha generates a heinous evil that lasts for an aeon and is boiled in hell for an aeon. But whoever, Devadatta, unites a divided Saṅgha generates sublime merit and rejoices in heaven for an aeon.” This talk was suitable and appropriate for Devadatta and the monks.

411. Samaggassāti sahitassa cittena ca sarīrena ca aviyuttassāti attho. Padabhājanepi hi ayameva attho dassito. Samānasaṃvāsakoti hi vadatā cittena aviyogo dassito hoti. Samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhitoti vadatā sarīrena. Kathaṃ? Samānasaṃvāsako hi laddhinānāsaṃvāsakena vā kammanānāsaṃvāsakena vā virahito samacittatāya cittena aviyutto hoti. Samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhito kāyasāmaggidānato sarīrena aviyutto.

411. Samaggassa (of the united) means of that which is together, not separated in mind and body. For in the Padabhājana (word analysis), this very meaning is shown. By saying samānasaṃvāsako (having a common communion), non-separation of mind is shown. By saying samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhito (established within a common boundary), non-separation of body is shown. How? One with a common communion, being free from a different communion based on view or a different communion based on formal acts, is not separated in mind due to having a common mind. One established within a common boundary is not separated in body because this provides bodily unity.

Bhedanasaṃvattanikaṃ vā adhikaraṇanti bhedanassa saṅghabhedassa atthāya saṃvattanikaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Imasmiñhi okāse [P 3.0608] “kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇa”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.168) viya kāraṇaṃ adhikaraṇanti adhippetaṃ. Tañca yasmā aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ hoti, tasmā padabhājane “aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūnī”ti vuttaṃ. Tāni pana “idhūpāli, bhikkhu adhammaṃ dhammoti dīpetī”tiādinā [M 2.0193] (cūḷava. 352) nayena khandhake āgatāni, tasmā tatreva nesaṃ atthaṃ vaṇṇayissāma. Yopi cāyaṃ imāni vatthūni nissāya aparehipi kammena, uddesena, vohārena, anusāvanāya, salākaggāhenāti pañcahi kāraṇehi saṅghabhedo hoti, tampi āgataṭṭhāneyeva pakāsayissāma. Saṅkhepato pana bhedanasaṃvattanikaṃ vā adhikaraṇaṃ samādāyāti ettha saṅghabhedassa atthāya saṃvattanikaṃ saṅghabhedanipphattisamatthaṃ kāraṇaṃ gahetvāti evamattho veditabbo. Paggayhāti paggahitaṃ abbhussitaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā. Tiṭṭheyyāti yathāsamādinnaṃ yathāpaggahitameva ca katvā accheyya[V 2.0174]. Yasmā pana evaṃ paggaṇhatā tiṭṭhatā ca taṃ dīpitañceva appaṭinissaṭṭhañca hoti, tasmā padabhājane “dīpeyyā”ti ca “nappaṭinissajjeyyā”ti ca vuttaṃ.

Bhedanasaṃvattanikaṃ vā adhikaraṇaṃ (or a matter conducive to schism): This refers to a cause (kāraṇaṃ) that is conducive to the schism of the Saṅgha. For in this context, the term adhikaraṇa is intended to mean ‘cause,’ as in phrases like “caused by desire…” Since this is of eighteen kinds, in the Padabhājana it is said, “the eighteen grounds for causing schism.” These are found in the Khandhaka, in the section beginning, “Here, Upāli, a monk explains non-Dhamma as Dhamma…” Therefore, we will explain their meaning in that very place. Furthermore, this schism of the Saṅgha also occurs based on these grounds through five other causes: by a formal act (kamma), by recitation (uddesa), by speech (vohāra), by proclamation (anusāvanā), and by the taking of voting sticks (salākaggāha). We will also clarify this where it appears. In brief, however, the meaning of “having undertaken a matter conducive to schism” should be understood as “having taken up a cause that is conducive to schism and capable of bringing it about.” Paggayha (having upheld) means having made it upheld, raised up, and manifest. Tiṭṭheyya (he would persist) means he would remain just as he has undertaken it and just as he has upheld it. And because one who thus upholds and persists has both declared (dīpita) and not relinquished (appaṭinissaṭṭha) that matter, in the Padabhājana it is said, “he would declare” and “he would not relinquish.”

Bhikkhūhi evamassa vacanīyoti aññehi lajjīhi bhikkhūhi evaṃ vattabbo bhaveyya. Padabhājane cassa ye passantīti ye sammukhā paggayha tiṭṭhantaṃ passanti. Ye suṇantīti yepi “asukasmiṃ nāma vihāre bhikkhū bhedanasaṃvattanikaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ samādāya paggayha tiṭṭhantī”ti suṇanti.

Bhikkhūhi evamassa vacanīyo (He should be spoken to thus by the monks) means he should be spoken to thus by other conscientious monks. In the Padabhājana (word analysis) for this, ye passanti (those who see) means those who see him in their presence upholding and persisting in that matter. Ye suṇanti (those who hear) means those who hear a report such as: “In such-and-such a monastery, monks are upholding and persisting in a matter conducive to schism.”

Sametāyasmā saṅghenāti āyasmā saṅghena saddhiṃ sametu samāgacchatu ekaladdhiko hotūti attho. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Samaggo hi saṅgho sammodamāno avivadamāno ekuddeso phāsu viharatīti.

Sametāyasmā saṅghena (May the venerable one be reconciled with the Saṅgha) means: may the venerable one be reconciled with the Saṅgha, come together with the Saṅgha, and become one in view. What is the reason? Because a united Saṅgha, rejoicing together, without disputes, and with a single recitation, dwells in comfort.

Tattha sammodamānoti aññamaññaṃ sampattiyā saṭṭhu modamāno. Avivadamānoti “ayaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo”ti evaṃ na vivadamāno. Eko uddeso assāti ekuddeso, ekato pavattapātimokkhuddeso, na visunti attho. Phāsu viharatīti sukhaṃ viharati.

Therein, sammodamāno (rejoicing together) means greatly rejoicing in one another’s accomplishments. Avivadamāno (without disputes) means not disputing thus: “This is Dhamma; this is not Dhamma.” Ekuddeso (with a single recitation) means it has one recitation (eko uddeso assa); that is, having a Pātimokkha recitation that occurs together, not separately. Phāsu viharati (dwells in comfort) means dwells happily.

Iccetaṃ kusalanti etaṃ paṭinissajjanaṃ kusalaṃ khemaṃ sotthibhāvo tassa bhikkhuno. No ce paṭinissajjati āpatti dukkaṭassāti tikkhattuṃ vuttassa appaṭinissajjato dukkaṭaṃ. Sutvā na vadanti āpatti dukkaṭassāti ye sutvā na vadanti, tesampi [P 3.0609] dukkaṭaṃ. Kīvadūre sutvā avadantānaṃ dukkaṭaṃ? Ekavihāre tāva vattabbaṃ natthi. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ “samantā addhayojane bhikkhūnaṃ bhāro. Dūtaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā pesetvā vadatopi āpattimokkho natthi. Sayameva gantvā ‘garuko kho, āvuso, saṅghabhedo[M 2.0194], mā saṅghabhedāya, parakkamī’ti nivāretabbo”ti. Pahontena pana dūrampi gantabbaṃ agilānānañhi dūrepi bhāroyeva.

'This is skillful' means this relinquishing is skillful, safe, and for the well-being of that bhikkhu. 'If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing' means for one who does not relinquish it after being told three times, there is an offense of wrong-doing. 'Those who hear but do not speak incur an offense of wrong-doing' means for those who hear but do not speak, there is also an offense of wrong-doing. How far away does hearing without speaking incur an offense of wrong-doing? Firstly, within a single monastery, there is nothing to be said. But in the commentary, it is said: 'The responsibility for bhikkhus extends up to half a yojana all around. Even for one who speaks by sending a messenger or a letter, there is no escape from the offense. One should go oneself and restrain him, saying, "Friend, schism in the Sangha is a grave matter; do not strive for schism in the Sangha."' But one who is capable should go even far, for indeed, for those who are not ill, the responsibility exists even at a distance.

Idāni “evañca so bhikkhu bhikkhūhi vuccamāno”tiādīsu atthamattameva dassetuṃ “so bhikkhu saṅghamajjhampi ākaḍḍhitvā vattabbo”tiādimāha. Tattha saṅghamajjhampi ākaḍḍhitvāti sace purimanayena vuccamāno na paṭinissajjati hatthesu ca pādesu ca gahetvāpi saṅghamajjhaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā punapi “mā āyasmā”tiādinā nayena tikkhattuṃ vattabbo.

Now, in the passage beginning 'And if that bhikkhu, being spoken to by the bhikkhus...,' to show the meaning only, the passage beginning 'That bhikkhu should be dragged even into the midst of the Sangha and spoken to...' was stated. Therein, 'dragged even into the midst of the Sangha' means that if, when spoken to in the previous manner, he does not relinquish, he should be seized by the hands and feet, dragged into the midst of the Sangha, and spoken to again three times in the manner beginning, 'Venerable sir, do not...'

Yāvatatiyaṃ samanubhāsitabboti yāva tatiyaṃ samanubhāsanaṃ tāva samanubhāsitabbo. Tīhi samanubhāsanakammavācāhi kammaṃ kātabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Padabhājane panassa atthameva gahetvā samanubhāsanavidhiṃ [V 2.0175] dassetuṃ “so bhikkhu samanubhāsitabbo. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, samanubhāsitabbo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'He should be admonished up to the third time' means he should be admonished up to the third admonishment. This means that the formal act should be done with three formal acts of admonishment. But in the analysis of terms, taking the meaning alone to show the procedure of admonishment, the passage beginning 'That bhikkhu should be admonished. And thus, bhikkhus, he should be admonished...' was stated.

414. Tattha ñattiyā dukkaṭaṃ dvīhi kammavācāhi thullaccayā paṭippassambhantīti yañca ñattipariyosāne dukkaṭaṃ āpanno, ye ca dvīhi kammavācāhi thullaccaye, tā tissopi āpattiyo “yassa nakkhamati so bhāseyyā”ti evaṃ yya-kārappattamattāya tatiyakammavācāya paṭippassambhanti saṅghādisesoyeva tiṭṭhati. Kiṃ pana āpannāpattiyo paṭippassambhanti anāpannāti? Mahāsumatthero tāva vadati “yo avasāne paṭinissajjissati, so tā āpattiyo na āpajjati, tasmā anāpannā paṭippassambhantī”ti. Mahāpadumatthero pana liṅgaparivattena asādhāraṇāpattiyo viya āpannā paṭippassambhanti, anāpannānaṃ kiṃ paṭippassaddhiyā”ti āha.

414. Herein, 'the offense of wrong-doing from the motion and the grave offenses from the two formal acts subside' means that both the offense of wrong-doing incurred at the conclusion of the motion, and the grave offenses incurred from the two formal acts—these three offenses subside with the third formal act, merely upon reaching the letter 'yya' in the phrase 'Whoever does not approve should speak.' Only the Saṅghādisesa offense remains. But do incurred offenses subside, or do un-incurred offenses subside? The Elder Mahāsumata first says: 'Whoever relinquishes at the end will not incur those offenses; therefore, un-incurred offenses subside.' But the Elder Mahāpaduma says: 'Like the uncommon offenses due to a change of gender, incurred offenses subside. Of what use is the subsiding of un-incurred offenses?'

415. Dhammakamme dhammakammasaññīti tañce samanubhāsanakammaṃ dhammakammaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ dhammakammasaññīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Idha saññā na rakkhati, kammassa dhammikattā [P 3.0610] eva appaṭinissajjanto āpajjati.

415. 'Perceiving a legal act as a legal act' means: if that act of admonishment is a legal act, he perceives it as a legal act. This is the method in all cases. Here, perception does not protect one; because the act itself is lawful, one who does not relinquish it incurs an offense.

416. Asamanubhāsantassāti asamanubhāsiyamānassa appaṭinissajjantassāpi saṅghādisesena anāpatti.

416. 'For one not being admonished' means: for one who is not being admonished, even if one does not relinquish it, there is no Saṅghādisesa offense.

Paṭinissajjantassāti [M 2.0195] ñattito pubbe vā ñattikkhaṇe vā ñattipariyosāne vā paṭhamāya vā anusāvanāya dutiyāya vā tatiyāya vā yāva yya-kāraṃ na sampāpuṇāti, tāva paṭinissajjantassa saṅghādisesena anāpatti.

'For one who relinquishes' means: for one who relinquishes—whether before the motion, at the moment of the motion, at the conclusion of the motion, or during the first, second, or third proclamation—so long as the letter 'yya' is not reached, there is no Saṅghādisesa offense.

Ādikammikassāti. Ettha pana “devadatto samaggassa saṅghassa bhedāya parakkami, tasmiṃ vatthusmi”nti parivāre (pari. 17) āgatattā devadatto ādikammiko. So ca kho saṅghabhedāya parakkamanasseva, na appaṭinissajjanassa. Na hi tassa taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ. Kathamidaṃ jānitabbanti ce? Suttato. Yathā hi “ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo yāvatatiyaṃ samanubhāsanāya na paṭinissajji, tasmiṃ vatthusmi”nti parivāre (pari. 121) āgatattā ariṭṭhassa kammaṃ katanti paññāyati, na tathā devadattassa. Athāpissa katena bhavitabbanti koci attano rucimattena vadeyya, tathāpi appaṭinissajjane ādikammikassa anāpatti nāma [V 2.0176] natthi. Na hi paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamantassa aññatra uddissa anuññātato anāpatti nāma dissati. Yampi ariṭṭhasikkhāpadassa anāpattiyaṃ “ādikammikassā”ti potthakesu likhitaṃ, taṃ pamādalikhitaṃ. Pamādalikhitabhāvo cassa “paṭhamaṃ ariṭṭho bhikkhu codetabbo, codetvā sāretabbo, sāretvā āpattiṃ ropetabbo”ti (cūḷava. 65) evaṃ kammakkhandhake āpattiropanavacanato veditabbo.

'For the first offender.' Here, because it is stated in the Parivāra, 'Devadatta strove to cause a schism in a united Sangha; in that case,' Devadatta is the first offender. And he was one who strove to cause a schism, not one who did not relinquish it. For that formal act was not performed on him. How is this to be known? From the Sutta. For just as it is known from what is stated in the Parivāra, 'The bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trapper, did not relinquish his view despite being formally admonished up to the third time; in that case,' that the formal act was performed on Ariṭṭha, it is not known in the same way for Devadatta. And even if someone were to say, merely from their own preference, that the act must have been performed, even so, there is no such thing as 'no offense' for the first offender in the case of not relinquishing. Indeed, for one who transgresses a laid-down training rule, no 'no offense' is seen, except where specifically permitted. And that which is written in the books in the no-offense section of Ariṭṭha’s training rule, 'for the first offender,' is a careless writing. That it is a careless writing should be understood from the statement about imposing the offense in the Kammakkhandhaka: 'First, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha should be accused; having been accused, he should be reminded; having been reminded, the offense should be imposed on him.'

Iti bhedāya parakkamane ādikammikassa devadattassa yasmā taṃ kammaṃ na kataṃ, tasmāssa āpattiyeva na jātā. Sikkhāpadaṃ pana taṃ ārabbha paññattanti katvā “ādikammiko”ti vutto. Iti āpattiyā abhāvatoyevassa anāpatti vuttā. Sā panesā kiñcāpi asamanubhāsantassāti imināva siddhā, yasmā pana asamanubhāsanto nāma yassa kevalaṃ samanubhāsanaṃ na karonti, so [P 3.0611] vuccati, na ādikammiko. Ayañca devadatto ādikammikoyeva, tasmā “ādikammikassā”ti vuttaṃ. Etenupāyena ṭhapetvā ariṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ sabbasamanubhāsanāsu vinicchayo veditabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

Thus, for Devadatta, the first offender in striving for schism, because that formal act was not performed, no offense arose at all. However, because the training rule was laid down concerning him, he was called 'the first offender.' Thus, his 'no offense' was stated precisely because of the absence of an offense. Although this 'no offense' is established by the phrase 'for one not being admonished,' 'one not being admonished' refers to someone on whom they simply do not perform the admonishment; it does not refer to the first offender. And this Devadatta is the first offender himself; therefore, it was stated 'for the first offender.' By this method, setting aside the Ariṭṭha training rule, the decision in all cases of admonishment should be understood. The rest is clear in all respects.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu tivaṅgikaṃ ekasamuṭṭhānaṃ, samanubhāsanasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāmametaṃ, kāyavācācittato samuṭṭhāti. Paṭinissajjāmīti kāyavikāraṃ vā vacībhedaṃ vā [M 2.0196] akarontasseva pana āpajjanato akiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dukkhavedananti.
