Regarding the origins and so forth: this training rule has three factors and one origin. It is called 'having its origin in admonition' and arises from body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, because one incurs the offense by merely intending, 'I will not renounce it,' without making any bodily gesture or change in speech, it is classified as non-action. It is subject to release through perception, is intentional, a fault in the world, a bodily action, a verbal action, involves unwholesome consciousness, and is accompanied by painful feeling.

Paṭhamasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first training rule on causing schism in the Saṅgha is concluded.

11. Dutiyasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Causing Dissension in the Saṅgha

417-8. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti dutiyasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha anuvattakāti tassa diṭṭhikhantiruciggahaṇena anupaṭipajjanakā. Vaggaṃ asāmaggipakkhiyavacanaṃ vadantīti vaggavādakā. Padabhājane pana “tassa vaṇṇāya pakkhāya ṭhitā hontī”ti vuttaṃ, tassa saṅghabhedāya parakkamantassa vaṇṇatthāya ca pakkhavuḍḍhiatthāya ca ṭhitāti attho. Ye hi vaggavādakā, te niyamena īdisā honti, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana tiṇṇaṃ uddhaṃ kammārahā na honti, na hi saṅgho saṅghassa kammaṃ karoti, tasmā eko vā dve vā tayo vāti vuttaṃ.

At that time the Blessed One laid down the second training rule on causing dissension in the Saṅgha. Therein, 'followers' means those who act in accordance by adopting his view, his approval, and his preference. 'Speakers for a faction' means those who speak words belonging to the side of disunity. In the word-by-word analysis, however, it is said, “They stand for his praise and for his faction.” This means they stand for the sake of the praise and for the sake of the increase of the faction of him who strives to cause dissension in the Saṅgha. For those who speak for a faction are invariably of this nature—hence it is stated thus. Furthermore, since those numbering more than three are not fit for a formal act—for a Saṅgha does not perform a formal act upon a Saṅgha—it is said, “one, two, or three.”

Jānāti [V 2.0177] noti amhākaṃ chandādīni jānāti. Bhāsatīti “evaṃ karomā”ti amhehi saddhiṃ bhāsati. Amhākampetaṃ khamatīti yaṃ so karoti, etaṃ amhākampi ruccati.

“He knows our…” means he knows our wishes and so on. “He speaks” means he speaks with us, saying, “Let us do thus.” “This is agreeable to us as well” means what he does is also pleasing to us.

Sametāyasmantānaṃ saṅghenāti āyasmantānaṃ cittaṃ saṅghena saddhiṃ sametu samāgacchatu, ekībhāvaṃ yātūti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha paṭhamasikkhāpade vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca pākaṭameva.

“May the venerable ones be in harmony with the Saṅgha” means the venerable ones’ minds should be in harmony with the Saṅgha, they should come together, and they should attain oneness—this is what is said. The rest here is evident because it was stated in the manner of the first training rule and because its meaning is plain.

Samuṭṭhānādīnipi paṭhamasikkhāpadasadisānevāti.

The origins and so on are also just like those of the first training rule.

Dutiyasaṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule on causing dissension in the Saṅgha is concluded.

12. Dubbacasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

12. Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Difficult to Admonish

424. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti dubbacasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha anācāraṃ ācaratīti anekappakāraṃ kāyavacīdvāravītikkamaṃ karoti. Kiṃ nu kho nāmāti vambhanavacanametaṃ. Ahaṃ kho nāmāti ukkaṃsavacanaṃ. Tumhe vadeyyanti [P 3.0612] “idaṃ karotha, idaṃ mā karothā”ti ahaṃ tumhe vattuṃ [M 2.0197] arahāmīti dasseti. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā amhākaṃ buddho bhagavā kaṇṭakaṃ āruyha mayā saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā pabbajitotievamādimatthaṃ sandhāyāha. “Amhākaṃ dhammo”ti vatvā pana attano santakabhāve yuttiṃ dassento “amhākaṃ ayyaputtena dhammo abhisamito”ti āha. Yasmā amhākaṃ ayyaputtena catusaccadhammo paṭividdho, tasmā dhammopi amhākanti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṅghaṃ pana attano veripakkhe ṭhitaṃ maññamāno amhākaṃ saṅghoti na vadati. Upamaṃ pana vatvā saṅghaṃ apasādetukāmo “seyyathāpi nāmā”tiādimāha. Tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇasaṭanti tattha tattha patitaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇaṃ. Atha vā tiṇañca nissārakaṃ lahukaṃ kaṭṭhañca tiṇakaṭṭhaṃ. Paṇṇasaṭanti purāṇapaṇṇaṃ. Ussāreyyāti rāsiṃ kareyya.

424. At that time the Blessed One laid down the training rule about being difficult to admonish. Therein, “behaves improperly” means he commits various kinds of transgressions through the doors of body and speech. “What now indeed?”—this is a contemptuous expression. “I indeed”—this is an expression of self-praise. “You should say” shows “I am worthy to tell you, ‘Do this, do not do this.’” If asked why, he spoke referring to such a meaning as: “Because our Buddha, the Blessed One, mounted Kaṇṭhaka, went forth with me, and became an ascetic.” Furthermore, having said “our Dhamma,” and showing the justification for it being his own possession, he said, “The Dhamma has been fully realized by our noble son.” Because the Dhamma of the Four Truths has been penetrated by our noble son, therefore it is said, “The Dhamma is also ours.” But, thinking the Saṅgha stands on the side of his enemies, he does not say “our Saṅgha.” Furthermore, wishing to disparage the Saṅgha by stating a simile, he said, “Just as…” and so on. ‘Grass, sticks, and old leaves’ means grass, sticks, and leaves fallen here and there. Alternatively, ‘grass-and-sticks’ means grass and insubstantial, light sticks; ‘old leaves’ means old leaves. “Would sweep up” means would make a pile.

Pabbateyyāti pabbatappabhavā, sā hi sīghasotā hoti, tasmā tameva gaṇhāti. Saṅkhasevālapaṇakanti ettha saṅkhoti dīghamūlako paṇṇasevālo vuccati. Sevāloti nīlasevālo, avaseso udakapappaṭakatilabījakādi sabbopi paṇakoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Ekato ussāritāti ekaṭṭhāne kenāpi sampiṇḍitā rāsīkatāti dasseti.

‘A mountain stream’ means originating from a mountain; indeed, its current is swift, therefore it is taken as the example. Regarding ‘saṅkha-sevāla-paṇaka,’ herein ‘saṅkha’ is said to be a long-rooted, leafy water plant. ‘Sevāla’ is blue-green moss. The remainder—all kinds of aquatic plants such as water-scum and those the size of sesame seeds—is counted as ‘paṇaka.’ ‘Swept up together’ shows that they have been gathered and piled up in one place by some force.

425-6. Dubbacajātikoti dubbacasabhāvo vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyoti attho. Padabhājanepissa [V 2.0178] dubbacoti dukkhena kicchena vaditabbo, na sakkā sukhena vattunti attho. Dovacassakaraṇehīti dubbacabhāvakaraṇīyehi, ye dhammā dubbacaṃ puggalaṃ karonti, tehi samannāgatoti attho. Te pana “katame ca, āvuso, dovacassakaraṇā dhammā? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pāpiccho hotī”tiādinā nayena paṭipāṭiyā anumānasutte (ma. ni. 1.181) āgatā pāpicchatā, attukkaṃsakaparavambhakatā, kodhanatā, kodhahetu upanāhitā, kodhahetuabhisaṅgitā, kodhahetukodhasāmantavācānicchāraṇatā, codakaṃ paṭippharaṇatā, codakaṃ apasādanatā, codakassa paccāropanatā, aññena aññaṃpaṭicaraṇatā[P 3.0613], apadānena na sampāyanatā, makkhipaḷāsitā, issukīmaccharitā, saṭhamāyāvitā, thaddhātimānitā, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsiādhānaggahiduppaṭinissaggitāti ekūnavīsati dhammā veditabbā.

‘Of a nature difficult to admonish’ means having a nature that is difficult to speak to; the meaning is one who cannot be admonished. In its word-analysis, ‘difficult to admonish’ means one who is to be spoken to with difficulty and with trouble; the meaning is that it is not possible to speak to them easily. ‘By the factors that make one difficult to admonish’ means by the things that cause the state of being difficult to admonish; the meaning is being endowed with those qualities that make a person difficult to admonish. These nineteen qualities, which have come in sequence in the Anumāna Sutta in the passage beginning, “And what, friends, are the qualities that cause one to be difficult to admonish? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is of corrupt wishes…,” should be understood: corrupt wishes; self-praise and disparagement of others; anger; harboring resentment due to anger; being consumed by anger; uttering words bordering on anger due to anger; retaliating against the accuser; discrediting the accuser; turning the accusation back on the accuser; evading one thing with another; failing to resolve the matter by citing a pretext; denigration and rivalry; envy and miserliness; deceit and craftiness; obstinacy and excessive pride; and wrongly grasping one’s own views, holding to them tenaciously, and relinquishing them with difficulty.

Ovādaṃ [M 2.0198] nakkhamati na sahatīti akkhamo. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ appaṭipajjanato padakkhiṇena anusāsaniṃ na gaṇhātīti appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ.

‘Intolerant’ is so called because he does not endure or tolerate advice. ‘One who does not receive instruction respectfully’ is so called because, by not practicing as instructed, he does not take instruction respectfully.

Uddesapariyāpannesūti uddese pariyāpannesu antogadhesu. “Yassa siyā āpatti, so āvikareyyā”ti evaṃ saṅgahitattā anto pātimokkhassa vattamānesūti attho. Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamānoti sahadhammikena vuccamāno karaṇatthe upayogavacanaṃ, pañcahi sahadhammikehi sikkhitabbattā tesaṃ vā santakattā sahadhammikanti laddhanāmena buddhapaññattena sikkhāpadena vuccamānoti attho.

‘Included in the recitation’ means included and contained within the recitation. The meaning is ‘occurring within the Pātimokkha,’ because they are all included by the statement, ‘Whatever offense there may be for someone, they should declare it.’ ‘Being addressed in accordance with the Dhamma’ means being addressed by that which is ‘sahadhammika’—this is a term used in the instrumental sense. The meaning is: being addressed by a training rule laid down by the Buddha, which has received the name ‘sahadhammika’ either because it is to be trained in by the five kinds of co-religionists or because it is their possession.

Viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāyāti yena vacanena maṃ vadatha, tato mama vacanato viramatha. Mā maṃ taṃ vacanaṃ vadathāti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Venerable sirs, refrain from speaking to me” means: refrain from those words with which you address me. It is said: “Do not speak those words to me.”

Vadatu sahadhammenāti sahadhammikena sikkhāpadena sahadhammena vā aññenapi pāsādikabhāvasaṃvattanikena vacanena vadatu. Yadidanti vuḍḍhikāraṇanidassanatthe nipāto. Tena “yaṃ idaṃ aññamaññassa hitavacanaṃ āpattito vuṭṭhāpanañca tena aññamaññavacanena aññamaññavuṭṭhāpanena ca saṃvaḍḍhā parisā”ti evaṃ parisāya vuḍḍhikāraṇaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

“Let him speak in accordance with the Dhamma” means: let him speak by a training rule that is common to fellow practitioners, or with reason, or by any other words that lead to inspiring confidence. The word ‘yadidaṃ’ is a particle in the sense of indicating the cause for growth. By this, the cause for the community’s growth is shown thus: “That is, the beneficial speech for one another and the raising from an offense; by that mutual speech and by that mutual raising, the community grows.”

Samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamasaṅghabhedasadisānevāti.

The origins and so on are similar to those of the first schism in the Saṅgha.

Dubbacasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Training Rule on Being Difficult to Admonish is concluded.

13. Kuladūsakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

13. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Corrupting Families

431. Tena [V 2.0179] samayena buddho bhagavāti kuladūsakasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha assajipunabbasukā nāmāti assaji ceva punabbasuko ca. Kīṭāgirisminti evaṃnāmake janapade. Āvāsikā hontīti ettha āvāso etesaṃ atthīti āvāsikā. “Āvāso”ti vihāro vuccati. So yesaṃ āyatto navakammakaraṇapurāṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇādibhārahāratāya, te āvāsikā. Ye pana kevalaṃ vihāre vasanti, te nevāsikāti vuccanti. Ime āvāsikā ahesuṃ. Alajjino pāpabhikkhūti [P 3.0614] nillajjā lāmakabhikkhū, te hi chabbaggiyānaṃ jeṭṭhakachabbaggiyā.

431. “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One…” is the Training Rule on Corrupting Families. Therein, “Assaji and Punabbasuka” means Assaji and Punabbasuka. “At Kīṭāgiri” means in a country of that name. “They were resident monks” means that they had a residence, hence they are “resident monks.” A “residence” is said to be a monastery. Those who are responsible for it by way of undertaking new construction, repairing the old, and so on, are resident monks. But those who merely live in the monastery are called mere residents. These were resident monks. “Shameless, evil monks” means shameless, base monks; for they were the eldest of the group of six.

Sāvatthiyaṃ [M 2.0199] kira cha janā sahāyakā “kasikammādīni dukkarāni, handa mayaṃ sammā pabbajāma! Pabbajantehi ca uppanne kicce nittharaṇakaṭṭhāne pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sammantayitvā dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ santike pabbajiṃsu. Te pañcavassā hutvā mātikaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā mantayiṃsu “janapado nāma kadāci subhikkho hoti kadāci dubbhikkho, mayaṃ mā ekaṭṭhāne vasimha, tīsu ṭhānesu vasāmā”ti. Tato paṇḍukalohitake āhaṃsu – “āvuso, sāvatthi nāma sattapaññāsāya kulasatasahassehi ajjhāvutthā, asītigāmasahassapaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ tiyojanasatikānaṃ dvinnaṃ kāsikosalaraṭṭhānaṃ āyamukhabhūtā, tatra tumhe dhuraṭṭhāneyeva pariveṇāni kāretvā ambapanasanāḷikerādīni ropetvā pupphehi ca phalehi ca kulāni saṅgaṇhantā kuladārake pabbājetvā parisaṃ vaḍḍhethā”ti.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, six friends conferred, saying, “Agricultural work and so on are difficult. Come, let us go forth properly! And when going forth, should a need arise, it is proper to go forth under someone who can see us through.” Having conferred, they went forth in the presence of the two chief disciples. After five years, having mastered the Mātikā, they conferred, “A country is sometimes prosperous and sometimes afflicted by famine. Let us not live in one place; let us live in three places.” Then they said to Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka: “Friends, Sāvatthī is inhabited by fifty-seven hundred thousand families and is the gateway for revenue for the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala, which span three hundred leagues and are adorned with eighty thousand villages. There, in a prominent location, you should have monastic dwellings made, plant mango, jackfruit, coconut trees and so on, and by means of their flowers and fruits, win over families, give the going-forth to their sons, and increase the community.”

Mettiyabhūmajake āhaṃsu – “āvuso, rājagahaṃ nāma aṭṭhārasahi manussakoṭīhi ajjhāvutthaṃ asītigāmasahassapaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ tiyojanasatikānaṃ dvinnaṃ aṅgamagadharaṭṭhānaṃ āyamukhabhūtaṃ, tatra tumhe dhuraṭṭhāneyeva…pe… parisaṃ vaḍḍhethā”ti.

To Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, they said: “Friends, Rājagaha is inhabited by eighteen crores of people and is the gateway for revenue for the two kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, which span three hundred leagues and are adorned with eighty thousand villages. There, you should… and increase the community.”

Assajipunabbasuke āhaṃsu – “āvuso, kīṭāgiri nāma dvīhi meghehi anuggahito tīṇi sassāni pasavanti, tatra tumhe dhuraṭṭhāneyeva pariveṇāni kāretvā…pe… parisaṃ vaḍḍhethā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Tesu ekamekassa pakkhassa pañca pañca bhikkhusatāni parivārā, evaṃ samadhikaṃ diyaḍḍhabhikkhusahassaṃ hoti. Tatra paṇḍukalohitakā saparivārā sīlavantova bhagavatā saddhiṃ janapadacārikampi caranti, te akatavatthuṃ uppādenti, paññattasikkhāpadaṃ pana na maddanti, itare sabbe alajjino akatavatthuñca uppādenti, paññattasikkhāpadañca maddanti, tena vuttaṃ – “alajjino pāpabhikkhū”ti.

To Assaji and Punabbasu, they said: “Friends, Kīṭāgiri is favored by two kinds of rain and produces three crops. There, you should… and increase the community.” They did so. Each faction had a retinue of five hundred monks; thus, there were more than fifteen hundred monks. Among them, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, with their retinues, were virtuous and even went on tour through the country with the Blessed One. They would originate a matter that had not yet been made a rule, but they would not transgress a training rule that had been laid down. All the others were shameless; they would both originate a matter that had not yet been made a rule and transgress a training rule that had been laid down. Therefore, it was said: “shameless, evil monks.”

Evarūpanti [P 3.0615][V 2.0180] evaṃjātikaṃ. Anācāraṃ ācarantīti anācaritabbaṃ ācaranti, akātabbaṃ karonti. Mālāvacchanti taruṇapuppharukkhaṃ, taruṇakā hi puppharukkhāpi pupphagacchāpi mālāvacchā tveva vuccanti, te ca anekappakāraṃ mālāvacchaṃ sayampi ropenti, aññenapi ropāpenti, tena vuttaṃ – “mālāvacchaṃ ropentipi ropāpentipī”ti. Siñcantīti sayameva udakena siñcanti. Siñcāpentīti aññenapi siñcāpenti.

“Of such a kind” means of such a nature. “They engage in misconduct” means they practice what should not be practiced; they do what should not be done. “A young plant” means a young flowering tree. For young flowering trees and flowering shrubs are both called “young plants.” And they themselves plant various kinds of young plants, and they have others plant them. Therefore, it was said: “they plant young plants and have them planted.” “They water” means they themselves water with water. “They have them watered” means they have others water them.

Ettha [M 2.0200] pana akappiyavohāro kappiyavohāro pariyāyo obhāso nimittakammanti imāni pañca jānitabbāni. Tattha akappiyavohāro nāma allaharitānaṃ koṭṭanaṃ koṭṭāpanaṃ, āvāṭassa khaṇanaṃ khaṇāpanaṃ, mālāvacchassa ropanaṃ ropāpanaṃ, āḷiyā bandhanaṃ bandhāpanaṃ, udakassa secanaṃ secāpanaṃ, mātikāya sammukhakaraṇaṃ kappiyaudakasiñcanaṃ hatthamukhapādadhovananhānodakasiñcananti. Kappiyavohāro nāma “imaṃ rukkhaṃ jāna, imaṃ āvāṭaṃ jāna, imaṃ mālāvacchaṃ jāna, ettha udakaṃ jānā”ti vacanaṃ sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇañca. Pariyāyo nāma “paṇḍitena nāma mālāvacchādayo ropāpetabbā nacirasseva upakārāya saṃvattantī”tiādivacanaṃ. Obhāso nāma kudālakhaṇittādīni ca mālāvacche ca gahetvā ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ ṭhitañhi sāmaṇerādayo disvā thero kārāpetukāmoti gantvā karonti. Nimittakammaṃ nāma kudāla-khaṇitti-vāsi-pharasu-udakabhājanāni āharitvā samīpe ṭhapanaṃ.

Here, five things should be understood: improper transaction, proper transaction, circumlocution, giving a hint, and making a sign. Among these, “improper transaction” refers to: cutting or having cut fresh green plants; digging or having dug a pit; planting or having planted a young plant; building or having built a dike; watering or having watered; directing a water channel towards something; sprinkling with allowable water; or sprinkling with water for washing the hands, face, or feet, or for bathing. “Proper transaction” refers to saying, “Take note of this tree,” “Take note of this pit,” “Take note of this young plant,” “Take note of the water here,” and the straightening of a dry water channel. “Circumlocution” refers to speech such as, “A wise person should have young plants and the like planted; they soon become beneficial.” “Giving a hint” refers to taking a hoe, a digging stick, and so on, and the young plants, and standing in a place. For when novices and others see him standing thus, they think, “The elder wishes to have it done,” and they go and do it. “Making a sign” refers to bringing a hoe, digging stick, adze, axe, and water pot and placing them nearby.

Imāni pañcapi kulasaṅgahatthāya ropane na vaṭṭanti, phalaparibhogatthāya kappiyākappiyavohāradvayameva na vaṭṭati, itarattayaṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “kappiyavohāropi vaṭṭati. Yañca attano paribhogatthāya vaṭṭati, taṃ aññapuggalassa vā saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā atthāyapi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

These five are not allowable in planting for the purpose of supporting the families. For the purpose of enjoying the fruit, only the pair of proper and improper speech is not allowable; the other three are allowable. However, in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'Even proper speech is allowable. And that which is allowable for one's own use is also allowable for the benefit of another person, or the Sangha, or a cetiya.'

Ārāmatthāya pana vanatthāyaca chāyatthāya ca akappiyavohāramattameva na ca vaṭṭati, sesaṃ vaṭṭati, na kevalañca sesaṃ yaṃkiñci mātikampi ujuṃ kātuṃ kappiyaudakaṃ siñcituṃ nhānakoṭṭhakaṃ katvā nhāyituṃ hatthapādamukhadhovanudakāni [P 3.0616] ca tattha chaḍḍetumpi vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kurundiyañca “kappiyapathaviyaṃ sayaṃ ropetumpi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ārāmādiatthāya pana ropitassa vā ropāpitassa vā phalaṃ paribhuñjitumpi vaṭṭati.

However, for the sake of a monastery, a forest, or shade, only improper speech is not allowable; the rest is allowable. And not only is the rest allowable, but it is also allowable to straighten any small water channel, to sprinkle allowable water, to make a bathing chamber and bathe, and also to discard there the water from washing hands, feet, and face. However, in the Mahāpaccarī and the Kurundī it is said: 'It is also allowable to plant oneself on allowable ground.' Moreover, for the sake of a monastery and so forth, it is also allowable to enjoy the fruit of a tree that one has planted or caused to be planted.

Ocinanaocināpane pakatiyāpi pācittiyaṃ. Kuladūsanatthāya pana pācittiyañceva dukkaṭañca. Ganthanādīsu ca uracchadapariyosānesu kuladūsanatthāya aññatthāya vā karontassa dukkaṭameva[V 2.0181]. Kasmā? Anācārattā, “pāpasamācāro”ti ettha vuttapāpasamācārattā ca. Ārāmādiatthāya rukkharopane viya vatthupūjanatthāya kasmā na anāpattīti ce? Anāpattiyeva. Yathā hi tattha kappiyavohārena pariyāyādīhi ca anāpatti tathā vatthupūjatthāyapi anāpattiyeva.

In plucking or causing to pluck, there is ordinarily a pācittiya offense. However, for the purpose of destroying the faith of the families, there is both a pācittiya and a dukkaṭa offense. And in matters beginning with making garlands and ending with chest-covering flowers, for one who does so for the purpose of destroying the faith of the families or for another purpose, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. Why? Because it is improper conduct, and because it is the evil conduct spoken of here in the passage 'pāpasamācāro'. If it is asked: 'Just as there is no-offense in planting trees for the sake of a monastery and so forth, why is there not no-offense for the purpose of venerating an object?' It is indeed no-offense. For just as there, there is no-offense through proper speech, indirect speech, and so forth, so too for the purpose of venerating an object, it is indeed no-offense.

Nanu [M 2.0201] ca tattha “kappiyapathaviyaṃ sayaṃ ropetumpi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttanti? Vuttaṃ, na pana mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Athāpi maññeyyāsi itarāsu vuttampi pamāṇaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyañca kappiyaudakasecanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ kathanti? Tampi na virujjhati. Tatra hi avisesena “rukkhaṃ ropentipi ropāpentipi, siñcantipi siñcāpentipī”ti vattabbe “mālāvaccha”nti vadanto ñāpeti “kulasaṅgahatthāya pupphaphalūpagameva sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ, aññatra pana pariyāyo atthī”ti. Tasmā tattha pariyāyaṃ, idha ca pariyāyābhāvaṃ ñatvā yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, taṃ suvuttameva. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Is it not the case that it was said there, 'It is also allowable to plant oneself on allowable ground'? It was said, but not in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Still, you might think that what is said in the other commentaries is also authoritative. And in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, the sprinkling of allowable water is mentioned; how can that be? That also does not conflict. For there, when it should have been said generally, 'They plant trees or cause them to be planted; they water them or cause them to be watered,' the Blessed One, by saying 'a flower-plant,' makes it known that 'This was said referring only to a tree that bears flowers and fruit for the purpose of supporting the families, but elsewhere there is an indirect method.' Therefore, having understood that there is an indirect method there, and that there is no indirect method here, what is said in the commentaries is indeed well-said. And this is said:

“Buddhena dhammo vinayo ca vutto;

Yo tassa puttehi tatheva ñāto;

So yehi tesaṃ matimaccajantā;

Yasmā pure aṭṭhakathā akaṃsu.

“The Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha; which was known in that very way by his sons; therefore, not transgressing their understanding, they composed the commentaries of old.

“Tasmā hi yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ;

Taṃ vajjayitvāna pamādalekhaṃ;

Sabbampi sikkhāsu sagāravānaṃ;

Yasmā pamāṇaṃ idha paṇḍitāna”nti.

Therefore, whatever is said in the commentaries—setting aside any careless writing—is entirely the standard here for the wise who are reverent in the trainings.”

Sabbaṃ [P 3.0617] vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tattha siyā yadi vatthupūjanatthāyapi ganthānādīsu āpatti, haraṇādīsu kasmā anāpattīti? Kulitthīādīnaṃ atthāya haraṇato haraṇādhikāre hi visesetvā te kulitthīnantiādi vuttaṃ, tasmā buddhādīnaṃ atthāya harantassa anāpatti.

Everything should be understood according to the method that has been stated. There, an objection might arise: 'If there is an offense in making garlands and so forth even for the purpose of venerating an object, why is there no-offense in carrying and so forth?' Indeed, it is because in the section on carrying, having specified, the Blessed One said, 'They, for women of good families...' and so forth. Therefore, for one who carries for the sake of the Buddha and so forth, there is no-offense.

Tattha ekatovaṇṭikanti pupphānaṃ vaṇṭe ekato katvā katamālaṃ. Ubhatovaṇṭikanti ubhohi passehi pupphavaṇṭe katvā katamālaṃ. Mañjarikantiādīsu pana mañjarī viya katā pupphavikati mañjarikāti vuccati. Vidhūtikāti sūciyā vā salākāya vā sinduvārapupphādīni [V 2.0182] vijjhitvā katā. Vaṭaṃsakoti vataṃsako. Āveḷāti kaṇṇikā. Uracchadoti hārasadisaṃ ure ṭhapanakapupphadāmaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva ettha padavaṇṇanā.

Therein, 'ekatovaṇṭikaṃ' means a bouquet made by gathering the stems of flowers together. 'Ubhatovaṇṭikaṃ' means a garland made with flower stems on both sides. In 'mañjarikā' and so forth, a special flower arrangement made like a flower cluster is called 'mañjarikā'. 'Vidhūtikā' is made by piercing sinduvāra flowers and so forth with a needle or a bamboo sliver. 'Vaṭaṃsako' is a head-ornament. 'Āveḷā' is a flower worn in the ear. 'Uracchado' is a flower garland placed on the chest, similar to a pearl necklace. This, for now, is the explanation of the terms here.

Ayaṃ pana ādito paṭṭhāya vitthārena āpattivinicchayo. Kuladūsanatthāya akappiyapathaviyaṃ mālāvacchaṃ ropentassa pācittiyañceva dukkaṭañca, tathā akappiyavohārena ropāpentassa. Kappiyapathaviyaṃ ropanepi [M 2.0202] ropāpanepi dukkaṭameva. Ubhayatthāpi sakiṃ āṇattiyā bahunnampi ropane ekameva sapācittiyadukkaṭaṃ vā suddhadukkaṭaṃ vā hoti. Paribhogatthāya hi kappiyabhūmiyaṃ vā akappiyabhūmiyaṃ vā kappiyavohārena ropāpane anāpatti. Ārāmādiatthāyapi akappiyapathaviyaṃ ropentassa vā akappiyavacanena ropāpentassa vā pācittiyaṃ. Ayaṃ pana nayo mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ na suṭṭhu vibhatto, mahāpaccariyaṃ vibhattoti.

This, however, is the detailed determination of offenses from the beginning. For one who plants a flower-plant on unallowable ground for the purpose of destroying the families' faith, there is both a pācittiya and a dukkaṭa offense; likewise for one who causes it to be planted by means of unallowable speech. On allowable ground, in both planting and causing to be planted, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. In both cases, by a single command, in planting even many trees, only one offense is incurred: either a dukkaṭa together with a pācittiya, or a pure dukkaṭa. Indeed, for the purpose of use, there is no-offense in causing something to be planted by means of allowable speech, whether on allowable or unallowable ground. Also, for the sake of a monastery and so forth, for one who plants on unallowable ground or causes it to be planted by means of unallowable speech, there is a pācittiya offense. This method, however, is not well analyzed in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā; it is analyzed in the Mahāpaccarī.

Siñcanasiñcāpane pana akappiyaudakena sabbattha pācittiyaṃ, kuladūsanaparibhogatthāya dukkaṭampi. Kappiyena tesaṃyeva dvinnamatthāya dukkaṭaṃ. Paribhogatthāya cettha kappiyavohārena siñcāpane anāpatti. Āpattiṭṭhāne pana dhārāvacchedavasena payogabahulatāya āpattibahulatā veditabbā.

However, in watering or causing to water with unallowable water, there is a pācittiya offense in all cases; for the purpose of destroying the families' faith and for use, there is also a dukkaṭa offense. With allowable water, for the purpose of only those two, there is a dukkaṭa offense. And here, for the purpose of use, there is no-offense in causing to water by means of allowable speech. However, in a situation where an offense is incurred, the multiplicity of offenses should be understood by way of the multiplicity of effort, according to the interruption of the stream.

Kuladūsanatthāya ocinane pupphagaṇanāya dukkaṭapācittiyāni aññattha pācittiyāneva. Bahūni pana pupphāni ekapayogena ocinanto payogavasena kāretabbo. Ocināpane kuladūsanatthāya [P 3.0618] sakiṃ āṇatto bahumpi ocinati, ekameva sapācittiyadukkaṭaṃ, aññatra pācittiyameva.

In plucking for the purpose of destroying the families' faith, dukkaṭa and pācittiya offenses are incurred according to the count of flowers; elsewhere, there are only pācittiya offenses. However, one who plucks many flowers with a single effort should be dealt with according to the effort. In causing to pluck for the purpose of destroying the families' faith, if one who is commanded once plucks many, there is only one dukkaṭa offense together with a pācittiya; elsewhere, there is only a pācittiya offense.

Ganthanādīsu sabbāpi cha pupphavikatiyo veditabbā – ganthimaṃ, gopphimaṃ, vedhimaṃ, veṭhimaṃ, pūrimaṃ, vāyimanti. Tattha “ganthimaṃ” nāma sadaṇḍakesu vā uppalapadumādīsu aññesu vā dīghavaṇṭesu pupphesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Daṇḍakena daṇḍakaṃ vaṇṭena vā vaṇṭaṃ ganthetvā katameva hi ganthimaṃ. Taṃ bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā kātumpi akappiyavacanena kārāpetumpi na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ jāna, evaṃ kate sobheyya, yathā etāni pupphāni na vikiriyanti tathā karohītiādinā pana kappiyavacanena kāretuṃ vaṭṭati.

In tying and so forth, all six kinds of specially made flowers should be understood: knotted (ganthima), plaited (gopphima), pierced (vedhima), wrapped (veṭhima), filled (pūrima), and woven (vāyima). Among these, that which is called 'knotted' should be seen in flowers with stalks, such as water lilies and lotuses, or in other flowers with long stems. Indeed, that which is made by tying stalk to stalk or stem to stem is called 'knotted'. For a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, it is not allowable to make this, nor to have it made with improper wording. However, it is allowable to have it made with proper wording, such as: 'Know it thus'; 'It would be beautiful if made thus'; 'Do it in such a way that these flowers are not scattered,' and so on.

“Gopphimaṃ” nāma suttena vā vākādīhi vā vassikapupphādīnaṃ ekatovaṇṭikaubhatovaṇṭikamālāvasena gopphanaṃ, vākaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā diguṇaṃ katvā tattha avaṇṭakāni [V 2.0183] nīpapupphādīni pavesetvā paṭipāṭiyā bandhanti, etampi gopphimameva. Sabbaṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati.

That which is called 'plaited' is the plaiting of vassika flowers and so on with thread or with bark-fiber and so on, in the manner of a single-stemmed or double-stemmed garland. Or, having made a bark-fiber or a cord double, and having inserted stemless flowers such as nīpa flowers into it, they bind them in sequence; this too is indeed 'plaited'. All of this is not allowable, according to the preceding method.

“Vedhimaṃ” nāma savaṇṭakāni vassikapupphādīni vaṇṭesu, avaṇṭakāni vā vakulapupphādīni antochidde sūcitālahīrādīhi vinivijjhitvā āvunanti, etaṃ vedhimaṃ nāma, tampi purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati. Keci pana kadalikkhandhamhi kaṇṭake vā [M 2.0203] tālahīrādīni vā pavesetvā tattha pupphāni vijjhitvā ṭhapenti, keci kaṇṭakasākhāsu, keci pupphacchattapupphakūṭāgārakaraṇatthaṃ chatte ca bhittiyañca pavesetvā ṭhapitakaṇṭakesu, keci dhammāsanavitāne baddhakaṇṭakesu, keci kaṇikārapupphādīni salākāhi vijjhanti, chattādhichattaṃ viya ca karonti, taṃ atioḷārikameva[P 3.0619]. Pupphavijjhanatthaṃ pana dhammāsanavitāne kaṇṭakampi bandhituṃ kaṇṭakādīhi vā ekapupphampi vijjhituṃ puppheyeva vā pupphaṃ pavesetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Jālavitānavedika-nāgadantaka pupphapaṭicchakatālapaṇṇaguḷakādīnaṃ pana chiddesu asokapiṇḍiyā vā antaresu pupphāni pavesetuṃ na doso. Etaṃ vedhimaṃ nāma na hoti. Dhammarajjuyampi eseva nayo.

That which is called 'pierced' is when they pierce stemmed flowers like vassika flowers on their stems, or stemless flowers like bakula flowers in their inner hole, with a needle, palm-fiber, and so on, and string them; this is called 'pierced'. This too is not allowable according to the preceding method. However, some, having inserted thorns or palm-fibers and so on into a banana trunk, pierce flowers onto them and place them there. Some pierce and place flowers on thorny branches. Some, for the purpose of making a flower-umbrella or a flower-pinnacle, pierce and place flowers on thorns that have been inserted and placed in an umbrella and on a wall. Some pierce and place flowers on thorns fastened to the canopy of a Dhamma-seat. Some pierce kaṇikāra flowers and so on with splinters and make it like a tiered umbrella. All that is indeed very coarse. However, for the purpose of piercing flowers, it is not allowable to fasten even a thorn to the canopy of a Dhamma-seat, or to pierce even a single flower with thorns and so on, or to insert one flower into another flower. However, there is no fault in inserting flowers into the holes of latticed canopies, railings, elephant-tusk pegs, flower-vases, palm leaves, balls, and so on, or in the spaces within a cluster of asoka flowers. This is not called 'pierced'. This is the same method for a Dhamma-cord.

“Veṭhimaṃ” nāma pupphadāmapupphahatthakesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci hi matthakadāmaṃ karontā heṭṭhā ghaṭakākāraṃ dassetuṃ pupphehi veṭhenti, keci aṭṭhaṭṭha vā dasa dasa vā uppalapupphādīni suttena vā vākena vā daṇḍakesu bandhitvā uppalahatthake vā padumahatthake vā karonti, taṃ sabbaṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati. Sāmaṇerehi uppāṭetvā thale ṭhapitauppalādīni kāsāvena bhaṇḍikampi bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Tesaṃyeva pana vākena vā daṇḍakena vā bandhituṃ aṃsabhaṇḍikaṃ vā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Aṃsabhaṇḍikā nāma khandhe ṭhapitakāsāvassa ubho ante āharitvā bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā tasmiṃ pasibbake viya pupphāni pakkhipanti, ayaṃ vuccati aṃsabhaṇḍikā, etaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Daṇḍakehi paduminipaṇṇaṃ vijjhitvā uppalādīni paṇṇena veṭhetvā gaṇhanti, tatrāpi pupphānaṃ upari paduminipaṇṇameva bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhā daṇḍakaṃ pana bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati.

That which is called 'wrapped' should be seen in flower-garlands and flower-bouquets. Indeed, some, when making a head-garland, wrap it with flowers below to show a pot-like shape. Some, having tied eight or ten water lilies and so on to their stalks with thread or bark-fiber, make water lily bouquets or lotus bouquets. All of that is not allowable according to the preceding method. It is not allowable to tie with a saffron robe a bundle of water lilies and so on that have been plucked by sāmaṇeras and placed on the ground. However, it is allowable to tie them with their own bark-fiber or with their stalks, or to make a shoulder-bundle. A shoulder-bundle is known thus: having brought together both ends of the saffron robe placed on the shoulder and made a bundle, they put flowers into it as if into a bag. This is called a shoulder-bundle. It is allowable to make this. They pierce a lotus leaf with sticks, and having wrapped water lilies and so on with the leaf, they take them. In that case, too, it is allowable to tie only the lotus leaf above the flowers. However, it is not allowable to tie the stalk below.

“Pūrimaṃ” nāma mālāguṇe ca pupphapaṭe ca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yo hi mālāguṇena cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā vedikaṃ vā parikkhipanto puna ānetvā pūrimaṭhānaṃ atikkāmeti, ettāvatāpi pūrimaṃ nāma hoti. Ko pana vādo anekakkhattuṃ parikkhipantassa, nāgadanta-kantarehi pavesetvā haranto olambakaṃ katvā puna nāgadantakaṃ parikkhipati, etampi pūrimaṃ nāma. Nāgadantake pana pupphavalayaṃ pavesetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mālāguṇehi pupphapaṭaṃ karonti. Tatrāpi ekameva mālāguṇaṃ [V 2.0184] harituṃ vaṭṭati. Puna paccāharato pūrimameva hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati. Mālāguṇehi pana bahūhipi kataṃ pupphadāmaṃ labhitvā āsanamatthakādīsu [P 3.0620] bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Atidīghaṃ pana mālāguṇaṃ [M 2.0204] ekavāraṃ haritvā vā parikkhipitvā vā puna aññassa bhikkhuno dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāpi tatheva kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

That which is called 'filled' should be seen in a string of flowers and in a flower-cloth. Indeed, a bhikkhu who, while encircling a cetiya, a Bodhi tree, or a railing with a string of flowers, brings it around again and makes it go beyond the original place, by even that much it becomes what is called 'filled'. What, then, is to be said in the case of one who encircles it many times? Having inserted it through the spaces between elephant-tusk pegs and carried it along, making it hang down, one then encircles the elephant-tusk peg again; this too is called 'filled'. However, it is allowable to insert a flower-wreath onto an elephant-tusk peg. They make a flower-cloth with strings of flowers. In that case, too, it is allowable to lay out only one string of flowers. For one who brings it back again, it becomes 'filled'. All of that is not allowable according to the preceding method. However, having received a flower-festoon made with many strings of flowers, it is allowable to tie it on the top of a seat and so on. However, having used a very long string of flowers once, or having encircled something with it, it is allowable to then give it to another bhikkhu. It is allowable for him also to do likewise.

“Vāyimaṃ” nāma pupphajālapupphapaṭapuppharūpesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cetiyesu pupphajālaṃ karontassa ekamekamhi jālacchidde dukkaṭaṃ. Bhitticchattabodhitthambhādīsupi eseva nayo. Pupphapaṭaṃ pana parehi pūritampi vāyituṃ na labbhati. Gopphimapuppheheva hatthiassādirūpakāni karonti, tānipi vāyimaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhanti. Purimanayeneva sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Aññehi kataparicchede pana pupphāni ṭhapentena hatthiassādirūpakampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kalambakena aḍḍhacandakena ca saddhiṃ aṭṭhapupphavikatiyo vuttā. Tattha kalambakoti aḍḍhacandakantare ghaṭikadāmaolambako vutto. “Aḍḍhacandako”ti aḍḍhacandākārena mālāguṇaparikkhepo. Tadubhayampi pūrimeyeva paviṭṭhaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana “dve tayo mālāguṇe ekato katvā pupphadāmakaraṇampi vāyimaṃyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi idha pūrimaṭṭhāneyeva paviṭṭhaṃ, na kevalañca pupphaguḷadāmameva piṭṭhamayadāmampi geṇḍukapupphadāmampi kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ, kharapattadāmampi sikkhāpadassa sādhāraṇattā bhikkhūnampi bhikkhunīnampi neva kātuṃ na kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pūjānimittaṃ pana kappiyavacanaṃ sabbattha vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Pariyāyaobhāsanimittakammāni vaṭṭantiyeva.

The term 'woven' (vāyima) should be understood in the context of flower-nets, flower-cloth, and flower-figures. For one who makes a flower-net at a cetiya, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each and every hole in the net. This same principle applies to walls, parasols, Bodhi trees, pillars, and the like. Regarding flower-cloth, however, it is not allowable to weave crosswise even that which has been filled lengthwise by others. They make figures of elephants, horses, and so on, only with gopphima flowers; these too are categorized as 'woven'. By the former principle, none of it is allowable. However, it is allowable for one placing flowers within a boundary made by others to also make figures of elephants, horses, and so on. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, eight kinds of flower arrangements are mentioned, along with kalambaka and aḍḍhacandaka. Therein, kalambaka is said to be a garland hanging down with a pot-like shape below, within a half-moon shape. Aḍḍhacandaka is the encircling with a string of garlands in the shape of a half-moon. Both of these are included in the 'strung' (pūrima) category. In the Kurundī, however, it is said: 'Making a flower festoon by joining two or three strings of garlands is also indeed "woven".' That too is included here in the 'strung' category. And not only a festoon of flower-balls, but also a festoon made of flour, a festoon of flowers shaped like a ball, and a festoon of tinsel are mentioned in the Kurundī. Because the training rule is common to both, it is not allowable for either bhikkhus or bhikkhunīs to make them or to have them made. However, for the purpose of worship, it is allowable to use permissible speech everywhere. Acts of indirect speech, making a hint, and giving a sign are indeed allowable.

Tuvaṭṭentīti nipajjanti. Lāsentīti pītiyā uppilavamānā viya uṭṭhahitvā lāsiyanāṭakaṃ nāṭenti, recakaṃ denti. Naccantiyāpi naccantīti yadā nāṭakitthī naccati, tadā tepi tassā purato vā pacchato vā gacchantā naccanti. Naccantiyāpi gāyantīti yadā sā naccati, tadā naccānurūpaṃ gāyanti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Aṭṭhapadepi kīḷantīti aṭṭhapadaphalake jūtaṃ kīḷanti. Tathā dasapade, ākāsepīti aṭṭhapadadasapadesu [P 3.0621] viya ākāseyeva kīḷanti. Parihārapathepīti bhūmiyaṃ nānāpathamaṇḍalaṃ katvā tattha pariharitabbapathaṃ pariharantā kīḷanti. Santikāyapi kīḷantīti santikakīḷāya kīḷanti, ekajjhaṃ ṭhapitā sāriyo vā pāsāṇasakkharāyo vā acālentā nakheneva apanenti ca upanenti ca, sace tattha kāci calati, parājayo hoti. Khalikāyāti jūtaphalake pāsakakīḷāya kīḷanti. Ghaṭikāyāti ghaṭikā vuccati daṇḍakakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Dīghadaṇḍakena rassadaṇḍakaṃ paharantā vicaranti.

‘Tuvaṭṭenti’ means they lie down. ‘Lāsenti’ means, rising up as if floating with joy, they perform a graceful dance and make elegant gestures. ‘They also dance while she is dancing’ means when a female dancer dances, they too dance, going in front of her or behind her. ‘They also sing while she is dancing’ means when she dances, they sing in accordance with the dance. This is the principle in all cases. ‘They also play on an eight-squared board’ means they play dice on an eight-squared board. Likewise on a ten-squared board. ‘Also in the air’ means they play just in an open space, as if on eight-squared and ten-squared boards. ‘On a path of avoidance’ means, having made various circular paths on the ground, they play there by avoiding the path that should be avoided. ‘They also play santikā’ means they play the game of santikā; without moving the counters or pebbles that have been placed together, they remove them and bring them near with just their fingernails. If any piece moves, it is a loss. ‘By khalikā’ means they play a game with dice on a dice board. ‘By ghaṭikā’: ghaṭikā is called the game of sticks; they play with that. They wander about, striking a short stick with a long stick.

Salākahatthenāti [M 2.0205][V 2.0185] lākhāya vā mañjaṭṭhiyā vā piṭṭhaudake vā salākahatthaṃ temetvā “kiṃ hotū”ti bhūmiyaṃ vā bhittiyaṃ vā taṃ paharitvā hatthiassādīrūpāni dassentā kīḷanti. Akkhenāti guḷena. Paṅgacīrenāti paṅgacīraṃ vuccati paṇṇanāḷikā, taṃ dhamantā kīḷanti. Vaṅkakenāti gāmadārakānaṃ kīḷanakena khuddakanaṅgalena. Mokkhacikāyāti mokkhacikā vuccati samparivattakakīḷā, ākāse vā daṇḍaṃ gahetvā, bhūmiyaṃ vā sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā heṭṭhupariyabhāvena parivattantā kīḷantīti attho. Ciṅgulakenāti ciṅgulakaṃ vuccati tālapaṇṇādīhi kataṃ vātappahārena paribbhamanacakkaṃ, tena kīḷanti. Pattāḷhakenāti pattāḷhakaṃ vuccati paṇṇanāḷi, tāya vālikādīni minantā kīḷanti. Rathakenāti khuddakarathena. Dhanukenāti khuddakadhanunā.

‘By salākahattha’ means: having moistened a bundle of bamboo splints in lac, madder juice, or flour-water, they ask, 'What shall it be?' and, striking it on the ground or a wall, they play by showing figures of elephants, horses, and so on. ‘By akkha’ means: with a ball. ‘By paṅgacīra’ means: paṅgacīra is called a small leaf-pipe; they play by blowing it. ‘By vaṅkaka’ means: with a small plow, a plaything of village boys. ‘By mokkhacikā’ means: mokkhacikā is called the game of turning somersaults; the meaning is that they play by turning upside down, either by holding a stick in the air or by placing their head on the ground. ‘By ciṅgulaka’ means: ciṅgulaka is called a wheel made from palm leaves and so on, which spins when struck by the wind; they play with it. ‘By pattāḷhaka’ means: pattāḷhaka is called a small leaf-cup; they play by measuring sand and so on with it. ‘By rathaka’ means: with a small chariot. ‘By dhanuka’ means: with a small bow.

Akkharikāyāti akkharikā vuccati ākāse vā piṭṭhiyaṃ vā akkharajānanakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Manesikāyāti manesikā vuccati manasā cintitajānanakīḷā, tāya kīḷanti. Yathāvajjenāti yathāvajjaṃ vuccati kāṇakuṇikakhañjādīnaṃ yaṃ yaṃ vajjaṃ taṃ taṃ payojetvā dassanakīḷā tāya kīḷanti, velambhakā viya. Hatthismimpi sikkhantīti hatthinimittaṃ yaṃ sippaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ sikkhanti. Eseva nayo assādīsu. Dhāvantipīti parammukhā gacchantā dhāvanti. Ādhāvantipīti yattakaṃ dhāvanti, tattakameva [P 3.0622] abhimukhā puna āgacchantā ādhāvanti. Nibbujjhantīti mallayuddhaṃ karonti. Nalāṭikampi dentīti “sādhu, sādhu, bhaginī”ti attano nalāṭe aṅguliṃ ṭhapetvā tassā nalāṭe ṭhapenti. Vividhampi anācāraṃ ācarantīti aññampi pāḷiyaṃ anāgataṃ mukhaḍiṇḍimādivividhaṃ anācāraṃ ācaranti.

‘By akkharikā’ means: akkharikā is called the game of recognizing letters in the sky or on one's back; they play that game. ‘By manesikā’ means: manesikā is called the game of knowing what is thought in the mind; they play that game. ‘By yathāvajja’ means: yathāvajja is called the game of demonstrating whatever fault there is of the blind, the crooked-limbed, the lame, and so on, by imitating it, like contortionists. ‘They also train in elephant-lore’ means they train in whatever skill should be learned concerning elephants. The same principle applies to horses and so on. ‘They also run’ means they run while going with their faces turned away. ‘They also run back’ means having run a certain distance, they run back that same distance, coming face-to-face again. ‘They wrestle’ means they engage in a wrestling match. ‘They also give a forehead-sign’ means, saying, 'Excellent, excellent, sister!', having placed a finger on their own forehead, they then place it on her forehead. ‘They practice various kinds of misconduct’ means they practice various other kinds of misconduct not mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as beating the mouth like a drum.

432. Pāsādikenāti pasādāvahena, sāruppena samaṇānucchavikena. Abhikkantenāti gamanena. Paṭikkantenāti nivattanena. Ālokitenāti purato dassanena. Vilokitenāti ito cito ca dassanena. Samiñjitenāti pabbasaṅkocanena. Pasāritenāti tesaṃyeva pasāraṇena. Sabbattha itthambhūtākhyānatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, satisampajaññehi abhisaṅkhatattā pāsādika abhikkanta-paṭikkanta-ālokita-vilokita-samiñjita-pasārito hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Okkhittacakkhūti heṭṭhā-khittacakkhu[M 2.0206]. Iriyāpathasampannoti tāya pāsādikaabhikkantāditāya sampannairiyāpatho.

432. ‘Pāsādikena’ means inspiring confidence, suitable, and befitting a recluse. ‘Abhikkantena’ means by going forward. ‘Paṭikkantena’ means by returning. ‘Ālokitena’ means by looking ahead. ‘Vilokitena’ means by looking from side to side. ‘Samiñjitena’ means by bending the limbs. ‘Pasāritena’ means by stretching them out. In all these cases, the instrumental case is used to describe a state. Because these actions are conditioned by mindfulness and clear comprehension, it is said that one is inspiring confidence in going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking around, bending, and stretching. ‘Okkhittacakkhu’ means having eyes cast down. ‘Iriyāpathasampanno’ means endowed with deportment through that state of inspiring confidence in going forward and so on.

Kvāyanti ko ayaṃ. Abalabalo viyāti abalo kira bondo vuccati, atisayatthe ca idaṃ āmeḍitaṃ, tasmā atibondo viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Mandamandoti abhikkantādīnaṃ anuddhatatāya [V 2.0186] atimando. Atisaṇhoti evaṃ guṇameva dosato dassenti. Bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko viyāti okkhittacakkhutāya bhakuṭiṃ katvā saṅkuṭitamukho kupito viya vicaratīti maññamānā vadanti. Saṇhāti nipuṇā, “amma tāta bhaginī”ti evaṃ upāsakajanaṃ yuttaṭṭhāne upanetuṃ chekā, na yathā ayaṃ; evaṃ abalabalo viyāti adhippāyo. Sakhilāti sākhalyena yuttā. Sukhasambhāsāti idaṃ purimassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yesañhi sukhasambhāsā sammodanīyakathā nelā hoti kaṇṇasukhā, te sakhilāti vuccanti. Tenāhaṃsu – “sakhilā sukhasambhāsā”ti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – amhākaṃ ayyā upāsake disvā madhuraṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathenti, tasmā sakhilā sukhasambhāsā, na yathā ayaṃ; evaṃ mandamandā viyāti. Mihitapubbaṅgamāti mihitaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etesaṃ vacanassāti mihitapubbaṅgamā, paṭhamaṃ sitaṃ katvā pacchā vadantīti attho. Ehisvāgatavādinoti upāsakaṃ disvā “ehi svāgataṃ [P 3.0623] tavā”ti evaṃvādino, na yathā ayaṃ; evaṃ saṅkuṭitamukhatāya bhākuṭikabhākuṭikā viya evaṃ mihitapubbaṅgamāditāya abhākuṭikabhāvaṃ atthato dassetvā puna sarūpenapi dassento āhaṃsu – “abhākuṭikā uttānamukhā pubbabhāsino”ti. Uppaṭipāṭiyā vā tiṇṇampi ākārānaṃ abhāvadassanametanti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ettha hi “abhākuṭikā”ti iminā bhākuṭikabhākuṭikākārassa abhāvo dassito. “Uttānamukhā”ti iminā mandamandākārassa, ye hi cakkhūni ummiletvā ālokanena uttānamukhā honti, na te mandamandā. Pubbabhāsinoti iminā abalabalākārassa abhāvo dassito, ye hi ābhāsanakusalatāya “amma tātā”ti paṭhamataraṃ ābhāsanti, na te abalabalāti.

What kind of monk is this? Like one who is very dull—a dull, sluggish person, it is said, is called `abalo` (weak/dull), and this is a repetition for emphasis; therefore, it means 'like one who is very dull'. 'Very gentle' means, due to the unagitatedness in going forward and so on, he is very gentle, very subtle; thus they point out a virtue as if it were a fault. 'Like one who is constantly frowning' means, thinking that due to his downcast eyes, he goes about with a frown and a contracted face as if angry, they speak thus. 'Skillful' means they are adept, clever at drawing the lay community near in a suitable place by saying, 'Mother, Father, Sister'; not like this one. Thus, the intention is: 'like one who is very dull'. 'Affable' means endowed with friendliness. 'Pleasant in speech' is a term explaining the reason for the preceding one. For those whose speech is pleasant to engage with, whose conversation is agreeable, faultless, and pleasant to the ear, they are called 'affable'. Therefore they said, 'affable, pleasant in speech'. Herein, this is the intention: 'Our venerable ones, upon seeing laypeople, speak sweet and agreeable words; therefore, they are affable and pleasant in speech, not like this one, who is thus like one who is very gentle.' 'Preceded by a smile' means a smile is the forerunner of their speech; the meaning is that they first smile and then speak. 'Saying, “Come, you are welcome”' means, upon seeing a layperson, they are ones who say, 'Come, your arrival is welcome'; not like this one, who, due to a contracted face, is like one who is constantly frowning. Thus, having shown by implication the state of not frowning by means of their being preceded by a smile and so on, and then showing it again in its own form, they said: 'not frowning, with open faces, speaking first'. Alternatively, it should be understood that this shows the absence of all three characteristics in reverse order. How so? Here, by 'not frowning', the absence of the characteristic of one who is constantly frowning is shown. By 'with open faces', the absence of the characteristic of one who is very gentle is shown; for those who, by opening their eyes and looking, have open faces are not very gentle. By 'speaking first', the absence of the characteristic of one who is very dull is shown; for those who, due to their skill in addressing, are the first to speak, saying 'Mother, Father', are not very dull.

Ehi, bhante, gharaṃ gamissāmāti so kira upāsako “na kho, āvuso, piṇḍo labbhatī”ti vutte “tumhākaṃ bhikkhūhiyeva etaṃ kataṃ[M 2.0207], sakalampi gāmaṃ vicarantā na lacchathā”ti vatvā piṇḍapātaṃ dātukāmo “ehi, bhante, gharaṃ gamissāmā”ti āha. Kiṃ panāyaṃ payuttavācā hoti, na hotīti? Na hoti. Pucchitapañho nāmāyaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā idāni cepi pubbaṇhe vā sāyanhe vā antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ koci puccheyya – “kasmā, bhante, carathā”ti? Yenatthena carati, taṃ ācikkhitvā “laddhaṃ na laddha”nti vutte sace na laddhaṃ, “na laddha”nti vatvā yaṃ so deti, taṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Regarding 'Come, venerable sir, we will go to the house': that lay follower, it is said, when told, 'Friend, alms are not obtained,' replied, 'This was done by your monks; even wandering the entire village, you will not receive anything.' Then, wishing to give alms, he said, 'Come, venerable sir, let us go to the house.' Now, is this speech connected with requisites, or not? It is not. This is called a question that has been asked, and it is proper to answer it. Therefore, even now, if someone should ask a monk who has entered a village in the morning or evening, 'Venerable sir, why do you wander?', he should explain the purpose for which he wanders. When asked, 'Have you obtained it or not?', if he has not obtained it, having said, 'I have not obtained it,' it is proper to accept whatever that person gives.

Duṭṭhoti na pasādādīnaṃ vināsena duṭṭho, puggalavasena duṭṭho. Dānapathānīti dānāniyeva vuccanti. Atha vā dānapathānīti dānanibaddhāni dānavattānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Upacchinnānīti dāyakehi [V 2.0187] upacchinnāni, na te tāni etarahi denti. Riñcantīti visuṃ honti nānā honti, pakkamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṇṭhaheyyāti sammā tiṭṭheyya, pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ patiṭṭhā bhaveyya.

“Corrupted” does not mean corrupted by the destruction of faith and so on, but corrupted with respect to the person. “Paths of giving” refers simply to gifts. Alternatively, “paths of giving” means established giving, the observances of giving. “Cut off” means cut off by the donors; they do not give them now. “They are abandoned” means they become separate, they become distinct; it is said they depart. “Should be established” means should stand rightly, should become a support for monks of amiable virtue.

Evamāvusoti kho so bhikkhu saddhassa pasannassa upāsakassa sāsanaṃ sampaṭicchi. Evarūpaṃ kira sāsanaṃ kappiyaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā “mama vacanena bhagavato pāde vandathā”ti vā “cetiyaṃ paṭimaṃ bodhiṃ saṅghattheraṃ vandathā”ti vā “cetiye gandhapūjaṃ karotha, pupphapūjaṃ karothā”ti vā “bhikkhū sannipātetha, dānaṃ dassāma[P 3.0624], dhammaṃ sossāmāti vā īdisesu sāsanesu kukkuccaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Kappiyasāsanāni etāni na gihīnaṃ gihikammapaṭisaṃyuttānīti. Kuto ca tvaṃ, bhikkhu, āgacchasīti nisinno so bhikkhu na āgacchati atthato pana āgato hoti; evaṃ santepi vattamānasamīpe vattamānavacanaṃ labbhati, tasmā na doso. Pariyosāne “tato ahaṃ bhagavā āgacchāmī”ti etthāpi vacane eseva nayo.

“So it is, friend.” The monk accepted the message of the faithful, devoted lay follower. It is indeed proper to carry such a proper message. Therefore, concerning messages like “At my word, pay homage to the Blessed One’s feet,” or “Pay homage to the stupa, the image, the Bodhi tree, or the elder of the Sangha,” or “Make offerings of incense and flowers at the stupa,” or “Gather the monks; we will give a donation; we will listen to the Dhamma”—in such messages, scrupulousness should not be practiced. These are proper messages, not connected with the household affairs of laypeople. Regarding “And where do you come from, monk?”: that monk is seated, he is not in the process of coming. But in meaning, he has come. Even so, for the recent past, a present tense verb is used; therefore, there is no fault. At the end, in the statement “From there… I come,” this same principle applies.

433. Paṭhamaṃ assajipunabbasukā bhikkhū codetabbāti “mayaṃ tumhe vattukāmā”ti okāsaṃ kāretvā vatthunā ca āpattiyā ca codetabbā. Codetvā yaṃ na saranti, taṃ sāretabbā. Sace vatthuñca āpattiñca paṭijānanti, āpattimeva vā paṭijānanti, na vatthuṃ, āpattiṃ ropetabbā. Atha vatthumeva paṭijānanti, nāpattiṃ; evampi “imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ ayaṃ nāma āpattī”ti ropetabbā eva. Yadi neva vatthuṃ, nāpattiṃ paṭijānanti, āpattiṃ na ropetabbā ayamettha vinicchayo. Yathāpaṭiññāya pana āpattiṃ [M 2.0208] ropetvā; evaṃ pabbājanīyakammaṃ kātabbanti dassento “byattena bhikkhunā”tiādimāha, taṃ uttānatthameva.

433. First, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are to be charged. Having requested permission by saying, “We wish to speak to you,” they are to be charged with both the matter and the offense. After charging them, if there is something they do not remember, they should be reminded of it. If they admit both the matter and the offense, or if they admit the offense but not the matter, the offense should be established. Or if they admit only the matter and not the offense, even then the offense should be established, stating, “In this matter, there is such-and-such an offense.” If they admit neither the matter nor the offense, the offense should not be established. This is the decision here. Then, having established the offense according to the admission, to show that the act of banishment should be performed, he says, “by a competent monk,” etc. The meaning of that is plain.

Evaṃ pabbājanīyakammakatena bhikkhunā yasmiṃ vihāre vasantena yasmiṃ gāme kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ hoti, tasmiṃ vihāre vā tasmiṃ gāme vā na vasitabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ vihāre vasantena sāmantagāmepi piṇḍāya na caritabbaṃ. Sāmantavihārepi vasantena tasmiṃ gāme piṇḍāya na caritabbaṃ. Upatissatthero pana “bhante nagaraṃ nāma mahantaṃ dvādasayojanikampi hotī”ti antevāsikehi vutto “yassā vīthiyā kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ tattheva vārita”nti āha. Tato “vīthipi mahatī nagarappamāṇāva hotī”ti vutto “yassā gharapaṭipāṭiyā”ti āha, “gharapaṭipāṭīpi vīthippamāṇāva hotī”ti vutto ito cito ca satta gharāni vāritānī”ti āha. Taṃ pana sabbaṃ therassa manorathamattameva. Sacepi vihāro tiyojanaparamo hoti dvādasayojanaparamañca nagaraṃ, neva vihāre vasituṃ labbhati, na nagare caritunti.

Thus, a monk upon whom the act of banishment has been performed should not dwell in the monastery where he was residing, nor in the village where the act of corrupting families was committed. While dwelling in that monastery, he should not go for alms even in a nearby village. While dwelling in a nearby monastery, he should not go for alms in that village. However, the Elder Upatissa, when told by his resident pupils, “Venerable sir, a city can be large, even twelve yojanas in extent,” replied, “It is prohibited only in that very street where the act of corrupting families was committed.” Then, when told, “A street can also be large, the size of a city,” he replied, “In whichever row of houses…” When told, “A row of houses can also be the size of a street,” he replied, “Seven houses on this side and that side are prohibited.” But all of this was merely the Elder’s own inclination. Even if the monastery is at most three yojanas in extent and the city at most twelve yojanas, it is not permitted to dwell in the monastery, nor is it permitted to go for alms in the city.

435. Te [P 3.0625][V 2.0188] saṅghena pabbājanīyakammakatāti kathaṃ saṅgho tesaṃ kammaṃ akāsi? Na gantvāva ajjhottharitvā akāsi, atha kho kulehi nimantetvā saṅghabhattesu kayiramānesu tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne therā samaṇapaṭipadaṃ kathetvā “ayaṃ samaṇo, ayaṃ assamaṇo”ti manusse saññāpetvā ekaṃ dve bhikkhū sīmaṃ pave setvā etenevupāyena sabbesaṃ pabbājanīyakammaṃ akaṃsūti. Evaṃ pabbājanīyakammakatassa ca aṭṭhārasa vattāni pūretvā yācantassa kammaṃ paṭippassambhetabbaṃ. Paṭippassaddhakammenāpi ca tena yesu kulesu pubbe kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ, tato paccayā na gahetabbā, āsavakkhayappattenāpi na gahetabbā, akappiyāva honti. “Kasmā na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitena “pubbe evaṃ katattā”ti vutte, sace vadanti “na mayaṃ tena kāraṇena dema idāni sīlavantatāya demā”ti gahetabbā. Pakatiyā dānaṭṭhāneyeva kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ hoti. Tato pakatidānameva gahetuṃ vaṭṭati, yaṃ vaḍḍhetvā denti, taṃ na vaṭṭati.

435. They were subjected to the act of banishment by the Sangha—how did the Sangha perform this act in their case? Not by going and overwhelming them directly, but rather, when families had invited them and Sangha meals were being prepared, in various places the elders spoke about the practice of ascetics, making people understand, “This one is an ascetic, this one is not an ascetic.” Then, having sent one or two monks into the boundary, by this very means they performed the act of banishment for all. For one who has been subjected to the act of banishment, after fulfilling the eighteen duties and requesting, the act should be revoked. Even after the act has been revoked, that monk should not accept requisites from those families where he previously committed the act of corrupting families. Even if he has attained the destruction of the taints, he should not accept them; they remain unsuitable. If asked, “Why do you not accept?” and he replies, “Because of what was done previously,” if they then say, “We are not giving for that reason; now we give because of your virtuous conduct,” they may be accepted. The act of corrupting families is committed at a regular place of giving. From there, it is permissible to accept only the regular gift; what they give as an addition is not permissible.

Na sammā vattantīti te pana assajipunabbasukā aṭṭhārasasu vattesu sammā na vattanti. Na lomaṃ pātentīti anulomapaṭipadaṃ appaṭipajjanatāya na pannalomā honti. Na netthāraṃ vattantīti attano nittharaṇamaggaṃ na paṭipajjanti[M 2.0209]. Na bhikkhū khamāpentīti “dukkaṭaṃ, bhante, amhehi, na puna evaṃ karissāma, khamatha amhāka”nti evaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khamāpanaṃ na karonti. Akkosantīti kārakasaṅghaṃ dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti. Paribhāsantīti bhayaṃ nesaṃ dassenti. Chandagāmitā…pe… bhayagāmitā pāpentīti ete chandagāmino ca…pe… bhayagāmino cāti evaṃ chandagāmitāyapi…pe… bhayagāmitāyapi pāpenti, yojentīti attho. Pakkamantīti tesaṃ parivāresu pañcasu samaṇasatesu ekacce disā pakkamanti. Vibbhamantīti ekacce gihī honti. Kathañhi nāma assajipunabbasukā bhikkhūti ettha dvinnaṃ pamokkhānaṃ vasena sabbepi “assajipunabbasukā”ti [P 3.0626] vuttā.

They do not behave properly: these Assaji and Punabbasukas do not behave properly in the eighteen observances. They do not let their pride fall: because they do not practice the compliant path, they do not become those whose pride has fallen. They do not follow the path of deliverance: they do not practice the path leading to their own deliverance. They do not ask the bhikkhus for forgiveness: they do not ask the bhikkhus for forgiveness, saying, “Venerable sirs, we have done wrong; we will not do so again; please forgive us.” They abuse: they abuse the Sangha that performed the act with the ten grounds for abuse. They threaten: they show them danger. They cause them to fall into partiality based on desire… based on fear: this means they cause them to be partial due to desire… and partial due to fear; they involve them. They depart: of their retinue of five hundred monks, some depart to other regions. They fall away: some become householders. How indeed could the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka…: here, on account of the two leaders, all are called “the Assaji and Punabbasuka bhikkhus.”

436-7. Gāmaṃ vāti ettha nagarampi gāmaggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ. Tenassa padabhājane “gāmopi nigamopi nagarampi gāmo ceva nigamo cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha apākāraparikkhepo saāpaṇo nigamoti veditabbo.

436-7. In the phrase “to a village,” a city is also included by the term “village.” Therefore, in its word analysis, it is said: “A village, a market town, and a city are a village and a market town.” In this context, a market town should be understood as a settlement without a surrounding wall but with a market.

Kulāni dūsetīti kuladūsako. Dūsento ca na asucikaddamādīhi dūseti, atha kho attano duppaṭipattiyā tesaṃ pasādaṃ vināseti. Tenevassa padabhājane “pupphena vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo haritvā vā harāpetvā vā pakkositvā vā pakkosāpetvā vā sayaṃ vā upagatānaṃ [V 2.0189] yaṃkiñci attano santakaṃ pupphaṃ kulasaṅgahatthāya deti, dukkaṭaṃ. Parasantakaṃ deti, dukkaṭameva. Theyyacittena deti, bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Eseva nayo saṅghikepi. Ayaṃ pana viseso, senāsanatthāya niyāmitaṃ issaravatāya dadato thullaccayaṃ.

He who corrupts families is a corrupter of families. And in corrupting, he does not corrupt with things like filth and mud, but rather he destroys their confidence through his own misconduct. For that reason, in the word analysis of this term, it is said, “with a flower,” and so on. In this context, any monk who gives any flower belonging to himself—whether having brought it, having had it brought, having invited them, having had them invited, or to those who have come of their own accord—for the purpose of winning over families, commits a dukkaṭa offense. If he gives what belongs to another, it is also a dukkaṭa offense. If he gives with a thieving mind, he must be made to pay the price of the goods. This same principle applies to what belongs to the Sangha. This, however, is the distinction: for one who, acting as if he were the master, gives what has been designated for the purpose of lodgings, it is a thullaccaya offense.

Pupphaṃ nāma kassa dātuṃ vaṭṭati, kassa na vaṭṭatīti? Mātāpitūnnaṃ tāva haritvāpi harāpetvāpi pakkositvāpi pakkosāpetvāpi dātuṃ vaṭṭati, sesañātakānaṃ pakkosāpetvāva. Tañca kho vatthupūjanatthāya, maṇḍanatthāya pana sivaliṅgādipūjanatthāya vā kassacipi dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Mātāpitūnañca harāpentena ñātisāmaṇereheva harāpetabbaṃ. Itare pana yadi sayameva icchanti, vaṭṭati. Sammatena pupphabhājakena bhājanakāle sampattānaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Kurundiyaṃ sampattagihīnaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ “cūḷakaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Asammatena apaloketvā dātabbaṃ.

To whom is it permissible to give a flower, and to whom is it not permissible? To one’s parents, it is permissible to give, whether by bringing it oneself, having it brought, inviting them, or having them invited. To other relatives, it is permissible only after having had them invited. And this is for the purpose of honoring a sacred object; it is not permissible to give to anyone for the purpose of decoration or for worshiping a sivaliṅga and the like. And when having them brought for one’s parents, one should have them brought only by novices who are relatives. As for other novices, however, if they themselves wish to bring them, it is permissible. An appointed flower distributor may give a half share to novices who have arrived at the time of distribution. In the Kurundī commentary, it is said that a half share may be given to laypeople who have arrived. In the Mahāpaccariya commentary, it is said, “a small amount may be given.” One who is not appointed should give after having sought authorization.

Ācariyupajjhāyesu [M 2.0210] sagāravā sāmaṇerā bahūni pupphāni āharitvā rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapenti, therā pātova sampattānaṃ saddhivihārikādīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ vā “tvaṃ idaṃ gaṇha, tvaṃ idaṃ gaṇhā”ti denti, pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti. “Cetiyaṃ pūjessāmā”ti gahetvā gacchantāpi pūjaṃ karontāpi tattha tattha sampattānaṃ cetiyapūjanatthāya denti, etampi pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti. Upāsake akkapupphādīhi pūjente disvā “vihāre kaṇikārapupphādīni atthi, upāsakā tāni gahetvā pūjethā”ti vattumpi [P 3.0627] vaṭṭati. Bhikkhū pupphapūjaṃ katvā divātaraṃ gāmaṃ paviṭṭhe “kiṃ, bhante, atidivā paviṭṭhatthā”ti pucchanti, “vihāre bahūni pupphāni pūjaṃ akarimhā”ti vadanti. Manussā “bahūni kira vihāre pupphānī”ti punadivase pahūtaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ gahetvā vihāraṃ gantvā pupphapūjañca karonti, dānañca denti, vaṭṭati. Manussā “mayaṃ, bhante, asukadivasaṃ nāma pūjessāmā”ti pupphavāraṃ yācitvā anuññātadivase āgacchanti, sāmaṇerehi ca pageva pupphāni ocinitvā ṭhapitāni honti, te rukkhesu pupphāni apassantā “kuhiṃ, bhante, pupphānī”ti vadanti, sāmaṇerehi ocinitvā ṭhapitāni tumhe pana pūjetvā gacchatha, saṅgho aññaṃ divasaṃ pūjessatīti. Te pūjetvā dānaṃ datvā gacchanti, vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kurundiyañca “therā sāmaṇerehi dāpetuṃ na labhanti. Sace sayameva tāni pupphāni tesaṃ denti, vaṭṭati. Therehi pana ‘sāmaṇerehi ocinitvā ṭhapitānī’ti ettakameva vattabba”nti vuttaṃ. Sace pana pupphavāraṃ yācitvā anocitesu pupphesu yāgubhattādīni ādāya āgantvā sāmaṇere “ocinitvā dethā”ti vadanti. Ñātakasāmaṇerānaṃyeva ocinitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Aññātake ukkhipitvā rukkhasākhāya [V 2.0190] ṭhapenti, na orohitvā palāyitabbaṃ, ocinitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana koci dhammakathiko “bahūni upāsakā vihāre pupphāni yāgubhattādīni ādāya gantvā pupphapūjaṃ karothā”ti vadati, tasseva na kappatīti mahāpaccariyañca kurundiyañca vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “etaṃ akappiyaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti avisesena vuttaṃ.

The novices, respectful toward their teachers and preceptors, gather many flowers and arrange them in piles. The elders, early in the morning, distribute them to their co-residents, disciples, or lay devotees who have arrived, saying, 'You take this, you take this.' This is not called a giving of flowers. Even when, having taken them saying, 'We will worship the cetiya,' they, while going or while worshipping, give them to those who have arrived here and there for the purpose of cetiya worship, this too is not called a giving of flowers. Seeing lay devotees worshipping with Akka flowers and the like, it is permissible to say, 'Lay devotees, there are Kaṇikāra flowers and others in the monastery; take them and worship.' If bhikkhus, after performing flower worship, enter the village rather late in the day and are asked, 'Venerable sirs, why have you entered so late?' they may reply, 'We were performing worship with many flowers in the monastery.' The people, thinking, 'It seems there are many flowers in the monastery,' on the next day, bring abundant hard and soft food, go to the monastery, perform flower worship, and give alms; this is permissible. If people say, 'Venerable sirs, we will worship on such-and-such a day,' and, having requested a turn for offering flowers, they arrive on the permitted day, and the novices have already picked and set aside the flowers, and those people, not seeing flowers on the trees, ask, 'Venerable sirs, where are the flowers?' They are told, 'The novices have collected and set them aside; you may worship and go, the Sangha will worship on another day.' They worship, give alms, and depart; this is permissible. However, in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundi it is said: 'The elders cannot have the novices give them. If the novices themselves give those flowers to them, it is permissible. But the elders should only say this much: "They have been picked and set aside by the novices."' If, however, having requested a turn for offering flowers, people arrive with rice gruel, cooked rice, and other items while the flowers are still unpicked and tell the novices, 'Pick them and give them to us,' it is permissible only for related novices to pick and give. If they lift up a non-relative novice and place him on a tree branch, he should not descend and run away; it is permissible for him to pick and give. But if some Dhamma preacher says, 'Lay devotees, there are many flowers in the monastery; go there with rice gruel, cooked rice, and other items and perform flower worship,' it is not allowable for him, as stated in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundi. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is stated without distinction, 'This is improper and not permissible.'

Phalampi attano santakaṃ vuttanayeneva mātāpitūnaṃñca sesañātakānañca dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Kulasaṅgahatthāya pana dentassa vuttanayeneva attano santake parasantake saṅghike senāsanatthāya niyāmite ca dukkaṭādīni veditabbāni. Attano santakaṃyeva gilānamanussānaṃ vā sampattaissarānaṃ vā [M 2.0211] khīṇaparibbayānaṃ vā dātuṃ vaṭṭati, phaladānaṃ na hoti. Phalabhājakenāpi sammatena saṅghassa phalabhājanakāle sampattamanussānaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Asammatena apaloketvā dātabbaṃ. Saṅghārāmepi [P 3.0628] phalaparicchedena vā rukkhaparicchedena vā katikā kātabbā. Tato gilānamanussānaṃ vā aññesaṃ vā phalaṃ yācantānaṃ yathāparicchedena cattāri pañca phalāni dātabbāni. Rukkhā vā dassetabbā “ito gahetuṃ labbhatī”ti. “Igha phalāni sundarāni, ito gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ pana na vattabbaṃ.

Fruits, too, being one's own property, it is permissible to give them to parents and other relatives in the manner stated above. However, for the sake of maintaining good relations with a family, when giving, offenses such as dukkaṭa should be understood as explained above, whether the property is one's own, another's, or belonging to the Sangha, or designated for lodging purposes. It is permissible to give only one's own property to sick persons, visiting dignitaries, or those with exhausted provisions; this is not considered a giving of fruit. Even an appointed fruit distributor, during the Sangha's fruit distribution, it is permissible to give half a share to those people who have arrived. If not appointed, permission should be requested before giving. In a Sangha monastery, an agreement should be made either by defining the fruit area or the tree area. Then, when sick persons or others request fruit, four or five fruits should be given according to the agreement. Alternatively, trees may be shown, saying, 'It is permissible to take from here.' But one should not say, 'Here the fruits are beautiful; take from here.'

Cuṇṇenāti ettha attano santakaṃ sirīsacuṇṇaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kasāvaṃ yaṃkiñci kulasaṅgahatthāya deti, dukkaṭaṃ. Parasantakādīsupi vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – idha saṅghassa rakkhitagopitāpi rukkhacchalli garubhaṇḍameva. Mattikadantakaṭṭhaveḷūsupi garubhaṇḍūpagaṃ ñatvā cuṇṇe vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Paṇṇadānaṃ pana ettha na āgataṃ, tampi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Paratopi garubhaṇḍavinicchaye sabbaṃ vitthārena vaṇṇayissāma.

Regarding 'cuṇṇa' (powder): Here, giving one's own property, such as sirīsa powder or any other astringent substance, whatever it may be, for the sake of maintaining good relations with a family, is a dukkaṭa offense. The same principle should be understood to apply to property belonging to others, and so forth, according to the method already stated. But here there is this distinction: even tree bark protected and guarded by the Saṅgha is indeed a weighty item. Similarly, knowing that even clay, tooth-sticks, and bamboo are included among weighty items, the determination regarding powder should be understood according to the method stated. The giving of leaves, however, is not mentioned here; that too should be understood in the same manner. Furthermore, we will describe everything in detail in the determination of weighty items later.

Vejjikāya vāti ettha vejjakammavidhi tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Regarding 'vejikāya' (medical practice): Here the procedure of medical practice should be understood in the same way as explained in the commentary on the third Pārājika.

Jaṅghapesanikenāti ettha jaṅghapesaniyanti gihīnaṃ dūteyyasāsanaharaṇakammaṃ vuccati, taṃ na kātabbaṃ. Gihīnañhi sāsanaṃ gahetvā gacchantassa pade pade dukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ kammaṃ nissāya laddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi ajjhohāre ajjhohāre dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ sāsanaṃ aggahetvāpi pacchā “ayaṃ dāni so gāmo handa taṃ sāsanaṃ ārocemī”ti maggā okkamantassāpi pade pade dukkaṭaṃ. Sāsanaṃ ārocetvā laddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjato purimanayeneva dukkaṭaṃ. Sāsanaṃ aggahetvā āgatena pana “bhante tasmiṃ gāme itthannāmassa kā pavattī”ti pucchiyamānena kathetuṃ [V 2.0191] vaṭṭati, pucchitapañhe doso natthi. Pañcannaṃ pana sahadhammikānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ paṇḍupalāsassa attano veyyāvaccakarassa ca sāsanaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati, gihīnañca pubbe vuttappakāraṃ kappiyasāsanaṃ. Idañhi jaṅghapesaniyakammaṃ nāma na hoti. Imehi pana aṭṭhahi [P 3.0629] kuladūsakakammehi uppannapaccayā pañcannampi sahadhammikānaṃ na kappanti, abhūtārocanarūpiyasaṃvohārehi uppannapaccayasadisāva honti.

Regarding `jaṅghapesanikena`: here, the act of carrying messages or errands for householders is called `jaṅghapesaniya`; that should not be done. Indeed, for one who goes having taken a message from householders, there is a `dukkaṭa` offense at every step. For one who eats food obtained on account of that act, there is also a `dukkaṭa` offense with every mouthful. Even if one has not taken the message at first, but later thinks, 'This is that village now. Come, I will deliver that message,' and steps off the path, there is a `dukkaṭa` offense at every step. For one who eats food obtained after having delivered the message, there is a `dukkaṭa` offense in the same way as before. However, for one who has come without having taken a message, when asked, 'Venerable sir, in that village, what is the news of so-and-so?', it is permissible to speak; there is no fault in answering a question that is asked. However, it is permissible to carry a message for the five kinds of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, for one's mother and father, for a candidate for ordination, and for one's own attendant; and for householders, a suitable message of the kind mentioned before. Indeed, this is not called the act of a leg-messenger. However, requisites that have arisen from these eight family-corrupting acts are not allowable even for the five kinds of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma; they are just like requisites that have arisen from falsely declaring superhuman states and from transactions in gold and silver.

Pāpā [M 2.0212] samācārā assāti pāpasamācāro. Te pana yasmā mālāvaccharopanādayo idha adhippetā, tasmā “mālāvacchaṃ ropentipī”tiādinā nayenassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tirokkhāti parammukhā. Kulāni ca tena duṭṭhānīti ettha pana yasmā “kulānī”ti vohāramattametaṃ, atthato hi manussā tena duṭṭhā honti, tasmāssa padabhājane “pubbe saddhā hutvā”tiādimāha. Chandagāminoti chandena gacchantīti chandagāmino. Esa nayo sesesu. Samanubhāsitabbo tassa paṭinissaggāyāti ettha kuladūsakakammena dukkaṭameva. Yaṃ pana so saṅghaṃ paribhavitvā “chandagāmino”tiādimāha. Tassa paṭinissaggāya samanubhāsanakammaṃ kātabbanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva.

One is of evil conduct (`pāpasamācāro`) because one has evil conduct. However, since those evil conducts, such as the planting of flowering plants, are intended here, the word-analysis for this term is therefore stated by the method beginning with 'they plant flowering plants...' `Tirokkhā` means out of sight. However, in the phrase 'and the families are corrupted by him,' since this word 'families' is a mere convention—for in reality, it is the people who are corrupted by him—therefore, in its word-analysis, it states the phrase beginning with 'having formerly been faithful...' `Chandagāmino` means they follow a wrong course out of desire; thus they are called `chandagāmino`. This is the method for the remaining terms. Regarding 'he should be admonished for his abandoning [of that view]': for the act of corrupting families, there is only a `dukkaṭa` offense. But as for what he said, beginning with 'they follow a wrong course out of desire,' having disparaged the Saṅgha, the meaning should be seen thus: the act of admonition should be done for the abandoning of that statement. The rest everywhere has a plain meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīnipi paṭhamasaṅghabhedasadisānevāti.

The origins and so forth are just like those of the first offense of creating a schism in the Saṅgha.

Kuladūsakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on the corrupter of families is concluded.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Conclusion

442. Uddiṭṭhā kho…pe… evametaṃ dhārayāmīti ettha paṭhamaṃ āpatti etesanti paṭhamāpattikā, paṭhamaṃ vītikkamakkhaṇeyeva āpajjitabbāti attho. Itare pana yathā tatiye catutthe ca divase hotīti jaro “tatiyako catutthako”ti ca vuccati; evaṃ yāvatatiye samanubhāsanakamme hontīti yāvatatiyakāti veditabbā.

442. In the passage beginning, “It has been recited… Thus I maintain it,” the term `paṭhamāpattikā` (of the first-offense category) refers to those rules for which an offense occurs first. The meaning is that they are offenses to be incurred at the very first moment of transgression. As for the other offenses, just as a fever that occurs on the third and on the fourth day is called “tertian” and “quartan” respectively, so too, because these offenses occur up to the third formal admonition, they should be known as `yāvatatiyakā` (up-to-the-third-time offenses).
