Yāvatīhaṃ jānaṃ paṭicchādetīti yattakāni ahāni jānanto paṭicchādeti, “ahaṃ itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno”ti sabrahmacārīnaṃ nāroceti. Tāvatīhanti tattakāni ahāni. Akāmā parivatthabbanti na kāmena, na vasena, atha kho akāmena avasena parivāsaṃ samādāya vatthabbaṃ. Uttari chārattanti parivāsato uttari cha rattiyo. Bhikkhumānattāyāti bhikkhūnaṃ mānanabhāvāya, ārādhanatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vīsatisaṅgho gaṇo assāti vīsatigaṇo[V 2.0192]. Tatrāti yatra sabbantimena [P 3.0630] paricchedena vīsatigaṇo bhikkhusaṅgho atthi tatra. Abbhetabboti abhietabbo sampaṭicchitabbo, abbhānakammavasena osāretabboti vuttaṃ hoti[M 2.0213], avhātabboti vā attho. Anabbhitoti na abbhito, asampaṭicchito, akatabbhānakammoti vuttaṃ hoti, anavhātoti vā attho. Sāmīcīti anudhammatā, lokuttaradhammaṃ anugatā ovādānusāsanī, sāmīci dhammatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha vuttanayamevāti.

`Yāvatīhaṃ jānaṃ paṭicchādeti` (For as long as one knowingly conceals): for as many days as one knowingly conceals, not informing one’s fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, “I have fallen into such-and-such an offense.” `Tāvatīhaṃ` (For that long) means for that many days. `Akāmā parivatthabbaṃ` (Probation is to be undertaken unwillingly): it is not to be undertaken by one’s desire, not by one’s own will; rather, having undertaken the probation unwillingly, without one’s own will, one should live it out. `Uttari chārattanti` (Beyond six nights) means six nights beyond the probation period. `Bhikkhumānattāyāti` (For the purpose of `mānatta` for the bhikkhu) means for the sake of being esteemed by the bhikkhus, for the purpose of pleasing them, is what is said. `Vīsatigaṇo` (a group of twenty) is a Saṅgha that has a group of twenty as its number. `Tatrā` (There) means where, by the very last determination, there is a Saṅgha of bhikkhus that is a group of twenty. `Abbhetabbo` (He is to be rehabilitated) means he is to be accepted, to be received; it is said that he is to be brought back into the fold by means of the act of rehabilitation, or the meaning is, he is to be called. `Anabbhito` (Not rehabilitated) means not accepted, not received; it is said that the act of rehabilitation has not been performed for him, or the meaning is, he has not been called. `Sāmīcī` (Proper) means conformity with the Dhamma, an instruction and admonition that follows the supramundane Dhamma; it is said to be the proper custom. The rest here is just as has been explained.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Terasakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Thirteen Rules is concluded.

3. Aniyatakaṇḍaṃ

3. The Chapter on the Indeterminate Rules

1. Paṭhamaaniyatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Indeterminate Training Rule

443. Tena [P 3.0631][M 2.0214][V 2.0193] samayena buddho bhagavāti paṭhamaaniyatasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha kālayuttaṃ samullapantoti kālaṃ sallakkhetvā yadā na añño koci samīpena gacchati vā āgacchati vā tadā tadanurūpaṃ “kacci na ukkaṇṭhasi, na kilamasi, na chātāsī”tiādikaṃ gehassitaṃ kathaṃ kathento. Kālayuttaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇantoti kālaṃ sallakkhetvā yadā añño koci samīpena gacchati vā āgacchati vā tadā tadanurūpaṃ “uposathaṃ kareyyāsi, salākabhattaṃ dadeyyāsī”tiādikaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathento.

443. The passage beginning, “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One…” is the first indeterminate training rule. Therein, `kālayuttaṃ samullapanto` (speaking what is suitable to the occasion) means, having considered the time, when no one else is going or coming nearby, then, speaking talk suitable to that situation, connected with the household, such as, “Are you not discontented? Not weary? Not hungry?” `Kālayuttaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇanto` (speaking the Dhamma that is suitable to the occasion) means, having considered the time, when someone else is going or coming nearby, then, speaking Dhamma talk suitable to that situation, such as, “You should observe the Uposatha,” “You should give ticket-food.”

Bahū dhītaro ca puttā ca assāti bahuputtā. Tassā kira dasa puttā dasa dhītaro ahesuṃ, bahū nattāro assāti bahunattā. Yatheva hi tassā evamassā puttadhītānampi vīsati vīsati dārakā ahesuṃ, iti sā vīsuttaracatusataputtanattaparivārā ahosi. Abhimaṅgalasammatāti uttamamaṅgalasammatā. Yaññesūti dānappadānesu. Chaṇesūti āvāhavivāhamaṅgalādīsu antarussavesu. Ussavesūti āsāḷhīpavāraṇanakkhattādīsu mahussavesu. Paṭhamaṃ bhojentīti “imepi dārakā tayā samānāyukā nirogā hontū”ti āyācantā paṭhamaṃyeva bhojenti, yepi saddhā honti pasannā, tepi bhikkhū bhojetvā tadanantaraṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ taṃyeva bhojenti. Nādiyīti tassā vacanaṃ na ādiyi, na gaṇhi, na vā ādaramakāsīti attho.

Because she has many daughters and sons, she is known as `Bahuputtā`. It is said that she had ten sons and ten daughters. Because she has many grandchildren, she is known as `Bahunattā`. Indeed, just as she had her own children, so too did each of her sons and daughters have twenty children; thus she had an entourage of four hundred and twenty children and grandchildren. `Abhimaṅgalasammatā` means esteemed as supremely auspicious. `Yaññesu` means in small and large acts of giving. `Chaṇesu` means in minor festivals, such as auspicious marriage ceremonies. `Ussavesu` means in great festivals, such as the Āsāḷhī and Pavāraṇā star festivals. `Paṭhamaṃ bhojenti` means people feed her first, wishing, “May these children, too, have a lifespan equal to yours and be free from illness.” And those who are faithful and have confidence, they too, having fed the monks, immediately thereafter feed her first of all. `Nādiyi` means he did not take her word, did not accept it, or did not show respect; this is the meaning.

444-5. Alaṃkammaniyeti kammakkhamaṃ kammayogganti kammaniyaṃ, alaṃ pariyattaṃ kammaniyabhāvāyāti alaṃkammaniyaṃ, tasmiṃ alaṃkammaniye, yattha ajjhācāraṃ karontā sakkonti, taṃ kammaṃ [P 3.0632] kātuṃ tādiseti attho. Tenevassa padabhājane vuttaṃ – “sakkā hoti methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitu”nti, yattha methunaṃ dhammaṃ sakkā hoti paṭisevitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Nisajjaṃ [V 2.0194] kappeyyāti nisajjaṃ kareyya, nisīdeyyāti attho. Yasmā pana nisīditvāva [M 2.0215] nipajjati, tenassa padabhājane ubhayampi vuttaṃ. Tattha upanisinnoti upagantvā nisinno. Evaṃ upanipannopi veditabbo. Bhikkhu nisinneti bhikkhumhi nisinneti attho. Ubho vā nisinnāti dvepi apacchā apurimaṃ nisinnā. Ettha ca kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “sotassa raho”ti āgataṃ, cakkhussa raheneva pana paricchedo veditabbo. Sacepi hi pihitakavāṭassa gabbhassa dvāre nisinno viññū puriso hoti, neva anāpattiṃ karoti. Apihitakavāṭassa pana dvāre nisinno anāpattiṃ karoti. Na kevalañca dvāre antodvādasahatthepi okāse nisinno, sace sacakkhuko vikkhittopi niddāyantopi anāpattiṃ karoti. Samīpe ṭhitopi andho na karoti, cakkhumāpi nipajjitvā niddāyanto na karoti. Itthīnaṃ pana satampi anāpattiṃ na karotiyeva.

444-5. `Alaṃkammaniya` means fit for the act, suitable for the act, hence `kammaniya`; it is sufficient and adequate for being suitable for the act, thus it is `alaṃkammaniya`. In that `alaṃkammaniya` place means in such a place where those committing a transgression are able to perform that act. Therefore, in its word-analysis it is said: “It is possible to engage in sexual intercourse,” which means, where it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse. `Nisajjaṃ kappeyya` means one should arrange a seat, that is, one should sit down. But since one lies down only after having sat down, both sitting and lying down are mentioned in its word-analysis. Therein, `upanisinno` means having gone near, one is seated. `Upanipanno` should be understood in the same way. `Bhikkhu nisinne` means when the bhikkhu is seated. `Ubho vā nisinnā` means both are seated at the same time, not one after the other. And here, although in the Pāḷi text it says “secluded from the ear,” the determination should be understood as being by seclusion from the eye only. Indeed, even if an intelligent man is sitting at the door of a room with closed door-leaves, he does not constitute a non-offense. But an intelligent man sitting at the door of a room with open door-leaves does constitute a non-offense. And it is not only a man sitting at the door; an intelligent man with eyesight sitting even in a space within twelve cubits, even if he is distracted or dozing, constitutes a non-offense. A blind person, even though standing nearby, does not constitute a non-offense, nor does a person with eyesight if he is lying down and sleeping. But even a hundred women certainly do not constitute a non-offense.

Saddheyyavacasāti saddhātabbavacanā. Sā pana yasmā ariyasāvikāva hoti, tenassa padabhājane “āgataphalā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āgataṃ phalaṃ assāti āgataphalā paṭiladdhasotāpattiphalāti attho. Abhisametāvinīti paṭividdhacatusaccā. Viññātaṃ sikkhattayasāsanaṃ etāyāti viññātasāsanā. Nisajjaṃ bhikkhu paṭijānamānoti kiñcāpi evarūpā upāsikā disvā vadati, atha kho bhikkhu nisajjaṃ paṭijānamānoyeva tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ aññatarena kāretabbo, na appaṭijānamānoti attho.

`Saddheyyavacasā` means one whose word is to be believed. And since she is in fact a noble female disciple, in the word-analysis for this term it is said, “one who has attained the fruit” (`āgataphalā`), and so on. Therein, `āgataphalā` is explained as ‘the fruit has been attained by her’; the meaning is one who has obtained the fruit of stream-entry. `Abhisametāvinī` means one who has penetrated the Four Truths. `Viññātasāsanā` means one by whom the teaching of the threefold training has been understood. `Nisajjaṃ bhikkhu paṭijānamāno` (if the bhikkhu acknowledges the sitting): the meaning is that although such a female lay disciple speaks upon seeing him, the bhikkhu is to be dealt with according to one of the three rules only if he acknowledges the sitting, and not if he does not acknowledge it.

Yena vā sā saddheyyavacasā upāsikā vadeyya tena so bhikkhu kāretabboti nisajjādīsu ākāresu yena vā ākārena saddhiṃ methunadhammādīni āropetvā sā upāsikā vadeyya, paṭijānamānova tena so bhikkhu kāretabbo. Evarūpāyapi upāsikāya vacanamattena na kāretabboti attho. Kasmā? Yasmā diṭṭhaṃ nāma tathāpi hoti, aññathāpi hoti.

The phrase `Yena vā... kāretabbo` means: regarding the modes of conduct such as sitting, by whatever manner that laywoman whose word is to be believed might speak, having made an accusation involving sexual intercourse and so on, that monk is to be dealt with according to that accusation only if he acknowledges it. The meaning is that he is not to be dealt with by the mere word of even such a laywoman. Why? Because what is seen can be so, and it can also be otherwise.

Tadatthajotanatthañca idaṃ vatthuṃ udāharanti – mallārāmavihāre [P 3.0633] kira eko khīṇāsavatthero ekadivasaṃ upaṭṭhākakulaṃ gantvā antogehe nisīdi, upāsikāpi sayanapallaṅkaṃ nissāya ṭhitā hoti. Atheko piṇḍacāriko dvāre ṭhito disvā “thero upāsikāya saddhiṃ ekāsane nisinno”ti saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā punappunaṃ olokesi. Theropi “ayaṃ mayi asuddhaladdhiko jāto”ti sallakkhetvā katabhattakicco vihāraṃ gantvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā antova nisīdi. Sopi bhikkhu “theraṃ codessāmī”ti [M 2.0216] āgantvā ukkāsitvā dvāraṃ vivari. Thero tassa cittaṃ ñatvā ākāse uppatitvā kūṭāgārakaṇṇikaṃ nissāya pallaṅkena nisīdi. Sopi bhikkhu [V 2.0195] anto pavisitvā mañcañca heṭṭhāmañcañca oloketvā theraṃ apassanto uddhaṃ ullokesi, atha ākāse nisinnaṃ theraṃ disvā “bhante, evaṃ mahiddhikā nāma tumhe mātugāmena saddhiṃ ekāsane nisinnabhāvaṃ vadāpetha evā”ti āha. Thero “antaragharasseveso āvuso doso, ahaṃ pana taṃ saddhāpetuṃ asakkonto evamakāsiṃ, rakkheyyāsi ma”nti vatvā otarīti.

And to illuminate that meaning, they cite this story: It is said that in the Mallārāma monastery, an elder who was an Arahant went to a supporter's home one day and sat inside the house. The laywoman, too, was standing leaning on a couch. Then a certain monk on alms-round, standing at the door, saw this and acquired the perception, “The elder is seated on one seat with the laywoman,” and looked again and again. The elder, too, marking that “This one has acquired an impure view of me,” finished his meal, went to the monastery, entered his own dwelling place, and sat inside. That monk, thinking, “I will reprove the elder,” came, cleared his throat, and opened the door. The elder, knowing his mind, rose into the air and sat cross-legged, leaning against the pinnacle of the gabled building. That monk entered, looked at the bed and under the bed, and not seeing the elder, looked up. Then, seeing the elder seated in the air, he said: “Venerable sir, being one of such great psychic power, would you allow it to be said that you were sitting on one seat with a woman?” The elder said: “Friend, this is the fault of being inside a house. But I, being unable to make you believe, have done this. You should protect me.” Having said this, he descended.

446. Ito paraṃ sā ce evaṃ vadeyyātiādi sabbaṃ paṭiññāya kāraṇākāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, tattha mātugāmassa methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantoti mātugāmassa magge methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantoti attho. Nisajjāya kāretabboti nisajjaṃ paṭijānitvā methunadhammapaṭisevanaṃ appaṭijānanto methunadhammapārājikāpattiyā akāretvā nisajjāmattena yaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati tāya kāretabbo, pācittiyāpattiyā kāretabboti attho. Etena nayena sabbacatukkesu vinicchayo veditabbo.

446. After this, all that begins with “If she should say thus...” was said for the purpose of showing, by way of confession, the manner of dealing with the case. Therein, “engaging in the sexual act with a woman” means engaging in the sexual act in the woman's sexual organ. “He should be dealt with for the sitting” means: while confessing to the sitting but not confessing to engaging in the sexual act, without being dealt with for the Pārājika offense for the sexual act, he should be dealt with for whatever offense he incurs by the mere sitting. The meaning is that he should be dealt with for a Pācittiya offense. By this method, the decision should be understood in all the tetrads.

451. Sikkhāpadapariyosāne pana āpattānāpattiparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttesu gamanaṃ paṭijānātītiādīsu gamanaṃ paṭijānātīti “rahonisajjassādatthaṃ gatomhī”ti evaṃ gamanaṃ paṭijānāti, nisajjanti nisajjassādeneva nisajjaṃ paṭijānāti. Āpattinti tīsu aññataraṃ āpattiṃ. Āpattiyā kāretabboti tīsu yaṃ paṭijānāti, tāya kāretabbo. Sesamettha catukke uttānādhippāyameva. Dutiyacatukke pana gamanaṃ na paṭijānātīti raho nisajjassādavasena na paṭijānāti[P 3.0634], “salākabhattādinā attano kammena gatomhi, sā pana mayhaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ āgatā”ti vadati. Sesametthāpi uttānādhippāyameva.

451. Now, at the end of the training rule, among the things said to show the distinction between an offense and non-offense, such as “He confesses to going”: “He confesses to going” means he confesses to going thus: “I went for the sake of enjoying a secluded sitting.” As for “the sitting,” he confesses to the sitting only through the enjoyment of sitting. As for “an offense,” it means one offense among the three. “He should be dealt with for the offense” means he should be dealt with for whichever of the three he confesses to. The rest in this tetrad has a clear meaning. Now, in the second tetrad, “he does not confess to going” means he does not confess in the sense of enjoying a secluded sitting; he says, “I went for my own task, such as for a ticket-meal, but she came to the place where I was sitting.” Here too, the rest has a clear meaning.

Ayaṃ pana sabbattha vinicchayo – raho nisajjassādoti methunadhammasannissitakileso vuccati. Yo bhikkhu tenassādena mātugāmassa santikaṃ gantukāmo akkhiṃ añjeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Nivāsanaṃ nivāseti, kāyabandhanaṃ bandhati, cīvaraṃ pārupati, sabbattha payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Gantvā nisīdati, dukkaṭameva. Mātugāme āgantvā nisinnamatte [M 2.0217] pācittiyaṃ. Sace sā itthī kenaci karaṇīyena uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya punappunaṃ nisīdati, nisajjāya nisajjāya pācittiyaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya gato, sā na diṭṭhā, aññā āgantvā nisīdati, assāde uppanne pācittiyaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “gamanakālato paṭṭhāya asuddhacittattā āpattiyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Sace sambahulā āgacchanti, mātugāmagaṇanāya pācittiyāni. Sace uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya punappunaṃ nisīdanti, nisajjāgaṇanāya pācittiyāni. Aniyametvā [V 2.0196] diṭṭhadiṭṭhāya saddhiṃ rahassādaṃ kappessāmīti gantvā nisinnassāpi āgatāgatānaṃ vasena punappunaṃ nisajjāvasena ca vuttanayeneva āpattiyo veditabbā. Sace suddhacittena gantvā nisinnassa santikaṃ āgantvā nisinnāya itthiyā rahassādo uppajjati anāpatti.

Now, this is the decision in all cases: “enjoyment of a secluded sitting” is the name for the defilement connected with the sexual act. Whatever monk, with that enjoyment, desiring to go into a woman's presence, applies eyeliner, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. He puts on his lower garment, fastens his waistband, drapes his robe—for each and every effort, it is a Dukkaṭa. He goes—for each and every step, it is a Dukkaṭa. Having gone, he sits—it is just a Dukkaṭa. At the mere moment a woman has come and sat down, it is a Pācittiya offense. If that woman, for some reason, gets up again and again and sits down repeatedly, for each and every sitting, it is a Pācittiya. He went with a certain woman in mind, but she is not seen; another comes and sits down—when enjoyment arises, it is a Pācittiya. But in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: “From the time of going, because of an impure mind, it is indeed an offense.” If many women come, there are Pācittiya offenses according to the count of women. For one who, without specifying, goes and sits thinking, “I will arrange for the enjoyment of seclusion with whichever woman I see,” the offenses should be understood in the manner stated, by way of those who have come and come, and by way of repeated sittings. If, for one who has gone and sat with a pure mind, the enjoyment of seclusion arises when a woman comes and sits in his presence, there is no offense.

Samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamapārājikasadisānevāti.

The origins and so forth are just like those of the first Pārājika offense.

Paṭhamaaniyatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first Aniyata training rule is concluded.

2. Dutiyaaniyatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Second Aniyata Training Rule

452. Tena samayena buddho bhagavāti dutiyaaniyatasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha bhagavatā paṭikkhittantiādimhi “yaṃ eko ekāya raho paṭicchanne āsane alaṃkammaniye nisajjaṃ kappeyya, taṃ nisajjaṃ kappetuṃ paṭikkhitta”nti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Itarathā hi “ekassa ekāyā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, kasmā? “Paṭikkhitta”nti vuttattā. Sāmiatthe vā etaṃ paccattavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

452. “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One…” is the second Aniyata training rule. Therein, regarding the initial phrase “prohibited by the Blessed One,” the connection of the words should be understood thus: “Whatever sitting a monk might arrange with one woman in a secluded, concealed seat suitable for the act of sexual intercourse, it is prohibited to arrange that sitting.” For otherwise, it would have to be said “of one, with one.” Why? Because it was said, “prohibited.” Alternatively, this nominative case should be understood in the sense of the agent.

453. Na heva kho pana paṭicchannanti ettha pana yampi bahi parikkhittaṃ anto vivaṭaṃ pariveṇaṅgaṇādi, tampi [P 3.0635] antogadhanti veditabbaṃ. Evarūpañhi ṭhānaṃ appaṭicchanneyeva gahitanti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ paṭhamasikkhāpadanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi idha itthīpi purisopi yo koci viññū anandho abadhiro antodvādasahatthe okāse ṭhito vā nisinno vā vikkhittopi niddāyantopi anāpattiṃ karoti. Badhiro pana cakkhumāpi andho vā abadhiropi na karoti. Pārājikāpattiñca parihāpetvā duṭṭhullavācāpatti vuttāti ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Ubhayatthāpi ummattakaādikammikānaṃ anāpatti.

453. However, regarding the phrase “not necessarily concealed,” here, whatever place, such as the grounds of a monastery, is enclosed on the outside but open on the inside, that too should be understood as included. For it is said in the Mahāpaccarī that such a place is taken only as “unconcealed.” The rest should be understood according to the method of the first training rule. It is only here that if any discerning person, whether woman or man, who is not blind and not deaf, is standing or sitting in a space within twelve cubits, even if distracted or drowsing, they make for a non-offense. However, a deaf person, even one with sight, or a blind person, even one who is not deaf, does not make for a non-offense. And the offense of coarse speech is stated, having set aside the Pārājika offense—this is the distinction.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu [M 2.0218] idaṃsikkhāpadaṃ tisamuṭṭhānaṃ – kāyacittato, vācācittato, kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, sukhamajjhattavedanāhi dvivedanaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Regarding its origins and so on, this training rule has three origins: it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action, dependent on perception, intentional, a worldly fault, a bodily action, a verbal action, arising from an unwholesome mind, and is felt with two feelings: pleasant and neutral. The rest is of clear meaning.

Dutiyaaniyatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second Aniyata training rule is concluded.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya,

Aniyatavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Aniyata section is concluded.

4. Nissaggiyakaṇḍaṃ

4. The Section on Forfeiture

1. Cīvaravaggo

1. The Chapter on Robes

1. Paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the First Kathina Training Rule

Tiṃsa [P 3.0636][M 2.0219] nissaggiyā dhammā, ye vuttā samitāvinā;

Tesaṃ dāni karissāmi, apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ.

The thirty Nissaggiya rules that were spoken by the Tranquil One; of these, I shall now provide an explanation of terms not previously explained.

459. Tena [V 2.0197] samayena buddho bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati gotamake cetiye. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ ticīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ hotīti ettha ticīvaranti antaravāsako uttarāsaṅgo saṅghāṭīti idaṃ cīvarattayaṃ paribhuñjituṃ anuññātaṃ hoti. Yattha panetaṃ anuññātaṃ, yadā ca anuññātaṃ, yena ca kāraṇena anuññātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ cīvarakkhandhake jīvakavatthusmiṃ (mahāva. 326 ādayo) āgatameva. Aññeneva ticīvarena gāmaṃ pavisantīti yena vihāre acchanti nhānañca otaranti, tato aññena, evaṃ divase divase nava cīvarāni dhārenti.

459. “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Gotamaka Shrine. Now at that time, the Blessed One had allowed the monks three robes.” Here, “three robes” means the lower robe, the upper robe, and the outer robe; this set of three robes was permitted to be used. As to where this was permitted, when it was permitted, and for what reason it was permitted, all that has already appeared in the Robe Chapter, in the story of Jīvaka. “They enter the village with another set of three robes” means: with a different set of robes from the one with which they stay in the monastery and go down to bathe. Thus, day by day, they wear nine robes.

460. Uppannaṃ hotīti anupaññattiyā dvāraṃ dadamānaṃ paṭilābhavasena uppannaṃ hoti, no nipphattivasena.

460. “It had arisen” means: giving an opening for a subsequent enactment, it had arisen by way of acquisition, not by way of completion.

Āyasmato sāriputtassa dātukāmo hotīti āyasmā kira ānando bhagavantaṃ ṭhapetvā añño evarūpo guṇavisiṭṭho puggalo natthīti guṇabahumānena āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ atimamāyati. So sadāpi manāpaṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā rajitvā kappabinduṃ datvā therasseva deti, purebhatte paṇītaṃ yāgukhajjakaṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ vā labhitvāpi therasseva deti, pacchābhatte madhuphāṇitādīni labhitvāpi therasseva deti, upaṭṭhākakulehi dārake nikkhāmetvā pabbājetvāpi therassa [V 2.0198] santike upajjhaṃ gāhāpetvā sayaṃ anusāvanakammaṃ karoti. Āyasmāpi sāriputto “pitu kattabbakiccaṃ nāma jeṭṭhaputtassa bhāro, taṃ mayā bhagavato kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ ānando karoti, ahaṃ [P 3.0637] ānandaṃ nissāya appossukko viharituṃ labhāmī”ti āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ ativiya mamāyati, sopi manāpaṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā ānandattherasseva detīti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva[M 2.0220]. Evaṃ guṇabahumānena mamāyanto tadā uppannampi taṃ cīvaraṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa dātukāmo hotīti veditabbo.

‘He wished to give it to the Venerable Sāriputta.’ It is said that the Venerable Ānanda, out of great respect for his virtue, esteemed the Venerable Sāriputta exceedingly, thinking: ‘Setting aside the Blessed One, there is no other person so distinguished in virtue.’ Whenever he received a pleasing robe, he would dye it, mark it with a kappabindu, and give it only to the Elder. When he received excellent gruel, snacks, or alms-food in the forenoon, he would give it only to the Elder. When he received honey, molasses, and so on in the afternoon, he would give it only to the Elder. Having led forth boys from supporter families and given them the going-forth, he would have them take the Elder as their preceptor, while he himself performed the act of proclamation. The Venerable Sāriputta, too, esteemed the Venerable Ānanda exceedingly, thinking: ‘The duty to be done for one’s father is the burden of the eldest son. Ānanda performs that duty which ought to be done by me for the Blessed One. Relying on Ānanda, I am able to dwell without anxiety.’ He too, upon receiving a pleasing robe, would give it only to the Elder Ānanda. All this is the same as before. Thus it should be understood that, esteeming him out of great respect for his virtue, he wished to give that robe which had then arisen to the Venerable Sāriputta.

Navamaṃ vā bhagavā divasaṃ dasamaṃ vāti ettha pana sace bhaveyya “kathaṃ thero jānātī”ti? Bahūhi kāraṇehi jānāti. Sāriputtatthero kira janapadacārikaṃ pakkamanto ānandattheraṃ āpucchitvāva pakkamati “ahaṃ ettakena nāma kālena āgacchissāmi, etthantare bhagavantaṃ mā pamajjī”ti. Sace sammukhā na āpucchati, bhikkhū pesetvāpi āpucchitvāva gacchati. Sace aññattha vassaṃ vasati, ye paṭhamataraṃ bhikkhū āgacchanti, te evaṃ pahiṇati “mama vacanena bhagavato ca pāde sirasā vandatha, ānandassa ca ārogyaṃ vatvā maṃ ‘asukadivase nāma āgamissatī’ti vadathā”ti sadā ca yathāparicchinnadivaseyeva eti. Apicāyasmā ānando anumānenapi jānāti “ettake divase bhagavatā viyogaṃ sahanto adhivāsento āyasmā sāriputto vasi, ito dāni paṭṭhāya asukaṃ nāma divasaṃ na atikkamissati addhā āgamissatī”ti. Yesaṃ yesañhi paññā mahatī tesaṃ tesaṃ bhagavati pemañca gāravo ca mahā hotīti iminā nayenāpi jānāti. Evaṃ bahūhi kāraṇehi jānāti. Tenāha – “navamaṃ vā bhagavā divasaṃ dasamaṃ vā”ti. Evaṃ vutte yasmā idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ, na lokavajjaṃ; tasmā āyasmatā ānandena vuttasadisameva paricchedaṃ karonto “atha kho bhagavā…pe… dhāretu”nti. Sace pana therena addhamāso vā māso vā uddiṭṭho abhavissa, sopi bhagavatā anuññāto assa.

Regarding 'On the ninth day, O Blessed One, or the tenth day,' if the question should arise, 'How does the Elder know?'—he knows for many reasons. It is said that when the Elder Sāriputta set out on a journey through the country, he would take leave of the Elder Ānanda before departing, saying, 'I will return by such and such a time; in the meantime, do not be heedless regarding the Blessed One.' If he did not take leave in person, he would send monks to convey his farewell before leaving. If he spent the rains-residence elsewhere, he would send word with the first monks who returned, saying, 'In my name, venerate the Blessed One’s feet with your heads, and after telling Ānanda of my well-being, say, “He will return on such-and-such a day.”' And he always arrives precisely on the appointed day. Moreover, the Venerable Ānanda also knows by inference: 'The Venerable Sāriputta has endured separation from the Blessed One for so many days; from now on, he will not exceed such-and-such a day—he will surely return.' For of those whose wisdom is great, their love and reverence for the Blessed One are also great—he knows by this method as well. In this way, he knows for many reasons. Therefore, he said: 'On the ninth day, O Blessed One, or the tenth day.' When this was said, because this training rule is an offense by enactment and not a worldly offense, the Blessed One, making a determination similar to what had been stated by the Venerable Ānanda, said: 'Then... let him keep it.' However, if the Elder had specified half a month or a month, that too would have been allowed by the Blessed One.

462-3. Niṭṭhitacīvarasminti yena kenaci niṭṭhānena niṭṭhite cīvarasmiṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ cīvaraṃ karaṇenapi niṭṭhitaṃ hoti, nassanādīhipi tasmāssa padabhājane atthamattameva [P 3.0638] dassetuṃ bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ kataṃ vā hotītiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha katanti sūcikammapariyosānena kataṃ, sūcikammapariyosānaṃ nāma yaṃkiñci sūciyā kattabbaṃ pāsapaṭṭagaṇṭhikapaṭṭapariyosānaṃ katvā sūciyā paṭisāmanaṃ. Naṭṭhanti corādīhi haṭaṃ, etampi hi karaṇapalibodhassa niṭṭhitattā niṭṭhitanti vuccati. Vinaṭṭhanti upacikādīhi khāyitaṃ. Daḍḍhanti agginā daḍḍhaṃ. Cīvarāsā vā upacchinnāti [V 2.0199] “asukasmiṃ nāma kule [M 2.0221] cīvaraṃ labhissāmī”ti yā cīvarāsā uppannā hoti, sā vā upacchinnā, etesampi hi karaṇapalibodhasseva niṭṭhitattā niṭṭhitabhāvo veditabbo.

462-3. 'When the robe is finished' means when the robe is completed by any means of completion. However, since that robe is finished by being made, or by being lost, and so on, in the analysis of the term, 'the monk's robe is made...' and so on is stated merely to indicate the meaning. Here, 'made' means completed by the finishing of needlework; the finishing of needlework means having done whatever is to be done with a needle—ending with the loop-fastener and button-fastener—and then putting the needle away. 'Lost' means carried off by thieves, etc.; indeed, even this is called 'finished' because the obstacle of making it is finished. 'Destroyed' means eaten by termites, etc. 'Burned' means burned by fire. 'Or the hope for a robe is cut off' means that the hope for a robe which had arisen, such as 'I will receive a robe from such-and-such a family,' is cut off. In these cases too, the state of being 'finished' should be understood as being due to the finishing of the obstacle of making it.

Ubbhatasmiṃ kathineti kathine ca ubbhatasmiṃ. Etena dutiyassa palibodhassa abhāvaṃ dasseti. Taṃ pana kathinaṃ yasmā aṭṭhasu vā mātikāsu ekāya antarubbhārena vā uddharīyati, tenassa niddese “aṭṭhannaṃ mātikāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “aṭṭhimā, bhikkhave, mātikā kathinassa ubbhārāya – pakkamanantikā, niṭṭhānantikā, sanniṭṭhānantikā, nāsanantikā, savanantikā, āsāvacchedikā, sīmātikkantikā, sahubbhārā”ti evaṃ aṭṭha mātikāyo kathinakkhandhake āgatā. Antarubbhāropi “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho; yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho kathinaṃ uddhareyya, esā ñatti. Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho; saṅgho kathinaṃ uddharati, yassāyasmato khamati, kathinassa ubbhāro, so tuṇhassa; yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya. Ubbhataṃ saṅghena kathinaṃ, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (pāci. 926) evaṃ bhikkhunīvibhaṅge āgato. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ taṃ āgataṭṭhāneyeva vaṇṇayissāma. Idha pana vuccamāne pāḷi āharitabbā hoti, atthopi vattabbo. Vuttopi ca na suviññeyyo hoti, aṭṭhāne vuttattāya.

'When the kathina is lifted' means when the kathina has been lifted. By this, it shows the absence of the second obstacle. However, since that kathina is lifted by one of eight grounds or by an interim lifting, therefore in its explanation, 'of the eight grounds,' etc., was stated. Herein, 'Monks, these are the eight grounds for the lifting of the kathina: departure-bound, completion-bound, finalization-bound, destruction-bound, hearing-bound, hope-cutting, boundary-crossing, and shared lifting'—thus these eight grounds appear in the Kathina Section. The interim lifting also appears in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga thus: 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should lift the kathina. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha is lifting the kathina. Whoever of the venerable ones approves of the lifting of the kathina should be silent; whoever does not approve should speak. The kathina has been lifted by the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold it.' (Pāci. 926). What should be said about that, we will explain in the place where it appears. Here, however, if it were to be discussed, the Pāḷi would have to be cited, and the meaning would have to be stated. And even if stated, it would not be easily understood, because it would be stated out of place.

Dasāhaparamanti dasa ahāni paramo paricchedo assāti dasāhaparamo, taṃ dasāhaparamaṃ kālaṃ dhāretabbanti attho. Padabhājane [P 3.0639] pana atthamattameva dassetuṃ “dasāhaparamatā dhāretabba”nti vuttaṃ. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti “dasāhaparama”nti ettha yā dasāhaparamatā dasāhaparamabhāvo, ayaṃ ettako kālo yāva nātikkamati tāva dhāretabbanti.

'Ten days at most' (dasāhaparamaṃ) means that because ten days are its utmost limit (paramo paricchedo), it is called dasāhaparama. The meaning is that it should be kept for that period of ten days at most. In the word analysis, however, merely to show the meaning, it is stated: 'it should be kept with a ten-day maximum' (dasāhaparamatā dhāretabbaṃ). For this is what is said: Here, in 'ten days at most,' as long as the state of having a ten-day maximum—the condition of having a ten-day maximum—is not exceeded, for that long it should be kept.

Adhiṭṭhitavikappitesu apariyāpannattā atirekaṃ cīvaranti atirekacīvaraṃ. Tenevassa padabhājane vuttaṃ “anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappita”nti.

Because it is not included among those that are determined or shared, it is an extra robe; thus, it is called an 'extra robe' (atirekacīvara). For that very reason, in its word analysis, it is stated: 'undetermined and unshared' (anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitaṃ).

Channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataranti khomaṃ, kappāsikaṃ, koseyyaṃ, kambalaṃ, sāṇaṃ, bhaṅganti imesaṃ channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ. Etena cīvarassa jātiṃ dassetvā idāni pamāṇaṃ dassetuṃ “vikappanupagaṃ pacchima”nti āha. Tassa pamāṇaṃ dīghato [M 2.0222] dve vidatthiyo, tiriyaṃ vidatthi. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āyāmena aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ sugataṅgulena caturaṅgulavitthataṃ pacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358).

'One of the six robes' means any one of these six robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, or mixed fabric. Having shown the kind of robe by this, now to show its measure, it is said: 'the smallest, suitable for sharing.' Its measure is two spans in length and one span in width. Herein, this is the Pāli: 'Monks, I allow the smallest robe—eight finger-breadths in length by the Sugata's finger-breadth, and four finger-breadths in width—to be shared.'

Taṃ [V 2.0200] atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti taṃ yathāvuttajātippamāṇaṃ cīvaraṃ dasāhaparamaṃ kālaṃ atikkāmayato, etthantare yathā atirekacīvaraṃ na hoti tathā akubbato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, tañca cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti, pācittiyāpatti cassa hotīti attho. Atha vā nissajjanaṃ nissaggiyaṃ, pubbabhāge kattabbassa vinayakammassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Nissaggiyamassa atthīti nissaggiyamicceva. Kintaṃ? Pācittiyaṃ. Taṃ atikkāmayato sanissaggiyavinayakammaṃ pācittiyaṃ hotīti ayamettha attho. Padabhājane pana paṭhamaṃ tāva atthavikappaṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ hotī”ti mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā “ekādase aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ hoti, nissajjitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Puna yassa ca nissajjitabbaṃ, yathā ca nissajjitabbaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “saṅghassa vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ekādase aruṇuggamaneti ettha yaṃ divasaṃ cīvaraṃ uppannaṃ tassa yo aruṇo, so uppannadivasanissito, tasmā cīvaruppādadivasaena saddhiṃ ekādase aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Sacepi bahūni ekajjhaṃ bandhitvā vā veṭhetvā vā ṭhapitāni ekāva āpatti. Abaddhāveṭhitesu vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo.

For one who allows it to be exceeded, it is an offense entailing forfeiture. The meaning is: for one who allows that robe of the aforementioned kind and size to exceed the maximum period of ten days, and who does not act within that interval in such a way that it does not become an extra robe, it is an offense entailing forfeiture. That robe becomes subject to forfeiture, and a pācittiya offense is incurred by him. Alternatively, 'nissaggiya' means forfeiture; it is the name of a disciplinary act to be performed beforehand. It is called 'nissaggiya' because it has this forfeiture. What is that? A pācittiya offense. The meaning here is that for one who allows it to be exceeded, a pācittiya offense occurs together with the disciplinary act of forfeiture. In the word-analysis, however, to first show the alternative meaning, having set down the summary rule, "for one who allows it to be exceeded, it becomes subject to forfeiture," it is then said: "At the eleventh sunrise, it becomes subject to forfeiture and must be relinquished." Furthermore, to show to whom it must be relinquished and how it must be relinquished, it is said, "to the Saṅgha, or..." and so on. Therein, regarding "at the eleventh sunrise": the dawn of the day on which the robe arose is related to the day of its arising; therefore, it should be understood that it becomes subject to forfeiture at the eleventh sunrise, including the day the robe arose. Even if many robes are placed having been tied or wrapped up together, there is only one offense. For those that are not tied or wrapped, there are offenses according to the count of the items.

Nissajjitvā [P 3.0640] āpatti desetabbāti kathaṃ desetabbā? Yathā khandhake vuttaṃ, kathañca tattha vuttaṃ? Evaṃ vuttaṃ – “tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vuḍḍhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo – ‘ahaṃ, bhante, itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ paṭidesemī’”ti (cūḷava. 239). Idha pana sace ekaṃ cīvaraṃ hoti “ekaṃ nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti vattabbaṃ. Sace dve, “dve”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace bahūni “sambahulānī”ti vattabbaṃ. Nissajjanepi sace ekaṃ yathāpāḷimeva “idaṃ me, bhante, cīvara”nti vattabbaṃ. Sace dve vā bahūni vā, “imāni me, bhante, cīvarāni dasāhātikkantāni nissaggiyāni, imānāhaṃ saṅghassa nissajjāmī”ti vattabbaṃ. Pāḷiṃ vattuṃ asakkontena aññathāpi vattabbaṃ.

Regarding 'Having relinquished, the offense should be confessed': how should it be confessed? As it is stated in the Khandhaka. And how is it stated there? It is stated thus: 'Monks, that bhikkhu should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior bhikkhus, sit in a squatting position, raise his joined palms, and say this: "Venerable sir, I have incurred such-and-such an offense. I confess it."' Here, however, if there is one robe, it should be said, 'one pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture.' If there are two, it should be said, 'two.' If there are many, it should be said, 'many.' Also in the act of relinquishing, if there is one, it should be said just as in the Pāli: 'Venerable sir, this is my robe...' If there are two or many, it should be said: 'Venerable sirs, these robes of mine, having exceeded ten days, are subject to forfeiture; I relinquish these to the Saṅgha.' By one who is unable to say the Pāli, it may also be said in another way.

Byattena [M 2.0223] bhikkhunā paṭibalena āpatti paṭiggahetabbāti khandhake vuttanayeneva paṭiggahetabbā. Evañhi tattha vuttaṃ – “byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

Regarding 'The offense should be received by a competent and able bhikkhu': it should be received in the very manner stated in the Khandhaka. For it is stated there thus: 'The Saṅgha should be informed by a competent and able bhikkhu—'

‘Suṇātu me bhante saṅgho, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu āpattiṃ sarati vivarati uttāniṃ karoti deseti, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno āpattiṃ paṭiggaṇheyya’nti.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. This bhikkhu, named so-and-so, remembers an offense, reveals it, makes it plain, and confesses it. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, I would receive the offense from this bhikkhu, named so-and-so.'

Tena [V 2.0201] vattabbo ‘passasī’ti? ‘Āma, passāmī’ti. Āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsī”ti (cūḷava. 239). Dvīsu pana sambahulāsu vā purimanayeneva vacanabhedo ñātabbo.

He should be asked by that bhikkhu: 'Do you see it?' 'Yes, I see it.' 'You should restrain yourself in the future.' However, in the case of two or many offenses, the variation in wording should be understood in the same way as before.

Cīvaradānepi “saṅgho imaṃ cīvaraṃ imāni cīvarānī”ti vatthuvasena vacanabhedo veditabbo. Gaṇassa ca puggalassa ca nissajjanepi eseva nayo.

Also in the giving of the robe, the variation in wording should be understood according to the item(s): 'The Saṅgha [gives] this robe... these robes.' And in the relinquishment to a group and to an individual, this is the same method.

Āpattidesanāpaṭiggahaṇesu panettha ayaṃ pāḷi – “tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā sambahule bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā vuḍḍhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘ahaṃ, bhante, itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno taṃ paṭidesemī’ti. Byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena te bhikkhū ñāpetabbā –

Herein, in the matters of confessing and accepting offenses, this is the Pāli: 'Monks, that bhikkhu should approach several bhikkhus, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior bhikkhus, sit in a squatting position, raise his joined palms, and they should be addressed thus: "Venerable sirs, I have incurred such-and-such an offense; I confess it." Those bhikkhus should be informed by a competent and able bhikkhu—'

‘Suṇantu me āyasmantā, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu āpattiṃ sarati vivarati uttāniṃ karoti deseti. Yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno āpattiṃ paṭiggaṇheyya’nti.

'Venerable sirs, may you hear me. This bhikkhu, named so-and-so, remembers an offense, reveals it, makes it plain, and confesses it. If it is the proper time for the venerable ones, I would receive the offense from this bhikkhu, named so-and-so.'

Tena vattabbo ‘passasī’ti? ‘Āma, passāmī’ti. ‘Āyatiṃ [P 3.0641] saṃvareyyāsī’ti.

He should be asked by that bhikkhu: 'Do you see it?' 'Yes, I see it.' 'You should restrain yourself in the future.'

Tena bhikkhunā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo – ‘ahaṃ, āvuso, itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno taṃ paṭidesemī’ti. Tena vattabbo ‘passasī’ti, āma passāmīti āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsī”ti (cūḷava. 239). Tattha [M 2.0224] purimanayeneva āpattiyā nāmaggahaṇaṃ vacanabhedo ca veditabbo.

That bhikkhu, having approached one bhikkhu, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, sat in a squatting position, and raised his joined palms, should say this to him: 'Friend, I have incurred such-and-such an offense. I confess it.' He should be asked by that bhikkhu: 'Do you see it?' 'Yes, I see it.' 'You should restrain yourself in the future.' (Cūḷavagga 239). Therein, the naming of the offense and the variation in wording should be understood in the same way as before.

Yathā ca gaṇassa nissajjane evaṃ dvinnaṃ nissajjanepi pāḷi veditabbā. Yadi hi viseso bhaveyya, yatheva “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tiṇṇannaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kātuṃ, evañca pana, bhikkhave, kātabbo. Byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena te bhikkhū ñāpetabbā”tiādinā nayena “tiṇṇannaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kātu”nti vatvā puna “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dvinnaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kātuṃ, evañca pana, bhikkhave, kātabbo. Therena bhikkhunā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅga”ntiādinā (mahāva. 168) nayena visuṃyeva dvinnaṃ pārisuddhiuposatho vutto, evamidhāpi [V 2.0202] visuṃ pāḷiṃ vadeyya, yasmā pana natthi, tasmā avatvā gatoti, gaṇassa vuttā pāḷiyevettha pāḷi.

Just as the Pāḷi for relinquishment for a group, so too should the Pāḷi for relinquishment for two be understood. For if there were a difference, just as—after having stated, 'to perform the purification Uposatha for three,' by the method beginning, 'I allow, bhikkhus, for three to perform the purification Uposatha. And it should be done in this way, bhikkhus: a competent and able bhikkhu should inform those bhikkhus'—the purification Uposatha for two was spoken of separately by the method beginning, 'I allow, bhikkhus, for two to perform the purification Uposatha. And it should be done in this way, bhikkhus: the senior bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder...' (Mahāvagga 168), so too here a separate Pāḷi would have been spoken. However, since there is no difference, it was therefore passed over without being stated. Thus, the Pāḷi spoken for the group is indeed the Pāḷi here.

Āpattipaṭiggahaṇe pana ayaṃ viseso, yathā gaṇassa nissajjitvā āpattiyā desiyamānāya āpattipaṭiggāhako bhikkhu ñattiṃ ṭhapeti, evaṃ aṭṭhapetvā dvīsu aññatarena yathā ekapuggalo paṭiggaṇhāti, evaṃ āpatti paṭiggahetabbā. Dvinnañhi ñattiṭṭhapanā nāma natthi, yadi siyā dvinnaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ visuṃ na vadeyya.

However, in the acceptance of an offense, this is the distinction: just as when an offense is being confessed after it has been relinquished to the group, the bhikkhu receiving the offense places a motion (ñatti), so too, without placing a motion, the offense should be accepted by one of the two, just as a single individual accepts it. Indeed, for two there is no such thing as placing a motion; if there were, the purification Uposatha for two would not have been spoken of separately.

Nissaṭṭhacīvaradānepi yathā “imaṃ cīvaraṃ āyasmato dammī”ti eko vadati, evaṃ “imaṃ mayaṃ cīvaraṃ āyasmato demā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Ito garukatarāni hi ñattidutiyakammānipi “apaloketvā kātabbānī”ti vuttāni atthi, tesaṃ etaṃ anulomaṃ nissaṭṭhacīvaraṃ pana dātabbameva adātuṃ na labbhati, vinayakammamattañhetaṃ. Na taṃ tena saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā puggalassa vā dinnameva hotīti.

Also in the giving of a relinquished robe, just as one person says, 'I give this robe to the Venerable Sir,' so too is it proper to say, 'We give this robe to the Venerable Sir.' For there are formal acts requiring a motion and a second announcement that are more serious than this and are stated as 'to be done after seeking consent.' This is in conformity with those. However, a relinquished robe must be given back; it is not allowable not to give it, for this is merely a Vinaya procedure. It is not that it has thereby been truly given by him to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.

468. Dasāhātikkante atikkantasaññīti dasāhaṃ atikkante cīvare “atikkantaṃ ida”nti evaṃsaññī, dasāhe vā atikkante “atikkanto [P 3.0642] dasāho”ti evaṃsaññī. Nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti na idha saññā rakkhati. Yopi evaṃsaññī, tassapi taṃ cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyāpatti ca. Sanissaggiyavinayakammaṃ vā pācittiyanti ubhopi atthavikappā yujjanti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

468. Perceiving as transgressed when ten days are transgressed: Regarding a robe for which ten days have been transgressed, one has the perception, 'This is transgressed'; or, when ten days have been transgressed, one has the perception, 'Ten days are transgressed.' It is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya: here, perception does not protect from the offense. For even one who perceives it as not transgressed, that robe is still subject to relinquishment and a pācittiya offense is incurred. Alternatively, it is a pācittiya that involves the Vinaya act of relinquishment; both interpretations of the meaning are suitable. This is the method in all cases.

Avissajjite [M 2.0225] vissajjitasaññīti kassaci adinne apariccatte “pariccattaṃ mayā”ti evaṃsaññī.

Perceiving as relinquished what is not relinquished: Regarding something not given or not relinquished to anyone, one has the perception, 'It has been relinquished by me.'

Anaṭṭhe naṭṭhasaññīti attano cīvarena saddhiṃ bahūni aññesaṃ cīvarāni ekato ṭhapitāni corā haranti. Tatresa attano cīvare anaṭṭhe naṭṭhasaññī hoti. Esa nayo avinaṭṭhādīsupi.

Perceiving as lost what is not lost: When thieves take many robes of others that were placed together with one's own robe, in that case, one perceives one’s own robe as lost, although it was not lost. This method also applies to what is not destroyed, and so on.

Avilutteti ettha pana gabbhaṃ bhinditvā pasayhāvahāravasena avilutteti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, in the phrase 'not plundered' (avilutta), it should be understood as 'not plundered' in the sense of being forcibly carried away after breaking into a chamber.

Anissajjitvā paribhuñjati āpatti dukkaṭassāti sakiṃ nivatthaṃ vā sakiṃ pārutaṃ vā kāyato amocetvā divasampi vicarati, ekāva āpatti. Mocetvā mocetvā nivāseti vā pārupati [V 2.0203] vā payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Dunnivatthaṃ vā duppārutaṃ vā saṇṭhapentassa anāpatti. Aññassa taṃ paribhuñjatopi anāpatti, “anāpatti aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjatī”ti (pārā. 570) ādivacanañcettha sādhakaṃ. Anatikkante atikkantasaññino vematikassa ca dukkaṭaṃ paribhogaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

If one uses it without relinquishing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing: If one wears a lower robe once or drapes an upper robe once and wanders for a whole day without removing it from the body, there is only one offense. If one repeatedly removes it and wears or drapes it again, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each instance of use. There is no offense for one who adjusts an improperly worn or improperly draped robe. There is also no offense for another who uses it; the initial words of the text, 'There is no offense for one who acquires and uses what was made by another,' serve as proof here. The offense of wrong-doing for one who perceives as transgressed what has not been transgressed, and for one who is in doubt, is stated with reference to the usage.

469. “Anāpatti antodasāhaṃ adhiṭṭheti, vikappetī”ti ettha pana adhiṭṭhānupagaṃ vikappanupagañca veditabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – atha kho bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “yāni tāni bhagavatā anuññātāni ‘ticīvara’nti vā ‘vassikasāṭikā’ti vā ‘nisīdana’nti vā ‘paccattharaṇa’nti vā ‘kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī’ti vā mukhapuñchanacoḷakanti vā parikkhāracoḷanti vā sabbāni tāni adhiṭṭhātabbānīti nu kho udāhu vikappetabbānī”ti, bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ –

469. Furthermore, in the phrase, 'There is no offense if one determines or assigns it within ten days,' it should be understood that this refers to a robe suitable for determination and suitable for assignment. In that regard, this is the Pāḷi: Then this thought occurred to the bhikkhus: 'Regarding those things permitted by the Blessed One—such as the triple robe, the rainy-season cloth, the sitting cloth, the spread, the scab-covering cloth, the face-wiping cloth, or the requisite cloth—should all of them be determined, or should they be assigned?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ; vassikasāṭikaṃ vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ; nisīdanaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ; paccattharaṇaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ; kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ yāvaābādhā adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ; mukhapuñchanacoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ [P 3.0643] na vikappetuṃ; parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358).

“I allow, bhikkhus, the triple robe to be determined, not assigned; the rainy-season cloth to be determined for the four months of the rains, and thereafter to be assigned; the sitting cloth to be determined, not assigned; the spread to be determined, not assigned; the scab-covering cloth to be determined for as long as the ailment lasts, and thereafter to be assigned; the face-wiping cloth to be determined, not assigned; the requisite cloth to be determined, not assigned.” (Mahāvagga 358).

“Tattha [M 2.0226] ticīvaraṃ” adhiṭṭhahantena rajitvā kappabinduṃ datvā pamāṇayuttameva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Tassa pamāṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena sugatacīvarato ūnakaṃ vaṭṭati, lāmakaparicchedena saṅghāṭiyā uttarāsaṅgassa ca dīghato muṭṭhipañcakaṃ tiriyaṃ muṭṭhittikaṃ pamāṇaṃ vaṭṭati. Antaravāsako dīghato muṭṭhipañcako tiriyaṃ dvihatthopi vaṭṭati. Pārupaṇenapi hi sakkā nābhiṃ paṭicchādetunti. Vuttappamāṇato pana atirekaṃ ūnakañca parikkhāracoḷanti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ.

Therein, one determining the triple robe should, after dyeing it and applying the marking-spot, determine only a robe that is of the proper measurements. Its measurement, by the highest limit, is proper if it is less than the Sugata's robe. By the lowest limit, for the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), a measurement of five cubits in length and three cubits in width is proper. The inner robe (antaravāsaka) is proper if it is five cubits in length and two cubits in width, for indeed it is possible to cover the navel even by wearing it. However, a robe that is larger or smaller than the stated measurements should be determined as a 'requisite cloth'.

Tattha yasmā “dve cīvarassa adhiṭṭhānā – kāyena vā adhiṭṭheti, vācāya vā adhiṭṭhetī”ti (pari. 322) vuttaṃ, tasmā purāṇasaṅghāṭiṃ “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmī”ti paccuddharitvā navaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ hatthena gahetvā “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena kāyena adhiṭṭhātabbā. Idaṃ kāyena adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena aphusantassa na vaṭṭati. Vācāya adhiṭṭhāne pana vacībhedaṃ katvā vācāya adhiṭṭhātabbā. Tatra duvidhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ – sace hatthapāse hoti “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā. Atha antogabbhe vā uparipāsāde vā sāmantavihāre vā hoti ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā [V 2.0204] bhinditabbā. Esa nayo uttarāsaṅge antaravāsake ca. Nāmamattameva hi viseso. Tasmā sabbāni saṅghāṭiṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ antaravāsakanti evaṃ attano nāmeneva adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Sace adhiṭṭhahitvā ṭhapitavatthehi saṅghāṭiādīni karoti, niṭṭhite rajane ca kappe ca imaṃ “paccuddharāmī”ti paccuddharitvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Adhiṭṭhitena pana saddhiṃ mahantatarameva dutiyapaṭṭaṃ vā khaṇḍaṃ vā saṃsibbantena puna adhiṭṭhātabbameva. Same vā khuddake vā adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi.

Herein, because it has been said, “There are two determinations of a robe: one determines by body, or one determines by speech,” therefore, having relinquished the old outer robe by stating, “I relinquish this outer robe,” one should take the new outer robe in hand, and having made the mental resolve, ‘I determine this outer robe,’ and making a bodily gesture, should determine it by body. This is determination by body; it is not proper for one who does not touch it with some part of the body. In the case of determination by speech, however, it should be determined by speech, having articulated the words. Therein, the determination is twofold: if it is within hand’s reach, the words, “I determine this outer robe,” should be articulated. If, however, it is in an inner chamber, on an upper story of a mansion, or in a nearby monastery, having noted the place where it is kept, the words, “I determine that outer robe,” should be articulated. This is the method for the upper robe and the inner robe as well. Indeed, the only difference is in the name. Therefore, all robes should be determined by their own names, thus: ‘outer robe,’ ‘upper robe,’ and ‘inner robe.’ If one makes an outer robe or the like from cloths that have been determined and set aside, then when the dyeing and the marking are finished, having relinquished the previous determination by stating, “I relinquish this,” they should be determined again. Furthermore, one who sews a second layer or a piece that is larger onto an already determined robe must determine it again. If the piece is of the same size or smaller, there is no need for determination.

Ticīvaraṃ pana parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati [P 3.0644] na vaṭṭatīti? Mahāpadumatthero kirāha – “ticīvaraṃ ticīvarameva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Sace parikkhāracoḷādhiṭṭhānaṃ labheyya udositasikkhāpade parihāro niratthako bhaveyyā”ti. Evaṃ vutte kira avasesā bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “parikkhāracoḷampi bhagavatāva adhiṭṭhātabbanti vuttaṃ, tasmā vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpaccariyampi vuttaṃ “parikkhāracoḷaṃ nāma pāṭekkaṃ nidhānamukhametanti ticīvaraṃ [M 2.0227] parikkhāracoḷanti adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Udositasikkhāpade pana ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā pariharantassa parihāro vutto”ti. Ubhatovibhaṅgabhāṇako puṇṇavālikavāsī mahātissattheropi kira āha – “mayaṃ pubbe mahātherānaṃ assumha, araññavāsino bhikkhū rukkhasusirādīsu cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā padhānaṃ padahanatthāya gacchanti. Sāmantavihāre dhammasavanatthāya gatānañca nesaṃ sūriye uṭṭhite sāmaṇerā vā daharabhikkhū vā pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā gacchanti, tasmā sukhaparibhogatthaṃ ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷanti adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpaccariyampi vuttaṃ pubbe āraññikā bhikkhū abaddhasīmāyaṃ dupparihāranti ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷameva adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjiṃsū”ti.

Furthermore, is it proper to determine the triple robe as a requisite-cloth, or is it not? The Elder Mahāpaduma, it is said, stated: “The triple robe should be determined only as the triple robe. If the determination as a requisite-cloth were permitted, the safeguard in the Udosita training rule would become meaningless.” When this was said, it is said, the remaining monks stated: “It has been said by the Blessed One himself that a requisite-cloth should also be determined; therefore, it is proper.” In the Mahāpaccarī also it is said: “This requisite-cloth is a separate means of storing robes. Therefore, it is proper to determine the triple robe as a requisite-cloth and use it. However, in the Udosita training rule, the safeguard is stated for one who carries about the triple robe after having determined it as the triple robe.” The Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavālika and a reciter of the Ubhatovibhaṅga, it is said, also stated: “We have heard from the great elders of the past that forest-dwelling monks, having placed their robes in tree hollows and so on, go to strive in their practice. And for those who have gone to a nearby monastery to listen to the Dhamma, when the sun has risen, novices or young monks take their bowl and robe and go to them. Therefore, for the sake of convenient use, it is proper to determine the triple robe as a requisite-cloth.” In the Mahāpaccarī also it is said: “In the past, forest-dwelling monks in an area without a consecrated boundary, thinking ‘it is difficult to look after,’ determined the triple robe only as a requisite-cloth and used it.”

“Vassikasāṭikā” anatirittappamāṇā nāmaṃ gahetvā vuttanayeneva cattāro vassike māse adhiṭṭhātabbā, tato paraṃ paccuddharitvā vikappetabbā. Vaṇṇabhedamattarattāpi cesā vaṭṭati. Dve pana na vaṭṭanti. “Nisīdanaṃ” vuttanayena adhiṭṭhātabbameva, tañca kho pamāṇayuttaṃ ekameva, dve na vaṭṭanti. “Paccattharaṇa”mpi adhiṭṭhātabbameva, taṃ pana mahantampi vaṭṭati, ekampi vaṭṭati, bahūnipi vaṭṭanti. Nīlampi pītakampi sadasampi pupphadasampīti sabbappakāraṃ vaṭṭati. Sakiṃ adhiṭṭhitaṃ adhiṭṭhitameva hoti. “Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi” yāva ābādho atthi, tāva pamāṇikā adhiṭṭhātabbā. Ābādhe vūpasante paccuddharitvā vikappetabbā, ekāva vaṭṭati[P 3.0645]. “Mukhapuñchanacoḷaṃ” adhiṭṭhātabbameva, yāva ekaṃ dhoviyati, tāva aññaṃ paribhogatthāya icchitabbanti [V 2.0205] dve vaṭṭanti. Apare pana therā “nidhānamukhametaṃ bahūnipi vaṭṭantī”ti vadanti. Parikkhāracoḷe gaṇanā natthi, yattakaṃ icchati tattakaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbameva. Thavikāpi parissāvanampi vikappanupagaṃ pacchimacīvarappamāṇaṃ “parikkhāracoḷaka”nti adhiṭṭhātabbameva. Bahūni ekato katvā “imāni cīvarāni parikkhāracoḷāni adhiṭṭhāmī”ti adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Bhesajjanavakammamātāpituādīnaṃ atthāya ṭhapentenapi adhiṭṭhātabbameva. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Mañcabhisi pīṭhakabhisi bimbohanaṃ pāvāro kojavoti etesu pana senāsanaparikkhāratthāya dinnapaccattharaṇe ca adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthiyeva.

A rains-cloth, not exceeding the specified measure, should be determined for the four rainy-season months by taking its name, in the manner already stated. After that, it should be relinquished and made subject to vikappana. And this is allowable even if dyed just enough to spoil its color. But two are not allowable. A sitting-cloth should be determined in the manner stated, and that too, only one that is of the specified measure; two are not allowable. A ground-covering also should be determined. But that is allowable even if large; one is allowable, and many are also allowable. Blue, yellow, with a fringe, with a floral fringe—all kinds are allowable. Once determined, it remains determined. An itch-covering cloth of the specified measure should be determined for as long as the illness exists. When the illness has subsided, it should be relinquished and made subject to vikappana; only one is allowable. A face-wiping cloth should be determined. Because while one is being washed, another is desired for use, two are allowable. But other elders say, “This is a means of storing; many are also allowable.” For requisite-cloths, there is no number limit; as many as one wishes may be determined. A bag and a water-strainer, if they are of a size suitable for vikappana—the measure of the smallest robe—should be determined as a “requisite-cloth.” It is also allowable to gather many together and determine them, saying, “I determine these cloths as requisite-cloths.” It should also be determined by one who keeps it for the sake of medicine, new construction work, mother and father, and so on. But in the Mahāpaccarī it is stated, “There is no offense.” However, in the case of these—a mattress for a bed, a mattress for a chair, a pillow, a blanket, a woolen rug—and a ground-covering given for the sake of lodging requisites, there is no need for determination at all.

Adhiṭṭhitacīvaraṃ pana paribhuñjato kathaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti? Aññassa dānena, acchinditvā gahaṇena, vissāsaggāhena, hīnāyāvattanena, sikkhāpaccakkhānena[M 2.0228], kālaṃkiriyāya, liṅgaparivattanena, paccuddharaṇena, chiddabhāvenāti imehi navahi kāraṇehi vijahati. Tattha purimehi aṭṭhahi sabbacīvarāni adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahanti, chiddabhāvena pana ticīvarasseva sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ vuttaṃ, tañca nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇena chiddena. Tattha nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ kaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhavasena veditabbaṃ, chiddañca vinibbiddhachiddameva. Chiddassa hi abbhantare ekatantu cepi acchinno hoti, rakkhati. Tattha saṅghāṭiyā ca uttarāsaṅgassa ca dīghantato vidatthippamāṇassa tiriyantato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, parato na bhindati. Antaravāsakassa pana dīghantato vidatthippamāṇasseva tiriyantato caturaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, parato [P 3.0646] na bhindati. Tasmā jāte chidde taṃ cīvaraṃ atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, sūcikammaṃ katvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Mahāsumatthero panāha – “pamāṇacīvarassa yattha katthaci chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, mahantassa pana pamāṇato bahi chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhindati, antojātaṃ bhindatī”ti. Karavīkatissatthero āha – “khuddakaṃ mahantaṃ na pamāṇaṃ, dve cīvarāni pārupantassa vāmahatthe saṅgharitvā ṭhapitaṭṭhāne chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhindati, orabhāge bhindati. Antaravāsakassapi ovaṭṭikaṃ karontena saṅgharitaṭṭhāne chiddaṃ na bhindati, tato oraṃ bhindatī”ti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ticīvare mahāsumattheravādaṃ pamāṇaṃ katvā uttarimpi idaṃ vuttaṃ “pacchimappamāṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ rakkhatī”ti. Parikkhāracoḷe dīghaso aṭṭhaṅgule sugataṅgulena tiriyaṃ caturaṅgule yattha katthaci chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahati. Mahante coḷe tato parena chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ na vijahati. Esa nayo sabbesu adhiṭṭhātabbakesu cīvaresū”ti.

Furthermore, how is the determination of a determined robe abandoned? It is abandoned by these nine causes: by giving it to another, by taking it through theft, by taking it through trust, by reverting to a lower state, by renouncing the training, by death, by change of gender, by revocation, and by the presence of a hole. Among these, by the first eight causes, the determination of all robes is abandoned, but by the presence of a hole, the abandonment of determination is stated in all the commentaries for the three robes only. And that is by a hole the size of the back of a fingernail. Therein, the size of the back of a fingernail should be understood by way of the nail of the little finger, and the hole must be a completely perforated hole. For if even a single thread inside the hole is not broken, it protects the determination. Therein, for the double-layered robe and the upper robe, a hole on the inner side of a section measuring a span from the long end and eight finger-widths from the crosswise end breaks the determination; on the outer side, it does not break it. As for the inner robe, a hole on the inner side of a section measuring a span from the long end and four finger-widths from the crosswise end breaks the determination; on the outer side, it does not break it. Therefore, when a hole has arisen, that robe stands in the category of an extra robe; after mending it, it must be determined again. However, the Elder Mahāsuma said: “For a robe of standard measure, a hole anywhere breaks the determination, but for a large robe, a hole outside the standard measure does not break the determination; one that has arisen inside does break it.” The Elder Karavīkatissa said: “Small or large is not the standard. For one wearing two robes, a hole in the place where they are folded and placed in the left hand does not break the determination; one in the inner part does break it. Even for the inner robe, for one making a roll, a hole in the folded place does not break the determination; one inside that does break it.” But in the Andhaka commentary, having taken the view of the Elder Mahāsuma regarding the three robes as the standard, this is further stated: “The minimum measure protects the determination.” For a requisite-cloth, a hole anywhere within a length of eight Sugata-fingers and a width of four Sugata-fingers causes the determination to be abandoned. In a large cloth, a hole beyond that does not cause the determination to be abandoned. This is the method for all robes that are to be determined.

Tattha yasmā sabbesampi adhiṭṭhātabbakacīvarānaṃ vikappanupagapacchimappamāṇato aññaṃ pacchimappamāṇaṃ [V 2.0206] nāma natthi, yañhi nisīdana-kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi-vassikasāṭikānaṃ pamāṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ, tato uttari paṭisiddhattā na pacchimaṃ tato heṭṭhā appaṭisiddhattā. Ticīvarassāpi sugatacīvarappamāṇato ūnakattaṃ ukkaṭṭhappamāṇameva. Pacchimaṃ pana visuṃ sutte vuttaṃ natthi. Mukhapuñchanapaccattharaṇaparikkhāracoḷānaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo natthiyeva. Vikappanupagapacchimena pana pacchimaparicchedo vutto. Tasmā yaṃ tāva andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 2.0229] “pacchimappamāṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ rakkhatī”ti vatvā tattha parikkhāracoḷasseva sugataṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulacaturaṅgulapacchimappamāṇaṃ dassetvā itaresaṃ ticīvarādīnaṃ muṭṭhipañcakādipabhedaṃ [P 3.0647] pacchimappamāṇaṃ sandhāya “esa nayo sabbesu adhiṭṭhātabbakesucīvaresū”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na sameti.

Herein, since for all robes that are to be determined there is no other minimum measure apart from the minimum measure suitable for sharing—for the measure stated for the sitting-cloth, the itch-covering cloth, and the rainy-season robe is the maximum, because anything beyond it is prohibited; it is not the minimum, because anything below it is not prohibited. For the three robes also, the Sugata-robe measure is only the maximum measure. A separate minimum measure, however, is not stated in the Suttas. For face-wiping cloths, spreads, and requisite-cloths, there is no defined maximum limit at all. The minimum limit, however, is stated by means of the minimum measure suitable for sharing. Therefore, that which is stated in the Andhaka commentary—first saying, “The minimum measure protects the determination,” and then, having shown the minimum measure for the requisite-cloth as eight Sugata-fingers by four Sugata-fingers, and referring to the minimum measure of the other robes, the three robes and so on, which is of the five-fist-lengths division and so forth, it was said, “This is the method for all robes that are to be determined”—that does not accord.

Karavīkatissattheravādepi dīghantatoyeva chiddaṃ dassitaṃ, tiriyantato na dassitaṃ, tasmā so aparicchinno. Mahāsumattheravāde “pamāṇacīvarassa yattha katthaci chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, mahantassa pana pamāṇato bahi chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhindatī”ti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ pana na vuttaṃ – “idaṃ nāma pamāṇacīvaraṃ ito uttari mahantaṃ cīvara”nti. Apicettha ticīvarādīnaṃ muṭṭhipañcakādibhedaṃ pacchimappamāṇanti adhippetaṃ. Tattha yadi pacchimappamāṇato bahi chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhindeyya, ukkaṭṭhapattassāpi majjhimapattassa vā omakappamāṇato bahi chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhindeyya, na ca na bhindati. Tasmā ayampi vādo aparicchinno.

In the view of the Elder Karavīkatissa also, a hole is indicated only lengthwise, not crosswise; therefore, that view is not delimited. In the view of the Elder Mahāsuma, it is stated: “For a robe of standard measure, a hole anywhere breaks the determination; but for a large robe, a hole outside the standard measure does not break the determination.” This, however, was not stated: “This is called a robe of standard measure; a robe larger than this is a large robe.” Moreover, herein, the division of the three robes and so on into five-fist-lengths, etc., is intended as the minimum measure. In that case, if a hole outside the minimum measure did not break the determination, then for a superior bowl or a medium bowl, a hole outside the lowest measure would not break the determination—and yet it does break it. Therefore, this view also is not delimited.

Yo panāyaṃ sabbapaṭhamo aṭṭhakathāvādo, ayamevettha pamāṇaṃ. Kasmā? Paricchedasabbhāvato. Ticīvarassa hi pacchimappamāṇañca chiddappamāṇañca chidduppattidesappamāṇañca sabbaaṭṭhakathāsuyeva paricchinditvā vuttaṃ, tasmā sveva vādo pamāṇaṃ. Addhā hi so bhagavato adhippāyaṃ anugantvā vutto. Itaresu pana neva paricchedo atthi, na pubbāparaṃ sametīti.

But this very first commentary view is the authority in this matter. Why? Because of the existence of delimitation. For the minimum measure of the three robes, the measure of the hole, and the measure of the location where a hole occurs are all stated in all the commentaries after having been precisely defined. Therefore, that very view is the authority. Indeed, it was stated in accordance with the Blessed One's intention. In the other views, however, there is no precise definition, nor do the earlier and later statements accord.

Yo pana dubbalaṭṭhāne paṭhamaṃ aggaḷaṃ datvā pacchā dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā apaneti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati. Maṇḍalaparivattanepi eseva nayo. Dupaṭṭassa ekasmiṃ paṭale chidde vā jāte gaḷite vā adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati, khuddakaṃ cīvaraṃ mahantaṃ karoti, mahantaṃ vā khuddakaṃ karoti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati. Ubho koṭiyo majjhe karonto sace paṭhamaṃ chinditvā pacchā ghaṭeti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhijjati. Atha ghaṭetvā chindati, na bhijjati, rajakehi dhovāpetvā setaṃ kārāpentassāpi adhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānamevāti[P 3.0648]. Ayaṃ tāva “antodasāhaṃ adhiṭṭheti vikappetī”ti ettha adhiṭṭhāne vinicchayo.

Furthermore, for one who, having first applied a patch on a weak or worn-out spot, afterwards cuts off and removes the weak spot, the determination is not broken. This same principle applies also to exchanging the large and small panels. If a hole appears in one layer of a double-layered robe, or if it becomes worn out, the determination is not broken. If one makes a small robe large, or a large robe small, the determination is not broken. If, while making both ends meet in the middle, one first cuts and then joins them, the determination is broken. But if one joins them first and then cuts, it is not broken. Even for one who has it washed by launderers and made white, the determination remains a determination. This, first of all, is the decision regarding determination in the phrase 'he determines or allocates within ten days'.

Vikappane [M 2.0230][V 2.0207] pana dve vikappanā – sammukhāvikappanā ca parammukhāvikappanā ca. Kathaṃ sammukhāvikappanā hotīti? Cīvarānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “‘imaṃ cīvara’nti vā ‘imāni cīvarānī’ti vā ‘etaṃ cīvara’nti vā ‘etāni cīvarānī’”ti vā “tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ, ayamekā sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhuñjituṃ pana vissajjetuṃ vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. “Mayhaṃ santakaṃ, mayhaṃ santakāni paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti evaṃ pana vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti. Tatopabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

Regarding allocation, however, there are two kinds of allocation: face-to-face allocation and indirect allocation. How does face-to-face allocation occur? Having known whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are present or not present, one should say, 'This robe,' or 'These robes,' or 'That robe,' or 'Those robes,' and 'I allocate to you.' This is one kind of face-to-face allocation. By this much, it is allowable to store them, but it is not allowable to use, give away, or determine them. However, when it is said, 'My property, my belongings; use, or give away, or do as is suitable,' this is called a withdrawal. From then on, use and so forth are also allowable.

Aparopi nayo – tatheva cīvarānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā tasseva bhikkhuno santike “‘imaṃ cīvara’nti vā ‘imāni cīvarānī’ti vā ‘etaṃ cīvara’nti vā ‘etāni cīvarānī’”ti vā vatvā pañcasu sahadhammikesu aññatarassa attanā abhirucitassa yassa kassaci nāmaṃ gahetvā “‘tissassa bhikkhuno vikappemī’ti vā ‘tissāya bhikkhuniyā, sikkhamānāya, tissassa sāmaṇerassa, tissāya sāmaṇeriyā vikappemī’”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ aparāpi sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā “tissassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ…pe… tissāya sāmaṇeriyā santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti. Tatopabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

There is also another method. In the same way, having known whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are present or not present, and having said in the presence of that same bhikkhu, 'This robe,' or 'These robes,' or 'That robe,' or 'Those robes,' then, having taken the name of any one of the five co-religionists whom one likes, one should say, 'I allocate to the bhikkhu Tissa,' or 'to the bhikkhunī Tissā,' 'to the sikkhamānā Tissā,' 'to the sāmaṇera Tissa,' or 'to the sāmaṇerī Tissā.' This is also another face-to-face allocation. By this much, it is allowable to store them, but regarding use and so forth, not even one is allowable. But when that bhikkhu says, 'The property of the bhikkhu Tissa... (etc.)... the property of the sāmaṇerī Tissā; use it, or give it away, or do with it as is suitable,' this is called a withdrawal. From then on, use and so forth are also allowable.

Kathaṃ parammukhāvikappanā hotīti? Cīvarānaṃ tatheva ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “‘imaṃ cīvara’nti vā ‘imāni cīvarānī’ti vā ‘etaṃ cīvara’nti vā ‘etāni cīvarānī’”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappanatthāya dammī”ti vattabbaṃ. Tena vattabbo – “ko te mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā”ti? Tato itarena purimanayeneva “tisso bhikkhūti vā…pe… tissā sāmaṇerī”ti vā vattabbaṃ. Puna tena bhikkhunā [P 3.0649] “ahaṃ tissassa bhikkhuno dammīti vā…pe… tissāya sāmaṇeriyā dammī”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ parammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā dutiyasammukhāvikappanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva “itthannāmassa santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti. Tatopabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

How does indirect allocation occur? In the same way, having known whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are present or not present, and having said, 'This robe,' or 'These robes,' or 'That robe,' or 'Those robes,' one should say, 'I give this to you for the purpose of allocation.' He (the owner) should be asked by him (the proxy): 'Who is your friend or acquaintance?' Then the other (the owner), following the previous method, should say, 'The bhikkhu Tissa,' or... (etc.)... 'the sāmaṇerī Tissā.' Again, that bhikkhu (the proxy) should say, 'I give to the bhikkhu Tissa,' or... (etc.)... 'I give to the sāmaṇerī Tissā.' This is indirect allocation. By this much, it is allowable to store them, but regarding use and so forth, not even one is allowable. But when that bhikkhu (the proxy), following the method stated for the second face-to-face allocation, says, 'The property of so-and-so; use it, or give it away, or do as is suitable,' this is called a withdrawal. From then on, use and so forth are also allowable.

Dvinnaṃ [M 2.0231] vikappanānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ? Sammukhāvikappanāyaṃ sayaṃ vikappetvā parena paccuddharāpeti[V 2.0208]. Parammukhāvikappanāya pareneva vikappāpetvā pareneva paccuddharāpeti, idamettha nānākaraṇaṃ. Sace pana yassa vikappeti, so paññattikovido na hoti, na jānāti paccuddharituṃ, taṃ cīvaraṃ gahetvā aññassa byattassa santikaṃ gantvā puna vikappetvā paccuddharāpetabbaṃ. Vikappitavikappanā nāmesā vaṭṭati. Ayaṃ “vikappetī”ti imasmiṃ pade vinicchayo.

What is the difference between the two kinds of allocation? In allocation in the presence of the recipient, one allocates it oneself and has it de-allocated by another. In allocation in the absence of the recipient, one has it allocated by another and has it de-allocated by that same other person; this is the difference here. But if the one to whom one allocates is not skilled in the regulations and does not know how to perform the de-allocation, then taking that robe, one should go to another who is competent, allocate it again, and have it de-allocated. This is called re-allocation of what was allocated, and it is allowable. This is the decision on the word 'allocates'.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetu”ntiādivacanato ca idaṃ “vikappetī”ti avisesena vuttavacanaṃ viruddhaṃ viya dissati, na ca viruddhaṃ tathāgatā bhāsanti. Tasmā evamassa attho veditabbo, ticīvaraṃ ticīvarasaṅkhepeneva pariharato adhiṭṭhātumeva anujānāmi, na vikappetuṃ. Vassikasāṭikaṃ pana cātumāsato paraṃ vikappetumeva na adhiṭṭhātuṃ. Evañca sati yo ticīvare ekena cīvarena vippavasitukāmo hoti, tassa ticīvarādhiṭṭhānaṃ paccuddharitvā vippavāsasukhatthaṃ vikappanāya okāso dinno hoti. Dasāhātikkame ca anāpattīti etenupāyena sabbattha vikappanāya appaṭisiddhabhāvo veditabbo.

And from the statement beginning, 'Monks, I allow the triple robe to be determined, not to be allocated,' this word 'allocates,' spoken without distinction, appears as if contradictory. But the Tathāgatas do not speak in contradiction. Therefore, its meaning should be understood thus: for one who wears the triple robe only as the set of three robes, I allow only its determination, not its allocation. But regarding the rains-bathing cloth, after four months, I allow only its allocation, not its determination. This being so, for one who wishes to dwell apart from one robe of his triple robe, having withdrawn the determination of the triple robe, the opportunity for allocation is given for the sake of comfort while dwelling apart. And there is no offense in exceeding ten days. By this method, the non-prohibition of allocation in all cases should be understood.

Vissajjetīti aññassa deti. Kathaṃ pana dinnaṃ hoti, kathaṃ gahitaṃ? “Imaṃ tuyhaṃ demi dadāmi dajjāmi oṇojemi pariccajāmi nissajjāmi vissajjāmīti vā “itthannāmassa demi…pe… nissajjāmī”ti vā vadati, sammukhāpi [P 3.0650] parammukhāpi dinnaṃyeva hoti. “Tuyhaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vutte “mayhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti vadati, sudinnaṃ suggahitañca. “Tava santakaṃ karohi, tava santakaṃ hotu, tava santakaṃ karissasī”ti vutte “mama santakaṃ karomi, mama santakaṃ hotu, mama santakaṃ karissāmī”ti vadati, duddinnaṃ duggahitañca. Neva dātā dātuṃ jānāti, na itaro gahetuṃ. Sace pana “tava santakaṃ karohī”ti vutte “sādhu, bhante, mayhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ. Sace pana “eko gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, itaro “na gaṇhāmī”ti puna so “dinnaṃ mayā tuyhaṃ, gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, itaropi “na mayhaṃ iminā attho”ti vadati. Tato purimopi “mayā dinna”nti dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, pacchimopi “mayā paṭikkhitta”nti. Kassa āpattīti? Na kassaci āpatti. Yassa pana ruccati, tena adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

‘He gives it away’ means he gives it to another. Now then, how is it given, and how is it taken?
