When one says, ‘I give this to you, I offer it, I would give it, I renounce it, I abandon it, I relinquish it, I give it away,’ or ‘I give it to so-and-so… (and so on)… I relinquish it,’ whether in the recipient's presence or absence, it is indeed given. If, when told, ‘Take this for yourself,’ one replies, ‘I take it for myself,’ it is well-given and well-taken. If, when told, ‘Make it your possession, let it be your possession, will you make it your possession?’ one replies, ‘I make it my possession, let it be my possession, I will make it my possession,’ it is badly given and badly taken. The giver does not know how to give, nor does the other know how to take. If, however, when told, ‘Make it your possession,’ one takes it, saying, ‘Very well, venerable sir, I take it for myself,’ it is well-taken. If, however, one says, ‘Take it,’ and the other says, ‘I will not take it,’ and the first one says again, ‘It has been given by me to you, take it,’ and the other also says, ‘I have no need of this,’ and thereafter the first one lets ten days pass, thinking, ‘It was given by me,’ and the latter also lets ten days pass, thinking, ‘It was rejected by me’—whose offense is it? There is no offense for anyone. But for whomever it is agreeable, it should be determined and used by him.

Yo [M 2.0232] pana adhiṭṭhāne vematiko, tena kiṃ kātabbaṃ? Vematikabhāvaṃ ārocetvā sace anadhiṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati, evaṃ me kappiyaṃ hotīti vatvā vuttanayeneva nissajjitabbaṃ. Na hi evaṃ [V 2.0209] jānāpetvā vinayakammaṃ karontassa musāvādo hoti. Keci pana “ekena bhikkhunā vissāsaṃ gahetvā puna dinnaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati. Na hi tassetaṃ vinayakammaṃ, nāpi taṃ ettakena aññaṃ vatthuṃ hoti.

Furthermore, if a monk is doubtful about the determination, what should be done by him? Having declared his state of doubt, if the robe should be undetermined, he should say, ‘Thus it becomes allowable for me,’ and then it should be forfeited in the manner already stated. Indeed, for one who performs a formal act of the Vinaya after making it known in this way, there is no false speech. Some, however, say, ‘It is allowable for it to be taken on trust by a monk and given again,’ but that is not correct. For this is not a formal act of the Vinaya for that monk, nor by that much does the article become a different object.

Nassatītiādi uttānatthameva. Yo na dadeyya āpatti dukkaṭassāti ettha “mayhaṃ dinnaṃ iminā”ti imāya saññāya na dentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Tassa santakabhāvaṃ pana ñatvā lesena acchindanto bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabboti.

The passage beginning ‘It is lost’ has an obvious meaning. Regarding the phrase, ‘For one who would not give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing,’ here it means: for one who does not give it back with the perception, ‘It was given to me by this monk,’ there is a dukkaṭa offense. However, one who, knowing it is the other's property, seizes it with a pretext, should be made to have the goods valued and to make restitution.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma kāyavācāto ca kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti, anadhiṭṭhānena ca avikappanena ca āpajjanato akiriyaṃ, saññāya abhāvepi na muccati, ajānantopi āpajjatīti nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding its origins and so forth, this training rule is called ‘of Kathina origin’. It arises from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind. Because it is incurred through non-determination and non-allocation, it is classified as non-action. One is not freed even in the absence of perception; even one who does not know incurs the offense, thus it is not a case of liberation through perception. It is unintentional, a fault by convention, a bodily action, a verbal action, associated with three kinds of consciousness, and with three kinds of feeling.

Paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first Kathina training rule is concluded.

2. Udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Udosita Training Rule

471. Tena [P 3.0651] samayena buddho bhagavāti udositasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha santaruttarenāti antaranti antaravāsako vuccati, uttaranti uttarāsaṅgo, saha antarena uttaraṃ santaruttaraṃ, tena santaruttarena, saha antaravāsakena uttarāsaṅgenāti attho. Kaṇṇakitānīti sedena phuṭṭhokāsesu sañjātakāḷasetamaṇḍalāni. Addasa kho āyasmā ānando senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantoti thero kira bhagavati divā paṭisallānatthāya gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe taṃ okāsaṃ labhitvā dunnikkhittāni dārubhaṇḍamattikābhaṇḍāni paṭisāmento asammaṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ sammajjanto gilānehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [M 2.0233] senāsanaṭṭhānaṃ sampatto addasa. Tena vuttaṃ – “addasa kho āyasmā ānando senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍanto”ti.

471. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... this is the Udosita training rule. Therein, regarding `santaruttarena`: `antara` is said to be the lower robe; `uttara` is said to be the upper robe. The upper robe that goes together with the lower robe is `santaruttara`. Thus, `tena santaruttarena` means: by the upper robe together with the lower robe. `Kaṇṇakitāni` means: having black and white circles that have arisen in the places touched by sweat. Regarding 'The Venerable Ānanda, wandering on a tour of the lodgings, saw': it is said that when the Blessed One had entered the Fragrant Abode for the purpose of daytime seclusion, the Elder, having gotten that opportunity, while putting away the wooden and clay items that were badly placed, while sweeping the unswept place, and while making courteous conversation with the sick monks, arrived at the dwelling place of those monks and saw. Therefore, it was said: 'The Venerable Ānanda, wandering on a tour of the lodgings, saw.'

473. Avippavāsasammutiṃ dātunti avippavāse sammuti avippavāsasammuti, avippavāsāya vā sammuti avippavāsasammuti. Ko panettha ānisaṃso? Yena cīvarena vippavasati, taṃ nissaggiyaṃ na hoti, āpattiñca nāpajjati. Kittakaṃ kālaṃ? Mahāsumatthero tāva āha – “yāva rogo na vūpasamati, vūpasante pana roge sīghaṃ cīvaraṭṭhānaṃ āgantabba”nti[V 2.0210]. Mahāpadumatthero āha – “sīghaṃ āgacchato rogo paṭikuppeyya, tasmā saṇikaṃ āgantabbaṃ. Yato paṭṭhāya hi satthaṃ vā pariyesati, ‘gacchāmī’ti ābhogaṃ vā karoti, tato paṭṭhāya vaṭṭati. ‘Na dāni gamissāmī’ti evaṃ pana dhuranikkhepaṃ karontena paccuddharitabbaṃ, atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhassatī”ti. Sace panassa rogo paṭikuppati, kiṃ kātabbanti? Phussadevatthero tāva āha – “sace soyeva rogo paṭikuppati, sā eva sammuti, puna sammutidānakiccaṃ natthi. Athañño kuppati, puna dātabbā sammutī”ti. Upatissatthero āha – “so vā rogo hotu, añño vā puna sammutidānakiccaṃ natthī”ti.

473. Regarding 'to give the consent for non-separation': consent because of non-separation is 'avippavāsasammuti'; or, consent for the purpose of non-separation is 'avippavāsasammuti'. What is the benefit here? The robe from which one is separated does not become subject to forfeiture, and one does not fall into an offense. For how long? First, the Elder Mahāsuma said: 'As long as the illness does not subside; but when the illness has subsided, one must come quickly to the place of the robe.' The Elder Mahāpaduma said: 'For one coming quickly, the illness might recur; therefore, one must come slowly. For, from when one seeks a caravan companion or makes the reflection, "I will go," from then on it is allowable. But by one who lays down the burden thus, "Now I will not go," it must be revoked; it will stand in the category of an extra robe.' But if his illness recurs, what is to be done? First, the Elder Phussadeva said: 'If that very same illness recurs, it is that same consent; there is no need to give consent again. But if another illness arises, consent must be given again.' The Elder Upatissa said: 'Be it that illness or another, there is no need to give consent again.'

475-6. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunāti idha pana purimasikkhāpade viya atthaṃ aggahetvā niṭṭhite cīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunoti evaṃ sāmivasena karaṇavacanassa attho veditabbo. Karaṇavasena [P 3.0652] hi bhikkhunā idaṃ nāma kātabbanti natthi. Sāmivasena pana bhikkhuno cīvarasmiṃ niṭṭhite kathine ca ubbhate evaṃ chinnapalibodho ekarattampi ce bhikkhu ticīvarena vippavaseyyāti evaṃ attho yujjati. Tattha ticīvarenāti adhiṭṭhitesu tīsu cīvaresu yena kenaci. Ekena vippavutthopi hi ticīvarena vippavuttho hoti, paṭisiddhapariyāpannena vippavutthattā. Tenevassa padabhājane “saṅghāṭiyā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vippavaseyyāti vippayutto vaseyya.

Regarding 'niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā': Here, however, without taking the meaning as in the previous training rule, the meaning of the instrumental expression should be understood in the genitive sense, thus: 'when the robe of the bhikkhu is finished.' For, in the instrumental sense, there is nothing that says, 'this so-and-so must be done by a bhikkhu.' But in the genitive sense, the meaning is suitable thus: 'when the bhikkhu's robe is finished and the kathina is withdrawn, having thus cut off the impediments, if a bhikkhu should be separated from the three robes for even one night.' Therein, 'ticīvarena' means by any one among the three robes that have been determined. For, even one who is separated from one robe is one who is separated from the three robes, because of being separated from that which is included among the prohibited items. For that very reason, in its word-analysis, 'by the outer-robe, or...' and so on was said. 'Vippavaseyya' means one would dwell separated.

477-8. Gāmo ekūpacārotiādi avippavāsalakkhaṇavavatthāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ yathākkamena tāneva pannarasa mātikāpadāni vitthārento “gāmo ekūpacāro nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha ekakulassa gāmoti ekassa rañño vā bhojakassa vā gāmo. Parikkhittoti yena [M 2.0234] kenaci pākārena vā vatiyā vā parikkhāya vā parikkhitto. Ettāvatā ekakulagāmassa ekūpacāratā dassitā. Antogāme vatthabbanti evarūpe gāme cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā gāmabbhantare yathārucite ṭhāne aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aparikkhittoti iminā tasseva gāmassa nānūpacāratā dassitā. Evarūpe gāme yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tattha vatthabbaṃ. Hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbanti atha vā taṃ gharaṃ samantato hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ, aḍḍhateyyaratanappamāṇappadesā uddhaṃ na vijahitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Aḍḍhateyyaratanabbhantare pana vatthuṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā sacepi iddhimā bhikkhū ākāse aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpeti, nissaggiyameva hoti. Ettha ca yasmiṃ ghareti gharaparicchedo “ekakulassa nivesanaṃ hotī”tiādinā (pārā. 480) lakkhaṇena veditabbo.

'A village with a single precinct,' etc., was said for the purpose of defining the characteristic of non-separation. After that, wishing to elaborate in sequence on those same fifteen matrix-headings, he said, 'A village with a single precinct is called...,' etc. Therein, 'a village of a single family' is a village of one king or village headman. 'Enclosed' means enclosed by some wall, or fence, or moat. By this much, the state of having a single precinct for a single-family village is shown. 'One should dwell within the village' means: in such a village, having deposited the robe, it is allowable to cause the dawn to arise in any desired place within the village. By 'unenclosed,' the state of having various precincts for that same village is shown. In such a village, in whichever house the robe was deposited, there one must dwell. 'Or one should not abandon the hand's reach' means: alternatively, one must not abandon the hand's reach all around that house; it is said that one must not go beyond a space measuring two and a half cubits. But it is allowable to dwell within two and a half cubits. Having transgressed that measure, even if a bhikkhu with psychic power causes the dawn to arise in the sky, it becomes subject to forfeiture. And here, regarding 'in which house,' the definition of a house should be understood by the characteristic 'it is the dwelling of a single family,' etc. (Pārā. 480).

479. Nānākulassa [V 2.0211] gāmoti nānārājūnaṃ vā bhojakānaṃ vā gāmo, vesālikusinārādisadiso. Parikkhittoti iminā nānākulagāmassa ekūpacāratā dassitā. Sabhāye vā dvāramūle vāti ettha sabhāyanti liṅgabyattayena sabhā vuttā. Dvāramūleti nagaradvārassa samīpe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ [P 3.0653] hoti – evarūpe gāme yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tattha vā vatthabbaṃ. Tattha saddasaṅghaṭṭanena vā janasambādhena vā vasituṃ asakkontena sabhāye vā vatthabbaṃ nagaradvāramūle vā. Tatrapi vasituṃ asakkontena yattha katthaci phāsukaṭṭhāne vasitvā antoaruṇe āgamma tesaṃyeva sabhāyadvāramūlānaṃ hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ. Gharassa pana cīvarassa vā hatthapāse vattabbameva natthi.

479. 'A village of various families' means a village of various kings or village headmen, like Vesālī or Kusinārā. By 'enclosed,' the state of having a single precinct for a village of various families is shown. Regarding 'in an assembly hall or at the root of a gate': here, 'sabhā' is stated as 'sabhāyaṃ' by a change of gender. 'Dvāramūle' means near the city gate. This is what is said: In such a village, one must dwell in the house where the robe was deposited. If unable to dwell there because of the clashing of sounds or because of the crowding of people, one must dwell in the assembly hall or near the city gate. If unable to dwell even there, having dwelt in any comfortable place and having come back before dawn, one must not abandon the hand's reach of that very assembly hall and gate-vicinity. However, regarding the hand's reach of the house or of the robe, there is nothing at all to be said.

Sabhāyaṃ gacchantena hatthapāse cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvāti sace ghare aṭṭhapetvā sabhāye ṭhapessāmīti sabhāyaṃ gacchati, tena sabhāyaṃ gacchantena hatthapāseti hatthaṃ pasāretvā “handimaṃ cīvaraṃ ṭhapemī”ti evaṃ nikkhepasukhe hatthapāsagate kismiñci āpaṇe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā purimanayeneva sabhāye vā vatthabbaṃ dvāramūle vā, hatthapāsā vā na vijahitabbaṃ.

Regarding 'having placed the robe within arm's reach while going to the assembly hall': If, not placing it in the house, a bhikkhu goes to the assembly hall with the thought, 'I will place it in the assembly hall,' then for him, while going to the assembly hall, 'within arm's reach' is as follows: stretching out his hand and thinking, 'Here, let me place this robe,' he should, for the ease of placing it, deposit the robe in some shop that is within arm's reach. Then, according to the previous method, he should stay either in the assembly hall or near the city gate, and he should not abandon the arm's reach.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – phussadevatthero tāva āha – “cīvarahatthapāse vasitabbaṃ natthi, yattha katthaci vīthihatthapāsepi sabhāyahatthapāsepi dvārahatthapāsepi [M 2.0235] vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Upatissatthero panāha – “nagarassa bahūnipi dvārāni honti bahūnipi sabhāyāni, tasmā sabbattha na vaṭṭati. Yassā pana vīthiyā cīvaraṃ ṭhapitaṃ yaṃ tassā sammukhaṭṭhāne sabhāyañca dvārañca tassa sabhāyassa ca dvārassa ca hatthapāsā na vijahitabbaṃ. Evañhi sati sakkā cīvarassa pavatti jānitu”nti. Sabhāyaṃ pana gacchantena yassa āpaṇikassa hatthe nikkhittaṃ, sace so taṃ cīvaraṃ atiharitvā ghare nikkhipati, vīthihatthapāso na rakkhati, gharassa hatthapāse vatthabbaṃ. Sace mahantaṃ gharaṃ hoti, dve vīthiyo pharitvā ṭhitaṃ purato vā pacchato vā hatthapāseyeva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sabhāye nikkhipitvā pana sabhāye vā tassa sammukhe nagaradvāramūle vā tesaṃyeva hatthapāse vā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ.

Herein is the determination. First, the Elder Phussadeva said: 'It is not necessary to stay only within arm's reach of the robe; it is permissible to stay anywhere within arm's reach of a street, an assembly hall, or a gate.' The Elder Upatissa, however, said: 'A city has many gates and many assembly halls; therefore, it is not permissible everywhere. But on whichever street the robe has been placed, one should not abandon the arm's reach of the assembly hall and the gate that are in the location opposite it. For, this being so, it is possible to know the status of the robe.' Furthermore, if, while going to an assembly hall, a monk deposits the robe in the hands of a shopkeeper, and if that shopkeeper carries the robe away and places it in his house, the arm's reach of the street does not protect it; one must stay within arm's reach of the house. If it is a large house that stands spanning two streets, dawn should be made to arise only within its arm's reach, whether in front or behind. But having deposited the robe in an assembly hall, dawn should be made to arise either in that assembly hall, or opposite it at the base of the city gate, or within the arm's reach of those very places.

Aparikkhittotiiminā tasseva gāmassa nānūpacāratā dassitā. Etenevupāyena sabbattha ekūpacāratā ca nānūpacāratā ca veditabbā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “gāmo ekūpacāro [P 3.0654] nāmā”ti evaṃ ādimhi “ajjhokāso ekūpacāro nāmā”ti evaṃ ante ca ekameva mātikāpadaṃ uddharitvā padabhājanaṃ vitthāritaṃ. Tasmā tasseva padassānusārena sabbattha parikkhepādivasena ekūpacāratā ca nānūpacāratā ca veditabbā.

By this word 'unenclosed,' the state of having various vicinities for that very village is shown. By this same method, the state of having a single vicinity and the state of having various vicinities should be understood in all cases. In the Pāḷi, however, by extracting only one matrix term—at the beginning, 'A village is called one of a single vicinity,' and at the end, 'An open space is called one of a single vicinity'—the analysis of the term has been expanded. Therefore, in accordance with that very term, the state of having a single vicinity and the state of having various vicinities should be understood in all cases by way of enclosure and so forth.

480-1. Nivesanādīsu [V 2.0212] ovarakāti gabbhānaṃyevetaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ. Hatthapāsā vāti gabbhassa hatthapāsā. Dvāramūle vāti sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇe gharadvāramūle. Hatthapāsā vāti gabbhassa vā gharadvāramūlassa vā hatthapāsā.

480-1. In the context of dwellings and so forth, this word 'ovaraka' is a synonym for 'gabbhas' (inner rooms). 'From arm's reach' means from the arm's reach of the inner room. 'At the base of the door' means at the base of the house-door that is common to all. 'From arm's reach' means from the arm's reach of either the inner room or the base of the house-door.

482-7. Udositoti yānādīnaṃ bhaṇḍānaṃ sālā. Ito paṭṭhāya ca nivesane vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Aṭṭoti paṭirājādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ iṭṭhakāhi kato bahalabhittiko catupañcabhūmiko patissayaviseso. Māḷoti ekakūṭasaṅgahito caturassapāsādo. Pāsādoti dīghapāsādo. Hammiyanti muṇḍacchadanapāsādo.

482-7. 'Udosita' is a hall for goods such as vehicles. And from this point onwards, the determination should be understood by the very method stated for a dwelling. 'Aṭṭa' is a special type of residence with four or five stories and thick walls, made of bricks for the purpose of repelling enemy kings and so forth. 'Māḷa' is a square storied building encompassed by a single pinnacle. 'Pāsāda' is a long storied building. 'Hammiya' is a storied building with a flat roof.

489. Sattabbhantarātiettha ekaṃ abbhantaraṃ aṭṭhavīsatihatthaṃ hoti. Sace sattho gacchanto gāmaṃ vā nadiṃ vā pariyādiyitvā tiṭṭhati antopaviṭṭhena saddhiṃ ekābaddho hutvā orañca pārañca pharitvā ṭhito hoti, satthaparihārova labbhati. Atha gāme vā nadiyā vā pariyāpanno hoti antopaviṭṭho[M 2.0236], gāmaparihāro ceva nadīparihāro ca labbhati. Sace vihārasīmaṃ atikkamitvā tiṭṭhati, antosīmāya ca cīvaraṃ hoti, vihāraṃ gantvā vasitabbaṃ. Sace bahisīmāya cīvaraṃ hoti satthasamīpeyeva vasitabbaṃ. Sace gacchanto sakaṭe vā bhagge goṇe vā naṭṭhe antarā chijjati, yasmiṃ koṭṭhāse cīvaraṃ tattha vasitabbaṃ.

489. Herein, in the phrase 'seven abbhantaras,' one abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits. If a caravan, while traveling, stops, having encompassed a village or a river, and stands united with those who have entered, pervading both this bank and the other bank, then only the caravan's perimeter is obtained. Or, if the caravan is included within the village or river, having entered inside, then both the village's perimeter and the river's perimeter are obtained. If one stops after having crossed the monastery boundary, but the robe is within the boundary, one must go to the monastery and stay. If the robe is outside the boundary, one must stay right near the caravan. If, while traveling, the caravan is split midway because a cart is broken or an ox is lost, one must stay in whichever section the robe is.

490. Ekakulassa khette hatthapāso nāma cīvarahatthapāsoyeva, nānākulassa khette hatthapāso nāma khettadvārassa hatthapāso. Aparikkhitte cīvarasseva hatthapāso.

490. In a field belonging to a single family, 'arm's reach' is the arm's reach of the robe itself. In a field belonging to various families, 'arm's reach' is the arm's reach of the field's entrance. In an unenclosed field, it is the arm's reach of the robe itself.

491-4. Dhaññakaraṇanti khalaṃ vuccati. Ārāmoti pupphārāmo [P 3.0655] vā phalārāmo vā. Dvīsupi khette vuttasadisova vinicchayo. Vihāro nivesanasadiso. Rukkhamūle antochāyāyanti chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsassa anto eva. Viraḷasākhassa pana rukkhassa ātapena phuṭṭhokāse ṭhapitaṃ nissaggiyameva hoti, tasmā tādisassa sākhācchāyāya vā khandhacchāyāya vā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace sākhāya vā viṭape vā ṭhapeti, upari aññasākhācchāyāya phuṭṭhokāseyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Khujjarukkhassa chāyā dūraṃ gacchati, chāyāya gataṭṭhāne ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Idhāpi hatthapāso cīvarahatthapāsoyeva.

491-4. 'Dhaññakaraṇa' (a place for grain) is called a threshing floor. 'Ārāma' is either a flower park or a fruit park. In both these cases, the determination is just like that stated for a field. A monastery is similar to a dwelling. At the foot of a tree, 'within the shade' means precisely inside the place touched by the shade. However, a robe placed in a spot touched by the sun under a tree with sparse branches becomes subject to forfeiture. Therefore, under such a tree, it should be placed in the shade of a branch or in the shade of the trunk. If one places it on a branch or a forked branch, it must be placed only in a spot above that is touched by the shade of another branch. The shade of a crooked tree goes far; it is indeed permissible to place the robe in the spot where the shade has gone. Here too, 'arm's reach' is the arm's reach of the robe itself.

Agāmake araññeti agāmakaṃ nāma araññaṃ viñjhāṭavīādīsu vā samuddamajjhe vā macchabandhānaṃ agamanapathe dīpakesu labbhati. Samantā sattabbhantarāti majjhe ṭhitassa samattā sabbadisāsu [V 2.0213] sattabbhantarā, vinibbedhena cuddasa honti. Majjhe nisinno puratthimāya vā pacchimāya vā disāya pariyante ṭhapitacīvaraṃ rakkhati. Sace pana aruṇuggamanasamaye kesaggamattampi puratthimaṃ disaṃ gacchati, pacchimāya disāya cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Esa nayo itarasmiṃ. Uposathakāle pana parisapariyante nisinnabhikkhuto paṭṭhāya sattabbhantarasīmā sodhetabbā. Yattakaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho vaḍḍhati, sīmāpi tattakaṃ vaḍḍhati.

Regarding 'in a non-village, in the wilderness': a wilderness called 'non-village' is found either in places such as the Vindhya forest, or on small islands in the middle of the ocean where there is no path for fishermen to travel back and forth. Regarding 'within seven abbhantaras all around': for one standing in the middle, there are seven abbhantaras in all directions all around; by penetration, there are fourteen. One sitting in the middle protects a robe placed at the limit of either the eastern or western direction. However, if at the time of sunrise he goes even a hair's breadth toward the eastern direction, the robe in the western direction becomes subject to forfeiture. This same principle applies to the other. Furthermore, at the time of the Uposatha, the boundary of seven abbhantaras should be cleared, starting from the bhikkhu seated at the edge of the assembly. To the extent that the community of monks grows, the boundary also expands to that extent.

495. Anissajjitvā paribhuñjati āpatti dukkaṭassāti ettha sace padhāniko bhikkhu sabbarattiṃ padhānamanuyuñjitvā paccusasamaye “nhāyissāmī”ti tīṇipi cīvarāni tīre ṭhapetvā nadiṃ otarati, nhāyantasseva cassa aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahati, kiṃ kātabbaṃ. So hi yadi uttaritvā cīvaraṃ nivāseti, nissaggiyacīvaraṃ [M 2.0237] anissajjitvā paribhuñjanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Atha naggo gacchati, evampi dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatīti? Na āpajjati. So hi yāva aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā vinayakammaṃ na karoti, tāva tesaṃ [P 3.0656] cīvarānaṃ aparibhogārahattā naṭṭhacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhito hoti. Naṭṭhacīvarassa ca akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā ekaṃ nivāsetvā dve hatthena gahetvā vihāraṃ gantvā vinayakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace dūre vihāro hoti, antarāmagge manussā sañcaranti. Ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ aṃsakūṭe ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ. Sace vihāre sabhāgabhikkhū na passati, bhikkhācāraṃ gatā honti, saṅghāṭiṃ bahigāme ṭhapetvā santaruttarena āsanasālaṃ gantvā vinayakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace bahigāme corabhayaṃ hoti, pārupitvā gantabbaṃ. Sace āsanasālā sambādhā hoti janākiṇṇā, na sakkā ekamante cīvaraṃ apanetvā vinayakammaṃ kātuṃ, ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ādāya bahigāmaṃ gantvā vinayakammaṃ katvā cīvarāni paribhuñjitabbāni.

495. Here, regarding 'Not having relinquished it, he uses it—there is an offense of wrong-doing': If a bhikkhu devoted to striving, having exerted himself all night, thinks at dawn, 'I will bathe,' and, having placed all three robes on the bank, enters the river, and while he is bathing the dawn breaks for him—what is to be done? For if he, having come out of the water, puts on a robe, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing on account of using a robe subject to forfeiture without having relinquished it. Or if he goes naked, does he also incur an offense of wrong-doing? He does not incur an offense. For as long as he does not see another bhikkhu and perform the formal act of the Vinaya, he is in the position of one whose robes are lost, because those robes are unfit for use. And for one whose robes are lost, there is nothing called 'improper'. Therefore, having put on one robe and taken the other two in his hand, he should go to the monastery and perform the formal act of the Vinaya. If the monastery is far away and people are traveling on the path in between, he should go having put on one robe, worn another as an upper garment, and placed one on the point of his shoulder. If he does not see fellow bhikkhus in the monastery because they have gone for alms, he should place the outer robe outside the village, go to the dining hall with the inner and upper robes, and perform the formal act of the Vinaya. If there is a fear of thieves outside the village, he should go wearing it. If the dining hall is crowded and thronged with people, and it is not possible to perform the formal act of the Vinaya in a secluded place after removing the robe, he should take one bhikkhu, go outside the village, perform the formal act of the Vinaya, and then the robes may be used.

Sace bhikkhū daharānaṃ hatthe pattacīvaraṃ datvā maggaṃ gacchantā pacchime yāme sayitukāmā honti, attano attano cīvaraṃ hatthapāse katvāva sayitabbaṃ. Sace gacchantānaṃyeva asampattesu daharesu aruṇaṃ uggacchati, cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti, nissayo pana na paṭippassambhati, daharānampi purato gacchantānaṃ theresu asampattesu eseva nayo. Maggaṃ virajjhitvā araññe aññamaññaṃ apassantesupi eseva nayo. Sace pana daharā “mayaṃ, bhante, muhuttaṃ sayitvā asukasmiṃ nāma okāse tumhe sampāpuṇissāmā”ti vatvā yāva aruṇuggamanā sayanti, cīvarañca nissaggiyaṃ hoti, nissayo ca paṭippassambhati, dahare uyyojetvā theresu sayantesupi eseva nayo. Dvedhāpathaṃ disvā therā “ayaṃ maggo” daharā “ayaṃ maggo”ti vatvā aññamaññassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā gatā, saha aruṇuggamanā cīvarāni ca nissaggiyāni honti[V 2.0214], nissayo ca paṭippassambhati. Sace daharā maggato okkamma “antoaruṇeyeva nivattissāmā”ti bhesajjatthāya gāmaṃ pavisitvā āgacchanti. Asampattānaṃyeva ca [P 3.0657] tesaṃ aruṇo uggacchati, cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo pana na paṭippassambhati. Sace pana dhenubhayena vā sunakhabhayena vā “muhuttaṃ ṭhatvā gamissāmā”ti ṭhatvā vā nisīditvā vā gacchanti, antarā aruṇe uggate cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo ca paṭippassambhati. Sace “antoaruṇeyeva āgamissāmā”ti antosīmāyaṃ [M 2.0238] gāmaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ antarā aruṇo uggacchati, neva cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, na nissayo paṭippassambhati. Sace pana “vibhāyatu tāvā”ti nisīdanti, aruṇe uggatepi na cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo pana paṭippassambhati. Yepi “antoaruṇeyeva āgamissāmā”ti sāmantavihāraṃ dhammasavanatthāya saussāhā gacchanti, antarāmaggeyeva ca nesaṃ aruṇo uggacchati, cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo pana na paṭippassambhati. Sace dhammagāravena “yāva pariyosānaṃ sutvāva gamissāmā”ti nisīdanti, saha aruṇassuggamanā cīvarānipi nissaggiyāni honti, nissayopi paṭippassambhati. Therena daharaṃ cīvaradhovanatthāya gāmakaṃ pesentena attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvāva dātabbaṃ. Daharassāpi cīvaraṃ paccuddharāpetvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace assatiyā gacchati, attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvā daharassa cīvaraṃ vissāsena gahetvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace thero nassarati, daharo eva sarati, daharena attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvā therassa cīvaraṃ vissāsena gahetvā gantvā vattabbo “bhante, tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjathā”ti attanopi cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ekassa satiyāpi āpattimokkho hotīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva[P 3.0658].

If bhikkhus, having given their bowl and robe into the hands of junior bhikkhus while traveling on a journey, wish to lie down in the last watch of the night, they should lie down only after having placed their own robes within arm's reach. If, while they are traveling, the dawn breaks before the junior bhikkhus have arrived, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture, but the dependence is not resolved. The same principle applies when the junior bhikkhus are traveling ahead and the senior bhikkhus have not yet reached them. Even if they stray from the path and do not see each other in the wilderness, the same principle applies. But if the junior bhikkhus say, “Venerable Sir, we will sleep for a moment and meet you at such and such a place,” and they sleep until the breaking of dawn, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture, and the dependence is resolved. The same principle applies if the senior bhikkhus sleep after sending the junior bhikkhus ahead. If, upon seeing a fork in the path, the senior bhikkhus say, “This is the path,” and the junior bhikkhus say, “This is the path,” and they depart without accepting each other’s word, then with the breaking of dawn, the robes become subject to forfeiture, and the dependence is resolved. If the junior bhikkhus leave the path, thinking, “We will return before dawn,” and enter a village for medicine, and the dawn breaks before they have returned, their robes become subject to forfeiture, but the dependence is not resolved. If, due to fear of a cow or fear of a dog, they stop or sit down, thinking, “We will go after a moment,” and the dawn breaks in the interim, the robes become subject to forfeiture, and the dependence is resolved. If, thinking, “We will return before dawn,” they enter a village that is within the boundary, and the dawn breaks in the interim, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture, nor is the dependence resolved. If, however, they sit down, thinking, “Let it dawn first,” even when the dawn breaks, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture, but the dependence is resolved. Those who, being zealous, go to a nearby monastery to hear the Dhamma, thinking, “We will return before dawn,” but the dawn breaks for them on the path in the interim, their robes become subject to forfeiture, but the dependence is not resolved. If, out of reverence for the Dhamma, they sit down, thinking, “We will go only after hearing it to the end,” then with the breaking of dawn, the robes also become subject to forfeiture, and the dependence is also resolved. When a senior bhikkhu sends a junior bhikkhu to a small village for washing a robe, he should give his own robe only after having withdrawn it from determination. The junior bhikkhu’s robe should also be caused to be withdrawn and set aside. If he goes unmindfully, the senior bhikkhu should withdraw his own robe and, with trust, take the junior bhikkhu's robe and set it aside. If the senior bhikkhu does not remember, but the junior bhikkhu does remember, the junior bhikkhu should withdraw his own robe and, with trust, take the senior bhikkhu's robe, go to him, and say, “Venerable Sir, please determine your robe and use it.” He should also determine his own robe. Thus, through the mindfulness of even one, there is release from the offense. The rest is clear in meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu paṭhamakathinasikkhāpade anadhiṭṭhānaṃ avikappanañca akiriyaṃ, idha apaccuddharaṇaṃ ayameva viseso. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayamevāti.

Regarding the origins and so forth, in the first Kathina training rule, non-determination and non-placing-under-shared-ownership are non-action; here, non-withdrawal is non-action. This is the only difference. The rest is in accordance with the method stated everywhere.

Udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Udosita training rule is finished.

3. Tatiyakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Third Kathina Training Rule

497. Tena samayenāti tatiyakathinasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha ussāpetvā punappunaṃ vimajjatīti “valīsu naṭṭhāsu idaṃ mahantaṃ bhavissatī”ti maññamāno udakena siñcitvā pādehi akkamitvā [V 2.0215] hatthehi ussāpetvā ukkhipitvā piṭṭhiyaṃ ghaṃsati, taṃ ātape sukkhaṃ paṭhamappamāṇameva hoti. So punapi tathā karoti, tena vuttaṃ – “ussāpetvā punappunaṃ vimajjatī”ti. Taṃ evaṃ kilamantaṃ bhagavā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova disvā nikkhamitvā senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍanto viya tattha agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “addasa kho bhagavā”tiādi.

497. By “At that time” is meant the third Kathina training rule. Therein, “having raised it, he rubs it again and again” means: thinking, “When the creases are gone, this will become large,” he sprinkles it with water, treads on it with his feet, lifts it with his hands, raises it up, and rubs it on its surface. When it is dry in the sun, it is just its original size. He does so again. Therefore it was said: “having raised it, he rubs it again and again.” The Blessed One, while sitting in the Perfumed Chamber, saw him toiling thus, and having come out, he went there as if wandering about the lodgings. Therefore it was said: “The Blessed One saw,” and so forth.

499-500. Ekādasamāseti [M 2.0239] ekaṃ pacchimakattikamāsaṃ ṭhapetvā sese ekādasamāse. Sattamāseti kattikamāsaṃ hemantike ca cattāroti pañcamāse ṭhapetvā sese sattamāse. Kālepi ādissa dinnanti saṅghassa vā “idaṃ akālacīvara”nti uddisitvā dinnaṃ, ekapuggalassa vā “idaṃ tuyhaṃ dammī”ti dinnaṃ.

By “eleven months” is meant a robe that has arisen in the remaining eleven months, having excluded the one last month of Kattika. By “seven months” is meant a robe that has arisen in the remaining seven months, having excluded the five months, that is, Kattika and the four months of the cold season. “Given, having specified, even in season” means a robe given to the Sangha, having pointed it out as, “This is an out-of-season robe,” or given to a single individual, saying, “I give this to you.”

Saṅghato vāti attano pattabhāgavasena saṅghato vā uppajjeyya. Gaṇato vāti idaṃ suttantikagaṇassa dema, idaṃ ābhidhammikagaṇassāti evaṃ gaṇassa denti. Tato attano pattabhāgavasena gaṇato vā uppajjeyya.

By “from the Sangha” is meant it may arise from the Sangha by way of one's own allotted share. By “from a group” is meant when they give to a group, saying, “We give this to the Suttantika group; this to the Ābhidhammika group.” From that, it may arise from the group by way of one's own allotted share.

No cassa pāripūrīti no ce pāripūrī bhaveyya, yattakena kayiramānaṃ adhiṭṭhānacīvaraṃ pahoti, tañce cīvaraṃ tattakaṃ na bhaveyya, ūnakaṃ bhaveyyāti attho.

By “And if it is not sufficient” is meant: if it should not be sufficient. That is, if the robe-cloth is not of the amount with which a determined robe, when being made, is sufficient, it would be deficient; this is the meaning.

Paccāsā hoti saṅghato vātiādīsu asukadivasaṃ nāma saṅgho cīvarāni labhissati, gaṇo labhissati, tato me cīvaraṃ uppajjissatīti evaṃ saṅghato vā gaṇato vā paccāsā hoti. Ñātakehi me cīvaratthāya pesitaṃ, mittehi pesitaṃ, te āgatā cīvare dassantīti evaṃ ñātito vā mittato vā paccāsā hoti. Paṃsukūlaṃ vāti ettha pana paṃsukūlaṃ vā lacchāmīti [P 3.0659] evaṃ paccāsā hotīti yojetabbaṃ. Attano vā dhanenāti attano kappāsasuttādinā dhanena, asukadivasaṃ nāma lacchāmīti evaṃ vā paccāsā hotīti attho.

In the phrases beginning with “There is expectation from the Sangha,” it means there is an expectation: “On such-and-such a day, the Sangha will receive robes, the group will receive robes, and from that a robe will arise for me.” Thus, there is an expectation from the Sangha or from the group. “My relatives have sent thread for the sake of a robe for me; my friends have sent thread. When the robe arrives, they will give it.” Thus, there is an expectation from relatives or from friends. In the phrase “or a rag-robe,” it should be construed as: “There is an expectation, ‘I will obtain a rag-robe.’” As for “or with one's own wealth,” the meaning is: with one's own wealth, such as cotton thread and so on, there is an expectation, “I will obtain it on such-and-such a day.”

Tato ce uttari nikkhipeyya satiyāpi paccāsāyāti māsaparamato ce uttari nikkhipeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti attho. Evaṃ pana avatvā yasmā antarā uppajjamāne paccāsācīvare mūlacīvarassa uppannadivasato yāva vīsatimo divaso tāva uppannaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ mūlacīvaraṃ attano gatikaṃ karoti, tato uddhaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ [V 2.0216] attano gatikaṃ karoti. Tasmā taṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ “tadahuppanne mūlacīvare”tiādinā nayena padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ uttānatthameva.

“If one should keep it beyond that, even with an expectation” means: if one should keep it beyond the limit of one month, it is an offense of relinquishment with confession. This is the meaning. However, this was not stated in this way in the division of words because when a robe of expectation arises in the interim, for as long as it is up to the twentieth day from the day the original robe arose, the arisen robe of expectation makes the original robe follow its own course. Beyond that, the original robe makes the robe of expectation follow its own course. Therefore, to show that distinction, the division of words was stated by the method beginning with, “When the original robe has arisen on that day…” That is clear in meaning.

Visabhāge uppanne mūlacīvareti yadi mūlacīvaraṃ saṇhaṃ, paccāsācīvaraṃ thūlaṃ, na sakkā yojetuṃ. Rattiyo ca sesā honti, na tāva māso pūrati[M 2.0240], na akāmā niggahena cīvaraṃ kāretabbaṃ. Aññaṃ paccāsācīvaraṃ labhitvāyeva kālabbhantare kāretabbaṃ. Paccāsācīvarampi parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Atha mūlacīvaraṃ thūlaṃ hoti, paccāsācīvaraṃ saṇhaṃ, mūlacīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā paccāsācīvarameva mūlacīvaraṃ katvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Taṃ puna māsaparihāraṃ labhati, etenupāyena yāva icchati tāva aññamaññaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ katvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

“When a dissimilar one has arisen in regard to the original robe”: if the original robe is fine and the robe of expectation is coarse, it is not possible to join them. And nights are remaining, the month is not yet complete; in that case, the robe should not be made unwillingly or by coercion. It should be made within the time limit only after obtaining another robe of expectation. The first robe of expectation should also be determined as a requisite-cloth. Or, if the original robe is coarse and the robe of expectation is fine, having determined the original robe as a requisite-cloth, the robe of expectation itself should be made the original robe and kept. That again receives the one-month allowance. By this method, for as long as one wishes, it is allowable to keep a robe by making one after another the original robe. The rest is clear.

Samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamakathinasadisānevāti.

The origins and so on are just like those of the first Kathina training rule.

Tatiyakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third Kathina training rule is concluded.

4. Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on an Old Robe

503-5. Tena samayenāti purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha yāva sattamā pitāmahayugāti pitupitā pitāmaho, pitāmahassa yugaṃ pitāmahayugaṃ. Yuganti āyuppamāṇaṃ vuccati. Abhilāpa mattameva cetaṃ. Atthato pana pitāmahoyeva pitāmahayugaṃ. Tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā. Evaṃ yāva sattamo puriso tāva yā asambaddhā sā yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā asambaddhāti [P 3.0660] vuccati. Desanāmukhameva cetaṃ. “Mātito vā pitito vā”tivacanato pana pitāmahayugampi pitāmahiyugampi mātāmahayugampi mātāmahiyugampi tesaṃ bhātubhaginībhāgineyyaputtapaputtādayopi sabbe idha saṅgahitā evāti veditabbā.

“At that time” refers to the training rule concerning an old robe. Therein, regarding “up to the seventh grandfather-generation”: the father's father is the “grandfather” (pitāmaha); the grandfather's generation is the “grandfather-generation” (pitāmahayuga). “Generation” (yuga) is said to mean the measure of a lifespan. And this is merely an expression. In terms of meaning, however, the grandfather himself is the “grandfather-generation.” Beyond him, all previous male ancestors are included by the term “grandfather.” Thus, up to the seventh man, any woman who is unrelated is called “unrelated up to the seventh grandfather-generation.” And this is merely the introduction to the discourse. However, from the statement “from the mother's side or from the father's side,” it should be understood that the paternal grandfather's generation, the paternal grandmother's generation, the maternal grandfather's generation, the maternal grandmother's generation, and all their relatives such as brothers, sisters, nephews, sons, grandsons, and so on, are included herein.

Tatrāyaṃ vitthāranayo – pitā pitupitā tassa pitā tassāpi pitāti evaṃ yāva sattamā yugā, pitā pitumātā tassā pitā ca mātā ca bhātā ca bhaginī ca puttā ca dhītaro cāti evampi uddhañca adho ca yāva sattamā yugā, pitā pitubhātā pitubhaginī pituputtā pitudhītaro tesampi puttadhītuparamparāti evampi yāva sattamā yugā, mātā mātumātā tassā mātā tassāpi mātāti evampi yāva sattamā yugā, mātā mātupitā tassa mātā ca pitā ca [V 2.0217] bhātā ca bhaginī ca puttā ca dhītaro cāti, evampi uddhañca adho ca yāva sattamā yugā, mātā mātubhātā mātubhaginī mātuputtā mātudhītaro tesampi puttadhītuparamparāti [M 2.0241] evampi yāva sattamā yugā, neva mātusambandhena na pitusambandhena sambaddhā, ayaṃ aññātikā nāma.

Herein, this is the detailed method: the father, the father's father, his father, and his father's father—thus up to the seventh generation; the father, the father's mother, her father and mother, brother and sister, sons and daughters—thus also upwards and downwards up to the seventh generation; the father, the father's brother, the father's sister, the father's sons, the father's daughters, and their succession of sons and daughters—thus also up to the seventh generation; the mother, the mother's mother, her mother, and her mother's mother—thus also up to the seventh generation; the mother, the mother's father, his mother and father, brother and sister, sons and daughters—thus also upwards and downwards up to the seventh generation; the mother, the mother's brother, the mother's sister, the mother's sons, the mother's daughters, and their succession of sons and daughters—thus also up to the seventh generation. One who is connected neither by relation on the mother's side nor by relation on the father's side—this one is called a non-relative.

Ubhato saṅgheti bhikkhunisaṅghe ñatticatutthena bhikkhusaṅghe ñatticatutthenāti aṭṭhavācikavinayakammena upasampannā.

‘By both Saṅghas’ means a bhikkhunī who has been fully ordained by a Vinaya act with eight recitations: that is, by a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and by a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

Sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampīti rajitvā kappaṃ katvā ekavārampi nivatthaṃ vā pārutaṃ vā. Antamaso paribhogasīsena aṃse vā matthake vā katvā maggaṃ gato hoti, ussīsakaṃ vā katvā nipanno hoti, etampi purāṇacīvarameva. Sace pana paccattharaṇassa heṭṭhā katvā nipajjati, hatthehi vā ukkhipitvā ākāse vitānaṃ katvā sīsena aphusanto gacchati, ayaṃ paribhogo nāma na hotīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘Even once worn as a lower garment or even once worn as an upper garment’ means a lower robe or an upper robe that, after being dyed and marked with the kappa point, has been worn or draped even one time. At the very least, if one has gone on a journey having placed it on one's shoulder or head by way of use, or has lain down having made it into a pillow, this too is an old robe. But if one lies down having placed it underneath a covering sheet, or if one goes along without it touching one's head after having lifted it with the hands and made it into a canopy in the open air, this is not called ‘use’—so it is said in the Kurundī commentary.

Dhotaṃ nissaggiyanti ettha evaṃ āṇattā bhikkhunī dhovanatthāya uddhanaṃ sajjeti, dārūni saṃharati, aggiṃ karoti, udakaṃ āharati yāva naṃ dhovitvā ukkhipati, tāva bhikkhuniyā payoge payoge bhikkhussa dukkaṭaṃ. Dhovitvā [P 3.0661] ukkhittamatte nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Sace duddhotanti maññamānā puna siñcati vā dhovati vā yāva niṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati tāva payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ. Esa nayo rajanākoṭanesu. Rajanadoṇiyañhi rajanaṃ ākiritvā yāva sakiṃ cīvaraṃ rajati, tato pubbe yaṃkiñci rajanatthāya karoti, pacchā vā paṭirajati, sabbattha payoge payoge bhikkhussa dukkaṭaṃ. Evaṃ ākoṭanepi payogo veditabbo.

Regarding ‘a washed robe is to be forfeited’: Herein, a bhikkhunī thus instructed prepares a stove for washing, gathers firewood, makes a fire, and fetches water. Until she has washed the robe and lifted it out, for every effort made by the bhikkhunī, the bhikkhu incurs a dukkaṭa offense. As soon as it is washed and lifted out, it becomes an item to be forfeited. If, thinking, ‘It is poorly washed,’ she sprinkles it or washes it again, then for every effort until the task is completed, there is a dukkaṭa. This is the same method for dyeing and beating. Indeed, in the case of a dyeing vat, having poured in the dye, until she dyes the robe once—whatever she does for the purpose of dyeing before that, or if she re-dyes it afterwards—in every case, for every effort, there is a dukkaṭa for the bhikkhu. In the same way, the analysis of the application should be understood for beating.

506. Aññātikāya aññātikasaññī purāṇacīvaraṃ dhovāpetīti no cepi “imaṃ dhovā”ti vadati, atha kho dhovanatthāya kāyavikāraṃ katvā hatthena vā hatthe deti, pādamūle vā ṭhapeti, upari vā khipati, sikkhamānāsāmaṇerīsāmaṇeraupāsakatitthiyādīnaṃ vā hatthe peseti, nadītitthe dhovantiyā upacāre vā khipati, antodvādasahatthe okāse ṭhatvā, dhovāpitaṃyeva hoti. Sace pana upacāraṃ muñcitvā orato ṭhapeti sā ce dhovitvā āneti, anāpatti. Sikkhamānāya vā sāmaṇeriyā vā upāsikāya vā hatthe dhovanatthāya deti, sā ce upasampajjitvā dhovati, āpattiyeva. Upāsakassa hatthe deti, so ce liṅge parivatte bhikkhunīsu [V 2.0218] pabbajitvā upasampajjitvā dhovati[M 2.0242], āpattiyeva. Sāmaṇerassa vā bhikkhussa vā hatthe dinnepi liṅgaparivattane eseva nayo.

506. If one has an old robe washed by a non-relative, while perceiving her as a non-relative: even if one does not say, ‘Wash this,’ but, for the purpose of having it washed, makes a bodily gesture and gives it from one's hand into her hand, or places it at her feet, or throws it near her, or sends it into the hands of a female probationer, female novice, male novice, lay follower, non-Buddhist ascetic, and so on, or throws it into the vicinity of someone washing at a river ford, while standing in a place within twelve cubits—it is indeed considered ‘having had it washed’. But if one places it outside that vicinity, and she washes it and brings it back, there is no offense. If one gives it into the hands of a female probationer, a female novice, or a laywoman for washing, and she washes it after receiving full ordination, there is still an offense. If one gives it into the hands of a layman, and he, after a change of sex, goes forth among the bhikkhunīs and washes it after receiving full ordination, there is still an offense. This same method applies if it is given into the hands of a male novice or a bhikkhu, in the case of a change of sex.

Dhovāpeti rajāpetītiādīsu ekena vatthunā nissaggiyaṃ, dutiyena dukkaṭaṃ. Tīṇipi kārāpentassa ekena nissaggiyaṃ, sesehi dve dukkaṭāni. Yasmā panetāni dhovanādīni paṭipāṭiyā vā uppaṭipāṭiyā vā kārentassa mokkho natthi, tasmā ettha tīṇi catukkāni vuttāni. Sacepi hi “imaṃ cīvaraṃ rajitvā dhovitvā ānehī”ti vutte sā bhikkhunī paṭhamaṃ dhovitvā pacchā rajati, nissaggiyena dukkaṭameva. Evaṃ sabbesu viparītavacanesu nayo netabbo. Sace pana “dhovitvā ānehī”ti vuttā dhovati ceva rajati ca, dhovāpanapaccayā eva āpatti, rajane anāpatti. Evaṃ sabbattha vuttādhikakaraṇe “avuttā dhovatī”ti iminā lakkhaṇena anāpatti veditabbā. “Imasmiṃ [P 3.0662] cīvare yaṃ kātabbaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ tuyhaṃ bhāro”ti vadanto pana ekavācāya sambahulā āpattiyo āpajjatīti.

In cases such as ‘has it washed, has it dyed,’ by one act there is an offense entailing forfeiture, and by the second, a dukkaṭa. For one who has all three things done, by one act there is an offense entailing forfeiture, and by the remaining two, there are two dukkaṭas. Since there is no escape from the offense for one who has these acts—washing and so on—done either in sequence or out of sequence, therefore three sets of four are stated here. For if, when a bhikkhunī is told, ‘Having dyed this robe, wash it and bring it,’ she first washes it and then dyes it, there is a dukkaṭa along with the offense entailing forfeiture. This method should be applied in all cases of reversed instructions. But if, when told, ‘Wash it and bring it,’ she both washes and dyes it, the offense is only on account of having it washed; for the dyeing, there is no offense. Thus, in all cases of doing more than what was stated, ‘no offense’ should be understood by the principle of ‘she washes without being told.’ However, one who says, ‘Whatever needs to be done to this robe, all of it is your responsibility,’ incurs multiple offenses with a single utterance.

Aññātikāya vematiko aññātikāya ñātikasaññīti imānipi padāni vuttānaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena vitthārato veditabbāni.

The terms ‘being doubtful about a non-relative’ and ‘perceiving a non-relative as a relative’—these too should be understood in detail by way of the three sets of four that have been mentioned.

Ekato upasampannāyāti bhikkhunīnaṃ santike upasampannāya dhovāpentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampannāya pana yathāvatthukameva, bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampannā nāma pañcasatā sākiyāniyo.

Regarding one ‘ordained by a single Saṅgha’: for a monk who has a robe washed by a bhikkhunī ordained in the presence of bhikkhunīs, it is an offense of wrong-doing. But for one who has it washed by a bhikkhunī ordained in the presence of bhikkhus, the offense is according to the case. Those ordained in the presence of bhikkhus are the five hundred Sakyan ladies.

507. Avuttā dhovatīti uddesāya vā ovādāya vā āgatā kilinnaṃ cīvaraṃ disvā ṭhapitaṭṭhānato gahetvā vā “detha, ayya, dhovissāmī”ti āharāpetvā vā dhovati ceva rajati ca ākoṭeti ca, ayaṃ avuttā dhovati nāma. Yāpi “imaṃ cīvaraṃ dhovā”ti daharaṃ vā sāmaṇeraṃ vā āṇāpentassa bhikkhuno sutvā “āharathayya ahaṃ dhovissāmī”ti dhovati, tāvakālikaṃ vā gahetvā dhovitvā rajitvā deti, ayampi avuttā dhovati nāma.

507. Regarding ‘washes without being told’: A bhikkhunī who has come for the purpose of recitation or for the purpose of receiving an exhortation, sees a soiled robe, and either takes it from the place where it was put, or has it brought to her, saying, ‘Venerable sir, give it, I will wash it,’ and then washes, dyes, and beats it—this is called ‘one who washes without being told.’ Also, a bhikkhunī who, having heard the words of a bhikkhu instructing a junior monk or a novice, ‘Wash this robe,’ says, ‘Venerable sirs, bring it, I will wash it,’ and washes it, or takes it for a time, washes it, dyes it, and gives it back—this one too is called ‘one who washes without being told.’

Aññaṃ parikkhāranti upāhanatthavikapattatthavikaaṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanamañcapīṭhabhisitaṭṭikādiṃ yaṃkiñci dhovāpeti, anāpatti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

Regarding 'another requisite': if one has whatsoever other item washed, such as a bag for sandals, a bowl-bag, a shoulder strap, a waistband, a couch, a chair, a bolster, a mat, and so on, there is no offense. The rest here has a clear meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu [M 2.0243][V 2.0219] pana idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding its origins and so on, this training rule has six origins. It is an action, not one from which there is release through misperception, unintentional, an offense by designation, involves bodily action and verbal action, arises from three mind-states, and is accompanied by three feelings.

Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on old robes is concluded.

5. Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving Robes

508. Tena samayenāti cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha piṇḍapātapaṭikkantāti piṇḍapātato paṭikkantā. Yena andhavanaṃ tenupasaṅkamīti apaññatte sikkhāpade yena andhavanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Katakammāti katacorikakammā, sandhicchedanādīhi parabhaṇḍaṃ haritāti vuttaṃ hoti. Coragāmaṇikoti corajeṭṭhako. So kira pubbe theriṃ [P 3.0663] jānāti, tasmā corānaṃ purato gacchanto disvā “ito mā gacchatha, sabbe ito ethā”ti te gahetvā aññena maggena agamāsi. Samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvāti therī kira paricchinnavelāyaṃyeva samādhimhā vuṭṭhahi. Sopi tasmiṃyeva khaṇe evaṃ avaca, tasmā sā assosi, sutvā ca “natthi dāni añño ettha samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā aññatra mayā”ti taṃ maṃsaṃ aggahesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho uppalavaṇṇā bhikkhunī”tiādi.

508. Regarding 'At that time': this introduces the training rule on receiving a robe. Here, 'returned from the alms-round' means having returned from the alms-round. 'She went to where the Andhavana was' refers to her going there before this training rule was laid down. 'Having done the deed' means having committed the act of theft; it is said that they took the belongings of others by means of house-breaking and so on. 'The robber chief' means the chief of the robbers. It is said that he knew the elder nun previously. Therefore, while going in front of the robbers, he saw her and said, 'Do not go this way. All of you, come this way,' and taking those robbers, he went by another path. Regarding 'having arisen from concentration': it is said the elder nun arose from concentration at the very time that had been determined. He too spoke thus at that very moment, so she heard. And having heard, she thought, 'Now, in this forest, there is no other ascetic or brahmin apart from me,' and she took that meat. Because of that, it was said: 'Then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā...' and so on.

Ohiyyakoti avahīyako avaseso, vihāravāraṃ patvā ekova vihāre ṭhitoti attho. Sace me tvaṃ antaravāsakaṃ dadeyyāsīti kasmā āha? Saṇhaṃ ghanamaṭṭhaṃ antaravāsakaṃ disvā lobhena, apica appako tassā antaravāsake lobho, theriyā pana sikhāppattā koṭṭhāsasampatti tenassā sarīrapāripūriṃ passissāmīti visamalobhaṃ uppādetvā evamāha. Antimanti pañcannaṃ cīvarānaṃ sabbapariyantaṃ hutvā antimaṃ, antimanti pacchimaṃ. Aññaṃ lesenāpi vikappetvā vā paccuddharitvā vā ṭhapitaṃ cīvaraṃ natthīti evaṃ yathāanuññātānaṃ pañcannaṃ cīvarānaṃ dhāraṇavaseneva āha, na lobhena, na hi khīṇāsavānaṃ lobho atthi. Nippīḷiyamānāti upamaṃ dassetvā gāḷhaṃ pīḷayamānā.

'One who was left behind' means one who remained, the remainder; the meaning is that having reached his turn to watch the monastery, he stayed in the monastery alone. Why did he say, 'If you would give me the inner robe'? He said it out of greed, having seen the soft, thick, and smooth inner robe. Moreover, his greed for the inner robe was slight, but the elder nun's perfection of bodily parts had reached its peak. Because of that, having aroused an improper greed with the thought, 'I will see the fullness of her body,' he spoke thus. 'The last one' means, of the five robes, it is the very last one, the final one. 'There is no other robe set aside, even by a hint, either by formal sharing or by revocation'—thus she spoke only in terms of wearing the five permitted robes, not out of greed. Indeed, for those whose cankers are destroyed, there is no greed. 'Being hard-pressed' means, showing a simile, being severely pressed.

Antaravāsakaṃ [M 2.0244] datvā upassayaṃ agamāsīti saṅkaccikaṃ nivāsetvā yathā tassa manoratho na pūrati, evaṃ hatthataleyeva dassetvā agamāsi.

Regarding 'Having given the inner robe, she went to her dwelling': having worn the breast-cloth as an undergarment so that his desire of mind would not be fulfilled, she showed the robe that was to be given on the back of her hand and went away.

510. Kasmā [V 2.0220] pārivattakacīvaraṃ appaṭigaṇhante ujjhāyiṃsu? “Sace ettakopi amhesu ayyānaṃ vissāso natthi, kathaṃ mayaṃ yāpessāmā”ti vihatthatāya samabhitunnattā.

510. Why did they complain about the monks not accepting the exchange-robe? Thinking, 'If the venerable sirs have not even this much trust in us, how then shall we be able to carry on?', they complained out of helplessness and because they were greatly agitated.

Anujānāmi bhikkhave imesaṃ pañcannanti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ sahadhammikānaṃ samasaddhānaṃ samasīlānaṃ samadiṭṭhīnaṃ pārivattakaṃ gahetuṃ anujānāmīti attho.

Regarding 'I allow, O bhikkhus, for these five': the meaning is, 'I allow the taking of an exchange-robe from these five co-religionists who are of equal faith, equal virtue, and equal view.'

512. Payoge dukkaṭanti gahaṇatthāya hatthappasāraṇādīsu dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭilābhenāti paṭiggahaṇena. Tattha ca hatthena vā hatthe detu, pādamūle vā ṭhapetu, upari vā khipatu, so ce sādiyati[P 3.0664], gahitameva hoti. Sace pana sikkhamānāsāmaṇerasāmaṇerīupāsakaupāsikādīnaṃ hatthe pesitaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti, anāpatti. Dhammakathaṃ kathentassa catassopi parisā cīvarāni ca nānāvirāgavatthāni ca ānetvā pādamūle ṭhapenti, upacāre vā ṭhatvā upacāraṃ vā muñcitvā khipanti, yaṃ tattha bhikkhunīnaṃ santakaṃ, taṃ aññatra pārivattakā gaṇhantassa āpattiyeva. Atha pana rattibhāge khittāni honti, “idaṃ bhikkhuniyā, idaṃ aññesa”nti ñātuṃ na sakkā, pārivattakakiccaṃ natthīti mahāpaccariyaṃ kurundiyañca vuttaṃ, taṃ acittakabhāvena na sameti. Sace bhikkhunī vassāvāsikaṃ deti, pārivattakameva kātabbaṃ. Sace pana saṅkārakūṭādīsu ṭhapeti, “paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhissantī”ti paṃsukūlaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

512. Regarding 'in the effort, a dukkaṭa': in stretching out the hand and so on for the purpose of taking, it is an offense of wrong-doing. Regarding 'on acquisition': this means by receiving. And in that case, whether one gives it from hand to hand, or places it at the feet, or throws it from above, if that monk consents, it is considered taken. But, if one receives a robe sent by the hand of a female probationer, a male novice, a female novice, a male lay-follower, a female lay-follower, and so on, there is no offense. While a monk is giving a Dhamma talk, the four assemblies may bring robes and various colored cloths and place them at his feet, or they may stand in the precincts or outside the precincts and throw them. Among those, for a monk who takes that which is the property of bhikkhunīs without an exchange, there is an offense. But if they are thrown during the night, and it is not possible to know, 'This is a bhikkhunī's, this is others',' it is said in the Mahāpaccarī and the Kurundī that there is no duty of exchange. That statement, however, does not accord with the principle of being unintentional. If a bhikkhunī gives a rains-residence robe, an exchange must be made. But if she places it on a rubbish heap and so on, thinking, 'They will take it as a dust-heap robe,' it is allowable to take it after having determined it as a dust-heap robe.

513. Aññātikāya aññātikasaññīti tikapācittiyaṃ. Ekato upasampannāyāti bhikkhunīnaṃ santike upasampannāya hatthato gaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampannāya pana pācittiyameva.

513. Regarding 'perceiving a non-relative as a non-relative': this is a threefold pācittiya. Regarding 'ordained in one assembly': for one who takes from the hand of a bhikkhunī ordained in the presence of bhikkhunīs, it is an offense of wrong-doing; but for one who takes from the hand of a bhikkhunī ordained in the presence of bhikkhus, it is a pācittiya offense.

514. Parittena vā vipulanti appagghacīvarena vā upāhanatthavikapattatthavikaaṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanādinā vā mahagghaṃ cetāpetvā sacepi cīvaraṃ [M 2.0245] paṭiggaṇhāti, anāpatti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “antamaso harītakīkhaṇḍenāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Vipulena vā parittanti idaṃ vuttavipallāsena veditabbaṃ. Aññaṃ parikkhāranti pattatthavikādiṃ yaṃ kiñci vikappanupagapacchimacīvarappamāṇaṃ pana paṭaparissāvanampi na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ neva adhiṭṭhānupagaṃ na vikappanupagaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Sacepi mañcappamāṇā bhisicchavi hoti, vaṭṭatiyeva; ko pana vādo pattatthavikādīsu. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

514. "With little or with much": Even if one receives a valuable robe after having caused it to be exchanged for a robe of little value, or for items such as a bag for sandals, a bowl-bag, a shoulder strap, a waistband, and so on, there is no offense. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said: "Even if one receives it after exchanging it for at least a piece of myrobalan fruit, there is no offense." The phrase "With much or with little" should be understood as the reverse of what has been said. "Other requisites": This refers to any item such as a bowl-bag and so on. However, any item that is of the size of the final robe subject to vikappana (shared ownership)—even a cloth water-strainer—is not allowable. Whatever is neither subject to adhiṭṭhāna (determination for personal use) nor subject to vikappana, all that is allowable. Even if there is a deer hide the size of a bed, it is indeed allowable; what then needs to be said of items like bowl-bags and so on? The rest is clear in meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu [V 2.0221] idaṃ chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyākiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ[P 3.0665], paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃvacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding origins and so on, this offense has six origins, arises from action and from inaction, is not a case of release through perception, is unintentional, is a transgression of a convention, is bodily and verbal action, involves three mind-states, and is felt with three kinds of feeling.

Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is concluded.

6. Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Soliciting from a Non-Relative

515. Tena samayenāti aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha upanando sakyaputtoti asītisahassamattānaṃ sakyakulā pabbajitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ patikiṭṭho lolajātiko. Paṭṭoti cheko samattho paṭibalo sarasampanno kaṇṭhamādhuriyena samannāgato. Kismiṃ viyāti kiṃsu viya kileso viya, hirottappavasena kampanaṃ viya saṅkampanaṃ viya hotīti attho.

515. "At that time": this begins the training rule on soliciting from a non-relative. Therein, Upananda the Sakyan son was the most despised among the eighty thousand bhikkhus who had gone forth from the Sakyan clan; he was of a greedy nature. "Like what?" means: What is it like? It is like a defilement, like a trembling, like a great trembling due to shame and moral dread—this is the meaning.

Addhānamagganti addhānasaṅkhātaṃ dīghamaggaṃ, na nagaravīthimagganti attho. Te bhikkhū acchindiṃsūti musiṃsu, pattacīvarāni nesaṃ hariṃsūti attho. Anuyuñjāhīti bhikkhubhāvajānanatthāya puccha. Anuyuñjiyamānāti pabbajjāupasampadāpattacīvarādhiṭṭhānādīni pucchiyamānā. Etamatthaṃ ārocesunti bhikkhubhāvaṃ jānāpetvā yo “sāketā sāvatthiṃ addhānamaggappaṭipannā”tiādinā nayena vutto, etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ.

"A long road" means a long road, so designated, not the streets of a city; this is the meaning. "Those bhikkhus were plundered" means they were robbed; it means their bowls and robes were taken from them. "Question them" means: ask in order to know their status as bhikkhus. "Being questioned" means: being asked about matters such as their going forth, higher ordination, and the determination of their bowl and robes. "They reported this matter" means: after making known their status as bhikkhus, they reported this matter, which was stated in the manner of the passage beginning, "They were traveling the long road from Sāketa to Sāvatthī..."

517. Aññātakaṃ gahapatiṃ vātiādīsu yaṃ parato “tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ ādiṃ katvā evaṃ anupubbakathā veditabbā. Sace core passitvā daharā pattacīvarāni gahetvā palātā, corā therānaṃ nivāsanapārupanamattaṃyeva haritvā gacchanti, therehi [M 2.0246] neva tāva cīvaraṃ viññāpetabbaṃ, na sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjitabbaṃ. Atha daharā sabbaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ chaḍḍetvā palātā, corā therānaṃ nivāsanapārupanaṃ tañca bhaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā gacchanti, daharehi āgantvā attano nivāsanapārupanāni na tāva therānaṃ dātabbāni, na hi anacchinnacīvarā attano atthāya sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjituṃ labhanti, acchinnacīvarānaṃ pana atthāya labhanti, acchinnacīvarāva attanopi paresampi atthāya labhanti. Tasmā therehi vā sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjitvā vākādīhi ganthetvā daharānaṃ dātabbaṃ, daharehi vā therānaṃ atthāya bhañjitvā ganthetvā tesaṃ hatthe datvā vā adatvā vā [P 3.0666] attanā nivāsetvā attano nivāsanapārupanāni therānaṃ dātabbāni, neva bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ hoti, na tesaṃ dhāraṇe dukkaṭaṃ.

517. In the passage beginning "a householder who is a non-relative...", taking as a starting point what is said later, "having covered with grass or with leaves," the step-by-step explanation should be understood as follows. If, upon seeing robbers, the junior monks flee, taking the bowls and robes, and the robbers depart after taking only the senior monks' lower and upper robes, the senior monks should not yet request a robe, nor should they break off branches and leaves. But if the junior monks flee, abandoning all the goods, and the robbers depart after taking the senior monks' lower and upper robes and those goods, the junior monks, upon returning, should not yet give their own lower and upper robes to the senior monks. For, monks whose robes have not been stolen are not permitted to break off branches and leaves for their own sake; however, they are permitted to do so for the sake of those whose robes have been stolen. Only those whose robes have been stolen are permitted to do so for their own sake and for the sake of others. Therefore, either the senior monks themselves should break off branches and leaves, tie them together with bark fibers and so on, and give them to the junior monks; or the junior monks should break them off for the sake of the senior monks, tie them together, and then—whether having placed them in the seniors' hands or not—wear them themselves, and then give their own lower and upper robes to the senior monks. There is no pācittiya offense for destroying plant life, nor is there a dukkaṭa offense for wearing them.

Sace [V 2.0222] antarāmagge rajakattharaṇaṃ vā hoti, aññe vā tādise manusse passanti, cīvaraṃ viññāpetabbaṃ. Yāni ca nesaṃ te vā viññattamanussā aññe vā sākhāpalāsanivāsane bhikkhū disvā ussāhajātā vatthāni denti, tāni sadasāni vā hontu adasāni vā nīlādinānāvaṇṇāni vā kappiyānipi akappiyānipi sabbāni acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhitattā tesaṃ nivāsetuñca pārupituñca vaṭṭanti. Vuttampihetaṃ parivāre –

If along the way there is a washerman’s spread, or if they see other such suitable people, a robe should be requested. Furthermore, whatever cloths are given to them—either by those people who were requested, or by others who become inspired upon seeing bhikkhus wearing garments of branches and leaves—all of those cloths, whether they have a fringe or not, whether they are of various colors such as blue, etc., and whether they are allowable or unallowable, are permissible for them to wear as a lower garment and to drape over themselves, because they are in the position of having had their robes stolen. Indeed, this is also said in the Parivāra:

“Akappakataṃ nāpi rajanāya rattaṃ;

Tena nivattho yena kāmaṃ vajeyya;

Na cassa hoti āpatti;

So ca dhammo sugatena desito;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 481);

"Not made allowable, nor dyed with dye;

Clothed in that, one may go wherever one wishes;

And there is no offense for him;

That Dhamma was taught by the Well-Gone One;

This question was pondered by the skillful."

Ayañhi pañho acchinnacīvarakaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya vutto. Atha pana titthiyehi sahagacchanti, te ca nesaṃ kusacīravākacīraphalakacīrāni denti, tānipi laddhiṃ aggahetvā nivāsetuṃ vaṭṭanti, nivāsetvāpi laddhi na gahetabbā.

Indeed, this question was spoken with reference to a bhikkhu whose robe has been stolen. Furthermore, if they are traveling with sectarians, and those sectarians give them garments made of kusa grass, bark fiber, or wooden planks, it is allowable to wear those too, without adopting their views. Even after wearing them, their views should not be adopted.

Idāni “yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ upagacchati, sace tattha hoti saṅghassa vihāracīvaraṃ vā”tiādīsu vihāracīvaraṃ nāma manussā āvāsaṃ kāretvā “cattāropi paccayā amhākaṃyeva santakā paribhogaṃ gacchantū”ti [M 2.0247] ticīvaraṃ sajjetvā attanā kārāpite āvāse ṭhapenti, etaṃ vihāracīvaraṃ nāma. Uttarattharaṇanti mañcakassa upari attharaṇakaṃ vuccati. Bhumattharaṇanti parikammakatāya bhūmiyā rakkhaṇatthaṃ cimilikāhi kataattharaṇaṃ tassa upari taṭṭikaṃ pattharitvā caṅkamanti. Bhisicchavīti mañcabhisiyā vā pīṭhabhisiyā vā [P 3.0667] chavi, sace pūritā hoti vidhunitvāpi gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Evametesu vihāracīvarādīsu yaṃ tattha āvāse hoti, taṃ anāpucchāpi gahetvā nivāsetuṃ vā pārupituṃ vā acchinnacīvarakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ labbhatīti veditabbaṃ. Tañca kho labhitvā odahissāmi puna ṭhapessāmīti adhippāyena na mūlacchejjāya. Labhitvā ca pana ñātito vā upaṭṭhākato vā aññato vā kutoci pākatikameva kātabbaṃ. Videsagatena ekasmiṃ saṅghike āvāse saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjanatthāya ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sacassa paribhogeneva taṃ jīrati vā nassati vā gīvā na hoti. Sace pana etesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ gihivatthādīnaṃ bhisicchavipariyantānaṃ kiñci na labbhati, tena tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabbanti.

Now, in passages such as, "the first monastery one arrives at, if there is a monastery robe belonging to the Saṅgha there," a 'monastery robe' is as follows: people have a monastery built and, preparing the three robes with the thought, 'Let the four requisites, being our own property, come into use,' they place them in the monastery they had built—this is called a 'monastery robe.' An 'upper covering' is said to be a covering placed on top of a small bed. A 'floor covering' is a covering made of coarse cloths for the protection of a prepared floor; spreading a fine mat over it, they walk. A 'cushion cover' is the outer layer of a bed cushion or a bench cushion; if it is filled, it is permissible to take it even after shaking it out. Thus, among these items such as monastery robes, whatever is in that monastery, it should be known that it is allowable for monks whose robes have been stolen to take it without asking and wear it as a lower robe or an upper robe. And this is with the intention, 'Having obtained it, I will put it back; I will place it again,' not for complete appropriation. And having obtained a new robe from a relative, a supporter, or from some other person, the borrowed item should be restored to its original condition. By a monk who has gone to another region, it should be placed in a Saṅgha monastery for the purpose of being used as a Saṅgha requisite. If it wears out or is lost through his use, he is not indebted. But if none of these aforementioned items, from householder's cloth up to a cushion cover, is available, then he should come having covered himself with grass or leaves.

519. Yehi [V 2.0223] kehici vā acchinnanti ettha yampi acchinnacīvarā ācariyupajjhāyā aññe “āharatha, āvuso, cīvara”nti yācitvā vā vissāsena vā gaṇhanti, tampi saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti vattuṃ yujjati.

519. Here, in the phrase 'snatched by whomever,' it is fitting to say that this also includes a robe that teachers, preceptors, or other fellow monks whose robes have been stolen take, either by requesting, 'Friend, bring a robe,' or through familiarity.

Paribhogajiṇṇaṃ vāti ettha ca acchinnacīvarānaṃ ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ attanā tiṇapaṇṇehi paṭicchādetvā dinnacīvarampi saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti vattuṃ yujjati. Evañhi te acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāne naṭṭhacīvaraṭṭhāne ca ṭhitā bhavissanti, tena nesaṃ viññattiyaṃ akappiyacīvaraparibhoge ca anāpatti anurūpā bhavissati.

And here, in the phrase 'or worn out through use,' it is fitting to say that even a robe given to teachers, preceptors, and others whose robes have been snatched away, by one who has covered himself with grass and leaves, is also included. For in this way, they will be established in the position of one whose robe has been snatched away and in the position of one whose robe has been lost. Therefore, for them, no-offense will be suitable in the case of requesting and in the case of using an improper robe.

521. Ñātakānaṃ pavāritānanti ettha “etesaṃ santakaṃ dethā”ti viññāpentassa yācantassa anāpattīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Na hi ñātakapavāritānaṃ āpatti vā anāpatti vā hoti. Attano dhanenāti etthāpi attano kappiyabhaṇḍena kappiyavohāreneva cīvaraṃ viññāpentassa cetāpentassa [M 2.0248] parivattāpentassa anāpattīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Pavāritānanti ettha ca saṅghavasena pavāritesu pamāṇameva vaṭṭati. Puggalikapavāraṇāya yaṃ yaṃ pavāreti, taṃ taṃyeva viññāpetabbaṃ. Yo catūhi paccayehi pavāretvā sayameva sallakkhetvā kālānukālaṃ cīvarāni divase divase yāgubhattādīnīti [P 3.0668] evaṃ yena yenattho taṃ taṃ deti, tassa viññāpanakiccaṃ natthi. Yo pana pavāretvā bālatāya vā satisammosena vā na deti, so viññāpetabbo. Yo “mayhaṃ gehaṃ pavāremī”ti vadati, tassa gehaṃ gantvā yathāsukhaṃ nisīditabbaṃ nipajjitabbaṃ, na kiñci gahetabbaṃ. Yo pana “yaṃ mayhaṃ gehe atthi, taṃ pavāremī”ti vadati. Yaṃ tattha kappiyaṃ, taṃ viññāpetabbaṃ, gehe pana nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā na labbhatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

521. Here, in the phrase 'of relatives who have invited,' the meaning should be understood thus: there is no offense for one who makes a request, for one who asks, saying, 'Give their property.' Indeed, for the relatives who have invited, there is neither an offense nor a no-offense. Also here, in 'with one's own wealth,' the meaning should be understood thus: there is no offense for a monk who requests a robe, has it bought, or has it exchanged with his own allowable goods and by proper transaction. And here, in 'of those who have invited,' among those who have invited on account of the Saṅgha, only a suitable measure is allowable. In the case of an individual invitation, whatever one invites with, that very thing should be requested. As for one who, having invited with the four requisites, himself takes note and from time to time gives robes, and day by day gives rice-gruel, meals, and so on—thus giving whatever is needed—for him, there is no need to make a request. But one who, having invited, does not give due to foolishness or due to a lapse of memory, he should be reminded by a request. For one who says, 'I invite you to my house,' one may go to his house and sit or lie down as one pleases, but nothing should be taken. But for one who says, 'Whatever is in my house, that I invite you with,' whatever there is that is allowable, that may be requested. In this case, however, it is not permitted to sit or lie down in the house—so it is said in the Kurundī.

Aññassatthāyāti ettha attano ñātakapavārite na kevalaṃ attano atthāya, atha kho aññassatthāya viññāpentassa anāpattīti ayameko attho. Ayaṃ pana dutiyo aññassāti ye aññassa ñātakapavāritā, te tasseva “aññassā”ti laddhavohārassa buddharakkhitassa vā dhammarakkhitassa vā atthāya viññāpentassa anāpattīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

Here, in 'for the sake of another,' this is one meaning: when requesting from one's own relatives and invited persons, there is no offense for one who makes the request not only for one's own sake, but also for the sake of another. But this is the second meaning: as for 'of another,' whoever are the relatives and invited persons of another, there is no offense for one who makes a request from them for the sake of that very person designated as 'another,' be it Buddharakkhita or Dhammarakkhita. The rest has a plain meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idampi chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding the origins and so on, this training rule is of six origins. It is functional, not a release by perception, non-intentional, a transgression by designation, an act of body and an act of speech, of three consciousnesses, and of three feelings.

Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from a non-relative is concluded.

7. Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Tatuttari Training Rule

522-4. Tena [V 2.0224] samayenāti tatuttarisikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha abhihaṭṭhunti abhīti upasaggo, haritunti attho, gaṇhitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Pavāreyyāti icchāpeyya, icchaṃ ruciṃ uppādeyya, vadeyya nimanteyyāti attho. Abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavārentena pana yathā vattabbaṃ, taṃ ākāraṃ dassetuṃ “yāvatakaṃ icchasi tāvatakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Atha vā yathā “nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato”ti (su. ni. 426, 1104; cūḷani. jatukaṇṇimāṇavapucchāniddesa 67) ettha disvāti attho, evamidhāpi “abhiaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā”ti abhiharitvā pavāreyyāti attho. Tattha [M 2.0249] kāyābhihāro vācābhihāroti duvidho abhihāro, kāyena vā hi vatthāni abhiharitvā pādamūle ṭhapetvā “yattakaṃ icchasi tattakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadanto pavāreyya, vācāya vā “amhākaṃ dussakoṭṭhāgāraṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, yattakaṃ icchasi tattakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadanto pavāreyya, tadubhayampi ekajjhaṃ katvā “abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā”ti vuttaṃ.

522-4. Tena samayena refers to the Tatuttari training rule. Therein, regarding abhihaṭṭhuṃ: abhi is a prefix; the meaning is 'to bring'; it is said to mean 'to take'. Pavāreyya means: he should cause to wish, he should cause a wish or liking to arise, he should say, he should invite—this is the meaning. However, to show the manner in which one who invites by bringing should speak, its word analysis is stated thus: 'Take as much as you wish.' Alternatively, just as in the phrase 'having seen renunciation as security,' the meaning is 'having seen,' so also here, abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā means 'having brought, he should invite.' Therein, the bringing is twofold: bringing with the body and bringing with speech. For one might invite by bringing robes with his body, placing them at the feet, and saying, 'Take as much as you wish.' Or one might invite with speech, saying, 'Our cloth storeroom is full; take as much as you wish.' Having combined both of these, it is said, 'he should invite by bringing.'

Santaruttaraparamanti saantaraṃ [P 3.0669] uttaraṃ paramaṃ assa cīvarassāti santaruttaraparamaṃ, nivāsanena saddhiṃ pārupanaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo assāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato cīvaraṃ sāditabbanti tato abhihaṭacīvarato ettakaṃ cīvaraṃ gahetabbaṃ, na ito paranti attho. Yasmā pana acchinnasabbacīvarena ticīvarikeneva bhikkhunā evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ, aññena aññathāpi, tasmā taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “sace tīṇi naṭṭhāni hontī”tiādinā nayenassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

Santaruttaraparamaṃ means: for this robe, an inner garment and an upper garment are the limit (paramaṃ); thus it is santaruttaraparamaṃ.
