It is said that for this, the upper garment together with the lower garment is the highest limit. Tato cīvaraṃ sāditabbaṃ means: from that offered robe, this much robe should be consented to; the meaning is 'not beyond this.' However, because a monk who possesses the three robes and has had all his robes stolen should practice in this way, while another may practice otherwise, therefore, to show that distinction, its word analysis is stated by the method beginning with, 'If the three are lost...'

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – yassa tīṇi naṭṭhāni, tena dve sāditabbāni, ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā aññaṃ sabhāgaṭṭhānato pariyesissati. Yassa dve naṭṭhāni, tena ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ. Sace pakatiyāva santaruttarena carati, dve sāditabbāni. Evaṃ ekaṃ sādiyanteneva samo bhavissati. Yassa tīsu ekaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, na sāditabbaṃ. Yassa pana dvīsu ekaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ. Yassa ekaṃyeva hoti, tañca naṭṭhaṃ, dve sāditabbāni. Bhikkhuniyā pana pañcasupi naṭṭhesu dve sāditabbāni. Catūsu naṭṭhesu ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ, tīsu naṭṭhesu kiñci na sāditabbaṃ, ko pana vādo dvīsu vā ekasmiṃ vā. Yena kenaci hi santaruttaraparamatāya ṭhātabbaṃ, tato uttari na labbhatīti idamettha lakkhaṇaṃ.

Herein, this is the decision: For one whose three robes are lost, two should be consented to; having worn one as a lower garment and draped one as an upper garment, he will search for another from a suitable source. For one whose two robes are lost, one should be consented to. If he is one who by nature goes about with an inner and upper garment, two should be consented to. Thus, he will be equal to one who consents to one. For one who has lost one of three, none should be consented to. However, for one who has lost one of two, one should be consented to. For one who has only one, and that is lost, two should be consented to. For a bhikkhunī, however, if all five are lost, two should be consented to. If four are lost, one should be consented to. If three are lost, nothing should be consented to—what then is to be said of two or one being lost? Indeed, one must by some means abide by the limit of an inner and upper garment; to consent to more than that is not allowed. This is the principle here.

526. Sesakaṃ āharissāmīti dve cīvarāni katvā sesaṃ puna āharissāmīti attho. Na acchinnakāraṇāti [V 2.0225] bāhusaccādiguṇavasena denti. Ñātakānantiādīsu ñātakānaṃ dentānaṃ sādiyantassa pavāritānaṃ dentānaṃ sādiyantassa attano dhanena sādiyantassa anāpattīti attho. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “ñātakapavāritaṭṭhāne pakatiyā bahumpi vaṭṭati, acchinnakāraṇā pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pāḷiyā na sameti. Yasmā panidaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃyeva paññattaṃ, tasmā idha “aññassatthāyā”ti na vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

526. Sesakaṃ āharissāmi means: having made two robes, 'I will bring the remainder back'—this is the meaning. Na acchinnakāraṇā means: they give on account of qualities such as great learning, not for the reason of one having been robbed. In Ñātakānaṃ, etc., the meaning is that there is no offense for one who consents when relatives give, when invited ones give, or when one consents with one's own wealth. However, in the commentaries it is said: 'In the case of relatives and invited ones, by nature even much is allowable; but for the reason of having been robbed, only the specified amount is allowable.' That does not agree with the Pāḷi. Furthermore, because this training rule was laid down specifically regarding an item requested for another's sake, therefore 'for another's sake' is not stated here. The rest is of clear meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu [M 2.0250] idampi chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding the origins and so on, this also is of six origins, is an action, is not a release through perception, is unintentional, is a transgression by designation, is bodily action and verbal action, arises from three kinds of consciousness, and is connected with three kinds of feeling.

Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tatuttari Training Rule is concluded.

8. Paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared

527. Tena [P 3.0670] samayenāti upakkhaṭasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha atthāvuso maṃ so upaṭṭhākoti āvuso, yaṃ tvaṃ bhaṇasi, atthi evarūpo so mama upaṭṭhākoti ayamettha attho. Api meyya evaṃ hotīti api me ayya evaṃ hoti, api mayyā evantipi pāṭho.

8. By 'at that time' is meant the training rule concerning what has been prepared. Therein, in the phrase 'Friend, that supporter is for me,' the meaning here is this: 'Friend, that supporter of such a kind whom you speak of, is mine.' As for 'Perhaps it might be so for me,' it means 'Venerable sir, perhaps it is so for me.' There is also the reading, 'Perhaps by me thus.'

528-9. Bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissāti ettha uddissāti apadissa ārabbha. Yasmā pana yaṃ uddissa upakkhaṭaṃ hoti, taṃ tassatthāya upakkhaṭaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmāssa padabhājane “bhikkhussatthāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

527. 'But with reference to a bhikkhu'—herein, 'with reference to' means indicating, concerning. Furthermore, because that which is prepared with reference to a certain bhikkhu is called 'prepared for his sake,' therefore in its word analysis, it is stated 'for the sake of a bhikkhu.'

Bhikkhuṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvāti bhikkhuṃ paccayaṃ katvā, yañhi bhikkhuṃ uddissa upakkhaṭaṃ, taṃ niyameneva bhikkhuṃ paccayaṃ katvā upakkhaṭaṃ hoti, tena vuttaṃ – “bhikkhuṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvā”ti. Paccayopi hi “labhati māro ārammaṇa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.243) ārammaṇanti āgato. Idāni “uddissā”ti ettha yo kattā, tassa ākāradassanatthaṃ “bhikkhuṃ acchādetukāmo”ti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhuṃ acchādetukāmena hi tena taṃ uddissa upakkhaṭaṃ, na aññena kāraṇena. Iti so acchādetukāmo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “bhikkhuṃ acchādetukāmo”ti.

'Having made a bhikkhu the object' means having made the bhikkhu the condition. Indeed, whatever is prepared with reference to a bhikkhu is invariably prepared having made the bhikkhu the condition. Therefore, it is said, 'having made a bhikkhu the object.' Indeed, 'condition' also appears as 'object' in passages such as 'Māra finds an object.' Now, herein, in 'with reference to,' in order to show the manner of the agent, it is said, 'desiring to clothe a bhikkhu.' Indeed, it was prepared with reference to him by one desiring to clothe the bhikkhu, not for any other reason. Thus, that person is one who desires to clothe. Therefore, it is said, 'desiring to clothe a bhikkhu.'

Aññātakassa [V 2.0226] gahapatissa vāti aññātakena gahapatinā vāti attho. Karaṇatthe hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Padabhājane pana byañjanaṃ avicāretvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “aññātako nāma…pe… gahapati nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Of an unrelated householder or...' means 'by an unrelated householder or...' Indeed, this genitive is in the sense of the instrumental. In the word analysis, however, without considering the expression and only to show the meaning, it is said, 'Unrelated means...' and so on.

Cīvaracetāpannanti cīvaramūlaṃ, taṃ pana yasmā hiraññādīsu aññataraṃ hoti, tasmā padabhājane “hiraññaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upakkhaṭaṃ hotīti sajjitaṃ hoti, saṃharitvā ṭhapitaṃ, yasmā pana “hiraññaṃ vā”tiādinā [M 2.0251] vacanenassa upakkhaṭabhāvo dassito hoti, tasmā “upakkhaṭaṃ nāmā”ti padaṃ uddharitvā visuṃ padabhājanaṃ na vuttaṃ. Imināti upakkhaṭaṃ sandhāyāha, tenevassa padabhājane “paccupaṭṭhitenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yañhi upakkhaṭaṃ saṃharitvā ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hotīti. Acchādessāmīti vohāravacanametaṃ “itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dassāmī”ti ayaṃ panettha attho. Tenevassa padabhājanepi “dassāmī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Robe-money' means the price of a robe. Furthermore, because that is one or another among gold and so on, therefore in the word analysis, 'gold or...' and so on is stated. 'Is prepared' means it is arranged, collected, and set aside. Furthermore, because by the statement 'gold or...' and so on its state of being prepared is shown, the term 'prepared means' is not taken up and given a separate word analysis. 'By this'—He said this referring to what was prepared. For that very reason, in its word analysis, 'by what is present' is stated. Indeed, that which is prepared, collected, and set aside is 'present.' 'I will clothe' is a conventional expression; the meaning here is, 'I will give to the bhikkhu named so-and-so.' For that very reason, in its word analysis also, 'I will give' is stated.

Tatra ce so bhikkhūti yatra so gahapati [P 3.0671] vā gahapatānī vā tatra so bhikkhu pubbe appavārito upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyya ceti ayamettha padasambandho. Tattha upasaṅkamitvāti imassa gantvāti imināva atthe siddhe pacuravohāravasena “ghara”nti vuttaṃ. Yatra pana so dāyako tatra gantvāti ayamevettha attho, tasmā punapi vuttaṃ “yattha katthaci upasaṅkamitvā”ti. Vikappaṃ āpajjeyyāti visiṭṭhakappaṃ adhikavidhānaṃ āpajjeyya, padabhājane pana yenākārena vikappaṃ āpanno hoti tameva dassetuṃ “āyataṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sādhūti āyācane nipāto. Vatāti parivitakke. Manti attānaṃ niddisati. Āyasmāti paraṃ ālapati āmanteti. Yasmā panidaṃ sabbaṃ byañjanamattameva, uttānatthameva, tasmāssa padabhājane attho na vutto. Kalyāṇakamyataṃ upādāyāti sundarakāmataṃ visiṭṭhakāmataṃ cittena gahetvā, tassa “āpajjeyya ce”ti iminā sambandho. Yasmā pana yo kalyāṇakamyataṃ upādāya āpajjati, so sādhatthiko mahagghatthiko hoti, tasmāssa padabhājane byañjanaṃ pahāya adhippetatthameva dassetuṃ tadeva vacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana na imassa āpajjanamatteneva āpatti sīsaṃ eti, tasmā “tassa vacanenā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

As for 'Therein, if that bhikkhu...': 'Wherever that householder or householder's wife is, if that bhikkhu, having approached uninvited beforehand, should make a specification regarding the robe'—this is the connection of the words here. Therein, regarding 'having approached,' although the meaning is established by 'having gone,' the word 'house' is stated due to common parlance. However, 'having gone wherever that donor is'—this alone is the intended meaning here. Therefore, it is also stated again, 'having approached anywhere whatsoever.' 'Should make a specification' means one would make a special arrangement, an excessive provision. Furthermore, in the word analysis, in order to show the manner in which one has made a specification, 'long or...' and so on is stated. 'Sādhu' is a particle used in requesting. 'Vata' is a particle used in deliberation. 'Maṃ' indicates oneself. 'Āyasmā' addresses or calls another. Furthermore, because all this is merely the expression and its meaning is plain, its meaning is not stated in the word analysis. 'On account of desiring what is fine' means having taken up with the mind the state of desiring what is beautiful, the state of desiring what is special; its connection is with 'if he should make.' Furthermore, because one who makes a specification on account of desiring what is fine is one who has need of what is good and costly, therefore in the word analysis, setting aside the literal expression to show only the intended meaning, that very statement was made. Furthermore, because an offense is not culminated by the mere act of making this specification, therefore 'by his statement...' and so on was stated.

531. Anāpatti ñātakānantiādīsu ñātakānaṃ cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjantassa anāpattīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Mahagghaṃ cetāpetukāmassa appagghaṃ cetāpetīti gahapatissa vīsatiagghanakaṃ cīvaraṃ cetāpetukāmassa “alaṃ mayhaṃ etena, dasagghanakaṃ vā aṭṭhagghanakaṃ vā dehī”ti vadati anāpatti. Appagghanti idañca atirekanivāraṇatthameva vuttaṃ, samakepi pana anāpatti[V 2.0227], tañca kho agghavaseneva na pamāṇavasena, agghavaḍḍhanakañhi idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ. Tasmā yo vīsatiagghanakaṃ antaravāsakaṃ cetāpetukāmo[M 2.0252], “taṃ ettakameva me agghanakaṃ cīvaraṃ dehī”ti vattumpi vaṭṭati. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

531. In 'No offense for relatives,' and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: there is no offense for one who makes a specification regarding a robe for relatives. As for 'For one who desires to have one of great value acquired, one has one of lesser value acquired': for a householder who desires to have a robe worth twenty acquired, if one says, 'Enough of this for me; give one worth ten or one worth eight,' there is no offense. And this 'of lesser value' is stated only for the purpose of preventing excess. Indeed, there is no offense even in the case of an item of equal value, and that is equal by way of value, not by way of measurement. For indeed, this training rule is about increasing the value. Therefore, for a donor who desires to have an inner robe worth twenty acquired, it is also allowable to say to him, 'Give me a robe of just this much value.' The rest has an obvious meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīnipi tatuttarisikkhāpadasadisānevāti.

The origins and so forth are also just the same as the subsequent training rule.

Paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared is finished.

9. Dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared

532. Dutiyaupakkhaṭepi [P 3.0672] imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Tañhi imassa anupaññattisadisaṃ. Kevalaṃ paṭhamasikkhāpade ekassa pīḷā katā, dutiye dvinnaṃ, ayamevettha viseso. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ paṭhamasadisameva. Yathā ca dvinnaṃ, evaṃ bahūnaṃ pīḷaṃ katvā gaṇhatopi āpatti veditabbāti.

532. In the second training rule on having something prepared also, the meaning should be understood by this very method. For it is like a supplementary regulation to this first one. Only, in the first training rule, the pressuring of one person was done; in the second, the pressuring of two. This alone is the difference here. The rest is all the same as the first. And just as for two, so too for one who takes after having pressured many, an offense should be understood.

Dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Prepared is finished.

10. Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Kings

537. Tena samayenāti rājasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha upāsakaṃ saññāpetvāti jānāpetvā, “iminā mūlena cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā therassa dehī”ti evaṃ vatvāti adhippāyo. Paññāsabandhoti paññāsakahāpaṇadaṇḍoti vuttaṃ hoti. Paññāsaṃ baddhotipi pāṭho, paññāsaṃ jito paññāsaṃ dāpetabboti adhippāyo. Ajjaṇho, bhante, āgamehīti bhante, ajja ekadivasaṃ amhākaṃ tiṭṭha, adhivāsehīti attho. Parāmasīti gaṇhi. Jīnosīti jitosi.

537. At that time—this refers to the training rule concerning kings. There, 'having informed a lay follower' means having caused him to know, the intention being, 'Having bought a robe with this money, give it to the elder.' 'Fifty-bound' means it is said to be a penalty of fifty kahāpaṇas. There is also the reading 'bound by fifty,' the intention being, 'he has lost fifty, he must be made to give fifty.' 'Venerable sir, please wait for today' means, 'Venerable sir, stay for us for one day, please consent.' 'He touched' means he took. 'You have conquered' means you are defeated.

538-9. Rājabhoggoti rājato bhoggaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ assatthīti rājabhoggo, rājabhogotipi pāṭho, rājato bhogo assa atthīti attho.

'One who enjoys royal patronage' (rājabhoggo) means: because there is for him wealth, which is to be used and enjoyed, obtained from the king, he is 'one who enjoys royal patronage.' There is also the reading 'royal patronage' (rājabhogo); the meaning is: there is for him patronage obtained from the king.

Pahiṇeyyāti peseyya, uttānatthattā panassa padabhājanaṃ na vuttaṃ. Yathā ca etassa, evaṃ “cīvaraṃ itthannāmaṃ bhikkhu”ntiādīnampi padānaṃ uttānatthattāyeva padabhājanaṃ na vuttanti veditabbaṃ[V 2.0228]. Ābhatanti ānītaṃ. Kālena kappiyanti [M 2.0253] yuttapattakālena, yadā no attho hoti, tadā kappiyaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhāmāti attho.

'Should send' (pahiṇeyya) means 'should dispatch' (peseyya). However, because its meaning is obvious, its word analysis was not stated. And just as for this word, so too for words beginning with 'a robe... a monk named so-and-so,' it should be understood that the word analysis was not stated precisely because their meaning is obvious. 'Brought' (ābhataṃ) means 'it has been brought' (ānītaṃ). 'Allowable at the right time' (kālena kappiyaṃ) means at a suitable and proper time; the meaning is: 'When we have a need, then we take the allowable robe.'

Veyyāvaccakaroti kiccakaro, kappiyakārakoti attho. Saññatto so mayāti āṇatto so mayā, yathā tumhākaṃ cīvarena atthe sati cīvaraṃ dassati, evaṃ vuttoti attho. Attho me āvuso cīvarenāti codanālakkhaṇanidassanametaṃ, idañhi vacanaṃ vattabbaṃ, assa vā attho [P 3.0673] yāya kāyaci bhāsāya; idaṃ codanālakkhaṇaṃ. “Dehi me cīvara”ntiādīni pana navattabbākāradassanatthaṃ vuttāni, etāni hi vacanāni etesaṃ vā attho yāya kāyaci bhāsāya na vattabbo.

'One who performs services' (veyyāvaccakaro) means one who does duties (kiccakaro); the meaning is one who makes things allowable (kappiyakārako). 'He has been informed by me' (saññatto so mayā) means he has been instructed by me; the meaning is he has been told in such a way that when you have need of a robe, he will give a robe. 'Friend, I have need of a robe' (attho me āvuso cīvarena)—this is an illustration of the characteristic of a prompting. For this statement should be spoken, or its meaning in any language; this is the characteristic of a prompting. However, phrases beginning with 'Give me a robe' (dehi me cīvaraṃ) are stated for the purpose of showing the manner of what should not be said. For these statements, or their meaning in any language, should not be spoken.

Dutiyampi vattabbo tatiyampi vattabboti “attho me āvuso cīvarenā”ti idameva yāvatatiyaṃ vattabboti. Evaṃ “dvattikkhattuṃ codetabbo sāretabbo”ti ettha uddiṭṭhacodanāparicchedaṃ dassetvā idāni “dvattikkhattuṃ codayamāno sārayamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṃ kusala”nti imesaṃ padānaṃ saṅkhepato atthaṃ dassento “sace abhinipphādeti, iccetaṃ kusala”nti āha. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ codento taṃ cīvaraṃ yadi nipphādeti, sakkoti attano paṭilābhavasena nipphādetuṃ, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ sādhu suṭṭhu sundaraṃ.

'A second time it should be spoken, and a third time it should be spoken' means this very statement, 'Friend, I have need of a robe,' should be spoken up to the third time. Thus, in the context of 'he should be prompted and reminded two or three times,' having shown the directly indicated limit of prompting, now, while showing the meaning of these words in brief—'if, while prompting and reminding two or three times, he should accomplish the getting of that robe, this is skillful'—he said, 'if he accomplishes it, this is skillful.' Thus, while prompting up to the third time, if he accomplishes the getting of that robe—if he is able to accomplish it by means of his own receiving—this is skillful, good, very good, beautiful.

Catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūtena uddissa ṭhātabbanti ṭhānalakkhaṇanidassanametaṃ. Chakkhattuparamanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakavacanametaṃ, chakkhattuparamañhi etena cīvaraṃ uddissa tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbaṃ, na aññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ, idaṃ ṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha yo sabbaṭṭhānānaṃ sādhāraṇo tuṇhībhāvo, taṃ tāva dassetuṃ padabhājane “tattha gantvā tuṇhībhūtenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha na āsane nisīditabbanti “idha, bhante, nisīdathā”ti vuttenāpi na nisīditabbaṃ. Na āmisaṃ paṭiggahetabbanti yāgukhajjakādibhedaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ “gaṇhatha, bhante”ti yāciyamānenāpi na gaṇhitabbaṃ. Na dhammo bhāsitabboti maṅgalaṃ vā anumodanaṃ vā bhāsathāti yāciyamānenāpi kiñci na bhāsitabbaṃ, kevalaṃ “kiṃ kāraṇā āgatosī”ti pucchiyamānena “jānāsi, āvuso”ti vattabbo. Pucchiyamānoti idañhi karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Atha vā pucchaṃ kurumāno pucchiyamānoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yo hi pucchaṃ karoti, so ettakaṃ vattabboti ṭhānaṃ bhañjatīti āgatakāraṇaṃ bhañjati.

'One should stand silently, indicating the robe, four times, five times, with six times as the utmost'—this is an illustration of the characteristic of standing. And 'with six times as the utmost' (chakkhattuparamaṃ) is an adverbial neuter term. For, with six times as the utmost, one should stand silently indicating the robe; nothing else should be done. This is the characteristic of standing. Therein, to show first the silence that is common to all standings, in the word analysis it was said, 'Having gone there, one should be silent,' and so on. There, 'one should not sit on a seat' means one should not sit even when told, 'Venerable sir, please sit here.' 'One should not accept material food' means one should not accept any material food, such as gruel or solid food, even when entreated, 'Venerable sir, please accept.' 'The Dhamma should not be spoken' means nothing should be spoken even when entreated, 'Please speak on a blessing or a dedication of merit.' Only when asked, 'For what reason have you come?' should one say, 'You know, friend.' 'Being asked' (pucchiyamāno): this is a present participle in the instrumental case with the sense of the agent. Or alternatively, the meaning should be understood here as 'one who is asking a question' is meant by 'being asked.' For whoever asks a question, to him this much should be said. But whoever speaks further than that, he breaks the standing. 'He breaks the standing' means he spoils the reason for his coming.

Idāni [P 3.0674][M 2.0254] yā tisso codanā, cha ca ṭhānāni vuttāni. Tattha vuḍḍhiñca hāniñca dassento [V 2.0229] “catukkhattuṃ codetvā”tiādimāha. Yasmā ca ettha ekacodanāvuḍḍhiyā dvinnaṃ ṭhānānaṃ hāni vuttā, tasmā “ekā codanā diguṇaṃ ṭhāna”nti lakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Iti iminā lakkhaṇena tikkhattuṃ codetvā chakkhattuṃ ṭhātabbaṃ, dvikkhattuṃ codetvā aṭṭhakkhattuṃ ṭhātabbaṃ, sakiṃ codetvā dasakkhattuṃ ṭhātabbanti. Yathā ca “chakkhattuṃ codetvā na ṭhātabba”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ “dvādasakkhattuṃ ṭhatvā na codetabba”ntipi vuttameva hoti. Tasmā sace codetiyeva na tiṭṭhati, cha codanā labbhanti. Sace tiṭṭhatiyeva na codeti, dvādasa ṭhānāni labbhanti. Sace codetipi tiṭṭhatipi, ekāya codanāya dve ṭhānāni hāpetabbāni. Tattha yo ekadivasameva punappunaṃ gantvā chakkhattuṃ codeti, sakiṃyeva vā gantvā “attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti chakkhattuṃ vadati. Tathā ekadivasameva punappunaṃ gantvā dvādasakkhattuṃ tiṭṭhati, sakiṃyeva vā gantvā tatra tatra ṭhāne tiṭṭhati, sopi sabbacodanāyo sabbaṭṭhānāni ca bhañjati. Ko pana vādo nānādivasesu evaṃ karontassāti evamettha vinicchayo veditabbo.

Now, the three promptings and six standings have been stated. Therein, showing increase and decrease, he said, “having prompted four times,” and so on. And because herein, by the increase of one prompting, the decrease of two standings is stated, therefore the characteristic ‘one prompting is a twofold standing’ is shown. Thus, by this characteristic: having prompted three times, one should stand six times; having prompted twice, one should stand eight times; having prompted once, one should stand ten times. And just as it is said, “Having prompted six times, one should not stand,” so too, “Having stood twelve times, one should not prompt,” is also said. Therefore, if one only prompts and does not stand, six promptings are obtained. If one only stands and does not prompt, twelve standings are obtained. If one both prompts and stands, for one prompting, two standings should be abandoned. Therein, a monk who, in a single day, going again and again, prompts six times, or going just once, says, “Friend, I have need of a robe,” six times; similarly, who in a single day, going again and again, stands twelve times, or going just once, stands in various places—that monk also breaks all promptings and all standings. What, then, is there to say of one who does so on different days? Thus, the judgment here should be understood.

Yatassa cīvaracetāpannaṃ ābhatanti yato rājato vā rājabhoggato vā assa bhikkhuno cīvaracetāpannaṃ ānītaṃ. Yatvassātipi pāṭho. Ayamevattho. “Yatthassā”tipi paṭhanti, yasmiṃ ṭhāne assa cīvaracetāpannaṃ pesitanti ca atthaṃ kathenti, byañjanaṃ pana na sameti. Tatthāti tassa rañño vā rājabhoggassa vā santike; samīpatthe hi idaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Na taṃ tassa bhikkhuno kiñci atthaṃ anubhotīti taṃ cīvaracetāpannaṃ tassa bhikkhuno kiñci appamattakampi kammaṃ na nipphādeti. Yuñjantāyasmanto sakanti āyasmanto attano santakaṃ dhanaṃ pāpuṇantu. Mā vo sakaṃ vinassāti tumhākaṃ santakaṃ mā vinassatu. Yo pana neva sāmaṃ gacchati, na dūtaṃ pāheti, vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati.

‘For whom a robe-fund is brought’ means from whichever king or royal official a robe-fund is brought for that monk. There is also the reading ‘yatvassā’; this is the meaning. They also recite ‘yatthassā,’ and explain the meaning as ‘in which place the robe-fund was sent for him,’ but the phrasing does not fit. ‘There’ means in the presence of that king or royal official; for this is a locative expression in the sense of proximity. ‘It does not serve any purpose for that monk’ means that robe-fund does not accomplish even the slightest task for that monk. ‘Venerable donors, may you obtain your own’ means may the venerable donors get back their own wealth. ‘Let not your own be lost’ means may your own property not be lost. But the monk who neither goes himself nor sends a messenger incurs a dukkaṭa offense for a breach of duty.

Kiṃ [P 3.0675] pana sabbakappiyakārakesu evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Na paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Ayañhi kappiyakārako nāma saṅkhepato duvidho niddiṭṭho ca aniddiṭṭho ca. Tattha niddiṭṭho duvidho – bhikkhunā niddiṭṭho, dūtena niddiṭṭhoti. Aniddiṭṭhopi duvidho – mukhavevaṭika kappiyakārako, parammukhakappiyakārakoti. Tesu bhikkhunā [M 2.0255] niddiṭṭho sammukhāsammukhavasena catubbidho hoti. Tathā dūtena niddiṭṭhopi.

But should one act thus with all kappiyakārakas? One should not act thus. For this so-called kappiyakāraka is, in brief, of two kinds: the designated and the undesignated. Therein, the designated is of two kinds: designated by a monk, and designated by a messenger. The undesignated is also of two kinds: a sammukhavevaṭika kappiyakāraka and a parammukhakappiyakāraka. Among these, the one designated by a monk is fourfold, by way of being in the presence and not in the presence. Similarly, the one designated by a messenger is also fourfold.

Kathaṃ? Idhekacco bhikkhussa cīvaratthāya dūtena akappiyavatthuṃ pahiṇati, dūto taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā “idaṃ, bhante, itthannāmena tumhākaṃ cīvaratthāya pahitaṃ, gaṇhatha na”nti vadati, bhikkhu “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, dūto “atthi pana te, bhante, veyyāvaccakaro”ti [V 2.0230] pucchati, puññatthikehi ca upāsakehi “bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karothā”ti āṇattā vā, bhikkhūnaṃ vā sandiṭṭhā sambhattā keci veyyāvaccakarā honti, tesaṃ aññataro tasmiṃ khaṇe bhikkhussa santike nisinno hoti, bhikkhu taṃ niddisati “ayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti. Dūto tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti gacchati, ayaṃ bhikkhunā sammukhāniddiṭṭho.

How? Here, a certain person sends an unallowable item through a messenger to a monk for a robe. The messenger approaches that monk and says, “Venerable sir, this has been sent by so-and-so for your robe. Please accept it.” The monk refuses, saying, “This is not allowable.” The messenger then asks, “Venerable sir, do you have a steward?” And there are some stewards who are either lay followers desiring merit who have been instructed, “Perform services for the monks,” or are acquaintances or companions of the monks. One of them is sitting near the monk at that moment. The monk points him out, saying, “This is a steward for the monks.” The messenger, having given the unallowable item into his hand, says, “Having bought a robe for the elder, give it,” and departs. This is one designated by the monk in his presence.

No ce bhikkhussa santike nisinno hoti, apica kho bhikkhu niddisati – “asukasmiṃ nāma gāme itthannāmo bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti, so gantvā tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā dadeyyāsī”ti āgantvā bhikkhussa ārocetvā gacchati, ayameko bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭho.

If there is no one sitting near the monk, but the monk points out, “In such-and-such a village, the one named so-and-so is a steward for the monks,” he goes, gives the unallowable item into that person's hands, saying, “You should buy a robe for the elder and give it,” and having returned and informed the monk, he departs. This is the first case of one designated by the monk not in his presence.

Na heva kho so dūto attanā āgantvā āroceti, apica kho aññaṃ pahiṇati “dinnaṃ mayā, bhante, tassa hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ, cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti, ayaṃ dutiyo bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭho.

That messenger does not come and inform him himself, but rather sends another, saying, “Venerable sir, the robe-fund has been given by me into his hand; you may take the robe.” This is the second case of one designated by the monk not in his presence.

Na heva kho aññaṃ pahiṇati, apica kho gacchantova bhikkhuṃ vadati “ahaṃ tassa hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ dassāmi, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti, ayaṃ tatiyo bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho tayo asammukhāniddiṭṭhāti ime cattāro bhikkhunā niddiṭṭhaveyyāvaccakarā [P 3.0676] nāma. Etesu imasmiṃ rājasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

He does not send another, but rather, just as he is going, he tells the monk, “I will give the robe-fund into his hand; you may take the robe.” This is the third case of one designated by the monk not in his presence. Thus, one designated in his presence and three designated not in his presence—these four are called stewards designated by the monk. With these, one should act only in the way stated in this training rule concerning the king.

Aparo bhikkhu purimanayeneva dūtena pucchito natthitāya vā, avicāretukāmatāya vā “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti vadati, tasmiñca khaṇe koci manusso āgacchati, dūto tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “imassa hatthato cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā gacchati, ayaṃ dūtena sammukhāniddiṭṭho.

Another monk, having been asked by the messenger in the same way as before, says, “We have no steward,” either because there is none or due to an unwillingness to arrange it. And at that moment, some person arrives. The messenger, having given the unallowable item into his hand, says, “You may take the robe from this person's hand,” and departs. This is one designated by the messenger in his presence.

Aparo [M 2.0256] dūto gāmaṃ pavisitvā attanā abhirucitassa kassaci hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā purimanayeneva āgantvā āroceti, aññaṃ vā pahiṇati, “ahaṃ asukassa nāma hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ dassāmi, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā vā gacchati, ayaṃ tatiyo dūtena asammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho, tayo asammukhāniddiṭṭhāti ime cattāro dūtena niddiṭṭhaveyyāvaccakarā [V 2.0231] nāma. Etesu meṇḍakasikkhāpade vuttanayena paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “santi, bhikkhave, manussā saddhā pasannā, te kappiyakārakānaṃ hatthe hiraññaṃ upanikkhipanti – ‘iminā ayyassa yaṃ kappiyaṃ taṃ dethā’ti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ tato kappiyaṃ taṃ sādituṃ, na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kenaci pariyāyena jātarūparajataṃ sāditabbaṃ pariyesitabbanti vadāmī”ti (mahāva. 299). Ettha ca codanāya pamāṇaṃ natthi, mūlaṃ asādiyantena sahassakkhattumpi codanāya vā ṭhānena vā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ sādituṃ vaṭṭati. No ce deti, aññaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetvāpi āharāpetabbaṃ. Sace icchati mūlasāmikānampi kathetabbaṃ; no ce icchati na kathetabbaṃ.

Another messenger enters the village and gives an unallowable object into the hand of someone he personally favors, and having returned, informs as before; or he sends another; or, having said, 'I will give the robe-fund into the hand of so-and-so; you may take the robe,' he departs. This is the third who is 'designated not in the presence by the messenger'. Thus, one is 'designated in the presence' and three are 'designated not in the presence'—these four are called 'attendants designated by the messenger'. Regarding these, one should act according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka training rule. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, there are faithful, devoted people who deposit gold with attendants, saying: "With this, give the venerable one whatever is allowable." I allow, bhikkhus, that you consent to what is allowable from that. But I do not say, bhikkhus, that in any way gold and silver should be sought or consented to.' (Mahāvagga 299). And here, there is no limit to the prompting. By one not consenting to the principal, it is allowable to consent to an allowable requisite even a thousand times, whether by prompting or by standing there. If the attendant does not give it, having appointed another attendant, it should be brought. If one wishes, the original owners of the fund may also be told; if one does not wish, they should not be told.

Aparo bhikkhu purimanayeneva dūtena pucchito “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti vadati, tadañño samīpe ṭhito sutvā “āhara bho ahaṃ ayyassa cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā dassāmī”ti vadati. Dūto “handa bho dadeyyāsī”ti tassa hatthe datvā bhikkhussa anārocetvāva gacchati, ayaṃ mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako. Aparo bhikkhuno upaṭṭhākassa vā aññassa vā hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ dadeyyāsī”ti [P 3.0677] ettova pakkamati, ayaṃ parammukhakappiyakārakoti ime dve aniddiṭṭhakappiyakārakā nāma. Etesu aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Sace sayameva cīvaraṃ ānetvā dadanti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce, kiñci na vattabbā. Desanāmattameva cetaṃ “dūtena cīvaracetāpannaṃ pahiṇeyyā”ti sayaṃ āharitvāpi piṇḍapātādīnaṃ atthāya dadantesupi eseva nayo. Na kevalañca attanoyeva atthāya sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati, sacepi koci jātarūparajataṃ ānetvā “idaṃ saṅghassa dammi, ārāmaṃ vā karotha cetiyaṃ vā bhojanasālādīnaṃ vā aññatara”nti vadati, idampi sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Yassa kassaci hi aññassatthāya sampaṭicchantassa dukkaṭaṃ hotīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Another bhikkhu, when asked by a messenger in the same way as before, says, 'We have no attendant.' Another person standing nearby, hearing this, says, 'Bring it, sir, I will have a robe procured for the venerable one and give it.' The messenger, saying, 'Here, sir, you may give it,' places it in that person's hand and departs without informing the bhikkhu. This is a 'word-of-mouth attendant'. Another person gives an unallowable object into the hand of the bhikkhu's regular attendant or someone else, saying, 'You should give a robe to the elder,' and departs from that very spot. This is an 'attendant in absence'. These two are called 'undesignated attendants'. Regarding these, one should act as one would towards non-relatives who have not given an invitation. If they themselves bring a robe and give it, it should be accepted. If not, nothing should be said to them. And this, 'One may send a messenger with a robe-fund,' is merely a teaching. This same principle applies also to those who bring it themselves and give it for the sake of alms-food and so on. And it is not only for one's own sake that it is not allowable to accept; even if someone brings gold and silver and says, 'I give this to the Saṅgha; build a monastery, or a cetiya, or a dining hall, or something else,' this too is not allowable to accept. For it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that for one who accepts on behalf of any other whatsoever, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

Sace [M 2.0257] pana “nayidaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitte “vaḍḍhakīnaṃ vā kammakarānaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, kevalaṃ tumhe sukatadukkaṭaṃ jānāthā”ti vatvā tesaṃ hatthe datvā pakkamati, vaṭṭati. Athāpi “mama manussānaṃ hatthe bhavissati mayhameva vā hatthe bhavissati, kevalaṃ tumhe yaṃ yassa dātabbaṃ, tadatthāya peseyyāthā”ti vadati, evampi vaṭṭati.

If, however, when it is refused with the words, 'It is not allowable for bhikkhus to accept this,' the donor says, 'It will be in the hands of the carpenters or the laborers; you should only know what is well-done and badly-done,' and having given it into their hands, he departs, it is allowable. Or if he says, 'It will be in the hands of my people, or it will be in my own hands; you should only send word for the purpose of giving whatever should be given to whomever,' this too is allowable.

Sace pana saṅghaṃ vā gaṇaṃ vā puggalaṃ vā anāmasitvā “idaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ cetiyassa dema, vihārassa dema, navakammassa demā”ti vadanti, paṭikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati. “Ime idaṃ bhaṇantī”ti [V 2.0232] kappiyakārakānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. “Cetiyādīnaṃ atthāya tumhe gahetvā ṭhapethā”ti vuttena pana “amhākaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitabbaṃ.

If, however, without addressing the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, they say, 'We give this gold and silver for the cetiya, for the vihāra, for new works,' it is not allowable to refuse. The attendants should be told, 'These people are saying this.' But if told by them, 'You should take and keep it for the sake of the cetiya and so on,' it should be refused, saying, 'It is not allowable for us to take it.'

Sace pana koci bahuṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ ānetvā “idaṃ saṅghassa dammi, cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vadati, taṃ ce saṅgho sampaṭicchati, paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpatti. Tatra ce eko bhikkhu “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, upāsako ca “yadi na kappati, mayhameva bhavissatī”ti gacchati. So bhikkhu “tayā saṅghassa lābhantarāyo kato”ti na kenaci kiñci vattabbo. Yo hi taṃ codeti, sveva sāpattiko hoti, tena pana ekena bahū anāpattikā katā. Sace [P 3.0678] pana bhikkhūhi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitte “kappiyakārakānaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, mama purisānaṃ vā mayhaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, kevalaṃ tumhe paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati.

If, however, someone brings a large amount of gold and silver and says, 'I give this to the Saṅgha; you may make use of the four requisites,' and if the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the acceptance and in the use. If, in that situation, one bhikkhu objects, saying, 'This is not allowable,' and the lay follower says, 'If it is not allowable, it will remain mine,' and departs, that bhikkhu should not be told anything by anyone, such as, 'You have caused an obstruction to the Saṅgha's gain.' For whoever reproaches him, that very one incurs an offense, whereas by that one bhikkhu, many have been made free of offense. If, however, when it is refused by the bhikkhus with the words, 'It is not allowable,' the lay follower says, 'It will be in the hands of the attendants, or in the hands of my men, or in my own hands; you just make use of the requisites,' it is allowable.

Catupaccayatthāya ca dinnaṃ yena yena paccayena attho hoti, tadatthaṃ upanetabbaṃ, cīvaratthāya dinnaṃ cīvareyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace cīvarena tādiso attho natthi, piṇḍapātādīhi saṅgho kilamati, saṅghasuṭṭhutāya apaloketvā tadatthāyapi upanetabbaṃ. Esa nayo piṇḍapātagilānapaccayatthāya dinnepi, senāsanatthāya dinnaṃ pana senāsanassa garubhaṇḍattā senāsaneyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace pana bhikkhūsu senāsanaṃ chaḍḍetvā gatesu senāsanaṃ vinassati, īdise kāle senāsanaṃ vissajjetvāpi bhikkhūnaṃ paribhogo anuññāto, tasmā senāsanajagganatthaṃ mūlacchejjaṃ akatvā yāpanamattaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

What is given for the sake of the four requisites should be applied for the purpose of whichever requisite is needed. What is given for the sake of robes should be applied only for robes. If there is no such need for robes and the Saṅgha is afflicted regarding alms-food and so on, then for the sake of the Saṅgha's well-being, having made a formal declaration, it may be applied for that purpose also. This is the principle also for what is given for the sake of alms-food and requisites for the sick. What is given for the sake of lodgings, however, because a lodging is a weighty item, should be applied only for lodgings. But if, when the bhikkhus have departed and abandoned the lodging, the lodging is perishing, at such a time, having disposed of the lodging, the use of its value by the bhikkhus is permitted. Therefore, for the sake of maintaining the lodging, without exhausting the principal, only what is sufficient for sustenance should be used.

Na [M 2.0258] kevalañca hiraññasuvaṇṇameva, aññampi khettavatthādi akappiyaṃ na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Sace hi koci “mayhaṃ tisassasampādanakaṃ mahātaḷākaṃ atthi, taṃ saṅghassa dammī”ti vadati, taṃ ce saṅgho sampaṭicchati, paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpattiyeva. Yo pana taṃ paṭikkhipati, so purimanayeneva na kenaci kiñci vattabbo. Yo hi taṃ codeti, sveva sāpattiko hoti, tena pana ekena bahū anāpattikā katā.

And it is not only gold and silver that should not be accepted, but also other unallowable things such as fields and land. For if someone says, 'I have a great reservoir that yields three harvests; I give it to the Sangha,' and the Sangha accepts it, there is an offense both in receiving and in using it. But whoever refuses it should not be spoken to by anyone in any way, in accordance with the previous method. For whoever reproves him is himself the one who commits an offense, while by that one person, many are made blameless.

Yo pana “tādisaṃyeva taḷākaṃ dammī”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto vadati “asukañca asukañca saṅghassa taḷākaṃ atthi, taṃ kathaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So vattabbo – “kappiyaṃ katvā dinnaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Kathaṃ dinnaṃ kappiyaṃ hotīti? “Cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vatvā dinnanti. So sace “sādhu, bhante, cattāro paccaye saṅgho paribhuñjatū”ti [V 2.0233] deti, vaṭṭati. Athāpi “taḷākaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto “kappiyakārako atthī”ti pucchitvā “natthī”ti [P 3.0679] vutte “idaṃ asuko nāma vicāressati, asukassa vā hatthe, mayhaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, saṅgho kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ paribhuñjatū”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Sacepi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto “udakaṃ paribhuñjissati, bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovissati, migapakkhino pivissantī”ti vadati, evampi vaṭṭati. Athāpi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto vadati “kappiyasīsena gaṇhathā”ti. “Sādhu, upāsaka, saṅgho pānīyaṃ pivissati, bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovissati, migapakkhino pivissantī”ti vatvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

But if a donor, having said, 'I give just such a reservoir,' is refused by the monks with the words, 'It is not allowable,' and then says, 'The Sangha has such and such a reservoir; how is that allowable?' He should be told: 'It will have been given after being made allowable.' How is it given so that it becomes allowable? By being given with the words, 'Use the four requisites.' If that donor then gives it, saying, 'Very well, venerable sirs, let the Sangha use the four requisites,' it is allowable. Furthermore, if, having said, 'Take the reservoir,' and being refused with, 'It is not allowable,' he asks, 'Is there a steward?' and upon being told, 'There is not,' he then says, 'So-and-so by name will manage this, or it will be in the hands of so-and-so, or in my hands; let the Sangha use the allowable goods,' it is allowable. Even if, being refused with, 'It is not allowable,' he says, 'The Sangha will use the water, wash their requisites, and beasts and birds will drink,' even so it is allowable. Or if, being refused with, 'It is not allowable,' he says, 'Accept it under the heading of what is allowable.' Then, having replied, 'Very well, lay supporter, the Sangha will drink the water, wash their requisites, and beasts and birds will drink,' it is allowable to use it.

Athāpi “mama taḷākaṃ vā pokkharaṇiṃ vā saṅghassa dammī”ti “vutte, sādhu, upāsaka, saṅgho pānīyaṃ pivissatī”tiādīni vatvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Yadi pana bhikkhūhi hatthakammaṃ yācitvā sahatthena ca kappiyapathaviṃ khanitvā udakaparibhogatthāya taḷākaṃ kāritaṃ hoti, taṃ ce nissāya sassaṃ nipphādetvā manussā vihāre kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ denti, vaṭṭati. Atha manussā eva saṅghassa upakāratthāya saṅghikabhūmiṃ khanitvā taṃ nissāya nipphannasassato kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ denti, evampi vaṭṭati. “Amhākaṃ ekaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapethā”ti vutte ca ṭhapetumpi labbhati. Atha pana te manussā rājabalinā upaddutā pakkamanti, aññe paṭipajjanti, na ca bhikkhūnaṃ kiñci denti, udakaṃ vāretuṃ labbhati. Tañca kho kasikammakāleyeva, na sassakāle. Sace te vadanti “nanu, bhante, pubbepi manussā imaṃ nissāya sassaṃ akaṃsū”ti[M 2.0259]. Tato vattabbā – “te saṅghassa imañca imañca upakāraṃ akaṃsu, idañcidañca kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ adaṃsū”ti. Sace vadanti – “mayampi dassāmā”ti, evampi vaṭṭati.

Furthermore, if it is said, 'I give my reservoir or my lotus pond to the Sangha,' it is indeed allowable to use it after replying, 'Very well, lay supporter, the Sangha will drink the water,' and so on. If, however, a reservoir is caused to be made by monks for the purpose of using water—after they have requested manual labor and dug on allowable ground with their own hands—and if, relying on it, people produce crops and give allowable goods to the monastery, it is allowable. Or, if people themselves, for the benefit of the Sangha, dig on Sangha land and, from the crops produced in reliance on that, they give allowable goods, even so it is allowable. And when it is said, 'Appoint for us a steward,' it is also permitted to appoint one. But if those people, oppressed by the king's tax, depart, and others take their place but give nothing to the monks, it is permitted to withhold the water. This, however, should be done only at the time of cultivation, not at the time of the harvest. If they say, 'Venerable sirs, did not people previously also cultivate crops in reliance on this?' they should then be told: 'They performed this and that service for the Sangha and gave this and that allowable good.' If they say, 'We too will give,' even so it is allowable.

Sace pana koci abyatto akappiyavohārena taḷākaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti vā kāreti vā, taṃ bhikkhūhi na paribhuñjitabbaṃ, taṃ nissāya laddhaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍampi akappiyameva. Sace bhikkhūhi pariccattabhāvaṃ ñatvā sāmiko vā tassa puttadhītaro vā añño vā koci vaṃse uppanno puna kappiyavohārena deti, vaṭṭati. Pacchinne kulavaṃse yo tassa janapadassa sāmiko, so acchinditvā [P 3.0680] puna deti, cittalapabbate bhikkhunā nīhaṭaudakavāhakaṃ aḷanāgarājamahesī viya, evampi vaṭṭati.

But if some monk who is unskilled in the Vinaya accepts a reservoir or has one made by means of an unallowable transaction, it should not be used by the monks; even allowable goods obtained in reliance on it are indeed unallowable. If, having learned that it has been relinquished by the monks, the original owner, or his sons and daughters, or some other person born in the lineage gives it again by means of an allowable transaction, it is allowable. When the family lineage has been cut off, whoever is the lord of that district may give it again after having taken possession of it—just as the chief queen of King Aḷanāga did with the water channel brought down from Cittalapabbata by a monk. Even so, it is allowable.

Kappiyavohārepi udakavasena paṭiggahitataḷāke suddhacittānaṃ mattikuddharaṇapāḷibandhanādīni [V 2.0234] ca kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ nissāya pana sassaṃ karonte disvā kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yadi te sayameva kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ denti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce denti, na codetabbaṃ, na sāretabbaṃ. Paccayavasena paṭiggahitataḷāke kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mattikuddharaṇapāḷibandhanādīni pana kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace kappiyakārakā sayameva karonti, vaṭṭati. Abyattena pana lajjibhikkhunā kārāpitesu kiñcāpi paṭiggahaṇe kappiyaṃ, bhikkhussa payogapaccayā uppannena missakattā visagatapiṇḍapāto viya akappiyamaṃsarasamissakabhojanaṃ viya ca dubbinibbhogaṃ hoti, sabbesaṃ akappiyameva.

Also, regarding the procedure for allowable transactions: in a reservoir that was accepted on the basis of its water, it is allowable for those with pure minds to do such things as removing earth and building embankments. But, upon seeing people cultivating crops in reliance on it, it is not allowable to appoint a steward. If they give allowable goods of their own accord, it should be accepted. If they do not give, they should not be urged or reminded. In a reservoir that was accepted on the basis of requisites, it is allowable to appoint a steward. But it is not allowable for monks to do such things as removing earth and building embankments. If the stewards do these things of their own accord, it is allowable. But when a conscientious monk who is unskilled in the Vinaya has caused such things as removing earth and building embankments to be done, then even though the initial acceptance was allowable, because it is mixed with that which has arisen from the monk's effort, it becomes difficult to use separately—like alms-food into which poison has entered, or like food mixed with the broth of unallowable meat—and is therefore unallowable for all.

Sace pana “udakassa okāso atthi, taḷākassa pāḷi thirā, yathā bahuṃ udakaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ karohi, tīrasamīpe udakaṃ karohī”ti evaṃ udakameva vicāreti, vaṭṭati. Uddhane aggiṃ na pātenti, “udakakammaṃ labbhatu upāsakā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Sassaṃ katvā āharathā”ti vattuṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Sace pana taḷāke atibahuṃ udakaṃ disvā passato vā piṭṭhito vā mātikaṃ nīharāpeti, vanaṃ chindāpetvā kedāre kārāpeti, porāṇakedāresu vā pakatibhāgaṃ aggahetvā atirekaṃ gaṇhāti, navasasse vā akālasasse vā aparicchinnabhāge “ettake kahāpaṇe dethā”ti kahāpaṇe uṭṭhāpeti, sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ.

Furthermore, if one manages only the water, saying, 'There is space for water, the embankment of the reservoir is firm; make it so that it can hold much water; make the water near the shore,' it is allowable. They do not place fire on the hearth; it is allowable to say, 'Lay devotees, may the water-related work be accomplished.' However, it is not allowable to say, 'Having cultivated the crop, bring it.' Furthermore, if, having seen too much water in the reservoir, one has a channel brought out from the side or from the back; or has the forest cleared and has fields made; or, in old fields, not taking the normal share, one takes the excess; or, in a field with a new crop, or an out-of-season crop, or with an unapportioned share, one establishes a demand for coins, saying, 'Give this many kahāpaṇas'—it is unallowable for all.

Yo [M 2.0260] pana “kassatha vapathā”ti avatvā “ettakāya bhūmiyā, ettako nāma bhāgo”ti evaṃ bhūmiṃ vā patiṭṭhapeti, “ettake bhūmibhāge amhehi sassaṃ kataṃ, ettakaṃ nāma bhāgaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadantesu kassakesu bhūmippamāṇaggahaṇatthaṃ [P 3.0681] rajjuyā vā daṇḍena vā mināti, khale vā ṭhatvā rakkhati, khalato vā nīharāpeti, koṭṭhāgāre vā paṭisāmeti, tasseva taṃ akappiyaṃ.

Furthermore, if a monk, without saying, 'Plow, sow,' establishes the land, saying, 'For this much land, such-and-such is the share'; or, when the farmers say, 'We have cultivated the crop in this much portion of land; take such-and-such a share,' he, for the purpose of taking the measure of the land, measures it with a rope or a stick; or, standing at the threshing floor, guards it; or has it brought out from the threshing floor; or stores it in the granary—that is unallowable for that monk alone.

Sace kassakā kahāpaṇe āharitvā “ime saṅghassa āhaṭā”ti vadanti, aññataro ca bhikkhu “na saṅgho kahāpaṇe khādatī”ti saññāya “ettakehi kahāpaṇehi sāṭake āhara, ettakehi yāguādīni sampādehī”ti vadati. Yaṃ te āharanti, sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattā.

If farmers, having brought kahāpaṇas, say, 'These have been brought for the Sangha,' and a certain monk, with the thought, 'The Sangha does not eat kahāpaṇas,' says, 'With this many kahāpaṇas, bring cloths; with this many, prepare gruel and so on'—whatever they bring is unallowable for all. Why? Because of having managed the kahāpaṇas.

Sace dhaññaṃ āharitvā idaṃ saṅghassa āhaṭanti vadanti, aññataro ca bhikkhu purimanayeneva “ettakehi vīhīhi idañcidañca āharathā”ti vadati. Yaṃ te āharanti, tasseva akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Dhaññassa vicāritattā.

If, having brought grain, they say, 'This has been brought for the Sangha,' and a certain monk, in the same way as before, says, 'With this much paddy, bring this and that requisite'—whatever they bring is unallowable for him alone. Why? Because of having managed the grain.

Sace [V 2.0235] taṇḍulaṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā āharitvā “idaṃ saṅghassa āhaṭa”nti vadanti, aññataro ca bhikkhu purimanayeneva “ettakehi taṇḍulehi idañcidañca āharathā”ti vadati. Yaṃ te āharanti, sabbesaṃ kappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Kappiyānaṃ taṇḍulādīnaṃ vicāritattā. Kayavikkayepi anāpatti, kappiyakārakassa ācikkhitattā.

If, having brought husked rice or pulses, they say, 'This has been brought for the Sangha,' and a certain monk, in the same way as before, says, 'With this much husked rice, bring this and that requisite'—whatever they bring is allowable for all. Why? Because of having managed allowable things such as husked rice. There is also no offense in regard to buying and selling, because it has been told to the one who makes things allowable.

Pubbe pana cittalapabbate eko bhikkhu catusāladvāre “aho vata sve saṅghassa ettakappamāṇe pūve paceyyu”nti ārāmikānaṃ saññājananatthaṃ bhūmiyaṃ maṇḍalaṃ akāsi, taṃ disvā cheko ārāmiko tatheva katvā dutiyadivase bheriyā ākoṭitāya sannipatite saṅghe pūvaṃ gahetvā saṅghattheraṃ āha – “bhante, amhehi ito pubbe neva pitūnaṃ na pitāmahānaṃ evarūpaṃ sutapubbaṃ, ekena ayyena catussāladvāre pūvatthāya saññā katā, ito dāni pabhuti ayyā attano attano cittānurūpaṃ vadantu, amhākampi phāsuvihāro bhavissatī”ti. Mahāthero tatova nivatti, ekabhikkhunāpi pūvo na gahito. Evaṃ pubbe tatruppādampi na paribhuñjiṃsu. Tasmā –

Furthermore, in the past, on Cittalapabbata, a certain monk at the four-gated hall, for the purpose of making a sign for the monastery attendants, made a circle on the ground, thinking, 'Oh, if only tomorrow they would cook cakes of this size for the Sangha!' A clever monastery attendant, having seen that, did just so. On the second day, when the drum was beaten and the Sangha had assembled, he took the cake and said to the Sanghatthera: 'Venerable sir, before this, we have never heard such a thing from our fathers, nor have we heard such a thing from our grandfathers. A certain venerable one made a sign at the four-gated hall for the sake of cake. From now on, let the venerable ones say what is in accordance with their own minds; for us too, there will be a comfortable abiding.' The Mahāthera turned back from that very spot; the cake was not accepted by even a single monk. Thus, in the past, they did not make use of even what was produced there. Therefore:

Sallekhaṃ [M 2.0261] accajantena, appamattena bhikkhunā;

Kappiyepi na kātabbā, āmisatthāya lolatāti.

By a heedful monk who does not abandon the practice of effacement, fickleness for the sake of material gain should not be engaged in, even in regard to what is allowable.

Yo [P 3.0682] cāyaṃ taḷāke vutto, pokkharaṇī-udakavāhakamātikādīsupi eseva nayo.

And this ruling which was stated in regard to a reservoir—this same principle applies also to lotus ponds, water conduits, channels, and so on.

Pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇaucchuphalāphalādīnaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ yaṃ kiñci khettaṃ vā vatthuṃ vā dammīti vuttepi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitvā taḷāke vuttanayeneva yadā kappiyavohārena “catupaccayaparibhogatthāya dammī”ti vadati, tadā sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, “vanaṃ dammi, araññaṃ dammī”ti vutte pana vaṭṭati. Sace manussā bhikkhūhi anāṇattāyeva tattha rukkhe chinditvā aparaṇṇādīni sampādetvā bhikkhūnaṃ bhāgaṃ denti, vaṭṭati; adentā na codetabbā. Sace kenacideva antarāyena tesu pakkantesu aññe karonti, na ca bhikkhūnaṃ kiñci denti, te vāretabbā. Sace vadanti – “nanu, bhante, pubbepi manussā idha sassāni akaṃsū”ti, tato te vattabbā – “te saṅghassa idañcidañca kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ adaṃsū”ti. Sace vadanti – “mayampi dassāmā”ti evaṃ vaṭṭati.

Even when it is said, 'I give whatever field or land is a place for the growing of early grain, pulses, sugarcane, minor fruits, major fruits, and so on,' having rejected it by saying, 'It is not allowable,' it should be accepted only when, by the same principle stated for the reservoir, one says, using allowable speech, 'I give it for the use of the four requisites.' But when it is said, 'I give a forest, I give a wilderness,' it is allowable. If people, uninstructed by the monks, cut down trees there, prepare pulses and so on, and give a share to the monks, it is allowable; those who do not give should not be asked for it. If, due to some obstacle, they depart and others do the work but give nothing to the monks, they should be stopped. If they say, 'Venerable sir, did not people in the past cultivate crops here?' then they should be told, 'They gave this and that allowable item to the Sangha.' If they reply, 'We too will give,' then it is allowable.

Kañci [V 2.0236] sassuṭṭhānakaṃ bhūmippadesaṃ sandhāya “sīmaṃ demā”ti vadanti, vaṭṭati. Sīmā paricchedanatthaṃ pana thambhā vā pāsāṇā vā sayaṃ na ṭhapetabbā. Kasmā? Bhūmi nāma anagghā appakenāpi pārājiko bhaveyya, ārāmikānaṃ pana vattabbaṃ – “iminā ṭhānena amhākaṃ sīmā gatā”ti. Sacepi hi te adhikaṃ gaṇhanti, pariyāyena kathitattā anāpatti. Yadi pana rājarājamahāmattādayo sayameva thambhe ṭhapāpetvā “cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti denti, vaṭṭatiyeva.

Referring to some plot of land where crops arise, if they say, 'We give a boundary,' it is allowable. However, for the purpose of demarcating the boundary, posts or stones should not be set up by oneself. Why? Land is priceless; even for a small amount, one could commit a pārājika offense. But the monastery attendants should be told, 'Our boundary goes by this place.' For even if they take more, because it was stated indirectly, there is no offense. But if kings, royal ministers, and so on, having had posts set up themselves, give it, saying, 'Make use of the four requisites,' it is certainly allowable.

Sace koci antosīmāya taḷākaṃ khanati, vihāramajjhena vā mātikaṃ neti, cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇādīni dussanti, vāretabbo. Sace saṅgho kiñci labhitvā āmisagarukatāya na vāreti, eko bhikkhu vāreti, sova bhikkhu issaro. Sace eko bhikkhu na vāreti, “netha tumhe”ti tesaṃyeva pakkho hoti, saṅgho vāreti, saṅghova issaro. Saṅghikesu hi kammesu yo dhammakammaṃ karoti, sova issaro. Sace vāriyamānopi karoti, heṭṭhā gahitaṃ paṃsuṃ heṭṭhā pakkhipitvā, upari gahitaṃ paṃsuṃ upari pakkhipitvā pūretabbā.

If anyone digs a pond within the boundary, or leads a water-channel through the middle of the monastery, and the shrine-courtyard, Bodhi-tree-courtyard, and so on are damaged, he should be stopped. If the Saṅgha, having received something, does not stop him out of attachment to material gain, but a single bhikkhu does stop him, that very bhikkhu is the authority. If a single bhikkhu does not stop him and, saying, 'You may lead it,' becomes their partisan, but the Saṅgha does stop him, then the Saṅgha is the authority. For in matters of the Saṅgha, whoever performs an act in accordance with the Dhamma, that very one is the authority. If he proceeds even while being stopped, the ditch should be filled by putting the soil taken from below back below, and the soil taken from above back above.

Sace [M 2.0262] koci yathājātameva ucchuṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā alābukumbhaṇḍādikaṃ [P 3.0683] vā valliphalaṃ dātukāmo “etaṃ sabbaṃ ucchukhettaṃ aparaṇṇavatthuṃ valliphalāvāṭaṃ dammī”ti vadati, saha vatthunā parāmaṭṭhattā “na vaṭṭatī”ti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero pana “abhilāpamattametaṃ sāmikānaṃyeva hi so bhūmibhāgo tasmā vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

If someone, wishing to give sugarcane, or pulses, or vine-fruits such as bottle-gourds and pumpkins just as they have grown, says, 'I give this entire sugarcane field, this plot of pulses, and this vine-fruit garden,' the Great Elder Suma said: 'It is not allowable, because it is considered together with the land.' The Great Elder Paduma, however, said: 'This is merely a manner of speaking. Indeed, that portion of land belongs to the owners themselves; therefore, it is allowable.'

“Dāsaṃ dammī”ti vadati, na vaṭṭati. “Ārāmikaṃ dammi, veyyāvaccakaraṃ dammi, kappiyakārakaṃ dammī”ti vutte vaṭṭati. Sace so ārāmiko purebhattampi pacchābhattampi saṅghasseva kammaṃ karoti, sāmaṇerassa viya sabbaṃ bhesajjapaṭijagganampi tassa kātabbaṃ. Sace purebhattameva saṅghassa kammaṃ karoti, pacchābhattaṃ attano kammaṃ karoti, sāyaṃ nivāpo na dātabbo. Yepi pañcadivasavārena vā pakkhavārena vā saṅghassa kammaṃ katvā sesakāle attano kammaṃ karonti, tesampi karaṇakāleyeva bhattañca nivāpo ca dātabbo. Sace saṅghassa kammaṃ natthi, attanoyeva kammaṃ katvā jīvanti, te ce hatthakammamūlaṃ ānetvā denti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce denti, na kiñci vattabbā. Yaṃ kiñci rajakadāsampi pesakāradāsampi ārāmikanāmena sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati.

If one says, 'I give a slave,' it is not allowable. When it is said, 'I give a monastery attendant,' 'I give a service-provider,' or 'I give an attendant who makes things allowable,' it is allowable. If that monastery attendant performs work for the Saṅgha both in the forenoon and in the afternoon, all care with medicine should be provided for him, just as for a novice. If he performs work for the Saṅgha only in the forenoon and performs his own work in the afternoon, the evening provision should not be given. For those who, having worked for the Saṅgha on a five-day or a fortnightly rotation, do their own work in the remaining time, for them too, a meal and provision should be given only at the time of their work. If there is no work for the Saṅgha and they make a living by doing their own work, should they bring and give the wage from their manual labor, it should be accepted. If they do not give, nothing should be said. It is allowable to accept anyone, even a slave of a washerman or a slave of a weaver, under the designation of 'monastery attendant'.

Sace “gāvo demā”ti vadanti, “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitabbā. Imā gāvo kutoti [V 2.0237] paṇḍitehi pañca gorasaparibhogatthāya dinnāti, “mayampi pañcagorasaparibhogatthāya demā”ti vutte vaṭṭati. Ajikādīsupi eseva nayo. “Hatthiṃ dema, assaṃ mahisaṃ kukkuṭaṃ sūkaraṃ demā”ti vadanti, sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace keci manussā “appossukkā, bhante, tumhe hotha, mayaṃ ime gahetvā tumhākaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ dassāmā”ti gaṇhanti, vaṭṭati. “Kukkuṭasūkarā sukhaṃ jīvantū”ti araññe vissajjetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Imaṃ taḷākaṃ, imaṃ khettaṃ, imaṃ vatthuṃ, vihārassa demā”ti vutte paṭikkhipituṃ na labbhatīti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

If they say, 'We give cows,' they should be rejected with, 'It is not allowable.' It is said that these cows were given by the wise for the purpose of enjoying the five dairy products; when it is said, 'We too give for the purpose of enjoying the five dairy products,' it is allowable. This same method applies to goats and so on. If they say, 'We give an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a chicken, or a pig,' it is not allowable to accept. If some people take them, saying, 'Venerable sirs, be without anxiety; we will take these and give you allowable items,' it is allowable. It is allowable to release chickens and pigs into the forest, saying, 'May chickens and pigs live in happiness.' When it is said, 'We give this pond, this field, this plot to the monastery,' it cannot be rejected. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idampi chasamuṭṭhānaṃ kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ[P 3.0684], ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding origins and so on, this offense has six origins. It is an action, not a release through perception, is without thought, a fault by convention, is a bodily and verbal action, involves three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is concluded.

Niṭṭhito cīvaravaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter, the Robe Chapter, is concluded.

2. Kosiyavaggo

2. The Chapter on Silk

1. Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Silk

542. Tena [M 2.0263] samayenāti kosiyasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha santharitvā kataṃ hotīti same bhūmibhāge kosiyaṃsūni uparūpari santharitvā kañjikādīhi siñcitvā kataṃ hoti. Ekenapi kosiyaṃsunā missitvāti tiṭṭhatu attano rucivasena missitaṃ, sacepi tassa karaṇaṭṭhāne vāto ekaṃ kosiyaṃsuṃ ānetvā pāteti, evampi missetvā katameva hotīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

542. At that time: this is the training rule on silk. Herein, “spread out and made” means: on an even ground, silk threads are spread out layer upon layer, sprinkled with rice gruel and the like, and made. “Even mixed with a single silk thread” means: let alone a thread mixed according to one’s own liking; even if, at the place of making, the wind brings and drops a single silk thread, even so, it is considered made by mixing. The rest is clear in meaning.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ,

It has six origins; it is an action; it is not released by perception; it is unintentional; it is an offense by designation; it is a bodily action and a verbal action.

Ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Silk is concluded.

2. Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Pure Black

547. Tena samayenāti suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha suddhakāḷakānanti suddhānaṃ kāḷakānaṃ[V 2.0238], aññehi amissitakāḷakānanti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Samuṭṭhānādīnipi kosiyasikkhāpadasadisānevāti.

547. At that time: this is the training rule on pure black. Herein, “of pure black” means of pure, black wool, that is, black unmixed with others—this is the meaning. The rest is clear in meaning. The origins and so forth are also just like those of the training rule on silk.

Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Pure Black is concluded.

3. Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Two Parts

552. Tena samayenāti dvebhāgasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha ante ādiyitvāti santhatassa ante anuvātaṃ viya dassetvā odātaṃ alliyāpetvā.

552. At that time: this is the training rule on two parts. Herein, “having taken at the edge” means: having applied white wool at the edge of the spread-out rug, showing it like a border along the length.

Dve bhāgāti dve koṭṭhāsā. Ādātabbāti gahetabbā. Gocariyānanti kapilavaṇṇānaṃ. Dve tulā ādātabbāti catūhi tulāhi kāretukāmaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atthato pana yattakehi eḷakalomehi kātukāmo hoti, tesu dve koṭṭhāsā kāḷakānaṃ eko odātānaṃ, eko gocariyānanti idameva dassitaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

“Two parts” means two portions. “Should be taken” means should be acquired. “Of tawny color” means of a brownish color. “Two tulā should be taken” is said with reference to one who wishes to have it made with four tulā. In terms of meaning, however, it should be understood that this very point is shown: of however much sheep’s wool one wishes to make it, two portions should be of black, one of white, and one of tawny. The rest is clear in meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīnipi [M 2.0264] kosiyasikkhāpadasadisāneva. Kevalaṃ idaṃ ādāya anādāya ca karaṇato kiriyākiriyaṃ veditabbanti.

The origins and so forth are just like those of the training rule on silk. Only, this should be understood as an action or non-action depending on whether it is made by procuring or by not procuring the materials.

Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Two Parts is concluded.

4. Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Six Years

557. Tena [P 3.0685] samayenāti chabbassasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha ūhadantipi ummihantipīti santhatānaṃ upari vaccampi passāvampi karontīti vuttaṃ hoti.

557. At that time: this is the training rule on six years. Herein, “they defecate or urinate” means it is said that they pass feces and urine on the spreads.

Dinnā saṅghena itthannāmassa bhikkhuno santhatasammutīti evaṃ laddhasammutiko bhikkhu yāva rogo na vūpasammati, tāva yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati, tattha tattha santhataṃ kātuṃ labhati. Sace arogo hutvā puna mūlabyādhināva gilāno hoti, soyeva parihāro, natthaññaṃ sammutikiccanti phussadevatthero āha. Upatissatthero pana “so vā byādhi paṭikuppatu, añño vā, ‘sakiṃ gilāno’ti nāmaṃ laddhaṃ laddhameva, puna sammutikiccaṃ natthī”ti āha.

“The permission for a spread has been given by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so.” A monk who has thus obtained permission may make a spread wherever he goes, for as long as the illness does not subside. If, having become healthy, he falls ill again with the very same root illness, that same allowance applies; there is no need for another act of permission—so said the Elder Phussadeva. The Elder Upatissa, however, said: “Whether that illness recurs or another arises, once the designation ‘one who is ill’ has been obtained, it remains obtained. There is no further need for an act of permission.”

Orena [V 2.0239] ce channaṃ vassānanti channaṃ vassānaṃ orimabhāge, antoti attho. Padabhājane pana saṅkhyāmattadassanatthaṃ “ūnakachabbassānī”ti vuttaṃ.

“If within six years” means in the hither part of six years, that is, within. In the word analysis, however, it is said “less than six years” for the purpose of showing the mere number.

Anāpatti chabbassāni karotīti yadā chabbassāni paripuṇṇāni honti, tadā santhataṃ karoti. Dutiyapadepi “yadā atirekachabbassāni honti, tadā karotī”ti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Na hi so chabbassāni karotīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

There is no offense if he makes it after six years: this means that when six years are complete, then he makes a spread. In the second phrase also, the meaning should be understood thus: “When it is more than six years, then he makes it.” For he does not make it during the six years. The rest is clear in meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīni kosiyasikkhāpadasadisānevāti.

The origins and so forth are just like those of the training rule on silk.

Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Six Years is concluded.

5. Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Felt Rug for Sitting

565. Tena samayenāti nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha icchāmahaṃ bhikkhaveti bhagavā kira taṃ temāsaṃ na kiñci bodhaneyyasattaṃ addasa, tasmā [M 2.0265] evamāha. Evaṃ santepi tantivasena dhammadesanā kattabbā siyā. Yasmā panassa etadahosi – “mayi okāsaṃ kāretvā paṭisallīne bhikkhū adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ karissanti, taṃ upaseno bhindissati. Ahaṃ tassa pasīditvā bhikkhūnaṃ dassanaṃ anujānissāmi, tato maṃ passitukāmā bahū bhikkhū dhutaṅgāni samādiyissanti, ahañca tehi ujjhitasanthatapaccayā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmī”ti, tasmā evamāha. Evaṃ bahūni hi ettha ānisaṃsānīti.

565. “At that time” introduces the training rule concerning the felt rug for sitting. Therein, regarding “I wish, O bhikkhus”: it is said that the Blessed One, for those three months, did not see any being worthy of enlightenment, and therefore he spoke thus. Even so, a Dhamma discourse should have been given according to the textual lineage. However, because it occurred to him: “When I have created an opportunity and am in seclusion, the bhikkhus will make an unlawful communal agreement. Upasena will break it. Being pleased with him, I will permit the bhikkhus an audience. Then, many bhikkhus desiring to see me will undertake the ascetic practices. And I, on account of the felt rugs abandoned by them, will lay down a training rule,” therefore he spoke thus. Indeed, there are many benefits in this.

Sapariso yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti [P 3.0686] thero kira “na, bhikkhave, ūnadasavassena upasampādetabbo, yo upasampādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 75) imasmiṃ khandhakasikkhāpade “kathañhi nāma tvaṃ moghapurisa aññehi ovadiyo anusāsiyo aññaṃ ovadituṃ anusāsituṃ maññissasī”ti evamādinā nayena garahaṃ labhitvā “satthā mayhaṃ parisaṃ nissāya garahaṃ adāsi, so dānāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ teneva puṇṇacandasassirīkena sabbākāraparipuṇṇena mukhena brahmaghosaṃ nicchāretvā parisaṃyeva nissāya sādhukāraṃ dāpessāmī”ti suhadayo kulaputto atirekayojanasataṃ paṭikkamitvā parisaṃ cinitvā pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi parivuto puna bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamanto. Tena vuttaṃ – “sapariso yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”ti. Na hi sakkā buddhānaṃ aññathā ārādhetuṃ aññatra vattasampattiyā.

Regarding “With his retinue, he approached the Blessed One”: it is said that the elder, in this training rule from the Khandhaka, “Bhikkhus, ordination should not be given by one who is less than ten years in seniority. Whoever should give ordination commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāva. 75), having received censure by way of such statements as, “How indeed, foolish man, could you, who should be advised and instructed by others, think to advise and instruct another?”, thought: “The Teacher censured me on account of my retinue. Now I shall cause the Blessed One, with that very mouth glorious as the full moon and perfect in every aspect, to utter a sublime voice and give his approval on account of this very retinue.” Being a noble son with a good heart, he went back more than a hundred yojanas, gathered a retinue, and, surrounded by about five hundred bhikkhus, approached the Blessed One again. Therefore it was said: “With his retinue, he approached the Blessed One.” For it is not possible to please the Buddhas in any other way than through the accomplishment of virtuous conduct.

Bhagavato [V 2.0240] avidūre nisinnoti vattasampattiyā parisuddhabhāvena nirāsaṅko sīho viya kañcanapabbatassa bhagavato avidūre nisinno. Etadavocāti kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ etaṃ avoca. Manāpāni te bhikkhu paṃsukūlānīti bhikkhu tava imāni paṃsukūlāni manāpāni, attano ruciyā khantiyā gahitānīti attho. Na kho me, bhante, manāpānīti, bhante na mayā attano ruciyā gahitāni, galaggāhena viya matthakatāḷanena viya ca gāhitomhīti dasseti.

Regarding “seated not far from the Blessed One”: through his accomplishment in virtuous conduct and his state of purity, he was without apprehension, and like a lion near a golden mountain, he sat not far from the Blessed One. Regarding “he said this”: he said this for the purpose of initiating a conversation. Regarding “Bhikkhu, are these rag-robes pleasing to you?”: the meaning is, “Bhikkhu, are these rag-robes of yours pleasing, taken according to your own liking and preference?” Regarding “Indeed, venerable sir, they are not pleasing to me”: this shows, “Venerable sir, they were not taken according to my own liking; I was made to take them as if seized by the throat and as if struck on the head.”

Paññāyissatīti paññāto abhiññāto bhavissati, tattha sandississatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na mayaṃ apaññattaṃ paññapessāmāti mayaṃ sāvakā nāma apaññattaṃ na paññapessāma, buddhavisayo hi eso yadidaṃ [M 2.0266] “pācittiyaṃ dukkaṭa”ntiādinā nayena apaññattasikkhāpadapaññapanaṃ paññattasamucchindanaṃ vā. Samādāyāti taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā, “sādhu suṭṭhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā yathāpaññattesu sabbasikkhāpadesu sikkhissāmāti dasseti. Tassa [P 3.0687] āraddhacitto punapi “sādhu sādhū”ti sādhukāramadāsi.

Regarding “It will be known”: it will be known, fully known; this means it will become apparent there. Regarding “We will not lay down what has not been laid down”: we who are disciples will not lay down what has not been laid down, for this is the domain of a Buddha—that is, the laying down of a training rule that has not been laid down, by way of saying “this is a pācittiya offense,” “this is a dukkaṭa offense,” and so on, or the abolishing of what has been laid down. Regarding “Having undertaken”: having undertaken that particular training rule and having accepted it with “good, very good,” it shows, “we will train in all the training rules as they have been laid down.” The Blessed One, his mind pleased with him, again gave his approval, saying, “Excellent, excellent!”

566. Anuññātāvusoti anuññātaṃ, āvuso. Pihentāti pihayantā. Santhatāni ujjhitvāti santhate catutthacīvarasaññitāya sabbasanthatāni ujjhitvā. Dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā bhikkhū āmantesīti bhagavā santhatāni vippakiṇṇāni disvā “saddhādeyyavinipātane kāraṇaṃ natthi, paribhogupāyaṃ nesaṃ dassessāmī”ti dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā bhikkhū āmantesi.

566. Regarding “Permitted, friends”: this means, “It is permitted, O friends.” Regarding “Desiring”: this means “desiring.” Regarding “Having abandoned the felt rugs”: this means having abandoned all the felt rugs due to perceiving a felt rug as a fourth robe. Regarding “Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus”: the Blessed One, seeing the felt rugs scattered about, thought, “There is no reason for this ruin of what is given in faith; I will show them a way to use them,” and having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus.

567. Sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampīti sakiṃ nisinnañceva nipannañca. Sāmantāti ekapassato vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā chinditvā gahitaṭṭhānaṃ yathā vidatthimattaṃ hoti, evaṃ gahetabbaṃ, santharantena pana pāḷiyaṃ vuttanayeneva ekadese vā santharitabbaṃ, vijaṭetvā vā missakaṃ katvā santharitabbaṃ, evaṃ thirataraṃ hotīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

567. Regarding “Even once worn as a lower garment, even once worn as an upper robe”: this means once sat upon and once lain upon. Regarding “From the border”: having cut a circle or a square from one side, it should be taken in such a way that the piece taken is the size of a span. However, by one who is making a new felt rug, it should be made in one part according to the method stated in the Pāḷi, or it should be made by unraveling the old material, mixing it with new, and felting it together; in this way, it becomes firmer. The rest has a clear meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīni kiriyākiriyattā imassa sikkhāpadassa dvebhāgasikkhāpadasadisānīti.

The origins and so forth of this training rule, because it involves both commission and omission, are similar to those of the training rule concerning the two parts.

Imesu pana pañcasu santhatesu purimāni tīṇi vinayakammaṃ katvā paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭanti, pacchimāni dve vaṭṭantīti veditabbānīti.

Now, among these five kinds of felt rugs, it should be understood that the first three are not allowable to be used, even after having performed a formal act of the Vinaya and having received them back; the latter two are allowable.

Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the felt rug for sitting is finished.

6. Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sheep's Wool

571. Tena [V 2.0241] samayenāti eḷakalomasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha uppaṇḍesunti “kittakena, bhante, kītānī”tiādīni vadantā avahasiṃsu. Ṭhitakova āsumbhīti yathā manussā araññato mahantaṃ dārubhāraṃ ānetvā kilantā ṭhitakāva pātenti, evaṃ pātesīti attho.

571. “At that time” (tena samayena): this refers to the training rule concerning sheep’s wool. Therein, “they mocked” (uppaṇḍesuṃ) means they ridiculed him by saying, “How much, Venerable Sir, were these bought for?” and so on. “Stood and threw it down” (ṭhitakova āsumbhī) means just as people bring a large load of wood from the forest and, being tired, throw it down while still standing, so he threw it down—this is the meaning.

572. Sahatthāti [M 2.0267] sahatthena, attanā haritabbānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bahitiyojanaṃ pātetīti tiyojanato bahi pāteti. Anantarāyena patanake hatthato muttamatte lomagaṇanāya nissaggiyapācittiyāni. Sace bahitiyojane rukkhe vā thambhe vā paṭihaññitvā puna anto patanti, anāpatti[P 3.0688]. Bhūmiyaṃ patitvā ṭhatvā ṭhatvā vaṭṭamānā eḷakalomabhaṇḍikā puna anto pavisati, āpattiyeva. Anto ṭhatvā hatthena vā pādena vā yaṭṭhiyā vā vaṭṭeti ṭhatvā vā aṭhatvā vā vaṭṭamānā bhaṇḍikā gacchatu, āpattiyeva. “Añño harissatī”ti ṭhapeti, tena haritepi āpattiyeva. Suddhacittena ṭhapitaṃ vāto vā añño vā attano dhammatāya bahi pāteti, āpattiyeva. Saussāhattā acittakattā ca sikkhāpadassa. Kurundiyādīsu pana “ettha anāpattī”ti vuttā, sā anāpatti pāḷiyā na sameti. Ubhatobhaṇḍikaṃ ekābaddhaṃ katvā ekaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ antosīmāya ekaṃ bahisīmāya karonto ṭhapeti, rakkhati tāva. Ekābaddhe kājepi eseva nayo. Yadi pana abandhitvā kājakoṭiyaṃ ṭhapitamattameva hoti, na rakkhati. Ekābaddhepi parivattetvā ṭhapite āpattiyeva.

572. “By his own hand” (sahatthā) means with his own hand; it is said that they are to be carried by oneself. “He causes it to fall beyond three yojanas” (bahitiyojanaṃ pāteti) means he causes it to fall outside of three yojanas.
