If it falls without obstruction, as soon as it is released from the hand, there are offenses of nissaggiya pācittiya according to the count of the wool-hairs. If, beyond three yojanas, it strikes a tree or a post and then falls back inside, there is no offense. If the bundle of sheep's wool, having fallen to the ground and stopped, then rolls back inside, it is still an offense. If, standing inside, he rolls it with his hand, foot, or a stick, and the bundle, whether it has stopped or not, continues to roll away, it is still an offense. If he places it thinking, “Another will carry it,” even when it is carried by that person, it is still an offense. If something placed with a pure mind is caused to fall outside by the wind or another, by its own nature, it is still an offense. This is because of the presence of effort and because this training rule can be transgressed even without intention. However, in the Kurundī and other commentaries, it is said, “Here there is no offense,” but that statement of no offense does not accord with the Pāḷi. If, having made two bundles bound as one, he places one bundle inside the boundary and one outside the boundary, he is protected for the time being. In the case of a carrying pole with things bound as one, this is the same method. However, if it is merely placed on the end of a carrying pole without being bound, he is not protected. Even if bound as one, if it is placed having been turned around, it is still an offense.

Aññassa yāne vāti ettha gacchante yāne vā hatthipiṭṭhiādīsu vā sāmikassa ajānantasseva harissatīti ṭhapeti, tasmiṃ tiyojanaṃ atikkante āpatti. Agacchantepi eseva nayo. Sace pana agacchante yāne vā hatthipiṭṭhiyādīsu vā ṭhapetvā abhiruhitvā sāreti, heṭṭhā vā gacchanto codeti, pakkosanto vā anubandhāpeti, “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti vacanato anāpatti. Kurundiyādīsu pana “āpattī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti iminā na sameti. Adinnādāne pana suṅkaghāte āpatti hoti. Yā hi tattha āpatti, sā idha anāpatti. Yā idha āpatti, sā tattha anāpatti. Taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā aññavihito vā corādīhi vā upadduto gacchati, āpattiyeva. Sabbattha lomagaṇanāya āpattiparicchedo veditabbo.

Regarding the phrase “or in another’s vehicle” (aññassa yāne vā): here, if he places it on a moving vehicle or on the back of an elephant, etc., thinking, “It will be carried,” while the owner does not know, there is an offense when that vehicle has crossed three yojanas. This is the same method even for a non-moving vehicle. However, if, having placed it on a non-moving vehicle or on the back of an elephant, etc., he mounts and drives it; or if, while going along below, he urges it on; or if, while calling out to it, he makes it follow along, there is no offense, because of the Pāḷi phrase “he has another carry it.” However, in the Kurundī and other commentaries, it is said, “There is an offense,” but that does not accord with this phrase, “he has another carry it.” In the case of taking what is not given, however, there is an offense in evading customs duty. Indeed, what is an offense there is not an offense here. What is an offense here is not an offense there. Having reached that place, if he goes on, being distracted or being harassed by thieves, etc., it is still an offense. In all cases, the determination of the offense should be understood by the count of the wool-hairs.

575. Tiyojanaṃ vāsādhippāyo gantvā tato paraṃ haratīti yattha gato, tattha uddesaparipucchādīnaṃ [V 2.0242] vā paccayādīnaṃ vā alābhena tato [M 2.0268] paraṃ aññattha gacchati, tatopi aññatthāti evaṃ yojanasatampi harantassa anāpatti. Acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvāti corā acchinditvā niratthakabhāvaṃ ñatvā paṭidenti, taṃ harantassa anāpatti. Nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvāti vinayakammakataṃ paṭilabhitvāti [P 3.0689] attho.

575. Regarding the phrase 'having gone for three yojanas with the intention of residing, he carries it further than that': wherever he has gone, if, due to not obtaining opportunities for learning the Pāḷi, asking about the commentary, etc., or not obtaining requisites like almsfood, etc., he goes from that place to another place beyond, and from that place to yet another—in this way, there is no offense for the monk who carries it even for a hundred yojanas. “Recovering what was seized” (acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvā): if thieves, having seized it and then realizing its worthlessness, give it back, there is no offense for the one who carries it. “Recovering what was relinquished” (nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvā): the meaning is 'having recovered what has been subjected to a Vinaya act'.

Katabhaṇḍanti kataṃbhaṇḍaṃ kambalakojavasanthatādiṃ yaṃ kiñci antamaso suttakena baddhamattampi. Yo pana tanukapattatthavikantare vā āyogaaṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanādīnaṃ antaresu vā pipphalikādīnaṃ malarakkhaṇatthaṃ sipāṭikāya vā antamaso vātābādhiko kaṇṇacchiddepi lomāni pakkhipitvā gacchati, āpattiyeva. Suttakena pana bandhitvā pakkhittaṃ katabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, veṇiṃ katvā harati, idaṃ nidhānamukhaṃ nāma, āpattiyevāti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

“A made-up item” (katabhaṇḍa) means any kind of made-up item, such as a blanket, a rug, a floor-covering, etc., or even something merely bound with a small thread. However, if a monk places wool-hairs in the space of a thin bowl-bag, or in the spaces of a chest-band, shoulder-strap, or waistband, etc., or for the purpose of protecting from rust things like a scraping knife, etc., or in a small bag, or at the very least, being one who has a wind-disease, puts wool-hairs in his ear-hole and goes, it is still an offense. However, wool that is bound with a small thread and put away stands in the place of a made-up item. If he carries it having made a braid, this is called a 'means of hiding', and it is still an offense. The rest has a clear meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu idaṃ eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma, kāyato ca kāyacittato ca samuṭṭhāti, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

In terms of origin, etc., this is called the origin of the sheep's wool offense. It arises from the body, and from the body and mind. It is an action, not one that is absolved by perception, can be transgressed without intention, a fault by formulation, a bodily action, involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning sheep’s wool is concluded.

7. Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Having Sheep's Wool Washed

576. Tena samayenāti eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha riñcantīti ujjhanti vissajjenti, na sakkonti anuyuñjitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha purāṇacīvarasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva saddhiṃ samuṭṭhānādīhīti.

576. “At that time…” is the training rule on having sheep's wool washed. Therein, `riñcanti` means they discard, they abandon; they are not able to practice, is what is said. The rest here, together with its origin and so forth, is in the same manner as stated in the training rule on old robes.

Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Having Sheep's Wool Washed is concluded.

8. Rūpiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Currency

582. Tena samayenāti rūpiyasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha paṭivisoti koṭṭhāso.

582. “At that time…” is the training rule on currency. Therein, `paṭiviso` means a share.

583-4. Jātarūparajatanti [M 2.0269] ettha jātarūpanti suvaṇṇassa nāmaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā tathāgatassa vaṇṇasadisaṃ hoti, tasmā “satthuvaṇṇo vuccatī”ti padabhājane vuttaṃ. Tassattho – “yo [V 2.0243] satthuvaṇṇo lohaviseso, idaṃ jātarūpaṃ nāmā”ti rajataṃ pana “saṅkho, silā, pavāla, rajataṃ, jātarūpa”ntiādīsu (pāci. 506) rūpiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Idha pana yaṃ kiñci vohāragamanīyaṃ kahāpaṇādi adhippetaṃ. Tenevassa padabhājane “kahāpaṇo lohamāsako”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kahāpaṇoti sovaṇṇamayo vā rūpiyamayo vā pākatiko vā. Lohamāsakoti tambalohādīhi katamāsako. Dārumāsakoti sāradārunā vā veḷupesikāya vā antamaso tālapaṇṇenāpi rūpaṃ [P 3.0690] chinditvā katamāsako. Jatumāsakoti lākhāya vā niyyāsena vā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā katamāsako. “Ye vohāraṃ gacchantī”ti iminā pana padena yo yo yattha yattha janapade yadā yadā vohāraṃ gacchati, antamaso aṭṭhimayopi cammamayopi rukkhaphalabījamayopi samuṭṭhāpitarūpopi asamuṭṭhāpitarūpopi sabbo saṅgahito.

583-4. In the phrase `jātarūparajataṃ`, `jātarūpa` is a name for gold. And since it is similar in color to the Tathāgata, it is said in the Padabhājana, 'It is called the Teacher's color.' The meaning of this is: 'Whatever special metal has the Teacher's color, that is called `jātarūpa`.' As for `rajata` (silver), in passages such as 'conch, rock-crystal, coral, silver (`rajata`), gold (`jātarūpa`)' and so on, it is called `rūpiya`. Here, however, any `kahāpaṇa` or other item that is used in trade is intended. For that very reason, in the Padabhājana for this term, it is said, 'a `kahāpaṇa`, a metal `māsaka`,' and so on. Therein, a `kahāpaṇa` is one made of gold, or made of silver, or a standard one. A metal `māsaka` is a `māsaka` made of copper, bronze, or other metals. A wooden `māsaka` is a `māsaka` made by cutting a figure from hardwood, or from a bamboo strip, or even from a palm leaf. A lac `māsaka` is a `māsaka` made by forming a figure from lac or resin. And by this phrase, 'whatever is used in trade,' all is included: whatever is used in trade in whatever region at whatever time, even if made of bone, or of leather, or of tree-fruit seeds, whether it has a figure stamped on it or does not have a figure stamped on it.

Iccetaṃ sabbampi rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ jātarūpamāsako, vuttappabhedo sabbopi rajatamāsakoti catubbidhaṃ nissaggiyavatthu hoti. Muttā, maṇi, veḷuriyo, saṅkho, silā, pavāla, lohitaṅko, masāragallaṃ, satta dhaññāni, dāsidāsakhettavatthupupphārāmaphalārāmādayoti idaṃ dukkaṭavatthu. Suttaṃ phālo paṭako kappāso anekappakāraṃ aparaṇṇaṃ sappinavanītatelamadhuphāṇitādibhesajjañca idaṃ kappiyavatthu. Tattha nissaggiyavatthuṃ attano vā saṅghagaṇapuggalacetiyānaṃ vā atthāya sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Attano atthāya sampaṭicchato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ hoti, sesānaṃ atthāya dukkaṭaṃ. Dukkaṭavatthuṃ sabbesampi atthāya sampaṭicchato dukkaṭameva. Kappiyavatthumhi anāpatti. Sabbampi nikkhipanatthāya bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena sampaṭicchato upari ratanasikkhāpade āgatavasena pācittiyaṃ.

Thus, all silver, gold, a gold `māsaka`, and all silver `māsaka` of the aforementioned types—these four kinds are objects that require relinquishment. Pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, conch shells, rock-crystal, coral, rubies, cat's-eye gems, the seven kinds of grain, female and male slaves, fields, building sites, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so on—these are objects entailing a `dukkaṭa` offense. Thread, cotton cloth, other textiles, raw cotton, various kinds of pulses, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and other such medicines—these are allowable objects. Among these, it is not permissible to accept an object that requires relinquishment for oneself, or for the Sangha, a group, an individual, or a cetiya. For one who accepts it for oneself, there is a `nissaggiya pācittiya` offense; for the others, a `dukkaṭa` offense. Regarding an object entailing a `dukkaṭa` offense, for one who accepts it for anyone at all, it is just a `dukkaṭa` offense. Regarding an allowable object, there is no offense. For one who accepts any item at all in the capacity of head storekeeper for the purpose of depositing it, there is a `pācittiya` offense, according to what is stated in the Ratanasikkhāpada above.

Uggaṇheyyāti gaṇheyya. Yasmā pana gaṇhanto āpattiṃ āpajjati, tenassa padabhājane “sayaṃ gaṇhāti nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesapadesupi.

`Uggaṇheyya` means one should accept. But since one who accepts falls into an offense, it is therefore said in the Padabhājana for this term: 'If one accepts it oneself, it is a `nissaggiya pācittiya` offense.' This is the method for the remaining terms as well.

Tattha [M 2.0270] jātarūparajatabhaṇḍesu kahāpaṇamāsakesu ca ekaṃ gaṇhato vā gaṇhāpayato vā ekā āpatti. Sahassaṃ cepi ekato gaṇhāti, gaṇhāpeti, vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kurundiyañca sithilabaddhāya thavikāya sithilapūrite vā bhājane rūpagaṇanāya āpatti. Ghanabaddhe pana ghanapūrite vā ekāva āpattīti vuttaṃ.

Therein, regarding gold and silver goods, and `kahāpaṇa` and `māsaka` coins, for one who accepts one or causes one to be accepted, there is one offense. Even if one accepts or causes to be accepted a thousand at once, there are offenses according to the count of the items. But in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundī it is said: in the case of a loosely tied bag or a loosely filled vessel, the offense is according to the count of the coins; but in the case of a tightly bound or tightly filled one, there is only one offense.

Upanikkhittasādiyane pana “idaṃ ayyassa hotū”ti vutte sacepi cittena sādiyati, gaṇhitukāmo hoti, kāyena vā vācāya vā “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, anāpatti. Kāyavācāhi [V 2.0244] vā appaṭikkhipitvāpi [P 3.0691] suddhacitto hutvā “nayidaṃ amhākaṃ kappatī”ti na sādiyati, anāpattiyeva. Tīsu dvāresu hi yena kenaci paṭikkhittaṃ paṭikkhittameva hoti. Sace pana kāyavācāhi appaṭikkhipitvā cittena adhivāseti, kāyavācāhi kattabbassa paṭikkhepassa akaraṇato akiriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyadvāre ca vacīdvāre ca āpattiṃ āpajjati, manodvāre pana āpatti nāma natthi.

But regarding delighting in something placed nearby: when it is said, 'May this be for the venerable one,' even if one delights in it with the mind and is desirous of taking it, if one rejects it with the body or with speech, saying, 'This is not allowable,' there is no offense. Or, even without rejecting it with body and speech, if, being of pure mind, one does not delight, thinking, 'This is not allowable for us,' there is still no offense. For indeed, what is rejected by any one of the three doors is truly rejected. But if, without rejecting it with body and speech, one consents with the mind, then due to not making the rejection that should be made with body and speech, one falls into an offense at the body-door and the speech-door, which arises from non-action. At the mind-door, however, there is no such thing as an offense.

Eko sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā pādamūle ṭhapeti “tuyhidaṃ hotū”ti, bhikkhū “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, upāsako pariccattaṃ mayā tumhākanti gato, añño tattha āgantvā pucchati – “kiṃ, bhante, ida”nti? Yaṃ tena attanā ca vuttaṃ, taṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. So ce vadati – “gopayissāmi, bhante, guttaṭṭhānaṃ dassethā”ti, sattabhūmikampi pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā “idaṃ guttaṭṭhāna”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ, “idha nikkhipāhī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Ettāvatā kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitaṃ hoti. Dvāraṃ pidahitvā rakkhantena vasitabbaṃ. Sace kiñci vikkāyikabhaṇḍaṃ pattaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā āgacchati, “idaṃ gahessatha bhante”ti vutte “upāsaka atthi amhākaṃ iminā attho, vatthu ca evarūpaṃ nāma saṃvijjati, kappiyakārako natthī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace so vadati, “ahaṃ kappiyakārako bhavissāmi, dvāraṃ vivaritvā dethā”ti, dvāraṃ vivaritvā “imasmiṃ okāse ṭhapita”nti vattabbaṃ, “idaṃ gaṇhā”ti na vattabbaṃ. Evampi kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitameva hoti, so ce taṃ gahetvā tassa kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. Sace adhikaṃ gaṇhāti, “na mayaṃ tava bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāma, “nikkhamāhī”ti vattabbo.

A certain lay supporter places a hundred or a thousand [coins] at a bhikkhu's feet, saying, 'May this be for you.' The bhikkhu rejects it, saying, 'This is not allowable.' The lay follower departs, saying, 'It has been relinquished by me to you.' Another person arrives there and asks, 'Venerable sir, what is this?' What was said by that donor and by oneself should be related. If that person says, 'Venerable sir, I will guard it; show me a safe place,' one may ascend even a seven-storied palace and point it out, saying, 'This is a safe place.' It should not be said, 'Place it here.' By this much, it stands depending on what is allowable and what is not allowable. One may stay there, guarding it with the door closed. If any merchandise for sale, such as a bowl or a robe, arrives, and it is said, 'Venerable sir, will you take this?' it should be said, 'Lay follower, we have a need for this, and such an object [i.e., the money] exists, but there is no steward.' If that person says, 'I will be the steward; open the door and give it,' the door should be opened, and it should be said, 'It is placed in this spot.' It should not be said, 'Take this.' Even so, it stands depending on what is allowable and what is not allowable. If that person, having taken that [money], gives the bhikkhu allowable goods, it is allowable. If he takes an excess, it can be said, 'We do not take your goods. Depart!'

Saṅghamajjhe nissajjitabbanti ettha yasmā rūpiyaṃ nāma akappiyaṃ, “tasmā nissajjitabbaṃ saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā puggalassa vā”ti na vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ paṭiggahitamattameva na tena kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ cetāpitaṃ, tasmā upāyena [M 2.0271] paribhogadassanatthaṃ “saṅghamajjhe nissajjitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Kappiyaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ sappi vāti “pabbajitānaṃ sappi vā telaṃ vā vaṭṭati upāsakā”ti evaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ.

Regarding 'it should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha': since what is called gold and silver is unallowable, it was not said, 'Therefore, it should be relinquished to the Sangha, or to a group, or to an individual.' But since it was merely accepted and no allowable goods have yet been acquired with it, therefore, for the purpose of showing a way of using it, it was said, 'it should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha.' Regarding 'An allowable item should be pointed out, such as ghee': it should be pointed out thus, 'Lay follower, ghee or oil is allowable for the gone-forth.'

Rūpiyapaṭiggāhakaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbeheva paribhuñjitabbanti [P 3.0692] sabbehi bhājetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Rūpiyapaṭiggāhakena bhāgo na gahetabbo. Aññesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vā ārāmikānaṃ vā pattabhāgampi labhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati, antamaso makkaṭādīhi tato haritvā araññe ṭhapitaṃ vā tesaṃ hatthato gaḷitaṃ vā tiracchānagatapariggahitampi paṃsukūlampi na vaṭṭatiyeva, tato [V 2.0245] āhaṭena phāṇitena senāsanadhūpanampi na vaṭṭati. Sappinā vā telena vā padīpaṃ katvā dīpāloke nipajjituṃ kasiṇaparikammampi kātuṃ, potthakampi vācetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Telamadhuphāṇitehi pana sarīre vaṇaṃ makkhetuṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Tena vatthunā mañcapīṭhādīni vā gaṇhanti, uposathāgāraṃ vā bhojanasālaṃ vā karonti, paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Chāyāpi gehaparicchedena ṭhitā na vaṭṭati, paricchedātikkantā āgantukattā vaṭṭati. Taṃ vatthuṃ vissajjetvā katena maggenapi setunāpi nāvāyapi uḷumpenapi gantuṃ na vaṭṭati, tena vatthunā khanāpitāya pokkharaṇiyā ubbhidodakaṃ pātuṃ vā paribhuñjituṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Anto udake pana asati aññaṃ āgantukaṃ udakaṃ vā vassodakaṃ vā paviṭṭhaṃ vaṭṭati. Kītāya yena udakena saddhiṃ kītā taṃ āgantukampi na vaṭṭati, taṃ vatthuṃ upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā saṅgho paccaye paribhuñjati, tepi paccayā tassa na vaṭṭanti. Ārāmo gahito hoti, sopi paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Yadi bhūmipi bījampi akappiyaṃ neva bhūmiṃ na phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace bhūmiṃyeva kiṇitvā aññāni bījāni ropitāni phalaṃ vaṭṭati, atha bījāni kiṇitvā kappiyabhūmiyaṃ ropitāni, phalaṃ na vaṭṭati, bhūmiyaṃ nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā vaṭṭati.

Regarding 'It should be used by all except for the acceptor of gold and silver': it should be divided and used by all. The acceptor of gold and silver should not take a share. It is not allowable for him to use it, even having received the share that has come to other bhikkhus or monastery attendants. Even if it is taken from there by monkeys or other animals and placed in the forest, or dropped from their hands—thus becoming like something possessed by an animal or like a dust-heap cloth—it is still not allowable. Even fumigating a lodging with molasses brought from that share is not allowable. It is not allowable to make a lamp with ghee or oil and lie down in its light, or to perform the preliminary work for a kasiṇa, or to have a book recited. Furthermore, it is certainly not allowable to anoint a wound on the body with oil, honey, or molasses. If, with that object, they acquire beds, chairs, and so forth, or build an Uposatha hall or a dining hall, it is not allowable for him to use them. Even the shadow, when it stands within the boundary of the building, is not allowable; having passed beyond the boundary, it is allowable because it is adventitious. It is not allowable for him to travel by a road, bridge, boat, or raft made with that object after it has been relinquished. It is not allowable for him to drink or use the spring water of a pond dug with that object. However, if there is no water inside, and other adventitious water or rainwater enters, it is allowable. If a pond is bought, the water with which it was bought is not allowable, even if it is adventitious. If the Sangha uses requisites by placing that object as a deposit, those requisites are also not allowable for him. If a monastery is acquired, it too is not allowable for him to use. If both the land and the seed are unallowable, it is not allowable to use either the land or the fruit. If only the land is bought and other seeds are planted, the fruit is allowable. But if the seeds are bought and planted on allowable land, the fruit is not allowable; however, it is allowable to sit or lie on the land.

Sace so chaḍḍetīti yattha katthaci khipati, athāpi na chaḍḍeti, sayaṃ gahetvā gacchati, na vāretabbo. No ce chaḍḍetīti atha neva gahetvā gacchati, na chaḍḍeti, kiṃ mayhaṃ iminā byāpārenāti yena kāmaṃ pakkamati, tato yathāvuttalakkhaṇo rūpiyachaḍḍako sammannitabbo.

Regarding 'If he discards it': this means he throws it anywhere. Or even if he does not discard it, but taking it himself, he goes away, he should not be stopped. Regarding 'If he does not discard it': this means he neither takes it and goes away, nor discards it, but thinking, 'What have I to do with this affair?' he departs wherever he wishes. Then, a 'discarder of gold and silver' with the aforementioned characteristics should be appointed.

Yo [M 2.0272] na chandāgatintiādīsu lobhavasena taṃ vatthuṃ attano vā karonto attānaṃ vā ukkaṃsento chandāgatiṃ nāma gacchati[P 3.0693]. Dosavasena “nevāyaṃ mātikaṃ jānāti, na vinaya”nti paraṃ apasādento dosāgatiṃ nāma gacchati. Mohavasena muṭṭhapamuṭṭhassatibhāvaṃ āpajjanto mohāgatiṃ nāma gacchati. Rūpiyapaṭiggāhakassa bhayena chaḍḍetuṃ avisahanto bhayāgatiṃ nāma gacchati. Evaṃ akaronto na chandāgatiṃ gacchati, na dosāgatiṃ gacchati, na mohāgatiṃ gacchati, na bhayāgatiṃ gacchatīti veditabbo.

In the phrase 'one who does not go by way of favor,' etc.: one who, through greed, either makes that object his own or exalts himself, goes by what is called the way of favor. Through hatred, one who disparages another, saying, 'This one knows neither the mātikā nor the Vinaya,' goes by what is called the way of hatred. Through delusion, one who falls into a state of lost and confused mindfulness goes by what is called the way of delusion. One who, through fear of the acceptor of gold and silver, does not dare to have it discarded, goes by what is called the way of fear. One who does not act thus, it should be understood, does not go by way of favor, does not go by way of hatred, does not go by way of delusion, and does not go by way of fear.

585. Animittaṃ katvāti nimittaṃ akatvā, akkhīni nimmīletvā nadiyā vā papāte vā vanagahane vā gūthaṃ viya anapekkhena patitokāsaṃ asamannāharantena pātetabbanti attho. Evaṃ jigucchitabbepi rūpiye bhagavā pariyāyena bhikkhūnaṃ paribhogaṃ ācikkhi. Rūpiyapaṭiggāhakassa pana kenaci pariyāyena tato uppannapaccayaparibhogo na vaṭṭati. Yathā cāyaṃ etassa na vaṭṭati, evaṃ asantasambhāvanāya vā kuladūsakakammena vā kuhanādīhi vā uppannapaccayā [V 2.0246] neva tassa na aññassa vaṭṭanti, dhammena samena uppannāpi appaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭanti.

585. ‘Making it without a sign’ means not making a sign, closing one's eyes, and dropping it in a river, on a precipice, or in a dense forest without any concern, like one would with excrement, not paying attention to the place where it has fallen; this is the meaning of 'it should be dropped.' Thus, even regarding gold and silver, which are so detestable, the Blessed One, by way of an expedient, taught the bhikkhus its use. However, for one who accepts gold and silver, the use of requisites arisen from it is not permissible by any means. And just as this is not permissible for him, so too, requisites arisen from praising oneself for non-existent qualities, or from an act that corrupts families, or from deceit and so forth, are not permissible either for him or for another. Even requisites obtained righteously and equitably are not permissible to use without reflection.

Cattāro hi paribhogā – theyyaparibhogo, iṇaparibhogo, dāyajjaparibhogo, sāmiparibhogoti. Tattha saṅghamajjhepi nisīditvā paribhuñjantassa dussīlassa paribhogo “theyyaparibhogo” nāma. Sīlavato appaccavekkhitaparibhogo “iṇaparibhogo” nāma. Tasmā cīvaraṃ paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ, piṇḍapāto ālope ālope. Tathā asakkontena purebhattapacchābhattapurimayāmapacchimayāmesu. Sacassa appaccavekkhatova aruṇo uggacchati, iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Senāsanampi paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ, bhesajjassa paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi satipaccayatā vaṭṭati, evaṃ santepi paṭiggahaṇe satiṃ katvā paribhoge akarontasseva āpatti, paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpatti.

Indeed, there are four kinds of use: use that is theft, use as a debt, use by inheritance, and use as a master. Among these, the use by an immoral person, even while sitting and partaking in the midst of the Sangha, is called 'use that is theft.' The use of unreflected requisites by a virtuous person is called 'use as a debt.' Therefore, a robe should be reflected upon at each and every use, and almsfood at each and every mouthful. If one is unable to do so, it should be reflected upon in the forenoon, in the afternoon, during the first watch, and during the last watch of the night. If dawn breaks for him while they are still unreflected upon, he stands in the position of 'use as a debt.' Lodgings too should be reflected upon at each and every use. For medicine, the condition of mindfulness is proper both at the time of receiving and at the time of using. Even so, there is an offense only for one who, having been mindful at the time of receiving, does not do so at the time of using. However, for one who is not mindful at the time of receiving but is so at the time of using, there is no offense.

Catubbidhā hi suddhi – desanāsuddhi, saṃvarasuddhi, pariyeṭṭhisuddhi, paccavekkhaṇasuddhīti. Tattha desanāsuddhi nāma pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ[P 3.0694], tañhi desanāya sujjhanato [M 2.0273] “desanāsuddhī”ti vuccati. Saṃvarasuddhi nāma indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ, tañhi na puna evaṃ karissāmīti cittādhiṭṭhānasaṃvareneva sujjhanato “saṃvarasuddhī”ti vuccati. Pariyeṭṭhisuddhi nāma ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ, tañhi anesanaṃ pahāya dhammena samena paccaye uppādentassa pariyesanāya suddhattā “pariyeṭṭhisuddhī”ti vuccati. Paccavekkhaṇasuddhi nāma paccayaparibhogasannissitasīlaṃ, tañhi “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) nayena vuttena paccavekkhaṇena sujjhanato “paccavekkhaṇasuddhī”ti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ – “paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpattī”ti.

Indeed, purity is fourfold: purity by confession, purity by restraint, purity of search, and purity by reflection. Herein, purity by confession is the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint; indeed, because it is purified by confession, it is called 'purity by confession.' Purity by restraint is the virtue of sense-faculty restraint; indeed, because it is purified only by the restraint of resolving in one's mind, 'I will not do so again,' it is called 'purity by restraint.' Purity of search is the virtue of purity of livelihood; indeed, because it is purified by the search of one who, having abandoned improper searching, produces requisites righteously and equitably, it is called 'purity of search.' Purity by reflection is the virtue dependent on the use of requisites; indeed, because it is purified by the reflection spoken of in the manner of 'Wisely reflecting, he uses the robe,' and so on, it is called 'purity by reflection.' Therefore it was said: 'However, for one who uses requisites without being mindful at the time of receiving, there is no offense'.

Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ paccayaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo nāma, te hi bhagavato puttā, tasmā pitusantakānaṃ paccayānaṃ dāyādā hutvā te paccaye paribhuñjanti. Kiṃ pana te bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjanti, gihīnaṃ paccaye paribhuñjantīti? Gihīhi dinnāpi bhagavatā anuññātattā bhagavato santakā honti, tasmā te bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjantīti (ma. ni. 1.29) veditabbaṃ, dhammadāyādasuttañcettha sādhakaṃ.

The use of requisites by the seven trainees is called 'use by inheritance,' for they are indeed the sons of the Blessed One; therefore, having become heirs to the requisites belonging to their father, they use those requisites. But do they use the requisites of the Blessed One, or do they use the requisites of householders? Even though given by householders, because they have been permitted by the Blessed One, they become the property of the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that they use the requisites of the Blessed One. And the Dhammadāyāda Sutta is a supporting text in this matter.

Khīṇāsavānaṃ [V 2.0247] paribhogo sāmiparibhogo nāma, te hi taṇhāya dāsabyaṃ atītattā sāmino hutvā paribhuñjantīti. Imesu paribhogesu sāmiparibhogo ca dāyajjaparibhogo ca sabbesampi vaṭṭati. Iṇaparibhogo na vaṭṭati, theyyaparibhoge kathāyeva natthi.

The use by those whose taints are destroyed is called 'use as a master'; indeed, because they have transcended the state of being a slave to craving, they use requisites having become masters. Among these kinds of use, 'use as a master' and 'use by inheritance' are permissible for all. 'Use as a debt' is not permissible, and as for 'use that is theft,' there is nothing even to be said.

Aparepi cattāro paribhogā – lajjiparibhogo, alajjiparibhogo, dhammiyaparibhogo, adhammiyaparibhogoti.

There are also four other kinds of use: use by one with a sense of shame, use by one without a sense of shame, righteous use, and unrighteous use.

Tattha alajjino lajjinā saddhiṃ paribhogo vaṭṭati, āpattiyā na kāretabbo. Lajjino alajjinā saddhiṃ yāva na jānāti, tāva vaṭṭati. Ādito paṭṭhāya hi alajjī nāma natthi, tasmā yadāssa alajjībhāvaṃ jānāti tadā vattabbo “tumhe kāyadvāre ca vacīdvāre ca vītikkamaṃ karotha, taṃ appatirūpaṃ mā evamakatthā”ti. Sace anādiyitvā karotiyeva, yadi tena saddhiṃ paribhogaṃ karoti, sopi alajjīyeva hoti. Yopi attano bhārabhūtena alajjinā saddhiṃ paribhogaṃ karoti, sopi nivāretabbo. Sace [P 3.0695] na oramati, ayampi alajjīyeva hoti. Evaṃ eko alajjī alajjīsatampi karoti. Alajjino [M 2.0274] pana alajjināva saddhiṃ paribhoge āpatti nāma natthi. Lajjino lajjinā saddhiṃ paribhogo dvinnaṃ khattiyakumārānaṃ suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ bhojanasadisoti.

Herein, for a shameless person, use together with a person with a sense of shame is permissible; the latter should not be made to incur an offense. For a person with a sense of shame, use together with a shameless person is permissible as long as he does not know. Indeed, from the beginning, there is no one called 'shameless'; therefore, when one knows his state of being shameless, he should be told: 'You commit transgressions through the body-door and the speech-door; that is improper. Do not act in that way.' If, not taking this to heart, he continues to do so, and if one continues to use things together with him, that person too becomes shameless. Whoever uses things together with a shameless person who is his own responsibility should also be prevented. If he does not desist, this one too becomes shameless. Thus, one shameless person can make even a hundred shameless. However, for a shameless person using things together with another shameless person, there is no offense. The use of a person with a sense of shame together with another person with a sense of shame is like two Khattiya princes eating from a golden bowl.

Dhammiyādhammiyaparibhogo paccayavasena veditabbo. Tattha sace puggalopi alajjī piṇḍapātopi adhammiyo, ubho jegucchā. Puggalo alajjī piṇḍapāto dhammiyo, puggalaṃ jigucchitvā piṇḍapāto na gahetabbo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana dussīlo saṅghato uddesabhattādīni labhitvā saṅghasseva deti, etāni yathādānameva gatattā vaṭṭantīti vuttaṃ. Puggalo lajjī piṇḍapāto adhammiyo, piṇḍapāto jeguccho na gahetabbo. Puggalo lajjī, piṇḍapātopi dhammiyo, vaṭṭati.

Righteous and unrighteous use should be understood according to the requisites. Herein, if the person is shameless and the almsfood is also unrighteous, both are to be detested. If the person is shameless but the almsfood is righteous, having detested the person, the almsfood should not be accepted. However, in the Mahāpaccarī commentary, it is said: an immoral person, having received designated meals and so on from the Sangha, gives it to the Sangha itself; because these have gone according to the original donation, they are permissible. If the person has a sense of shame but the almsfood is unrighteous, the almsfood is to be detested and should not be accepted. If the person has a sense of shame and the almsfood is also righteous, it is permissible.

Apare dve paggahā; dve ca paribhogā – lajjipaggaho, alajjipaggaho; dhammaparibhogo āmisaparibhogoti.

There are two other kinds of support and two kinds of use: support of the scrupulous and support of the unscrupulous; use related to the Dhamma and use related to material things.

Tattha alajjino lajjiṃ paggahetuṃ vaṭṭati, na so āpattiyā kāretabbo. Sace pana lajjī alajjiṃ paggaṇhāti, anumodanāya ajjhesati, dhammakathāya ajjhesati, kulesu upatthambheti[V 2.0248]. Itaropi “amhākaṃ ācariyo īdiso ca īdiso cā”ti tassa parisati vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, ayaṃ sāsanaṃ osakkāpeti antaradhāpetīti veditabbo.

Among these, it is permissible for an unscrupulous one to support a scrupulous one; he should not be made to incur an offense. But if a scrupulous one supports an unscrupulous one, invites him to give the blessing, invites him to give a Dhamma talk, or upholds him among the families; or if another scrupulous one speaks his praise in the assembly of that unscrupulous one, saying, 'Our teacher is of such and such a kind,' this one should be understood as causing the Dispensation to decline and to disappear.

Dhammaparibhoga-āmisaparibhogesu pana yattha āmisaparibhogo vaṭṭati, tattha dhammaparibhogopi vaṭṭati. Yo pana koṭiyaṃ ṭhito gantho tassa puggalassa accayena nassissati, taṃ dhammānuggahena uggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ.

Now, regarding the use related to the Dhamma and the use related to material things, wherever use related to material things is permissible, there use related to the Dhamma is also permissible. But it is said that if a text that is on the verge of extinction will be lost with the passing away of that person, it is permissible to learn it out of concern for the Dhamma.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – mahābhaye kira ekasseva bhikkhuno mahāniddeso paguṇo ahosi. Atha catunikāyikatissattherassa upajjhāyo mahātipiṭakatthero nāma mahārakkhitattheraṃ āha – “āvuso mahārakkhita, etassa santike mahāniddesaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. “Pāpo kirāyaṃ, bhante, na gaṇhāmī”ti. “Gaṇhāvuso, ahaṃ te santike nisīdissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante, tumhesu nisinnesu gaṇhissāmī”ti paṭṭhapetvā rattindivaṃ nirantaraṃ pariyāpuṇanto [M 2.0275] osānadivase heṭṭhāmañce itthiṃ disvā “bhante, sutaṃyeva me pubbe, sacāhaṃ evaṃ jāneyyaṃ, na īdisassa santike dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇeyya”nti āha. Tassa pana santike [P 3.0696] bahū mahātherā uggaṇhitvā mahāniddesaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

On this, there is this story: It is said that during the great danger, only a single monk was proficient in the Mahāniddesa. Then the preceptor of the Elder Tissa, the expert in the four Nikāyas, the Elder named Mahātipiṭaka, said to the Elder Mahārakkhita: 'Friend Mahārakkhita, learn the Mahāniddesa from him.' 'Venerable sir, it is said this one is wicked; I will not learn.' 'Learn, friend, I will sit near you.' 'Very well, venerable sir, I will learn while you are seated near.' Having thus begun, he studied continuously day and night. On the final day, seeing a woman under the low couch, he said: 'Venerable sir, I had only heard of this before. If I had known it was like this, I would not have learned the Dhamma from such a one.' But many great elders learned from him and established the Mahāniddesa.

586. Rūpiye rūpiyasaññīti ettha sabbampi jātarūparajataṃ rūpiyasaṅgahameva gatanti veditabbaṃ.

586. "Perceiving what is money as money": Herein, it should be understood that all gold and silver is included in the category of 'money'.

Rūpiye vematikoti “suvaṇṇaṃ nu kho, kharapattaṃ nu kho”tiādinā nayena saṃsayajāto.

"Being doubtful about what is money": this is when doubt has arisen in such ways as, 'Is this gold, or is it a base metal coin?'

Rūpiye arūpiyasaññīti suvaṇṇādīsu kharapattādisaññī. Apica puññakāmā rājorodhādayo bhattakhajjakagandhapiṇḍādīsu pakkhipitvā hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ denti, coḷabhikkhāya carantānaṃ dassante baddhakahāpaṇādīhiyeva saddhiṃ coḷakāni denti, bhikkhū bhattādisaññāya vā coḷakasaññāya vā paṭiggaṇhanti, evampi rūpiye arūpiyasaññī rūpiyaṃ gaṇhātīti veditabbo. Paṭiggaṇhantena pana “imasmiṃ gehe idaṃ laddha”nti sallakkhetabbaṃ. Yena hi assatiyā dinnaṃ hoti, so satiṃ paṭilabhitvā puna āgacchati, athassa vattabbaṃ – “tava coḷakaṃ passāhī”ti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

“Perceiving what is money as not money” means perceiving gold and so on as base metal coins and so on. Furthermore, those desirous of merit, such as women of the royal harem, give gold and silver after placing it inside cooked rice, snacks, fragrant balls, and so on. To those wandering to ask for a robe, they give robes together with kahāpaṇas and so on tied to the fringe. The monks accept them with the perception of it being food or a robe. Even so, it should be understood that one who perceives what is money as not money accepts money. But one who accepts should take note, 'This was received in this house.' For if someone has given it through mindlessness, that person, on regaining mindfulness, comes again. Then he should be told, 'Examine your robe.' The rest here has a plain meaning.

Samuṭṭhānādīsu chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, siyā kiriyaṃ gahaṇena āpajjanato, siyā akiriyaṃ paṭikkhepassa [V 2.0249] akaraṇato rūpiyaaññavādakaupassutisikkhāpadāni hi tīṇi ekaparicchedāni, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Regarding the origins and so on: this training rule has six origins. It can be by action, as it is incurred through accepting; it can be by inaction, as it is incurred through not rejecting. Indeed, the three training rules—on money, on prevarication, and on eavesdropping—are a single section. There is no offense for one who is not perceiving, there is no offense for one who is out of his mind, it is an offense by regulation, it is an act of body and an act of speech, it arises from three mind-states, and it is experienced with three feelings.

Rūpiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning money is concluded.

9. Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Transactions in Gold and Silver

587. Tena samayenāti rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha nānappakārakanti katākatādivasena anekavidhaṃ. Rūpiyasaṃvohāranti jātarūparajataparivattanaṃ. Samāpajjantīti paṭiggahaṇasseva paṭikkhitattā paṭiggahitaparivattane dosaṃ apassantā karonti.

587. At that time: the training rule concerning transactions in gold and silver. Herein, 'of various kinds' means of many sorts, by way of wrought and unwrought, etc. 'Transaction in gold and silver' means the exchange of gold and silver. 'They engage in': Because only the receiving itself is prohibited, not seeing a fault in exchanging what has been received, they do so.

589. Sīsūpagantiādīsu [M 2.0276] sīsaṃ upagacchatīti sīsūpagaṃ, potthakesu pana “sīsūpaka”nti likhitaṃ, yassa kassaci sīsālaṅkārassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Katena katantiādīsu suddho rūpiyasaṃvohāroyeva.

589. In phrases such as 'sīsūpaga,' it means 'that which goes to the head,' thus it is 'sīsūpaga.' However, in books it is written as 'sīsūpaka'; this is a designation for any head ornament. This is the method in all cases. In phrases such as 'wrought for wrought,' it is purely a transaction of gold and silver.

Rūpiye rūpiyasaññītiādimhi purimasikkhāpade vuttavatthūsu nissaggiyavatthunā nissaggiyavatthuṃ cetāpentassa [P 3.0697] mūlaggahaṇe purimasikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, aparāparaparivattane iminā nissaggiyapācittiyameva. Nissaggiyavatthunā dukkaṭavatthuṃ vā kappiyavatthuṃ vā cetāpentassapi eseva nayo. Yo hi ayaṃ arūpiye rūpiyasaññī rūpiyaṃ cetāpetītiādi dutiyo tiko vutto, tassānulomattā avuttopi ayamaparopi rūpiye rūpiyasaññī arūpiyaṃ cetāpetītiādi tiko veditabbo. Attano vā hi arūpiyena parassa rūpiyaṃ cetāpeyya attano vā rūpiyena parassa arūpiyaṃ, ubhayathāpi rūpiyasaṃvohāro katoyeva hoti, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ ekantena rūpiyapakkhe ekoyeva tiko vuttoti.

In the cases stated in the previous training rule, beginning with 'perceiving gold and silver as gold and silver,' for one who causes an object entailing relinquishment to be acquired with an object entailing relinquishment, at the initial acceptance, there is an offense of pācittiya entailing relinquishment by the previous training rule; in subsequent exchanges, by this rule, there is precisely an offense of pācittiya entailing relinquishment. For one who causes an object of wrongful conduct or a permissible object to be acquired with an object entailing relinquishment, this is the same method. Indeed, the second triad which is stated, beginning with 'perceiving what is not gold and silver as gold and silver, one causes gold and silver to be acquired,' because of its correspondence, this other triad, though not stated, should be understood, beginning with 'perceiving gold and silver as gold and silver, one causes what is not gold and silver to be acquired.' For one might cause another's gold and silver to be acquired with one's own non-gold-and-silver, or another's non-gold-and-silver with one's own gold and silver; in both ways, a transaction in gold and silver has indeed been done. Therefore, in the Pāli, on the side of gold and silver, only one triad is stated exclusively.

Dukkaṭavatthunā pana nissaggiyavatthuṃ cetāpentassa mūlaggahaṇe purimasikkhāpadena dukkaṭaṃ, pacchā parivattane iminā nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, garukassa cetāpitattā. Dukkaṭavatthunā dukkaṭavatthumeva, kappiyavatthuṃ vā cetāpentassa mūlaggahaṇe purimasikkhāpadena dukkaṭaṃ, pacchā parivattanepi iminā dukkaṭameva. Kasmā? Akappiyavatthunā cetāpitattā. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sace kayavikkayaṃ samāpajjeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti bhāsitaṃ, taṃ dubbhāsitaṃ. Kasmā? Na hi dānaggahaṇato añño kayavikkayo nāma atthi, kayavikkayasikkhāpadañca kappiyavatthunā [V 2.0250] kappiyavatthuparivattanameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, tañca kho aññatra sahadhammikehi. Idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ rūpiyena ca rūpiyārūpiyacetāpanaṃ arūpiyena ca rūpiyacetāpanaṃ. Dukkaṭavatthunā pana dukkaṭavatthuno cetāpanaṃ neva idha na tattha pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, na cettha anāpatti bhavituṃ arahati. Tasmā yatheva dukkaṭavatthuno paṭiggahaṇe dukkaṭaṃ, tatheva tassa vā tena vā cetāpanepi dukkaṭaṃ yuttanti bhagavato adhippāyaññūhi vuttaṃ.

However, for one who causes an object entailing relinquishment to be acquired with an object of wrongful conduct, at the initial acceptance, there is an offense of wrongful conduct by the previous training rule; afterwards, in the exchange, by this rule, there is a pācittiya entailing relinquishment, because a grave object was caused to be acquired. For one who causes an object of wrongful conduct itself, or a permissible object, to be acquired with an object of wrongful conduct, at the initial acceptance, there is an offense of wrongful conduct by the previous training rule; afterwards, in the exchange, by this rule, there is only an offense of wrongful conduct. Why? Because it was caused to be acquired with an unallowable object. However, in the Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: 'If one were to engage in buying and selling, there is a pācittiya entailing relinquishment.' That is poorly stated. Why? Because there is no such thing as buying and selling other than giving and taking. And the training rule on buying and selling was stated in reference to the exchange of a permissible object for a permissible object, and that, too, except with co-religionists. This training rule was stated concerning causing gold-and-silver or non-gold-and-silver to be acquired with gold-and-silver, and causing gold-and-silver to be acquired with non-gold-and-silver. However, causing an object of wrongful conduct to be acquired with an object of wrongful conduct is stated neither here nor there in the Pāli, and it is not fit that there be no offense in this case. Therefore, just as there is an offense of wrongful conduct in accepting an object of wrongful conduct, so too it is proper that there is an offense of wrongful conduct in causing acquisition of it or with it. Thus it was stated by those who know the intention of the Blessed One.

Kappiyavatthunā [M 2.0277] pana nissaggiyavatthuṃ cetāpentassa mūlaggahaṇe purimasikkhāpadena anāpatti, pacchā parivattane iminā nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “arūpiye arūpiyasaññī rūpiyaṃ cetāpeti nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti[P 3.0698]. Teneva kappiyavatthunā dukkaṭavatthuṃ cetāpentassa mūlapaṭiggahaṇe tatheva anāpatti, pacchā parivattane iminā dukkaṭaṃ. Kasmā? Akappiyassa cetāpitattā. Kappiyavatthunā pana kappiyavatthuṃ aññatra sahadhammikehi cetāpentassa mūlaggahaṇe purimasikkhāpadena anāpatti, pacchā parivattane upari kayavikkayasikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Kayavikkayaṃ mocetvā gaṇhantassa uparisikkhāpadenapi anāpatti, vaḍḍhiṃ payojentassa dukkaṭaṃ.

However, for one who causes an object entailing relinquishment to be acquired with a permissible object, at the initial acceptance, there is no offense by the previous training rule; afterwards, in the exchange, by this rule, there is a pācittiya entailing relinquishment. For this has been stated: 'Perceiving what is not gold-and-silver as not gold-and-silver, one causes gold-and-silver to be acquired: it is a pācittiya entailing relinquishment.' For that very reason, for one who causes an object of wrongful conduct to be acquired with a permissible object, at the initial acceptance, there is likewise no offense; afterwards, in the exchange, by this rule, there is an offense of wrongful conduct. Why? Because an unallowable object was caused to be acquired. However, for one who causes a permissible object to be acquired with a permissible object, except with co-religionists, at the initial acceptance, there is no offense by the previous training rule; afterwards, in the exchange, by the subsequent training rule on buying and selling, there is a pācittiya entailing relinquishment. For one who takes it, having avoided buying and selling, there is no offense even by the subsequent training rule. For one who engages in usury, there is an offense of wrongful conduct.

Imassa ca rūpiyasaṃvohārassa garukabhāvadīpakaṃ idaṃ pattacatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yo hi rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhitvā tena ayabījaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, taṃ koṭṭāpetvā tena lohena pattaṃ kāreti, ayaṃ patto mahāakappiyo nāma, na sakkā kenaci upāyena kappiyo kātuṃ. Sace hi taṃ vināsetvā thālakaṃ kāreti, tampi akappiyaṃ. Vāsiṃ kāreti, tāya chinnaṃ dantakaṭṭhampi akappiyaṃ. Baḷisaṃ kāroti, tena māritā macchāpi akappiyā. Vāsiphalaṃ tāpetvā udakaṃ vā khīraṃ vā uṇhāpeti, tampi akappiyameva.

And this tetrad of bowls should be known as illustrating the gravity of this transaction in gold and silver. For a monk who, having accepted gold and silver, produces iron-seed with it, has it forged, and causes a bowl to be made with that metal—this bowl is called 'greatly unallowable,' and it is not possible to make it allowable by any means. Indeed, if one destroys it and has a dish made, that too is unallowable. If one has an adze made, even a tooth-stick cut with it is unallowable. If one has a fishhook made, even the fish killed with it are unallowable. If one heats the blade of the adze and has water or milk warmed, that too is indeed unallowable.

Yo pana rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhitvā tena pattaṃ kiṇāti, ayampi patto akappiyo. “Pañcannampi sahadhammikānaṃ na kappatī”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sakkā pana kappiyo kātuṃ, so hi mūle mūlasāmikānaṃ patte ca pattasāmikānaṃ dinne kappiyo hoti. Kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ datvā gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

However, a monk who, having accepted gold and silver, buys a bowl with it—this bowl is also unallowable. 'It is not allowable for the five fellows in the Dhamma,' is stated in the Mahāpaccarī. However, it is possible to make it allowable; for when the price is given to the owners of the price and the bowl to the owners of the bowl, it becomes allowable. It is proper to use it, having taken it in exchange for an allowable item.

Yopi rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā kappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ ruccatī”ti vadati. Kappiyakārako ca taṃ rūpiyaṃ datvā kammāraṃ saññāpeti, ayampi [V 2.0251] patto kappiyavohārena gahitopi dutiyapattasadisoyeva, mūlassa sampaṭicchitattā akappiyo. Kasmā sesānaṃ na kappatīti? Mūlassa anissaṭṭhattā.

Also, a monk who, having caused gold and silver to be accepted, goes with a steward to the blacksmith's workshop, and seeing a bowl, says, 'This one pleases me.' And the steward gives that gold and silver and makes the blacksmith agree. This bowl also, even though acquired through an allowable transaction, is just like the second bowl; it is unallowable because the price was accepted. Why is it not allowable for the others? Because the price was not relinquished.

Yo pana rūpiyaṃ asampaṭicchitvā “therassa pattaṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti pahitakappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā “ime kahāpaṇe [M 2.0278] gahetvā imaṃ dehī”ti kahāpaṇe dāpetvā gahito, ayaṃ patto etasseva bhikkhuno na vaṭṭati dubbicāritattā, aññesaṃ pana vaṭṭati, mūlassa asampaṭicchitattā.

However, a monk who, without accepting money himself, goes to the blacksmith's workshop with an attendant sent with the instruction, 'Buy a bowl for the elder and give it,' and upon seeing a bowl, has the kahāpaṇas given, saying, 'Take these kahāpaṇas and give this [bowl],' and takes it—this bowl is not allowable for that very monk due to his improper conduct. For others, however, it is allowable, because the principal [money] was not accepted [by him].

Mahāsumattherassa kira upajjhāyo anuruddhatthero nāma ahosi. So attano evarūpaṃ [P 3.0699] pattaṃ sappissa pūretvā saṅghassa nissajji. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherassapi saddhivihārikānaṃ evarūpo patto ahosi. Taṃ theropi sappissa pūrāpetvā saṅghassa nissajjāpesīti. Idaṃ akappiyapattacatukkaṃ.

It is said that the preceptor of the Elder Mahāsumana was named the Elder Anuruddha. He filled such a bowl of his with ghee and relinquished it to the Sangha. The pupils of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga also had such a bowl. That Elder too, having caused it to be filled with ghee, had it relinquished to the Sangha. This is the tetrad of unallowable bowls.

Sace pana rūpiyaṃ asampaṭicchitvā “therassa pattaṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti pahitakappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ ruccatī”ti vā “imāhaṃ gahessāmī”ti vā vadati, kappiyakārako ca taṃ rūpiyaṃ datvā kammāraṃ saññāpeti, ayaṃ patto sabbakappiyo buddhānampi paribhogārahoti.

However, if a monk, without accepting money himself, goes to the blacksmith's workshop with an attendant sent with the instruction, 'Buy a bowl for the elder and give it,' and upon seeing a bowl, says either, 'This one pleases me,' or, 'I will take this one,' and the attendant gives that money and completes the purchase from the blacksmith, this bowl is entirely allowable and is worthy of use even by the Buddhas.

591. Arūpiye rūpiyasaññīti kharapattādīsu suvaṇṇādisaññī. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti sace tena arūpiyaṃ cetāpeti dukkaṭāpatti hoti. Esa nayo vematike. Arūpiyasaññissa pana pañcahi sahadhammikehi saddhi “idaṃ gahetvā idaṃ dethā”ti kayavikkayaṃ karontassāpi anāpatti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

591. 'Perceiving what is not money as money' means having the perception of gold, etc., in relation to base metals and the like. 'An offense of wrong-doing': if with that [item perceived as money] one causes another non-money item to be acquired, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This is the principle in a case of doubt. However, for one who perceives it as not money, there is no offense even when engaging in buying and selling with the five [classes of] fellows in the Dhamma, saying, 'Taking this, give that.' The rest is self-evident.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It has six origins, is functional, is not absolved through perception, is non-intentional, is a transgression by convention, involves bodily action and verbal action, is of three consciousnesses, and is of three feelings.

Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning transactions with money is concluded.

10. Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Buying and Selling

593. Tena [V 2.0252] samayenāti kayavikkayasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha kati hipi tyāyanti kati te ayaṃ, hikāro panettha padapūraṇo, pikāro garahāyaṃ, ayaṃ dubbalasaṅghāṭi tava kati divasāni bhavissatīti attho. Atha vā katihampi tyāyantipi pāṭho. Tattha katihanti kati ahāni, kati divasānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Katihipi myāyanti idampi [M 2.0279] eteneva nayena veditabbaṃ. Gihīpi naṃ gihissāti ettha nanti nāmatthe nipāto, gihī nāma gihissāti vuttaṃ hoti.

593. 'At that time' introduces the training rule on buying and selling. Therein, in the phrase `kati hipi tyāyanti`, the word division is `kati te ayaṃ`. Here, the particle `hi` is a metrical filler, and the particle `pi` is used in the sense of censure. The meaning is: 'This weak outer robe of yours, for how many days will it last?' Alternatively, there is also the reading `katihampi tyāyanti`. Therein, `katihanti` means 'how many days.' The rest is according to the method stated. The phrase `Katihipi myāyanti` should also be understood in this same way. In the phrase `Gihīpi naṃ gihissāti`, the particle `naṃ` is in the sense of a name; it means, 'a layperson, by name, gives to a layperson.'

594. Nānappakārakanti cīvarādīnaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍānaṃ vasena anekavidhaṃ. Tenevassa padabhājane cīvaraṃ ādiṃ katvā dasikasuttapariyosānaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍameva dassitaṃ. Akappiyabhaṇḍaparivattanañhi kayavikkayasaṅgahaṃ na gacchati. Kayavikkayanti kayañceva vikkayañca. “Iminā imaṃ dehī”tiādinā hi nayena parassa kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhanto kayaṃ samāpajjati, attano kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ dento vikkayaṃ[P 3.0700].

594. 'Of various kinds' means of many types, by way of allowable goods such as robes and so on. For that very reason, in its word analysis, only allowable goods are shown, beginning with robes and ending with thread for fringes. Indeed, the exchange of unallowable goods does not come under the category of buying and selling. 'Buying and selling' means both buying and selling. For, by the method of saying, 'With this, give this,' and so on, one who takes another's allowable goods engages in buying; one who gives one's own allowable goods engages in selling.

595. Ajjhācaratīti abhibhavitvā carati, vītikkamavācaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Yato kayitañca hoti vikkayitañcāti yadā kayitañca hoti parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagataṃ karontena, vikkītañca attano bhaṇḍaṃ parahatthagataṃ karontena. “Iminā ima”ntiādivacanānurūpato pana pāṭhe paṭhamaṃ attano bhaṇḍaṃ dassitaṃ.

595. 'He transgresses' means he acts having overcome [the rule]; he speaks words of transgression—this is the meaning. 'From when there is both buying and selling' means: when buying has occurred, by one making another's goods come into one's own hand, and selling has occurred, by one making one's own goods come into another's hand. However, in the text, in accordance with the phrasing 'With this, this,' and so on, one's own goods are shown first.

Nissajjitabbanti evaṃ parassa hatthato kayavasena gahitakappiyabhaṇḍaṃ nissajjitabbaṃ. Ayañhi kayavikkayo ṭhapetvā pañca sahadhammike avasesehi gihipabbajitehi antamaso mātāpitūhipi saddhiṃ na vaṭṭati.

'It is to be relinquished' means: thus, the allowable goods taken from another's hand by way of purchase are to be relinquished. Indeed, this buying and selling, excepting the five [classes of] fellows in the Dhamma, is not allowable with the remaining laypeople and renunciants, not even with one's mother and father.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – vatthena vā vatthaṃ hotu bhattena vā bhattaṃ, yaṃ kiñci kappiyaṃ “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti vadati, dukkaṭaṃ. Evaṃ vatvā mātuyāpi attano bhaṇḍaṃ deti, dukkaṭaṃ. “Iminā imaṃ dehī”ti vutto vā “imaṃ dehi, imaṃ te dassāmī”ti vatvā vā mātuyāpi bhaṇḍaṃ attanā gaṇhāti, dukkaṭaṃ. Attano bhaṇḍe parahatthaṃ parabhaṇḍe ca attano hatthaṃ sampatte nissaggiyaṃ. Mātaraṃ pana pitaraṃ vā “imaṃ dehī”ti vadato viññatti na hoti. “Imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ na hoti. Aññātakaṃ “imaṃ dehī”ti vadato viññatti [V 2.0253] hoti. “Imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ hoti. “Iminā imaṃ dehī”ti kayavikkayaṃ āpajjato nissaggiyaṃ. Tasmā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ parivattentena mātāpitūhipi saddhiṃ kayavikkayaṃ aññātakehi saddhiṃ tisso āpattiyo mocentena parivattetabbaṃ.

Herein, this is the legal decision: Whether it is cloth for cloth, or food for food, if one says of any allowable item, 'With this, give this,' it is an offense of wrong-doing. Having said this, if one gives one's own goods even to one's mother, it is an offense of wrong-doing. Having been told, 'With this, give this,' or having said, 'Give this, I will give you this,' if one takes goods even from one's mother, it is an offense of wrong-doing. When one's own goods have reached another's hand and another's goods have reached one's own hand, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. However, for one who says to one's mother or father, 'Give this,' there is no offense of improper requesting. For one who says, 'Take this,' there is no offense of destroying an offering of faith. For one who says to a non-relative, 'Give this,' there is an offense of improper requesting. For one who says, 'Take this,' there is an offense of destroying an offering of faith. For one who engages in buying and selling by saying, 'With this, give this,' it is an offense requiring relinquishment. Therefore, when exchanging allowable goods, one should exchange them while avoiding the offense of buying and selling with one's parents, and the three offenses with non-relatives.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 2.0280] parivattanavidhi – bhikkhussa pātheyyataṇḍulā honti, so antarāmagge bhattahatthaṃ purisaṃ disvā “amhākaṃ taṇḍulā atthi, na ca no imehi attho, bhattena pana attho”ti vadati. Puriso taṇḍule gahetvā bhattaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. Tissopi āpattiyo na honti. Antamaso nimittakammamattampi na hoti. Kasmā? Mūlassa atthitāya. Parato ca vuttameva “idaṃ amhākaṃ atthi, amhākañca iminā ca iminā ca atthoti bhaṇatī”ti. Yo pana evaṃ akatvā “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti parivatteti; yathāvatthukameva[P 3.0701]. Vighāsādaṃ disvā “imaṃ odanaṃ bhuñjitvā, rajanaṃ vā dārūni vā āharā”ti vadati, rajanachalligaṇanāya dārugaṇanāya ca nissaggiyāni honti. “Imaṃ odanaṃ bhuñjitvā idaṃ nāma karothā”ti dantakārādīhi sippikehi dhamakaraṇādīsu taṃ taṃ parikkhāraṃ kāreti, rajakehi vā vatthaṃ dhovāpeti; yathāvatthukameva. Nhāpitena kese chindāpeti, kammakārehi navakammaṃ kāreti; yathāvatthukameva. Sace pana “idaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā idaṃ karothā”ti na vadati “idaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñja bhuttosi bhuñjissasi, idaṃ nāma karohī”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Ettha ca kiñcāpi vatthadhovane vā kesacchedane vā bhūmisodhanādinavakamme vā parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagataṃ nissajjitabbaṃ nāma natthi. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana daḷhaṃ katvā vuttattā na sakkā etaṃ paṭikkhipituṃ, tasmā yathā nissaggiyavatthumhi paribhutte vā naṭṭhe vā pācittiyaṃ deseti, evamidhāpi desetabbaṃ.

Herein, this is the method of exchange: A bhikkhu has rice for his journey. On the way, he sees a man with cooked rice in his hand and says, 'We have rice, but we have no need for this rice; we have a need for cooked rice.' The man takes the rice and gives the cooked rice; this is allowable. The three offenses also do not occur. Not even a mere act of making a sign occurs. Why? Because of the existence of the original basis. And later on, it is indeed stated: '“We have this, and we have need of this and that,” he says.' But any bhikkhu who, not doing it thus, exchanges by saying, 'With this, give this,' the offense is just according to the object. Seeing one who eats leftovers, if he says, 'Having eaten this cooked rice, bring dye or firewood,' the items become subject to forfeiture according to the count of cakes of dye and the count of pieces of firewood. Saying, 'Having eaten this cooked rice, do such-and-such work,' if he has artisans such as ivory carvers make various requisites like fans, or has washermen wash a robe, the offense is just according to the object. If he has a barber cut his hair, or has laborers do new work, the offense is just according to the object. But if he does not say, 'Having eaten this food, do this work,' but says, 'Eat this food. You have eaten. You will eat. Do such-and-such work,' it is allowable. And here, although in the washing of robes, or in the cutting of hair, or in new work such as sweeping the ground, there is no such thing as an item to be forfeited that, being another's property, has come into one's own hand, however, because it is stated firmly in the Great Commentary, it is not possible to reject this. Therefore, just as when a forfeitable object has been used up or is lost, one confesses a pācittiya offense, so also here it must be confessed.

596. Kayavikkaye kayavikkayasaññītiādimhi yo kayavikkayaṃ samāpajjati, so tasmiṃ kayavikkayasaññī vā bhavatu vematiko vā, na kayavikkayasaññī vā nissaggiyapācittiyameva. Cūḷattike dvīsu padesu dukkaṭamevāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

596. In the passage beginning 'perceiving it as buying and selling in buying and selling': any bhikkhu who engages in buying and selling, whether he perceives it as buying and selling, is in doubt, or does not perceive it as buying and selling, it is only a nissaggiya pācittiya offense. In the Minor Triad, in the two preceding cases, it is only a dukkaṭa offense; thus the meaning should be understood.

597. Agghaṃ pucchatīti “ayaṃ tava patto kiṃ agghatī”ti pucchati. “Idaṃ nāmā”ti vutte pana sace tassa kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ mahagghaṃ hoti, evañca naṃ paṭivadati “upāsaka, mama idaṃ vatthu mahagghaṃ, tava pattaṃ aññassa dehī”ti. Taṃ sutvā itaro “aññaṃ thālakampi dassāmī”ti vadati gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, “idaṃ amhākaṃ atthī”ti vuttalakkhaṇe patati[V 2.0254]. Sace so patto mahaggho, bhikkhuno vatthu appagghaṃ, pattasāmiko cassa appagghabhāvaṃ na jānāti, patto na gahetabbo, “mama vatthu appaggha”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ. Mahagghabhāvaṃ ñatvā [M 2.0281] vañcetvā gaṇhanto hi gahitabhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbataṃ āpajjati. Sace pattasāmiko “hotu, bhante, sesaṃ mama puññaṃ bhavissatī”ti deti, vaṭṭati.

597. As for 'he asks the price': he asks, 'What is this bowl of yours worth?' If, when it is said, 'It is worth such-and-such,' that bhikkhu's allowable requisite is of great value, he replies to him thus: 'Lay follower, this item of mine is of great value; give your bowl to someone else.' Hearing that, if the other says, 'I will also give another small bowl,' it is allowable to take it; it falls into the category described by 'We have this.' If that bowl is of great value, and the bhikkhu's item is of little value, and the bowl's owner does not know its low value, the bowl should not be taken. It should be declared, 'My item is of little value.' For a bhikkhu who, knowing its great value, takes it by deceiving, becomes liable to have the taken item appraised and the value made up. If the bowl's owner gives it, saying, 'Let it be, venerable sir, the remainder will be my merit,' it is allowable.

Kappiyakārakassa [P 3.0702] ācikkhatīti yassa hatthato bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāti, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ antamaso tassa puttabhātikampi kappiyakārakaṃ katvā “iminā imaṃ nāma gahetvā dehī”ti ācikkhati. So ce cheko hoti, punappunaṃ apanetvā vivaditvā gaṇhāti, tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbaṃ. No ce cheko hoti, na jānāti gahetuṃ, vāṇijako taṃ vañceti, “mā gaṇhā”ti vattabbo.

As for 'he informs the one who makes things allowable': setting aside the merchant from whose hand he wishes to take the goods, having made another—even that merchant's son or brother—the one who makes things allowable, he informs him, saying, 'With this, take such-and-such an item and give it.' If that person is skillful and takes it after repeatedly rejecting and disputing, the bhikkhu should stand by silently. If he is not skillful and does not know how to take it, and the merchant deceives him, he should be told, 'Do not take it.'

Idaṃ amhākantiādimhi “idaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ telaṃ vā sappi vā amhākaṃ atthi, amhākañca aññena appaṭiggahitakena attho”ti bhaṇati. Sace so taṃ gahetvā aññaṃ deti, paṭhamaṃ attano telaṃ na mināpetabbaṃ. Kasmā? Nāḷiyañhi avasiṭṭhatelaṃ hoti, taṃ pacchā minantassa appaṭiggahitakaṃ dūseyyāti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

In the passage beginning 'This is ours': he says, 'This oil or ghee, which has been received, we have, and we have need of other oil or ghee that has not been received.' If that person takes that and gives another, one's own oil should not be measured out first. Why? Because in the measuring vessel there is leftover oil, and that might spoil the unreceived oil of the one measuring afterwards. The rest is self-evident.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It has six origins, is an action, is not a case of release through perception, is unintentional, is a transgression of a formulated rule, is an action of body and speech, involves three states of consciousness, and three feelings.

Kayavikkayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on buying and selling is concluded.

Niṭṭhito kosiyavaggo dutiyo.

The second chapter, the Kosiyavagga, is concluded.

3. Pattavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Bowl

1. Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Bowl

598. Tena samayenāti pattasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha pattavāṇijjanti gāmanigamādīsu vicarantā pattavāṇijjaṃ vā karissanti. Āmattikāpaṇaṃ vāti amattāni vuccanti bhājanāni, tāni yesaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ te āmattikā, tesaṃ āmattikānaṃ āpaṇaṃ āmattikāpaṇaṃ, kulālabhaṇḍavāṇijakāpaṇanti attho.

598. At that time: the training rule on the bowl. Herein, 'bowl trade' means that, wandering in villages, towns, and so on, they will engage in the bowl trade. 'Or a pottery shop': vessels are called 'amatta'; those whose wares these are, they are 'āmattikā'; the shop of those āmattikā is an 'āmattikāpaṇa', meaning the shop of merchants of potter's wares.

602. Tayo [V 2.0255] pattassa vaṇṇāti tīṇi pattassa pamāṇāni. Aḍḍhāḷhakodanaṃ gaṇhātīti magadhanāḷiyā dvinnaṃ taṇḍulanāḷīnaṃ odanaṃ gaṇhāti. Magadhanāḷi [M 2.0282] nāma aḍḍhaterasapalā hotīti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīhaḷadīpe pakatināḷi mahantā, damiḷanāḷi khuddakā, magadhanāḷi pamāṇayuttā, tāya magadhanāḷiyā diyaḍḍhanāḷi ekā sīhaḷanāḷi hotīti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Catubhāgaṃ khādananti odanassa catutthabhāgappamāṇaṃ khādanaṃ, taṃ hatthahāriyassa muggasūpassa [P 3.0703] vasena veditabbaṃ. Tadupiyaṃ byañjananti tassa odanassa anurūpaṃ macchamaṃsasākaphalakaḷīrādibyañjanaṃ.

602. There are three kinds of bowls: these are three measurements of a bowl. 'It holds half an āḷhaka of cooked rice' means, by the Magadhan nāḷī measure, it holds the cooked rice from two nāḷīs of rice grains. It is said in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā that the Magadhan nāḷī is twelve and a half palas. In the island of Sri Lanka, the native nāḷi is large, the Damiḷa nāḷi is small, and the Magadhan nāḷi is of appropriate size. In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, it is said that one and a half Magadhan nāḷīs make one Sinhalese nāḷī. 'A fourth part as relish' means a relish of the measure of a fourth part of the cooked rice; that should be understood by way of mung bean soup that can be taken by hand. 'Suitable relish' means a relish suitable for that cooked rice, such as fish, meat, vegetables, fruits, and shoots.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – anupahatapurāṇasālitaṇḍulānaṃ sukoṭṭitaparisuddhānaṃ dve magadhanāḷiyo gahetvā tehi taṇḍulehi anuttaṇḍulaṃ akilinnaṃ apiṇḍitaṃ suvisadaṃ kundamakuḷarāsisadisaṃ avassāvitodanaṃ pacitvā niravasesaṃ patte pakkhipitvā tassa odanassa catutthabhāgappamāṇo nātighano nātitanuko hatthahāriyo sabbasambhārasaṅkhato muggasūpo pakkhipitabbo. Tato ālopassa ālopassa anurūpaṃ yāvacarimālopappahonakaṃ macchamaṃsādibyañjanaṃ pakkhipitabbaṃ, sappitelatakkarasakañjikādīni pana gaṇanūpagāni na honti, tāni hi odanagatikāneva, neva hāpetuṃ na vaḍḍhetuṃ sakkonti. Evametaṃ sabbampi pakkhittaṃ sace pattassa mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, suttena vā hīrena vā chindantassa suttassa vā hīrassa vā heṭṭhimantaṃ phusati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti, antogatameva hoti, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho nāma patto.

Herein, this is the determination: Take two Magadhan nāḷīs of well-pounded, pure, unbroken, old sāli rice grains. With these grains, cook rice that is not undercooked, not soggy, not lumpy, very clear, like a heap of jasmine buds, and from which the water has been drained. Place all of it into the bowl without remainder. Then, add mung bean soup, equal to a fourth part of that cooked rice, that is not too thick, not too thin, can be taken by hand, and is prepared with all ingredients. After that, add a curry of fish, meat, and so on, suitable for each morsel and sufficient up to the last morsel. However, ghee, oil, buttermilk, sour gruel, and so on, do not come into the reckoning, for they are of the same nature as the cooked rice; they can neither decrease nor increase it. When all this has been placed, if it stands level with the lower line of the bowl's rim, such that when leveling with a thread or a fiber, it touches the lower edge of the thread or fiber, this is called a 'superior' bowl. If it stands exceeding that line in a mound, this is called a 'superior-inferior' bowl. If it does not reach that line and remains within, this is called a 'superior-superior' bowl.

Nāḷikodananti magadhanāḷiyā ekāya taṇḍulanāḷiyā odanaṃ. Patthodananti magadhanāḷiyā upaḍḍhanāḷikodanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana nāmamatte viseso – sace nāḷikodanādi sabbampi pakkhittaṃ vuttanayeneva heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimo nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti antogatameva hoti, ayaṃ majjhimukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace patthodanādi sabbampi pakkhittaṃ heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ omako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ omakomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na pāpuṇāti antogatameva hoti, ayaṃ [P 3.0704] omakukkaṭṭho nāma pattoti evamete nava pattā. Tesu dve apattā ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho [M 2.0283] ca omakomako ca. “Tato ukkaṭṭho [V 2.0256] apatto omako apatto”ti idañhi ete sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho hi ettha ukkaṭṭhato ukkaṭṭhattā “tato ukkaṭṭho apatto”ti vutto. Omakomako ca omakato omakattā tato omako apattoti vutto. Tasmā ete bhājanaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbā, na adhiṭṭhānupagā, na vikappanupagā. Itare pana satta adhiṭṭhahitvā vā vikappetvā vā paribhuñjitabbā, evaṃ akatvā taṃ dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti taṃ sattavidhampi pattaṃ dasāhaparamaṃ kālaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

Nāḷikodana means the cooked rice from one Magadhan nāḷī of rice grains. Patthodana means the cooked rice from half a nāḷī by the Magadhan nāḷī measure. The rest should be understood in the way already stated. This, however, is a distinction in name only. If the nāḷikodana, etc., when all is placed within, stands level with the lower line in the way already stated, this is a bowl named 'middle'. If it stands exceeding that line, mounded up, this is a bowl named 'middle-inferior'. If it does not reach that line and is just inside, this is a bowl named 'middle-superior'. If the patthodana, etc., when all is placed within, stands level with the lower line, this is a bowl named 'inferior'. If it stands exceeding that line, mounded up, this is a bowl named 'inferior-inferior'. If it does not reach that line and is just inside, this is a bowl named 'inferior-superior'. Thus, these are nine bowls. Among them, two are not proper bowls: the superior-superior and the inferior-inferior. For it was said in reference to these: 'Superior to that is not a proper bowl; inferior to that is not a proper bowl.' Herein, the superior-superior is called 'superior to that is not a proper bowl' because it is superior to the superior. And the inferior-inferior is called 'inferior to that is not a proper bowl' because it is inferior to the inferior. Therefore, these should be used as mere vessels; they are not fit for determination or for sharing. The other seven, however, should be used after having determined or shared them. For one who does not do so and lets ten days pass with it, there is a pācittiya offense requiring forfeiture. Thus, for one who lets the period limited to ten days pass with regard to any of those seven kinds of bowls, there is a pācittiya offense requiring forfeiture.

607. Nissaggiyaṃ pattaṃ anissajjitvā paribhuñjatīti yāguṃ pivitvā dhote dukkaṭaṃ, khañjakaṃ khāditvā bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā dhote dukkaṭanti evaṃ payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ.

607. Regarding 'one uses a bowl subject to forfeiture without having forfeited it': after drinking gruel and washing the bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing; after eating hard food, eating a meal, and washing the bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Thus, for each and every instance of use, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

608. Anāpatti antodasāhaṃ adhiṭṭheti vikappetīti ettha pana pamāṇayuttassapi adhiṭṭhānavikappanupagattaṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – ayopatto pañcahi pākehi mattikāpatto dvīhi pākehi pakko adhiṭṭhānupago, ubhopi yaṃ mūlaṃ dātabbaṃ, tasmiṃ dinneyeva. Sace ekopi pāko ūno hoti, kākaṇikamattampi vā mūlaṃ adinnaṃ, na adhiṭṭhānupago. Sacepi pattasāmiko vadati “yadā tumhākaṃ mūlaṃ bhavissati, tadā dassatha, adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjathā”ti neva adhiṭṭhānupago hoti, pākassa hi ūnattā pattasaṅkhaṃ na gacchati, mūlassa sakalassa vā ekadesassa vā adinnattā sakabhāvaṃ na upeti, aññasseva santako hoti, tasmā pāke ca mūle ca niṭṭhiteyeva adhiṭṭhānupago hoti. Yo adhiṭṭhānupago, sveva vikappanupago, so hatthaṃ āgatopi anāgatopi adhiṭṭhātabbo vikappetabbo vā. Yadi hi pattakārako mūlaṃ labhitvā sayaṃ vā dātukāmo hutvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ pattaṃ katvā asukadivase nāma pacitvā ṭhapessāmī”ti vadati, bhikkhu ca tena paricchinnadivasato dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ [P 3.0705] pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana pattakārako “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pattaṃ katvā pacitvā sāsanaṃ pesessāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, tena pesitabhikkhu pana tassa bhikkhuno na āroceti, añño disvā vā sutvā vā “tumhākaṃ, bhante, patto niṭṭhito”ti āroceti, etassa ārocanaṃ napamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana tena pesitoyeva [M 2.0284] āroceti, tassa vacanaṃ sutadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pattakārako “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pattaṃ katvā pacitvā kassaci hatthe pahiṇissāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, pattaṃ gahetvā āgatabhikkhu pana attano pariveṇe ṭhapetvā tassa na āroceti, añño koci bhaṇati “api, bhante, adhunā ābhato patto sundaro”ti! “Kuhiṃ, āvuso, patto”ti? “Itthannāmassa hatthe pesito”ti. Etassapi vacanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana so bhikkhu pattaṃ deti[V 2.0257], laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Tasmā dasāhaṃ anatikkāmetvāva adhiṭṭhātabbo vikappetabbo vā.

608. Regarding the phrase, 'There is no offense if one determines or formally disposes of a bowl within ten days,' the decision here is as follows: even for a bowl of the proper size, its suitability for determination and formal disposal should be understood thus: an iron bowl that has been fired five times, or a clay bowl fired twice, is suitable for determination, and for both, only when the price that should be given has been given. If even one firing is incomplete, or if a price of even a `kākaṇika` is not given, it is not suitable for determination. Even if the owner of the bowl says, 'When you have the price, then give it; determine it and use it,' it is still not suitable for determination. Indeed, due to the incompleteness of the firing, it does not count as a bowl, and since the price—whether in whole or in part—has not been given, it does not become one's own property; it remains the property of another. Therefore, only when both the firing and the price are complete does it become suitable for determination. That which is suitable for determination is also suitable for formal disposal. It should be determined or formally disposed of, whether it has come to hand or not. Indeed, if the bowl-maker, having received the price or wishing to give it himself, says, 'Venerable sir, I will make your bowl and, after firing it, will set it aside on such-and-such a day,' and the monk exceeds ten days from that specified day, it is an offense entailing forfeiture and confession. If, however, the bowl-maker says, 'I will make your bowl, fire it, and send a message,' and does so, but the monk who was sent does not inform that monk, and another, having seen or heard, says, 'Venerable sir, your bowl is finished,' this notification is not authoritative. But when the one who was sent by him informs him, for one who exceeds ten days from the day he heard the words, it is an offense entailing forfeiture and confession. If the bowl-maker says, 'I will make your bowl, fire it, and send it by the hand of someone,' and does so, but the monk who brought the bowl places it in his own monastic cell and does not inform him, and someone else says, 'Venerable sir, is the bowl that was just brought beautiful?' and he asks, 'Friend, where is the bowl?' and is told, 'It was sent by the hand of so-and-so,' the words of this one are also not authoritative. But when that monk gives the bowl, for one who exceeds ten days from the day it was received, it is an offense entailing forfeiture and confession. Therefore, one must determine or formally dispose of it without exceeding ten days.

Tattha dve pattassa adhiṭṭhānā – kāyena vā adhiṭṭhāti, vācāya vā adhiṭṭhāti. Tesaṃ vasena adhiṭṭhahantena ca “imaṃ pattaṃ paccuddharāmī”ti vā “etaṃ pattaṃ paccuddharāmī”ti vā evaṃ sammukhe vā parammukhe vā ṭhitaṃ purāṇapattaṃ paccuddharitvā aññassa vā datvā navaṃ pattaṃ yattha katthaci ṭhitaṃ hatthena parāmasitvā “imaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena kāyena vā adhiṭṭhātabbo, vacībhedaṃ katvā vācāya vā adhiṭṭhātabbo. Tatra duvidhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ – sace hatthapāse hoti “imaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā. Atha antogabbhe vā uparipāsāde vā sāmantavihāre vā hoti, ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā.

In this matter, there are two kinds of determination of a bowl: one determines by body or one determines by speech. By means of these, one who is determining, having first revoked an old bowl that is present either in front of one or elsewhere by saying, 'I revoke this bowl' or 'I revoke that bowl,' or having given it to another, should then determine a new bowl. To determine by body, one should touch the new bowl, wherever it may be, with the hand, and while making a mental advertence, 'I determine this bowl,' make a distinct bodily gesture. Or, one should determine it by speech, making an utterance.
