In this regard, determination by speech is twofold: if the bowl is within hand's reach, the words 'I determine this bowl' should be uttered. If, however, it is inside a room, on an upper story, or in a neighboring monastery, having noted its location, the words 'I determine that bowl' should be uttered.

Adhiṭṭhahantena pana ekakena adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭati, aññassa santike adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭati. Aññassa santike ayamānisaṃso – sacassa “adhiṭṭhito nu kho me, no”ti vimati uppajjati, itaro sāretvā vimatiṃ chindissatīti. Sace koci dasa patte labhitvā sabbeva attanāva paribhuñjitukāmo hoti, na sabbe adhiṭṭhātabbā. Ekaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāya punadivase taṃ paccuddharitvā añño [P 3.0706] adhiṭṭhātabbo. Etenupāyena vassasatampi pariharituṃ sakkā.

However, when determining, it is permissible to determine alone, and it is permissible to determine in the presence of another. The advantage of being in the presence of another is this: if doubt arises for him, thinking, 'Has it been determined by me or not?' the other person, by reminding, will cut off the doubt. If someone obtains ten bowls and wishes to use all of them himself, not all should be determined. One bowl should be determined, and on the following day, having revoked it, another should be determined. By this means, it is possible to manage them for even a hundred years.

Evaṃ appamattassa bhikkhuno siyā adhiṭṭhānavijahananti? Siyā. Sace hi ayaṃ pattaṃ aññassa vā deti, vibbhamati vā sikkhaṃ vā paccakkhāti, kālaṃ vā karoti, liṅgaṃ vāssa parivattati, paccuddharati vā, patte vā chiddaṃ hoti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Could the determination of a heedful monk be abandoned? It could. Indeed, if this monk gives the bowl to another, or disrobes, or renounces the training, or dies, or his gender changes, or he revokes the determination, or a hole appears in the bowl, the determination is abandoned. And this has also been said:

“Dinnavibbhantapaccakkhā[M 2.0285], kālaṃkiriyakatena ca;

Liṅgapaccuddharā ceva, chiddena bhavati sattama”nti.

By giving, disrobing, and renouncing the training; and by the act of dying; also by change of gender and by revoking; the seventh is by a hole.

Coraharaṇavissāsaggāhehipi vijahatiyeva. Kittakena chiddena adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhijjati? Yena kaṅgusitthaṃ nikkhamati ceva pavisati ca. Idañhi sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ lāmakadhaññasitthaṃ, tasmiṃ ayacuṇṇena vā āṇiyā vā paṭipākatike kate dasāhabbhantare puna adhiṭṭhātabbo. Ayaṃ tāva “antodasāhaṃ adhiṭṭheti vikappetī”ti ettha adhiṭṭhāne vinicchayo.

The determination is also abandoned by being carried away by a thief or by being taken by a trusted person. By what size of hole is the determination broken? By one through which a cooked grain of millet can both exit and enter. Indeed, this is a cooked grain of the least among the seven kinds of grains. When that bowl has been repaired with iron filings or a rivet, it must be determined again within ten days. This, so far, is the decision concerning determination in the context of the phrase, 'one determines or formally disposes of within ten days.'

Vikappane [V 2.0258] pana dve vikappanā – sammukhāvikappanā ca parammukhāvikappanā ca. Kathaṃ sammukhāvikappanā hoti? Pattānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ. Ayamekā sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhuñjituṃ vā vissajjetuṃ vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. “Mayhaṃ santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti evaṃ pana vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tatopabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

However, regarding relinquishment, there are two kinds of relinquishment: face-to-face relinquishment and relinquishment in absence. How is face-to-face relinquishment done? Having known the state of the bowl or bowls as one or many, and as present or not present, and having said, “this bowl,” or “these bowls,” or “that bowl,” or “those bowls,” one should say, “I relinquish to you.” This is one kind of face-to-face relinquishment. By this much, it is permissible to store it, but it is not permissible to use it, give it away, or determine it. However, when it is said, “Use what is mine, or give it away, or do with it as is suitable,” this is called revocation; from then on, use and so forth are also permissible.

Aparo nayo – tatheva pattānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā tasseva bhikkhuno santike “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā pañcasu sahadhammikesu aññatarassa attanā abhirucitassa yassa kassaci nāmaṃ gahetvā “tissassa bhikkhuno vikappemī”ti vā “tissāya bhikkhuniyā sikkhamānāya sāmaṇerassa tissāya [P 3.0707] sāmaṇeriyā vikappemī”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ aparāpi sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā “tissassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ…pe… tissāya sāmaṇeriyā santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti. Tatopabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

Another method: similarly, having known the state of the bowl or bowls as one or many, and as present or not present, and having said in the presence of that very monk, “this bowl,” or “these bowls,” or “that bowl,” or “those bowls,” and having taken the name of any one of the five co-religionists whom one prefers, one should say, “I relinquish to the monk Tissa,” or “I relinquish to the nun Tissā, to the probationer Tissā, to the novice monk Tissa, or to the novice nun Tissā.” This is also another face-to-face relinquishment. By this much, it is permissible to store it, but among uses and so forth, not even one is permissible. However, when that monk says, “Use what belongs to the monk Tissa… or what belongs to the novice nun Tissā, or give it away, or do with it as is suitable,” this is called revocation. From then on, use and so forth are also permissible.

Kathaṃ parammukhāvikappanā hoti? Pattānaṃ tatheva ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappanatthāya dammī”ti vattabbaṃ. Tena vattabbo – “ko te mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā”ti? Tato itarena purimanayeneva [M 2.0286] “tisso bhikkhūti vā…pe… tissā sāmaṇerī”ti vā vattabbaṃ. Puna tena bhikkhunā “ahaṃ tissassa bhikkhuno dammī”ti vā…pe… “tissāya sāmaṇeriyā dammī”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ parammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvattā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā dutiyasammukhāvikappanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva “itthannāmassa santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti. Tatopabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

How is relinquishment in absence done? In the same way, having known the state of the bowl or bowls as one or many, and as present or not present, and having said, “this bowl,” or “these bowls,” or “that bowl,” or “those bowls,” one should say, “I give this to you for the purpose of relinquishment.” That person should be asked, “Who is your friend or acquaintance?” Then the other, in the same way as before, should say, “The monk Tissa,” or… up to… “the novice nun Tissā.” Again, that monk should say, “I give to the monk Tissa,” or… up to… “I give to the novice nun Tissā.” This is relinquishment in absence. By this much, it is permissible to store it, but among uses and so forth, not even one is permissible. However, when that monk, in the manner stated for the second face-to-face relinquishment, says, “Use what belongs to so-and-so, or give it away, or do with it as is suitable,” this is called revocation. From then on, use and so forth are also permissible.

Imāsaṃ [V 2.0259] pana dvinnaṃ vikappanānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ, avaseso ca vacanakkamo sabbo paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo saddhiṃ samuṭṭhānādīhīti.

However, the distinction between these two kinds of relinquishment, and the entire remaining sequence of words, should be understood together with their arising and so forth, in the very way it was stated in the commentary on the first Kathina training rule.

Pattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the bowl is finished.

2. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Less Than Five Bonds

609. Tena samayenāti ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha na yāpetīti so kira yadi ariyasāvako nābhavissā, aññathattampi agamissā, evaṃ tehi ubbāḷho, sotāpannattā pana kevalaṃ sarīreneva na yāpeti, tena vuttaṃ – “attanāpi na yāpeti, puttadārāpissa kilamantī”ti.

609. ‘At that time’ refers to the training rule concerning less than five bonds. Therein, regarding 'he does not get by,' it is said that if he had not been a noble disciple, being so oppressed by them, he would have reached a different state. However, because he was a stream-enterer, he was merely unable to get by in a bodily sense. Therefore, it was said: ‘He himself does not get by, and his wife and children are also weary.’

612-3. Ūnapañcabandhanenāti ettha ūnāni pañca bandhanāni assāti ūnapañcabandhano, nāssa pañca bandhanāni pūrentīti attho, tena ūnapañcabandhanena. Itthambhūtassa lakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tattha yasmā abandhanassāpi pañca bandhanāni na pūrenti, sabbaso natthitāya, tasmā padabhājane “abandhano vā”tiādi vuttaṃ[P 3.0708]. “Ūnapañcabandhanenā”ti ca vuttattā yassa pañcabandhano patto hoti, tassa so apatto, tasmā aññaṃ viññāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Bandhanañca nāmetaṃ yasmā bandhanokāse sati hoti, asati na hoti, tasmā tassa lakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “abandhanokāso nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding ‘with a bowl that has less than five bonds’: here, ‘a bowl that has less than five bonds’ is so called because its bonds are less than five. The meaning is that its five bonds are not complete; hence, ‘with a bowl that has less than five bonds.’ The instrumental case is in the sense of indicating a characteristic of one who has come to be in such a state. Therein, because for a bowl with no bonds at all the five bonds are not complete—due to their total absence—it is therefore said in the word-analysis, ‘or without bonds,’ and so on. And since it is said ‘with a bowl that has less than five bonds,’ for a monk who has a five-bonded bowl, that other bowl is not a valid bowl. Therefore, it is allowable to request another. And this, called a ‘bond,’ exists when there is a place for binding and does not exist when there is not. Therefore, to show its characteristic, it is said, ‘a place with no opportunity for a bond is called…’ and so on.

Dvaṅgulā rāji na hotīti mukhavaṭṭito heṭṭhā dvaṅgulappamāṇā ekāpi rāji na hoti. Yassa dvaṅgulā rāji hotīti yassa pana tādisā ekā [M 2.0287] rāji hoti, so tassā rājiyā heṭṭhimapariyante pattavedhakena vijjhitvā pacitvā suttarajjuka-makacirajjukādīhi vā tipusuttakena vā bandhitabbo, taṃ bandhanaṃ āmisassa alagganatthaṃ tipupaṭṭakena vā kenaci baddhasilesena vā paṭicchādetabbaṃ. So ca patto adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjitabbo, sukhumaṃ vā chiddaṃ katvā bandhitabbo. Suddhehi pana madhusitthakalākhāsajjulasādīhi bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Phāṇitaṃ jhāpetvā pāsāṇacuṇṇena bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Mukhavaṭṭisamīpe pana pattavedhakena vijjhiyamāno kapālassa bahalattā bhijjati, tasmā heṭṭhā vijjhitabbo. Yassa pana dve rājiyo ekāyeva vā caturaṅgulā, tassa dve bandhanāni dātabbāni. Yassa tisso ekāyeva vā chaḷaṅgulā, tassa tīṇi. Yassa catasso ekāyeva vā aṭṭhaṅgulā, tassa cattāri. Yassa pañca [V 2.0260] ekāyeva vā dasaṅgulā, so baddhopi abaddhopi apattoyeva, añño viññāpetabbo. Esa tāva mattikāpatte vinicchayo.

‘There is no crack of two fingers’ length’ means that not even a single crack of two fingers’ measure exists below the rim. As for a bowl that has a crack of two fingers’ length, meaning it has one such crack, it should be pierced at the lower end of that crack with a bowl-awl, fired, and then bound with things such as thread-cord or bark-cord, or with a lead thread. That binding, to prevent food from sticking to it, should be covered with a lead patch or with some binding adhesive. And that bowl should be determined and then used. Or, a small hole may be made and bound. However, it is not allowable to bind it with pure substances like beeswax, lac, or resin. It is allowable to bind it with stone powder after burning molasses. When being pierced near the rim with a bowl-awl, it may break due to the thickness of the bowl's shell; therefore, it should be pierced lower down. For a bowl that has two cracks, or a single one of four fingers’ length, two bonds should be applied. For one that has three cracks, or a single one of six fingers’ length, three bonds. For one that has four cracks, or a single one of eight fingers’ length, four bonds. A bowl that has five cracks, or a single one of ten fingers’ length, is not a valid bowl at all, whether it is bound or unbound; another should be requested. This, for a start, is the ruling concerning an earthen bowl.

Ayopatte pana sacepi pañca vā atirekāni vā chiddāni honti, tāni ce ayacuṇṇena vā āṇiyā vā lohamaṇḍalakena vā baddhāni maṭṭhāni honti, sveva patto paribhuñjitabbo, na añño viññāpetabbo. Atha pana ekampi chiddaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, lohamaṇḍalakena baddhampi maṭṭhaṃ na hoti, patte āmisaṃ laggati, akappiyo hoti, ayaṃ apatto. Añño viññāpetabbo.

In the case of an iron bowl, however, if there are five or even more holes, and if they are mended and made smooth with iron powder, a rivet, or a small iron plate, that same bowl should be used; another should not be requested. But if even one hole is large, and even when mended with a small iron plate it is not smooth, food sticks in the bowl, and it becomes unsuitable. This is an invalid bowl. Another should be requested.

615. Thero vattabboti patte ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā “ayaṃ, bhante, patto pamāṇayutto sundaro therānurūpo, taṃ gaṇhathā”ti vattabbo. Yo na gaṇheyyāti anukampāya na gaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Yo pana santuṭṭhiyā “kiṃ me aññena pattenā”ti na gaṇhāti, tassa anāpatti. Pattapariyantoti evaṃ parivattetvā [P 3.0709] pariyante ṭhitapatto.

615. ‘The elder should be told’ means that one should point out the benefits of the bowl and say: ‘Venerable sir, this bowl is of the right size, is beautiful, and is suitable for an elder. Please take it.’ Regarding ‘If one does not take it’: for one who does not take it out of compassion for the owner, there is an offense of wrong-doing. But for one who does not take it out of contentment, thinking, ‘What use have I for another bowl?’, there is no offense. ‘The final bowl’ (pattapariyanto) is the bowl that remains at the end after having exchanged in this way.

Na adeseti mañcapīṭhachattanāgadantakādike adese, na nikkhipitabbo. Yattha purimaṃ sundaraṃ pattaṃ ṭhapeti, tattheva ṭhapetabbo. Pattassa hi nikkhipanadeso “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ādhāraka”ntiādinā nayena khandhake vuttoyeva.

‘Not in an unsuitable place’ means it should not be placed in an unsuitable place, such as on a bed, a chair, under a parasol, on an ivory peg, and so on. It should be placed in the very same place where one keeps a previous, fine bowl. For the place for setting down a bowl has indeed been stated in the Khandhaka by the method beginning with, ‘I allow, O monks, a stand…’

Na [M 2.0288] abhogenāti yāgurandhanarajanapacanādinā aparibhogena na paribhuñjitabbo. Antarāmagge pana byādhimhi uppanne aññasmiṃ bhājane asati mattikāya limpetvā yāguṃ vā pacituṃ udakaṃ vā tāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

‘Not for improper use’ means it should not be used improperly for things such as cooking gruel, boiling dye, and so on. However, on a journey, if one becomes ill and there is no other vessel available, it is allowable to coat the bowl with clay to cook gruel or to heat water.

Na vissajjetabboti aññassa na dātabbo. Sace pana saddhivihāriko vā antevāsiko vā aññaṃ varapattaṃ ṭhapetvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ sāruppo, ayaṃ therassā”ti gaṇhāti, vaṭṭati. Añño vā taṃ gahetvā attano pattaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. “Mayhameva pattaṃ āharā”ti vattabbakiccaṃ natthi.

‘It should not be given away’ means it should not be given to another. However, if a co-resident or a pupil places another, better bowl and takes the elder's, saying, ‘This one is suitable for me, this one is for the elder,’ it is allowable. Or if another monk takes that bowl and gives his own bowl in return, it is allowable. There is no need to say, ‘Bring back my own bowl.’

617. Pavāritānanti ettha saṅghavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne pañcabandhaneneva vaṭṭati. Puggalavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne ūnapañcabandhanenāpi vaṭṭatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

617. Regarding those who have been invited (pavāritānaṃ): here, when invited by the Sangha, it is allowable to request a new bowl only if one's current bowl has five bonds. When invited as an individual, it is allowable to request one even with a bowl that has less than five bonds; so it is said in the Kurundī commentary. The rest here has a clear meaning.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ[V 2.0261], kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

Six origins; functional; not-release-by-perception; unintentional; a transgression by designation; bodily and verbal action; threefold consciousness; threefold feeling.

Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Less Than Five Bonds is concluded.

3. Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Medicine

618. Tena samayenāti bhesajjasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha attho, bhanteti rājā bhikkhū uyyuttappayutte therassa leṇatthāya pabbhāraṃ sodhente disvā ārāmikaṃ dātukāmo pucchi.

618. The training rule on medicine begins with 'At that time'. Therein, the king, seeing the monks diligently and exceedingly engaged in clearing a mountain slope for the elder's cave, wished to give a monastery attendant and asked.

619-21. Pāṭiyekkoti visuṃ eko. Mālākiteti katamāle mālādhare, kusumamālāpaṭimaṇḍiteti attho. Tiṇaṇḍupakanti tiṇacumbaṭakaṃ. Paṭimuñcīti ṭhapesi. Sā ahosi suvaṇṇamālāti dārikāya sīse ṭhapitamattāyeva therassa adhiṭṭhānavasena suvaṇṇapadumamālā ahosi. Tañhi tiṇaṇḍupakaṃ sīse ṭhapitamattameva “suvaṇṇamālā hotū”ti thero adhiṭṭhāsi. Dutiyampi kho…pe…. Tenupasaṅkamīti dutiyadivaseyeva upasaṅkami.

Pāṭiyekko: separately, one. Mālākiteti: having made garlands, bearing garlands, adorned with flower garlands—this is the meaning. Tiṇaṇḍupakanti: a coil of grass. Paṭimuñcīti: he placed. Sā ahosi suvaṇṇamālāti: merely upon being placed on the girl's head, by the elder’s resolve, it became a golden lotus garland. For that coil of grass, merely upon being placed on the head, the elder resolved, 'Let it be a golden garland.' Dutiyampi kho…pe…. Tenupasaṅkamīti: he approached on the very second day.

Suvaṇṇanti [M 2.0289] adhimuccīti “sovaṇṇamayo hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Pañcannaṃ bhesajjānanti sappiādīnaṃ. Bāhulikāti [P 3.0710] paccayabāhulikatāya paṭipannā. Kolambepi ghaṭepītiettha kolambā nāma mahāmukhacāṭiyo vuccanti. Olīnavilīnānīti heṭṭhā ca ubhatopassesu ca gaḷitāni. Okiṇṇavikiṇṇāti sappiādīnaṃ gandhena bhūmiṃ khanantehi okiṇṇā, bhittiyo khanantehi upari sañcarantehi ca vikiṇṇā. Antokoṭṭhāgārikāti abbhantare saṃvihitakoṭṭhāgārā.

Suvaṇṇanti adhimuccīti: he resolved, 'Let it be made of gold.' Pañcannaṃ bhesajjānanti: of ghee and so forth. Bāhulikāti: they were disposed to an abundance of requisites. Kolambepi ghaṭepītiettha: herein, 'kolambā' are called large-mouthed pots. Olīnavilīnānīti: they had dripped down below and on both sides. Okiṇṇavikiṇṇāti: strewn about by mice digging the ground due to the smell of ghee and so forth, and scattered by mice digging into the walls and moving about above. Antokoṭṭhāgārikāti: those with storehouses prepared inside.

622. Paṭisāyanīyānīti paṭisāyitabbāni, paribhuñjitabbānīti attho. Bhesajjānīti bhesajjakiccaṃ karontu vā mā vā, evaṃ laddhavohārāni. “Gosappī”tiādīhi loke pākaṭaṃ dassetvā “yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappatī”ti iminā aññesampi migarohitasasādīnaṃ sappiṃ saṅgahetvā dassesi. Yesañhi khīraṃ atthi, sappipi tesaṃ atthiyeva, taṃ pana sulabhaṃ vā hotu dullabhaṃ vā, asammohatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ navanītampi.

622. Paṭisāyanīyānīti: things that should be used with pleasure, that is, things that should be consumed. Bhesajjānīti: whether they perform a medicinal function or not, they are medicines that have thus received the designation. By showing what is well-known in the world with 'cow's ghee' and so forth, and with the text 'of those whose flesh is allowable,' it also includes the ghee of other animals like deer, roe-deer, and hares. For indeed, of whichever beings there is milk, of them ghee also certainly exists; whether that ghee is easy to obtain or difficult to obtain, this is stated for the purpose of non-bewilderment. The same applies to fresh butter.

Sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjitabbānīti sannidhiṃ katvā nidahitvā paribhuñjitabbāni. Kathaṃ? Pāḷiyā āgatasappiādīsu sappi tāva purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ tadahupurebhattaṃ sāmisampi nirāmisampi [V 2.0262] paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sattāhātikkame sace ekabhājane ṭhapitaṃ, ekaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Sace bahūsu vatthugaṇanāya nissaggiyāni, pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā uggahitakaṃ katvā nikkhittaṃ ajjhoharituṃ na vaṭṭati; abbhañjanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti, anajjhoharaṇīyataṃ āpannattā. “Paṭisāyanīyānī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Sace anupasampanno purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitanavanītena sappiṃ katvā deti, purebhattaṃ sāmisaṃ vaṭṭati. Sace sayaṃ karoti, sattāhampi nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitanavanītena pana yena kenaci katasappi sattāhampi nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Uggahitakena kate pubbe vuttasuddhasappinayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo.

Sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjitabbānīti: they are to be consumed after having been stored. How so? Regarding ghee and so forth mentioned in the Pāḷi: ghee received before noon is allowable to be consumed on that day before noon either with or without staples. From after noon onwards, it is to be consumed without staples for seven days. If it exceeds seven days, should it be kept in one container, it is one item for forfeiture. If in many containers, they are items for forfeiture according to the count of items. Ghee received after noon is allowable for seven days only without staples. Ghee that was taken without formal acceptance, whether before or after noon, and then put aside, is not allowable to be consumed; it should be applied for purposes such as anointing. Even after exceeding seven days, there is no offense, because it has become non-consumable. For it was said, 'to be used with pleasure' (paṭisāyanīyāni). If an unordained person makes ghee from fresh butter received before noon and gives it, it is allowable with staples before noon. If one makes it oneself, it is allowable for seven days only without staples. However, ghee made by anyone from fresh butter received after noon is allowable for seven days only without staples. For ghee made from that which was taken without formal acceptance, the ruling is to be understood according to the method previously stated for pure ghee.

Purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitakhīrena vā dadhinā vā katasappi [P 3.0711] anupasampannena kataṃ sāmisampi tadahupurebhattaṃ vaṭṭati. Sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati[M 2.0290]. Navanītaṃ tāpentassa hi sāmaṃpāko na hoti, sāmaṃpakkena pana tena saddhiṃ āmisaṃ na vaṭṭati. Pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya ca na vaṭṭatiyeva. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti, savatthukassa paṭiggahitattā, “tāni paṭiggahetvā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitehi kataṃ pana abbhañjanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Purebhattampi ca uggahitakehi kataṃ ubhayesampi sattāhātikkame anāpatti. Eseva nayo akappiyamaṃsasappimhi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yattha pāḷiyaṃ āgatasappinā nissaggiyaṃ, tattha iminā dukkaṭaṃ. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ vatvā manussasappi ca navanītañca paṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ duppaṭikkhittaṃ, sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu anuññātattā. Parato cassa vinicchayopi āgacchissati.

Ghee made by an unordained person from milk or curds received before noon is allowable with staples on that day before noon. If made by oneself, it is allowable only without staples. For one heating fresh butter, it is not considered 'cooking by oneself'; however, with that which is self-cooked, staples are not allowable. And from after noon onwards, it is not allowable at all. Even after exceeding seven days, there is no offense, because it was received together with its base-substance; for it is said, 'having received them'. However, ghee made from substances received after noon should be applied for purposes such as anointing. And for ghee made from items taken without formal acceptance even before noon—in both of these cases, there is no offense if seven days are exceeded. This is the same method for ghee from unallowable flesh. This, however, is the distinction: where for ghee mentioned in the Pāḷi there is an offense of forfeiture, here with this there is a dukkaṭa offense. In the Andhaka commentary, having stated a specious reason, human ghee and fresh butter are rejected. That is badly rejected, because it is allowed in all commentaries. And a ruling on this will come later.

Pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ navanītampi purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ tadahupurebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva. Sattāhātikkame nānābhājanesu ṭhapite bhājanagaṇanāya ekabhājanepi amissetvā piṇḍapiṇḍavasena ṭhapite piṇḍagaṇanāya nissaggiyāni. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sappinayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ettha pana dadhiguḷikāyopi takkabindūnipi honti, tasmā taṃ dhotaṃ vaṭṭatīti upaḍḍhattherā āhaṃsu. Mahāsīvatthero pana “bhagavatā anuññātakālato paṭṭhāya takkato uddhaṭamattameva khādiṃsū”ti āha. Tasmā navanītaṃ paribhuñjantena dhovitvā dadhitakkamakkhikākipillikādīni apanetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Pacitvā sappiṃ katvā paribhuñjitukāmena adhotampi pacituṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ tattha dadhigataṃ vā takkagataṃ vā taṃ khayaṃ gamissati, ettāvatā hi savatthukapaṭiggahitaṃ nāma na hotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Āmisena [V 2.0263] saddhiṃ pakkattā pana tasmimpi kukkuccāyanti kukkuccakā. Idāni uggahetvā ṭhapitanavanīte ca purebhattaṃ khīradadhīni [P 3.0712] paṭiggahetvā katanavanīte ca pacchābhattaṃ tāni paṭiggahetvā katanavanīte ca uggahitehi katanavavīte ca akappiyamaṃsanavanīte ca sabbo āpattānāpattiparibhogāparibhoganayo sappimhi vuttakkameneva gahetabbo.

Fresh butter mentioned in the Pāḷi, if received before noon, is allowable on that day before noon even with staples, but from after noon onwards, it is allowable only without staples. If it exceeds seven days, when placed in various vessels, it becomes subject to forfeiture according to the count of the vessels; even in one vessel, if placed unmixed as separate lumps, it becomes subject to forfeiture according to the count of the lumps. What is received after noon should be understood according to the method for ghee. Here, however, there are also small lumps of curd and drops of buttermilk; therefore, it is allowable if washed, so said half of the elders. The Elder Mahāsīva, however, said, 'From the time permitted by the Blessed One, they ate only what had been skimmed from the buttermilk.' Therefore, one consuming fresh butter should consume it after washing it and removing curd, buttermilk, flies, ants, and so on. By one who wishes to consume it after cooking it and making it into ghee, it is allowable to cook it even unwashed. Whatever curd or buttermilk is in it will perish; indeed, by that much it is not called 'received with its substance'—this is the intention here. However, because it is cooked together with an accompanying substance, the scrupulous have scruples even about that. Now, regarding fresh butter that was taken up and stored; fresh butter made from milk and curds received before noon; fresh butter made from those received after noon; fresh butter made from items that were taken up; and fresh butter from unallowable meat—in all these cases, the entire method concerning offenses, non-offenses, use, and non-use should be understood in the same way as stated for ghee.

Telabhikkhāya paviṭṭhānaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ tattheva sappimpi navanītampi pakkatelampi apakkatelampi ākiranti, tattha takkadadhibindūnipi bhattasitthānipi taṇḍulakaṇāpi makkhikādayopi honti. Ādiccapākaṃ katvā [M 2.0291] parissāvetvā gahitaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ hoti, paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitabhesajjehi saddhiṃ pacitvā natthupānampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vaddalisamaye lajji sāmaṇero yathā tattha patitataṇḍulakaṇādayo na paccanti, evaṃ sāmisapākaṃ mocento aggimhi vilīyāpetvā parissāvetvā puna pacitvā deti, purimanayeneva sattāhaṃ vaṭṭati.

However, for monks who have entered for the alms-round for oil, people pour right into their bowls ghee, fresh butter, cooked oil, and uncooked oil. In that, there may also be drops of buttermilk and curd, lumps of cooked rice, fragments of raw rice, dead flies, and so on. Oil that is prepared by sun-heating, strained, and taken is a seven-day allowable. Having received it, it is allowable to cook it together with stored medicines and to make it into a nasal inhalation or a drink. If, during a time of drizzling rain, a scrupulous novice—in order that the fallen fragments of raw rice and so on in it are not cooked—avoids cooking the accompanying substances by melting it over a fire, straining it, cooking it again, and then giving it, it is allowable for seven days according to the previous method.

Telesu tilatelaṃ tāva purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva. Sattāhātikkame panassa bhājanagaṇanāya nissaggiyabhāvo veditabbo. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Uggahitakaṃ katvā nikkhittaṃ ajjhoharituṃ na vaṭṭati, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Purebhattaṃ tile paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ hoti, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Pacchābhattaṃ tile paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ anajjhoharaṇīyameva, savatthukapaṭiggahitattā, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā uggahitakatilehi katatelepi eseva nayo.

Among oils, first, sesame oil: if received before the meal, it is allowable before the meal even with relish; from after the meal onwards, it is allowable only without relish. If seven days are exceeded, it should be understood as being subject to forfeiture by the counting of vessels. If received after the meal, it is allowable for seven days only without relish. If taken up and set aside, it is not allowable to consume; it should be used for anointing the head and so on, and even if seven days are exceeded, there is no offense. Oil made from sesame seeds received before the meal is allowable before the meal even with relish; from after the meal onwards, it is not to be consumed but should be used for anointing the head and so on, and even if seven days are exceeded, there is no offense. Oil made from sesame seeds received after the meal is simply not to be consumed, because it was received with its substance; it should be used for anointing the head and so on, and even if seven days are exceeded, there is no offense. This same method applies also to oil made from sesame seeds that were taken up, whether before or after the meal.

Purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitakatile bhajjitvā vā tilapiṭṭhaṃ vā sedetvā uṇhodakena vā temetvā katatelaṃ sace anupasampannena kataṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati. Attanā katatelaṃ pana nibbaṭṭitattā purebhattaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Sāmaṃpakkattā [P 3.0713] sāmisaṃ na vaṭṭati, savatthukapaṭiggahitattā pana pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya ubhayampi anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Yadi pana appaṃ uṇhodakaṃ hoti abbhukkiraṇamattaṃ, abbohārikaṃ hoti, sāmapākagaṇanaṃ na gacchati. Sāsapatelādīsupi avatthukapaṭiggahitesu avatthukatilatele vuttasadisova vinicchayo.

If oil is made from sesame seeds received before the meal—by frying them, or by steaming sesame flour, or by soaking it with hot water—and if it is made by one who is not fully ordained, it is allowable before the meal even with relish. However, oil made by oneself, because it has been extracted, is allowable before the meal only without relish. Because it is self-cooked, it is not allowable with relish. Furthermore, because it was received with its substance, from after the meal onwards, both types are not to be consumed; they should be used for anointing the head and so on. Even if seven days are exceeded, there is no offense. If, however, there is only a little hot water, just enough for sprinkling, it is negligible and does not count as self-cooking. For mustard oil and so on, when received without their substance, the ruling is just like that stated for sesame oil without its substance.

Sace [V 2.0264] pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitānaṃ sāsapādīnaṃ cuṇṇehi ādiccapākena sakkā telaṃ kātuṃ, taṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva, sattāhātikkame nissaggiyaṃ. Yasmā pana sāsapamadhukacuṇṇādīni sedetvā eraṇḍakaṭṭhīni ca bhajjitvā eva telaṃ karonti, tasmā tesaṃ telaṃ anupasampannehi kataṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati. Vatthūnaṃ yāvajīvikattā pana savatthukapaṭiggahaṇe doso natthīti. Attanā kataṃ [M 2.0292] sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogeneva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Uggahitakehi kataṃ anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ bāhiraparibhoge vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti.

If, however, it is possible to make oil by sun-heating the powders of mustard seeds and so on, received before the meal, that oil is allowable before the meal even with relish; from after the meal onwards, it is allowable only without relish. If seven days are exceeded, it is subject to forfeiture. Since they make oil by steaming the powders of mustard, madhuka, and so on, and by frying castor beans, their oil, when made by those not fully ordained, is allowable before the meal even with relish. Furthermore, because the substances themselves are lifelong allowables, there is no fault in receiving them with their substance. Oil made by oneself must be consumed for seven days only without relish. Oil made from items that were taken up is not to be consumed; it is allowable for external use, and even if seven days are exceeded, there is no offense.

Telakaraṇatthāya sāsapamadhukaeraṇḍakaṭṭhīni vā paṭiggahetvā kataṃ telaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ. Dutiyadivase kataṃ chāhaṃ vaṭṭati. Tatiyadivase kataṃ pañcāhaṃ vaṭṭati. Catuttha-pañcama-chaṭṭhasattāmadivase kataṃ tadaheva vaṭṭati. Sace yāva aruṇassa uggamanā tiṭṭhati, nissaggiyaṃ. Aṭṭhame divase kataṃ anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ. Anissaggiyattā pana bāhiraparibhoge vaṭṭati. Sacepi na karoti, telatthāya gahitasāsapādīnaṃ sattāhātikkamane dukkaṭameva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana anāgatāni aññānipi nāḷikeranimbakosambakakaramandaatasīādīnaṃ telāni atthi, tāni paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ atikkāmayato dukkaṭaṃ hoti. Ayametesu viseso. Sesaṃ yāvakālikavatthuṃ yāvajīvikavatthuñca sallakkhetvā sāmaṃpākasavatthukapurebhattapacchābhattapaṭiggahitauggahitakavatthuvidhānaṃ sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

If mustard, madhuka, or castor seeds are received for the purpose of making oil, the oil made from them is a seven-day allowable. If made on the second day, it is allowable for six days. If made on the third day, it is allowable for five days. If made on the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, it is allowable only for that day. If it remains until the rising of dawn, it is subject to forfeiture. If made on the eighth day, it is not to be consumed. However, since it is not subject to forfeiture, it is allowable for external use. Even if one does not make the oil, keeping mustard seeds and so forth received for this purpose beyond seven days incurs a wrongdoing. Furthermore, there are other oils not mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as those from coconut, neem, kosamba, karamanda, and linseed; if these are received and kept beyond seven days, a wrongdoing is incurred. This is the distinction among these. The rest, concerning items for temporary use and items for lifelong use, should all be understood in the same way as previously explained, by considering the rules for self-cooked items, items received with their substance, items received before or after the meal, and items that have been taken up.

623. Vasātelanti [P 3.0714] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni, acchavasaṃ, macchavasaṃ, susukāvasaṃ, sūkaravasaṃ, gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) evaṃ anuññātavasānaṃ telaṃ. Ettha ca “acchavasa”nti vacanena ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ sabbesaṃ akappiyamaṃsāna vasā anuññātā. Macchaggahaṇena ca susukāpi gahitā honti, vāḷamacchattā pana visuṃ vuttaṃ. Macchādiggahaṇena cettha sabbesampi kappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasā anuññātā. Maṃsesu hi dasamanaussa-hatthi-assa-sunakha-ahi-sīha-byaggha-dīpi-accha-taracchānaṃ maṃsāni akappiyāni. Vasāsu ekā manussavasāva. Khīrādīsu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi.

623. ‘Fat-oil’ means oil from fats thus permitted: ‘Monks, I allow fats as medicines: bear fat, fish fat, crocodile fat, pig fat, and donkey fat’ (Mahāvagga 262). And here, by the statement ‘bear fat,’ the fats of all creatures with impermissible meat are permitted, with the exception of human fat. By the inclusion of ‘fish,’ crocodiles are also included, but because they are a type of fierce fish, they are mentioned separately. And by the inclusion of fish and so forth, the fats of all creatures with permissible meat are permitted here. Indeed, among meats, the flesh of ten is impermissible: human, elephant, horse, dog, snake, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, and hyena. Among fats, only human fat is impermissible. Among milk and so forth, there is nothing that is impermissible.

Anupasampannehi katanibbaṭṭitavasātelaṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati. Pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana tattha sukhumarajasadisaṃ maṃsaṃ vā nhāru vā aṭṭhi vā lohitaṃ vā hoti, taṃ abbohārikaṃ. Sace pana vasaṃ paṭiggahetvā sayaṃ karoti, purebhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā pacitvā parissāvetvā sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbaṃ[V 2.0265]. Nirāmisaparibhogañhi sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ – “kāle [M 2.0293] paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 262). Tatrāpi abbohārikaṃ abbohārikameva. Pacchābhattaṃ pana paṭiggahituṃ vā kātuṃ vā na vaṭṭatiyeva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

If fat-oil is made and extracted by those not fully ordained, and received before the meal, it is allowable before the meal even with relish. From after the meal onwards, it is allowable for seven days only without relish. However, whatever fine substance like dust—be it flesh, sinew, bone, or blood—is present therein, that is considered negligible. But if one receives fat and prepares it oneself, having received it before the meal, cooked it, and strained it, it should be consumed for seven days only without relish. For it is with reference to consumption without relish that this was stated: ‘If received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, it should be consumed in the manner of oil’ (Mahāvagga 262). Even in that case, what is negligible remains negligible. However, it is simply not allowable to receive or prepare it after the meal. For it was said—

“Vikāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, anāpattī”ti.

“If, monks, something is received at the wrong time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of three wrongdoings. If, monks, something is received at the right time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of two wrongdoings. If, monks, something is received at the right time, cooked at the right time, but mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of one wrongdoing. If, monks, something is received at the right time, cooked at the right time, and mixed at the right time, and one consumes it, there is no offense.”

Upatissattheraṃ pana antevāsikā pucchiṃsu – “bhante, sappinavanītavasāni [P 3.0715] ekato pacitvā nibbaṭṭitāni vaṭṭanti, na vaṭṭantī”ti? “Na vaṭṭanti, āvuso”ti. Thero kirettha pakkatelakasaṭe viya kukkuccāyati. Tato naṃ uttari pucchiṃsu – “bhante, navanīte dadhiguḷikā vā takkabindu vā hoti, etaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Etampi, āvuso, na vaṭṭatī”ti. Tato naṃ āhaṃsu – “bhante, ekato pacitvā saṃsaṭṭhāni tejavantāni honti, rogaṃ niggaṇhantī”ti? “Sādhāvuso”ti thero sampaṭicchi.

However, the disciples asked the Elder Upatissa: “Venerable sir, if ghee, fresh butter, and fat are cooked together and extracted, are they permissible or not?” “They are not permissible, friends,” he replied. Indeed, the elder was scrupulous here, as if it were the dregs of cooked oil. Then they further asked him: “Venerable sir, if there is a curd ball or a drop of buttermilk in fresh butter, is that permissible?” “This too, friends, is not permissible,” he replied. Then they said to him: “Venerable sir, when cooked together and mixed, they become potent and suppress disease.” “Well said, friends,” the elder agreed.

Mahāsumatthero panāha – “kappiyamaṃsavasā sāmisaparibhoge vaṭṭati, itarā nirāmisaparibhoge vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpadumatthero pana “idaṃ ki”nti paṭikkhipitvā “nanu vātābādhikā bhikkhū pañcamūlakasāvayāguyaṃ acchasūkaratelādīni pakkhipitvā yāguṃ pivanti, sā tejussadattā rogaṃ niggaṇhātī”ti vatvā “vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

However, the Elder Mahāsumana said: “Fat from permissible meat is permissible for consumption with relish; other fat is permissible for consumption without relish.” However, the Elder Mahāpaduma, rejecting this with “What is this?”, said: “Do not monks afflicted with wind ailments drink gruel mixed with bear fat, pig fat, and so forth, in gruel made from the decoction of the five roots? That, being potent, subdues the disease.” Thus, he said, “It is permissible.”

Madhu nāma makkhikāmadhūti madhukarīhi nāma madhumakkhikāhi khuddakamakkhikāhi bhamaramakkhikāhi ca kataṃ madhu. Taṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaparibhogampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogameva vaṭṭati. Sattāhātikkame sace silesasadisaṃ mahāmadhuṃ khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ, itaraṃ vā nānābhājanesu, vatthugaṇanāya nissaggiyāni. Sace ekameva khaṇḍaṃ, ekabhājane vā itaraṃ ekameva nissaggiyaṃ. Uggahitakaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, arumakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Madhupaṭalaṃ [M 2.0294] vā madhusitthakaṃ vā sace madhunā amakkhitaṃ [V 2.0266] parisuddhaṃ, yāvajīvikaṃ. Madhumakkhitaṃ pana madhugatikameva. Cīrikā nāma sapakkhā dīghamakkhikā, tumbalanāmikā ca aṭṭhipakkhā kāḷamahābhamarā honti, tesaṃ āsayesu niyyāsasadisaṃ madhu hoti, taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

Honey is what is produced by bees, namely honeybees, small bees, and bumblebees. Honey received in the forenoon may be consumed with food items in the forenoon. From the afternoon onwards, it may be consumed only without food items for seven days. If it exceeds seven days, and if large honey resembling gum is broken into pieces and stored, or if other honey is stored in various containers, they become forfeitable by the count of items. If there is only one piece, or other honey in one container, only that one is forfeitable. What has been taken up without being offered should be understood in the same way as explained, and it should be applied to anointing wounds and so forth. A honeycomb or beeswax, if not smeared with honey and is pure, is allowable for life. But if smeared with honey, it follows the same rule as honey. Cīrikā refers to long-winged flies, and tumbalanāmikā refers to large black bumblebees with bone-like wings. The substance in their dwellings, resembling resin, is honey and is allowable for life.

Phāṇitaṃ nāma ucchumhā nibbattanti ucchurasaṃ upādāya apakkā vā avatthukapakkā vā sabbāpi avatthukā ucchuvikati phāṇitanti veditabbā. Taṃ phāṇitaṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Sattāhātikkame vatthugaṇanāya [P 3.0716] nissaggiyaṃ. Bahū piṇḍā cuṇṇetvā ekabhājane pakkhittā honti ghanasannivesā, ekameva nissaggiyaṃ. Uggahitakaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, gharadhūpanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitena aparissāvitaucchurasena kataphāṇitaṃ sace anupasampannena kataṃ, sāmisampi vaṭṭati. Sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya pana savatthukapaṭiggahitattā anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Pacchābhattaṃ aparissāvitapaṭiggahitena katampi anajjhoharaṇīyameva, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Esa nayo ucchuṃ paṭiggahetvā kataphāṇitepi. Purebhattaṃ pana parissāvitapaṭiggahitakena kataṃ sace anupasampannena kataṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva. Sayaṃkataṃ purebhattampi nirāmisameva. Pacchābhattaṃ parissāvitapaṭiggahitena kataṃ pana nirāmisameva sattāhaṃ vaṭṭati. Uggahitakakataṃ vuttanayameva. “Jhāmaucchuphāṇitaṃ vā koṭṭitaucchuphāṇitaṃ vā purebhattameva vaṭṭatī”ti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Phāṇita is the name for what is produced from sugarcane. Taking sugarcane juice as the basis, any sugarcane product—whether uncooked, or cooked without its substance [pulp], or any product without its substance—is to be known as 'phāṇita'. That phāṇita, if received in the forenoon, is allowable even with food items in the forenoon; from the afternoon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only without food items. Upon exceeding seven days, it becomes an item for forfeiture according to the count of items. If many lumps are crushed and placed in a single vessel, forming a solid mass, it is a single item for forfeiture. That which is taken up without being offered should be understood in the manner already stated; it should be used for things like fumigating a house. If phāṇita made from unstrained sugarcane juice received in the forenoon is made by an unordained person, it is allowable even with food items. If made by oneself, it is allowable only without food items. But from the afternoon onwards, because it was received together with its substance, it is not to be consumed; there is no offense even upon exceeding seven days. Even if made from unstrained juice received in the afternoon, it is not to be consumed; there is no offense even upon exceeding seven days. This is the same principle for phāṇita made after receiving sugarcane stalks. But if it is made from strained juice received in the forenoon, and if it is made by an unordained person, it is allowable even with food items in the forenoon; from the afternoon onwards, it is for seven days only without food items. If made by oneself, even in the forenoon, it is only without food items. But if made from strained juice received in the afternoon, it is allowable for seven days only without food items. That which is made from what was taken up without being offered is as stated before. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā it is said: 'Phāṇita from burnt sugarcane or phāṇita from chopped sugarcane is allowable only in the forenoon.'

Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “etaṃ savatthukapakkaṃ vaṭṭati, no vaṭṭatī”ti pucchaṃ katvā “ucchuphāṇitaṃ pacchābhattaṃ novaṭṭanakaṃ nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ. Sītudakena kataṃ madhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaṃ vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva. Sattāhātikkame vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Khīraṃ pakkhipitvā kataṃ madhukaphāṇitaṃ yāvakālikaṃ. Khaṇḍasakkharaṃ pana khīrajallikaṃ apanetvā sodhenti, tasmā vaṭṭati. Madhukapupphaṃ pana purebhattaṃ allaṃ vaṭṭati, bhajjitampi vaṭṭati. Bhajjitvā tilādīhi missaṃ vā [M 2.0295] amissaṃ vā katvā koṭṭitampi vaṭṭati. Yadi pana taṃ gahetvā merayatthāya yojenti, yojitaṃ bījato paṭṭhāya na vaṭṭati. Kadalī-khajjūrī-amba-labuja-panasa-ciñcādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ yāvakālikaphalānaṃ [P 3.0717] phāṇitaṃ yāvakālikameva. Maricapakkehi phāṇitaṃ karonti, taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

However, in the Mahāpaccarī, after asking the question, 'Is this, cooked with its substance, allowable or not allowable?', it was said: 'There is no such thing as sugarcane molasses that is not allowable in the afternoon.' That is correct. Molasses of madhuka flowers made with cold water is allowable with food items in the forenoon; from the afternoon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only without food items. Upon exceeding seven days, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each item. Madhuka molasses made by adding milk is a yāvakālika. As for lump sugar, they purify it by removing the milk scum; therefore, it is allowable. Furthermore, fresh madhuka flowers are allowable in the forenoon; even if fried, they are allowable. Having been fried, whether mixed with sesame and so on or unmixed, and then pounded, it is also allowable. But if they take it and prepare it for the purpose of an intoxicant, once so prepared, it is not allowable from the seed onwards. The molasses of all yāvakālika fruits—such as banana, date palm, mango, breadfruit, jackfruit, tamarind, and so on—is itself a yāvakālika. They make molasses from ripe peppers; that is a yāvajīvika.

Tāni paṭiggahetvāti sacepi sabbānipi paṭiggahetvā eka ghaṭe avinibbhogāni katvā nikkhipati[V 2.0267], sattāhātikkame ekameva nissaggiyaṃ. Vinibhuttesu pañca nissaggiyāni. Sattāhaṃ pana anatikkāmetvā gilānenapi agilānenapi vuttanayeneva yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sattavidhañhi odissaṃ nāma – byādhiodissaṃ, puggalodissaṃ, kālodissaṃ, samayodissaṃ, desodissaṃ, vasodissaṃ, bhesajjodissanti.

Regarding 'having received those': even if one receives all of them and places them in one pot, having made them inseparable, upon exceeding seven days, only one item for forfeiture is incurred. If they are separated, five items for forfeiture are incurred. However, without exceeding seven days, it should be consumed at will by one who is sick as well as by one who is not sick, in the manner already stated. For there are seven kinds of specific allowance, namely: specific allowance for illness, for a person, for a time, for an occasion, for a place, for fat, and for medicine.

Tattha byādhiodissaṃ nāma – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, amanussikābādhe āmakamaṃsaṃ āmakalohita”nti (mahāva. 264) evaṃ byādhiṃ uddissa anuññātaṃ, taṃ teneva ābādhena ābādhikassa vaṭṭati, na aññassa. Tañca kho kālepi vikālepi kappiyampi akappiyampi vaṭṭatiyeva.

Therein, 'specific allowance for illness' refers to what was permitted with reference to an illness, as in: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, in the case of a non-human affliction, raw meat and raw blood.' That is allowable for the one afflicted with that very illness, not for another. And that is allowable indeed, whether at the proper time or the improper time, and whether the item itself is permissible or impermissible.

Puggalodissaṃ nāma – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, romanthakassa romanthanaṃ. Na ca, bhikkhave, bahimukhadvāraṃ nīharitvā ajjhoharitabba”nti (cūḷava. 273) evaṃ puggalaṃ uddissa anuññātaṃ, taṃ tasseva vaṭṭati, na aññassa.

'Specific allowance for a person' refers to what was permitted with reference to a person, as in: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, rumination for one who ruminates. But, O bhikkhus, it should not be swallowed after having been brought out from the mouth.' Thus, what is permitted with reference to that individual is allowable for that one alone, not for another.

Kālodissaṃ nāma – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cattāri mahāvikaṭāni dātuṃ – gūthaṃ, muttaṃ, chārikaṃ, mattika”nti (mahāva. 268) evaṃ ahinā daṭṭhakālaṃ uddissa anuññātaṃ, taṃ tasmiṃyeva kāle appaṭiggahitakampi vaṭṭati, na aññasmiṃ.

'Specific allowance for a time' refers to what was permitted with reference to the time of a snakebite, as in: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, four great abnormal substances: excrement, urine, ashes, and clay.' That is allowable only at that specific time, even if not formally received, but not at any other time.

Samayodissaṃ nāma – “gaṇabhojane aññatra samayā”tiādinā (pāci. 217) nayena taṃ taṃ samayaṃ uddissa anuññātā anāpattiyo, tā tasmiṃ tasmiṃyeva samaye anāpattiyo honti, na aññadā.

'Specific allowance for an occasion' refers to the exemptions from offense permitted with reference to a particular occasion, by the principle beginning, 'In a group meal, except on an occasion…' Those are exemptions from offense only on that particular occasion, and not at other times.

Desodissaṃ nāma – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, evarūpesu paccantimesu janapadesu vinayadharapañcamena gaṇena upasampada”nti (mahāva. 259) evaṃ paccantadese uddissa anuññātāni upasampadādīni, tāni tattheva vaṭṭanti, na majjhimadese.

'Specific allowance for a place' refers to ordination and so on, permitted with reference to a border region, as in: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, in such border regions, ordination by a chapter of five, with one versed in the Vinaya as the fifth.' These are allowable only there, not in the Middle Country.

Vasodissaṃ [M 2.0296] nāma – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjānī”ti (mahāva. 262) evaṃ vasānāmena anuññātaṃ[P 3.0718], taṃ ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ sabbesaṃ kappiyākappiyavasānaṃ telaṃ taṃtadatthikānaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

'Specific allowance for fat' refers to what is permitted by the name 'fat' (vasā), as in: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, fats as medicines.' This refers to the oil from the fat of all animals—whose flesh may be permissible or impermissible—with the exception of human fat. For those who have need of it, it is allowable to consume it by way of consuming oil.

Bhesajjodissaṃ [V 2.0268] nāma – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca bhesajjānī”ti (mahāva. 260-261) evaṃ bhesajjanāmena anuññātāni āhāratthaṃ pharituṃ samatthāni sappinavanītatelamadhuphāṇitanti. Tāni paṭiggahetvā tadahupurebhattaṃ yathāsukhaṃ pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sati paccaye vuttanayeneva sattāhaṃ paribhuñjitabbāni.

'Specific allowance for medicine' refers to what is permitted by the name 'medicine', as in: 'I allow, O bhikkhus, five kinds of medicine.' Thus, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses are allowed, being capable of fulfilling the purpose of food. Having received them, they may be consumed at will in the forenoon on that day; from the afternoon onward, if there is a reason, they should be consumed for seven days in the manner stated.

624. Sattāhātikkante atikkantasaññī nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti sacepi sāsapamattaṃ hoti sakiṃ vā aṅguliyā gahetvā jivhāya sāyanamattaṃ nissajjitabbameva, pācittiyañca desetabbaṃ.

624. If, after seven days have passed, one perceives it as having passed, it is an item to be forfeited and entails a pācittiya offense. Even if it is only a mustard-seed amount, or an amount just for tasting once with the tongue by taking it with a finger, it must be forfeited, and the pācittiya offense must be confessed.

Na kāyikena paribhogena paribhuñjitabbanti kāyo vā kāye aru vā na makkhetabbaṃ. Tehi makkhitāni kāsāvakattarayaṭṭhiupāhanapādakathalikamañcapīṭhādīnipi aparibhogāni. “Dvāravātapānakavāṭesupi hatthena gahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ na makkhetabba”nti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Kasāve pana pakkhipitvā dvāravātapānakavāṭāni makkhetabbānī”ti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

They should not be used for bodily application; neither the body nor a wound on the body should be smeared with them. Items smeared with them, such as dyed robes, a walking stick, sandals, a foot-wiper, a couch, or a chair, also become unusable. In the Mahāpaccarī it is said: “Even on the leaves of doors and windows, the place grasped by the hand should not be smeared.” In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā it is said: “But having put them in dye, the doors and windows may be smeared.”

Anāpatti antosattāhaṃ adhiṭṭhetīti sattāhabbhantare sappiñca telañca vasañca muddhanitelaṃ vā abbhañjanaṃ vā madhuṃ arumakkhanaṃ phāṇitaṃ gharadhūpanaṃ adhiṭṭheti, anāpatti. Sace adhiṭṭhitatelaṃ anadhiṭṭhitatelabhājane ākiritukāmo hoti, bhājane ce sukhumaṃ chiddaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ telaṃ purāṇatelena ajjhottharīyati, puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Atha mahāmukhaṃ hoti, sahasāva bahutelaṃ pavisitvā purāṇatelaṃ ajjhottharati, puna adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi. Adhiṭṭhitagatikameva hi taṃ hoti, etena nayena adhiṭṭhitatelabhājane anadhiṭṭhitatelākiraṇampi [P 3.0719] veditabbaṃ.

There is no offense if one determines it within seven days. Within seven days, if one determines ghee, oil, or animal fat as head-oil or as an ointment; honey as a wound-salve; or molasses as house-incense, there is no offense. If one wishes to pour determined oil into a vessel of undetermined oil, and if the vessel has a fine opening and the oil that enters each time is overwhelmed by the old oil, it must be determined again. But if the opening is large and much oil enters at once and overwhelms the old oil, there is no need for a new determination, for it takes on the status of what has been determined. By this method, the pouring of undetermined oil into a vessel of determined oil should also be understood.

625. Vissajjetīti ettha sace dvinnaṃ santakaṃ ekena paṭiggahitaṃ avibhattaṃ hoti, sattāhātikkame dvinnampi anāpatti, paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Sace yena paṭiggahitaṃ, so itaraṃ bhaṇati – “āvuso, imaṃ telaṃ sattāhamattaṃ paribhuñja tva”nti. So ca paribhogaṃ na karoti, kassa āpatti? Na kassacipi āpatti[M 2.0297]. Kasmā? Yena paṭiggahitaṃ tena vissajjitattā, itarassa appaṭiggahitattā.

625. Regarding 'one should relinquish': if an undivided item belonging to two monks is received by one, there is no offense for either of them when seven days have passed, but it is not allowable to consume it. If the one who received it says to the other, “Friend, you may consume this oil for seven days,” and that other monk does not consume it, whose offense is it? It is no one's offense. Why? Because it has been relinquished by the one who received it, and it has not been accepted by the other.

Vinassatīti aparibhogaṃ hoti. Cattenātiādīsu yena cittena bhesajjaṃ cattañca vantañca muttañca hoti, taṃ cittaṃ cattaṃ vantaṃ muttanti vuccati. Tena cittena puggalo anapekkhoti vuccatti, evaṃ anapekkho sāmaṇerassa datvāti attho. Idaṃ kasmā vuttaṃ? “Evaṃ [V 2.0269] antosattāhe datvā pacchā labhitvā paribhuñjantassa anāpattidassanattha”nti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero panāha – “nayidaṃ yācitabbaṃ, antosattāhe dinnassa hi puna paribhoge āpattiyeva natthi. Sattāhātikkantassa pana paribhoge anāpattidassanatthamidaṃ vutta”nti. Tasmā evaṃ dinnaṃ bhesajjaṃ sace sāmaṇero abhisaṅkharitvā vā anabhisaṅkharitvā vā tassa bhikkhuno natthukammatthaṃ dadeyya, gahetvā natthukammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace bālo hoti, dātuṃ na jānāti, aññena bhikkhunā vattabbo – “atthi te, sāmaṇera, tela”nti “āma, bhante, atthī”ti. “Āhara, therassa bhesajjaṃ karissāmā”ti. Evampi vaṭṭati. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

‘It is spoiled’ means it becomes unusable. In ‘by what is given up,’ etc., the mind with which the medicine is given up, vomited, and released is called ‘given up,’ ‘vomited,’ and ‘released.’ A person with such a mind is called ‘unconcerned.’ Thus, the meaning is giving it to a novice while being unconcerned. Why was this said? The Elder Mahāsumatthera said: “This was said to show there is no offense for one who, having given it away within seven days, receives it back later and consumes it.” But the Elder Mahāpadumatthera said: “This should not be requested back, for there is no offense in again consuming what was given away within seven days. Rather, this was said to show there is no offense in consuming it after seven days have passed.” Therefore, if a novice gives such medicine that has been given away—whether he has prepared it or not—to that monk for the purpose of nasal treatment, it should be taken and the nasal treatment should be done. If the novice is young and does not know how to give it, he should be told by another monk: “Novice, do you have oil?” “Yes, venerable sir, I have.” “Bring it, we will make medicine for the elder.” This is also allowable. The rest has a plain meaning.

Kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ, akiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ,

It arises from the Kathina; it is non-action; there is no exemption through perception; it is unintentional; it is an offense by formulation; it is a bodily action and a verbal action.

Ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It involves three mind-states and three kinds of feeling.

Bhesajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning medicine is concluded.

4. Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rains-Robe

626. Tena samayenāti vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha vassikasāṭikā anuññātāti cīvarakkhandhake visākhāvatthusmiṃ (mahāva. 349 ādayo) anuññātā. Paṭikaccevāti pureyeva.

626. ‘At that time’ refers to the training rule on the rains-robe. Therein, as for the words ‘a rains-robe is permitted,’ it was permitted in the Visākhā story in the Chapter on Robes (Mahāvagga 349 ff.). ‘Paṭikacceva’ means ‘beforehand’.

627. Māso seso gimhānanti catunnaṃ gimhamāsānaṃ eko pacchimamāso seso. Katvāti sibbanarajanakappapariyosānena niṭṭhapetvā. Karontena [P 3.0720] ca ekameva katvā samaye adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, dve adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vaṭṭanti.

627. ‘One month remains of the summer’ means that of the four summer months, one last month remains. ‘Having made’ means having completed it by finishing the sewing, dyeing, and making of the determination mark. And by one who is making it, only one should be made and determined at the proper time; it is not permissible to determine two.

Atirekamāse sese gimhāneti gimhānanāmake atirekamāse sese.

‘When an extra month of summer remains’ means when the extra month named ‘summer’ remains.

Atirekaddhamāse [M 2.0298] sese gimhāne katvā nivāsetīti ettha pana ṭhatvā vassikasāṭikāya pariyesanakkhettaṃ karaṇakkhettaṃ nivāsanakkhettaṃ adhiṭṭhānakkhettanti catubbidhaṃ khettaṃ, kucchisamayo piṭṭhisamayoti duvidho samayo, piṭṭhisamayacatukkaṃ kucchisamayacatukkanti dve catukkāni ca veditabbāni.

Now, regarding the phrase, ‘When there is more than half a month of the hot season remaining, having made it, he wears it’: here, with regard to the rains-robe, the following should be understood: the fourfold field—the field of seeking, the field of making, the field of wearing, and the field of determination; the twofold time—the belly-time and the back-time; and the two sets of four—the fourfold division of the back-time and the fourfold division of the belly-time.

Tattha jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva kāḷapakkhuposathā, ayameko addhamāso pariyesanakkhettañceva karaṇakkhettañca. Etasmiñhi antare vassikasāṭikaṃ aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ laddhaṃ kātuñca vaṭṭati, nivāsetuṃ adhiṭṭhātuñca na vaṭṭati. Kāḷapakkhuposathassa pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva āsāḷhīpuṇṇamā, ayameko [V 2.0270] addhamāso pariyesanakaraṇanivāsanānaṃ tiṇṇampi khettaṃ. Etasmiñhi antare pariyesituṃ kātuṃ nivāsetuñca vaṭṭati, adhiṭṭhātuṃyeva na vaṭṭati. Āsāḷhīpuṇṇamāsiyā pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva kattikapuṇṇamā, ime cattāro māsā pariyesanakaraṇanivāsanādhiṭṭhānānaṃ catunnaṃ khettaṃ. Etasmiñhi antare aladdhaṃ pariyesituṃ laddhaṃ kātuṃ nivāsetuṃ adhiṭṭhātuñca vaṭṭati. Idaṃ tāva catubbidhaṃ khettaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, from the day after the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla up to the observance day of the dark fortnight, this one half-month is both a field for seeking and a field for making. For during this interval, it is permissible to seek for a rains-robe that has not been obtained and to make one that has been obtained, but it is not permissible to wear it or determine it. From the day after the observance day of the dark fortnight up to the full moon of Āsāḷhī, this one half-month is a field for all three: seeking, making, and wearing. For during this interval, it is permissible to seek, make, and wear it; only determining it is not permissible. From the day after the full moon of Āsāḷhī up to the full moon of Kattika, these four months are a field for all four: seeking, making, wearing, and determining. For during this interval, it is permissible to seek for one that has not been obtained, and to make, wear, and determine one that has been obtained. This, in the first place, is to be understood as the fourfold field.

Kattikapuṇṇamāsiyā pana pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamā, ime satta māsā piṭṭhisamayo nāma. Etasmiñhi antare “kālo vassikasāṭikāyā”tiādinā nayena satuppādaṃ katvā aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ nipphādentassa iminā sikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. “Detha me vassikasāṭikacīvara”ntiādinā nayena viññattiṃ katvā nipphādentassa aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Vuttanayeneva satuppādaṃ katvā ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato nipphādentassa imināva sikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ[P 3.0721]. Viññattiṃ katvā nipphādentassa aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena anāpatti. Vuttañhetaṃ parivāre –

Then, from the day after the full moon of Kattika until the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla, these seven months are called the back-time. For during this period, for one who, having given a hint in the manner of, ‘It is time for the rains-robe,’ etc., acquires a rains-robe from an unrelated, uninvited source, there is an offense of forfeiture with confession by this training rule. For one who, having made a request in the manner of, ‘Give me a rains-robe,’ etc., acquires it from an unrelated person, there is an offense of forfeiture with confession by the training rule concerning soliciting. For one who, having given a hint in the manner stated, acquires it from a related or invited source, there is an offense of forfeiture with confession by this very training rule. For one who, having made a request, acquires it from a related or invited person, there is no offense under the training rule concerning soliciting from an unrelated person. For this was said in the Parivāra:

“Mātaraṃ cīvaraṃ yāce, no ca saṅghe pariṇataṃ;

Kenassa hoti āpatti, anāpatti ca ñātake;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 481);

‘He asks his mother for a robe, and it is not one dedicated to the Saṅgha; by what is there an offense for him, and no offense regarding a relative? This is a question considered by the wise.’ (pari. 481);

Ayañhi [M 2.0299] pañho imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttoti. Evaṃ piṭṭhisamayacatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For this question was spoken with reference to this matter. Thus, the fourfold division of the back-time should be understood.

Jeṭṭhamūlapuṇṇamāsiyā pana pacchimapāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva kattikapuṇṇamā, ime pañca māsā kucchisamayo nāma. Etasmiñhi antare vuttanayena satuppādaṃ katvā aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ nipphādentassa vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ. Ye manussā pubbepi vassikasāṭikacīvaraṃ denti, ime pana sacepi attano aññātakaappavāritā honti, vattabhedo natthi, tesu satuppādakaraṇassa anuññātattā. Viññatiṃ katvā nipphādentassa aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Idaṃ pana pakatiyā vassikasāṭikadāyakesupi [V 2.0271] hotiyeva. Vuttanayeneva satuppādaṃ katvā ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato nipphādentassa iminā sikkhāpadena anāpatti. Viññattiṃ katvā nipphādentassa aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena anāpatti. “Na vattabbā detha me”ti idañhi pariyesanakāle aññātakaappavāriteyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evaṃ kucchisamayacatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, from the day of the latter first waning moon of Jeṭṭhamūla up to the full moon of Kattika, these five months are called the 'urgent period'. Indeed, during this interval, for one who, having aroused mindfulness in the manner described, has a rains-bathing cloth made by an unrelated and uninvited person, there is an offense of wrong-doing for a breach of conduct. However, regarding those people who have also previously given rains-bathing cloths, even if they are unrelated and uninvited, there is no breach of conduct, because arousing mindfulness in them is permitted. For one who, having made a request, has it made, there is an offense of expiation with forfeiture according to the training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person. This, however, applies even to regular donors of rains-bathing cloths. For one who, having aroused mindfulness in the manner stated, has it made by a related or invited person, there is no offense under this training rule. For one who, having made a request, has it made, there is no offense under the training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person. For the statement, ‘They are not to be told, “Give me,”’ was indeed spoken with reference only to unrelated, uninvited people during the time of seeking. Thus, the fourfold division of the urgent period should be understood.

Naggo kāyaṃ ovassāpeti, āpatti dukkaṭassāti ettha udakaphusitagaṇanāya akatvā nhānapariyosānavasena payoge payoge dukkaṭena kāretabbo. So ca kho vivaṭaṅgaṇe ākāsato patitaudakeneva nhāyanto. Nhānakoṭṭhakavāpiādīsu ghaṭehi āsittaudakena vā nhāyantassa anāpatti.

Regarding the phrase, ‘If one, being naked, lets the body be rained on, there is an offense of dukkaṭa’: herein, the offense is not incurred by counting the drops of water, but a dukkaṭa should be incurred for each act of bathing, determined by its completion. And this applies only to one bathing in an open space with water falling from the sky. There is no offense for one who bathes in places such as bathing enclosures or reservoirs, or with water poured from pots.

Vassaṃ ukkaḍḍhiyatīti ettha sace katapariyesitāya vassikasāṭikāya gimhānaṃ pacchima māsaṃ khepetvā puna vassānassa paṭhamamāsaṃ ukkaḍḍhitvā gimhānaṃ pacchimamāsameva karonti, vassikasāṭikā dhovitvā nikkhipitabbā. Anadhiṭṭhitā avikappitā dve māse parihāraṃ [P 3.0722] labhati, vassūpanāyikadivase adhiṭṭhātabbā. Sace satisammosena vā appahonakabhāvena vā akatā hoti, te ca dve māse vassānassa ca cātumāsanti cha māse parihāraṃ labhati. Sace pana kattikamāse kathinaṃ attharīyati, aparepi cattāro māse labhati, evaṃ dasa māsā honti. Tato parampi satiyā paccāsāya mūlacīvaraṃ katvā ṭhapentassa ekamāsanti [M 2.0300] evaṃ ekādasa māse parihāraṃ labhati. Sace pana ekāhadvīhādivasena yāva dasāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya antovasse vā laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca, kadā adhiṭṭhātabbāti etaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu na vicāritaṃ. Laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya antodasāhe niṭṭhitā pana tasmiṃyeva antodasāhe adhiṭṭhātabbā. Dasāhātikkame niṭṭhitā tadaheva adhiṭṭhātabbā. Dasāhe appahonte cīvarakālaṃ nātikkametabbāti ayaṃ no attanomati. Kasmā? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ; vassikasāṭikaṃ vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ, tato paraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā vassūpanāyikato pubbe dasāhātikkamepi anāpatti. “Dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti (pārā. 462) ca vuttaṃ. Tasmā ekāhadvīhādivasena yāva dasāhānāgatāya vassūpanāyikāya antovasse vā laddhā ceva niṭṭhitā ca vuttanayeneva antodasāhe vā tadahu vā adhiṭṭhātabbā, dasāhe appahonte cīvarakālaṃ nātikkametabbā.

Herein, regarding 'the Rains is postponed': if, when the rains-bathing cloth has been sought and made, they, having passed the last month of the hot season, then postpone the first month of the Rains and make it the last month of the hot season itself, in that case, the rains-bathing cloth should be washed and put away. If undetermined or unshared, it obtains a two-month allowance; it should be determined on the day of the Rains-residence. If, due to forgetfulness or insufficiency, it has not been made, it obtains an allowance for those two months and the four months of the Rains, thus six months. However, if the Kathina is spread in the month of Kattika, another four months are obtained, thus making ten months. Beyond that, for one who, with hopeful anticipation, makes a basic robe and keeps it, an allowance for one month is obtained, thus making eleven months. But if it is both obtained and completed within one day, two days, and so on, up to ten days before the Rains-residence, or within the Rains, when should it be determined? This has not been examined in the commentaries. However, if completed within ten days from the day it was obtained, it should be determined within those very ten days. If completed after ten days have passed, it should be determined on that very day. If it is insufficient within ten days, the robe-period should not be overstepped—this is our own opinion. Why? For it is said: ‘I allow, monks, the determination of the triple robe, not its assignment; the rains-bathing cloth is to be determined for the four months of the Rains, and beyond that, it is to be assigned.’ Therefore, even if ten days are exceeded before the Rains-residence, there is no offense. And it is said: ‘An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days.’ Therefore, if it is both obtained and completed within one day, two days, and so on, up to ten days before the Rains-residence, or within the Rains, it should be determined, according to the method stated, either within those ten days or on that very day. If it is insufficient within ten days, the robe-period should not be overstepped.

Tattha siyā “vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātu”nti vacanato “cātumāsabbhantare yadā vā tadā [V 2.0272] vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Yadi evaṃ, “kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ yāva ābādhā adhiṭṭhātu”nti vuttaṃ sāpi, ca dasāhaṃ atikkāmetabbā siyā. Evañca sati “dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti idaṃ virujjhati. Tasmā yathāvuttameva gahetabbaṃ, aññaṃ vā acalaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā chaḍḍetabbaṃ. Apica kurundiyampi nissaggiyāvasāne [P 3.0723] vuttaṃ – “kadā adhiṭṭhātabbā? Laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya antodasāhe niṭṭhitā pana tasmiṃyeva antodasāhe adhiṭṭhātabbā. Yadi nappahoti yāva kattikapuṇṇamā parihāraṃ labhatī”ti.

Herein, there might be the view: 'Because it is said, "to be determined for the four months of the Rains," it is permissible to determine it at any time whatsoever within the four months.' If so, then regarding the statement, 'the itch-covering cloth is to be determined for as long as the illness lasts,' that too could be made to exceed ten days. And if this were so, this statement, ‘An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days,’ would be contradicted. Therefore, it should be taken just as stated, or, having found another unshakeable reason, this should be discarded. Moreover, in the Kurundī commentary as well, it is stated at the end of the Nissaggiya section: 'When should it be determined? If it is completed within ten days from the day it is obtained, it must be determined within those very ten days. If it is insufficient, an allowance is obtained until the full moon of Kattika.'

630. Acchinnacīvarassāti etaṃ vassikasāṭikameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tesañhi naggānaṃ kāyovassāpane anāpatti. Ettha ca mahagghavassikasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā nhāyantassa corupaddavo āpadā nāma. Sesamettha uttānameva.

630. This phrase 'of one whose robe has been snatched away' is said with reference to the rains-bathing cloth itself. For indeed, for them, being naked, there is no offense in letting the body be drenched by the rain. And here, for one bathing having put on an expensive rains-bathing cloth, the danger from thieves is called a 'calamity'. The rest here is self-evident.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ[M 2.0301], kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It arises from six sources, is an action, is not exempt through perception, is unintentional, is an offense by regulation, is an action of body and speech, involves three states of consciousness, and involves three kinds of feeling.

Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Rains-Bathing Cloth is concluded.

5. Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Snatching of a Robe

631. Tena samayenāti cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha yampi tyāhanti yampi te ahaṃ. So kira “mama pattacīvaraupāhanapaccattharaṇāni vahanto mayā saddhiṃ cārikaṃ pakkamissatī”ti adāsi. Tenevamāha. Acchindīti balakkārena aggahesi, sakasaññāya gahitattā panassa pārājikaṃ natthi, kilametvā gahitattā āpatti paññattā.

631. ‘At that time’ introduces the training rule concerning the snatching of a robe. Therein, `yampi tyāhaṃ` means `yampi te ahaṃ`. He, it is said, gave it thinking, ‘Carrying my bowl, robes, sandals, and bed-coverings, he will depart on a journey with me.’ Therefore, he spoke thus. ‘Snatched’ means he took it by force; however, because it was taken with the perception that it was his own, there is no pārājika offense for him, but because it was taken after causing distress, an offense was laid down.

633. Sayaṃ acchindati nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti ekaṃ cīvaraṃ ekābaddhāni ca bahūni acchindato ekā āpatti. Ekato abaddhāni visuṃ visuṃ ṭhitāni ca bahūni acchindato “saṅghāṭiṃ āhara, uttarāsaṅgaṃ āharā”ti evaṃ āharāpayato ca vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo. “Mayā dinnāni sabbāni āharā”ti vadatopi ekavacaneneva sambahulā āpattiyo.

633. Regarding 'If one personally snatches, it is an offense of pācittiya entailing forfeiture': for one who snatches one robe, and for one who snatches many robes bound together as one, there is a single offense. For one who snatches many robes not bound together and standing separately, and for one who has them brought by saying, ‘Bring the double-layered robe; bring the upper robe,’ there are offenses according to the count of the items. Even for one who says, ‘Bring all that were given by me,’ there are multiple offenses with just a single utterance.

Aññaṃ āṇāpeti āpatti dukkaṭassāti “cīvaraṃ gaṇhā”ti āṇāpeti, ekaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Āṇatto bahūni gaṇhāti, ekaṃ pācittiyaṃ “saṅghāṭiṃ gaṇha, uttarāsaṅgaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadato vācāya [V 2.0273] vācāya dukkaṭaṃ. “Mayā dinnāni sabbāni gaṇhā”ti vadato ekavācāya sambahulā āpattiyo.

Regarding 'If one orders another, it is an offense of wrong-doing': if one commands, ‘Take the robe,’ there is one offense of wrong-doing. If the one who is commanded takes many robes, there is one pācittiya offense. For one who says, ‘Take the double-layered robe; take the upper robe,’ there is an offense of wrong-doing for each utterance. For one who says, ‘Take all that were given by me,’ there are multiple offenses with a single utterance.

634. Aññaṃ parikkhāranti vikappanupagapacchimacīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā yaṃ kiñci antamaso sūcimpi. Veṭhetvā ṭhapitasūcīsupi vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭāni. Sithilaveṭhitāsu evaṃ. Gāḷhaṃ katvā baddhāsu pana ekameva dukkaṭanti mahāpaccariyaṃ [P 3.0724] vuttaṃ. Sūcighare pakkhittāsupi eseva nayo. Thavikāya pakkhipitvā sithilabaddha gāḷhabaddhesu tikaṭukādīsu bhesajjesupi eseva nayo.

634. ‘Another requisite’ means anything whatsoever, excepting the last robe that is suitable for vikappana, even down to a needle. Even for needles stored after being wrapped, there are offenses of wrong-doing according to the count of the items. It is the same for those loosely wrapped. But for those that are made tight and bound, there is only one offense of wrong-doing—thus it is said in the Mahāpaccarī. This is the same principle for those placed in a needle case. This is also the same principle for medicines such as the three pungent spices, etc., placed in a bag, whether loosely bound or tightly bound.

635. So [M 2.0302] vā detīti “bhante, tumhākaṃyeva idaṃ sāruppa”nti evaṃ vā deti, atha vā pana “āvuso, mayaṃ tuyhaṃ ‘vattapaṭipattiṃ karissati, amhākaṃ santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhissati, dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇissatī’ti cīvaraṃ adamha, so dāni tvaṃ na vattaṃ karosi, na upajjhaṃ gaṇhāsi, na dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāsī”ti evamādīni vutto “bhante, cīvaratthāya maññe bhaṇatha, idaṃ vo cīvara”nti deti, evampi so vā deti. Disāpakkantaṃ vā pana daharaṃ “nivattetha na”nti bhaṇati, so na nivattati. Cīvaraṃ gahetvā rundhathāti, evaṃ ce nivattati, sādhu. Sace “pattacīvaratthāya maññe tumhe bhaṇatha, gaṇhatha na”nti deti. Evampi so vā deti, vibbhantaṃ vā disvā “mayaṃ tuyhaṃ ‘vattaṃ karissatī’ti pattacīvaraṃ adamha, so dāni tvaṃ vibbhamitvā carasī”ti vadati. Itaro “gaṇhatha tumhākaṃ pattacīvara”nti deti, evampi so vā deti. “Mama santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhantasseva demi, aññattha gaṇhantassa na demi. Vattaṃ karontasseva demi, akarontassa na demi, dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇantasseva demi, apariyāpuṇantassa na demi, avibbhamantasseva demi, vibbhamantassa na demī”ti evaṃ pana dātuṃ na vaṭṭati, dadato dukkaṭaṃ.
