Āharāpetuṃ pana vaṭṭati. Cajitvā dinnaṃ acchinditvā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

635. Regarding ‘Or he gives it’: he gives it saying, ‘Venerable sir, this is suitable only for you,’ or else, having been told such things as, ‘Friend, we gave you a robe thinking, “He will perform his duties and observances, he will take a preceptor from us, he will study the Dhamma,” but now you do not perform your duties, you do not take a preceptor, you do not study the Dhamma,’ he says, ‘Venerable sirs, I think you speak for the sake of the robe; this is your robe,’ and gives it. In this way too, it is ‘or he gives it’. Or else, one says of a junior monk who has departed to another region, ‘Have him return.’ He does not return. One says, ‘Take his robe and stop him.’ If he returns because of this, it is good. If he says, ‘I think you speak for the sake of the bowl and robe; take them,’ and gives them, in this way too, it is ‘or he gives it’. Or, having seen one who has disrobed, one says, ‘We gave you a bowl and robe thinking, “He will perform his duties,” but now you have disrobed and go about.’ The other says, ‘Take your bowl and robe,’ and gives them; in this way too, it is ‘or he gives it’. However, it is not proper to give saying, ‘I give only to one who takes a preceptor from me; I do not give to one who takes one elsewhere. I give only to one who performs his duties; I do not give to one who does not. I give only to one who studies the Dhamma; I do not give to one who does not study it. I give only to one who does not disrobe; I do not give to one who disrobes.’ For one who gives thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, it is proper to have it brought back. One who snatches and takes what was given after it was relinquished should be made to pay its value. The rest here is self-evident.

Tisamuṭṭhānaṃ – kāyacittato vācācittato kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti, kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, dukkhavedananti.

It has three origins – it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action, subject to release through perception, intentional, a worldly fault, a bodily action and verbal action, with unwholesome consciousness, and has a painful feeling.

Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the snatching of robes is concluded.

6. Suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread

636. Tena [V 2.0274] samayenāti suttaviññattisikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha khomanti khomavākehi katasuttaṃ. Kappāsikanti kappāsato nibbattaṃ. Koseyyanti kosiyaṃsūhi kantitvā katasuttaṃ. Kambalanti eḷakalomasuttaṃ. Sāṇanti sāṇavākasuttaṃ. Bhaṅganti pāṭekkaṃ vākasuttamevāti eke. Etehi pañcahi [P 3.0725] missetvā katasuttaṃ pana “bhaṅga”nti veditabbaṃ.

636. The training rule on requesting thread begins with the words 'At that time'. Herein, 'khoma' means thread made from flax fibers. 'Kappāsika' means thread produced from cotton. 'Koseyya' means thread made by spinning silk filaments. 'Kambala' means thread from sheep's wool. 'Sāṇa' means thread from hemp fibers. 'Bhaṅga' means a distinct type of bark fiber thread, according to some. However, thread made by mixing these five should be understood as 'bhaṅga'.

Vāyāpeti payoge payoge dukkaṭanti sace tantavāyassa turivemādīni natthi, tāni “araññato āharissāmī”ti vāsiṃ vā pharasuṃ vā [M 2.0303] niseti, tato paṭṭhāya yaṃ yaṃ upakaraṇatthāya vā cīvaravāyanatthāya vā karoti, sabbattha tantavāyassa payoge payoge bhikkhussa dukkaṭaṃ. Dīghato vidatthimatte tiriyañca hatthamatte vīte nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “yāva pariyosānaṃ vāyāpentassa phalake phalake nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ. Tampi idameva pamāṇaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Vikappanupagapacchimañhi cīvarasaṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti.

Regarding 'When one causes to be woven, there is a dukkaṭa offense at every effort': if a weaver lacks tools such as the shuttle and loom, and thinking, 'I will bring them from the forest,' he sharpens an adze or an axe, then from that point onward, for whatever he does for the purpose of making tools or for weaving the robe, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the bhikkhu at every effort of the weaver. When a piece is woven to the length of one span and the breadth of one cubit, it becomes a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said: 'For one who has weaving done until its completion, at each roll, there is a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture.' This should be understood as being stated with reference to this very same measurement, for it is the final cloth fit for vikappana that is reckoned as a robe.

Apicettha evaṃ vinicchayo veditabbo – suttaṃ tāva sāmaṃ viññāpitaṃ akappiyaṃ, sesaṃ ñātakādivasena uppannaṃ kappiyaṃ. Tantavāyopi aññātakaappavārito viññattiyā laddho akappiyo, seso kappiyo. Tattha akappiyasuttaṃ akappiyatantavāyena vāyāpentassa pubbe vuttanayena nissaggiyaṃ. Teneva pana kappiyasuttaṃ vāyāpentassa yathā pubbe nissaggiyaṃ, evaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Teneva kappiyaṃ akappiyañca suttaṃ vāyāpentassa yadi pacchimacīvarappamāṇena eko paricchedo suddhakappiyasuttamayo, eko akappiyasuttamayoti evaṃ kedārabaddhaṃ viya cīvaraṃ hoti, akappiyasuttamaye paricchede pācittiyaṃ, itarasmiṃ tatheva dukkaṭaṃ. Yadi tato ūnaparicchedā honti, antamaso acchimaṇḍalappamāṇāpi, sabbaparicchedesu paricchedagaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Atha ekantarikena vā suttena dīghato vā kappiyaṃ tiriyaṃ akappiyaṃ katvā vītaṃ hoti, phalake phalake dukkaṭaṃ. Kappiyatantavāyenapi akappiyasuttaṃ vāyāpentassa yathā pubbe nissaggiyaṃ, evaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Teneva kappiyañca akappiyañca suttaṃ vāyāpentassa sace pacchimacīvarappamāṇā ūnakā vā akappiyasuttaparicchedā honti, tesu paricchedagaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Kappiyasuttaparicchedesu [P 3.0726] anāpatti. Atha ekantarikena vā suttena dīghato vā kappiyaṃ tiriyaṃ akappiyaṃ katvā vītaṃ hoti, phalake phalake dukkaṭaṃ.

Furthermore, the ruling here should be understood thus: Firstly, thread requested by oneself is unallowable; the rest, which has arisen through relatives and so on, is allowable. A weaver, too, who is not a relative and not invited, if obtained by request, is unallowable; the rest are allowable. Therein, for one who has unallowable thread woven by an unallowable weaver, it is an offense entailing forfeiture according to the method previously stated. However, for one who has allowable thread woven by that same weaver, just as there was an offense entailing forfeiture before, so there is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who has both allowable and unallowable thread woven by that same weaver, if the robe is like a paddy field divided by embankments, such that one section of the size of the minimum robe is made purely of allowable thread and one section is made of unallowable thread, then in the section made of unallowable thread, there is a pācittiya offense, and in the other, likewise a dukkaṭa offense. If the sections are smaller than that, even down to the size of the pupil of an eye, in all sections, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each section counted. Or, if it is woven with alternating threads, or by making the warp allowable and the weft unallowable, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each roll. For one who has unallowable thread woven by an allowable weaver, just as there was an offense entailing forfeiture before, so there is a dukkaṭa offense. For one who has both allowable and unallowable thread woven by that same weaver, if there are sections of unallowable thread of the size of the minimum robe or smaller, in those sections, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each section counted. In the sections made of allowable thread, there is no offense.

Yadi [V 2.0275] pana dve tantavāyā honti, eko kappiyo eko akappiyo, suttañca akappiyaṃ, te ce vārena vinanti, akappiyatantavāyena vīte phalake phalake pācittiyaṃ, ūnatare dukkaṭaṃ. Itarena vīte ubhayattha dukkaṭaṃ. Sace dvepi vemaṃ gahetvā ekato vinanti, phalake phalake pācittiyaṃ. Atha suttaṃ kappiyaṃ, cīvarañca kedārabaddhādīhi saparicchedaṃ, akappiyatantavāyena vīte paricchede paricchede dukkaṭaṃ, itarena vīte anāpatti. Sace dvepi [M 2.0304] vemaṃ gahetvā ekato vinanti, phalake phalake dukkaṭaṃ. Atha suttampi kappiyañca akappiyañca, te ce vārena vinanti, akappiyatantavāyena akappiyasuttamayesu pacchimacīvarappamāṇesu paricchedesu vītesu paricchedagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ. Ūnakataresu kappiyasuttamayesu ca dukkaṭaṃ. Kappiyatantavāyena akappiyasuttamayesu pamāṇayuttesu vā ūnakesu vā dukkaṭameva. Kappiyasuttamayesu anāpatti.

If, however, there are two weavers, one allowable and one unallowable, and the thread is unallowable, and they weave in turns: for each roll woven by the unallowable weaver to the size of the minimum robe, there is a pācittiya offense; for a smaller amount, a dukkaṭa offense. For what is woven by the other weaver, there is a dukkaṭa offense in both cases. If both, taking the shuttle, weave together, there is a pācittiya offense for each roll. Or, if the thread is allowable, and the robe has sections like a paddy field: for each section woven by the unallowable weaver, there is a dukkaṭa offense; for what is woven by the other, there is no offense. If both, taking the shuttle, weave together, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each roll. Or, if the thread is both allowable and unallowable, and they weave in turns: when sections made of unallowable thread of the size of the minimum robe are woven by the unallowable weaver, there is a pācittiya offense for each section counted. For smaller sections and for those made of allowable thread, there is a dukkaṭa offense. When woven by the allowable weaver, in sections made of unallowable thread, whether of the full size or smaller, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. In sections made of allowable thread, there is no offense.

Atha ekantarikena vā suttena dīghato vā akappiyaṃ tiriyaṃ kappiyaṃ katvā vinanti, ubhopi vā te vemaṃ gahetvā ekato vinanti, aparicchede cīvare phalake phalake dukkaṭaṃ, saparicchede paricchedavasena dukkaṭānīti. Ayaṃ pana attho mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ apākaṭo, mahāpaccariyādīsu pākaṭo. Idha sabbākāreneva pākaṭo.

Or, if they weave with alternating thread, or by making the warp unallowable and the weft allowable; or if both of them, taking the shuttle, weave together: in a robe without sections, there is a dukkaṭa offense for each roll; in one with sections, there are dukkaṭa offenses according to the sections. This meaning, however, is not evident in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, but it is evident in the Mahāpaccarī and other commentaries. Here, it is evident in every way.

Sace suttampi kappiyaṃ, tantavāyopi kappiyo ñātakappavārito vā mūlena vā payojito, vāyāpanapaccayā anāpatti. Dasāhātikkamanapaccayā pana āpattiṃ rakkhantena vikappanupagappamāṇamatte vīte tante ṭhitaṃyeva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Dasāhātikkamena niṭṭhāpiyamānañhi nissaggiyaṃ bhaveyyāti. Ñātakādīhi tantaṃ āropetvā “tumhākaṃ, bhante, idaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti niyyātitepi eseva nayo.

If the thread is allowable, and the weaver is also allowable—being a relative, one who has been invited, or one who has been engaged for a price—there is no offense on account of causing it to be woven. However, one who is guarding against an offense on account of exceeding ten days should make a determination over the cloth while it is still on the loom, once a piece of the size fit for vikappana has been woven. For if it were to be completed after exceeding ten days, it would become subject to forfeiture. This is the same method to be applied even when relatives and others have put the cloth on the loom and have handed it over, saying, 'Venerable sirs, you may take this robe.'

Sace tantavāyo evaṃ payojito vā sayaṃ dātukāmo vā hutvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ [P 3.0727] asukadivase nāma vāyitvā ṭhapessāmī”ti vadati, bhikkhu ca tena paricchinnadivasato dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

If a weaver, having been engaged in this way or being desirous of giving it himself, says, 'Venerable sir, I will weave a robe for you and set it aside on such-and-such a day,' and the bhikkhu lets ten days pass from the day specified by the weaver, it is a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture.

Sace pana tantavāyo “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ vāyitvā sāsanaṃ pesessāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, tena pesitabhikkhu pana tassa bhikkhuno na āroceti, añño disvā vā sutvā vā “tumhākaṃ, bhante, cīvaraṃ niṭṭhita”nti āroceti, etassa ārocanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā [V 2.0276] pana tena pesitoyeva āroceti, tassa vacanaṃ sutadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

Furthermore, if a weaver, having said, 'I will weave a robe for you and send a message,' does just so, but the monk sent by him does not inform that monk (for whom the robe was intended), and another person, having seen or heard, informs him, saying, 'Venerable sir, your robe is finished,' the announcement of this person is not the standard. However, when the very one sent by him informs him, for the monk who lets ten days pass starting from the day he heard that statement, it is a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture.

Sace tantavāyo “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ vāyitvā kassaci hatthe pahiṇissāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, cīvaraṃ gahetvā gatabhikkhu pana attano pariveṇe ṭhapetvā tassa na āroceti, añño koci bhaṇati [M 2.0305] “api, bhante, adhunā ābhataṃ cīvaraṃ sundara”nti? “Kuhiṃ, āvuso, cīvara”nti? “Itthannāmassa hatthe pesita”nti. Etassapi vacanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana so bhikkhu cīvaraṃ deti, laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana vāyāpanamūlaṃ adinnaṃ hoti, yāva kākaṇikamattampi avasiṭṭhaṃ, tāva rakkhati.

If a weaver, having said, 'I will weave a robe for you and send it by the hand of someone,' does just so, but the monk who took the robe, having placed it in his own monastic cell, does not inform him (the owner), and some other person says, 'Venerable sir, is the robe just brought beautiful?' and he asks, 'Friend, where is the robe?' and the reply is, 'It was sent by the hand of so-and-so.' The statement of this person is also not the standard. However, when that monk (who brought it) gives the robe, for the one who lets ten days pass starting from the day it was received, it is a pācittiya offense entailing forfeiture. But if the payment for weaving has not been given, and as long as even the amount of a kākaṇika remains, he may keep it.

640. Anāpatti cīvaraṃ sibbetunti cīvarasibbanatthāya suttaṃ viññāpentassa anāpattīti attho. Āyogetiādīsupi nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ, āyogādinimittaṃ viññāpentassa anāpattīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

640. There is no offense: 'To sew a robe' means there is no offense for one who requests thread for the purpose of sewing a robe. Also in such phrases as 'āyoge' (for a weaver's beam), the locative case is used in the sense of purpose; it is said that there is no offense for one who makes a request for the purpose of a weaver's beam and so on. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It has six origins, is an action, is not absolved by perception, is unintentional, is an offense by designation, is a bodily action and a verbal action, arises from three states of consciousness, and is accompanied by three kinds of feeling.

Suttaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning requesting thread is concluded.

7. Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Master Weavers

641. Tena samayenāti mahāpesakārasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha suttaṃ dhārayitvāti suttaṃ tuletvā palaparicchedaṃ katvā. Appitanti ghanaṃ. Suvītanti suṭṭhu vītaṃ, sabbaṭṭhānesu samaṃ katvā vītaṃ. Suppavāyitanti suṭṭhu pavāyitaṃ sabbaṭṭhānesu samaṃ katvā tante pasāritaṃ. Suvilekhitanti lekhaniyā suṭṭhu vilikhitaṃ. Suvitacchitanti kocchena suṭṭhu vitacchitaṃ, suniddhotanti attho. Paṭibaddhanti vekallaṃ[P 3.0728]. Tanteti tante dīghato pasāraṇeyeva upanetvāti attho.

641. 'At that time' introduces the training rule concerning master weavers. Therein, 'having weighed the thread' means having weighed the thread and determined its measure in palas. 'Appita' means dense. 'Suvīta' means well-woven, made even in all places and woven. 'Suppavāyita' means well-spread, spread out evenly in all places on the loom. 'Suvilekhita' means well-scratched with a shuttle. 'Suvitacchita' means well-combed with a brush; the meaning is well-cleaned. 'Paṭibaddha' means defective. 'Tante' means having brought it onto the loom only by stretching it lengthwise; this is the meaning.

642. Tatra ce so bhikkhūti yatra gāme vā nigame vā te tantavāyā tatra. Vikappaṃ āpajjeyyāti [V 2.0277] visiṭṭhaṃ kappaṃ adhikavidhānaṃ āpajjeyya. Pāḷiyaṃ pana yenākārena vikappaṃ āpanno hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ kho, āvuso”tiādi vuttaṃ.

642. 'And if that monk there': 'there' means in whatever village or market town those weavers are. 'Should arrive at a special arrangement' means he should undertake a distinguished arrangement, an additional provision. Furthermore, in the Pāḷi text, to show in what manner he arrived at this special arrangement, the passage beginning, 'This, friend...' was spoken.

Dhammampi bhaṇatīti dhammakathampi katheti, “tassa vacanena āyataṃ vā vitthataṃ vā appitaṃ vā”ti suttavaḍḍhanaākārameva dasseti.

'He also speaks the Dhamma' means he also gives a Dhamma talk. The phrase 'by his word... long, or wide, or dense' shows only the manner of increasing the thread.

Pubbe [M 2.0306] appavāritoti cīvarasāmikehi pubbe appavārito hutvā. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

'Not having been invited beforehand' means not having been invited beforehand by the owners of the robe. The rest is of clear meaning.

Chasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ,

It has six origins, is an action, is not absolved by perception, is unintentional, is an offense by designation, and is a bodily action and a verbal action.

Ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It arises from three states of consciousness and is accompanied by three kinds of feeling.

Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning master weavers is concluded.

8. Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning an Emergency Robe

646-9. Tena samayenāti accekacīvarasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha dasāhānāgatanti dasa ahāni dasāhaṃ, tena dasāhena anāgatā dasāhānāgatā, dasāhena asampattāti attho, taṃ dasāhānāgataṃ, accantasaṃyogavasena bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tenevassa padabhājane “dasāhānāgatāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Pavāraṇāyāti idaṃ pana yā sā dasāhānāgatāti vuttā, taṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ asammohatthaṃ anupayogavacanaṃ.

'At that time' refers to the training rule concerning an emergency robe. Therein, 'not arrived within ten days' (`dasāhānāgata`) means: ten days are a ten-day period (`dasāha`); not yet arrived within that ten-day period is `dasāhānāgatā`; not yet reached within ten days, this is the meaning. That term, `dasāhānāgataṃ`, is a word in the accusative case used in the locative sense by way of continuous connection. For that very reason, in its word analysis, it is stated as `dasāhānāgatāyā`. As for this word `pavāraṇāya`, it is a word not in direct grammatical construction, stated in order to show, in its own form and for the purpose of non-bewilderment, that which was called `dasāhānāgatā`.

Kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamanti paṭhamakattikatemāsikapuṇṇamaṃ. Idhāpi paṭhamapadassa anupayogattā purimanayeneva bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “‘yato paṭṭhāya paṭhamamahāpavāraṇā dasāhānāgatā’ti vuccati, sacepi tāni divasāni accantameva bhikkhuno accekacīvaraṃ uppajjeyya, ‘accekaṃ ida’nti jānamānena bhikkhunā sabbampi paṭiggahetabba”nti. Tena pavāraṇāmāsassa juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭhāya uppannassa cīvarassa nidhānakālo dassito hoti. Kāmañcesa “dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti imināva siddho, atthuppattivasena pana apubbaṃ viya atthaṃ dassetvā sikkhāpadaṃ [P 3.0729] ṭhapitaṃ.

'The Kattika three-month full moon' means the first Kattika three-month full moon. Here too, because the first word (`dasāhānāgataṃ`) is used as a qualifier, just as by the previous method, it is a word in the accusative case used in the locative sense. This is what is said: 'Starting from when the first great Pavāraṇā is said to be ten days away, if during those days an emergency robe should arise for a bhikkhu without interruption, a bhikkhu, knowing, “This is an emergency robe,” should accept all of it.' By that, the time for keeping a robe that has arisen starting from the fifth day of the waxing moon of the Pavāraṇā month is shown. And although this is indeed established by this very rule, “An extra robe is to be kept for ten days at most,” the training rule was laid down, showing a meaning as if it were new, by way of the arising of the matter.

Accekacīvaranti accāyikacīvaraṃ vuccati, tassa pana accāyikabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “senāya vā gantukāmo hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saddhāti iminā saddhāmattakameva dassitaṃ. Pasādoti [V 2.0278] iminā suppasannā balavasaddhā. Etaṃ accekacīvaraṃ nāmāti etaṃ imehi kāraṇehi dātukāmena dūtaṃ vā pesetvā sayaṃ vā āgantvā “vassāvāsikaṃ dassāmī”ti evaṃ ārocitaṃ cīvaraṃ accekacīvaraṃ nāma hotī. Chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāya [M 2.0307] pana uppannaṃ anaccekacīvarampi paccuddharitvā ṭhapitacīvarampi etaṃ parihāraṃ labhatiyeva.

'An emergency robe' (`accekacīvara`) is called a robe for an urgent matter (`accāyikacīvara`). However, to show its nature as being for an urgent matter, “or he wishes to go with an army,” etc., is said. Therein, by this word `saddhā` (faith), mere faith is shown. By this word `pasādo` (confidence), very clear, strong faith is shown. This is what is called an emergency robe: a robe that is announced thus, “I will give a rains-residence robe,” by one who wishes to give for these reasons, having either sent a messenger or come in person, is called an emergency robe. However, starting from the sixth day, even a non-emergency robe that has arisen, and a robe that has been set aside after having been withdrawn from determination, certainly obtains this allowance.

Saññāṇaṃ katvā nikkhipitabbanti kiñci nimittaṃ katvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Kasmā etaṃ vuttaṃ? Yadi hi taṃ pure pavāraṇāya vibhajanti. Yena gahitaṃ, tena chinnavassena na bhavitabbaṃ. Sace pana hoti, taṃ cīvaraṃ saṅghikameva hoti. Tato sallakkhetvā sukhaṃ dātuṃ bhavissatīti.

'Having made a sign, it should be set aside' means it should be set aside after making some mark. Why was this said? For if they divide it before the Pavāraṇā, the one by whom it was taken should not be one with a broken rains-residence. But if he is, that robe belongs only to the Saṅgha. Then, having taken note of the mark, it will be easy to give it back.

650. Accekacīvare accekacīvarasaññīti evamādi vibhajitvā gahitameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace pana avibhattaṃ hoti, saṅghassa vā bhaṇḍāgāre, cīvarasamayātikkamepi anāpatti. Iti atirekacīvarassa dasāhaṃ parihāro. Akatassa vassikasāṭikacīvarassa anatthate kathine pañca māsā, vasse ukkaḍḍhite cha māsā, atthate kathine apare cattāro māsā. Hemantassa pacchime divase mūlacīvarādhiṭṭhānavasena aparopi eko māsoti ekādasa māsā parihāro. Satiyā paccāsāya mūlacīvarassa eko māso, accekacīvarassa anatthate kathine ekādasadivasādhiko māso, atthate kathine ekādasadivasādhikā pañca māsā, tato paraṃ ekadivasampi parihāro natthīti veditabbaṃ.

650. “Perceiving an emergency robe as an emergency robe,” and so on, is said with reference only to that which has been taken after being divided. But if it is undivided, or in the Saṅgha's storeroom, there is no offense even when the robe-time has passed. Thus, for an extra robe, the allowance is ten days. For an unmade rains-cloth robe: when the Kathina is not spread, five months; when the rains-residence is postponed, six months; when the Kathina is spread, another four months. On the last day of the cool season, by way of determining it as the basic robe, there is another one month; thus, the allowance is eleven months. When there is expectation of a robe, for the basic robe, the allowance is one month. For an emergency robe: when the Kathina is not spread, the allowance is one month plus eleven days; when the Kathina is spread, the allowance is five months plus eleven days. Beyond that, it should be understood that there is no allowance for even one day.

Anaccekacīvareti accekacīvarasadise aññasmiṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

'Regarding a non-emergency robe' (`anaccekacīvare`): this refers to another robe similar to an emergency robe. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ – akiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

It has its origin in the Kathina, is non-action, is not absolved by perception, is unintentional, is an offense by designation, is a bodily action and a verbal action, arises from three states of consciousness, and is accompanied by three kinds of feeling.

Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning an Emergency Robe is concluded.

9. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Peril

652. Tena [P 3.0730] samayenāti sāsaṅkasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha vutthavassā āraññakesūti te pubbepi araññeyeva vihariṃsu. Dubbalacīvarattā pana paccayavasena gāmantasenāsane vassaṃ vasitvā niṭṭhitacīvarā hutvā “idāni nippalibodhā samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmā”ti āraññakesu senāsanesu [M 2.0308][V 2.0279] viharanti. Kattikacorakāti kattikamāse corā. Paripātentīti upaddavanti, tattha tattha ādhāvitvā uttāsenti palāpenti. Antaraghare nikkhipitunti antogāme nikkhipituṃ. Bhagavā yasmā paccayā nāma dhammena samena dullabhā, sallekhavā hi bhikkhu mātarampi viññāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā cīvaraguttatthaṃ antaraghare nikkhipituṃ anujānāti. Bhikkhūnaṃ pana anurūpattā araññavāsaṃ na paṭikkhipi.

652. At that time—this is the training rule concerning peril. Therein, those who had spent the rains in wilderness dwellings means: those monks lived only in the wilderness even before. However, because their robes were inadequate, due to the need for requisites they spent the rains retreat in lodgings at the edge of a village. Having completed their robes, thinking, “Now, free from anxiety, we will practice the ascetic’s duty,” they live in wilderness dwellings. Kattika thieves means thieves in the month of Kattika. They assault means they harass; running here and there, they frighten them and cause them to flee. To deposit it within an inhabited area means to deposit it within a village. Because requisites are difficult to obtain righteously and properly—indeed, a monk practicing effacement cannot even make a request of his mother—therefore, for the sake of protecting the robe, the Blessed One allows it to be deposited within an inhabited area. However, he did not forbid wilderness dwelling, as it was suitable for monks.

653. Upavassaṃ kho panāti ettha upavassanti upavassa; upavasitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasampajjantiādīsu viya hi ettha anunāsiko daṭṭhabbo. Vassaṃ upagantvā vasitvā cāti attho. Imassa ca padassa “tathārūpesu bhikkhu senāsanesu viharanto”ti iminā sambandho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Vassaṃ upagantvā vasitvā ca tato paraṃ pacchimakattikapuṇṇamapariyosānakālaṃ yāni kho pana tāni āraññakāni senāsanāni sāsaṅkasammatāni sappaṭibhayāni; tathārūpesu bhikkhu senāsanesu viharanto ākaṅkhamāno tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ antaraghare nikkhipeyyāti. Yasmā pana yo vassaṃ upagantvā yāva paṭhamakattikapuṇṇamaṃ vasati, so vuṭṭhavassānaṃ abbhantaro hoti, tasmā idaṃ atigahanaṃ byañjanavicāraṇaṃ akatvā padabhājane kevalaṃ cīvaranikkhepārahaṃ puggalaṃ dassetuṃ “vuṭṭhavassāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tassāpi “bhikkhu senāsanesu viharanto”ti iminā sambandho. Ayañhi ettha attho “vuṭṭhavassānaṃ bhikkhu senāsanesu viharanto”ti evarūpānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abbhantare yo koci bhikkhūti vuttaṃ hoti.

653. In the phrase Upavassaṃ kho pana, `upavassaṃ` means having approached the rains (`upavassa`); it is said to mean having stayed (`upavasitvā`). Indeed, as in words like `upasampajjanti`, the nasal sound should be understood here. The meaning is: having approached the rains (`vassaṃ upagantvā`) and having stayed (`vasitvā ca`). And this phrase is connected with “a bhikkhu dwelling in such lodgings.” What is being said? Having approached the rains and having stayed, thereafter, until the time ending with the later Kattika full moon, with regard to those wilderness lodgings that are regarded as perilous and are fraught with danger, a bhikkhu dwelling in such lodgings may, if he wishes, deposit one of the three robes within an inhabited area. However, because one who, having entered upon the rains, dwells until the first Kattika full moon is included among those who have completed the rains, therefore, without making this very complex analysis of the wording, in the word-analysis, simply to show the person eligible to deposit a robe, the term of those who have completed the rains (`vuṭṭhavassānaṃ`) is used. That term, too, is connected with “a bhikkhu dwelling in lodgings.” For this is the meaning here: “a bhikkhu dwelling in lodgings, from among those who have completed the rains.” This means any bhikkhu among such bhikkhus who have completed the rains.

Araññalakkhaṇaṃ adinnādānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – sace vihāro parikkhitto hoti, parikkhittassa [P 3.0731] gāmassa indakhīlato aparikkhittassa parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya yāva vihāraparikkhepā minitabbaṃ. Sace vihāro aparikkhitto hoti, yaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ senāsanaṃ vā bhattasālā vā dhuvasannipātaṭṭhānaṃ vā bodhivā cetiyaṃ vā dūre cepi senāsanato hoti, taṃ paricchedaṃ katvā minitabbaṃ. Sacepi āsanne gāmo hoti, vihāre ṭhitehi gharamānusakānaṃ saddo sūyati, pabbatanadīādīhi pana antaritattā na sakkā ujuṃ gantuṃ, yo cassa pakatimaggo hoti, sacepi nāvāya sañcaritabbo, tena maggena gāmato [M 2.0309] pañcadhanusatikaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Yo āsannagāmassa aṅgasampādanatthaṃ tato tato maggaṃ pidahati, ayaṃ “dhutaṅgacoro”ti veditabbo.

The characteristic of the wilderness is explained in the commentary on taking what has not been given. Here, however, is the distinction: if the monastery is enclosed, it should be measured from the boundary pillar of an enclosed village or, for an unenclosed village, from the place suitable for an enclosure, up to the monastery’s enclosure. If the monastery is unenclosed, then having determined as the boundary whichever comes first—the dwelling, the refectory, the regular assembly place, the Bodhi tree, or the shrine—it should be measured from there, even if that point is far from the other dwellings. Even if a village is nearby and the sound of people in their houses is heard by those staying in the monastery, but one cannot go directly because it is obstructed by mountains, rivers, and so on, then the distance of five hundred bow-lengths should be taken from the village along its natural path, even if one must travel on it by boat. Whoever, for the sake of fulfilling the factors of a wilderness dwelling with respect to a nearby village, blocks the path here and there, that person is to be known as a 'thief of the ascetic practices.'

Sāsaṅkasammatānīti [V 2.0280] “sāsaṅkānī”ti sammatāni; evaṃ saññātānīti attho. Padabhājane pana yena kāraṇena tāni sāsaṅkasammatāni, taṃ dassetuṃ “ārāme ārāmūpacāre”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Regarded as perilous” means they are considered to be “perilous”; this is the meaning, that is, they are thus known. In the word analysis, however, to show the reason why they are regarded as perilous, it is said: “in the monastery or the vicinity of the monastery,” and so on.

Saha paṭibhayena sappaṭibhayāni, sannihitabalavabhayānīti attho. Padabhājane pana yena kāraṇena tāni sappaṭibhayāni; taṃ dassetuṃ “ārāme ārāmūpacāre”tiādi vuttaṃ.

With danger, they are fraught with danger; the meaning is that they have powerful, imminent dangers. In the word analysis, however, to show the reason why they are fraught with danger, it is said: “in the monastery or its vicinity,” and so on.

Samantā gocaragāme nikkhipeyyāti āraññakassa senāsanassa samantā sabbadisābhāgesu attanā abhirucite gocaragāme satiyā aṅgasampattiyā nikkhipeyya.

He may deposit it in a village for alms in the vicinity means: around the wilderness dwelling, in any direction, he may deposit it in a village for alms that he approves of, when the factors are fulfilled.

Tatrāyaṃ aṅgasampatti – purimikāya upagantvā mahāpavāraṇāya pavārito hoti, idamekaṃ aṅgaṃ. Sace pacchimikāya vā upagato hoti chinnavasso vā, nikkhipituṃ na labhati. Kattikamāsoyeva hoti, idaṃ dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ. Kattikamāsato paraṃ na labhati, pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchimameva pamāṇayuttaṃ senāsanaṃ hoti, idaṃ tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ. Ūnappamāṇe vā gāvutato atirekappamāṇe vā na labhati, yatra hi piṇḍāya caritvā puna vihāraṃ bhattavelāyaṃ sakkā āgantuṃ, tadeva idha adhippetaṃ. Nimantito pana addhayojanampi yojanampi gantvā vasituṃ pacceti, idamappamāṇaṃ. Sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayameva hoti, idaṃ catutthaṃ [P 3.0732] aṅgaṃ. Anāsaṅkaappaṭibhaye hi aṅgayuttepi senāsane vasanto nikkhipituṃ na labhatīti.

Herein, this is the accomplishment of the factors: Having entered upon the earlier rains-retreat, one has performed the Pavāraṇā at the great Pavāraṇā ceremony; this is the first factor. If one has entered upon the later rains-retreat or has had an interrupted rains-retreat, one is not permitted to deposit it. It must be the month of Kattika; this is the second factor. After the month of Kattika, one is not permitted. The dwelling must be of the proper measure, a maximum of five hundred bow-lengths; this is the third factor. One is not permitted if it is of a lesser measure or of a measure exceeding a gāvuta. For here, only that dwelling is intended from which it is possible, after going for alms, to return to the monastery by mealtime. However, if invited, one may go half a yojana or even a yojana to stay and then return; this is not subject to the standard measure. The dwelling must be perilous and fraught with danger; this is the fourth factor. For one is not permitted to deposit a robe while dwelling in a dwelling that is secure and free from danger, even if the other factors are met.

Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyāti yā udositasikkhāpade kosambakasammuti (pārā. 475) anuññātā tassā sammutiyā aññatra; sace sā laddhā hoti, chārattātirekampi vippavasituṃ vaṭṭati.

Except by the bhikkhus’ agreement—meaning, apart from that Kosambaka agreement that was permitted in the Udosita training rule (Pārā. 475). If that agreement has been obtained, it is allowable to remain away even beyond six nights.

Puna gāmasīmaṃ okkamitvāti sace gocaragāmato puratthimāya disāya senāsanaṃ; ayañca pacchimadisaṃ gato hoti, senāsanaṃ āgantvā sattamaṃ aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkontena gāmasīmampi okkamitvā [M 2.0310] sabhāyaṃ vā yattha katthaci vā vasitvā cīvarappavattiṃ ñatvā pakkamituṃ vaṭṭatīti attho. Evaṃ asakkontena tattheva ṭhitena paccuddharitabbaṃ, atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhassatīti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

Herein, regarding 'Again, having entered the village boundary': If the lodging is to the east of the alms-resort village, and this monk has gone in the western direction, then a monk who is unable to return to the lodging to cause the seventh dawn to arise may enter even the village boundary, stay in an assembly hall or anywhere whatsoever, and after learning the situation of the robe, it is allowable to depart—this is the meaning. By a monk unable to do so, it should be withdrawn while staying right there, reflecting, 'It will remain in the place of an extra robe.' The rest is clear.

Kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0281] – kāyavācato kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti, akiriyā, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

The origin of the Kathina—it arises from body and speech, or from body, speech, and mind. It is non-action, not a release by perception, mindless, a conventional transgression, bodily and verbal action, involving three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning what is perilous is concluded.

10. Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on What Has Been Dedicated

657. Tena samayenāti pariṇatasikkhāpadaṃ. Tattha pūgassāti samūhassa; dhammagaṇassāti attho. Paṭiyattanti paṭiyāditaṃ. Bahū saṅghassa bhattāti saṅghassa bahūni bhattāni anekāni lābhamukhāni; na saṅghassa kenaci parihānīti dīpenti. Oṇojethāti detha. Kiṃ panevaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti kasmā na vaṭṭati? Ayañhi abhihaṭabhikkhā abhiharitvā ekasmiṃ okāse saṅghassatthāya paṭiyattā abhihaṭapaṭiyatte ca uddissa ṭhapitabhāge ca payuttavācā nāma natthi.

657. 'At that time' refers to the training rule on what has been dedicated. Therein, 'for the group' means for the assembly; the meaning is 'for the righteous group.' 'Prepared' means made ready. 'Much food for the Sangha' means many meals for the Sangha, numerous sources of gain; they indicate that there is no loss for the Sangha in any way. 'Offer' means 'give.' But is it allowable to speak thus? Why would it not be allowable? For with regard to almsfood brought forward and prepared in one place for the Sangha's benefit, and to a portion set aside with designation, there is no such thing as speech constituting a request.

658. Saṅghikanti saṅghassa santakaṃ. So hi saṅghassa pariṇatattā hatthaṃ anārūḷhopi ekena pariyāyena saṅghassa santako hoti, padabhājane pana “saṅghikaṃ nāma saṅghassa dinnaṃ hoti pariccatta”nti evaṃ atthuddhāravasena nippariyāyatova saṅghikaṃ dassitaṃ. Lābhanti paṭilabhitabbavatthuṃ [P 3.0733] āha. Tenevassa niddese “cīvarampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pariṇatanti saṅghassa ninnaṃ saṅghassa poṇaṃ saṅghassa pabbhāraṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ. Yena pana kāraṇena so pariṇato hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “dassāma karissāmāti vācā bhinnā hotī”ti padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

658. 'Belonging to the Sangha' means the property of the Sangha. For because it is dedicated to the Sangha, even though it has not yet come into hand, in one way it is the property of the Sangha. But in the word-analysis, 'belonging to the Sangha' is shown directly, not figuratively, by way of clarifying the meaning as 'given to the Sangha, relinquished.' By 'gain,' it speaks of an object to be obtained. For that very reason, in its explanation, 'a robe, etc.' is stated. 'Dedicated' means having become inclined towards the Sangha, sloping towards the Sangha, leaning towards the Sangha. But to show the reason why it is dedicated, the word-analysis states, 'the declaration "we will give, we will do" is made.'

659. Payoge [M 2.0311] dukkaṭanti pariṇatalābhassa attano pariṇāmanapayoge dukkaṭaṃ, paṭilābhena tasmiṃ hatthaṃ ārūḷhe nissaggiyaṃ. Sace pana saṅghassa dinnaṃ hoti, taṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati, saṅghasseva dātabbaṃ. Yopi ārāmikehi saddhiṃ ekato khādati, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo. Pariṇataṃ pana sahadhammikānaṃ vā gihīnaṃ vā antamaso mātusantakampi “idaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti saṅghassa pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā attano pariṇāmetvā gaṇhantassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. “Imassa bhikkhuno dehī”ti evaṃ aññassa pariṇāmentassa suddhikapācittiyaṃ. Ekaṃ pattaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā attano, ekaṃ aññassa pariṇāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyañceva suddhikapācittiyañca. Eseva nayo bahūsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

659. Regarding 'In the effort, a dukkaṭa': in the effort to divert a gain dedicated to the Sangha for oneself, there is a dukkaṭa; upon acquisition, when it comes into hand, it is an offense entailing forfeiture. But if it has been given to the Sangha, it is not allowable to take it; it must be given to the Sangha. And whoever eats together with the monastery attendants should be made to pay the value of the goods. However, for a monk who, knowing that something has been dedicated to the Sangha—even if it is the property of fellow monastics, laypeople, or at the very least, one's mother—diverts it for himself, saying, 'Give this to me,' and takes it, there is an offense of pācittiya entailing forfeiture. For one who diverts it for another, saying, 'Give this to this bhikkhu,' there is a simple pācittiya. If one diverts one bowl or robe for oneself, and one for another, there is both an offense of pācittiya entailing forfeiture and a simple pācittiya. The same principle applies to many items. And this has been stated:

“Nissaggiyena [V 2.0282] āpattiṃ, suddhikena pācittiyaṃ;

Āpajjeyya ekato;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 480);

"One incurs an offense of relinquishment,

And a simple pācittiya;

Both at once;

This question has been pondered by the skilled."

Ayañhi pariṇāmanaṃ sandhāya vutto. Yopi vassikasāṭikasamaye mātugharepi saṅghassa pariṇataṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ ñatvā attano pariṇāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Parassa pariṇāmeti, suddhikapācittiyaṃ. Manussā “saṅghabhattaṃ karissāmā”ti sappitelādīni āharanti, gilāno cepi bhikkhu saṅghassa pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā kiñci yācati, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyameva. Sace pana so “tumhākaṃ sappiādīni ābhaṭāni atthī”ti pucchitvā “āma, atthī”ti vutte “mayhampi dethā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Athāpi naṃ kukkuccāyantaṃ upāsakā vadanti – “saṅghopi amhehi dinnameva labhati; gaṇhatha, bhante”ti evampi vaṭṭati.

For this was stated with reference to diversion. And whoever, during the time of the rains-cloth, knowing that a rains-cloth has been dedicated to the Sangha even in his mother's house, diverts it for himself, there is an offense of pācittiya entailing forfeiture. If he diverts it for another, there is a simple pācittiya. People, thinking, 'We will make a meal for the Sangha,' bring ghee, oil, and so on. If a sick monk, knowing that these have been dedicated to the Sangha, should ask for anything, it is indeed an offense of pācittiya entailing forfeiture. But if he, after asking, 'Do you have ghee and other items that have been brought?' and upon being told, 'Yes, there is,' says, 'Give some to me too,' it is allowable. Furthermore, if the lay followers say to him who is feeling scrupulous, 'The Sangha too receives only what is given by us; take it, venerable sir'—if they speak thus, this too is allowable.

660. Saṅghassa pariṇataṃ aññasaṅghassāti ekasmiṃ vihāre saṅghassa pariṇataṃ aññaṃ vihāraṃ uddisitvā “asukasmiṃ nāma mahāvihāre saṅghassa dethā”ti pariṇāmeti[P 3.0734].

660. Regarding what is dedicated to the Sangha being diverted to another Sangha: In one monastery, a gain dedicated to the Sangha is diverted by pointing to another monastery, saying, 'Give it to the Sangha in such-and-such a great monastery.' This entails an offense of wrong conduct.

Cetiyassa vāti “kiṃ saṅghassa dinnena, cetiyassapūjaṃ karothā”ti evaṃ cetiyassa vā pariṇāmeti.

Or for a shrine: Saying, 'What is the use of what is given to the Sangha? Make an offering to the shrine,' thus one diverts it for a shrine. This entails an offense of wrong conduct.

Cetiyassa [M 2.0312] pariṇatanti ettha niyametvā aññacetiyassatthāya ropitamālāvacchato aññacetiyamhi pupphampi āropetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekassa cetiyassa pana chattaṃ vā paṭākaṃ vā āropetvā ṭhitaṃ disvā sesaṃ aññassa cetiyassa dāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Herein, regarding what is dedicated to a shrine: It is not allowable to offer at another shrine even a flower from a small flowering plant planted for the benefit of a specific, different shrine. But having seen an umbrella or a banner being raised for one shrine, it is allowable to have the remainder given to another shrine.

Puggalassa pariṇatanti antamaso sunakhassāpi pariṇataṃ “imassa sunakhassa mā dehi, etassa dehī”ti evaṃ aññapuggalassa pariṇāmeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana dāyakā “mayaṃ saṅghassa bhattaṃ dātukāmā, cetiyassa pūjaṃ kātukāmā, ekassa bhikkhuno parikkhāraṃ dātukāmā, tumhākaṃ ruciyā dassāma; bhaṇatha, kattha demā”ti vadanti. Evaṃ vutte tena bhikkhunā “yattha icchatha, tattha dethā”ti vattabbā. Sace pana kevalaṃ “kattha demā”ti pucchanti, pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayeneva vattabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

Regarding what is dedicated to an individual: If one diverts what is dedicated even to a dog at the very least to another individual, saying, 'Do not give to this dog, give to that one,' it is an offense of wrong conduct. But if donors say, 'We wish to give a meal to the Sangha, make an offering to a shrine, or give requisites to a single monk; we will give according to your preference. Tell us, where should we give?' When this is said, that monk should say, 'Give wherever you wish.' But if they simply ask, 'Where should we give?' one should speak only according to the method that has come down in the Pāḷi. Herein, the rest has a clear meaning.

Tisamuṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0283] – kāyacittato vācācittato kāyavācācittato ca samuṭṭhāti, kiriyaṃ, saññāvimokkhaṃ, sacittakaṃ, lokavajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, akusalacittaṃ, tivedananti.

It has three origins—it arises from body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind; it is functional, a release by perception, intentional, blameworthy in the world, a bodily action, a verbal action, of unwholesome consciousness, and with threefold feeling.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on What Has Been Dedicated is concluded.

Niṭṭhito pattavaggo tatiyo.

The third, the Bowl Chapter, is concluded.

Nissaggiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Nissaggiya rules is concluded.

Pārājikakaṇḍa-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pārājika Section is concluded.
